text:
The simmering row over the introduction of Irish language signage in the North has once again laid bare the contradictions at the heart of the so-called ‘shared future’ narrative for the Six Counties. While the Stormont Executive continues to trumpet its commitment to diversity and cultural respect, the ongoing disputes at local level expose just how shallow much of this rhetoric remains.

This week, tempers flared at a council meeting in Mid and East Antrim, where unionist councillors objected in force to proposals for new bilingual road signs. The council ultimately voted against the measure, with some representatives branding the move as “provocative” and an attempt to “rewrite history.” Nationalists, in turn, accused their opponents of clinging to outdated prejudices and failing to recognise the legitimacy of the Irish identity in public life.

This is hardly the first such standoff. Last year saw similar discord in Ards and North Down, while even in Belfast, disputes over Irish language street names regularly tie the city council in knots. Every time such issues surface, they are painted – in the North and from the south – as growing pains: uncomfortable but necessary steps towards the elusive goal of a genuinely inclusive society.

Yet it is worth asking who is being included, and on what terms. The Irish language, for all the advocates’ protestations that it is ‘for everyone,’ remains deeply bound up with nationalist identity. Attempts by Sinn Féin and the SDLP to normalise Irish in public space are frequently understood by unionists as marking territory, or worse, as a subtle form of one-upmanship. The politics of language in the North are still, in many respects, zero-sum.

The impasse is further complicated by the British Government’s commitment, under the New Decade, New Approach deal, to introduce long-awaited protections for the Irish language. The Identity and Language (Northern Ireland) Act 2022, passed in Westminster after years of bickering at Stormont, set out ambitious plans for language commissioners and new rights for Irish speakers – but its practical impacts have so far been patchy, with implementation left to already-stretched councils.

There is a deep irony here. Government at every level proclaims a vision of coexistence and equal citizenship, but the lived reality is that any assertion of identity is immediately interpreted as a provocation by the other side. The Irish language, far from being a neutral marker of ‘diversity,’ is instead a recurring flashpoint.

Some commentators in the Republic are quick to blame unionist intransigence. But this is a blinkered view. If ‘diversity’ in the North simply means the expansion of one tradition at the expense of another, it cannot be a foundation for peace or mutual respect. Rather, it risks perpetuating the cycle of grievance and symbolic contestation that has marred Northern politics for generations.

True reconciliation will not be achieved through top-down legislation or by imposing cultural markers on unwilling communities. If policymakers in both Stormont and Dublin are serious about a genuinely inclusive future, they must acknowledge that identity in the North is inherently plural, and that any scheme for diversity must accommodate, not override, profound differences of outlook and allegiance. The row over road signs is only the latest reminder of how far there is yet to go.
headline: Dispute over Irish language signage exposes flaws in the scheme for a diverse Six Counties

A fundraising campaign has been launched in memory of a 14-year-old girl who lost her life in a tragic incident in the River Shannon at the weekend. The teenager, named locally as Aoife O’Callaghan, drowned after getting into difficulty whilst swimming with friends near the quayside in Athlone on Saturday afternoon.

Emergency services were called to the scene shortly after 3pm, with units from the local fire brigade, ambulance service, and Gardaí all responding rapidly. Despite efforts from first responders and members of the public who entered the water, Aoife was pronounced dead at the scene. The area was cordoned off as Gardaí initiated a detailed investigation.

Aoife, a first-year pupil at Our Lady’s Bower secondary school, has been described as a “gentle and caring soul” by heartbroken friends and neighbours. Her family, well-known in the area, have been left devastated by the sudden loss. Messages of condolence have poured in from across Athlone and beyond, with classmates and teachers expressing their shock at the tragedy.

A JustGiving fundraiser, established on Sunday evening by friends of the O’Callaghan family, aims to assist with funeral costs and to support Aoife’s bereaved relatives in the coming weeks. Organisers said that, “Aoife brought light and kindness to everyone who knew her. The whole community is in mourning.” The appeal has already raised more than €8,000 at the time of writing, with donations continuing to climb.

Local parish priest Fr Tomás Kennedy spoke at Mass on Sunday about Aoife’s “quiet strength and infectious laughter”, leading prayers for her family and friends. “No words can adequately express the pain we feel as a parish,” he said.

Gardaí have confirmed that the incident is being treated as a tragic accident and are not seeking anyone else in connection with the death. Officers have again warned of the dangers associated with swimming in rivers, particularly during the warmer weather.

The school Aoife attended has activated its critical incident response plan, with counsellors and support staff available for pupils and staff struggling to come to terms with her loss. The HSE has advised parents to be mindful of the emotional impact such tragedies can have on young people.

Funeral arrangements have yet to be finalised, but those wishing to support the O’Callaghan family can do so through the online fundraiser, details of which are available on social media.
headline: Fundraiser for “gentle” girl who died in River tragedy

A public meeting in Navan, Co Meath, on Thursday night heard claims from local residents and business owners that there has been “a spiral of crime and anti-social behaviour” in the area in recent months, with several speakers expressing frustration at what they described as an inadequate Garda response and a lack of political will to address the problem.

The meeting, which was organised by members of the Meath Crime Concern group, took place in a local community centre and drew a crowd of more than 200 people, including local councillors and representatives of the Gardaí. Attendees described a series of incidents in recent weeks, ranging from burglaries to muggings, theft, public drinking, and vandalism, with many claiming recent months had seen a “marked increase” in such offences.

A number of business owners spoke of a “marked decline” in footfall in the town centre, blaming what they described as a prevailing atmosphere of intimidation and fear, particularly in the evenings. Several warned that unless the problem is addressed, more jobs could be lost in the town and local businesses may be forced to close their doors.

One pensioner recounted being accosted outside her home in broad daylight, while another resident described repeated break-ins on her street and expressed frustration that calls to Gardaí often resulted in slow or no response. She told the meeting: “People just don’t feel safe in Navan any more. We’re told there aren’t enough Gardaí, but that’s not good enough. There’s a duty of care owed to the people living here.”

Inspector Michael Finnerty, representing Navan Garda Station, acknowledged concerns raised, saying resources were “under pressure” but that Gardaí were “doing their best” within constraints. He insisted a number of ongoing investigations were being prioritised and encouraged residents to continue reporting incidents, to build a clearer picture of crime trends.

Local Fianna Fáil TD, Thomas Byrne, attended the meeting and said he would raise constituents’ concerns with the Minister for Justice in the Dáil, promising to lobby for an increased Garda presence and greater support for community safety initiatives. Independent councillor Sharon Keogan called for a government review of policing allocations in Meath, claiming the current system “simply isn’t working for the people on the ground”.

Some speakers blamed national government policies for what they perceived as a “breakdown in law and order”, while others accused the judicial system of failing to impose meaningful consequences for offenders. There were calls for stricter bail conditions and mandatory sentences for repeat offenders, which they argued would act as a greater deterrent.

A representative of Meath Crime Concern said the group was not interested in “scapegoating” or “vigilantism”, but wanted to see “proper action” from authorities. “We want a town where people of every background can walk safely and business can thrive,” he said.

The meeting concluded with agreement to form a voluntary neighbourhood watch committee and a petition calling on the Department of Justice to allocate additional Gardaí to the area. Organisers said a further public meeting would be planned if progress was not seen in the coming weeks.
headline: Public meeting in Meath to hear there has been ‘spiral’ of crime and anti-social behaviour

text:
A newly published study has found that 95% of young women prescribed testosterone as part of gender transition treatment developed some form of pelvic floor dysfunction, sparking renewed debate over current approaches to transgender healthcare and raising serious questions about the long-term effects of cross-sex hormones on women’s health.

The peer-reviewed research, published in the European Journal of Translational Myology last month, followed 50 biological females aged 18-25 who had undergone testosterone therapy for at least one year. Researchers reported that nearly all participants experienced symptoms typically associated with pelvic floor dysfunction, including urinary incontinence, pain during intercourse, constipation, and pelvic pain. Only three women in the study reported no change in pelvic function after starting testosterone.

The authors suggested testosterone may weaken pelvic muscles or alter nerve function, but called for further investigation to clarify the precise mechanisms involved. While the sample size is small, the authors stressed that the findings warrant immediate attention from medical professionals providing gender-affirming care.

Pelvic floor problems can have a devastating impact on daily life, leading to chronic pain, social embarrassment, and increased risk of infections. The study’s lead author, Dr Alessandra Rucci, stated: “Given the significant rates of dysfunction observed, clinicians should routinely inform female patients of potential risks and carefully monitor pelvic health after commencing testosterone therapy.”

The findings come amid sharp international debate about the appropriateness of prescribing cross-sex hormones to young people, particularly minors. Health authorities in several European countries have taken a more cautious stance in recent years, with Sweden, Finland and the UK all rolling back access to puberty blockers and hormones for children, citing a lack of long-term data.

In Ireland, the number of young people presenting with gender dysphoria has risen sharply, though recent waiting list data from the HSE shows that young women seeking medical interventions outnumber their male counterparts by a significant margin. The National Gender Service, based at St Columcille’s Hospital in Loughlinstown, is currently the primary provider of adult transgender care in the State, but has faced criticism for lengthy wait times and lack of specialist support.

Gript has previously reported on gaps in the evidence base for gender medicine in Ireland, including the lack of locally published data on outcomes for those prescribed cross-sex hormones. The HSE told Gript it is “monitoring emerging international research closely” and will “continue to review clinical protocols in line with best practice.”

However, some campaigners are calling for an immediate moratorium on the prescription of cross-sex hormones for young people until more research is available. Speaking to Gript, Independent Senator Rónán Mullen said: “This study is deeply alarming. Instead of blindly following trends from abroad, we need to put a stop to potentially irreversible treatments that could do permanent harm to healthy young women.”

Transgender advocacy groups, meanwhile, argue that gender-affirming care is vital and often lifesaving for those experiencing gender dysphoria. Transgender Equality Network Ireland (TENI) said in a statement that “rigorous informed consent and continuous medical evaluation are already standard in Irish clinical settings.”

The new research, though not without its limitations, is likely to increase calls for greater transparency and a more cautious, evidence-based approach to transgender healthcare in Ireland. The Oireachtas Health Committee is due to debate the future of transgender medicine later this year, with medical professionals and advocacy groups both expected to make submissions.
headline: Study: 95% of young women on testosterone for sex change developed pelvic floor dysfunction

text:
Elon Musk, the billionaire owner of Twitter (recently rebranded as X), has claimed that the social media platform “interfered in elections” prior to his acquisition of the company last October. The Tesla and SpaceX chief made the remarks in response to a discussion on the Joe Rogan Experience podcast, where the host accused Twitter of acting as an “arm of the Democratic Party” in the United States.

Musk, who has frequently been critical of what he calls the “woke mind virus” and censorship by big tech companies, said: “Twitter has had a massive impact on elections, not just in the US but globally.” He went on to accuse previous management of suppressing dissenting voices and prioritising certain political viewpoints over others. “The degree to which Twitter was acting as an arm of the government was not well understood by the public,” he stated.

Twitter’s role in shaping political debate has long been a controversial issue. The platform had previously banned former US President Donald Trump following the Capitol riot in January 2021 and was accused of suppressing stories, such as those relating to Hunter Biden’s laptop, during the 2020 US presidential campaign. Documents released in the so-called “Twitter Files” last year appeared to show direct requests from government officials and political campaigns for content moderation.

Musk’s comments have triggered new debate over the role of social media firms both in the United States and internationally. In Ireland, the topic is of particular significance as government ministers are in the process of implementing the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act, which would grant a new Media Commission regulatory powers over tech companies. Concerns have previously been raised in the Oireachtas regarding censorship and the suppression of free speech online, with some TDs warning of the dangers of allowing unaccountable foreign corporations to influence Irish political debate.

In response to Musk’s latest claims, critics have argued that he is overstating the platform’s influence and attempting to absolve his own stewardship of responsibility. Supporters, however, say that greater transparency is needed regarding social media moderation practices and their impact on democratic processes.

Musk concluded his remarks by stating his commitment to free speech and promising that under his ownership, the platform would strive for greater openness and viewpoint diversity. Irish users and policymakers will be watching closely as these global debates continue to affect the national conversation on regulation, media freedom, and public trust in the digital sphere.
headline: Musk says Twitter interfered in elections

Fianna Fáil’s justice spokesman, Jim O’Callaghan TD, has said that while he supports a tough approach to law and order, he would not introduce an automatic deportation policy for non-EU migrants who serve prison sentences in Ireland. O’Callaghan, who has been increasingly vocal on issues relating to asylum and immigration, made the remarks as the Government faces mounting pressure to address what many see as a system struggling to cope with rising numbers of international protection applicants and high-profile incidents involving foreign nationals.

O’Callaghan stated that he "would favour, where appropriate, deportation" of convicted non-EU nationals, but cautioned against a blanket policy that would see all non-Irish prisoners removed from the State upon release, regardless of circumstances. Speaking to Gript, the Dublin Bay South TD argued: “We have to be careful not to undermine our own legal principles. The right approach is to consider each case on its merits, taking into account the nature of the offence, the length of sentence, and individual factors such as family ties or risk to life.”

Pressure for automatic deportation has mounted following several high-profile criminal cases involving foreign nationals, and as recent figures showed that the proportion of non-Irish citizens in Irish prisons has increased. Latest statistics from the Irish Prison Service indicate that nearly 20% of inmates are foreign-born, with the majority of these coming from outside the EU. Justice Minister Helen McEntee, meanwhile, has insisted that anyone with a deportation order on release is subject to removal, but opposition figures and members of the public have questioned the consistency and effectiveness of existing policies, amid reports of hundreds of deportation orders not being enforced each year.

O’Callaghan noted Ireland’s obligations under EU law and various international treaties, which prevent the State from deporting individuals to countries where they face persecution or death, or where family unity would be disproportionately affected. “It is easy to call for blanket measures, but our Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights bind us to a fair process,” he said. “That does not mean being soft — it means being effective and just.”

The Government has faced criticism from Sinn Féin, the Independent Group, and activists on both sides of the immigration debate. Some, such as Deputy Michael Collins of Cork South-West, have called for automatic deportation to be written into law for anyone convicted of a serious criminal offence. Opponents, including the Irish Council for Civil Liberties, argue that such measures could breach human rights and damage Ireland’s standing internationally.

O’Callaghan rejected suggestions that the State is powerless to act, pointing to the existing legal framework which empowers the Minister for Justice to issue a deportation order against any non-EU national whose presence is no longer deemed “conducive to the public good.” However, he conceded that enforcement is "patchy" and that delays in processing applications and orders remain a “serious problem” for the Department of Justice and the Garda National Immigration Bureau.

Calls for reform have also arisen from Gardaí, with one senior officer telling Gript that the current system is “overly bureaucratic” and can see dangerous individuals released before removal arrangements are finalised. “We need faster, tougher processes for those who have demonstrably abused our hospitality,” the source said, “but also safeguards to ensure no injustices are committed.”
headline: O’Callaghan won’t automatically deport all jailed migrants

Concerns that ageing populations will inevitably create economic disaster for Western countries such as Ireland may be overstated, new international research suggests. A study published this week in the journal Nature Ageing finds that the negative economic impact of global ageing is likely to be “much smaller” than widely assumed, and in some cases, the trend could even bring benefits.

The study challenges the prevailing narrative articulated by many governments and economic commentators, who warn that Ireland and other developed countries face an unsustainable burden as the proportion of older people grows. Advocates for this view have cited projected increases in healthcare and pension costs, as well as warnings of labour shortages, falling productivity, and stagnant economic growth. These fears have been repeatedly referenced in Dáil debates and policy papers issued by the Department of Finance and the ESRI.

However, researchers from the University of Oxford, the London School of Economics, and several other institutions argue that such predictions often ignore key factors, such as improvements in older people’s health, longer working lives, and technological advances that boost productivity.

The team analysed data from 180 countries over six decades. Their findings indicate that while ageing does modestly slow economic growth, the effect is significantly smaller than that of other issues, such as declining investment, reduced innovation, or restrictive economic policies. The negative impact, they say, is “not large enough” to justify the alarmism often seen in media reports and political discourse.

Professor Sarah Harper, one of the study’s authors, told Gript: “What we find is that people in older societies are healthier and more capable than previous generations. Many can and do work longer, and higher education levels mean older workers are often more productive.”

In Ireland, the Central Statistics Office (CSO) projects that those over 65 will make up more than a quarter of the population by 2051, up from just under 15% today. Government reports have warned that this trend may threaten the funding of the State pension and place “unprecedented” pressure on the HSE and social care services. Earlier this year, the Pensions Commission recommended raising the State pension age from 66 to 68, citing longer life expectancy and sustainability concerns—an issue that has become a flashpoint for trade unions and opposition parties.

But the Nature Ageing study contends that with proper planning, these challenges can be managed. The authors point to the potential for automation, targeted immigration policies, and labour force participation among older workers to help offset the demographic shift. Importantly, the research also finds that societies with higher proportions of elderly people have, on average, better social cohesion and lower crime rates.

Irish demographer Dr Anne Nolan of the Economic and Social Research Institute, commenting on the findings, said: “While there are real issues to address, especially in healthcare and infrastructure, the idea of an ‘ageing crisis’ is often exaggerated. With the right policies, older populations can be a resource rather than a burden.”

The study’s authors urge policymakers in Ireland and elsewhere to focus on “evidence-based adaptation” rather than alarmism. They recommend measures such as investing in lifelong learning, flexible retirement options, and redesigning workplaces to accommodate a more age-diverse workforce.

Nonetheless, critics argue that the findings could be used to justify pushing back pension ages or reducing entitlements.
headline: Study: Economic fears of ageing societies overblown

An 85-year-old man has appeared in court charged with the murder of Patricia Aust (81) at a residence in Bangor, Co Down. Jim Moore, of Birch Hill Park in the town, was brought before Newtownards Magistrates Court on Tuesday morning following his arrest by the PSNI over the weekend.

Officers were called to a house in Bangor’s Birch Hill Park area shortly before 6.30pm on Saturday evening, where Mrs Aust was discovered with serious injuries. Despite the efforts of emergency services, the pensioner was pronounced dead at the scene. A post-mortem examination is understood to have confirmed the cause of death as blunt force trauma.

Detective Inspector Foreman, speaking on Monday, described the incident as a “domestic-related matter” and urged anyone with information to come forward. Gardaí in the Republic monitored developments closely, given the close ties between Bangor and Dublin, particularly among families with members in both jurisdictions.

Mr Moore, appearing in court on crutches and accompanied by a solicitor, spoke only to confirm his name, address, and date of birth. The court heard that police have gathered forensic evidence from the scene and are continuing to interview neighbours and potential witnesses as part of their investigation.

A PSNI detective told the judge that Mr Moore had been living in the house with Mrs Aust and that the accused had been arrested at the scene. He added that the incident was “deeply shocking” for the local community.

No application for bail was made. Defence counsel confirmed that Moore has age-related health issues, and indicated that a psychiatric assessment is likely to be requested.

District Judge Mark Hamill remanded the accused in custody to appear again via video link next week.

Neighbours in the quiet residential area have expressed shock and sadness at news of the tragedy. Floral tributes have been placed outside the property, with one local resident describing Patricia Aust as “a lovely woman, always friendly and full of stories from her younger days in Dublin before she moved north.” Another neighbour said, “It’s heartbreaking. You don’t expect such things to happen here.”

Mrs Aust’s family, some of whom travelled from the Republic, have requested privacy as the investigation continues. The Department of Foreign Affairs confirmed it is providing consular assistance.

Police have appealed for anyone with relevant information, including dash-cam or CCTV footage from the area on Saturday, to contact detectives in Newtownards.

The case has reignited debate about the adequacy of support for elderly people in domestic circumstances and has prompted renewed calls for closer cross-border cooperation on elder protection. Both the HSE and the Department of Health in Northern Ireland have issued statements expressing condolences and encouraging those affected to seek support.
headline: Jim Moore (85) charged with murder of Patricia Aust (81) in Bangor

Independent TD Michael Fitzmaurice and Fianna Fáil Senator Eugene Mullooly travelled to Brussels this week to voice strong objections to the proposed EU-Mercosur trade agreement, warning that the deal would have “devastating consequences” for Irish farmers and rural communities. The two Oireachtas members joined a delegation of Irish farming representatives and rural campaigners at a protest outside the European Commission headquarters on Tuesday morning, organised to coincide with a high-level meeting of EU trade ministers.

Deputy Fitzmaurice, who represents Roscommon-Galway, described the EU-Mercosur deal as “a betrayal of Irish agriculture” and accused the European Commission of “selling out” Irish beef and suckler farmers in favour of imported South American products produced under lower environmental and welfare standards. “We have some of the highest standards in the world, and instead of supporting us, Brussels is negotiating deals that will flood the European market with beef that doesn’t meet the same criteria,” he told Gript. “It’s hypocrisy that beggars belief, and Irish farmers will pay the price.”

Senator Mullooly echoed the concerns, highlighting the special vulnerability of rural Ireland. “This isn’t just about individual farmers,” he said. “It’s about the future of rural towns, local economies, and the viability of family farms that have been at the heart of Irish life for generations. The small price advantage promised to consumers will not make up for the devastation to communities.”

The EU-Mercosur agreement, first announced in principle in 2019, would allow increased imports of beef, poultry, and other agricultural products from Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay into the EU in exchange for greater access for European exports. Irish farming unions and industry bodies, including the IFA and ICMSA, have long opposed the deal, citing concerns over traceability, environmental damage in the Amazon, and the potential impact on Irish beef prices and market share.

The protest in Brussels saw participants display placards and banners bearing slogans such as “Stop Mercosur Betrayal” and “Protect Irish Family Farms”. Addressing the crowd, Fitzmaurice and Mullooly called on the Irish Government to “stand firm” against EU pressure to ratify the deal. They criticised what they described as “doublespeak” from European Commission officials, who have insisted that Mercosur imports will be subject to strict controls. “There’s no way these imports will be held to our standards,” Fitzmaurice said. “We’ve seen before that once a deal is signed, enforcement vanishes when money talks.”

Both representatives met with MEPs from across Ireland’s political spectrum, urging them to reject the agreement if it comes to the European Parliament for a vote. They also called on Minister for Agriculture Charlie McConalogue to reaffirm the Government’s opposition and to push for a formal veto if necessary. “Ireland has the right to defend our interests. Anything less is not acceptable to the people we represent,” Mullooly said.

The Department of Agriculture has previously stated that it maintains “strong reservations” about the agreement, but critics argue that Dublin’s stance has softened in recent months amid growing pressure from Brussels and the business lobby. With France and Austria recently indicating renewed opposition, Irish campaigners now believe there is a fresh opportunity to block the deal.

As negotiations continue, farming groups have announced plans for further demonstrations both at home and on the continent.
headline: Fitzmaurice, Mullooly protest EU-Mercosur deal in Brussels

Across the country, the housing crisis looms large, from inner-city flats to rural boreens, but nowhere is its impact felt more acutely – or insidiously – than in the Gaeltacht. There, the shortage of affordable and available homes is not simply an economic or planning issue. It is a direct threat to the survival of the Irish language and, by extension, to the communities which have carried the language into the twenty-first century despite centuries of neglect, bureaucracy, and anglicisation.

Politicians are fond of proclaiming support for Irish, whether in the Dáil chamber or on the campaign trail. Yet, when it comes to meaningful protection of the Gaeltacht, it is clear that words have not translated into action. In Gaeltacht regions – from Connemara to Donegal and West Kerry – an acute shortage of housing is resulting in a slow-motion exodus of young people. Those who might otherwise remain and raise families in their own communities are increasingly faced with the impossible choice of moving away or remaining in overcrowded, unsuitable or even unsafe accommodation.

It is not uncommon to hear of young couples, both with steady jobs, unable to afford to buy or rent in the very townlands where they grew up. This is not the result of lack of ambition or “wanting it all.” It is the consequence of a market utterly skewed by external demand, holiday homes, and, in recent years, a spike in short-term lettings to tourists. Many houses in these areas now stand empty for much of the year, while local families are left in limbo, unable to secure even the most basic accommodation.

The statistics underline the scale of the problem. According to the CSO and the most recent surveys by Údarás na Gaeltachta, home ownership amongst young adults in Gaeltacht regions has plummeted, while the number of vacant or seldom-used houses continues to rise. All the while, the proportion of the population speaking Irish daily continues to decline. There is a direct link between affordable, secure housing and the health of any language community. If young Gaeltacht residents are forced to move to Galway, Cork or even further afield to find a home, the social network that sustains Irish-speaking life is irreparably damaged.

Government responses to date have been remarkably inadequate. Leases of public land at knockdown rates to developers have yielded little for local needs. Planning laws, supposedly adapted to protect Gaeltacht interests, are easily circumvented by well-resourced buyers from outside the region. Local authorities plead poverty and blame “the market,” while the Department of Housing and the Department of the Gaeltacht point the finger at each other.

If the State wishes to be serious in its commitments to the Irish language, this is the frontline. Solutions are possible. Designating Gaeltacht regions as “special planning zones,” increasing restrictions on non-local and non-permanent ownership, and shifting incentives away from short-term holiday lettings towards long-term local tenancies are all well within the capacity of the Oireachtas – if there were the will.

At stake is more than bricks and mortar. It is the living future of communities where Irish is spoken as a native tongue; where centuries-old traditions and networks are sustained by a way of life rooted in place. If these are allowed to wither because young people cannot find a home, the blame will lie squarely at the door of those who prefer platitudes to policy.
headline: The housing crisis threatening An Ghaeltacht

text:
Amid the mince pies and tinsel, there’s always a touch of mystery about Santa Claus. His red suit, white beard, and gravity-defying mode of transport—reindeer or otherwise—have been pored over by experts and sceptics alike. Yet, buried under the avalanche of Coca-Cola adverts and Hollywood films, lies an oft-overlooked thread in the tapestry of his legend: the curious, enduring association between Saint Nicholas and cats.

This connection may seem fanciful, or even the fevered invention of some contemporary influencer looking to spice up their Instagram feed, but the truth is more complex—and more interesting. In medieval Europe, where the cult of Saint Nicholas first flourished, cats played a larger-than-life role in both folklore and the rhythms of domestic life. They were guardians of the home, warriors against vermin in larders and granaries, and, in many places, regarded as creatures with a touch of the supernatural.

The roots of the association go deep. In the chilly north of Europe, where the traditions of Christmas as we know it were largely shaped, cats were not mere household pets. The Norse goddess Freyja, revered throughout Scandinavia, rode a chariot pulled by formidable cats. It was widely believed that caring for cats during the hard winter months would curry favour with Freyja, bringing prosperity and even gifts. When Christianity spread across the continent, old pagan customs were absorbed, repurposed, and dressed in Christian garb. Saint Nicholas, the gift-giver, in many places inherited the feline motif.

By the Middle Ages, celebrations of the feast of Saint Nicholas (on 6 December) were widespread throughout northern Europe. In parts of Germany and the Low Countries, children left out shoes or stockings not just for sweets or small gifts, but sometimes with a saucer of milk for the cats that kept Saint Nicholas company on his rounds. To do so was to demonstrate kindness, and to ensure good fortune for the coming year. Some depictions from the time even show Nicholas accompanied by a sleek cat, or bearing gifts for the household animal as well as the children.

Closer to home, Irish mummers’ plays and Christmas traditions also feature animals as important figures, if not always centre-stage. Cats, with their feisty independence and ability to fend for themselves, were esteemed in rural Ireland for keeping the peace in kitchens and stables alike. Folklore from counties Cork and Galway associates the ‘cóiste bodhar,’ the phantom death coach, with black cats—a reminder that the line between the sacred and the uncanny was never entirely clear.

Some scholars point to the Yule Cat of Icelandic legend, a fearsome creature that prowls the snow, rewarding industrious children with gifts and punishing the idle. While the Yule Cat is not Santa Claus, the context is telling: gifts and cats, benevolence and threat, all tangled together in a mythic winter landscape. Over centuries, as Christmas became more homogenised under Victorian influence, elements like cats receded into the background, replaced by the more universal imagery of reindeer, elves, and snowy fir trees.

Yet, echoes remain. In parts of continental Europe, especially in rural communities, it is still common to remember house cats at Christmas—leaving scraps of ham or fresh milk in a small dish on Christmas Eve, in the hope of a year without bad luck or spoiled grain.
headline: Why Santa Claus is historically associated with cats

A man has appeared before a sitting of Dundalk District Court charged with the murders of his parents and younger brother. The accused, Michael O’Driscoll, aged 29, was brought to the court under heavy Garda escort on Wednesday evening, following his arrest on Tuesday after the bodies of three members of the O’Driscoll family were discovered at their home in rural Co Louth.

Gardaí were alerted shortly after midday on Tuesday, after a neighbour raised concerns about the welfare of the family, who had not been seen in several days. On arrival at the scene, officers discovered the bodies of John O’Driscoll (60s), his wife Joan (late 50s), and their son Patrick (22), all with apparent stab wounds.

The accused, who resided at the same address, was located a short distance away and arrested without incident. He was detained at Dundalk Garda Station under Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act and questioned throughout Tuesday night before being charged.

Dressed in a grey tracksuit and flanked by two Gardaí, Mr O’Driscoll remained silent throughout the brief hearing. The court heard from Detective Garda Seamus Reddin, who gave evidence of arrest, charge and caution. When charged with three counts of murder, Mr O’Driscoll made no reply.

Judge Grainne Malone remanded the accused in custody to Cloverhill Prison to appear again by video link next week for directions from the DPP. Legal aid was granted following an application by defence solicitor, Ms Aisling Hayes.

There was a heavy Garda presence both inside and outside the court building, as members of the local community gathered in shock at the events. Friends and neighbours have paid tribute to the O’Driscoll family, describing them as “quiet, decent people” who had lived in the area for over 30 years.

Gardaí say they are not seeking anyone else in connection with the case. Scenes of crime officers remain at the house, and a post-mortem examination is underway at Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital in Drogheda.

In a statement, the Minister for Justice, Helen McEntee TD, expressed her condolences to the family and said that Gardaí would receive whatever resources were necessary for the investigation.

Any witnesses or anyone with information are asked to contact Dundalk Garda Station on 042 9388400, the Garda Confidential Line, or any Garda station. 

The tragic deaths have sent shockwaves through the Co Louth community, with local councillors and clergy calling for privacy for surviving relatives and support services to be made available. Grief counsellors from the HSE have been deployed locally as the investigation continues.
headline: BREAKING: Son charged with murder of parents, brother

The Dáil has voted to accept the Oireachtas Committee on Assisted Dying’s final report, recommending that legislation be drawn up to allow for assisted suicide in Ireland, following months of heated debate, emotional testimony, and strong lobbying from both sides of the issue.

TDs were given a free vote on the report’s recommendations late on Wednesday night, with the government not imposing a whip. The result—passed by 88 votes to 59—paves the way for the Minister for Health to begin work on a Bill which, if enacted, would for the first time permit both assisted suicide and euthanasia under what the committee describes as “strict eligibility criteria and robust safeguards.”

The Committee's work, launched last March, heard detailed evidence from medical professionals, patient advocacy groups, pro-life and pro-euthanasia campaigners, and people with lived experience of terminal illness. It noted strong divisions in public opinion, but ultimately recommended legalising assisted dying for those deemed to have a terminal illness with a prognosis of six months or less to live and who are “suffering unbearably.”

Opponents, including a number of Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and Independent TDs, raised grave concerns throughout the debate about the potential for a “slippery slope,” coercion of vulnerable individuals, and the adequacy of palliative care services. “We are sending a message that some lives are not worth living,” Clare TD Michael McNamara said, urging the Dáil to reject the report in what he described as “a fundamental matter of ethics and human dignity.”

Vocal supporters, including Sinn Féin’s Louise O’Reilly and Social Democrats TD Holly Cairns, argued that the State has a duty to respect personal autonomy and respond compassionately to those suffering from unbearable pain. “We cannot continue to criminalise people whose only crime is wanting to die with dignity,” Deputy O’Reilly said. She rejected claims that human life would be devalued, insisting that “strict protocols and oversight” could protect against abuse.

Among the report’s key recommendations is the creation of a new regulatory authority to oversee applications and ensure that psychological and medical assessments are carried out before approval is granted. The committee also called for a mandatory waiting period, mechanisms to allow individuals to withdraw consent, and safeguards to ensure that requests are voluntary and free from external pressure.

Health Minister Stephen Donnelly welcomed the Dáil’s decision, but cautioned that “a careful and considered approach” will be taken in preparing the legislation, with further consultation and legal advice promised before a general scheme is brought to Cabinet. “There are profound ethical, legal, and social implications that must be fully examined,” he said.

The Catholic Church, along with several disabilities and elder’s rights groups, expressed “deep disappointment” at the outcome, warning that vulnerable populations could feel pressured to end their lives prematurely. The Irish Cancer Society and the Irish Palliative Medicine Consultants’ Association also questioned whether adequate resources have been devoted to end-of-life care, renewing calls for investment in palliative services nationwide.

Meanwhile, pro-assisted dying campaigns applauded the vote as a “historic step” and called on the government to move swiftly. “The public has waited long enough for compassion and choice at the end of life,” said Tommy Roche, spokesperson for End of Life Ireland.

The issue remains deeply controversial and is expected to dominate public discourse as draft legislation begins its journey through the Dáil and Seanad.
headline: Dáil votes to accept report recommending legislating for assisted suicide

Sinn Féin has come under fire from critics after it emerged that senior party activists organised a fundraising event in support of Mermaids, a UK-based charity which has advocated for the prescription of puberty blockers to children experiencing gender distress. The event, promoted by members of the party’s LGBTQ+ network, took place virtually last weekend, drawing attention among campaigners concerned about the charity’s controversial position on medical intervention for minors.

Mermaids has been the subject of significant scrutiny in recent years for backing the use of so-called “puberty blockers” for children, a practice that has since been criticised by health experts, including in the UK, over questions regarding long-term safety and efficacy. The NHS and a major independent review, the Cass Report, have pulled back from recommending puberty blockers outside of clinical trials, citing insufficient evidence and concerns about irreversible effects on adolescent development.

A spokesperson for Sinn Féin confirmed party members had been involved in the online fundraiser and said the party “stands in solidarity with the trans community and supports organisations that work to protect vulnerable young people.” However, the move has prompted a backlash from some parents’ groups, medical bodies, and politicians who claim the party is showing “reckless disregard” for child safety in the face of mounting evidence against the unfettered use of hormone treatments.

Independent Senator Rónán Mullen told Gript: “Sinn Féin is either ignorant of the real harms associated with puberty blockers for children or they simply don’t care. To fundraise for an organisation under investigation for its practices is indefensible.” He added: “Irish parents are becoming increasingly alarmed as international evidence comes out about the dangers of social and medical transitioning for children, yet political parties like Sinn Féin seem to be doubling down.”

The HSE has also updated its own clinical guidelines for the treatment of gender dysphoria in minors, adopting a far more cautious approach in line with international best practice. The Department of Health last year confirmed that Irish clinicians would not prescribe puberty blockers outside the context of specialised multidisciplinary teams and ongoing review.

Parents’ advocacy group The Countess released a statement calling on the party’s leadership to distance itself from Mermaids and clarify its position. “By associating themselves with an organisation under such a cloud, Sinn Féin are sending the wrong message to Irish families,” the group said.

Gript understands that fundraising for UK-based advocacy groups is not unprecedented among Irish political activists, but the controversy around Mermaids places fresh scrutiny on party policy as the general election approaches. Senior party figures, including health spokesperson David Cullinane TD, have not publicly commented on the matter, despite requests for clarification.

Meanwhile, critics say that while Sinn Féin presents itself as a champion of children’s rights and public health, its support of Mermaids undermines confidence in its ability to formulate policy based on evidence rather than ideology.

The issue is likely to add fuel to the ongoing national debate over gender identity services for young people, with the Oireachtas Health Committee expected to discuss updates to care pathways later this year. With public awareness growing and a series of recent court cases in the UK highlighting the risks, pressure is mounting for all Irish political parties to make their positions clear.

Sinn Féin’s position paper on gender identity, released last year, broadly supports access to gender-affirming healthcare for minors, provided it is clinically guided and subject to “robust safeguarding.”
headline: Sinn Féin slammed for Mermaids fundraiser over puberty blocker stance

New statistics released this week by the EU’s asylum agency paint a stark and uncomfortable picture for Ireland’s policymakers, as the latest figures show a Europe-wide fall in the number of people seeking asylum – just as Ireland reports another significant increase.

Across the EU, the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) has confirmed that the number of asylum applications lodged between January and May of this year has decreased by over 12% compared to the same period in 2023. The decline is widespread, with countries such as Germany, France, and Sweden each reporting double-digit percentage falls. In contrast, the data indicate that Ireland is bucking the trend, with a rise of over 20% in new asylum claims so far this year.

Officials in the Department of Justice have sought to play down the sharp contrast, citing the “fluctuating nature” of migration and international protection trends. However, the explanation has failed to ring true for critics who accuse the government of presiding over a failed and unsustainable asylum system.

As the rest of the EU implements tighter border controls and more restrictive asylum policies, the Irish government, and Minister for Integration Roderic O’Gorman, have remained committed to what they frame as a humane and open approach. But even as the government talks up its “international obligations,” mounting social and political tensions at home tell a different story.

Communities from Clare to Dublin have seen repeated protests in recent months, with local residents voicing opposition to the housing of asylum claimants in hotels, former office blocks, and even tented camps. The government’s promise last spring of “decompression” and a more even distribution of arrivals across the country has not materialised. Instead, the crisis appears to have deepened, with the number of people arriving to claim international protection standing at over 3,000 in the first quarter alone – more than double the same period in 2022.

While the EUAA has noted that a decrease in arrivals is the result of concerted policy efforts across several member states – including border checks, agreements with third countries, and faster processing times – Ireland has so far avoided any substantial tightening of its procedures. Critics say this has turned the country into a “soft touch,” attracting more asylum seekers even as other states act to deter new arrivals.

There is little sign that the government’s messaging is resonating with the public. Confidence in the government’s handling of immigration, and particularly the international protection process, has collapsed in recent opinion polls, and some rural TDs have warned colleagues privately that the issue is now dominating local politics to a degree not seen since the economic crash.

What is clear is that the government is now boxed in: determined to avoid the scenes at the Greek or Polish borders – and to uphold Ireland’s “reputation for compassion” – but facing a hardening of public attitudes and a growing sense that the system is out of control. With accommodation options exhausted, the use of tents, makeshift hostels, and even disused Garda stations is likely to continue.

As Ireland’s EU neighbours take action to stem the flow, the government here faces a choice: stay the course and risk a backlash at the ballot box, or confront the challenges of reforming a system that is no longer fit for purpose. Either way, the numbers are now impossible to ignore.
headline: Numbers claiming asylum across EU fall, but rise in Ireland

text:
The decades-long stand-off between the United States and Venezuela has moved into a new and dangerous phase, raising fears that two of the Americas’ largest countries might be closer than ever to open conflict. While many Irish readers may have grown used to American foreign entanglements, recent developments have brought simmering hostilities in the Caribbean to the fore, with the Biden administration and the Maduro regime exchanging barbs and military manoeuvres on an unprecedented scale.

The immediate flashpoint has been Venezuela’s renewed claim over the oil-rich Essequibo region of neighbouring Guyana. In December, President Nicolás Maduro staged a referendum asserting Venezuela’s rights over this vast tract of land, and in the months since, Caracas has moved troops and equipment closer to the disputed border. The United States, which has key interests in Guyana’s newly discovered offshore oil reserves through companies such as ExxonMobil, responded by flying in military aircraft and naval assets, as well as hosting joint exercises with the Guyanese Defence Force.

Washington’s stance is both strategic and symbolic. The United States has not recognised the results of Venezuela’s recent referendum and sees any attempt to seize Essequibo by force as a grave threat to regional stability and to the legal order of the Americas. American officials have warned directly that military action against Guyana would “not be tolerated,” deploying what they call a “deterrence posture.” For its part, Venezuela accuses the US of “imperialist interference” and backing its enemies, with Maduro stoking nationalist fervour and warning of a “Yankee plot” to steal Venezuela’s rightful territory.

This dangerous escalation comes against a backdrop of deeper tensions between the two countries. The US has imposed repeated economic sanctions on Venezuela in response to what it calls rigged elections and human rights abuses under Maduro’s socialist government. Although there were fleeting hopes of rapprochement last year—when Washington relaxed oil sanctions to secure Venezuelan cooperation on migration—relations soured again after Caracas allegedly failed to abide by its electoral promises.

From Dublin’s vantage point, Ireland has a limited but not insignificant stake in the crisis. The Department of Foreign Affairs has expressed “serious concern” over the prospect of military conflict and called for dialogue, in line with the EU position. NGOs working in the Venezuelan diaspora have warned that a new war would risk an even greater exodus from a region already facing economic and political instability.

Irish analysts, including some in the Oireachtas Foreign Affairs Committee, believe the real risk is that the dispute could spiral wider. Russian and Iranian advisors are known to be active in Venezuela, raising the spectre of a proxy contest of the type seen elsewhere. Others point to the risk of US domestic politics heating up, with Republican critics accusing President Biden of being “soft on socialism” and urging tougher action.

The underlying causes are manifold: the collapse of Venezuela’s economy and its desperate need for new revenue streams, the irresistible lure of Guyana’s untapped oil, and America’s determination not to cede influence in what it still considers its own backyard. For now, both sides insist they want to avoid war, but the rhetoric is heating up and the military presence on the ground is growing. As one Irish diplomat put it this week, “It only takes a spark.”

For Irish citizens living or travelling in the region, the Department of Foreign Affairs has advised caution, particularly near the border areas.
headline: Why are America and Venezuela on the cusp of war?

text:
The latest by-election in Newbridge offered all the tension and theatre that might be expected of a county final, and, as the final count ticked well past midnight on Tuesday, Tom McDonnell emerged victorious, clutching the Tricolour with characteristic gusto. In a contest often painted in muted shades by national media, Newbridge voters bucked expectations, with turnout figures of just over 61% ensuring that this was not merely a coronation, but a battle worthy of the name. 

McDonnell’s campaign, underestimated by many, drew together an eclectic coalition of locals – farmers, small business owners, and the quietly disgruntled silent majority who have felt increasingly left behind by the political establishment in the Dáil. While other candidates poured resources into glossy social media campaigns and the now-predictable calls for more “investment” and “inclusivity”, McDonnell kept his message hard-edged and direct: a full-throated defence of local industry, an uncompromising stance on securing greater Garda resources, and, crucially, a vigorous critique of what he called “Dublin-centred groupthink”.

What was most interesting, and perhaps most telling, was the sharp increase in first preference votes for McDonnell among younger voters—voters that, according to the wisdom of the “experts”, are expected to embrace every social trend wafting across from Brussels. Instead, many openly cited rising rents and open-door immigration as reasons for marking their 1 beside McDonnell’s name. The local canvass, it turns out, still matters—people wanted to be heard about practical issues, not handed pamphlets about climate targets or pronoun policies. 

His closest rival, the party-blessed favourite, ran what some characterised as a by-the-numbers campaign, relying on endorsements from party HQ and the now almost mandatory photo-ops with the Tánaiste or, briefly, the Taoiseach. In contrast, McDonnell’s rallies resembled something closer to the old céilí, with GAA stalwarts rubbing shoulders with local businesspeople and the occasional priest in the crowd—an overlooked Ireland, perhaps, but an Ireland that has delivered a stinging message about what matters outside the M50.

The reaction from official Dublin has been predictable. An Taoiseach, in a carefully worded statement, congratulated the winner while reiterating Government “commitment to progressive values”. On social media, the usual suspects have attempted to paint McDonnell’s victory as some sort of “populist backlash”, with plenty of hand-wringing over the “direction” the region has taken. Yet, for those who spent time knocking on doors during this contest, the result was no mystery. If anything, it was a delayed reckoning.

For now, Tom McDonnell’s camp is riding high—the Tricolour, once again, waving over a field of well-earned victory. The real test, though, will be whether his victory in Newbridge marks the start of something larger, or whether official Ireland will, as usual, ignore the warning bells rung so loudly this week. For many across the country, all eyes are now on Newbridge, and on whether McDonnell will be allowed to keep the promises that brought him triumph in the nail-biting battle that will be spoken of in Kildare for years to come.
headline: Tom McDonnell emerges with Tricolour flying in the nail-biting Battle of Newbridge

text:
The month of June comes round, and with it, the now-familiar spectacle of rainbow flags rising over every public building, every major brand, and every possible space in civic life. Across the media, in schools, and emblazoned upon Garda cars, the Pride colours have become less an emblem of individual liberty and more a compulsory badge of allegiance to a prevailing ideology. In a country that once held debate and dissent as values worth defending, the phenomenon we might fairly call “Big Gay” now brooks no opposition.

Let’s be honest: what was once a movement demanding equality has morphed into an all-encompassing social force, eager to police thought and punish heretics. State-funded NGOs, quangos, and advocacy groups enjoy an outsize influence on politicians, government department directives, and even judicial attitudes. The annual Pride parade—now sponsored by banks, tech giants and Government alike—has little to do with the rights of ordinary gay men and women, and everything to do with enforcing a top-down consensus that goes well beyond sexual orientation or discrimination.

Look no further than recent rows over the redefinition of gender in Irish law, curriculum changes in schools prompted by activist groups, or the taxpayer money poured into Pride events by city and county councils. Dissenters—whether they are parents concerned about explicit sex education, or professionals simply unwilling to display the latest rainbow pin—are immediately tarred as “hateful” or “bigoted”. Debate has been replaced by diktat, with the weight of official Ireland, from the Oireachtas to An Post, thrown behind every Pride initiative.

Meanwhile, ordinary people—who may support the right of anyone to live as they choose, but who object to compelled speech or indoctrination—are left in an impossible position. Question the wisdom of teaching gender identity to eight-year-olds, and you may find yourself accused of “hate”. Question the saturation of sexual politics in public life, and you will be told that “visibility saves lives”—as if flying a flag and painting a zebra crossing constitutes the defence of the vulnerable.

All of this comes at a real cost, both financial and cultural. There is, by now, an entire ecosystem of activist groups, DEI (Diversity, Equity, Inclusion) officers, and State-funded campaigns whose existence depends on the constant ratcheting up of claimed oppression. The HSE, for example, can scarcely staff basic health services, but spares no expense lavishing resources on new “inclusivity” initiatives. The Gardaí find themselves spending more time patrolling social media for perceived “hate” than preventing real-world crime. The ordinary taxpayer is paying for a culture war most never voted for.

The net effect is a chilling one: it is no longer enough to “live and let live”, nor to respect the rights of others. Instead, we are expected to participate in a compulsory affirmation of the latest activist dogma, or risk social and even legal sanction. That is not progress; it is the imposition of ideological conformity by a powerful new establishment—one with the full collusion of official Ireland.

It is time for someone to say: enough. The rainbow flag should not be more sacrosanct than the tricolour, nor should any Irish citizen be compelled to celebrate or promote what they do not believe. We have allowed a well-funded, media-savvy movement to dictate the terms of our national conversation.
headline: MCGUIRK: It’s time to stand up to “Big Gay”

The European Union is moving ahead with controversial measures to tie citizens’ online access to a so-called ‘Digital Identity Wallet’ – a sequel to the much-criticised EU COVID pass that divided Europe during the pandemic and sparked widespread debate about civil liberties. Backed by major industry players and European bureaucrats, the new regulation will see digital ID technology not only facilitating travel or banking, but potentially becoming a prerequisite for the use of online services, including social media, e-commerce, and news platforms.

Supporters in Brussels claim the proposal will “streamline” online verification and make internet use more “secure.” Critics, however, warn that the Digital Identity Wallet’s true impact would be to create a centralised, government-controlled gatekeeper to citizens’ digital lives. Civil liberties groups across Europe have raised the alarm about the potential for centralised tracking and surveillance, as well as the ever-present risk that access to online platforms could be restricted by authorities in the name of “safety” or “combating misinformation.”

Irish MEPs have largely lined up behind the EU Commission, with only a handful expressing concern at the implications for privacy and free expression. The Department of Justice in Dublin has said the Government “welcomes EU efforts to harmonise digital identification,” while not addressing the risks for online freedom. The Digital Identity Wallet will reportedly be compatible with the COVID pass infrastructure – raising fears that digital passes, once portrayed as an emergency pandemic measure, are now morphing into a permanent fixture of everyday life.

Central to the controversy is the European Commission’s stated ambition to combat “disinformation” and “illegal content” online. New EU laws such as the Digital Services Act already require platforms to delete content deemed unlawful or misleading. Now, campaigners warn, the digital wallet could allow Brussels and national governments to link users’ online identities to their published opinions – and even block access to critical voices.

Tech companies, including several receiving EU contracts, have welcomed the move, claiming it will reduce fraud. But small publishers, privacy advocates, and independent journalists are sounding the alarm. They argue that tying identity verification to digital speech will chill debate, stifle dissent, and threaten press freedom – especially in smaller countries like Ireland, where the media landscape is already under pressure from political and corporate interests.

The shift to mandatory digital identification for major online services is happening rapidly, with trials already running in Germany and plans to roll out the system EU-wide by 2026. While the European Commission insists participation will be “voluntary,” leaked documents and statements from officials have suggested access to banking, government services, and even everyday websites could soon require a valid digital wallet.

Many Irish citizens remember being told that the COVID pass was a “temporary” measure. With the same infrastructure now poised to underpin online censorship, questions are being asked in the Dáil – but answers remain thin on the ground. While Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil TDs parrot EU talking points, opposition voices such as Independent TDs and some from Sinn Féin have demanded more transparency about the legislation’s scope and potential for abuse.

The EU Digital Identity Wallet raises pressing issues about the balance between convenience and liberty, and whether Irish values of individual privacy and free speech will ultimately be sacrificed on the altar of Brussels’ regulations. With the Government showing little sign of pushing back, and many mainstream media outlets silent on the real implications, it may fall to citizens and the few remaining voices of dissent to keep the debate alive.
headline: EU to Use COVID Pass Sequel for Online Censorship
