A Boil Water Notice has been issued by Uisce Éireann (formerly Irish Water) for more than 22,000 residents and businesses served by the Adamstown Public Water Supply in Co Wexford, following concerns over the quality of treated water produced at the local water treatment plant. The notice, which was announced on Thursday evening, affects homes, farms, and commercial premises across Adamstown, Clonroche, Taghmon, Wellingtonbridge, and a number of surrounding rural areas.

Uisce Éireann said the decision was taken as a precaution, after consultation with the HSE and Wexford County Council, “to protect the health of all our customers.” The public utility said that routine monitoring had detected elevated levels of cryptosporidium, a microscopic parasite that can cause illness, particularly among young children, the elderly and people with compromised immune systems. While no reports of illness associated with the water supply have been confirmed, customers are being advised as a matter of urgency to boil water intended for drinking, preparing food, brushing teeth, or making infant formula.

The HSE has urged residents to remain vigilant for symptoms of gastrointestinal upset, such as nausea, vomiting, cramps, or diarrhoea, and to seek medical advice if they are concerned. Dr Catherine Donnelly of the HSE’s Public Health Department said the risk to the general population remains low as long as the instructions are followed, but stressed the importance of adhering to the guidelines. “It’s essential that all water used for consumption or food preparation is brought to a rolling boil and allowed to cool. Vulnerable people, including young children and those with underlying health conditions, should take particular care,” she said.

Uisce Éireann has not yet indicated how long the Boil Water Notice is likely to remain in place, but said its engineers and water quality specialists are working urgently to identify and resolve the underlying treatment issue. Tankered water supplies will be made available at key locations throughout the affected area for those who cannot boil water at home, although residents are reminded to bring their own clean containers.

The ongoing water quality and infrastructure issues in Wexford have drawn sharp criticism from local representatives. Independent TD Verona Murphy said the situation again highlights serious deficiencies in Ireland’s rural water infrastructure, calling for “immediate investment and support” for smaller treatment schemes. “People in rural Wexford should not be expected to cope with repeated water notices in the 21st century. This is a public health matter and needs to be addressed at the highest level,” Deputy Murphy said.

Cllr Frank Staples (FG), whose electoral area includes some affected communities, said businesses and farmers will face additional costs and difficulties as long as the notice remains in place, and called for a clear timeline for repairs. Several schools in the area have also informed parents of the precautions in place, with some switching to bottled water for drinking and food preparation.

This is the second Boil Water Notice issued for parts of the south Wexford region within twelve months, after a separate incident last summer affected hundreds of customers near New Ross. Uisce Éireann said it will provide daily updates via its website and social media channels until the matter is resolved.

Customers with queries can contact the Uisce Éireann customer care centre at 1800 278 278, or visit water.ie for further information.
headline: Wexford: Boil Water Notice issued for 22,000 customers

text:
Business owners in Ennis say the much-vaunted Ennis 2040 plan has become a source of acute concern, arguing that the proposals, aimed at revitalising the Clare county town, could spell the end for independent traders and drastically alter the fabric of the community. Far from being a blueprint for progress, the draft plans—particularly those for Abbey Street car park and the so-called ‘River Fergus Experience’—have prompted a groundswell of local opposition, with many characterising the approach of the Ennis 2040 DAC (Designated Activity Company) as tone-deaf to the realities on the ground.

Several retailers and café owners contacted by Gript describe a process in which consultation is “pitched as a box-ticking exercise” while major decisions are driven by consultants and distant planners rather than those who live and work in the town every day. “Their vision is our nightmare,” said one longstanding shop proprietor, preferring not to be named for fear of council retribution. “They want to bulldoze what gives Ennis its heart and soul to put in another generic plaza and more offices nobody has asked for. If this is progress, spare us.”

At the heart of the furore is the plan to demolish most of Abbey Street car park, replacing it with a plaza and multi-storey building, alongside new walkways by the river. Supporters say it will make Ennis more attractive for visitors and future business, in line with the aspirations of the 2040 strategy to make the town “Ireland’s first climate-adaptive urban centre.” However, traders warn that the removal of convenient parking is already driving footfall down, with business “on the floor” since the plans were mooted.

“People don’t want hassle,” said another retailer, whose family have been trading in the town for three generations. “If parking disappears, they’ll just go to Limerick or shop online. We can’t survive on tourists dropping in for a stroll along the river in July. What about the other eleven months?”

Community and heritage activists have also raised concerns about the potential loss of character, warning that the town’s medieval lanes, independent shops and lived-in streetscape could be threatened by what they term “template regeneration.” Recent public meetings have drawn large crowds, and campaigners have presented Clare County Council with thousands of petition signatures urging a rethink. Yet many fear that the outcome is preordained, with decisions driven from Dublin, or even Brussels, rather than reflecting the wishes of Ennis residents.

The Ennis 2040 DAC, a special-purpose company owned by Clare County Council, insists that its plans are subject to public consultation and environmental assessment, and that the changes are necessary to meet future challenges like climate action and economic resilience. Its board is composed of local councillors, council officials, and select business representatives. However, local critics point to a lack of transparency, with minutes and correspondence often only available after repeated requests. It has not gone unnoticed that some board members have interests in construction or property sectors, fuelling accusations that the plans are being shaped for profit rather than people.

As the debate heats up, local TDs and councillors are under increasing pressure to take a stand. While some back the plan as a way to secure investment, others have called for a pause and a meaningful review. “People feel they’re being steamrolled,” said one Independent member of the Oireachtas.
headline: Local businesses on Ennis 2040 plan: “Their vision is our nightmare”

text:
A new State-backed initiative, announced this week by Minister for Community Development, Joe O’Brien TD, has sparked debate after channelling €5 million towards what is being described as “systemic reform” led by “marginalised” communities. The scheme, titled the Inclusive Leadership Fund, will distribute grants to individuals and groups from backgrounds purportedly underrepresented in public decision-making, with the stated aim of supporting “leadership towards structural change.”

According to information released by the Department of Rural and Community Development, the fund will be administered through Pobal, the semi-state body frequently tasked with overseeing government diversity and inclusion programmes. The department claims the initiative will “empower leaders from minority and disadvantaged groups,” thereby increasing influence for these groups in areas such as social policy, housing, and education.

However, critics argue that the vague criteria and opaque goals of the fund raise questions about its efficacy, as well as its potential to foster divisions instead of resolving them. “We’re seeing a trend of public money being channelled into identity-based programmes with little evidence that they deliver concrete improvements for the wider community,” said one opposition TD, who added that existing supports for community leaders should already be accessible to all, regardless of background.

The fund will prioritise applicants who “self-identify as marginalised on the grounds of race, ethnicity, disability, sexual orientation, or socio-economic disadvantage,” a requirement some say risks excluding voices with alternative perspectives. “Ireland has always prided itself on a tradition of local leadership drawing on all sections of society,” said community worker Joan O’Reilly. “Targeting funding this way could inadvertently sideline capable leaders who don’t tick a specific box.”

Department officials maintain that the Inclusive Leadership Fund will foster “collaborative projects to drive reform in government policy and public services,” with applicants required to demonstrate an intention to “challenge systemic barriers.” Grants may be used for training, advocacy campaigns, or establishing pilot initiatives in local communities. Applicants must also commit to “engaging with policymakers,” raising concerns among some observers about the potential for lobbying and activism underwritten by the taxpayer.

The launch is the latest in a series of government moves aimed at meeting diversity targets, in line with EU equality frameworks. The Taoiseach, Simon Harris, has previously stated that the Government “must reflect the diversity of today’s Ireland.” The new fund’s announcement follows recent controversy over the State’s funding for advocacy NGOs, with several Government-funded organisations now among the strongest campaigners for changes to immigration, education and healthcare policies.

Despite questions over accountability and oversight, Minister O’Brien has defended the scheme. “If we are to build a fairer and more inclusive Ireland, then we need to ensure that those with lived experience of marginalisation have a seat at the table,” he said. The Department said successful applicants will be subject to standard financial and reporting requirements.

The first round of funding is expected to open for applications in July, with grants to be distributed by the end of the year. The Department has not provided a breakdown of projected outcomes but said it hopes the programme will “inspire long-term cultural and systemic change.” Critics, meanwhile, say the need for rigorous evaluation and transparency will be vital to ensure the scheme delivers results for all sections of society.
headline: New fund aims to help “marginalised” leaders to “support systemic reforms”

text:
A TD has called for an explicit ban on nursing home staff convicted of violently abusing residents, stating that only a “zero-tolerance approach” can restore public trust in Ireland’s long-term care sector. The call follows recent reports of assaults and mistreatment in several care facilities, sparking renewed concern over the safeguarding of vulnerable elderly people.

Fianna Fáil’s Éamon Ó Cuív, speaking in the Dáil on Tuesday, said the Government must introduce legislation to ensure any care worker found guilty of physical abuse is automatically barred from working with older or at-risk adults in the future. “Families entrust their loved ones to nursing homes, expecting dignity and safety,” he told TDs. “One incident of violence is one too many, and no abuser should ever be allowed to return to this sector.”

The HSE and the Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) have received an increased number of complaints in recent years, with 293 notifications of alleged abuse in private nursing homes in 2023, up from 217 in 2021. Only a fraction of cases result in prosecutions under current law, and there is no centralised register preventing those with criminal convictions for abuse from being re-employed within the sector.

Minister for Older People, Mary Butler, confirmed that her department is “actively reviewing” the possibility of a statutory register similar to the Vetting and Barring Scheme in the UK. She said any reforms must balance “the rights of staff with the need to provide absolute assurance to families” and acknowledged that “there is a gap in the current oversight regime that must be addressed.”

HIQA inspectors identified several cases last year in which staff subject to disciplinary proceedings or criminal investigations had moved between facilities undetected due to poor sharing of information. One such case in County Meath saw a healthcare assistant found guilty of assaulting two residents, only to be re-employed months later in another home elsewhere in Leinster.

Age Action, the advocacy group, welcomed Deputy Ó Cuív’s intervention, arguing that “too much leniency” persists regarding staff misconduct and that lifetime bans for violent offenders are “the minimum reasonable standard.” Its chief executive, Paddy Connolly, warned that “vulnerable people are at risk if we allow known abusers to slip through the net.”

However, some unions representing care workers urged caution, pointing to the need for fair investigation processes and safeguards against false allegations. “Workers must not be subjected to summary dismissal without due process,” said SIPTU’s Paul Bell, while emphasising the union’s support for “robust measures against anyone proven to have caused harm.”

The Department of Health has indicated that a draft amendment to strengthen vetting and barring provisions could be brought to Cabinet before the summer recess. The Oireachtas Health Committee will hear submissions on the issue in the coming weeks, as families of affected residents say they want to see urgent action, not another “lengthy review”.

A spokesperson for the Taoiseach’s office said: “There can be no place for violence or abuse in any care setting. The Government is committed to closing loopholes and upholding the highest standards of safeguarding for all residents.”
headline: TD: Ban nursing home staff who violently abuse residents

text:
The Department of Justice has confirmed it is “actively engaging” with 19 airlines operating out of Dublin Airport, following revelations that hundreds of international passengers have arrived in Ireland with false or inadequate travel documentation. The move comes amid heightened concerns over the State’s ability to verify the identities of those claiming international protection, and mounting political pressure to tighten border controls.

A spokesperson for the Department told Gript that ongoing discussions with airline representatives are aimed at reinforcing existing protocols and exploring additional measures to “mitigate the risk” of individuals travelling to Ireland without proper papers. “All carriers have a legal obligation under EU and Irish law to ensure passengers are in possession of the appropriate documentation before boarding,” the spokesperson said. “We are working collaboratively with the airlines to uphold those responsibilities.”

The engagement follows a series of reports highlighting the scale of the problem. According to data released in response to parliamentary questions, over 80 percent of international protection applicants arriving at Dublin Airport in 2023 either presented with false documents or none at all. Most of these cases involved passengers who boarded flights in safe European countries, only to discard their identification en route or upon arrival — a practice that complicates the asylum process and raises security concerns.

The Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) has established a dedicated unit within Dublin Airport to intercept and process arrivals suspected of document fraud. However, sources within law enforcement told Gript that the sheer volume of cases is placing “significant pressure” on resources and contributing to bottlenecks in the system. “It’s a constant game of catch-up,” said one Garda member familiar with operations. “We’re dealing with sophisticated tactics, and the lack of cooperation from some airlines is not helping.”

The International Air Transport Association (IATA) rules require airlines to check the validity of passenger documents before departure, but enforcement appears patchy. Airlines can be liable for the cost of repatriating passengers denied entry, but penalties for non-compliance are rarely imposed, according to industry insiders.

Minister for Justice Helen McEntee has faced sustained criticism from opposition TDs and government backbenchers alike, with several members of the Rural Independent Group demanding immediate action. “It’s not credible to allow this situation to continue. The Department needs to get tough with the airlines,” said Independent TD for Laois-Offaly Carol Nolan. There have also been calls for the Oireachtas Justice Committee to launch an inquiry into the extent of document fraud and the efficacy of government responses.

In a statement, Dublin Airport’s operator DAA said it was supporting the authorities and working closely with airline partners to address the issue. “We are fully cooperating with the Gardaí and Department of Justice in their efforts to ensure the integrity of the State’s borders,” a spokesperson said.

The Department has not published a list of the 19 airlines involved, citing “operational sensitivities,” but it is understood that most major carriers connecting with European and Middle Eastern hubs are included in the talks. Internal HSE and Department of Integration memos seen by Gript confirm that the problem has also placed additional strain on accommodation and social services, with hundreds of new arrivals requiring urgent assessment and housing each month.

Government sources maintain that a combination of technology upgrades, greater intelligence-sharing, and stiffer sanctions for non-compliant airlines are under consideration. However, critics argue that progress has been “painfully slow” and that Ireland remains a soft target for document fraud compared with other EU countries.
headline: Dept engaging with 19 airlines to address false documents scandal

text:
Reports circulating on Wednesday evening claimed that Ishmail Haniyah, the political leader of Hamas, has been killed in a missile strike in Iran, in what would mark a significant escalation in the ongoing conflict across the Middle East.

Initial details remain unclear, with conflicting accounts coming from regional media and authorities. State-affiliated news sources in Iran have neither confirmed nor denied the incident, though social media accounts associated with Hamas published statements mourning Haniyah and warning of an “unprecedented response.” There has been no official statement issued by the group’s press office as of yet.

According to reports, the missile strike allegedly targeted a high-level meeting in Tehran attended by senior figures from Hamas and other aligned organisations. Iranian news agencies reported explosions in the vicinity of Tehran’s central district around 17:30 local time, but did not specify the cause.

Speculation is rife regarding responsibility for the attack. Some commentators point to Israel, which has previously vowed to dismantle Hamas’s foreign leadership structures following the October 7th attacks last year. However, the Israeli Defence Forces refused to comment when questioned by international media. Iranian security sources, quoted by semi-official outlets, blamed “external actors,” without further elaboration.

Haniyah has led the political bureau of Hamas since 2017 and is regarded as the chief architect of the group’s diplomatic initiatives abroad. Based outside Gaza for several years, he has travelled widely across the region, cultivating links with Iran, Qatar, and Turkey. He is considered a key intermediary between the core leadership in Gaza and international backers.

If verified, Haniyah’s death would leave a significant vacuum within the movement and could spark further destabilisation both in the Palestinian territories and throughout the Middle East. The timing of the reported strike comes at a moment of heightened tensions, with Israel recently engaging in tit-for-tat exchanges with Iranian-backed militias.

The Department of Foreign Affairs in Dublin said it was monitoring the situation closely and urged Irish citizens in the region to remain vigilant. A spokesperson for the Taoiseach described the reports as “deeply concerning,” calling for “restraint on all sides.”

Analysts warn the ramifications could extend well beyond Gaza. Iran’s Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, has previously pledged full support to the “Palestinian cause,” and any attack on Iranian soil is likely to provoke a sharp response. The United States, which has a significant troop presence in the region, has not commented on the matter, though Pentagon sources said they were “assessing the veracity” of the reports.

The UN Secretary-General has called for an immediate investigation and an urgent de-escalation, but with the facts still emerging, the prospect of retaliatory action remains high.

As of Wednesday night, neither the HSE nor the Irish Embassy in Tehran had reported any casualties among Irish citizens. The Department of Justice said there were no immediate indications of increased threats to the Irish diaspora, but that security protocols were being reviewed in light of the fast-developing situation.

More information is expected as authorities and international observers attempt to verify the details of the strike and its implications for the broader geopolitical landscape.
headline: Political leader of Hamas, Ishmail Haniyah, killed in Iran missile strike

Dr Hilary Cass, the leading paediatrician behind the landmark independent review of gender identity services for young people in the UK, has sharply criticised the politicisation of gender medicine, warning that children are being “weaponised” by activists and interest groups on both sides of the trans debate. Speaking to British media following the release of her long-awaited final report, Dr Cass said that the current discourse around gender identity has “become so toxic that it is children and their families who are suffering most.”

Dr Cass’s review, commissioned by NHS England and concluded last week, examined the evidence and clinical practice in treating children and adolescents distressed about their gender. The deeply divisive issue has also resonated in Ireland, where the State has no dedicated gender identity service for minors, but where heated public and political debates echo many of the concerns raised in the Cass report.

In her review, Dr Cass found “remarkably weak” evidence for puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones in children, and called for a cautious, case-by-case approach in treatment. She also condemned the climate of polarisation and intimidation affecting both clinicians and families. “We must stop weaponising children in a debate driven by ideology rather than evidence,” she said. “Children deserve care based on the best clinical standards, not campaigns or slogans.”

In Ireland, the Department of Health said it would study the Cass recommendations, after the HSE confirmed that a “clinical pathway” for gender care in young people remains under development. In the absence of domestic services, scores of Irish children have been referred to the UK’s now-closed Tavistock clinic in recent years. The Cass report was scathing of Tavistock’s practices, finding that some children were prescribed hormone interventions after just a handful of appointments, with scant attention paid to underlying mental health or family issues.

The Irish government has faced mounting calls for an independent review of any future gender identity services, with some Oireachtas members highlighting concerns about “affirmation-only” approaches and the long-term impact of medical interventions. Social Protection Minister Heather Humphreys told RTÉ that the government “will take on board” the key findings of the Cass Review. However, advocacy groups such as TENI (Transgender Equality Network Ireland) continue to press for easier access to medical transition for minors, warning against what they describe as “scare tactics” and “moral panic.”

Meanwhile, organisations like The Iona Institute and Women’s Space Ireland have welcomed Dr Cass’s warnings, urging the State to prioritise evidence-based practice over ideology. They say the experience in England should set off alarm bells here, given the potential for long-term harm if children are put on a medical pathway without robust safeguards.

Amid the heated rhetoric, Dr Cass has appealed for civility and perspective, stressing that her review is driven by concern for children’s wellbeing, not by partisan interests. “We all want the same thing: that any young person distressed about their gender receives safe, kind, and effective care,” she said. “But we must not allow children to become pawns in adult arguments.”

The fallout from the Cass Review is set to reverberate in Ireland, where more parents are voicing uncertainty about the pathway ahead, and clinicians warn that a lack of clear guidelines is leaving families in limbo.
headline: Dr Cass: children “weaponised” by toxic trans debate

text:
A significant new study has found mounting evidence that viral infections may play a key role in the development of neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's. The research, published this week in the journal Neuron, offers fresh insight into long-standing concerns within medical circles that certain viruses could be triggering or accelerating brain disorders that have, until now, largely been attributed to genetics and lifestyle factors.

The international team behind the study, led by scientists at the University of Helsinki, examined decades of anonymised health records from over 450,000 individuals, spanning both Nordic and North American populations. Their analysis identified a clear statistical link between previous viral infections—particularly influenza, shingles (herpes zoster), and viral encephalitis—and the subsequent onset of Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

According to the researchers, those with a history of certain viral infections were up to twice as likely to develop an associated neurodegenerative disease within 15 years of their initial illness. Flavio De Marco, a senior researcher involved in the study, said the findings "strengthen the hypothesis that common viruses may be among the environmental triggers for these brain disorders."

While a direct causal relationship has yet to be definitively established, the study did uncover compelling immunological patterns. Post-mortem brain tissue from Alzheimer's and Parkinson's patients frequently showed traces of viral DNA, suggesting that viruses may inflame the nervous system and set off a cascade of immune responses, ultimately damaging neural tissue. Previous Irish research funded by the Health Research Board has pointed to similar pathways.

Medical experts have called for policy makers and the HSE to take notice and update public health guidance, particularly concerning the importance of adult vaccination programmes. Dr Eimear Dunne, a neurologist at St James’s Hospital, commented that "if further studies confirm this association, it could change how we think about prevention and early intervention for Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s in Ireland."

The findings come amid increased scrutiny of long COVID and other post-viral syndromes that have left thousands of Irish patients struggling with neurological symptoms. While the study did not specifically examine COVID-19, the authors believe the pandemic offers a "unique natural experiment" to further test the viral hypothesis.

Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s are both major causes of disability and death in Ireland. According to the Alzheimer Society of Ireland, more than 64,000 people here are living with dementia, most commonly caused by Alzheimer’s, while Parkinson’s Association estimates 12,000 people in Ireland are living with Parkinson’s disease. The HSE has repeatedly called for greater investment in neurodegenerative disease research and services as the population ages.

The study’s implications will also feed into wider debates about the role of viral exposure in chronic disease development and the need for robust data linking infection surveillance with long-term health outcomes.

In the Dáil this week, opposition TDs urged the Government to commit additional funding to brain health research and to ensure the latest findings are rapidly translated into clinical practice. Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly has said the Department is reviewing the study in conjunction with the Chief Medical Officer.

Although experts caution that no single viral infection can be blamed for these complex diseases, the study’s authors stress that their work provides "the strongest evidence yet" that preventing and managing viral illnesses could have benefits that extend far beyond the acute phase, potentially reducing the future burden of devastating neurodegenerative conditions.
headline: New Study: link between Alzheimer’s/Parkinson’s and viral infection

More than €1.7 million of taxpayers’ money has been spent promoting Garda recruitment campaigns since 2019, new figures reveal, prompting criticism from opposition TDs and policing commentators who question the effectiveness of the high-profile advertising blitz during a period marked by a severe recruitment crisis.

According to data obtained by Gript, the money was expended on a mix of national radio, outdoor, digital, social media and print campaigns encouraging applications to An Garda Síochána. The figures, provided in response to a parliamentary question from Carol Nolan TD, show €1,704,656 has been spent on advertising and promotional activities since the start of 2019.

Despite the investment, the number of serving Gardaí remains below Government targets, with fewer than 13,900 currently active—well short of the 15,000 threshold set out in the last Programme for Government. The force has struggled to attract suitable new recruits, with intake figures falling short in multiple consecutive classes at Templemore. Most recent recruitment campaigns, widely trailed as refreshes of the Garda’s public image, have seen a steady drop-off between initial applications and new members actually taking up training places.

Speaking to Gript, former Assistant Commissioner Michael O’Sullivan said: “This level of spending would be questionable at the best of times, but it’s absolutely pointless when there’s little sign it’s making any meaningful difference. If people don’t see the Gardaí as an appealing or respected career, you can’t fix that with flashy adverts. The issues go much deeper—pay, morale, and public support are all part of it.”

Carol Nolan TD described the advertising spend as “farcical,” arguing that the Department of Justice and Garda management are “throwing good money after bad.” “If you ask serving members, they’ll tell you the real issues are a lack of support from the courts, anti-social policies from Government, and poor retention—not a lack of awareness about the job itself. This money would be better spent actually supporting frontline Gardaí or addressing morale,” she said.

An analysis of the recruitment ads shows a strong emphasis on diversity and modernisation, themes heavily promoted by Garda Commissioner Drew Harris. However, representatives from the Garda Representative Association (GRA) have warned repeatedly that aspiring recruits are being put off by negative media coverage, concerns about safety, and perceptions of political interference in policing.

One serving member in Dublin told Gript: “Putting up posters with smiling faces and new slogans is little comfort when there aren’t enough boots on the ground. Morale is at rock bottom and people are bailing out. Any ad campaign that doesn’t acknowledge that reality is doomed.”

The latest round of advertising began in February this year, after the force confirmed it had missed even its revised, lower recruitment targets for 2023. Minister for Justice Helen McEntee announced a streamlined application process amid warnings from her own officials that fewer people were applying to the service than at any point in the last decade.

A spokesman for the Department of Justice defended the spending, stating that “broad, multi-platform recruitment campaigns are a necessary part of modern public service recruitment,” and that ongoing efforts to raise awareness are essential to maintaining Garda numbers.

But public trust in the sustainability of such campaigns appears to be waning.
headline: “Absolutely pointless”: €1.7m spent on Garda recruitment ads since 2019

text:
Footage has emerged online showing the moment a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the Danube port town of Galați in Romania late on Saturday, marking a significant escalation in hostilities along NATO’s eastern frontier.

The incident, captured on a resident's security camera and widely circulated on social media, reveals a drone rapidly descending before a powerful explosion engulfs several storeys of a residential building. Romanian officials have since confirmed that the blast occurred shortly before midnight, injuring three civilians, including a child, and causing extensive damage to at least 40 apartments. Emergency services, backed by the Romanian Army, responded swiftly, with local authorities evacuating residents in the aftermath.

The Romanian Ministry of National Defence issued a statement condemning the attack, which it described as a “flagrant violation of national sovereignty,” and confirmed that fragments retrieved from the scene are consistent with the Shahed-136 drones used by Russian forces in Ukraine. The Ministry said Romania would be raising the incident at NATO and European Union level, and called for “greater vigilance and defensive measures” along the Black Sea corridor.

The attack occurred less than 16km from the border with war-torn Ukraine, where Russia has repeatedly targeted infrastructure near the Danube in attempts to disrupt grain shipments. Until now, outlying drone debris had been found in Romanian territory on several occasions, leading to heightened tensions and aerial warnings in the border counties of Tulcea and Galați. However, this marks the first recorded instance of a Russian drone directly striking a residential building on NATO soil since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022.

Speaking to local media, residents described scenes of panic and disbelief as the drone approached. “There was a loud buzzing, then the window shattered and we ran to the corridor,” said one witness, whose flat was among those damaged. “We never thought something like this would happen here.”

Romania’s President, Klaus Iohannis, condemned the attack as “utterly unacceptable” and called for a robust response from NATO allies. The Romanian government has requested an emergency meeting of the North Atlantic Council, invoking Article 4, which allows member states to bring security concerns for collective consultation.

The Taoiseach, Simon Harris, expressed Ireland’s solidarity with Romania in a statement released on Sunday. “An attack on a NATO member is an attack on the security architecture of all of Europe. We stand with our Romanian colleagues and call for respect for international law,” he said, urging diplomatic pressure to prevent further escalation.

The incident has renewed debate within the Oireachtas over Ireland’s policy of military neutrality and the adequacy of state responses to hybrid and aerial threats, especially given the country’s own limited air defence capabilities and reliance on NATO partners for surveillance.

In Brussels, the Secretary General of NATO, Jens Stoltenberg, warned Russia that “NATO territory will be defended,” and said that consultations with the Romanian government were under way. EU officials have also condemned the act, insisting on accountability for breaches of sovereignty.

No group or individual claimed responsibility for the drone, but Russian defence authorities confirmed overnight drone operations in southern Ukraine, claiming to have targeted military facilities and logistical hubs near the border. Moscow has denied deliberately attacking Romanian territory, insisting that any cross-border incidents were unintentional.

As of Sunday afternoon, engineers and Gardaí from the scene were carrying out investigations alongside NATO liaison officers. Initial reports indicate that while power and water supply have resumed, several dozen residents remain displaced.
headline: WATCH: Russian drone hits apartment block in NATO member Romania

Tributes have poured in from across the country following the sudden passing of Scarlett Faulkner, an outspoken commentator and activist known for her dedication to family values and her fearless defence of free expression. Faulkner, originally from County Down, passed away peacefully in her Belfast home on Sunday, according to a statement released by her family.

Colleagues and friends alike have described Faulkner as a woman of conviction who never shied away from challenging the political establishment, both in Northern Ireland and the Republic. Over the past decade, she became a familiar face on social media and in print, contributing regular opinion pieces to publications and engaging in lively debates on radio programmes.

Speaking to Gript, Aontú leader Peadar Tóibín TD said, “Scarlett was a powerful advocate for the pro-life cause, always willing to stand up for her beliefs, no matter the backlash. She brought clarity and compassion to public debate, and her passing is a great loss to the movement.”

Faulkner first rose to prominence during the 2018 campaign to retain the Eighth Amendment, participating in rallies across the island and gaining a reputation for incisive commentary. Her campaign work extended to issues of education and parental rights, where she called for greater respect for traditional family structures. She was also regarded as a staunch defender of religious freedom and frequently addressed Oireachtas committees on matters relating to faith and conscience.

A regular contributor to Gript and other alternative news outlets, Faulkner was praised for her willingness to question mainstream narratives and her commitment to what she described as “truth without compromise”. Many pointed to her courage in facing public criticism for her stances, particularly on social media, where she was unafraid to engage with those holding opposing views.

Former MEP Dana Rosemary Scallon said, “Scarlett was a beacon of hope for so many who felt their values were under siege. She spoke for the voiceless and did so with grace and determination.”

Messages of condolence have flooded social media, with many sharing stories of how Faulkner’s writing and public speaking inspired them to speak out on issues of conscience. Her family have thanked the public for their support and have asked for privacy as they make funeral arrangements.

Scarlett Faulkner is survived by her husband, two sons, and a wide circle of friends and supporters across Ireland. Her death marks the loss of a distinctive voice in Irish public discourse, and her legacy is likely to resonate for many years to come.
headline: Tributes flood in after Scarlett Faulkner passes away

text:
In recent years, a remarkable number of media outlets, NGOs, and even government departments have embraced the notion that young children and teenagers should be routinely consulted on matters of public policy. Campaigns abound urging the Dáil or Cabinet to "centre youth voices" on issues from climate change to education, and various youth assemblies have been staged with great fanfare. While this might offer politicians a photo opportunity and NGOs a pat on the back, it is worth asking whether the growing demand for child involvement in policymaking is anything more than a feel-good exercise—or, worse, whether it’s actively detrimental to public life.

Let’s begin with an axiom that should be obvious: policymaking in a democracy is the responsibility of elected adults, answerable to the public at the ballot box. Children, by definition, are not permitted to vote, and for good reason. Would anyone seriously suggest that a 12-year-old is equipped with the maturity, knowledge and long-term perspective to make decisions that may affect the nation’s economic, legal or moral framework for decades to come? The answer, surely, is no—and society recognises this in countless ways, from prohibitions on underage drinking to rules on driving and contractual responsibility. Involving children in governance is not an act of empowerment; it is an abdication of adult responsibility.

Supporters of child participation often claim that “children are experts in their own lives,” or that policy should be designed with those it will impact most in mind. No doubt, a child knows what it feels like to be a secondary school student or a member of a sports club. But insight into one’s personal experience is not evidence of an ability to weigh up complex trade-offs, to balance rights and responsibilities, or to understand the law of unintended consequences. Asking children to contribute to policy debates on matters like national budgeting, criminal justice, or international relations is not just performative—it undermines the seriousness with which those issues should be treated.

Worse, the practice risks politicising childhood. Instead of protecting children from the cut-and-thrust of political rows, activist organisations and educational programmes now encourage them to lobby the State on everything from carbon taxes to hate speech laws. This is a dangerous blurring of roles. It’s all too easy for adults—particularly those with an ideological agenda—to exploit children as mouthpieces for their own views. When a group of primary school students is paraded in front of an Oireachtas committee to demand legislative change, it is not a triumph of democracy; it is a spectacle in which children’s innocence is harnessed for propaganda.

Some might say that including youth voices fosters engagement and teaches civic responsibility. But true civic responsibility means understanding the limitations of one’s experience and respecting the processes by which society is governed. No one is saying that young people should be silenced, or that their concerns are irrelevant. There is a world of difference between listening to children in the family or classroom, and deputising them to shape national policy.

Ireland faces enough challenges without outsourcing decision-making to those with neither the experience nor the mandate to bear such weight. The role of children is to learn, and the role of adults is to lead—not vice versa. If we are to have mature, effective governance, we ought to return to that simple principle.
headline: No, kids shouldn’t be involved in policy-making

text:
The Irish Council for Civil Liberties (ICCL) has renewed its calls for a comprehensive “human rights review” of the Covid-19 lockdowns, warning that the exceptional emergency powers used by the Government should not become a “new normal” in Irish public life.

In a statement issued this week, the ICCL urged the Oireachtas to establish an independent inquiry into the sweeping restrictions imposed during the pandemic. The group argued that, while public health was a legitimate concern, the measures taken had “significantly curtailed” basic rights and freedoms guaranteed under Bunreacht na hÉireann and international law, including freedom of movement, association, and the right to earn a livelihood.

Executive Director Liam Herrick said that Ireland had witnessed “unprecedented interference with personal autonomy” over the course of the pandemic, from the mandatory closure of churches and businesses to the heavy-handed enforcement of travel limits by the Gardaí. “We were told at the time that these were temporary, justified by the public health emergency. Now is the time to look back and ask: were they really necessary? Were they proportionate? And how do we prevent such broad powers from being misused in future?” Herrick said.

The ICCL statement highlighted the fact that many of the legal instruments underpinning lockdown—such as the Health (Preservation and Protection and other Emergency Measures in the Public Interest) Act 2020—were passed in a matter of days, with little scrutiny by TDs or Senators. In some cases, opposition TDs voiced concerns about the lack of sunset clauses and the speed at which Ministerial powers were extended, but the Government insisted that robust oversight mechanisms were in place.

During the two years of rolling restrictions, thousands of people were stopped and fined by Gardaí under emergency powers. Critics, including senior legal academics, have since argued that many of these fines were legally questionable, with several being overturned when challenged in the District Court. ICCL claims these cases underline the need for a formal process of accountability.

Last month, the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Health heard submissions from legal and rights experts on the legacy of Covid regulations, but as yet, no decision has been made on establishing a statutory inquiry. The Department of Health has said any review would be “premature” while the World Health Organisation’s own pandemic review is ongoing.

Victims’ advocacy groups and business owners, many of whom suffered severe losses or closures during the restrictions, have joined calls for an inquiry, stating that lessons must be drawn from what they describe as a “traumatising” period for Irish society.

Meanwhile, Government ministers have largely defended their record, with Tánaiste Micheál Martin last week stating that Ireland’s response had “saved lives”, and that all decisions were guided by public health advice. Taoiseach Simon Harris has indicated that he is “open to a review in principle”, but warned against politicising the issue.

While some TDs have called for a “truth and reconciliation-style commission” to examine the impact of the lockdown, others have accused the ICCL of “playing into the hands of conspiracy theorists”. Sinn Féin’s health spokesperson, David Cullinane, said, “There are legitimate questions about proportionality, but we must not forget the context of the time—people were dying, hospitals were under siege.”

The ICCL insists that a non-partisan, rights-focused inquiry is necessary to restore public trust.
headline: ICCL calls for “human rights review” of Covid lockdown

text:
When the Government is challenged on its handling of any contentious issue nowadays, the phrase “misinformation” is trotted out with growing frequency. This defence, which is becoming almost a reflex from Ministers and spokespersons, appears designed to silence criticism, rather than provide clarity or accountability. But in reality, invoking “misinformation” as a catch-all excuse is not only unconvincing, it is deeply insulting to the public’s intelligence.

Recent weeks have seen the “misinformation” smear deployed to dismiss concerns about Ireland’s migration system, the housing crisis, and even debates on the new Hate Speech legislation. Rather than engaging with the substance of objections—be they from Opposition TDs, community groups, or ordinary citizens—the Taoiseach and Cabinet regularly brand such questions as the product of “online misinformation” or “far-right narratives.” The effect is to shut down debate, while painting all critics with the same brush.

Is there genuinely a great surfeit of false information out there? Of course, in the age of social media, some claims do circulate which are inaccurate or misleading. No reasonable person disputes that. But the Government’s eagerness to invoke the term “misinformation” at every turn is transparently self-serving. It allows Ministers to avoid engaging with hard questions: Why did Ireland receive over 141,000 new arrivals last year without adequate infrastructure or services? Why are thousands of Irish citizens still languishing on housing lists or enduring record hospital waits? Why are genuine concerns about freedom of expression under the Hate Speech Bill being waved away as the product of Facebook conspiracy theorists?

Moreover, this stance is downright hypocritical. Recall, for instance, official pronouncements during the pandemic that repeatedly shifted and even contradicted the available evidence, particularly on issues such as mandatory mask wearing or vaccine passports. When citizens expressed legitimate worries, they too were accused of “misinformation”—only for some of those same “conspiracy theories” to be vindicated months later by the evolving scientific consensus.

The Irish public is perceptive, and it has not failed to notice that the charge of “misinformation” most often follows a familiar pattern: when the facts are uncomfortable, or when public anger is mounting, suddenly the Government invokes the spectre of fake news. It’s a rhetorical shield to duck scrutiny—not a genuine attempt to promote informed debate.

This is not a healthy way for a democracy to function. The Oireachtas is supposed to be a forum for robust argument, not a club for those who toe the line. And outside Leinster House, citizens are entitled to challenge official narratives without being dismissed as dupes or extremists. If the Government wishes to retain any credibility, it must stop the waffle about “misinformation” and start answering the hard questions, honestly and directly. Otherwise, all the pious talk about fighting “fake news” is less about truth, and more about simply suppressing dissent.
headline: The Government’s “misinformation” defence is utter waffle

text:
A row has erupted after a news team covering events at Citywest accused Gardaí of “attacking” them during a protest on Friday evening. Members of the group, said to be documenting unrest at the controversial Citywest transit hub, claimed they were forcibly removed from the scene and that equipment was damaged in the process.

Footage widely shared on social media appears to show Gardaí forming a cordon at the entrance to the centre during heightened tensions between demonstrators and officers. In a statement released late on Friday night, the news team alleged that they were “physically shoved” away from the main entrance, despite identifying themselves as journalists, and that one camera was knocked to the ground during the incident.

The news team, who describe themselves as independent reporters, said: “We were there to document the demonstration and relay the concerns of local residents, but were instead subjected to an unwarranted attack by members of An Garda Síochána.” They are calling for an immediate investigation into what they describe as a breach of press freedom, and say the actions of Gardaí amounted to “an assault on journalism”.

Gardaí, for their part, have said they “engaged with all individuals present on the basis of public order” and that “no arrests were made” during the protest, which saw more than 60 people gather outside the accommodation centre. In a statement to Gript, a Garda spokesperson said: “An Garda Síochána recognises and respects the important role played by the media. Any complaints will be fully examined in accordance with Garda policy and procedure.”

The protest at Citywest comes amid growing concern in the community at the continued use of the facility to house asylum seekers. Local representatives have raised questions in the Dáil about the lack of consultation and oversight, while government insists that the centre is a necessary response to the housing and migration crisis.

Speaking to Gript, one protest organiser, who asked not to be named, criticised the conduct of the Gardaí at the event. “There was no need for force to be used against journalists. The community has a right to be heard and the media a right to report without interference,” they said.

Supporters of the Citywest accommodation centre have meanwhile condemned what they describe as “intimidation tactics” by some demonstrators, and called for dialogue rather than confrontation.

It is not the first time allegations of heavy-handed policing have surfaced in relation to immigration-related protests. Last month, TDs from constituencies in Dublin called for increased transparency following reports of journalists and local citizens being prevented from filming outside similar facilities.

The National Union of Journalists (NUJ) released a short statement on Saturday morning calling for “clarity and respect for media access” at all public demonstrations. The union noted that any interference with news reporting should be subject to “immediate scrutiny”.

As of Saturday afternoon, the equipment allegedly damaged during the incident remains with the news team, who say they are considering legal options and will be lodging a formal complaint with the Garda Ombudsman.

A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said “all individuals’ rights, including those of the press, must be upheld during protests,” and that the Department would be monitoring the situation at Citywest closely.
headline: CITYWEST: news team accuse Gardaí of ‘attack’

text:
The Taoiseach this week announced yet another suite of measures aimed at boosting housing supply, reaffirming Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil’s seemingly endless faith in the capacity of Government to fix a crisis which, at this stage, stands as the nation’s greatest policy failure in decades. If there is one thing every party in the Dáil appears to agree on, it is that the solution to the ongoing housing shortage is more Government intervention — more spending, more targets, more launches, more red tape. But the evidence from the last twenty years suggests exactly the opposite: the more the State has tried to fix the housing market, the worse it has got.

Consider the record: In 2007, the last year that housing supply remotely kept up with demand, private developers built almost 80,000 homes. Today, with the Government the dominant player in housing, we’re lucky to manage half that, despite population growth and sky-high demand. Since the crash, the State’s obsession with ‘affordable housing’, ‘social homes’, and now ‘cost-rental’ schemes has distorted the market, driven up costs, and crowded out private investment. The result is a dysfunctional system where prices keep rising, but neither aspiring owners nor renters can find a home.

The cause is not a mystery. Government policy — from excessive planning regulation, to spiralling construction levies, to endless environmental and social ‘requirements’ — has made it almost impossible to build in Ireland without the consent and patronage of officialdom. Large swathes of land are zoned but unserviced, or tied up in bureaucratic limbo. Every year, new initiatives are rolled out: Help-to-Buy, First Home, Land Development Agencies, the Shared Equity Scheme, and more. Each one is touted as a game-changer; each one makes the system more byzantine, and increases the dependence of the construction industry on public subsidy and permission.

Successive Ministers for Housing, from Simon Coveney to Darragh O’Brien, have realised that they cannot build their way out of this crisis, yet they cannot bring themselves to step back and let the market respond to demand. Instead, the Department of Housing acts as both umpire and player: setting the rules, distributing the money, and picking which projects get built and where. The result is a housing policy designed to avoid political pain, not to deliver homes. 

Even the so-called ‘Land Value Sharing’ measures and recent Government moves to buy up derelict and unfinished developments reflect the same statist approach, hoovering up what little opportunity remains for private actors and channelling it through State agencies and quangos. Meanwhile, ordinary people, be they renters or would-be first-time buyers, are left with the same old story: long waiting lists, soaring rents, and zero certainty.

What Ireland needs is not another round of centralised plans and announcements, but a radical reduction in Government involvement. Abolish restrictive planning rules that freeze land supply. Cut taxes and levies that add tens of thousands to the cost of each home. Scrap arbitrary targets and mandates for ‘social’ or ‘affordable’ units that only slow down projects and make them unviable. Let private enterprise do what it does best: build where there is demand, for the people who need homes, not to tick bureaucratic boxes.

Of course, there will be claims from the Opposition benches that the market ‘failed’ before — but it did not.
headline: MCGUIRK: Want more houses? Get the Government out of housing.

text:
Alastair Campbell, the former Downing Street press secretary and infamous spin-doctor for Tony Blair, has declared that the public “don’t see us as politicians,” in conversation with Tánaiste Micheál Martin. The remarks were made during a wide-ranging discussion at the Irish Government’s new Global Ireland Summit, held in Dublin on Wednesday. The event, which was attended by senior officials, diplomats, and a number of opposition TDs, focused on Ireland’s international standing and the future of Irish foreign policy.

Campbell, now a high-profile commentator and columnist, offered his reflections on the shifting relationship between public trust and political leadership in Ireland and the UK. Addressing the Tánaiste directly during a panel discussion, Mr Campbell asserted: “People don’t see us as politicians anymore. They see us as something else entirely – part of a system that no longer represents them.”

Martin, who has led Fianna Fáil since 2011 and previously served as Taoiseach, responded by acknowledging the deepening mistrust between politicians and the electorate, but emphasised the need for politicians to “work harder than ever” to rebuild trust. He pointed to Ireland’s unique political landscape, where party allegiances are less tribal and the electorate highly engaged, but noted that even here, “people’s faith in political processes has taken a knock.”

The exchange comes amid recent findings from the Electoral Reform Commission showing a continuing decline in public trust in Irish political institutions, with just 27% of Irish adults surveyed last month saying they believe politicians “put the public interest first.” In contrast, nearly half of respondents described TDs as being “out of touch with ordinary people.”

Mr Campbell, whose legacy remains fiercely debated in British and Irish circles, cited the “professionalisation” of politics as a root cause of this estrangement. “When the main ambition is to survive the next news cycle, something crucial is lost,” he said, drawing a comparison to the declining faith in state institutions seen in the wake of the UK’s Brexit referendum.

Tánaiste Martin defended the Irish system’s record, highlighting recent reforms to Dáil committee structures and transparency measures introduced by the Standards in Public Office Commission (SIPO). However, he admitted that the work “has a long way to go,” and said that “improving the visibility and accountability of national decision-making” would remain a government priority.

The summit, organised by the Department of Foreign Affairs, also heard from representatives of the Irish diaspora, business leaders, and human rights advocates who called for greater transparency and responsiveness from Leinster House. Sinn Féin’s foreign affairs spokesperson, John Brady TD, said that “if people are losing faith in politicians, it is because politicians have failed to address issues that matter—cost of living, migration, rural decline.”

Audience members questioned both Campbell and Martin about the impact of social media, political polarisation, and allegations of spin and “groupthink” at the heart of government. Campbell, for his part, admitted that the tactics he popularised in the Blair years have contributed to wider cynicism, but insisted that “tough messaging” was necessary “in an age of relentless misinformation.”

As the summit concluded, the Tánaiste said the Irish government “cannot ignore” the growing gulf between voters and elected representatives, and promised that “the days of politics as usual are over.”
headline: “People don’t see us as politicians”: Alastair Campbell to Micheál Martin

A Fianna Fáil councillor who had been outspoken in his criticism of the government’s approach to immigration and accommodation has resigned from the party, saying it is “hopelessly detached from ordinary people and their everyday concerns”.

Cllr Seán O’Dowd, elected in 2019 to the Louth County Council, announced his departure on Friday, stating he can “no longer, in good conscience, represent a party that refuses to listen to the communities it claims to serve.” Speaking to Gript, Cllr O’Dowd said the final straw came with what he described as “a pattern of dismissing any dissent on the immigration issue,” after his interventions at recent council meetings calling for “greater transparency and consultation with local residents” about the sudden arrival of international protection applicants in small towns and rural areas.

“The leadership doesn’t want to hear about the impact their policies are having on rural Ireland,” O’Dowd said. “When local people raise genuine worries about resources, services, or the pace and scale of change, they are labelled as bigots by Dublin-based party managers who haven’t a clue what life is like outside the M50.” 

O’Dowd, who represents the Ardee Municipal District, had previously tabled motions calling for a cap on numbers of asylum seekers accommodated in any one locality, and had publicly criticised Minister for Integration Roderic O’Gorman and officials at the Department of Children for what he called “a total lack of engagement” with elected representatives.

Fianna Fáil HQ did not respond directly to O’Dowd’s resignation, but a party spokesperson reiterated the coalition’s “commitment to a fair and compassionate approach to migration in line with Ireland’s international obligations”. Privately, party sources expressed frustration that O’Dowd had “chosen to grandstand rather than work within the party to achieve real change”.

Local reaction in Ardee was largely supportive of the councillor’s move, with one resident telling Gript: “He’s only voicing what half the country is saying. People feel ignored.” O’Dowd said he would continue to serve on Louth County Council as an Independent, and confirmed he will seek re-election in 2024.

Political analysts said the departure will raise fresh questions within Fianna Fáil about its grassroots support, particularly in rural constituencies where immigration has become a flashpoint. The party has faced recent defections in Wexford and Mayo on similar grounds, and senior TDs have privately warned of an “existential crisis” for the party outside metropolitan areas.

O’Dowd concluded: “Fianna Fáil once stood for the ordinary Irish person. I don’t believe that’s true anymore – and many lifelong supporters know it in their bones.”
headline: Fianna Fáil Cllr who criticised immigration policy resigns, says party “detached from ordinary person”

text:
Reports of disturbing trends in social policy often reach the public cloaked in the language of care and progress. The steady drift of Irish public discourse around “compassionate” initiatives regularly hides the harsh consequences that follow in their wake. Of late, the expansion of so-called rights and entitlements, particularly around social issues, has been driven less by a genuine concern for those involved and more by a political class eager to signal their virtue and their alignment with global trends—no matter the impact on Irish society.

Consider, for example, the recent advocacy efforts around euthanasia and the calls to introduce assisted dying into the healthcare system. Proponents argue for “choice,” for the “right to die with dignity,” but these slogans mask a far more unsettling reality. Once the door is opened to legal doctor-assisted suicide, it sends a message to the vulnerable—our elderly, our disabled, those suffering from depression—that their lives are burdensome or less valuable than those of the healthy and able-bodied. International experience, from Canada to the Netherlands, has already demonstrated these risks, with cases of people opting for assisted death not because medicine failed them, but because society did.

The same principle applies to Ireland’s ongoing debates over migration and asylum policies. Official narratives, repeated faithfully by government spokespeople and much of the media, appeal to our historic memory of emigration and hardship. Yet these pleas for “compassion” ignore the actual needs and concerns of local communities, particularly in rural towns where unplanned and unmanaged arrivals have caused significant social strain, stretched public services, and undermined cohesion. Gardaí are left under-resourced, primary schools are overwhelmed, and local populations feel voiceless as the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth pushes ahead with relocations announced at short notice and with little consultation.

This same phenomenon is evident in the area of gender ideology. Activists, cheered on by the Department of Education and many NGOs, stress the need to “protect” transgender children and adults. But the result of this ideology is a dramatic surge in children presenting to gender clinics like the controversial Tavistock centre in the UK, now disbanded after a torrent of clinical failures. Ireland has begun importing these policies, despite mounting evidence of their dangers and the distress caused to children and families left to navigate irreversible medical interventions. Still, to object or even raise concerns is deemed “cruel,” the debate swiftly shut down by those who claim the mantle of compassion.

Too often in recent years, talk of empathy and progress has meant shutting down dissent, bypassing public debate, and dismissing the legitimate worries of ordinary people. Compassion is not demonstrated by reflexive openness to every proposal that arrives from Brussels or the UN, nor by prioritising the demands of activist groups over thoughtful, community-centred policymaking. True care means considering the long-term consequences, protecting the vulnerable from the unintended outcomes of careless reforms, and ensuring that the voices of all Irish citizens—not just a select cadre of campaigners—are respected in the process.

Ireland has, for centuries, been a country defined by community, by looking out for neighbours and cherishing life at every stage. The rush to endorse every new “progressive” cause, especially when done under the guise of compassion, risks undermining that heritage. Policy that is truly compassionate is honest, prudent, and rooted in reality—not just in slogans and sentiment.
headline: Cruelty Cloaked in Compassion

text:
Last week, the Central Statistics Office (CSO) released its latest survey on sexual violence in Ireland, sparking a fresh round of reaction and headlines. The Sexual Violence Survey 2022 follows on from the 2021 survey and paints a picture of Irish society that is both confronting and, in parts, open to interpretation. As with all statistics, context and nuance matter, and there is a real risk that the raw figures may be misunderstood—or deliberately misrepresented—by campaigners or the political class.

The headline findings are stark. According to the CSO, 40% of adults in Ireland report experiencing some form of sexual violence in their lifetime, with women significantly more likely than men to report such experiences. The overall figure for women is given as 55%, compared to 24% for men. These numbers have been described as “shocking” by advocacy groups and politicians alike, and there are calls for further funding for services and for a re-examination of government policy.

No-one would seriously dispute that sexual violence is a grave and serious problem. But when figures seem to suggest that over half of all Irish women and one in four Irish men have experienced some form of sexual violence, it is essential to look more closely at what is being measured, and how those results are being presented.

The CSO survey uses a broad definition of “sexual violence,” covering not just acts that would constitute a criminal offence under Irish law, such as rape or sexual assault, but also a range of other experiences: unwanted touching, forced viewing of sexual images, or sexual harassment in the workplace or in public. For example, “unwelcome sexual comments, jokes, or gestures” are counted in the same category as physical assault. This approach is not unique to the CSO—similar definitions are used in many modern surveys—but it does mean that the figures being quoted combine a wide spectrum of behaviour, from the criminal to the inappropriate or objectionable.

This is not to downplay the impact of any of these experiences on individuals, but to suggest that the public and policymakers should be precise when interpreting what is being reported. The danger is that, by grouping all these behaviours together, we create the impression that sexual violence, in the most serious sense of the term, is happening to the majority of people in the country. That simply is not borne out by the Gardaí’s own figures, nor by the annual crime statistics.

In 2022, for example, the Gardaí recorded just over 3,800 sexual offences, including rape, sexual assault, and other offences, across the State. While it is widely acknowledged that sexual crimes are under-reported, the difference between the official figures and the CSO’s survey data suggests more than just under-reporting—it reflects the broad expansion of what is being included under the heading of “sexual violence.”

Some campaigners argue that redefining sexual violence in this way is itself an achievement, bringing to light behaviours previously ignored or minimised. That is a reasonable point, but when Government departments, statutory bodies, and the media repeat the 40% figure without qualification, there is a real risk of creating a sense of moral panic, and of undermining the public’s trust in statistics and reporting.

There is another issue, too. The CSO survey was based on self-reporting, and the responses were voluntary.
headline: Premium: Making sense of the CSO figures on sexual violence

text:
As the dust settles on the latest controversy surrounding RTÉ’s erroneous reporting of a so-called “far-right” conspiracy about an alleged “arson epidemic” sweeping the country, questions must be asked about the role of Ireland’s mainstream media in scrutinising facts—or, indeed, dodging inconvenient truths. Yesterday’s grovelling “clarifications” from both Prime Time and the station’s social media accounts came only after days of mounting public pressure, as the narrative spun from the original allegations about activist-led misinformation to an embarrassing admission that much of the programme’s own coverage relied on dubious figures and incomplete data.

For weeks, RTÉ and several other outlets insisted that claims of a significant rise in arson attacks targeting properties earmarked for migrants, asylum seekers, or government accommodation plans were not only exaggerated but rooted in “far-right disinformation.” Garda sources were invoked—anonymously, of course—to assure viewers that there was little or no evidence of arson targeting, and that, in any case, far-right activists were deliberately inflaming tensions through spurious online rumours.

However, as independent journalists and citizen sleuths compiled fire service call-outs, published and unpublished Garda records, and photographic evidence from around the country, it quickly became apparent that the lion’s share of supposed “misinformation” was, in fact, entirely accurate. A string of fires—from Galway to Dublin, Wicklow to Cork—have, since late last year, either been confirmed or are under active Garda investigation as suspected arson, in many cases on properties newly announced for refugee or asylum seeker accommodation.

The plain facts show that, while investigations are ongoing in numerous cases, outright dismissals by media of even the possibility of arson were simply not supported by available evidence. Yet, rather than issue prompt corrections, RTÉ initially doubled down. When critics pointed to the growing number of suspicious blazes, the broadcaster retreated behind vague statements about “ongoing investigations” and the need to avoid “speculation.”

But speculation, it seems, was fair game if it pointed in only one direction: blaming the so-called far right. This week’s u-turn, with Prime Time quietly updating its reporting after the horse had long bolted, raises a deeper concern about the willingness of media to serve as gatekeepers of information, rather than as relayers of facts. The public, increasingly distrustful of official sources and national broadcasters, have had to do the basic legwork that journalists once prided themselves on.

Of course, it does not excuse or condone genuine hate-mongering or threats towards individuals, nor does it imply every fire is politically motivated. But it should not be the job of ordinary people to keep the country informed while the taxpayer-funded broadcaster—and much of the rest of the media—spend their time editorialising rather than investigating.

If RTÉ is to have any credibility left with the public, it must realise that “fighting misinformation” does not mean suppressing inconvenient truths in the service of a political or ideological narrative. As the events of this week have shown, wilful misrepresentation of facts is not just counterproductive, it is dangerous; it hands easy ammunition to those who would claim the entire system is rotten. The response to this debacle will tell much about the future of Irish media—and, perhaps, the future of public trust in our national institutions.
headline: A black day for media misinformation

text:
US President Joe Biden has pledged to ensure a “peaceful transition of power” after failing to secure re-election in the 2024 contest, conceding defeat as Republican Donald Trump claimed victory amid a divisive and closely-fought race.

In a brief address from the White House, President Biden, 81, said he accepted the will of the American people, citing the importance of maintaining stability and respect for democratic norms. “While today is not the outcome I had hoped for, I have always believed in the sanctity of America’s democracy. I will ensure a peaceful transition, as has been the tradition of this country,” he told reporters.

The concession comes after a dramatic night in which Mr Trump, 78, declared victory following projections showing him securing the necessary majority in the Electoral College. While final counts are still pending in some states, major broadcasters, including the Associated Press and Reuters, have called the election in favour of Mr Trump, who previously served as president from 2017 to 2021.

President Biden acknowledged deep political divisions, urging calm amid reports of sporadic protests in cities including Washington DC, New York, and Portland. State authorities, including the National Guard in several swing states, have been placed on alert to deter potential disturbances.

The Taoiseach Simon Harris welcomed President Biden’s “gracious” remarks, stating that Ireland’s relationship with the United States “transcends any one administration.” Mr Harris, who met President Biden during his St Patrick’s Day visit to Washington earlier this year, said he looked forward to “working with President-elect Trump and his team on vital issues for the Irish people, including immigration, trade, and the Good Friday Agreement.”

European Union leaders, who voiced unease about the possibility of Trump’s return to power, also congratulated the former president on his apparent victory. Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, said the EU “stood ready to cooperate with the next administration on the basis of mutual respect and shared values.”

The Biden campaign has called on supporters to respect the outcome, despite concerns expressed over alleged voting irregularities in a handful of states. Legal representatives for the Democratic National Committee indicated that, while they would monitor ongoing recounts and legal challenges, they did not expect any major change in the result.

Mr Trump, speaking at a rally in Mar-a-Lago, Florida, hailed the win as a “return to American greatness” and suggested he would seek to reverse a number of the Democratic policies enacted under the Biden administration, including climate regulations and immigration reforms.

Biden’s concession and the outgoing administration’s emphasis on an orderly transition stand in stark contrast to the aftermath of the 2020 election, when Trump’s refusal to concede led to unprecedented turmoil, culminating in the Capitol riots of January 2021.

Irish citizens residing in the US have voiced mixed reactions. John O’Sullivan, an emigrant from Cork living in Chicago, said he hoped the transition would be “dignified and peaceful for everyone’s sake,” while others expressed anxiety about policy changes affecting the undocumented Irish community.

Gardaí in Ireland said they were not expecting any immediate security concerns related to the US election, but would continue to monitor international developments. The Department of Foreign Affairs has issued updated travel advice, urging Irish nationals in the US to “remain aware of local developments and follow guidance from local authorities” during the transition period.

President Biden is expected to remain in office until the inauguration in January 2025.
headline: President Biden promises “peaceful transition” following Trump victory
