As the second year of the Russia-Ukraine war draws to a close, there is little sign of either the military or diplomatic breakthroughs so often promised by Western leaders. Instead, the conflict grinds on, day after bloody day, with no end in sight. Despite the billions poured in by the EU, the US, and NATO countries—including Ireland’s own €122 million in non-lethal aid and contributions—Ukraine has lost territory in incremental Russian advances, and the once-vaunted counter-offensive has faltered.

From the outset, the dominant narrative offered by Western media and many of our own politicians was that Russia would be swiftly brought to its knees by unprecedented sanctions and a show of democratic unity. When Moscow’s initial drive towards Kyiv stalled, this was trumpeted as proof of Russian incompetence and Ukrainian superiority. But twelve months on, that optimism has evaporated—replaced by a grim acceptance that both sides are dug in for a long fight, and the economic war has failed to cripple Putin’s regime.

Ukraine’s much-anticipated summer counteroffensive was to be the turning point, according to numerous defence analysts and former generals wheeled out on RTÉ and quoted in the Irish Times. Yet it barely dented Russian lines, at a cost in lives that President Zelenskyy himself has called “painful”. Western-supplied tanks and armoured vehicles, including cutting-edge German and American kit, are now a familiar sight among the burned-out wreckage along the front. In spite of record arms shipments, the old Soviet lines held, and the maps have changed little since the winter of 2022.

On the diplomatic front, we have witnessed a year of missed opportunities. Ukraine’s Western backers insist that only Kyiv can decide when to negotiate, while repeatedly urging escalation—including long-range missiles and even controversial cluster munitions. Meanwhile, Russia, for all its brutality, appears increasingly confident that the West’s patience is waning. Polling in key EU states, including France and Germany, shows declining public support for further military spending. In the United States, where $75 billion has already been spent, Congress is now openly debating whether to cut future aid.

Ireland’s own position has become increasingly muddled. The Government has tried to square neutrality with rhetorical support for Ukraine, offering training and medical support through the EU’s so-called “peace facility”. Yet, as the cost-of-living crisis deepens, with rents rising and hospitals under pressure, more Irish people are asking: where is the limit? And what is the endgame?

Perhaps worst of all, the year has been marked by a stubborn refusal to reckon with reality. We have heard repeated warnings of impending Russian military collapse, only for each to be quietly dropped from the news cycle. The EU embargo on Russian oil was supposed to choke off funding, but Moscow simply sold more to China and India, while energy prices at home soared. The mantra that “Ukraine is winning” has proved not merely premature, but dangerously misleading—fuel for a war that looks set to drag on indefinitely.

It is all too easy, in Dublin or Brussels, to cheerlead for a distant war. But the consequences are very real: destroyed Ukrainian cities, a hollowing-out of Europe’s defence stockpiles, staggering economic costs, and a growing risk of further escalation.
headline: A year of getting it wrong. A review of the Russia-Ukraine War

text:
A Dublin mother has said she feels she has “more chance of winning the lotto” than securing a social house for her family, as the housing crisis continues to bite in the capital.

Sarah Doyle, a 34-year-old mother of three from Ballyfermot, has been on the social housing list for over seven years. Despite making regular contact with Dublin City Council and providing updated details of her growing family, her rank on the list has barely shifted.

Speaking to Gript, Ms Doyle described spending years in cramped temporary accommodation, sofa-surfing with relatives and friends, and at times fearing for her children’s safety and stability. “My eldest is starting secondary school in September, and we’re still living out of suitcases. We go from my mam’s to a friend’s flat to my sister-in-law’s — all because there’s nowhere for us,” she said.

The family’s experience is not unique. Latest figures from the Department of Housing show more than 14,500 people, including over 4,000 children, are currently registered as homeless nationwide, with the majority in Dublin. The number of families living in so-called ‘family hubs’ and emergency accommodation reached a new high in May, according to the charity Focus Ireland.

Ms Doyle said the promises made by successive ministers and parties about tackling the crisis have failed to materialise. “Every election they say they’ll sort it out, but nothing changes. Sometimes I think I’d have a better chance if I did the Euromillions every week than waiting on the council to come calling,” she said.

She questioned the allocation process and criteria used by local authorities. “It’s not clear how they’re deciding who gets a house. I know families who got sorted quickly, and others like us still waiting years. It feels like a lottery — only at least with lotto, you eventually see a winner.”

Opposition TDs have raised concerns in the Dáil that the government’s Housing for All strategy is failing to meet targets, particularly when it comes to social and affordable homes. The Taoiseach, Simon Harris, has echoed assurances made by his predecessors that the government is “committed to ending homelessness,” but many affected families remain sceptical.

The current government’s target is to deliver 9,100 new social homes in 2024. However, housing campaigners argue the pace is too slow to address both current homelessness and the mounting backlog on waiting lists. “The situation is critical,” said Fr Peter McVerry, founder of the Peter McVerry Trust. “Families are being failed by a system that just can’t keep up.”

Ms Doyle said she has reached breaking point: “You try to stay positive for the kids, but it’s hard when they ask why their friends have homes and they don’t. I feel forgotten. It’s like everyone’s given up — except us mums, who have no choice but to keep fighting.”

In a statement, Dublin City Council said it is “doing everything possible to increase the supply of social and affordable housing”, but acknowledged demand “heavily outstrips supply.”

For families like the Doyles, the odds — and their patience — are wearing thin.
headline: Dublin mum says she feels she has more chance of winning the lotto than being housed

Two men have died and two others are being treated in hospital following a shooting incident in Co Fermanagh late on Saturday evening. The attack occurred in the small rural area of Lisnaskea, with emergency services called to the scene shortly after 8pm.

It is understood that the victims were gathered at a private residence near the Drumhaw Fold area when several shots were fired. The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) confirmed that two men died at the scene, despite the efforts of paramedics. Two others, a man and a woman, sustained injuries described as serious but not life-threatening, and were transferred to South West Acute Hospital in Enniskillen.

Forensic officers remained at the cordoned-off scene overnight, with investigators carrying out door-to-door enquiries in the quiet Fermanagh community on Sunday morning. The area, a close-knit locality known for its strong community ties, has been left in shock. Locals told Gript that gun violence is almost unheard of in this part of Ulster.

Chief Superintendent Gillian Kearney, PSNI District Commander for Fermanagh and Omagh, appealed for witnesses to come forward. “This was a reckless and violent attack. Our thoughts are with the families of the deceased and those injured. We are urging anyone who was in the area at the time, or who may have dashcam or CCTV footage, to contact us.”

Political reaction was swift, with the Taoiseach, Simon Harris, expressing his condolences to the families affected. “Such violence has no place on our island,” he said. The Tánaiste, Micheál Martin, echoed those sentiments, offering government support to the authorities in the North and to the local community.

The Gardaí have confirmed that they are in close contact with their PSNI counterparts, given the proximity of the border and the potential for cross-border implications. Additional patrols were visible in the border zone on Sunday.

No arrests have yet been made and the motive for the shooting remains unclear. Security sources told Gript that all lines of enquiry are being pursued, including the possibility of a local dispute or links to organised criminality.

Sinn Féin MP for Fermanagh and South Tyrone, Michelle Gildernew, described the incident as “deeply disturbing”, calling for calm and urging anyone with information to cooperate with the PSNI investigation. The DUP’s Arlene Foster, a native of the area, said she was “heartbroken” for the families and praised the “quiet courage” of locals in the face of tragedy.

This latest incident will once again raise concerns about rural policing and community safety along the border, with calls for additional resources for both the PSNI and the Gardaí. A major investigation is now underway, and the PSNI have appealed to anyone with information or relevant footage to contact detectives on the non-emergency number 101, quoting incident reference 1847 of 1 June 2024.

The names of the deceased have not yet been released pending notification of next of kin. Further updates are expected as the investigation continues.
headline: Co Fermanagh: Two dead, two injured in shooting incident

text:
The chorus from many mainstream commentators, following the recent European Parliament elections, is that Europe is decisively “shifting to the right.” It is a phrase that has rung out across radio airwaves and been pasted on the front pages from Berlin to Dublin. But is it true? Does the surge in votes for certain parties signal an unabashed continental embrace of what many would call right-wing values—or does it reflect a more complicated and localised reaction to the present political and economic malaise?

Let us start with a fact: in France, Marine Le Pen’s National Rally trounced Emmanuel Macron’s party, prompting the French President to gamble on dissolving the National Assembly and calling a snap parliamentary election. In Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD), despite being shunned by the establishment and engulfed in scandals, increased its vote share and now sits in second place nationally. Even in Ireland, the election revealed growing dissatisfaction with traditional power blocs, with the “big three” parties haemorrhaging support and the election of three candidates affiliated with the right-populist group Identity & Democracy.

At first glance, this might seem to justify the headlines. But Europe is not a homogenous bloc and the so-called “right” is far from united or even consistent. The issues that animate voters in Hungary or Italy are not identical to those that move voters in Finland or Spain. In Hungary, Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party is motivated by opposition to EU centralisation and what it sees as an assault on national sovereignty. In Italy, Giorgia Meloni pitches herself as a defender of order and stability, but also maintains a pragmatic approach within the EU.

If there is a common thread, it is popular frustration: frustration with a technocratic elite that voters feel are indifferent to their concerns; anger at escalating living costs, the ongoing immigration crisis, the deteriorating sense of security, and—perhaps most fundamentally—a feeling that the EU’s grand projects are out of touch with the daily lives of its citizens.

Yet often lost in the debate is what is meant by the “right.” Under this label, much of the media now includes anything from hard Eurosceptics to moderate economic realists who merely question the wisdom of overambitious climate targets or unchecked migration. Even the centre-right European People’s Party, led by Ursula von der Leyen, has tacked right on rhetoric around migration and security. But are these stances genuinely “far right”—or simply a belated recognition by mainstream politicians of concerns that have been bubbling up for years?

Within Ireland, the emergence of non-traditional voices reflects growing disenchantment. The coalition government, led by Fine Gael, Fianna Fáil and the Greens, suffered heavy losses. Issues around housing, immigration, and the rising cost of living were repeatedly cited by voters. The old certainties—the assumption that governments could manage these issues without serious challenge—have been shaken. But while Sinn Féin failed to capitalise as expected, the growth of smaller parties and independents suggests that many voters are seeking solutions outside the old club, and some are looking to newer right-leaning or anti-establishment figures.

So, is Europe turning to the right, or is it wobbling on its axis, searching for new answers after decades of stagnant wages, eroded public services, and a political establishment seemingly unmoored from ordinary life?
headline: Is Europe really shifting to the right?

text:
Doctors from across Ireland have written to every TD in the Oireachtas, urging the Government to make ultrasound scanning compulsory before any abortion is carried out under Irish law. The move follows recent revelations in a Limerick case, where a woman was left without her unborn child after an abortion was performed despite what turned out to be a misdiagnosis of miscarriage.

The letter, seen by Gript, is signed by over 150 healthcare professionals, including obstetricians, GPs and nurses. It expresses deep concern about the lack of mandatory access to ultrasound scanning for women seeking terminations under the Health (Regulation of Termination of Pregnancy) Act 2018. The letter comes after a much-publicised incident last year in University Maternity Hospital Limerick, where a pregnant woman underwent a termination based on a clinical assessment that her baby had died. A subsequent scan indicated that the foetus had shown a heartbeat, casting serious doubt on the original diagnosis.

The signatories argue that without a legal requirement for an ultrasound, there is a real risk of misdiagnosis and “potentially irreversible tragedies” for parents and their children. They cite guidance from both the Health Service Executive and the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, which advise that ultrasound is the gold standard in determining foetal viability, especially in early pregnancy complications.

“In any other area of medicine, such a safeguard would be basic practice,” said Dr. Miriam O’Donoghue, a Cork-based GP who co-ordinated the letter. “No woman should undergo a procedure as serious as abortion without every effort being made to confirm the clinical facts. We are deeply concerned that the current process puts women at risk.”

The group says that current HSE protocols recommend, but do not require, access to scanning, and that availability varies from county to county, with rural areas particularly under-resourced. Several women and couples have shared accounts with Gript of being told that no scan was available before proceeding with a termination, sometimes resulting in ongoing emotional distress and, in one case, legal proceedings against the State.

Opposition parties, including Sinn Féin and the Social Democrats, have previously called for improvements to diagnostic facilities in maternity hospitals, but the Government has stopped short of amending legislation to make pre-abortion scanning compulsory. Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly confirmed in the Dáil last week that the matter was under review, but said the Government must “balance access to services with clinical best practice.”

Campaigners for more liberal abortion law argue that making ultrasounds mandatory would cause unnecessary delays and distress for women seeking terminations, and could amount to an extra barrier to care, especially in rural areas with limited staffing and equipment. Groups such as the National Women’s Council maintain that doctors are best placed to decide when scans are necessary, and that blanket requirements undermine clinical judgement.

However, Dr. O’Donoghue and her colleagues contend that in the wake of the Limerick case, it is clear that universal scanning is necessary to prevent further tragedies. “This is a basic safety issue, not a political football,” she said. “The Irish public were promised the highest standards of care when the law changed. We are simply asking the Government to honour that promise.”

The letter calls on the Government to urgently review the legislation and to allocate funding for scanning equipment and staff in every county.
headline: After Limerick case, medics write to every TD to warn ultrasounds must be provided before abortion

A 34-year-old expectant father who stole a bicycle from a teenage boy in a Dublin suburb has avoided a custodial sentence after telling the court he acted out of desperation to provide for his growing family.

Dublin District Court heard that Martin O’Reilly, with an address at St Ronan’s Drive, Clondalkin, approached a 16-year-old boy on his way home from school on 23 February this year. The youth had stopped at a local shop when O’Reilly, described by witnesses as “agitated”, forcibly took the boy’s bike and cycled away.

The court was told that Gardaí later recovered CCTV footage showing O’Reilly leaving the area on the stolen bicycle, valued at €450. He was identified by officers familiar with the accused and arrested a week later at his home address, where the bike was subsequently retrieved.

O’Reilly, who has six previous convictions including theft and public order offences, pleaded guilty to the charge of theft under Section 4 of the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001.

His solicitor, Ms Orla O’Donovan, told the court that her client was “under considerable stress” at the time of the offence and that his partner was expecting their first child in a matter of weeks. She said that O’Reilly had lost his job shortly after Christmas and “panicked”, feeling unable to provide for his family.

Judge Pauline Codd noted the seriousness of the offence and the impact it had on the young victim, who told the court he was left “afraid to cycle in the area” since the incident. She also noted O’Reilly’s early plea and remorse, as well as his cooperation with Gardaí.

In her remarks, Judge Codd said: “The court needs to send a message that theft, and particularly the taking of property from young people, cannot be tolerated. However, I must also weigh the genuine remorse demonstrated and the steps taken to make amends.”

O’Reilly offered to pay €300 in compensation to the boy, which the court accepted. Judge Codd imposed a four-month suspended sentence on condition that O’Reilly engage with Probation Services and stay out of further trouble for twelve months.

The judge admonished O’Reilly to “take responsibility as a father” and to ensure he was a better example for his child. She warned any breach of the suspended sentence would likely lead to imprisonment.

O’Reilly left court with his partner, declining to comment to waiting reporters. The family of the teenage boy expressed disappointment at the sentence but welcomed the return of the bicycle and the compensation paid.
headline: Dad to be stole bike from teenage boy

Mourners gathered in St Patrick’s Church, Skerries, on Friday morning for the funeral of Tadgh Farrell, whose family and friends spoke movingly of “a lifetime of love” shared with all who knew him. Mr Farrell, 78, who died peacefully at his home on Tuesday, was remembered as a man deeply devoted to his family, proud of his town, and steadfast in his Catholic faith.

A native of Skerries, Mr Farrell was described by parish priest Fr Michael O’Sullivan as “a fixture of the town”, beloved for his “generosity, quiet wit, and decency”. During the packed Requiem Mass, the congregation heard eulogies from his children and grandchildren, who recalled his “constant presence and unwavering support”. His eldest daughter, Aisling, told mourners that her father taught by example, saying: “He never needed to preach. Instead, he showed us in every act of kindness and every moment shared.”

Symbols of Mr Farrell’s life were brought to the altar by his grandchildren, including a football scarf in the colours of Skerries Harps, a rosary beads, and a weathered fishing cap. His son, Ciarán, described his father as “a man who worked hard, laughed easily, and always put others before himself”.

Mr Farrell worked for over four decades with CIÉ before retiring in 2005. His neighbours recalled his “willingness to help, no matter what the weather”, remembering him as a familiar figure cycling to morning Mass or tending to his garden.

Among those in attendance were representatives of local voluntary organisations, including the Skerries Community Association and St Vincent de Paul, both of which Mr Farrell supported for many years. Fine Gael TD for Dublin Fingal, Alan Farrell (no relation), sent condolences to the family, describing Mr Farrell as “a true community man”.

Fr O’Sullivan spoke of “the quiet power of a good man’s life” and encouraged the congregation to follow Mr Farrell’s example of compassion and neighbourliness. Hymns included ‘Be Not Afraid’ and ‘Lady of Knock’, and the Mass was offered for the repose of Mr Farrell’s soul.

Following the funeral, Mr Farrell was laid to rest in Holmpatrick Cemetery, accompanied by his family and friends. The Farrell family expressed thanks for the support received from the local community, the HSE carers, and the staff of Beaumont Hospital.

Mr Farrell is survived by his wife, Mary, his three children, five grandchildren, a wide circle of relatives and friends, and all those in Skerries who will remember him for the love he gave so freely throughout his life.
headline: Funeral of Tadgh Farrell hears of “a lifetime of love”

text:
A senior paediatrician has strongly criticised claims that restricting access to puberty blockers for children leads to suicide, describing such assertions as “dangerous” and unsupported by available evidence.

The controversy follows recent high-profile coverage in international media and on social platforms, in which advocates have linked the introduction of stricter guidelines on puberty blockers to increased risk of suicide among children diagnosed with gender dysphoria. In the UK, the decision by the NHS to halt routine use of puberty blockers for children outside of formal research has sparked similar criticism.

Speaking to Gript, Dr Catherine O’Neill, consultant paediatrician and member of the College of Paediatrics and Child Health, said it was “deeply irresponsible” to invoke child suicide in order to lobby for medical treatments whose safety and efficacy remain under scrutiny.

“No reputable study has shown a cause-and-effect relationship between limits on the use of puberty blockers and suicide rates in children,” Dr O’Neill stated. “The available data is much more nuanced, and many national health bodies—such as the NHS in England and the Swedish National Board of Health—have concluded that the evidence base for these interventions is weak.”

The Irish Health Service Executive (HSE) last month tightened internal protocols for referring children for puberty blockers, following legal actions in the UK and growing concerns from clinicians and parents. HSE guidance now states that hormone treatments should not be given to those under 16 except in rare cases and only within the context of clinical research or after multi-disciplinary assessment.

A review by the National Gender Service in Tallaght University Hospital earlier this year found that “the evidence for the benefits and harms of puberty blockers remains limited,” echoing the findings of the Cass Review in the UK. The Cass Review, an independent report commissioned by the NHS, cited a lack of long-term data on mental health outcomes for children given puberty blockers.

However, some advocacy groups have claimed that failure to provide puberty blockers amounts to “denying life-saving care.” In a widely shared social media post circulated by a campaign group, it was alleged that “puberty blockers prevent suicide in trans youth,” and that “removing access puts children at risk.”

Dr O’Neill rejected these claims as “scare tactics,” saying: “No health authority in Ireland, or internationally, is seeking to deny care to vulnerable young people. Rather, we have a duty to ensure treatments are truly in patients’ best interests. To suggest that caution over puberty blockers is driving children to take their own lives is not only baseless, but may itself increase anxiety and distress among affected families.”

Internationally, academic studies on puberty blockers and suicide risk are inconclusive. A recent review published in the British Medical Journal concluded that “evidence of mental health benefits is very low certainty.” Several studies used to support the claim of lowered suicide risk have been criticised for methodological weaknesses, such as small sample sizes and lack of long-term tracking.

Irish parents and clinicians have described pressure from advocacy groups to prescribe puberty blockers as “intense.” One mother, who asked not to be named, told Gript her family were told “if you don’t accept it, your child could die.” She said the experience left her feeling “coerced and frightened,” but added that careful assessment later showed her child did not have persistent gender dysphoria.

“Responsible debate means engaging honestly with the evidence,” said Dr O’Neill.
headline: Claim puberty blocker ban causing suicide in children unfounded and “dangerous”

text:
The latest fashionable suggestion to grace Irish media pages is the call for “childfree zones”, urging cafes, restaurants, and even public amenities to reserve spaces where children—and, strikingly, their parents—are not permitted. The pitch, imported from already over-regulated corners of the US and Europe, is that those without children deserve “peace and quiet” away from the supposed cacophony of family life. This, apparently, is progress.

But is it really? Behind the polite language of “zones” and “choice”, the demand boils down to a polite form of social exclusion: a move to further hive off the messy business of families from polite society and reinforce the regrettable notion that children are, fundamentally, a nuisance. Irish culture, for all its modernisation, has always held fast to the belief that children are a blessing, rather than a bother. Even now, regardless of low birth rates, our towns and villages still pulse with the sound of children at play—a sign, surely, of a society with a sense of future.

Certainly, nobody enjoys the shrill ring of a tantrum over their cappuccino, but is the answer really to cordon off the young as though they were lepers? Already, families face mounting obstacles—soaring childcare costs, housing shortages, and the struggle to find a place in the workforce for parents balancing responsibilities. The message from the “childfree zone” lobby seems to be: not only are families to bear the burden of demographic renewal, but they must do so apologetically, in the margins, lest they intrude on the tranquil brunches of the voluntarily childless.

There is an irony here. The very people most vocally advocating for “childfree” spaces often style themselves as champions of inclusivity—while backing the deliberate exclusion of one of the most vulnerable segments of society and their carers. Would they endorse similar exclusion for the elderly, the disabled, or those whose behaviour—through no fault of their own—sometimes jars with the urbanite’s taste for serenity?

There may be rare instances—a late-night restaurant, a high-end hotel—where it is reasonable to expect an adult atmosphere. But the enthusiasm for blanket bans betrays a deeper attitude: a discomfort with the realities of community and a desire to curate urban life into something frictionless, predictable, and, ultimately, sterile.

If Ireland is to remain a society rather than just an economy, we must be careful about the values we enshrine. The sounds of children—sometimes boisterous, sometimes grating—are not evidence of a failing in public life, but proof that Irish life still exists. Those who find families so objectionable as to warrant legal exclusion might do well to examine their own priorities. The alternative is a country that grows, inexorably, quieter—and not in a way that bodes well for any of us.
headline: PERRINS: No to childfree zones for the child-free

text:
The HSE has confirmed that an external review will be conducted into a recent case at the National Maternity Hospital in Holles Street, where a couple underwent a termination following what was later revealed to be a misdiagnosis of a fatal foetal abnormality. The case, which has already sparked strong public reaction, involved the mistaken belief by medical practitioners that the unborn child had Edwards’ syndrome, a condition that is normally considered incompatible with life. 

Sources familiar with the matter have told Gript that the couple were informed of the diagnosis following a first round of tests and subsequently consented to a termination under the Health (Regulation of Termination of Pregnancy) Act 2018. However, further genetic testing which arrived after the procedure revealed that the foetus did not, in fact, have the genetic disorder.

In a statement to Gript, the HSE confirmed that an "independent, external review" has been commissioned to establish how the misdiagnosis occurred and to ensure that lessons are learned for future practice. The statement read: “The HSE acknowledges the distress caused to those involved in this case, and is committed to a thorough and transparent independent review of the clinical, laboratory and communications processes.”

The statement continued, “We wish to extend our deepest sympathies to the family affected, and are engaging with them through the appropriate channels.” The HSE also confirmed that all relevant material from hospitals, laboratories, and clinicians involved will be made available to the review panel.

The case has attracted criticism from campaigners on both sides of the abortion debate. Pro-life groups say it highlights the irreversible consequences of Ireland’s abortion regime and have called for a moratorium on terminations for fatal foetal abnormality until protocols are overhauled. Spokesperson for the Life Institute, Niamh Uí Bhriain, said, “This is a tragedy that could have been avoided. The rush to legislate for abortion in Ireland has created a situation where devastating mistakes can be made, and families are left to deal with unimaginable grief.”

Pro-choice advocates, on the other hand, have argued that clear guidelines and adequate time for diagnostic procedures are necessary so that families are not forced into making rushed decisions. The National Women’s Council of Ireland released a statement urging that the review focus on best practice in pre-natal diagnosis and communication, rather than seeking to restrict access to services.

The Minister for Health, Stephen Donnelly TD, speaking at Leinster House, said he was “deeply concerned” by the report and that the Department of Health would fully cooperate with the review. “It is absolutely essential that families can trust the information and advice they receive at the most vulnerable moments in their lives. I will be seeking assurances that robust protocols are in place as a matter of urgency,” the Minister said.

The external review will be led by an expert from the UK, according to the HSE, to ensure independence and “international best practice”. The findings are expected to be presented to the HSE Board and the Minister for Health before being shared with the Oireachtas Committee on Health.

This is the second high-profile case of misdiagnosis in maternity services since the repeal of the Eighth Amendment in 2018, and comes as abortion law in Ireland continues to be a divisive issue. Calls for increased investment in diagnostic infrastructure were made in the Dáil on Wednesday, with several TDs saying the incident showed the need for caution and comprehensive support for both patients and clinicians.
headline: HSE confirms external review into abortion misdiagnosis case

text:
Ciara Mageean, Ireland’s queen of the middle distance, was achingly close to gold in Rome on Sunday night. For the better part of four minutes, right across the Foro Italico’s blue track, Mageean looked every inch the champion the country so desperately wants to see. When the bell rang for the final lap, she surged and stretched the field, and held the lead with bravura until the last, only to be overtaken in the dying meters by Great Britain’s Jemma Reekie.

That split-second loss, to so many, can feel like heartbreak. But Mageean herself was anything but shattered in the aftermath. Instead, she spoke with warmth and exuberance, smiling through her post-race interviews, wearing her silver medal with pride, and making clear that she recognises what her performance means for Irish sport: “I know I can come home to everybody and know I gave it absolutely everything,” she said.

It is, perhaps, easy to focus on the glory of winning. Ireland is a country starved of athletic gold on the continental stage since Sonia O’Sullivan’s heyday. Our national longing for another idol is palpable. Yet, there is a different kind of magnificence in defeat—especially when it is met with the poise and positivity Mageean displayed on Sunday night.

She has, after all, travelled a long and winding road. The Portaferry woman has faced injuries, setbacks, and the constant comparisons to her legendary predecessors. And yet, at 32, she has not only endured but improved, setting Irish records and consistently challenging the world’s best. Rome was the culmination of years of perseverance, and she delivered a tactical masterclass, only undone by a world-class rival in the absolute final stretch.

Mageean’s conduct in the aftermath also stands in stark contrast to the too-frequent sourness seen in elite sport. While others might look for excuses, or dwell on the knife-edge nature of defeat, she only had words of congratulations for her competitors and gratitude for her team. In doing so, she set a standard that aspiring Irish athletes, and indeed fans, would do well to emulate.

There is also something to be said for the rare sense of national unity her achievements inspire. As Irish athletes arrived home from Rome to a hero’s welcome, Mageean’s medal—silver or not—was celebrated in Tallaght, Tralee, and her own Down homeplace alike. At a time when the headlines are too often dominated by political quarrels or social division, sport offers a rare moment of uncomplicated pride.

Of course, Mageean will go again. Paris looms large this summer, and the Olympic 1500m is perhaps the most competitive event in world athletics. No one can promise her that elusive gold. But what is certain is that—that in victory or defeat—she will once again carry herself with the kind of grace that speaks to the best of Ireland.

Ciara Mageean’s run in Rome was magnificent, even if it ended in second place. But her positivity in defeat may well prove to be her greatest legacy, and it is a lesson for all who watch her: that the character forged in striving, and the humility in accepting outcomes beyond one’s control, matter at least as much as medals do. The tricolour raised for silver in Rome flew for an athlete who gave her all, and reminded Ireland, once again, what sporting greatness truly means.
headline: Ciara Mageean magnificent and positive in defeat

Figures released by Eurostat and the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) this week reveal what has become evident to communities across Ireland and the continent alike: illegal immigration is rising at a rate not seen in decades, and the European Union’s approach to border management is proving wholly inadequate.

According to Frontex, the number of irregular crossings into the EU soared to over 380,000 in 2023 alone—the highest tally since the height of the migrant crisis in 2016. While attention has often focused on the Mediterranean routes, the statistics show significant upticks across multiple entry points, including a doubling of arrivals via the Western Balkans and notable increases in arrivals via the Atlantic route to Spain’s Canary Islands.

Ireland, supposedly insulated by its island status and the Common Travel Area, is feeling the impact. Official data show record numbers seeking international protection here, with applications tripling since 2021. The Department of Justice confirmed over 13,000 asylum applications in 2023, not including undocumented arrivals the authorities are unable to track reliably. This comes even as many of those arriving admit to having transited through safe EU countries without applying for protection before reaching Irish shores—in clear contravention of both the Dublin Regulation and the widely touted EU solidarity mechanisms.

At the same time, deportation and removal statistics make for equally troubling reading. The Oireachtas Public Accounts Committee heard recently that of the tens of thousands issued with deportation orders over the past decade, only a small fraction were actually removed. Gardaí and the immigration authorities face mounting backlogs and challenges in enforcing the law, often because individuals simply abscond or because returns are blocked by legal appeals. The State has become, in effect, a magnet for those seeking to circumvent standard procedures, knowing that the risk of actual removal is vanishingly small.

Meanwhile, Minister for Justice Helen McEntee and other government figures continue to insist that Ireland’s systems are robust and that the integrity of the asylum process is being preserved. Yet, the lived reality for local communities tells a different story. The sight of protesters at accommodation centres across the country is a testament to grassroots frustration at the lack of consultation and perceived lack of control over who is entering and settling in Ireland. Many Irish people feel that their concerns are dismissed as “far right” rhetoric, even when they arise from genuine worries about resource allocation, community cohesion, and the capacity of health, housing and education services already under severe strain.

The EU’s statistical revelations also put paid to the claim that Ireland simply faces the same challenges as every other member state. Our numbers, relative to population, are among the highest in Western Europe. The Government’s insistence on “doing our part” must be weighed against the clear evidence that loopholes in the system are being widely exploited. Critics of government policy have long warned that so-called temporary protections can become permanent, and that the failure to enforce returns is one of the major drivers of continued illegal entries.

If the EU is serious about addressing illegal immigration, talk of solidarity and “fair share” must be matched with meaningful border control and enforcement. For Ireland, the first step is to acknowledge the scale of the problem—rather than hoping that statistics and lived experience alike can be wished away by official platitudes. As the numbers climb, public confidence in the immigration system continues to erode, and the Government’s credibility on this issue hangs in the balance.
headline: EU statistics reflect vastly increased levels of illegal immigration

text:
A Catholic bishop has been attacked and four people stabbed in a shocking incident during a Sunday evening church service in Sydney, Australia, with the violent assault captured on video and circulating widely across social media.

The attack took place at Christ The Good Shepherd Church in the Wakeley suburb of western Sydney. Bishop Mar Mari Emmanuel, a prominent Assyrian Christian leader, was delivering a livestreamed sermon shortly after 7pm local time when a man approached the altar and launched an assault. Witnesses say the attacker produced a knife and lunged at the bishop, wounding him and three other men who attempted to intervene.

Footage of the incident shows parishioners screaming and rushing to restrain the attacker as chaos erupts inside the church. Blood is visible on the floor and panic is evident among the congregation, which included families and children attending the regular service.

Australian emergency services arrived promptly, and the local police confirmed four men, including Bishop Emmanuel, suffered injuries in the attack. A statement from New South Wales Police said all four were being treated in hospital for non-life-threatening wounds. The attacker, a young man believed to have been known to some members of the congregation, was detained at the scene by parishioners before being arrested by responding officers.

Australian authorities have declared the attack as “extremely serious” and confirmed that a counter-terrorism investigation is underway. Early indications suggest the motive is still being probed, with police not ruling out hate crime or sectarian violence, particularly given ongoing tensions in multicultural western Sydney.

In the aftermath of the incident, crowds gathered outside the church. Later, unrest broke out, with some congregants clashing with police and emergency workers as frustration and concern ran high among the local community. Reports from the scene describe bottles and other objects being thrown as police attempted to restore order.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described the stabbing as a “shocking attack on a man of faith and his congregation,” and called for calm, unity, and respect for law enforcement. “There is no place for violent extremism or religious intolerance in Australia,” Mr Albanese said.

Bishop Emmanuel is a well-known religious figure, with a significant following online and among Australia’s Assyrian Christian diaspora. His sermons, often shared on social platforms, are known for their forthright style and strong positions on contemporary issues, including religious freedoms and moral decline in Western societies.

The Irish Embassy in Canberra said it is monitoring the situation closely, but there are no indications at this time of any Irish citizens involved in the incident.

The attack comes just days after a separate mass stabbing in Sydney’s Bondi Junction shopping centre, in which six people were killed and several others seriously injured, leading to a heightened state of alert across the city.

Australian police have stepped up patrols outside places of worship and community hubs, as authorities urge people not to share graphic footage of the attack online and to seek information from official sources.

As investigations continue, the faithful in Sydney and further afield are being asked to pray for Bishop Emmanuel and all those injured. The incident has also reignited debate on the security of religious gatherings, freedom of worship, and the impact of social media in spreading both awareness and panic during crisis events.
headline: BREAKING: Video captures Bishop attacked as 4 stabbed during church service

text:
Lisa Smith’s return to Ireland continues to provoke public outcry – and with good reason. The former Irish soldier who left her family and homeland to join the so-called Islamic State in Syria now seeks a fresh start in a country she abandoned with shocking ease. The narrative put out by her supporters paints Smith as a lost soul, a victim of manipulation, even a naive woman led astray by radicalisation. But what cannot be overlooked is the central fact: Smith made a conscious choice to turn her back on Ireland and the values we hold dear, pledging herself instead to a murderous cult whose actions horrified the civilised world.

There are those who argue that she has “paid her debt” – that time in a Syrian detention camp, time served in Limerick Prison, and her ongoing surveillance by the Gardaí are penance enough for her past. But forgiveness is not a mechanical process in a civil society. It depends on trust, on a sense of shared belonging – of which the Lisa Smith saga leaves precious little. To ask the Irish people to now welcome her as “one of our own”, to extend the warmth of home after all that has happened, is – at best – wishful thinking and, at worst, a wilful disregard for national security and societal cohesion.

In court, Smith insisted she never fired a shot for ISIS, never picked up a weapon. Yet her conviction for membership of a terrorist organisation was not the product of hearsay or tabloid sensationalism, but the result of a lengthy Garda investigation and the scrutiny of the Special Criminal Court. Whatever the nuances of her particular case, the fact remains that she saw nothing wrong in marrying an ISIS fighter, living amongst some of the most brutal men on the planet, and raising her child in that atmosphere. How can such a person credibly claim to represent, or even want, what ordinary Irish people believe in?

Government officials, NGOs, and certain elements in the media may wring their hands over Smith’s plight and urge compassion in the spirit of “rehabilitation.” But there is a profound difference between charity for the marginalised and blind amnesty for those who consciously spurned the country that nurtured them. The Oireachtas has a duty to draw a clear line, lest the message go out that there are no real consequences for betraying Ireland. If citizenship, with all its rights and privileges, means anything, then crossing that line should not be treated as a mere blunder to be papered over when it becomes inconvenient.

It is not “hateful” or “Islamophobic” to feel that Smith, and others like her, have broken an essential bond of trust with their fellow citizens. The rights of returning extremists—however they might be dressed up in legalese—cannot outweigh the rights of ordinary people to feel secure in their homes. If the Irish state is now to be seen as a revolving door for those who would join our enemies when it suits, then be shocked when they want to “come home” again, we are in deeper trouble than we realise.

Lisa Smith may hold an Irish passport, but she long since abandoned the deeper, truer sense of belonging that binds a nation together. She may wish to “come home”, but in truth, home is not waiting for her. Whether she or her legal team want to admit it, she is not one of us – for that was a choice she made herself, when she boarded the plane to Syria.
headline: Lisa Smith is not one of us, no matter how much she wants to “come home”

text:
Ireland’s political class has been quietly content to let the country drift into a gerontocracy – rule by the old for the old – and, as ever, it is the young and the future who pay the price. Every Budget is measured by how it plays in the bingo halls and the parish pumps. The Department of Finance releases glossy breakdowns of pension increases before it even addresses rents, mortgage traps, or childcare. TDs scurry to add a fiver to the pension every year, while young families grind their teeth wondering how they will ever save enough for a deposit or pay for schoolbooks.

We are told, in the most pious tones, that this is merely respect for our elders – an “age friendly” society. In reality, it is cowardice and moral laziness from a political establishment that is unwilling to ask hard questions or think beyond the next general election. The Dáil is a reflection of this: the average age of TDs is now over 50, and the Seanad is, if anything, an even more exclusive retirement club. Young people, meanwhile, are leaving in droves. More than 70,000 Irish citizens emigrated in the last year alone; the vast majority are under 30. They do not see a place for themselves here. Why would they? Housing is unaffordable, childcare is the highest in Europe, and every call for reform is met with a beige denial that things could ever be any different.

The grip of the older generation on power and decision-making is not accidental. It is the result of decades of deliberate policy: artificially inflated house prices keep assets in the hands of the over-55s; rent controls protect sitting tenants, not families trying to find a first home; and a social care system creaks along, propped up by the unpaid labour of daughters and daughters-in-law. Meanwhile, the language of “fairness” and “solidarity” is invoked to dismiss any suggestion that prioritising the needs of the young is necessary for Ireland’s future. The Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation has pointed out the acute staffing shortages in the HSE. Who is going to staff the hospitals and care homes when all the young nurses and carers have left for Australia or Canada?

This is not an argument for pitting one generation against another. There is no justice in scapegoating older people for structural problems created by government choices. But it is utter folly to pretend that a country can thrive when its policy agenda is driven by short-term electoral calculations and the fear of annoying the “grey vote.” If the best that can be said for the Programme for Government is that it has protected those who already own a house or have a public sector pension, it has failed half the country.

Ireland cannot be at peace with itself if it remains a society where the needs and aspirations of the young are perpetually subordinated to those of the old. The malaise is visible in the failure to build, to plan, to risk. Demographics are destiny, we are told. But it is not destiny – it is a failure of courage and imagination by those who claim to lead. The question now is whether we want a future at all, or just a comfortable present for those lucky enough to have been born at the right time. An honest debate is long overdue – one that dares to imagine what Ireland could be if we stopped mortgaging tomorrow to pay for yesterday.
headline: Ireland a gerontocracy will never be at peace

text:
The National Gender Service (NGS), the HSE’s principal body for gender medicine, has called for the provision of “affirming” surgical breast removal—double mastectomies—for individuals identifying as transgender men or non-binary, according to documents seen by Gript. The proposal comes amid ongoing controversy surrounding the HSE’s approach to gender identity and medical interventions.

The NGS, based at St Columcille’s Hospital in Loughlinstown, has for some time been the centre of heated debate regarding its handling of gender dysphoria in adults. Now, in submissions to the Department of Health, it has pressed for the establishment of dedicated facilities in Ireland for what is termed “top surgery”, whereby healthy breast tissue is surgically removed in the name of “affirming” a new gender identity.

Currently, patients seeking such procedures are advised that they may have to travel abroad, chiefly to private clinics in the UK or further afield. The NGS argues this amounts to a form of discrimination and is inconsistent with “affirming models of care” promoted by international activists and advocacy organisations.

However, the submission sidesteps key questions about the dramatic and irreversible nature of such surgeries, and whether sufficient safeguards are in place to protect vulnerable patients, especially younger adults. Critics, including many Irish clinicians and campaigners, have voiced concern regarding the speed and pressure with which “affirming” approaches are now being championed without fully transparent debate or a robust evidence base.

Dr Paul Moran, consultant psychiatrist and lead clinician at the NGS, has previously spoken in favour of expanding access to irreversible medical interventions for transgender patients, despite the fact that no long-term Irish studies exist on the outcomes or rates of regret among those who undergo double mastectomies for gender dysphoria. He and his colleagues state that “the absence of accessible surgical facilities in Ireland constitutes a health inequity for transgender and gender diverse people.”

Yet, international evidence is far from settled. Several European countries, including Sweden, Finland, and the UK, have substantially revised their approach to medicalised gender transitions, citing concerns over side effects, growing rates of post-surgery regret, and poor quality evidence. The Cass Review, commissioned by the NHS in England, recently found little proof for the safety and efficacy of rapid “affirming” medical and surgical pathways, especially for younger people.

Here in Ireland, the HSE’s policy framework continues to be shaped by pressure from international lobby groups and a small number of vocal advocacy organisations. Critics argue the push for expanded surgical interventions highlights the HSE’s ongoing failure to consult with a broader cross-section of Irish society, medical professionals, and especially those who have suffered negative consequences following medical transition.

There is also an ongoing lack of clarity regarding funding—would these surgeries, if provided in Irish hospitals, be fully paid for by the taxpayer, and if so, what criteria and oversight would be in place? To date, no cost-benefit or risk analysis has been published by the Department of Health or the HSE.

A spokesperson for the Department would only say that “considerations around surgical pathways for transgender healthcare are ongoing and guided by clinical best practice,” without specifying which clinical sources or what independent scrutiny, if any, is being applied.

Ireland has already seen the introduction of self-declaration for legal gender recognition, and the quiet expansion of puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for children and adults, yet the public debate remains muted compared to other European nations.
headline: National Gender Service calls for ‘affirming’ surgical breast removal facilities

Thousands of people have signed an online petition in a last-ditch effort to save a family dog from being put down, following an order granted by the District Court in recent days. The case, which has sparked heated debate about Ireland’s dog control laws and the rights of pet owners, centres on a beloved Labrador mix, "Buddy", from Co. Meath.

The petition was set up earlier this week by the Clifford family, who say the dog has never shown aggression and pose no threat to the public. Within 48 hours, signatures topped 15,000, with supporters calling on the Gardaí, the Department of Agriculture, and animal welfare groups to intervene and prevent the destruction of the animal.

The controversy began after a neighbour alleged that Buddy bit their young son last November, resulting in a minor injury. The incident was reported to the local Gardaí, who subsequently issued a Dog Control Notice and referred the case for prosecution. Evidence presented to Trim District Court included medical reports and witness statements. Judge Gerard Fanning, citing his statutory obligations under the Control of Dogs Act 1986, granted the destruction order last Friday.

The Clifford family say the court proceedings did not allow for a full account of the dog's background, and that mitigation factors—including the lack of any previous complaint and the manner in which the incident occurred—were not given due weight. “Our dog has been a part of our family for nine years. He’s gentle with the children and neighbours’ pets. This order is disproportionate,” said Mary Clifford outside the courthouse.

Supporters have flooded social media with messages of solidarity, sharing stories of similar destruction orders being issued for what they view as minor incidents. Several local TDs have also weighed in on the matter, with Sinn Féin TD Johnny Guirke calling for an urgent review of the legislation. “People are rightly worried that a single incident, with little room for appeal, can lead to a loved pet’s death,” Deputy Guirke told Gript. “The law is too rigid. There has to be a common-sense approach.”

The Department of Agriculture, which has responsibility for national animal control policy, told Gript it could not comment on individual cases, but noted that dog attacks are taken seriously and that current law is under ongoing review. The HSE would not comment on the specifics of the child’s injury for privacy reasons, but confirmed the matter was treated and no long-term consequences were reported.

Animal welfare organisations have highlighted a significant increase in destruction orders in recent years, with Dogs Trust Ireland saying there is a lack of clarity and transparency in how such decisions are made. “We regularly see families devastated by these court orders, sometimes over minor incidents with no serious harm,” said spokesperson Aoife Ryan. “We urge authorities to consider alternatives to destruction, such as mandatory training or secure rehoming.”

Meanwhile, a stay on the court order has been granted, giving the Clifford family until the end of the month to appeal the decision to the Circuit Court. The family are being represented by solicitor Ciarán O’Dowd, who said they will be presenting new evidence and seeking an independent behavioural assessment of Buddy.

The campaign to save Buddy has led to renewed calls for a more nuanced and evidence-based approach to dog control in Ireland, and prompted a wider discussion about the rights of pet owners and the limits of state intervention in family life. The Clifford family say they are hopeful common sense will prevail.
headline: Thousands sign petition to Save Dog from Being Put Down

Recent polling figures from Ireland’s European Parliament elections point to a stable consensus: the vast majority of Irish voters remain enthusiastic about the State’s EU membership. With support hovering comfortably above the 80% mark, it is easy—too easy, perhaps—to dismiss those who remain sceptical or outright opposed. But that dismissed minority, this year amounting to 12%, represent a significant voice in our democracy. To brush them aside as outliers or “cranks” is both intellectually lazy and at odds with the core claims of pluralism that the European project itself purports to champion.

There is no denying the material and social realities that have helped shape Ireland’s strongly pro-EU stance. Structural funds in the 1990s, access to the single market, and the freedom to travel and work across member states have all undeniably benefited many. But enthusiasm should not melt into uncritical adulation, and voices of concern deserve to be heard—especially at a time when the EU’s own direction is subject to growing debate across the continent.

The 12% tally for anti-EU sentiment, as measured by the Irish Times/Ipsos B&A exit poll, cannot be written off as mere ignorance or populist backlash. Among them are those who watch the creeping expansion of EU competencies with unease, who recall the bruises of the bailout, the dilution of national sovereignty or the imposition of policies—from migration quotas to agricultural regulation—that clash with local preferences and priorities. The social, political, and economic impacts of these policies are not abstractions; they are lived realities in communities from Donegal to Kerry.

Moreover, to ignore or mock this minority is to invite the very alienation and polarisation that has upended politics elsewhere. A mature democracy requires not just tolerating dissenting views, but engaging with them. There are legitimate questions to be asked about the European Commission’s increasing power, about “ever closer union”, about the lack of democratic accountability in Brussels, and about the drift toward federalism that many Irish people—though currently a minority—find alarming.

It is especially ironic that the same guardians of pluralism who routinely invoke “diversity” and “inclusion” as democratic virtues are too often the first to anathematise critics of EU integration. Such double standards only deepen distrust. The point is not to claim a majority where there is none, nor to champion EU exit as a panacea. Rather, it is to insist that a healthy democracy makes room for robust debate and that even a small minority has the right to scrutiny, scepticism, and public debate.

It is also worth recalling that Irish enthusiasm for the EU has not always been unchecked or unconditional. The Nice and Lisbon treaties were both initially rejected at the ballot box, forcing the government of the day to seek approval a second time after institutional and political pressure from Brussels. That memory—of referendums rerun until the “right” answer emerges—should serve as a reminder that Ireland’s pro-EU orientation is resilient but not immune to challenge.

As the EU faces its own crossroads, with questions swirling over defence policy, migration, agricultural reform, and enlargement, it is more important than ever that those with concerns are listened to, not just tolerated but actively engaged. That is not just a service to democracy in Ireland, but a signal to Europe that Irish support is not a blank cheque—and that the 12% deserve more than silence or sneers.
headline: On EU membership, the 12% deserve a voice

As Europe grapples with stubbornly high energy prices and rolling warnings of insecurity in supply, a growing chorus is questioning the wisdom of the continent’s relentless push towards so-called “green” policies. The narrative from Brussels and officialdom, echoed faithfully by Irish government leaders, trumpets a coming green utopia; but the reality for ordinary households and businesses is all too often bills they struggle to pay, industries shutting up shop, and families shivering in the winter cold. It’s high time to confront an uncomfortable truth: the European Union’s approach to energy – including Ireland’s – has played a pivotal role in creating the very crisis it claims to be fighting.

For over a decade, the EU, backed by governments from Dublin to Berlin, has prioritised climate targets over secure and affordable energy. Massive subsidies and regulations were directed towards wind and solar, but little heed was paid to ensuring baseload power – the type that keeps the lights on when the wind doesn’t blow and the sun doesn’t shine. The result: shutdowns of coal and nuclear plants, declining investment in reliable generation, and growing reliance on volatile imports, especially Russian gas.

Ireland’s situation is a microcosm of the wider European malaise. The government has spent countless millions on wind farms dotting the countryside, while ruling out nuclear power entirely and closing down peat stations long before alternatives were ready. The ESB has repeatedly warned about the risk of blackouts, an outcome unthinkable in an advanced economy. Yet, official policy ploughs ahead, with ever-more ambitious green targets taking precedence over practical realities.

Supporters of the EU’s Green Deal insist that renewables make energy cheaper in the long run, but the evidence from the last two years says otherwise. As soon as the war in Ukraine broke out, Europe – having made itself dependent on Russian gas, while banning domestic fossil fuel and nuclear options – found itself exposed. Energy prices soared across the continent, and Ireland was not immune: households saw bills double or triple, and competitive Irish industry was left scrambling to survive.

Green policies have also stifled investment elsewhere. The regulatory war on fossil fuels has made it riskier and less profitable to maintain or build conventional generating capacity. At the same time, the much-vaunted green alternatives simply aren’t reliable enough to pick up the slack. Interconnectors to Britain and beyond are a sticking plaster, not a solution, and leave Ireland exposed to the exact same price volatility and shortages seen elsewhere.

Proponents will argue that the energy crisis is the result of geopolitics, not green policy. There’s no denying that Russian aggression played a role, but it was policy decisions made in European capitals – not Moscow – that left the continent so vulnerable in the first place. The drive to decarbonise, pursued at all costs, created a situation where energy grids became brittle and dependent on factors beyond any Irish or European government’s control.

Now, with Irish and European leaders still promoting impossible deadlines for net zero, the risk is that things will get worse before they get better. The government’s own Climate Action Plan admits that demand for electricity will double by 2030, yet also calls for shutting down the very sources of power that currently keep Ireland’s lights on.

It is not “anti-environment” to point out these hard truths. Real conservation and sensible environmental protection require reliable energy and thriving economies. Policies that undermine both do nothing to help the planet or the people living on it.
headline: How European green policies caused the energy crisis

Kanye West has never shied away from controversy, but his bold declaration that “Jesus Is King” – which he has made the name of his 2019 album and something of a public mantra since – has ignited a debate that stretches well beyond the world of celebrity gossip or pop culture. The statement, short as it is, invites both derision and applause, but it stands as a challenge to a culture which increasingly seems to want to excise faith, and Christianity in particular, from the public square.

West’s journey to Christianity has been as public as it has been tumultuous. Once known for his brashness, headline-grabbing stunts, and music that glorified the here and now, West’s pivot to overtly Christian themes was met with surprise, not to mention scepticism, from much of the music press. Yet for all the raised eyebrows, there can be little doubt that his sincerity is having an impact, not least among his millions of fans, many of them young and immersed in a culture that sees religious faith as at best a private affair, and at worst something to be ridiculed.

The album “Jesus Is King” itself is a departure from West’s previous work: gospel-inspired, infused with Biblical references, and replete with the kind of open-hearted evangelism rarely seen at the top of the charts. Critics might sneer that it is merely a phase, or a marketing ploy, but it has already spawned “Sunday Service” gatherings in the United States that draw crowds in their thousands, creating a kind of pop culture revival meeting. It’s hard to argue with that kind of reach.

Why does this matter to Ireland? The answer lies in the country’s own evolving relationship with Christianity. For years, Ireland was known as the “land of saints and scholars”, and in living memory the Catholic Church was at the heart of Irish identity. Today, after scandals, a collapse in vocations, and a steady drumbeat of criticism – some justified, some less so – church attendance has declined, and faith is more private than ever. The powers that be, from RTÉ to politicians in the Dáil, take pains to stress Ireland’s “modern” and “inclusive” credentials, usually understood to mean a movement away from any public assertion of Christian belief.

In that context, West’s unapologetic embrace of faith in the spotlight is almost radical. It has become common, even in Ireland, to see figures mocked for taking religion seriously. Young people, certainly, are rarely exposed to role models who speak about faith with conviction. But here is one of the world’s most famous musicians, refusing to be cowed by derision, and instead using his influence to re-open a conversation about spiritual things – and not just any spirituality, but Christianity itself.

This is not to say that Kanye West is a model of orthodoxy, or that his personal life is free from controversy. But his courage in declaring that “Jesus Is King” challenges the notion that faith is something to be hidden. It invites questions: what would happen if more public figures in Ireland – not least those in politics or media – were so open about their beliefs? Would that be met with the same mixture of hostility and curiosity? Or would it help expand the boundaries of what is permissible in Irish public discourse?

More importantly, West’s approach underscores that the hunger for the transcendent has not disappeared, even in cultures that pride themselves on their secularism.
headline: Kanye West says “Jesus Is King”. Here’s why that matters

The Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) has scored yet another windfall from the public purse, it has emerged, as the Government signs off on a staggering €10 million for a single, standalone research “study”. The sum, which would be the envy of any ordinary research department—or for that matter, any typical Irish SME—has been allocated for the ESRI to investigate the “social determinants of health and wellbeing”. If readers are struggling to recall a day when they did not hear about social determinants, they are not alone.

This latest payout, announced quietly by the Department of Health, continues a trend where the ESRI, along with a growing cadre of policy-aligned research bodies, occupy a privileged position in guiding policy while being funded handsomely by the people for their efforts. The Dáil has always been keen to commission research in support of its preferred narratives, but €10 million for a report is the kind of sum that would raise eyebrows even at the European Central Bank.

It is no secret that the ESRI has become a darling of the Irish political establishment, with its staff regularly appearing before Oireachtas committees to lend technical sheen and scholarly weight to government proposals. Its research is rarely far from the speeches of the Minister for Health or the Tánaiste, and its headlines almost always underpin calls for more spending, more intervention, and more bureaucracy. The self-reinforcing cycle is obvious: tax money funds the ESRI, the ESRI writes a report recommending more government, the government implements the findings, and more money is sent the ESRI’s way.

Meanwhile, questions remain about the true independence of Ireland’s research ecosystem. Academics with dissenting views, particularly around issues like migration, family structure, or the effectiveness of welfare initiatives, often find it difficult to secure similar levels of funding—or indeed, any funding at all. The ESRI, in contrast, has become the reliable go-to for any and all questions, its reports regularly setting the terms of debate in media and the corridors of power alike.

One might reasonably ask, with record spending on the HSE and public health, record contributions to NGOs, and billions allocated annually to health promotion, what precisely the taxpayer is getting for the ESRI’s additional €10 million. Will it solve our waiting lists, or merely provide another round of reports and recommendations to be cited in next year’s funding campaign? It is hard to avoid the suspicion that public money is being used less to inform policy than to manufacture consent for policies already decided. 

There was a time when “evidence-based policy” meant a robust debate, with Government, Opposition, and civil society able to draw on a breadth of analysis and data. Today, the pipeline flows almost exclusively one way, through a handful of well-compensated research organisations whose findings, by happy coincidence, nearly always align with government goals.

As hospital trolleys line up in Emergency Departments and parents wait months for basic assessments for their children, one must wonder how much practical value all these “evidence bases” are delivering for real people. For the ESRI’s researchers at least, the answer is obvious: the social scientists are indeed doing alright. As for the rest of us, the jury is still out—pending a report.
headline: The social scientists are doing alright: ESRI get €10 million for report

Sinn Féin Vice President and First Minister-designate Michelle O’Neill has rejected renewed criticism regarding her attendance at the funeral of veteran republican Bobby Storey, insisting that she did not break social distancing guidance despite photographic and video evidence to the contrary. The event, which took place in June 2020 at the height of Covid-19 restrictions in Northern Ireland, was attended by a significant number of senior Sinn Féin figures, including Ms O’Neill herself, Mary Lou McDonald and Gerry Adams. 

In a statement this week following fresh scrutiny of her role in the high-profile funeral, Ms O’Neill maintained that her actions on the day were guided by public health advice. “I did not breach social distancing. I respected the guidelines as they were understood at the time,” Ms O’Neill told reporters during a stormy press conference at Stormont.

However, photos from the event show Ms O’Neill and other mourners in close proximity, with little evidence of the two-metre distance recommended by both the Northern Ireland Executive and the HSE at that time. The funeral, which drew crowds estimated at over 1,800 people, led to public outrage and accusations of ‘one rule for them, another for the rest of us’ from members of the public and opposition politicians. Many ordinary families across the island were prevented from attending the funerals of loved ones due to the strict regulations in place.

The controversy as been reignited amid the ongoing formation of the Northern Executive and renewed debates over Sinn Féin’s adherence to public health rules while in office. DUP representatives have called on Ms O’Neill to apologise for what they describe as a “flagrant disregard” for public health restrictions. Ulster Unionist MLA Doug Beattie said the incident “undermined confidence in the Executive’s messaging at a critical moment in the pandemic.”

For her part, Ms O’Neill continues to refuse to issue an apology, instead emphasising the need for “collective leadership” and remembering those who died during the pandemic. “I understand the hurt felt by families. I lost family members myself during Covid-19. We all had to make sacrifices and I did not intend to cause any pain,” she said.

A previous Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) investigation concluded that no criminal offences were committed by those in attendance at the Storey funeral, provoking further anger among critics who argue that ordinary citizens suffered penalties for breaches of less severe nature.

Public confidence in the Executive’s handling of pandemic measures remains a contentious issue. Many on the ground in both the North and the Republic remember the incident as a turning point in perceptions of political accountability during crisis. With Michelle O’Neill in line to become First Minister once again, questions over her leadership and judgement have resurfaced. 

Opposition TDs in the Dáil have also weighed in, with Fine Gael’s Neale Richmond describing the episode as “deeply damaging” to inter-community trust. Sinn Féin, for their part, insist that the matter is closed and have accused political opponents of “opportunistic point-scoring.”

Bereaved families across the island continue to express their frustration. One Dublin woman whose father died of Covid-19 in April 2020 told Gript: “We couldn’t even go into the church. Politicians set the rules and then break them. There’s no real justice in that.”
headline: Michelle O’Neill: No, you didn’t see me breach social distancing at that funeral

A rural Meath community has mounted a campaign against plans for a modular housing development intended to accommodate refugees from Ukraine, warning that the project would fundamentally alter the character of the area and has not been subject to adequate local consultation.

Residents of the small village of Ballinabrackey, close to the Offaly border, say they were blindsided by news that over 100 modular units are to be constructed by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, as part of the government’s rapid-build accommodation programme for those fleeing the conflict in Ukraine.

Locals told Gript that work at the greenfield site, which lies on the edge of the village, began last month. Several expressed anger that there was “no warning or consultation” before machinery arrived to clear ground and install temporary infrastructure. They argue that amenities in Ballinabrackey, home to fewer than 400 people, are already stretched and that local services — including the primary school, medical centre, and water supply — would not cope with the proposed influx.

A spokesperson for the residents’ action group said the community supports offering shelter to people fleeing war, but that “foisting a development of this scale onto a tiny village, without so much as a public meeting, is both unfair and irresponsible.” The group has launched a petition and is pursuing legal advice regarding possible breaches in the planning process.

The Department has defended the project, stating that the modular units are urgently needed to fulfil the State’s obligations to provide accommodation, and that measures to integrate new arrivals with the existing community will be put in place. A spokesperson said the development will contain family units and communal facilities, and that those arriving will be offered “comprehensive supports.”

However, Ballinabrackey residents are unconvinced. “We understand and sympathise with Ukrainian families, but this is about lack of transparency and disregard for rural communities,” said local parent Siobhan O’Neill. “Our children’s school is already full. Where are they supposed to go? Who will pay for the upgrades needed for water and sewage? Nobody from the Department is giving us answers.”

A public meeting in the village hall this week drew a large turnout, with several TDs from Meath West and Offaly present. Sinn Féin TD Johnny Guirke said the Government had yet again “failed to communicate properly with ordinary people,” while Fine Gael TD Damien English called for an immediate halt to works pending further consultation.

The issue comes as communities around the country grapple with what some describe as the “hidden consequences” of the Government’s efforts to house tens of thousands of international protection applicants and refugees, many of whom are now being accommodated in rural or small-town settings. The Oireachtas Committee on Children and Integration is expected to hear fresh calls for reform of the placement system when it meets next week.

Meanwhile, Ballinabrackey residents have vowed to continue their campaign and have not ruled out further protests. The Department maintains the project is proceeding as planned, with the first modular homes expected to be completed by autumn.
headline: Meath village seeks to stop Ukrainian refugee village being built on its doorstep
