AstraZeneca, the pharmaceutical giant behind one of the world’s main Covid-19 vaccines, appears poised to end its much-touted "no profit" commitment on jab sales, according to a leaked legal agreement seen by this publication. The document, first reported by international media, strongly indicates that the company's promise to supply its vaccine “at cost” was bound by specific contractual terms relating to the end of the pandemic period — terms that may be set to expire soon.

The agreement, made between AstraZeneca and a major vaccine manufacturer, defines the “Pandemic Period” as lasting until July 2021, or until AstraZeneca determines on its own that Covid-19 is no longer a pandemic emergency. Once that period ends, the company is at liberty to begin charging “commercial pricing” for its vaccine — a move that could potentially see prices rise sharply in countries reliant on the jab to continue their immunisation programmes.

The revelation comes as governments across Europe, including the Department of Health in Ireland, have been under pressure over the cost and procurement of Covid-19 vaccines. The HSE's roll-out strategy relied heavily on the AstraZeneca vaccine, especially during the first half of 2021, although its use was later curtailed due to concerns about rare side effects.

AstraZeneca had previously promoted its “at cost” model as a sign of its commitment to global health, with CEO Pascal Soriot telling media that the company had no intention of profiting “during the pandemic.” However, the leaked contract raises questions about how long that promise was ever intended to last, and whether the company could now move to profit from ongoing booster campaigns or future variants.

Campaign groups and some opposition TDs have already voiced concern, warning that profits should not come before public health. “This is exactly what we feared might happen,” said People Before Profit TD Gino Kenny. “Taxpayers have already funded the research and development – lifesaving vaccines should not become a profit machine for massive corporations.”

For its part, AstraZeneca maintains that it has kept to the letter of its commitments. In a statement to international press, the company confirmed that its original pledge was always tied to the pandemic period, and that it may "consider introducing a modest commercial price" as the world transitions into an endemic phase of Covid-19.

Industry analysts say any price rise could have significant effects on the developing world, where governments have often depended on the lower cost of the AstraZeneca jab to protect vulnerable populations. Critics also point out that much of the underlying research for the vaccine was carried out at the University of Oxford with significant public funding, before AstraZeneca took on manufacturing and distribution.

The Department of Health has so far declined to comment on specific contract terms, but has reiterated the government’s commitment to securing "fair and equitable access" to vaccines as required.

As the pandemic enters yet another uncertain winter, the potential for higher vaccine costs is likely to prompt fierce debate in the Dáil over the government’s procurement strategy, and renew calls for greater transparency and public oversight over pharmaceutical contracts negotiated on the State’s behalf.
headline: Leaked document: AstraZeneca can end no-profit pledge soon

For years, Ireland has been told by government and climate activists alike that our car culture is spiralling out of control, with dire warnings about emissions, gridlock, and the alleged dangers of simply owning a family car. Whether it’s the relentless push for congestion charges, extra taxes, or outright bans on certain vehicles, motorists have been painted as the villains in the fight against climate change. Yet, when we look past the hype and actually examine the figures, the narrative often used to justify these policies begins to unravel.

Latest statistics from the European Automobile Manufacturers Association (ACEA) show that Ireland has one of the lowest rates of private car ownership in Western Europe. With approximately 470 cars per 1,000 inhabitants according to their 2023 report, Ireland sits well below the EU average, and far behind neighbours like Germany and Italy where the rate is over 600 per 1,000 people. Even the UK, which is often cited as a model, has a significantly higher level of car ownership per capita.

For a country where life outside a handful of urban centres is dependent on private transport, these figures make for uncomfortable reading for those pushing ever-harsher restrictions on driving. Dublin may have Luas lines and a patchwork of bus corridors, but in the rest of the country, options are either sparse or non-existent. Take rural Cork, Mayo, or Donegal—without your own car you are at the mercy of infrequent bus services, if there is a service at all.

The reality, for most Irish people, is that a vehicle is not a luxury or a status symbol, but a necessity. This is especially true for families, carers, shift workers, or anyone who does not live directly on a train or bus route. The idea that the majority are frivolously hopping in SUVs every morning for a two-minute jaunt when they could easily walk or cycle is, frankly, a myth. The car is often the only practical way to access work, health services, or even a local shop.

Those fixated on demonising motorists should also consider the demographics at play. Young people are less likely than ever to own cars, not because of virtue but because of affordability. The cost of insurance, NCT, and fuel, coupled with some of the highest vehicle taxes in Europe, have already put car ownership out of reach for many. Instead of reflecting on these challenges, politicians and campaigners are keen to pile on further, either through proposed “road usage charges” or plans to limit parking spaces in new developments—while simultaneously failing to deliver viable alternatives.

And yet, for all the noise about Ireland’s emissions, private vehicles account for less than one-fifth of national greenhouse gas output. Agriculture remains the largest source of emissions by a considerable margin, a fact that seems conveniently forgotten when car bans or “decarbonisation initiatives” are discussed in the Dáil.

The fixation on cars is part of a wider pattern: blaming ordinary people for problems created by policy failures elsewhere. Rather than investing seriously in rural transport, or recognising the real, lived circumstances of families and workers, government action seems determined to make life that bit harder for anyone who relies on their car.

It is time for a bit more honesty in the national conversation. Ireland, far from being a country with a runaway car culture, is actually well behind our peers in Europe when it comes to car ownership.
headline: Despite Climate Hysteria, figures show Ireland has low car ownership rate

A majority of Irish people are not in favour of allowing biological males who identify as female to compete in women’s sports, according to a new poll commissioned by Gript.

The poll, carried out by Red C, asked a representative sample of 1,001 adults across the country for their views on transgender participation in women’s sporting competitions. Respondents were presented with the statement: “Transgender women (that is, biologically male people who identify and live as women) should be allowed to compete in women's sports competitions.” Just 15% said they agreed with the statement, while 65% disagreed. A further 20% said they did not know or had no strong opinion.

Opposition to transgender participation in women’s sport was strongest among older age groups, with 72% of those aged 55 and over expressing disagreement. Among younger adults aged 18 to 34, opposition was less pronounced but still in the majority, with 52% saying they disagreed with the statement. The poll also found no significant difference between men and women in their responses.

Supporters of transgender participation tended to cite inclusion and equality as their primary reasons, with a small minority of respondents saying they believed sporting bodies should make their own rules rather than being bound by government regulation. Those opposed, however, cited concerns about fairness, safety, and the perceived physical advantages held by biological males.

The results are likely to reignite debate in the Oireachtas, as several sporting organisations, including the FAI and the IRFU, have reviewed their policies on transgender athletes in recent years. The Irish Rugby Football Union in 2022 ruled that players who were born male and had gone through puberty would not be eligible to play in women’s contact rugby for safety reasons. Nonetheless, critics have argued that existing policies in other sports remain too permissive, and have called for more robust guidance from Sports Ireland and government departments.

Speaking to Gript, Senator Sharon Keogan (Independent), a vocal critic of gender self-ID legislation, said the figures reflected a growing public unease. “These numbers show that the Irish public is increasingly unhappy with woke ideology being imposed on women’s sport. It’s about fairness and safety—nothing else,” she said.

Transgender advocacy groups, however, have challenged the framing of the debate. Trans Equality Together, a coalition of NGOs, described the poll question as “misleading” and “designed to sow fear.” In a statement, the group said: “The reality is that trans people are already present in sports at every level and face significant barriers to participation.”

Meanwhile, Government ministers have so far shown little appetite to legislate on the issue, preferring to leave decisions in the hands of national sporting bodies. Sports Minister Thomas Byrne said in a recent interview that “it’s a matter for each sporting organisation to ensure fairness and inclusion in line with international best practice.”

However, campaigners say the issue is not going away, as rising numbers of women’s teams and athletes raise concerns about the impact of transgender participation on competition, safety and the future of women’s sport.

The poll has been conducted as part of a wider Gript investigation into the rapidly-evolving policy landscape surrounding gender and sport in Ireland. With 65% of the public now opposed, the findings will intensify pressure on both politicians and sporting organisations to provide clear policies—and perhaps, in time, new legislation.
headline: Poll: Irish public not real keen on the transgender sports stuff

A row broke out in the Canadian House of Commons this week after an MP was abruptly cut off while raising questions about the influence of the World Economic Forum (WEF) on the country’s government—a move which has fuelled fresh concerns over transparency and free debate in Canadian parliamentary proceedings.

Conservative MP Colin Carrie was speaking during a Monday session when he began to ask about the WEF’s involvement in Canadian government affairs. Almost immediately, Speaker Anthony Rota interjected, halting Carrie’s question mid-sentence and citing “disinformation” as a reason to move the discussion on.

Dr Carrie had attempted to ask the government to clarify its relationship with the Davos-based WEF, noting that many Canadians hold concerns about the group’s potential sway over national policy. "I had constituents ask me about outside influence, including the WEF," he began, before the Speaker interrupted, insisting that Carrie “cease the line of questioning”.

The incident was quickly picked up by media outlets and commentators across North America and further afield, with critics arguing that it is indicative of a wider unwillingness among political elites to permit open discussion of influential international organisations such as the WEF—a forum widely associated with global policy agendas on issues including environmental regulation, digital identity, and public health.

In a statement following the exchange, Carrie described the Speaker’s intervention as “deeply troubling”, adding that “Canadians deserve answers about who is influencing their government and why certain topics are considered off-limits in Parliament”.

Opposition to the WEF has mounted in several countries, with critics expressing concern about the group’s unelected status and its annual gathering of global leaders, business magnates, and policymakers in Davos, Switzerland. The WEF has publicly stated that it works to “improve the state of the world in collaboration with stakeholders from government, business, and civil society”, but suspicions persist among both left and right-wing groups about the potential for backroom agreements and policy alignment outside of normal democratic channels.

Parallels have been drawn by some Irish commentators to recent debates in the Oireachtas regarding the growing influence of international bodies in Irish policy formation, particularly in the realms of climate legislation and digital regulation. Critics have warned that shutting down uncomfortable lines of questioning sets a worrying precedent for parliamentary democracy, regardless of jurisdiction.

Government ministers in Canada had not commented on the matter at time of writing, but social media reaction has been swift and polarised, with supporters of Carrie demanding further debate on the WEF and its reach, while others dismissed the focus as an exercise in conspiracy-mongering.

The episode highlights a growing global tension between elected representatives and supranational organisations, raising questions about where the line should be drawn between legitimate policy collaboration and undue influence by outside entities.
headline: Canadian MP cut off in parliament while asking about WEF

text:
As Ireland marks a decade since the legalisation of same-sex marriage and observes the rapid social change that has reshaped the national landscape, it is worth pausing to ask whether the liberal consensus that now underpins most aspects of Irish society truly stands up to scrutiny—or whether it is long overdue for serious interrogation. In the rush to embrace new orthodoxies, have we lost sight of the warnings sounded by thinkers who understood both the promise and the peril of liberal modernity?

Among the most prescient critics was John Henry Newman, the English theologian and convert to Catholicism who spent crucial years founding and nurturing the Catholic University of Ireland, the institution that would ultimately become UCD. Newman’s warnings about the limitations of liberalism, aired in his celebrated lectures and writings in mid-19th century Dublin, have become only more relevant as Ireland has morphed into what its leaders now hail as an “open, tolerant, liberal democracy”—as if these terms were immune to contradiction or excess.

Newman, it must be remembered, was no enemy of genuine freedom. He recognised the importance of liberty of conscience and speech. However, he was also deeply sceptical about the idea—now almost dogmatic amongst our commentariat and political class—that truth is best served when all opinions are flattened into equivalence, and that institutions (be they universities or parliaments) should neuter their capacity to say anything definite or enduring about the good, the true, or the beautiful.

“If in a search for truth it is enough to ascertain what is new, then the search itself will go astray,” Newman warned. He astutely observed the “suicidal” tendency of liberalism to undermine its own foundations, by refusing to assert any authority for fear of being thought “intolerant” or “outdated.” He saw what would happen when the very concepts of truth and virtue became passe, and when universities (then, as now) took pride in producing clever sceptics rather than citizens formed in character and conviction.

In recent years, Ireland has seen precisely this dynamic unfold at breathtaking speed. The Oireachtas routinely rushes through legislation on matters of life, family, and identity, often with little more than a nod to meaningful debate. University campuses once charged with the pursuit of truth routinely cancel speakers who do not fit prevailing fashions. The HSE and Department of Education issue guidelines on gender and sexuality that brook no dissent. Media outlets self-censor or demonise those who ask the “wrong” questions. Meanwhile, politicians from every party insist that “liberal Ireland” represents the natural end-point of history, as if any alternative vision were not simply wrong but morally reprehensible.

But as Newman warned, a society that refuses to assert the real existence of truth—both moral and philosophical—will soon find itself unable to justify its own institutions. Right now, the only heresy is to suggest that there might be limits to liberalism itself: to question whether children benefit when every value is treated as equal, or whether a country needs more than procedural fairness to bind it together. The very suggestion that there are goods and truths that are not up for endless re-negotiation is now greeted with suspicion, if not outright hostility.

Newman’s prescience lies in his insistence that liberalism, left unchecked, becomes not a friend of reasoned debate but its gravedigger.
headline: Holding liberalism to account: the prescience of John Henry Newman

Maria Bailey, the Fine Gael TD for Dún Laoghaire who became a focus of controversy over her now infamous personal injury claim against a Dublin hotel, has stepped down from her role as chairwoman of the Oireachtas Committee on Members’ Interests. The decision, announced late Wednesday evening, comes amid mounting pressure from within her own party and ongoing criticism from opposition benches questioning her suitability for the ethics watchdog role.

Ms Bailey confirmed her resignation in a statement to Gript, citing what she described as a need to “end distractions” and allow the committee “to continue its important work without the cloud of unrelenting political and media commentary.” Sources within Fine Gael indicated that the Taoiseach personally called Ms Bailey earlier this week, expressing the view that her continued presence at the helm threatened to overshadow the committee’s remit and undermine public confidence in the Oireachtas’ standards in public office.

The resignation comes two months after details emerged of Ms Bailey’s 2015 legal action against the Dean Hotel, in which she claimed to have suffered injuries after falling from a swing. The case, which was ultimately withdrawn, sparked a national debate over “compo culture” and calls for reform of personal injury claims. Ms Bailey has previously apologised for her handling of the matter, but her appointment as chair of the Members’ Interests Committee drew renewed criticism, with opposition TDs accusing Fine Gael of failing to grasp the seriousness of public concerns.

Labour leader Brendan Howlin called the resignation “inevitable”, saying, “You cannot have someone under the shadow of a questionable legal claim overseeing ethical standards in the Oireachtas.” Sinn Féin’s Mary Lou McDonald echoed those sentiments, insisting the issue “should never have arisen in the first place.” Members of the committee itself had reportedly raised concerns informally, with at least two TDs threatening to resign rather than serve under Ms Bailey.

Sources within Fine Gael have indicated that the party’s National Executive discussed the matter at length, with a view to minimising fallout in the lead-up to the next general election. Senior party figures remain anxious about the optics of the ongoing controversy at a time when scrutiny over standards in public office remains high. The Taoiseach is expected to nominate a new chairperson in the coming days, with backbenchers privately speculating that the party will select a member with a reputation for probity to “steady the ship”.

For her part, Ms Bailey insisted that she remains committed to serving her constituents in Dún Laoghaire and intends to contest the next general election. “I have made mistakes, but I will not be defined by one incident. I look forward to continuing my work as a public representative,” she said.

The Members’ Interests Committee, which is responsible for overseeing compliance with ethics rules by TDs and Senators, is expected to reconvene next week to elect a new chair. Opposition parties have called for a wider review of appointments to key oversight roles in the wake of the controversy, arguing that political appointments must be subject to greater scrutiny if public confidence in the Oireachtas is to be restored.
headline: Ouch: Maria Bailey resigns from chairmanship of Oireachtas ethics committee

Traditional Irish music and sean-nós singing fans are in for a treat this weekend as two major events in the cultural calendar move online, ensuring the spirit of the tradition endures despite ongoing public health restrictions.

The Patrick Ó’Keeffe Traditional Music Festival, usually a lively draw to Castleisland, Co Kerry, has adapted to the challenges of Covid-19 by migrating its events to virtual platforms. Meanwhile, the much-anticipated Oireachtas na Gaeilge, the premier festival of the Irish-speaking world, is also hosting its competitions, workshops and performances over the internet, connecting communities at home and abroad.

Organisers of the Patrick Ó’Keeffe festival have arranged a full programme of streamed performances, interviews and workshops, with fiddler Matt Cranitch and accordion player Jackie Daly among those taking centre stage online. The festival, named after the famed Sliabh Luachra fiddle master, is renowned among traditional musicians as a place to honour the unique style and repertoire of the region. In a statement to Gript, festival director Cormac O’Mahony said, “We’re determined to keep the festival flame burning, even from a distance. The music may be online, but the heart of Sliabh Luachra is still beating strong.”

Music-lovers can tune in for interactive workshops as well as live-streamed sessions, many of which are free. The committee said the transition to a digital format had the benefit of allowing fans from around the world to take part. “It’s a real opportunity to showcase the tradition to a wider audience. We’ve viewers logging in from the US, Australia and across Europe.”

Not to be outdone, Oireachtas na Gaeilge is also embracing the online format, bringing the colour and pageantry of the annual festival to living rooms from Donegal to Dún Laoghaire. The Oireachtas has been a staple in the Irish-language calendar since 1897, renowned for its sean-nós singing, dancing and storytelling, as well as the fiercely contested agallamh beirte and lúibíní competitions. Oireachtas CEO Máirín Nic Dhonnchadha told Gript that while the move online posed logistical challenges, it also offered new possibilities for engagement. “We wanted to ensure that the Gaeltacht and the diaspora felt part of the celebration. There’s a huge appetite for connecting with our language and arts, especially among younger generations.”

The festival’s opening ceremony, competitions and performances are being broadcast via the official Oireachtas website and social media channels, with participants joining from their homes. While the lack of in-person mingling is a loss, organisers have emphasised the positives. “The Oireachtas is more than just a festival, it’s a homecoming for Gaels everywhere. Even though we can’t gather in person, we’re delighted that people can still experience the richness of our culture,” Nic Dhonnchadha added.

Both festivals have called on audiences to support performers, many of whom have faced a difficult year with little or no live work. Donations are encouraged, and the hope is that this year’s online events will only deepen the appreciation for one of the island’s most deeply-rooted cultural traditions.

Details of the Patrick Ó’Keeffe Festival and Oireachtas na Gaeilge’s online programmes can be found on their respective websites.
headline: Enjoy trad and sean-nós this weekend as Patrick Ó’Keeffe Festival and Oireachtas na Gaeilge move online

Farmers from across the country have vowed to bring “thousands of tractors” back into the centre of Dublin if the Government fails to address what they describe as “years of neglect and betrayal of rural Ireland”.

Speaking to Gript, protest organisers said they were “ready to escalate” their campaign following what they claim was a lacklustre response from agriculture officials and the Taoiseach to their concerns on CAP reform, nitrates restrictions, and spiralling compliance costs. The Irish Farmers’ Association (IFA), the Irish Cattle and Sheep Farmers’ Association (ICSA), and the Irish Creamery Milk Suppliers Association (ICMSA) are among several groups considering coordinated mass convoys, warning of “serious disruption” if action is not taken.

“We brought 100 tractors and 500 farmers to the city centre in January – next time it’ll be five or six times that if needs be,” said a farmer from Westmeath, who helped coordinate previous Dublin demonstrations. “The Government need to realise we’re not backing down. Rural communities have been ignored for too long by the Dáil.”

Farmers say they are facing mounting pressure from Department of Agriculture clampdowns, with new EU-imposed caps on livestock numbers and pesticide use, and what they describe as “impossible” paperwork. One ICSA representative from Tipperary said: “We’re not the villains here – we’re just trying to feed the country, but they want to cut our herds and tie us up in red tape.”

Sources within farming organisations told Gript that recent meetings with the Tánaiste and Minister for Agriculture, Charlie McConalogue, were “frustratingly vague”, leaving the farming sector with “no option but to up the ante”. Farmers have highlighted what they say is a “double standard”, with large agri-corporations and meat processors allegedly favoured over family farms.

Gardaí are said to be preparing for the potential return of farm convoys and road blockades similar to those seen in Paris and Amsterdam, with an Assistant Garda Commissioner telling Gript that “public order plans are under review”. Previous tractor protests led to major traffic delays in the capital, with streets around Leinster House, Merrion Square and St Stephen’s Green brought to a standstill. Dublin City Council has warned that another large demonstration would mean “significant disruption” to Luas and Dublin Bus services.

Minister McConalogue has called for dialogue, saying he recognises “the vital role farmers play in Irish life” and wants “all stakeholders” at the negotiating table. However, the message has not reassured the rural community. “We’re tired of being fobbed off,” said a Kerry beef farmer who travelled to Dublin for Thursday’s demonstration. “We don’t want sympathy – we want policies that will allow us to make a living.”

Many in rural Ireland have expressed solidarity with the planned escalation and accused the Government and opposition alike of “urban bias”. As farming groups meet this weekend to finalise plans, there is growing anticipation — and some unease—about the prospect of a city paralysed by wheel after wheel of agricultural machinery. Organisers have not ruled out an overnight occupation, with one warning: “We’ll stay as long as it takes. If they won’t listen to us in the countryside, we’ll bring the countryside to their door.”
headline: Call for thousands of tractors in Dublin: farmers’ protest escalates

One of Denmark’s highest-circulation newspapers has issued an apology to its readers for what it described as “hypnotic” and uncritical coverage of the government’s Covid-19 response, reigniting debate over the media’s role during the pandemic. Ekstra Bladet, renowned for its tabloid edge and wide readership, published the editorial mea culpa at the weekend, admitting that it had failed to ask hard questions about Danish health authorities’ data and policies.

In a strikingly candid piece, the paper wrote that its journalists had “failed to be vigilant enough at the garden gate” and “not sufficiently questioned” the official information coming from Denmark’s health authorities and politicians. The editorial singled out a reliance on government case tallies and hospitalisation numbers that, it now acknowledged, may have “painted a more frightening picture” than was warranted. It further admitted to echoing government messaging without adequately investigating the complexities behind daily case numbers— especially given the role of incidental positive tests among patients hospitalised for other reasons.

While Danish authorities have been praised in some quarters for a relatively swift vaccine rollout and comparatively light lockdowns, the media’s handling of pandemic information has faced mounting criticism. Ekstra Bladet’s recalibration follows similar critiques emerging elsewhere in Europe relating to trust in media and the need for rigorous oversight of rapidly changing scientific and political statements. The editor noted that at times, the public were “practically hypnotised” by official statistics, and that journalists should have “stood firmer on our own two feet.”

In Ireland, the episode has resonance with ongoing debates about balance and scrutiny in pandemic reporting. Irish outlets faced regular demands both to bolster government health communications and to provide platforms for contrarian voices. Notable frustration among sections of the public and several TDs arose over the HSE’s daily briefings and how media organisations relayed this information. Oireachtas committees in late 2021 heard expert testimony calling for greater transparency in the communication of Covid numbers, particularly distinguishing between those in hospital because of Covid versus those who simply tested positive while admitted.

While the Danish paper stopped short of accusing officials of deliberate misinformation, the editorial suggests an institutional lesson about the media’s role as a check on government power during crises. “We should have done more to challenge the narrative, especially where the data was not as clear as it seemed,” the editorial concluded.

International watchdogs, such as Reporters Without Borders, have repeatedly stressed the necessity of independent journalism in the face of government health directives. Trust in Irish media has fluctuated throughout the pandemic, with surveys indicating significant portions of the public feeling that coverage was either too alarmist or insufficiently sceptical of official policy. Some Irish commentators have likewise encouraged self-reflection among journalists, warning against “groupthink” and calling for robust public debate as Ireland moves through the next phase of the pandemic.

Ekstra Bladet’s admission is likely to be welcomed by those in Denmark and abroad who have called for more nuanced and questioning scrutiny of pandemic policies. It may also serve as a prompt for Irish news organisations to revisit their own editorial decisions during the emergency, as societies across Europe reckon with the extraordinary challenges faced—and lessons learned—since Covid-19 first arrived.
headline: Danish newspaper sorry for “hypnotic” reporting of Covid narrative

text:
Periods of social and economic upheaval have long acted as unlikely incubators for artistic innovation. The Irish experience is a clear testament to this paradox: adversity has often summoned forth some of the nation’s most enduring and powerful cultural contributions, as creative minds channel uncertainty, anxiety, or outright hardship into works that resonate for generations.

The times in which we live are, by almost any measure, turbulent. Few could have predicted five years ago the scale of societal change that would roll across the country: the tail end of austerity, Brexit, the pandemic, and the ongoing cost-of-living crisis. Yet among the widespread anxiety and disillusionment, one can discern a renewed energy among Ireland’s artists, musicians, and writers—many of whom find that their creative drive is only intensified by the backdrop of societal unrest.

It is hardly a new phenomenon. Looking back, the Irish literary renaissance at the turn of the 20th century—a time marked by political struggle and economic deprivation—produced a galaxy of talent, from Yeats and Synge to Lady Gregory and O’Casey. In the 1980s, during a period of recession, unemployment, and mass emigration, Irish music and theatre flourished, with acts like U2, The Pogues, and writers such as Roddy Doyle gaining international recognition. Even in the darkest days of the Troubles, poetry, song, and drama provided a voice for those whose stories might otherwise have gone unheard.

For the creative, hardship is not necessarily a barrier but often a catalyst. Many will recall the rush of online performances and inventive projects that emerged during the lockdowns—virtual céilís, living room concerts, and digital galleries—demonstrating not only the resilience but the adaptability of Irish culture. These were not always grand productions, but they captured the raw immediacy of the moment, often with a wit and irreverence that is uniquely Irish.

It is also the case that, in straitened times, there is an appetite for new voices—those willing to challenge the status quo or articulate what many feel but cannot express. The rise of small presses and independent film-makers in recent years is evidence of this, as is the proliferation of podcasts, zines and grassroots arts initiatives set up by people frustrated with traditional gatekeepers. The Arts Council has reported a notable increase in applications for funding in the past three years, with a marked rise in projects exploring themes of housing, migration, and national identity.

Yet, this creative ferment is not simply a silver lining to national hardship. It also serves as a kind of collective therapy and a means of social cohesion. Shared stories, whether told on stage, in song, or on the page, allow for the airing of grievances and the forging of solidarity. In a small country like Ireland, where almost everyone knows someone in the creative arts, the knock-on effect can be profound—not just for individual artists, but for communities who find their own struggles reflected and honoured in the national conversation.

Of course, such a flowering of creativity cannot be divorced from the necessity of public and private support. While hardship may inspire, chronic underfunding threatens to sap the energy of even the most determined artists. The ongoing debate over arts funding in the Dáil is no mere sideshow, and many creative organisations warn that without sustained investment, Ireland risks losing its next generation of cultural innovators to better opportunities abroad.

For now, though, Irish creativity continues to defy the gloom.
headline: For the creative, the worst of times can be the best of times

text:
A criminal court in the United States has acquitted two police officers who shot and killed a man with Down Syndrome, prompting an outpouring of grief and anger among disability rights campaigners and the family of the deceased.

Robert “Bobby” Eaton, a 28-year-old man with Down Syndrome, was shot multiple times by officers responding to a call about a disturbance in a suburban neighbourhood in Tucson, Arizona last year. Eaton’s family and eyewitnesses say he was unarmed at the time, holding only a soft drink can, and was not a threat to anyone present.

The jury’s decision late on Thursday found that Officers Mark Pelley and Tanya Dorsey had acted in accordance with police “training and procedures” and were not criminally liable for Eaton’s death. Throughout the two-week trial, the defence argued that the officers had “feared for their safety.” However, body camera footage played during the hearing showed Eaton moving slowly, with one hand raised, as officers fired a total of six rounds.

The verdict sparked sharp criticism from disability rights groups, with advocates accusing the American justice system of endangering vulnerable people. “What this says is that killing us is ok — that our lives are worth less,” said Ellen Doyle, spokesperson for the National Down Syndrome Advocacy Network. “It is impossible to understand how any jury could see that video and think those officers were in danger.”

The Eaton family were visibly distressed following the verdict. Speaking outside the courthouse, Bobby’s sister, Jessica Eaton, called on the US Department of Justice to launch a wider inquiry. “Bobby needed help, not bullets. Instead, we have to bury our brother and watch those responsible walk free,” she said.

Legal experts in both the US and Ireland noted that American police officers generally enjoy broad legal protections in cases involving the use of deadly force, an issue that has come under increasing scrutiny after several high-profile police shootings in recent years. In contrast, Gardaí in Ireland are subject to stricter oversight and do not routinely carry firearms.

The US case has also reignited debate about police training and interactions with those who have intellectual disabilities. According to data compiled by the disability justice group Dignity Now, more than 150 Americans with intellectual or developmental disabilities have been killed by police since 2015. Campaigners are demanding mandatory disability awareness training for all frontline officers.

The Irish Centre for Disability Law and Policy at University of Galway said the verdict was “deeply concerning.” In a statement, the Centre called for international pressure on US authorities to reform police practices. “No one should have to fear for their life because of their disability,” the statement read.

As the US faces fresh calls for police and justice reform, the Eaton family say they will pursue a civil case against the city of Tucson and the police department. They have also vowed to campaign for stronger protections for people with disabilities, holding up Bobby’s picture as a reminder of what they call a “tragic injustice.”
headline: “Killing us is ok?” – grief as cops who shot man with Down Syndrome acquitted

text:
The emergence of self-appointed “anti-misinformation” bodies, particularly those with high-profile funding and access to media platforms, is a defining feature of our era. The latest controversy surrounds the UK-based Full Fact, a think-tank which bills itself as an impartial bulwark against online falsehoods, but whose recent foray into transgender issues exposes more than a few cracks in its claimed neutrality.

On social media this week, Full Fact published an “explainer” about gender identity, doubling down on ideological talking points rather than sticking with facts. The piece, widely shared by Irish activists and even picked up by a handful of local journalists, claims flatly that “trans women are women” and characterises any discussion of biological sex as, at best, a “debate” and, at worst, “harmful disinformation.” The irony of a misinformation watchdog indulging in the same sleight of hand it claims to police is apparently lost on its authors.

Irish people are keenly aware of the impact foreign lobby groups can have on domestic policy. The Oireachtas has spent months deliberating on gender recognition, single-sex spaces, sport, and the rights of children. Many here, regardless of personal view, expect these debates to be guided by clear evidence and respect for plural opinions. Yet, Full Fact’s framing is anything but clear. It refers consistently to “assigned sex at birth,” a phrase that began as activist jargon and is now taken up as if it were a neutral scientific reality. In fact, sex is observed and recorded at birth, not “assigned,” and intersex conditions (often cited in these arguments) do not disprove the binary nature of human biology.

Crucially, the content produced by Full Fact fails to distinguish between gender identity (a matter of subjective feeling) and biological sex (an observable reality). This is not merely semantic: Irish law, sports competitions, healthcare access and safeguarding are all affected by these definitions. Full Fact’s “explainer” not only refuses to acknowledge scientific and legal consensus on sex differences, but goes further, branding dissenting opinion as “potentially harmful,” thereby chilling legitimate public discussion.

It is worth questioning how a group that claims to safeguard “the facts” could come to such a position. The answer lies, perhaps, in the ideological capture of mainstream institutions. Ireland has seen a surge in activism-driven policy, much of it propelled by NGOs and think-tanks with little regard for the electorate’s actual views. As Full Fact’s recent misstep demonstrates, “misinformation” is often in the eye of the beholder – and when the beholder is in thrall to gender ideology, inconvenient facts get swept aside.

Irish citizens deserve debate that is transparent and anchored in reality, not dictated by unaccountable foreign bodies parroting activist lines. The Oireachtas, schools, sports organisations, and families face difficult and complex decisions in the years ahead. They are ill-served by fact-checkers who appear incapable of distinguishing between facts, ideology, and wishful thinking. Full Fact, by spreading its own brand of misinformation on this issue, reveals the urgent need for greater scrutiny not just of what we believe, but also of who gets to decide what is “true.”
headline: Anti-misinformation think-tank spreads trans misinformation

Fianna Fáil stalwart Eamon Ó Cuív has broken ranks once again, this time declaring his opposition to the emerging coalition deal currently being hammered out at the top table of Irish politics. Ó Cuív, never shy of striking a discordant note with the party leadership, made it clear to Gript that he cannot support an alliance which, in his words, “fails to reflect the core values and legacy of Fianna Fáil as a republican and grassroots movement”.

Ó Cuív, a grandson of party founder Éamon de Valera, is no stranger to challenging the Fianna Fáil hierarchy. He has repeatedly voiced concerns that the party has drifted too far from its original mission in pursuit of power. “Fianna Fáil has always represented the broad sweep of Irish society – urban and rural, rich and poor. We cannot, in all honesty, tell our supporters that this arrangement is in line with our core beliefs,” he said.

The proposed coalition, involving elements of Fine Gael, the Greens and possibly independents, has been widely criticised, not least by the party’s traditional base. Many grassroots members view the arrangement as a betrayal of Fianna Fáil’s distinct identity, particularly after years of bitter contest with Fine Gael. Ó Cuív’s intervention is likely to stoke further debate within the party, already divided after a bruising general election.

Ó Cuív, who has represented Galway West for decades and who carries the weight of his family legacy in the Oireachtas, argues that the party is in danger of becoming indistinguishable from its rivals. “We are at a crossroads. If we compromise too much, we risk losing the trust of our voters, especially in rural Ireland where Fianna Fáil’s roots run deepest. There is no point in being in government if it means abandoning what we stand for,” he said.

He also took aim at what he calls the “Dublin-centric” policies dominating the coalition talks, particularly on housing, agriculture, and rural development. “We have had enough of one-size-fits-all solutions dictated from Dublin. The new government must realise that the needs of families and communities in Galway or Donegal are not always the same as those in the capital,” he stated.

While Ó Cuív has often found himself on the losing side of intra-party debates, his views command respect among members disillusioned by the leadership’s direction. He insisted his stance is not about personalities but about principle: “Fianna Fáil was established to defend the interests of ordinary people. If we cannot do that in this coalition, then we should not enter it.”

With the Fianna Fáil parliamentary party scheduled to meet later this week, pressure is mounting on Taoiseach Micheál Martin to allay the concerns of dissidents like Ó Cuív and to convince members that the party’s soul will not be sold for a seat at the Cabinet table.

Ó Cuív’s words will resonate with many who fear that, by leaping into bed with old rivals, Fianna Fáil is surrendering its independence – and, perhaps, sealing its fate with voters who already feel abandoned. The question, now, is whether his warning will be heeded, or whether it will be brushed aside by a leadership intent on clinching a deal at almost any cost.
headline: Eamon O’Cuiv says: I am against this proposed coalition

text:
The Great Barrier Reef has recorded its highest levels of hard coral cover in decades, according to a new survey released by the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS). The findings confound ongoing concerns about the reef’s imminent collapse, with researchers reporting “remarkable” resilience in the face of recent environmental pressures.

The annual survey, which has monitored the health of the reef since 1985, shows significant coral growth across two-thirds of the 2,300 kilometre structure off Queensland’s coast. The northern and central sections in particular are at their highest coral cover since records began, with some reefs reporting up to 36% hard coral coverage.

Scientists involved in the research attribute the rebound to a temporary lull in severe weather events, such as cyclones and mass bleaching episodes, which have battered the reef repeatedly in recent years. Dr Mike Emslie, lead author of the AIMS Long-Term Monitoring Programme, described the results as “cause for cautious optimism”, while noting that the southern part of the reef experienced some declines due to crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks.

The report comes as international commentary continues to paint the reef as a near-lost cause, fuelling ongoing debates about the scale and urgency of interventions required. In 2022, a United Nations monitoring mission recommended the Great Barrier Reef be added to the World Heritage “in danger” list, citing concerns over climate change and water quality.

Minister for the Environment, Tanya Plibersek, welcomed the positive news but warned that the reef’s recovery is fragile, highlighting the need for ongoing investment in conservation and management programmes. Environmental groups have responded with caution, arguing that one good year does not offset the long-term threats posed by global warming and ocean acidification.

Nevertheless, the findings have reignited debate over the accuracy of some of the more alarmist claims about the reef’s decline, with some critics accusing international bodies of exaggeration to push a broader climate agenda. Senator Matt Canavan, a prominent sceptic, said the report “vindicates those who have called for a more balanced and evidence-based approach to reporting on the reef”.

Tourism operators and local businesses have also welcomed the results, saying they reinforce the reef’s enduring value as one of the world’s most iconic natural attractions. The tourism sector, a major employer in Queensland, had suffered steep declines in visitor numbers amid negative coverage of the reef’s health and the Covid-19 pandemic.

Irish marine scientists have followed developments at the Great Barrier Reef with interest, as Irish reefs and marine ecosystems face similar pressures from warming waters and pollution. The Marine Institute in Galway has pointed to the AIMS survey as an example of the importance of long-term, consistent monitoring in shaping effective conservation policy.

While AIMS scientists stress that the reef remains vulnerable to further setbacks, particularly as climate change drives increasingly frequent and intense marine heatwaves, the latest figures offer hope that with targeted management and favourable conditions, recovery is possible even in delicate ecosystems.

The Great Barrier Reef remains under close scrutiny as nations prepare for the next United Nations Climate Change Conference, with policymakers weighing up the relative impacts of local action versus global emissions targets. For now, the reef’s unexpected resilience stands as a reminder of nature’s capacity for renewal, given the right circumstances.
headline: Great Barrier Reef has record levels of coral, says survey

text:
The arrival of the swallows each year is a signal of hope for many throughout Ireland—a reassurance that, despite storms and setbacks, the world continues on as it always has. Their return is woven into the story of Irish place and family, a signifier of continuity and belonging. It is fitting, then, that this spring, as swallows trace their arcs over towns and townlands, the Irish news cycle is full once more of the seemingly intractable crisis around Irish housing—another story of home, exile, and return.

The image of the emigrant Irish was once an emblem of economic hardship, of forced absence, of a nation unable to mind its own. In recent years, the narrative from government benches has been one of recovery, boom, and progress. Yet, for tens of thousands of young Irish people, the prospect of home—of settling, of family, of rooting themselves here—remains as elusive as it was for previous generations. The swallows have a place to return. For many unable to buy or rent in Ireland’s overheated market, there is no such certainty.

Since the start of the year, more than 4,000 Irish people have left the country—a figure that, while perhaps lower than the darkest days of the recession, is still a damning indictment. These are not mere statistics. They are sons and daughters, newlyweds and young families, graduates and tradesmen. The reason most often cited? The cost and scarcity of housing. The latest figures from the Central Statistics Office show that average house prices continue to rise, and even the most basic rentals in Dublin, Cork, or Galway are now beyond the reach of most earning an average salary. Local authority waiting lists stretch into the years, and government targets for new builds remain just that: targets, rarely realised.

The reply from Leinster House is depressingly familiar: yet more targets, yet more plans, yet more announcements of schemes and initiatives that never seem to bite. The Housing for All plan, trumpeted as a coordinated solution, has proved as fragile as a swallow’s nest in a winter gale. The numbers simply do not stack up: with net inward migration outstripping housing completions, demand is not merely outpacing supply, it is leaving it in the dust.

Meanwhile, much is made of “progressive” solutions: co-living pods, micro-apartments, and the reclassification of hotels and offices as temporary accommodation. For any Irish person who grew up with even the faintest notion of what a home should mean—not simply a place to sleep, but a site of permanence, privacy, and rootedness—these are meagre offerings. The State’s growing reliance on Housing Assistance Payment and other rent supports is only a sticking plaster over a wound that continues to bleed.

In the countryside, villages hollow out as the young move to cities, or, more frequently now, abroad. The Government proclaims its commitment to rural regeneration, yet fails to address the basic infrastructure and investment deficit that keeps young families from settling beyond the M50. Urban centres cram ever more people into ever smaller, ever more unaffordable spaces, while ghost estates and derelict buildings rot in plain sight.

The question that ought to keep ministers awake at night is not just about supply and demand, but about the kind of country Ireland is becoming. We are a nation that once sent its children to the four winds out of necessity.
headline: Irish housing, and the flight of the swallows

The Irish Red Cross has issued a stark warning to elderly citizens after reports emerged of a scam in which fraudsters are charging vulnerable individuals €100 for bogus Coronavirus tests. The organisation has received several accounts of people being approached at their homes by individuals claiming to be connected with either the Red Cross or the HSE.

The perpetrators, reportedly targeting older persons living alone, arrive wearing makeshift uniforms and carrying forged identification. They claim to offer a “rapid Covid-19 screening test” for a fee of €100, insisting that failure to be tested could result in fines or the withdrawal of essential services.

The Red Cross, in a statement issued this morning, emphasised that it does not conduct any form of door-to-door virus testing and never requests payment for any medical service or public health intervention. Furthermore, the HSE has confirmed to Gript that all legitimate Covid-19 testing through the public health system remains entirely free of charge, and that staff will never ask for payment or entry to a person’s home unannounced.

Patsy Toland, National Community Support Officer for the Irish Red Cross, called the scam “particularly despicable” given the fear and confusion caused by the pandemic, and urged neighbours and family members to check in on elderly relatives and friends to ensure they are not being targeted.

“We are very concerned about the safety and wellbeing of our senior citizens, particularly those who may be isolated during this time. No Red Cross volunteer or HSE worker will ever come to your home requesting payment for a Covid-19 test. If you are approached by individuals claiming otherwise, close the door and contact the Gardaí immediately,” Mr Toland said.

Gardaí have also appealed to the public to remain vigilant, particularly in rural communities and housing estates where older people might be more susceptible to this type of doorstep fraud. Anyone who receives an unsolicited visit or phone call offering coronavirus tests for a fee is asked to report the incident to their local Garda station.

The scam comes as concern grows nationally about criminals exploiting the ongoing public health crisis. Both the Office for Internet Safety and the HSE have issued separate alerts about online tricksters selling counterfeit masks, supposed cures, and fake test kits.

Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly TD condemned those responsible for preying on the elderly and vulnerable. “This kind of behaviour is utterly reprehensible. Nobody should be asked to pay for a Covid-19 test in Ireland. If in doubt, contact the HSE helpline or your GP, but never hand over cash at your door,” Minister Donnelly noted.

The Red Cross is reminding the public that any official visit from the HSE or voluntary support group will have prior arrangement and proof of identity. Community and parish groups have been asked to disseminate this information widely, ensuring those most at risk are properly informed.

As the country continues to navigate the unpredictable challenges of the pandemic, authorities are urging citizens to watch out for one another and to report any suspicious behaviour without delay.
headline: Red Cross warn against Coronavirus scam charging elderly €100 for fake test

The Canadian government has officially lifted its Covid-19 vaccination requirement for entry at its border, marking a significant policy shift more than three years after the start of the pandemic. The update, announced by federal officials in Ottawa late yesterday, came into effect immediately, allowing foreign nationals to travel into Canada without providing proof of vaccination against Covid-19.

The move brings Canada’s border protocols closer in line with most European nations, including Ireland, which phased out similar restrictions last year. Canadian authorities said the change reflected the current epidemiological situation and widespread population immunity.

Previously, the requirement, in place since autumn 2021, meant that most travellers – including Irish citizens – needed to show documentation of at least two Covid-19 vaccinations, or face being turned back at the border or denied boarding on flights. The rule applied not only to air travel but also to entry by land and sea, affecting visitors, temporary workers, and even returning residents.

The restrictions were a source of frustration and controversy for many, particularly after the World Health Organisation (WHO) downgraded its global emergency status for the virus in May 2023. International travel industry groups, along with some Canadian provincial leaders and opposition MPs, repeatedly called on Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s government to end the “outdated and punitive” measure.

Business groups and travel agencies have welcomed the change, saying it will boost economic activity and restore family connections disrupted by the policy. Irish community organisations in Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal – home to large Irish diaspora populations – have also expressed relief that relatives can now visit more freely.

However, some Canadian public health officials have urged continued caution, especially during periods of higher respiratory illness transmission. The Public Health Agency of Canada still “strongly recommends” that visitors be up-to-date with their Covid-19 and other routine vaccinations.

Ireland dropped its Covid-19 entry requirements in March 2022. The US, which shares its only land border with Canada, withdrew its own vaccine requirement for international arrivals last May.

The Canadian government retained the right to reimpose vaccine checks should a new variant of concern emerge. For now, the Department of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship said that “all travellers, regardless of vaccination status, are welcome to enter Canada as of today.”

No significant changes are expected for travel into or out of Ireland as a result of the Canadian decision. The Irish Embassy in Ottawa has updated its travel advice to reflect the new rules. 

With the removal of one of the Western world’s last major Covid-era border requirements, observers say the move signals the final chapter in Canada’s pandemic border policies – though Canadians are being reminded of the need for ongoing vigilance as winter approaches in the northern hemisphere.
headline: Canada finally drops Covid vaccine requirement for entry at border

text:
The storm of public outrage that greeted both the “Golfgate” scandal and the more recent revelations surrounding RTÉ’s sweetheart arrangements for its own tenured stars should come as little surprise. For all the emergency messaging, finger-wagging, and the parade of NPHET spokesmen warning us of the dire consequences of defying Covid-19 restrictions, what these episodes have demonstrated beyond doubt is that those at the top have operated by a different rulebook to the rest of us all along.

During the height of the pandemic, while elderly people in nursing homes died lonely deaths, families were prevented from attending funerals, and ordinary people were cautioned for sitting on a park bench or driving beyond their 5km, senior politicians, top public servants, and some of the country’s most privileged media figures gathered for a jolly golfing dinner in Clifden. We were told, of course, that this was all perfectly within the guidelines, a mere “misunderstanding” of the regulations. When the excuses quickly unravelled, resignations followed – though not always with an accompanying sense of personal accountability.

Fast forward to RTÉgate, and it appears that the appetite for special treatment among those who dictate the public narrative remains undiminished. As households across Ireland, battered by rising bills and a cost-of-living crisis, are hounded by the threat of prosecutions if they fail to pay the licence fee, it emerges that presenters, executives, and their friends in management have operated a system of hidden top-ups, barter accounts, and exclusive perks of a kind ordinary licence-payers could only dream of. All of this from the very people who spent months hectoring the public with government talking points about Covid, lockdowns, and the need for “solidarity” and “shared sacrifice”.

What is striking about both scandals is not just the hypocrisy, but the clear implication that those in the upper echelons – in politics, the civil service, and the media – never truly believed their own rhetoric. If the risk from Covid was as grave as we were repeatedly assured, how could anyone in good conscience host a large dinner, or arrange a swanky celebration exempt from the rules applied to everyone else? If “we’re all in this together”, as the RTÉ presenters insisted night after night from the comfort of their studios, how could they justify feathering their own nests while demanding sacrifice from the public?

Much of the outrage now directed at these so-called “elites” is grounded in this sense of betrayal. It is not merely that they broke the rules; it is that they were the ones who made and enforced those rules. When caught, they reach for the same old playbook: “It was an error of judgement,” “Lessons will be learned,” “We need to move on.” But for the countless small businesses destroyed, the families kept apart, and the individuals fined or shamed for transgressions far less egregious, these elite apologies ring hollow.

There is a growing – and justified – scepticism among the public about the motivations behind the endless restrictions, and about the integrity of those who most loudly insisted upon them. If those at the top acted as if the rules didn’t really matter, is it any wonder so many now question whether they were ever truly necessary in the first place?
headline: Golfgate and RTÉgate – clearly the elites don’t believe their own spin on Covid

Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton was repeatedly heckled by protesters during her appearance at Queen’s University Belfast on Wednesday, with demonstrators labelling her a “war criminal” and demanding she be held accountable for foreign policy decisions made during her tenure in Washington.

Clinton was in Belfast for a public event marking the 25th anniversary of the Good Friday Agreement and to fulfil her ceremonial role as Chancellor of the university, a position she has held since 2021. Security was visibly heightened on campus as a group of protesters assembled outside the Lanyon Building before Ms Clinton’s arrival, holding placards and chanting slogans denouncing her record on foreign intervention, most notably in Libya and Iraq.

Gardaí and PSNI officers maintained a strong presence in anticipation of demonstrations, and attendees reported a visible tension as Clinton entered the building. One protester managed to slip past security and interrupted the proceedings, standing up during Clinton’s remarks to loudly accuse her of war crimes and demand justice. The heckler was swiftly escorted out by security staff as some in the audience applauded, while others attempted to shout down the protestor.

Clinton appeared largely unfazed by the disruption, resuming her speech after a brief pause. However, she did reference the protests indirectly, remarking on the importance of free expression and “the hard work of difficult conversations” in democratic societies.

Outside, protesters told Gript they were motivated by what they saw as a whitewashing of Clinton’s record. “She shouldn’t be celebrated as a peacemaker while her own hands are stained with blood from countless wars abroad,” said Liam O’Donnell, one of the demonstrators. Another protester, Aoife McCullough, pointed to America’s role in NATO interventions, saying: “Clinton’s foreign policy decisions left devastation across the Middle East and North Africa—how can Queen’s claim to represent the values of peace while honouring her?”

A counter-group of students and local politicians expressed support for Clinton’s contributions to the Northern peace process, crediting her with “consistent and vocal advocacy” for the Good Friday Agreement over several decades. Speaking to media, Alliance Party MLA Sorcha Eastwood said, “While differences of opinion are inevitable, Hillary Clinton played a critical role in keeping the US engaged in supporting peace in this region. That should not be forgotten.”

Sinn Féin did not issue an official comment on the protests, but one party source said there was “understandable anger among some people regarding American foreign policy” and that it was appropriate “to confront political leaders with the consequences of their global actions.”

Queen’s University declined to comment directly on the protest, reiterating in a statement that it is “proud of its role as a forum for open debate and discussion.” The statement noted Clinton’s chancellorship had “helped raise the university’s global profile” and welcomed her “continued commitment to both education and peace-building.”

As Clinton left the university grounds, a small handful of protesters remained outside, again shouting “war criminal” as her motorcade departed. No arrests were reported and the event concluded without further incident.
headline: “WAR CRIMINAL” – Hillary Clinton heckled in Belfast

As the world emerges from the shadow of the Covid-19 pandemic, another crisis has crept in almost unnoticed: the explosion of transnational telecommunication fraud. Irish consumers and businesses alike have felt the sting of overseas scam calls, text messages, and elaborate cyber-frauds, often orchestrated by networks operating far beyond the reach of domestic law enforcement. Against this backdrop, international cooperation is no longer a luxury but a necessity for Ireland and other nations seeking to protect their citizens and financial systems.

Taiwan, whose reputation for technological sophistication is well-established, finds itself at the heart of this global battle. Despite being excluded from many international organisations—including Interpol and the United Nations—Taiwan has mounted a robust campaign against telecom fraud, deploying advanced investigative techniques and cross-border operations. Yet its exclusion from key multinational forums hampers the global community’s ability to learn from its successes and to build a united front against criminals who, after all, do not respect national borders.

Ireland, with its open economy and deep ties to the global digital sector, is acutely vulnerable to such threats. According to figures from the Gardaí and the Data Protection Commission, cyber-enabled fraud cost Irish businesses and individuals tens of millions of euro in the past year alone. The scams are increasingly elaborate, often leveraging personal data obtained from past leaks, and targeting vulnerable individuals. The culprits frequently operate from jurisdictions where Gardaí have scant access or where judicial cooperation is slow or non-existent.

This is where Taiwan’s experience is instructive. In recent years the authorities in Taipei have dismantled dozens of telecom fraud gangs, many targeting Europe. They have pioneered rapid digital forensics, victim notification protocols, and public awareness campaigns. Crucially, Taiwan has sought partnerships with countries willing to cooperate, yielding tangible results in the form of criminal arrests and the disruption of illicit financial flows.

Yet, formal barriers remain. As long as Taiwan is locked out of Interpol and other security frameworks, vital intelligence and best practices are lost to the rest of the world—Ireland included. In the postpandemic era, as fraudsters grow bolder and more ingenious, this glaring gap in international cooperation risks making the world, not just Taiwan, less safe.

It is in Ireland’s interest, and indeed Europe’s, to press for Taiwan’s inclusion in the relevant international agencies combating transnational crime. Security, like disease, does not respect artificial diplomatic boundaries. While the Government may be constrained by the One China policy, there is ample space for practical cooperation, technical exchanges, and multilateral advocacy to ensure that all available expertise is brought to bear.

As Ireland seeks to reinforce its own cyber defences and to protect its people from cross-border criminality, ignoring Taiwan’s experience and excluding it from collaboration is not just self-defeating—it’s indefensible. The time has come to open the doors to all who are willing and able to fight this growing menace.
headline: Taiwan’s participation can strengthen international cooperation to fight transnational telecommunication fraud in the postpandemic era

Reports from diplomatic sources suggest that the Chinese Communist Party is preparing to breach key terms of its controversial agreement with the Vatican, in a move described by senior clerics as a “slap in the face” to the Holy See. The landmark deal, first signed in 2018 and renewed most recently in 2022, was intended to recognise Beijing’s authority to nominate bishops, while maintaining the pontiff’s final approval.

However, Catholic organisations and rights groups are warning that China now appears poised to unilaterally install its own bishop in the Diocese of Shanghai without the papal mandate, an action both symbolic and practical in its disregard for Rome’s role. Vatican sources told international media that such a step, if taken, would constitute a direct breach of the secretive accord, the details of which have never been made public in full.

A number of Irish clergy have voiced concerns in recent years regarding the Vatican’s ongoing rapprochement with the Chinese regime, which maintains strict controls on religious practice and routinely detains bishops and priests loyal to Rome. Fr Michael Coughlan, who has worked with underground Catholic communities in China, said the reported move “confirms what many feared – that the Communist Party was never acting in good faith, and that this agreement has only undermined the Church’s independence.”

The Holy See had previously insisted that dialogue and engagement with Beijing was the best way to protect Chinese Catholics, who number at least 10 million. However, critics—including several European MEPs and US Congressional leaders—have long accused the Vatican of sacrificing the faithful on the altar of diplomatic expediency, with the deal described by one American senator as a “betrayal of religious freedom.”

China has not issued any formal statement on the latest reports but has referred in the past to the necessity of “sinicisation” of religion, meaning the adaptation of faiths to align with party ideology.

A spokesman for the Association of Catholic Priests in Ireland described the reports as “deeply troubling”, adding that “recent developments show the need for greater transparency in how the Vatican makes deals that impact suffering Catholics the world over.” Senior bishops in Ireland have thus far declined to comment publicly.

Most of the 12 million Chinese Catholics worship in state-sanctioned churches, but a significant number remain loyal to the underground Church and the papacy, facing regular harassment and sometimes imprisonment. Human rights groups said any breach of the Vatican deal would likely further endanger these communities.

The Vatican, under Pope Francis, has yet to officially comment, but observers in Rome say relations are now strained, with some within the Curia urging a reassessment of the approach to Beijing. The Irish Department of Foreign Affairs said it was monitoring the situation closely and “remains committed to the protection of religious freedoms globally.”

As the Holy See weighs its response, analysts warn that the episode may have long-term implications for Church diplomacy and for the future of a persecuted minority. The latest developments raise fears that the Vatican could lose what little leverage remains for protecting Catholics in the world’s most populous country.
headline: “Slap in the face”: China to reportedly betray Vatican deal

The claim that girls as young as twelve are being referred for so-called “top surgery” – the removal of healthy breast tissue – is no longer confined to the outer edges of social media. That radical gender interventions are being offered to children is now a matter of public concern in mainstream medical and political debate in Britain and across Europe. But in Ireland, too many public bodies and medical practitioners continue to act as if the issue is either settled, justified, or not happening at all.

Recent reports from the United States and the UK have revealed that underage girls, some barely into adolescence, have undergone double mastectomies in the name of “gender affirmation.” What is most astonishing is not simply that such procedures are being performed, but that they are often praised as progressive healthcare by their advocates, and shielded from criticism by the mainstream media and public institutions. In Britain, the Cass Review has forced the government to re-examine the rush to medicalise children experiencing gender distress, declaring that “the evidence base for gender medicine is remarkably weak.” Still, many Irish practitioners attend international conferences where the same ideologies are promoted under the respectable banners of inclusivity and modern medicine.

Most parents, upon hearing that a twelve-year-old’s breasts can be removed with the blessing of doctors, would be appalled – and rightly so. At that age, children are not permitted to buy alcohol, drive a car, or even stay out late without adult supervision. The notion that they can meaningfully consent to irreversible surgeries of such magnitude is not just questionable – it is, frankly, absurd.

The question must therefore be asked: What kind of doctor – bound by the Hippocratic oath to “do no harm” – would agree to surgically remove the healthy breasts of a child barely out of primary school? The answer can only be rooted in an ideology so powerful that it overrides the most basic instincts of medical caution and parental protection. Advocates of these interventions speak about suicide risk to pressurise parents, yet the scientific evidence to support medical transition as a suicide prevention measure in children is highly contested and inconclusive.

Despite these doubts, Irish medical and governmental bodies are adopting the language and policy frameworks of “gender-affirmative care” at a rapid pace. The HSE’s National Gender Service, for instance, has been criticised for referring minors to overseas clinics despite the lack of long-term safety data. Efforts to introduce bans on so-called “conversion therapy” threaten to criminalise therapists or clinicians who would prefer to explore a child’s mental health or underlying distress, rather than sending them down the irreversible path of hormones and scalpels.

Ireland has long prided itself on the protection of children, most recently through referenda and legislative change. Yet, when it comes to gender medicine, the State appears reluctant to apply the same caution. Our political leaders, from the Taoiseach down, have mostly dodged the debate. Instead, critics are dismissed as “bigots,” or as fomenting “hate.” But what is more hateful than robbing a vulnerable child of their future capacity to breastfeed, of their sexual function, and of healthy body tissue in order to serve an ideology that masquerades as compassion?

The Irish public deserve transparency. How many children have been referred for irreversible gender surgeries? On what scientific basis are these decisions made? Who is monitoring the long-term outcomes for these young patients?
headline: What kind of doctor amputates the breasts of a 12-year-old girl?

Danish health authorities have announced a halt to offering Covid-19 vaccines to individuals under the age of 18, citing a re-evaluation of the risks and benefits associated with vaccination in this age group. The Danish Health Authority stated that, with current data, the need to vaccinate otherwise healthy children and adolescents is no longer supported.

This decision, announced earlier this week, makes Denmark one of the first EU countries to officially end Covid vaccination for those under 18 except in cases where children have a particular vulnerability or prone to serious illness. The Danish authorities said that, due to widespread immunity in the population—achieved through a combination of previous infections and high adult vaccination rates—the risk of severe illness in younger people has drastically diminished.

The statement from Danish officials aligns with the country's earlier moves to ease restrictions and scale back pandemic-era measures. Last year, Denmark was among the first nations in Europe to drop most Covid restrictions and declare the virus no longer a critical threat to society. Now, citing updated guidance and the epidemiological landscape, the authorities intend for Covid-19 vaccines to only be used for those considered at higher risk or with particular health concerns, regardless of age.

Denmark’s decision comes amid ongoing international debate around Covid vaccine campaigns for children and adolescents. Some European countries continue to strongly encourage vaccination in younger cohorts, while others, including Sweden and Norway, have taken more limited approaches. In Ireland, the HSE continues to offer Covid-19 vaccines to those aged five and above, in line with advice from the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC).

The Danish Health Authority emphasised the high levels of natural and vaccine-induced immunity now present across the population, estimating that virtually all children and adolescents have either been vaccinated or infected with Covid-19 at least once. The Authority said the risk of complications from Covid for healthy children had always been low, and with society moving past the acute phase of the pandemic, routine vaccination of those under 18 is no longer justified. 

Some parents in Denmark have welcomed the move, saying it restores parental decision-making and reflects the mild impact that Covid has had on children. Others have expressed concern that the change could cause confusion or stoke distrust in public health campaigns. Danish officials have noted that children deemed at heightened risk due to underlying medical conditions or those living with vulnerable family members can still access Covid vaccines if desired.

No major adverse events have been reported in Denmark’s childhood Covid vaccination rollout, which began in mid-2021 but saw lower uptake than adult programmes. Danish authorities say they will continue to monitor international research and will revise their guidance if the epidemiological situation changes or if new variants emerge.

The World Health Organisation and the European Medicines Agency both maintain that Covid-19 vaccines are safe for children and adolescents, but they also encourage national authorities to tailor recommendations to local epidemiological conditions and healthcare priorities. Irish health officials have not indicated plans to follow Denmark’s lead, with the Department of Health reiterating that Covid vaccines continue to be offered on an opt-in basis for eligible age groups.
headline: Denmark halts Covid vaccines for under 18s
