A leading abortion provider has failed to produce any tangible evidence to support claims of harassment by pro-life activists, despite repeated assertions in national media interviews and before an Oireachtas committee.

Dr Mary Favier, a prominent campaigner for expanded abortion access and spokesperson for Doctors for Choice, appeared before the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Health last month. She alleged that medical colleagues and patients have faced “intimidation and harassment” from protesters outside clinics and GP surgeries providing terminations. However, when pressed for specifics, Dr Favier was unable to provide details or examples of reported incidents to the committee.

In subsequent interviews, including with RTÉ and the Irish Times, Dr Favier claimed a “persistent campaign of harassment” was ongoing, but again cited no incidents being reported to the Gardaí, nor were any formal complaints submitted to the Medical Council, HSE, or Department of Health.

A spokesperson for the Gardaí confirmed to Gript that while protests outside some clinics have taken place since the introduction of abortion services in 2019, there have been “no recorded incidents of criminal harassment or intimidation” relating to these demonstrations to date. The Gardaí stated that all protests have remained peaceful and that they “continue to monitor such events in order to ensure public order is maintained.”

When contacted by Gript, the HSE could not provide any records of complaints filed by staff or patients regarding pro-life demonstrations at abortion providers. The Medical Council likewise confirmed no complaints alleging harassment from protesters have been received from any registered practitioner.

Irish pro-life groups, including the Life Institute and Pro Life Campaign, have strongly rejected the claims of intimidation. Spokesperson Niamh Uí Bhriain described Dr Favier’s allegations as “completely unsubstantiated and designed to stoke division.” Uí Bhriain said pro-life volunteers “stand in silent witness, offer support and information to women entering clinics, and at all times comply with the law.”

The apparent lack of evidence comes as the government faces increasing pressure to introduce exclusion zones around abortion facilities, with the Health (Safe Access to Termination of Pregnancy Services) Bill currently before the Oireachtas. Supporters of the Bill insist it is a necessary response to alleged harassment, though opposition TDs have questioned whether such legislation is justified without proof of a problem.

TDs speaking to Gript underlined the need for “clear evidence, not mere assertion” before moving to limit the right to peaceful assembly and free speech around medical facilities. “This is a question of civil liberties as well as public safety,” said one independent TD. “We need to see facts, not just hearsay, before we consider restricting basic freedoms.”

With the government still considering amendments to the Bill, the controversy is set to continue. Pro-life campaigners have called on the Taoiseach, Simon Harris, to insist that any future legislation be based on “evidence, not claims that cannot be substantiated.” Dr Favier has yet to respond to repeated requests from Gript to provide the evidence she says exists.
headline: Abortion doctor provides no tangible evidence of harassment claim

text:
Laura Whitmore, the Bray-born television presenter who has become one of Ireland’s most recognisable cultural exports, has spent the better part of the last decade in the glare of the British tabloid spotlight. It’s a position that, for many, would be as much curse as blessing. Once celebrated for her charm and wit – first on MTV and then as the face of *Love Island* and other primetime fixtures – Whitmore now finds herself a lightning rod for online abuse and media scrutiny to a degree that borders on persecution.

In recent months, following her new career moves, including presenting the true-crime programme *Laura Whitmore Investigates* and a run on the West End, the familiar cycle has resumed: every outfit, opinion, and photo dissected by tabloid writers and social media ‘critics’. As is now the norm with high-profile women at the top of their field, the coverage rarely stops at professional evaluation. Instead, both the online commentariat and entertainment media have revived old complaints about her accent, her appearance, and her perceived right to the spotlight.

What is most alarming is how quickly commentary crosses the boundary from fair criticism into personal attack. Whitmore’s recent RTE interview about the pressures of presenting *Love Island* and about her own mental health was seized upon by Twitter users and columnists alike, with many dismissing her experiences and others going so far as to claim she was courting victimhood. This is not the first time Whitmore has faced such reactions. During her time on *Love Island*, she spoke candidly about the emotional toll of the role, particularly after the tragic suicide of her friend and predecessor, Caroline Flack. Despite the well-publicised realities of the job and its impact, much of the coverage remained unsympathetic, if not downright hostile.

It is not just the British press and public who have taken aim. In Ireland, too, Whitmore’s level of success sometimes appears to inspire begrudgery rather than admiration. Where once the Irish media might have claimed her as one of our own, celebrating her rise in a notoriously difficult industry, now the familiar pattern of tearing down those who make it abroad is at play. It reflects a broader problem within Irish culture – one that sees the celebrated quickly become the scorned, particularly if they are women. The British tabloids are infamous for their appetite for scandal, real or manufactured, but the Irish establishment has its own ways of warning ‘too big for your boots’.

The relentless criticism of Whitmore reaches into wider questions about the culture of online abuse and the treatment of women in the media. It is a broader problem that has attracted the attention of the Oireachtas in recent years, with several TDs calling for increased regulation of online platforms, and the establishment of initiatives aimed at countering misogynistic abuse online. Yet progress is slow, and the vast majority of high-profile Irish women in media, politics, and sport continue to report a higher volume of online abuse than their male counterparts.

Whitmore herself has acknowledged these difficulties, calling for more support for public figures exposed to the ‘pile-ons’ of social media. However, she has refused to allow the negativity to define her. “There are times when you have to block out the noise and focus on the work,” she told a recent podcast audience. “But I’d be lying if I said it doesn’t get to you sometimes.”
headline: The persecution of Laura Whitmore

text:
Suicide remains the leading cause of death among Irish men under the age of 25, according to the latest figures from the Central Statistics Office (CSO). Despite major government initiatives and the work of numerous mental health organisations, the rate of young male suicide has stubbornly refused to fall, with campaigners warning that Ireland’s suicide crisis is deteriorating for young men.

Data released by the CSO shows that in the most recent full year, 76 young men under 25 died by suicide—accounting for more than a third of all deaths in that demographic. The figure is significantly higher than deaths caused by road accidents, illnesses, or drug overdoses for young males, making suicide the single biggest killer of young Irish men.

The figures have led to renewed calls for a radical overhaul of the HSE’s mental health services, amid concerns that existing strategies are not reaching those most at risk. Critics point out that despite increased government funding and the launch of awareness campaigns such as “Connecting for Life”, front-line services are struggling to meet demand, and many young men continue to fall through the cracks.

Aidan McCarthy, founder of the support group Irish Men’s Network, said: “If you’re a young man in Ireland today, you’re more likely to die at your own hand than from any illness or accident. We’ve spoken to dozens of families who lost sons and brothers who were crying out for help but couldn’t access support when they needed it. The system is failing them.”

In rural counties, the problem is particularly acute, with rates of young male suicide consistently higher than in Dublin or other urban areas. Studies have pointed to factors including social isolation, lack of local mental health services, and the decline of traditional community supports as contributing to the crisis. The stigma attached to mental health struggles, particularly among young men, remains a major barrier to seeking help.

Speaking in the Dáil last week, Independent TD Michael Collins criticised the government’s approach: “We have report after report, strategy after strategy, but our suicide rate among young men shows no signs of coming down. The funding is there, but bureaucracy and inertia in the HSE mean that too many are left without intervention at the critical moment.”

The government, meanwhile, defends its record, citing an increase of €72 million in mental health funding for 2024 and claiming that recruitment of additional counsellors and psychiatrists is underway. The Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly said: “Every death by suicide is a tragedy. We are working intensively with the HSE and NGOs to ensure that support is available to anyone who needs it, no matter where they live.”

However, families affected by suicide warn that support remains patchy and often comes too late. “We lost our son because he couldn’t get seen by anyone in time,” said one mother from Co. Clare, whose 22-year-old son took his own life last year. “He was waiting six weeks for a counselling appointment. Those six weeks were the difference between life and death.”

Experts advise that early intervention and community-based approaches are crucial. Dr. Louise O’Hanlon, a consultant psychiatrist at St. Patrick’s Mental Health Services, said: “If we normalise discussion of mental health, and ensure fast access to assessment and treatment, we will save lives. But right now, young men are telling us—often in their own words or actions—that they feel abandoned.”
headline: Suicide the biggest killer of Irish men under the age of 25

text:
The last few years have tested the very limits of what it means to live in a free and democratic society, not only in Ireland but across the Western world. In Sweden, a country long lauded for its robust welfare state and tolerant social values, the script has been flipped. Sweden was once the poster child for “following the science” — or rather, for their controversial decision to take a light-touch approach to managing the pandemic while others locked down. Ironically, the same nation is now being quietly transformed by a surge of government intervention and an increasingly heavy-handed approach to regulation.

In 2020, as Ireland endured some of the strictest COVID-19 restrictions in Europe, with checkpoints manned by the Gardaí, mandatory mask-wearing, shuttered businesses, and curfews, our government often pointed to other countries’ “successful” tough measures as examples to be copied. Sweden, in contrast, made global headlines for refusing to impose full-scale lockdowns and allowing much of daily life to continue – an approach which drew ire and condescension from Brussels, Dublin, and every Irish “expert” on Twitter.

Now, as the dust settles and the data becomes clear, Sweden’s model looks, at the very least, defensible – and it certainly didn’t generate the dystopian headlines many predicted. Yet, in a curious twist, it is Sweden that is now grappling with a spate of policy over-reach: proposals for expanded surveillance powers, identity checks, and government monitoring in the name of tackling both crime and “misinformation”. The Swedish government, like many of its European counterparts, has shifted from a “light touch” on public health to an increasingly interventionist stance in other spheres.

This is a pattern we ought to pay close attention to in Ireland. It is always in the name of “safety” that freedoms are chipped away. During COVID, the justification was public health. Today, the threats are terrorism, cybercrime, hate speech, or, as with the recent push for wider hate speech legislation here at home, the amorphous danger of “harmful content”. Each time, the public is asked to accept diminishing privacy, more intrusive bureaucracy, and fewer avenues for dissent.

If Sweden, so recently a global synonym for progressive liberalism, can slide down this slope, what does it portend for countries like ours? Our own government has shown little hesitation when it comes to curbing freedoms: remember the proposals for pandemic “amnesty passes”, the pointless criminalisation of beach walkers, or the Garda power to break up Easter family dinners. These were not the product of crisis, but of a political class that has grown used to the taste of power – and is loath to relinquish it.

Yet, just as Sweden resisted the initial calls for lockdown, perhaps the lesson for us now is to demand a lockdown of a different kind: a lockdown against government over-reach, against the slide towards the kind of constant scrutiny and regulation that no Irish citizen has ever voted for. It is easier to impose than to undo. The next time the Dáil debates a Bill that trims our rights or hands more power to unaccountable agencies, we should ask: is this really necessary, or is it just another brick in the wall of a new, technocratic normal?

The Irish people have, historically, shown a healthy scepticism towards authority, whether in the hands of the Church or the State.
headline: Does Sweden show we need a lockdown against the spread of government over-reach?

The Government jet has been in the air for over 125 hours so far this year, at a cost to the taxpayer of nearly half a million euro, new figures obtained by Gript reveal. The Air Corps Learjet 45, which is operated out of Baldonnel and primarily used for official state business, has seen a notable uptick in usage compared to previous years, raising questions about the necessity and prudence of its deployment by government ministers and officials.

According to data provided in response to Parliamentary Questions, the jet’s operational costs in the first five months of 2024 have already surpassed €480,000, with flight logs detailing trips to European capitals and beyond, including Brussels, London and Paris. The Taoiseach and Tánaiste have each availed of the service on multiple occasions, with further use attributed to ministers and senior civil servants travelling for EU summits, diplomatic meetings, and international conferences.

The figures do not include routine maintenance, crew salaries or the capital cost of replacing or upgrading the jet, which is now in its 20th year of service. Aviation experts estimate that the total cost of operating and maintaining the Government’s official aircraft could be substantially higher when all factors are included.

Critics have questioned whether the frequency and nature of the flights represent good value for money, particularly in a year when the Government is urging public sector workers and ordinary families to tighten their belts amid rising inflation and ongoing concerns about public spending. Socialist TDs, as well as opposition figures from Sinn Féin and the Rural Independents, have called for greater transparency and a full review into official travel arrangements, with some arguing for greater use of commercial flights or video conferencing to reduce costs.

A spokesperson for the Department of Defence defended the usage, saying that the jet provides “essential flexibility for urgent and sensitive government business, including attendance at critical EU and international meetings where commercial travel is not feasible.” The spokesperson added that the current arrangement “ensures the safe and efficient travel of the Taoiseach, Tánaiste and other Ministers, with due regard for security and time constraints.”

Nonetheless, the disclosure comes as public confidence in government expenditure faces fresh scrutiny, with recent controversies around spending on consultancy, HSE management fees, and the National Children’s Hospital overruns still reverberating. Opposition TDs are expected to raise the matter again in the Dáil next week, pressing for detailed logs of all flights and justification for each journey undertaken on the state jet.

With over half a million euro in costs already accrued before the halfway point of the year, the question remains whether ministers will heed calls to curtail official air travel, or if the government jet will continue to rack up both miles and taxpayer expense as political and diplomatic business resumes apace.
headline: Government Jet has flown for 125 hours this year, costing half a million

text:
The European Union is set to unveil plans for bloc-wide “vaccine passports” this week, as Brussels seeks to salvage the summer holiday season and revive the struggling tourism sector across the 27 member states.

Under a draft proposal, which is expected to be formally published on Wednesday, proof of COVID-19 vaccination would allow EU residents to travel more freely between countries, potentially bypassing current restrictions such as quarantine or negative test requirements. The so-called “Digital Green Certificate” would also include information on recent negative tests or recovery from COVID-19, offering a wider range of options for those who have not yet received a jab.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said last week that the scheme is intended “to enable Europeans to move safely and freely within the European Union this summer.” She insisted that any system would “respect data protection, security and privacy.”

The draft proposal is expected to recommend that each member state decide for itself whether to exempt vaccine certificate holders from quarantine regulations and other travel curbs. However, officials in Dublin have already indicated caution over the move, with Tánaiste Leo Varadkar warning that the introduction of vaccine passports would need to be “very carefully considered” given Ireland’s ongoing slow vaccine rollout and concerns around the potential for new variants.

Many southern EU countries, including Greece, Spain, and Italy, whose economies rely heavily on summer tourism, have urged the bloc to accelerate the rollout of vaccine passports to rescue what is left of the holiday season. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has been particularly vocal in his support, calling for a standardised EU-wide approach to avoid a patchwork of national measures.

In contrast, several northern and western countries, including France, Belgium and Germany, have voiced concerns about fairness and the risk of discrimination against those who have not yet been vaccinated, as well as the potential for technical and data privacy issues.

Brussels faces a tight timetable if the vaccine passport scheme is to be operational before peak summer months. With Ireland’s vaccine programme still lagging behind other EU countries, the Government is expected to seek “robust guarantees” on non-discrimination for those who cannot yet access vaccination, and will likely urge that recent negative tests and proof of recovery be given equal weight.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has not yet signalled when or how Ireland might participate in any proposed EU-wide scheme. However, Ministers are under pressure from sectors such as airlines and the hospitality industry to support any initiative that might reopen international travel and stem deepening job losses.

Debate is also underway about the potential use of vaccine certificates for domestic activities, such as attending gigs, sports matches, or dining indoors, although the Department of Health has so far ruled out any decision until more is known about the vaccine’s ability to prevent transmission.

The European Commission hopes to secure political agreement on the proposal at a virtual summit of EU leaders scheduled for later this month. Any system would then be subject to approval by the European Parliament and individual national governments, a process that is likely to be contentious and could face legal challenges.

Irish civil liberties organisations have warned against the “creeping normalisation” of health passports, with Digital Rights Ireland describing the idea as “fraught with risks to privacy and equality.”

As the EU’s vaccination drive continues to face criticism over supply shortfalls and distribution delays, some officials have questioned whether a summer relaunch of tourism is realistic.
headline: EU to propose vaccine passports for summer travel

The average monthly rent in Dublin has now risen to €1,997, according to the latest figures released by property website Daft.ie this morning – a record high and marking yet another sharp increase in what tenants are being forced to pay in the capital. The new data, covering the first quarter of 2024, shows rents in Dublin are now almost double what they were ten years ago, and well above levels witnessed during the Celtic Tiger peak.

The national average rent now stands at €1,850, with rents in every county showing continued growth, but nowhere near the steep increases seen across Dublin. In Cork city, the average rent is €1,636 per month, Galway city is €1,613, and rents in Limerick and Waterford now average €1,452 and €1,267 respectively.

Daft.ie’s analysts have pointed to the chronic lack of supply in the rental sector as the main driver of the ongoing price hikes. As of 1 May, there were just 1,100 homes available to rent nationwide on the website, among the lowest figures recorded since Daft.ie began tracking data in 2006. In Dublin, only 426 properties were listed as available, with some localities, such as South Dublin and Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown, showing less than 100 homes for rent.

The ongoing shortage has put immense pressure on existing renters, with many young people and families reporting being priced out of the market or unable to find suitable accommodation. Speaking to Gript, UCD student Anna McNulty said: “I’ve been looking for a place since last year, and even for a shared room, I’m expected to pay €800 or more. It’s near impossible to find anything affordable.”

Various housing charities and advocates have renewed calls for government intervention amid what they describe as a worsening crisis. Threshold chief executive John-Mark McCafferty said the figures “once again prove the government’s housing and rental policies are failing ordinary people,” and warned that families are at risk of homelessness as rents climb.

The Department of Housing has pointed to its Housing for All programme and a recent uptick in the number of new builds, but critics say these measures are not keeping pace with demand. The government’s controversial decision last year to end the eviction ban has also been cited by opposition TDs as exacerbating the situation.

Solidarity TD Mick Barry said: “The government talks about progress but the facts speak for themselves. Rents are out of control and, for many, home ownership is now completely out of reach.”

Meanwhile, landlords’ representatives have argued that stricter regulations and tax changes are driving small landlords out of the market, reducing supply further. The Irish Property Owners’ Association said the figures show that “without meaningful incentives and regulatory easing, more landlords will leave, deepening the crisis.”

The Minister for Housing, Darragh O’Brien, said the government “understands the pressures renters are facing,” and insisted the state is “on track to deliver a significant increase in supply this year.” However, for Dublin renters already struggling with the near-€2,000 monthly average, relief remains elusive.
headline: Average rent now almost €2,000 per month in Dublin

text:
England’s Chief Medical Officer, Professor Sir Chris Whitty, has warned that the United Kingdom should prepare for another surge of Covid-19 infections by the autumn, adding to concerns about the ongoing impact of the virus as public health systems remain under pressure.

Speaking to the Health and Social Care Committee at Westminster on Tuesday, Sir Chris stated that although current infection rates have stabilised and society has largely returned to pre-pandemic life, a further uptick in cases is likely as the colder months approach. He noted that respiratory viruses, including Covid-19, have a well-established pattern of increased transmission in winter, and cautioned against complacency.

“We must be realistic: Covid-19 has not disappeared,” Sir Chris told MPs. “We expect that, as with influenza and other respiratory viruses, there will be a significant increase in cases in the autumn and winter months, and the NHS needs to remain ready to respond.”

The warning comes amid concerns across the NHS about ongoing staff shortages, long waiting lists, and rising demand for hospital beds. Sir Chris confirmed that measures such as vaccination programmes and antiviral treatments remain crucial tools in managing the pandemic’s impact, but did not advocate for a return to widespread restrictions at this time. “The approach now is living with the virus, using the tools we have, rather than reverting to the measures of the past,” he said.

Irish public health officials have so far not commented directly on Sir Chris’s remarks, but the HSE has previously echoed similar concerns about the potential for a resurgence of Covid-19 cases later in the year. The Department of Health continues to monitor infection rates and hospital admissions, with the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC) reviewing booster schedules for vulnerable groups.

Covid-19 hospital admissions in Ireland have remained stable in recent weeks, but the HSE has warned that even a moderate surge in cases could put additional pressure on already-stretched services. The Taoiseach, Simon Harris, has indicated that the Government will follow public health advice on further booster campaigns if the need arises.

In the UK, Sir Chris also highlighted the risks to individuals with underlying health conditions, the elderly, and those with weakened immune systems, urging eligible groups to avail of booster vaccines when available. He noted that the virus continues to evolve, with new variants regularly identified, which complicates long-term planning.

This latest warning from the UK’s top medical advisor underscores the ongoing nature of the pandemic, even as attention has shifted to other health and economic challenges. For the public, it is a reminder that, despite the end of most restrictions, the virus remains a factor in health policy and planning for the foreseeable future.
headline: UK CMO expects another Covid surge by autumn

Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov has issued a stark warning that Moscow would consider deploying nuclear weapons to the Baltic region should Sweden and Finland proceed with joining NATO. The threat, described by Western observers as an escalation in rhetoric, comes as both Nordic countries debate ending decades of military neutrality in response to the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Ryabkov, speaking to Russian state media on Thursday, stated that “there can be no more talk of any nuclear-free status for the Baltic” if Sweden and Finland join the Western military alliance. The comments follow mounting speculation in Stockholm and Helsinki over whether the time has come to formalise ties with NATO, after Russian military aggression brought security concerns to the fore.

Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin and Swedish Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson have acknowledged a “new security reality” in Europe. Both countries have seen public opinion polls swing significantly in favour of joining NATO in recent months, something the Kremlin has insisted would be considered a “hostile act” with “serious military and political consequences”.

In a statement, Ryabkov accused the West of pushing Russia into a corner, and claimed that Moscow “will have to restore military balance” in the region if Finland and Sweden turn to NATO for protection. He did not specify the exact nature or location of any nuclear deployments, but referenced the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which borders Lithuania and Poland and is already heavily militarised.

NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg has reiterated that the alliance’s door remains open, and that Sweden and Finland would be welcomed should they choose to apply. Both countries have been close NATO partners for years, participating in joint exercises, but have held back from seeking full membership up to now.

European Union officials dismissed Moscow’s remarks as sabre-rattling. A spokesperson for the European Commission said, “It is up to sovereign nations to decide their security policy. No external actor can dictate their choices.”

The Nordic nations are bound by close economic and political ties to the EU, with both having condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Their armed forces are considered among the most capable in Europe, but membership of NATO would commit them to collective defence, including the alliance’s Article 5 guarantee that an attack on one is considered an attack on all.

The Russian warning has also raised concerns in the Oireachtas. Sinn Féin’s Matt Carthy TD, speaking at Leinster House, called for the government to uphold Ireland’s policy of military neutrality, warning that “rising tensions and nuclear threats show the dangers of military blocs and escalation”. The Green Party’s Patrick Costello TD similarly called for diplomatic solutions.

The Department of Foreign Affairs in Dublin has said Ireland stands with Sweden and Finland’s right to determine their own security arrangements, but acknowledged the “alarming escalation” in Russian rhetoric.

Meanwhile, the United States State Department described Russia’s threats as “unhelpful and destabilising”, stating that it would support NATO’s decision if Sweden and Finland apply to join.

Amid the backdrop of the conflict in Ukraine, the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania—which joined NATO in 2004—have also voiced alarm at the Russian threats. Lithuanian Defence Minister Arvydas Anušauskas described Russian nuclear posturing as “nothing new” but emphasised the need for unity among NATO and EU partners.
headline: Russia threatens to deploy nukes if Sweden & Finland join NATO

text:
The Irish Council for Civil Liberties (ICCL) has issued a stark warning that the Government’s proposed Hate Speech Bill could have a “chilling effect on the free expression of opinion,” raising fresh questions about the balance between tackling incitement to hatred and upholding fundamental freedoms in Ireland.

The remarks, delivered in a submission to the Oireachtas Joint Committee on Justice, come as the Criminal Justice (Incitement to Violence or Hatred and Hate Offences) Bill 2022 progresses through the legislative process. The Bill, which the Minister for Justice, Helen McEntee, has prioritised, is intended to modernise Ireland’s hate speech laws and broaden existing provisions dating from 1989.

However, the ICCL submission states that the proposed legislation risks criminalising “expressions of opinion that may be unpopular or controversial, but do not amount to incitement to hatred or violence.” The advocacy group contends that the Bill deploys “overbroad and vague” language which could, in practice, stifle freedom of speech and restrict legitimate debate on social and political issues.

In particular, the ICCL highlights Section 7 of the Bill, which introduces a new offence of preparing or possessing material with intent to incite hatred or violence. The group warns that the intent requirement is insufficiently clear, and that the proposed wording “could result in the criminalisation of people who possess or share material for reasons other than incitement, including satire, academic research or robust commentary.” The Council urged the Committee to “ensure that the law is targeted at genuinely harmful conduct, and does not unduly restrict the right to freedom of expression protected by the Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights.”

Speaking to Gript, ICCL Executive Director Liam Herrick said the organisation has consistently supported strong laws to address hate crime, but emphasised the need to avoid “unintended consequences which could undermine public debate and democratic participation.” Mr Herrick added: “We’re concerned that under the current drafting, there is the real possibility that people expressing opinions—however contentious—could find themselves subject to Garda questioning or even prosecution. That’s not a society we want to live in.”

The Department of Justice, however, has defended the Bill, arguing that the changes are necessary to bring Irish law in line with EU and international obligations. In a statement, the Department said the legislation “strikes a careful balance between protecting individuals and groups from harm and safeguarding the right to freedom of expression.” The Department further noted that the Bill explicitly provides for defences in cases of “reasonable and genuine contribution to literary, artistic, political, scientific or academic discourse.”

The political response to the ICCL’s intervention has been mixed. Some Government backbenchers have indicated they will seek to amend the Bill to include more robust protections for free speech, while opposition TDs have called for a broader public debate before the law is finalised. Aontú leader Peadar Tóibín said: “We cannot have a situation where legitimate debate or critique, even if it offends some, is subject to criminal sanction.”

Civil society groups supporting the Bill, including the Irish Network Against Racism, have insisted that strong measures are needed to combat hate speech and protect vulnerable communities. Dr Lucy Michael, speaking on behalf of the Network, said: “We have seen a rise in hate-fuelled incidents in Ireland, both online and offline. The law must be equipped to offer meaningful protection.”
headline: ICCL Flags “chilling effect on the free expression of opinion” in Government Bill

Protestors in Mulhuddart have expressed “shock and dismay” after a sitting judge in the Circuit Court indicated that “other agencies” connected with child welfare could be drawn into ongoing proceedings concerning the occupation of council-owned houses in the area.

The case, which has seen several local families and their supporters resisting attempts by Fingal County Council to evict them from properties earmarked for social housing, took a new turn this week when Judge James O’Donovan said he might have “no option” but to refer matters concerning the welfare of children in one of the households to Tusla, the Child and Family Agency, if the current occupation continued.

Campaigners supporting the families, who have mounted regular demonstrations outside the council offices and on the Avondale estate, said the judge’s comments were “deeply worrying”. “Bringing Tusla into a housing dispute is an escalation none of us expected,” said Alice Byrne, who has acted as a spokesperson for the “Homes for Mulhuddart” group. “Many here are worried about the trauma this could cause children who are already dealing with upheaval and uncertainty.”

The case concerns three families who entered vacant council properties late last year, arguing that years on the social housing waiting list and persistent overcrowding in their previous accommodation had left them with no alternative. Fingal County Council obtained injunctions requiring the occupiers to vacate the houses, but these orders have been challenged in the courts. 

During Wednesday’s hearing, the council’s legal team claimed the continued unauthorised occupation was preventing genuine applicants on the list from accessing desperately needed accommodation. They asked for immediate enforcement of the injunction, warning the court that the situation could set a precedent for similar “takeovers” elsewhere in Dublin.

In response, legal representatives for the defendants argued that the families had not set out to break the law, but had been “driven to desperation” by failures in the housing system. They described the prospect of children being uprooted again as “cruel and unnecessary”.

Addressing both sides, Judge O’Donovan said he was “concerned for the welfare of the children involved” and noted that if the situation persisted, “other agencies” with responsibility for child protection “may have to become engaged”. He adjourned the case for two weeks to allow further negotiations between the parties, but warned that the authority of the court could not be “continually disregarded”.

Speaking to Gript, Ms Byrne claimed the council and the legal system were “using the threat of Tusla” to browbeat families into compliance. “We’re angry that hard-pressed parents are being threatened with interventions that should be about child safety, not used as a stick in a housing dispute,” she said.

A spokesperson for Tusla confirmed to Gript that the agency was not currently involved in the case, but said it “takes any referral from the courts seriously and will always assess the situation based on the best interests of the child”.

Fingal County Council did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.

As the housing crisis deepens and tensions flare in communities across Dublin, the situation in Mulhuddart is rapidly becoming a rallying point for activists who accuse the government of “utterly failing” working families. Further demonstrations are planned in the coming days, with protestors demanding an immediate halt to all evictions from public land until adequate accommodation is provided.
headline: Mulhuddart protestors “shocked” as judge says “other agencies” related to children may become involved in housing case

text:
For over six years, survivors and families bereaved by the Glenanne Gang have persistently sought meetings with successive Taoisigh, but say their appeals have been repeatedly ignored. The group, which represents victims of a notorious loyalist paramilitary unit believed to have operated with the collusion of elements within British security forces during the Troubles, have written to Enda Kenny, Leo Varadkar, and Micheál Martin, but report having received either no response or generic acknowledgements from government staff.

The Glenanne Gang is linked to more than 120 murders across counties Armagh and Tyrone, as well as in south Down and Monaghan, between 1972 and 1978. Families say cross-border attacks, including the 1974 Dublin and Monaghan bombings, have never been properly investigated or acknowledged, leaving survivors feeling abandoned by both Irish and British governments.

Speaking to Gript, Eugene Reavey, whose three brothers were murdered at their home near Whitecross, County Armagh, in 1976, said: "We have written countless times, and not once has a Taoiseach sat down to talk to us. We are Irish citizens, and we have lost family members to this campaign of terror. Surely we deserve the courtesy of a meeting."

The families say their requests have included calls for the Irish government to push the British authorities on outstanding inquests and the full disclosure of documents, as well as asking Dublin to press for the implementation of court rulings on independent investigations. In 2018, the families received a letter from then-Taoiseach Leo Varadkar's office expressing "sympathy" but offering no commitment to meet or to take new action.

More recently, the group wrote to current Taoiseach Simon Harris following his appointment. As of this week, they say they have not received any reply.

The families have accused the Department of Foreign Affairs of "passing the buck" and of prioritising diplomatic relations with London over truth and justice for Irish victims. Margaret Urwin of Justice for the Forgotten, which has supported the Glenanne families, said: "There is a clear pattern of avoidance. These families are being treated as an inconvenience. It is shameful."

When asked for comment by Gript, a spokesperson for the Department of the Taoiseach did not confirm if any of the three former or current Taoisigh had received or replied to correspondence from Glenanne Gang victims' groups. The spokesperson said the government "remains committed to supporting victims and survivors of the Troubles" and continues to press the British government "at every opportunity" for full disclosure and cooperation in outstanding cases.

For campaigners like Mr Reavey, such assurances ring hollow. "We have had promises for decades, but no real engagement," he said. "We are not going away. We will keep asking for the meeting we deserve — until a Taoiseach has the courage to face us."
headline: 3 Taoisigh Have Ignored Requests to Meet with Victims and Survivors of the Glenanne Gang

text:
A 17 year old girl died in hospital in March 2021 after recording a positive Covid-19 swab, despite initially testing negative on admission, an inquest at Dublin Coroner’s Court has heard.

The teenager, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was admitted to a Dublin hospital in acute respiratory distress. She reportedly presented with a history of asthma and complained of severe shortness of breath. Her family told the inquest that she had been “generally healthy” aside from underlying asthma, but her condition deteriorated rapidly.

According to evidence given at the hearing, the girl arrived at the emergency department with severe respiratory symptoms. A Covid-19 antigen test returned negative, and she was subsequently transferred to a ward for further monitoring and treatment. However, medical staff noted that her oxygen requirements were increasing, and she was reviewed by a consultant who ordered a PCR swab as her health failed to improve.

Within 24 hours, the PCR test returned positive for Covid-19. Despite aggressive medical intervention, including ventilation and intensive care support, the teenager’s condition continued to worsen. She died less than two days after her initial admission.

A consultant respiratory physician told the court that while initial antigen tests can sometimes yield false negatives, PCR swabs remain the “gold standard” for detecting the virus, particularly in patients with worsening symptoms. He described a “catastrophic decline in lung function consistent with severe viral pneumonia,” complicated by her pre-existing asthma.

Family members raised concerns at the inquest about whether delays in recognising her infection or delays in providing certain treatments may have contributed to the rapid deterioration. In response, hospital representatives stated that all necessary protocols were followed and that care was escalated according to best practice guidelines from the HSE.

The case comes amid ongoing debate about the efficacy of rapid Covid-19 testing in acute settings, with experts warning that negative results do not always rule out infection in cases where clinical suspicion remains high.

The inquest heard that the girl was not eligible for vaccination at the time under Government guidelines, as the national rollout had not yet reached her age cohort. The coroner recorded a verdict of death due to natural causes, namely Covid-19 pneumonia, aggravated by underlying asthma.

The girl’s family has called for greater awareness among clinicians and parents about the possibility of false negatives in initial testing, especially in the context of rapidly worsening respiratory symptoms. The hospital, for its part, expressed condolences to the family and reiterated its commitment to ongoing staff training and adherence to national protocols. 

The case has been referred to the HSE’s incident management team for internal review, and no further comment was provided pending the completion of that process.
headline: 17 year old girl died in hospital following a positive covid 19 swab after initially testing negative on admission.
