A large crowd of parents and concerned locals packed into the local parish hall last night for a public meeting on the controversial new Relationships and Sexuality Education (RSE) programme being introduced to primary and secondary schools. Organised by a group of local parents and supported by a number of national advocacy groups, the event heard repeated expressions of worry and anger from parents who said they were never consulted on the content of the new programme and were shocked by what they have since discovered.

Several speakers outlined in detail what they described as “highly explicit” material being introduced to children as young as eight, expressing fears about the appropriateness and potential psychological impact on pupils. One mother told the meeting: “These are children—our children—and what we’re hearing is that they’re being taught about sexual practices, gender identity and concepts that most parents would consider totally inappropriate for primary school kids. Where is the parental say in all this?”

Another speaker, a father of three, warned that the Department of Education had failed in its duty to consult parents and communities before rolling out the new RSE content. “We are being sidelined. It’s as if the State believes it owns our children. There needs to be real consultation, not box-ticking exercises,” he said, to loud applause from the gathered crowd.

Also present were representatives of advocacy groups including the National Parents Council and the Catholic Primary Schools Management Association, both of whom echoed concerns about the lack of transparency and the direction of the curriculum review. A spokesperson for the Catholic Primary Schools Management Association told Gript: “Many boards of management, and indeed many teachers, are very uneasy with the instructions coming from the Department regarding the new RSE programme. There is a real risk that parental rights are being undermined here.”

During the meeting, copies of some of the educational materials, obtained by parents, were circulated among the attendees. Many expressed shock at what they described as graphic diagrams and explicit language. A local teacher, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said that staff in several schools had also raised objections but felt they were being pressured not to speak out publicly.

The meeting heard repeated calls for the Department of Education to pause the rollout of the new programme, and to engage in “genuine, open consultation” with parents, boards of management, and school staff. Several parents also called for the right to opt their children out of any classes they deemed inappropriate. Local TD John Murphy, who attended the meeting, said he would be raising the matter in the Dáil this week, calling for Minister for Education Norma Foley to address parents’ concerns directly.

In a statement issued to Gript after the meeting, a spokesperson for the Department of Education said the new RSE curriculum is being developed “following extensive engagement with educational stakeholders” and is “in line with best international practice.” The statement also stressed that schools have discretion in how the material is delivered, and that parents retain a right to withdraw their child from any aspect of the sex education programme.

However, parents at last night’s meeting said that had not been their experience so far, with many stating that information had been difficult to obtain and that they felt the process lacked transparency and accountability. “This is about the rights of parents, and the innocence of children,” one attendee said. The meeting concluded with a motion calling for an immediate suspension of the rollout, which was passed unanimously. Organisers said further meetings and protests would take place in the coming weeks.
headline: Packed meeting on explicit RSE course hears parents’ anger and concern

text:
A total of 12,776 people received a COVID-19 vaccine in the State on Tuesday, according to the latest data published this morning by the Health Service Executive (HSE). The figures, updated as part of the national VACTRACK initiative, include first, second and booster doses administered across vaccination centres, GP practices and participating pharmacies.

Tuesday’s figure marks a moderate increase on the previous day's total, with 10,804 doses reported on Monday, as the ongoing campaign continues to target at-risk groups and health and social care workers. Demand for vaccination has fluctuated in recent weeks, with the HSE citing seasonal factors and the conclusion of some community outreach programmes.

Among those vaccinated on Tuesday, the breakdown shows 7,256 booster doses, 2,436 initial doses for adults, and 3,084 paediatric doses for children aged 5 to 11. The HSE said uptake among the over-65 cohort remains ‘steady’, while officials have encouraged parents of children with chronic medical conditions to attend for vaccination.

The Minister for Health, Stephen Donnelly, has welcomed what he called “continued engagement with the vaccination programme,” urging anyone who has yet to avail of vaccination to come forward. “It remains the best protection we have against severe illness,” the Minister said.

Walk-in clinics continue to operate in major urban areas including Dublin, Cork, Limerick and Galway, as well as a number of rural locations. GP-led clinics reported a rise in appointments this week, ahead of the Easter holidays. Pharmacies participating in the rollout are also providing appointments, with the Irish Pharmacy Union (IPU) calling it a “vital service for communities”.

Questions persist regarding the long-term strategy for vaccination. Speaking in the Dáil on Tuesday, Sinn Féin health spokesperson David Cullinane TD asked when an updated plan for autumn boosters will be published. The Department of Health has yet to provide a timeline, but sources indicate planning is underway, pending further guidance from the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC).

To date, more than 8.3 million COVID-19 vaccine doses have been administered in Ireland. The HSE continues to monitor vaccine uptake by county and age group, with public health officials reiterating the importance of vaccination, particularly for those with underlying conditions.

Information regarding eligibility and clinic opening times is available on the HSE website, and the national helpline remains open for queries.
headline: Vaccine Update: 12,776 vaccinated on Tuesday

text:
Fianna Fáil TD Willie O’Dea has called for a full removal of mask mandates for children in Irish primary and secondary schools, arguing that the policy is both unnecessary and damaging to young people’s development.

Deputy O’Dea, the long-serving Limerick City representative, told Gript that the mask requirement imposed during the Covid-19 pandemic was an “extraordinary measure” that is now out of step with current public health realities. He said, “It’s well past time we ended these mandates for children. The science is increasingly clear that the risks to children are low, and the harms of masking—on communication, learning, and social interaction—are significant.”

The TD’s comments come as the Department of Education has yet to formally rescind guidance recommending face coverings for pupils aged nine and above in certain settings. While enforcement has eased across many schools, some boards of management continue to cite the guidelines as a reason for their retention, particularly during the winter months or local outbreaks.

O’Dea said, “We have to recognise the reality: adults are living normally, masks are all but gone in most public spaces, and yet we’re still asking children to cover their faces for hours on end. It’s not fair, and it’s not evidence-based at this stage.”

While the HSE and officials in the Department of Health have recently stated that mask mandates may be reimposed if a new wave of Covid-19 or another respiratory illness arises, O’Dea argues that the indefinite threat of reintroduction is “making school a place of constant anxiety for some children and parents” and discouraging open debate on the topic within the Oireachtas.

Several parent groups have also called for the blanket mask rules to be dropped, citing concerns around speech development, special educational needs, and children for whom English is not the first language. Experts, including speech therapists and psychologists, have voiced similar worries, particularly in the context of early years education. “Children rely on nonverbal cues—facial expressions, lip movements—to learn and connect. These are crucial years, and the impact of prolonged masking is not yet fully understood,” said Dr. Maeve O’Sullivan, a paediatric psychologist interviewed by Gript.

Opponents of the mandate also point to international evidence from countries such as Sweden and Norway, which did not impose widespread masking on younger children and reported no significant difference in school-based transmission or community outcomes.

Asked about the argument that masks provide an extra layer of protection for vulnerable staff members or families, O’Dea was clear: “Vulnerable adults deserve all necessary protections, but the responsibility shouldn’t be placed on children indefinitely. Vaccinations are widely available, treatments have improved, and we have to balance risks with children’s right to a normal education.”

The Department of Education did not respond to Gript’s request for comment on whether an update to mask guidance is planned before the next academic year. However, a spokesperson noted that all public health advice is kept under continuous review in conjunction with the HSE.

The Taoiseach Leo Varadkar recently signalled the government’s intention to “learn the lessons of the pandemic” but stopped short of commenting on any specific reversal of regulations, saying only that “future measures would be based on up-to-date science and the context at the time.”

For now, the issue remains a point of contention among teachers, parents, and policymakers.
headline: Willie O’Dea TD: Mask mandates for school children must go

text:
A major new study by University College London has found that the prevalence of depression in the United Kingdom has more than doubled during the coronavirus lockdowns, with researchers warning of a “looming crisis” in mental health. The longitudinal study, considered the largest of its kind in Britain, tracked over 70,000 adults and found that rates of depressive symptoms soared from 9.7% before the pandemic to 19.4% during the strictest periods of restrictions.

The study’s findings suggest that the mental health impact of lockdowns has been especially severe among young adults, women, and those living alone or on lower incomes. Researchers noted that these groups, already more vulnerable to mental health difficulties, bore the brunt of isolation, financial strain and disruption to daily life. While the British government provided some measures of support, charities and advocacy groups argue that these interventions have been insufficient to stave off a mounting crisis.

Dr Daisy Fancourt of UCL, the study’s lead author, said the results should serve as a “wake-up call” for policymakers. “We’re facing a tidal wave of mental health issues, with many people experiencing depression for the first time. It is vital that we prepare health and support services for the aftermath of the pandemic as well as for any future restrictions.”

Similar concerns are echoed in Ireland, where the HSE has reported increased demand for mental health services since the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic. Charities such as Pieta House and Samaritans have also noted a surge in contacts, as Irish citizens grapple with the social and economic consequences of restrictions. Although the current government has pledged to increase funding to mental health, service capacity remains a challenge, particularly outside main urban centres.

The UK study raises serious questions about the collateral effects of public health measures such as lockdowns. While intended to protect vulnerable groups from the coronavirus, the measures imposed have themselves created new forms of vulnerability. The authors of the UCL research called for a balanced approach, recommending that future public health policies weigh the mental health costs of restrictions, particularly for those most at risk.

As other countries in Europe and beyond contemplate retaining or re-introducing restrictions amidst new variants, the findings are likely to fuel debate about the best path forward. With the World Health Organisation urging governments to treat mental health as a priority, pressure is growing on both London and Dublin to ensure that psychological wellbeing is not sidelined in the ongoing response to the pandemic.
headline: ‘Looming crisis’ as depression DOUBLES in lockdown: UK study

text:
It is a rare thing in the contemporary cultural landscape for a writer born in the Victorian era to find fresh relevance, but G.K. Chesterton—essayist, novelist, poet, and self-described “orthodox”—has found his way into the Irish conversation once more. The continuing interest in Chesterton is not merely the idle pastime of academic circles, nor the preserve of the nostalgic. Rather, it is Irish men and women on the ground—those frustrated by modernity’s contradictions—who are asking if the old English essayist’s critiques of progress and his defence of common sense might have something to offer in 2024.

Chesterton himself never set foot in Ireland, but he wrote extensively about the Irish people, most memorably in “Irish Impressions” (1919), a travelogue composed during the tail-end of the Irish War of Independence. He saw in Ireland something that had already been stamped out in England—a stubbornness, a preservation of faith, custom, and family life in the face of both British and continental progressivism. Chesterton’s suspicion of the fashionable ideologies of his own time—social Darwinism, secular materialism, and a kind of technocratic optimism—reads, in the current context, as a prescient warning.

In Dublin today, where tech companies dominate the skyline and “progressive” is ever the watchword, a Chestertonian counter-point is surprisingly resonant. He was wary of progress for its own sake, writing: “The business of progressives is to go on making mistakes. The business of the conservatives is to prevent the mistakes from being corrected.” The phrase could well apply to much of the current Irish political debate, where parties compete in proposing change, but seldom pause to reckon with what, precisely, is being left behind in the rush.

Chesterton’s vision was not regressive in the pejorative sense, but restorative—a call back to what the modern world might have lost: rootedness, neighbourliness, the primacy of the family, and above all, the reality of objective moral truths. He was a Catholic convert, and in that role, he saw the value of small nations and cultures, like Ireland’s, as bulwarks against flattening global forces. “A nation with a soul,” he wrote after passing through Cork and Waterford, “has something worth defending.” Today, with the increased secularisation of Irish life and the marginalisation of native traditions, his assessment rings with a new urgency.

The “future” Chesterton points toward, paradoxically, is one where society looks backwards—not in nostalgia, but in search of firm ground. He argued that “tradition is the democracy of the dead,” suggesting that the wisdom of our forebears deserves a vote in present deliberations. Whether it is the erosion of religious observance, the breakdown of the family, or the push for ever more radical social experiments, the Chestertonian warning is consistent: the newest solution is not always superior to the settled wisdom of the past.

There are hints, even within the Oireachtas, of a growing sense that something has been lost. While Dáil debates rarely cite Victorian authors, the questions raised about loneliness, community breakdown, and the hollowing out of rural Ireland are ones that Chesterton would have recognised.
headline: Back to the future with G.K. Chesterton

text:
Volunteers at Dublin’s leading suicide helpline say they have been forced to double their shifts as calls for help surge to record levels during the latest lockdown, with many callers citing isolation, job loss and mounting anxiety over the future.

The Dublin Suicide Helpline, run from the city centre, reports a 130% spike in calls since Level 5 restrictions were announced in January, with callers ranging from teenagers to pensioners. Volunteers, most of whom work remotely under current HSE guidelines, say the sheer “desperation and loneliness” expressed by callers is unlike anything they’ve encountered before.

“It’s relentless,” one long-serving volunteer told Gript. “We’re getting calls around the clock, and the stories are getting harder. People have lost businesses, or they live alone, and now they’re facing another few months of it. You can hear the despair in their voices.”

In a bid to keep up, the helpline team – which numbers fewer than 20 regular volunteers – has doubled shift hours, with many now working late into the night to ensure the phone is always answered.

The helpline’s coordinator, Mary Mulcahy, says the organisation simply cannot afford to miss any call. “We see every call as a life that could depend on us. Some people ring because they have no-one else. We have volunteers doing double-time, no complaints, no questions asked – because they know how critical this is.”

Incoming calls often spike in the late evening, volunteers say, as the reality of isolation and lockdown curfews sink in. Callers have raised worries about financial stress, relationship breakdowns, delayed medical appointments, and in some cases domestic violence. Many have told volunteers they are struggling without in-person community supports, closed under public health guidelines.

The Department of Health has acknowledged a “concerning” rise in mental health issues since the onset of Covid-19 restrictions. While the HSE points to investment in online mental health supports, Mulcahy says these are no substitute for a human voice. “People are overwhelmed by digital. They want to talk to someone who’ll listen, not fill out an online form.”

She also voiced frustration at the uncertainty around government funding for volunteer-based services, which she says have become essential since the pandemic began. “We get by on donations and some small grants, but the need has never been greater and we’re stretched to breaking point.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Health told Gript that additional funding for mental health services is “under review” and pointed to new telephone and web-based resources launched by the HSE. However, Mulcahy insists the government response is far from sufficient: “There’s a gap that needs to be filled, and volunteers are trying to fill it – but we can’t do it alone forever.”

Meanwhile, volunteers are bracing for another spike in calls as new restrictions are announced and social isolation deepens in the coming weeks. “We do this because we care,” said one. “But after a year of this, we’re exhausted. Still, we’ll pick up the phone. It’s what we have to do.”
headline: Dublin suicide helpline volunteers DOUBLE their hours as calls skyrocket amid lockdown

text:
A Dublin school asked a 13-year-old girl whether she had “said anything racist” after she was physically assaulted by a black classmate, according to the student’s mother. The incident, which occurred earlier this year, has left the family “shocked and disappointed” by the school’s handling of the matter.

Speaking to Gript, the mother said her daughter, who attends a co-educational secondary school in the capital, was punched in the face and taunted during class by a fellow student. The girl’s mother claimed that when her daughter reported the assault to a member of staff, the first question asked was, “Did you say anything racist to her?” The mother alleges that her daughter, who was left with visible bruising, denied making any such remarks.

According to the mother, the school did not initially contact her directly about the incident. “She rang me herself, crying, and told me what happened. When I went in, a teacher told me they needed to check whether she had ‘provoked’ the other child with any racist comments. I couldn’t believe what I was hearing,” the mother said.

The family have alleged that school authorities seemed more concerned about the possibility of racism than the physical assault. “It felt like they wanted to excuse what happened to my daughter before even asking if she was alright,” the mother added.

When asked for comment, the Department of Education said it does not comment on individual cases but that “all reports of bullying and assault in schools should be dealt with in accordance with school policy and national guidelines.” The Gardaí confirmed they had not received a formal complaint in relation to the incident.

The school, when contacted by Gript, said it does not comment on individual students but that it was “committed to providing a safe and inclusive learning environment.”

The incident has highlighted concerns among parents about how schools are responding to violence and the role played by diversity and inclusion policies. Some parents have claimed that such policies are leading to a reluctance to address certain types of misconduct for fear of accusations of discrimination.

“It’s simple,” the mother said. “My daughter was punched in the face. That should be condemned, whatever the backgrounds of the students involved. Instead, we were made to feel like we had to defend ourselves.”

The mother said she is considering moving her daughter to another school and called for “common sense” in how schools handle incidents of violence. “No child should feel unsafe at school, or feel that their complaints won’t be taken seriously just because of who was involved.”

The school’s Board of Management is understood to be reviewing its policies in light of the incident.
headline: School asked student (13) if she had said anything racist after she was assaulted by black classmate

text:
A woman at the centre of the ongoing SaveKim controversy has refused to speak to journalists, telling reporters “no comment” when approached at her home in north Dublin earlier this week.

The woman, who cannot be named for legal reasons, has become embroiled in a heated national debate after her involvement in a campaign surrounding the deportation of South Korean national Kim Seong-hyeon was brought to public attention. The SaveKim campaign claims it is seeking to prevent the deportation of Mr Kim, whose visa expired last year, but critics allege that influential campaigners are misleading the public and encouraging breaches of immigration law.

Minister for Justice Helen McEntee has faced pressure in the Dáil to clarify the State’s position, with opposition TDs raising questions about how immigration cases are handled by the Department of Justice. Advocacy groups insist that Ireland’s reputation as a welcoming nation is at stake, while others, including local residents, have voiced frustration over what they see as a lack of proper enforcement and transparency.

When Gript visited the address linked to the campaign’s principal organiser on Tuesday morning, the woman in question declined to answer any questions. She emerged briefly to retrieve post before shutting her door when approached by a reporter, repeating, “No comment, thank you.”

The campaign has attracted significant social media attention, with supporters sharing appeals for “compassion” and calling on the government to intervene on Mr Kim’s behalf. However, others are asking pointed questions about the accuracy of the claims being circulated and the motivations behind the campaign.

Speaking to Gript, a local resident who wished to remain anonymous said: “People want to help, absolutely, but there needs to be honesty about what’s actually happening. Some of us are worried the rules are just being ignored if there’s enough noise online.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Justice told Gript that it does not comment on individual immigration cases, but stated: “Ireland’s immigration processes are fair and robust, with all applicants given a full opportunity to present their case.”

The SaveKim campaign’s organisers have not responded to further requests for comment, and have instead directed the public to a series of online petitions and fundraising platforms.

As speculation continues, the case has sparked renewed debate about Ireland’s immigration policy and the role of online activism in influencing ministerial decisions. Government sources have indicated there will be no change to current procedures, saying that the rule of law must be respected. 

The matter is expected to be raised again in the Oireachtas in the coming days.
headline: “No comment” – woman in SaveKim saga refuses to speak

text:
Cherry Orchard, in west Dublin, has for years been a byword for social deprivation, anti-social behaviour, and, more recently, highly publicised incidents involving stolen cars and reckless driving. Yet for all the headlines, it is an area where successive Governments have poured resources—brand new schools, a state-of-the-art family resource centre, multiple playgrounds, and a €5 million community centre opened in 2020. The local parish and charities run childcare services, clubs, sports teams, and afterschool activities. The Council funds youth projects and supports. The HSE operates clinics and addiction outreach. If amenities alone were the answer, Cherry Orchard would be thriving.

So why, amid the sports pitches and freshly painted community halls, is social breakdown so painfully evident? In Garda reports and local testimony alike, the story is about teenagers—almost always boys—who are out of school, and out of control, their parents struggling or unwilling to rein them in. The question, as one elderly resident puts it, is not about facilities but families: “Who is raising these children? Where are their fathers?”

Official data is stark. According to the 2022 Census, nearly two-thirds of households with children in Cherry Orchard are headed by single parents, most of them mothers. Many fathers are absent or have minimal involvement. In far too many cases, this is compounded by intergenerational unemployment, the legacy of urban “regeneration” schemes which saw communities broken up, and, in some instances, ongoing drug use and criminality that undermine any attempts at stability.

State agencies are not blind to these realities, but their responses are shaped by the priorities of the moment. The local TDs speak of “investment” and “inclusion,” the City Council launches consultation after consultation, and the Department of Children and Youth Affairs trumpets new intervention programmes. But the one form of intervention that dare not speak its name is family structure. The evidence, both international and domestic, could not be clearer: children raised by their married, biological parents in a stable home are far less at risk of educational failure, drug use, violence, or contact with the criminal justice system. Yet this is never part of the “solutions” tabled in Oireachtas committee rooms or City Council briefing notes.

Nobody is saying that single parents are the problem, or that all two-parent families are perfect. Life is messy; tragedy and hardship intervene. But to ignore the centrality of intact families—or to pretend that a new AstroTurf pitch can substitute for a present father and a stable home—is an abdication of responsibility. For too long, policy in Cherry Orchard has focused on amenities and interventions, rather than supporting the family as the basic unit of society.

There are brave volunteers, often from the area itself, who do heroic work mentoring young people, running clubs, and trying to keep some kind of order. The Gardaí work tirelessly, often putting themselves in harm’s way. But all agree, privately if not publicly, that the root problem is cultural as much as infrastructural. It is not a lack of money, per se, but a lack of social capital—and that capital is built, first and foremost, in the home.

As new cycles of anti-social behaviour play out on social media, and new press releases are issued from Government Buildings, the tragedy of Cherry Orchard is not that it is without amenities.
headline: Falling down in Cherry Orchard: lots of amenities but few intact families

text:
As Ireland settles into a new political era, two things are becoming increasingly clear: first, that the spectre of COVID-19 restrictions still looms insidiously over public life, and second, that a vocal tranche of the Irish Left appears disturbingly unwilling to let this power slip. While many had assumed that the end of the worst of the pandemic would prompt a return to ordinary freedoms, there remains a notable clique who have grown attached to the lockdown mentality, not as a public health necessity, but as a blueprint for indefinite social control.

This phenomenon is hardly unique to Ireland, but it has found particularly fertile ground here, nurtured by the institutional strength of the NGO sector, the dominance of progressive orthodoxy in media and academia, and the willingness of certain politicians to indulge every cry for greater state authority. Consider the language that continues to be deployed months after the emergency: “public safety”; “protecting the vulnerable”; “following the science.” Each phrase, once a call to collective action in extraordinary times, now risks serving as a perpetual justification for restrictions on civil liberties.

From proposals for “permanent pandemic preparedness” legislation, to the regular calls for misinformation crackdowns, to suggestions that “temporary” powers over movement and assembly might need extension in the face of future threats, the pattern is consistent. Those on the Left who previously railed against Gardaí powers, lamented the erosion of privacy, and championed personal autonomy, now appear remarkably unconcerned by new forms of state surveillance and regulation—so long as these are said to advance progressive ends.

A glance at recent debates in the Oireachtas is instructive. No sooner had the mask mandates been lifted than a flurry of comment pieces, open letters, and Dáil interventions began calling for even stricter public health laws “just in case.” Sinn Féin and the Social Democrats, among others, have floated the idea that “emergency” should become the norm: an ever-present rationale for increased funding, centralised decision-making, and sweeping intervention into private life. The Government, for its part, has proven more than happy to keep the option open.

What underpins all of this is a deeper ideological reflex: distrust of the public, coupled with certainty in the righteousness of elite expertise. The ordinary person, in this view, cannot be trusted to exercise common sense or behave with compassion unless guided by bureaucratic fiat. Freedoms that took centuries to win—the right to assemble, to worship, to protest, to earn a living—are seen as privileges, contingent on compliance with whatever “crisis” happens to be declared.

To be clear: COVID-19 was and remains a deadly threat to many. The State was justified in extraordinary measures when hospitals creaked under the strain. But the Irish left’s fixation on lockdown, and its fantasy of endless government diktat, is not about evidence or science anymore. It is about power: who wields it, who is allowed to dissent, and whether individual liberty is to mean anything at all.

The Taoiseach declared the “end” of the emergency, but listen carefully to the most ideological voices on the Left, and you’ll hear a different refrain. For them, lockdown is not a nightmare to be escaped, but an opportunity never to be wasted.
headline: The Left wants the Lockdown to be forever

text:
Ireland could face a staggering €375 billion bill if the State pursues its ambition to become carbon neutral, Independent TD Mattie McGrath has claimed, warning that the scale of the financial burden is not being honestly discussed by Government or the opposition.

Speaking to Gript, Deputy McGrath said the figure is based on preliminary assessments and international comparisons, as well as consultations with energy and infrastructure experts. He argued that the ongoing shift to a net zero emissions economy by 2050, as set out in the Programme for Government and backed by the Green Party, risks placing an unmanageable strain on Irish businesses and households, while also exposing communities in rural Ireland to disproportionate costs.

“The Green agenda has been steamrolled into legislation without a full accounting of what it will mean for ordinary people. If all of the Climate Action Plan measures and targets go ahead as planned, we are looking at a price tag of €375 billion over the coming decades. That’s more than double the entire national debt,” Deputy McGrath said.

While Government figures have not publicly costed the full implementation of carbon neutrality, official projections by the Department of Environment and estimates from the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council have put the annual costs of decarbonisation in the range of €7bn to €12bn per year over the next quarter century. The costs include retrofitting housing stock, upgrading the electricity grid, scaling up public transport, transitioning agriculture, and investment in renewable energy.

Deputy McGrath pointed out that the figure does not account for the indirect costs to the wider economy, such as job losses in traditional sectors and increased energy prices for consumers.

“The entire agriculture sector is being told to halve emissions, but there’s no honest debate about how this will devastate family farms. If carbon neutrality means shutting down large parts of our rural economy, we have a duty to ask whether that price is worth paying, especially when Ireland’s emissions are less than 0.1% of the global total,” he said.

Government officials have argued that the long-term costs of inaction on climate change, including extreme weather, damage to coastal infrastructure, and increased health costs, would outweigh the expense of decarbonising the country. The Taoiseach this year described climate action as “the greatest economic and social transformation of our generation”, but acknowledged the scale of the challenge in a recent Dáil debate.

Sinn Féin and Labour have backed ambitious climate targets, though both have called for greater support for affected sectors and regions. However, McGrath contends that none of the main parties are “level with the public about just how much this will cost and who will pay for it.”

“People on low or fixed incomes, especially in counties like Tipperary and Donegal, simply cannot absorb the soaring costs for home heating, energy, or transport that come with pushing this agenda. We will see people left behind and deeper regional divides if there is not a complete rethink,” he added.

The Government is expected to update its Climate Action Plan later this year, with sectoral carbon ceilings and draft legislation on emissions reporting due before the Oireachtas in the autumn. Environmental groups have dismissed the €375 billion figure as “wildly inflated”, arguing that the net benefits of cleaner air, green jobs, and climate resilience outweigh up-front investment costs.
headline: TD: Ireland going carbon neutral could cost €375 billion

text:
Independent TD Michael Collins has accused the Government of overseeing an “act of piracy” following the recent seizure of a foreign trawler off the Cork coast. Deputy Collins said that the detention of the Spanish-registered fishing vessel, which occurred earlier this week near Castletownbere, amounted to “the criminalisation of traditional fishing” and posed a serious threat to the livelihoods of Irish fishermen.

The operation, carried out by the Naval Service and the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority (SFPA), saw the vessel boarded and escorted to port on suspicion of breaches of EU fisheries regulations. However, Deputy Collins claims the dramatic action was not only heavy-handed but also indicative of the “outsourcing of Irish fisheries policy to Brussels” at the expense of local communities.

“The reality is that Irish fishermen are being driven out of their own waters while foreign vessels are favoured and then targeted in this way under EU diktats,” the Cork South-West TD told Gript. “The Government has stood idly by as our natural resources have been handed over, and now they allow this sort of act, which to me resembles piracy. It’s shameful.”

In the Dáil yesterday, the Taoiseach, Simon Harris, defended the actions of the Naval Service and the SFPA, stressing the importance of upholding fisheries laws and sustainable management. “Ireland has obligations under the Common Fisheries Policy, and our agencies act to protect those resources on behalf of all citizens,” Mr Harris said.

Mr Collins disputes that approach, arguing that enforcement has become “overzealous”. “What happened off the Cork coast was a hostile intervention. Fishermen, both Irish and foreign, are being treated like criminals for carrying on a way of life that sustained our coastal communities for generations. The Government is more interested in pleasing bureaucrats than standing up for Irish jobs,” he said.

Fishing representative groups have long protested the impact of EU quotas and regulatory measures, arguing they disproportionately affect Irish vessels. The Irish South and West Fish Producers Organisation has previously described enforcement practices, including frequent boardings and lengthy detentions, as “harassment”.

A spokesperson for the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine said all fisheries enforcement actions are based on “intelligence-led risk assessment” and consistent with Ireland’s legal and EU obligations. “The monitoring of fishing activity is essential to safeguard fish stocks and ensure a level playing field,” the spokesperson said.

Deputy Collins called for an immediate review of fisheries enforcement and for greater national control over Irish waters. “We need an Irish solution for Irish fisheries. The Government must stop bowing to Brussels,” he said.

The detained trawler remains at Castletownbere, pending an investigation. No charges have yet been brought. The Department confirmed that seizures and boardings are subject to oversight and that any breaches identified by the SFPA are handled according to due process in the District Court.
headline: TD says government allowed “act of piracy” off Cork coast

text:
A north Dublin TD has claimed “organised gang violence” is fuelling chaos in the town of Balbriggan, with residents enduring a litany of attacks including “stabbings, arson, and the takeover of a local shopping centre”. The comments, made by Independent TD for Dublin Fingal, Joe O’Brien, during a Dáil debate on Wednesday, have heightened pressure on government and Gardaí to respond to spiralling disorder in the growing commuter town.

O’Brien said the situation in Balbriggan has deteriorated rapidly over the past year, attributing the escalation of violence to “a lack of effective policing and a failure by the State to provide adequate resources”. According to the TD, “gangs of youths—some barely in their teens—are effectively in control after dark, terrorising families, damaging businesses, and attacking other youths”.

“People are afraid to go to the SuperValu after 6pm,” O’Brien told the Dáil. “There have been stabbings outside the cinema, cars torched beside schools, groups running rampant with weapons. There was a case only last Friday of thirty lads storming the shopping centre, intimidating staff and shoppers.”

Figures released to Gript show Gardaí recorded at least 47 public order incidents in Balbriggan so far this year, up from 29 over the same period in 2023. Several knife assaults have taken place since Easter, with one 18-year-old still recovering in hospital from a stabbing near Bremore Castle in May. Arson attacks have targeted cars and bins in residential estates, and the management of Millfield Shopping Centre have had to hire private security after what staff described as “frightening, organised mob behaviour”.

Local business owners say trade has plummeted. “Staff are too scared to close up after dark, and we’ve had to replace our windows three times,” says one shop manager who asked not to be named for fear of reprisals. “It’s out of control.”

Gardaí have responded by increasing visible patrols and setting up a new community policing office, but residents and public representatives say it has not been enough. “There are not enough Gardaí on the beat, plain and simple,” said Cllr Tony Murphy (independent). “It’s gone beyond anti-social behaviour now. These are serious criminal acts—stabbings, firebombings, businesses being ransacked in broad daylight.”

Gript understands that a number of suspects linked to recent attacks are known to Gardaí and have appeared before the District Court, but bail conditions have failed to stem the problem, with at least two reoffending within weeks. There is particular concern about the recruitment of very young teenagers into local gangs, fuelled by social media and a lack of youth services.

Local schools and parent groups have pleaded with authorities for an urgent, multi-agency intervention. The HSE has not commented on whether additional youth mental health resources will be provided, but the Department of Justice said Minister Helen McEntee is “monitoring the situation closely” and that a dedicated Garda operation is “under active consideration”.

In the Dáil, O’Brien criticised “years of State neglect”, and called for a task force modelled on the one set up in Drogheda following similar outbreaks of violence there. “We cannot abandon families who just want to raise their children in safety,” he said. “Balbriggan needs urgent action, not more promises.”
headline: TD admits ‘gang violence’ causing mayhem in Ballbriggan: ‘stabbings, arson, shopping centre taken over’

News this week from Tehran should give pause to policymakers far beyond the Middle East. Iran’s government has announced a raft of pro-family incentives in response to plummeting birth rates and mounting anxieties over a looming “baby drought.” The move, while predictable in a country where the median age is rising fast and the population is forecast to shrink, stands as a stark contrast to the dominant currents in most of Europe, Ireland included, where concerns about falling birth rates are rarely met with anything but hand-wringing or resort to increased inward migration.

Iran’s newly unveiled measures include expanded parental leave, subsidised housing loans for young couples, and direct financial support for families welcoming children. Authorities have gone so far as to restrict access to contraception and abortion, drawing the ire of Western NGOs but reflecting the seriousness with which the Islamic Republic views its demographic predicament. Their Health Minister has warned publicly of an unsustainable future with fewer workers, more pensioners, and an eroding base of national self-reliance—echoing, incidentally, the same demographic warnings quietly circulating within EU think-tanks and Ireland’s Department of Finance.

It’s easy to scoff at Iranian social policy or to tut-tut about cultural differences, but the underlying reality is not lost on the world’s more clear-eyed demographers. UN projections show that, by 2050, a fifth of the global population will be over 60, and Iran’s fertility rate—now hovering around 1.6, well below replacement level—is hardly unique. Ireland, for now, maintains a modestly higher fertility rate (1.75 in the latest CSO figures), but that’s a steep drop from the post-boom years and still well below the minimum needed to ensure long-term population stability without resorting to ever more migration.

Yet, Ireland’s approach remains firmly stuck in denial. There is little sign of the pro-natalist thinking seen in Hungary, Poland, or now Iran. Mention of our demographic woes, when it is made at all, is typically framed as a reason to further liberalise immigration policy or to trumpet the “diversity dividend” to the Dáil. There is scant talk of removing tax penalties faced by single-income families, of rebalancing child benefit to encourage larger families, or of seriously addressing the exorbitant cost of childcare and housing that deters so many from having children.

Iran’s response, while certainly top-down and heavy-handed by Western standards, at least attempts to treat the roots of the problem rather than simply importing a temporary fix. If the Islamic Republic—hardly a bastion of Western family values—can openly acknowledge demographic crisis and act accordingly, what does it say about the Irish political establishment that any similar discussion about birth rates is immediately branded reactionary or “regressive”?

Far too often, the Irish Government prefers to paper over demographic cracks with policies that boost GDP but do little to address the underlying issues of community, continuity, and social cohesion. The future for Ireland—if our leaders continue to ignore the demographic writing on the wall—may well be determined not by the values we cherish, but by our stubborn refusal to defend them.

The Iranian case is a reminder that acknowledging birth rate decline is neither old-fashioned nor extreme: it is an unavoidable fact. Pretending otherwise or relying solely on migration to fill the gap risks transforming our society in unpredictable ways.
headline: Baby drought fears prompt introduction of pro-family incentives in Iran

The government has repeatedly boasted of its “game-changing” cost rental housing programme, promising affordable homes for “ordinary working people” squeezed out of the market by sky-high rents. Yet the reality, as experienced by many Irish families on modest incomes, is far removed from those glossy photo ops and upbeat press releases.

This week, social media lit up with heated reaction to the now-viral video showing an African national, recently arrived in Ireland, giving a tour of his brand-new cost rental home in west Dublin. The excitement was palpable – not among the Irish people who have grown up here and worked hard for years, but among those who see Ireland as a land of opportunity, even in the middle of a housing crisis. “It’s brand new, it’s perfect, I am so grateful,” the young man declared, panning the camera to show the spotless kitchen and pristine bedrooms.

For thousands of Irish families – some living with relatives, others facing eviction from the private rental sector, and many more languishing on endless housing lists – the reaction ranged from disbelief to despair. The question on everybody’s lips: how does a newly-arrived migrant access a cost rental property almost overnight, while citizens and long-term residents are left to compete for a limited supply, often with little hope of success?

The Department of Housing insists the cost rental system is “open to all who meet the criteria” – an income cap, no property ownership and a commitment to use the home as a principal residence. But these boxes are easily ticked by a new arrival, especially when the system itself makes little distinction between the newly-arrived, and those who have paid taxes and contributed to Irish society for decades.

Data on how many cost rental homes have gone to Irish citizens versus new arrivals is not being published. When pressed, the Housing Agency and Approved Housing Bodies cite privacy and data protection. What we do know is that the country is facing a record influx of international protection applicants – over 10,000 so far this year – and that housing pressure has never been more acute. Meanwhile, the government continues to insist there is “no queue-jumping”, even as stories of newly-arrived migrants accessing social and affordable housing ahead of locals multiply.

This has led many to compare the government’s approach to the world of Willy Wonka – a magical land where rules are made up as they go along, and golden tickets are handed out to the lucky few. If you are a long-term resident, the message is clear: keep playing, keep hoping, but don’t expect fairness or transparency.

Minister for Housing Darragh O’Brien has labelled the criticism “divisive” and “unfair”. Yet for a growing number of would-be homeowners and renters, these are not just talking points but lived reality. The anger is palpable at local meetings, on the doorsteps, and across social media. People see a government willing to make lavish promises to the world, but unable – or unwilling – to defend the interests of the Irish people themselves.

Nobody blames individual migrants for seeking a better life. But there is a growing sense that government policy has become detached from the needs and expectations of its own citizens. While TDs announce new funding packages and unveil yet more “affordable” schemes, ordinary families are told to wait, to be patient, to “trust the process.”

The gap between government spin and everyday experience grows wider.
headline: The migrant, the cost rental house, and the Willy Wonka Government

Figures released by Eurostat and the Department of Children show that Ireland continues to accept Ukrainian refugees at a rate significantly higher than many other Western countries, including France and the United States, raising fresh questions about the sustainability of the Government’s ongoing response to the crisis.

As of June 2024, over 105,000 Ukrainians have entered Ireland since the Russian invasion in February 2022. This places the State second in the EU on a per capita basis, with the UNHCR noting that Ireland, population just over 5 million, is now accommodating almost 21 arrivals per 1,000 residents. By contrast, the United States – with a population of over 330 million – has accepted around 200,000 Ukrainians under its Uniting for Ukraine programme, a rate of just 0.6 per 1,000. France, meanwhile, has taken in approximately 135,000 displaced Ukrainians, a much lower per capita figure than Ireland.

Minister for Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth Roderic O’Gorman told the Oireachtas last week that “Ireland’s response remains among the most generous in Europe.” He also conceded that “continued arrivals are placing severe strain” on already-stretched resources. The Department of the Taoiseach has acknowledged mounting logistical challenges, particularly regarding accommodation, education, and healthcare, with the HSE reporting increased pressure on local GP services and emergency departments.

Accommodation pressures have led to ongoing protests in several towns, including Inch, Co Clare and Dublin’s East Wall, with residents expressing frustration at the lack of consultation and the impact on local infrastructure. Gardaí have attended a number of demonstrations, though overall incidents remain small in scale.

Industry groups and opposition TDs remain divided on the Government’s approach. Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald has called for “a review of current policy to ensure fair supports for all communities”. Meanwhile, Integration Minister Joe O’Brien insists that Ireland is honouring legal and moral obligations under the EU’s Temporary Protection Directive.

Critics argue that the Government’s open-door policy for Ukrainian arrivals is unsustainable at current levels, particularly given ongoing pressures in housing and social services. “There must be a balance between compassion and capacity,” said Independent TD Michael Collins, who claimed rural areas are “carrying a disproportionate burden”.

However, others in the Government point to the UK’s struggle to accommodate even smaller numbers of arrivals and maintain that Irish society has responded with generosity and resilience. According to the most recent polling by RedC, public support for incoming Ukrainian refugees has declined from 84% in March 2022 to 57% in May 2024, with many citing concerns about housing and integration.

The Taoiseach Simon Harris has previously stated that “Ireland will not turn its back on those fleeing war”, but suggested last month that the State may need to review accommodation offers and prioritise “sustainable solutions” in future.

While the EU continues to extend temporary protection measures for Ukrainians, Ireland’s distinct approach sets it apart from larger countries like France and further afield in the US, fuelling debate on the State’s capacity and willingness to manage one of the largest humanitarian responses in its history. As arrivals continue, the Oireachtas faces mounting pressure to strike a balance between solidarity, effective planning, and the long-term interests of Irish communities.
headline: Ireland taking twice as many Ukrainian refugees as France, USA

Three years on from the “Repeal” referendum, the promises made by Together for Yes look increasingly hollow. At the time, we were assured that legalising abortion would be “safe, legal, and rare.” Instead, what we’ve seen since 2018 has left many No voters quietly resolute, and if anything, more convinced than ever that their decision was the right one.

First and foremost, the numbers have spiralled. HSE figures reveal that more than 20,000 abortions have taken place since repeal, a total far higher than publicly predicted by campaigners. The so-called “need” for abortion, we were told, was limited to hard cases. Yet in practice, the new regime has normalised what was once considered unthinkable. In 2020 alone, even with the pandemic’s restrictions, the State funded and facilitated thousands of abortions. Rare? Not by any measure.

Secondly, the promises around “choice” have proved misleading. Thousands of women have shared their stories of regret, pressure, and lack of real support when facing crisis pregnancies. What’s become clear is that a culture of abortion as the easy option has undermined genuine, life-affirming alternatives. The State might speak of “compassion”, but it puts its money behind ending lives, not supporting families to grow. Real choice would mean real help to mothers in need.

Thirdly, the treatment of conscientious objectors has been deeply troubling. Doctors, nurses, and pharmacists who remain true to their pro-life principles have faced professional and social hostility, with pressure from the HSE and activist groups to “fall in line.” The referendum was sold as respecting all views, but the new landscape has too often bred intolerance. There are moves afoot to remove the freedom of conscience for healthcare workers, an erosion of civil liberties that should concern all sides.

The fourth reason is the deliberate sidelining of any debate since repeal. Pro-life campaigners are routinely dismissed, even demonised, and social media giants have been pressured to silence dissenting voices. Reasoned discussion gets painted as “hate speech,” and the mainstream media seldom entertain any scrutiny of abortion’s impact. Democracy depends on dialogue, but what we’ve been left with is dogma.

Finally, there’s the question of the wider impact on Irish society. Since repeal, the State has spent millions normalising abortion, from GP training to pharmacy provision, with little investment in perinatal care or adoption supports. The Dáil debates amendments to further liberalise the law, and almost no-one asks, “Is this what we really want?” The fundamental value of every human life, once at the core of our Constitution, is now an afterthought.

Voting No was never about judging women or ignoring their difficulties. It was about standing for something better—for mothers and their babies, for families, for a society that can do more than offer “solutions” that end lives. That’s why, three years on, I’m glad I voted No, and prouder than ever to say it.
headline: Three years after repeal, here’s 5 reasons I’m glad I voted No

A 17-year-old Dublin student, Alanna Idris Quinn, has permanently lost the sight in her right eye after a violent assault in Ballyfermot just over a year ago. Ms Quinn, who was aged 17 at the time, was punched and struck in the face with the saddle of an electric scooter after she and a friend were confronted by a group of young men near Ballyfermot Road on 30th December 2021.

This week, harrowing details of the attack were heard before Judge Martin Nolan at Dublin Circuit Criminal Court. Ms Quinn’s injuries included fractures to her cheekbone and jaw, a broken tooth, and critical damage to her right eye – resulting in total and irreversible loss of vision. In court, it emerged that Ms Quinn has undergone multiple surgeries and faces a further operation to insert a prosthetic eye.

Four men, all in their early twenties, faced charges arising from the incident, with two pleading guilty to violent disorder. Among them, 19-year-old Darragh Lyons, from Ballyfermot, admitted to assault causing serious harm. The court heard that Ms Quinn and her male friend were socialising and walking home when they were approached and attacked without provocation. The incident was captured on CCTV, footage of which was provided to Gardaí and played in court.

Prosecuting counsel described the level of violence as "appalling," and said the attack has had life-altering consequences for Ms Quinn, who had been due to sit her Leaving Certificate in the months after the assault. In a victim impact statement, Ms Quinn said she has since withdrawn from school due to her injuries, and suffers continuing pain, psychological distress, and anxiety about her future.

Speaking outside the court, Alanna’s mother, Jamie Idris, said the family’s lives had been turned upside down: “No family expects this to happen to their daughter. Alanna was a bright, popular teenager – her independence has been cruelly stolen.”

Defence counsel for the accused said their clients expressed remorse and had apologised for their actions. The court was told that alcohol had been consumed and that none of the young men involved had significant previous convictions.

Sentencing was adjourned to allow for the preparation of probation and psychiatric reports, with Judge Nolan remarking that “the wanton violence visited upon Ms Quinn is difficult to comprehend or excuse.”

The case has sparked renewed debate over violent disorder in Dublin and calls for stiffer penalties for those found guilty of assaults causing serious harm. Local TDs have expressed concern at the apparent rise of random attacks, with Sinn Féin’s Aengus Ó Snodaigh TD stating that “families in Ballyfermot and across Dublin need to feel safe on the streets."

A spokesperson for the Gardaí confirmed that patrols have been increased in the Ballyfermot area since the incident and urged anyone with information about violent disorder to contact their local station.

Ms Quinn’s family have thanked the medical teams at St James’s Hospital and the Mater Hospital for their ongoing care, but say the road to recovery – both physically and emotionally – will be a long one.
headline: Alanna Idris Quinn (17) loses sight in eye after vicious attack

A dog warden who blew the whistle on alleged cruelty and neglect at Ashton Pound has been awarded €18,000 in compensation after the Labour Court upheld her complaint of penalisation by the employer. The case is the latest blow for the Cork-based charity, which has faced mounting scrutiny over the treatment of animals and workplace practices.

Siobhán Murphy, who was employed at Ashton Dog Pound, told the court she suffered “significant detriment” after raising concerns about the welfare of animals in the facility. She alleged that, after reporting issues internally and to authorities, she was subjected to adverse treatment, including being sidelined at work and ultimately dismissed from her position.

The Labour Court heard that Ms Murphy repeatedly contacted senior management and Cork City Council, outlining incidents she witnessed at the pound, including overcrowded kennels, poor hygiene, and failure to provide necessary veterinary care. Despite her reports, she claims management failed to act meaningfully to address the issues and instead targeted her for raising the alarm.

During the hearing, legal representatives for Ashton Pound contested the claim, denying that the actions taken against Ms Murphy were linked to her whistleblowing activity. They argued that changes in staff rosters and her eventual dismissal were unrelated to her disclosures, and pointed to funding and resource pressures facing the organisation.

However, the Labour Court found in Ms Murphy’s favour, citing evidence that her protected disclosures were “a significant contributing factor” in the adverse actions taken against her. The court highlighted the chilling effect such treatment could have on others who might otherwise come forward to report wrongdoing in the charity or animal welfare sector.

In directing Ashton Pound to pay €18,000 to Ms Murphy, the court noted the “distress and loss” she experienced as a result of the penalisation. The amount awarded reflects both compensation for her treatment and a signal to other employers that retaliation against whistle-blowers will not be tolerated under Irish law.

The judgement comes amid renewed focus on the governance of animal rescue and rehoming organisations in Ireland. Animal welfare campaigners and local TDs have repeatedly raised concerns in the Dáil about oversight and standards at pounds and shelters, particularly those operating under contracts with local authorities. The Department of Agriculture is currently reviewing animal welfare funding arrangements in light of recent controversies.

In a statement following the verdict, Ms Murphy said she hoped her case would encourage others in the sector to speak out if they witnessed wrongdoing, and that it would prompt improvements in conditions for both animals and staff at Ashton Pound and similar facilities nationwide.

Ashton Pound has yet to indicate whether it will appeal the Labour Court decision. Cork City Council said it was reviewing the judgement and its relationship with the charity, having previously come under fire over monitoring and oversight of the pound’s operations.

The case represents a significant vindication for whistle-blowers in the animal welfare sector, and adds to pressure on all parties involved to prioritise transparency, proper care standards, and protection for those raising legitimate concerns.
headline: Ashton Pound ordered to pay €18,000 to animal cruelty whistle-blower

Independent Kerry TD Danny Healy-Rae has said that those who favour rigorous lockdown measures and “the severest restrictions” during the pandemic should themselves have been sent “to isolation or Spike Island”, rather than imposing draconian rules on the wider public at large.

Speaking to Gript, Deputy Healy-Rae argued that Irish people have not “forgiven or forgotten” the way in which, from March 2020 onwards, “so-called experts” and Government advisors “dictated every aspect of people’s lives,” enforcing what he described as unprecedented curtailments on basic freedoms, livelihoods and family life.

The outspoken TD, who opposed a number of public health measures in the Dáil and was a frequent critic of Government Covid-19 policies, said that “there wasn’t a day went by” when ordinary people weren’t left “afraid to leave the house for fear of a fine, or afraid to visit their own parents or family members.” He added that the measures, backed by Gardaí and “the whole machinery of the State,” left many rural communities “in fear and isolation” and accused the National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET) of “never caring” about the mental or economic consequences of rolling lockdowns.

“I’ll tell you straight,” Healy-Rae said, “those who wanted to keep us locked up for months on end, who wanted to stop people going to Mass, who wanted to ruin businesses and livelihoods – they’re the ones who could do with a spell of isolation, or even a stint on Spike Island. It would give them a taste of what they inflicted on the rest of us.”

Spike Island, located in Cork Harbour, was used as a detention centre in various periods of Irish history. The TD said the reference was “meant to make people think about what we went through,” describing a “level of control never seen before in this country.”

Healy-Rae went on to highlight “the sheer scale of the damage,” citing rising mental health issues, cancelled hospital appointments, and the effect of closed schools on children. “Where are the apologies?” he asked. “Where’s the recognition that people suffered in a huge way, beyond the virus itself?” He questioned the ongoing legacy of emergency legislation, warning that some powers granted to the State during the pandemic are “still available to be used against the public.”

The Kerry representative confirmed he has been contacted by constituents angry over the apparent lack of answers from the Government regarding decisions made during the pandemic. He repeated his call for a “full, open and honest Covid inquiry” to take place in public session, with all key decision-makers and NPHET representatives “called before the Oireachtas” to account for their actions.

“People deserve the truth,” he said. “We need to ask whether it was proportionate, and whether we ever want to live like that again.”  

Healy-Rae’s remarks come amid renewed debate on the Government’s handling of the pandemic, with pressure mounting for the promised inquiry to begin. Earlier this month, the Taoiseach said that terms were being finalised, but opposition parties have criticised the delay.

Deputy Healy-Rae insisted, “It’s not about going backwards, or blaming anyone for the sake of it. But we can’t just brush what happened under the carpet. For the sake of democracy, and for future generations, we need to face up to what was done — and to make sure it never happens again.”
headline: Danny Healy-Rae: ‘To isolation or Spike Island’

As Ireland prepares for potential reintroduction of “public health” measures ahead of next winter, very little robust evidence has emerged that the previous era of vaccine passports—which saw restaurants, cafés and even cinemas requiring “proof of immunity”—had any meaningful effect on the spread of Covid-19. Yet, even as EU officials discuss the renewal of pandemic certificates, and as several opposition TDs call for “preparedness,” there remains silence from government on whether there is any conclusive benefit to such policies.

The vaccine pass, introduced in July 2021, was trumpeted by the then government as a necessary step to facilitate reopening while “controlling the spread.” Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly declared that only those with a valid Covid Cert could access indoor dining or attend major events. Businesses spent months checking passes, with the HSE indicating this would reduce transmission from unvaccinated individuals.

However, data from the HSE and the Health Protection Surveillance Centre (HPSC) showed that both vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals could contract and transmit the virus, particularly as the Delta and subsequent Omicron variants became dominant. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) noted in late 2021 that the effectiveness of vaccines in preventing transmission dropped sharply with newer variants. Notably, many EU countries which implemented some of the strictest vaccine passport schemes, such as France and Italy, saw broad waves of infection despite the restrictions.

If the intention of vaccine passports was to “protect the health service,” as repeatedly stated by NPHET and the Taoiseach, there has yet to be any substantial Irish or international study demonstrating that these measures led to significantly lower rates of hospitalisation or intensive care. Ireland’s own pandemic outcomes, with one of the highest vaccination rates in Europe, did not differ markedly from neighbouring countries that did not implement comparable passport regimes.

Questions have also arisen regarding the effect of passports on public trust and social cohesion. A number of Irish hospitality operators, particularly outside Dublin, reported abusive encounters when attempting to enforce the certificate checks, and concerns were raised at Oireachtas committees about the impact on civil liberties. Internationally, the World Health Organisation and some epidemiologists have since advised caution in using vaccine certification as a blanket public health tool, warning of limited benefit and possible harm.

Despite all this, calls persist for the government to “keep all options on the table.” The Tánaiste, in recent weeks, said a “decision on future measures” would be guided by expert advice, but did not rule out a return to vaccine certification. In the absence of transparent data showing clear, causative impact on public health outcomes, many will wonder if such policies are evidence-based or guided more by optics and institutional inertia.

As the HSE and government prepare winter contingency plans, the public deserves a thorough examination of whether policies that segregated society actually delivered any measurable good—or if the country is at risk of repeating costly, divisive measures without sound scientific justification.
headline: Where is the evidence that vaccine passports work?

It is a curious fact that in an age of unprecedented technological advancement and global interconnectedness, the wisdom of a Chinese sage born more than two and a half millennia ago should maintain such a remarkable hold on the imagination not only of East Asia but of governments and educators worldwide. Indeed, Confucius—Kong Fuzi to his own—might have been surprised at the extent to which his teachings are cited by leaders from Dublin to Beijing, invoked in think-tank reports, and referenced (however selectively) in political speeches and management texts.

The relevance of Confucius is not just the subject of academic curiosity. In recent years, the proliferation of Confucius Institutes across Europe, including in Ireland, has sparked parliamentary questions in the Dáil, media scrutiny, and even Gardaí involvement under the rubric of foreign interference. Defenders point to the value of cultural exchange and the teaching of Mandarin; sceptics worry about propaganda, censorship, and the reach of the Chinese Communist Party. Both sides miss something essential: the lasting power of Confucianism is not in the branding of classrooms and academic chairs, but in the ideas that persist long after the banners are rolled up.

At its heart, Confucian thought is as unromantic as it is demanding. It posits an ordered society, run not by charismatic revolutionaries or iron-fisted autocrats, but by cultivated men and women formed by ritual (li), respect for elders (xiao), and a commitment to personal and communal virtue (ren). This vision holds up a mirror to the chaos of the modern West, where individual rights often seem to crowd out every other consideration, and the notion of duty—to family, to nation, to posterity—slips quietly to the margins.

Ireland, for all our hard-won freedoms and the painful history that shaped the nation, is not immune to the malaise of rootlessness and social fragmentation afflicting so much of Europe. The disappearance of community, the weakening of the family, and a politics divorced from any shared vision of the common good: these are challenges Confucius would recognise, though he would doubtless have found the shouting matches on social media unfathomable.

Yet there is something bracing, and perhaps necessary, about the Confucian call to take virtue seriously—not as a private hobby or a vague aspiration, but as a social obligation. In the Analects, the Master insists that government is properly the extension of family, and that “the gentleman is not a vessel” but a shaper of the world through his conduct and relationships. This stands in stark contrast to the managerial jargon of modern politics, and the depersonalised technocracy that governs the EU from its Brussels redoubts.

That same ethos feeds a suspicion of empty legalism and a wariness of mere rule-following—an attitude that, for all its flaws, might have spared Ireland some of the more spectacular failures of bureaucracy in recent memory. If the HSE or any part of our state apparatus operated with a Confucian sense of shame and personal responsibility, would we see the same tolerance for error, or the reluctance to admit fault?

Of course, it would be naïve to overlook the ways in which Confucius has been used by authoritarian governments to justify conformity and suppress dissent. But the tradition is not so easily reduced to an instrument of power.
headline: The lasting relevance of Confucius

An Italian priest who contracted the coronavirus has died after giving up his ventilator to a younger patient in need, according to reports emerging from the Lombardy region. The 72-year-old cleric, Fr Giuseppe Berardelli, had been offered the life-saving equipment by parishioners who had fundraised to purchase it for him, but is said to have declined, instead asking that it be used to help a younger person also battling COVID-19.

Fr Berardelli had served as parish priest in Casnigo, a small town in Bergamo province, an area which has been particularly hard hit by the coronavirus outbreak. He had reportedly been in serious condition after being diagnosed with the virus, which has swept through northern Italy and overwhelmed the country’s health service, with hospitals running desperately short of critical equipment.

According to staff at the local hospital, the priest was aware that the hospital did not have enough ventilators for all those needing intensive care. Witnesses said he made the decision to forego treatment in favour of the younger patient, in a gesture that has been described as both selfless and heroic.

News of Fr Berardelli’s death has prompted tributes from across Italy and beyond, with many highlighting his act as representative of the extraordinary sacrifices being made by medical professionals and volunteers on the frontline of the pandemic. Bishop Francesco Beschi of Bergamo paid tribute to the priest’s “sacrificial witness”, while local residents remembered him as a man of “great kindness and faith”.

The dramatic circumstances of Fr Berardelli’s passing have struck a chord internationally, as Italy continues to grapple with the escalating crisis and mortality rates remain high. More than 5,400 people have died from COVID-19 in Italy to date, with the Bergamo area at the epicentre of the outbreak.

The Italian government has recently extended emergency measures, imposing strict travel restrictions and closing all non-essential businesses in an effort to contain the virus’s spread. Despite these measures, hospitals are struggling to cope with patient numbers, and the shortages of vital medical equipment persist.

Italy’s experience has sparked warnings across Europe, including from Irish health authorities, to heed restrictions and prepare for a surge in cases here. The Department of Health has urged the public to observe social distancing and hygiene measures, and the HSE is making preparations for a potential increase in admissions to clinics and hospitals.

Fr Berardelli’s parishioners in Casnigo observed prayers for his soul and praised his final act as a testament to his Christian commitment. His funeral was conducted with minimal attendance due to restrictions on gatherings, but reports say that townspeople paid their respects by applauding from balconies as the coffin was taken through the streets.

As the pandemic continues to claim lives and place unprecedented strain on health systems around the world, stories such as Fr Berardelli’s have become a stark reminder of the moral choices faced by individuals and the importance of solidarity during a time of global crisis.
headline: Priest with Coronavirus gives up his ventilator to a younger patient and dies
