Fine Gael’s Regina Doherty has this week stepped back into the limelight to warn ominously of the so-called “gender pay gap”, calling for renewed government action against “inequality” in the workplace. It seems the former Minister has chosen to dust off a well-worn script beloved of progressive campaigners, without pausing to question whether the statistics justify the sense of crisis being peddled.

For years now, political parties and a large swathe of the media have treated the “gender pay gap” as if it were beyond dispute that Irish women are systematically underpaid for the same work as their male counterparts. This narrative, conveniently, is rarely challenged in public debate, even though the Central Statistics Office itself has confirmed repeatedly that the headline “pay gap” statistic simply measures the difference between average earnings of men and women overall—not the difference in pay for the same job with the same qualifications and the same hours.

Doherty’s intervention relies on the discredited claim that women “earn less than men”, glossing over the reality that differences in average pay arise mainly from differences in hours worked, occupations chosen, and years of experience. Numerous reputable studies, including those by the European Commission, have found that when like is compared with like—when all relevant factors such as job type, education and experience are controlled for—the so-called “gap” all but vanishes. In other words, men and women in Ireland are already paid the same for the same work.

Yet facts appear to matter little when the politics of grievance are so profitable. For politicians hoping to burnish their progressive credentials, the pay gap myth provides a handy stick with which to beat employers and to demand ever more expansion of costly bureaucratic oversight. In 2022, the government introduced mandatory gender pay gap reporting for Irish firms, a move cheered on by groups like the National Women’s Council. Predictably, the first round of figures confirmed what was already widely known—no evidence of widespread, deliberate discrimination exists.

It is worth asking why Doherty and others persist in framing the issue as “paying women less”, when the real issues—childcare costs, part-time work and career choices—are much more complex and nuanced. Is it because confronting these factors would require political courage, and perhaps an acceptance that not every statistical disparity is a result of unfairness or sexism? Or is it that the narrative of oppression is just too useful to let go?

The result is a policy environment increasingly obsessed with identity politics at the expense of evidence-based decision-making. Businesses are forced to allocate resources to producing reports that prove what we already know, while genuine issues that might foster prosperity for women and men—affordable housing, family supports, and investment in skills—are left on the long finger.

Doherty, like many of her colleagues in Leinster House, appears more interested in competing for progressive credibility than in grappling honestly with social and economic realities. By resuscitating the feminist pay gap myth yet again, she does a disservice to public debate and to the goal of genuine equality. Ireland deserves better than policies built on half-truths and slogans. If the government wants to help working women, it should start by treating them—and the Irish public in general—as adults, capable of understanding the full picture, rather than feeding them the same tired myths.
headline: Regina Doherty revives feminist pay gap myth

Leo Varadkar’s position within Fine Gael, and indeed as Taoiseach, has rarely been so openly scrutinised as it is now. Recent weeks have seen both internal dissent and external criticism intensify, with questions swirling around whether Varadkar retains the confidence of his own parliamentary party. The abysmal results in successive opinion polls, combined with a prevailing sense among party members that Fine Gael is adrift, have raised the inevitable: is Leo safe as leader?

The latest figures make grim reading for party loyalists. Fine Gael’s poll numbers have consistently trailed Sinn Féin, with the government parties collectively struggling to reach support levels seen prior to the 2020 general election. The electorate’s disillusionment appears particularly acute on issues of immigration, housing, and law and order—areas where grassroots members are privately saying the government has lost the run of itself. It is no secret that the local and European elections in June are now viewed as a make-or-break moment for Varadkar’s leadership.

TDs spoken to by Gript, on condition of anonymity, emphasise that patience is wearing thin among the parliamentary ranks. “There’s a sense that the party isn’t being listened to, that the leadership doesn’t understand where the public mood is,” one rural FG TD commented. “If we get hammered in June, it’s hard to see how Leo stays on.” Several cited the government’s handling of the recent crisis at the International Protection Office on Sandwith Street, along with the increasingly visible anti-immigration protests, as proof that the Taoiseach is out of touch with ordinary voters.

Varadkar, for his part, has doubled down on Fine Gael’s centrist, liberal-progressive branding. His recent Dáil speeches have shown little sign of shifting to address the party’s critics. There’s a stubborn, even ideological, refusal to acknowledge the scale of opposition to the government’s asylum and migration policies. Some party veterans remember a time when Fine Gael saw itself as the voice of rural and small-town Ireland: Varadkar’s embrace of social-liberal talking points, they argue, has alienated that traditional base.

What matters now is whether those grumbles turn to open revolt. The party has always had a pragmatic instinct for self-preservation; leaders from Garret FitzGerald to Enda Kenny have been dispatched with little ceremony when the numbers turned. Despite that history, Varadkar’s own calculation seems to rest on the lack of a viable alternative—the would-be challengers, Simon Coveney and Paschal Donohoe, are either tainted by association or lack the appetite for a civil war. The party’s younger, up-and-coming TDs are yet to build the networks needed for a tilt at the leadership.

Nevertheless, history shows that when it comes to crunch time, Fine Gael TDs tend to prioritise their own seats before loyalty to the leader. Many will be watching June’s results with a keen eye for the direction of the political wind. Should the party’s share collapse below the already poor showings, a heave against Varadkar could move from private mutterings to public action in a matter of days.

Varadkar himself has shown little inclination to back down or alter course, brushing aside criticism with the familiar confidence that has so often defined his career.
headline: Is Varadkar safe as FG leader?

Pharmaceutical company Moderna has announced that it is advancing clinical trials for a potential HIV vaccine utilising its pioneering mRNA technology, the same platform that underpinned its Covid-19 vaccine. According to company statements, early-phase studies are underway with initial results expected to be released within the coming year. The news has prompted global interest and cautious optimism among public health specialists, who have long struggled against the persistent challenge of HIV/AIDS.

The development comes after decades of failed attempts to produce a reliable vaccine for HIV, a virus which continues to affect millions worldwide and remains a significant issue in both Western countries and the developing world. Moderna’s approach, leveraging messenger RNA technology, aims to instruct the body’s immune system to recognise and fight the virus if exposed.

Researchers say that one of the unique hurdles to creating an HIV vaccine is the virus’s tendency to mutate rapidly, evading traditional vaccine responses. The mRNA platform offers the potential for more adaptable vaccines, which can be modified more swiftly in response to emerging viral variants. Early data from phase 1 trials, which began in the United States late last year, indicate that the vaccine candidate is safe and induces a measurable immune response in recipients, although it remains too soon to confirm its efficacy in preventing HIV infection.

The centres of HIV infection and activism, including those in Ireland, have taken note of the developments. The HSE recorded over 500 new HIV diagnoses in Ireland in 2023, a figure broadly stable over the last five years, and advocacy organisations here have highlighted the urgent need for new prevention strategies. Speaking to Gript, a spokesperson for HIV Ireland said, “A vaccine has always been the holy grail for the HIV community. If the mRNA approach yields results, it could transform the global response to HIV.”

Irish researchers are observing the international trials closely, with the National Virus Reference Laboratory at UCD confirming ongoing collaboration with European partners. Dr Lorraine O’Gorman, a virologist at Trinity College Dublin, notes that while progress is encouraging, any potential roll-out would be years away and dependent on successful, large-scale clinical trials. “While the science behind mRNA gives us hope, caution is necessary before we talk about timelines or eradication,” Dr O’Gorman warned.

Moderna’s technology drew widespread acclaim during the Covid-19 pandemic, when the company’s vaccine was rolled out at scale in Ireland and globally. Many scientists believe the platform’s flexibility could revolutionise not only HIV prevention but also vaccines for flu, cytomegalovirus, and other infectious diseases.

Nevertheless, some have raised concerns about the potential for pharmaceutical companies to dominate the market and about equitable access, especially in lower-income countries most affected by HIV. The company has committed to “broad global access” should the vaccine prove successful, but activists remain sceptical until details of pricing and distribution are confirmed.

For now, the world’s attention remains fixed on the results of Moderna’s upcoming trials. Should the mRNA approach prove effective, it could mark a significant turning point in the long fight against HIV/AIDS. Irish public health authorities and advocacy groups alike will be watching developments with a mixture of hope and hard-earned prudence.
headline: Moderna developing vaccine for HIV using mRNA technology

With the leadership of Fine Gael hanging in the balance following Leo Varadkar’s shock resignation, one name has leapt to the front of the pack: Simon Harris. At just 37 years old, the Minister for Further and Higher Education is being spoken of as the clear favourite, with many party insiders already counting the numbers and foretelling a coronation rather than a contest. But one has to ask: would Fine Gael be mad to make Harris their leader? The answer is a resounding yes.

The party is at a crossroads. After over a decade in government, its support has haemorrhaged, and its vote share at an all-time low. The party that once boasted a rural base, and attracted the middle ground, is now widely seen as a home for the Dublin urban professional and little else. The Varadkar years, for all the slick PR and international media fawning, left Fine Gael looking like an out-of-touch clique, more interested in rainbow-coloured Twitter avatars and the latest Brussels fashion than the concerns of ordinary Irish people. The results are plain for all to see: mass emigration, a housing crisis, out-of-control crime and a health service in perpetual crisis.

And now, as the party considers who should fill Varadkar’s shoes, the name being most touted is Harris—a man who, as Minister for Health, presided over the HSE’s mounting disasters, who became a social media fixture for his Covid monologues, and who has never encountered an EU policy he didn’t wholeheartedly endorse. Harris is the darling of a certain section of the media and the party’s liberal wing, but is he the man to win back the farmers, the small business owners, and the hard-pressed young families?

There is a certain madness in the idea that Fine Gael’s fortunes will be revived by doubling down on what has failed before. The party’s drift on issues like immigration, crime and the cost of living has alienated vast swathes of its traditional base. Harris’s instincts, as demonstrated time and again, are for more government, more Brussels, and more deference to the advice of “experts” and NGOs. In the face of public concerns about asylum seekers and lawlessness in Dublin, Harris’s response has been to scold the public rather than listen to them. It is the mentality that has pushed Fine Gael into the electoral gutter.

If Fine Gael are intent on further narrowing their appeal to the chattering classes of South Dublin, then yes, Harris is their man. But if they have any interest in reconnecting with the voters who made them the largest party in the country for decades, they would do well to look elsewhere. The Irish public are weary of managerial technocrats reading from the same tired script. What’s needed—now more than ever—is a leader with the courage to speak plainly, admit past mistakes, and put the interests of Ireland and ordinary Irish people first.

A coronation for Harris might please the party’s HQ and the Twitterati, but it would be a disaster at the ballot box. If Fine Gael want to write their own obituary, crowning Simon Harris is the best way to do it.
headline: SCALLAN: Fine Gael would be mad to make Simon Harris leader

The Irish justice system once again stands accused of prioritising the so-called “rehabilitation” of violent offenders over the safety and wellbeing of the public, as news emerges that a teenager, convicted of a brutal rape at just 14 years of age, will be released at 21. This chilling case, which has left a trail of trauma in its wake, has reignited the debate about how our courts handle the most serious crimes, and whether the rights of victims and society are being trampled in a myopic pursuit of reforming young criminals.

Despite the severity of the crime—a vicious and premeditated act that has left lifelong scars—the judicial system appears determined to draw a line under the matter in just a few short years. The offender, now shielded from public scrutiny by strict reporting restrictions due to his age at the time of the offence, will be free to walk among us before he is even old enough to hire a car.

One has to ask: what message does this send to victims, to their families, and to society at large? Where is the deterrence, the sense that justice is being done? Instead, we are told that the system must focus on “second chances” and that a young age absolves one of ultimate responsibility. Are we so sure of our ability to “turn lives around” that we are willing to gamble with the safety of others?

This is not an isolated incident. Across Ireland, we have seen a pattern emerge where those found guilty of the most serious, life-altering crimes are routinely given sentences that seem, to ordinary Irish people, grossly insufficient. All the while, victims are left to live with the consequences, often denied any sense of closure or justice.

Is it any wonder that public confidence in the courts is at an all-time low? Victims and their advocates have repeatedly voiced their concerns, but these are regularly brushed aside in favour of academic theories about rehabilitation and reintegration. Politicians, meanwhile, seem content to wring their hands and take shelter behind “separation of powers”, avoiding any meaningful scrutiny of sentencing policy or legislation that would put victims’ rights at the centre of the system.

There is, of course, a place for rehabilitation, for second chances and redemption. But it is not unreasonable to ask whether someone capable of such a violent act should have to prove themselves worthy of that second chance over a much longer period, rather than being released while still barely an adult.

As the debate continues, the voices of those most directly affected—the victims—are conspicuously absent from the decision-making process. Instead, academic and legal elites speak in abstract terms about reform, rarely pausing to consider the devastated lives left behind by such crimes.

Unless the Oireachtas finds the backbone to address the balance between rights of victims and offenders, the cycle will continue. For now, the rest of us are left to wonder exactly how safe our streets are when those who commit the most heinous acts are so quickly afforded their freedom.
headline: The boy who brutally raped at 14 will be just 21 when he gets out

Most Irish citizens assume that the State keeps some kind of basic tabs on who comes into the country and for how long they are meant to stay. When the Government says a ‘stamp’ has an expiry date, the average person would believe there’s at least some mechanism for making sure that when that date arrives, the person either renews their visa or leaves. However, documents released to Gript under FOI reveal that the Department of Justice cannot say, with any confidence, what actually happens to thousands of migrants and international students once their permission lapses.

The email exchange, dating to early February 2024 between Department officials, explicitly states: “We do not have a tracking mechanism for people whose permissions expire. We are not in a position to know if they then leave, overstay, or regularise via other means.” This comes from the very section tasked with overseeing immigration permissions and is an astonishing admission for any country, but it is particularly jarring here, where immigration is now a major issue among the public—and a running sore for the Government.

The context is vital. In recent years, the number of people arriving to the State on study, work, or short-term visas has soared. The expectation is that these individuals will respect their permission and depart when their time is up. But as the Department’s own staff say, “there is no automated outbound check” at ports or airports. In practice, someone could simply melt away into the population.

If this were a small number, perhaps some might argue the impact is limited. But as of last year, over 20,000 non-EEA students were registered at Irish institutions. The number of non-EU nationals with short-term work permits continues to rise. Even before the recent asylum surge, the Department was repeatedly warned by the Comptroller and Auditor General about failings in the system to monitor overstays.

The standard political response is that Ireland’s “friendly” Common Travel Area with the UK, and “open” approach to movement, are part of our charm and advantage. But that position is wearing thin as the State struggles with a severe housing shortage, pressure on public services, and what is now acknowledged across Europe as a border crisis. Ireland, we are told, must “do its bit”—but there is little appetite among the Government to discuss the consequences.

Notably, the current Tánaiste, Micheál Martin, has said in the Dáil that “our immigration system is robust” and “continually reviewed.” These FOI documents suggest otherwise. Behind the scenes, officials admit that the basic information of who is still, legally, in the country is simply not available.

For years, Ministers have dismissed concerns about overstaying as “scaremongering.” Today, with border controls in disarray and public confidence at a low ebb, the Government’s insistence that “all is in order” rings hollow.

If you have ever wondered how it is that people fall out of the system, remain for years without status, or only turn up again when seeking leave to remain, now you have your answer: the State doesn’t know, doesn’t check, and doesn’t seem to care. Until that changes, calls for a serious debate on immigration policy will only grow louder.
headline: We don’t have a clue if people leave when visas expire says Department

International hopes have risen for a further extension of the fragile truce between Israel and Hamas, after another group of hostages was released in Gaza overnight. The latest exchange, the sixth since the ceasefire began last Friday, saw 12 hostages, including two dual nationals, returned to Israel in exchange for 30 Palestinian detainees freed from Israeli prisons.

The temporary halt in fighting, brokered by Qatar, Egypt, and the United States, has brought a tentative calm to the besieged territory after seven weeks of conflict. The Israeli Government confirmed the latest group of hostages had been safely brought back from captivity and were undergoing medical evaluation. Many had been held in Gaza since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7th, which sparked the most severe round of violence in the region in years.

Negotiations are continuing over a fresh extension to the truce, after both sides signalled a willingness to consider further releases. An Israeli government spokesperson said there remained “the possibility of an additional day or more”, provided Hamas could identify more women and children to be freed. The Qatari foreign ministry said mediators were in close contact with both parties in the hope of prolonging the pause in hostilities.

The Palestinian Red Crescent reported that much-needed aid had continued to flow into Gaza during the cessation of fighting, but warned that the level of humanitarian relief remained far below urgent needs. The United Nations has called the situation in the enclave “catastrophic”, with the population facing severe shortages of food, water, and medical supplies.

In Dublin, the Minister for Foreign Affairs, Micheál Martin, welcomed the release of hostages and detainees as “a positive step”, and reiterated the Government’s call for “an immediate and sustained ceasefire leading to renewed dialogue and a political solution”. The Department of Foreign Affairs confirmed that officials remain engaged with EU and international partners on the crisis.

However, there is continuing uncertainty over how long the truce can hold. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has repeatedly stated that military operations will resume in Gaza once the pause concludes, vowing to “eliminate Hamas’ capabilities”. Hamas, meanwhile, insists further exchanges must form part of a broader ceasefire agreement.

The initial truce was originally due to end on Monday but has been extended in increments as negotiators have secured further releases. More than 100 hostages have now been freed, and over 200 Palestinian prisoners released.

International observers say the extension of the pause remains delicately balanced. With mounting international pressure for a longer-term cessation of violence, diplomats warn that a return to conflict would have grave consequences for civilians on both sides. As hopes remain pinned on the fragile negotiations, families in Israel and Gaza alike are waiting anxiously for news of their loved ones’ fate.
headline: Hopes for extension of Israel-Hamas truce as more hostages released

A legal challenge has been lodged in Belfast’s High Court against the UK Government’s contentious Northern Ireland legacy legislation, with applicants arguing that the new act is incompatible with the European Convention on Human Rights and undermines victims’ rights.

The Legacy Act, officially known as the Northern Ireland Troubles (Legacy and Reconciliation) Act, came into force earlier this year despite widespread opposition from victims’ groups, political parties across the island, and the Irish Government. It moves to end all inquests, civil actions, and criminal prosecutions relating to conflict-era killings and instead establishes a new Independent Commission for Reconciliation and Information Recovery.

Solicitors representing the bereaved families claim the act violates Article 2 of the European Convention—protecting the right to life—and obstructs proper investigation of historic crimes. Families of victims have expressed outrage, saying the legislation shuts down avenues to justice that they have pursued for decades.

The legal proceedings are being brought forward by a group of individual families as well as advocacy organisations, backed by Amnesty International and the Committee on the Administration of Justice. A preliminary hearing was heard yesterday, with further dates expected to be scheduled over the summer.

Gráinne Teggart, Northern Ireland Deputy Director of Amnesty International, said, “This law prioritises the interests of the state over the rights of victims and families of those killed. It signals to perpetrators that they are above the law and denies families the truth and justice they so desperately seek.”

While the British Government maintains that the measures are necessary to allow Northern Ireland to move forward, the Irish Government has been vocal in its opposition. Taoiseach Simon Harris reiterated last week that his government “cannot accept any amnesty for serious offences,” and confirmed that the State is separately pursuing its own inter-state case against the Act at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.

The legislation has also drawn criticism from across the political spectrum in the Dáil, as well as from Sinn Féin, the SDLP, and Alliance in the North. Ulster Unionist and DUP leaders have also expressed concern about its impact on victims’ rights.

During Wednesday’s proceedings, counsel for the applicants argued that the Act deprives families of their right to effective investigations and that the new Commission lacks adequate powers to compel evidence or ensure accountability. The court heard that more than 30 ongoing inquests—many delayed for years—will now be terminated under the new framework.

A spokesperson for the Northern Ireland Office said the Government “remains confident that the Legacy Act complies with its international obligations and provides the best way to help society move beyond the legacy of the Troubles.”

The High Court is expected to issue directions on the management of the consolidated cases in the coming weeks, with substantive arguments anticipated in the autumn. In the meantime, families have pledged to continue their campaign for justice, insisting the fight is “far from over.”
headline: Legal challenge lodged over controversial Northern Ireland legacy legislation

Pop star Rita Ora was spotted enjoying a brief visit to Cork city this week before taking to the stage at a private event for Apple headquarters staff.

The British singer-songwriter, best known for hits including “Anywhere” and “Let You Love Me,” spent several hours soaking up the sights in the city centre on Tuesday. Ora is understood to have arrived early ahead of a scheduled performance at Apple’s European headquarters in Hollyhill.

A number of eagle-eyed fans shared images on social media of Ora walking along Oliver Plunkett Street and posing for photos near the English Market. Though the singer’s team kept her itinerary under wraps, sources confirmed she visited a number of local boutiques during her “short but sweet” stay.

Staff at a popular Cork café described Ora as “relaxed and friendly,” stopping for coffee and pastries with two members of her entourage. “She was really down to earth and happy to chat. She loved the vibe of the place and said the people here were so welcoming,” one employee said.

Later that evening, Ora performed an intimate set for Apple staff at the technology giant’s Hollyhill campus in what was described as a “morale-boosting” event. With Apple employing over 6,000 people in Cork, such private performances are a rare treat, and tickets were in high demand among employees.

Posting to Instagram after her visit, the singer wrote: “Had the best time in Cork — thank you for the warm welcome and good craic! Hope to be back soon.”

Ora, who has previously spoken of her love for Ireland, is expected to travel on to further engagements in London and Paris later this week as part of her European tour.

Her visit comes as Cork continues to draw major international stars, both for public appearances and exclusive corporate events. Local tourism representatives welcomed the attention, with one commenting: “Every time a major artist spends time in Cork, it helps to highlight all the city has to offer. We’re delighted to see performers of Rita Ora’s calibre enjoying what’s unique about Cork.”

Ora’s fleeting trip marks the latest in a string of high-profile celebrity visits to the city, with recent months also seeing Ed Sheeran and Saoirse Ronan making headlines during their own stints in the Rebel County.
headline: Rita Ora spends 'short' stint exploring Cork ahead of Apple HQ gig

Raja Shehadeh’s reflection brings into sharp focus the gulf between the longed-for peace of the past and the daily reality now faced by Palestinians. For those of us watching from Ireland — itself no stranger to the painful legacies of partition, conflict, and contested land — the descent from hope to despair in the Holy Land is both painfully familiar and profoundly sobering.

Ireland’s own history of negotiation, intermittent violence, and the eventually hard-won compromises of the Good Friday Agreement give us both a sense of the potential for resolution and the fragility of peace. The Oslo Accords in the 1990s were an echo of such possibility for Israel and Palestine. Shehadeh’s memories recall a time when the international community, including successive Irish governments, invested diplomatic energy in supporting a two-state solution. Irish civil society, too, marched and lobbied for dialogue, humanitarian aid, and recognition of Palestinian rights.

Yet hopes have been repeatedly dashed with every cycle of violence, expansion of settlements, and breakdown in talks. The recent bloodshed in Gaza and Israel, with soaring civilian casualties and retaliatory rocket barrages, has made stark the terrible cost of a peace process left moribund. Families mourning in Rafah and Tel Aviv, and images of destruction streamed into Irish sitting rooms, bring home the very personal consequences of diplomatic failure and political intransigence.

Shehadeh’s account is crucial because it refuses the comforting distance of abstraction. He reminds us that the people living this conflict are not merely victims or combatants, but communities once buoyed by hope — parents, students, shopkeepers who sought ordinary lives. Their despair today is a direct response to broken promises: the international community’s inability or unwillingness to enforce agreed frameworks; the relentless expansion of settlements; and the steady disappearance of the space for negotiation and trust.

Ireland, as a small neutral country with its own experience of peace-building, has continued to advocate at the United Nations and within the EU for adherence to international law and the protection of civilians. The recognition of Palestine as a state by the Dáil this year is both a symbolic act and a call to others to take practical steps in support of negotiations, human rights, and reconstruction.

But as Shehadeh implies, gestures alone, however principled, cannot rebuild the edifice of hope. If Ireland’s own history tells us anything, it is that peace is not simply the absence of violence, but constant, painstaking work: sustained dialogue, the inclusion of all sides, and guarantees that the agreements reached will be honoured. The current moment demands not only humanitarian aid but a renewal of political will for real engagement — from Israelis and Palestinians, and from the wider international community.

Without this, Shehadeh’s painful question — how did it come to this? — risks becoming not just a reflection on the past, but a grim prophesy for the future. For the sake of those living the consequence of this conflict, and for all who dare to hope for peace, that must not be allowed to happen.
headline: Raja Shehadeh: I remember when Palestinians dared to hope for peace. How did it come to this?

Former Taoiseach Leo Varadkar has paid tribute to the United States’ pioneering activism on LGBT rights, saying he doubts he would have come out publicly as gay without “the path that America forged.”

Speaking at an event in Dublin to mark the 55th anniversary of the Stonewall Riots, Mr Varadkar acknowledged the profound influence the US civil rights movement had on Ireland’s journey towards LGBT equality. “I don’t think I’d be here today – not just as a former Taoiseach, or a public figure, but as an openly gay man – if it wasn’t for the work that was done by activists, campaigners, and ordinary people in America,” he told the audience gathered at the Mansion House.

Mr Varadkar, who was Ireland’s first openly gay head of government, referenced milestones such as the decriminalisation of homosexuality in Ireland in 1993, the civil partnership legislation of 2010, and the landmark marriage equality referendum in 2015. He said progress in the US, particularly legal victories and the visibility of LGBT leaders, gave Irish campaigners a sense of what was possible and inspired change at home.

“We saw court rulings in America, we watched people like Harvey Milk, Ellen DeGeneres, and so many others speak out,” he said. “That had a profound impact, even in a small country thousands of miles away. It made people like me realise there was a different way to live, that there was nothing wrong with us, and that we deserved equal respect.”

He recalled travelling to New York as a young medical student and experiencing the city’s “out and proud” LGBT culture, which contrasted with the more conservative Ireland of the late 1990s and early 2000s. “I remember standing in Christopher Street, looking at the Stonewall Inn, and thinking about how brave those people must have been. It made it seem possible, though not easy, to come out in Ireland.”

Mr Varadkar came out as gay in 2015 while serving as Minister for Health, ahead of the marriage equality referendum. He has regularly cited the support of family and friends, as well as the growing climate of acceptance in Ireland, but said US developments had provided a crucial blueprint. “Ireland didn’t just import American TV shows or economics – we imported hope, visibility and the language of rights.”

The Fine Gael TD also noted ongoing challenges for the LGBT community in Ireland and worldwide. “Equality isn’t a destination, it’s a process,” he said. “There are still kids growing up here feeling isolated. There are trans people facing hostility. The lesson from America is that you have to keep pushing, and you can’t take rights for granted.”

He welcomed the recent appointment of Ireland’s first full-time LGBT rights envoy and called on the Department of Foreign Affairs to strengthen links with groups in the US and Europe. “Ireland has a role to play now too,” he said. “We can be a beacon, just as America was to us.”

The event, which was attended by senior politicians from across the Oireachtas, US Embassy officials, and local LGBT organisation representatives, also featured a panel discussion on the global future of LGBT rights. Tánaiste Micheál Martin praised Mr Varadkar’s leadership and said Ireland’s progress “stands as a testament to the power of international solidarity.”
headline: Leo Varadkar: I don't think I'd be here without America’s work on LGBT rights

text:
In the late 1980s, the American Dream was alive and well in our Irish households, beamed in through the cathode rays of Dallas, Dynasty, and Baywatch. America was not just a far-off land then, but a dazzling promise. Our streets were narrower, our weather grimmer, and the future felt as grey as the North Atlantic sky. America was colour TV—bigger, brighter, louder and, crucially, possible. 

When I was a teenager, the Leaving Cert results arrived with a sliver of hope that a J1 visa might follow, or maybe a Green Card if you were lucky, or an au pair gig in Boston if you had a cousin willing to write a letter. I made my first trip in my twenties—New York laid out like a mythical board game, endless blocks and avenues, yellow taxis, Central Park, and the Statue of Liberty promising unlimited horizons. America was the place you went to stretch your ambition, especially if you were Irish and restless.

It was more than concrete and neon—America was mythic. We’d grown up with JFK on the mantelpiece, The Fields of Athenry on the radio, and stories of uncles and grandparents who’d escaped the stifling constraints of 1950s Ireland for a place where they might remake themselves. For many Irish, emigration was necessity, but it turned into romance. America was where you could become something else; a rebel, a success, a part of history.

But for my children, growing up in a different Ireland—one richer, more connected, more self-confident—the America of my imagination barely exists. Their notion of the US is filtered through the lens of TikTok, climate anxiety, mass shootings, and the January 6th insurrection. For them, it’s a country of deep contradictions, a place as likely to be feared as admired. 

They watch American politics drift into chaos—polarisation, conspiracy, vitriol, and gun violence that seems unimaginable here. My youngest, still in primary school, asks how it’s possible that children in America need “active shooter drills”, the phrase sounding as alien and chilling to her as air raid sirens did to my parents. My eldest, already climate-conscious, notes that the US is a leading carbon emitter, and that irony isn’t lost on her.

Gone, too, is that old excitement about a summer in Boston or Chicago. The J1, once a rite of passage for Irish students, is now just one option among many—Australia, Canada, or simply staying close to home. Cheap flights, Erasmus, and social media have brought the world to our doorstep. America isn’t the beacon it was; it’s just one country among many, no longer a singular escape hatch.

There’s a sadness in that, perhaps mostly for myself, in realising that something I once revered has lost its shine for this new generation. But there’s also relief. Ireland itself has changed—a country with choices, one where my children can hope for a future not only here, but on their own terms. The necessity of leaving, the longing for a better life far away, no longer defines us. We have a greater sense of what it means to belong, not just in America’s shadow, but under our own sky.

Where once the American Dream was a necessity, now it is an option—and often, not the first choice.
headline: Jennifer Horgan: My children will never see America as I did

text:
Sinn Féin members have voted on a series of contentious issues including hare coursing, cannabis legalisation, and the party’s stance on political prisoners, at its Ard Fheis in Athlone this weekend.

The annual gathering, which drew several hundred delegates from across the island, saw lively debate on animal welfare, drug policy, and legacy issues stemming from the conflict in the North.

A motion to support a ban on hare coursing was carried after a robust exchange on the floor, with delegates citing concerns for animal welfare and the party’s record on progressive social issues. In her address, Sinn Féin spokesperson on animal welfare, Deputy Pauline Tully, described hare coursing as “outdated and cruel”, emphasising the “need for stronger protections for Ireland’s native wildlife”.

The decision is likely to draw criticism from coursing enthusiasts and rural sports groups, who have traditionally opposed any move to prohibit the practice. Sinn Féin’s rural affairs spokesperson, Matt Carthy TD, acknowledged the party’s challenge in balancing animal welfare and the traditions of rural communities, but said the position reflected “the evolving values of Irish society”.

Delegates also debated the legalisation of cannabis for personal use. The motion to support decriminalisation was narrowly defeated, with several speakers citing the dangers of drug misuse and the lack of adequate support services. However, the party reaffirmed its commitment to a health-led approach to drug addiction, with public support for additional resources for the HSE’s addiction services and a review of current drug laws.

On the issue of political prisoners, the Ard Fheis adopted a motion calling for the immediate release of what it described as “republican prisoners of conscience” in the North and Britain. The text, debated late on Saturday evening, reaffirms Sinn Féin's longstanding position on prisoners linked to legacy offences. Some senior figures, including Pearse Doherty TD, stressed the importance of supporting the Good Friday Agreement and the peace process, while others underlined what they termed the “unfinished business” of legacy justice.

The votes come as Sinn Féin prepares for an expected general election later this year, and at a time when the party faces renewed scrutiny over its past and policy positions. Party leader Mary Lou McDonald, addressing the Ard Fheis, said “Sinn Féin is ready for government”, but cautioned delegates that the party must remain “open to new ideas, while holding firm to our republican principles”.

Opposition parties have criticised Sinn Féin’s positions, with Labour’s Ivana Bacik TD calling on the party to clarify its policy on drug reform, and Fine Gael accusing Sinn Féin of “sending mixed messages” on rural issues.

The motions adopted at the Ard Fheis will now form part of Sinn Féin’s official policy platform going into election season, as the party seeks to broaden its appeal across rural and urban constituencies.
headline: Sinn Féin members vote on hare coursing, cannabis, and political prisoners

text:
The Irish Government’s latest package of immigration reforms, announced this week by the Department of Justice, has reignited public debate over the future direction of Irish society and the place of immigrants within it. Against a backdrop of escalating international protection applications, increasing political pressure, and recent high-profile protests directed at accommodation centres, the reforms have been presented as all but inevitable. Yet the scope and pace of the proposed changes raise urgent questions as to whether Ireland is at risk of abandoning its traditionally open, if cautious, approach in favour of a more exclusionary regime.

While the Taoiseach, Simon Harris, has framed the measures as a pragmatic response to an evolving European migration landscape, the content bears the stamp of rapid policymaking informed by fear as much as foresight. Proposals for accelerated deportation procedures, tighter eligibility criteria, and the controversial idea of so-called “processing centres” situated outside the State’s borders have unsettled not only advocacy groups but also some within coalition parties themselves.

It is essential to recognise the context: Ireland has experienced a surge in applications for international protection, with provisional figures showing a near-doubling since 2022. Local communities have felt the strain, and integration, especially in rural Ireland, remains an ongoing challenge. These pressures are real and deserve a policy response. But the spectre haunting the current debate is that of conflation: the risk that all immigrants, regardless of their reason for coming here, become caught in the crossfire of political reaction.

A nation forged by emigration, Ireland has long prided itself on its offering of céad míle fáilte. It is no mere cliché; up to now, this ethos has informed both policy and the everyday experience of newcomers. That welcome has not always been uncomplicated—the Direct Provision system and bottlenecks in family reunification have rightly drawn criticism—but the basic presumption has been one that distinguishes between those in need of protection, economic migrants, and the Irish diaspora returning home.

The proposed reforms threaten to upend this distinction. The tone of official communication has shifted palpably—from cautious welcome to guarded suspicion. The very language, invoking “abuse of the system” and the need to act as a “deterrent”, risks painting all immigrants with the same brush. There is a real danger that the immigrant, in the public imagination, becomes synonymous with crisis—rather than with the opportunity, dynamism, and demographic renewal that immigration brings.

Moreover, the involvement of the Gardaí in enforcing expedited removals, as outlined in the reforms, risks further eroding public trust and amplifying tensions. For immigrants already in Ireland, often contributing significantly to the economy and culture, the anxiety is palpable. Many of those individuals and families, who have built lives in Irish towns and cities, now face renewed uncertainty as they wait to see how these reforms will be implemented on the ground.

Legal analysts have pointed out that some elements of the proposed legislation may face challenge in the High Court or even at European level, particularly with respect to international obligations under the Refugee Convention and EU law. Yet the wider concern is not just about legalities; it is about the social fabric of the country.

If the current trajectory continues, Ireland could find itself joining a growing list of European countries where immigration policy has become a proxy battleground over national identity.
headline: Colin Sheridan: New reforms risk transforming what it means to be an immigrant in Ireland

Israeli naval forces have intercepted nearly half of the vessels attempting to reach Gaza as part of a humanitarian aid flotilla, according to organisers of the mission. The coalition of activists, which includes representatives from several European countries as well as Ireland, said on Monday that three out of seven ships had been stopped by the Israeli navy in international waters and were now being escorted toward the port of Ashdod.

Footage shared online showed commandos boarding the ships just north of Egyptian waters, with participants alleging the interceptions took place outside Israel’s declared maritime exclusion zone. Campaigners on board, some of whom include medical volunteers and politicians, asserted that their mission was strictly non-violent and intended to deliver desperately needed food, medicines and medical supplies to the besieged Gaza Strip.

Irish participants in the flotilla have called on the Government and the Department of Foreign Affairs to intervene, amid fears for the safety of those detained. The Sinn Féin TD John Brady, who has previously met flotilla organisers, described the move as “a clear violation of international law”, calling for the immediate release of the vessels and all on board. At least two Irish nationals are believed to be among the passengers.

The Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) said in a statement that their actions were necessary to “prevent unauthorised entry” into Gaza and to stop supplies that have not been vetted by Israeli authorities. The IDF insisted that the crews would be treated in accordance with international regulations before being deported.

Organisers said the intercepted ships were carrying hundreds of tonnes of aid, including baby formula, water purification tablets and wound dressings. They said the remaining four vessels have not yet reached the exclusion zone, but warned that they too risk being boarded.

Attempts by international activists to break the Israeli naval blockade on Gaza have been ongoing since 2010, when a similar mission — the Mavi Marmara — ended in fatal clashes. Since then, most aid destined for Gaza has been directed through the Egyptian border crossing at Rafah or the Israeli-controlled Kerem Shalom.

The Department of Foreign Affairs said it was providing consular assistance to Irish citizens involved with the flotilla, and reiterated the Government’s call for unimpeded humanitarian access to Gaza. The incident comes days after the Oireachtas passed a motion urging further EU action to alleviate the humanitarian crisis in the region.

The United Nations has repeatedly warned of looming famine in Gaza, where over 30,000 people have been killed since the outbreak of war last October. Aid agencies say restrictions at Israel’s border crossings and a lack of safe corridors have made it impossible to meet the basic needs of the strip’s population. 

As diplomatic pressure mounts, activists say they will continue making efforts to deliver aid by sea, insisting it is a vital channel in the face of ongoing land restrictions.
headline: Activists say Israeli navy has intercepted almost half of Gaza aid flotilla

text:
People Before Profit-Solidarity TD Paul Murphy has begun a High Court challenge aimed at preventing so-called super junior ministers from attending Cabinet meetings.

In proceedings launched on Tuesday, Deputy Murphy is seeking an order quashing Government decisions that have allowed three Ministers of State—Jack Chambers, Ossian Smyth, and Hildegarde Naughton—to attend meetings of the Cabinet. He contends this practice is unconstitutional and undermines the principle of collective Cabinet responsibility.

Under current arrangements, the trio hold the formal status of “super junior ministers,” permitting them to participate in Cabinet discussions, though they do not hold voting rights. Minister Chambers attends in relation to transport and climate policy, Minister Smyth for digital and communications policy, and Minister Naughton for government legislation.

Deputy Murphy, who represents Dublin South-West, argues in his statement of claim that the Constitution, specifically Article 28.4, restricts participation in Cabinet to full ministers, who collectively bear responsibility for decisions taken. He claims the attendance of super juniors dilutes this responsibility, as Ministers of State are not answerable in the same way and are not party to collective decision-making.

The case, against the State and the Government, was brought following the expansion of the number of super junior roles in recent years, which has drawn criticism from opposition parties and some constitutional law experts. The three current attendees are each paid an additional €17,205 on top of their ministerial salaries for their Cabinet role.

During the brief High Court hearing, Senior Counsel for Deputy Murphy, Michael Lynn, said the proceedings raise “important constitutional issues” about the functioning of government and the separation of powers. He stated that the presence of super juniors at Cabinet “represents an incremental erosion of constitutional protections.”

Counsel for the State argued in response that the Constitution does not explicitly bar Ministers of State from attending as observers and that only voting Cabinet members are involved in decision-making.

The court agreed to give the State several weeks to file a response. The case is expected to be heard in full later this year.

Speaking outside the Four Courts, Deputy Murphy said: “This is not about personalities, it’s about upholding the clear constitutional safeguards around Cabinet secrecy and collective responsibility. The Cabinet should be made up solely of responsible Ministers answerable to the Dáil, not expanded by political arrangement.”

The Attorney General’s office declined to comment, citing ongoing legal proceedings.

Cabinet composition has become increasingly contentious since the 2020 General Election, when the coalition agreed to appoint three super junior ministers with the right to attend Cabinet meetings, an apparent increase from previous governments. The opposition has argued the move was designed to satisfy internal party politics rather than public interest.

If Deputy Murphy’s challenge is successful, the Government could be compelled to change the way Cabinet meetings are conducted, with possible implications for current and future office holders. The case is watched closely across the political spectrum for any potential precedent it may set regarding Cabinet procedure.

The matter returns to the High Court on 16 July for directions.
headline: Paul Murphy takes High Court case to block super junior ministers from Cabinet meetings

At least 32 Palestinians have been killed and dozens more injured in Gaza after Israeli strikes and gunfire targeted crowds gathered near food distribution sites, according to local health officials. The incidents, which occurred in different areas across the north and centre of the besieged enclave on Saturday, come amid mounting warnings from aid organisations of catastrophic levels of hunger and desperation.

Dr Ashraf al-Qudra, spokesperson for Gaza’s health ministry, said most of the casualties were a result of Israeli shelling and live fire directed at civilians waiting to receive desperately needed food aid. “People are dying just trying to get a bag of flour,” he told reporters, adding that the number of people injured has risen past 50.

Eyewitnesses said hundreds had gathered in multiple locations where lorries carrying flour and other basic supplies were expected to arrive. “We receive alerts that food would be distributed. Everyone here is hungry. So, despite the danger, people come out because we have no choice,” said Mahmoud al-Hasna, a resident in northern Gaza.

Israel’s military stated it is investigating reports of civilian deaths in the area and reiterated its assertion that Hamas militants have been seizing aid and using civilian crowds as cover. However, United Nations officials have pointed to a breakdown in law and order and escalating violence along aid routes, which has hampered the delivery of relief to the hardest-hit neighbourhoods.

The latest violence comes on the back of repeated warnings by the UN and other humanitarian agencies that malnutrition and starvation are rife in Gaza after five months of intense conflict. Last week, the European Commission and the Department of Foreign Affairs both called for an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, urging Israel to ensure safe and unimpeded access for life-saving aid.

The Taoiseach, Leo Varadkar, described recent images from Gaza as “harrowing” and repeated Ireland’s calls for an end to the violence and for all parties to respect international law. “The Irish Government is appalled at the targeting of civilians and the ongoing suffering in Gaza,” he said.

More than 30,000 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the conflict last October, according to Gaza health officials, and the UN says at least 576,000 people in Gaza – a quarter of the population – are on the brink of famine.

Aid agencies including Médecins Sans Frontières and the World Food Programme have repeatedly warned that a “man-made famine” is unfolding. On Thursday, a team from the International Committee of the Red Cross said the levels of hunger they witnessed were “unprecedented in modern conflict”. 

Irish MEPs have urged the European Union to suspend arms exports to Israel and offer greater support for humanitarian operations. The Tánaiste, Micheál Martin, said he would raise the issue at the next meeting of EU foreign ministers, and reaffirmed Ireland’s commitment to increasing its humanitarian funding for Gaza.

The Israeli government has so far resisted calls for a ceasefire, insisting its operations target Hamas fighters and are necessary for national defence. However, international pressure has grown in recent days, with US President Joe Biden stating that insufficient aid is reaching civilians and that protection of non-combatants must improve immediately.

Meanwhile, daily life in Gaza remains dangerous and unpredictable as basic supplies run dangerously low and health infrastructure lies in ruins. Local hospitals, struggling with shortages and damage, say their workers are overwhelmed by both the scale of injuries and the growing number of children suffering severe malnutrition.
headline: 32 Palestinians killed ‘while trying to reach food distribution sites in Gaza’

text:
The Government faces mounting pressure to address barriers preventing average earners from buying a home, after auctioneers and estate agents warned that current schemes do not go far enough to support the majority of would-be buyers.

The Institute of Professional Auctioneers and Valuers (IPAV) has called on Minister for Housing Darragh O’Brien to introduce targeted measures that would enable more middle-income earners to enter the property market. The group claims that, while existing supports such as the Help to Buy and First Home schemes have had some impact, the main impediments for most prospective buyers remain unresolved.

Speaking on RTÉ’s Morning Ireland, IPAV chief executive Pat Davitt argued that rising house prices, stricter mortgage lending criteria, and a chronic shortage of affordable new homes have combined to put homeownership out of reach for many. He described the current situation as “unsustainable,” warning that a growing cohort of young workers are being forced to delay or abandon plans to buy, despite earning above the national average wage.

“We are seeing people earning €50,000 to €70,000 per year – nurses, teachers, gardaí – who simply cannot get on the property ladder in their own communities,” Mr Davitt said. “The Government must look at new solutions to remove these impediments, whether that is through supporting first-time buyers with deposits, freeing up more land for building, or relaxing some lending rules, particularly for those with secure employment.”

IPAV is also calling for an urgent review of the mortgage lending limits introduced by the Central Bank. Under current rules, buyers are generally required to have a deposit of 10% and can only borrow up to four times their gross annual income, a cap Mr Davitt said was “entirely out of step with prevailing market conditions, especially outside Dublin where prices have surged in recent years.”

Separately, the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland (SCSI) echoed concerns about affordability, suggesting that spiralling construction costs and delays in the planning system are exacerbating the supply crisis. SCSI’s most recent report found that the median price of a new three-bedroom semi-detached home now exceeds €370,000 nationally, with prices in Cork, Limerick, and Galway all recording significant annual increases.

Latest CSO figures show that home prices rose by 5.4% nationwide in the year to April. Meanwhile, the number of new homes completed remains well below Housing for All targets, with just under 7,000 finished in the first quarter.

Opposition TDs have seized on the latest warnings, with Sinn Féin’s housing spokesperson Eoin Ó Broin declaring that, “Average earners are being squeezed out while vulture funds and institutional investors snap up what little supply is available. The Government must take urgent action to make home ownership a realistic prospect, not just an aspiration.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Housing said the Government is “committed to increasing supply and supporting homeownership through a range of schemes,” adding that ministerial engagement with stakeholders is ongoing.

However, industry sources say that unless further steps are taken in the forthcoming Budget, efforts to help ordinary buyers onto the ladder risk falling short, as rents and prices continue to climb.
headline: Government must help average earners overcome 'impediments' to homebuying, say auctioneers

text:
When a film with as much pre-hype and political charge as Kneecap finally arrives, you expect to be put through your paces. But the debut feature from director Rich Peppiatt, which opened to a standing ovation in Belfast last week and has packed cinemas up and down the country since, is so electrifying and fresh that it feels like an adrenaline shot to the Irish film scene. It’s also simply one of the best, and most riotously entertaining, films I have seen in years.

Kneecap, for those who have somehow missed the commotion, is based on the real-life exploits of the eponymous Belfast hip-hop trio — Mo Chara, Móglaí Bap, and DJ Próvaí — whose irreverent, Irish-language anthems have made them both cult heroes and lightning rods for controversy. The film, shot in a dizzying blend of Gaeilge and English, tells the fictionalised origin story of the group, set against the backdrop of a post-Good Friday Agreement Belfast that still thrums with tension, humour, and possibility.

What sets Kneecap apart is its refusal to be pinned down. From the first scene, it’s clear that we are not in for a po-faced republic-of-virtue biopic, nor a tired Troubles retread. Instead, we get a wild, scabrous comedy-drama, equal parts Trainspotting and The Commitments, with a dash of Derry Girls’ anarchic wit. It pulses with the beat of the city and, crucially, with the musical energy of Kneecap themselves, who star as lightly fictionalised versions of their onstage personas.

Every frame of the film fizzes with a sense of place and time. There are moments of jaw-dropping cheek: graffiti daubed on peace walls, clandestine gigs in community centres, and subversive run-ins with Gardaí and the PSNI alike. Yet Peppiatt never lets the pace flag, and at no point does the film tip into caricature. Belfast is depicted in all its complexity — a city still reckoning with the legacies of violence, but also bursting with creativity and black humour.

The performances are a revelation. The three Kneecap lads, none of whom have acted professionally before, carry the film with a swagger that is never forced. Supporting turns from Michael Fassbender, playing a world-weary teacher, and Simone Kirby as the indomitable principal, lend the proceedings a gravitas that never wavers from the central joke. But it is the chemistry between Mo Chara and Móglaí Bap — by turns hilarious, touching, and infuriating — that anchors the story.

Kneecap’s use of language is, frankly, inspirational. The dialogue crackles with Belfast slang and street Gaeilge, riffing on the idea of the Irish language as a weapon of rebellion, but also as the living, breathing vernacular of a new generation. There are moments when the subtitles play catch-up with the pace, but you never lose the thread; the energy is in the delivery.

There will be those who see Kneecap’s refusal to mollify or sanitise as a provocation. Certainly, it goes places few Irish films dare, poking fun at political and cultural sacred cows with the same gleeful disregard that made the group themselves famous. But to reduce it to a stunt would be a grave mistake.
headline: Tom Dunne: Here's why Kneecap is already my favourite film of the year

text:
Hundreds of Oasis fans descended on Manchester last night for the band’s highly anticipated reunion, with some devoted followers travelling from as far afield as Australia for what was the group’s first live performance in over sixteen years.

Queues snaked around the iconic Co-Op Live arena hours before doors opened, as enthusiasts young and old braved the brisk June air. Many arrived clad in bucket hats and parkas, recreating the signature look of the Gallagher brothers, Liam and Noel, whose famously tempestuous relationship had fuelled years of speculation about a possible reunion.

Amongst the crowd were several Irish contingents, with fans from Dublin, Cork and Belfast waving tricolours and chanting Oasis classics ahead of the show. “It’s been an unreal trip,” said Conor O’Shea, who, along with three friends, flew from Dublin Airport on Thursday night. “We grew up listening to Oasis. Seeing them together again is something I never thought would happen. For a lot of us, this is bigger than any football match.”

However, it was Australians Emily Rhodes and Tom McMahon, both originally from Perth, who had perhaps the longest journey. “I’ve been obsessed with Oasis since I was a teenager,” Ms Rhodes told the Irish Examiner. “We booked our flights as soon as the rumours started back in February. Everyone thought we were mad coming all the way to Manchester, but it’s been completely worth it.”

The concert itself lived up to its billing, with the Gallagher brothers taking to the stage amid deafening cheers. The set opened with ‘Rock ‘n’ Roll Star’ and featured classics such as ‘Wonderwall’, ‘Don’t Look Back In Anger’, and ‘Champagne Supernova’. There was a certain poignancy in the air as the crowd belted out lyrics that have become anthems for a generation.

The event was as much a celebration of the band’s legacy as it was of the enduring power of music to unite people across continents and cultures. “Tonight’s about more than nostalgia,” said Aoife O’Donnell, who travelled from Limerick for the gig. “It’s about everyone coming together after everything we’ve all been through these last few years. That first chord of ‘Live Forever’—you could feel the whole place lift.”

Organisers said demand for tickets had been unprecedented, with over 40,000 people in attendance. The Gardaí reported no major incidents overnight, though air traffic at Manchester Airport saw a noticeable spike in flights arriving from Dublin, Cork and Shannon.

Speculation is already mounting about further dates, with bookies slashing odds on an Irish show before the end of the year. While there has been no official confirmation from the band’s management, fans remain hopeful a Croke Park or Marlay Park gig could be on the cards.

For now, those lucky enough to attend the Manchester reunion are left with memories to last a lifetime—and the hope that, after sixteen years, Oasis might just be ready to roll with it once again.
headline: Oasis fans travel from Australia for band’s first gig in 16 years
