Mary Crilly, the founder and long-time head of the Sexual Violence Centre Cork, is set to retire from her formal role at the organisation after more than four decades of advocacy and frontline support for survivors of sexual violence. However, Ms Crilly has pledged to remain active as a campaigner and to continue her work highlighting the needs of victims and lobbying for systemic change.

Ms Crilly established the centre in 1983, making it the first dedicated sexual violence support service outside Dublin. Under her leadership, the centre has provided crisis support, counselling and advocacy to thousands of people across Cork city and county, and has played a major part in shifting public attitudes about sexual violence and consent. The centre, which is largely funded by the HSE and the Department of Justice, also works closely with Gardaí and runs educational and prevention programmes in schools, workplaces and communities.

In a statement on Wednesday, Ms Crilly said the decision to step back from her directorship had not been easy, but that she would not be “silenced or stepping away” from the fight for justice and support for survivors. “I’m leaving at a time of immense change, with more understanding now than ever about the impact of sexual violence, but there is still a long way to go. I’ll keep using my voice wherever it’s needed – for survivors, for better services, and for a criminal justice system that actually listens,” she said.

Paying tribute to Ms Crilly, Taoiseach Simon Harris described her as “a tireless force for change not just in Cork but nationwide”, while Green Party TD for Cork South Central, Dan Boyle, said she had “transformed the conversation on sexual violence in Ireland”. The centre’s board said it would begin the process of recruiting a new director over the coming months.

Staff at the centre said Ms Crilly’s legacy included not only the service she built, but also the countless survivors who finally felt able to seek support due to outreach efforts led by her and her team. “She never gave up – not on a person, not on an issue,” said long-time colleague Christine O’Callaghan. “She fought hard for every client who came through the door.”

News of Ms Crilly’s retirement comes as the latest data show a continued rise in the number of people seeking support after experiencing sexual violence in Munster. The centre said it had received more than 2,200 contacts last year, with the biggest increase among those under 25.

Ms Crilly, who was made a Freeman of Cork City in 2022 and is a member of the National Women’s Council, said she would use her next chapter to focus on education, prevention, and advocacy at a national level. She called on the Government to ensure promised reforms to the criminal justice system and to increase funding for supports outside Dublin.

“The fight isn’t over,” she said. “Survivors still face barriers every day – in accessing justice, in getting the help they need, and in being believed. I’ll keep standing with them as long as I can.”
headline: Mary Crilly to retire from Sexual Violence Centre Cork but says she will continue campaigning

text:
Thousands of locals and visitors alike descended on Dungarvan this weekend as the Waterford Festival of Food returned to the harbour town, promising a feast for all the senses and serving up a powerful showcase for the region’s rich culinary talent. Now in its 15th year, the festival has established itself as one of the country’s leading food events, drawing foodies from across Ireland and beyond to the Déise to sample artisan wares, street eats, and the best of local hospitality.

Strolling through the bustling market on Grattan Square on Sunday, it was impossible not to be swept up by the aroma of freshly baked breads, sizzling local sausages, and the distinctive tang of seaweed snacks. More than 100 vendors, many from within a short spin of Dungarvan, lined the square and surrounding streets, their stalls piled high with everything from award-winning cheeses and craft butters, to plant-based treats and Waterford Blaa sandwiches stuffed with slow-roasted lamb. There was even a collection of Dungarvan’s famous soft serve ice cream, served with a drizzle of Blackwater gin syrup for the grown-ups.

Festival chairperson Paul Flynn, chef-owner of The Tannery and a tireless champion of the Waterford food scene, said the event is as much about community and connection as it is about cuisine. “There’s a great grá for food here, but it’s the sense of togetherness that really sets this festival apart,” he told the Irish Examiner. “It’s a chance for local producers to meet their customers, for people to take pride in our food heritage, and for families to make memories around the table – or in the middle of Grattan Square.”

As well as the street market, visitors flocked to cookery demonstrations hosted by well-known chefs such as Eunice Power, Edward Hayden, and more recent stars from Waterford’s own kitchens. The Festival Table on The Green was packed for long-table suppers, where guests tucked into tasting menus celebrating the region’s seafood, vegetables, and foraged delights, all paired with craft ales from Dungarvan Brewing Company and small-batch ciders.

Children were kept entertained with workshops on everything from pizza-making to chocolate tempering in the family marquee, while grown-ups sipped locally roasted coffee or cooling pints under the April sun. There were food trails to Ardmore, bread-baking masterclasses in the Quay, and for those feeling adventurous, the much-anticipated wild food foraging walk along the Copper Coast.

Sustainability was at the heart of this year’s programme, with the organisers partnering with Waterford City and County Council and local environmental groups to keep waste to a minimum. Reusable cups and compostable plates were the order of the day, while many stallholders offered plastic-free packaging and tips on minimising food waste at home.

For festival-goer Siobhán O’Sullivan from Tramore, the event is a highlight of the year. “We come every spring – the kids love it, and I get ideas for my own cooking. But it’s also about supporting local people and tasting things you won’t find anywhere else,” she said, tucking into a wood-fired Ballybeg pizza.
headline: Delicious Déise delights: How Waterford Festival of Food brings fun to Dungarvan

text:
Fewer homebuyers have been lining up for new properties in Douglas as the second phase of the Bayly residential development hit the market this week, with local estate agents indicating a noticeable cooling compared to the frenzied demand seen in 2023.

The Bayly scheme, located off the well-established Grange Road, brought its latest phase of three- and four-bed homes to the public, following the rapid sell-out of its initial release last year. Agents at Sherry FitzGerald reported that while there was steady interest and some bookings had been registered, the queues and late-night camp-outs that characterised last year’s launch were notably absent.

According to industry sources, just over 35 homes were released in the latest phase, priced from €415,000 for a three-bed semi, which is around €30,000 higher than similar units in the first phase. Four-bed units are on the market from €470,000. While these prices remain in line with the Douglas and Grange market, the increase comes at a time when cost-of-living pressures and heightened interest rates are weighing on potential buyers.

“It’s a solid turnout, but not the kind of frenzied opening we saw last year,” said one agent, who asked not to be named. “Buyers are being far more measured. They’re booking viewings, taking their time, and there’s less of the panic to secure a property that we saw in 2023.”

The change in buyer behaviour comes against the backdrop of a broader cooling in Cork’s housing market, with the latest MyHome.ie report showing a slowdown in price growth and an increase in the number of available properties for sale in Munster, especially in suburban areas such as Douglas, Ballincollig and Glanmire.

Local TD Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire (Sinn Féin) said the softer demand reflects “the deepening affordability crisis for working families and first-time buyers in Cork”. He added: “The price rises and higher mortgage costs are shutting more people out, at a time when the need for homes remains immense.”

The developer, O’Flynn Construction, did not respond to requests for comment on sales performance but sources close to the project said they expect “steady and sustainable” absorption of stock.

Potential buyers attending the opening described a different atmosphere from previous launches. One couple, hoping for their first home, said they had been able to view the showhouse at leisure and make an offer without “feeling under pressure or forced into a snap decision”.

Neighbouring developments in Grange and Frankfield have also seen fewer bidders for recent phases, agents confirmed, but added that finished, well-insulated homes in prime school catchments remain in demand.

The new Bayly phase includes A-rated energy-efficient houses and is due for completion by late 2024. Local councillors have called on Cork City Council’s planning department to ensure infrastructure keeps pace with the increased population in Grange and Douglas, citing ongoing pressures on schools, roads, and public transport.

Mortgage brokers in the city report that while interest remains strong among those with loan approval, some are hesitating to commit, concerned about further interest rate rises or the prospect of better value later in the year.

The Irish Home Builders Association has warned that continuing cost increases, particularly for materials and labour, could keep pressure on prices even if demand continues to soften.
headline: Fewer buyers queue for Douglas homes as second phase of Bayly development goes on sale

text:
Photographs, personal letters and a series of rare documents linked to one of Ireland’s key Treaty Ports negotiators are set to go on public display for the first time on Spike Island. The exhibition will shine a spotlight on Commandant Michael J. Kavanagh, a prominent member of the 1938 commission which oversaw the historic transfer of the ports from British to Irish control.

The artefacts, gifted to the island’s museum by Kavanagh’s descendants, include previously unpublished photographs of Irish and British military officers during the handovers at Berehaven, Cobh, and Lough Swilly. The collection also contains letters written between Kavanagh and then Taoiseach Éamon de Valera, as well as communications with British government officials during the protracted negotiations.

“This collection offers a unique window into a transformative moment in Irish history,” said Tom O’Neill, heritage manager at Spike Island. “The Treaty Ports handover in 1938 marked the completion of Ireland’s gradual emergence from British rule. Commander Kavanagh was at the heart of this process, and his documents provide fresh insights into both the tense negotiations and the ceremonial aspects of the handover.”

The Treaty Ports, retained by Britain under the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921, were seen as vital strategic outposts for the Royal Navy. Their relinquishment was considered a major diplomatic victory for de Valera’s administration and a turning point for Irish sovereignty on the eve of the Second World War.

Among the newly revealed materials is Kavanagh’s own diary, chronicling the long days spent at the negotiating table, as well as invitations to official dinners, and photographs of the Irish Defence Forces taking up position in Cobh’s fortified harbour. The family also contributed a set of medals awarded to Kavanagh in recognition of his service.

Members of the public will be able to view the collection at Spike Island’s museum from 27 June, as part of a wider exhibition marking the 85th anniversary of the Treaty Ports handover. The opening will be attended by members of the Kavanagh family, military historians and representatives of the Defence Forces.

Local historian Dr Jennifer O’Mahony said the display is “a significant addition to the public record, putting names and faces to an often-overlooked chapter of Munster and Irish history.” She added that the presence of primary documents “deepens our understanding of how the Treaty Ports return was experienced on the ground, in communities like Cobh and beyond.”

The exhibition runs through September and is included in the general admission to Spike Island, with guided tours exploring the legacy of the Treaty Ports for both Cork Harbour and the wider region. Further details are available on the Spike Island website.
headline: Photos and letters belonging to Treaty Ports negotiator to go on display on Spike Island

text:
The head of Oxfam Ireland has urged political parties and candidates to put the humanitarian crisis in Gaza at the forefront of debate during the coming General Election campaign.

Jim Clarken, chief executive of the development agency, said Ireland has a unique role to play in advocating for an immediate ceasefire, and that Irish voters are demanding clarity on what steps parties would take to end the conflict and address the ongoing suffering of Palestinian civilians.

Speaking on Thursday, Mr Clarken called on party leaders, including the Taoiseach Simon Harris and Tánaiste Micheál Martin, to go beyond statements of concern and commit to “meaningful diplomatic action” at EU and UN level. “Irish people are horrified by what they are seeing in Gaza — the destruction of homes, the loss of life, the threat of famine,” he said. “They want to see leadership that goes beyond words.”

Oxfam Ireland has seen a surge in public engagement and fundraising for its humanitarian programmes in Gaza since October, Mr Clarken said, adding that thousands of people have contacted the agency seeking advice on how to urge politicians to press for a lasting ceasefire.

The Government has repeatedly called for an immediate and sustained ceasefire in Gaza, with the Dáil passing several motions in support of Palestinian civilians. However, campaigners have criticised what they see as a lack of pressure on international partners, notably the United States and EU member states, to pursue stronger action against Israel over alleged breaches of international humanitarian law.

Mr Clarken said this election is “an opportunity for Ireland to use its voice on the world stage” and urged candidates from all parties to set out “clear policy positions” on arms embargoes, financial aid, and accountability measures. “We have a tradition of standing up for justice and peace. Most Irish people want to see our government do the same today,” he said.

According to the UN, more than 36,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel began its military operation in response to the Hamas attacks of 7 October. The Department of Foreign Affairs has pledged €29 million in humanitarian aid to Gaza and the wider region so far in 2024.

The ongoing conflict has featured prominently at protests across Ireland, with thousands gathering in Dublin and Cork in recent weeks to call for an immediate ceasefire. Several sitting TDs have faced questions from constituents on their stance and actions regarding the crisis.

Mr Clarken said it was “crucial” that, over the coming weeks, all political leaders “listen to the voices of voters, humanitarian workers, and survivors,” and prioritise the demand for peace and accountability in Gaza alongside domestic election issues.
headline: Oxfam Ireland chief calls for Gaza to be central issue in General Election campaign

text:
When it comes to supporting children and teenagers online, the impulse for many parents is to seek out the latest app or parental control tool, hoping that technological solutions can keep pace with the digital lives of young people. But as anyone who has been handed a smartphone by a nine-year-old for “technical support” can attest, the speed at which children adapt to new technologies often outstrips their parents’ own digital know-how.

Dr Colman Noctor, child and adolescent psychotherapist, believes it’s time for a wider conversation about how Irish families and communities engage with online safety. “We have become fixated on finding the perfect piece of software or control — some magic bullet — that will protect our children from everything the internet has to throw at them,” he says. “But digital safety, like every other kind of safety, comes back to community. It’s something we need to tackle collectively.”

According to statistics from CyberSafeKids, over 90% of eight- to twelve-year-olds in Ireland own a smart device, and many have unsupervised access to messaging apps, gaming platforms and the vast corners of the internet. This reality presents a challenge for parents who feel ill-equipped to supervise every interaction or anticipate every threat.

Noctor notes that attempts to “out-tech” young people are rarely successful for long. “Children are brilliant at finding workarounds. When we rely on apps to do the parenting for us, we are always one step behind,” he says. Instead, he advocates for open dialogue within families, and a community approach across schools, clubs, and neighbourhoods. “We need a space where parents can compare notes, ask questions, and decide together what is age-appropriate for our children.”

This community ethos is not new to Ireland. In the past, parents often looked to each other for guidance and backup, whether it was navigating the walk to school or dealing with playground politics. The digital world, Noctor argues, should be no different. “If your child says, ‘everyone in my class is on Snapchat’, it’s vital that parents have a way to verify that. Is it really everyone? Or just a few? When parents talk to each other, they realise that their concerns are shared, and they can make informed choices together.”

Despite resources from the Department of Education and workshops run by the HSE and voluntary groups, many parents still feel isolated with these issues. The pressure to allow children access to social media — often before the official age limit of 13 — can be immense. “No one wants their child to be the only one left out, but the more parents speak openly to each other, the more possible it becomes to set boundaries that are realistic and consistent,” Noctor says.

He also acknowledges the limits of control. “It’s not about pretending we can keep children away from all risk. Instead, we should be equipping them to manage risk. That means lots of conversations about what’s out there, how to respond, and knowing they can come to you if something goes wrong.”

In practice, building this ‘digital village’ can be as simple as starting a WhatsApp group with other parents, comparing notes on games and apps, and agreeing shared rules where possible. Schools can facilitate information sessions, and local youth organisations can involve young people in discussions about what makes them feel safe online.
headline: Colman Noctor: Digital safety needs a village, not an app

text:
The Irish fishing industry has called for urgent Government intervention as soaring fuel costs threaten the viability of the country’s fishing fleet. Sector representatives warn the combination of spiralling diesel prices and declining catch quotas is pushing many vessels to the brink, with some owners forced to consider tying up their boats indefinitely.

Industry leaders say fuel costs have risen by as much as 60% in the past 18 months, eroding already tight margins and jeopardising employment in coastal communities. The Irish South and West Fish Producers’ Organisation (IS&WFPO) said this week that some skippers are spending over €1,000 per day on fuel alone, leaving “very little incentive to leave port”.

Patrick Murphy, the organisation’s chief executive, said: “Irish fishing families are being squeezed from every angle. We are facing a situation now where it is becoming impossible to even break even, never mind make a living. The Government needs to step in as a matter of urgency.”

Mr Murphy has called on the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine to introduce a fuel rebate similar to schemes operating in France and Spain, where state supports have kept much of their fleets operational. “We are not seeking a handout, but a recognition that Irish boats are already facing reduced quotas and higher operational costs than our European counterparts,” he said.

Skippers operating out of Castletownbere and Killybegs, two of the country’s busiest fishing ports, report that smaller vessels in particular are struggling to cover basic costs. Captain Sean O’Driscoll, a Castletownbere fisherman with 30 years’ experience, said: “We are battling rising costs not just for fuel but also for insurance, repairs and bait. It’s getting to the stage where some lads are thinking it’s not worth going out at all.”

The industry’s plight comes amid broader concerns over the impact of Brexit and the Common Fisheries Policy on Ireland’s quota allocation. Marine Minister Charlie McConalogue has acknowledged the difficulties facing the sector and has indicated that officials are examining potential support measures.

Speaking in the Dáil on Wednesday, Mr McConalogue said: “I recognise the enormous pressure fuel prices are placing on the fleet. My department is engaging with stakeholders and we are looking at options to assist during this challenging period.” He added that any measures would have to comply with European Union state aid rules.

Fianna Fáil TD Jackie Cahill, chair of the Oireachtas agriculture committee, called for “meaningful support from Government” to maintain jobs and the future of rural fishing communities. “Fishing is a cornerstone of the coastal economy and we cannot allow this industry to be decimated by circumstances beyond its control,” he said.

The fishing industry directly employs approximately 3,700 people in Ireland, with thousands more jobs dependent on the sector through processing and ancillary services.

Industry groups are seeking an urgent meeting with the Taoiseach to discuss their concerns, warning that a failure to act could see much of the Irish fleet “left tied up at the pier this summer” with serious social and economic consequences for coastal Ireland.
headline: Fishing industry seeks Government help as soaring fuel costs threaten Irish fleet

text:
Learner drivers who book their driving tests through unofficial third-party websites risk losing their test appointments, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has warned.

The authority said it has become aware of increasing numbers of online platforms and intermediaries offering fast-track driving test bookings, often at inflated prices, to candidates around the country. According to the RSA, these sites are not authorised to provide driving test appointments, and any bookings secured through such means are liable to be cancelled without refund.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the RSA clarified that the only legitimate way to book the official driver theory test or practical driving test is directly through its designated website and customer service channels.

“We are urging all learner drivers and their families to be on alert for these third-party websites. They are not affiliated with the RSA, and bookings made through these channels are not valid,” said a spokesperson. “Unfortunately, candidates who use unofficial brokers risk losing both their money and their place on the waiting list.”

The warning comes as demand for driving test appointments remains high nationally. Many learners, frustrated by long waiting times, are reportedly turning to online services promising early slots for additional fees. The authority confirmed that it has identified patterns where individuals or organisations use multiple email addresses and false information to secure test dates, which are then resold online at a profit.

Minister of State at the Department of Transport, Jack Chambers, said the practice undermines the fairness of the system. “The driving test is an essential public service and the process of allocating appointments must be equitable. The Department and the RSA are working together to identify and cancel appointments made through these unofficial channels, and where appropriate, refer matters to the Gardaí for further investigation.”

The RSA has also reminded the public that genuine rescheduling or cancellation of tests—where slots may become available at short notice—can only be done through the official portal. The authority provides free access to a cancellation system for those who wish to secure an earlier appointment, based on real-time availability.

A spokesperson for Insurance Ireland echoed the warning, saying that only those with valid, officially booked test appointments should present themselves for an examination, and that any irregular booking practices could lead to complications for learners seeking to obtain cover.

The RSA said it will continue to monitor online activity closely and take steps as required to protect the integrity of the testing system. It advised anyone who suspects they may have been targeted by third-party booking scams to contact its customer service team or report the issue to the Gardaí.
headline: RSA warns learner drivers tests booked through third-party platforms will be cancelled

text:
Hollywood actor Robert De Niro has spoken publicly for the first time about his daughter’s gender identity, expressing his “love and support” for his eldest child, Drena, who is transgender.

In an interview with US network CBS Mornings, De Niro said he fully supports Drena, now 52, in her journey and hopes that public expressions of acceptance might encourage other families facing similar challenges. “You love your children, unconditionally. That’s what it is. And I want her to live her truth and be happy in her life,” he told presenter Gayle King.

The Oscar-winning actor, a frequent visitor to Ireland through his work and personal ties, said he recognises the difficulties faced by transgender people, particularly in the public eye. “She’s dealt with a lot,” De Niro said. “I just want to be there for her, and for all my kids, no matter what.”

Drena De Niro, a film producer and actress, publicly identified as transgender earlier this year, posting on social media about her experiences. The news was welcomed by many in the LGBTQ+ community and prompted a fresh conversation about acceptance and understanding for transgender people and their families.

In Ireland, support groups such as TENI (Transgender Equality Network Ireland) and BeLonG To Youth Services have noted a growing openness from some public figures in supporting transgender children and adults, but say that many still face discrimination and misunderstanding.

De Niro, who has six other children and recently became a father again at age 79, has previously been outspoken on matters of civil rights and mental health, but has kept much of his family life private. “I know it’s not always easy, particularly in the world we live in now,” he said during the interview, “but we have to give our kids all the love we can.”

Friends and colleagues in Hollywood and beyond shared messages of support online, praising the actor’s candour and compassion. Irish fans have also voiced encouragement, with many saying it is important to see such high-profile figures speak openly about their families.

The actor’s comments come amid ongoing debate in Ireland and internationally around gender recognition, healthcare access, and the rights of transgender people. Last year, the Oireachtas heard submissions from advocacy organisations and parents on the need for increased resources for trans and non-binary young people.

As De Niro concluded, “At the end of the day, all that matters is that your children know you’re with them. That’s what I hope everyone realises.”
headline: Robert De Niro expresses ‘love and support’ for transgender daughter

text:
Patients across Ireland will for the first time be able to access their personal health records using a new smartphone app launched today by the Health Service Executive (HSE). The move marks a significant step towards digitising the State’s health system, as the HSE aims to modernise the way health information is managed and shared.

The “My Health” app, available for download from Wednesday, allows patients in participating projects to view records such as hospital appointments, laboratory results, and prescribed medications. The HSE said the initial rollout will focus on select hospitals, GP practices and community clinics in Dublin, Cork and Galway, with plans for a phased national expansion over the coming year.

Announcing the launch at Cork University Hospital, Chief Executive of the HSE Bernard Gloster described the app as “a milestone in empowering patients and improving transparency in the health service.” Mr Gloster said: “For too long, patients have struggled to access their own health information or have had to rely on paper records. This is about giving people ownership of their health data, and ultimately supporting better health outcomes.”

Access to the new service will require patients to register and verify their identity using their PPS number and a MyGovID account. The HSE has confirmed that the app complies with all GDPR requirements and has undergone third-party security testing. Officials also stressed that the system will continue to be developed with input from patient advocacy groups and healthcare providers.

The move was welcomed by Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly, who said it would “transform how people engage with their own health,” and promised further investments in eHealth solutions. “This is a vital step towards creating an integrated digital health record for every person in Ireland,” the Minister said.

However, patient groups have cautioned that the digital divide must be considered. Rachel Flynn of the Irish Patients’ Association said: “We are supportive of greater access and transparency, but there needs to be real support for older people and those less comfortable with technology.”

Healthcare professionals have also raised concerns about the additional workload that may arise from having to explain records or test results to patients accessing them in real-time. Dr Brendan O’Shea, a Kildare GP, said: “Most patients want clear, simple information, and there will be questions and anxiety. The HSE needs to invest in supporting clinicians as well as the technology itself.”

The HSE said it has established a dedicated support helpline and will provide training for health professionals on communicating digital health information.

The launch comes after years of criticism over the pace of health digitisation in Ireland, including delays in rolling out a universal electronic health record system. Previous attempts have faced technical and procurement challenges, as well as concerns about cyber security following the 2021 ransomware attack on HSE IT systems.

Despite these setbacks, the HSE maintains that the “My Health” app is secure and future-proofed, and represents a foundation for further digital innovations, including the long-awaited national electronic health record.

The pilot phase will be closely monitored, with feedback from patients and clinicians shaping future updates. The HSE says it expects the majority of the population to have access to their records online by the end of 2025.
headline: HSE launches app allowing patients access to their health data

text:
As Americans head to the polls this November for what promises to be one of the most consequential elections of their lifetimes, the view from Ireland is marked by both keen interest and a sense of personal connection. For generations, ties between the two countries have run deep, shaped by shared history, culture, and, for many, family. In President Joe Biden, these connections are not just diplomatic slogans but lived reality: the US President has consistently underlined his Irish ancestry, and his tenure in the White House has come with more than a little green in the mix.

The relationship between Ireland and the United States has always been more than transactional. At times, it has been a source of practical benefit—support for the peace process in Northern Ireland being a prime example. At other moments, it is a question of the values and aspirations both nations hold dear: democracy, respect for human rights, and a commitment to stability and peace in an increasingly uncertain world.

Biden’s presidency has been watched closely in Ireland, with political leaders across the spectrum, from the Taoiseach to opposition TDs, welcoming his administration’s engagement, particularly in the context of Brexit and its implications for the Good Friday Agreement. The appointment of Joe Kennedy III as Special Envoy to Northern Ireland was well received, reinforcing the White House’s hands-on approach, and contrasting starkly with the reticence of the previous Trump administration.

The prospect of a second term for Donald Trump brings with it a different tone: unpredictability, a transactional approach to international affairs, and a style at odds with the collaborative, values-driven relationship Ireland traditionally enjoys with Washington. It is little wonder, then, that polling consistently shows overwhelming Irish support for President Biden. While the Irish electorate does not have a vote in the US election, there is no doubting where hearts and hopes lie.

This is not, however, to say there is no critique of the Biden administration among the Irish public or political class. Concerns have been raised over US foreign policy, particularly in relation to the conflict in Gaza, and Labour, Sinn Féin, and other parties have called for stronger responses from Ireland and Europe. Yet, in terms of the fundamental question facing American voters—who should serve as President for the next four years—Irish sentiment is clear: Biden is seen not just as an ally, but as a friend who understands this country’s unique story and its place in the world.

As election day approaches, Ireland will follow events with acute attention. The outcome in November will have direct consequences for this island, from economic links to our standing in matters of peace and diplomacy. Whatever the result, the expectation is that the bonds will endure, but it is unmistakable that, in 2024, Joe Biden will have the backing of the Irish.
headline: Irish Examiner view: Biden will have backing of the Irish

text:
It’s a common scenario witnessed at many a playgroup or family gathering: a small fist reaches out, and in a flash, someone’s hair is being tugged with surprising force. Many Irish parents find themselves apologising for their baby’s sudden interest in other people’s locks, often feeling both mortified and mystified about what to do next.

Joanna Fortune, psychotherapist and author specialising in child development, says it’s important for parents to realise that hair pulling in infants is neither unusual nor intentionally aggressive, but rather a stage of curiosity and exploration.

"Babies explore their world through their senses," explains Fortune. "For young children, touch is a key way of learning. Hair, with its interesting texture and response, is naturally intriguing for them." Pulling hair isn’t about causing harm—more often, it’s an experiment in cause and effect.

Yet, Fortune acknowledges, while the behaviour is typical, that doesn’t mean parents shouldn’t address it—especially when it risks tears, hurt feelings, or tension among friends and relatives.

“The first step is to intervene gently but consistently,” she advises. “Saying ‘No pulling’ in a calm but firm tone, while freeing the hair from their grip, helps your baby begin to connect the action with your response.” Repetition is key, as is reinforcing gentle touch immediately after. "If possible, demonstrate a soft stroke and praise your baby when they imitate the gesture," she adds.

Sometimes, children repeat the hair-pulling because they enjoy the reaction it provokes, particularly if it leads to an uproar or much attention. Fortune recommends keeping reactions as low-key as possible, redirecting your baby’s attention to an appropriate toy or activity instead. "Remember, big reactions can unintentionally reinforce the behaviour," she cautions.

For parents worried about social situations, transparency helps. Letting other adults know that your child is at a sensory-exploratory stage can defuse embarrassment and encourage understanding.

“It’s important not to scold or shame a young child for hair pulling,” Fortune says. “Babies lack impulse control at this stage of development. What they need is gentle, consistent guidance over time.”

Should the behaviour persist beyond toddlerhood or become aggressive, parents are encouraged to consult their public health nurse or GP for advice. In most cases, however, with patience and gentle redirection, the phase passes naturally.

For now, Fortune suggests, focus on modelling gentle touch, using positive language, and ensuring your baby has plenty of other sensory experiences – squishy balls, textured books, and supervised water play can all satisfy that innate curiosity.

Above all, she urges parents to be kind to themselves. “Every parent has been there,” Fortune reassures. “This too will pass, and it doesn’t define your child or your parenting.”

For further support, organisations such as Barnardos and local parent and toddler groups can offer advice and a listening ear. Remember, you are not alone—and your baby is simply learning about the world, one curious handful at a time.
headline: Joanna Fortune: My baby keeps pulling other people's hair

text:
A rift has emerged at Cabinet level after a senior minister questioned the feasibility of further reductions in third-level student fees, despite ongoing calls from coalition partners to accelerate cost-of-living measures for families.

The Minister for Public Expenditure, Paschal Donohoe, told reporters yesterday that the current fiscal environment is “challenging”, and cautioned against making promises that may not be deliverable ahead of October’s Budget. “We must be prudent and ensure that any commitments to further cut the student contribution are matched by sustainable revenue streams,” the Dublin Central TD said.

His remarks came in apparent contrast to statements made by Minister for Higher and Further Education, Simon Harris, who reiterated his “absolute commitment” to working towards a €1,000 cut in the student contribution charge, currently set at €3,000 per year.

Pressure has grown from backbenchers in both Fianna Fáil and the Green Party, with some expressing concern that students and their families will “bear the brunt” of rising costs if the Government does not deliver further relief. Speaking to the Irish Examiner, one Fianna Fáil TD said, “We made a commitment to support families. Pushing back on this would send entirely the wrong message before a general election.”

Tánaiste Micheál Martin has previously described reducing the student fee as “a core aim” of this Government’s legacy, while Taoiseach Simon Harris, upon his election, pledged to “work tirelessly to ease the financial burden” on those entering third-level education.

A spokesperson for the Department of Further and Higher Education said that budgetary negotiations are ongoing and that no final decision has been made. The spokesperson added: “Minister Harris continues to advocate for students and their families. Any decision will be made in the context of the overall Budget and available resources.”

However, senior sources in Fine Gael pointed to “significant spending pressures” elsewhere, including in health and housing, and warned that the State must “balance ambition with affordability.”

Student unions have reacted with concern. The Union of Students in Ireland President, Jessica Smyth, called the minister’s comments “deeply disappointing”, saying that “students cannot wait for action on the cost of education.”

The issue is expected to come before the Cabinet Committee on Economic Recovery next week. It is understood Minister Harris will seek to secure agreement from his coalition colleagues to prioritise a fee cut as part of the Government’s broader cost-of-living response.

The Government previously reduced the student contribution fee by €1,000 in Budget 2024, with more than 40,000 students benefitting. However, campaigners and opposition parties have insisted that one-off interventions are no substitute for structural reform of third-level funding.

Labour’s Education spokesperson, Aodhán Ó Ríordáin, accused the Government of “dithering” and called for third-level fees to be phased out entirely. “We are one of the few countries in the EU still charging such high fees. The uncertainty must end,” he said.

The latest disagreement comes as the coalition faces increasing scrutiny over the pace of progress on key Programme for Government pledges, with speculation mounting that further disputes could threaten unity in the run-up to the next general election.
headline: Government split as minister casts doubt on further student fee cut

text:
A 34-year-old man has been remanded in custody after appearing before Cork District Court charged with the murder of a Ukrainian national in Cork city earlier this week.

Oleksandr Kovalenko, of no fixed abode, was formally charged with the murder of Yevhenii Bondarenko, who was found with fatal injuries at a flat on Boreenmanna Road in Ballinlough on Sunday night.

Detective Garda Michelle Walsh gave evidence of arrest, charge and caution, telling the court that Mr Kovalenko made no reply when the single charge was put to him at Bridewell Garda Station shortly after 11pm on Monday.

The court heard that Mr Bondarenko, who was in his 40s and had been living in Cork since arriving to Ireland from Ukraine more than a year ago, was pronounced dead at the scene after emergency services were called to the apartment complex around 8.30pm on Sunday.

Defence solicitor Eddie Burke applied for legal aid, telling Judge Olann Kelleher that his client is unemployed and has no means. Judge Kelleher granted the application and directed that an interpreter be made available, noting Mr Kovalenko’s limited English.

There was no application for bail, as the District Court does not have jurisdiction to grant bail in murder cases.

Judge Kelleher remanded Mr Kovalenko in custody to appear before a sitting of Cork District Court via video link on 21 June, to allow for the preparation of a file for the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Inspector John O’Donovan asked the court to note that the investigation remains ongoing.

Mr Bondarenko’s body was taken to Cork University Hospital for a post-mortem examination, the results of which are not being released for operational reasons.

Gardaí have appealed for anyone with information or who may have witnessed anything suspicious in the Boreenmanna Road area on Sunday evening to contact Anglesea Street Garda Station.

A number of Mr Bondarenko’s relatives attended the brief hearing.

Legal aid was also extended to cover consultations with counsel, given the seriousness of the charge.
headline: Man accused of murdering Ukrainian in Cork city remanded

text:
A powerful earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 6.2 struck central Japan on Monday, killing at least four people and injuring dozens more. The tremor, which hit at 6.31pm local time, was centred near Suzu City in Ishikawa prefecture and was felt across much of the Chubu region, including the major city of Kanazawa.

Authorities said that homes had collapsed and landslides blocked roads in several rural areas, leaving some communities cut off. Emergency crews worked through the night to reach those trapped beneath debris. The Fire and Disaster Management Agency confirmed four fatalities as of Tuesday morning, with local media reporting that at least 60 people had received treatment for injuries ranging from broken bones to minor cuts.

Japanese government officials held an emergency meeting in Tokyo, mobilising military and rescue personnel to the affected areas. Prime Minister Fumio Kishida expressed condolences to the families of the victims and pledged full support for recovery efforts, warning that strong aftershocks could continue for several days.

The Meteorological Agency ruled out the risk of a tsunami but urged residents to keep vigilant for further tremors and to avoid entering damaged buildings. More than 2,000 people have been evacuated to community centres and schools amid concerns over ongoing landslides and the possibility of building collapses.

Japan sits atop the so-called Ring of Fire, a seismically active region prone to frequent earthquakes. Monday’s quake raised concerns about the safety of infrastructure in the region, which includes several ageing dams and a nuclear power station in neighbouring Fukui prefecture, although officials said there were no reports of damage or radiation leaks.

The Department of Foreign Affairs said it was not aware of any Irish citizens directly affected but urged anyone with concerns about family members in the region to contact the Embassy in Tokyo.

As search and rescue operations continued in cold and wet conditions, local authorities appealed for additional support from the national government. Many roads remained impassable due to fallen trees and landslides, complicating efforts to deliver relief supplies to isolated mountain communities.

The long-term impact on the region’s economy, already hit hard by population decline and last year’s typhoon season, remains uncertain. Local officials said a full assessment of damage to homes, businesses, and public infrastructure would not be possible until after aftershocks subside.
headline: Deadly 6.2-magnitude earthquake strikes central Japan

text:
It’s a dilemma that will resonate in many Irish households, especially as our population ages and families become more dependent on each other for support. “I love my husband,” writes one reader. “But his mother is in declining health and I’m terrified I’ll end up responsible for her day-to-day care. I’m only in my mid-forties, our children are leaving home, and I’d hoped for more freedom, not another layer of duty. Am I wrong to feel resentful?”

The issue of caring for ageing parents-in-law arises frequently in Irish relationships. Traditionally, our culture expected families — particularly wives — to shoulder the responsibility of elder care. Yet today, more people feel conflicted, caught between their own needs and those of extended family. According to latest HSE figures, over half a million people in Ireland provide unpaid care to a loved one, with the majority of carers being women.

Clinical psychologist Dr Anne O’Reilly says it’s important to acknowledge the emotional weight this prospect can bring. “There’s a deep expectation, especially on Irish women, to put family care before personal aspirations,” she says. “But these feelings of resentment or anxiety are not selfish — they’re a signal that your own boundaries need to be respected too.”

For couples, the key is honest and ongoing communication. “Sit down with your husband and discuss your fears openly, before the situation becomes urgent,” Dr O’Reilly advises. “Try to avoid accusations or defensiveness. Focus on how you see your own life over the next five or ten years, and what you’re realistically able and willing to do.”

She adds that it’s also reasonable to explore external options for care, such as home help, day centres, or long-term residential care if necessary. The HSE provides assessment and supports, but many families remain unaware of what’s available or assume there’s no alternative to taking on the work themselves.

“Remember, being a loving spouse doesn’t mean sacrificing your health or happiness,” says Dr O’Reilly. “It’s about partnership, not martyrdom. If you feel under pressure, reach out to a counsellor or support group. Your feelings are valid and you’re not alone — thousands of families are having these conversations every day.”

Above all, she encourages couples to plan ahead. A frank conversation now, while everyone is able to take part, can prevent bitterness and misunderstandings later. With compassion, clear boundaries, and knowledge of the supports available, it’s possible to look after your loved ones — and yourself — with dignity and care.
headline: Dear Dáithí: I'm worried I'll end up as a carer for my mother-in-law

text:
A man is set to face criminal charges after a fire caused damage to the official residence of the governor of Pennsylvania, authorities in the US state confirmed on Thursday.

The incident occurred late Wednesday night at the governor’s mansion in Harrisburg, the state capital, with emergency services responding to reports of a blaze at the historic property shortly after 1am local time. Firefighters managed to contain the fire before it could spread throughout the building. No injuries were reported, and the governor, Josh Shapiro, his family, and staff members were unharmed.

State police in Pennsylvania stated that the suspect, a 30-year-old man from the local area, was taken into custody at the scene. He faces charges including arson, criminal mischief, reckless endangerment, and burglary. The suspect’s identity has not yet been released, pending the formal filing of charges. Officials said the investigation remains ongoing, but there is no indication at this stage that the incident was politically motivated.

The governor’s office confirmed that minor damage was sustained to part of the property’s exterior, with no significant harm reported to the main living quarters or historic artefacts within the mansion. A spokesperson for Governor Shapiro thanked first responders for their swift action and expressed relief that no one had been injured.

The Pennsylvania governor’s mansion, which overlooks the Susquehanna River, has served as the residence of the state’s chief executive since 1968. It regularly hosts official events, receptions, and international dignitaries.

Local authorities are expected to provide further updates as the investigation progresses. In the meantime, security measures at the property have been increased as a precaution.

The incident is likely to prompt a review of security protocols at other official residences across the United States. The governor’s office said it remains fully operational, and no disruptions to state business are anticipated.
headline: Man to face charges after fire damages Pennsylvania governor’s mansion

text:
The Government has given the green light to the long-awaited M28 Cork to Ringaskiddy motorway, approving an allocation of €456 million for the project at Cabinet on Tuesday. The development, which has been in the pipeline for over a decade, is set to deliver a vital transport corridor connecting Cork city with the deepwater port at Ringaskiddy, with significant implications for industry, commuters, and local communities throughout the region.

Minister for Transport Eamon Ryan confirmed the decision following the Cabinet meeting, describing the project as "critical infrastructure for the South and for the national economy". He said construction is expected to begin in late 2024, subject to finalised tendering, with the motorway scheduled for completion by 2028.

The M28 will stretch for approximately 12.5km, providing a high-capacity, high-quality dual carriageway from the existing South Ring Road at Bloomfield through Carrigaline to the Port of Cork’s Ringaskiddy facility. The scheme also includes the upgrade of junctions, new cycleways and footpaths, and environmental mitigation measures to address local concerns over noise and biodiversity.

The decision comes after a protracted planning process, with An Bord Pleanála granting approval in 2018 following a lengthy oral hearing and several High Court challenges from residents and environmental groups. The National Development Plan lists the M28 as a priority for the southern region, and it is seen as essential to unlocking further job creation and investment at the expanding Ringaskiddy port.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin, who is a TD for Cork South-Central, welcomed the move, saying it marked "a new era of connectivity for Cork and the wider region". He acknowledged that while the project will bring disruption during construction, "the benefits for residents, businesses and commuters will be immense in the years ahead".

However, some local residents remain opposed, expressing concerns about increased traffic, noise and potential impacts on their communities. The M28 Steering Group, representing several affected estates, said it would continue to seek assurances regarding mitigation measures and road safety.

The HSE has also noted that the motorway will improve ambulance access to both Cork University Hospital and the planned elective hospital at the Cork Science and Innovation Park, reducing journey times on what is currently a heavily congested route.

Ringaskiddy is home to some of the world’s largest pharmaceutical firms, as well as the National Maritime College of Ireland. The Port of Cork Authority said the upgraded road will support growth in freight and cruise ship operations and will be "transformative for both the local and national economy".

Transport Infrastructure Ireland will oversee the project, with input from Cork County Council, and a public information campaign is due to begin in the coming weeks outlining timelines and what residents can expect during construction. 

Environmental campaigners have called for full transparency around the project’s impact, while business groups in Cork have said the Government’s commitment will “future-proof” the region’s economy by improving access to critical transport hubs.

The M28 project represents the largest single investment in roads infrastructure in Munster in over a decade. The Minister for Public Expenditure Paschal Donohoe said the Cabinet’s approval underlines the Government’s commitment to balanced regional development and to delivering on the ambitions of Project Ireland 2040.
headline: Cabinet approves €456m M28 Cork to Ringaskiddy motorway project

Gaeltacht communities are facing a severe housing shortage, with newly published figures revealing that the number of Airbnbs vastly outstrips available long-term rental accommodation in the majority of these areas.

According to an analysis by advocacy group Uplift, in 25 out of 26 designated Gaeltacht regions, there are at least 100 times more entire homes listed on Airbnb than there are homes available to rent on Daft.ie, Ireland’s largest property website. In some Gaeltacht districts, there are no permanent rental properties listed at all.

The disparity has raised concerns about the future sustainability of Gaeltacht communities, where the Irish language and culture are protected under government policy. Critics say the proliferation of short-term holiday lets is contributing to an exodus of young people and families who are unable to find homes in their native areas.

In Connemara, one of the largest Gaeltacht regions, Uplift found just two homes available for long-term rent on Daft.ie, compared to 237 properties listed on Airbnb. On Donegal’s Gaeltacht coast, only one long-term rental was identified, alongside 287 entire homes on Airbnb.

The figures come amid a broader national debate over the impact of short-term letting platforms on Ireland’s housing crisis. New laws requiring most landlords to register short-term lets are set to come into force in September, but housing campaigners say enforcement will be crucial to address the imbalance in high-demand rural and coastal locations.

Speaking to the Irish Examiner, Uplift campaigner Aoife O’Leary called for urgent action. “The Irish language and the culture of the Gaeltacht are under threat if people cannot afford or find homes where they were raised. Short-term lets must be regulated much more strictly in these vulnerable regions,” she said.

Local representatives echoed the concerns. Donegal TD Thomas Pringle said: “Our young people are being forced out because they can’t rent or buy. The Government’s failure to control the spread of short-term lets is hollowing out our rural communities.”

The Department of Housing told the Irish Examiner it recognises the acute pressures facing Gaeltacht areas and pointed to upcoming regulations as part of the State’s efforts to redress the issue.

The new short-term letting rules will require property owners to secure planning permission before advertising for short stays in designated rent pressure zones, a measure that will cover several Gaeltacht areas. However, critics argue that without sufficient resources for local authorities and enforcement by the relevant agencies, the rules will have limited effect.

A spokesperson for Conradh na Gaeilge, the Irish language advocacy organisation, said: “Housing is a cornerstone of community life. If we want the Irish language to not only survive but thrive, families must be able to secure affordable, long-term homes in the Gaeltacht.”

The Department of Tourism said it is “working closely with the Department of Housing and Údarás na Gaeltachta to strike a balance between the needs of communities and tourism in the region”.

As peak summer holiday season approaches, the issue has come into sharper focus, with local schools and sports clubs warning of a long-term decline in numbers if young families continue to be priced out.

Housing Minister Darragh O’Brien is expected to face questions on the matter in the Dáil this week, with opposition TDs set to demand stronger regulatory and enforcement measures.
headline: Gaeltacht areas have 100 times more Airbnbs to let than permanent rental properties, new data shows

Former US president Donald Trump has issued a stark warning to Iran, stating “watch what happens” as tensions continue to simmer in the Middle East in the wake of recent attacks and diplomatic manoeuvring.

Speaking at a campaign rally in Michigan, Trump criticised the current US administration’s approach to Iran, accusing President Joe Biden of “weakness” and vowing that a potential Trump return to the White House would mark a dramatic shift in policy. “If Iran does something bad, they will pay a price like never before,” he said to cheers from supporters, adding: “Just watch what happens.”

Trump’s remarks follow heightened concerns over Iranian involvement in regional conflicts, particularly amid ongoing violence in the Gaza Strip and cross-border exchanges between Israel and Hezbollah. Last month, Iran launched a missile and drone barrage at Israel, prompting global condemnation and calls for restraint from Ireland and other European nations.

His comments have been widely circulated by US media outlets and have drawn criticism from political opponents, who accused Trump of inflaming tensions and engaging in “dangerous posturing”. Senior Democrats urged the Republican frontrunner to exercise caution, warning that strong rhetoric could further destabilise the situation in the Middle East.

The Irish Department of Foreign Affairs has not commented directly on Trump’s latest statements, but a spokesperson reiterated Ireland’s continued support for diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions in the region. “We condemn all acts of violence and urge all parties to show maximum restraint and respect for international law,” the department said.

Ireland has maintained an active interest in Middle East affairs, with the Tánaiste Micheál Martin calling for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza and reiterating Ireland’s support for a two-state solution. Irish NGOs and humanitarian organisations have also called for greater international action to prevent further conflict.

Trump’s renewed focus on Iran comes as the US presidential election campaign intensifies, with foreign policy and American influence abroad set to feature prominently in debates leading up to November’s poll. The Biden administration, meanwhile, has reaffirmed its commitment to working with international partners to contain Iranian aggression and support stability in the region.

While Trump’s statements have been dismissed by White House officials as campaign rhetoric, analysts warn that the risk of miscalculation between the US, Iran and regional actors remains high. The coming months are expected to see further diplomatic efforts, with the European Union and the United Nations urging all sides to avoid escalation.
headline: ‘Watch what happens’ – Donald Trump issues new threat to Iran

text:
Students sitting Higher Level Accounting in this year’s Leaving Certificate were generally positive about Wednesday’s paper, with teachers and exam experts saying it favoured candidates who were “match fit” and well-rehearsed in past questions.

The two-and-a-half hour paper, which kicked off at 9.30am across the country, was described as “fair with a sting in the tail” by teachers, with strong overlap between key topics and the published exam guidelines. Many students left exam centres at midday with a sense of relief, reporting familiar formats and manageable calculations, though some expressed concern about time pressure and the need for “plenty of practice”.

Question 1, the ever-present Company Final Accounts, offered a typically structured challenge, with a focus on the sale of fixed assets and bonus issue of shares. This question, worth 100 marks, proved time-consuming for some, but students who had worked through previous years’ papers found the layout familiar. According to John McCarthy, Accounting teacher at a Cork secondary school, “Anyone who had put in the hours with past paper practice would have felt at home, but there was little scope for guesswork.”

Other topics included Interpretation of Accounts, Correction of Errors, and Cash Flow Statements. There were few surprises, with the expected appearance of Club Accounts and Tabular Statements, in line with the assessment arrangements outlined by the State Examinations Commission. However, Question 5, often referred to as the ‘wildcard’, this year presented a less common scenario, requiring candidates to adjust for investment income received in advance, which left some students “momentarily caught out”, as one Leaving Cert candidate from Dublin put it.

The Irish Business Teachers’ Association (IBTA) described the exam as “well balanced”, acknowledging that “students with solid preparation and exam technique would have been well able for it.” They warned, however, that “those relying on rote learning or hoping for a predictable pattern would have found themselves under pressure, especially on the time-consuming calculation sections.”

With approximately 5,000 students sitting Higher Level Accounting this year, the subject remains a popular choice for those aiming for business or commerce programmes at third level. The majority of students spoken to outside centres in Cork, Limerick and Dublin said they felt “reasonably confident” about securing their grades, with one adding, “It was tough in parts, but if you’ve done your study, you’d have managed.”

Marking is now underway, with provisional results due for release alongside all other Leaving Certificate papers in late August. Guidance counsellors have advised students to focus attention on their remaining exams and “not to dwell on yesterday’s paper”, with Home Economics, Construction Studies and German still to come this week.
headline: Accounting exam suited 'match fit' students who had done 'plenty of practice'

text:
None of the victims killed in Wednesday’s shooting at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas (UNLV) were students, university authorities have confirmed, with all three fatalities being faculty members. The announcement comes as the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police continue their investigation into the campus attack, which also left one person critically injured.

The suspected gunman, identified by US media as Anthony Polito, a 67-year-old former college professor, was shot dead by police minutes after opening fire near the university’s business school during late morning classes. The attack sent students and staff scrambling to secure themselves in classrooms and prompted a large-scale response from law enforcement. A fourth victim remains in hospital with critical injuries.

UNLV President Dr Keith E. Whitfield, in a statement released on Thursday, described the shootings as a “devastating loss” for the university. “We have lost valued colleagues, mentors, and friends. Our hearts are broken for the families of the victims and our entire campus community,” Dr Whitfield said.

Authorities have not formally released the names of the victims, citing notification of families. However, US media outlets have identified at least one of the deceased as a business professor. No motive for the shooting has been confirmed, but reports suggest the suspect had previously applied unsuccessfully for a position at the university.

Clark County Sheriff Kevin McMahill told reporters that the swift response by campus police prevented further tragedy. “Our officers engaged the suspect within minutes, likely saving many lives,” Sheriff McMahill said. He confirmed that there were no fatalities or injuries reported among students during the incident.

The Gardaí have warned Irish citizens in Nevada to remain mindful of developments and to heed local instructions. The Department of Foreign Affairs updated its travel advice for Irish citizens in Las Vegas as a “precautionary measure” but said no Irish nationals were known to be affected by the shooting.

The incident is the latest in a series of gun violence outbreaks on US campuses in recent years, prompting renewed calls for gun control reforms amid widespread public concern. President Joe Biden issued a statement expressing condolences to the families of those killed, saying the “epidemic” of gun violence must be addressed.

Classes at UNLV have been cancelled for the remainder of the week, and counselling services have been made available for students and staff. The university has asked anyone affected to reach out to support organisations as the campus community begins to come to terms with the tragedy.
headline: No students killed in Las Vegas shooting with victims all faculty members, university says
