Former US president Donald Trump is due to address a hastily convened gathering of high-ranking military officials, according to a senior US administration source. The meeting, which was announced with little public notice late on Wednesday, is set to take place at an undisclosed location in Washington, DC.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, stated that the purpose of the meeting had not been disclosed to the broader defence community, with details tightly held among Trump’s inner circle and key Pentagon staff. The development comes amid mounting political tension as the US heads into a highly charged election season, with Mr Trump seeking to reclaim the White House in November.

A spokesperson for the US Department of Defense declined to comment on the agenda for the meeting, but confirmed that senior military commanders, including Joint Chiefs of Staff chair General Charles Brown, have been summoned. It is understood that members of the National Security Council have also been asked to attend.

Observers in Washington have speculated the meeting may relate to ongoing foreign policy challenges faced by the US, including the continuing war in Ukraine and heightened tensions in the Middle East. Some analysts have suggested Mr Trump may seek to outline a revised national security approach should he secure victory in the upcoming presidential race.

Democratic party leaders have criticised the lack of transparency around the meeting, with Senator Chuck Schumer calling for greater clarity on the issues to be discussed. “At a time of significant global instability, the American people have a right to know what their leaders are discussing behind closed doors,” he said.

This latest move comes days after Mr Trump was acquitted in a high-profile court case in New York, further fuelling speculation over his influence within the Republican party and the broader US political system. His campaign team has dismissed suggestions that the meeting is intended to signal his return to active political life, insisting instead that it is focused on “ensuring the security and prosperity of the American nation”.

Irish officials at the Department of Foreign Affairs are understood to be monitoring developments closely, with one source indicating that the Irish Embassy in Washington has sought clarification from US authorities on the nature and potential implications of the talks.

As Washington braces for further political drama in the weeks ahead, diplomatic sources say international partners—including Ireland—will be watching carefully for any signals of a shift in US military or foreign policy direction.
headline: Donald Trump to speak at hastily called meeting of top military leaders, says official

text:
The stabbing attack in Blanchardstown, which the Gardaí have confirmed was motivated by Islamist extremism, marks a sobering first for Ireland—and shatters long-held assumptions about the nation’s immunity to such violence. While Irish society has, until now, largely watched the spread of jihadist-inspired attacks across Europe from a safe distance, last Thursday’s events draw a stark line under how far the country can no longer consider itself merely a bystander.

It’s worth recalling that Ireland, despite its open borders within the European Union and increasingly diverse communities, has always prided itself on social cohesion and the relative absence of the kind of radicalisation seen elsewhere. Yet the suspect—who, according to Garda sources, appears to have acted alone and was not previously on the State’s terrorism radar—demonstrates the limitations of that comforting narrative. The details emerging from the ongoing inquiry, overseen by the Garda National Immigration Bureau and the Special Detective Unit, point to a self-radicalisation process largely conducted online and outside the scope of established extremist networks.

For the authorities, this raises urgent questions. How resilient is Ireland’s counter-terrorism apparatus to the “lone wolf” model—a scenario vexing security services across Europe for years? The Gardaí have made notable progress in inter-agency cooperation, relying on established links with Europol and counterparts in the UK and elsewhere. Yet Ireland’s intelligence resources, relative to those of larger neighbours, remain comparatively small. Garda Commissioner Drew Harris has publicly acknowledged the increased workload and sophistication required in tracking potential threats, calling for additional resources and updated legislative frameworks to keep pace with evolving risks.

While the Minister for Justice, Helen McEntee, has moved to reassure the public and underlined that there is no evidence of a wider threat, a more searching discussion about national preparedness is now inevitable. The rapid radicalisation potential on social media, as illustrated by this attack, challenges conventional methods of detection. Monitoring online spaces—within the bounds of privacy and rights—is a fraught but unavoidable reality.

The response at political level has, thus far, wisely avoided knee-jerk reactions. Calls for calm have been matched by a commitment to review existing counter-terrorism legislation, including the Criminal Justice (Terrorist Offences) Acts. However, some opposition TDs are likely to press for a more robust approach, including enhanced Garda resources and more stringent community engagement measures.

It is crucial that this debate steers clear of stigmatising Ireland’s Muslim community, who have repeatedly condemned extremist violence and who, in many cases, are among the first to feel the consequences of increased suspicion. Community leaders and inter-faith organisations have already responded with statements of solidarity for the victims and reaffirmed a commitment to dialogue.

From a policy perspective, Ireland’s challenge now is to recalibrate its security response without sacrificing the values of openness and inclusivity that have defined the State for decades. Investment in intelligence, better community outreach, and partnerships with international agencies will all form part of that evolving toolkit. Above all, the events in Blanchardstown must prompt a sober reappraisal of the Irish context—one that recognises the reality of extremist threats without abandoning the principles that set Ireland apart.

The attack may be an isolated incident, but it has ended the assumption that Ireland is somehow uniquely insulated from global trends. The next steps taken by the State will define whether that realisation results in a more resilient, yet still open, society.
headline: Ireland’s first Islamist-inspired knife attack raises urgent questions about extremist threats

text:
Older people are facing significantly higher costs for private health insurance, with policyholders aged over 65 paying on average 43% more than younger adults, according to a new report from the Health Insurance Authority (HIA). 

The regulator’s annual market review, published on Thursday, reveals that people over 65 are paying €1,946 per person on average for private medical cover, compared to an average of €1,361 for adults aged between 18 and 65. This disparity occurs despite the system of community rating, which is designed to prevent insurers from charging older customers more for the same cover.

The HIA said the price gap is mainly due to older consumers choosing plans with wider cover, including access to private hospitals and reduced or no excess charges. However, the authority has raised concerns about the affordability of cover for those approaching or in retirement, particularly in the context of ongoing premium increases across the sector.

Chief executive Laura Brien said the system remains “broadly effective” but warned that “significant differentials” have emerged due to the proliferation of policy choice and plan complexity. “While the community rating system continues to protect older and sicker consumers, the market has developed a wide variety of plans. Many older people are opting for more comprehensive and therefore more expensive policies, but a lack of clear information and advice can make it difficult for consumers to assess value for money,” Ms Brien said.

The HIA has called on health insurers to do more to proactively communicate options to customers, particularly those approaching renewal, and to simplify product offerings. The authority also urged consumers to review their policies regularly, as many could save by switching plans or insurers.

This year has seen a series of health insurance price hikes, with the country’s three main providers — VHI, Laya Healthcare, and Irish Life Health — all announcing increases of between 4% and 7% from the spring. Insurers have cited rising costs due to increased claims volumes, medical inflation, and higher demand for private care after the Covid-19 pandemic.

Industry analysts say the increasing reliance on private insurance to access hospital care is placing pressure on older people to maintain cover as they age. “There is a real fear among over-65s about giving up health insurance, particularly given the waiting lists in the public system,” said Dermot Goode, a health insurance adviser. “However, it’s vital that people are aware that there are cheaper plans available, and switching does not mean losing out on key benefits,” he added.

The HIA estimates that three in four over-65s in Ireland hold some form of private health cover, compared to two in five adults overall. The report also found that the number of health insurance customers has reached 2.5 million, the highest level since records began.

Responding to the findings, Age Action called for “urgent action” to protect older people from being priced out of the market. “Health insurance should not become a luxury for the wealthy or a cause of financial worry for those on modest pensions,” the group said.

The Department of Health said it is working with the HIA to ensure “fairness and transparency” in the market, and to support consumers to make informed decisions. Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly said the Government remains committed to strengthening public health services so older people do not feel dependent on private insurance to access timely care.
headline: Over 65s pay 43% more for health insurance, watchdog finds

text:
Kathleen MacMahon admits there are mornings when she still aches for the urgent thrill of the newsroom. “There’s a certain buzz you get from not knowing what story will land in your lap, what will break next,” she says, recalling her two decades with RTÉ News. “I do sometimes miss the camaraderie, and the sense of events unfolding right before your eyes.” Yet, as her latest novel, The Home Scar, hits bookshop shelves, MacMahon says she’s found another way to chase truth—through fiction.

Speaking to the Irish Examiner at her bright, book-lined home in Sandymount, MacMahon describes the odd comfort and solitude of the novelist’s life. “I suppose it’s not as lonely as people imagine. You’re always in conversation—just with your characters, rather than a producer shouting in your ear,” she laughs. Since the seismic success of her 2012 debut, This is How it Ends, MacMahon has become a steady presence on the Irish literary scene, her work praised for its subtlety, wit, and the sharpness of emotion threading through apparently ordinary lives.

Her new novel is no exception. The Home Scar is, at its heart, about mothers and daughters: the stories we inherit, the ones we’re desperate to tell, and those we never quite manage to say aloud. “I’ve always been fascinated by the push and pull between generations of Irish women,” MacMahon says. “That sense of closeness, but also of things withheld.” The novel follows two women—one Irish, one Nigerian—whose lives intersect unexpectedly, revealing fault lines that stretch back decades.

For MacMahon, whose own mother, Val Joyce, was a much-loved radio broadcaster, the theme is deeply personal. “Growing up in a house where words mattered, I became aware of the power of what’s left unsaid. My relationship with my mother was complicated, in the way all mother-daughter bonds are.” She pauses, turning over her words. “It’s never simple, is it? I think Irish women, especially, are taught to be strong, to get on with things. But that can come at a cost.”

The writer sees echoes of those dynamics in Irish society more broadly. “Look at how the stories of women have come to the fore in recent years—the Mother and Baby Homes, the Repeal campaign,” she says. “There’s a hunger in Ireland to look at our past, to confront things.” Fiction, she believes, can be a way to break down walls that journalism sometimes cannot. “When you’re writing news, you’re bound by verifiable facts. With fiction, you can explore emotional truths—the things people think but don’t voice, the secrets that shape families.”

Though she’s left the daily cut and thrust of RTÉ behind, MacMahon believes her broadcasting background still informs her writing. “You learn that everyone has a story—often more complicated than you expect.” She credits her time covering everything from elections at Leinster House to summer stories of community life for fostering empathy and curiosity, tools that now serve her at the desk where she drafts each morning.

As for where Irish fiction goes next, MacMahon is optimistic. “We’re living in a golden age, really. There’s a new confidence—you see it in younger writers, in those taking on topics once considered taboo.”
headline: Kathleen MacMahon on missing journalism, the mother/daughter relationship and her latest novel

A woman in her 30s has appeared before Carlow District Court charged in connection with the murder of a man in the town earlier this week.

Gardaí arrested the accused, who cannot be named for legal reasons, after a man in his late 40s was discovered with fatal injuries at a residential property on the outskirts of Carlow town in the early hours of Sunday morning.

Emergency services were called to the scene shortly after midnight, where the victim was pronounced dead despite efforts by paramedics and Gardaí. The man’s body was removed to University Hospital Waterford where a post-mortem examination was conducted by State Pathologist Dr Linda Mulligan.

During a brief hearing this morning, Detective Garda Eoin O’Donnell gave evidence of arrest, charge and caution. He told Judge Geraldine Carthy that the woman made no reply when the charge was put to her at Carlow Garda Station on Monday evening.

Defence solicitor John Murphy applied for legal aid, noting that his client is not currently in employment and has limited means. He also requested that the woman receive appropriate medical attention while in custody, telling the court that she has a history of mental health difficulties.

Judge Carthy remanded the accused in custody to appear again before the District Court via videolink on 18 June. She directed that all necessary medical and psychiatric assessments be carried out.

An incident room has been established at Carlow Garda Station and a Senior Investigating Officer has been appointed to oversee the investigation, which Gardaí say is ongoing. Officers are appealing for any witnesses who may have been in the area of the Burrin Road between 11pm and 1am on Sunday to contact them.

The deceased has not yet been formally identified, but Gardaí said efforts are ongoing to contact next of kin.

The court was told that the Director of Public Prosecutions has been notified and further charges may follow as the investigation progresses.
headline: Woman, 30s, appears in court in connection with murder of man in Carlow

text:
Sara Ochs’ debut novel, *The Resort*, arrives with the kind of quietly assured craft and confidence that belies its author’s newcomer status. A legal academic by background, Ochs brings forensic precision to both her prose and the tightly-wound plotting of this atmospheric thriller, set against the intoxicating backdrop of a luxury Thai island.

From the opening pages, Ochs envelops the reader in the languor and latent menace of her sun-drenched setting. The story revolves around Cass, a young American woman fleeing a traumatic past, who finds herself working at the eponymous resort. The staff are a motley but close-knit crew of international escapees, each with secrets of their own, while the privileged guests flit in and out, alternately oblivious and all-seeing. When a guest is found dead under suspicious circumstances, suspicion falls on every side, and Cass is drawn inexorably into a tangle of intrigue, suspicion, and danger.

Ochs excels in conjuring both place and atmosphere, painting the resort and its surroundings in lush, evocative detail, so that the island itself emerges as a character: seductive, claustrophobic, and faintly sinister. Yet she balances this with deft psychological insight, exploring the motivations and wounds of Cass and her cohort with empathy and nuance.

What most distinguishes *The Resort*—and what marks Ochs out as a talent to watch—is the quiet assurance of her narrative voice. The pacing, taut and deliberate, never falters; the plot, while twisty, never strains credulity. Ochs also threads timely questions about privilege, exploitation, and what it means to belong through the narrative, giving her story a bracing contemporary edge.

Irish readers may find particular resonance in the novel’s themes of exile and reinvention, and in Cass’s uneasy search for community in a place both inviting and fundamentally alien. The spectre of trauma—personal and collective—hovers over the action, but Ochs resists simple resolutions, preferring instead to dwell in the ambiguous spaces between guilt and innocence, victim and perpetrator.

Though *The Resort* has all the trappings of an escapist beach read—sweeping beaches, forbidden romance, and a murder mystery at its core—it is elevated by Ochs’ sharp, elegant prose and her refusal to shy away from the darker undercurrents of her characters’ experiences. The result is a novel that lingers in the mind, as unsettling as it is immersive.

With this strikingly accomplished debut, Sara Ochs stakes a compelling claim in the crowded landscape of contemporary thrillers. Readers will be left eagerly anticipating where her talent will take her next.
headline: Book Review: Sara Ochs' debut is strikingly assured and accomplished

A large-scale polio vaccination campaign was launched on Sunday across the Gaza Strip, as health officials and international organisations rush to prevent the spread of the crippling disease amid deteriorating sanitary conditions.

The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), in partnership with the World Health Organisation (WHO) and local authorities, is coordinating the initiative in response to recent confirmation of poliovirus in wastewater samples. While no cases of paralysis have yet been reported, experts warn that the risk of an outbreak is heightened by the ongoing conflict, mass displacement, and severe disruption of health services.

The campaign aims to immunise over 500,000 children under the age of five, with mobile vaccination teams moving through refugee camps, shelters, and makeshift population centres. Gaza’s health system, already battered by months of Israeli bombardment and shortages, is struggling to maintain basic services, and routine vaccination programmes have been heavily disrupted.

Speaking on Sunday, Dr Hanan Balkhy, WHO Regional Director for the Eastern Mediterranean, said: “The conditions in Gaza create an urgent need for action. The vaccination drive is vital to protect children from a disease we know how to prevent but can devastate communities if left unchecked.”

The campaign comes amid surges in other infectious diseases, including measles and hepatitis A, as hundreds of thousands of people are crammed into overcrowded, unsanitary locations after fleeing violence in the north of the territory. Aid agencies report that children are particularly vulnerable, with safe water, food, and shelter in critically short supply.

Irish humanitarian organisations, including Trócaire and Concern Worldwide, have called for sustained access for medical and aid teams. The Department of Foreign Affairs this week reiterated Ireland’s support for international relief efforts, with Tánaiste Micheál Martin urging all parties to allow unfettered humanitarian access.

Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, launched after the 7th October attacks by Hamas, has left the enclave’s health infrastructure in ruins. Many clinics and hospitals have been destroyed or are operating far beyond capacity. UNICEF warned that the risk of vaccine-preventable diseases is now “extremely high”.

The UN and its partners are appealing for additional funding to support vaccination logistics and medical supplies. Local Palestinian health workers, assisted by international staff, are working in difficult and sometimes dangerous conditions. The UN has described Gaza as “on the brink of catastrophe” and called for an immediate ceasefire to facilitate medical and humanitarian operations.

In recent years, polio has re-emerged in several conflict zones globally, as war and instability undermine disease control efforts. Gaza’s last reported case of wild poliovirus was in 1996, but experts say the current situation could reverse decades of progress.

Parents in Gaza are being urged to bring children to vaccination points or wait for mobile teams, with health officials emphasising the safety and necessity of immunisation. With limited electricity and fuel, maintaining the cold chain for vaccines presents an ongoing challenge.

International monitors, including the HSE’s overseas arm, have been deployed to assist with surveillance and reporting. Irish diplomats have reiterated the government’s commitment to supporting child health in emergencies, saying that “no child should suffer from a disease we can prevent”. 

The campaign is expected to run for two weeks, with a follow-up round planned if needed. Aid agencies warn that without sustained support and access, the risks to Gaza’s children will continue to grow.
headline: Massive polio vaccination campaign begins in Gaza

text:
RTÉ has confirmed the addition of a new face to the judging panel of Dancing With The Stars, following Loraine Barry’s surprise departure after seven seasons at the helm. After weeks of speculation among fans and insiders, the national broadcaster announced that esteemed choreographer and TV personality, Julian Benson, will join Brian Redmond and Arthur Gourounlian for the forthcoming series, set to air in early January.

Benson, well known to Irish audiences from his previous stint as a judge on the hit show and for his advocacy as founder of the Julian Benson Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, is making a much-anticipated return to the ballroom. His lively on-screen presence and expertise in dance promise to bring both continuity and a fresh energy to the judging line-up.

Loraine Barry, who cited personal reasons for her decision to step back, played a pivotal role in establishing Dancing With The Stars as a fixture of the Irish television calendar since its launch in 2017. The Dubliner, herself a four-time world ballroom champion, endeared herself to viewers with her wit, warmth and unwavering devotion to dance. In a statement released by RTÉ, Barry thanked the show's fans, fellow judges and crew for their support, and wished the new panel well, expressing her confidence that the series “will continue to showcase the very best of Irish dance and talent”.

Benson expressed his excitement at the opportunity to return, saying: “It’s an honour to be invited back to a show that means so much to me and to so many people across Ireland. I look forward to seeing all the glitz, glamour, and incredible talent on the dancefloor this season.”

The move comes as RTÉ seeks to continue the programme’s strong performance in the Sunday night schedule, with last year’s grand final drawing an average audience of over half a million viewers, according to figures released by TAM Ireland. Sources within the production hinted that Benson’s appointment was in part a response to audience feedback, following his popular appearances as a guest judge in previous years.

While the full line-up of celebrity contestants will not be announced until later this month, the producers have promised “some of Ireland’s most recognisable faces” will take to the floor for the new series. Presenter Jennifer Zamparelli returns to host, and the show's professional dancers are also expected to remain largely unchanged.

For many, the reintroduction of Julian Benson signals an intent by RTÉ to maintain the fun and inclusive spirit that has made Dancing With The Stars a highlight of the winter TV schedule. Industry commentators point to the enduring appeal of the dance contest, especially at a time when homegrown entertainment is facing increasing competition from international streaming platforms.

Tickets for studio recordings are expected to be in high demand once again, with audiences eager to see how the new judging dynamic plays out live each week in Donnybrook. The show’s producers say they are “working closely with RTÉ to ensure the magic, excitement and high standard of production audiences expect”.

As preparations gather pace for the new season, the broadcaster faces both the challenge of living up to the legacy set by Loraine Barry and the promise of a new era for one of Ireland’s best-loved family favourites.
headline: Revealed: New Dancing With The Stars judge confirmed following Loraine Barry's exit

Latest JNLR listenership figures have confirmed RTÉ Radio 1’s Morning Ireland as the most listened-to radio programme in the country, while Cork's own Neil Prendeville has retained his leading position locally.

Morning Ireland, broadcast weekdays on RTÉ Radio 1, continues to attract a national audience, with 491,000 listeners tuning in each morning, according to the Joint National Listenership Research (JNLR) survey for the period from April 2023 to March 2024. The news and current affairs flagship remains the country’s clear radio leader, maintaining its grip at the top for yet another year.

Meanwhile, in Cork, RedFM’s The Neil Prendeville Show remains the most popular programme for Rebel County listeners, with 123,000 tuning in each week. Prendeville, who returned to RedFM in 2014 after a brief stint at 96FM, continues to command a strong following, particularly among listeners aged 25-54.

Nationally, radio continues to play a central role in Irish daily life, with more than 3.3 million adults listening across the country every weekday. RTÉ Radio 1 remains the most popular station, with 864,000 daily listeners, followed by Today FM and Newstalk, which also recorded steady numbers.

There were gains for several RTÉ Radio 1 programmes, with Liveline, hosted by Joe Duffy, reaching 364,000 listeners, and The Ryan Tubridy Show—now helmed by Oliver Callan—at 334,000. However, the survey period also encompasses the fallout from the RTÉ payments controversy and management shake-ups, which have prompted significant public debate on the future of public service broadcasting.

RedFM and the Neil Prendeville Show continue to outpace local rivals in Cork, with the station highlighting its ongoing commitment to locally-focused content. C103 and 96FM, the other key players in the Cork market, also maintained strong weekly audiences, but Prendeville’s morning slot remains the most listened to in the region.

Industry observers noted that talk and news programmes continue to perform strongly, with Irish listeners showing a consistent appetite for current affairs and interactive formats. The JNLR survey is compiled by Ipsos B&A for the Irish radio industry and remains the definitive source for radio listenership data.

RTÉ Director-General Kevin Bakhurst welcomed the latest figures, saying they were “a testament to the trust Irish audiences place in our news and current affairs teams”. Meanwhile, RedFM management hailed Prendeville’s unwavering popularity as evidence of “the enduring strength of local voices in Cork radio”.

The survey also found that digital platforms, including streaming and podcasts, continue to supplement traditional listenership, particularly among younger audiences, but the radio dial remains dominant for large swathes of the population.

With the next JNLR figures due in the autumn, stations across the country will be watching closely to see if the dominance of Morning Ireland and Prendeville’s local reign can be sustained.
headline: Morning Ireland the country's most popular radio show as Neil Prendeville on top in Cork

Poet Michael Longley’s ability to “touch souls with just a few words” was remembered fondly at his funeral service in Belfast on Saturday. Mourners gathered at St Anne’s Cathedral to pay tribute to the revered writer, who died earlier this week at the age of 84, following a short illness.

A number of leading figures from Ireland’s literary and artistic communities joined family and friends in the packed cathedral. Among those in attendance were President Michael D Higgins, poet Paul Muldoon, and representatives of the Arts Council of Northern Ireland.

During the service, Longley’s daughter, Sarah, described him as “the best of fathers: witty, gentle, endlessly curious, and always encouraging”. She said, “He had the rare gift of saying so much with so little. He touched countless souls with just a handful of words.” She recalled his deep love for the Irish landscape and wildlife, as well as his devotion to his wife Edna, their children, and grandchildren.

Longley was born in Belfast in 1939 and was educated at the Royal Belfast Academical Institution and Trinity College Dublin. Over a career spanning six decades, he became one of the island’s most highly regarded poets, winning numerous awards, including the Queen’s Gold Medal for Poetry and the Griffin International Poetry Prize. In 2017, he was made a Freeman of the City of Belfast, and in 2022, he received the Freedom of Dublin for his contribution to literature.

The Dean of Belfast, the Very Reverend Stephen Forde, told mourners that Longley’s poems “gave voice to the silences of our lives and drew attention to the beauty in the everyday”. He said the poet had a unique ability to address themes of love, war, and loss “with a clarity and simplicity that made the complex feel approachable”.

Longley’s close friend and fellow poet, Sinéad Morrissey, read his poem “The Ice Cream Man”, recalling how his words offered comfort and hope during the Troubles in Northern Ireland. She told the congregation: “Michael taught us that poetry is not a luxury but a necessity, especially in difficult times.”

Among personal tributes, President Higgins praised Longley as “an artist whose work drew people together, north and south, and reminded us of our shared humanity”. The President added that Longley’s contribution to Irish culture would continue to “echo through the generations”.

After the service, Mr Longley’s coffin was carried from the cathedral to the gentle strains of a traditional Irish air, performed by uilleann piper Liam O’Flynn. Burial took place privately.

Longley is survived by Edna, their three children, and six grandchildren. The family expressed their gratitude for the many messages of support and condolences received from all over Ireland and beyond.
headline: Poet Michael Longley touched souls with just a few words, funeral hears

A man in his 20s has died following a single-vehicle crash in County Tipperary in the early hours of Sunday morning.

The incident occurred shortly before 1am on the R664 at Ballykisteen, near Tipperary Town. Gardaí and emergency services attended the scene after the car, in which the man was the sole occupant, left the road and struck a ditch.

The man, who was pronounced dead at the scene, was removed to University Hospital Limerick for a post-mortem examination. The stretch of road remains closed on Sunday morning to facilitate a forensic collision investigation, with local diversions in place.

Gardaí have appealed for witnesses to come forward, particularly any road users with dashcam footage from the area between midnight and 1.30am.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Tipperary Garda Station on 062 80670, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.

A Garda spokesperson extended condolences to the man’s family and said enquiries are ongoing. The tragedy brings to 73 the number of people who have lost their lives on Irish roads so far this year.
headline: Man, 20s, dies in single-vehicle crash in Tipperary

Elon Musk’s brain-implant company, Neuralink, is under investigation by US authorities amid concerns about “unsafe” methods used to ship devices potentially contaminated with hazardous materials, including pathogens. The US Department of Transportation (DoT) has confirmed it is conducting an inquiry after receiving claims of possible violations of regulations relating to the transport of dangerous goods.

The scrutiny centres on shipments from Neuralink’s facilities in California and Texas. Documents obtained by US news outlets indicate a former Neuralink employee alleged that the company failed to properly label and package materials contaminated with biohazards such as animal tissue, as well as transmit the necessary documentation to carriers.

The DoT said it “takes these allegations very seriously” and is reviewing whether the company’s observed practices meet federal requirements for the safe and legal transport of infectious substances. If the probe finds significant breaches, Neuralink could face penalties of up to several hundred thousand dollars.

Neuralink is developing a brain-computer interface device that aims to allow direct interaction between the human brain and digital devices. The company’s research has involved implanting devices in animal test subjects, including monkeys and pigs. Musk has repeatedly stated that the technology could one day help people with severe neurological conditions regain movement or communicate more easily.

Last year, Neuralink announced it had received approval from the US Food and Drug Administration to launch its first human trials. However, the company has faced criticism from animal welfare groups and researchers who accuse it of causing unnecessary harm to animals and failing to adhere to industry best practices for ethical research and safety.

In December, a separate federal investigation was launched into potential breaches of animal welfare standards, after reports surfaced of rushed and poorly executed experiments resulting in animal suffering. Neuralink has denied wrongdoing, insisting its facilities are subject to rigorous oversight, and has said it is cooperating fully with all regulatory enquiries.

The latest investigation comes as scrutiny of the intersection between technology, biotechnology, and public health rises globally. While Neuralink is a US-based firm, Irish regulators and research institutions are likely to monitor the outcome closely, given Ireland’s role as a European hub for medical technology and pharmaceutical innovation.

Neither Elon Musk nor Neuralink responded to requests for comment on the DoT investigation by the time of publication. The DoT declined to provide a timeline for the completion of its enquiry.
headline: Elon Musk’s brain-implant company investigated over ‘unsafe’ shipping methods

text:
A notable 74-acre farm outside Limerick city has changed hands for an accumulated sum exceeding €3.8 million, after a drawn-out sale process that attracted significant interest from both local farmers and outside investors.

Located at Clonmacken, just two kilometres from Limerick city centre, the land was presented for sale in late 2023 by GVM Auctioneers. The farm, renowned for its fertile limestone soils and good road frontage, had been owned for several decades by a local farming family, who decided to dispose of the holding as part of a wider restructuring of their agricultural interests.

Originally offered in three separate lots, the property was ultimately sold in two tranches. The majority of the acreage—approximately 54 acres of high-quality grazing land with road frontage—was sold by private treaty at the start of the year. According to auctioneers, fierce competition among bidders saw the price rise well above the initial guide, with the parcel eventually realising almost €52,000 per acre.

The remaining 20-acre parcel, which comprises a mix of arable and pasture land, as well as several derelict outbuildings, was sold to a different buyer for a figure in excess of €37,000 per acre. Both transactions were completed by late May, with contracts exchanged and title transferred last week. The combined sale price across both lots exceeded €3.8 million, making it one of the highest-value agricultural disposals in the county in recent years.

According to Tom Crosse of GVM Auctioneers, the sale demonstrates continued robust demand for prime agricultural land in Limerick, particularly close to the urban fringe, where land is increasingly sought both for farming and as a strategic investment amid ongoing city expansion. “We had viewers travelling from as far as Kilkenny and Cork,” he said. “Local farmers were very interested but so too were businesspeople and investors looking for land with long-term potential.”

The farm had been operated for beef and silage production in recent years, but neighbours expect part of the holding may now move to higher-value uses. Some speculation exists in the locality about a possible application for a change in land use, given the proximity to major roadways and urban amenities, though no planning submissions have yet been lodged with Limerick City and County Council.

The sector as a whole continues to see upward pressure on land values, with the most recent Irish Farmers Journal Land Price Report showing the average price for farmland in Munster rising to €14,709 per acre last year—though exceptional parcels, such as the Clonmacken holding, continue to attract premiums. Nationwide, land agents report a tight supply of large, quality blocks coming to market, with inheritance and restructuring the common triggers for sales.

The purchasers of both lots have not been named. It is understood that one is a well-established farmer with existing holdings in the county, while the other is a company with interests in land and property development.

Across the county, smaller farm holdings continue to change hands generally between €10,000 and €18,000 per acre, and experts predict the strong demand will persist for the foreseeable future, particularly on the periphery of Limerick city where pressure for development land is expected to intensify.

The sale at Clonmacken is regarded by many as a benchmark for future transactions in the region, with local estate agents predicting that holdings with similar location and quality could command equally strong prices in the coming months.
headline: Limerick farm sold for accumulated sum of over €3.8m

text:
A mural believed to be the work of the elusive street artist Banksy has appeared overnight at the base of one of London’s tallest skyscrapers, sparking fresh debate over public art and the city’s rapidly changing landscape.

The monochrome image, depicting a small child planting a sapling amid a backdrop of cranes and tower blocks, was spotted early on Tuesday on a hoarding at the foot of the 48-storey Heron Tower in the City. The style and execution have prompted speculation among art enthusiasts and local residents that the piece may, in fact, be an authentic Banksy.

Security staff initially attempted to cordon off the area but were quickly joined by passers-by eager to take photographs, with the site drawing a steady crowd throughout the morning. Local businesses reported a noticeable uptick in foot traffic soon after images began circulating on social media.

A spokesperson for Heron Tower said they were “aware of an unauthorised artwork” on their property and were “consulting with relevant authorities” regarding its preservation. No decision has yet been made on whether the mural will be kept or removed.

Noted art dealer Jonathan Shortall, who has previously authenticated Banksy pieces, told the Irish Examiner that the mural bears “the unmistakable hallmarks of Banksy’s political wit and technical skill,” but cautioned that “until the artist claims responsibility, its provenance remains uncertain.”

Banksy, whose true identity remains shrouded in mystery after more than two decades, is renowned for his satirical works addressing themes such as consumerism, inequality, and environmental degradation. The appearance of the new mural follows a spate of high-profile developments in central London, which have faced criticism from local campaigners who argue that rapid construction is undermining community identity.

The Metropolitan Police said they had received no complaints in relation to the artwork but were liaising with the building’s management, while officials in the London borough of Hackney, who have previously taken a hands-off approach to Banksy’s pieces, issued a statement urging “responsible stewardship of street art that contributes to the city’s cultural fabric.”

The piece’s potential value has already been raised among art collectors, with some experts suggesting it could be worth in excess of €1 million if authenticated.

Banksy customarily confirms new works via his official social media channels. As of press time, no such acknowledgement has been posted. Whether the mural will be allowed to remain or meet the same fate as several of Banksy’s previous interventions – swiftly removed or covered up – remains to be seen. 

For now, the curious and the devoted continue to flock to the Heron Tower, hoping to witness what may be the artist’s latest commentary on the ever-changing face of London.
headline: Artwork thought to be by Banksy appears at foot of London skyscraper

text:
Emma Donoghue’s 2016 novel, The Pull of the Stars, unfolds amid the chaos of the 1918 flu pandemic in Dublin. Now, transformed for the stage by Landmark Productions in collaboration with Dublin Theatre Festival, its resonance feels newly acute in a post-Covid Ireland, where the collective memory of crisis is still painfully fresh. The adaptation, directed by Louise Lowe and staged at the Project Arts Centre, is both urgent and intimate—drawing out connections between past and present that are impossible to ignore.

The story centres on Nurse Julia Power (Caoimhe Coburn Gray), working in a makeshift maternity ward at a Dublin hospital as the city, and the world beyond, reels from the twin traumas of war and pandemic. Over three harrowing days, Julia tends to pregnant women with influenza, some of whom will not live to see their children. Donoghue’s finely observed characters—Nurse Power, the idealistic volunteer Bridie Sweeney (Killian Filan), and the formidable Dr Kathleen Lynn (Sarah Morris)—are vividly realised, their fates intertwining in a cramped space heavy with the scent of fear, disinfectant, and hope.

The production’s design is spare yet immersive: beds lined up beneath stark lighting, the set adorned with ominous shadows. The audience’s proximity to the action, with seats arranged around the hospital ward, intensifies the sense of vulnerability. Lowe’s direction keeps the tension taut and the pace unrelenting, refusing to sanitise the exhaustion, the grief, or the fleeting moments of joy that punctuate the struggle for survival.

Coburn Gray is remarkable as Julia, anchoring the production with a performance that is both quietly authoritative and deeply compassionate. Filan’s Bridie brings warmth and humour, her innocence a poignant counterpoint to the horrors unfolding, while Morris imbues Dr Lynn with steely integrity—her activism and radicalism subtly evoked in every decisive movement.

Throughout, the script foregrounds the inequalities exposed by crisis. The mothers’ stories lay bare the poverty and neglect that persisted even as politicians debated in the Dáil, and the city’s most vulnerable paid the heaviest price. Echoes of the recent pandemic—staff shortages, public health messaging, suspicion of authority—are unmistakeable.

Yet the production resists simple analogies. Donoghue and Lowe let the human drama take precedence over polemics, allowing the audience to draw its own conclusions about what has changed, and what has not. The Pull of the Stars is a powerful reminder of the endurance and fragility of hope in the midst of catastrophe, told with unsentimental clarity. It is a gripping piece of theatre made all the more vital by the times we live in—haunted by a century-old story whose prescience now feels inescapable.
headline: Theatre review: Emma Donoghue's tale of 1918 has a renewed prescience

text:
This week’s Five For Your Radar brings together a blend of homegrown talent, international stardom, and community celebration, as summer kicks into gear across the arts. With choices spanning music, film, literature, and local festivals, there’s something to draw out the culture vulture in us all.

First up, Cork’s own Mick Flannery returns to the live stage for a string of intimate gigs around the country, including a sold-out date at the Everyman. The troubadour, long admired for his gravelly sincerity and razor-sharp lyrics, will showcase favourites from his acclaimed back catalogue alongside newer material. Flannery’s live shows have become something of a rite for Irish audiences—expect an emotional, occasionally mischievous, night.

On the cinema front, Emma Stone leads the highly anticipated Poor Things, released in Irish cinemas this Friday. Directed by Yorgos Lanthimos, with whom Stone previously collaborated on The Favourite, the film is a surreal, darkly comic take on female autonomy, based on the novel by Alasdair Gray. Early reviews hail Stone’s performance as fearless and wickedly funny. With Mark Ruffalo and Willem Dafoe rounding out the cast, it is tipped as a contender for next year’s big awards.

Literary fans will be flocking to Listowel for the 52nd annual Listowel Writers’ Week, running from 1–4 June. This year’s programme boasts a melting pot of established and emerging voices, including Roddy Doyle, Sinéad Gleeson, and Michael Harding. There are workshops, readings, and walking tours, cementing the Kerryman town’s reputation as the beating heart of Irish letters. Tickets are still available for select events, but advance booking is advised given the festival’s perennial popularity.

Back in Cork, the Midsummer Festival lights up the city from 12–23 June with a kaleidoscopic array of performance, visual art, and spoken word. Highlights include the European premiere of Clare Keegan’s Small Things Like These, adapted for stage, and a participatory dance spectacle taking over the Coal Quay. A genuine showcase for the region’s creative pulse, the festival invites families and seasoned theatregoers alike to soak up the midsummer magic.

Finally, for those seeking something a little offbeat, the Westport Sea Sessions kicks off the summer festival season along the Mayo coast. Running from 21–23 June, the event blends music, surfing, and street art in a lively, relaxed setting. Acts this year include Gavin James, Dec Pierce’s Block Rockin’ Beats, and Cian Ducrot. With tickets ranging from €59, and the sea breeze on tap, it’s a festival with a true sense of place.

Whatever your taste, this week’s picks affirm the vibrancy of Irish culture—rooted in tradition, global in reach, and always ready to surprise.
headline: Five For Your Radar: Mick Flannery, Emma Stone film, book festival...

text:
A seafood processing company in West Cork has been fined a total of €18,000 at Cork District Court after it was found guilty of six breaches of emissions regulations relating to its wastewater discharges.

The court heard how Banner Seafoods Ltd, based in Bantry, was prosecuted by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) following an inspection in June last year, which uncovered a series of non-compliances at the facility. Inspector Michael Donohoe of the EPA told the court that officers found “significantly elevated levels” of chemical oxygen demand, ammonia and suspended solids in samples taken from the plant’s final discharge point.

The company holds a waste water discharge licence under the Water Pollution Act, with strict conditions attached concerning the treatment and monitoring of effluent prior to its release into Bantry Bay. However, according to Mr Donohoe, Banner Seafoods had failed to maintain key treatment infrastructure and had not undertaken the stipulated self-monitoring tests for over four months.

Solicitor for the EPA, Eileen Murphy, said the breaches had the potential to cause “serious environmental damage” to the receiving waters and posed risks both to marine habitats and public health. She noted that the EPA had engaged with the company through warning letters and site visits, but “significant remedial action” was not taken until after proceedings commenced.

Defence solicitor John Lacey said Banner Seafoods “deeply regretted” the breaches, citing “serious financial challenges” linked to rising energy costs and staff shortages in the seafood sector. He told Judge Mary Dorgan that the company had since invested €45,000 in upgrading its water treatment systems and engaged an external consultant to oversee compliance.

Judge Dorgan remarked that the court “must send a strong message” regarding the protection of Ireland’s natural resources. She convicted Banner Seafoods on all six counts and imposed fines totalling €18,000, as well as ordering the company to pay €3,200 in prosecution costs.

In a statement, the EPA welcomed the outcome, saying it would continue to “vigorously enforce” environmental regulations to protect communities and ecosystems. Banner Seafoods declined to comment when contacted by the Irish Examiner.
headline: West Cork company fined for six breaches of emissions regulations

text:
When the Government finally gave the green light to auto-enrolment for private sector pensions this spring, campaigners for women’s economic equality had every reason to celebrate. Long overdue, Ireland’s new retirement savings scheme promises for the first time to capture the vast swathe of workers—particularly women—who have historically reached pension age reliant solely on the State Pension and patchwork personal savings.

For decades, the gender pension gap has been one of the most stubborn indicators of ongoing inequality in Irish society and the workplace. Recent CSO data reveals that women in Ireland continue to receive markedly lower pension income than men, a legacy of broken work histories, part-time employment, and caring responsibilities often undertaken for little or no financial reward. In 2022, only about a third of women working in the private sector were paying into an occupational pension, as opposed to almost half of men.

The Minister for Social Protection, Heather Humphreys, has hailed auto-enrolment as a “game-changer” for those without occupational pensions, the majority of whom are women. The scheme will see more than 750,000 workers automatically signed up for a workplace pension for the first time, with phased contributions from employees, employers, and the State. This compulsory approach is designed to close coverage gaps where traditional incentives—like tax breaks—have failed to encourage sufficient numbers of lower-paid and part-time workers into the pension system.

Auto-enrolment, on paper, is a critical plank in catching women who have thus far slipped through the cracks. It responds to decades of calls from the National Women’s Council and the Irish Congress of Trade Unions to help those with fragmented careers build up a modest retirement pot. The State’s own position as an employer already offers certain protections—which is why the most acute disadvantage has persisted among the private sector workforce, in retail, hospitality, and caring professions.

But auto-enrolment is not, on its own, the answer to the gender pension gap. A scheme whose ultimate rate is around 14% of qualifying earnings is unlikely to fully right systemic wrongs baked into a labour market structured around male working patterns. The new system offers a floor, not a ceiling, and it leaves unresolved the more fundamental problem of Ireland’s low pay, precarious work, and the undervaluation of unpaid care.

Crucially, the scheme will not cover everyone—those earning less than €20,000 per annum, many of whom are women in part-time or seasonal jobs, fall outside the remit. The same is true for those aged under 23, even as recent evidence from the ESRI suggests the pension gap starts accruing from those earliest years of employment. And while interrupted service is less harshly penalised than under some legacy private pensions, auto-enrolment still cannot fully compensate women who step out of the workforce to care for children, parents, or loved ones.

Ireland is late to auto-enrolment; the UK’s experience since 2012 shows the model can boost participation and encourage pension saving across the board. But British data also shows that the lowest earners and those with interrupted working lives remain most at risk of pension poverty—groups which, here as there, are disproportionately made up of women.

The expansion of auto-enrolment must be matched by further reform. That means a renewed policy focus on paid parental leave, affordable childcare, flexible working, and revaluing the social and economic contribution of unpaid carers.
headline: Ireland’s pension auto-enrolment is a turning point for women but it's not the whole story

text:
Taoiseach Simon Harris has called on US multinationals to deepen their investment in Ireland, citing the country’s skilled workforce, stable business environment, and close ties with both the United States and European Union as key advantages.

Speaking at an Enterprise Ireland-hosted event in New York, Mr Harris highlighted the Government’s ongoing commitment to creating an attractive environment for international businesses and pointed to recent reforms in the Irish education and skills sector as evidence of Ireland’s readiness to support high-value expansion. “Ireland stands at the heart of Europe, offering unrivalled access to the Single Market alongside a young, innovative workforce. We want US firms to see Ireland not just as a place to do business, but as a home for growth,” he told the gathering, which included senior executives from the technology, life sciences, and financial services sectors.

The Taoiseach’s comments come amidst heightened competition across Europe to attract foreign direct investment (FDI), with several EU member states recently announcing new incentives for multinationals. Despite this, Ireland continues to outperform many of its peers, with more than 900 US companies currently employing over 190,000 people directly across the country.

Mr Harris also moved to reassure executives over recent changes in Ireland’s corporate tax regime, which has seen the country align with new international standards on minimum effective tax rates. He insisted that the core attractions of Ireland for FDI remain unchanged. “Our commitment to talent, innovation and a clear, predictable regulatory environment goes far beyond taxation,” he said. “We understand the importance of providing certainty to our partners, and Ireland remains one of the most pro-enterprise locations globally.”

The visit to New York forms part of a week-long trade mission to the US, during which Mr Harris is expected to meet with leaders in technology, biopharma, and the green energy sector. He will also visit Boston and San Francisco for engagements with existing investors and Irish diaspora business networks.

IDA Ireland, the state agency responsible for attracting FDI, has reported a steady pipeline of interest from US firms in both expansion and new investments, particularly in regional locations outside Dublin. IDA chief executive Michael Lohan, who accompanied the Taoiseach on the trip, said: “We’re seeing tremendous opportunities in emerging sectors such as AI, fintech, and sustainable technologies. Ireland is ready to support companies as they scale and innovate.”

The Taoiseach’s trip comes as the Government seeks to maintain Ireland’s competitive edge against a backdrop of global economic uncertainty, with ongoing concerns within Cabinet over US tax reforms and the international outlook for the tech industry. Mr Harris acknowledged these challenges but argued that Ireland’s adaptability and reputation for partnership placed it in a strong position.

The Tánaiste, Micheál Martin, welcomed the Taoiseach’s efforts, stating that Ireland’s close economic links with the US are “crucial for jobs, innovation, and the continued growth of our economy.” Opposition parties, while generally supportive of FDI, have called on the Government to ensure that investment benefits the wider community and is matched by improvements in housing and infrastructure.

Mr Harris is due to address the United Nations later this week, where he is expected to reinforce Ireland’s commitment to multilateralism and international cooperation.
headline: Taoiseach urges US firms to expand operations to Ireland

text:
The children of Ireland depend on us all. That phrase is so often trotted out, usually when discussing education or the funding of frontline services. But rarely do we truly pause to consider what depending on us actually means. How does a society show it values its young people? The answer, I believe, is simple: we must show up for the adults who care for them.

In a country ever-proud of its supposed family values, it is striking how little is invested in the scaffolding around children—be it the childcare sector, schools, special education assistants, social care workers, or those staffing the crèches that allow parents to work. The foundation of a child’s wellbeing lies in the quality of relationships with the trusted grown-ups in their lives. But too many of those adults—childcare workers, SNAs, teachers, youth workers—are stretched thin, underpaid, and, crucially, undervalued.

Take the ongoing crisis in early years care. This week, the Early Childhood Ireland organisation laid bare the cold facts: staff turnover at record highs, services closing due to soaring insurance and energy costs, and new parents scrabbling for places in creches and naíonraí. Meanwhile, pay remains stubbornly low. In what other sector is a qualification in early childhood education met with a wage that barely clears thirteen euro an hour? Is it any wonder that staff leave for retail or hospitality, where the stress is lower and the pay often better?

It is not just about pay. The daily reality for many carers of children is an absence of respect in both rhetoric and policy. Special needs assistants, the backbone of so many classrooms, are battling a constant tide of precarious hours and short-term contracts. Child protection social workers face caseloads that make meaningful intervention all but impossible. And, in our schools, teachers double up as social workers, therapists, and, often, the only reliable adult presence in a child’s life.

The disconnect is galling. Politicians and officials queue up to insist that ‘children are a priority’, while budget after budget scrimps on investment in those who support them most closely. We see it in the difficulty parents face securing places for their children with additional needs. We see it in the frustration of educators forced to manage complex needs without adequate supports. And we see it in the fatigue etched onto the faces of over-stretched staff, who continue to show up for our children despite the odds.

This is not something to mourn in the abstract. It is, as parents know, a matter that affects the everyday lives of families. When a preschool closes in a rural town, when an SNA post goes unfilled, when a youth club shutters for want of funding, the ripple effects are real and immediate. It is children—isolated, anxious, denied basic opportunities—who pay the greatest price.

That is why, when carers take to the streets, they deserve not just our sympathy but our solidarity. When early years educators march on Leinster House, it is not just for a fair wage—it is for the future of every child who passes through their hands. When SNAs strike, it is a call for dignity and sustainability, for themselves and for the young people who rely on them for inclusion and daily care. Their struggle is not separate from parents’ struggle for affordable, reliable care; nor is it distinct from the campaign for better mental health services or smaller class sizes.
headline: Jennifer Horgan: For the sake of Ireland's children, let's march in solidarity with their carers

text:
A Cork-based mental health author who was the target of an online blackmail scam has spoken out about the experience, expressing his disappointment at victim-blaming attitudes encountered after the incident.

The author, who has published several books on mental wellbeing and regularly gives talks in schools and workplaces throughout Munster, said he was approached by a person purporting to be a fan via a popular social media platform. Initially, the contact appeared benign, but after a period of conversation, the individual threatened to release sensitive personal information unless a payment was made.

Speaking to the Irish Examiner, the author—who asked that his name not be printed to protect his privacy—said, "My first thought was shock, and then the fear set in. As someone who encourages openness about mental health, I never expected to find myself in this situation. The pressure was immense."

He reported the attempted blackmail to the Gardaí, who confirmed they are investigating the matter. "I was advised not to engage further with the account and to preserve all communications," he said.

He described feeling “let down” not only by the perpetrator, but also by the reaction of some acquaintances and online commentators. "When I confided in a few people, the first questions were about what I must have done to put myself in this position, or why I interacted online at all. There was a clear suggestion that it was somehow my fault. That's deeply disappointing, especially in an era when we’re supposed to be supporting people who speak up about these issues."

The author said the experience underscored the need for greater awareness around cybercrime and the dangers of blaming victims. "This can happen to anyone, regardless of their background, education, or intentions. The focus should be on supporting survivors and holding the criminals to account, not on questioning the victim’s actions."

He encouraged others who experience similar incidents to come forward and seek help, stressing the importance of early intervention and reporting. "There is help available, both from the Gardaí and support organisations. I’d urge anyone affected not to suffer in silence or let shame prevent them from reaching out."

The HSE has previously warned of the growing prevalence of online scams and extortion attempts, noting a rise in incidents in recent years, particularly during the pandemic when online communication surged. Cybercrime units continue to investigate such cases, but authorities say public understanding and support for victims remain crucial.

A Garda spokesperson confirmed they are investigating a report of an online blackmail threat received in recent weeks, and that "enquiries are ongoing." No arrests have been made at this time.

The author plans to address the topic in his next public talks, aiming to promote open conversation around digital safety. "If sharing my experience helps even one person avoid this, it will have been worthwhile," he said.
headline: Cork mental health author blackmailed online 'disappointed by victim-blaming'

text:
UN Secretary-General António Guterres has called on world leaders to provide clear solutions to the current series of global crises, stating that “people are looking to leaders for a way out of the mess” confronting societies across the globe.

Speaking at a summit in Geneva on Tuesday, Mr Guterres emphasised the responsibility of governments to respond to the combined challenges of war, climate change, and economic instability, warning that “trust in institutions is crumbling and despair is taking root” among citizens.

“The world today is in turmoil. We are facing multiple emergencies – conflict, poverty, devastating weather events, and a cost-of-living crisis that threatens to push millions more into hardship. People are not simply asking for help, they are demanding leadership,” Mr Guterres said.

He noted that the prospect of further international unrest, exacerbated by ongoing fighting in Ukraine, turmoil in Gaza, and political polarisation in countries including the United States, has left many feeling uncertain about the future.

“We must all work to rebuild trust – in governments, in international cooperation, and in the promise of a better tomorrow,” Mr Guterres urged, calling for increased humanitarian aid, urgent climate action, and a renewed commitment to peace-building efforts.

The UN chief’s remarks come ahead of next week’s annual meeting of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, where Taoiseach Simon Harris is expected to attend and address the assembly. Ireland has consistently advocated at the UN for stronger international action on issues including global food security and conflict resolution.

Mr Guterres also highlighted the recent devastating flooding in southern Brazil and persistent drought across East Africa as “stark reminders” of the growing impact of climate disruption, emphasising that developed nations must honour their pledge to provide €100 billion annually to help vulnerable countries adapt and respond.

“People everywhere are looking to governments to put aside short-term interests and think in terms of a common future. The solutions are there – what is lacking is the political will to act,” he concluded.

Irish NGOs, including Concern Worldwide and Trócaire, have echoed these concerns in recent statements, appealing for both increased international support and swifter action from the Irish Government on overseas aid commitments.

The Department of Foreign Affairs said it continues to work closely with Irish Aid partners and the UN, noting that Ireland’s overseas development assistance now exceeds €2.3 billion per annum.

Meanwhile, the UN General Assembly is set to focus on global security, sustainable development, and climate finance during its upcoming session, with member states facing growing public pressure to deliver tangible progress on long-standing challenges.
headline: UN chief says people are looking to leaders for way out of ‘mess’

text:
Ireland’s tillage farmers have watched anxiously for months as the fate of the United Nations-brokered grain deal between Ukraine and Russia remains uncertain. The Black Sea Grain Initiative, struck in July 2022, was intended to facilitate the safe export of grain and foodstuffs from Ukrainian ports, despite the ongoing conflict. Its future is now mired in diplomatic wrangling, with implications that range far beyond the war-torn region.

The most recent negotiations, mediated by Türkiye and the UN, failed to secure a renewal after Russia withdrew from the deal in July 2023, citing Western sanctions as a barrier to its own agricultural exports. Since then, the UN has issued warnings about rising food prices and the risk of shortages in countries dependent on Ukrainian grain, notably in Africa and the Middle East. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization, global wheat prices have fluctuated significantly, with each announcement from Moscow and Kyiv rippling through commodity markets.

For Irish growers, the uncertainty has translated into volatility in both markets and input costs. IFA President Tim Cullinan has repeatedly stressed the need for stability, noting that global price swings, combined with rising fertiliser and fuel costs, are undermining confidence in the native grain sector. “We’re very much affected by world events,” he told the Irish Examiner this week. “Irish farmers have seen costs rise steadily since the outset of the war. The lack of a secure grain corridor puts further pressure on an already vulnerable industry here.”

In the absence of the deal, Ukraine has shifted to exporting grain via EU land routes and through the Danube, but these alternatives are significantly less efficient. Logistical bottlenecks and increased insurance premiums for Black Sea shipping have sent global grain prices higher at times, though large harvests elsewhere have tempered the effect in recent months. The European Commission has pledged support for affected Member States, and in September authorised temporary trade measures to help move Ukrainian grain more freely through Europe, including ports in Romania, Poland and Slovakia.

Irish importers and millers have adjusted sourcing strategies, drawing on alternative markets in France and Germany, and, to a lesser extent, South America. However, these changes have brought their own challenges. “We’ve had more variability in quality and delivery timelines,” noted one Cork-based grain merchant. “It requires a lot of flexibility in our supply chains.”

At the same time, competition from cheap imports has led some Irish farmers to call for stronger supports from the Department of Agriculture. The tillage sector – which had targeted an area of 400,000 hectares under the government’s Food Vision 2030 plan – is now under fresh pressure, with Central Statistics Office data showing a modest reduction in cereal acreage for 2024.

As the global community awaits further developments from Moscow, Kyiv, and the UN, the outlook for the coming year remains clouded with uncertainty. For Irish farmers, the knock-on effects of diplomatic stalemate in the Black Sea are likely to persist, reinforcing calls for targeted government intervention and a renewed focus on food security at home.
headline: Against the grain: What's the latest with the UN's grain deal?

text:
Former US President Donald Trump has said he is “fine” after sustaining an injury in an apparent assassination attempt during a campaign rally in Pennsylvania on Saturday evening. The incident, which left at least one spectator dead and several others injured, has sparked widespread condemnation and heightened security concerns in the run-up to November’s presidential election.

Mr Trump, the presumptive Republican nominee, was addressing supporters in Butler, north of Pittsburgh, when gunshots rang out just after 6pm local time. Video footage shows Mr Trump clutching his right ear before ducking behind the lectern as Secret Service agents rushed to shield him and escort him from the stage. Blood could be seen on the former president’s face as he was hurried to safety.

The Secret Service later confirmed that Mr Trump had suffered a minor injury but was not seriously hurt. In a statement shortly after the incident, Mr Trump said: “I was shot with a bullet that pierced the upper part of my right ear. I am fine.” He expressed his thanks to the Secret Service and first responders and offered condolences to the family of the deceased rally attendee.

Authorities identified the suspected shooter as a 20-year-old local man who fired from a nearby rooftop. Officials said the assailant was “neutralised” by Secret Service personnel at the scene. The FBI has opened a federal investigation, with local law enforcement and state police assisting.

US President Joe Biden, who is seeking re-election and is Mr Trump’s rival in the upcoming vote, denounced the attack as “abhorrent” and called for calm. “There is no place in America for this kind of violence,” Mr Biden said, adding that he had spoken to Mr Trump by phone after the shooting.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin condemned the attack, describing it as “shocking and deeply troubling for democracy everywhere”. He said the government’s thoughts were with those affected and noted that the Consulate General in New York had received no reports of any Irish citizens injured.

Political leaders and international organisations have expressed concern that the shooting could further inflame political tensions in the US. Security has been stepped up for both candidates, with the Democratic National Convention due to take place in Chicago in August.

The attempted assassination comes amid one of the most polarised election campaigns in recent US history. Mr Trump, who survived a four-year presidency marked by controversy and a subsequent series of legal challenges, was holding one of his first major rallies since formally accepting the Republican nomination.

Local hospitals reported treating several people for gunshot injuries, but details have yet to be confirmed. The names of the victim and the suspected shooter have not been officially released.

The White House said President Biden would address the nation in a televised statement on Sunday. The Taoiseach Simon Harris is expected to issue a further response over the weekend.

Gardaí have said there is no indication of any heightened threat to US interests in Ireland, but the Embassy in Ballsbridge remains in “close contact” with Irish authorities. The Department of Foreign Affairs has advised Irish citizens living or travelling in the US to exercise caution and monitor local media.

The Oireachtas Foreign Affairs Committee has called for a special sitting to discuss the implications for Irish-US relations and the safety of the Irish diaspora in America.

The campaign trail in the US is expected to remain on high alert, with both Republican and Democratic teams reviewing security protocols in light of Saturday’s events.
headline: Trump injured but ‘fine’ after attempted assassination at rally

text:
Migrants living in Ireland are more likely to be in employment than their Irish-born counterparts, yet continue to face heightened risks of poverty and deprivation, a new report from the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) has found.

The study, published today, analyses the most recent data from the Central Statistics Office and highlights significant disparities in living standards among Ireland’s foreign-born population. According to the research, just under 70% of migrants of working age were in employment, compared to 66% of people born in Ireland. However, the report notes that migrants remain overrepresented in lower-paid sectors such as accommodation, food service, and cleaning, with many still experiencing poor pay and insecure working conditions.

The ESRI report reveals that almost a fifth of non-EU migrants and 14% of EU migrants were living below the relative poverty line in 2022, compared to 11% of Irish nationals. Migrant households are also more likely to face enforced deprivation, with 25% of non-EU migrants lacking basic necessities such as adequate heating or the ability to afford new clothes, versus 17% among the Irish-born population.

While employment rates among migrants have recovered strongly since the pandemic, the report finds that many continue to face challenges integrating into the labour market. Barriers include the non-recognition of overseas qualifications, language difficulties, and limited social networks, all of which can restrict access to higher-paid and more secure roles.

The research also points to a gender gap in employment, with women from some migrant backgrounds less likely to be in work than both Irish-born women and male migrants. The ESRI warns that this gulf could have long-term ramifications for the economic independence and wellbeing of these women and their families.

Dr Frances McGinnity, lead author of the report, said while it is positive that migrants are securing work, more needs to be done to address persistent inequalities. “The high employment rates among migrants demonstrate their contribution to Ireland’s economy, but the elevated poverty and deprivation rates underline the need for targeted policy interventions,” she said. The study makes several recommendations, including improved access to English language support, recognition of qualifications, and stronger pathways to permanent residency and citizenship.

The findings come amid ongoing debate over migration and integration policy, with the Government recently committing to a review of Ireland’s International Protection system and promising increased resources for the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth.

Responding to the report, a spokesperson for the Department said the Government is working to ensure all residents, regardless of origin, can participate equally in economic and social life. “We recognise the importance of reducing barriers for migrants, particularly in relation to employment and access to services,” the spokesperson said.

Several advocacy groups including the Immigrant Council of Ireland and Migrant Rights Centre Ireland have called on the State to act on the ESRI’s recommendations. They say the report’s findings highlight ongoing inequalities and the need for reforms to support integration, combat discrimination, and ensure decent work for all.

The report concludes that tackling these disparities will be crucial if Ireland is to ensure prosperity and social cohesion as the country’s demographic profile changes in the years ahead.
headline: Migrants more likely to work but face higher poverty rates, ESRI study finds

text:
When my aunt Mary sat our family down one Sunday afternoon and told us she had been diagnosed with breast cancer, the air seemed to vanish from the room. We clustered around her in the sitting room, rain pattering against the windows, and tried our best to lend comfort. Nobody likes to imagine cancer coming so close. But while her diagnosis was shocking, it set in motion a chain of events that, unexpectedly, may have saved my own life.

Mary was 52 when she found a lump in her left breast. She’d always been diligent about attending her regular mammogram appointments with BreastCheck, the HSE’s national screening programme, but this time she’d noticed something herself between scheduled appointments. She was swiftly referred by her GP to the Breast Clinic in Cork University Hospital, where further tests confirmed the diagnosis. She had surgery within weeks, followed by chemotherapy.

As her niece, I was 39 at the time, well below the usual age for automatic screening in Ireland. But hearing her diagnosis prompted our family to talk more openly about health. It emerged that my grandmother, who had died young, had also suffered from breast cancer, though this was never discussed when I was a child.

Mary’s team at CUH recommended genetic counselling, emphasising the importance of understanding whether her cancer could have been hereditary. Our family GP referred those of us with blood ties for genetic testing, available through the HSE for individuals with a strong family history of certain cancers. I went for testing at the genetics clinic at St. James’s Hospital in Dublin. Some weeks later, I received the news: I carried the BRCA1 gene mutation, known to increase the risk of both breast and ovarian cancers.
