Suddenly, the statistics took on a new significance. According to the Irish Cancer Society, approximately one in nine women in Ireland will develop breast cancer during their lifetime. For BRCA carriers, the lifetime risk is significantly higher, and can approach 70%.

With the advice of my consultant, I began yearly MRI scans – far earlier than the usual screening schedule. Just months later, a small, early-stage tumour was detected in my right breast. It was too small to feel and would almost certainly have gone unnoticed for several years without the increased surveillance prompted by Mary’s diagnosis.

Treatment was swift. I had a lumpectomy at the Mater Hospital, followed by radiotherapy, and I was able to return to work after a few months. My prognosis is excellent, for which I am deeply grateful.

Mary’s openness changed my life and, potentially, saved it. It also encouraged my younger cousins and siblings to speak more frankly about their health and to advocate for themselves with their GPs. In Ireland, family histories are often shrouded in silence, with illnesses euphemised or left unspoken, but breaking that silence can be lifesaving.

The experience has left me an advocate, not just for genetic testing but for open, honest discussions about family health history. The Irish Cancer Society and the Marie Keating Foundation both offer information and support for families wanting to learn more about hereditary cancer risk.

Mary is now cancer-free and back to her old self, presiding over Sunday roasts and slipping fivers to her grandchildren. She and I have become closer, bound by this strange twist of fate, and grateful for each ordinary day. Her diagnosis was the hardest thing our family ever faced, but in a way none of us could have imagined, it was also the reason I am here today.
headline: My aunt's breast cancer diagnosis saved me

text:
A talented young chef died after striking his head off a tumble dryer when he lost his balance at a house in Cork city, an inquest at Cork Coroner’s Court has heard.

Gardaí were called to the rented accommodation on the south side of the city in the early hours of 15 October 2022, after friends discovered the body of Emmet O’Shea, aged 26, inside the utility room of the property. The deceased, originally from Ballinlough, had been socialising with housemates when the tragic incident occurred.

The court was told that Mr O’Shea had been in good spirits throughout the evening and had consumed a moderate amount of alcohol. Statements read by Inspector Donal O’Connell indicated no evidence of a physical altercation or any suspicious circumstances.

Housemate Aoife McCarthy gave evidence that she saw Mr O’Shea laughing and joking minutes before the fall. “He went into the utility room to grab a pair of shoes from the dryer. I heard a bang and when I went in, he was on the floor,” she told the coroner. “There was blood coming from his head. We called emergency services straight away.”

Paramedics arrived within minutes but were unable to revive Mr O’Shea, and he was pronounced dead at the scene.

State Pathologist Dr Margot Bolster, who carried out the post-mortem examination at Cork University Hospital, testified that death was due to blunt force trauma to the back of the head, consistent with a fall onto a hard surface. Dr Bolster confirmed that toxicology results showed Mr O’Shea was over the legal driving limit, but that his level of intoxication would not have caused unconsciousness.

“Even a minor loss of balance, in the right circumstances, can lead to a tragic outcome,” Dr Bolster said.

Gardaí investigating the death confirmed there was no evidence of foul play or third party involvement, and that the incident would not be subject to further criminal investigation.

Coroner Philip Comyn returned a verdict of accidental death, expressing his condolences to the family and friends of Mr O’Shea. Mr Comyn remarked upon the “devastating effect” the sudden loss had had on the close-knit circle of friends and on Cork’s hospitality community, in which Mr O’Shea was a popular figure.

Speaking after the hearing, Mr O’Shea’s father, John, described his son as “a hard-working, kind-hearted young man with a big future ahead of him”. The family have asked for privacy as they continue to grieve his loss.
headline: Chef, 26, died after falling and hitting his head off dryer

text:
There are few things guaranteed to raise family tensions quite like a holiday home. Whether it’s the inevitable squabbles over who gets the good week in August, or the silent score-keeping over changed lightbulbs and gutters left uncleared, the family bolthole often becomes a lightning rod for all the old grievances that have quietly simmered since childhood.

This week, I’ve received a letter from a reader whose patience has finally evaporated. She writes: "Dear Dáithí, our parents were always generous with their holiday home in West Cork. After they passed, my siblings and I agreed to keep the place going as a shared retreat. Last month, a cousin – invited as a favour – left it in an awful state: bins overflowing, beds unmade, and broken crockery hidden away. I’m furious, but my sister says it’s not worth the row. What should I do?"

First of all, let’s acknowledge the heartbreak. The death of parents changes the atmosphere around any family home, and the holiday place is no exception. Where before there was the guiding hand of Mam or Dad, there’s now just a rota on the fridge and, it seems, the hope that everyone behaves themselves.

But the question here isn’t really about a cousin who can’t manage the basic decencies of cleaning up after themselves; it’s about where the lines are drawn, and who has the right – or the courage – to enforce them.

Irish families, in particular, are famous for their reluctance to confront. We’d rather mutter all the way back to Dublin than risk a scene at the kitchen table. Yet, someone has to say something – because if you let a mess go unremarked, it becomes the new normal. Before you know it, the ‘lovely’ house is the one no one wants to use.

You have a few options. The soft one is to drop your cousin a gentle note, perhaps with a list of the things you found, couching it in humour but making clear that the house relies on everyone mucking in. If that feels like too much, you could suggest, at the next siblings’ WhatsApp or family call, that a set of house rules be agreed. This depersonalises the issue and sets expectations. It also lets you see who, if anyone, objects – often, it’s the ones who didn’t do their share in the first place.

Your sister says it’s not worth the row. She may be right, but only if you never want to use the place again. If it matters to you, then it’s worth standing up for. The house represents more than bricks and mortar – it’s your parents’ memory, and a little piece of your own childhood. It deserves better than being left to go to rack and ruin because nobody wants to risk an awkward chat.

And if all else fails? Next time your cousin wants a stay, suggest they try Airbnb. At least then someone else will collect the cleaning fee.
headline: Dear Dáithí: A relative left our parents' lovely holiday home in an awful state

text:
Sir, – The recent revelations concerning ongoing problems within the Health Service Executive (HSE) are sadly unsurprising to many patients and families who have endured the system first-hand. Your recent coverage highlighting chronic delays in diagnostics, miscommunication, and administrative failures has ignited an important national conversation about accountability in our health services. While I have no doubt that many frontline HSE staff are hardworking and dedicated, it is increasingly clear that certain individuals, particularly within management and administration, are failing in their roles, to the detriment of those in their care.

My own experiences as a patient, and those of several family members, reinforce the sense that some staff act as though they are untouchable, immune to scrutiny, and more focused on bureaucracy than patient wellbeing. Repeated phone calls and requests for basic information frequently go ignored. Appointments are cancelled without reason and often without notice, and follow-up is patchy at best. In one instance, my elderly mother’s referral was misplaced twice, resulting in a six-month delay for a vital scan. Such inefficiency and lack of accountability are not just frustrating: they have real, tangible effects on people’s health and quality of life.

The HSE in its annual reports highlights the vast sums spent on staff training and “continuous improvement”, but there is precious little evidence of improvement on the ground. Instead, patients are left to navigate a labyrinthine system, with little transparency and few avenues for meaningful complaint or redress. Many will have seen senior HSE officials defend their operations before Oireachtas committees, but these public displays rarely translate into change where it matters most.

We must be honest and acknowledge that not all staff are suited to their roles. The public sector ethos, so often invoked, cannot excuse mediocrity or incompetence. It is unfair to those who give their all every day, and even more unfair to patients whose trust in the health system is constantly eroded. Other European health services with similar or fewer resources manage better outcomes and higher satisfaction rates. It is time to face the uncomfortable reality that some HSE employees are simply not fit for purpose, and that the culture of tolerating poor performance must end.

Meaningful reform will require more than strategic plans or glossy press releases. There must be genuine oversight, with real consequences for those who fail repeatedly or show disregard for the people they are supposed to serve. Until then, the public will continue to pay the price for a health system that too often puts its own interests before those of its patients.
headline: Letters to the Editor: Some HSE workers are not fit for purpose

text:
Ronan Keating has spoken candidly about the profound impact the death of his brother, Ciarán, has had on him and his family, describing the past months as “the hardest time” of his life.

The Boyzone star and broadcaster offered an emotional update this week, several months after Ciarán Keating died in a car crash in Co Mayo last July. The tragic incident, which happened as Ciarán was on his way to watch his son Ruairí play football for Cork City, left the Keating family “heartbroken” and brought an outpouring of sympathy from across the country.

Speaking in a recent interview, Ronan, 46, admitted the grief has been “all-consuming” at times. “It’s been the hardest time. Grief is such a strange thing – it takes hold of you when you least expect it. We’re still trying to come to terms with it as a family,” he said.

Keating, who is based in the UK where he presents on Magic Radio and appears on The One Show, travelled home to Ireland immediately following the crash to support his loved ones. In the months since, he said he has drawn strength from the “amazing support” offered by friends, colleagues, and fans.

“Our family and friends in Mayo, and around Ireland, have been incredible. The amount of messages and kindness – it’s been a comfort, really, in the darkest moments,” he said.

Ciarán Keating, who was in his 50s, was laid to rest in July following a funeral Mass at St Patrick’s Church in Louisburgh, attended by hundreds of mourners including GAA and League of Ireland figures. Ronan gave a moving eulogy, remembering his brother as “a good man with a great heart”.

Reflecting on how he and his siblings have coped, Ronan acknowledged that life has changed irrevocably: “You never expect something like this to happen. We’re all just taking it day by day, minding each other.”

He also spoke of the importance of seeking help and talking about grief, urging others who are struggling after a loss to reach out. “We need to look out for one another and not be afraid to say we’re not okay. That’s something I’d encourage anyone who’s in that position to do,” he said.

Ronan has resumed work commitments gradually, but said his priority remains his family, especially his parents and Ciarán’s wife and children. “Family is everything now – more than ever,” he said. “We’re all just trying to keep Ciarán’s memory alive in whatever way we can.”

A Garda investigation into the circumstances of the collision remains ongoing. The Keating family have requested privacy as they continue to grieve and thanked the public for their continued support.
headline: ‘It’s been the hardest time:’ Ronan Keating shares update following death of his brother

text:
Growing tensions have emerged between the Department of Health and hospital consultants, as waiting lists for public patients continue to escalate despite record levels of funding. 

Figures published last week by the National Treatment Purchase Fund (NTPF) reveal that more than 897,000 people are now waiting for outpatient, inpatient, or day case appointments in hospitals across the country. This marks a 4% increase on last year’s numbers, with children and older patients disproportionately affected.

Senior hospital doctors, represented by the Irish Hospital Consultants Association (IHCA), have openly criticised the Department of Health for what they describe as “persistent failures” to address staff shortages, provide adequate theatre capacity, and invest in diagnostic equipment. The IHCA claims that despite repeated warnings, the Government’s Sláintecare reforms have stalled, and that excessive bureaucracy is hampering efforts to address the backlog.

Professor Robert Landers, president of the IHCA, told the Irish Examiner that the health service is “at breaking point.” “Consultants, nurses, and all frontline staff are doing everything they can. We have highlighted time and again that without resolving chronic consultant vacancies, opening extra theatres, and tackling blockers in the system, waiting times will only worsen,” he said. “The Department has focused on plans and targets, but the reality on the ground is a worsening crisis for patients.”

However, the Department has rejected accusations of inaction, insisting that it is implementing a “multi-annual waiting list action plan.” A spokesperson said: “Budget 2024 allocated an unprecedented €23.3 billion to health, with specific measures to reduce waiting lists. We are recruiting extra consultants and investing in community diagnostics. Progress is being made, but pressure on the system remains due to increased demand and the legacy of Covid-19 disruptions.”

The HSE’s Chief Operations Officer, Damien McCallion, also pointed to a surge in referrals and ongoing difficulties in discharging patients who require social care supports. “We are working closely with hospitals and community services to improve patient flow and capacity. The target is to bring waiting lists down to pre-pandemic levels by the end of 2025,” he said.

Opposition parties have criticised both the Government and senior medics, calling for greater urgency and transparency. Sinn Féin’s health spokesperson, David Cullinane TD, accused the Coalition of “empty promises and missed deadlines,” while Labour’s Duncan Smith TD said the HSE must “hold hospital management to account” where targets are missed.

Patients’ groups say delays are causing “real distress” for people waiting months or even years for routine appointments or life-changing procedures. Marie O’Connor, Chairwoman of the Patients Association of Ireland, said more families are travelling abroad for treatment or seeking private care due to lengthy delays: “The system is failing those who need it most.”

The Oireachtas Health Committee is due to meet next week to hear evidence from both consultants’ representatives and Department officials, as pressure mounts for an agreed approach to tackling growing lists. While agreement remains elusive, all sides acknowledge that the situation is unsustainable and that urgent action is needed to restore timely access to care.
headline: Department of Health and hospital doctors at odds over growing waiting lists

text:
Ireland is set to experience unseasonably mild weather over the coming weekend, with temperatures predicted to reach as high as 15 degrees Celsius in parts of the country, according to Met Éireann. The unusual warmth comes following a period of unsettled conditions that brought prolonged rain and localised flooding to many areas earlier this week.

Met Éireann meteorologist Joanna Donnelly said the country can expect “a marked improvement in conditions,” especially in the midlands and the east. “We’re looking at values in the low to mid-teens, which is well above the seasonal average for early March. Some areas, particularly in the south and east, may see temperatures reach up to 15 degrees on Saturday and Sunday,” she said.

Despite the milder temperatures, forecasters warn that occasional showers are still likely, especially along Atlantic coastal counties. “It won’t be wall-to-wall sunshine,” noted Ms Donnelly. “Cloud cover may persist in places and there’s still a risk of patchy rain or drizzle, particularly in the west and northwest. However, most areas will see drier intervals and some sunny spells.”

The balmy weather is attributed to a southerly airflow drawing warmer air from continental Europe. Met Éireann’s latest outlook suggests this pattern will persist into early next week, with above-average temperatures set to continue at least until Tuesday. Night-time temperatures are also forecast to remain relatively high, dipping no lower than 6 or 7 degrees in most places.

Farmers and outdoor enthusiasts are being advised to make the most of the improved conditions following a wet and blustery start to March. The Irish Farmers’ Association said that the extended dry spell would provide a welcome window for fieldwork after recent flooding hampered activity in many rural areas.

Meanwhile, public health officials have reminded the public that, despite the mild weather, the risk of seasonal illnesses such as colds and flu remains. The HSE has urged those most vulnerable to continue taking precautions, including regular handwashing and vaccination if eligible.

Irish Water says reservoirs and rivers remain at satisfactory levels following heavy rainfall over recent weeks and there are currently no plans for restrictions.

Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) confirmed that planned road works in several counties will proceed as scheduled, with the settled spell expected to facilitate progress.

With the St Patrick’s Day festival season approaching, many organisers have welcomed the news, although it remains to be seen whether the mild weather will hold for the bank holiday.

Met Éireann will issue an updated forecast on Friday, but for now, the advice is to enjoy the rare spell of spring warmth while it lasts.
headline: Unusually mild temperatures predicted for weekend, with highs of 15C forecast

text:
A major fundraising drive has been launched in Ireland to support relief efforts in eastern Libya, where authorities fear at least 5,300 people have died following catastrophic flooding. The devastation comes after Storm Daniel battered the region, unleashing torrential rain that overwhelmed dams and swept away entire neighbourhoods in the city of Derna.

Irish aid organisations, including the Irish Red Cross and Trócaire, have called on the public to donate urgently as emergency services in Libya struggle to cope with the scale of the disaster. With thousands more missing and tens of thousands displaced, officials warned the true human cost is likely to rise in the days ahead.

Libyan officials said the collapse of two dams above Derna late on Sunday night unleashed a torrent of water that tore through the city, washing buildings, vehicles, and residents out to sea. A spokesman for the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies described the situation as "disastrous beyond comprehension", with search and rescue teams overwhelmed by the extent of the destruction.

Irish people with family links to Libya have also appealed for assistance, with concerns mounting for loved ones who are unaccounted for. The Department of Foreign Affairs said it was providing consular assistance where possible, although there have been no reports so far of Irish citizens directly affected.

Taoiseach Leo Varadkar extended condolences to the people of Libya, stating, "Ireland stands in solidarity with all those affected by this terrible tragedy. Our thoughts and prayers are with the victims and their families." The Government said it was monitoring the situation closely and considering additional humanitarian aid.

Access to the stricken region has been severely hampered by damaged infrastructure and ongoing political instability. Many survivors have been forced to sleep in the open, with limited access to drinking water, electricity, and medical care. International agencies warned of the risk of diseases spreading due to contaminated water supplies.

The United Nations and the European Union have both pledged support, with rescue and medical teams being sent from neighbouring countries. The Irish Red Cross said donations would help supply emergency shelter, food, and healthcare for those most in need.

The full scale of the disaster remains unclear as large parts of Derna are still cut off. Local authorities have declared the city a disaster zone and appealed for international assistance, warning that the death toll could rise sharply as floodwaters recede and debris is cleared.

Irish aid workers are expected to travel to the region in the coming days, coordinating with international partners to deliver supplies. The fundraising appeal comes amid growing recognition of the role of climate change in fuelling extreme weather events, with meteorologists calling Storm Daniel the deadliest storm to hit Libya in living memory.
headline: Fundraising appeal launched as 5,300 feared dead in flood-hit eastern Libya

text:
Parents of children attending a Cork primary school have called for a full safety audit of the local school transport fleet after a bus driver was hospitalised following an incident on Wednesday morning. The driver, a man in his 50s, sustained injuries in what parents described as a “serious and avoidable” mechanical fault as he was preparing to collect pupils in the Douglas area.

Emergency services attended the scene shortly after 8am when the bus reportedly lurched forward unexpectedly as the driver performed a routine safety check. He was treated at the scene before being transferred to Cork University Hospital, where his injuries are understood to be non-life threatening.

Parents at St Mary’s School in Douglas expressed concern over what they termed “an ongoing pattern” of issues with the contracted fleet, including reports in recent months of malfunctioning doors and heating failures on several vehicles transporting pupils from the surrounding area.

“It’s not the first time we’ve had to raise the alarm,” said Aisling Murphy, whose two children travel on the affected route daily. “We’ve spoken to Bus Éireann and to the Department of Education, but we don’t feel reassured. If it was a child near the bus this morning, it could have been a tragedy. What’s it going to take before a proper audit is carried out?”

The Parents’ Association has written to Bus Éireann seeking an immediate review of the entire fleet used for school transport in Cork city and suburbs, calling for clear timelines and publication of inspection records. They have also requested an urgent meeting with the principal and board of management of St Mary’s, alongside representatives from the Department of Education.

Bus Éireann confirmed in a statement that the company is “aware of an incident involving one of our contracted school transport vehicles in Cork,” and said it is cooperating fully with the Gardaí and relevant authorities as part of the investigation. “The safety of students and our drivers is our priority, and we are reviewing procedures around fleet maintenance and driver checks,” the statement read.

The Gardaí confirmed they are carrying out enquiries into the circumstances of the incident. “There is no indication of foul play, but we are ensuring all appropriate safety protocols were followed,” a spokesperson said.

Meanwhile, parents say they are considering keeping their children home until they receive assurances regarding the inspection and maintenance regime for school buses. The Department of Education said it is in contact with Bus Éireann and the board of management regarding the concerns raised, and will “monitor the situation closely.”

Local Sinn Féin TD Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire said: “It’s not acceptable for families to have to worry if their children’s journey to school is safe. There are serious questions about oversight and standards, and it’s time for a thorough review.”

St Mary’s principal, Marie O’Connell, said the school is “deeply concerned” about the incident and will support parents in their requests for improved safety measures. 

No children were on board at the time of the incident.
headline: Parents call for fleet safety audit after Cork school bus driver injured

text:
Donald Trump’s return to the centre of US politics has sounded alarms far beyond America’s borders, but nowhere are his policies likely to inflict more immediate harm than on the country’s most vulnerable. His track record and campaign promises reveal a calculated assault on the fragile supports underpinning the health and wellbeing of millions. The deliberate undermining of healthcare, food assistance, and public health infrastructure is no mere byproduct of ideological fervour—it is a strategy with profound social, economic and political consequences.

During his presidency, Trump made repeated, headline-stealing attempts to dismantle the Affordable Care Act, threatening the insurance coverage of tens of millions. While those efforts were only partially successful, the message was clear: health was not a right for all, but a privilege for those who could pay. Programmes that benefitted the poor and working class—Medicaid, food stamps (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Programme), and support for children and people with disabilities—were all subjected to budget cuts or new, punishing conditions. The result? Higher numbers of uninsured, a rise in hospital closures in rural areas, delayed treatment for chronic illnesses, worsening maternal and infant mortality, and a stark increase in food insecurity.

For an Irish reader, the scale is staggering. Ireland has never been perfect in its provision of services, and the HSE is frequently battered for its failings, but the underlying social contract—however threadbare—remains. The notion that government would deliberately restrict access to GP care, hospital treatment, or nutrition for the poorest might be debated around the Committee tables of Leinster House, but here it rarely becomes overt policy. In the US, Trump’s approach has mainstreamed such thinking. This has left one of the world’s wealthiest societies with child hunger at rates far eclipsing anything seen in Europe, and a population with the lowest life expectancy among rich nations.

It is not just about immediate privation. A sick and hungry population, experts warn, is a less resilient population. The people most affected by these targeted rollbacks are also those most likely to challenge government failings, to take to the streets, or to organise. By cutting the ground from under them—literally taking food off tables and medicine off pharmacy shelves—Trump’s project weakens civic opposition and manufactured apathy out of suffering. It is an old playbook, seen in societies where the goal is not to govern for all, but to secure power by demobilising critics.

The ripple effects have been felt here in Ireland, too. US policy decisions echo through global health, migration, and economic systems. Campaigns to restrict access to reproductive health or slash pandemic preparedness budgets have emboldened similar movements in Europe, with knock-on effects for international aid and public health cooperation. The cost of living and health crises faced by many Irish families are reminders that the logic behind Trump’s policies is not confined to American shores.

Ireland’s own experience with austerity, homelessness, and health inequities provides no room for smugness. But Trump’s targeting of health and food support is a chilling reminder of the dangers inherent when political calculation trumps the basic rights of citizens. The legacy is stark: a nation where millions wake up sick or hungry, and where their ability to demand better is systematically undermined. For democracies everywhere, it is a warning that dismantling the safety net is not just a policy choice—it is a strategy for keeping power by keeping people down.
headline: Trump's targeting of health keeps people hungry, sick and less likely to fight back

text:
Every parent knows that time with young children can feel both endless and fleeting. The days of sleepless nights and busy school runs stretch long, yet the years seem to rush by in a blur. As families across Ireland navigate the return to school and the rhythm of daily routines, finding time to mark milestones and make memories can be both a challenge and a joy.

Milestones come in many forms, not just the big ones like a first day at primary school or a Leaving Cert result. For many Irish families, occasions such as a child’s first solo journey on the Luas or cycling unaided in the local park are moments to treasure. These ordinary achievements often hold as much weight as more formal rites of passage. “When my daughter made her Communion, we celebrated with the extended family, but I’ll never forget the pride I felt watching her tie her own shoes for the first time,” says Mary O’Donoghue, a mother of three in Cork.

Family life in Ireland is shaped by tradition but constantly evolving. With the growing popularity of all-day breakfast cafes and forest schools, parents are increasingly opting for new ways to celebrate family life. Instead of the grand birthday parties in play centres, some are choosing simple gatherings in the local GAA club or picnics at the beach. There is a shift towards marking occasions with shared experiences rather than expensive gifts.

Creating these memories doesn’t have to involve elaborate planning or significant expense. Experts advise that what children remember most is not the price tag, but the sense of togetherness. Dr Sinéad Murphy, a child psychologist with the HSE, says, “Children feel secure and cherished when their achievements are noticed, no matter how small. Taking a moment to share a treat from the corner shop or having a chat after school can have a lasting impact.”

Social media can often give the impression that memorable moments require picture-perfect backdrops and matching outfits. Yet, according to a recent survey by Barnardos, Irish children rated shared family rituals—like Sunday walks or bedtime stories—as their happiest memories. Parents themselves often recall the same: simple pleasures like picking blackberries on a country lane or summers spent in a caravan in Tramore.

Photographs and keepsakes have their place, of course, but memory-making is as much about being present as it is about recording the moment. For some families, this means switching off phones during meals or setting aside time at the weekend for a family game or walk. The important thing is consistency and attention. Even a trip to the local library or helping with a bake sale at school can become a cherished memory.

Irish schools and communities also play a key role. From local camogie matches to transition year musicals, these shared events allow children to feel part of something bigger. The ritual of the annual school photo or the excitement of St Patrick’s Day parades are milestones that form the patchwork of childhood.

As the pace of life quickens and schedules fill up, parents may feel pressure to do more, buy more, be more. But the evidence—and the testimony of countless Irish families—suggests that the most enduring memories are forged in the quiet, ordinary moments. Mark the milestones, by all means, but also look for the magic in the everyday. In Ireland’s changeable weather, a spontaneous family walk in the rain may turn out to be the memory your child holds onto, long after the big occasions fade.
headline: Marking milestones and making memories

text:
A majority of officers in the Defence Forces would not recommend a career in the organisation to friends or family, according to the findings of a confidential survey circulated among serving personnel.

The survey, conducted by the Representative Association of Commissioned Officers (RACO), points to deepening dissatisfaction with pay, conditions, and career progression, with more than two-thirds of respondents stating they would actively discourage others from joining. The results come as government pledges of Defence Forces reform and pay improvements remain slow to materialise.

Out of more than 600 commissioned officers surveyed, 77% said they would not advise friends or relatives to pursue a career in the Defence Forces. Among the reasons cited were ongoing recruitment and retention issues, increased workloads, and “unacceptable” rates of pay compared to other State agencies and the private sector.

Morale across the ranks is described as being at “crisis point.” Senior officers who participated in the survey said many are being compelled to work excessive hours due to chronic staff shortages, with several reporting regular breaches of the Organisation of Working Time Act. A number of respondents said they are handling the workload of two or more positions at once.

The survey also revealed that nearly 60% of officers are considering leaving before the end of their current engagement, with one in five reporting active plans to depart within the next 12 months if no significant improvements are made.

RACO general secretary Commandant Conor King said the survey highlights “a systemic failure by the State to meet its obligations towards military personnel.” He urged the government to accelerate implementation of recommendations from the Commission on the Defence Forces, particularly those on pay parity, allowances, and career progression.

“We are seeing officers leave the organisation for opportunities abroad or in other sectors at a rate not seen in decades,” Comdt King said. “The State simply cannot afford to ignore this crisis any longer if it wants to maintain an effective and credible Defence Forces.”

The findings come even as the Department of Defence has insisted that measures are being put in place to address the exodus from the army, air corps, and naval service. A spokesperson for the Department pointed to recent increases in starting pay and the rolling-out of new recruitment campaigns, but acknowledged “significant challenges remain.”

The Defence Forces’ current strength is estimated at just over 7,500 personnel—well below the Government’s minimum establishment figure of 9,500. Retention issues are particularly pronounced among experienced mid-ranking officers, whose departures leave gaps in command and specialist roles.

Opposition TDs have called on the Minister for Defence, Micheál Martin, to treat the matter as urgent. Sinn Féin’s defence spokesperson, Sorca Clarke TD, described the survey results as “deeply worrying,” and called for an “immediate and comprehensive response from government.”

The Department of Defence is preparing to submit an updated implementation plan for the Defence Forces transformation programme to the Oireachtas Committee on Foreign Affairs and Defence later this month. In the meantime, Defence Forces personnel have warned that unless swift action is taken, the crisis is likely to deepen further, compromising the organisation’s ability to meet its domestic and international commitments.
headline: Officers would not recommend Defence Forces career to friends or relatives, survey shows

text:
Two brothers from Co Kildare have begun an extraordinary challenge to run 33 marathons in as many days, hoping to raise over €1 million for dementia research in Ireland.

David and Conor O’Flaherty, originally from Naas, set off on their first marathon at dawn on Monday morning. The pair, who are both in their early thirties, are undertaking the mammoth fundraising effort in honour of their late grandmother, Mary O’Flaherty, who lived with Alzheimer’s disease before her death in 2020.

Over the next month, the brothers will clock up a total of 1,390km, running the marathon distance each day in different towns and cities across the country. The route includes stops in Cork, Limerick, Galway, Letterkenny and Dublin, with the final marathon scheduled to finish at the Phoenix Park on 11th July.

Speaking to the Irish Examiner as they completed their opening 42.2km stretch in Naas, Conor described the challenge as “daunting but deeply personal.” He said, “Every family in Ireland has been touched by dementia in some way. We saw first-hand the toll it takes—not just on the person living with the disease but on everyone around them. This is our way to honour Gran and try to make a difference.”

Funds raised will go to leading Irish dementia charities and research initiatives, including the Alzheimer Society of Ireland and the Dementia Research Network Ireland, supported in part by Science Foundation Ireland. The brothers’ campaign, called ‘Miles for Memories’, has already garnered significant public support, with donations surpassing €320,000 in the first week.

David, a former competitive triathlete, said the support from local communities has been “incredible”. “People have been turning out to run a few kilometres with us each day. The encouragement keeps us going, especially when the legs start to go,” he added.

Dementia is estimated to affect over 64,000 people in Ireland, a number projected to double in the next 25 years according to the HSE. The O’Flahertys hope their effort will raise not only funds but also awareness about the urgent need for increased research and improved care for those living with Alzheimer’s and related conditions.

The pair are being supported by a volunteer crew, including a physiotherapist and nutritionists, and have received backing from local businesses along the route. The brothers are also inviting members of the public to join them for sections of the runs, in adherence with guidance from Gardaí regarding road safety at each location.

Minister of State for Mental Health and Older People, Mary Butler TD, praised the initiative, saying, “This is an outstanding example of Irish community spirit and the power of personal experience to make a wider social impact. The Government is committed to increasing funding for dementia services and research, and it’s inspiring to see families leading the charge.”

Donations to ‘Miles for Memories’ can be made through the campaign’s official website or via collection points at each marathon location. The O’Flahertys say they will continue to update supporters daily through social media and hope that, with the country’s backing, they can cross the €1 million mark by the end of their journey.
headline: Brothers hope running 33 marathons in 33 days will raise over €1m for dementia research

text:
As New Year’s Eve approaches, many of us will be thinking about popping a cork or two to ring in 2025. While prosecco and cava have their place at Irish tables, there’s something uniquely festive about Champagne – the real deal from France’s fabled region, with its fine bubbles and unmistakable elegance.

Champagne is more than just a celebratory drink; it’s a symbol of shared moments and tradition. In Ireland, our relationship with Champagne stretches back centuries, with storied houses such as Bollinger and Pol Roger counting notable Irish figures among their greatest admirers. There’s a heritage to our enjoyment of Champagne, and never is this more keenly felt than at New Year.

True Champagne must come from the eponymous region, following stringent rules on grapes and production. It’s typically crafted from pinot noir, pinot meunier, and chardonnay, and aged for at least 15 months. The result is that ethereal combination of crisp acidity, fine mousse, and flavours ranging from green apple and brioche to toasted almonds and citrus zest.

Irish off-licences and supermarkets offer an ever-improving range, catering for different tastes and budgets. For those looking to spend a little extra, a bottle from a recognised house – say, Moët & Chandon, Veuve Clicquot, or Louis Roederer – offers a safe bet. Their non-vintage expressions, reliably stocked across Ireland, bring lively fruit and toasty notes that work as well with seafood starters as they do on their own.

Smaller grower Champagnes are increasingly available through specialist wine shops in Dublin, Cork and Galway. These producers, who farm and bottle their own grapes, are worth seeking out. Names like Pierre Gimonnet and Laherte Frères offer superb quality at keen prices – and add a dash of individuality to your toast.

For those watching the budget but still wanting authentic Champagne, supermarket own-label bottles sourced from reputable growers – such as Aldi’s Veuve Monsigny or Lidl’s Comte de Senneval – often punch above their weight at around €25 to €30. They make an accessible entry point to the style and sparkle of Champagne.

When it comes to serving, a chilled but not icy bottle (about 8°C) and proper glassware make all the difference. Opt for a tulip-shaped flute or white wine glass, which preserves the bubbles and lets the aromas shine. And don’t be afraid to pair Champagne with food beyond canapés: its freshness cuts beautifully through fish and chips, oysters, or even a curry.

As the clock strikes midnight, there are few rituals as uplifting as sharing a glass of Champagne with family and friends. It is a moment to savour, a fitting tribute to the year behind and the possibilities ahead. Whatever your choice of bottle this year, here’s wishing you a Nollaig shona agus athbhliain faoi mhaise daoibh. Sláinte!
headline: Wine with Leslie: Toast the New Year with time-tested Champagne

text:
The Dublin Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (DSPCA) has issued an appeal to the public to help identify a man who was caught on CCTV footage shoving a severely injured dog under the gates of their Rathfarnham facility earlier this week.

Staff arriving for work on Tuesday morning discovered the animal, a young female lurcher cross, wedged between the metal bars at the entrance. According to the charity, the dog was in significant distress and bore injuries consistent with blunt force trauma.

Security footage released by the DSPCA shows a man arriving at the gates in the early hours, carrying the dog by the scruff of the neck before forcing her through the narrow gap and leaving the area on foot. The charity described the man as being of average build, wearing dark clothing and a hood pulled over his head.

Gillian Bird, head of education and media at the DSPCA, said the incident left staff “shocked and heartbroken”, noting the animal could have suffered further harm if staff had not arrived in time. “There’s no excuse for abandoning an animal in such a state. This was a deliberate act that showed a total disregard for her welfare,” she said.

The DSPCA has made a formal report to the Gardaí and is now working with officers from Rathfarnham station to trace the individual’s movements. “We’re appealing to anyone who may recognise this man, or who might have witnessed suspicious activity in the area during the early hours of Tuesday, to come forward,” said Ms Bird.

Veterinary teams at the shelter say the dog remains under observation, having undergone emergency treatment for multiple fractures and lacerations. Her condition is described as stable, but she is facing a “long road to recovery”.

The DSPCA is reminding members of the public that there are proper channels for surrendering animals, and that leaving a pet in a vulnerable state can result in prosecution under the Animal Health and Welfare Act. Penalties for breaches of the legislation include fines of up to €250,000 or imprisonment.

A spokesperson for the charity urged anyone with information to contact the DSPCA directly or Rathfarnham Garda Station. Staff emphasised the importance of holding those who mistreat animals to account, and repeated their commitment to pursuing a prosecution if the perpetrator is identified.

The charity says it has seen a marked increase in animal abandonment cases in recent months, blaming cost-of-living pressures and a lack of awareness about animal welfare resources. They are encouraging pet owners struggling to care for their animals to seek help rather than leaving them in harm’s way.
headline: DSPCA looking to identify man who shoved injured dog under their gates

text:
A woman who was sexually abused as a child has told Cork Circuit Criminal Court she has been left “living in fear” after being attacked by a stranger in Cork city centre last summer.

The victim, now in her early 30s, was walking home on the evening of 15 June 2023 when she was set upon by 28-year-old Mark Farrell, of no fixed abode. The court heard Mr Farrell followed the woman after she had left a pub on Oliver Plunkett Street, before grabbing her and dragging her into a laneway, where he attempted to sexually assault her.

The woman, who cannot be named for legal reasons, managed to scream for help, attracting the attention of two passers-by, who intervened and detained Mr Farrell until Gardaí arrived at the scene. Mr Farrell was arrested and taken to Bridewell Garda Station, where he was later charged with assault with intent to commit a sexual offence and false imprisonment.

The court heard that the woman had previously suffered long-term trauma following childhood abuse, which had already affected her ability to trust others and to feel safe in public spaces. In her victim impact statement, which was read to the court, she described how the attack by Mr Farrell had “brought back all the nightmares” she had worked hard to overcome.

“I find it hard to leave my home now. I’m constantly looking over my shoulder,” she said through tears, describing the lasting psychological impact of the assault. “I thought the worst was behind me, but now I realise I still live in fear, every day.”

Detective Garda Siobhán O’Leary told the court that CCTV footage showed Mr Farrell following the victim for several minutes before the attack. When confronted by Gardaí, Mr Farrell, who has 12 previous convictions including for public order and assault, was intoxicated and became aggressive.

Defence counsel, Donal O’Sullivan BL, told the court that Mr Farrell was “deeply remorseful” and had expressed his regret in a letter to the victim. Mr O’Sullivan said his client had struggled with addiction and homelessness, and was engaging with addiction services since his remand in custody.

Judge Helen Boyle said the psychological harm caused by the assault was “grave” and compounded by the woman’s previous experiences of abuse. “This was a frightening and unprovoked attack on a vulnerable woman simply trying to get home,” she said.

Judge Boyle imposed a sentence of five years’ imprisonment, with the final year suspended, and ordered Mr Farrell to engage with addiction and rehabilitation services upon his release.

Mr Farrell, who appeared via video link from Cork Prison, thanked the court for what he described as “a fair hearing.” The woman was supported in court by members of her family and staff from the Sexual Violence Centre Cork.
headline: Woman who was sexually abused as child attacked by stranger in Cork city

text:
Gardaí have issued an appeal for information regarding the whereabouts of a missing man from County Meath, expressing growing concern for his welfare. 

Mark O’Connor, aged 43, was last seen in the Navan area at approximately 10pm on Tuesday night. He is described as being 1.82 metres (6 feet) in height, of medium build, with short brown hair and blue eyes. At the time of his disappearance, Mr O’Connor was wearing dark jeans, a navy jacket, and black trainers.

Family members reported Mark missing after he failed to return home or make contact, which they said was out of character. Relatives told the Irish Examiner they are extremely worried for his safety and urged anyone with information to come forward.

A Garda spokesperson said: “Gardaí and Mark’s family are concerned for his wellbeing. We are appealing to anyone who may have seen Mark or who may have information on his movements since Tuesday evening to contact us without delay.”

Gardaí have carried out local searches in Navan and surrounding areas, including checks of local parks and riversides. CCTV footage from the town centre is being reviewed as part of the ongoing enquiry.

Navan Garda Station can be contacted at 046 9036100. Alternatively, information can be provided to the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or at any Garda station.

No further details are available at this time. Gardaí have asked members of the public to refrain from sharing unverified information on social media, and to respect the privacy of Mr O’Connor’s family during this difficult period.
headline: Gardaí concerned for welfare of missing Meath man

text:
A man pointed an imitation firearm at a van driver’s face during a frightening incident in broad daylight, a court has heard.

Conor Murphy (22), with an address at Dolphin House, Dublin 8, appeared before Judge Sinéad Ní Chúlacháin at Dublin District Court, charged with possession of an imitation firearm with intent to cause fear, and with threatening and abusive behaviour under the Firearms and Public Order Acts.

Gardaí told the court that on 28 March last, the accused approached a delivery van parked on Cork Street, Dublin 8. Murphy, who was wearing a black hoodie, is alleged to have opened the passenger door and pointed what appeared to be a handgun directly into the face of the driver, a man in his 40s, and shouted at him to get out.

The van driver, fearing for his safety, managed to run from the vehicle and flag down a passing Garda patrol. The imitation gun was later recovered nearby, and Murphy was arrested at the scene a short time afterwards. He made no reply when formally charged.

The court heard that the driver has been unable to return to work due to stress following the incident, and has required counselling through his employer’s support service.

Garda evidence outlined that the firearm was later established to be a realistic replica, incapable of firing live rounds. However, both the victim and a number of witnesses believed it was genuine at the time.

Murphy has no previous convictions. His solicitor, Ms Mary Finn, told the court her client suffers with addiction issues and mental health difficulties, and that he had not intended to cause serious harm, but accepted the trauma caused. She said Murphy has expressed remorse and is engaging with addiction services.

Judge Ní Chúlacháin ordered a probation report and remanded Murphy on continuing bail to appear again in four weeks’ time for sentencing.
headline: Man pointed imitation gun into van driver's face

text:
A man in his thirties has been arrested by Gardaí following a burglary at a pharmacy in Cork city in the early hours of Thursday morning.

The incident occurred at a premises on the south side of the city shortly after 2am. Gardaí were alerted when an intruder alarm was triggered at the pharmacy, located on a busy suburban street. On arrival, officers discovered evidence of forced entry at the rear of the building.

A short time later, a man was located in the vicinity and arrested in connection with the break-in. It is understood that a quantity of prescription medication was recovered at the scene. The suspect was brought to Bridewell Garda Station where he is currently being detained under Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act, 1984.

A technical examination of the premises was conducted by Garda crime scene investigators on Thursday morning. CCTV footage from the area is also being reviewed as part of the ongoing investigation.

In a statement, a Garda spokesperson confirmed: “Gardaí in Cork are investigating a burglary that occurred at a pharmacy in the early hours of 13 June. One male in his 30s has been arrested and investigations are ongoing.”

The pharmacy remained closed to the public on Thursday morning but is expected to reopen later in the day. No injuries were reported during the incident.

Gardaí have appealed to anyone who noticed suspicious activity in the area or who may have information relevant to the investigation to contact Bridewell Garda Station on 021 494 3330, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda Station.
headline: Man arrested following burglary at Cork pharmacy

text:
The Russian ambassador to Ireland, Yury Filatov, has rejected accusations that he misled the public over his country’s actions in Ukraine. Speaking at a press briefing at the Russian Embassy in Dublin on Thursday afternoon, Mr Filatov insisted his government’s narrative around the ongoing conflict is “accurate and truthful.”

The ambassador faced a series of questions from Irish reporters regarding Russia’s justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, alleged war crimes, and disinformation campaigns.

Mr Filatov said: “We have been very open about our goals in Ukraine from the beginning. We are not hiding anything from the Irish public or the international community.” He claimed Western media outlets and governments, including Ireland, have promoted “falsehoods” about Russian military operations and intentions, dismissing reports of targeted attacks on civilians and evidence of atrocities as “fabricated.”

When pressed to respond to criticism from Irish politicians, including Taoiseach Simon Harris and Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin, who have accused Russia of spreading propaganda and lying to justify aggression, the ambassador was defiant.

“That is simply not true. Ireland is entitled to its view, but we have always provided factual information,” Mr Filatov said.

He repeated the Kremlin’s position that Russia is acting in self-defence and seeking to “denazify” Ukraine, a claim widely dismissed by the international community and by the United Nations. The ambassador denied that Russia’s actions amount to an illegal invasion, arguing that NATO expansion and Western support for Ukraine left Russia with “no alternative.”

Asked about the impact of the war on the Irish community, particularly Ukrainian refugees who have arrived in Ireland since 2022, Mr Filatov expressed “regret for any suffering” but blamed the Ukrainian government and Western allies for prolonging the conflict.

Earlier this week, the Department of Foreign Affairs summoned Mr Filatov to Iveagh House, where he was presented with the Government’s “grave concerns” over recent Russian missile strikes on civilian infrastructure in Kyiv and other cities. Minister Martin described Russia’s conduct as “outrageous and indefensible,” saying Ireland stands with Ukraine “for as long as it takes.”

Opposition parties, including Sinn Féin and Labour, have called for stronger measures against the Russian Embassy in Dublin, with some TDs demanding a further reduction in diplomatic staff.

The ambassador’s remarks come as the Oireachtas Foreign Affairs Committee prepares to hear from Ukrainian representatives in the coming days. More than 100,000 people fleeing the war have come to Ireland since February 2022, with the HSE and various local authorities providing accommodation and support services.

Gardaí have maintained a visible presence outside the Russian Embassy on Orwell Road in Rathgar since protests began at the outset of the invasion. Demonstrations have continued intermittently, with activists calling for the expulsion of the embassy and an end to the war.

The Department of Foreign Affairs reiterated on Thursday that the Government’s policy is “clear and unwavering” in support of Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. A spokesperson said: “We reject Russian attempts to distort the truth about the war and call for accountability for those responsible for war crimes.”
headline: Russian ambassador to Ireland denies lying to public over Ukraine

text:
Fine Gael spent more on its campaign for the European Parliament elections than any other party, according to figures filed with the Standards in Public Office Commission (Sipo). The party reported an outlay of just over €1 million for the June 2024 polls, significantly outstripping Sinn Féin, Fianna Fáil and other rivals.

Sipo returns, published on Monday, reveal total campaign spending by all parties just shy of €3.5 million, with Fine Gael accounting for almost 30% of the total. Fine Gael fielded candidates in all three European constituencies and increased its number of seats to five, matching Fianna Fáil’s total after the latter lost two sitting MEPs.

Sinn Féin, which suffered unexpected losses in the European elections, spent €670,000, while Fianna Fáil’s bill came in at €650,000. The Green Party reported spending close to €400,000, while smaller parties such as the Social Democrats and Labour each recorded expenditure below €200,000.

Fine Gael’s operation included a series of national advertising campaigns, significant online spend and logistics for canvasses across the large European constituencies. Its bill was buoyed by high-profile endorsements, events and professional consultancy services, according to the documents.

Parties are required under law to file detailed expenditure reports with Sipo within 56 days of the poll. The spending cap for each candidate is €230,000, but party-wide totals can vary depending on the number of candidates run and additional central spending.

The documents also show that Fine Gael received the highest amount of donations, with €150,000 raised in the form of compliant donations from individuals and companies. Sinn Féin reported €95,000 in donations, while Fianna Fáil disclosed almost €70,000. No party exceeded the legal donation limits, Sipo confirmed.

The sharp contrast in spending mirrors the political stakes attached to the European campaign as parties sought to consolidate support ahead of the next general election. While Fine Gael’s heavy investment delivered seat gains, Sinn Féin's returns have prompted internal reviews and questions about the party’s election strategy.

The Green Party, defending two incumbent MEPs, narrowly retained a single seat in Dublin, with leader Eamon Ryan conceding the party faces a “difficult period” after local and European election setbacks.

A Fine Gael spokesperson said the party’s financial commitments "reflected its ambition to provide strong Irish representation in Europe" and were in line with all statutory requirements. Opposition parties have called for “greater transparency” in the reporting of centrally-coordinated campaign spending by the main parties.

Sipo is now undertaking a routine audit of all campaign finance returns and will publish its compliance report in the autumn.
headline: Fine Gael's €1m European election spend outstrips other parties

text:
As thousands of holidaymakers prepare to travel abroad from Irish airports this summer, concerns remain over what recourse is available if their getaway doesn’t go according to plan. From cancelled flights to lost luggage and hotel nightmares, it’s important to know your entitlements under Irish and EU law.

The most common issues for Irish consumers relate to flight delays and cancellations. Under EU Regulation 261/2004, passengers departing from EU airports, or flying into the EU on an EU-based carrier, may be entitled to compensation if their flight is significantly delayed or cancelled. Compensation can range from €250 to €600, depending on the length of the delay and the distance travelled.

Fionnuala Meehan, spokesperson for the European Consumer Centre Ireland, told the Irish Examiner that “passengers should always contact the airline first, as they are obliged to either provide an alternative flight or refund the ticket if your flight is cancelled.” She emphasised that in cases of lengthy delays, airlines must also offer meals, refreshments, and, if necessary, hotel accommodation and transport to and from the hotel.

Lost, delayed, or damaged baggage remains an ongoing source of frustration. Under the Montreal Convention, you may claim up to approximately €1,500 for lost or delayed luggage, provided you submit your claim within 21 days of receiving the bag, or within seven days if it is damaged. Airlines usually require proof of purchase for valuable items, so keeping receipts from your holiday shopping is advisable.

For those who book package holidays, the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018 offer robust protections. If a package holiday is significantly changed or cancelled by the organiser before departure, you are entitled to a full refund or a suitable replacement. Should problems arise during the holiday — such as substandard accommodation or misrepresented activities — operators are required to resolve the issue or offer appropriate compensation.

The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission advises holidaymakers to keep records of all correspondence and to take photographs of any problems encountered. If an issue remains unresolved, complaints should be escalated to the operator in writing. If you are dissatisfied with their response, the Commission can offer further guidance.

Travel insurance remains crucial. Policies differ, but standard cover typically includes trip cancellation, medical expenses, personal liability, and baggage loss. However, most policies exclude claims arising from events already known at the time of booking, such as ongoing industrial action.

Minister for Transport, Eamon Ryan, TD, urged consumers to check the terms and conditions of their travel insurance and be aware of their rights. “Planning ahead is the best defence against disappointment,” he said.

Travellers are also reminded to check their European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) is valid, granting access to public healthcare in the EU at local rates.

For those who encounter issues abroad, the Department of Foreign Affairs operates a 24/7 consular assistance service, though its remit is limited to emergencies rather than holiday complaints.

With demand for travel rebounding after years of pandemic disruption, consumer organisations are reminding holidaymakers that knowing your rights is the best way to ensure that a holiday mishap does not ruin your summer plans.
headline: What you're entitled to if your holiday goes wrong

Irish businesses may face costs of up to €1.5bn and significant operational disruption due to ongoing “chaotic” delays and uncertainty in the Brexit transition, according to a new report published on Thursday.

The report, commissioned by business advocacy group Ibec, warns that supply chain bottlenecks, new customs procedures, and divergences in regulation are already driving up costs and threatening competitiveness for Irish firms that trade with Britain. Ibec’s analysis estimates that additional compliance, administrative, and logistics expenses could total as much as €1.5bn over the coming year if current conditions persist.

Danny McCoy, chief executive of Ibec, said the “piecemeal” implementation of post-Brexit rules was leaving firms in a “constant state of limbo”. He called on the Government to intensify diplomatic engagement with British authorities and the European Commission to streamline procedures and protect Ireland’s economic interests.

“Businesses are dealing with a moving target — every month brings new paperwork, shifting requirements, and uncertainty over what the rules will actually look like in practice,” Mr McCoy said. “For many SMEs in particular, this raises very serious questions about viability and jobs.”

The report highlights issues such as delays at ports, increased checks on goods, and complex customs documentation, which are causing disruption for importers and exporters. Sectors worst affected include agri-food, pharmaceuticals, and manufacturing, all of which depend heavily on the UK market and cross-border supply chains.

While the Government has allocated funding for Brexit readiness and customs infrastructure, Ibec says much more is needed to support affected firms and ensure Ireland remains an attractive location for trade and investment. It is also calling for expanded training for customs agents, streamlined IT systems, and targeted financial supports.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin, speaking on Thursday, acknowledged the pressures facing the business community and said the Government “remains fully committed to safeguarding Ireland’s position”. He pledged to raise concerns with UK counterparts at the next Joint Committee meeting under the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement.

Opposition TDs accused the Government of complacency in its Brexit preparations. Sinn Féin’s finance spokesperson, Pearse Doherty, said more direct supports were needed for businesses “caught up in red tape”, while Labour’s Aodhán Ó Ríordáin called for an “urgent review” of customs and logistics procedures.

The Ibec report warns that, without action to resolve outstanding protocol issues and improve regulatory clarity, Irish export performance could suffer sustained damage. It also notes a rising risk of border delays and trading friction once additional UK controls come into effect later this year.

Business leaders have urged the Oireachtas to convene an emergency committee hearing to examine the risks and recommend immediate interventions. Mr McCoy said: “It’s vital that Irish jobs and competitiveness are not collateral damage in a Brexit process that continues to be anything but smooth.”
headline: Businesses could face €1.5bn costs amid ‘chaotic’ Brexit transition

ALONE, the national organisation supporting older people to age at home, is set to hold its inaugural ‘Donation Day’ in Dublin this Thursday. The fundraising event, which takes place at St Stephen’s Green Shopping Centre from 9am to 9pm, marks the first time ALONE has organised a dedicated donation drive in the city centre.

Organisers said the campaign was launched in response to rising demand for ALONE’s services as the cost-of-living crisis continues to affect many older people across the capital and beyond. The charity is calling on members of the public to give what they can in order to help fund vital supports including befriending, housing, and practical assistance.

Speaking ahead of the event, ALONE CEO Seán Moynihan said: “Every day, more and more older people are reaching out to us for help. Many are struggling with energy bills, housing insecurity, and feelings of isolation. Our services are needed now more than ever, and public donations are crucial in enabling us to be there for those who need us most.”

Volunteers and staff will be present throughout the day at collection points, providing information about ALONE’s work and accepting both cash and contactless donations. There will also be a ‘Wall of Support’ where donors can leave messages of encouragement for older people availing of the charity’s services.

Mr Moynihan emphasised that all funds raised on the day will go directly towards ALONE’s frontline programmes, including the nationwide Support and Befriending service that matches older people with trained volunteers for weekly visits or phone calls.

According to ALONE, requests for support have increased by over 30% in the last year, with the organisation receiving upwards of 50,000 calls to its national helpline in 2023. Issues most commonly reported include loneliness, difficulty accessing healthcare or transport, and financial hardship.

Several well-known figures have pledged their backing for the campaign, with Minister for Older People Mary Butler TD urging the public to “spare a thought and a few euro” for vulnerable older neighbours. “ALONE does exceptional work in communities all over Ireland. Every donation will make a real difference this winter,” she said.

Members of the public who are unable to attend can also contribute online via the ALONE website. The charity is hopeful that ‘Donation Day’ will become an annual fixture, helping to secure sustainable funding at a time when the number of people aged over 65 in Ireland continues to rise.

For further information on ALONE’s services or to make a donation, visit alone.ie or call 0818 222 024.
headline: ALONE holding first ever 'Donation Day' in Dublin

text:
Phil Hogan’s reported interest in the top job at the World Trade Organisation comes at a complex and highly charged moment for both Ireland and the international trading system. The former EU Trade Commissioner and ex-Minister for the Environment has signalled he is “keeping an open mind” about seeking the WTO Director-Generalship, yet the prospect of an Irish candidate at the heart of global trade governance warrants careful consideration.

Mr Hogan’s experience is not in doubt. As EU Agriculture Commissioner, he built a reputation as an effective deal-broker, winning deep respect among his counterparts across the bloc and abroad. His subsequent spell as Trade Commissioner, though curtailed by the so-called ‘Golfgate’ controversy, placed him at the forefront of Europe’s response to escalating trade tensions with the United States and the increasingly assertive stance of China. His breadth of contacts and his understanding of both the Irish and European political landscapes position him among the most seasoned candidates to emerge for the WTO post.

For Ireland, the elevation of a domestic figure to such a prominent international stage would carry real significance, both symbolic and substantive. In the wake of Brexit, Irish trade policy has had to adapt at pace, with the country more reliant than ever on the multilateral system to underpin access to international markets. An Irish influence at the top of the WTO could bring welcome focus to the needs of smaller trading nations and an agricultural exporting economy. Given the critical role of the WTO in adjudicating trade disputes and setting global rules, an Irish director-general could serve as a moderating force at a time when protectionist pressures threaten the very basis of open trade.

But the case for Mr Hogan’s candidacy is not straightforward. While his expertise is acknowledged, the legacy of Golfgate has not faded from public memory. His resignation from the European Commission under pressure from both Brussels and the Irish Government underscored the importance of public trust in those holding high office. For many, the manner of his departure raises questions around judgment and the responsibilities attending leadership at the highest level.

It is also important to note the scale of challenge facing the WTO itself. The body has become increasingly paralysed, with key functions—most notably its appellate dispute mechanism—blocked by great power rivalry. Whoever succeeds to the Director-Generalship must find a way to restore relevance to the organisation, broker compromise between competing economic powerhouses, and ensure that the benefits of trade accrue more equitably across developed and developing nations. That is no small task, and any candidate must command the confidence not only of Washington and Beijing, but also of the many smaller states whose futures depend upon global rules.

Mr Hogan has yet to declare any formal candidacy, and it remains to be seen whether the Irish Government would throw its full weight behind him. The process will be lengthy, political, and, as ever, subject to the wider machinations of European and global diplomacy. Nonetheless, the possibility of an Irish figure at the helm of the world’s trade rulebook is a reminder that Irish expertise can command attention on the international stage, for all the complexities that might entail.

As Ireland continues to navigate an increasingly uncertain global economic environment, the national interest will be best served by thoughtful engagement rather than simple cheerleading. If Mr Hogan does choose to seek the WTO role, both his supporters and detractors would do well to weigh his credentials and his record in full, conscious of the consequences for Ireland’s standing far beyond these shores.
headline: The Irish Examiner View: Hogan’s hat in the WTO ring?

text:
Irish consumers are increasingly bombarded with advice on skincare and beauty routines, much of it coming from celebrities and so-called influencers. The glossy sheen of celebrity endorsements, coupled with slick social media campaigns, has led many to believe that these personalities possess expert knowledge on how best to care for their skin. But dermatologists and registered skin therapists are cautioning the public to be mindful of whose advice they follow.

Recent trends see celebrities sharing intricate skincare routines, sometimes involving dozens of steps or expensive products. From international stars like Gwyneth Paltrow to homegrown talents, the message is often the same: if you use what they use, you too can achieve flawless skin. However, according to the Irish Skin Foundation, this approach can be misleading and, in some cases, harmful.

Speaking to the Irish Examiner, Dr Nuala Tierney, Consultant Dermatologist at Tallaght University Hospital, warns that celebrity routines rarely take into account the unique needs of each individual. “What works for one person, especially someone with access to private dermatologists and cosmetic procedures, is unlikely to translate for the average person,” she said. “People often forget that celebrities may also use filters, editing, and even professional lighting, so the results you see on screen are not always a fair reflection.”

The rise of so-called ‘skinfluencers’ has also complicated matters, particularly among younger consumers. The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) has expressed concern about the promotion of unregulated skincare products online. In some cases, influencers have encouraged the use of products not authorised for sale in Ireland or the wider EU, with potential risks to consumers’ health.

Jennifer Rock, also known as The Skin Nerd and founder of Skingredients, notes that many celebrity-endorsed products are chosen for their branding rather than their efficacy. “There’s a perception that celebrities are experts, but unless they hold relevant qualifications, their opinion is just that—an opinion,” Rock told the Irish Examiner. “When it comes to skincare, evidence-based advice is what we should prioritise.”

In recent years, the number of people seeking help for adverse reactions to popular skincare trends has increased, according to the Irish Association of Dermatologists. The mistakes range from chemical burns caused by unregulated face peels to allergic reactions from fragrances and essential oils that are commonly recommended by non-experts online.

The HSE has encouraged the public to consult with registered professionals for skin health advice, particularly for those with underlying conditions like eczema, psoriasis or acne. “It is important to remember that the skin is the body’s largest organ and should be treated with respect,” a HSE spokesperson said. “Misinformation online can create unrealistic expectations and sometimes leads to more harm than good.”

While celebrities can bring attention to the importance of good skincare, the consensus among Irish experts is clear: when it comes to your health, particularly something as vital as skin, it’s best to turn to those with relevant expertise rather than the latest celebrity trend. Just because your favourite star swears by a certain serum, doesn’t mean it’s the right choice for you—or indeed, safe at all.
headline: The Skin Nerd: Coming clean- celebrities don’t always know best

text:
Ceremonies were held in Nagasaki early on Monday to mark the 76th anniversary of the atomic bombing by the United States, which killed over 70,000 people and hastened the end of the Second World War. Survivors, bereaved families and officials gathered at the city’s Peace Park, with attendance scaled back due to Covid-19 restrictions.

The annual event began with a moment of silence at 11.02am, the exact time when the bomb detonated above the city on 9 August 1945. Representatives laid wreaths and paper cranes in memory of victims, while the Peace Bell tolled.

Nagasaki’s mayor, Tomihisa Taue, addressed the gathering, urging world leaders to pursue dialogue and concrete action for nuclear disarmament. He called upon the Japanese government to sign and ratify the UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which came into effect earlier this year. Mr Taue reflected on the suffering caused by the attack and warned against forgetting the lessons of the past.

Prime Minister Yoshihide Suga attended the commemoration, emphasising Japan’s commitment to a nuclear-free world while reiterating the policy of relying on the US nuclear deterrent as part of its security arrangements. The ceremony also included statements from hibakusha, atomic bomb survivors, some of whom criticised Japan’s refusal to join the treaty, citing the continuing threat posed by nuclear weapons.

Only three days separate the bombings of Hiroshima on 6 August and Nagasaki, which together killed an estimated 214,000 people by the end of 1945, either instantly or from subsequent injuries and illness. The majority of those who died in Nagasaki were civilians, including schoolchildren and medical workers. The events remain a source of deep trauma and a focal point in debates over disarmament and historical responsibility.

Due to the ongoing pandemic, the number of participants at the 2021 memorial was limited, with social distancing in place and many people watching the proceedings remotely. President Michael D Higgins sent a message of solidarity, highlighting Ireland’s longstanding advocacy for nuclear disarmament, and commending the resilience of the hibakusha in their struggle for peace.

The commemoration comes against a backdrop of rising global tensions and concern over the risk of a new arms race. Japan, the only country to have suffered atomic bombings in war, continues to walk a delicate line between its security policies and the calls from survivors and campaigners for a comprehensive ban on nuclear weapons.
headline: Nagasaki marks 76th anniversary of US atomic bombing
