Four new cases of coronavirus have been confirmed in the west of Ireland, according to the latest figures released by the Department of Health last night. The cases, which bring the total number of confirmed Covid-19 infections in the region to 62, were identified following laboratory testing carried out by the HSE’s regional public health teams.

The individuals affected are understood to be from counties Galway and Mayo, with two cases each reported in those areas. All four people are currently self-isolating at home and are being monitored closely by HSE officials. It is believed that three of the new cases are linked to previously confirmed infections, while the fourth was detected through the contact tracing programme.

Dr Ronan Glynn, the Acting Chief Medical Officer, appealed again to members of the public to remain vigilant and to continue following public health advice. “These new cases show that while the incidence rate remains low, the virus continues to circulate in our communities,” he said. “Anyone experiencing symptoms such as a cough, fever, or loss of taste or smell should immediately contact their GP and self-isolate.”

Gardaí in the region have renewed calls for people to adhere strictly to current social distancing measures and restrictions on gatherings, as well as the advice to wear face coverings in indoor public spaces. In recent weeks, there have been a number of reports of house parties and other social events in violation of current guidelines.

The Minister for Health, Stephen Donnelly TD, said the situation is being closely monitored and that additional testing resources will be deployed in the west if needed. “We are grateful to the vast majority of people who are following the public health advice, but these new cases underline the importance of remaining cautious,” he said.

Meanwhile, University Hospital Galway and Mayo University Hospital have confirmed that they are continuing to operate normal services, but have urged members of the public not to attend emergency departments unless absolutely necessary.

Public health teams are now working with the families and close contacts of those affected to limit further spread of the virus. The latest figures from the HSE indicate that there have been over 1,200 tests conducted in the region in the past week, with health officials warning that continued vigilance will be needed to avoid a further rise in cases.

The National Public Health Emergency Team is due to meet tomorrow to consider the latest data and to provide updated guidance to the Government on the phased reopening of society.
headline: Four new coronavirus cases confirmed in west of Ireland

Fianna Fáil leader Micheál Martin is facing mounting pressure from both opposition parties and elements within his own party to clarify his position on Government formation, as inter-party talks enter a period of uncertainty.

Senior figures within Fianna Fáil have privately voiced concerns over what has been described as a “lack of public leadership”, with some party colleagues urging Mr Martin to “come out of hiding” amid growing confusion over coalition negotiations.

The calls come after a week marked by stalled discussions between Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael, and the Green Party, with disagreements over issues such as climate targets, housing, and the proposed programme for government. The uncertainty has fuelled speculation over whether Mr Martin’s leadership remains secure, particularly in advance of the expected reconvening of the Dáil next week.

Opposition parties, including Sinn Féin and Labour, have seized on the delays, accusing the establishment parties of “dragging their feet” and lacking transparency. Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said: “The public deserves honesty and clarity. Micheál Martin needs to make himself available and explain Fianna Fáil’s position on the key issues facing the country.”

Within Fianna Fáil, backbench TDs and councillors have grown increasingly restless as the party’s grassroots express frustration at the protracted process. A number of Fianna Fáil TDs who spoke to the Irish Examiner on condition of anonymity said that local members are “losing patience” and fear lasting reputational damage if a deal is not concluded soon.

One senior party source said: “We’ve been left in the dark. There’s a feeling that Micheál needs to be out front, showing leadership, not behind closed doors. People want to hear directly from him, not through leaks or spin.”

Amid the mounting criticism, Mr Martin has maintained a relatively low profile, declining several invitations to speak publicly on the state of the negotiations since last weekend. Sources close to the Fianna Fáil leader argue that he is “deeply engaged” in discussions and is “fully committed” to forming a stable government.

The Taoiseach, Leo Varadkar, and Green Party leader, Eamon Ryan, have both given media interviews in recent days outlining their respective parties’ positions, increasing pressure on Mr Martin to similarly brief the public.

Meanwhile, a meeting of the Fianna Fáil parliamentary party, expected later this week, is likely to be dominated by questions on the state of the talks and Mr Martin’s strategy. Several TDs are expected to seek assurances on key policy issues, including health and housing, amid fears that further delays could embolden calls for a change in leadership.

Political analysts suggest that unless a breakthrough is reached soon, the current impasse could force the parties back to the electorate or see fresh attempts made to form a minority government.

As the deadlock continues, public attention is focusing on whether Mr Martin will step forward to address concerns and reaffirm his leadership at a critical juncture for both his party and the country.
headline: Micheál Martin urged to 'come out of hiding' amid Government formation confusion

text:
New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern looked set for a landslide victory as early results rolled in from the country's general election on Saturday, with her Labour Party on course for an outright majority in parliament for the first time in decades.

With just over half of the votes counted, preliminary tallies indicated Labour was polling close to 50%, far ahead of the centre-right National Party, which trailed on around 26%. If the trend continued, Ms Ardern could form the next government without needing to rely on coalition partners, an unprecedented result since New Zealand adopted its proportional voting system in 1996.

Support for Labour surged in the wake of Ms Ardern’s widely praised handling of the Covid-19 pandemic. Swift and decisive action during the crisis saw the country avoid the high infection rates and fatalities experienced elsewhere, allowing much of New Zealand’s economy and daily life to return to normal. The government’s response has resonated strongly with voters, analysts said.

Ms Ardern, 40, addressed supporters in Auckland, calling for unity and promising to deliver on pledges to build affordable housing, tackle climate change and boost the economy. She urged New Zealanders to “keep the faith” as official counts continued into the evening.

Opposition leader Judith Collins conceded that the National Party faced a disappointing result, but vowed to continue fighting for voters’ concerns in the next parliament. Other opposition parties, including the Greens and the populist New Zealand First, hovered near the 5% threshold required to secure seats under the proportional system.

The projected outcome would cement Ms Ardern’s status as one of the world’s most prominent progressive leaders, admired internationally for her compassionate approach to governance. She rose to global prominence after her response to the Christchurch mosque attacks in 2019, and again during the coronavirus outbreak.

The official result is expected in the coming days, pending counting of special votes including those cast by New Zealanders overseas. Turnout appeared to be robust, with tens of thousands of voters casting ballots ahead of election day.

Irish citizens resident in New Zealand have closely monitored the contest, with Ireland’s Ambassador to New Zealand, Peter Ryan, encouraging all to participate in the democratic process. The Department of Foreign Affairs has maintained regular contact with the local Irish community, providing updated travel advice and support throughout the pandemic.

Political analysts said a strong mandate for Ms Ardern would give her greater scope to push ahead with Labour’s reform agenda, though she may opt to continue working with smaller parties to ensure stability. The final outcome—and the make-up of the next government—will be confirmed once all votes are counted early next week.
headline: Ardern heading for big win as votes counted in New Zealand poll

text:
Jerry Harris, the US television personality best known for his appearance on the Netflix documentary series *Cheer*, has been sentenced to 12 years in prison in an American federal court. The 22-year-old, who rose to international fame with the 2020 hit series, faced charges relating to the possession and distribution of child sexual abuse imagery, as well as sex offences involving underage boys.

Harris appeared before a US District Court in Chicago on Wednesday, where he delivered an emotional statement to the court, insisting: “I am not an evil person.” Harris, who had earlier pleaded guilty to two of the most serious counts, apologised to his victims and acknowledged the damage he had caused to their lives and families.

“I take responsibility for the hurt I have caused,” Harris told the judge. “I realise that what I did was wrong, and I am deeply sorry for the pain I have caused these families and children. I am not an evil person. I am someone who made terrible mistakes.”

The judge, in handing down the 12-year sentence, said Harris’s actions had “wreaked havoc” on the lives of his victims and described the crimes as “grave violations of trust”. Following the custodial sentence, Harris will also be subject to a further eight years of supervised release, US prosecutors confirmed.

Harris became a familiar face to Irish audiences through his enthusiastic presence on *Cheer*, which followed a competitive cheerleading squad in Navarro College, Texas. His arrest in 2020 shocked fans, and the programme later addressed his case in a follow-up episode.

During the sentencing, statements from victims and their families were read into the record, describing the “devastating” impact of Harris’s offences. The defence argued that Harris’s own background of abuse and hardship should be taken into account, but prosecutors insisted the seriousness of the crimes merited a substantial custodial sentence.

Netflix, which produced the documentary series, issued a brief statement, saying it “condemns all forms of sexual abuse and stands with the survivors”. There was no immediate comment from Harris’s representatives following the sentencing.

The case has prompted renewed discussions in the US and internationally about child safety in sports and the responsibilities of organisations to protect young people. In Ireland, youth advocacy groups have called for greater education and awareness in local sports and youth activities.

Harris will be eligible for early release only after serving the minimum required term, according to court records. He had no prior criminal record before these offences came to light.

The *Cheer* series, while still available on Netflix in Ireland, now features an onscreen disclaimer referencing the allegations and subsequent criminal proceedings involving Harris.
headline: Jerry Harris says ‘I am not an evil person’ as he receives 12-year sentence

text:
Ireland’s fashion community is calling for a more inclusive and diverse approach to style, saying the industry must better reflect the country’s changing face and meet the needs of people of all backgrounds, ages and body types. At the centre of this shift are Irish designers, influencers and campaigners who say the traditional boundaries around what is fashionable are outdated and exclusionary, and who are championing a message of ‘fashion for all’.

Aisling O’Connor, a plus-size model from Cork, believes the Irish market has long ignored people outside the narrow sample sizes seen on catwalks and high street posters. “For years, I struggled to find clothes that didn’t just fit, but actually made me feel seen and included,” she says. “There’s a huge appetite for stylish, well-made clothes in bigger sizes, and thankfully Irish brands are starting to catch up.”

Organisations like Bodywhys and the Irish Wheelchair Association have welcomed the growing conversation about making fashion accessible for people with various needs, including those with disabilities. A recent show at Dublin’s Mansion House featured models with physical and sensory disabilities, in collaboration with adaptative clothing label No Bounds. Co-founder Clodagh McNamara says the response has been overwhelming. “People want to see themselves on the runway. Fashion should never be about exclusion,” she says.

The call for inclusivity goes beyond size and ability. Irish designers like Aoife Fitzpatrick, whose label is stocked in Brown Thomas, are incorporating gender-neutral collections and unisex lines. “There’s a shift happening, especially among younger shoppers. They want options that aren’t dictated by gender or societal norms,” says Fitzpatrick.

Fashion influencers and stylists are also playing a key role in changing perceptions. Limerick-based stylist Eoin Murphy says the growth of social media has given a platform to voices once shut out by mainstream fashion. “Instagram and TikTok are full of Irish creators celebrating different shapes, genders and backgrounds. The message is clear: fashion is for everyone, whether you’re in Ennis or Enniskerry.”

The high street is responding, albeit slowly. Penneys has recently launched dedicated plus-size lines and accessible ranges in selected stores, and Dunnes Stores has collaborated with local designers on limited-edition inclusive collections. International brands present in Ireland, such as H&M and Zara, are also under pressure from Irish consumers and advocacy groups to expand their sizing and adaptive fashion ranges.

Industry insiders say more work remains to be done, particularly in rural areas, where choice can still be limited. “It can be isolating if you don’t fit the mould and your only options are online,” says O’Connor. Campaigners are calling for tax incentives for adaptive fashion lines, and for government grants to support Irish designers focused on inclusion.

The push for a more open and accessible industry is also being felt at the educational level. The National College of Art and Design and Limerick School of Art and Design have both added modules on body diversity and adaptative design to their courses, signalling a generational change in how the next crop of designers are thinking.

For those in the sector, the hope is that the message of ‘fashion for all’ becomes standard, not a slogan. “Irish fashion has a history of creativity and resilience,” says McNamara. “Now, it’s about building an industry where everyone is welcome in the fitting room.”
headline: The Fitting Room: Irish fashionistas advocate fashion for all

text:
Emilie Pine’s debut novel, Ruth & Pen, arrives with considerable anticipation following the success of her acclaimed essay collection, Notes to Self. Readers familiar with Pine’s previous work will recognise the same keenly observed humanity and emotional intelligence that made her essays stand out. In this first work of fiction, Pine turns her attention to two women in Dublin whose lives are, on the surface, quite separate but are quietly shaped by forces of longing, anxiety and hope.

Set over the course of a single day, Ruth & Pen draws explicit inspiration from James Joyce’s Ulysses, but while the canvas here is smaller, Pine brings a modern sensibility to her depiction of contemporary Dublin. The city is rendered in tactile, lived-in detail: Luas journeys, cafés on Camden Street, the uneasy hum of traffic, and the private aches of those moving through it. For readers in Ireland, these settings are instantly recognisable, yet Pine avoids cliché, instead weaving them into the fabric of her characters’ inner lives.

Ruth, a therapist in her late thirties, wakes to uncertainty as her marriage hangs in the balance. Pen, a teenager on the autism spectrum, is navigating the labyrinth of adolescence with acute sensitivity. The two women’s stories unfold in parallel, never directly intersecting, yet the patterns of their experience—alienation, connection, and hope—echo across the novel in subtle, affecting ways.

Pine’s writing is remarkable for its compassion, particularly in her rendering of Pen. The challenges Pen faces in communicating her needs and navigating an unforgiving world are explored with nuance and honesty, never tipping into sentimentality. Ruth’s sections, too, are marked by the author’s skill in revealing the vulnerabilities that lie beneath the surface of adult life. Pine is attentive to the small details of daily existence—the missed phone call, the shared silences, the significance of a quiet gesture—and it is in these moments that her empathy shines brightest.

There is a virtuosic control to Pine’s prose, which is clear and unshowy, yet suffused with warmth. The narrative structure, with its dual perspectives and compressed timeline, serves to heighten the emotional stakes. Readers are drawn into the private worlds of Ruth and Pen, urged to consider not only what it means to be seen and known, but also the quiet courage it takes to reach out when one feels alone.

While the plot eschews melodrama, focusing instead on internal change, Pine’s background as a writer of personal narrative is evident in the authenticity and depth she brings to her characters. The result is a novel which is both intimate and universal, inviting readers to reflect on their own relationships and the hidden stories of those around them.

Ruth & Pen reaffirms Emilie Pine’s place as one of Ireland’s most empathetic and perceptive writers. It is a sensitive, finely crafted debut, brimming with insight into the private struggles and small triumphs that shape everyday life. For those drawn to character-driven fiction, and to stories which capture the spirit of modern Ireland, Pine’s novel will linger long after the final page.
headline: Book review: Emilie Pine's debut novel reinforces her reputation as an empathetic writer

text:
British armed forces are on standby to launch air strikes targeting Islamic State (IS) operatives in Afghanistan, according to senior UK defence sources, as heightened fears of terrorist activity in the region have prompted a review of Britain’s counter-terror capabilities.

The British government says forces stationed in the Middle East, including the Royal Air Force, have the capacity to conduct precision strikes against IS-Khorasan, the Afghan offshoot of the terrorist group. The move comes amid concerns that Afghanistan is once again serving as a haven for terrorist groups following the withdrawal of Western troops in 2021 and the Taliban’s return to power.

Speaking to the House of Commons on Thursday, the UK defence secretary, Grant Shapps, confirmed that the government was prepared to act if presented with credible intelligence about IS activities. He said protecting British citizens, as well as international partners, remained the “highest priority”.

“We have the assets in place and we have the will to act where necessary,” Mr Shapps told MPs. He added that any operation would be conducted in close cooperation with Britain’s allies, including the United States and other NATO partners.

The announcement follows the deadly massacre in Moscow last weekend, for which IS-Khorasan claimed responsibility. The group, which has targeted both Afghan civilians and Western interests in recent years, is believed by Western intelligence agencies to have regrouped and strengthened capabilities since the Taliban takeover.

While Downing Street has not specified whether any imminent action is planned, officials say contingency plans have been put in place for rapid response. Reports indicate that RAF Typhoon and Reaper drones are stationed in Qatar and Cyprus, capable of reaching Afghanistan with missile and surveillance support.

The UK assessment mirrors concerns raised earlier this week by US President Joe Biden and the Pentagon, who warned that IS-Khorasan retains the capacity to carry out major attacks against Western targets, including within Europe. The Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs, Micheál Martin, said on Wednesday that Ireland would remain vigilant and work closely with international partners on counter-terrorism.

Meanwhile, the United Nations has reported a significant increase in IS-K attacks within Afghanistan, where Taliban authorities have faced repeated challenges in curbing rival militant groups. The international community has repeatedly called on the Taliban to prevent Afghanistan from becoming a launchpad for global terrorism.

Dublin Airport authorities and Garda security units said on Thursday that current threat levels remain unchanged, but that “continuous monitoring” is underway in line with advice from the National Security Analysis Centre. The Department of Foreign Affairs continues to advise Irish citizens to avoid all travel to Afghanistan, citing terrorism and the volatile security situation across the country.

British officials have not indicated that ground troops would be deployed in any such operation, and emphasised that any military response would focus on targeted air strikes against terrorist positions. The developments come as Western powers attempt to adapt their counter-terror strategies in the face of evolving threats from non-state actors in unstable regions.
headline: British forces prepared to launch air strikes to target Islamic State terrorists in Afghanistan

text:
A man in his thirties remains in stable condition after sustaining stab wounds during an incident in Dublin city centre on St Stephen's Day. Gardaí have launched an investigation following the altercation, which occurred shortly after 9pm on Tuesday night on Dame Street, a busy thoroughfare frequented by revellers and shoppers at this time of year.

Emergency services were alerted to the scene after reports of a row involving a group of individuals outside a premises near the junction with South Great George's Street. Upon arrival, Gardaí discovered a man with apparent stab injuries. He received treatment from paramedics before being rushed to St James's Hospital, where his injuries are not understood to be life-threatening.

Garda forensic officers carried out a technical examination of the area overnight, and an incident room has been established at Pearse Street Garda station. Detectives are appealing for witnesses who may have been in the vicinity between 8.45pm and 9.30pm, particularly anyone who may have video or dashcam footage.

No arrests have been made to date, but inquiries are ongoing. A Garda spokesperson confirmed that the injured man is assisting with the investigation. The motive for the attack is not yet clear, though sources indicated that the parties involved are believed to have been known to one another.

Dame Street was partially cordoned off for several hours as investigations continued, causing minor traffic disruptions in the city centre on one of the busiest shopping days of the Christmas period. Local representatives have expressed concern at the rise in violent incidents in the capital in recent months and called for a visible Garda presence in the area.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Pearse Street Garda station on (01) 666 9000, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.
headline: Man stabbed in St Stephen's Day attack

text:
Boris Johnson has warned colleagues to brace for a “huge spike” in Omicron cases in the coming days, as the UK’s Covid-19 response intensified amid mounting concern over the new variant’s rapid spread.

The British Prime Minister addressed ministers at a special virtual Cabinet meeting on Sunday evening, convened as the government sought to accelerate its booster vaccination programme. His comments come as Britain reported 1,239 cases of the Omicron variant on Sunday, nearly doubling the previous day’s figure and prompting fears of a significant wave of infections in the run-up to Christmas.

Mr Johnson told ministers that the UK faces a “tidal wave” of Omicron cases and warned of renewed strain on the health system. He urged citizens to come forward for booster jabs, announcing that the government aims to offer a third dose to every eligible adult by the end of December.

The UK Health Security Agency has estimated that Omicron infections may be doubling every two or three days, suggesting the potential for a steep rise in cases. Early data indicates the variant is more transmissible than previous strains, though questions remain about its severity and the level of protection conferred by vaccines.

The Prime Minister stopped short of announcing further restrictions on movement or gatherings in England, but introduced a new Covid alert level 4, the second highest, across the country. Mask-wearing indoors and guidance to work from home are set to remain in place through the festive season.

Northern Ireland’s executive is monitoring developments closely, with the Department of Health confirming a number of Omicron cases. The HSE and Irish health officials have similarly warned the public to remain vigilant.

Tánaiste Leo Varadkar told RTÉ on Sunday that the Irish Government is “watching the UK situation very carefully”, and that additional public health measures cannot be ruled out if a surge in Omicron cases threatens to overwhelm local hospitals.

The World Health Organisation reiterated its advice to accelerate vaccine rollout and maintain public health measures. Scientists have cautioned that while booster doses appear to offer enhanced protection, high case numbers could still lead to increased hospitalisations and pressure on health services.

Travel restrictions remain in place between the UK and Ireland, with pre-departure testing requirements set to continue for the immediate future. Public health officials have appealed for continued compliance with guidelines to curtail the spread of Omicron, urging eligible individuals to avail of booster vaccines as soon as possible.

As Christmas approaches, the prospect of new restrictions casts uncertainty over social plans and retail activity on both sides of the Irish Sea. The government in London has not ruled out further measures, with Mr Johnson insisting decisions will be guided by the “evolving science and data”.
headline: Johnson warns ‘huge spike’ of Omicron cases on way at virtual Cabinet

text:
Minister for Finance, Paschal Donohoe, has said the next government will face the daunting challenge of rebuilding the Irish economy in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic, warning that economic recovery will be “the dominant concern” for the incoming administration.

Speaking yesterday after the Cabinet’s weekly meeting, Mr Donohoe acknowledged that while Ireland had made significant progress in curbing the spread of the virus, the road ahead for jobs and businesses remained uncertain. “No matter what shape the next government takes, restoring the economy will be central to its work,” he said.

The Minister expressed hope that the phased reopening of the country, which began this week, would bring some relief to businesses forced to close their doors during the lockdown, but cautioned that economic activity would likely remain subdued for some time. “We are seeing the impact on every sector. Small firms, the hospitality sector, and exporters have all been hit hard. The priority must be to support viable businesses and get people back to work as soon as it is safe to do so,” he said.

Unemployment surged to almost 30% at the height of the pandemic crisis, with more than 1.2 million people receiving support through the Pandemic Unemployment Payment and the Temporary Wage Subsidy Scheme. The Department of Finance estimates the economy will contract by 10.5% this year, with a public deficit of up to €23 billion expected.

Mr Donohoe said the scale of the fiscal intervention so far was “unprecedented”, noting that government supports totalling more than €12 billion had been rolled out to cushion the blow to workers and businesses. He indicated that further support measures would be considered as the situation evolves, particularly for sectors likely to face prolonged disruption, such as tourism and retail.

On the question of how long emergency measures could be sustained, the Minister said the “extraordinary state” of public finances could not last indefinitely. “We cannot maintain this level of support forever, but it is the correct response, for now, to the extraordinary circumstances our country is facing,” he said.

Mr Donohoe, who was first elected as a TD in 2011, also called for “political certainty” as negotiations between Fine Gael, Fianna Fáil, the Green Party and other potential partners continue. “A new government is urgently needed to make decisions about the next phase of our recovery. The Oireachtas needs to be able to legislate quickly in response to an evolving economic landscape,” he said.

Meanwhile, business groups welcomed the Minister’s comments as a sign that the next government would keep economic recovery at the forefront of its agenda. However, they warned that clarity was needed on plans for future wage supports, tax reliefs, and investment in training and infrastructure.

Opposition parties have called for targeted investment in public health as well as the economy, arguing that any recovery package must address long-standing issues in housing, healthcare and childcare exposed by the crisis.

As coalition talks continue, Mr Donohoe insisted that Ireland retains the capacity to borrow at low cost due to its strong pre-crisis economic position, but stressed that “difficult decisions” would lie ahead. “The choices we make now will shape the kind of recovery we have, and what sort of society emerges from this crisis,” he said.
headline: Donohoe: Next government will be concerned with restoring economy after Covid-19

text:
A close associate of Florida congressman Matt Gaetz has pleaded guilty to a series of federal charges, including the sex trafficking of a minor, in a development likely to increase pressure on the embattled Republican and intensify scrutiny from US authorities.

Joel Greenberg, the former tax collector for Seminole County, Florida, entered the plea in a federal court in Orlando on Monday to six felony counts, including sex trafficking of a minor, identity theft, and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Greenberg admitted to soliciting and paying a 17-year-old girl for sex, as well as introducing her to other adult men “who engaged in commercial sex acts.”

The plea agreement comes as part of a deal with prosecutors, under which Greenberg has agreed to cooperate fully with investigators. The court filing states that Greenberg will provide “substantial assistance” as federal authorities continue their probe into the wider network surrounding the case. The development is seen as potentially significant for Matt Gaetz, a high-profile ally of former US president Donald Trump.

Gaetz, who has denied any wrongdoing, is reportedly under investigation by the US Department of Justice over possible violations relating to sex trafficking and the possible use of campaign funds to facilitate travel for women with whom he had relationships. The congressman has not been charged with any crime. In repeated public statements, Gaetz claims he is the victim of a politically motivated smear campaign.

Greenberg’s admissions in court highlight a wider pattern of criminal conduct, including an attempt to obtain fraudulent IDs for underage girls and the misuse of public office for personal financial gain. In exchange for his cooperation, prosecutors agreed to drop 27 other charges against him. He now faces a minimum mandatory sentence of 12 years’ imprisonment, with sentencing set for later this year.

The scandal has reverberated through Washington, with some members of the US Republican Party calling on Gaetz to resign from Congress if allegations are proven true. US House leadership has said their response will depend on the outcome of the ongoing investigation.

Irish politicians have previously expressed concern over developments in the Gaetz investigation, with Sinn Féin TDs raising questions in the Dáil regarding the transatlantic impact of political scandals. The Department of Foreign Affairs said it continues to monitor the situation as it unfolds.

In the US, the Justice Department has declined to comment on the status of the Gaetz investigation. Gaetz continues to serve in Congress, representing Florida’s 1st district.

The case is one of the most high-profile US political scandals in recent years, attracting international attention amid ongoing concerns over the handling of allegations of sexual misconduct by powerful figures. Greenberg now remains in custody awaiting sentencing as the fallout from the case continues.
headline: Matt Gaetz associate pleads guilty to sex trafficking charges

text:
A further 53 cases of Covid-19 have been confirmed in the Republic, with no new deaths reported, according to the Department of Health.

The latest figures, released on Monday evening, bring the total number of confirmed cases in Ireland to 26,768 since the beginning of the pandemic. The death toll remains at 1,774.

Acting Chief Medical Officer Dr Ronan Glynn said that while the majority of the new cases were located in the east and south of the country, there are still instances of community transmission being identified.

“Covid-19 has not gone away and, as we have seen in recent days, it continues to pose a serious risk. It is vital that we all keep up our efforts in adhering to the public health advice, particularly in light of recent outbreaks,” Dr Glynn said.

Of the 53 additional cases, 27 are associated with known outbreaks or close contacts of a confirmed case. Eight cases have been identified as community transmission, while the remaining are still under investigation by public health officials.

The National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET) has expressed concern over the increase in the number of clusters associated with private gatherings and events, urging the public to exercise caution.

Dr Glynn reiterated the importance of limiting contacts, maintaining a distance of two metres, washing hands regularly, and wearing face coverings in situations where social distancing cannot be guaranteed.

“The virus spreads quickly in crowds, enclosed spaces, and households. Each and every one of us can make a difference to the trajectory of Covid-19 in Ireland,” he said.

The HSE is continuing to ramp up its testing programme, with mobile testing units deployed in affected areas to address potential outbreaks swiftly.

Meanwhile, the Cabinet met today to discuss the possibility of further restrictions in counties with rising case numbers. Taoiseach Micheál Martin has said that the Government will follow the advice of public health experts and stands ready to introduce additional measures if required.

The latest update comes as the country continues its phased approach towards reopening, with certain restrictions remaining in place for travel, social gatherings, and businesses.

The Department of Health has urged anyone experiencing symptoms of Covid-19, including cough, fever, or shortness of breath, to contact their GP and self-isolate pending test results.

The Government is expected to provide a further update on the situation later in the week.
headline: Covid-19: 53 additional cases with no new deaths recorded

text:
Northern Ireland’s Chief Medical Officer, Dr Michael McBride, has warned that residents should be prepared for a potential second lockdown if Covid-19 infection rates continue to rise across the region. The stark message comes as the Department of Health confirmed a sharp increase in daily case numbers, sparking fresh concerns among public health officials about community transmission.

Dr McBride said that while the Executive was working hard to avoid a return to the severe restrictions imposed earlier this year, the public must remain vigilant and compliant with the existing guidance. “We are at a crucial juncture. If the current trajectory continues, further and significant interventions, up to and including another widespread lockdown, cannot be ruled out,” he said.

His comments came amid growing anxiety about localised outbreaks, particularly in the Derry and Strabane district, where clusters of cases have led to renewed restrictions on household visits and hospitality venues. The total number of cases in Northern Ireland has now surpassed 10,000 since the start of the pandemic, with hospital admissions also beginning to climb after several weeks of relative stability.

The Northern Ireland Executive will meet later this week to consider whether additional measures are required to curb the spread of the virus. First Minister Arlene Foster and Deputy First Minister Michelle O’Neill have both echoed the chief medical officer’s call for continued public cooperation and said that every effort would be made to avoid blanket restrictions unless absolutely necessary.

Dr McBride emphasised the personal responsibility of individuals, urging people to continue wearing face coverings, maintaining physical distance, and practising good hand hygiene, as well as adhering to the restrictions on gatherings. “We know what works. We managed to suppress the virus before, but complacency is our enemy. Our actions in the coming days and weeks will determine whether more severe steps are required.”

Retailers, business organisations and unions have expressed deep concern at the prospect of a second lockdown, warning that it could have devastating consequences for the already fragile economy. “Businesses are only starting to get back on their feet after the first lockdown,” said Glyn Roberts, chief executive of Retail NI. “A return to full closures would be catastrophic for jobs and livelihoods.”

Health authorities have also issued reminders about the importance of self-isolation for those who display symptoms and the need for anyone contacted by the Public Health Agency’s test and trace service to comply fully with the advice given.

Dr McBride’s warning follows the introduction of new restrictions in several parts of Britain and the Republic of Ireland, where local lockdowns and tightened rules have become necessary in recent weeks in response to surges in case numbers.

The Department of Health in the Republic confirmed an additional 334 new cases on Monday, bringing the total number of cases to 33,444, while two further deaths were reported. The National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET) has said it is closely monitoring developments both North and South of the border.

The Taoiseach, Micheál Martin, has said that cross-border co-operation remains vital in the effort to contain the virus, and discussions are ongoing between public health authorities in Dublin and Belfast.

Dr McBride stated: “No one wants to see a second lockdown. But we must all be realistic and prepare for the possibility, should it prove necessary to protect lives and our health service.”
headline: Prepare for potential second lockdown, medical chief tells Northern Ireland

text:
Few issues are as potent or as perennially relevant as global surveillance, and the world of espionage has long exerted a peculiar fascination over Irish readers. From John le Carré to contemporary tales of cyber snooping, the stakes have steadily mounted. James Ball’s latest offering, *The Other Side of the World: The Rise of the Surveillance Industry and How It Is Changing Our Lives*, arrives at a time when public attention is sharply fixed on the growing power wielded by both state and corporate actors in the business of watching.

Ball, a journalist well known for his work on the Snowden leaks and years with The Guardian, steers readers through a marketplace that is not just lucrative, but virtually unregulated. This forensic examination stretches from Israeli spyware firms, to the shadowy world of corporate malfeasance on the streets of Dublin, London and Washington DC. Ball is especially strong on drawing the lines between the personal and the political, tracking how seemingly innocuous data — a WhatsApp message here, a location ping there — becomes a commodity in a global trade worth billions of euro annually.

Much of the book’s appeal lies not just in shocking revelations — though there are many — but in Ball’s ability to cut through jargon and make complex technology accessible. His case studies, ranging from Pegasus spyware to the use of surveillance tools against journalists, activists and ordinary citizens, make for sobering reading. The role of official secrecy, Ball argues, has allowed certain actors to operate with near-total impunity, as oversight mechanisms struggle to keep pace.

From an Irish perspective, there are familiar concerns. The book references European data protection regimes and the work of the Data Protection Commission in co-ordinating cross-border privacy actions, a subject that has frequently put Ireland in the European spotlight. Ball is unafraid to probe the political implications: the tension between safeguarding the public from terrorism and criminality, and protecting individual rights in a republic with a long memory of surveillance abuses.

Ball delivers his analysis in brisk, readable prose, and perhaps the most chilling aspect is his insistence that the real power in the 'spying game' now rests as much in private hands as it does with governments. Tech firms and data brokers, largely based in the US but with significant operations in Ireland, have become major players. For policymakers in Dublin, the book’s underlying message is clear: legal frameworks are racing to keep up with an industry that is moving at breakneck speed.

If *The Other Side of the World* is occasionally unsettling in its implications, it is also a brisk call to action. Ball’s background as both a technologist and a sceptic serves him well in an environment often clouded by secrecy. For Irish readers, this book is an invitation to look beyond the headlines and consider where the real profits — and power — now reside. It will be of particular interest to those following the work of Irish privacy campaigners, legislators, and anyone concerned about the future shape of our digital society.
headline: Book Review: Big profits in the global spying game

text:
Former South African president FW de Klerk, who played a pivotal role in bringing about the end of apartheid, has died at the age of 85. The FW de Klerk Foundation confirmed that Mr de Klerk passed away peacefully at his home in Cape Town following a long illness.

Mr de Klerk served as South Africa’s president from 1989 to 1994 and was widely recognised for initiating the process that dismantled the country’s deeply entrenched system of racial segregation. In 1990, he took the ground-breaking step of releasing Nelson Mandela from prison after 27 years and began negotiations with the African National Congress and other groups to transition the nation towards democracy.

Alongside Mr Mandela, Mr de Klerk was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993 for his efforts in ending apartheid and guiding South Africa through its first democratic elections in 1994. Those elections resulted in Mr Mandela becoming the country’s first Black president, marking a new era for South Africa.

Born Frederik Willem de Klerk in Johannesburg in 1936, he came from a prominent Afrikaans political family and initially supported the system he would later help to abolish. Having risen through the ranks of the ruling National Party, Mr de Klerk succeeded PW Botha as president at a time of growing unrest and international sanctions.

Although praised by many internationally for his role in ending apartheid, Mr de Klerk’s legacy remains a source of contention. Many South Africans, particularly from the Black majority, have criticised him for not going far enough to dismantle all aspects of apartheid and for failing to prevent political violence during the transition period.

Nonetheless, tributes have poured in from across the globe, acknowledging his contribution to peace and reconciliation. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa described Mr de Klerk’s passing as “the end of an era” and expressed condolences to his family.

A statement issued by the Department of Foreign Affairs in Ireland noted that Mr de Klerk’s actions “helped to shape a path towards democracy in South Africa,” while adding that “Ireland stands in support of South Africa’s ongoing journey towards justice and equality for all its people.”

Details regarding funeral arrangements have yet to be announced. Mr de Klerk is survived by his wife Elita, his children and grandchildren.
headline: South Africa’s last apartheid president FW de Klerk dies at 85

text:
A woman reported missing from Dublin earlier this week has been found safe and well, Gardaí have confirmed.

The 45-year-old woman had last been seen in the Drumcondra area on Sunday evening, prompting a public appeal by Gardaí for assistance in tracing her whereabouts. Family members had raised concerns for her welfare after she failed to make contact as expected.

In a statement issued this morning, a Garda spokesperson said the woman has since been located and is receiving support.

“Gardaí wish to thank the public and the media for their assistance in this matter. No further action is required,” the statement read.

The missing person appeal has now been stood down.

Gardaí had earlier asked anyone with information to contact Mountjoy Garda Station, but have said the case is now closed.

No further details have been released.
headline: Woman, 45, missing from Dublin located safe and well

text:
Now is the ideal time to consider planting a native tree, according to biodiversity expert and author Juanita Browne, who says that autumn’s gentle weather and moist, settling soils provide perfect conditions for young saplings to take root.

The mild, damp days typical of the Irish autumn allow roots to establish before the harsher winter frosts arrive. Seasonal rainfall also ensures a steady supply of water, helping to reduce transplant shock. Browne argues that by putting a native species into the ground now, householders and community groups alike can give their tree the best possible start.

Native trees – such as oak, birch, rowan, hazel and holly – are encouraged by the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, and supported through various local authority biodiversity grants. Browne highlights that these species have evolved over millennia to thrive in Irish conditions and, crucially, to support our native wildlife.

“Planting a native tree is one of the most effective actions any of us can take to help our environment. It’s the ultimate gesture for future generations, but the benefits start right away – birds, insects, and mammals will move in as soon as the new tree becomes established,” Browne says.

She cautions, however, that species choice is important. “Non-natives like leylandii or cherry laurel grow quickly, but they don’t support the same number of Irish birds, insects or fungi. A native oak, by contrast, can host hundreds of different native species.”

In recent years, the State has set ambitious targets for tree planting in response to the twin emergencies of climate change and biodiversity loss. The Dáil’s Climate Action Plan outlines a commitment to increasing native woodland cover, while community-based schemes funded by local authorities are helping to put thousands of new trees in the ground nationwide.

For those wishing to plant a tree in a garden or community space, Browne recommends sourcing a sapling from a reputable supplier that guarantees Irish provenance. “It’s important to buy from a nursery that specialises in native trees grown from Irish seed. That way you are supporting local biodiversity and ensuring your tree is better adapted to our conditions.”

She suggests that even a small garden can accommodate at least one native species. “A rowan or holly will fit in most spaces, and birds will thank you for it come next autumn when the berries appear.”

Browne also reminds would-be planters to consider the long-term impact. “Give your tree room to grow, and think about where roots and branches will go in time.”

With the mornings now sharp and the earth still warm, this weekend could be the perfect moment to make a practical contribution to Ireland’s landscape and wildlife. As Browne puts it, “Planting a native tree is a simple act. But it’s an act of hope for the future.”
headline: Juanita Browne: It's the perfect time to plant a native tree

text:
Pat Shortt’s distinctive wit and affable stage presence have endeared him to Irish audiences for more than three decades. As an actor, comedian, and musician, he is a fixture of Ireland’s cultural landscape, his career spanning from the legendary D’Unbelievables double act to acclaimed dramatic turns in film and television. Yet, for all the attention, Shortt is quick to locate his roots firmly in the everyday, rural Ireland of his upbringing.

Raised in Thurles, Co Tipperary, Shortt’s early years were shaped by a household filled with music and laughter. The son of a baker, he recalls Saturday mornings assisting in the family shop, tuning in to the cacophony of local characters, a community tapestry that would later colour much of his comedy. “My father was a great storyteller, my mother too,” he says. “There was always a sense that if you could make each other laugh, you were on to something.”

Shortt’s first stage was the parochial hall, where he played saxophone with the local brass band. The connection between music and community remains vital to him. “Music in rural Ireland isn’t just for performance, it’s a way of bringing people together, sharing in something bigger; that sense of belonging seeped into everything I’ve done,” he says.

His breakthrough came with Jon Kenny in D’Unbelievables, whose sketches—like the beloved Smalltown—skewered the idiosyncrasies of small parish life. For Shortt, inspiration was never far away. “Every village has a lad who’s a bit of a chancer or a local legend with a story no one believes. That’s universal in Ireland,” he says, “and it’s something I always try to celebrate rather than send up.”

Shortt credits the Abbey Theatre and RTÉ’s commitment to home-grown programming with giving him creative opportunities as he moved into solo work. He speaks warmly of the collaborative culture among Irish performers and writers. “There’s a generosity in Irish theatre and comedy. People help each other, whether you’re starting out at the Cat Laughs festival or taking a punt on a new play in Smock Alley,” he notes, citing the importance of festivals and venues outside Dublin in nurturing new talent.

When Shortt’s dramatic performance in Lenny Abrahamson’s Garage won him an IFTA and widespread praise, he took satisfaction in showing a different facet of rural life—one marked by isolation and quiet dignity. “I think Irish culture values empathy,” he reflects. “We respond to stories that show the soul of a place, and that’s what keeps me going: making people feel seen.”

Shortt’s career is now a patchwork quilt of panto, television (including The Late Late Show and Father Ted), and sell-out live tours, often alongside his daughter, Faye. He sees the Irish tradition of the family business as alive and well in their partnership. “She brings a fresh energy, but also that same love of making people laugh.”

For a man whose work has been rooted in the rhythms and rituals of Irish life, Shortt is philosophical about the changes rapid modernisation has brought. “Ireland is always evolving, but I think we hold on to our need for stories, music, a bit of craic.
headline: Culture that made me: Pat Shortt

text:
In a year where the ordinary has been turned on its head, it’s no surprise that Christmas, too, will look different. As November shuffles into December, and those familiar jingles begin to rise from television sets across the country, the peculiarities of pandemic-era advertising are revealing themselves. Never has the art of persuasion had to be so careful, so coded, so aware.

This season, Irish advertisers face a challenge unlike any before. The heart of festive marketing — families gathering, hands clasped, crowds bustling through shopping centres; even Santa’s lap — must be remade under the sharp gaze of social distancing. The result is a new kind of Christmas message, one that tiptoes between hope and realism, nostalgia and responsibility.

It’s no use pretending nothing’s changed. The scenes of last-minute scrambles in town, the cacophony of office parties, the hugs in crowded pubs — gone, or at least banished from our screens. In their place, four distinct strategies are emerging, each offering a window into how we want to see ourselves, and how we hope to see the weeks ahead.

The first is the More of the Same, But With Masks approach. Here, familiar festive tropes endure, but with subtle pandemic signifiers: a masked shop assistant, a hint of hand sanitiser on the counter, greetings exchanged with a cautious nod rather than a hug. These ads are desperate for normality, but can’t avoid the world outside. It’s an optimistic route, but sometimes feels a shade too eager — as if by simply dropping in a mask, the advertisers can will the pandemic away.

Next is the Intimate Homecoming. These campaigns zoom in on the small domestic moments: toast popping up in the kitchen, fairy lights coiled around a single banister, gifts passed through windows and garden gates. They lean on the idea that Christmas is, at its core, about the people directly beside us, not the big gatherings. Where before the focus was on excess, now it’s on presence — who’s at the table, rather than how many.

A more overt response is the Nostalgic Time Capsule. With current realities too tender, some advertisers have fled backwards in time, to a sepia-toned Ireland of train sets and turf fires. There’s comfort in familiarity, and an escape from the masked world outside. Yet the risk here is in papering over present anxieties. Sometimes, these campaigns edge close to denial — as if 2020 never happened at all.

Finally, there is the New Normal Embrace. A handful of brands are braving it: acknowledging the hardship, even the heartbreak, of this year. Their adverts feature grandparents waving through glass, friends gathering over video calls, young children grumbling about missing Santa’s grotto. Tissues are provided, but so is a sense of solidarity: we’re all muddling through, together. If Christmas is about hope, these campaigns suggest, it’s a hope made more necessary by adversity.

All of this sits against the backdrop of national uncertainty: questions over travel, over restrictions, over whether the Dáil’s latest guidance will reach homes in Letterkenny as swiftly as in Dún Laoghaire. The advertising world, rarely accused of subtlety, is now tasked with providing reassurance without inciting rebellion; joy, without irresponsibility.
headline: Caroline O'Donoghue: Four ways to advertise Christmas in a pandemic

text:
As the festive season draws near, many of us are faced with the perennial challenge of choosing meaningful gifts that won’t end up gathering dust on a shelf or, worse, hastily rewrapped and regifted next year. This Christmas, why not look beyond the usual offerings and consider presents that celebrate the wild beauty of Ireland and encourage friends and family to connect with nature?

Wildlife author and broadcaster Juanita Browne is urging people to think outside the box when it comes to Christmas shopping. “So often, we opt for token gifts that lack real impact or longevity,” she says. “Gifts that foster a sense of wonder for the outdoors can have a lasting effect – on individuals and on wildlife.”

Browne, whose recent projects include working with the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan and writing the much-loved ‘Ireland’s Mammals’, says that Ireland’s ecosystems are under increasing pressure. “Small actions, like giving a bird feeder or a wildflower seed mix, can inspire someone to become more aware of the creatures sharing our towns and gardens. Those small changes add up, and Christmas is the perfect time to spark those interests.”

Among Browne’s practical suggestions are native tree saplings – such as hazel, rowan, or hawthorn – which can be easily sourced from reputable Irish nurseries or local tidy towns initiatives. “A tree is a gift that grows year on year, providing food and shelter for birds, insects and mammals,” she says. “It’s a present that connects people to the land, and one that the recipient can nurture for decades.”

For budding botanists or younger children, Browne recommends simple wildlife guides or bug hunt kits. “A pocket guide to Ireland’s butterflies or birds can ignite a lifelong interest. And things like magnifying glasses or pond-dipping nets will get children outside and learning through discovery.”

Those looking to make a difference on a larger scale could consider supporting Irish environmental charities on behalf of someone else. “A membership to BirdWatch Ireland, the Irish Wildlife Trust or the Vincent Wildlife Trust doesn’t just help to safeguard species – it keeps people connected to conservation events, nature walks and citizen science projects throughout the year.”

Experience-based gifts are also gaining popularity, and Browne notes there are countless ways to enjoy Ireland’s great outdoors. “Nature walks, wildlife safaris and bushcraft days make brilliant presents,” she says. “You’re giving your loved ones memories as well as skills, and supporting local guides and communities into the bargain.”

Not all gifts require a trip to the shops. Browne points out that even a homemade ‘wildlife promise’ – such as committing to leave a patch of the garden unmown for pollinators, or building a hedgehog highway – can bring joy, at no cost. “Nature doesn’t care about receipts or packaging – it cares about small acts of kindness that add up to real benefits. Sometimes the most heartfelt gifts are the ones we make ourselves.”

By giving a gift that celebrates the richness of Ireland’s wildlife, this Christmas can be greener in every sense – for both the giver and the receiver. As Browne puts it, “A wild gift is a hopeful gift, one that says the future – for people and for nature – really does matter.”
headline: Juanita Browne: Give some really wild Christmas gifts this year

text:
Public health officials have expressed concern over a growing trend of individuals failing to answer calls from HSE contact tracers, warning that it could undermine efforts to stem the spread of Covid-19. The development comes as Ireland experiences a rise in daily case numbers, with the Department of Health confirming 647 new infections on Tuesday and four further deaths associated with the virus.

Officials from the HSE’s National Contact Management Programme have reported that an increasing proportion of people are not engaging when contacted, in some cases dismissing calls without listening to voicemails or inadvertently blocking unfamiliar numbers. Dr Breda Smyth, Director of Public Health in the HSE West, described the situation as “concerning”, adding that delays in reaching positive cases and their close contacts can have knock-on effects for communities.

“We rely on people answering their phones and engaging honestly with contact tracers, so we can quickly identify and inform close contacts who may be at risk,” Dr Smyth said. “The sooner we can make those calls, the sooner we can break chains of transmission. If people don’t engage, the virus has more opportunity to spread.”

The HSE said it has increased capacity in its contact tracing teams in recent weeks in response to the growing case numbers. However, the system’s effectiveness depends on public cooperation. In some incidents, tracers have made repeated attempts to reach individuals over several days without success, delaying vital public health interventions.

The Taoiseach, Leo Varadkar, urged the public to “answer the phone to a call you may not recognise,” stressing that calls from the HSE’s contact tracing centres are critical to the national effort. “You may be helping to protect the health of your family and the wider community,” he said.

The HSE is reminding people that calls from contact tracers will come from an 01 or 021 number, depending on the tracing centre, and that they will never ask for bank details or payment information. Officials also encouraged members of the public who have tested positive for Covid-19, or who have been identified as a close contact, to keep their phones charged and nearby and to respond to calls from the service as quickly as possible.

In recent weeks, some cases have been referred to the Gardaí after repeated failures to make contact with individuals connected to clusters, although officials stress that enforcement remains a last resort and that the emphasis is on cooperation.

The HSE also noted that the public health system continues to face pressure from both Covid-19 cases and the seasonal flu, with hospitals nationwide reporting high levels of admissions. As part of ongoing efforts, antigen testing is now being utilised more widely in schools and workplaces, alongside PCR testing in community settings.

Immunisation rates remain high, with more than 90 per cent of the adult population fully vaccinated, but public health experts warn that complacency could threaten progress made in recent months. Dr Tony Holohan, the Chief Medical Officer, appealed once again for the public’s support, saying, “The small acts – answering the phone, isolating when required, getting tested and following the guidance – all help to keep each other safe.”

The Department of Health is expected to update the Oireachtas Covid-19 Committee on the latest developments later this week.
headline: Covid-19: 'Concerning' trend of some people not answering calls from contact tracers

text:
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has declared his readiness to “extend the hand of friendship” to Turkey, signalling a potential thaw in decades of strained relations between the two neighbours. Speaking ahead of a summit with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Ankara, Mr Mitsotakis said both countries had “much more to gain from cooperation than from confrontation”.

Greece and Turkey, both NATO members, have long-standing disputes over maritime boundaries, energy exploration rights, and the status of Greek islands in the Aegean Sea. Tensions have led to several military standoffs, most recently in 2020, when both sides deployed naval ships to disputed waters.

However, relations have improved in recent months, with Mr Mitsotakis and President Erdoğan meeting on the sidelines of international summits and resuming bilateral talks. The Greek PM described the current moment as a “window of opportunity to build a climate of trust” and urged both sides to focus on economic cooperation, tackling irregular migration, and disaster response.

“We do not ignore our differences, but we must manage them with respect for international law and mutual understanding,” Mr Mitsotakis said in an interview on Greek state broadcaster ERT. He added that confidence-building measures could pave the way for future agreements, and insisted Greece would defend its sovereign rights “with calm determination”.

The rapprochement comes as both countries face pressing challenges, including the aftermath of last year’s earthquakes in Turkey and the ongoing migration crisis in the Eastern Mediterranean. The Greek and Turkish foreign ministers have visited each other’s countries in recent months, and the two governments have agreed to strengthen cooperation on border security and emergency response.

Despite the positive signals, significant obstacles remain. Turkey continues to dispute the extent of Greek territorial waters and airspace, and there have been periodic accusations of airspace violations. Athens, meanwhile, has accused Ankara of encouraging migrant crossings into Greece, a claim Turkey denies.

Analysts say any real breakthrough would require both governments to withstand domestic criticism and nationalist pressure. Nonetheless, European leaders have welcomed the diplomatic overtures. The European Commission President, Ursula von der Leyen, described dialogue between Greece and Turkey as “essential for the stability of the wider region”.

Ireland, which maintains diplomatic relations with both countries, has previously called for the disputes to be resolved peacefully in accordance with international law. The Department of Foreign Affairs said it “strongly encourages dialogue and cooperation between our EU partner Greece and Turkey, in the interests of peace and security in the Mediterranean”.

Mr Mitsotakis’ visit to Ankara is seen as a significant gesture, as it marks the first time a Greek leader has visited the Turkish capital in five years. Both sides have indicated they hope to sign a series of minor agreements on economic and cultural exchange as part of the visit. However, officials in Athens have cautioned against expectations of any immediate, sweeping breakthroughs, noting that “trust is built step by step”.

As the leaders prepare to meet, the international community will be watching closely for signs that the historic rivals can turn rhetoric into lasting reconciliation.
headline: Greek PM willing to extend ‘hand of friendship’ to long-time rival Turkey

text:
Achieving flawless skin may seem like a tall order, given the realities of Irish weather, city living and the daily stressors that can take their toll on our complexions. Still, with so many innovations in skincare and make-up, foundations now offer not just coverage, but active ingredients that work throughout the day to hydrate, protect and illuminate.

For many, the search for the right base starts with texture and finish. If your skin veers towards the dry side, formulas enriched with hyaluronic acid—such as Lancôme’s Teint Idole Ultra Wear Care & Glow or Clarins’ Skin Illusion foundation—will offer moisture alongside medium coverage, leaving a radiant finish without settling into lines. Those with oilier skin may prefer oil-free, mattifying options like Estée Lauder Double Wear Stay-in-Place or MAC’s Studio Fix Fluid, both of which have dedicated cult followings among Irish make-up artists for their longevity and ability to withstand a day’s wear, even if you’re dashing from meetings on O’Connell Street to a walk along the prom in Salthill.

Skin tone and undertone are also crucial. Irish complexions can range from porcelain with cool undertones to medium with a peach or golden hue. Brands such as Fenty Beauty and NARS have made strides in offering inclusive shade ranges, making it easier to find a genuine match. If possible, always test your chosen shade in natural daylight and along the jawline—a tip many Irish beauty advisors at Brown Thomas or Arnotts swear by—to ensure a seamless blend.

For those who favour a natural, ‘your skin but better’ look, lightweight, buildable formulas like Chanel’s Les Beiges Healthy Glow Foundation or the affordable L’Oréal True Match offer a barely-there effect, perfect for daytime wear or work. Meanwhile, the beauty community is abuzz with praise for Irish brand Sculpted by Aimee’s Second Skin foundation, which offers both dewy and matte variants, created with the Irish climate and skin in mind.

Application techniques have also evolved. While a brush offers the most polished finish, many find that using a damp beauty sponge or even fingertips helps the foundation melt into the skin for a fresh effect. A light dusting of setting powder down the t-zone will help lock everything in place, but don’t be tempted to overdo it—radiant, touchable skin remains on-trend this season.

With SPF now a non-negotiable, many foundations—such as IT Cosmetics Your Skin But Better CC+ Cream or Shiseido Synchro Skin Self-Refreshing Foundation—include built-in sun protection. However, dermatologists and the HSE continue to advise layering a standalone facial sunscreen under your make-up for optimal defence against Ireland’s often underestimated UV rays.

Ultimately, flawless skin is less about hiding and more about enhancing what’s already there. With the right foundation, a gentle hand, and a nod to individual needs, the perfect canvas is within reach—come rain or shine.
headline: Get The Look: flawless skin is possible with a little help from these foundations

text:
Russia has issued a stern warning to Ukraine against the use of force in the country’s breakaway eastern regions, further escalating tensions amid continuing conflict and stalling peace talks.

The Russian Foreign Ministry on Wednesday cautioned Kyiv against any “provocations” in the self-declared republics of Donetsk and Luhansk, where pro-Russian separatists have held swathes of territory since 2014. In a statement, the ministry said the use of military force in these regions would have “grave consequences” and accused the Ukrainian government of undermining ongoing diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis.

“We are monitoring the situation closely and would urge the Ukrainian authorities to refrain from any actions that could lead to a further escalation,” the statement read. “Responsibility for any new outbreak of violence will rest squarely with Kyiv.”

The move comes against a backdrop of intensifying clashes along the line of contact in eastern Ukraine, raising fears that the conflict, which has claimed more than 14,000 lives since it began, could spiral into a broader confrontation. Ukrainian officials have recently reported a build-up of Russian military forces near the border, a claim Russia has denied, insisting that any deployments are routine exercises within its own territory.

Ukraine’s President, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has called for renewed international support and the strengthening of sanctions against Moscow, accusing the Kremlin of stoking unrest and refusing to abide by the Minsk peace accords. Speaking in Kyiv, he stated: “Ukraine has the right to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity. We seek a diplomatic solution, but will not tolerate the threat of violence.”

The European Union has urged both sides to show restraint, with the Taoiseach, Leo Varadkar, joining calls for de-escalation and reaffirming Ireland’s backing for Ukraine’s sovereignty. Meanwhile, the United Nations has appealed for fresh negotiations to avert a humanitarian crisis in the region, where thousands remain displaced and dependent on international aid.

Analysts say the latest warning from Moscow signals little appetite for compromise as Russia seeks to retain influence over its neighbour and contests western involvement in the region. The warning is likely to further strain already fraught relations with the West, which continues to support Ukraine diplomatically and, in some cases, with defensive military aid.

With diplomatic channels under strain and violence threatening to flare anew, the international community faces mounting pressure to mediate a solution before the situation deteriorates further.
headline: Russia warns Ukraine against use of force in rebel regions

text:
A letter sent by Mary Lowry’s solicitor to Patrick Quirke in the months before the disappearance of Bobby Ryan outlined her concerns about Quirke’s lease on her land and set out terms for its termination, the Central Criminal Court has heard.

During the latest day of the so-called “love triangle” murder trial, the jury was shown correspondence dated January 2011, in which Ms Lowry’s legal representative notified Quirke, a tenant farmer, of her intention to end his lease agreement. The issue of the lease became central to the prosecution’s case, with the State alleging that Quirke had a financial motive in connection with the killing of Mr Ryan, whose body was found concealed in an underground tank on Ms Lowry’s farm near Tipperary two years after he was reported missing.

Detective Garda Paul Fitzpatrick read out the letter in court. It indicated that Ms Lowry wished to regain possession of the land for her own use, and expressed concern about conditions on the farm. The letter also referenced Quirke’s obligations regarding notice periods and the proper care of the property.

Patrick Quirke, of Breanshamore, Co Tipperary, denies the murder of Bobby Ryan. The prosecution allege that Quirke, then a married man, had been involved in a clandestine relationship with Ms Lowry before she began seeing Mr Ryan, and that Quirke’s resentment over the loss of the relationship and his lease prompted him to plan Mr Ryan’s death.

Under cross-examination, Ms Lowry told the court she felt uncomfortable about Quirke’s continued presence on her land and had become increasingly unhappy after the end of their affair. Her solicitor’s letter, she said, was a formal step to clarify the boundaries of their arrangement and ensure her wishes were respected.

The court also heard Quirke continued to farm the land following receipt of the letter. Defence counsel challenged the suggestion that the dispute over the lease was a significant factor, arguing that Quirke’s farming activities were legitimate and that there was no evidence he had reacted improperly to the legal notice.

The trial, now in its eighth week, has gripped public attention with its revelations of secret relationships and rural intrigue. Gardaí investigations revealed that Quirke was the person who eventually reported the discovery of Mr Ryan’s body in the farm’s underground tank in April 2013, claiming he had stumbled upon it while attempting to source water for cattle.

The case continues before Mr Justice Eileen Creedon and a jury of seven men and five women.
headline: Love triangle trial: Letter from Mary Lowry's lawyer outlined 'concerns' over Patrick Quirke's lease on her land

text:
A Kerryman believed to be the oldest man in Ireland has died at the age of 108, prompting an outpouring of tributes in his home community and beyond.

Michael O'Donoghue, who lived in the village of Ballyduff in North Kerry, passed away peacefully on Sunday surrounded by his family. Born in 1916, the year of the Easter Rising, Mr O'Donoghue witnessed more than a century of Irish history, spanning from the War of Independence through to the modern digital age.

The late Mr O'Donoghue, a retired farmer, was described as a quiet but deeply respected figure in Ballyduff, known for his sharp mind and love of local history. He celebrated his 108th birthday in January, becoming a source of pride for the local community and recognised nationwide as Ireland's oldest living man.

Ballyduff parish priest, Fr Pat Moore, said Mr O'Donoghue was “a true gentleman with a remarkable memory”, recalling his ability even in his later years to recount stories from his youth and to reference local events going back to the 1920s.

“He had a great interest in what was going on in the world but always stayed rooted in his community,” Fr Moore said. “Michael was a witness to so many changes in rural Ireland, from the demise of the horse and cart, to the coming of electricity, and the arrival of the internet in the village.”

President Michael D Higgins extended his condolences to the O'Donoghue family, noting that few have spanned a period of such dramatic change in Irish society with such grace and dignity.

Mr O'Donoghue is survived by three children, nine grandchildren, and a wide circle of friends and neighbours. His wife, Mary, predeceased him in 1999.

Local historian Bríd Stack paid tribute to Mr O'Donoghue’s wealth of knowledge about the parish, which she said was “invaluable to the community”. “He was our living link with the past,” she said, “and it is hard to imagine Ballyduff without him.”

The funeral Mass will take place at St Peter and Paul’s Church, Ballyduff, on Wednesday morning, followed by burial in the adjoining cemetery. A large attendance is expected, with mourners travelling from across Munster and beyond to pay their respects.

Mr O'Donoghue’s family have expressed gratitude for the care he received at home in recent years, particularly from his neighbours, the HSE community nurses, and his GP.

Gardaí will be on hand to manage traffic in the village, as local businesses prepare to close for the funeral as a mark of respect.
headline: Kerry native believed to be Ireland's oldest man dies at 108

text:
A suspected Estonian hitman linked to the Kinahan cartel will challenge his extradition from Ireland later this year. The man, who has been remanded in custody, is wanted by Estonian authorities on serious organised crime charges and appeared before the High Court in Dublin on Thursday.

The accused, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was arrested last month on foot of a European Arrest Warrant (EAW) issued in Tallinn. He is alleged to have been recruited by the Kinahan crime gang to carry out a contract killing in Estonia as part of an ongoing feud with a rival criminal organisation.

Detectives from the Garda National Bureau of Criminal Investigation (GNBCI) detained the Estonian national at a property in south Dublin following a joint operation with Europol and the Estonian Police and Border Guard Board. Gardaí told the court that the suspect has significant links to the Kinahan group, which is the subject of several transnational organised crime investigations.

Lawyers for the accused indicated that he will oppose the extradition application on multiple grounds, including potential breaches of his rights under European and Irish law. Legal representatives said the man fears for his safety if returned to Estonia, given the notoriety of the ongoing feud and threats to his life.

Mr Justice Paul Burns set a date in October to hear full arguments in the extradition challenge. The man will meanwhile remain in custody at Cloverhill Prison. The court ordered that all legal documents be exchanged by both parties by the end of September.

Irish authorities have ramped up co-operation with their European counterparts amid concerns about the movement of serious criminals across EU borders. The Kinahan cartel, which has been the focus of Garda and international law enforcement attention, is suspected of directing various hit squads for illegal activities abroad.

A spokesperson for the Department of Justice declined to comment on the specific case but said Ireland “remains fully committed to co-operating with our European partners in tackling organised crime and ensuring that fugitives face justice”.

The extradition hearing comes as gardaí continue to disrupt the Kinahan network’s international operations. Senior sources say “substantial progress” is being made in targeting cartel members believed to be using Ireland as a base or safe haven. The case is expected to be closely watched by both Irish and Estonian authorities.

The accused is due to appear again before the High Court in October, when a final decision on his extradition will be made.
