headline: Estonian Kinahan hitman will challenge extradition bid in October

text:
A man has taken legal action against EBS and Ulster Bank, alleging that they failed to properly forward maintenance payments to his former partner as instructed, potentially leaving him exposed to legal and financial repercussions.

The plaintiff, who cannot be named for legal reasons, claims that both financial institutions neglected their duty to process standing orders set up for child maintenance payments, leading to missed or delayed payments to his ex-partner. The case was brought before the High Court, where the man argues that the banks’ alleged failures have caused him significant distress and have impacted his relationship with his children.

In documents lodged before the court, the man asserts that he set up monthly standing orders through EBS and Ulster Bank, following a District Court order requiring him to pay maintenance to his former partner after their separation. He claims to have received assurances at the time that the funds would be transferred automatically and on time each month, in accordance with the court order.

However, according to his legal representatives, the payments were either not executed or not received in the manner required by the court, resulting in his former partner initiating enforcement proceedings against him. The man maintains that he was at risk of being found in contempt of court due to the banks’ alleged negligence, and that he incurred additional legal costs in defending his position.

The case centres on whether the banks fulfilled their obligations in processing the standing orders, with the plaintiff alleging that both institutions failed to adequately inform him of any issues with the payments or to rectify them in a timely manner.

EBS and Ulster Bank are contesting the claims, with legal representatives for both institutions stating that their systems operated according to standard banking practice and that they acted in good faith based on the information available to them. The banks argue that any disruptions to the payments may have arisen from issues outside their control, such as account details provided by the plaintiff or actions taken by the payee’s bank.

The High Court heard that the alleged failures have had ongoing repercussions for the plaintiff, who claims to have suffered reputational damage and emotional distress as a result of the missed payments and subsequent legal proceedings.

Justice Mary Faherty has directed both parties to engage in further discussions in an effort to resolve the dispute, noting the sensitive nature of the issues and the importance of ensuring compliance with court-ordered maintenance. The case is due to return to the High Court later this month.

Both EBS and Ulster Bank said they would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.
headline: Man sues EBS and Ulster Bank over alleged failure to forward payments to former partner

text:
Johnny Depp’s legal team are set to argue before the Court of Appeal in London that the Hollywood actor was denied a fair trial in his high-profile libel case against a British newspaper, it has emerged. Lawyers for Depp, who has a strong following in Ireland and has visited the country on numerous occasions, will contend that “significant procedural irregularities” and the “exclusion of crucial evidence” led to a “manifestly unjust outcome”.

Depp, best known for his roles in films such as Pirates of the Caribbean and Edward Scissorhands, lost a libel action in the High Court in 2020 after suing The Sun newspaper over an article that described him as a “wife-beater” in reference to allegations made by his former wife Amber Heard. The judge found the article was “substantially true”, a verdict Depp’s legal representatives have vigorously contested ever since.

Now, after several failed attempts to overturn the decision, his legal counsel will today tell a panel of senior judges that new evidence and failures in the original proceedings undermined the fairness of the trial. In documents submitted to the Court of Appeal, Depp’s lawyers allege that key witness testimony and relevant documentation were either omitted or improperly handled during the original hearing.

Sources close to the actor’s legal team told the Irish Examiner that they will seek to demonstrate that “material errors” were made by Mr Justice Nicol in conducting the trial and in his assessment of the evidence. They claim that these alleged errors “fatally compromised” Mr Depp’s right to a fair hearing and that, had the judge properly considered the evidence, the outcome would have been different.

The case has drawn keen interest in Ireland and abroad, with many fans of Depp expressing support online and debating the fairness of the English legal system. The actor, who filmed scenes for his 2004 film Finding Neverland in Co Wicklow, retains a loyal Irish fanbase, which has followed the proceedings closely.

Amber Heard’s representatives have maintained that the High Court judgment should stand, arguing that the evidence against Depp was “overwhelming”. They have previously described the repeated legal challenges as “an attempt to re-litigate matters already decided”.

A decision by the Court of Appeal could have significant implications for the future conduct of libel trials in England and Wales, and could determine whether the original verdict is quashed or a retrial is ordered.

The court is expected to reserve its decision, with a ruling likely to follow in the coming months.
headline: Johnny Depp ‘did not receive a fair trial’, lawyers to tell Court of Appeal

text:
A further 4,141 cases of Covid-19 have been confirmed by the Department of Health, as the Omicron variant continues its rapid spread across the country. The number of people currently hospitalised with the virus stands at 443, with 108 patients receiving treatment in intensive care units.

Chief Medical Officer Dr Tony Holohan warned that the trajectory of the Omicron variant poses a significant challenge to the health service in the weeks ahead. He urged members of the public to exercise caution in the run-up to Christmas, encouraging everyone to limit their social contacts, follow public health advice, and avail of booster vaccinations where eligible.

“We continue to see a concerning trend in the daily case numbers, driven largely by Omicron,” Dr Holohan said. “While early indications suggest it may cause less severe disease than previous strains, its high transmissibility means it has the potential to cause significant disruption and place further strain on our hospitals.”

Latest data from the Health Protection Surveillance Centre indicates that Omicron now accounts for an estimated 35% of new cases, with officials anticipating that the variant will become dominant before the New Year. Health Service Executive CEO Paul Reid said the HSE’s testing and tracing systems are under considerable strain, with positivity rates surging and demand for testing at record highs.

Vaccination centres nationwide have reported high turnout in recent days, as thousands queue for booster doses in a renewed effort to curb the spread of the virus. The Minister for Health, Stephen Donnelly, welcomed the public’s “strong response” to the booster campaign, but cautioned that vaccination alone will not be enough to control transmission during the festive period.

In a statement, the Tánaiste, Leo Varadkar, said: “We all have a role to play in slowing the spread of Omicron and protecting those most at risk. The government is keeping all options under review and will not hesitate to act if further measures are deemed necessary.”

The National Public Health Emergency Team is due to meet later this week to assess the latest data and consider any additional recommendations to the government.

Meanwhile, the Irish Hotels Federation has reported a wave of cancellations for Christmas bookings, as concerns grow among businesses about the economic impact of new public health guidelines. Publicans and restaurateurs have called for additional supports to help offset losses during the traditionally busy season.

The Department of Health also confirmed that an additional 35 deaths related to Covid-19 have been notified in recent days, bringing the total number of pandemic-related fatalities in the State to 5,835.

Public health officials have urged anyone experiencing symptoms of Covid-19 to self-isolate immediately and arrange a test, as well as encouraging the continued use of face coverings, hand hygiene, and social distancing.

The latest figures come ahead of a Cabinet meeting to discuss potential restrictions on hospitality and events, as Ireland faces into an uncertain Christmas with the Omicron variant now firmly established in the community.
headline: 4,141 new Covid cases as Omicron spread continues

text:
Iraqis are making final preparations to welcome Pope Francis to Baghdad this Friday, with security tightened and anticipation running high ahead of his historic visit—the first ever by a pontiff to the war-scarred country.

The papal journey, set to last four days, has been described as unprecedented, both for its high-profile symbolism and its significant logistical and security challenges. Pope Francis, 84, is expected to deliver messages of hope and reconciliation to Iraq’s embattled Christian minority, while meeting with political and religious leaders amid the lingering threat of Covid-19 and sporadic violence.

Iraqi officials, led by President Barham Salih and Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi, have declared the visit a “national event”, with local authorities across Baghdad and other key stops, including Najaf, Erbil, and Mosul, overseeing preparations. Baghdad’s streets are adorned with Vatican and Iraqi flags, banners, and portraits of the Pope, while workers have rushed to spruce up main thoroughfares in anticipation.

The Ministry of Interior confirmed that more than 10,000 members of the security forces will be deployed along the Pope’s route, supplemented by road closures and increased surveillance. The route itself has not been publicised for security reasons, and the Vatican has insisted the trip will proceed despite ongoing concerns—most recently, a rocket attack on an air base housing international troops.

In a letter addressed to the Iraqi people ahead of his departure, Pope Francis said he was coming “as a pilgrim of peace, seeking fraternity and reconciliation”. He is expected to visit the Syriac Catholic Cathedral of Our Lady of Salvation, the scene of a deadly massacre in 2010, meet the revered Shia cleric Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani in Najaf, and travel to the ancient city of Ur, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of Abraham.

The visit is seen as a vital boost for Iraq’s Christians, whose numbers have plummeted from around 1.5 million before the US-led invasion in 2003 to as few as 250,000 today, driven by years of violence and persecution, most notably under the so-called Islamic State.

Local church leaders and community members voiced both excitement and nervousness. “This is a dream come true for Christians in Iraq,” said Fr. Pola Kasha, a Chaldean priest in Baghdad. “But we pray for his safety and for real change after his visit.” The Iraqi Government, together with the United Nations and international embassies, has issued joint appeals for calm, urging everyone to avoid large gatherings where possible due to the ongoing pandemic.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has updated its travel advice for Irish citizens in the region, emphasising the importance of vigilance and adherence to local security guidance throughout the duration of the papal trip.

Pope Francis is scheduled to celebrate Mass in a stadium in Erbil, in the Kurdish region, before returning to Rome on Monday. Organisers have limited attendance and urged strict mask-wearing, though public health experts have warned of the risk of Covid-19 transmission given Iraq’s fragile healthcare system.

The papal visit is expected to shine an international spotlight on Iraq’s struggle for stability and interfaith coexistence, and, for many Iraqis, represents a rare moment of optimism after years of conflict and unrest.
headline: Iraqis prepare to welcome Pope to Baghdad

text:
A member of An Garda Síochána charged with false imprisonment and sexual assault may now be named following a ruling at Cork District Court yesterday. Judge Olann Kelleher lifted interim reporting restrictions that had prevented identification of Garda James O’Connell (41), who is stationed in north Cork, after lawyers for the Irish Examiner successfully argued that there was a significant public interest in open reporting of the case.

Garda O’Connell, with an address in Kanturk, is accused of detaining a woman against her will and sexually assaulting her at a location in Cork city last August. He appeared before Judge Kelleher on Thursday morning, accompanied by his solicitor, and was formally served with a book of evidence outlining the charges against him.

The case was previously subject to reporting restrictions that shielded Garda O’Connell’s identity while the DPP considered whether to proceed with prosecution. Defence counsel, Michael O’Donnell BL, had argued last month that his client risked “irreparable harm” to his professional and personal life if named prior to trial, given the gravity of the accusations.

However, in his ruling, Judge Kelleher said: “There is a longstanding principle that justice be administered in public, and that members of the public, including gardaí, are subject to the law in the same manner as every citizen of the State.” The judge noted that the DPP had directed trial on indictment and that the evidence now before the court justified lifting the order.

The offences are alleged to have occurred in the early hours of 14 August 2023, when, according to the prosecution, Garda O’Connell detained a woman known to him in a car parked at a secluded location near the city centre. It is further alleged that he then attempted to force the woman to engage in sexual activity without her consent.

Detective Sergeant Linda Walsh of the Garda National Protective Services Bureau, who led the investigation, told the court that O’Connell was arrested in September following a complaint made by the alleged victim. He was suspended from duty on full pay pending the outcome of the criminal proceedings.

The accused was granted bail under strict conditions, including a curfew, surrender of his passport, and an undertaking not to contact witnesses in the case. Judge Kelleher remanded him to appear before Cork Circuit Court on 17 July for arraignment.

A spokesperson for the Garda Press Office said it would be inappropriate to comment on the case while legal proceedings are underway. The HSE has offered support services to the alleged victim.

If convicted, Garda O’Connell faces a maximum sentence of life imprisonment on the false imprisonment charge and up to 10 years for sexual assault. The case marks the first time in recent years that a sitting garda has faced such serious allegations in Cork.

Legal representatives for Garda O’Connell declined to comment outside court.
headline: Judge allows garda accused of false imprisonment and sexual assault to be named

text:
Visitors to Cork’s Crawford Art Gallery are being offered a fresh perspective on some of the city’s best-loved artworks as a major re-hang of the historic collection seeks to cast new light on more than two centuries of Irish and international art.

The ambitious reimagining of the gallery’s Long Room, which houses its permanent collection, comes as the building itself undergoes an extensive multi-million euro redevelopment, funded by the Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media.

Gallery director Mary McCarthy said the new display layout draws on recent scholarship and a growing awareness of the social and political contexts in which many of the works were created. “We are looking at these pieces with new eyes and asking how they speak to today’s Ireland,” she said. This includes reframing the gallery’s collection of 19th-century statuary casts—much of which arrived from the Vatican in 1818—and placing a renewed focus on works by female artists such as Letitia Hamilton and Norah McGuinness.

The re-hang is intended to invite audiences to consider the shifting tides of Irish identity, the influence of European movements, and the gallery’s own role in the development of artistic practice in the region. The collection now features a more prominent display of works from the Cork School, alongside modern and contemporary acquisitions by artists such as Hughie O’Donoghue and Rita Duffy.

Behind the scenes, the gallery’s curatorial team have undertaken a painstaking audit of the 3,000-piece collection, assessing each item for relevance and condition. Assistant curator Michael Waldron said the process had thrown up “delightful surprises”, enabling the team to bring lesser-known works out of storage and introduce them to a wider public.

As part of its commitment to community engagement, the Crawford will also host a series of workshops and talks exploring the themes raised by the new displays. The gallery, which is free to visit, expects to see visitor numbers further recover this year following a marked drop during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The ongoing refurbishment, which has necessitated some partial closures, is expected to be substantially complete by early 2025. In the meantime, the gallery remains open and staff are encouraging the public to experience the revitalised collection.

Minister for the Arts Catherine Martin TD welcomed the gallery’s efforts, stating that “access to our national collections and cultural heritage is essential for a vibrant, inclusive society.” The revitalisation of the Crawford is part of a broader government strategy to invest in cultural infrastructure across the country.

Crawford Art Gallery has been at the heart of Cork’s cultural life since 1884, and the current developments are seen as securing its role for generations to come. Gallery staff say the aim is to ensure that while the history of Irish art is honoured, its future is also imagined and made visible to all who pass through its historic halls.
headline: Crawford Gallery’s historic collection cast in new light

text:
Voters in Limerick could be heading to the polls sooner than expected to elect Ireland’s first directly-elected mayor, with Government sources indicating that an accelerated timeline is under active consideration.

The Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage is understood to be reviewing the original schedule, which had envisaged a November election, amid mounting pressure to establish the new mayoral post and deliver on a long-standing commitment made to the people of Limerick.

Sources close to Minister for Local Government, Kieran O’Donnell, confirmed that officials are examining the feasibility of holding the election in September instead. The review follows concerns from local representatives and community groups about prolonged uncertainty, as well as campaigners highlighting the importance of having an accountable mayor in place before the 2025 budget and planning cycle.

Speaking to the Irish Examiner, a Government spokesperson said, “Work on the Local Government (Mayor of Limerick) Bill has reached an advanced stage, and preparations for the election are well underway. The Minister is keen to ensure the people of Limerick have a voice in shaping their own governance as soon as practicable.”

The directly-elected mayor model, unique in Ireland, will see the new office-holder assume significant executive functions over housing, transport, and economic development, devolved from the City and County Council’s chief executive. The referendum approving the post was passed with a narrow majority in 2019, but progress stalled due to legislative delays and the Covid-19 pandemic.

Potential candidates—including sitting councillors, business leaders, and community activists—have already begun informal campaigning across the city and county. Several parties and independents are expected to field candidates, with Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael currently finalising their selection processes.

Council sources have also raised logistical questions for the returning officer should the election be brought forward, including the readiness of polling infrastructure and the need for comprehensive voter information campaigns.

Local TDs have broadly welcomed the move to expedite the election. Limerick City TD Maurice Quinlivan (Sinn Féin) described the potential September poll as “a positive step that would finally give Limerick a strong, accountable leader.”

Meanwhile, concerns remain among some councillors about the transfer of powers from the council chamber to the new mayoral office, with calls for additional scrutiny of the final legislation. The Department has indicated that further details will be published in the coming weeks and that public consultation sessions will continue over the summer.

If approved, the earlier election would mark the first time in the history of the State that any local authority directly elects its own mayor, setting a precedent other counties may seek to follow. With final decisions expected before the Dáil’s summer recess, the political landscape in Limerick is poised for significant change.
headline: Limerick City and County voters could cast ballots for directly-elected mayor ahead of schedule

text:
The incorporation of clover into Irish pastures is increasingly recognised as a practical and effective measure for improving both farm profitability and environmental performance, according to Teagasc’s Signpost Programme. As the twin challenges of reducing input costs and meeting stringent climate targets intensify, clover is being highlighted by agronomists and farmers alike as a key component in sustainable grassland management.

White and red clover, once a mainstay of traditional swards, have been making a steady comeback across the country as concerns around fertiliser costs and nitrate regulations grow. The nitrogen-fixing capacity of clover allows farmers to reduce reliance on chemical nitrogen fertilisers, which is a significant benefit both to the bottom line and in terms of reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

“Clover in the sward is a real win-win,” said Michael O’Donovan, Head of Grassland Research at Teagasc. “On average, incorporating clover can decrease nitrogen fertiliser use by up to 100kg per hectare annually on livestock farms. That’s a direct saving in fertiliser bills which, after last year’s price spikes, is not to be underestimated.”

Trials conducted by Teagasc at the Moorepark and Johnstown Castle research centres have consistently shown that swards containing at least 20% white clover can maintain similar levels of grass growth with less fertiliser applied. The resulting reduction in nitrous oxide emissions and runoff is regarded as an important contribution toward meeting Ireland’s commitments under the Climate Action Plan and the EU Nitrates Directive.

Farmers in every region are beginning to see the advantages. Tom Loughnane, a dairy farmer in Co Tipperary, has overseen the successful introduction of clover to over half of his grazing platform since 2021. “We’ve cut back on nitrogen use by about 30% already. The cows are milking well and the pastures are greening up earlier in the spring,” he said.

There are, however, management changes required. Establishing clover is most effective when swards are reseeded or oversown after a tight grazing rotation in late spring or early summer. Careful attention must be paid to grazing management and avoiding overly high nitrogen application, which can suppress clover. Experts advise that a targeted phosphorus and potassium plan, soil testing, and regular monitoring are crucial to ensure successful establishment.

Animal health concerns, such as bloat in cattle, need to be factored into grazing decisions, but these are manageable with appropriate planning and use of anti-bloat measures.

In line with the Government’s ambition to lower farm emissions, the Department of Agriculture has announced further support for the adoption of multi-species swards and clover mixes under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) Strategic Plan. The schemes are expected to encourage more farms to integrate clover, especially where fertiliser prices remain volatile and margins tight.

With Teagasc’s economic models forecasting significant savings at farm level and notable improvements to water and air quality, incorporating clover is seen as a sound step for Irish farmers seeking resilience in a changing regulatory and market landscape.

For further guidance on clover establishment and management, farmers are encouraged to attend local Signpost farm walks and consult their Teagasc advisors.
headline: Signpost: Incorporating clover offers a 'win win' for economic and environmental sustainability

text:
Mary Lou McDonald has emerged as a more popular party leader than Leo Varadkar, according to the latest Irish Examiner/Ipsos opinion poll, which shows the Sinn Féin president continuing to outpace the Tánaiste in public approval ratings.

The findings indicate that Ms McDonald is viewed favourably by 48% of those surveyed, compared to a 36% positive rating for Mr Varadkar, who stepped down as Taoiseach earlier this year. The poll, which gauged voter sentiment across the country, suggests the Sinn Féin leader’s personal appeal remains robust, even as her party’s overall support has ebbed slightly since its peak in 2022.

The survey also highlights a sharp generational divide, with Ms McDonald enjoying particularly strong support among voters under 35. More than half of respondents in this age bracket expressed a positive opinion of her leadership, underscoring the party’s enduring draw among younger cohorts anxious over issues such as housing and the cost of living.

Varadkar’s departure from the top job in March, citing personal and political reasons, has prompted renewed scrutiny of Fine Gael’s standing and leadership. While Mr Varadkar retains considerable support among Fine Gael voters, his favourability ratings have struggled to recover from the controversies and challenges experienced during his tenure, particularly on health and housing.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin, who now leads the Government in a caretaker capacity pending the selection of a new Fine Gael leader and Taoiseach, secured a 41% positive rating. The Fianna Fáil leader’s numbers have remained steady, reflecting a relatively even-handed public perception as the coalition navigates a crucial transition period.

Sinn Féin’s position as the main opposition force at Leinster House lends further weight to Ms McDonald’s standings. Political analysts note that while the party’s poll lead has narrowed in recent months, her personal popularity could prove decisive in the next general election, expected within the coming year.

The Irish Examiner poll points to enduring volatility in the electorate, with nearly a quarter of voters indicating they remain undecided on their party preference. Issues such as the housing crisis, healthcare waiting lists and immigration continue to dominate the political agenda, and party leaders’ ability to project competence and empathy may be increasingly important as campaigning intensifies.

A Sinn Féin spokesperson said the results demonstrated "a continued appetite for change" among the electorate. Fine Gael representatives meanwhile insisted that the party is “renewing and responding” to the challenges facing the country, citing recent measures on housing supply and cost-of-living supports.

The survey sampled 1,200 adults nationwide between 1st and 4th June, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.8 percentage points.
headline: Mary Lou McDonald 'more popular leader than Leo Varadkar'

text:
Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs Simon Coveney has urged UK Brexit Secretary Dominic Raab to present "credible, workable alternatives" to the contentious backstop arrangement, insisting that Ireland and the EU cannot accept vague promises in its place.

Speaking after bilateral talks in Brussels yesterday, Mr Coveney reaffirmed the Irish Government's position that the withdrawal agreement, including the backstop, remains "the only available solution" to prevent a hard border on the island of Ireland if future trade talks are unsuccessful. The Tánaiste said that the EU and Ireland remain open to examining fresh proposals from the British side, but stressed that any alternatives must be legally operable and realistic.

"The challenge for anyone who believes there is an alternative to the backstop is to put those alternatives forward in detail," Mr Coveney said. "What is not helpful is to simply talk about future optimism or about potential technical solutions that have not been tested or developed. The onus is on the UK Government—if they have alternatives, they need to present them—so that we can examine them to see if they do what the backstop is designed to do."

The Brexit Secretary had travelled to Brussels ahead of next week's crucial European Council summit, insisting the UK Government is "determined" to secure a deal that respects the peace process and the Good Friday Agreement, but without what he described as an "indefinite" Irish backstop. Mr Raab said progress is being made in negotiations and insisted there are "workable solutions" that would allow the UK to leave the EU customs union and single market while maintaining an open border in Ireland.

However, Irish and EU officials remain sceptical, arguing that technical solutions such as trusted trader schemes or advanced customs checks have yet to be proven feasible. "There is a growing sense of frustration at this stage," a senior Irish official told the Irish Examiner. "The backstop is there as an insurance policy. Ireland and the EU have shown a willingness to be flexible on its wording and scope, but what we cannot accept is its removal or replacement with something that is merely aspirational."

Meanwhile, political tensions continue to rise in London. DUP leader Arlene Foster reiterated her party's opposition to any backstop arrangement that would see Northern Ireland treated differently to the rest of the UK, warning the Prime Minister she cannot support any deal that "compromises the economic or constitutional integrity" of the union.

In Dublin, Government sources confirmed that contingency planning is being ramped up amid concerns over a possible 'no-deal' Brexit, including preparations across key departments and agencies. Taoiseach Leo Varadkar will travel to Paris for further talks with French President Emmanuel Macron, as the Government continues its diplomatic drive to maintain unity among EU member states.

The EU’s chief negotiator Michel Barnier has indicated progress but said a withdrawal agreement must include "a legally operative backstop" to guarantee there will be no return to a hard border regardless of the outcome of future trade relationships.

With just months remaining until the scheduled Brexit date at the end of March, pressure is mounting on both sides to break the deadlock. While talks are set to continue throughout the week, there remains no clear sign that the UK Government will present the "detailed and legally sound" alternatives demanded by Dublin and Brussels.
headline: Coveney tells Raab to produce viable alternatives to backstop

text:
The Guinness Cork Jazz Festival has unveiled what organisers describe as its most ambitious and wide-ranging programme to date for the 2022 edition, promising a dynamic blend of international stars, homegrown talent, and energetic newcomers to the genre. The much-anticipated festival, which returns to Leeside from Thursday, 27 October to Monday, 31 October, will see Cork City transformed into Ireland’s jazz capital for the October Bank Holiday weekend.

Among the headline acts announced this morning are Grammy-winning vocalist Gregory Porter, acclaimed British five-piece GoGo Penguin, and jazz-pop sensation Corinne Bailey Rae, who will each take to the stage at the iconic Cork Opera House. The Everyman Theatre will host genre-bending bluegrass virtuosos Punch Brothers and electrifying UK ensemble Nubiyan Twist, while the Metropole Hotel—the spiritual home of the festival—will once again thrum with music until the small hours, with dozens of acts scheduled across the weekend.

Festival Director Mark Murphy said the 2022 programme marks a major return to form after two years impacted by the pandemic. “Cork has always been Ireland’s beating heart of jazz, and this year’s line-up reflects the energy and excitement that live music brings back to the city,” he said. “We’re welcoming major international acts, but also providing a platform for emerging Irish artists and community groups who are vital to the festival’s spirit.”

In addition to ticketed headline concerts, music fans can expect a lively array of free gigs in over 60 venues citywide, with local pubs, hotels, and public spaces hosting improvisational sessions and street performances throughout the weekend. The Jazz Parade will make a welcome return on Saturday afternoon, with costumed bands and dancers bringing a carnival atmosphere to St Patrick’s Street and Oliver Plunkett Street.

Cork’s thriving jazz scene will also be celebrated, with local favourites like The Paul Dunlea Big Band and The New Irish Jazz Orchestra among those performing. The festival’s education strand is set to feature masterclasses and workshops with visiting musicians, in partnership with the Cork School of Music and University College Cork.

The economic impact of the festival is significant, with Fáilte Ireland estimating that jazz weekend brings in upwards of €35 million to the city and surrounding areas each year. Hoteliers and restaurateurs across Cork are already reporting strong early bookings, with many city centre hotels close to full occupancy for the weekend.

Tickets for headline events go on sale Friday at noon via the festival’s website and participating venues. Organisers have advised fans to book early amid strong demand. For the full programme and timetable, visit guinnesscorkjazz.com.

As festival-goers eager to return to the dancefloors and intimate club sessions that define Cork Jazz, this year’s edition is shaping up to be a jubilant homecoming for artists and audiences alike.
headline: Guinness Cork Jazz Festival announces stellar programme for 2022 event

text:
EU leaders gathered in Brussels on Friday for the latest European Council summit, with Taoiseach Simon Harris reaffirming Ireland’s commitment to Ukraine and discussing key issues including defence cooperation, migration, and the ongoing Middle East conflict. The Taoiseach told reporters that Ireland would not support the EU Treaty changes currently under discussion, reiterating the Government’s opposition to moves that could jeopardise the country’s neutrality. He also pushed for more robust humanitarian efforts for Gaza, calling for “an immediate ceasefire and full and unhindered humanitarian access.”

The summit comes as Ireland marks 26 years since the signing of the Good Friday Agreement, a landmark accord credited with bringing an end to decades of violence in Northern Ireland. Politicians from across the political spectrum paid tribute on Friday to the architects of the agreement, with Tánaiste Micheál Martin saying it “continues to underpin our peace and prosperity” and urging renewed efforts to protect the institutions established under its terms. Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald described the Agreement as “the foundation stone of a new Ireland” but warned that political stability in the North remains “fragile” in the face of ongoing disagreements over legacy issues and the operation of Stormont.

Meanwhile, a case of mistaken identity caused some amusement in Cork City after a suspected rat seen near Grand Parade prompted a call-out to City Council pest control services. Upon closer inspection, Council workers discovered not a rodent but an escaped pet ferret, which was successfully captured and returned to its owner. The incident, which briefly sparked debate on social media over the city’s ongoing efforts to tackle vermin, ended with City Hall confirming that “all appropriate procedures were followed” and reassuring the public that there was no wider infestation.

Elsewhere, delays were reported on the M50 northbound due to a multi-vehicle collision near Junction 6, with Gardaí and emergency services attending the scene. No serious injuries were reported, but motorists were advised to allow extra time for their journeys. In health news, the HSE has issued a statement on the ongoing outbreak of norovirus in several hospitals across the country, advising the public to restrict visits to vulnerable relatives and maintain strict hand hygiene.

Finally, Met Éireann has forecast a mostly dry weekend with some sunny spells, though scattered showers are expected on Sunday in the west. Temperatures are set to range from 12 to 16 degrees Celsius, offering a mild start to the month of May.
headline: Friday's Evening Round-Up: EU summit, Good Friday Agreement and mistaken identity of rodent

A baby was taken to hospital last night following a second suspected petrol bomb attack at a house in Cork city, Gardaí have confirmed.

Emergency services were called to the scene at a property in the Mayfield area shortly before 10pm on Thursday, after reports that an incendiary device had been thrown through a window. It is understood the device ignited, causing a fire in one of the rooms.

A woman and her infant child were in the house at the time. The baby, believed to be less than two years old, was assessed at the scene by paramedics and subsequently transported by ambulance to Cork University Hospital. The child's injuries are not thought to be life-threatening, and the woman was uninjured.

This incident marks the second such attack at the same address in recent weeks. A similar incident occurred on 28 May, prompting heightened Garda patrols in the locality.

Locals said they were “deeply shocked and frightened” by the escalation in violence. One neighbour told the Irish Examiner that families in the area are “living in fear” after the latest attack. “To target a home where a young child is sleeping is beyond comprehension,” she said.

Gardaí cordoned off the property overnight and an examination was carried out by Garda crime scene investigators on Friday morning. A number of items have been sent for forensic analysis.

A spokesperson for An Garda Síochána said: “Gardaí are investigating an incident of criminal damage by fire at a house in the Mayfield area of Cork city which occurred on Thursday, 6 June. A number of persons were present in the house at the time. No arrests have been made. Investigations are ongoing.”

Preliminary enquiries suggest the attack may be linked to an ongoing local dispute. Gardaí are appealing to anyone who may have witnessed any unusual activity in the area between 9.30pm and 10.30pm on Thursday to come forward.

Local Sinn Féin TD, Thomas Gould, condemned the attack and called for a “robust Garda response” to reassure residents. “The safety of our communities, especially vulnerable families and children, must be paramount,” he said.

Cork City Council has been notified and arrangements are being made to support the family affected by the incident.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Mayfield Garda Station on 021 455 8510 or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: Baby taken to hospital following second petrol bomb attack in Cork

Renewed calls have been made for greater enforcement of the car ban on Cork’s Patrick Street, amid ongoing concerns about compliance and the safety of pedestrians and cyclists.

Councillors and local businesses have voiced frustration that, despite the restrictions being in place since 2018, private vehicles continue to access the street during prohibited hours with few consequences. The so-called “car ban”, which was reintroduced and made permanent after a controversial pilot scheme, prohibits private cars from entering the city centre thoroughfare between 3pm and 6.30pm, Monday to Sunday, in a bid to prioritise public transport, promote active travel, and reduce congestion.

However, there have been repeated reports of motorists ignoring the restrictions, with little visible enforcement by An Garda Síochána or Cork City Council traffic wardens. This, some say, is undermining the objectives of the ban and endangering vulnerable road users.

Green Party councillor Dan Boyle said that, while the measures had delivered benefits in terms of reduced through traffic, a lack of enforcement was eroding public confidence in the scheme. “The issue is not with the regulation itself, but with its consistent and fair implementation. Without robust enforcement, the message goes out that compliance is optional,” he said.

Fine Gael councillor Derry Canty echoed these concerns, calling for the installation of automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) cameras to deter non-compliance. “We can’t expect Gardaí to stand on every corner, but technology can provide a solution. Other cities have shown how effective it can be,” he said.

Local business owners, meanwhile, are split on the issue. Some argue that stricter enforcement will make Patrick Street a more pleasant environment for shopping and dining, while others worry about a potential impact on trade if clients cannot easily access the area by car.

A spokesperson for Cork City Council said that the restrictions are clearly signposted, and that the council continues to work closely with Gardaí to monitor compliance. “We encourage all motorists to respect the regulations to ensure the safety of all road users and to support Cork’s city centre as a vibrant, people-friendly destination,” the spokesperson said.

An Garda Síochána stated that regular patrols are carried out in the area, and that fines have been issued where contraventions were observed. However, the Gardaí acknowledged that resource limitations mean officers cannot be present at all times.

Patrick Street is a key artery in the city’s transport strategy, and its future has become a focal point in the broader debate about mobility, climate action, and the post-pandemic recovery of Cork’s urban core. Campaigners for sustainable transport are calling on the council and Gardaí to ensure that regulations are enforced effectively, warning that the credibility of similar schemes citywide is at stake.

The issue is expected to be discussed at the next meeting of Cork City Council’s transport committee.
headline: Calls for more enforcement of Cork's Patrick St car ban

text:
As the electric anticipation builds in the wings of the Bord Gáis Energy Theatre, Máire Flavin breathes deeply, steadying herself for the torrent of emotion and sound that is Elektra. For the acclaimed Dublin-born soprano, this production with Irish National Opera marks not only a significant career milestone but also an extraordinary test of vocal and emotional stamina.

Richard Strauss’s Elektra is no ordinary opera. Composed in 1909, its relentless psychological intensity and demanding vocal lines have secured its reputation as one of the most challenging roles in the repertoire. Flavin, cast as Chrysothemis—the tragic heroine’s conflicted sister—describes stepping into Strauss’s world as “thrilling, terrifying, and utterly absorbing.” 

“It’s a privilege, honestly, but you really have to go to the edge,” Flavin says, smiling as she sits backstage, still in costume after a final rehearsal. “Chrysothemis is desperately caught between duty to her family and her longing for a normal life. That conflict is written right into the music—some of the lines soar, some are almost screamed. It’s wonderfully cathartic, but it takes everything you have.”

Flavin has become a familiar face to Irish audiences in recent years, building a reputation for fine lyricism and dramatic insight. Having trained at the prestigious Royal Irish Academy of Music and cut her teeth with Opera Theatre Company and Wexford Festival Opera, her career has blossomed with engagements across Europe, including in Vienna, London, and Munich. 

But returning home to perform, especially in a work as iconic as Elektra, carries a unique significance. “There’s a particular energy singing for an Irish audience,” she says. “It’s a bit like being among family—you want to make them proud, you want to reach them. And doing Strauss here with Irish National Opera, you feel that support all around you.”

Elektra itself is a stark tale of vengeance and grief, drawing on ancient Greek myth but rendered with a modernist’s psychological complexity. Strauss’s score, often described as relentless and overwhelming, tests the mettle of any singer. Flavin admits to feeling daunted by the role’s technical demands. 

“You can’t switch off for a second,” she explains. “The orchestra is massive, the harmonies are jagged and strange, and you have to ride above it all—keep the emotional truth while also thinking about breath support, pacing, not blowing out your voice. It’s very exposing, but it’s also exhilarating. There’s no hiding in Strauss.”

Despite the opera’s reputation for darkness, Flavin insists the process has been intensely rewarding. “It’s surprisingly uplifting, actually, because you go through so much with your colleagues. Sinéad Campbell Wallace, who sings Elektra, is extraordinary. We push each other, and the whole company pulls together—chorus, orchestra, technical teams. You feel part of something bigger.”

The Irish National Opera’s production, directed by the award-winning Tom Creed, leans into the work’s psychological undertones, setting the action in a timeless world of shadows and fractured light. Flavin credits Creed and conductor Fergus Sheil with fostering a supportive environment that allows the cast to take risks. “There’s a kind of bravery needed for this opera, and I think Irish artists have that in spades,” she laughs.
headline: Máire Flavin: Irish soprano on her role in Elektra, Strauss's famously dark opera

text:
Nurses are warning that the decision to end a Government-funded childcare scheme has left them facing daily childcare bills of up to €110, with the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO) describing the situation as “unsustainable and deeply unfair”.

The emergency childcare scheme, which was introduced in May 2020 at the height of the Covid-19 pandemic, provided subsidised childcare places for frontline healthcare workers. However, the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth confirmed earlier this month that the scheme would not be extended, citing the return to “normal” childcare operations.

Phil Ní Sheaghdha, General Secretary of the INMO, said that the sudden withdrawal of the scheme has put members under “enormous financial and personal strain”. She said some nurses are now paying as much as €110 per day for private childcare, particularly those working long and unpredictable shifts in the HSE.

“Our members already work unsocial hours and have little flexibility, but the removal of this support means many are having to make impossible decisions around their family’s welfare and their ability to work,” Ms Ní Sheaghdha said.

“We have nurses who are sole parents or have partners also working shifts in healthcare — they’re left with no affordable options and are forking out sums that just aren’t viable on a nurse’s wage.”

The average cost of full-time childcare in Ireland is now over €1,200 per month, according to figures from the Department of Children, but costs are significantly higher in Dublin and other urban centres. Nurses say that due to their rosters, many have to rely on more expensive private or flexible arrangements, as traditional crèches cannot accommodate shift work patterns.

A nurse working on a busy Dublin hospital ward, who did not wish to be named, told the Irish Examiner her childcare costs have doubled since the scheme ended. “I’m paying €100-€110 some days just to have my daughter minded from early in the morning until after my 12-hour shift. That’s half my daily wage gone before I’ve paid the mortgage or bills,” she said.

Opposition TDs have criticised the Government’s decision to wind down the scheme, with Sinn Féin’s health spokesperson, David Cullinane, describing it as “a step backwards for frontline health staff who kept this country going in the darkest days of the pandemic”. He called for an urgent review and for new targeted supports to be introduced for shift-working families.

In a statement, the Department of Children said the emergency measure was “always intended as a temporary response” and pointed to a recent increase in the National Childcare Scheme (NCS) subsidies as a move to improve affordability for all families. However, the INMO argues that the NCS does not address the unique needs of healthcare workers, whose hours often fall outside standard childcare provision.

The Irish Congress of Trade Unions (ICTU) and the HSE Staff Panel have both backed the INMO’s call for a tailored solution, warning that ongoing workforce shortages in nursing and midwifery could worsen if the situation is not addressed.

With record numbers of nursing vacancies reported in hospitals nationwide, the INMO is urging the Department of Health and the Department of Children to meet with unions to devise a scheme that recognises the realities of frontline shift work.

“Recruitment and retention are already at crisis point,” said Ms Ní Sheaghdha.
headline: INMO: Some nurses paying €110 per day for childcare as govt scheme scrapped

A North Yorkshire-based fertiliser company is on the verge of a significant global expansion, following a series of promising trials and growing international interest in its innovative products. The firm, Sirius Minerals, which operates from the Cleveland Potash mine near Whitby, has developed a fertiliser derived from polyhalite, a naturally occurring mineral found deep beneath the North Sea.

Irish farmers and agricultural co-operatives have been watching developments closely, with Teagasc, the State agriculture advisory body, confirming that polyhalite-based fertilisers have been undergoing evaluation at several sites across Munster and Leinster. Early indications suggest potential agronomic benefits, particularly for improving soil health and providing a multi-nutrient solution suitable for Irish grassland and tillage farms.

Polyhalite contains potassium, magnesium, calcium and sulphur in a single product, which Sirius Minerals says allows growers to meet essential crop requirements without separate applications. With fertiliser prices remaining volatile and Irish tillage farmers facing pressure to maximise yields while preserving soil quality, alternatives to conventional fertilisers are attracting considerable attention.

Interest in the North Yorkshire product has not been limited to Ireland. Sirius Minerals recently secured export agreements with distributors in Brazil, China, and the United States. Closer to home, UK and Continental European buyers are also assessing the polyhalite offering, with large-scale trials under way in France and Germany.

Dr Maria Gleeson, crop nutrition specialist at Teagasc, said that initial Irish field trials have been “encouraging”, citing improvements in grass growth and resilience, particularly in fields with historically low potassium and sulphur levels. “We’re seeing some positive responses, but as always, more work is required to tailor advice to specific Irish conditions,” Dr Gleeson said.

Representatives of the Irish Farmers’ Association have expressed cautious optimism, noting that any new fertiliser product will need to demonstrate cost-effectiveness and environmental compliance under new regulatory frameworks. An IFA spokesperson noted: “We’re open to any product that can help Irish farmers improve sustainability, but price and performance will ultimately decide uptake.”

Sirius Minerals has already invested heavily in extraction and transport infrastructure, including a 37km underground conveyor to move the raw material directly from the mine to Teesside port. The company claims its polyhalite has a lower carbon footprint compared to many traditional fertilisers, an attribute that could make it attractive to Irish buyers seeking to lower emissions per the Department of Agriculture’s climate targets.

Market analysts warn that global fertiliser markets remain fiercely competitive, dominated by established players with deep distribution networks. Yet, with increasing scrutiny on fertiliser sustainability and provenance, Sirius Minerals’ polyhalite could carve out a significant niche if agronomic results continue to impress.

As Irish farmers face uncertain times with price volatility, regulatory change and weather challenges, the arrival of a new fertiliser option from nearby shores will be closely monitored in the coming months. Further findings from Irish farm trials are expected later this year, which may determine whether this North Yorkshire product will become a familiar sight on Irish fields in the seasons ahead.
headline: Global success beckons for North Yorkshire fertiliser

text:
The board overseeing the National Children’s Hospital project was advised of escalating costs before the summer, with documentation confirming warnings were issued in June of last year, months before budget overruns became public. Correspondence seen by the Irish Examiner details briefings to the National Paediatric Hospital Development Board (NPHDB) outlining “significant financial pressures” on the project, then estimated at €1.4bn.

The revelations come as political attention continues to focus on the spiralling bill for the hospital on the St James’s site in Dublin, now expected to exceed €2bn when completed. The Oireachtas Public Accounts Committee is due to question senior HSE and development board officials later this week. Opposition TDs have called for greater transparency over the timeline of warnings, with Sinn Féin health spokesperson David Cullinane describing the situation as “a shambles for taxpayers and families alike”.

Documents from the June 2023 board meeting, obtained under Freedom of Information, record that members were told of “contractor claims and risk items likely to have material impact on the overall cost” and the need for “immediate escalation” of concerns to both the Department of Health and the HSE. The Department has reiterated that it is cooperating fully with the ongoing review, commissioned by Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly last month.

Meanwhile, more than 37,000 nurses and midwives across the country remained on picket lines for a third consecutive day in a dispute with the HSE over pay and conditions. Services at acute hospitals and community care centres were again heavily curtailed, with thousands of outpatient appointments and elective procedures cancelled. The Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO) said support for the action was holding firm, with union general secretary Phil Ní Sheaghdha stating that members “are determined to see this through for the future of nursing in Ireland”.

Efforts to break the deadlock are set to continue, with the Workplace Relations Commission expected to reconvene talks later this week. The HSE said it “regrets disruption to patients”, with Chief Executive Bernard Gloster repeating calls for both parties to “re-engage meaningfully”. The Department of Health has insisted that pay structures must fit within existing public service agreements.

Patient representative groups have urged both sides to resolve the dispute swiftly, warning of “severe and lasting damage” to waiting lists. Meanwhile, Taoiseach Simon Harris told the Dáil that the Government “remains committed to constructive engagement”, but stressed the need for “affordability and sustainability” in public sector pay. The INMO said further strike dates could not be ruled out if there is no breakthrough in negotiations.
headline: Bulletin: Children's hospital board told of rising costs last June; Over 37,000 nurses in third day of strike action

text:
Taoiseach Leo Varadkar has said he does not want Ireland to become a society where politicians are compelled to live "in a security bubble", following heightened concern over the safety of public representatives in recent months.

Speaking in the Dáil on Thursday, Mr Varadkar acknowledged an increase in threatening behaviour and intimidation directed at elected officials, but warned against the development of a political culture where TDs and ministers are isolated from their communities. He told the House: “We want politicians to be able to live among the people who elect them, to shop in their local supermarket, to attend local events and walk down the street. I don’t want a country where politicians live in a security bubble, separated from the people.”

His comments come after a number of high-profile security incidents, including the protest outside the then Taoiseach’s home in Castleknock last July, and recent cases where threats against TDs have resulted in Garda responses. The recent vandalism of constituency offices, as well as online abuse targeted at women in public life, have prompted calls from some quarters for greater protection for members of the Oireachtas.

Mr Varadkar confirmed that the Government is in ongoing discussions with the Gardaí regarding the adequacy of current security arrangements but emphasised the need for balance. “There must always be a proportionate response. While nobody should be intimidated or threatened for doing their job, we must be careful not to put up barriers that separate politicians from the people we serve,” he said.

Opposition parties, including Sinn Féin and Labour, have raised concerns about the safety of their members, with Labour leader Ivana Bacik calling for “urgent and effective steps” to protect public representatives, especially in their constituency offices. Ms Bacik said that while robust debate is an essential part of democracy, it must not cross the line into harassment or violence.

Justice Minister Simon Harris recently met with the Garda Commissioner to review existing protocols and said a formal review is under way to address security at public meetings, clinics, and politicians’ homes. “Intimidation of public representatives is an attack on democracy itself,” Mr Harris said.

The Irish Council for Civil Liberties has also warned that increasing security should not lead to the erosion of the public’s ability to access their representatives. A spokesperson said: “A functioning democracy relies on openness and accessibility. Any new measures should protect both the safety of politicians and the rights of citizens to engage.”

Figures from the Department of Justice show a rise in reported incidents against politicians since 2021, with a marked increase in online harassment. The Association of Garda Sergeants and Inspectors (AGSI) has called for additional resources to respond to threats against public figures, noting that “politicians, like all citizens, have a right to feel safe in their homes and workplaces”.

Mr Varadkar concluded his remarks by reiterating the importance of maintaining trust between elected officials and the electorate. “Ireland is a republic where public representatives are, and should remain, part of everyday society. We will protect our democracy by ensuring that remains the case,” he said.
headline: Varadkar: 'I don't want a country where politicians live in a security bubble'

text:
RTÉ’s legal challenge against a significant compensation award to a former broadcaster has collapsed in the High Court after the national broadcaster’s barrister conceded that inappropriate “ageist and sexist” remarks had been admitted as evidence during an earlier hearing.

The High Court had been due to hear RTÉ’s appeal against a ruling of the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) last year, which found in favour of former staff member Geraldine McNamara, 58, who claimed she had been discriminated against and unfairly dismissed. Ms McNamara, who worked as a producer in Montrose for more than two decades, was awarded €69,000 after the WRC accepted she had been denied promotion and subsequently let go on grounds related to her age and gender.

On Tuesday morning, barrister for RTÉ, Eoin McCarthy SC, told Mr Justice Charles Meenan that the broadcaster was withdrawing its appeal “with regret”, following the recent disclosure of internal emails containing remarks about Ms McNamara’s age and appearance. Counsel said it was now clear that material “not appropriate to be considered in any workplace, never mind in the context of a legal challenge, had become central to the WRC determination.”

RTÉ’s decision not to pursue its challenge comes after lawyers for Ms McNamara sought to introduce further evidence, including transcripts of internal conversations in which senior RTÉ managers referred to her as “past it” and “unfit for the new direction.” The emails, which were not disclosed to Ms McNamara during the WRC process, also alluded to concerns that she “wouldn’t present well on camera at her age.”

In his brief remarks, Justice Meenan welcomed the “pragmatic decision” by RTÉ, stating that “no employer, public or private, can justify defending discriminatory attitudes, much less when those attitudes are so clearly documented.”

Speaking outside the Four Courts, Ms McNamara said she hoped her experience would “shine a light on ageism and sexism in Irish workplaces, particularly in our national institutions.” She thanked her legal team and said she was “relieved” that the case had concluded after a lengthy and difficult process. “No one should have to listen to colleagues or managers discuss their age or appearance behind closed doors, especially not at a public broadcaster.”

In a statement, RTÉ apologised to Ms McNamara for any hurt or distress caused and said it would be reviewing its workplace procedures. “We acknowledge the findings of the WRC and the High Court, and are committed to ensuring that all staff are treated with respect, fairness, and equality in every aspect of their employment,” the statement read.

The compensation award, which RTÉ must now pay, comes at a sensitive time for the broadcaster amid ongoing scrutiny over workplace culture and employment practices. The case is one of several being monitored by the Oireachtas Committee on Media, which last year questioned senior management about allegations of discrimination and inappropriate comments within the organisation.

A spokesperson for the National Women’s Council welcomed the outcome, saying it “sends a strong signal that ageism and sexism will not be tolerated in Irish workplaces.” The HSE has also previously highlighted the damaging health impacts that discrimination in the workplace can have, particularly for women over 50.

Ms McNamara said she looked forward to “moving on to the next chapter” and urged other victims of discrimination not to be afraid to come forward.
headline: RTE challenge against compensation ruling collapses over 'ageist and sexist' remarks

text:
Future housing developments in Cork must prioritise traffic-calming measures and improved footpath connectivity if communities are to thrive and road safety is to be enhanced, local representatives and residents’ groups have insisted.

The call comes as Cork City Council prepares to consider several major housing plans, including schemes in the city’s fast-growing suburbs and satellite towns. With population increases projected across the metropolitan area under the Cork 2040 framework, concerns persist that the infrastructure of many new estates fails to support safe walking routes or manage increasing traffic volumes.

Fianna Fáil Cllr Mary Rose Desmond, who chairs the city’s Strategic Policy Committee on housing, said a ‘modal shift’ must underpin all planning decisions. “We cannot continue to design estates where footpaths are an afterthought, or where cars dominate every corner,” she said. “Traffic-calming measures, such as raised platforms, narrower carriageways and clear pedestrian linkages, need to be embedded from the outset.”

Her comments were echoed by the Grange-Frankfield Residents’ Association, which has long campaigned for safer crossings and continuous pavements in its area. Association spokesperson Liam O’Driscoll pointed to ongoing issues around Grange Road and the entrance to local schools: “Children and elderly residents are expected to cross busy roads or navigate broken footpaths. It’s simply not good enough in 2024.”

Recent traffic data from Cork City Council shows a sharp increase in car journeys originating in new developments across the southside, with residents frequently citing the lack of alternative transport infrastructure as the key reason for their reliance on private vehicles.

The current Cork City Development Plan requires developers to submit a Mobility Management Plan for any scheme above a certain scale. However, local TDs have warned that these requirements “are not always robustly enforced” at construction stage. Labour’s Sean Sherlock, who represents Cork East, stated: “There are plenty of examples where developers have paid lip service to pedestrian priority, but little has changed on the ground.”

The issue has also featured in submissions to the Oireachtas Committee on Housing, with the National Transport Authority urging a ‘whole neighbourhood’ approach to active travel provision, particularly in light of the Government’s commitment to halve transport emissions by 2030. The NTA’s recent audit of Cork estates identified ‘significant deficits’ in footpath widths, pedestrian crossings and permeability, especially in developments approved prior to 2018.

A spokesperson for the Department of Housing said that new statutory guidelines are being finalised and are due to issue to planning authorities later this year. “It is critical that new housing not only meets climate targets, but enables children, people with disabilities and older citizens to walk safely from their doorstep,” the Department said in a statement.

For many Cork residents, however, the urgency of the situation leaves little room for delay. “We’re not asking for anything radical,” said O’Driscoll. “Just neighbourhoods where people can walk to school, the shop or the bus stop without risking their lives.”
headline: Traffic-calming measures and footpath connectivity 'a must' for future Cork housing developments

text:
A Russian-based hacking collective widely accused of interfering in the 2016 US presidential election has renewed its attempts to infiltrate Western political organisations, according to security experts.

The group—known variously as APT28, Fancy Bear, or by Russian military intelligence monikers—has been observed attempting fresh intrusions into political targets in the United States and Europe since late last year. Security analysts say the campaign highlights ongoing concerns about foreign interference in democratic processes, particularly as several countries prepare for elections in 2024.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued a public advisory on Tuesday, warning political parties, think tanks, and advocacy groups to update security protocols in light of recent suspicious activity linked to APT28. The group, which Western intelligence agencies allege is operated by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service, utilises tailored phishing emails and malware to compromise systems and steal sensitive data.

In 2016, the hacking collective orchestrated a breach of the Democratic National Committee, leading to a leak of internal communications and allegations of coordinated efforts to influence the outcome of the presidential election. Moscow has repeatedly denied any involvement, dismissing the accusations as politically motivated.

Sources in the Irish National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) say there have been no confirmed attacks against Irish institutions by APT28 in recent months, but the organisation remains on heightened alert and is coordinating with European partners. “The tactics are becoming more sophisticated and difficult to detect,” a spokesperson told the Irish Examiner. “We are urging all political organisations to review their cyber defence measures ahead of the elections to the European Parliament and local authorities in June.”

UK and European officials have also raised the alarm, citing a growing wave of cyber-enabled espionage targeting politicians, diplomats and analysts. Last year, British authorities accused APT28 of attempting to gather information on MPs and peers. German authorities reported similar attempts to breach Bundestag systems earlier this spring.

Experts say the group often leverages publicly available information and exploits known software vulnerabilities to gain access to email accounts and internal documents. “It’s a matter of persistent, low-profile attacks rather than flashy, high-impact incidents,” said Dr. Aoife Whelan, a cyber security lecturer at University College Dublin. “The aim is often to collect intelligence rather than to disrupt or destroy.”

The Taoiseach, Simon Harris, has previously described cyber security as a “critical pillar” of national security, following ransomware attacks on the HSE in 2021. A report published by the Oireachtas Communications Committee last year called for increased investment in cyber defence measures for both state and civil society organisations.

With European and US elections looming, officials fear that disinformation and illicit information-gathering campaigns could influence public debate. CISA and the EU’s Cybersecurity Agency (ENISA) have urged all election-related organisations to upgrade cyber defences and to train staff to recognise email scams and other social engineering tactics.

While attribution of cyber attacks remains complex, Western intelligence services maintain high confidence in linking APT28 to past incidents. The Russian Embassy in Dublin did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the renewed allegations.

Irish officials have said there is no current evidence of a direct threat to this year’s elections, but warned that the evolving nature of cyber threats demands constant vigilance. The NCSC said it is working with the Department of Defence, the Gardaí, and international partners to mitigate risks and ensure the integrity of Ireland’s democratic processes.
headline: Russian group blamed for hacking Democrats in 2016 ‘attempting new intrusions’

text:
The former president of Waterford Institute of Technology (WIT), Dr Ruaidhrí Neavyn, has lost a High Court challenge against the decision of the Governing Body not to appoint him for a second term.

Mr Justice Michael Twomey delivered his judgment on Tuesday morning, ruling that the procedures followed by the Governing Body of WIT in 2015 were lawful and that Dr Neavyn was not entitled to be reinstated or compensated.

Dr Neavyn, who served as WIT president from 2011 to 2016, had sought to overturn the institution’s decision not to offer him a further five-year term. He took legal action against the Governing Body, as well as the Higher Education Authority (HEA) and the Minister for Further and Higher Education.

In his proceedings, Dr Neavyn argued that the process leading to the non-renewal of his contract was “flawed, unfair and lacked transparency”. He claimed he was not provided with adequate reasons for the decision, nor given a fair opportunity to respond to concerns raised by the Governing Body.

The court heard that, in April 2015, the Governing Body resolved not to reappoint Dr Neavyn, following an internal review of his performance and consultation with the then Department of Education and Skills. Minutes of meetings were furnished as evidence, as well as correspondence between WIT and the HEA.

Representing Dr Neavyn, Senior Counsel Michael Howard contended that the Governing Body relied on subjective impressions and failed to apply appropriate procedures, depriving his client of natural justice.

However, lawyers for WIT argued that there was no legal entitlement for a president to be reappointed, and that the Governing Body enjoyed wide discretion under the Institutes of Technology Acts. They said due process was followed, and that Dr Neavyn was aware from the outset that renewal was not automatic.

Delivering judgment, Mr Justice Twomey said it was clear the decision not to reappoint was “within the reasonable scope of the Governing Body’s authority”. He found no evidence of bias or procedural unfairness, and noted that Dr Neavyn had been informed of the concerns and given an opportunity to address them.

“The court is satisfied that the process was fair and the decision reached was one the Governing Body was entitled to make,” the judge stated.

Dr Neavyn’s case was dismissed in its entirety. Costs were awarded against him, though the court noted that “all parties acted in good faith and with the best interests of the institution in mind”.

The decision brings to a close a lengthy and at times acrimonious dispute, which had become a point of public debate in Waterford’s academic and political circles. Dr Neavyn, who has since taken up advisory roles in higher education elsewhere, was not present for the judgment.

The Department of Further and Higher Education, the HEA and Waterford IT all declined to comment in detail, citing the legal nature of the proceedings. However, a spokesperson for WIT welcomed “the clarity provided by the court and its endorsement of the institution’s governance procedures”.

Waterford IT is due to become part of the new South East Technological University, following a merger process with Institute of Technology Carlow. The transition is expected to be completed later this year.
headline: Former WIT president loses High Court action over college's decision not to reappoint him

text:
Green Party candidate Ciarán Cuffe has topped the poll in the European Parliament elections for the Dublin constituency, but no candidate has reached the quota following the first count. Mr Cuffe secured a strong lead, receiving just under 64,000 first preference votes, well ahead of his nearest rivals, but did not meet the required quota of 75,754 to be elected on the first count. 

The count took place at the RDS throughout Sunday, with returning officer James Barry confirming the results shortly after 8pm. Fianna Fáil’s Barry Andrews came in second, with Fine Gael's Frances Fitzgerald running a close third. Sinn Féin’s Lynn Boylan, who is seeking to retain her seat, finished in fourth, while Independent candidate Clare Daly is in contention in fifth place. 

The final allocation of the four available MEP seats is now set to go to further counts, as the distribution of Ciarán Cuffe’s substantial surplus and the elimination of lower-polling candidates will determine the outcome. 

Turnout in Dublin was reported to be just over 50%, with polling day coinciding with local elections and the plebiscite on directly elected mayors.

Speaking after the announcement, Mr Cuffe described his poll-topping performance as “a remarkable day for the Greens, and for the people who want action on climate change”. He said the party’s message resonated with voters who “want a greener, fairer Dublin, with better public transport and an end to homelessness”. 

In a statement, Barry Andrews said he was “delighted by the strong support”, adding that “it’s clear the voters want experienced representation in Brussels.” Frances Fitzgerald, who served as Tánaiste and Minister for Justice & Equality, called her tally “a strong endorsement of a pro-European approach.”

Lynn Boylan, for her part, said she remained hopeful of retaining her seat as transfers were distributed. Clare Daly pointed to the strength of her independent campaign, noting it was “hard-fought in the face of the larger parties” and that her “focus on housing, health and social justice” had won broad support.

With no candidate reaching the quota, counting staff will now begin the intricate process of transferring surpluses and eliminating the lowest-scoring candidates. This process is expected to continue into Monday, with all eyes on the distribution of votes between Sinn Féin, Independents, and the larger parties for the final seats.

The count for Dublin is closely watched as a barometer for national sentiment, with all major parties seeking to claim momentum ahead of the next general election. It also signals a remarkable resurgence for the Green Party, as voters appear to have prioritised environmental issues against the backdrop of ongoing debates about climate action and public transport in the capital.

The full results for the four Dublin European seats are not likely to be confirmed until later in the week following the completion of multiple counts. The final outcome will determine not just Dublin’s representation in Brussels, but also the standing of parties as the political landscape shifts in the wake of #Elections2019.
headline: #Elections2019: Ciaran Cuffe tops the poll but nobody reaches quota in Dublin

text:
A marked shift in public discourse has been observed in recent months, with a growing sense of dismay among communities across Ireland as headlines are dominated by reports of rising crime, political instability, and social challenges both at home and abroad. The phrase “What is the world coming to?” has become a regular refrain from community leaders, politicians, and ordinary citizens alike, reflecting concerns that the country, and indeed the global community, are navigating an unprecedented period of uncertainty.

Recent incidents have fuelled the debate, including the spate of high-profile assaults in Dublin city centre and ongoing anti-immigration protests in several towns. The Garda Commissioner, Drew Harris, has reassured the public that measures are being put in place to address safety concerns, with additional resources promised for areas most affected by crime. Despite these assurances, some business owners and residents have expressed frustration, saying they do not feel safer on the streets, especially after dark.

Internationally, wars in Ukraine and Gaza, political polarisation in the United States, and deepening economic inequalities have added to the prevailing mood of apprehension. Irish families with close ties to affected regions have spoken of their anxiety for loved ones, while the ongoing cost-of-living crisis has left many struggling at home. Charities have reported record numbers seeking assistance, and the Society of St Vincent de Paul warned last week that demand for food and fuel vouchers is outpacing supply.

Social media platforms, often a forum for both informed debate and misinformation, have amplified fears and frustrations, making it difficult for public authorities to counter false narratives. Minister for Social Protection Heather Humphreys told the Dáil that government is working to address disinformation, but cautioned that restoring trust is a “marathon, not a sprint.”

Commentators note that while pessimism is not itself new in Irish public life, the breadth and immediacy of current challenges is unusual.
