The Archbishop of Dublin, Dermot Farrell, spoke on Sunday of “an uneasy world, where rapid change and uncertainty unsettle us all.” Meanwhile, calls for greater solidarity have been echoed by community groups, with many encouraging local initiatives aimed at fostering inclusivity and resilience.

Despite the sense of unease, there are also stories of hope. Volunteer groups, youth organisations, and social enterprises continue to find innovative ways to support those most in need. Educators and mental health professionals, meanwhile, are urging parents and young people to talk openly about their concerns and remind them that, while the world may seem tumultuous, positive change is possible through engaged citizenship.

Analysts suggest that as the nation moves towards local and European elections, there is an opportunity for political leaders to articulate a shared vision for the future—one in which Irish values of compassion and community remain central, even as the world around us shifts in uncertain ways.
headline: 'What is the world coming to?'

text:
As Irish families prepare for the return to school, the humble cheese sandwich is set to reclaim its place in lunchboxes across the country. Cheddar remains the go-to cheese for many, prized for its versatility, value and a flavour profile that appeals to younger palates. With supermarket shelves offering an array of options—own-brand blocks, Irish farmhouse varieties, and value packs—choosing the right cheddar can prove daunting.

To help parents navigate the cheese aisle, the Irish Examiner conducted a blind taste test of eight supermarket cheddars widely available in Ireland. Judged by flavour, texture, meltability, and overall appeal, the cheddars were sampled both on their own and in the classic school sandwich: sliced between two pieces of batch loaf with a smattering of butter.

Tesco Irish Mature Red Cheddar scored highly for its creamy texture and approachable mildness, making it a favourite among younger tasters. Its meltability also impressed, performing well in a quick toastie, with no oily residue or rubberiness emerging.

Lidl’s own-brand Rathdaragh Mature Irish Cheddar emerged as a strong contender, offering a pleasing tang and a firm bite. At €2.79 for 400g, it represents solid value, and its robust flavour held up well when paired with both white and brown bread.

SuperValu’s Signature Tastes West Cork Cheddar stood out for its pronounced savoury notes and satisfying crumb. While slightly pricier at €3.80 per 300g, parents agreed it delivered a touch of luxury, ideal for teenagers seeking a little more depth in their lunch.

Aldi’s Dromona Extra Mature Cheddar divided opinion. While its sharper tang and drier texture appealed to adults, some children found its assertiveness overpowering. However, it shreds well for quick pasta bakes, providing versatility beyond the lunchbox.

Dunnes Stores Irish Cheddar Block offers a mild, accessible profile. Some testers felt the flavour faded quickly, but it wins points for its soft consistency and ease of slicing, making it a safe bet for fussier eaters.

Kilmeaden Mature Cheddar, produced in Co. Waterford and widely regarded as a staple, lived up to its reputation with a full-bodied, nutty edge. At €4.20 for 300g, it is at the higher end pricewise, but its flavour earned it high marks among the panel, particularly when sampled in a toasted sandwich.

Charleville Creamery Cheddar proved reliable, with a balanced profile and a smooth finish. Its widespread availability and mid-range price (€3.50 per 350g) make it a dependable inclusion for families seeking consistency week after week.

Finally, Ballymaloe Farmhouse Cheddar, while less commonly found and carrying a higher price tag, delivered on authenticity and character. Its crumbly texture and farmhouse tang won over adults, but the sharper notes may be less suited to very young children.

Whether opting for a locally-produced block or a good-value supermarket staple, Irish families are spoilt for choice when it comes to cheddar for school lunches. Ultimately, the best cheddar is the one that disappears fastest from the sandwich box. If time allows, a quick taste test at home may help ensure both value and happy faces come the first bell.
headline: Top 8: Supermarket cheddars put to the taste test for school lunches

text:
Victims of domestic abuse are being left “trapped” in dangerous homes due to unaffordable mortgage debt and a lack of viable housing alternatives, leading support organisations have warned. Campaigners say the current system effectively forces survivors to remain with abusive partners, as fears of financial ruin, complex legal barriers and an acute housing crisis combine to block their escape.

Safe Ireland, the national network of domestic violence services, has reported a significant rise in calls from women unable to leave abusive situations because their names are tied to joint mortgages. “We are seeing increasing numbers of women who are desperate to flee, but who face homelessness or crippling debt if they do,” said Mary McDermott, chief executive of Safe Ireland. “For many, the options are stark: stay and risk further violence, or leave and face destitution.”

The problem is exacerbated by the ongoing shortage of social and affordable housing, with local authority housing lists at record lengths and private rents continuing to climb. According to the most recent figures from the Department of Housing, over 13,000 people remain in emergency accommodation, with a significant proportion comprising women and children escaping domestic abuse.

Legal and financial advisors say that for many mortgage holders, the threat of joint and several liability means both parties are held responsible for the entire loan, even when a relationship has broken down. Removing a name from a mortgage typically requires agreement from both parties and the lender, as well as a court order in cases of family law disputes. In the meantime, missed payments can damage credit ratings and increase arrears, further limiting future housing options.

Sinn Féin’s spokesperson for housing, Eoin Ó Broin TD, said urgent action is needed to ensure survivors are not further penalised by the system. “Domestic abuse victims should never be faced with the choice between safety and financial solvency. The Government must prioritise supports for those who need to exit joint tenancies and mortgages, and guarantee access to safe accommodation,” he said.

The Irish Mortgage Holders Organisation (IMHO) has also seen an increase in queries from those seeking to disentangle themselves financially after experiencing domestic violence. David Hall, chief executive of IMHO, said banks need to show greater flexibility and compassion: “The rigid nature of mortgage contracts is at odds with the realities of abuse. Lenders should be more proactive in working with survivors to find solutions.”

The Department of Justice said it is aware of the challenges faced by domestic abuse survivors in accessing safe accommodation and is working with the Department of Housing to expand refuge capacity. A spokesperson said: “The Government is committed to progressing the Zero Tolerance strategy and delivering additional refuge spaces, as well as developing protocols to support victims in addressing legal and financial obstacles.”

However, frontline workers warn that change is not keeping pace with need. “We are seeing families stuck for months, sometimes years, waiting for safe, permanent accommodation,” said a support worker at a women’s refuge in Cork. “It is not enough to offer shelter for a few nights if survivors then have nowhere to go but back to their abusers.”

Safe Ireland has called for the Government to introduce a dedicated fund to assist those needing to exit joint mortgages due to domestic violence, and for the amendment of banking regulations to allow for “compassionate release” from mortgage liability in such cases. The group has also requested greater provision of legal aid to support victims through family law proceedings.
headline: Domestic abuse victims 'trapped' in dangerous homes by mortgages

text:
The armed attack on author Salman Rushdie has elicited a complex response in Iran, with conservative groups lauding the act while reform-minded commentators and ordinary citizens have voiced unease about the repercussions for the country’s global image. Rushdie, whose 1988 novel *The Satanic Verses* led to a fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini, was stabbed on stage in New York state last Friday, sustaining severe injuries but surviving the assault.

State-linked Iranian media outlets and some politicians were quick to describe the attack as a form of divine justice. The hardline newspaper *Kayhan*, whose editor is appointed by Iran’s Supreme Leader, declared its approval, stating: “A thousand bravos to the courageous and dutiful person who attacked the apostate and depraved Salman Rushdie in New York.” Other conservative voices hailed the incident as vindication of the still-unresolved fatwa, which has shadowed Rushdie for more than three decades.

However, Iranian officials have denied direct involvement in the attack. In the first official reaction, the foreign ministry in Tehran said, “No one has the right to accuse the Islamic Republic of Iran,” and described Rushdie as a person who had “exposed himself to the wrath and rage of the people” due to “insulting Islam and its sanctities.” The ministry did not clarify what level of support, if any, the Iranian authorities give to the ongoing bounty for Rushdie’s life, which was increased by some semi-official foundations following the attack.

Among Iran’s younger generation and in more reformist circles, the attack has been met with apprehension, particularly over its potential impact on already fraught diplomatic relations with the West. Many have taken to social media to express dismay and embarrassment, with some warning that the incident may reinforce negative perceptions of Iran and hinder efforts to revive the stalled nuclear talks with the US and European Union.

Artists and writers in Iran, some speaking anonymously for fear of reprisal, expressed concern that the attack would further restrict freedom of expression and cement the image of the country as intolerant of dissent. Mahsa, a writer in Tehran, told the *Irish Examiner*: “Whatever one thinks of Rushdie’s work, this violence makes life harder for Iranian artists and damages the search for understanding.”

Internationally, the attack has been broadly condemned, with the European Union, the British Prime Minister and US President Joe Biden all defending Rushdie’s right to free speech. In Ireland, President Michael D Higgins described the stabbing as “an appalling act against a celebrated voice for reason and literary freedom.”

The suspect, Hadi Matar, 24, from New Jersey and reportedly of Lebanese descent, has pleaded not guilty to charges of attempted murder and assault. The investigation is ongoing, with US authorities examining possible links between the suspect and extremist groups.

The episode has reignited debate over the legacy of the fatwa and the responsibility of governments in confronting threats to free expression. The Dáil is expected to discuss a motion condemning the attack later this week, with several TDs calling for a renewed commitment to the defence of writers and artists at risk worldwide.
headline: Salman Rushdie attack provokes both praise and anxiety in Iran

text:
At just 13 years old, Sorcha McMahon from Kildare is making waves in an industry where most seek only to find their feet. While her peers mull over the merits of TikTok trends, Sorcha has already attracted the notice of Irish fashion insiders with her self-designed collection showcased at last weekend's Young Creators Expo in Dublin’s RDS.

The young designer, whose creations feature clever upcycling and bold colour choices, was awarded a special commendation from the Irish Fashion Council. Judges were said to be particularly impressed by her signature patchwork jackets, created from repurposed vintage fabrics sourced from charity shops around Leinster.

Sorcha’s mother, Maeve, says her daughter’s fascination with design started early, and recalls her “drawing dresses on the backs of cereal boxes as soon as she could hold a pen.” By age ten, Sorcha was teaching herself sewing techniques on YouTube and crafting simple garments for her friends and family. “She’s an old soul — very focused and creative,” Maeve told the Irish Examiner.

The attention Sorcha’s work has garnered reaches beyond the Expo. Local boutiques in Naas and Newbridge have stocked some of her accessories on a trial basis, with one owner describing her as “the next Simone Rocha, mark my words.” Teachers at her school, St Mary’s College, have also rallied behind her ambitions, helping her balance the demands of first year maths with the opportunities to travel to fashion events.

According to industry watcher and stylist Aisling Byrne, the appetite for fresh, sustainably-minded voices in fashion is only growing. “It’s remarkable to see a young person not only demonstrating technical skill but also a deep sense of responsibility in how she sources her materials,” said Byrne. “It’s exactly the direction we need more established designers to go.”

Sorcha herself seems undaunted by the attention, saying she simply wants “to make things that people feel happy and comfortable in.” When pressed about her inspirations, she cited Irish designers Helen Steele and Richard Malone, as well as her grandmother, who taught her how to sew on her first machine.

As she looks forward to the summer holidays, Sorcha is already planning her next collection, with a view to applying for the Junk Kouture competition later this year. The family say they are keeping her feet firmly on the ground, with education her top priority. But for many in the fashion world, this Kildare teenager is already a name to watch.
headline: A name to watch in fashion at just 13 years old

text:
Minister for Education Norma Foley has unveiled a €1 million fund to expand the provision of free schoolbooks in primary schools across the country. The announcement was made at a primary school in Co Cork yesterday, where Minister Foley met with pupils and staff who have already benefitted from the pilot scheme introduced last year.

The funding, which will be allocated for the 2024/2025 academic year, aims to support schools in purchasing textbooks, workbooks, and essential classroom resources for all pupils in junior and senior infants up to sixth class. The initiative is expected to ease financial pressure on families ahead of the new term and is part of the Department of Education’s broader commitment to making education more accessible to all children.

Speaking in Cork, Minister Foley said the move would help close the gap between families of different means and ensure every child has the resources they need to participate fully in school life. “Cost should not be a barrier to education. This fund will ensure that every child in our primary schools can access the resources they need, regardless of their background,” she said.

The fund will be distributed directly to primary schools, with the Department providing guidelines to ensure that resources are allocated fairly and meet the specific needs of each school community.

The initiative has been broadly welcomed by parent groups and school principals. The National Parents’ Council said it would make “a real difference to families, particularly at a time when back-to-school costs are rising.” The Irish National Teachers’ Organisation also gave its backing, noting that teachers have seen first-hand the challenge faced by pupils who go without essential books due to financial constraints.

Sinn Féin’s spokesperson on Education, Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire TD, said that while the funding is welcome, “It is essential that the government moves faster towards a truly free education system. Parents are still struggling with other costs including uniforms and voluntary contributions.”

Minister Foley indicated that the Department of Education is examining ways to expand the free books programme into post-primary schools in the coming years, subject to budgetary approval.

Schools will receive communication from the Department in the coming weeks outlining how to apply for and administer the new funding. The Department has also set up a dedicated helpline for school principals to provide support during the rollout of the scheme.

The measure comes as part of a wider drive by the Government to address educational inequality and follows previous initiatives, such as the extension of the school meals programme and additional supports for pupils with special educational needs.

The Department of Education estimates that more than 500,000 children will benefit from the free schoolbooks scheme when fully implemented. Schools are expected to begin receiving funds in time to order materials ahead of the September term.
headline: Education Minister announces €1m fund for free books in primary schools

text:
Beef price protests intensified in several parts of the country on Monday, as farmers voiced frustration over what they describe as inadequate progress in talks with processors, despite last week’s move by factories to withdraw legal proceedings against protestors. Demonstrations at major processing plants in counties Offaly, Cavan, and Waterford saw large crowds gather, with tractors lining roads and delays to deliveries reported.

The renewed escalation comes after leading industry representatives and farming organisations struck a compromise at the weekend aimed at bringing an end to weeks of disruption. Meat Industry Ireland (MII) agreed to drop High Court injunctions against individuals and farming bodies, a gesture described by the Tánaiste Micheál Martin as “an important step towards restoring dialogue and stability”.

However, many protesting farmers said they remain dissatisfied with what was achieved at the talks, citing continued concern over the lack of a concrete increase in base beef prices. “The lifting of the legal threat is welcome, but it doesn’t put money in our pockets,” said Eddie O’Brien, a beef finisher from west Waterford, outside the Dawn Meats facility in Grannagh. “Unless there’s a clear move on price, we’ll have no choice but to keep demonstrating.”

The Irish Farmers' Association (IFA) and the Beef Plan Movement confirmed their members were participating in ongoing local action this week, but both organisations have distanced themselves from some protests that have sprung up outside the formally agreed process. Some pickets have been described as “unofficial”, with Gardaí monitoring the situation and urging adherence to the law.

Minister for Agriculture Charlie McConalogue urged all sides to “use the breathing space created by the withdrawal of legal action to build a lasting solution”, warning that “further disruption risks undermining the progress made”. Meat processors maintain they have limited margin to raise farmgate prices, pointing to competitive pressure in EU markets and increased compliance costs.

The situation has drawn the attention of opposition TDs, with Sinn Féin’s Matt Carthy accusing the Government of “failing to address the imbalance of power between farmers and factories”. Labour’s Seán Sherlock called for the establishment of a beef regulator with statutory oversight. 

Meanwhile, supermarkets have reported sporadic supply issues, with some butchers warning of reduced availability of certain cuts if stoppages persist. The Irish Cattle and Sheep Farmers Association (ICSA) has called on all parties to “redouble their efforts at the negotiating table and prioritise the viability of family farms”.

Further talks are expected later this week, but as of Monday evening, blockades remained in place at several plants, and farmers were adamant their campaign would continue until there is what they term a “fair price for Irish beef”.
headline: Beef price protests escalate in some areas despite agreement to remove legal threat

text:
Two people have been killed and eight others wounded in a shooting attack in central Tel Aviv, according to Israeli authorities, in what has been described as one of the most serious incidents in the city in recent years.

The shooting occurred late on Thursday evening in the busy Dizengoff Street area, a popular nightlife hub, when a gunman opened fire on patrons outside a series of bars and restaurants. Eyewitnesses reported scenes of panic as people scrambled for cover while shots rang out. Emergency medical teams arrived within minutes, providing treatment to the injured before transferring them to local hospitals. The HSE has confirmed that, to their knowledge, no Irish citizens were harmed in the incident.

Israeli police said the attacker was killed after a manhunt that lasted several hours. Footage broadcast on Israeli television showed security forces searching rooftops and alleyways as armed officers instructed people to stay indoors. The two fatalities have not been formally identified, but officials stated that all victims were civilians. Of the eight wounded, four are reported to be in a serious condition.

The attack comes amid heightened tensions across Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories, following a series of violent incidents in recent weeks. Prime Minister Naftali Bennett convened an emergency meeting of security chiefs following the shooting, vowing that “no act of terror will break our spirit or divide us”.

No group has so far claimed responsibility for the Tel Aviv shooting, but police stated that initial indications pointed to a lone attacker with connections to the occupied West Bank. The Palestinian President, Mahmoud Abbas, issued a statement condemning attacks on civilians, while also warning against what he called “continued Israeli escalation”.

In a statement, Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin condemned the attack and expressed condolences to the families of those killed. “Ireland stands against all acts of violence and urges restraint from all parties at this time of heightened tension,” he said.

Security has been stepped up across Israel, with additional police patrols deployed in major cities. The Department of Foreign Affairs has updated its travel advice for Irish citizens in the region, urging caution and advising to avoid large gatherings or areas with a heightened security presence.

The incident marks the latest in a spate of attacks in Israel which have left 13 people dead over the past three weeks. Israeli analysts have warned of the risk of further escalation as the holy month of Ramadan coincides this year with Passover and Easter, traditionally a time of increased friction in the region.
headline: Two killed and eight wounded in Tel Aviv shooting

text:
The Government has announced the allocation of an emergency €1.1 million funding package to Dublin Zoo and Fota Wildlife Park in a move aimed at averting the imminent threat of closure due to the severe impact of Covid-19 restrictions on visitor income.

The Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage, Darragh O’Brien, confirmed the decision this morning, saying the funding would be released immediately to allow the two sites to cover the “essential ongoing costs” of caring for their animal collections over the winter months.

Both Dublin Zoo and Fota Wildlife Park had warned in recent weeks that a combination of the pandemic-induced loss of income, ongoing running costs, and the uncertainty over reopening timelines had left their future “hanging in the balance”. Visitor numbers, both parks said, had dropped by as much as 90% at the height of the restrictions and remained well below average due to social distancing requirements.

Speaking on RTÉ’s Morning Ireland, Dublin Zoo director Dr Christoph Schwitzer welcomed the announcement and described the funding as “a lifeline” that would allow the park to maintain animal care standards while exploring other revenue options. “While we are so grateful for the public’s support after our ‘Save Dublin Zoo’ campaign, this State intervention is crucial to our immediate survival,” he said.

Fota Wildlife Park’s director, Sean McKeown, echoed the sentiment, noting that the Cork-based facility had also reached a crisis point. “Fota is in a similar situation — our gates were closed for long periods during the year and our reserves are exhausted. This funding gives us breathing space into early next year, but a long-term solution will be needed,” he said.

The Department of Housing has said the €1.1m will be split between the two parks, with Dublin Zoo to receive €800,000 and Fota €300,000. Minister O’Brien said the funding “recognises the unique importance of our zoos, not just for conservation and education, but as places of joy for so many families throughout the country.” He added that the Government is committed to working with both organisations to explore more sustainable funding models in future.

Opposition parties have broadly welcomed the announcement but called for a review of long-term funding arrangements for facilities engaged in significant conservation work. Sinn Féin spokesperson for Heritage, Aengus Ó Snodaigh TD, said: “These parks play a vital role in species preservation and education — the State must ensure this work is properly resourced, not just in times of crisis.”

Animal welfare groups also expressed relief at the intervention, but said it was “essential” that animal welfare standards and transparency on expenditure be maintained.

Both parks said that despite the new funding, ongoing fundraising campaigns would continue and called on the public to support through online donations and symbolic ‘adoptions’ of animals.

Dublin Zoo has operated since 1831 and is home to over 400 rare and endangered animals, while the Fota Wildlife Park opened in 1983 and plays a key role in international breeding programmes for threatened species. Both have relied heavily on ticket sales, on-site events, and education programmes for income — all of which were curtailed by Covid-19 restrictions.

The Government said it would review the situation in early 2021 and consider additional support if necessary, depending on evolving public health guidance and the progression of the pandemic.
headline: Emergency €1.1m fund to help prevent closure of Dublin Zoo and Fota

text:
Veteran broadcaster Larry King, renowned for his decades-long career in American television and radio, has died at the age of 87.

The widely respected talk show host passed away at Cedars-Sinai Medical Centre in Los Angeles on Saturday morning, as confirmed by Ora Media, the production company he co-founded. No cause of death was immediately released, but Mr King had faced various health issues in recent years, including a bout with Covid-19.

Best known for his iconic show “Larry King Live,” which ran on CNN for 25 years, King interviewed thousands of guests, from presidents and world leaders to celebrities and ordinary citizens, developing a reputation for his direct yet empathetic interview style. His trademark suspenders and gravelly voice made him instantly recognisable to audiences worldwide.

Across a broadcasting career that spanned more than six decades, King conducted an estimated 50,000 interviews. His guests read like a who’s who of global society, including US presidents from Richard Nixon to Barack Obama, as well as figures such as Nelson Mandela, Lady Gaga, and Vladimir Putin.

King’s conversational approach and willingness to ask simple, open-ended questions drew both praise and critique. His method, however, often prompted forthright and revealing answers and he was widely credited with making complex issues accessible to the public.

Born Lawrence Zeiger in Brooklyn, New York in 1933, King began his career in radio in Miami before making the transition to television. His laid-back style became his signature, and “Larry King Live” soon became a mainstay of American—and international—media culture.

Tributes have come in from across the world, with celebrities and politicians alike marking King’s passing. Michelle Obama wrote, “Larry King was a master of the interview. He made every guest feel at home.” Piers Morgan, who succeeded King on CNN, described him as “a brilliant broadcaster and masterful TV interviewer.”

In Ireland, tributes were also forthcoming, with RTÉ’s Miriam O’Callaghan calling him “a pioneer who set the bar for broadcasters everywhere.” President Michael D Higgins acknowledged King’s “extraordinary contribution to public discourse.”

King is survived by three sons. His family have thanked fans for their support and requested privacy at this difficult time. Funeral arrangements are expected to be announced in due course.
headline: Legendary talk show host Larry King dies aged 87

text:
Thousands are expected to descend on Cork city and county this weekend as a packed calendar of events delivers a significant boost for local businesses and the hospitality sector. The Bank Holiday atmosphere is set to be heightened by a diverse mix of music, sport, and family-focused activities across the Rebel County.

The highly anticipated return of Live at the Marquee continues, with international acts such as The Coronas and The Script drawing sell-out crowds to the Docklands. Venues across the city are reporting near full capacity, as music fans flock from across Munster and beyond. Organisers have urged concert-goers to plan ahead, with increased parking restrictions and additional public transport options in place to accommodate demand. The Gardaí have advised motorists to expect delays in the city centre, particularly on Saturday night, and to avail of park-and-ride services where possible.

Elsewhere, the Cork Summer Show in Curraheen is set to welcome upwards of 40,000 visitors over two days, with organisers confident the spell of dry weather will see numbers surpass last year’s total. Exhibitors from across the region will showcase the very best in agriculture, artisan food, crafts, and entertainment, while the new biodiversity zone is expected to attract particular interest from families and school groups. Children will have their pick of amusements, while sporting displays and live cooking demonstrations promise to keep adults entertained.

In sport, Páirc Uí Chaoimh hosts a double-header on Sunday, with Cork’s senior hurlers and footballers both in action in their respective All-Ireland championship qualifiers. Ticket demand remains strong, and the Cork County Board has encouraged supporters to purchase in advance to avoid queues. Local businesses are bracing themselves for an influx, with many city centre pubs and restaurants laying on extra staff and extending hours in anticipation of post-match crowds.

Meanwhile, a host of smaller festivals and community events are taking place throughout the city’s suburbs and the wider county, from the Ballydehob Jazz Festival to the East Cork Food Trail. Tourism industry representatives have welcomed the upturn in visitor numbers, saying it comes at a vital time for the sector. Hotels in the city are reporting occupancy close to 90%, with many rural guesthouses also benefiting from the increased footfall.

Cork Chamber CEO, Conor Healy, said the weekend’s array of events underlines the city’s status as a leading destination for cultural and sporting life. “This is an opportunity for Cork to showcase its vibrancy, creativity, and hospitality. The positive impact for local businesses and employment cannot be overstated,” he said.

The Gardaí have confirmed a visible policing presence will be maintained across major venues and city hot spots, with additional patrols focusing on public safety and anti-social behaviour. Weather conditions are set to remain favourable, with Met Éireann forecasting dry and mild conditions throughout the weekend.

Organisers across the board have called on festival-goers and sports fans to respect local communities and to dispose of litter responsibly. With Cork set to thrum to the beat of summer, the outlook is upbeat for what promises to be one of the busiest weekends in recent memory.
headline: Beat goes on for busy weekend in Cork

text:
A man has appeared in court charged in connection with the seizure of €6.5 million worth of cannabis herb at Rosslare Europort earlier this week.

The 37-year-old, who is originally from Eastern Europe but has an address in Co Meath, was arrested by Gardaí after Revenue officers discovered the drugs concealed in a shipment which arrived off a ferry from Cherbourg, France, on Wednesday.

Customs officials conducting routine examinations at the port uncovered the cannabis hidden in a consignment of what was declared as food products. The seizure, made as part of ongoing operations targeting organised criminal activity at the country’s main ferry ports, is one of the largest at Rosslare so far this year.

The man was detained at Wexford Garda Station under Section 2 of the Criminal Justice (Drug Trafficking) Act, 1996. He was subsequently charged last night and brought before a special sitting of Wexford District Court this morning.

Detective Garda Michael Byrne told the court that the accused made no reply when the charge was put to him after caution. The court heard an application for bail is to be made at a later date, with the man remanded in custody to appear again before the court next week.

Legal aid was granted by Judge Brian O’Shea. The man’s solicitor told the court that her client was co-operating fully with the investigation.

In a statement, the Revenue Commissioners said the seizure was the result of "intelligence-led" work and "excellent co-operation" between Revenue, the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau, and local Gardaí. The drugs have an estimated street value of €6.5 million, pending further analysis.

Investigations are ongoing, and Gardaí have not ruled out further arrests in connection with the incident. The HSE and other agencies have been notified and are monitoring any potential impact on drug activity in the region.
headline: Man charged over €6.5m drug seizure at Rosslare Europort

text:
A viable pipe bomb has been made safe by army technical officers after it was discovered in Co Down earlier today.

The suspicious device was located near a residential area in the Lower Dromore Road area of Warrenpoint, prompting a security alert that lasted for several hours. The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) evacuated a number of homes and established a security cordon shortly after the item was reported at approximately 10:30am.

Army bomb disposal experts were called to the scene and conducted a controlled examination of the device, which was confirmed to be a viable pipe bomb. It was later defused and removed for further forensic analysis.

Inspector Darren Hardy of the PSNI said, “This was a reckless and dangerous act that had the potential to cause serious injury or worse. We would like to thank local residents for their patience and cooperation as we worked to ensure their safety.”

Road closures were in place for several hours, causing some local disruption. Gardaí and emergency services in the Republic were informed as a precaution, given the proximity to the border. There have been no reports of injuries.

SDLP MLA Sinead Bradley condemned those responsible, saying, “There is absolutely no place for this kind of behaviour in our community. It has caused unnecessary fear and disruption to families and residents.”

The PSNI has appealed for anyone with information or who witnessed suspicious activity in the area to contact officers at Ardmore station on the non-emergency number 101, or to provide information anonymously via Crimestoppers.

The scene has since been declared safe and residents have returned to their homes.
headline: Pipe bomb defused after being found in Co Down

text:
Jozef Puska has been granted legal aid to appeal his conviction for the murder of Ashling Murphy in Co Offaly last year. The decision was made this morning at the Court of Appeal in Dublin, where Puska appeared via video link from Midlands Prison.

Puska, originally from Slovakia and with an address at Lynally Grove, Mucklagh, Tullamore, was last November found guilty by a jury at the Central Criminal Court of the murder of 23-year-old Ms Murphy as she jogged along the Grand Canal in Tullamore on 12 January 2022. He was subsequently sentenced to life imprisonment.

His legal representatives told the court that Puska does not have the means to fund a legal challenge and requested that he be granted a legal aid certificate for the appeal process. The application was not opposed by the State, and the three-judge panel approved the request.

In accordance with standard procedure, the next step will be for Puska’s legal team to lodge formal grounds of appeal. No date has yet been set for the hearing. Typically, appeal hearings in murder cases consider whether there were errors of law in the conduct of the trial or the judge’s directions to the jury.

Members of Ms Murphy’s family were not present in court for this morning’s brief procedural hearing. Outside the court, a solicitor for the family said they have been informed of developments and continue to take each stage of the legal process “one day at a time”.

The high-profile case led to a significant outpouring of public grief and renewed conversations about violence against women in Ireland. Ms Murphy, a primary school teacher and talented musician, was widely mourned.

Puska will remain in custody pending the outcome of the appeal process. If successful, the conviction could be set aside or a retrial ordered. However, legal experts say the threshold for overturning a murder conviction on appeal remains high.

The Legal Aid Board will now assign counsel to prepare Puska’s case. The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions is expected to respond to any grounds of appeal once they are lodged. The Court of Appeal has indicated it will list the case for mention when ready.
headline: Puska granted legal aid to appeal murder conviction

text:
A US military aircraft crashed in Kuwait this morning, with dramatic footage circulating widely on social media showing the plane losing control before plummeting to the ground in a remote desert area. The incident occurred near Ali Al Salem Air Base, a key site for US and coalition forces stationed in the Middle East.

According to reports from Kuwait’s civil defence authorities, emergency services were dispatched to the crash site, where a plume of smoke could be seen rising from the wreckage. The Kuwaiti Ministry of Interior confirmed the incident and said that search and rescue operations were underway. There has been no official statement so far regarding casualties, nor the specific type of aircraft involved.

US Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the region, acknowledged the crash in a brief statement, saying that an investigation is underway and promising further details “as soon as they are available”. It is understood that no Irish citizens were involved in the incident.

The cause of the crash remains unclear, although unverified video footage appears to show the aircraft descending rapidly before losing altitude and disappearing behind sand dunes. Aviation experts have indicated that weather conditions in the area were clear at the time, ruling out immediate concerns over visibility.

Local Kuwaiti authorities have cordoned off the area and urged the public to avoid sharing unverified information online. The US Embassy in Kuwait issued a statement thanking emergency responders and said it is cooperating fully with host nation officials.

Ali Al Salem Air Base is a strategic hub for US and NATO operations, and is frequently used for the transit of troops and military equipment to and from the region. The crash is likely to trigger a review of operational safety at the base, as well as renewed scrutiny of US military activities in the Middle East.

Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs, Micheál Martin, said the Department of Foreign Affairs was monitoring the situation closely and expressed relief that there were no indications of Irish citizens being affected. The Department advised any Irish nationals in the region to register with the Embassy and to follow official advice.

The Pentagon is expected to release further details on the circumstances of the crash later today. US military aircraft accidents in the Gulf region are rare, but not unprecedented, given the high tempo of operations and regional security challenges. The US maintains a significant military presence in Kuwait, as part of its broader strategic posture in the Middle East.
headline: Watch: US military plane plummets from sky in Kuwait

text:
North Korea has announced its intention to deploy new weapons along its border with South Korea, in a move that has raised tensions and prompted concern from the international community. The decision comes amid an escalation in hostile rhetoric between the two neighbouring states on the Korean Peninsula.

Pyongyang’s official Korean Central News Agency reported on Tuesday that the North Korean army will introduce “more powerful and advanced military hardware” to forward positions in response to what it described as “provocations” by South Korea and the United States. The statement did not specify the type or quantity of weapons to be deployed but warned that the North’s “counteractions will be immediate and overwhelming”.

The South Korean government condemned the announcement as an “unacceptable threat to regional peace and stability”. In a statement, Seoul’s Ministry of National Defence urged Pyongyang to halt military activities that could “further destabilise the region”.

Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin called for restraint and dialogue, expressing “deep concern” over the rising tensions. “Ireland, as a longstanding supporter of peace and disarmament, urges all parties to adhere to international norms and return to diplomatic engagement,” a spokesperson for the department said.

The United Nations Security Council convened an emergency session on the matter yesterday. UN Secretary-General António Guterres reiterated his “grave concern” regarding North Korea’s continued weapons development and urged both Koreas to “exercise maximum restraint”.

This latest development follows a series of recent missile tests carried out by North Korea, which the US and its allies say violate Security Council resolutions. Last week, North Korea claimed it had successfully tested new tactical guided weapon systems, while South Korea and the US have stepped up combined military drills in response.

Experts have warned that the deployment of new weaponry at the heavily fortified border, known as the Demilitarised Zone, could spark miscalculation and accidental clashes. Dr. Patricia Lee, senior fellow at the Institute for International and European Affairs, told RTÉ News: “An arms build-up along the DMZ increases the risk of escalation – both sides are on a hair trigger and the margin for error is very small.”

Irish nationals in South Korea have been advised by the Department of Foreign Affairs to monitor developments closely and follow the advice of local authorities. There are currently around 1,000 Irish citizens living in the country, according to DFA figures.

The border between North and South Korea, established following the Korean War armistice in 1953, remains one of the most militarised frontiers in the world. Despite several rounds of talks in recent years, there has been little progress towards denuclearisation or formal peace.

The Irish Government reiterated its support for diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions and building trust on the peninsula. “Only through dialogue can the two Koreas hope to achieve lasting peace and security for their peoples,” Minister Martin said.
headline: North Korea vows to deploy new weapons at border

text:
Financial services company BNY has announced plans to close its facility in Wexford, with the loss of approximately 170 jobs. Staff at the site, which operates under BNY’s investment services division, were informed of the decision today.

The company, formerly known as BNY Mellon, has had a presence in Wexford since 2002, originally operating under the name PNC International Bank before it was acquired by the US-based banking giant. The Wexford facility specialises in fund accounting, transfer agency and custody support for international clients.

A spokesperson for BNY said the company had taken the “difficult decision” to wind down operations in Wexford following a strategic review of its global footprint. The spokesperson cited the need to streamline operations and “drive efficiency” across its European network.

“We recognise the impact this announcement will have on our colleagues, their families and the wider community,” the spokesperson said. “We are committed to engaging with impacted employees and providing support, including redeployment opportunities in other offices where possible, as well as outplacement services.”

The closure is expected to be phased, with a wind-down period over the next 12 months. Some roles may be relocated to BNY’s Dublin office, while others could be absorbed into its European operations.

Local public representatives have described the news as a blow to the region. Labour TD Brendan Howlin said the announcement was “hugely disappointing,” with significant consequences for the local economy. “BNY has been a major employer in Wexford for over two decades,” he said. “We will be engaging with the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment and with the IDA to ensure every support is made available to affected workers.”

Sinn Féin TD Johnny Mythen echoed those concerns, calling on the Government to prioritise new investment in the South East. “We cannot allow these skilled jobs to be lost from the area without concerted action to attract alternative employers,” he said.

BNY employs more than 1,500 people in Ireland across offices in Dublin, Cork and Wexford. The company said it remained committed to its presence in Ireland, which it described as a key European centre for its investment services business.

Minister of State for Business, Neale Richmond, said he was “deeply disappointed” by the announcement and that the Government would mobilise support, including engagement with the Department of Social Protection and the Education and Training Boards to provide retraining options.

The IDA said it would work closely with BNY, relevant government departments, and local agencies to support affected employees and to “identify further opportunities for investment in the region.” The agency highlighted that the South East continues to be a strong location for financial services, with a skilled workforce and well-developed infrastructure.

Consultation with employees and their representatives is set to begin in the coming weeks. Union sources have called for a fair redundancy package and access to redeployment opportunities, while also pressing for increased government focus on regional employment.

The Wexford Chamber of Commerce said it was seeking a meeting with the company and local political representatives to discuss ways to mitigate the impact of the closure.
headline: Financial services firm BNY to close its Wexford facility

text:
A man arrested in connection with the murder of Sean Fox in west Belfast has been released, the PSNI have confirmed.

The man, aged in his 50s, had been detained on Wednesday for questioning by detectives from the Major Investigation Team. He was released on Thursday afternoon pending a report to the Public Prosecution Service.

Sean Fox, who was 42, was shot dead at point blank range in the Donegal Celtic Social Club in October 2022. Two masked gunmen entered the premises on the Suffolk Road in broad daylight and fired multiple shots, killing Mr Fox as he sat with friends.

Investigators believe the murder was carefully planned and linked to an ongoing feud involving organised criminal gangs in the city. Mr Fox was known to Gardaí and the PSNI.

In a statement issued today, the PSNI said their enquiries are continuing and have appealed for anyone with information to come forward.

The murder, carried out in front of numerous witnesses, sent shockwaves through the local community and renewed calls for increased action to tackle gun violence and organised crime in Belfast. Security sources have described the killing as “a brutal and calculated execution”.

The Gardaí are understood to be assisting their PSNI counterparts as part of a cross-border intelligence operation focusing on criminal networks with links in both jurisdictions.

To date, several people have been arrested and questioned in relation to the murder, but no one has been charged. Investigators are examining CCTV footage, forensic evidence and mobile phone data as part of the ongoing inquiry.

Mr Fox’s funeral last year was attended by hundreds of mourners, with his family pleading for justice and urging anyone with information to come forward. Detectives have again renewed their appeal for witnesses or those who may have recorded video footage at the scene to contact police directly or via the confidential Crimestoppers service.
headline: Man released in Sean Fox murder investigation

text:
Sir Keir Starmer has admitted he was mistaken in naming Lord Peter Mandelson as his preferred choice for Britain’s ambassador to the United States, following mounting criticism from within his own party and senior civil servants.

Speaking to journalists after a campaign event in Birmingham on Friday, the Labour leader acknowledged he had overstepped convention by discussing possible diplomatic appointments before the outcome of the general election is known. “I realise now it was inappropriate to name any individual for a role that is not in the gift of the opposition,” said Starmer. “I have spoken to Peter Mandelson and apologised for any embarrassment caused.”

Lord Mandelson, a former Minister under Tony Blair and one of the architects of New Labour, was widely tipped to be sent to Washington should Labour form the next government. However, Starmer’s comments sparked controversy, with opposition parties accusing him of taking the electorate for granted and senior officials warning that diplomatic posts should not be politicised.

The Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office also released a statement reminding all parties that ambassadors are appointed by the government of the day “in accordance with established procedures” and are subject to approval from the head of state in the host country.

Several Labour MPs expressed concern that the announcement fuelled perceptions of cronyism, with one backbencher telling RTÉ News: “If we’re serious about a fresh start, we can’t be handing out jobs to political insiders before we’ve even won.”

Political analysts said the gaffe could dent Starmer’s efforts to present himself as a steady hand ahead of next month’s election, in which Labour is currently leading the Conservatives in opinion polls. In Ireland, the Tánaiste Micheál Martin noted the importance of the UK maintaining close relationships with the US and said “it’s for the British authorities to decide on such matters.”

Lord Mandelson himself issued a brief statement on Friday evening, saying: “I am grateful for Sir Keir’s confidence in me, but I have made no commitments and will not comment further on speculation.”

The controversy comes as the campaign enters its final fortnight, with party leaders seeking to avoid missteps that could sway undecided voters. Starmer reiterated Labour’s commitment to restoring “standards and integrity” in public life, adding: “Ultimately, it is for the British people to decide who governs — and for the government to appoint ambassadors in due course.”
headline: Starmer says he was wrong to name Mandelson as US envoy

Tributes have been paid across Donegal and further afield to Joey Forker, the popular businessman and community stalwart who died suddenly on Sunday. Mr Forker, aged 58, from Ballybofey, was remembered as a “larger than life character” whose presence enlivened every room and event he attended.

Family, friends, and members of the business community have voiced their shock at his unexpected passing. The Forker family have operated Forker’s Hardware in Ballybofey for decades, with Joey’s good humour and generous spirit becoming well-known throughout the Finn Valley and beyond.

Local TD Pat the Cope Gallagher described Mr Forker as “a man who gave so much back to the community,” highlighting his involvement with numerous voluntary initiatives in the area. “Joey was the first to step forward whenever there was a need, whether it was a charity fundraising night or simply helping a neighbour in need. Donegal is poorer for his loss,” he said.

The president of the Ballybofey and Stranorlar Chamber of Commerce, Mary Friel, said that Mr Forker’s passion for the town and its people made him “a driving force for positive change.” She noted that his shop was “much more than a business—Joey made sure it was a hub for the community, a place where you’d always find a welcome and a bit of craic.”

Local GAA clubs and sports organisations paid tribute on social media, recalling Forker’s years of support for youth teams and events. “He never made a fuss, but he was always there when help was needed—on the sidelines, at the gate, or dropping supplies for fundraisers,” said Finn Harps chair Brian McElhinney.

Prayers were offered for Mr Forker at morning Mass in St. Mary’s Church, Stranorlar, where parish priest Fr Seamus Duffy told the congregation that “Joey’s big heart and big laugh will be greatly missed by all who knew him.”

The Forker family have asked for privacy as they make funeral arrangements. In a statement, they thanked the community for “the outpouring of love and support in this difficult time.”

Joey Forker is survived by his wife, Maureen, and three children. Funeral details are expected to be announced in the coming days.
headline: Tributes to 'larger than life' Joey Forker in Donegal

text:
The death toll from a fire that broke out at a ski resort in eastern Turkey has risen to 76, according to local authorities. Emergency services are continuing their search of the Palandöken Mountain resort in the city of Erzurum after the blaze swept through a section of the accommodation complex late last night.

Turkish Interior Minister Ali Yerlikaya confirmed the updated fatalities figure in a statement this morning, adding that a further 11 people have been hospitalised, with some in a critical condition. The cause of the fire is under investigation, but initial reports suggest it may have started in the sauna area of the building before spreading rapidly through several storeys.

Footage broadcast on national television showed firefighters battling the flames and rescuing guests from upper floors using ladders, as thick smoke enveloped much of the complex. Many of the victims are believed to be domestic tourists who had travelled to the popular resort for an annual winter festival.

Search teams, including members of the Turkish disaster and emergency management authority (AFAD), laboured throughout the night and into the morning to account for guests and staff who had been registered at the resort. Officials said the operation was hampered by heavy snowfall and freezing temperatures, which are common in the region at this time of year.

The Turkish President, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, expressed his condolences to the families of those who died, calling the fire a “devastating tragedy”. The local prosecutor’s office has opened an inquiry, and authorities have detained two people for questioning.

The Department of Foreign Affairs in Ireland said it is aware of the incident but has not received any requests for consular assistance so far. A spokesperson said the department is monitoring the situation and is ready to provide support to Irish citizens if needed.

The Erzurum ski area is a popular destination for visitors from across Turkey and abroad. This is understood to be the deadliest fire in the region for many years and the overall death toll is expected to rise, as emergency workers continue to sift through the damaged building.

The Turkish Red Crescent has deployed teams to the scene to provide psychological support to survivors and families impacted by the tragedy. Government officials say a full review of safety protocols at ski resorts across the country will take place in response to the disaster.
headline: Death toll in Turkish ski resort fire jumps to 76 people

Firefighters from Donegal County Council have been battling a significant wildfire on the Fanad Peninsula since early this morning. The blaze, which broke out on hillside gorse and scrubland near the village of Portsalon, has spread rapidly due to strong winds and dry conditions, prompting an urgent response from local fire services.

Crews from fire stations in Letterkenny, Milford and Buncrana were mobilised shortly after 9am when residents reported smoke and flames advancing towards houses in the Drumfad area. Firefighters have been using beaters and water tankers in an effort to contain the fire and prevent it from crossing local roads and threatening properties.

Local residents were advised by the Gardaí to remain indoors and keep doors and windows closed as a precaution, due to heavy smoke in the area. Some homes at risk were temporarily evacuated, though it is understood most residents have since returned once the immediate danger passed. No injuries have been reported.

A spokesperson for Donegal County Council said that fire crews were facing challenging conditions due to strong gusts and the remote terrain. “The priority is to protect homes and prevent the fire from spreading further into forestry and farmland. Our crews are working tirelessly and we are grateful for the support of the local community,” the spokesperson said.

The HSE has urged people with respiratory issues to be especially vigilant and to avoid the affected area if possible. The Gardaí have put diversions in place on several local roads to allow access for emergency vehicles.

The cause of the fire is not yet known. However, the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine has warned that the risk of wildfires remains high across the north-west due to the recent spell of dry weather.

Aerial support has not yet been requested, but council officials are monitoring the situation closely and will seek assistance from the Air Corps if conditions deteriorate.

Emergency services have appealed to the public to avoid lighting fires in rural areas and to report any suspicious activity to the Gardaí. Firefighting operations are expected to continue into the evening.
headline: Firefighters tackling wildfire on Fanad Peninsula

text:
A peculiar sense of déjà vu hangs over Leinster House this week, as echoes of political controversies past resurface amid an already fraught winter session. The intended business—debate of Budget measures, scrutiny of the HSE's winter plans, the escalating housing crisis—has been overshadowed by a series of reminders that for all talk of “new politics”, age-old issues persist at the heart of Irish governance.

The most striking apparition has been the unexpected return of public service pay disputes to the political centre stage. The scenes in committee rooms this week—detailing the HSE’s strained recruitment and retention, and the ongoing industrial unease among nurses and paramedics—have strong parallels with the difficult winters of a decade ago, when fiscal crisis and staff strikes repeatedly tested the patience of the public and the agility of ministers. The Government insists this time it is better prepared, pointing to contingency planning and a more robust fiscal position. Yet the language of “sacrifice”, “shared hardship”, and “difficult choices” has once again crept into ministerial statements, reminding many of the austerity years.

The passage of the Housing (Amendment) Bill, too, has brought up ghosts older and perhaps even more deeply rooted. Opposition TDs, especially from Sinn Féin and the Social Democrats, have seized the moment to invoke the collapse of the ‘Celtic Tiger’ property bubble, warning the current administration not to repeat the mistakes of the past. In the Dáil chamber, accusations of “developer-led policy” and “systematic neglect” of social housing echoed charges levelled at successive governments since the financial crash. It is clear the housing crisis, now in its second decade, continues to haunt the political class with no straightforward path towards either closure or consensus.

Not to be outdone, this week’s controversies around the conduct of certain office-holders—ranging from issues of political donations to the ongoing saga of ministerial expense claims—have spurred talk in the corridors of Leinster House of the kind not widely heard since the fallout from the Moriarty and Mahon Tribunals. While standards in public office have undoubtedly improved, there is a palpable anxiety among backbenchers and Cabinet alike that missteps, however minor by comparison, might quickly snowball in the current climate of distrust. The opposition has not hesitated to remind the Government of the need for vigilance and transparency: the lessons of history, it seems, are never truly forgotten.

A more literal haunting came when an Oireachtas tour guide, with more sense of humour than fear, recounted yet again the tales of roaming spirits said to pace the corridors after hours. It is, after all, a building steeped in centuries of Irish political life, from the birth of the State to the present day, carrying with it the accumulated memory of both triumph and scandal.

For all the talk of change, modernisation, and a move away from the era of “nod and wink” politics, events at Leinster House this Christmas confirm that the past remains a powerful—if unwelcome—presence. The challenge facing the Government in the year ahead will be not only to address the crises at hand, but to finally lay to rest the ghosts of previous failures still wandering the halls. Whether this can be achieved, or whether these spectres will continue to shape political reality, remains the central question haunting Irish political life as 2024 draws to a close.
headline: Leinster House visited by Ghost of Christmas Past

text:
The Government’s updated housing strategy, published this week, seeks to address mounting concerns over affordability, supply, and homelessness as the housing crisis continues to dominate Irish political discourse. With Housing Minister Darragh O’Brien under sustained spotlight, the plan’s revised targets and new measures aim to reassure both the public and coalition partners that progress can be made.

At the heart of the announcement is a commitment to increase new housing supply, targeting an average of 40,000 homes per year by 2026—up from the previous 33,000 annual target. The ambition acknowledges population growth projections and the record levels of net migration, but critics, including opposition TDs and housing advocates, are sceptical about whether these numbers are realistic, citing the persistent gap between announced targets and actual completions in recent years.

The plan introduces an expanded role for state agencies such as the Land Development Agency and the Housing Agency. Both bodies are being given additional resources and powers to expedite housing delivery on state-owned land. The Government argues this will accelerate the provision of social and affordable homes, but questions remain over how swiftly these institutions can overcome planning, legal, and infrastructural bottlenecks that have hampered progress to date.

A notable new policy lever is the extension and broadening of affordability schemes, including an increase in the income eligibility thresholds for the First Home Scheme and the expansion of the Tenant Purchase Scheme. The move is designed to assist more middle-income renters in accessing home ownership—a growing cohort squeezed by high rents and deposit requirements. However, there are ongoing warnings that such interventions risk pushing up house prices further unless accompanied by significant increases in supply.

On homelessness, the plan promises additional emergency accommodation and increased supports, as the number of people without a home reached yet another peak in recent Department of Housing figures. The Government maintains existing eviction protections for the most vulnerable and has signalled further investment in Housing First and wraparound services. Yet advocacy groups such as Focus Ireland and the Simon Communities stress that without rapid scaling up of social housing construction, the underlying pressures will persist.

Finally, the plan’s response to planning challenges is under close scrutiny. A new Planning Bill is pledged to streamline the system, reduce judicial review delays, and give local authorities greater autonomy in zoning and development. The industry and local government have broadly welcomed these proposed reforms, but environmental groups and residents’ associations are wary of any perceived weakening of public consultation or oversight.

The Government’s housing plan is therefore a balancing act—between ambition and deliverability, state intervention and market forces, and short-term crisis response and long-term reform. With a general election likely within the next eighteen months, its success or failure will have profound consequences not just for the current coalition, but for public confidence in the political system’s ability to tackle Ireland’s most urgent social challenge.
headline: 5 takeaways from Government's housing plan

text:
Several Gardaí were injured last night after violent unrest erupted in Dublin city centre in the aftermath of a stabbing incident that left three people hospitalised, including a young child.

The initial disturbance occurred shortly after 1pm on Parnell Square East, when a man allegedly attacked a woman and two children outside a primary school. Emergency services attended the scene and the injured parties were transferred to Temple Street Children’s Hospital and the Mater Hospital. The suspect, a man in his forties, was detained by Gardaí and is currently being treated for injuries in hospital under Garda custody.

In the hours following the incident, large crowds began to gather in the city centre. By early evening, the demonstration escalated, with groups engaging in violent clashes with Gardaí. Missiles, including stones and glass bottles, were thrown at officers and Garda vehicles. Several buses and a Luas tram were set alight near O’Connell Street, and numerous shops were looted or damaged in the area.

Sources in An Garda Síochána described the scenes as “unprecedented in recent years”, with reinforcement units, including the Public Order Unit, deployed in significant numbers in an effort to restore order. Pepper spray and batons were used amid tense confrontations.

Garda Commissioner Drew Harris condemned the violence, stating: “We are dealing with a serious public order situation, and our priority is to ensure the safety of the public, our officers, and the wider community.” He confirmed that a number of Gardaí sustained injuries, though none are believed to be life-threatening. At least 34 people have been arrested so far and are being held at various Garda stations across the city.

Public transport services through the city centre were suspended throughout the evening, and a number of city businesses closed early as a precaution. The HSE advised the public to avoid the affected area and confirmed that hospital emergency departments remained fully operational, though staff were on high alert.

Taoiseach Leo Varadkar expressed his shock at the events, saying: “Violence and destruction on our streets are unacceptable, and those responsible will be held to account.” The Minister for Justice, Helen McEntee, has pledged additional resources for An Garda Síochána as investigations continue.

Forensic officers have launched a major inquiry into both the stabbing and subsequent disorder. Gardaí are appealing for anyone with footage of the incidents to come forward, and have set up a dedicated incident room at Mountjoy Garda Station.

Dublin City Council is working to assess the damage and begin clean-up operations, with local representatives warning of the long-term impacts on businesses and the community. Gardaí have said a visible Garda presence will remain in place in the city centre for the coming days.
headline: Gardaí attacked during violent unrest after stabbing

text:
Twenty-seven individuals have been sentenced at Belfast Crown Court in what has been described as the largest tax fraud case ever prosecuted in Northern Ireland. The defendants, who operated as part of a network spanning across several counties in both Northern Ireland and the Republic, were convicted of a sophisticated VAT carousel fraud involving more than €25 million.

The prosecution was brought following a joint investigation by HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) and the Garda National Economic Crime Bureau. The court heard that the group established a series of shell companies which purported to trade in electronic goods, including mobile phones and computer components, in order to manipulate VAT returns and claim refunds to which they were not entitled.

Detectives described the operation as “highly organised”, with funds laundered through bank accounts in the North, Britain, and the Republic. The fraudulent activity was said to have taken place over a period of four years, from 2017 to 2021, and included dozens of fake invoices and the use of counterfeit documentation to evade detection.

Sentencing the defendants, Mr Justice O’Hara said the fraud represented a “serious and sustained attack on the public finances” and stressed the importance of deterrence in such cases. He handed down sentences ranging from two to seven years’ imprisonment, with several defendants receiving concurrent sentences for related money-laundering offences.

In a statement following the hearing, a spokesperson for HMRC welcomed the outcome, saying it demonstrated that “those who abuse the tax system face significant consequences.” The Gardaí also praised the cross-border co-operation, noting that several of the accused had addresses in counties Louth, Monaghan and Donegal. Extradition proceedings had earlier taken place in the High Court in Dublin for four of the main organisers, with warrants executed under the European Arrest Warrant Act.

The court was told that almost €10 million has been recovered so far, with further asset seizure proceedings ongoing in both jurisdictions. The judge also ordered confiscation hearings in respect of the principal organisers, which are expected to take place later this year.

Legal aid was granted to all defendants. There was a significant security presence at court, and proceedings were attended by representatives of Revenue, the Criminal Assets Bureau, and the PSNI. The case is regarded as a landmark in efforts to tackle organised financial crime on the island of Ireland.
headline: 27 people sentenced in biggest tax fraud case in NI

text:
The Archbishop of Canterbury, Justin Welby, is facing mounting pressure to resign following allegations of mishandling safeguarding concerns within the Church of England. Senior clergy, alongside members of the laity and victims’ advocacy groups, have called for Archbishop Welby to step aside pending an independent review into the Church’s procedures.

The controversy centres on several cases where survivors of clerical abuse claim their complaints were inadequately addressed by church authorities. While the Church of England’s National Safeguarding Team has stated that steps are being taken to improve its processes, critics argue that recent revelations point to “systemic failures” at the highest levels of leadership. Archbishop Welby, who was appointed in 2013, has previously apologised to survivors and acknowledged shortcomings within the institution, but has insisted that significant reforms are underway.

A letter signed by several senior figures within the Church, including two retired bishops, was delivered to Lambeth Palace yesterday, urging the Archbishop to consider his position. “As the principal leader of the Anglican Communion, the Archbishop must be beyond reproach with regard to safeguarding,” it read. “We feel that the time has come for Archbishop Welby to allow for new leadership to restore trust.”

The situation has drawn the attention of the British Parliament, with a cross-party group of MPs calling for an urgent debate. In Westminster today, Labour MP Sarah Owen said, “The public and the Church deserve full accountability. Survivors should not have to wait any longer for justice.”

The Gardaí have confirmed they have not received any requests for assistance from British authorities in relation to the allegations. The Department of Foreign Affairs has also stated that it is monitoring the situation, given the close relationship between the Church of Ireland and the wider Anglican Communion.

In Dublin, the Archbishop of Dublin, the Most Reverend Dr Michael Jackson, said that the Church of Ireland is committed to “full compliance with best practice in safeguarding” and expressed concern for all survivors of abuse. “The wellbeing and safety of parishioners must remain our paramount priority,” he said.

Archbishop Welby has declined to comment directly on calls for his resignation, but a spokesperson for Lambeth Palace said he “remains focused on implementing the recommendations from the recent independent safeguarding reviews”. The Archbishop is due to travel to Rome for an interfaith gathering next week but is expected to make a further statement upon his return.

Survivors’ groups across Ireland and Britain have said they will continue to campaign for greater transparency and accountability within the Church. The National Board for Safeguarding Children in the Catholic Church in Ireland said it would be engaging with Anglican counterparts “to share learning and ensure rigorous protections are in place in all faith communities”.

The controversy is the latest in a series of challenges facing the Church of England, which has seen declining attendance and internal divisions over social issues in recent years. The calls for Archbishop Welby’s resignation overshadow preparations for the upcoming General Synod, where safeguarding is expected to dominate the agenda.
headline: Archbishop of Canterbury urged to resign over scandal
