Concerns are mounting among parents, educators, and health professionals over the proliferation of so-called ‘SkinnyTok’ content on TikTok, with calls for greater accountability from the social media platform regarding the promotion of body image issues among young people in Ireland.

The trend, which involves users posting videos that glorify extreme thinness, strict calorie restriction, and rapid weight loss, has drawn criticism for its potential to fuel disordered eating behaviours, particularly among teenagers and young women. Posts associated with hashtags such as #SkinnyTok and #Thinspo have been viewed millions of times worldwide, with Irish users among those engaging with the content.

The Psychological Society of Ireland (PSI) has warned that such videos can negatively impact impressionable audiences, citing an increase in reports of anxiety and body dissatisfaction among adolescents. Dr Sinéad O’Malley, a clinical psychologist specialising in adolescent mental health, told RTÉ News that the trend “normalises unhealthy attitudes towards food and body image” and “may contribute to the rising number of eating disorder cases being seen by the HSE.”

According to the HSE, there has been a notable increase in referrals to eating disorder services in recent years, with over 2,000 young people receiving treatment in 2023, up from 1,300 in 2020. The service warned that social media is “an increasingly significant factor” in the development and maintenance of these disorders.

The Department of Education issued a statement on Monday, expressing concern over the trend and advising schools to “be vigilant and support students in developing critical media literacy skills.” The statement also called on parents to familiarise themselves with the content their children are exposed to online.

TikTok, which has over one billion users globally and lists Ireland as its European headquarters, has previously stated that it is “committed to protecting users” and removes content that violates its community guidelines, including the promotion of eating disorders. However, advocacy groups argue that the company is not doing enough.

The Irish Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (ISPCC) called for an “urgent review of TikTok’s algorithms and moderation practices,” saying the platform must take greater responsibility for harmful content. In a letter to Minister for Children Roderic O’Gorman, the ISPCC urged the Government to work with the forthcoming Media Commission to strengthen regulatory measures.

Fine Gael TD Emer Higgins, chair of the Oireachtas Committee on Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, said the committee would invite representatives from TikTok to appear before it to address concerns. “It’s vital that tech companies are held to account and that children’s wellbeing is put front and centre,” Deputy Higgins said.

TikTok said in a statement to RTÉ News that it “prohibits content promoting eating disorders and removes such material when identified,” and encouraged users to report harmful posts. The company added that it works closely with mental health organisations in Ireland and provides in-app resources to users searching for terms related to eating disorders.

However, critics remain sceptical about the effectiveness of such measures. Dr O’Malley said, “While guidelines and reporting mechanisms are important, the reality is that these videos are still highly visible, and the algorithms often push them toward vulnerable users.”

As concern grows, parents and campaigners are urging both regulators and social media companies to do more to protect children from online harms.
headline: Calls for TikTok accountability over 'SkinnyTok' trend

text:
Six children are currently awaiting placement in a special care unit, the Child and Family Agency, Tusla, has confirmed. The figures emerged at an Oireachtas committee meeting on Wednesday, amid ongoing concerns about the availability of places for vulnerable young people in crisis.

Special care units provide secure accommodation for children who are at serious risk to themselves or others, and for whom no other suitable care arrangement can be found. Placement in such units is ordered by the High Court, following an application by Tusla.

Speaking before the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, Tusla’s Chief Executive Officer Kate Duggan told TDs and Senators that the six children currently waiting for a space have already been approved for special care by the courts. Ms Duggan said that every effort was being made to identify placements as quickly as possible, and that the safety and welfare of the children remained the top priority.

"We absolutely acknowledge the distress this causes for the children and families involved," Ms Duggan said, adding that Tusla was actively working to expand capacity across the three special care units in the State.

There are currently 24 beds available across the three units — in Dublin, Limerick and Galway — but demand routinely outstrips supply. The committee heard that high staff turnover, recruitment difficulties, and the complex needs of the children involved have impacted the agency’s ability to provide timely placements.

Sinn Féin spokesperson for Children, Kathleen Funchion TD, described the waiting list as "deeply concerning" and called on Minister for Children Roderic O’Gorman to prioritise additional resources for special care provision in Budget 2025. "These are some of the most vulnerable children in the country and delays in accessing appropriate care can have lifelong consequences," Deputy Funchion said.

Tusla has faced criticism from advocacy groups for delays in securing placements, with the Children’s Rights Alliance warning that children waiting for special care were at heightened risk of harm, homelessness or exploitation.

In response, the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth said it was working with Tusla to address the challenges in the system. A spokesperson stated that the Department had provided additional funding of €6.5 million for special care services in the past year, and that a review of the service is due to be published before the end of 2024.

The High Court regularly hears urgent applications seeking special care orders for children presenting with acute mental health needs, experience of trauma, or at risk of absconding from other care settings. In the absence of immediate places, children may be accommodated in temporary arrangements, including hotels or foster care.

Children’s Ombudsman Dr Niall Muldoon has previously described the shortage of special care places as "a recurring crisis" and called for a long-term, sustainable strategy to ensure vulnerable children are not left waiting for appropriate intervention.

Tusla told the committee it was pursuing a recruitment drive for care staff, and that efforts were under way to deliver additional beds by the end of next year. The agency also committed to closer collaboration with the HSE and CAMHS to ensure an integrated approach to meeting the complex needs of children in the special care system.
headline: Six children waiting for special care unit place

text:
The Biden administration has filed a lawsuit against the state of California in the US District Court, challenging state regulations that it claims are contributing to higher egg prices nationwide. The federal government alleges that California’s animal welfare standards, which require all eggs sold in the state to come from cage-free hens with specific space allowances, are effectively setting rules for the rest of the country and placing an undue burden on egg producers in other states.

California’s laws, enacted through Proposition 12 and in force since 2020, have been lauded by animal rights campaigners but have drawn criticism from some farming and retail groups, who argue that the regulations drive up costs for producers and consumers alike. Under the rules, farms—regardless of their location—must comply with California’s cage-free standards if they wish to sell eggs in the state, which is America’s largest consumer market.

In its complaint, the US Department of Justice contends that California’s requirements overstep constitutional bounds, impeding interstate commerce and contributing to recent spikes in egg prices seen across the country. The federal government argues that by compelling out-of-state producers to adhere to California’s stricter standards, the state is dictating agricultural practices far beyond its borders.

California officials have defended the law, saying it reflects voters’ wishes and protects both consumers and animal welfare. The state’s Attorney General, Rob Bonta, said California would “vigorously defend” its standards in court, maintaining that states have the right to ensure products sold within their markets meet certain ethical and safety criteria.

The lawsuit comes amid broader concerns over food price inflation in the US, with the cost of eggs rising sharply last year due to supply chain disruptions, high feed prices, and outbreaks of avian flu. While prices have moderated in recent months, the conflict over California’s regulations has renewed debates over the role of state law in shaping national agricultural markets.

The case echoes previous legal challenges, including one in which several midwestern states unsuccessfully sued California in 2014. However, this time the involvement of the federal government heightens the stakes and could prompt a ruling from the US Supreme Court on the extent of state authority over goods sold across state lines.

Egg producers and retailers are closely watching the proceedings, which could have significant implications for the future of food regulation in the US. If the federal government succeeds, it may limit the ability of states to set conditions on products entering their markets. If California prevails, other states may follow its lead in imposing similar welfare or environmental standards, with potential knock-on effects for food prices and supply chains nationwide.

A hearing date has yet to be set. The outcome of the case could have far-reaching implications for farmers, consumers and policymakers across the United States.
headline: US government sues California over egg prices

text:
The Irish Farmers’ Association (IFA) has warned that the ongoing European Commission investigation into deforestation in Brazil could further undermine the EU-Mercosur trade deal, already facing mounting opposition from Irish agriculture.

IFA President Francie Gorman said today that the inquiry by the European Commission’s Food and Veterinary Office (FVO), under the guidance of the International Food and Joint Audit Service (IFJ), highlights the “glaring contradictions” at the heart of the proposed Mercosur agreement and puts Irish and EU standards at risk.

“This probe shows that Brazil is not meeting even the basic traceability and environmental requirements that we expect in Ireland and across the EU,” Mr Gorman said. “For the Commission to continue negotiating with Mercosur countries while simultaneously investigating breaches of fundamental standards is simply not credible.”

The EU-Mercosur deal, first agreed in principle in 2019, would see reduced tariffs on a range of goods exchanged between the EU and the Mercosur bloc, which consists of Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, and Paraguay. However, Irish farmers have long argued that the deal would expose local producers to unfair competition from countries with lower animal welfare and environmental standards.

The Commission audit, which began in May, will examine Brazil’s efforts to prevent illegal deforestation linked to beef exports. The IFJ team is expected to report back in the coming months. Ireland’s Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine, Charlie McConalogue, has previously expressed concerns over whether Brazil can provide adequate guarantees on sustainability and food safety standards.

In a statement today, the IFA repeated its call for the Irish Government to formally reject the Mercosur agreement when it comes before the Council of Ministers. Mr Gorman insisted that “now is the time for Ireland to show leadership in Europe and stand up for farm families and the rural economy.”

The IFA’s stance has been echoed by representatives from the Irish Cattle and Sheep Farmers’ Association and the Irish Creamery Milk Suppliers Association, both of which argue that Irish food exports could be seriously damaged by the introduction of South American beef and other products that do not meet EU traceability and environmental criteria.

A spokesperson for the Department of Agriculture said Minister McConalogue remains “deeply engaged” on the issue at both national and EU level, and reiterated the Government’s commitment to ensuring that any future trade deal will “fully protect the high standards demanded of Irish farmers and rural communities.”

The Mercosur agreement requires unanimous approval from all EU member states. France, Austria and the Netherlands have also signalled their opposition in light of ongoing environmental and animal welfare concerns. 

The Commission has not commented directly on the IFJ investigation, stating only that “robust and ongoing evaluations” are part of the EU’s due diligence process in all trade negotiations.

Opposition TDs including Sinn Féin’s Matt Carthy and the Social Democrats’ Holly Cairns have criticised what they term “double standards” in EU policy, arguing that Irish and European farming could be sacrificed for broader commercial interests.

The IFJ’s audit report is expected to be completed by the end of the summer, after which the European Commission will issue a public statement on its findings.
headline: IFJ probe 'undermines' EU-Mercosur trade deal, says IFA

The cost of the new IT system for Student Universal Support Ireland (SUSI) has exceeded initial estimates by over 40%, RTÉ News has learned. The overspend, totalling nearly €5 million, has prompted concerns among members of the Oireachtas Public Accounts Committee regarding governance and budgeting within the system that administers student grants nationwide.

Documents provided to RTÉ show that the original allocation for the modernisation of SUSI’s grant processing system stood at €11.7 million, but most recent figures supplied by the Department of Further and Higher Education confirm that the project’s final cost will exceed €16.5 million.

The Department attributed the escalation to “unanticipated complexities” encountered during the implementation phase, including integration with other Government platforms and adapting to evolving data protection requirements. It also cited delays brought about by the Covid-19 pandemic, which required remote development work and contributed to slower progress.

SUSI, which operates under the aegis of the City of Dublin Education and Training Board (CDETB), is responsible for the processing of approximately 100,000 student grant applications each year. The IT project was originally launched in 2021 with the aim of streamlining the application process and future-proofing the system for prospective changes in policy, such as the increased number of applicants and new eligibility criteria announced in recent Budgets.

In response to the overspend, the Chair of the Public Accounts Committee, Brian Stanley TD, said that while modern and robust IT systems are vital for the efficient functioning of public services, “serious questions” remain over project management and oversight. “We cannot have a situation where costs spiral in this fashion without a clear explanation or accountability,” he said.

The Department said that a lessons-learned review will be conducted in conjunction with the Office of Government Procurement. A spokesperson for Minister for Further and Higher Education Simon Harris TD acknowledged that “all major public IT projects carry a degree of risk” and claimed that the improved system would ultimately result in savings through administrative efficiencies.

Opposition parties criticised the handling of the project, with Labour’s Aodhán Ó Ríordáin TD describing the overspend as “another example of poor planning and weak control over public expenditure.” Sinn Féin’s Rose Conway-Walsh TD called for the Comptroller and Auditor General to scrutinise the matter, saying students and taxpayers deserved “clarity and assurance” around value for money.

SUSI said that while the transition to the new IT system caused “some limited delays” for a small number of applicants in the most recent round, most students experienced no disruption and the process is now running as intended.

The PAC is expected to recall senior officials from the Department before the Committee to address unanswered questions regarding the cost overruns, procurement process, and governance arrangements. The Comptroller and Auditor General may also be requested to carry out a special report. The Department has committed to keeping both the Oireachtas and the public informed as the review proceeds.
headline: Significant overspend in cost for SUSI IT system

text:
The World Health Organisation (WHO) recently classified the ongoing Ebola outbreak in Central Africa as a “high-risk emergency”, prompting heightened concern among public health authorities globally, including Ireland’s Health Service Executive (HSE). But what does such a designation mean, and how likely is the threat to spread beyond the affected region?

Ebola, a severe and often fatal viral illness, has been endemic to certain parts of Africa for decades. The current outbreak, concentrated in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, has seen a surge in cases in recent weeks, with the WHO confirming over 300 infections and more than 200 deaths since late March. This escalation has triggered a review of international protocols, and on Wednesday, the WHO upgraded the emergency level to high-risk, citing the outbreak’s proximity to major transport hubs and porous land borders.

The term “high-risk emergency” signals that, while the outbreak remains geographically localised, there is an elevated likelihood of cross-border transmission and subsequent international spread. This is particularly concerning given the region’s history of conflict, inadequate healthcare infrastructure, and limited access to medical supplies—all factors noted by the WHO as impediments to an effective local response.

For Ireland, the direct risk remains minimal, but not negligible. The HSE has issued updated guidance to hospitals and general practitioners, outlining protocols for isolating suspected cases and managing travellers returning from affected areas. The Department of Foreign Affairs has also amended its travel advice for the region, urging Irish citizens to exercise extreme caution and to register their details with the Embassy, given the unpredictable security situation.

The WHO’s declaration also has concrete implications for the international community’s response. It unlocks access to emergency funding and triggers the deployment of additional resources, including epidemiologists, laboratory technicians and emergency supplies. The Irish Government recently pledged an additional €500,000 to support Ebola containment efforts as part of its commitment to global health security.

However, both the WHO and the HSE emphasise that Ebola is not transmitted through casual contact. The virus spreads primarily via direct exposure to bodily fluids of symptomatic patients, or through contaminated medical equipment. Standard infection prevention and control measures are effective in reducing transmission risk, and European countries, including Ireland, have robust systems in place to detect and manage imported cases.

Speaking in the Dáil on Thursday, the Minister for Health stressed the importance of international cooperation and ongoing vigilance. “While the risk to people living in Ireland is currently considered very low, we cannot be complacent,” he said. “Our public health teams are monitoring the situation closely and are prepared to respond swiftly should the need arise.”

Previous Ebola outbreaks, notably the West Africa epidemic in 2014–2016, have demonstrated the potential for the virus to spark global alarm when containment measures falter. The current response is informed by those experiences, with rapid diagnostics, ring vaccination campaigns, and international coordination forming the backbone of efforts to halt the spread.

The situation in Central Africa remains fluid, and health authorities have warned that the risk designation could escalate further if containment fails. In the meantime, Irish officials are urging members of the public to remain informed through official channels and to consult their GP if they develop symptoms consistent with severe viral illness and have recently travelled to the affected region.

As the WHO and its partners work to curb the outbreak at source, attention will remain focused on preparedness and solidarity—key lessons drawn from past emergencies, and critical to preventing a local crisis from becoming a global health threat.
headline: Explained: WHO's high-risk Ebola emergency

text:
Hundreds of residents were evacuated from areas near Athens yesterday as a large forest fire swept through villages on the outskirts of the Greek capital, fuelled by strong winds and soaring summer temperatures.

The blaze, which broke out in the foothills of Mount Parnitha to the north-west of Athens, spread rapidly amid gusts of up to 50 kilometres per hour, prompting authorities to issue urgent evacuation orders for several nearby communities.

Firefighting aircraft and helicopters were deployed alongside more than 140 firefighters and 40 vehicles on the ground, as smoke billowed across the Attica region. Volunteers and local residents could be seen joining emergency teams in an effort to contain the flames and protect homes, with some using garden hoses and buckets of water as the fire approached inhabited areas.

Greek officials said at least five villages, including Fyli and Dervenochoria, had been evacuated as a precaution. Civil defence authorities used mobile phone alerts to urge people to leave, with many gathering in local stadiums and school buildings set up as temporary shelters.

No injuries have been reported, but fire service spokespersons confirmed that several houses and vehicles have been damaged. Efforts to contain the blaze continued into the night, with firefighters working in hazardous conditions.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis convened an emergency meeting last night to review the response, with officials warning that a combination of high temperatures, low humidity and strong winds would continue to pose a threat in the coming days.

Greece has experienced a succession of devastating wildfires in recent years, as climate change brings more frequent heatwaves and tinder-dry conditions. In 2023, at least 28 people died in wildfires across the country, and thousands were forced to flee their homes.

The Department of Foreign Affairs, meanwhile, advised any Irish citizens currently in Greece to monitor local media and follow the instructions of authorities. There have been no reports of Irish nationals affected by the fires.

Weather warnings remain in place across much of southern Greece, with officials urging the public to remain vigilant and avoid unnecessary travel in affected areas.
headline: Greece forest fire forces evacuations near Athens

text:
A 29-year-old man has been sentenced to seven years in prison at the Central Criminal Court for his role in a fatal shooting in Ballymun, Dublin, in 2021.

Karl Dunne, with an address at Belclare Park, Ballymun, pleaded guilty to a charge of manslaughter in connection with the death of 33-year-old Jamie Walsh. The court heard that Mr Walsh died after being shot outside an apartment complex on Belclare Terrace on 16 May 2021.

The court was told that Mr Dunne was part of a group that approached Mr Walsh, who had been living in the area but was not originally from Ballymun. During the confrontation, Dunne produced a handgun and fired a single shot, striking Mr Walsh in the chest. Emergency services arrived at the scene within minutes, but Mr Walsh was pronounced dead shortly afterwards at the Mater Hospital.

Prosecuting counsel outlined that the shooting arose from an ongoing dispute and noted that Mr Dunne had not intended to kill Mr Walsh, but accepted responsibility for his actions by entering an early guilty plea to manslaughter.

In a victim impact statement read to the court, Mr Walsh’s mother described her son as a "loving father and brother", and said his loss had left an "irreplaceable void" in the family’s life.

Defence counsel told the court that Mr Dunne had expressed genuine remorse and had co-operated with the Garda investigation. The court also heard that Dunne had a history of drug misuse and had experienced difficulties from a young age.

Mr Justice Paul McDermott described the offence as "entirely avoidable and tragic", and said it had "devastated" the Walsh family. He imposed a sentence of seven years’ imprisonment, backdated to when Dunne first went into custody in May 2021.

Gardaí welcomed the sentence, and said the outcome would bring some closure to the family and community. Dunne showed little reaction as he was led away from the court room.
headline: Man jailed for seven years over fatal Ballymun shooting

text:
UK police have confirmed they have received a number of "non-recent" sexual offence allegations relating to comedian and broadcaster Russell Brand.

The Metropolitan Police said it had received a report on Sunday alleging sexual assault, which is said to have occurred in the London area in 2003. Since then, officers have spoken with several other individuals who have come forward with additional allegations of sexual offences.

A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police said they will be "offering specialist support" to those who have made allegations and that the force is "in contact with the woman who originally reported" the matter. The spokesperson added: "We have also received a number of other allegations of sexual offences. These allegations are all non-recent and are being investigated by detectives in the Central Specialist Crime unit."

Brand, who denies all allegations of sexual assault, has said his relationships have always been consensual. The allegations were first aired in a joint investigation by Channel 4's Dispatches, The Times and The Sunday Times, which included accusations from four women, some dating back to 2006.

The comedian has not been arrested or charged with any offence. He has issued a statement saying he "absolutely refutes" the claims made against him. His publisher and a number of production companies have since suspended their work with Brand.

The UK Home Office has declined to comment on the ongoing police enquiries. The BBC has launched its own internal investigation into Brand's conduct during his time as a presenter at the broadcaster.

Police have encouraged anyone who believes they may have been a victim of sexual assault to come forward and contact them. The UK Government has also urged media organisations and employers to share any further information they may come across regarding the allegations.

Meanwhile, there have been calls in the House of Commons for a broader review of regulations around the welfare of young people and women in the entertainment industry.

No further details about the new allegations have been released by the police at this stage. The investigation remains open and ongoing.
headline: 'Non-recent' allegations against Brand made to police

text:
The United States has deployed a number of naval vessels to the southern Caribbean amid growing fears of an escalation in tensions between Venezuela and its neighbour Guyana. The move comes as concerns rise over a potential conflict between the two South American nations, after Venezuela renewed claims to the oil-rich Essequibo region, which is recognised internationally as part of Guyana.

US officials have described the deployment of warships, including a guided-missile destroyer and support vessels, as a “routine” operation linked to scheduled military exercises with regional partners. However, the show of force is being widely interpreted as a signal of support for Guyana and a caution to Venezuela not to act unilaterally in the ongoing border dispute.

In recent weeks, Venezuela has stepped up its rhetoric and military presence near the contested region, following a controversial referendum in December in which it claimed overwhelming domestic backing for the annexation of Essequibo. The government of President Nicolás Maduro maintains that the region, which comprises more than two-thirds of Guyanese territory and is believed to contain significant oil reserves, rightfully belongs to Venezuela.

Guyana, a former British colony, has protested against Venezuela’s actions and requested international assistance. The government in Georgetown has welcomed the US deployment, saying it helps “safeguard peace and stability” in the region and supports Guyana’s sovereignty.

The situation has drawn concern from the United Nations, the Organisation of American States, and CARICOM, all of whom have called for restraint and a peaceful resolution through dialogue. Brazil has also increased its military presence along its borders, amid fears of a wider regional fallout should hostilities erupt.

Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin said this morning that Ireland was closely monitoring the situation. He reiterated Ireland’s support for the principles of international law and called for “immediate de-escalation and respect for Guyana’s territorial integrity”.

While US military officials have played down the risk of imminent conflict, they have also stated that they stand “shoulder to shoulder” with Guyana. The Defence Department in Washington did not disclose the exact number of ships or personnel involved in the deployment.

Diplomatic efforts are ongoing, with talks brokered by the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC) scheduled to take place next week. Both Venezuela and Guyana claim to be committed to negotiations, but so far there has been little sign of compromise.

The dispute over Essequibo dates back to the 19th century, and the International Court of Justice is currently considering the case. However, the recent discovery of large offshore oil deposits by multinational firms, including ExxonMobil, has dramatically raised the stakes.

With regional stability now under threat, the coming days are expected to be critical in determining whether the crisis can be defused through diplomacy, or if the deployment of US warships will be the prelude to a greater confrontation.
headline: US deploys warships amid fears of Venezuela conflict

text:
The Minister for Enterprise, Trade and Employment, Peter Burke, has cautioned that the outcome of ongoing EU-US talks concerning the removal of tariffs remains "not certain", as negotiators face mounting pressure to reach an agreement before a crucial deadline next month.

Speaking to RTÉ News on Thursday, Minister Burke said that while the Government supports efforts to resolve outstanding disputes over steel and aluminium tariffs, there are still "significant hurdles" to overcome. "The European Union is engaging robustly with our American counterparts," Mr Burke said. "But it is not certain that a breakthrough will be achieved in the coming weeks."

Tariffs on steel and aluminium were originally imposed by the Trump administration in 2018, prompting retaliatory measures from the European Union. In 2021, both sides agreed to a temporary suspension of some duties as talks got under way to reach a lasting solution. However, that arrangement is set to expire at the end of March, with potential implications for Irish exporters.

The Irish Exporters Association has expressed concern over the prospect that, without a new agreement, tariffs could return as early as April. Simon McKeever, chief executive of the organisation, said: "Irish producers, especially in agri-food and manufacturing, rely heavily on transatlantic trade. Any renewal of tariffs would be damaging for Irish jobs and the wider economy."

Officials from the European Commission are due to hold further discussions with their US counterparts in Brussels next week. A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs said that Ireland remains in close contact with both EU negotiators and affected sectors at home. "Our priority is to safeguard Irish economic interests while supporting a rules-based international trading system," the statement read.

The talks have also been complicated by wider geopolitical tensions, with EU and US leaders clashing on unrelated issues such as subsidies for green technology and differences over approaches to China. 

Opposition parties have urged the Government to press for greater protection for Irish firms, with Sinn Féin spokesperson on Business, Enterprise and Innovation, Louise O’Reilly TD, calling for "clear assurances" that the interests of Irish workers will not be sacrificed in the negotiations.

The European Commission has said it is "committed to achieving a fair and balanced outcome" but warned the timeline is tight. If no agreement is reached by 31 March, tariff rates could automatically revert to their previous levels. 

Minister Burke said the Government would continue to monitor the situation closely and provide support to affected businesses if necessary.
headline: Outcome of EU-US tariff talks 'not certain'

text:
A pair of wolves previously unknown to the region has ignited controversy in rural France, after repeated sightings and reported livestock attacks in the foothills of the Massif Central. The animals, thought to be a male and female, were first spotted in late May by a group of hikers near Saint-Flour, prompting immediate concern among local farmers’ associations.

Local authorities have since confirmed the presence of the wolves through DNA analysis of sheep carcasses, with the prefecture of Cantal issuing fresh guidance on livestock safety and compensatory schemes. France’s Office national de la chasse et de la faune sauvage (ONCFS) is monitoring the pair, which experts believe may have migrated from Italy or the Alps, where wolf populations have been slowly increasing for the past two decades.

Many farmers had been reassured by government commitments to maintain a low national wolf population, but the emergence of an established pair well outside the species’ usual range has led to a renewed sense of unease across agricultural communities. “It’s not just the sheep they attack, it’s the psychological pressure on farmers and their families,” said Pierre Delacour, a local livestock breeder, who claims to have lost several ewes in recent weeks. “We feel abandoned by Paris.”

Conservation groups have urged restraint, arguing for the ecological benefits of wolf presence and describing the animals’ return as a natural consequence of rural depopulation and recovery of wild prey. “Wolves are part of our heritage. Their presence shows our environment is healing,” said Sonia Martin of Ferus, an organisation supporting predator reintroduction in France.

However, the dispute has grown political, with the president of the regional council calling on the government in Paris to review France’s obligations under the EU’s Habitats Directive. Some local TDs have also pressed the issue in the Assemblée Nationale, reflecting a broader rural unease that mirrors similar debates in Ireland over rewilding and livestock protection.

The French Minister for Agriculture, Marc Fesneau, has pledged additional resources for the region, including funding for electric fencing and guard dogs, as well as a review of compensation payments to affected farmers. “We must find a balance between biodiversity and the legitimate concerns of those who live and work on the land,” he said.

Meanwhile, wildlife rangers and local gardaí have warned against any attempts by concerned residents to take matters into their own hands, reminding the public that wolves are a protected species under French and EU law. Investigations are ongoing into recent rumours of unauthorised use of poison baits.

With the summer grazing season underway, both sides acknowledge that tensions are likely to persist, as the wolves’ unpredictable movements add a new twist to an old debate over the place of wild predators in a modern rural landscape.
headline: Unlikely wolf pair sparks row in rural France

text:
Gardaí seized nine mobile phones and a number of electronic devices during a search of a well-known celebrity’s home in Dublin yesterday, RTÉ News understands. The search was conducted as part of an ongoing investigation by the Garda National Economic Crime Bureau (GNECB) into allegations of fraud and money laundering.

Sources close to the inquiry said that officers from the bureau, supported by members of the local detective unit, executed a search warrant at the south Dublin residence shortly before 7am. The operation is believed to have lasted more than six hours. Gardaí also removed several laptops, USB drives, and a number of documents from the premises.

The individual at the centre of the investigation, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was present at the time of the search and is said to be cooperating fully with authorities. No arrests have been made at this stage and gardaí said their inquiries are ongoing.

In a statement, a garda spokesperson confirmed that “a planned search was carried out at a private residence in Dublin as part of an ongoing criminal investigation.” The spokesperson added that a number of items were seized for forensic examination but declined to comment further, citing operational reasons.

It is understood that the investigation focuses on suspected large-scale financial offences, including the use of multiple mobile phones and encrypted messaging platforms. Detectives are now expected to examine the seized devices to determine whether they contain evidence relevant to the inquiry.

The scene was preserved throughout the day yesterday and technical experts from the Garda Cyber Crime Bureau attended to assist with the examination of electronic media.

The high-profile figure at the centre of the probe is known for appearances on Irish television and radio, and is also active in business ventures.

Gardaí have appealed to anyone with information in relation to the investigation to contact them confidentially. The outcome of the forensic analysis of the devices is expected to determine the next steps in the case.

No charges have been brought, and the investigation is said to be at an early stage.
headline: Gardaí 'seized nine phones' from celebrity's home

text:
Voters in Israel are heading to the polls today in a closely watched election that could have significant implications not only for Israeli politics but also for the ongoing conflict with the Palestinians and wider regional stability. The poll, the country’s sixth in less than five years, comes against the backdrop of heightened tensions in Gaza and the West Bank, as well as domestic upheaval over government proposals targeting the judiciary.

The outcome is being closely monitored by Irish officials, with Foreign Affairs Minister Micheál Martin reiterating Ireland’s call for a just and lasting peace in the region, and for the upholding of international law. The Irish Government has been a strong proponent of a two-state solution, and recent violence has led to renewed calls in the Oireachtas for diplomatic efforts to be redoubled.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has dominated Israeli politics for much of the past quarter century, is facing one of his toughest challenges yet. His coalition government, mainly comprising right-wing and religious parties, has been criticised both at home and abroad for its handling of the war in Gaza, which has resulted in a humanitarian crisis and rising international scrutiny. Critics have accused Mr Netanyahu of prioritising his own political survival over efforts to secure a ceasefire, while his supporters argue that strong leadership is needed in a time of conflict.

Central to the election is the question of whether Mr Netanyahu’s leadership can endure, or whether the opposition, led by former defence chief Benny Gantz, can form an alternative coalition. Mr Gantz has campaigned on a platform of accountability and national unity, presenting himself as a more moderate voice capable of restoring trust among Israelis disillusioned by years of political gridlock.

The elections are also being viewed as a referendum on the government’s controversial judicial overhaul. Proposed changes to how judges are appointed, and to the power of the Supreme Court, have triggered mass protests and deepened divisions within Israeli society. The outcome will determine whether these reforms proceed, are moderated, or scrapped entirely.

For Palestinians, the Israeli elections are being watched with a mixture of scepticism and anxiety. Many fear that regardless of who forms the next government, the occupation and expansion of settlements in the West Bank will continue unabated, further dimming hopes for renewed peace talks. In recent months, the humanitarian situation in Gaza has continued to deteriorate, prompting repeated calls for an immediate ceasefire from the United Nations and EU member states, including Ireland.

Regional actors, including Egypt, Jordan, and the Gulf states, are also paying close attention, given concerns that further escalation could destabilise the wider Middle East. In the US and European capitals, the composition of the next Israeli government will have an impact on security cooperation, aid programmes, and diplomatic initiatives.

For Ireland, the stakes are particularly high given the strong historical ties to the region and the large number of Irish NGOs operating in both Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territories. The Department of Foreign Affairs has confirmed it will closely monitor the outcome, with a view to reassessing official policy depending on the political direction taken in Jerusalem.

Counting is expected to begin shortly after polls close, but with a fragmented political landscape and complex coalition maths, it may be some days before a new government is formed. As the world watches, the choices made by Israeli voters will have profound consequences, not only for the future direction of their own country, but for the quest for peace and stability in the wider region.
headline: What's at stake in Israel's elections?

text:
A 32-year-old man has been remanded in custody after appearing before Dublin District Court charged in connection with the assault of a tourist in the city centre at the weekend.

Gardaí told the court that the incident occurred on Saturday night on Dame Street, where a male tourist in his 20s was allegedly attacked while returning to his accommodation. It is understood the victim, who is visiting from France, suffered injuries to his face and ribs and was treated at St James’s Hospital.

The accused, who has an address at a hostel in the city, was arrested on Sunday afternoon and detained at Pearse Street Garda Station. He is charged with assault causing harm under Section 3 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act.

Objecting to bail, the Gardaí cited concerns that the defendant posed a flight risk and that he could interfere with witnesses. They also told the court that CCTV footage and several witness statements formed part of the investigation, which is ongoing.

Defence counsel argued that the accused had strong ties to the area and would comply with any bail conditions imposed by the court. However, Judge Bryan Smyth said he was not satisfied with the proposed surety and refused bail.

The man was remanded in custody to Cloverhill Prison and is due to appear again before the court next week. The injured tourist has since been discharged from hospital and has made a statement to investigating officers. The Department of Foreign Affairs has confirmed it is providing consular assistance to the victim.
headline: Man in court for assault on tourist in Dublin denied bail

text:
The Minister for Health, Stephen Donnelly, has announced an expansion of the State’s free contraception scheme, which will now extend to women and people with a uterus aged up to 35 years. The move, approved by Cabinet this week, aims to further support reproductive health and reduce the financial barriers to accessing contraception.

Since its initial launch in September 2022, the programme has provided free contraception to those aged 17 to 26. This was extended to include those up to the age of 30 last year. The latest move means that an estimated additional 128,000 people will be eligible to access the scheme.

The free contraception service covers prescription contraceptive pills, patches, injections, implants, intrauterine devices (IUDs), and contraceptive rings. The programme also covers consultations with GPs, family planning clinics, and fitting or removal procedures. Emergency contraception is included, and those availing of the service do not need a medical card.

Speaking at a press conference at Government Buildings, Minister Donnelly said the expansion reflects the Government’s commitment to enhancing women’s health services and advancing gender equality in healthcare. “This is a significant development that will help more people to make informed choices about their reproductive health, without cost being a barrier,” he stated.

The scheme is being funded through the Department of Health at an estimated annual cost of €31 million. The HSE will work with GPs and community pharmacies nationwide to facilitate the wider rollout, expected to take effect from 1 July.

Welcoming the announcement, the National Women’s Council said it would particularly benefit women who may otherwise have delayed seeking contraception due to financial constraints. Dr Cliona Murphy, a consultant obstetrician and gynaecologist, also praised the expansion, describing it as “a key step towards reducing unplanned pregnancies and supporting reproductive autonomy.”

The Irish College of General Practitioners (ICGP) said that demand for contraceptive services has increased since the scheme’s introduction, with many GPs reporting easier access for young women and a reduction in out-of-pocket costs.

The programme was one of several recommendations from the Oireachtas Committee on the Eighth Amendment and is a central part of the Government’s Women's Health Action Plan. The Department of Health stated that further expansions will be kept under review, with consideration potentially given to including other groups in future.

Opposition parties have welcomed the move, but some have called for increased public awareness campaigns to ensure eligible groups are fully informed of their entitlements. The Department of Health has indicated that an information campaign will be launched across print, broadcast, and online media in the coming weeks.

Free contraception for eligible age groups can be accessed through most GPs and participating pharmacies nationwide. Full details are available on the HSE website.
headline: Government expands free contraception scheme

text:
The European Court of Justice (ECJ) has ruled against the Irish Government’s interpretation of its obligations towards asylum seekers, rejecting claims that it could derogate from certain provisions related to the reception and processing of applications.

The judgment, delivered this morning in Luxembourg, centred on the application of the European Union’s Reception Conditions Directive in Ireland. The case was brought to the ECJ after a challenge in the Irish courts on whether the State was obliged to guarantee full reception standards, including access to employment, education, and healthcare, for all asylum applicants regardless of their status during appeal processes.

The Government had argued that, under exceptional circumstances and due to pressures on the asylum system, it could limit some supports, citing national security and capacity constraints. However, the ECJ found that Ireland could not restrict rights guaranteed under EU law, even in the event of significant increases in arrivals.

In its ruling, the court stated that Member States “cannot invoke practical difficulties or national emergencies as grounds for derogation from the minimum standards set out in the Directive.” The judgment stressed the importance of “ensuring that fundamental rights and dignity of applicants are safeguarded throughout the procedure.”

In a statement, the Department of Justice said it noted the ruling and would examine its implications for domestic policy. “Ireland remains committed to fulfilling its obligations under EU law and will review relevant reception arrangements in light of the judgment,” the Department said.

The case was originally referred to the ECJ after the High Court in Dublin sought clarification on the extent of State obligations under EU law. Legal experts have said the ruling could have significant ramifications for Ireland’s International Protection system, particularly as it faces ongoing challenges with accommodation for protection applicants.

Minister for Justice Helen McEntee acknowledged the judgment, noting that the Government’s priority remains to “ensure a fair, efficient and humane system for all seeking international protection.” She reiterated calls for EU-wide solutions to migration pressures, as the number of applicants in Ireland continues to rise.

Advocacy groups have welcomed the decision, urging the Government to move swiftly to provide adequate supports for all asylum seekers. Nick Henderson, CEO of the Irish Refugee Council, said the ruling “clarifies once and for all that Ireland must treat all international protection applicants with the dignity and rights guaranteed by EU law.”

Opposition TDs have called for an immediate review of current reception conditions, with Sinn Féin’s spokesperson on Justice, Pa Daly, describing the ruling as “a wake-up call for Government to address deficiencies in the system.”

It is understood that the Department will consult with the HSE and other relevant bodies in the coming weeks to determine the practical impact of the judgment on service provision.

The ECJ ruling comes as the State continues to contend with acute shortages in accommodation for new arrivals, with many asylum seekers currently accommodated in hotel rooms and repurposed facilities across the country.

The issue of Ireland’s obligations under EU asylum law has been the subject of significant debate in the Dáil, particularly over the last year as arrivals have increased sharply. Today’s ruling is expected to further shape that debate and prompt urgent policy responses from the Government.
headline: ECJ rejects Govt's claim over asylum seeker obligations

text:
The Irish husband of a woman who died following a botulism outbreak in Bordeaux remains in hospital in France, according to official sources.

The man, originally from the Cork area, travelled with his wife to France last month, where they attended a local wine bar that has since been linked to a cluster of botulism cases. His wife, a 32-year-old woman, passed away in hospital last week after contracting the rare but serious illness.

French health authorities have confirmed that several people became ill after consuming preserved sardines at the Tchin Tchin Wine Bar in Bordeaux. The restaurant has been closed as investigations continue. The strain of botulism involved has prompted a Europe-wide alert through the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).

The Department of Foreign Affairs has stated it is providing consular assistance to the man and his family. The HSE’s Health Protection Surveillance Centre has advised anyone who may have eaten at the restaurant and developed symptoms—including blurred vision, difficulty swallowing, and respiratory problems—to seek immediate medical attention.

Botulism, caused by a bacterial toxin, can lead to paralysis and is potentially fatal if not treated rapidly. French officials said the Irish man remains in a stable condition but continues to receive intensive medical care. Other affected patrons include individuals from North America, Spain, and Germany.

The Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs, Micheál Martin, extended his condolences to the bereaved family in a statement and thanked French medical teams for their work.

The HSE has reassured the public that there is no evidence of contaminated products reaching Ireland, and that the risk to Irish consumers is extremely low. However, Irish authorities are liaising with their French counterparts as the investigation continues.

The Oireachtas Health Committee is expected to be briefed on the incident next week, as public health officials continue to monitor developments closely.
headline: Irish husband of botulism victim remains hospitalised

text:
Pope Francis, the first pontiff from Latin America and the Southern Hemisphere, has marked more than a decade at the helm of the Catholic Church with a series of landmark gestures, reforms, and controversies. Selected as the 266th pope in March 2013, his papacy has been defined by an emphasis on mercy, a focus on the marginalised, and efforts to reform Church governance and engage with a fast-changing world. Here are ten notable moments from Francis’ pontificate so far:

The first days of his papacy set the tone for a new style of leadership. Pope Francis appeared on the balcony of St Peter's Basilica simply dressed, asking the faithful to pray for him. He chose to live in the modest Casa Santa Marta guesthouse, rather than the ornate Apostolic Palace, cementing his reputation for personal humility.

Francis’ 2015 encyclical *Laudato Si’* placed environmental stewardship at the heart of Catholic social teaching, calling climate change "one of the principal challenges facing humanity.” The document resonated worldwide, drawing praise from scientists and environmentalists, and influencing discussion at UN summits.

The pope has made significant efforts to address historical wrongs, particularly clerical sexual abuse scandals. While survivors and advocacy groups have sometimes criticised the Vatican’s response as insufficient, Francis created a dedicated commission for the protection of minors, updated Church law to address abuse, and met victims on several occasions.

In 2014, Francis facilitated a historic meeting of Israeli and Palestinian leaders in the Vatican Gardens, appealing for peace in the Middle East. The gesture was widely viewed as an attempt to use the moral authority of the papacy to foster dialogue.

The Extraordinary Jubilee Year of Mercy in 2016 invited Catholics worldwide to focus on forgiveness and reconciliation. Holy Doors, typically sealed except in jubilee years, were opened in cathedrals across the globe, including in the Pro-Cathedral in Dublin, drawing hundreds of thousands of Irish pilgrims.

Francis has travelled extensively, visiting over 50 countries. His 2015 visit to the United States included an address to the US Congress, while his trip to Myanmar in 2017 made him the first pope to visit the country. In 2018, he visited Ireland for the World Meeting of Families, where he acknowledged the “grave scandal” of abuse by clergy and met survivors in Dublin.

The Argentine pope has sought to open discussion on contentious topics, including the role of women in the Church and the possible ordination of married men in remote regions. In 2021, his apostolic letter *Spiritus Domini* expanded opportunities for women to serve as lectors and acolytes.

Francis has consistently spoken out in defence of refugees and migrants, denouncing a “globalisation of indifference.” In 2016, he brought three Syrian refugee families back to Rome after visiting a camp on the Greek island of Lesbos, a powerful symbolic act amid the ongoing European migrant crisis.

His handling of Vatican finances has included efforts at transparency and accountability, with high-profile trials of cardinals and lay officials for alleged embezzlement. The pope has established new frameworks for oversight, though Vatican finances remain under international scrutiny.

Finally, his focus on synodality has seen the global Church participate in an unprecedented consultation process ahead of the Synod on Synodality, with parishes and dioceses across Ireland and worldwide asked for input.
headline: 10 notable moments from Francis' pontificate so far

text:
The United Nations has called for a swift and thorough investigation after a reported Israeli airstrike in a suburb of Beirut struck close to a hospital, raising fears over civilian safety in the Lebanese capital.

The incident occurred on Wednesday night in the southern suburb of Chiyah, an area densely populated with residential buildings and home to the Al-Maamouri Hospital. According to Lebanese authorities, several buildings were damaged and at least seven people were killed as a result of the strike, with dozens more injured, including patients and hospital workers.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres, through his spokesperson, said he was “deeply concerned” by the escalation and urged all parties “to respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, including the protection of medical facilities and civilians.” The Secretary-General called for “a prompt, transparent, and impartial investigation into the circumstances surrounding the strike.” The UN’s Special Coordinator for Lebanon, Joanna Wronecka, also expressed alarm at the damage inflicted in a civilian area, stating that “any attacks endangering the safety of hospitals or impeding access to medical care are wholly unacceptable.”

The Lebanese Prime Minister, Najib Mikati, condemned the incident as a “flagrant aggression” and accused Israel of targeting civilian infrastructure. Israel, for its part, has said it is investigating the reports but alleged that the area was being used by Hezbollah operatives to launch attacks on northern Israel in recent days.

The HSE has confirmed that no Irish citizens are currently known to have been injured in the strike. Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin stated that Ireland “stands with the people of Lebanon at this difficult time” and fully endorses the UN’s call for an independent investigation. He reiterated Ireland’s commitment to supporting the work of UN peacekeepers in Lebanon, where Irish Defence Forces personnel are deployed as part of the UNIFIL mission.

The strike comes as tensions have sharply increased along the Israel-Lebanon border over recent weeks, with frequent exchanges of fire raising fears of a wider regional escalation. Lebanese sources have reported that several thousand people living in the southern districts of Beirut have moved to safer areas amid growing uncertainty.

International humanitarian organisations, including Médecins Sans Frontières and the International Committee of the Red Cross, have urged all parties to avoid targeting medical facilities and to ensure the delivery of aid to affected communities.

With investigations now underway, the Lebanese authorities have called on the international community to guarantee the protection of civilians and prevent further attacks on critical infrastructure. The UN meanwhile has called an emergency meeting of the Security Council to discuss the situation.
headline: UN demand 'prompt' probe into strike near Beirut hospital

text:
Kieran Cuddihy has been announced as the new presenter of RTÉ Radio 1’s flagship afternoon phone-in programme, Liveline. The broadcaster will take up his new role in early September, succeeding Joe Duffy, who steps down after more than 25 years at the helm.

Mr Cuddihy, originally from Kilkenny, has presented The Hard Shoulder on Newstalk since 2019 and previously worked as a reporter with Today FM and TV3. In a statement released by RTÉ, Mr Cuddihy described the appointment as “an immense honour and responsibility”, citing the long legacy of the programme in giving voice to callers on issues of national and personal concern.

Liveline, which broadcasts weekdays at 1.45pm, is widely regarded as a key platform for public debate and engagement, often leading the national conversation on social issues, consumer affairs, and matters of public policy. The show regularly attracts over 350,000 daily listeners.

RTÉ Director of Content, Jim Jennings, welcomed Mr Cuddihy’s appointment, saying: “Kieran brings a wealth of experience in current affairs and a deep understanding of the issues that matter to listeners. He has proven his ability to facilitate lively, respectful debate and brings fresh energy to the Liveline team.”

Joe Duffy, who announced his decision to step aside last month, endorsed his successor, saying he was “delighted” that Liveline would be in “safe hands” and wished Mr Cuddihy well as he began his tenure.

Reacting to the news, Mr Cuddihy said: “Liveline is unique in Irish broadcasting. The trust placed in the programme by listeners is something I take very seriously, and I look forward to continuing its tradition of reflecting real life in Ireland.”

RTÉ confirmed that the appointment follows an open recruitment process. Mr Cuddihy’s first show as Liveline presenter is scheduled for 2 September. The broadcaster said further details on his replacement on The Hard Shoulder will be provided in due course.
headline: Kieran Cuddihy named as new Liveline presenter

text:
Renowned Northern Irish mountaineer Noel Hanna has died after successfully reaching the summit of Mount Annapurna in Nepal, one of the world’s most treacherous peaks. The Newry native, aged 56, was reported to have passed away overnight at a camp shortly after descending from the 8,091-metre summit, according to officials from the Nepalese tourism ministry.

Hanna, an experienced climber and adventurer, had scaled the summit of Annapurna on Monday as part of an international expedition. Following his successful ascent, he returned to Camp IV where he was found unresponsive in his tent by Sherpa guides. Efforts to resuscitate him proved unsuccessful.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has confirmed it is aware of the incident and stands ready to provide consular assistance if requested. The cause of Hanna’s death has not yet been officially determined but high-altitude expeditions in the Himalayas are known for posing significant risks, including exhaustion, high-altitude sickness and extreme weather conditions.

Hanna was widely regarded as one of Ireland’s leading mountaineers, having previously summited Mount Everest ten times and completed a number of other challenging climbs around the globe. He was also the first person from the North to successfully summit and descend K2, the world’s second-highest mountain, and had forged a reputation for resilience and leadership in punishing conditions.

Tributes have poured in from across the Irish and international mountaineering community. Mourne Mountain Rescue Team, of which Hanna was a long-time member, described him as “an inspirational figure whose passion for adventure was matched only by his generosity and support for others”. Fellow climbers and friends have spoken of his dedication to training aspiring mountaineers and his regular charity fundraising efforts.

Hanna’s family, who reside in County Down, have requested privacy as they come to terms with the loss. His wife, Lynne Hanna, is herself a noted mountaineer, and together the couple had completed numerous expeditions.

The Himalayan Database, which records mountaineering activity across the region, reports that Mount Annapurna remains one of the deadliest peaks above 8,000 metres, with a summit-to-fatality ratio higher than that of Mount Everest. This climbing season has already been marked by a series of dangerous weather changes on Annapurna, with other climbers currently reported missing or rescued in recent days.

Arrangements to repatriate Mr Hanna’s remains are being coordinated by local authorities with the support of the Irish Embassy in New Delhi as well as the British Embassy in Kathmandu. The Department of Foreign Affairs is liaising with the family as the process continues.

Noel Hanna is remembered as an exceptional athlete and a passionate advocate for the outdoor community, who inspired many with his achievements on the world’s highest peaks.
headline: NI climber Noel Hanna dies after scaling Himalayan peak

text:
Belarus will begin hosting Russian tactical nuclear weapons on its territory following what President Alexander Lukashenko described as "unprecedented pressure" from western countries. The move, confirmed on Thursday, marks the first time Russian nuclear arms will be stationed outside Russian borders since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.

Russian and Belarusian officials signed key documents in Minsk on Thursday, formalising the deployment, with President Lukashenko stating that the weapons were already on their way. Russian Defence Minister Sergei Shoigu said Moscow would maintain control over the weapons, while Belarusian forces would receive training on their use. The weapons in question are short-range and not believed to be strategic nuclear missiles.

The Kremlin had previously announced its intention to deploy tactical nuclear arms in Belarus following a request from Minsk, which has remained a close ally of Moscow throughout its ongoing invasion of Ukraine. Western governments have condemned the move, warning that the deployment could further destabilise the region. The European Union's External Action Service has described it as "an irresponsible escalation" and called on Belarus to reconsider.

Taoiseach Simon Harris said today that Ireland remains "deeply concerned by any actions that increase nuclear risks in Europe." He called on "all parties to exercise restraint" and expressed Ireland's continued support for diplomatic efforts to end the conflict in Ukraine.

The deployment comes amid heightened tensions following recent gains by Russian forces around the embattled Ukrainian city of Avdiivka, and ahead of a widely anticipated Ukrainian counter-offensive. Ukrainian officials have described the move as a "nuclear blackmail" tactic.

Minsk has insisted that the weapons will act as a deterrent against what it termed "aggressive policies" from NATO member states, but NATO's secretary general Jens Stoltenberg said the alliance had seen no evidence of Russia preparing to use a nuclear weapon.

The Irish Department of Foreign Affairs reiterated its support for Ukraine's sovereignty and condemned the decision, stating that any deployment of nuclear weapons in Belarus is a "dangerous and unnecessary provocation."

As of now, there are no indications the presence of Russian nuclear arms in Belarus will alter Ireland's existing travel advice or its humanitarian and military support to Ukraine. The Oireachtas will debate the issue next week, with calls from opposition TDs for the government to step up pressure on Belarus through EU mechanisms and to review existing diplomatic channels. 

The International Atomic Energy Agency has not commented directly on the deployment, but continues to monitor the situation closely.
headline: Belarus to hold Russian nuclear arms after 'pressure'

text:
A rare Roman coin bearing the likeness of Marcus Junius Brutus, one of the key conspirators in the assassination of Julius Caesar, is due to go under the hammer in Geneva later this week. Numismatic experts have hailed the gold coin as one of the most historically significant pieces to ever emerge on the auction market, with estimates suggesting it could fetch up to €2.5 million.

The “Eid Mar” aureus—minted in 42 BC to commemorate Caesar’s killing on the Ides of March—features a striking portrait of Brutus on one side, while the reverse depicts two daggers flanking a liberty cap, a symbol of freedom in Roman iconography. Only three examples of the gold edition of this coin are known to exist, with the vast majority struck in silver. The piece is described as being in exceptional condition for its age.

The coin’s appearance at auction has generated considerable interest among both collectors and historians, many of whom view it as one of the earliest examples of political propaganda in coinage. Speaking to RTÉ News, Dr. Caitríona McCarthy, a lecturer in classics at UCD, described the coin as “a tangible link to one of history’s most dramatic turning points—it’s not just money, it’s a statement of intent.”

Auctioneers at Numismatica Genevensis, the firm handling the sale, said the coin had been part of a private European collection for decades before being consigned for sale. Its provenance has been verified by both Swiss authorities and international experts in antiquities, with full export documentation provided. The auction house has said it is co-operating with the authorities to ensure full compliance with heritage protection protocols.

Irish collectors are among those expected to participate in the international online sale, according to industry sources. The Irish market for rare coins and antiquities has grown steadily in recent years, with specialist sales in Dublin and Cork attracting significant interest.

Brutus’ depiction on coinage was unprecedented at the time, as living Romans were traditionally forbidden from placing their image on currency. The coin is therefore seen as an act of defiance, issued by Brutus’ supporters in the years of civil war that followed Caesar’s assassination.

The sale in Geneva will also feature a number of other important ancient pieces; however, all attention is expected to focus on the Brutus coin. The auction is scheduled to take place on Thursday, with bids being accepted in person and online.

The National Museum of Ireland has previously acquired similar historic coins for its collection, but it is not known if the institution intends to participate in this auction. Any successful bid would be subject to Swiss and European export regulations, as well as Irish law governing the import and private ownership of antiquities.
headline: Rare Roman coin featuring Brutus up for auction in Geneva

text:
Mark Rutte’s appointment as the next Secretary General of NATO comes at a pivotal moment for the alliance, with mounting geopolitical tensions and the question of continued US commitment looming large. The outgoing Dutch prime minister, who is set to take up the role in October, will step into the post just as NATO faces its most significant challenges since the end of the Cold War.

One of the foremost issues confronting Mr Rutte will be navigating the uncertainty surrounding the US presidential election. Donald Trump’s rhetoric, which has at times cast doubt on America’s commitment to the collective defence clause at the heart of NATO, has alarmed many European leaders. The prospect of a second Trump term raises concerns about Washington’s willingness to defend allies deemed not to be spending enough on defence, a message that has resonated with some but unsettled most.

Rutte, widely viewed as a pragmatic consensus builder and strong supporter of the transatlantic alliance, will need to reassure NATO’s eastern flank, particularly in the wake of Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine. Vladimir Putin’s recent threats and ongoing aggression have heightened anxieties in countries bordering Russia, with Poland and the Baltic states seeking more robust assurances and a clear strategy on deterrence and defence.

The war in Ukraine continues to serve as the most immediate test for NATO. While the alliance itself is not a direct party to the conflict, its unity and resolve are being tested by differing levels of support among member states. Funding and supplying military equipment to Kyiv, as well as maintaining a coordinated approach to sanctions against Moscow, will require deft diplomatic skills—an area in which Rutte has previously excelled as Dutch premier.

NATO’s pledge to increase defence spending to at least 2% of GDP by next year remains a contentious issue. Despite the Taoiseach Simon Harris confirming Ireland’s commitment to military neutrality, the Government has also agreed to boost spending on cyber defence and intelligence-sharing within the alliance’s framework. However, for many of NATO’s longstanding members, including Germany and Canada, reaching the 2% target is proving difficult. Rutte will face the delicate task of applying pressure on laggards without alienating key allies.

Emerging security domains represent another significant challenge. The alliance is playing catch-up in areas such as cyber warfare, disinformation campaigns, and hybrid threats, much of which are being deployed by Russia and other state actors. Rutte will be expected to bolster NATO’s resilience in the face of such tactics—as well as to address the technological and industrial gaps that have been exposed during the war in Ukraine.

Finally, internal cohesion remains a concern. The expansion of NATO to include Finland and Sweden has been hailed as a strategic win, but also contributed to friction with Turkey and Hungary, and domestic politics in several member countries threatens to complicate defence and enlargement policy further. Maintaining unity under such pressure will require careful management.

As he prepares to take up the post, Rutte’s experience as a seasoned negotiator and his reputation for consensus-building are likely to be tested to the limit. The stakes for the alliance—and for transatlantic security more broadly—have rarely been higher.
headline: Trump to Putin: what key challenges face Rutte at NATO?

text:
The European Space Agency’s (ESA) Euclid space telescope has today released its first set of scientific images, marking a major milestone in its mission to map the ‘dark universe’. The images, hailed as the deepest and sharpest wide-field views of the cosmos ever captured at visible and infrared wavelengths, showcase far-flung galaxies, star clusters, and previously unseen cosmic features.

Euclid, launched in July 2023 aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral, is tasked with investigating the universe’s mysterious dark matter and dark energy. These components are believed to comprise approximately 95% of the universe, yet remain poorly understood by scientists to date.

Speaking at a press conference in Paris, ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher described the images as “revolutionary”, adding that they demonstrated the telescope’s “immense potential to transform our understanding of the cosmos”. Over the course of its six-year primary mission, Euclid will create a three-dimensional map of the universe by observing billions of galaxies across more than a third of the sky.

One of the first images released shows a stunning panorama of the Perseus Cluster, revealing thousands of galaxies with unprecedented clarity. Other photographs highlight the Horsehead Nebula in infrared, uncovering star-forming regions obscured from terrestrial telescopes. ESA scientists noted that faint and distant galaxies—some more than 10 billion light years away—are visible in remarkable detail.

Professor Tom Ray of the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, a member of the Euclid consortium, said that today’s results would inspire astronomers in Ireland and around the world. “We’re glimpsing structures and phenomena that have never been witnessed before. This is a remarkable achievement for European science, and Irish researchers are playing a part in deciphering these cosmic mysteries.”

Euclid’s instruments, built in partnership with over 300 scientific institutions across Europe, are designed to measure the shapes and positions of galaxies with extreme precision. By analysing the subtle distortions caused by gravity—a phenomenon known as weak gravitational lensing—scientists hope to trace the influence of dark matter and map the acceleration of the universe’s expansion driven by dark energy.

Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin TD congratulated the ESA and all involved researchers, saying that Ireland’s support for ESA collaborative programmes continues to bring significant scientific returns.

The mission comes as global interest in astronomy and space science is surging, with ESA, NASA, and China all making significant investments in next-generation observatories. The Euclid images, now available to the public, are expected to prompt new research and excite astronomical societies and schools throughout the country.

ESA indicated that this is only the beginning of Euclid’s discoveries, with tens of thousands more images set to be captured and released over the coming years. The data will be used to further probe the texture, evolution, and fate of the universe—questions that have puzzled scientists, philosophers, and the public alike since time immemorial.
headline: Europe's Euclid space telescope releases first images

text:
An initiative aimed at promoting the safe use of e-scooters in Waterford has been launched this week, as concerns persist over their impact on road safety and public spaces. The campaign, jointly organised by Waterford City and County Council and the Gardaí, seeks to raise awareness among e-scooter users about traffic regulations and safe riding practices.

Local authorities say the initiative comes as a response to a significant increase in e-scooter usage across the city centre and surrounding areas, particularly among younger people and students. Gardaí in Waterford have reported a rise in incidents involving e-scooters, including collisions with pedestrians, near misses at junctions, and improper use on footpaths.

Under current legislation, most privately owned e-scooters are not permitted for use on public roads, cycle lanes or footpaths unless they comply with specific guidelines set out by the Department of Transport. However, many users remain unaware of these restrictions, prompting calls from councillors and community groups for greater clarity and enforcement.

Inspector James White of Waterford Garda Station said that while e-scooters offer an efficient and eco-friendly means of travel, users must be aware of their responsibilities: “We are urging all e-scooter owners to familiarise themselves with the rules of the road and to think of the safety of themselves and others. Inappropriate or reckless use can result in injury and potential prosecution.”

The council’s Road Safety Officer, Deirdre O’Shea, said educational outreach through local schools and colleges would be a key part of the effort. She added that the council is also exploring the possibility of designated e-scooter parking zones and clearer signage in high-traffic areas.

Several Waterford city residents have raised concerns about the lack of regulation, with some describing e-scooters being left obstructing pavements or travelling at excessive speeds. Parent groups have highlighted the dangers for children and those with limited mobility, while business owners in the city centre have spoken of increased risk to customers due to shared spaces.

The Department of Transport has indicated that proposed legislation to legalise and regulate e-scooters nationally is currently progressing through the Oireachtas, with new rules expected later in the year.
