Until then, Gardaí have confirmed they will continue to monitor e-scooter usage and enforce existing traffic laws, warning that offenders may have their vehicles seized or face fines.

The council has encouraged members of the public to report dangerous or anti-social use of e-scooters, as part of a broader effort to ensure Waterford remains accessible and safe for all.
headline: Waterford e-scooter initiative amid safety concerns

text:
A man in his thirties is due before the District Court this morning as part of an ongoing investigation into human trafficking in the south of the country.

Gardaí arrested the man yesterday following a planned operation in Cork city, which was carried out by members of the Garda National Protective Services Bureau in conjunction with local units. The investigation centres on the alleged trafficking of several non-Irish nationals for the purposes of exploitation.

The man was detained under Section 50 of the Criminal Justice Act, 2007 and questioned at a Garda station in Cork overnight. He is expected to face charges relating to the alleged recruitment, movement and exploitation of vulnerable individuals.

The operation follows a lengthy enquiry involving specialist officers from the bureau’s Human Trafficking Investigation and Co-ordination Unit, as well as support from international law enforcement agencies. It is understood that a number of individuals have been provided with assistance and support services under the auspices of the HSE, and are being cared for at a secure location.

In a statement, Gardaí said their investigation remains ongoing and that further arrests have not been ruled out. They have appealed for anyone with information on human trafficking or labour exploitation to contact the confidential Garda helpline.

The man is scheduled to appear before Cork District Court later today.
headline: Man due in court in human trafficking investigation

text:
Former US President Donald Trump has claimed credit for progress towards a ceasefire in Gaza, describing it as “my peace deal” in a new interview released this morning. Speaking on a US-based podcast, Mr Trump said his administration’s prior efforts in the region had laid the groundwork for the current negotiations, despite not holding office since January 2021.

Mr Trump, who is campaigning to return to the White House in November’s election, told host Steve Bannon on the War Room podcast that his Middle East policies, including the Abraham Accords, were instrumental in shaping recent diplomatic efforts. “They’re now finally coming around to what we started. We had peace in the Middle East like never before. This could have been resolved years ago if they’d kept my programme,” he said.

The remarks come amid mounting international pressure for a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas, as the conflict continues into its eighth month. Over 36,000 Palestinians have been killed since October, according to Gaza’s health authorities, with the humanitarian crisis deepening despite intermittent talks brokered by the US, Qatar and Egypt.

The Biden administration has circulated a new ceasefire proposal in recent weeks, with US Secretary of State Antony Blinken visiting the region for meetings with Israeli and Arab leaders. However, the path to an agreement remains uncertain, with major stumbling blocks including the release of Israeli hostages and guarantees for long-term security in the enclave.

Mr Trump, whose foreign policy legacy remains divisive, frequently cites the Abraham Accords—a set of normalisation agreements signed by Israel and several Arab states in 2020—as evidence of his success in the region. He has repeatedly criticised President Joe Biden’s handling of the Gaza crisis, arguing that his successor’s approach has “emboldened Hamas”.

In the podcast, Mr Trump did not provide specific details on how his administration would approach a ceasefire, but insisted that regional players “trusted” the US more during his tenure. “We had all sides talking. There was respect, there was understanding,” he asserted.

His comments have drawn criticism from Democratic Party officials, who argue that current US policy seeks to balance Israeli security interests with urgent humanitarian needs in Gaza. Meanwhile, Palestinian officials have dismissed the claim that the Abraham Accords contributed meaningfully to resolving the underlying issues between Israel and the Palestinians.

In Ireland, the Government and several Irish TDs have repeatedly called for an immediate ceasefire and increased humanitarian assistance for Gaza. Dáil Éireann recently backed a motion to support the recognition of a Palestinian state, in line with a coordinated announcement by Ireland, Spain and Norway last month.

As fighting intensifies in southern Gaza and the UN warns of an imminent famine, international pressure continues to mount for all parties to agree to a permanent end to hostilities. The likelihood of a breakthrough remains unclear, with both sides trading blame for the latest round of violence.

Mr Trump is expected to continue highlighting Middle East policy as a key plank of his presidential campaign, promising “peace through strength” if elected for a second term.
headline: Podcast: Trump praises his peace deal for Gaza

text:
The Government is adopting a “wait and see” approach to the introduction of further measures to shield consumers from rising energy costs, with senior sources indicating that any new supports are unlikely to be unveiled before the autumn.

Speaking at Leinster House on Wednesday, the Minister for the Environment, Climate and Communications, Eamon Ryan, said that while the recent drop in wholesale gas prices is welcome, prices remain high by historic standards. He pointed to the existing suite of energy credits and targeted supports already rolled out by the State during the winter as evidence of the Government’s ongoing commitment to assisting households through the energy crisis.

The current €450 energy credit, funded through the Department of Social Protection, is due to expire in March, with no official confirmation yet as to whether a similar scheme will be renewed for the next winter season. Minister Ryan reiterated that “the situation is being closely monitored”, and that any intervention would be “timely and proportionate to developments on the international energy markets”.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin struck a similar note, stating that any decision on renewed energy supports would be “informed by economic data and the evolving situation across Europe”. He highlighted the need for “prudence and flexibility,” noting that while the State’s finances remain robust, “rainy day funding” must be managed carefully in anticipation of potential further volatility.

Opposition parties have criticised the Government’s stance, with Sinn Féin’s spokesperson on energy, Darren O’Rourke TD, describing the response as “complacent” and calling for a renewed windfall tax on energy companies. The Social Democrats’ leader Holly Cairns also pressed for a “clear timeline” regarding future supports.

Consumer advocacy groups, including St Vincent de Paul and the Money Advice and Budgeting Service (MABS), have reported a “steady stream” of calls from households struggling with high utility bills, despite the mild winter. Both organisations have urged the Government to set out a comprehensive plan for energy poverty in advance of the next heating season.

For its part, the Department of the Environment has confirmed that the Cabinet will receive a detailed briefing on international energy price trends in April, as part of wider budgetary discussions.

Electric Ireland, Bord Gáis Energy and SSE Airtricity all indicated this week that further reductions in residential tariffs will depend on sustained wholesale price decreases, with no immediate plans for further cuts beyond those announced in recent months.

The European Commission has signalled that member states may phase out some extraordinary supports as prices stabilise, but acknowledged the need for “targeted measures” for vulnerable customers.

Meanwhile, the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) has urged consumers to continue to shop around for better deals and to avail of energy efficiency grants where possible. The CRU is conducting a review of standing charges and bill transparency, due to report in June.

As the summer approaches, the Government is expected to reassess the position, with decisions on possible new measures deferred until closer to Budget 2025.
headline: Govt taking 'wait and see' approach to energy protection

text:
Authorities have issued a renewed appeal for vigilance around water as the June bank holiday approaches, amid concerns over potential rises in incidents related to swimming, boating, and other water-based activities.

The Coast Guard, Water Safety Ireland, and the RNLI have all urged members of the public to take extra care in coastal areas, rivers, and lakes over the long weekend, which traditionally sees a surge in recreational activity as temperatures rise.

Over the past five years, an average of nine people have lost their lives to drowning during the month of June, according to Water Safety Ireland. In a statement today, the organisation said many of these cases involved sudden immersion in open water and highlighted the unpredictable nature of Irish weather, including rapidly changing sea and river conditions.

The appeal comes in the wake of several recent incidents where members of the public required assistance, including a number of rescues last weekend off the coasts of Wexford and Galway. Gardaí are also reminding families to be mindful of young children near water, noting that supervision and the use of appropriate flotation devices are key preventative measures.

Minister for Rural and Community Development, Heather Humphreys, said: “With the good weather forecast, we want everyone to enjoy their time outdoors safely. Whether you’re heading to the sea, lakes or rivers, please take sensible precautions and never underestimate the risks.”

The Coast Guard is advising those heading to beaches to swim only at lifeguarded locations and to remain within their depth. Swimmers should avoid jumping or diving into water where the depth is unknown and be aware of tides and currents.

The RNLI has echoed the call, asking people to check local weather and tide times, to wear lifejackets where appropriate, and to let someone know their plans before setting out on the water.

Emergency services have reminded the public that in the event of witnessing a person in difficulty on or near water, they should dial 112 or 999 and ask for the Coast Guard. 

Last year, almost 80 people lost their lives in water-related incidents across the country. Water Safety Ireland stressed the importance of education, preparation and adhering to basic safety advice to prevent further tragedies as people seek to make the most of the long weekend.
headline: Appeal for safety around water ahead over bank holiday

text:
A major breakthrough has been reported in efforts to halt the decline of Ireland’s native curlew population, as new figures show a significant rise in breeding pairs in areas targeted by a conservation programme.

The Curlew Conservation Programme, run by the National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS), has revealed that the number of breeding curlew pairs in selected project areas has increased by nearly 30% over the past two years. The findings come following an intensive effort involving landowners, volunteers, and NPWS staff across key habitats in the midlands, Connacht and Munster.

The curlew, a ground-nesting wader famous for its distinctive call, has experienced a dramatic decline in numbers over the past decades. Recent estimates suggested that fewer than 150 pairs remained in the Republic, down from several thousand in the late 20th century, due largely to habitat loss, predation, and agricultural intensification.

Minister of State for Heritage and Electoral Reform, Malcolm Noonan TD, welcomed the progress, describing it as “a real cause for hope” in what has been a grim story for one of Ireland’s most threatened birds. “This demonstrates what can be achieved where dedicated collaboration takes place between farmers, scientists and local communities,” he said.

Key measures implemented through the conservation scheme include predator control, such as the management of fox and mink populations, and habitat protection through agreements with farmers. The programme also provides support for delayed mowing and appropriate grazing, ensuring safer conditions for nesting curlew.

Project officer Dr Barry O’Donoghue said the recent fledging of multiple chicks in the boglands and wetlands of Roscommon, Galway and Kerry underlines the “real impact” being made at ground level. “Where this type of intensive management is in place, the difference is plain to see,” he said. “We’re now seeing more birds returning to sites where they’d completely vanished only a few years ago.”

Farmers involved in the scheme say support payments and advisory visits have helped offset the challenges of adapting farm practices to protect the species. “We all want to see the curlew survive here,” said Meath farmer John Flynn. “The changes are worth it when you hear them calling in the mornings again.”

The NPWS cautioned that while the results mark a positive step, the curlew remains critically endangered and that ongoing commitment will be required to avoid extinction. Conservationists have called for the expansion of the scheme and sustained funding to support the work.

The Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage has indicated it will seek to secure an increase in resources for the coming year to widen the programme’s reach. The Department also plans to publish a detailed review of the scheme before the end of 2024.

Ireland holds a special responsibility for the curlew’s survival, as it is home to a unique and genetically distinct population. The curlew is listed as a priority species under the EU Birds Directive, with the State obliged to safeguard its remaining habitats.

The breakthrough comes as environmental groups warn of the broader decline of biodiversity across the island, urging further action to protect threatened wildlife. The Dáil is expected to debate new measures on biodiversity later this month, as part of the Government’s response to the Citizens’ Assembly on Biodiversity Loss.
headline: Curlew conservation scheme makes breakthrough

text:
The Football Association of Ireland has issued a formal apology to a group of female former international players who spoke publicly this week about their experiences with the women’s national team during the 1990s and early 2000s, acknowledging what it called a “legacy of neglect and disregard”.

In a statement released on Thursday morning, the FAI’s chief executive, Jonathan Hill, said: “We have listened closely to the recent testimonies from our former internationals and are deeply sorry for the unacceptable conditions they endured, and for the lack of respect shown to them both on and off the pitch.”

The apology follows an RTÉ Investigates report in which a number of ex-internationals described playing in hand-me-down kit, being asked to wash their own jerseys, and travelling long distances for matches and training at their own expense, with little or no support from the association. Players also spoke of being denied basic facilities, such as separate changing rooms, and a lack of medical or coaching resources.

One former international, who played for Republic of Ireland between 1995 and 2002, told RTÉ News: “We felt like an afterthought. No one ever asked what we needed or how we were managing. It’s hard to see now how we were expected to perform at a high level in those circumstances.”

The FAI statement acknowledged “systemic failings” in its treatment of women’s football, admitting that, over many years, successive administrations “prioritised the men’s programme to the exclusion of all others”.

“Today’s apology is overdue, but it is sincere,” the FAI said. The association has also invited representatives from the ex-players’ group to meet with senior officials and current members of the women’s national squad.

Minister for Sport Catherine Martin TD welcomed the apology but said the government would be “monitoring closely” to ensure a new culture of “genuine respect and equality” for women and girls in football.

Labour TD Aodhán Ó Ríordáin, chairperson of the Oireachtas Committee on Tourism, Culture, Arts, Sport and Media, said the testimonies revealed “shocking failures by the FAI” and called for an independent audit of the association’s historical governance in respect of women’s football.

The FAI has in recent years increased funding to the women’s national team and the League of Ireland Women’s Premier Division, with senior players now on professional contracts and receiving parity of match fees. However, campaigners say more still needs to be done to address the disparity in resources at underage levels and in grassroots clubs across the country.

Some of the ex-players have indicated they may seek further redress and want assurances that the association will establish a formal process to hear their grievances. The FAI has said it will consider establishing an independent review panel to examine historical treatment of women’s football.

RTÉ News contacted the Department of Sport and the Sports Council for comment. The Department said it “expects all sporting bodies in receipt of public funding to uphold the highest standards of equality and inclusion”. The Sports Council said it would “continue to engage with the FAI and relevant stakeholders to ensure the ongoing improvement of conditions for women’s sport in Ireland”.

Current Republic of Ireland captain Katie McCabe, speaking on behalf of the present squad, said: “We stand in solidarity with the players who came before us. Their experiences should never be repeated.
headline: FAI apologises to female former players who have spoken out

text:
The Minister for Justice, Helen McEntee, is to publish a long-awaited review of Ireland’s sex work legislation this afternoon, following months of lobbying by advocacy groups and cross-party TDs. The report, commissioned in 2022, examines the effectiveness of the 2017 Sexual Offences Act provisions that criminalise the purchase of sex and brothel-keeping, but not the act of selling sex itself.

The review’s publication comes amid growing calls from sex workers’ organisations, human rights campaigners, and opposition TDs for the Government to address what they describe as unintended harms caused by the current legal framework. Critics of the legislation argue that it has pushed the sector further underground, increasing the dangers faced by those involved and making it more difficult to access Garda protection or support services.

Sources indicate the review, conducted by an independent expert panel, draws on extensive consultations with stakeholders, including An Garda Síochána, survivors of trafficking, healthcare professionals, and sex workers themselves. Early drafts suggest the panel found “mixed evidence” on whether the law has achieved its objectives of reducing demand and providing greater safety for vulnerable individuals.

Minister McEntee is expected to brief the Cabinet on the findings before publishing the report, which will be made available on the Department of Justice website. She has signalled her intention to consider legislative changes if warranted, but stressed the need for a balanced approach that continues to protect victims of trafficking and exploitation.

Speaking this morning, the Minister said, “My priority remains the safety and dignity of all those affected by sex work and the ongoing fight against organised crime and trafficking. This review provides a crucial evidence base for what steps might be necessary.”

The review is also expected to address the question of criminal sanctions for sex workers found working together for safety, a practice currently prohibited under brothel-keeping laws. Advocacy groups such as the Sex Workers Alliance Ireland (SWAI) have called these provisions “dangerous and counterproductive”, and urged the Government to move towards a harm-reduction model.

Opposition parties, including Sinn Féin and the Social Democrats, have called for comprehensive reform and the introduction of safeguards that ensure sex workers can report abuse or violence to the Gardaí without fear of prosecution.

The report’s publication is likely to reignite debate within the Oireachtas, with a number of TDs and Senators on the Justice Committee pledging to hold hearings on any proposed legislative amendments.

The Minister is due to make a statement in the Dáil later today, with further details on the review’s recommendations expected to follow.
headline: Minister to publish review of sex work legislation

text:
US Vice President Kamala Harris has criticised Donald Trump’s approach to foreign and domestic affairs, describing the former president’s vision for America as “self-serving” and harmful to international cooperation. Speaking at a security conference in Washington DC, Ms Harris said that the stakes in November’s presidential election could not be higher, warning that Mr Trump’s return to the White House would represent “a retreat from America’s responsibility” on the world stage.

Ms Harris accused Mr Trump of prioritising his personal interests and political ambitions at the expense of long-standing alliances and multilateral partnerships, including within NATO. “When America turns inward, when decisions are made for short-term, self-serving reasons, the world becomes less stable and less safe,” Ms Harris told delegates, which included representatives from EU member states and the United Nations.

Referring to Mr Trump’s recent comments questioning the US’s future commitment to NATO, Ms Harris said such statements “undermine the foundation of collective security” and embolden authoritarian regimes. She added that America’s leadership was “essential” in tackling challenges such as climate change, the war in Ukraine, and the defence of democracy globally.

The remarks come amid a deeply polarised political landscape in the US, where Mr Trump remains the leading Republican candidate for November’s election. President Joe Biden and his administration have sought to contrast their approach with that of Mr Trump, emphasising support for Ukraine and a multilateral foreign policy.

White House spokesperson Karine Jean-Pierre said afterwards that President Biden and Vice President Harris were “committed to strengthening America’s alliances and upholding the rules-based order”. She added that voters faced a “clear choice” between “responsible leadership and reckless isolationism”.

Mr Trump has repeatedly defended his ‘America First’ strategy, claiming it better serves the interests of US citizens and arguing that allies should do more to share the cost of international defence arrangements. His campaign has dismissed the criticism from Ms Harris as “political grandstanding”.

Observers in Europe and elsewhere are closely monitoring the campaign, given the implications for transatlantic cooperation and global security. Irish officials have previously raised concerns about Mr Trump’s stance on international agreements, particularly on climate action and NATO.

While Ms Harris did not directly refer to Ireland in her address, diplomatic sources suggest the Irish Government is expected to maintain close engagement with whichever administration emerges after the US election, while reiterating commitments to EU and UN-led responses to global challenges.
headline: Trump's America is 'self-serving', says Kamala Harris

text:
A meatball created using the resurrected genetic material of the woolly mammoth has been unveiled at a science museum in Amsterdam, in a world first that its creators say is designed to spark debate about the future of food.

The unusual culinary creation was produced by Australian cultivated meat company Vow, who worked with scientists to sequence mammoth DNA and insert it into sheep cells. The cells were then grown in a laboratory to create the meatball, which was presented under glass at the NEMO Science Museum on Wednesday.

Tim Noakesmith, a co-founder of Vow, said the intention was to highlight the possibilities opened up by cellular agriculture and to encourage discussion on sustainable food sources. “We wanted to create something that was both attention-grabbing and a conversation starter about what the future of food might look like,” he said.

The woolly mammoth roamed what is now Europe, Asia and North America, before going extinct around 4,000 years ago. Scientists extracted DNA sequences from preserved mammoth remains and used these sequences to fill in missing gaps with genes from the African elephant, the mammoth’s closest living relative.

The resulting mammoth protein was produced in sheep cells in the laboratory. The company has stressed that no one has yet tasted the meatball, as it is not yet established whether people would have an allergic or adverse reaction.

Professor Ernst Wolvetang of the University of Queensland said that the process was technologically straightforward. “We just synthesised the gene, based on the mammoth genome, and put it into yeast, which we then used to produce the protein in the laboratory,” he said.

Proponents of cultivated meat argue that such technology could significantly reduce the environmental impact of animal agriculture while providing alternative protein sources. Critics, however, point to existing challenges in scaling up production and achieving regulatory approval.

The unveiling comes amid growing international debate over how to feed a global population expected to reach 10 billion by 2050, with concerns about greenhouse gas emissions from livestock farming and the biodiversity impact of large-scale agriculture.

Irish researchers in the field have welcomed the project as a demonstration of the potential for cellular agriculture but have cautioned that significant hurdles remain before such products could appear on supermarket shelves. The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) has said that cultivated meat products would be subject to rigorous EU novel food regulations before being approved for sale.

The meatball will remain on display in Amsterdam, for now as a scientific curiosity — but its creators hope it will inspire further research and debate on the role of science and innovation in making the future of food more sustainable.
headline: Meatball made with mammoth DNA unveiled in Amsterdam

text:
Hundreds of demonstrators gathered in the centre of Dublin on Saturday afternoon to call for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza, urging the Irish Government to do more to press for the protection of civilians and an end to the ongoing conflict. Organised by the Ireland-Palestine Solidarity Campaign, the march began at the Garden of Remembrance and proceeded down O’Connell Street, with participants chanting slogans and carrying Palestinian flags and banners.

Protesters heard speeches from representatives of civil society groups, trade unions and several TDs, who condemned recent Israeli military operations in Gaza and expressed solidarity with the Palestinian population. The event comes amid growing international concern over the humanitarian situation in the region, where local health authorities say thousands have been killed and many more injured since the escalation of violence began last October.

Speaking at the demonstration, People Before Profit TD Richard Boyd Barrett renewed calls for the Government to expel the Israeli ambassador and sanction companies with links to the Israeli defence sector. “Ireland must take a stand against the slaughter in Gaza and demand the immediate release of hostages and unimpeded humanitarian access,” he said.

Labour Party leader Ivana Bacik also addressed the crowd, urging all sides to return to negotiations. “The loss of life in Gaza is unacceptable. We call for a permanent ceasefire and support all diplomatic efforts towards a just and lasting peace,” she said.

The protest was one of several taking place across Europe this weekend amid growing calls for international intervention to halt the violence. Gardaí say the Dublin demonstration passed off peacefully and no arrests were reported. Traffic delays occurred on several city centre routes as marchers made their way to a rally outside Leinster House, where a minute’s silence was held for victims of the conflict.

In a statement last week, the Department of Foreign Affairs reiterated Ireland’s support for a two-state solution and again called on both Israel and Hamas to cease hostilities. Taoiseach Simon Harris told the Dáil that the situation in Gaza was “deeply concerning” and said the Government would continue to advocate for increased humanitarian aid.

The UN has described the humanitarian situation in Gaza as “catastrophic”, with widespread shortages of food, clean water and medical supplies. Irish aid agencies including Trócaire and GOAL have appealed for increased support to help civilians caught up in the conflict.
headline: Dublin protesters call for end to Gaza conflict

text:
At least 61 migrants, including women and children, are believed to have drowned following a shipwreck off the coast of Libya, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). The tragedy occurred on Saturday when a vessel carrying around 86 people capsized near the port city of Zuwara, west of Tripoli.

Survivors reported that the boat, described as an overcrowded rubber dinghy, set off in poor weather conditions before encountering rough seas. The IOM said the victims comprised people predominantly from Nigeria, The Gambia and other sub-Saharan African countries. Twenty-five survivors were brought ashore by local authorities, where they remain in need of urgent humanitarian assistance.

The Mediterranean continues to be the world's deadliest migration route, with the IOM estimating that over 2,250 people have lost their lives or gone missing attempting the crossing so far this year. Many departing from Libya hope to reach Italy or Malta, but often face dangerous conditions, including unseaworthy vessels and the risk of interception by Libyan authorities.

Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) and other humanitarian agencies have reiterated calls for increased search and rescue operations, as well as safe and legal migration pathways. They warn that the lack of coordinated international response is leaving vulnerable people at the mercy of traffickers and perilous journeys.

The incident comes as European leaders continue to debate migration policy, with Italy and several other EU member states seeking to step up cooperation with North African countries to curb departures. The Irish Government has previously pledged support for EU efforts to address the crisis, while Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin has called for a fair and humane approach to migration management.

In a statement, the IOM called for urgent action to prevent further loss of life, saying: “We must not become numb to such tragedies, which are entirely preventable if states act in solidarity and in line with international law.”

An estimated 45,000 people have attempted the crossing from North Africa to Europe so far in 2024, according to the UN Refugee Agency. The latest disaster adds to mounting concerns about the dangers faced by those seeking safety and a better life in Europe.
headline: 61 migrants drown after shipwreck off Libya

text:
Israel’s Defence Minister, Yoav Gallant, has said his government is prepared to take “unilateral action” in Gaza if negotiations on a post-war arrangement with international and regional partners fail, raising fresh concerns about possible annexation of parts of the territory.

Speaking during a visit to Israel’s border with Gaza on Wednesday, Mr Gallant stated that if international parties cannot reach agreement on who would control the Palestinian enclave, Israel would consider establishing a “security buffer zone” along the Strip’s border and maintaining direct military control over certain areas.

“We prefer an arrangement with partners, but if that is not possible, we will act independently to ensure Israel’s security interests,” Mr Gallant told reporters. “This could involve establishing buffer zones and eradicating the threat from Hamas for good.”

His comments come amid ongoing discussions involving Israel, the United States, Egypt, and Gulf states, as well as the Palestinian Authority, concerning the governance of Gaza after months of conflict. International reaction to Mr Gallant’s remarks has been swift, with the US State Department reiterating its opposition to any reduction in the size of Gaza or permanent Israeli occupation of the territory.

A spokesperson for the European Union expressed “grave concern” at any suggestion of annexation, warning that unilateral measures could further destabilise the region and undermine prospects for a two-state solution.

Speaking in the Dáil this afternoon, Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin said any move by Israel to annex areas of Gaza would be “completely unacceptable” to the Irish Government and a violation of international law. He repeated Ireland’s call for “an immediate ceasefire, unimpeded humanitarian access, and a credible political process leading to Palestinian self-determination.”

Since the escalation of violence in October, more than 37,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli military operations in Gaza, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry. Over one million people have been displaced, with many now living in overcrowded shelters or makeshift camps.

Israel maintains its offensive is aimed at destroying Hamas, which carried out the 7th October attack that killed some 1,200 Israelis and led to the abduction of over 250 hostages. However, international aid agencies, including several Irish NGOs, have warned of a looming famine in parts of Gaza and called for greater protection of civilians and medical facilities.

Negotiations on a possible ceasefire, involving Egypt, Qatar, and the United States, have so far failed to reach a breakthrough. Meanwhile, the United Nations and other international bodies have repeatedly called for the protection of Gaza’s territorial integrity.

Mr Gallant’s remarks, which come as Israel faces growing diplomatic pressure, are likely to increase concerns in European capitals and could complicate efforts to broker an end to the current conflict. The situation remains tense on Israel’s northern border with Lebanon, where exchanges of fire with Hezbollah militants have continued.
headline: Israeli defence minister threatens to annex parts of Gaza

text:
Labour Party leader Ivana Bacik has criticised the Government’s handling of higher education funding, claiming that student budget plans are in “disarray” following the announcement of higher university fees for the next academic year.

Speaking in the Dáil today, Deputy Bacik said the proposed increase in student contribution charges—due to take effect in September—will place further financial strain on families already grappling with rising costs of living. She accused the coalition of failing to fulfil its commitment to easing the burden on students and their families.

“Students around the country are now faced with further uncertainty as they try to plan for the academic year ahead. The Government’s decision to raise fees undermines previous promises to make higher education more accessible,” Deputy Bacik told TDs.

The Department of Further and Higher Education last week confirmed that the student contribution fee for undergraduate courses will rise by €250, bringing the annual charge to €3,500. The department has defended the measure, stating that increased funding is needed to address inflationary pressures and to support the quality of teaching and campus services.

However, Deputy Bacik argued that the move will deter prospective students from lower-income backgrounds and add to the growing problem of student debt. She also referenced ongoing accommodation shortages and the cost of living crisis faced by those attending colleges in Dublin and other cities.

“Many students are already struggling to pay rent and meet day-to-day expenses. Forcing them to shoulder yet another increase in fees is deeply unfair,” she said.

A spokesperson for the Union of Students in Ireland (USI) described the decision as “a step backwards for access to education”, and called on the Government to reconsider. The USI has indicated plans to hold protests in the coming weeks.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin defended the increase during Leaders’ Questions, saying that additional resources are necessary to maintain standards but insisted the Government remains committed to long-term reform of higher education funding. He pointed to recent measures such as the extension of the SUSI grant and additional supports for disadvantaged students.

The Higher Education Authority has warned that Irish universities face a significant funding gap and has lobbied for a sustainable financing model. Meanwhile, opposition TDs have called on Minister for Further and Higher Education Simon Harris to engage with student representatives and explore alternatives to fee hikes.

The Government is expected to face continued pressure on the issue when the Oireachtas resumes its debate on the Education (Student Contributions) Bill next week.
headline: Bacik: Student's budget plans in 'disarray' over fee hike

text:
Irish marine scientists have identified microplastics in the breath exhaled by dolphins off the coast of west Cork, marking the first such discovery in these waters. The findings, published today by the Marine Institute and University College Cork (UCC), raise renewed concerns about the extent of plastic contamination along Ireland’s coastline and its potential impact on marine mammals.

Researchers working with the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group (IWDG) conducted a series of boat-based surveys in Roaringwater Bay, County Cork, where they collected exhaled breath samples — known as “blow” — from bottlenose dolphins using a custom device. The analysis detected microscopic fragments of plastics in over 65% of the samples.

Dr Simon Berrow, lead researcher and lecturer at the Atlantic Technological University, said the results were “deeply concerning” and highlighted that dolphins could be inhaling or ingesting microplastics both through the water they swim in and the air they breathe at the surface.

“This research shows that microplastics are entering dolphins’ bodies not just through their food, but from the very air above our waters. We have long known that marine mammals are threatened by larger pieces of plastic, but this study confirms that the smallest fragments are now an immediate hazard,” Dr Berrow said.

Microplastics are pieces of plastic less than five millimetres in length, often resulting from the breakdown of larger debris or from microbeads found in cosmetics and cleaning products. These particles have been found throughout Ireland’s marine environment, from remote beaches to deep sea sediments, but this is the first time they have been identified inside wild dolphins’ respiratory systems here.

Dr Amy Lusher, a microplastics specialist at the Marine Institute, said that while the health risks to dolphins are still being studied, microplastics can carry toxic chemicals and pathogens, potentially leading to respiratory and immune issues. “The presence of microplastics in dolphin blow raises serious questions about the long-term health implications for these animals, many of which are already facing pressure from other human activities,” Dr Lusher said.

Ireland is home to several resident populations of bottlenose and common dolphins, with the Shannon Estuary designated as a Special Area of Conservation for the species. The discovery has prompted calls from conservation groups for more stringent regulation of plastics entering the marine environment and for expanded monitoring by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage.

Responding to the findings, a spokesperson for the Department said the Government would “consider the latest scientific evidence as part of its ongoing Marine Strategy Framework Directive obligations” and stressed its commitment to reduce single-use plastics nationally.

The research team is now extending its study to include samples from Galway Bay and the Irish Sea, where microplastic levels may differ. They also plan to examine possible links between microplastic exposure and dolphin health outcomes.

The findings come just days before World Oceans Day, with campaigners urging stronger government action to tackle marine plastic pollution, warning that “Ireland’s unique marine life is quite literally struggling to breathe.”
headline: Microplastics discovered in dolphin breath

text:
Donegal county councillors have voted unanimously to support calls for a public inquiry into the Creeslough explosion, which claimed the lives of ten people in October 2022. The motion, proposed at a full meeting of Donegal County Council this afternoon, urges the Government to establish an immediate, independent public inquiry into the circumstances leading to the tragedy at the Applegreen service station.

Councillors from across party lines spoke in favour of the motion, with many highlighting the continued anguish experienced by the Creeslough community and bereaved families. Cllr Michael McClafferty (FG), who tabled the motion, said a public inquiry was “the only way to ensure transparency and accountability”, praising the dignity and resilience shown by those affected.

The motion follows a renewed campaign by victims’ families, supported by local clergy and community groups, who argue that the ongoing Garda investigation—now in its 20th month—has yet to provide answers. Representatives for the families have said they are frustrated at the lack of detailed information, and have called on Taoiseach Simon Harris to meet with them directly.

Cllr Marie Therese Gallagher (SF) told the chamber that the pain in Creeslough was “as raw as ever”, and that the demand for an inquiry was about justice and closure, not blame. She added: “People need to know what happened, and need to know everything was done to prevent such a tragedy.”

The Mayor of Donegal, Cllr Liam Blaney, echoed these concerns, saying that a public inquiry would not only examine the cause of the explosion but would also scrutinise regulatory practices and emergency responses.

In a statement, Donegal County Council said it would write to the Minister for Justice, Helen McEntee, and the Taoiseach, conveying the Council’s position and seeking an urgent response from the Government.

To date, investigations are being led by Gardaí, supported by the Health and Safety Authority and a team of specialist engineers. The findings have not yet been made public, and no timeframe has been given for the completion of the criminal probe.

Minister McEntee has previously indicated she would await the outcome of the Garda investigation before considering further steps. However, pressure has mounted in recent weeks, with TDs from Donegal raising the matter in the Dáil and calling for a comprehensive, independent process.

Locals in Creeslough have said they welcome the Council's support, but remain determined to press their case with Government. Family members gathered at the council offices in Lifford today to show their gratitude for the motion and said they hoped it would mark a turning point in their campaign.
headline: Donegal councillors back Creeslough public inquiry

text:
Gardaí in Co Mayo are appealing for witnesses following the death of a man in his forties in Ballina on Tuesday evening. Emergency services were alerted to the scene on Barrett Street at approximately 8:30pm, where the man was discovered with serious injuries. He was treated by paramedics and taken to Mayo University Hospital but was later pronounced dead.

The area was sealed off overnight to allow for a technical examination by Garda forensic teams. Gardaí have confirmed that the State Pathologist has been notified and a post-mortem examination is expected to be carried out later today. The results of the post-mortem will determine the course of the Garda investigation.

Local sources have indicated that the man, who was originally from the area, may have sustained his injuries in a serious assault. Gardaí, however, have not commented on the nature of the incident and are keeping an open mind as they examine all circumstances surrounding the death.

Speaking this morning, Superintendent Pat Diskin of Ballina Garda Station said: “We are appealing to anyone who may have been in the Barrett Street or Lord Edward Street area between 8pm and 9pm on Tuesday evening, or who may have dashcam or CCTV footage, to come forward.”

Local representatives have expressed shock at the incident, with Mayo County Council cathaoirleach Gerard McHale extending his condolences to the family and urging anyone with information to assist the Gardaí in their enquiries.

Gardaí can be contacted at Ballina Garda Station on 096 20560, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or at any Garda station.
headline: Gardaí appeal for witnesses following death of man

text:
With just days to go before voters across Ireland cast their ballots in the European Parliament elections, candidates from all parties are intensifying efforts to secure support in what is shaping up to be one of the most hotly contested races in recent memory. Campaign teams have fanned out across constituencies, canvassing door to door, attending local events, and stepping up their presence on social media in a final push to shore up undecided voters.

The main parties — Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael, Sinn Féin, Labour, and the Green Party — are joined by a record number of Independents and smaller groupings, making for a crowded field in each of the three constituencies: Dublin, Midlands–North-West, and South. Polls suggest that while incumbents enjoy some advantage, several seats remain too close to call, with the potential for shock results as transfers are distributed on counting day.

In Dublin, the contest has been described as “fluid” by party sources, with Sinn Féin’s Lynn Boylan hoping to reclaim a seat lost in 2019, while Fine Gael’s Regina Doherty and Labour’s Aodhán Ó Ríordáin compete with a strong showing from Independents Clare Daly and Ciarán Cuffe of the Greens. Social Democrats candidate Sinéad Gibney has also reported growing momentum during the final days of canvassing.

Tensions have surfaced as rival campaigns accuse each other of negative tactics and misinformation, particularly over issues such as housing policy, EU migration proposals, and the Government’s climate targets. Several candidates have faced confrontations at public meetings, while Gardaí have increased patrols at larger events amid concerns over security.

In Midlands–North-West, an extensive area spanning from Donegal to Laois, the ballot paper features 27 names, including sitting MEPs Luke ‘Ming’ Flanagan and Maria Walsh. Sinn Féin’s Michelle Gildernew is seeking to make gains, while Fianna Fáil’s Barry Cowen and Fine Gael councillor Nina Carberry are attempting to appeal beyond traditional party bases. Recent polls indicate that transfers will prove critical given the fragmented field.

The South constituency likewise remains unpredictable, with sitting MEPs Sean Kelly (Fine Gael) and Billy Kelleher (Fianna Fáil) under pressure from challengers including Sinn Féin’s Kathleen Funchion and Green Party councillor Grace O’Sullivan. Farmers’ concerns over CAP reforms and nitrates derogations have featured prominently, while cost-of-living and rural connectivity issues dominate doorstep conversations.

Turnout is expected to be pivotal amid fears of voter apathy, with several candidates urging the public to “make their voices heard” on Friday. The outcome will not only determine Ireland’s 14 seats in the next European Parliament, but is widely seen as a bellwether for the next general election, with party leaders closely monitoring the performance of their candidates.

Counting is due to begin on Saturday, with results expected to emerge over the weekend and early next week. The returning officers have urged patience, warning that the large number of candidates and lengthy ballot papers may delay the final declarations.
headline: Candidates jostle for position ahead of Euro Parl vote

text:
A new May temperature record has been set at Shannon Airport, where the mercury soared to 28.6 degrees Celsius on Monday afternoon, according to Met Éireann. The previous May high for the site was 27.9 degrees, recorded on 29 May 2017.

The national forecaster confirmed that Shannon’s reading is also the highest temperature recorded anywhere in Ireland for the month of May since reliable records began. The previous national May record was 28.4C, set in Ardfert, Co Kerry, in 1997.

The unusually warm weather has been attributed to a high-pressure system drawing up air from southern Europe and North Africa, resulting in clear skies and sustained sunshine across much of the country.

Large crowds flocked to beaches and parks across Munster and the west, with Gardaí warning of heavy traffic and urging caution on the roads. Emergency services responded to several incidents involving swimmers and sun-seekers, prompting renewed appeals for water safety.

Met Éireann has issued a Yellow High Temperature warning for Clare, Limerick, Galway, and surrounding counties, advising the public to take extra care during outdoor activities and to stay hydrated, particularly the elderly and young children.

The Health Service Executive has reminded people to take steps to avoid sunburn and heat exhaustion, including staying in the shade during peak afternoon hours and using high-factor sunscreen.

While temperatures are expected to dip slightly later in the week, forecasters say the warm spell will persist, with daytime highs in the mid-twenties likely through Thursday. Provisional data will be reviewed by Met Éireann to confirm the record but officials say the reading at Shannon is unlikely to be surpassed this month.

Minister for the Environment Eamon Ryan said the record-breaking temperature “is a stark reminder of the impacts of climate change in Ireland”, adding that the Government remains committed to delivering on its climate targets.

A decision on potential restrictions to water supplies will be made if the dry spell continues, Irish Water has said, but no immediate issues have been reported.
headline: 28.6C reached at Shannon, breaking May temperature record

text:
The use of Bloody Sunday footage in a new Conservative Party campaign video has been condemned as “disgusting” by relatives of those killed and by political representatives in the North.

The British Conservative Party launched an online advert on Tuesday which, among other historic events, showed a clip from the 1972 massacre in Derry, when British soldiers shot dead 13 civil rights marchers and injured many more. A fourteenth victim later died as a result of injuries sustained that day.

John Kelly, whose 17-year-old brother Michael was killed on Bloody Sunday, told RTÉ News that the Tories’ use of the footage was “shameless and deeply disrespectful”, adding that it “reopens wounds for families who are still seeking justice more than half a century on”.

The short video was published on the official social media accounts of the Conservative Party ahead of the British general election, scheduled for 4 July. The footage also features reference to the 1984 Brighton bombing by the IRA and other historic incidents.

SDLP leader Colum Eastwood said the inclusion of Bloody Sunday was “utterly crass” and demonstrated that the Conservative Party was “willing to use the blood of Irish citizens for electioneering ends”. Sinn Féin Vice President Michelle O’Neill called on the party to withdraw the advert immediately and apologise to those affected.

The Taoiseach, Simon Harris, speaking in Dublin, described the inclusion of Bloody Sunday footage as “deeply insensitive”, urging respect for the memory of those who lost their lives and their families. He said the Irish Government had raised its concerns through diplomatic channels.

Mayor of Derry City and Strabane District Council, Patricia Logue, called the video “profoundly hurtful” and said it would only increase the hurt and anger still felt in Derry and across the North.

Amnesty International’s Northern Ireland Programme Director Grainne Teggart also criticised the Tories, stating: “Electioneering should never come at the expense of victims or their families, particularly in the case of unresolved historic injustices.”

The Conservative Party declined to comment when contacted by RTÉ News on Wednesday, but a source pointed to the party's “longstanding commitment to national security”.

The full findings of the 2010 Saville Inquiry into Bloody Sunday found all of those shot dead were unarmed, and that the killings were “unjustified and unjustifiable”. The British Government issued a formal apology in the House of Commons following the publication of the report.

Families of those killed have called for the campaign material to be removed and for an apology from the Conservative Party leadership. As of Wednesday evening, the video remained online.
headline: Tories' use of Bloody Sunday footage 'disgusting'

text:
Thirty dogs have been rescued from a private residence in England following the discovery of their owner’s body, local authorities have confirmed.

The animals were found in “distressing conditions” at the property in the rural Lincolnshire area after police responded to reports of concern for the welfare of a woman in her 60s. Officers from Lincolnshire Police attended the scene on Monday morning, where they subsequently discovered the woman’s remains.

The deceased has not yet been formally identified, but next of kin have been informed. The death is not being treated as suspicious, police said.

Animal welfare officers were called in to assist, with the RSPCA leading the rescue operation. The charity stated that the dogs, a mixed group of breeds, were found living in cramped and unsanitary conditions. Veterinary checks are ongoing, but initial reports indicate many of the dogs are undernourished and suffering from neglect.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Lincolnshire Police said: "We are working closely with the RSPCA to ensure the animals receive the care they require. An investigation into the circumstances surrounding both the woman’s death and the condition of the dogs is underway."

Local residents expressed shock at the discovery, noting that the property had been the subject of complaints in the past due to noise and concerns about animal welfare. Council officials are now liaising with the RSPCA to assess whether further action will be taken regarding animal welfare standards in the area.

The dogs have been taken to a number of animal rescue centres in the region, where they will undergo further assessment and rehabilitation. The RSPCA has appealed for donations to help with the cost of veterinary treatment and rehoming the animals once they are ready.

It is understood that the local authority is reviewing procedures relating to the monitoring of private homes where a large number of animals are kept. A report will be prepared for the coroner as part of the formal inquiry into the woman’s death.
headline: 30 dogs rescued from home in UK after owner found dead

text:
James Watson, the American scientist renowned for his role in uncovering the structure of DNA, has died at the age of 97, his family has confirmed. Watson, who shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962 with Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins, was widely regarded as one of the most influential biologists of the 20th century.

His discovery, alongside Crick in 1953, of the double-helix structure of DNA revolutionised biological sciences and paved the way for advances in genetics, medicine, and biotechnology. The team’s findings, published in the journal Nature, built on the work of Rosalind Franklin, whose X-ray diffraction images of DNA were critical in identifying its structure.

Born in Chicago in 1928, Watson pursued his studies at the University of Chicago and later at Indiana University, before moving to the University of Cambridge, where he met Crick. Their collaboration, while groundbreaking, was later the subject of controversy regarding the recognition of Franklin's contributions.

Watson went on to lead the Human Genome Project during its early phases and served as director and later president of Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory in New York. However, his reputation was marred in later years by a series of remarks widely condemned as racist and sexist, leading to his removal from public roles and honours.

Despite the controversies, Watson’s scientific achievements left an indelible mark on genetics and molecular biology. Tributes have poured in from leading scientific institutions and colleagues, reflecting on both the magnitude of his contributions and the debates his career provoked.

Irish academics have acknowledged the importance of Watson’s discoveries for medical research in Ireland and globally, noting that the understanding of DNA has underpinned advances in genetics, forensic science, and numerous HSE programmes targeting genetic disorders.

The family have said that funeral arrangements will be private. Watson is survived by his sons and grandchildren.
headline: DNA pioneer James Watson dies aged 97

text:
Over half of homeowners whose properties were repaired under the Government’s defective concrete blocks scheme have reported that further remedial works are required, according to new figures presented to the Oireachtas Housing Committee.

The scheme, which was established in response to the mica and pyrite scandals, has seen more than 2,600 applications approved to date, primarily in counties Donegal and Mayo. However, correspondence received by the Department of Housing indicates that many homes that underwent initial repairs continue to show signs of cracking and structural deterioration.

A review commissioned by the Department and published today found that 53% of homes that availed of the initial Stage 1 grant for remedial works have since reported the need for additional intervention. Structural engineers cited ongoing exposure to defective blocks, incomplete removal of compromised material, and, in some cases, substandard repair techniques as contributing factors.

Speaking after the committee’s session, Minister for Housing Darragh O’Brien said the findings were “deeply concerning” and acknowledged the “continuing distress” faced by affected families. “Every homeowner who relies on this scheme expects the repair to be permanent and comprehensive,” he said. “We are engaging with local authorities and contractors to ensure lessons are learned and standards improved.”

Representatives from the Mica Action Group and the Donegal Defective Blocks campaign criticised what they described as “piecemeal approaches” to remediation, claiming that partial repairs favour cost-saving over certainty for homeowners. “It’s not enough to patch up walls and hope for the best,” said Lisa Hone, chair of the Mica Action Group. “Families need homes they can trust.”

The Department has committed to an urgent review of inspection and certification processes, and is considering the establishment of an independent quality assurance body. Homeowners affected by the need for repeat works expressed frustration, with several telling RTÉ News they fear for the long-term value and safety of their homes.

The State has already allocated over €200 million to the redress scheme, with the Tánaiste Micheál Martin stating in the Dáil last week that “no affected family will be left behind.” Opposition TDs including Sinn Féin’s Eoin Ó Broin have called for a full public inquiry and guaranteed 100% redress.

A spokesperson for the Construction Industry Federation said it was essential that new building control regulations, currently under consultation, be enforced robustly to prevent recurrence of the crisis.

The Department is due to report back to the Oireachtas Committee in early September on its proposed reforms, amid growing calls for greater oversight and support for affected homeowners across the northwest.
headline: Half of homes in defective blocks scheme need more work

text:
At a time when many families were facing the toughest of challenges, Cian’s Kennels continued to bring comfort and companionship to children and young people receiving hospital treatment by reuniting them with their beloved pets. The Longford-based charity, established in memory of 15-year-old Cian Neary who died of cancer in 2019, experienced a year of growth and impact in 2022, expanding its unique service to more hospitals and families around the country.

Cian’s parents, Evelyn and Enda Neary, launched the organisation after witnessing first-hand the difference their family dog, Cooper, made to Cian’s spirits during his treatments at CHI Crumlin. Since its foundation, the service has offered safe kennelling, transportation and visits for pets of sick children, allowing families to focus on treatment and recovery while keeping the bond between child and animal intact.

The charity’s work reached new milestones in 2022, with nearly 100 families across Ireland availing of the service over the year. Demand increased as word spread among paediatric units, oncology teams and social workers, with referrals coming from hospitals in Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford. Coordinating with hospital staff and veterinary partners, the team ensures that each pet’s health and welfare are prioritised, with vaccination and hygiene protocols in place so visits can proceed safely.

For families navigating lengthy or repeated hospital stays, seeing a treasured pet can provide vital emotional support. Parents describe moments of “pure joy” and “renewed strength” when children are surprised by a visit from their dog or cat. Speaking to RTÉ News, Evelyn Neary said, “We see children light up the minute they spot their pet coming down the corridor or into the grounds. It really means the world to them and gives them a boost in their recovery.”

Cian’s Kennels also provides logistical support, collecting animals from homes across the country, caring for them at their facility in Ballymahon, and arranging scheduled visits to hospital campuses where permitted. In 2022, the charity worked closely with CHI at Crumlin and Tallaght, as well as University Hospital Limerick, with hopes to expand further in 2023.

The organisation relies on donations, grant aid and the commitment of volunteers, and has seen a groundswell of community support, particularly in Longford, where Cian’s legacy continues to inspire fundraisers and awareness campaigns. The HSE, hospital trusts and local authorities have commended the project’s innovative approach to holistic paediatric care.

Looking to the future, Cian’s Kennels aims to establish a network of designated pet-friendly visiting areas at major children’s hospitals and to develop guidelines for similar schemes nationally. As families reflect on a year of difficult journeys, many credit the charity with making the “unbearable that bit more bearable,” ensuring that no child has to face a hospital stay without the comfort of their loyal companion by their side.
headline: Cian's Kennels reunites sick children with their pets

text:
The National Lottery has issued an urgent appeal to Lotto players in Co Mayo to check their tickets, as a €1 million prize from a draw held earlier this year remains unclaimed.

The winning ticket, which was purchased in a shop in Ballina, matched the numbers for the Lotto Plus 1 top prize in the draw on 17 March. However, despite repeated notifications, the holder of the ticket has yet to come forward. The deadline to claim the life-changing sum is approaching fast, with only two weeks left before the prize must be forfeited under the rules of the game.

A spokesperson for the National Lottery urged anyone who bought a ticket for the St Patrick’s Day draw in Ballina or the surrounding areas to search their homes, cars, and wallets to ensure they have not misplaced the valuable slip. “We are reminding players that the ticket was purchased in a busy retail premises in Ballina ahead of the St Patrick’s Day celebrations. There’s a genuine possibility that the winner may not realise they are in possession of this €1 million ticket. We are appealing to the public to check old coat pockets, handbags, and even under car seats.”

If the prize is not claimed before the deadline of 15 June, the money will be returned to the National Lottery’s unclaimed prize fund, to be distributed for future draws and National Lottery good cause projects across Ireland.

The winner is advised to sign the back of the ticket and contact the National Lottery offices in Dublin as soon as possible. They will need to make arrangements to present the winning ticket in person and to confirm their identity in line with Lottery procedures.

Retailers in Ballina say the story has created excitement and speculation in the area. “Everyone is hoping the winner steps forward soon. It would be a great boost for Ballina,” said one local shopkeeper.

The National Lottery is reminding all players to play responsibly and to keep their tickets safe at all times. Anyone with queries can contact the Lotto claims team on 1800 666 222 or by email.
headline: Appeal to find winner of unclaimed €1m Lotto prize

text:
There is growing concern among advocacy groups and politicians over the continuing rise in the number of children experiencing homelessness across the State. The latest figures from the Department of Housing show there were 4,206 children in emergency accommodation at the end of April, the highest monthly total recorded to date.

Focus Ireland described the trend as “deeply alarming” and called for the urgent implementation of measures to prevent families from losing their homes. The charity said that the rate at which children are entering homelessness is outpacing efforts to secure long-term accommodation, leaving many facing months or even years in hotels and family hubs.

Social Democrats TD Cian O’Callaghan said the Government’s response to the crisis lacked urgency and clarity, adding that the ongoing reliance on emergency accommodation was “utterly unacceptable”. Sinn Féin’s spokesperson on Housing, Eoin Ó Broin, called for a renewed focus on prevention, including an expansion of the tenant-in-situ scheme to keep more families in their current homes.

The Simon Communities of Ireland echoed these calls, noting that the latest statistics follow the expiration of the winter eviction ban at the end of March. They warned that deteriorating rental supply and rising rents would further increase the flow of families into homelessness unless additional safeguards are put in place.

The Department of Housing has said that work is ongoing to increase the supply of social and affordable homes, with more than 2,000 such units delivered in the first quarter of 2024. A spokesperson acknowledged the “particular vulnerability of children experiencing homelessness” and pointed to expanded supports for families at risk, including the Homeless HAP place finder services.

The Ombudsman for Children, Dr Niall Muldoon, reiterated his call for the Government to adopt a rights-based approach to housing children and families, stating that the increased numbers in emergency accommodation “represent a failure of the system to protect children’s welfare and development”. 

Meanwhile, school principals and teachers have reported an increase in the number of children struggling with attendance, concentration, and wellbeing, as a result of instability linked to homelessness.

The Tánaiste, Micheál Martin, speaking in the Dáil, said the housing crisis remained the Government’s top priority and that targeted measures to assist families in urgent need would be outlined in the coming weeks. However, opposition parties said that repeated promises had failed to deliver an end to what they described as a national emergency.

The Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth confirmed that it is working closely with the HSE and local authorities to provide additional support and services to homeless families, but acknowledged that the impact on children remains significant and far-reaching.

As the number of children experiencing homelessness continues to rise, charities, advocacy groups and opposition politicians are calling for more decisive action to prevent further escalation.
headline: Major concern over pace of child homelessness

text:
Two people have died and at least ten others have been hospitalised following a series of explosions at a steel manufacturing plant in Ohio, United States. Emergency services responded to the incident, which occurred yesterday afternoon local time, at the TimkenSteel facility in Canton.

Local authorities confirmed that the deceased were employees of the plant. Their names have not yet been released pending notification of next of kin. Ten further individuals, nine workers and one contractor, were transported to hospital with injuries ranging from burns to smoke inhalation. Two are understood to be in a serious condition.

The explosions, which began shortly before 2pm, caused significant damage to part of the plant’s furnace operations. Large plumes of smoke were visible for several kilometres and nearby residents were advised to remain indoors while emergency services brought the situation under control.

TimkenSteel, which employs more than 1,800 people in the region, said in a statement it was “deeply saddened” by the loss of life and was cooperating fully with investigators. The company has suspended all operations at the facility until further notice and has pledged to support affected families.

Local fire officials and representatives of the federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) are leading an inquiry into the cause of the explosions. Preliminary reports suggest a possible malfunction in one of the plant’s electric arc furnaces, but a full investigation is under way.

Ohio Governor Mike DeWine expressed condolences to the families of the victims and praised first responders for their swift action. “Our thoughts and prayers are with all those impacted by this terrible tragedy,” he said.

The TimkenSteel plant in Canton is a major employer and a key supplier of steel products for the automotive and energy industries. The last major industrial incident at a steel plant in the region occurred in 2017.

Irish officials confirmed that there were no Irish citizens known to be caught up in the incident. The Department of Foreign Affairs said it was monitoring the situation and remained in contact with local authorities.

Support services are being put in place for employees and their families. The company has also established a helpline for those seeking information about loved ones. Further updates are expected as the investigation progresses.
headline: Two dead, 10 hospitalised after US steel plant explosions

text:
The Centre Pompidou in Paris, one of the city’s most iconic modern art museums, is preparing to close its doors for a major renovation project expected to last five years. The closure, which will take effect from the end of 2024, has been described as essential by French authorities to address significant wear and tear, as well as to ensure the building meets modern safety and energy standards.

Designed by Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers, the Centre Pompidou was opened in 1977 and quickly garnered attention with its striking “inside-out” architectural style, featuring colourful exposed pipes and an external escalator. The museum, named after former French president Georges Pompidou, houses Europe’s largest collection of modern and contemporary art, including works by Picasso, Kandinsky, and Duchamp.

The institution receives more than three million visitors each year, making it one of Paris’s most popular cultural attractions. During the extensive renovation, all exhibitions and events will be suspended at the main site in the Beaubourg district. Officials have indicated, however, that off-site exhibitions and educational programmes will continue in other parts of France and abroad. Some items from its collection may be loaned internationally, with possible temporary exhibitions in venues including Brussels and Spain.

French Minister for Culture Rachida Dati said the works were “absolutely necessary” to preserve the building’s heritage and to address issues such as asbestos removal, energy efficiency, and accessibility. The renovation is scheduled to be completed by 2030, with an estimated cost of over €260 million.

For Irish visitors and the thousands who travel from Ireland to Paris each year, the closure may come as a disappointment, though the museum’s leadership says the revamp will enhance the overall visitor experience once works are finished. The Pompidou Centre’s closure comes as other Parisian institutions, such as Notre-Dame Cathedral, remain under restoration ahead of the Olympic Games this summer.

The museum has assured the public that its digital collections and online resources will remain available throughout the closure, aiming to maintain engagement with its international audience, including art lovers in Ireland.
headline: Pompidou Centre in Paris to close for 5-year renovation

text:
All Government departments will be required to accept cash payments for their services under a new strategy set to be formally announced later this week. The move comes amid growing concerns over the declining availability of cash-based payment options and increasing reliance on digital-only transactions across public services.

The Department of Finance is leading the initiative, which will set out guidelines to ensure that anyone wishing to pay for State services in cash will be able to do so at their local office or any point of contact where government payments are accepted. Officials have said the measure aims to safeguard access to the public service for those who do not have access to banking or digital payment methods, including older people and those living in rural areas with poor broadband connectivity.

Speaking to RTÉ News, Minister for Finance Michael McGrath said the updated strategy is intended to “provide certainty and reassurance” to the public that cash will continue to be an accepted and valued means of payment. “While Ireland is on the path to becoming one of the most cashless societies in Europe, we recognise the importance of inclusivity and fairness. Not everyone can, or wishes to, pay by card or online. This new direction is about making sure no one is left behind,” the Minister said.

The move follows reports that certain government offices and local authorities had begun accepting card-only payments for specific services, such as driving licence applications, local property tax, and passport fees. NGOs and advocacy groups have raised issues about potential exclusion, particularly for people on lower incomes or those experiencing digital poverty.

The National Payments Strategy, which is expected to be published by the end of the month, will include mandatory cash acceptance for all departments and non-commercial State bodies, as well as recommendations for best practice in the wider public sector. Departments will be required to provide at least one cash payment option either onsite or through an arrangement with An Post or other authorised agents.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin also welcomed the move, describing it as “a practical response to the real needs of citizens”. He said practical steps would be taken to implement the guidelines at all levels of public administration, adding that the Government is committed to balancing innovation with accessibility.

Opposition parties have broadly welcomed the policy, with Sinn Féin’s finance spokesperson, Pearse Doherty TD, saying it was a necessary response to growing concerns among vulnerable groups. However, he called for a clear implementation timeline and assurances that frontline staff would be adequately resourced.

The Department of Social Protection, the Revenue Commissioners, and the HSE have all indicated they are working to ensure compliance with the new requirements. The Department of Finance said it will monitor implementation and consult with stakeholders to address any operational challenges.

Recent figures from the Central Bank showed that cash withdrawals from ATMs remain substantial, with almost €20 billion withdrawn in 2023, despite the surge in contactless and online payments during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Consumer rights organisations, including Age Action and the Money Advice and Budgeting Service (MABS), have said the announcement is a “step in the right direction” but have called for ongoing review to ensure services remain accessible to all. The matter will be discussed in the Dáil later this week, with further details expected following the strategy’s official publication.
headline: All Govt depts to accept cash under new strategy

text:
Thousands of people marched in Budapest on Saturday in defiance of a government ban on Hungary’s annual Pride parade, with demonstrators waving rainbow flags and chanting slogans in support of LGBTQ+ rights.

Organisers said this was the first time in more than twenty years that authorities had refused to grant a permit for the event. The Budapest Metropolitan Police had cited security concerns and disruption to traffic for rejecting the application last month. The decision prompted widespread criticism from rights groups, the European Union, and the United Nations, who argued the ban contravenes Hungary's human rights obligations.

Despite the ban, activists pressed ahead with what they described as a “standing demonstration” along the banks of the Danube. Several thousand people gathered near the Parliament building, where speakers condemned Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s government for what they described as an increasingly hostile atmosphere for minorities.

Garda Representative Association president Brendan O'Connor, who attended the rally while on a private visit to Hungary, told RTÉ News that the heavy police presence was reminiscent of previous Pride events in Ireland, but that “the tension was markedly higher given the official ban”.

Police formed lines to block marchers from proceeding onto the originally planned parade route, but did not disperse the crowd. No major incidents were reported, although local media said several protesters were detained after attempting to display banners on nearby bridges.

Among those attending were diplomats from several EU member states, including officials from the Irish Embassy in Budapest, who stood alongside protesters in a show of solidarity. Eoin Lynch, a Dublin-based student currently studying in Hungary, said the turnout reflected “a real determination among young Hungarians to push back against discrimination”.
