The Pride parade ban comes amid a series of controversial measures by the Orbán government, including restrictions on LGBTQ+ content in schools and media, and a constitutional amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman. The European Commission has already initiated legal proceedings against Hungary over these laws.

Amnesty International’s Hungary office said in a statement that the government’s actions represented “a further erosion of fundamental freedoms”. The group urged EU leaders to intensify pressure on Budapest to reverse the ban and ensure the right to peaceful assembly is upheld.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin, speaking in Cork ahead of the weekend, said Ireland had raised “serious concerns” with Hungarian authorities over the clampdown on civil society, and called for “respect for European values of inclusivity and diversity”.

Organisers said that, despite the ban, the event had succeeded in drawing attention to the challenges facing LGBTQ+ people in Hungary. “The fact so many people showed up, even in the face of intimidation, is a message in itself,” said Anna Halász, a spokesperson for the Budapest Pride collective.

The crowd dispersed peacefully in the early evening, watched by a significant police presence. A number of smaller rallies are expected to take place in Budapest over the coming days, as activists continue to press for recognition of LGBTQ+ rights.
headline: Thousands march in banned Budapest Pride parade

text:
Tributes have been paid to a man who died following a road collision in Co Mayo earlier this week, with friends and family describing him as a “lovely guy” who was well known in the local community.

The man, named locally as 42-year-old Shane O’Malley from Ballina, died after his car struck a tree on the N59 at Knockmore shortly before midnight on Wednesday. Emergency services attended the scene, but Mr O’Malley was pronounced dead a short time later.

Gardaí closed the road overnight to facilitate a forensic collision investigation. The route reopened to traffic at midday on Thursday. Gardaí have appealed for any witnesses to the incident, as well as any motorists with dashcam footage from the area around the time, to come forward.

Mr O’Malley was a well-known figure in the Ballina area, having worked for a number of years with a local construction company. Friends described him as “hard-working” and “always up for a laugh”, while neighbours spoke of his involvement with community events and local sports.

“He was just a really lovely guy, someone you could always rely on,” said one neighbour. “There’s a real sense of shock around here this week. He’ll be badly missed.”

Local councillor Seamus Weir extended his sympathies to the O’Malley family, saying the tragedy had cast a shadow over the town. “Shane was a popular young man and well regarded,” he said. “Our thoughts are with his family and friends as they try to cope with this terrible loss.”

A funeral Mass for Mr O’Malley will take place at St Muredach’s Cathedral on Saturday morning, with burial afterwards in Leigue Cemetery.

Gardaí have asked anyone with information about the incident to contact Ballina Garda Station on 096 20560 or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: Man who died in Mayo collision was 'lovely guy'

text:
Thirty-six people have been killed and over 140 injured after waves of Russian missile and drone strikes targeted cities and infrastructure across Ukraine, including a major children’s hospital in Kyiv, according to Ukrainian authorities. The attacks, among the deadliest in recent months, struck multiple regions early on Monday morning, leaving scenes of devastation in the capital and elsewhere.

In Kyiv, a residential district and the Okhmatdyt children’s hospital, the country’s largest paediatric medical centre, were both hit by incoming missiles. Hospital staff and emergency workers spent hours clearing rubble and evacuating patients, many of them young children undergoing treatment for cancer and other serious conditions. The city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, confirmed at least 10 deaths in the capital alone, with fears the number could rise as search efforts continue.

President Volodymyr Zelensky described the attacks as “deliberate terror” and said Russia had used more than 40 missiles of various types against Ukrainian territory. He has called for an emergency meeting of the United Nations Security Council and renewed his appeal to Western leaders for additional air defence systems.

Elsewhere, strikes were reported in Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih, Sloviansk and Pokrovsk. Local authorities said residential buildings, energy installations and businesses had been hit, causing disruption to power and water supplies. The country’s energy operator warned that rolling blackouts would likely continue amid ongoing efforts to repair damaged infrastructure.

The Russian defence ministry said its forces had targeted Ukrainian military facilities and claimed that the strikes were successful. Moscow has repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians. However, footage from Kyiv’s Okhmatdyt hospital showed significant damage to surgical and intensive care wards, and the Ukrainian health ministry said at least two adults were killed and more than a dozen children were injured in that attack alone.

Ireland’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Micheál Martin, condemned the strikes as “abhorrent and unjustifiable”, expressing solidarity with the victims and their families. In a statement, the Department of Foreign Affairs reiterated Ireland’s support for Ukraine and called for an immediate cessation of hostilities.

The bombardments come ahead of a major NATO summit in Washington, where support for Ukraine’s defence is expected to be a key topic. Ukrainian officials have warned that without further support, including advanced missile defences, civilian casualties will continue to mount.

Gardaí have said there are no indications that any Irish citizens have been caught up in the attacks, but the Department of Foreign Affairs continues to advise against all non-essential travel to Ukraine. Ireland’s embassy in Kyiv remains operational, providing consular assistance where possible.

The European Commission has also issued a strong statement condemning the attacks and urging Russia to respect international law, including the protection of medical facilities under the Geneva Conventions. The government in Kyiv has vowed not to be “intimidated by terror” and to continue its resistance as the invasion enters its third year.
headline: 36 dead, Kyiv hospital hit in Russian strikes on Ukraine

text:
Members of the public have been advised to avoid the area around An Earagail (Mount Errigal) in Co Donegal over the coming days, as helicopter operations take place as part of ongoing path improvement works on the popular hiking route.

Donegal County Council, in conjunction with Transport Infrastructure Ireland and local contractors, has announced that a specialist helicopter will be used to transport stone and construction materials to and from the mountain from Monday, 10 June, for approximately five days, weather permitting.

The operations are part of a €1.2 million sustainable access project aimed at improving the safety and environmental impact of the well-trodden path leading to the summit of Errigal, Donegal’s highest peak. The works are designed to combat erosion and protect surrounding habitats, while also upgrading the route for the thousands of walkers and climbers who visit each year.

In a statement, the council said it is essential for public safety that all access routes to An Earagail, including car parks and walking trails, remain closed while the helicopter is in operation. Signage and barriers have been erected, and members of the public are being asked not to attempt to access the mountain or surrounding land until works have been completed.

Local gardaí in Gweedore have issued similar advice, urging visitors and hillwalkers to respect closures and cooperate with personnel on the ground. Gardaí said there will be additional patrols in the area during the helicopter lifts to ensure compliance.

The council has apologised for any inconvenience and has thanked the public and local community for their support and understanding. It said that safe and environmentally sensitive access to Errigal is expected to be fully restored once the helicopter phase is completed.

The path restoration is being carried out in close consultation with landowners, the National Parks and Wildlife Service, and Mountaineering Ireland. The works form part of a wider Donegal Outdoor Recreation Strategy, aimed at enhancing access to outdoor amenities across the county.
headline: Public asked to avoid An Earagail during helicopter work

text:
Nicaraguan authorities have detained two additional high-profile opposition figures, intensifying an ongoing crackdown on critics of President Daniel Ortega’s government. The latest arrests bring to at least half a dozen the number of potential challengers held by the authorities ahead of November’s presidential election.

According to statements released by the Nicaraguan police, Félix Maradiaga and Juan Sebastián Chamorro, both prominent opposition leaders and known critics of President Ortega, were taken into custody on Tuesday evening. Police have accused the pair of undermining national sovereignty and inciting foreign interference, allegations which both men and their legal representatives deny.

The latest detentions were carried out under sweeping security and sovereignty laws passed by the government late last year. International observers, including the United Nations and the Organisation of American States (OAS), have expressed grave concern about the crackdown, warning that the right to free and fair elections is under serious threat in the Central American country.

In recent weeks, at least four other opposition presidential hopefuls have been arrested or placed under house arrest. Among them is Cristiana Chamorro, a journalist and former NGO director seen by many as the most formidable challenger to Ortega in the November polls.

Local human rights organisations have described the situation as unprecedented since the end of Nicaragua’s civil conflict in the 1980s. Vilma Núñez, president of the Nicaraguan Centre for Human Rights, condemned the latest arrests as “politically motivated” and said they were a sign that “the electoral process is being manipulated to ensure no real competition.”

The Irish Department of Foreign Affairs issued a statement this morning calling on the Nicaraguan authorities to respect democratic norms and the rule of law, and to release all those detained for exercising their political rights. The European Union and the United States have also threatened sanctions if the crackdown continues.

President Ortega, who has been in power since 2007 and is seeking a fourth consecutive term, insists that the arrests are necessary to prevent what he describes as “foreign-backed destabilisation”. State media in Nicaragua echoed this line, accusing the detained opposition figures of plotting to overthrow the government with international support.

The wave of arrests has triggered widespread protests in Nicaragua’s capital, Managua, with demonstrators demanding the release of detainees and calling for the restoration of democratic freedoms. Security forces have reportedly used tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse some gatherings, though the full scale of the response remains unclear.

With less than five months until the election, international watchdogs say the climate of fear and intimidation is likely to persist, making it increasingly difficult for opposition candidates to organise or campaign. The OAS has called for an emergency session to discuss the situation, while Amnesty International described the events as a “new low” for human rights in the region.

The developments in Nicaragua come amid heightened scrutiny of electoral integrity and the suppression of dissent in several Latin American nations. Irish officials have said they will continue to monitor the situation closely and engage with EU partners on an appropriate response.
headline: Nicaraguan police arrest two more opposition contenders

text:
Three men have appeared before the Special Criminal Court in Dublin this morning charged in connection with the 2016 shooting at the Regency Hotel in the north of the city.

The three accused, all aged in their 30s and 40s, are charged with offences linked to the murder of David Byrne, who was shot dead during a boxing weigh-in at the hotel on the afternoon of 5 February 2016—a killing which escalated a violent feud between the Hutch and Kinahan crime gangs.

The men, whose addresses are in Dublin, Louth and Armagh, were arrested following investigations led by Gardaí attached to the Garda National Bureau of Criminal Investigation (GNBCI). The court heard that the men are charged with offences including participating in the activities of a criminal organisation and facilitating the murder of Mr Byrne.

All three were brought to the Special Criminal Court under heavy Garda escort shortly before 10am. Armed units secured the Four Courts complex throughout the proceedings, and extra security measures were in place around the court buildings.

Detective Garda testimony outlined how the accused were detained at separate Garda stations in the greater Dublin area last week as part of ongoing inquiries into the broader activities of the Hutch gang. The court was told that each man made no reply when charged.

State Solicitor Dara Hayes told the court that the Director of Public Prosecutions had directed trial on indictment before the non-jury court, citing the "exceptional security issues and the involvement of organised crime".

None of the accused applied for bail at this stage. Their respective defence solicitors indicated that applications may be brought at a later date, subject to the direction of counsel. They requested that their clients receive all necessary medical attention and that disclosure of all relevant evidence be provided as soon as possible.

The presiding judge, Mr Justice Tony Hunt, remanded the three men in custody to appear again before the court on 20 June for the service of the book of evidence.

Gardaí have confirmed that investigations into the Regency shooting and its aftermath remain ongoing, and further arrests have not been ruled out. The case continues to be a significant focus for An Garda Síochána, due to the impact of the subsequent feud on gun crime in the capital.
headline: Three men in court in connection with Regency shooting

text:
A man has escaped unharmed following a suspected petrol bomb attack on his home in Co Louth last night.

The incident occurred at a house in the Moneymore estate in Drogheda at approximately 11.30pm. Gardaí and emergency services were called to the scene after reports of an explosive device being thrown at the front of the property.

The man, who was in the house at the time, was not injured. Damage was caused to the front door and exterior of the building.

Members of the local fire service arrived promptly and extinguished a small fire at the scene. No other injuries have been reported.

A technical examination of the property was carried out by Gardaí overnight. Officers are appealing for witnesses or anyone with camera or dashcam footage from the area between 11.00pm and midnight to come forward.

No arrests have yet been made and enquiries are ongoing. Gardaí say they are keeping an open mind regarding the motive for the incident.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Drogheda Garda Station on 041 987 4200, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.
headline: Man uninjured after suspected petrol bomb attack

text:
Gardaí have issued an appeal to the public for assistance in tracing the whereabouts of a man who has been reported missing from Dundalk, Co Louth.

Patrick Foley, aged 37, was last seen in the town centre area on Monday afternoon, 17 June. He is described as approximately 1.78 metres (5’10”) tall, of medium build, with short brown hair and blue eyes.

It is understood that Mr Foley was wearing a navy zip-up jacket, grey tracksuit bottoms, and black trainers when he was last observed. His family and friends have expressed concern for his welfare, and Gardaí say they are anxious to locate him as soon as possible.

Gardaí are appealing to anyone who may have seen Patrick, or who may have information on his whereabouts, to contact Dundalk Garda Station on 042 938 8400, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.

In a statement this afternoon, a spokesperson for the force said: “We are concerned for Patrick’s safety and well-being and are urging anyone who might have seen him or have any information in relation to his disappearance to make contact.”

No further details are available at this time.
headline: Appeal issued to trace man missing from Dundalk

text:
Ken Starr, the former US independent counsel whose investigation led to the impeachment of President Bill Clinton in the late 1990s, has died at the age of 76.

A family statement said Mr Starr died in Houston, Texas, due to complications from surgery. He had a long career as a lawyer, judge and academic, but remains best known internationally for his role in the Whitewater investigation, which ultimately shifted to focus on President Clinton’s relationship with White House intern Monica Lewinsky.

His pursuit of the case culminated in the 1998 publication of the so-called Starr Report, detailing allegations of perjury and obstruction of justice against President Clinton. The revelations led to impeachment proceedings by the US House of Representatives, though President Clinton was acquitted by the Senate and completed his term in office.

Ken Starr’s legal career spanned several decades. He was appointed to the US Court of Appeals by President Ronald Reagan in 1983 before serving as solicitor general under President George H.W. Bush. In 1994, he was named independent counsel to investigate the Clintons’ real estate dealings in Arkansas, a mandate that eventually expanded to include multiple alleged scandals.

Mr Starr later became dean of Pepperdine Law School in California and served as president and chancellor of Baylor University in Texas. His tenure at Baylor was marred by controversy and ended in his dismissal over the handling of sexual assault allegations involving the university’s football team.

Paying tribute, former US President George W. Bush said Mr Starr was a “brilliant jurist and devoted public servant”. Monica Lewinsky also posted online, offering condolences to his family and saying, “My thoughts are with them for peace and comfort.”

In recent years, Mr Starr joined the legal team defending President Donald Trump during his first impeachment trial.

He is survived by his wife Alice, three children and several grandchildren. Funeral arrangements have not yet been announced.
headline: Ken Starr, who investigated Clinton, dies at 76

text:
Irish holidaymakers and families in the United States have begun preparations to return home as the travel ban on passengers from Europe was lifted this morning, bringing an end to restrictions that have been in place for nearly two years.

Transatlantic flights from Dublin and Shannon airports have resumed to full schedules, with airline operators reporting strong demand since the announcement that vaccinated travellers would once again be permitted to enter the US. Thousands of Irish citizens who had postponed trips or were separated from relatives have welcomed the easing of entry requirements.

Under the revised protocols, all passengers aged over 18 must be fully vaccinated and present a negative Covid-19 test taken within 72 hours before departure. Children under 18 are exempt from the vaccination requirement but must also provide a negative test.

Aer Lingus, Ireland’s national airline, said it had added extra capacity on key routes to New York, Boston and Chicago in response to the surge in interest. “The lifting of the US travel ban is a significant moment for families, businesses, and tourists on both sides of the Atlantic,” an Aer Lingus spokesperson said. “We are seeing strong bookings, particularly from those looking to reunite with loved ones for the first time since 2020.”

Irish travel agents have also reported a sharp rise in bookings for winter and spring. Pat Dawson, chief executive of the Irish Travel Agents Association, said the reopening of the US would provide a much-needed boost to the sector. “There’s a great sense of relief among people who have been waiting anxiously to see family or to resume business,” Mr Dawson said.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has updated its travel advice and is urging all travellers to check the latest guidelines before departure, with specific advice for those travelling with unvaccinated children.

Shannon Airport, which saw transatlantic flights suspended for much of the pandemic, had its first US-bound passengers depart this morning, with emotional scenes as families and friends were reunited. “It’s been a long wait. I haven’t seen my daughter in New York since before Christmas 2019,” said Mary O’Connor from Limerick, who travelled with her husband. “We’re very grateful to finally be able to go.”

Although the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) continues to recommend caution for international travel, the move has been welcomed by Irish business leaders and representatives of the tourism industry, who had lobbied for a clear roadmap to reopening.

The Minister for Foreign Affairs, Simon Coveney, said the resumption of travel marked “a significant step towards normality” and would strengthen ties between Ireland and the US. Gardaí and airport authorities advised passengers to arrive early and to have all documentation ready to ensure a smooth journey.

With hundreds of thousands of Irish people living in the United States, the return of regular flights is expected to see a busy winter of travel and family reunions in the lead-up to Christmas.
headline: Tourists prepare to return to US as travel ban lifted

text:
A total of 7,333 new cases of Covid-19 have been confirmed by the Department of Health today, bringing the number of confirmed cases in the ongoing wave to its highest level since late January.

There are currently 410 people in hospital receiving treatment for the virus, with 35 patients in intensive care units. This represents a rise in hospitalisations from 399 yesterday, while ICU admissions remain steady.

Chief Medical Officer Dr Tony Holohan expressed concern about the rise in cases, warning that the Omicron sub-variant BA.2 continues to drive infection rates. “The high level of transmission in the community means we must continue to adhere to public health advice, particularly for those who are more vulnerable to severe outcomes,” Dr Holohan said.

The HSE has reiterated that vaccination remains the best protection against serious illness. Booster uptake among adults has reached 61%, but authorities have urged those who have not yet received their third dose to come forward. Walk-in vaccination clinics remain open across the country.

Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly has appealed to people to isolate at the first sign of symptoms and to wear face coverings in crowded or poorly ventilated settings. “We are at a critical phase in managing Covid-19. It is essential that everyone plays their part to protect themselves, their families, and our health services,” the Minister said.

The latest figures come as schools around the country prepare for the final term, with updated guidance issued to principals on ventilation and cleaning regimes. No further changes to existing public health measures in schools are planned at this time, according to the Department of Education.

The latest data from the HSE also show 75 Covid-19 outbreaks in residential care settings in the past week. The National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET) is set to meet on Thursday to assess the situation, with ministers indicating that further action may be taken if hospital capacity becomes strained.

There have now been over 1.6 million confirmed cases of Covid-19 in Ireland since the start of the pandemic. Public health officials have again urged the public to continue practising hand and respiratory hygiene, and to avail of antigen testing if symptomatic.
headline: Covid-19: 7,333 cases, 410 patients in hospital

text:
Community leaders and tourism operators have renewed calls for the construction of a new pier on Great Blasket Island, citing safety concerns and repeated difficulties accessing the popular heritage site off the coast of Co Kerry.

Representatives from the Blasket Island Ferry and local councillors say that the existing landing arrangements, which rely on visitors transferring from ferries to rigid inflatable boats (RIBs) before reaching a small jetty, are inadequate and have on occasion resulted in tourists becoming stranded or injured.

Over 13,000 people visited the island last year, according to figures provided by Kerry County Council. However, poor weather and strong currents frequently make landings treacherous, with ferry operators sometimes forced to cancel sailings altogether at short notice.

“The Blaskets are a huge attraction and a vital part of the region’s cultural history, but the current facilities are simply not fit for purpose,” said Cllr Breandán Fitzgerald (FF). “A new pier is urgently needed to ensure safe and reliable access for visitors, locals and emergency services.”

Efforts to secure funding for a new pier have stalled over the past decade amid environmental concerns and uncertainties regarding ownership of the land. The Office of Public Works (OPW), which manages the island’s heritage village, stated that it is “aware of the issues raised” but stressed that any development must adhere to strict conservation guidelines given the island’s status as a Special Area of Conservation.

Tour operators have warned that unless the infrastructure is improved, the economic benefits of tourism to nearby communities on the Dingle Peninsula could be severely curtailed. “We regularly find ourselves having to turn people away because it’s just not safe to land. It’s disappointing, both for the visitors and for us as businesses,” said Tomás O’Driscoll, a local ferry operator.

The Department of Rural and Community Development confirmed to RTÉ News that it is in discussions with Kerry County Council and the OPW regarding possible plans to upgrade landing facilities. However, no timeline has yet been announced for a decision.

The Blasket Islands, famed for their literary heritage and rich wildlife, have long been a focal point for tourists and scholars. Advocates say investing in improved access is essential to preserving this legacy for future generations.
headline: Renewed calls for a new pier on Great Blasket Island

text:
The Indonesian navy has confirmed that its missing submarine, KRI Nanggala-402, which disappeared during a training exercise off the north coast of Bali last week, has been found split into three pieces at a depth of more than 800 metres. All 53 crew members on board are presumed dead, according to officials, in what is being described as one of the country’s worst naval disasters.

A multinational search operation involving vessels and aircraft from Indonesia, Australia, Singapore and the United States had been racing against time after the submarine lost contact in the early hours of Wednesday morning. Hopes of finding survivors diminished rapidly after the vessel's oxygen supply was believed to have run out by Saturday.

Rear Admiral Yudo Margono, the Indonesian navy’s chief of staff, told a press conference on Sunday that high-resolution images taken by remotely operated underwater vehicles from the Singaporean navy showed the submarine’s hull, stern and main body lying separately on the sea floor. Debris including life vests, prayer mat fragments and part of a torpedo tube had been recovered from the area earlier in the search.

President Joko Widodo has described the loss as a “national tragedy” and conveyed his condolences to the families of the crew. He thanked the international community for its support during the search, which included assistance from the US Navy’s Poseidon surveillance aircraft and an Australian warship.

Indonesian authorities are investigating the cause of the incident. The 44-year-old German-built submarine had undergone refitting in recent years, but officials say there had been no reports of major technical faults prior to the exercise. Naval analysts point to the potential for structural failure due to excessive pressure at greater depths than the vessel was rated for.

A military funeral for the lost submariners is being organised, with President Widodo ordering that the fallen sailors be posthumously promoted as a mark of respect for their service. The Indonesian parliament has called for a review of the country’s ageing naval fleet, while the defence minister has pledged to modernise maritime capabilities to prevent similar tragedies in future.

Irish navy representatives expressed condolences to their Indonesian counterparts, noting the risks faced routinely by submariners, and the Department of Foreign Affairs said there are no reports of Irish citizens among the crew or involved in the search operation.
headline: Sunken Indonesian submarine found broken in three

text:
The Road Safety Authority (RSA) has announced plans to recruit 80 additional driving testers in an effort to tackle the growing backlog of learner drivers awaiting their driving test.

The move comes after months of criticism from learner drivers, driving instructors, and public representatives about lengthy waiting times for a test appointment. In some centres, candidates have reported waiting up to nine months for a slot, while the average national wait time currently stands at approximately 22 weeks, well above the RSA’s target of ten weeks.

Minister of State at the Department of Transport, Jack Chambers TD, said the decision to hire more testers is a direct response to the unprecedented demand for driving tests since the pandemic. "We have listened to those impacted by these delays and are determined to address them as a matter of urgency," he said, adding that the new recruits should be in place and operational by the autumn.

The RSA said a nationwide recruitment campaign has already commenced and expects to begin training successful applicants in the coming weeks. The body has also indicated that extra focus will be placed on high-demand areas such as Dublin, Cork, and Galway where the waiting lists are longest.

Brian Farrell, spokesperson for the RSA, acknowledged the frustration experienced by learner drivers, many of whom rely on access to a full driving licence for work or education. "We recognise the impact these delays are having on people’s lives. Increasing our panel of testers is the most effective way to improve waiting times in the short term," he said.

In the Dáil last week, several TDs raised the issue of driving test backlogs, citing correspondence from constituents whose employment prospects are being hampered by their inability to sit the test.

Labour’s Duncan Smith TD said the delays were "completely unacceptable" and called for a dedicated taskforce to address what he termed a "chronic under-resourcing" of the system. Sinn Féin’s spokesperson on Transport, Darren O’Rourke TD, welcomed the announcement but stressed the need for a long-term strategy to prevent a recurrence of the backlog.

The RSA has processed record numbers of test applications in recent months, with over 150,000 already completed so far this year. Officials have attributed the current surge in demand to the backlog created by Covid-related cancellations, as well as a sharp rise in the number of learner permits issued since 2021.

The Department of Transport said it would continue to monitor the situation closely and work with the RSA to ensure the backlog is cleared as quickly as possible. Applicants are advised to keep checking the MyRoadSafety portal for updates on test availability in their area.
headline: 80 driving testers to be hired to tackle backlog

text:
The Japanese ambassador to Ireland has made an appeal for the elimination of nuclear weapons, warning of the catastrophic consequences of their use and urging the international community to redouble efforts towards nuclear disarmament.

Ambassador Norio Maruyama was speaking at a commemoration event in Dublin this Thursday, marking the 79th anniversary of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The event, organised by the Irish branch of the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, was attended by representatives of the Department of Foreign Affairs, members of the diplomatic corps and Irish anti-nuclear activists.

Addressing the gathering, Ambassador Maruyama recalled the devastation wrought by the bombings in August 1945, which resulted in the deaths of over 200,000 people and left lasting scars on survivors, known as hibakusha. He said their testimony underscores the urgent need for a world free of nuclear weapons.

“Japan, as the only country ever to have suffered atomic bombings during wartime, has a special mission to convey the inhumanity of nuclear weapons,” Ambassador Maruyama said. He called on all states, including the nuclear powers, to fulfil their obligations under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and to work constructively towards a comprehensive ban on nuclear arsenals.

Ireland played a key role in the negotiation of the 1968 Non-Proliferation Treaty and is a signatory to the 2017 Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. Officials from the Department of Foreign Affairs reaffirmed Ireland’s commitment to nuclear disarmament and welcomed the ambassador’s comments.

Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin, in a statement, said: “Ireland continues to advocate for a world without nuclear weapons. We urge all states to redouble their efforts in pursuit of the total elimination of these weapons of mass destruction.”

The ambassador’s remarks come amid heightened global tensions and renewed concerns about the risks of nuclear proliferation, particularly in the context of the war in Ukraine and North Korea’s recent missile launches.

The United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres also warned last week that the risk of nuclear conflict is at its highest in decades, calling on world leaders to “reverse course and work towards disarmament.”

The Hiroshima and Nagasaki commemorations in Dublin included testimonies from Irish peace campaigners and Japanese residents in Ireland, as well as a moment of silence in memory of those lost to the bombings. Organisers said the event aimed to remind the public and policymakers alike of the enduring threat posed by nuclear weapons and to renew calls for international action.
headline: Japanese ambassador appeals for end to nuclear weapons

text:
A man has died while climbing a mountain in Co Kerry.

The incident occurred on Saturday afternoon on Carrauntoohil, Ireland’s highest peak, in the MacGillycuddy’s Reeks range.

It is understood that the man, who was in his 60s and from Munster, was climbing with a group when he suffered a medical emergency at a high altitude.

Kerry Mountain Rescue Team (KMRT) was alerted shortly before 2pm. Rescue volunteers, supported by the Coast Guard’s Rescue 115 helicopter from Shannon, responded to the scene. Difficult conditions and poor visibility hampered the operation.

Despite efforts by rescuers and medics, the man was pronounced dead at the scene. His body was airlifted from the mountain and later transferred to University Hospital Kerry in Tralee, where a post-mortem examination will be carried out.

There were no reports of injuries to others in the group. The Gardaí in Killarney are liaising with the coroner and have confirmed they are treating the incident as a tragic accident.

The man’s name is not being released at this time, pending notification of family members.
headline: Man dies while climbing Kerry mountain

text:
Paris authorities have introduced stringent new measures to curb the rapid growth of electric scooter usage, citing concerns about pedestrian safety and urban congestion. The move comes after a surge in complaints from residents and visitors alike, as well as a series of high-profile accidents involving the popular mode of transport.

The city’s action plan, announced by mayor Anne Hidalgo, includes a ban on the use of rental e-scooters on pavements, stricter speed limits in busy areas, and new designated parking zones aimed at discouraging haphazard parking that has been blamed for accessibility issues and visual clutter.

Under the new regulations, rental e-scooters must now be left only in marked bays, while operators face the prospect of losing their licenses if they fail to ensure compliance. The city has capped the number of scooters permitted per operator and is threatening fines for breaches.

Dublin and other Irish cities have watched the developments in Paris with interest, as the Oireachtas continues to debate the Road Traffic and Roads Bill, which would provide scope for the regulation of e-scooters in Ireland. While privately-owned e-scooters remain illegal for use on public roads here, reports from the Department of Transport have indicated that legislation is likely to be enacted later this year.

Paris was an early adopter of e-scooter sharing schemes, with more than 15,000 such vehicles deployed by multiple operators at the height of their popularity. However, a public backlash grew as injuries increased and complaints mounted regarding the devices being abandoned on footpaths, blocking access for wheelchair users and prams.

In a statement, Mayor Hidalgo said the objective was not to “banish” the scooters, but to “take back control of the public space.” Local residents, meanwhile, have expressed mixed reactions, with some welcoming the clampdown as overdue, while others argue that e-scooters provide sustainable and flexible alternatives to cars and taxis.

French authorities report that in 2022, at least 24 people died in scooter-related incidents nationwide, including one Irish tourist, while hundreds more were injured. The rising casualty numbers have fuelled calls for an outright ban, although Paris City Hall has opted for stricter regulation rather than prohibition.

Irish road safety campaigners, including the Road Safety Authority (RSA), have previously warned that without robust legislation and enforcement, Irish cities could face similar issues as those witnessed in Paris and other European capitals.

The developments in the French capital are expected to inform policy discussions in Ireland, as urban planners and local authorities balance the need for sustainable transport against public safety concerns. The Department of Transport confirmed to RTÉ News that officials are monitoring the situation closely and have been in contact with their French counterparts regarding best practice.

The measures are scheduled to take effect in Paris this month, and are seen by observers as a landmark test of whether major European cities can successfully manage innovative but disruptive new forms of urban mobility.
headline: Paris aims to put the brakes on scooter proliferation

text:
Eight people have died after a private plane crashed in a field near Milan in northern Italy on Sunday, local authorities have confirmed.

The aircraft, a Pilatus PC-12 single-engine turboprop, had departed from Milan’s Linate airport shortly after 1pm local time and was bound for the island of Sardinia. Italian media report that the plane crashed in the town of San Donato Milanese, a residential area about ten kilometres south-east of the city centre, shortly after take-off.

Firefighters and emergency services responded to the scene and extinguished the blaze that engulfed the aircraft. The bodies of all those on board—six passengers and two crew—were recovered from the wreckage. Local officials said there were no survivors.

Witnesses told Italian television that the plane appeared to be in difficulty before it went down and hit a building undergoing renovation near an underground railway station. No one on the ground was injured, although several cars were damaged.

Authorities in Milan have opened an investigation into the cause of the crash. Italy’s National Agency for the Safety of Flight (ANSV) has sent investigators to the site. Preliminary reports suggest the aircraft had reached an altitude of around 600 metres before rapidly losing height.

The identities of the victims have not yet been released, but Italian officials indicated that foreign nationals are among the dead. Local media report that the plane was privately owned and had been chartered for leisure travel.

There was no immediate indication of technical failure, but investigators are examining flight data and speaking to air traffic controllers who had contact with the jet before the accident.

The Department of Foreign Affairs said it is aware of the incident and stands ready to provide consular assistance if any Irish citizens are found to have been involved. The crash has prompted expressions of sympathy from Italian leaders, with President Sergio Mattarella extending condolences to the families of the victims.

Air traffic at Milan’s Linate airport was not significantly affected by the incident. The site of the crash remains cordoned off as investigators continue their work.
headline: Eight die after private plane crashes in Italy

text:
Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across Ireland have lost an estimated €11.7 billion in revenue as a result of restrictions imposed during the Covid-19 pandemic, according to new research published today. The report, commissioned by the Small Firms Association (SFA) and conducted by economic consultants BDO, reveals that businesses in sectors such as hospitality, retail, and tourism suffered the most significant losses between March 2020 and June 2021.

The study found that over 80% of SMEs reported a reduction in turnover during periods of lockdown, with nearly a quarter stating their monthly income dropped by more than half. Micro enterprises—those with fewer than 10 employees—were hit particularly hard, while businesses outside the major urban centres experienced sharper declines.

The SFA has called for targeted supports to aid the recovery of small businesses, warning that the combined impact of lost revenue, wage bills, and outstanding debts threatens the long-term viability of thousands of firms. According to the report, nearly 30,000 jobs remain at risk unless further assistance is made available.

Speaking following the publication of the findings, SFA Director Sven Spollen-Behrens said the figures underline the urgent need for continued intervention from Government. “While supports such as the Employment Wage Subsidy Scheme and the Covid Restrictions Support Scheme provided a vital lifeline, many small businesses are now grappling with legacy debts, rising costs, and ongoing staff shortages. Without a coordinated effort to address these challenges, Ireland risks a wave of business closures,” he said.

The research also highlighted difficulties in accessing finance, with over 40% of SMEs surveyed stating that their existing debt levels made securing new credit more difficult. Many business owners expressed concern over the scheduled winding down of Government support schemes in the coming months.

Minister for Enterprise, Trade and Employment, Simon Coveney TD, said the Government remained committed to working with small businesses throughout the recovery period. “We recognise the sacrifices made by business owners during the pandemic and will continue to support those sectors that are still struggling,” Minister Coveney said.

The report recommends the introduction of a new grant scheme to assist SMEs in repaying legacy debt, as well as support for investment in digital tools and staff training. The SFA has also called for a review of commercial rates, with a view to providing additional relief to businesses most severely affected by the restrictions.

Representatives from the hospitality and retail sectors echoed the call for further action. Adrian Cummins, CEO of the Restaurants Association of Ireland, described the situation as “precarious” for many independent operators, while Lorraine Higgins of Digital Business Ireland said small retailers were still “feeling the aftershocks” of repeated closures.

The Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment said it would consider the report’s recommendations as part of ongoing discussions with SME stakeholders and enterprise groups. The next meeting of the SME and Entrepreneurship Taskforce is due to take place later this month.
headline: SMEs lose billions due to Covid-19 restrictions

text:
Senior Irish Government figures have called on the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) to re-engage with efforts to address outstanding issues arising from Brexit, following a series of fresh warnings over political paralysis at Stormont and continued disruptions to trade in Northern Ireland.

The Tánaiste, Micheál Martin, speaking after a cross-party Oireachtas meeting on Brexit implementation, said it was “imperative” that all parties in the North “take ownership of the current challenges and work collectively towards practical, durable solutions for all communities.” He described the recent impasse as “deeply concerning not only for the people of Northern Ireland, but for the stability of the power-sharing institutions.”

Tensions have persisted over the operation of the Windsor Framework, which was agreed between the UK and the EU last year to address concerns over the Northern Ireland Protocol. Unionist leaders, including DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson, have continued to insist that the revised post-Brexit arrangements undermine Northern Ireland’s place in the UK internal market, citing what they term “unacceptable barriers” to the movement of goods from Britain.

The DUP has refused to return to the Stormont Executive since February 2022, citing the need for “firm guarantees” on Northern Ireland’s constitutional status and trade. This has left the power-sharing arrangements in limbo, with legislation and key spending decisions on health and education stalled.

Tánaiste Martin urged unionists to “seize the opportunity” provided by the recent UK-EU agreements, warning that “prolonged disengagement will only deepen the practical difficulties faced by businesses and daily life in the North.” He called for the DUP to join ongoing technical discussions, involving the Irish Government, the British Government, and the European Commission.

Speaking in the Dáil, Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald accused the DUP of “holding Northern society to ransom for partisan ends” and urged Prime Minister Rishi Sunak to “step up and ensure that the institutions are restored as a matter of urgency.” Alliance Party deputy leader Stephen Farry stressed that the bulk of business groups in Northern Ireland have now adapted to the new trading regime, but “uncertainty and instability hampers investment and community cohesion.”

Meanwhile, Minister for Foreign Affairs, Simon Coveney, confirmed that the Irish Government remains in close contact with Brussels and London officials to press for any “flexibilities and mitigations” within the Windsor Framework, especially in relation to small businesses and agri-food movements. “We are aware that some teething problems remain and we are working constructively to address them,” he said.

A UK Government spokesperson said London remains committed to upholding the Good Friday Agreement “in all its dimensions” and was engaging with all parties. The spokesperson reiterated Prime Minister Sunak’s “full support for the Windsor Framework as a balanced and pragmatic outcome.”

However, DUP sources signalled no early return to Stormont, insisting that “further progress and meaningful engagement from the British Government are needed” before any decisions can be made.

Business leaders and civic groups across the North have repeatedly highlighted the negative impact of ongoing political uncertainty, warning that the absence of devolved government means vital decisions on funding, infrastructure, and public services are being left in limbo.

Irish, British and EU officials are due to meet again in Brussels next week to review implementation of the Windsor Framework, amid increasing calls for a renewed push to find compromise and restore power-sharing in Belfast.
headline: DUP urged to join search for post-Brexit solutions

text:
A British MP has accused Stanley Johnson, the father of former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson, of inappropriately touching her at a Conservative Party conference.

Caroline Nokes, the Conservative MP for Romsey and Southampton North, told Sky News that Mr Johnson had forcefully smacked her on the backside and made a crude remark during the 2003 party conference. She said the incident occurred when she was a prospective parliamentary candidate and that she was left "mortified" by his behaviour.

Speaking on the record, Ms Nokes said: "I can remember a really prominent man, at the Conservative Party conference in Blackpool in 2003, who completely inappropriately touched me, and I have no problem naming him, Stanley Johnson."

The allegations have prompted further scrutiny of the Conservative Party's handling of complaints about sexual harassment and inappropriate behaviour. Ms Nokes, who chairs the UK's Women and Equalities Committee, said she had struggled with whether to name Mr Johnson publicly, but decided it was important to highlight the continued challenges faced by women in politics.

In response to the accusation, Mr Johnson, who ran as a Conservative candidate for the European Parliament and is a well-known public figure in the UK, said he had "no recollection" of the incident. He told the media: "I have no recollection of Caroline Nokes or of any incident at all."

Another journalist, Ailbhe Rea of the New Statesman, also reported that Mr Johnson had groped her at a Conservative Party event. Ms Rea stated on social media that she had not intended to speak publicly but felt compelled to come forward in solidarity with Ms Nokes.

The allegations have led to calls for the Conservative Party to investigate the matter. A party spokesperson said all such complaints are taken seriously and should be reported through the appropriate channels.

Senior UK politicians, including Labour’s deputy leader Angela Rayner, have called for a formal inquiry and for political parties to take action to ensure a safe environment for women. No formal complaint has yet been lodged with the party or with the police.

The controversy comes amid wider concerns about the culture within British politics, following a series of high-profile cases involving allegations of misconduct by MPs and party officials.

Stanley Johnson, 81, is a former Member of the European Parliament and a longstanding media commentator. He has not responded in further detail to the specific allegations beyond his initial statement. The Conservative Party has not indicated whether disciplinary action will be considered in relation to the reports.
headline: MP accuses Stanley Johnson of inappropriate touching

text:
A Co Galway schoolboy who previously struggled with reading has found a new passion in the books of Roald Dahl, his parents and teachers have said. Nine-year-old Sean Murphy, from Loughrea, began reading Dahl’s stories earlier this year as part of a literacy programme at his local primary school.

Sean, who is in third class at St Brendan’s National School, had experienced difficulties with reading from an early age. His mother, Sarah Murphy, said that reading homework was often “a real battle” and that Sean lacked confidence with books. “He’d get frustrated or bored and say he couldn’t do it. We really worried he’d fall behind,” she told RTÉ News.

Last term, Sean’s teacher introduced the class to Roald Dahl classics including “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” and “Matilda”. According to his teacher, Ms Deirdre O’Grady, Sean became engrossed in the “adventurous worlds and mischievous characters” in Dahl’s writing. “He started to volunteer to read aloud in class and asked to bring the books home,” said Ms O’Grady.

Sean himself said he likes how “funny and a bit mad” the books are. “My favourite is The BFG because he talks in a silly way and he’s really nice,” he explained. Sean said he now reads for 15 or 20 minutes before bed every night, something his parents say has had a positive impact on his confidence and schoolwork.

Literacy specialist with the school, Evelyn Keane, said Roald Dahl’s use of humour and imaginative language can be a powerful tool for young readers who struggle with motivation. “Once a child finds a book or author they genuinely enjoy, it can make all the difference in developing a lifelong love of reading,” Ms Keane said.

The HSE recently launched a nationwide campaign to promote early literacy, encouraging parents to read regularly with their children. According to the Department of Education, approximately one in ten Irish children experience significant difficulties with reading during their primary school years.

Sean’s mother said she hopes his story encourages other parents to keep trying different books until something clicks. “It’s such a relief to see him associating reading with something fun now. He’s even started writing his own stories at home,” she said.

Staff at St Brendan’s National School say they plan to expand their reading initiative next term, using a wider range of authors to inspire pupils. Sean, meanwhile, is working his way through Dahl’s entire collection and says he hopes to finish “The Witches” before the end of the month.
headline: Schoolboy enjoys new chapter reading Roald Dahl books

text:
Hospitals across the country have welcomed the first babies of 2024, with maternity units reporting a night of celebration as families rang in the New Year with new arrivals.

The National Maternity Hospital on Holles Street, Dublin, marked the birth of its first baby of the year at 12.07am. Baby Aoife, weighing 3.2kg, was welcomed by her delighted parents, Sarah and Michael Byrne from Clondalkin. Staff said mother and baby are both doing well.

At Cork University Maternity Hospital, the first birth of the year occurred at 12.21am. Baby Oisín arrived to proud parents Emma and Colm Murphy from Ballincollig. Midwives at the hospital described a “festive atmosphere” on the wards as several families ushered in 2024 with the arrival of their newborns.

University Hospital Galway reported the arrival of twins shortly after midnight. The twins, a boy and a girl, were born to parents Aisling and David Conway from Oranmore. Dr Claire O’Shea, consultant obstetrician at the hospital, said staff were “delighted to share in such a special moment with the Conway family”.

Meanwhile, the Rotunda Hospital in Dublin welcomed its first baby of the year at 12.31am. Baby Hannah weighed in at 3.45kg. Her parents, Siobhan and Patrick Nolan from Skerries, expressed their gratitude to the staff for their support.

Hospitals in Limerick, Waterford, and Letterkenny also reported the arrival of several New Year’s Day babies. The HSE congratulated families across Ireland, with a spokesperson noting: “Each New Year’s birth is a moment of great joy for our maternity services and a sign of hope and renewal.”

Speaking to RTÉ News, Dr Mary Higgins, consultant obstetrician at the National Maternity Hospital, said: “There’s always a sense of excitement with the first babies of the year. It reminds us of the special role played by our maternity teams every day.”

Staff at all the hospitals praised the work of midwives, nurses and medical teams who ensured safe deliveries through the holiday period. 

As the country wakes to the first day of 2024, proud parents across Ireland are beginning the New Year with new additions to their families, and maternity wards continue to echo with the sound of newborn cries.
headline: Hospitals welcome first babies of the New Year

text:
President Michael D Higgins officially marked the beginning of the festive season this evening with the annual turning on of the Christmas lights at Áras an Uachtaráin. The event, attended by children from a number of local primary schools and representatives from a range of community organisations, took place in the grounds of the President’s official residence in the Phoenix Park.

Speaking at the ceremony, President Higgins said the lighting of the Áras Christmas tree was an opportunity to reflect on the importance of community, solidarity, and inclusiveness, particularly at a time when many across the country are facing challenges. He urged those present to remember vulnerable members of society, highlighting the efforts of charitable groups and volunteers who provide support during the winter months.

“Christmas offers us all a moment to pause and consider how we can help build a kinder, more inclusive Ireland,” the President said. “It is a time to extend a hand of friendship, and show support for those who may be struggling.”

The event featured seasonal music from the Garda Band and a choir comprised of pupils from St Mary’s Primary School, who joined in singing carols as the festive lights were illuminated. Among the guests were representatives from children’s advocacy organisations, members of the Defence Forces, and staff from healthcare and emergency services.

The Áras Christmas tree, a 10-metre Norway spruce sourced from Co Wicklow, was decorated with hundreds of energy-efficient LED lights and traditional ornaments. President Higgins and his wife, Sabina, greeted children in attendance, many of whom had written letters to Santa as part of the evening’s activities.

The ceremony concluded with hot chocolate and mince pies served in the State Dining Room, with President Higgins wishing all present a peaceful and happy Christmas. The lights at Áras an Uachtaráin will remain on display throughout the holiday period, with the annual Christmas tours of the residence scheduled to continue in the coming weeks.

In a statement, the President reiterated his gratitude to frontline workers and volunteers for their continued service, and extended his best wishes to people across Ireland and to the Irish diaspora abroad.
headline: President turns on Áras an Uachtaráin Christmas lights

text:
A leading European health agency has warned that ongoing mutations of the coronavirus could potentially undermine the effectiveness of existing vaccines, raising renewed concerns over the trajectory of the Covid-19 pandemic.

In a report published today, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) stated that several recent variants of the virus contain genetic changes that may allow it to partially evade the immune response triggered by current vaccines. The agency urged member states, including Ireland, to maintain robust surveillance and to accelerate vaccination campaigns.

The ECDC said there was "moderate evidence" that some mutations, particularly those identified in variants first detected in Brazil and South Africa, might reduce the efficacy of certain vaccines. However, it stressed that vaccination remains the best available defence against severe illness and hospitalisation.

The agency has called on European governments to continue genomic sequencing of virus samples, in order to rapidly identify and track new variants. Dr Andrea Ammon, ECDC director, said that ongoing vigilance was essential: "The evolution of the virus is not unexpected, but it means we must be ready to adapt our strategies if necessary."

The Department of Health said it is monitoring the situation closely and is in regular contact with European and international counterparts. The Minister for Health, Stephen Donnelly, said that Ireland’s vaccination programme would continue as planned, but acknowledged that future changes to the rollout may be necessary as the evidence evolves.

To date, over 500,000 people in Ireland have received their first vaccine dose, with the HSE aiming to ramp up distribution as more supplies become available. Health officials have repeatedly stressed the need for continued adherence to public health measures, including social distancing, mask wearing and limiting social contacts.

The Chief Medical Officer, Dr Tony Holohan, said that while the emergence of variants was concerning, Ireland’s public health infrastructure was well placed to respond. "It is essential that we continue to act cautiously and follow the guidance, even as the vaccination programme gathers pace," he said.

Experts have cautioned that further mutations are likely as long as the virus continues to circulate widely. They have called on the public to remain patient and to trust the scientific process as vaccine manufacturers work to adapt their formulations if necessary.

The Government is expected to discuss the ECDC findings at tomorrow’s Cabinet meeting, with officials saying they remain committed to the goal of vaccinating all adults by September.
headline: ECDC: Virus mutation could hamper vaccine effectiveness

text:
The Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine, Charlie McConalogue, has announced the establishment of a Seafood Sector Taskforce in response to the significant challenges posed by Brexit to the Irish fishing industry. The move comes after the conclusion of the recent EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement, which sees Ireland ceding quota shares in a number of key fish stocks and has sparked concern among coastal communities and industry representatives.

The new taskforce, chaired by Aidan Cotter, former Chief Executive of Bord Bia, is to assess the impacts of Brexit on the sector and make recommendations to ensure its long-term viability. Minister McConalogue said the loss of quota represents a “devastating blow” to many fishing-dependent areas, with estimates suggesting an annual loss of €43 million in fish landings, and called for a “co-ordinated and robust response” from government and stakeholders.

Membership of the taskforce will include representatives from the fishing and aquaculture industries, processors, coastal community groups, and State agencies such as Bord Iascaigh Mhara and the Marine Institute. The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine confirmed the group’s mandate will include identifying support measures to address the immediate financial impact, as well as strategies for longer-term sectoral adaptation.

Industry groups have welcomed the announcement but cautioned that urgent action is needed. The Irish South and West Fish Producers Organisation said the quota cuts would have “real and lasting consequences” for rural communities, and urged the taskforce to prioritise direct financial supports, fleet restructuring, and access to new markets.

The European Commission’s Brexit Adjustment Reserve is expected to be a key resource, with Ireland set to receive a significant allocation in recognition of the disproportionate effect of Brexit on the national seafood sector.

The taskforce will submit its final report to Minister McConalogue by the end of April, with recommendations expected to inform the Government’s approach to supporting one of the country’s most hard-hit industries in the months and years ahead.
headline: Seafood Sector Taskforce launched in wake of Brexit

text:
Lockdown drills have become “part of life” for an Irish teacher working in the United States, who says that such exercises are a routine feature of the school calendar across the country.

Aisling O'Brien, originally from Dublin, has been teaching in an elementary school in Massachusetts for the past five years. She told RTÉ News that she was initially taken aback by the frequency and seriousness with which US schools conduct lockdown drills, which simulate a response to an active shooter incident.

Ms O'Brien said the drills often involve students as young as five practising how to hide quietly in darkened classrooms, away from doors and windows, while teachers lock doors, lower blinds and instruct children to remain silent.

"At first, it was really surreal coming from Ireland, where the worst thing we’d prepare for might be a fire alarm," she said. "Here, lockdown drills are just a fact of life. We have them several times a year, and everyone takes them very seriously."

The teacher, who previously taught in south Dublin, said the level of preparation is “unlike anything” she experienced before moving to the US. "We’re drilled on specific protocols – how to secure the classroom, where the safest corners are, how to communicate with law enforcement, and, most importantly, how to keep the children calm," she said.

Ms O'Brien added that while most children treat the exercises as routine, some find them distressing. "You see the anxiety in some of the younger students. They have questions afterwards – sometimes they’re worried, sometimes they joke, but you can tell it’s on their minds," she said.

The prevalence of school shootings in the United States has prompted schools nationwide to introduce regular lockdown drills as part of safety measures. According to figures from the US National Centre for Education Statistics, over 95% of public schools in the country conducted lockdown drills in the 2021-22 school year.

Ms O'Brien said that parents are kept informed about the drills in advance, but she believes many Irish people would be shocked to see what is now considered standard practice. "When I tell friends and family at home, they’re horrified. It’s just not something that would cross your mind in an Irish school," she said.

Despite the added stress, Ms O'Brien says she remains passionate about teaching and emphasises the resilience of both staff and students. "It’s not something you ever get used to, but you adapt, because you have to. We all want to feel safe, and this is just part of life here now," she said.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has previously advised Irish citizens living in the US to be aware of local procedures for emergencies. The Department of Education has confirmed to RTÉ News that there are no plans to introduce similar lockdown drills in Irish schools.
headline: Lockdown drills 'part of life' for Irish teacher in US

text:
The British government has announced a relaxation of immigration rules for care workers, in an effort to tackle significant staff shortages in the United Kingdom’s social care sector. The move comes amid ongoing recruitment challenges exacerbated by Brexit and the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic.

Under the new measures, care workers from overseas—including Ireland and EU member states—will be able to apply for Health and Care Worker visas, allowing them to work in the UK for a period of at least 12 months. The announcement was welcomed by care sector organisations, who have long argued that post-Brexit restrictions made it more difficult to recruit staff from outside Britain.

The UK’s Home Secretary, James Cleverly, said the government recognised the "crucial role" played by care workers and hoped the changes would help alleviate pressure on the health and social care system. He stated: "We are acting to ensure vulnerable people get the care they need, while also ensuring the integrity of our immigration system."

Irish citizens were not subject to the same limitations as other EU nationals following Brexit, due to the Common Travel Area arrangements between Ireland and the UK. However, industry groups on both sides of the Irish Sea noted a marked reduction in EEA nationals taking up care jobs in Britain since the UK formally left the single market and customs union on 1 January 2021.

Patricia King, General Secretary of SIPTU, said the British move was overdue and called for similar recognition of the sector in Ireland, where care providers also report recruitment and retention difficulties. She said: "The pandemic exposed just how vital and undervalued care work is. While the UK is finally taking steps to attract more workers, we must also invest in pay and conditions at home to ensure Irish workers are not lured abroad."

According to British government figures, vacancies in the UK’s adult social care sector currently stand at around 150,000, with many care homes struggling to fill posts. The new visa route for care workers will be open to applicants from February, with successful candidates allowed to bring dependants.

The move faced criticism from some Conservative MPs, who said it risked undermining efforts to train domestic workers. However, sector leaders insist overseas recruitment remains essential unless the government addresses low pay and difficult working conditions within the industry.

Meanwhile, the Taoiseach, Leo Varadkar, said the government would monitor developments closely, but stressed that freedom of movement for Irish citizens between the two islands would not be affected by the UK’s policy change. He added: "The Common Travel Area arrangements continue to ensure strong links and opportunities for our people."

The Department of Foreign Affairs has advised Irish citizens considering care work in the UK to familiarise themselves with the new visa process and ensure potential employers comply with the latest regulations. Further details are available on the UK government’s website.
headline: UK to ease immigration rules for care workers

text:
The National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET) has warned that indoor dining may have remained closed beyond September had the Government not decided to proceed with a phased reopening linked to the EU Digital COVID Certificate.

In a briefing with the Oireachtas Committee on Health today, Chief Medical Officer Dr Tony Holohan outlined NPHET’s ongoing concerns regarding the spread of the Delta variant and the risk it poses to unvaccinated cohorts. Dr Holohan said the recommendation to delay the original reopening was made on public health grounds, as the trajectory of the virus in late June indicated a sharp increase in daily case numbers.

“Had we not adopted a cautious approach and introduced the new framework for indoor hospitality, it is likely that restrictions would have had to continue well into the autumn to prevent further waves of infection,” Dr Holohan told TDs.

Last week, the Taoiseach Micheál Martin announced that indoor dining could reopen for fully vaccinated people and those who have recovered from COVID-19, provided that venues adhere to strict guidelines. Children under 18 are permitted to accompany vaccinated adults.

NPHET’s modelling, published earlier this month, predicted that daily cases could reach between 2,000 and 4,000 by the end of July, with a significant risk of increased hospital admissions if restrictions were lifted without additional safeguards.

In his evidence to the committee, Dr Holohan emphasised the importance of the COVID certificate system as a temporary measure: “It is not our intention that these arrangements should continue any longer than necessary. We are responding to an unprecedented public health threat and must act with caution.”

The HSE’s Chief Clinical Officer, Dr Colm Henry, said 70% of adults are now fully vaccinated, with vaccine uptake strong among younger age groups. However, he cautioned that outbreaks linked to indoor settings could still occur, particularly given higher rates of transmission among unvaccinated individuals.

Representatives from the Restaurant Association of Ireland expressed concern about the continued impact on businesses, calling for further financial supports and a clear roadmap for the full reopening of hospitality.

Gardaí have confirmed that compliance checks will continue at licensed premises. The Department of Health also advised that ventilation, mask wearing, and social distancing remain key elements in limiting the spread of the virus.

Dr Holohan concluded that while significant progress has been made in the vaccination programme, vigilance is still required: “Our collective effort has brought us this far, but the coming weeks will be critical in determining how the situation evolves.”

The Government is expected to review the measures at the end of August, based on advice from NPHET and the latest epidemiological data.
headline: NPHET: Indoor dining could have closed beyond September

text:
The United States has threatened to impose new tariffs on a range of EU products, including cheese, pork, and whiskey, in a move that could have significant repercussions for Irish exporters. The announcement was made by the office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) late last night, citing ongoing disputes over agricultural subsidies and digital services taxes.

US officials said the proposed levies are being considered as a response to what they describe as “unfair trade practices by certain EU member states” and retaliatory measures in longstanding disputes at the World Trade Organisation (WTO). The list of goods outlined by the USTR includes Irish and EU cheeses, processed pork products, and whiskeys, among other items.

Industry representatives in Ireland have expressed concern at the news, warning that any tariffs could have a substantial impact on Irish food and drink exports. The US is a key export market for Irish agri-food businesses, with Bord Bia figures showing that more than €1 billion worth of Irish food and drink was exported to the US in the past year alone. Irish whiskey, in particular, has enjoyed rapid growth in the American market in recent years.

The Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine, Charlie McConalogue, said the Government was closely monitoring developments. “We are working with our EU partners and the European Commission to seek a resolution to these disputes, and we will be making strong representations to ensure Irish producers do not suffer as a result of issues beyond their control,” he said.

The Distilled Spirits Council of the US, a major trade body, has also called for a negotiated solution, warning that tariffs on whiskey would ultimately hurt both producers and consumers on both sides of the Atlantic.

A spokesperson for the European Commission described the US move as “regrettable,” and indicated that the EU would consider all available options in response if the tariffs are implemented.

The US administration has set a 30-day public consultation period before any final decision is made. An escalation of trade barriers would come at a challenging time for Irish exporters, who are already grappling with increased shipping costs and volatility in global markets.

The Department of Foreign Affairs said it was seeking further clarity from US authorities and coordinating with Irish embassies and the European Commission on the matter. The Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs, Micheál Martin, said protecting the interests of Irish exporters remained an “absolute priority” for the Government.

Trade officials in Brussels are expected to seek high-level talks with their US counterparts in the coming weeks in an effort to resolve the dispute before any tariffs take effect.
headline: US threatens tariffs on EU cheese, pork and whiskey

text:
Sinn Féin has announced that Martina Anderson will stand as its candidate in Northern Ireland for the upcoming European elections, confirming speculation that the former MEP would seek to return to Brussels.

Ms Anderson, a former Stormont MLA and ex-prisoner, previously represented Northern Ireland in the European Parliament from 2012 until Brexit in 2020, during which time she was a vocal advocate for Irish unity and the protection of citizens' rights post-Brexit. Her selection was ratified by party members at a special convention in Belfast on Friday evening.

Speaking after her confirmation, Ms Anderson expressed gratitude for the support she received from the party and outlined her priorities for the campaign ahead. “This election comes at a pivotal time for Ireland, North and South, as we navigate the fallout from Brexit and face into a cost-of-living crisis that is hitting families hard,” she said.

She added that she will work to defend the interests of all communities in Northern Ireland and push for stronger representation in Europe. “We need a determined voice in Brussels to ensure our people do not pay the price for political decisions taken elsewhere,” Ms Anderson said. She also pledged to focus on addressing regional economic disparities and supporting peace funding initiatives.

Sinn Féin party leader Mary Lou McDonald TD welcomed Ms Anderson’s candidacy, describing her as “a formidable campaigner and a passionate advocate for the people of the North.” Ms McDonald stressed the importance of having “a strong all-Ireland voice in Europe,” particularly in light of the ongoing discussions on the Protocol and future EU-UK relations.

The European Parliament elections are set to take place next month, with campaigning across all constituencies now underway. While Northern Ireland will return only one MEP under the current arrangements, the race is expected to attract significant attention, with the DUP and Alliance Party also poised to field high-profile candidates.

The confirmation of Ms Anderson’s candidacy signals Sinn Féin’s intent to retain its influence at a European level, despite the uncertainties posed by the UK’s departure from the EU. Party strategists believe her experience and profile will resonate with nationalist voters, while her track record on social issues and cross-community work is expected to broaden her appeal.

Northern Ireland voters go to the polls alongside the rest of Ireland on 7 June, with counting expected to begin the following day. The outcome will be closely watched both in Dublin and London, given the ongoing political sensitivities in the North and the wider implications for EU-UK relations.
headline: Anderson confirmed as Sinn Féin's NI Europe candidate

text:
Countries around the world are not on track to meet critical climate targets and must urgently raise their ambitions, the United Nations has warned. Speaking ahead of a key summit in Bonn, Germany, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said that current national commitments are falling well short of what is needed to limit global temperature increases and prevent disastrous consequences.

"Governments must move much faster – and with much greater ambition – if we are to keep the goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees alive," Mr Guterres said. He called for rapid reductions in fossil fuel use, increased investment in renewable energy, and more support for vulnerable countries facing the worst impacts of climate change.

The warning comes as delegates from nearly 200 countries gather in Bonn for two weeks of negotiations that will lay the groundwork for COP29, the United Nations climate conference scheduled for later this year in Baku, Azerbaijan. The talks will focus on closing gaps between existing pledges and the actions needed to avoid the most severe outcomes predicted by scientists.

Analysis published by the UN’s climate body earlier this year found that even if all countries delivered on their current pledges, global temperatures would still rise by around 2.5 degrees by the end of the century – well above the target set in the Paris Agreement.
