Scientists warn this would lead to more frequent extreme weather events, rising sea levels, and severe impacts on food and water security.

Climate activists and representatives from small island states have repeatedly called for wealthier nations to provide more financial and technical support to help developing countries reduce emissions and adapt to climate risks. Loss and damage funding, which aims to assist communities already suffering the effects of climate change, remains a key point of contention.

Ireland’s Minister for the Environment, Climate and Communications, Eamon Ryan, has said that Ireland supports efforts to increase climate ambition internationally and will continue to advocate for stronger targets at EU level. The Government recently launched a public consultation on its own Climate Action Plan, which sets out measures to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 51% by 2030.

Mr Guterres urged countries to submit strengthened national action plans ahead of COP29, and cautioned that “history will not be kind to those who delay” decisive action. “The science is clear, and the solutions are known. What is needed now is political will and real solidarity.”
headline: Countries must be more ambitious on climate goals: UN

text:
Authorities in Sydney have imposed stricter lockdown measures amid what has been described as a “stubborn” outbreak of Covid-19 cases, as Australia’s largest city grapples with rising infections fuelled by the highly transmissible Delta variant.

The New South Wales Premier, Gladys Berejiklian, announced a raft of new restrictions on Saturday following the detection of 111 new locally acquired cases, the highest daily increase yet in the current surge. The Premier warned that the virus was spreading quickly within households and essential workplaces, prompting fears that existing measures were not sufficient to contain the outbreak.

From midnight, residents in the worst-affected council areas in southwest Sydney face tighter stay-at-home orders. Only one person per household will be permitted to leave the home each day for essential shopping, and non-essential retail will be closed. Construction projects will be paused across the city, and all non-critical workplaces have been ordered to shut. The new restrictions are set to remain in place for at least two weeks.

Ms Berejiklian said the government has “no option” but to strengthen the lockdown, citing continued non-compliance with health guidelines and the persistently high numbers of unlinked cases. “We are in a very serious situation here in New South Wales and particularly in Sydney,” she said, calling on residents to follow public health advice.

The latest measures come as the state government faces criticism over the slow pace of the vaccine rollout, with only around 11% of Australia’s population fully vaccinated, according to official figures. Authorities have urged people over 40, health workers, and those with underlying conditions to register for vaccination, though supply constraints persist.

Police have increased patrols and checkpoints in the city’s southwest, where transmission rates have been highest. Officers have been authorised to issue €235 (AUD$200) fines to individuals breaching public health orders.

Since the start of the pandemic, Australia has kept case numbers relatively low through border closures and swift local lockdowns. However, the Delta variant has proved more difficult to contain, with health experts warning it poses new challenges to the country’s response.

The lockdown’s extension and tightening have prompted renewed calls for federal support for affected businesses and workers, with industry groups warning of significant economic impact. Prime Minister Scott Morrison has pledged further assistance, including income support for those unable to work due to restrictions.

The current outbreak, which began in mid-June, has accounted for more than 1,000 cases, with dozens of hospitalisations. Health officials are urging all Sydneysiders to get tested if they have any symptoms and to remain vigilant as the city works to bring the outbreak under control.
headline: Sydney tightens lockdown amid 'stubborn' outbreak

text:
China has revoked the press credentials of three Wall Street Journal correspondents, ordering them to leave the country in response to what it called a “racially discriminatory” headline in an opinion piece published by the US newspaper.

The action, announced by China’s Foreign Ministry on Wednesday, marks the first expulsion of multiple foreign journalists from the country in decades. The ministry said the reporters’ press cards were “cancelled” due to the Journal’s publication of a 3 February opinion headline referring to China as “the real sick man of Asia”.

The three correspondents—Josh Chin, Chao Deng and Philip Wen—were based in Beijing. The Foreign Ministry said their reporting had “nothing to do” with the government’s decision, which it insisted was taken solely over the editorial stance of the publication, but Western diplomatic sources have suggested the move represents an escalation in China’s restrictions on foreign media.

A spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry, Geng Shuang, said the article had “insulted the Chinese people” and accused the Journal of failing to issue a formal apology. “The Chinese people do not welcome media that publish racially discriminatory articles and maliciously slander China,” he told reporters at a regular press briefing.

The Wall Street Journal condemned the move, with editor-in-chief Matt Murray calling for the immediate reinstatement of the journalists’ visas. In a statement, the Journal said, “We are deeply disappointed with this action, which is unprecedented. The Journal’s news department has had no involvement with the opinion article that caused offence.”

International media watchdogs and foreign correspondents’ associations also criticised the expulsions, warning that they would further restrict access to independent information at a critical time, as China and the World Health Organisation respond to the ongoing coronavirus outbreak.

The United States government condemned the decision. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo urged China to respect freedom of the press, saying, “Mature, responsible countries understand that a free press reports facts and expresses opinions. The correct response is to present counter arguments, not restrict speech.”

One of the journalists, Chao Deng, is an American citizen, while Josh Chin holds US citizenship and Philip Wen is an Australian national. Their expulsion follows a warning from Beijing earlier this month that it would retaliate if the US tightened restrictions on Chinese journalists working in America.

The decision has raised concerns among foreign correspondents in China, where press freedom is routinely curtailed and visas are subject to lengthy approval processes. In 2019, several Irish and European outlets reported difficulties in securing or renewing press credentials for their staff in China.

The National Union of Journalists and Reporters Without Borders said the move by Chinese authorities set a worrying precedent and called on the Chinese government to review its approach to international media.

The Department of Foreign Affairs said it was monitoring developments and would continue to “raise concerns relating to media freedom and freedom of expression” in its engagements with Chinese officials.
headline: China revokes press credentials of three WSJ reporters

text:
Iceland will put an end to commercial whale hunting from next year, its Minister of Food, Agriculture and Fisheries has announced, marking a significant shift in the country’s long-controversial whaling policy.

In a statement issued today, Minister Svandís Svavarsdóttir said that the government would not issue new whaling licences once the current permits expire at the end of 2023. The minister cited evolving public attitudes, falling demand for whale meat internationally and domestically, and mounting scientific evidence of the impact on whale populations.

“Conditions have changed dramatically, and there is little justification to continue commercial whaling beyond next year,” Ms Svavarsdóttir said, adding that ethical considerations and the nation’s international reputation were also factors in the decision.

Iceland, alongside Norway and Japan, has been one of just a few countries to permit commercial whaling in defiance of the International Whaling Commission’s (IWC) global moratorium, which took effect in 1986. In recent years, the Icelandic fleet has primarily targeted fin and minke whales, but the industry has faced growing opposition at home and abroad.

Environmental groups such as the International Fund for Animal Welfare have welcomed the move, describing it as a “major victory for marine conservation.” Critics of whaling have long pointed to declining consumer interest, especially among younger Icelanders, and the fact that the vast majority of the meat is exported – mainly to Japan.

The last few hunting seasons in Iceland have been marked by reduced quotas and frequent interruptions, with only one company, Hvalur hf, actively engaged in whaling. According to official statistics, just one minke whale was caught in 2021, and no fin whales were hunted.

The government’s decision follows the conclusion of a comprehensive report into the social, economic and environmental aspects of whaling, which found that the benefits no longer outweighed the costs or reputational damage.

Tourism has overtaken whaling as an economic driver in recent decades, with whale-watching now attracting more visitors and revenue than the hunt itself. Industry groups and conservationists contend that the move will further boost Iceland’s eco-friendly image.

While those employed in the remaining whaling sector have expressed disappointment and accused the government of bowing to international pressure, the fisheries minister has promised support for affected workers.

The ban is set to take effect on 1 January 2024. With this decision, Iceland becomes the latest North Atlantic nation to phase out the practice of commercial whaling, in line with a growing global consensus on marine protection.
headline: Iceland to end whale hunting from 2024, says minister

text:
The Managing Director of Shannon Airport, Mary Considine, is to step down from her position later this year, it has been confirmed. Ms Considine, who has led the airport since 2019 and previously served as Chief Executive of Shannon Group, informed staff of her decision on Monday morning. 

Shannon Group said Ms Considine will remain in place until a successor is appointed, ensuring what it called a "smooth transition" during a period of increasing passenger numbers and route expansion. The Group’s Chair, Pádraig Ó Céidigh, paid tribute to Ms Considine, describing her as a “dedicated and visionary leader” who had steered Shannon through the significant challenges faced by the aviation sector during the Covid-19 pandemic and subsequent recovery.

During Ms Considine’s tenure, Shannon saw the restoration of transatlantic flights, the addition of several new European routes, and the advancement of major infrastructure projects, including the resurfacing of the main runway and the planned redevelopment of terminal facilities. Passenger numbers at the airport have rebounded strongly, with 2023 figures indicating a return to pre-pandemic levels.

In her message to staff, Ms Considine said it had been “the honour of a lifetime” to lead the airport and organisation, paying tribute to her colleagues and the wider community in the Mid-West region. She said she was proud of Shannon’s role in supporting the local economy and promoting regional connectivity.

Local representatives, including Clare TD Joe Carey, praised Ms Considine’s commitment, noting that she had “championed not only Shannon Airport but the wider region, especially during testing periods for the industry”. Business and tourism groups also hailed her stewardship.

The recruitment process for a new managing director will begin shortly, with the post to be advertised nationally and internationally. Shannon Group said it remains focused on its plans to further expand connectivity and enhance facilities for passengers and airlines.

Shannon Airport, which marked its 75th anniversary last year, is a key transport hub for the Mid-West and West of Ireland, serving over 30 destinations. The airport is also home to the world’s oldest duty-free shop and the International Aviation Services Centre.

Ms Considine is expected to leave her role in the autumn.
headline: Shannon Airport Managing Director is to leave his role

text:
A motorcyclist in his 20s has been hospitalised following a road traffic collision in Co Offaly last night.

Gardaí and emergency services attended the scene at Clonminch Road, Tullamore, shortly after 10pm on Thursday. The incident involved a motorcycle and a car.

The motorcyclist sustained what are understood to be serious but non-life threatening injuries. He was treated at the scene before being taken by ambulance to Midlands Regional Hospital Tullamore. The driver of the car was uninjured.

The scene was preserved overnight for a technical examination by Garda forensic collision investigators. Traffic diversions were in place but the road has since fully reopened.

Gardaí are appealing for witnesses, particularly any road users who may have camera footage, including dash cam, from the area at the time of the collision to come forward.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Tullamore Garda Station on 057 932 7600, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111 or any Garda station.
headline: Motorcyclist, 20s, injured in Offaly collision

text:
A locum general practitioner has appeared before a Fitness to Practise Inquiry of the Medical Council following allegations relating to the care of a patient at a rural practice in Co Clare. The inquiry heard that Dr Jonathan Mahon is alleged to have failed to adequately assess and manage a male patient who presented complaining of chest pain and shortness of breath in August 2022.

The patient, who was in his early fifties, is understood to have visited the surgery after experiencing persistent discomfort over several days. It is alleged Dr Mahon did not carry out a physical examination, did not record vital observations or an electrocardiogram (ECG), and failed to refer the patient for urgent hospital assessment, despite the risk factors present.

The patient’s symptoms reportedly worsened later that evening, and he attended the Emergency Department at University Hospital Limerick, where he was found to have suffered a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction, a form of heart attack. He subsequently underwent urgent intervention and has since recovered.

Counsel for the Medical Council, Grace O’Sullivan BL, told the inquiry that the case raises "serious concerns regarding the standard of care provided to a patient with potential cardiac symptoms." She said the central issues relate to alleged failures in assessment, record keeping, and timely referral.

Dr Mahon, through his legal representative, said he deeply regretted the outcome and had "at all times acted in good faith". He accepted that record keeping on the day in question did not meet the required standard, but argued he had assessed the patient’s symptoms to be musculoskeletal in origin based on the patient’s own account and the absence of acute distress. The inquiry heard that at the time, Dr Mahon was providing locum cover and was unfamiliar with the patient’s medical history.

The practice manager gave evidence describing the surgery’s protocols for managing acute presentations, and the inquiry was told that the practice has since implemented new procedures to ensure all chest pain cases are seen by a permanent GP and triaged for ECG and observation.

The hearing continues, with expert witnesses due to give evidence on Thursday regarding the appropriate standards of care and the obligations of locum GPs in out-of-hours or temporary cover scenarios. The outcome of the inquiry may result in sanctions ranging from advice to censure, or restrictions on Dr Mahon’s registration, should any breaches of professional standards be proven.
headline: Locum GP before Medical Council over care of patient

text:
Four Irish entrepreneurs are making a name for themselves by transforming their passion for baking and confections into successful small businesses, each serving up sweet treats and a generous helping of community spirit.

In County Galway, Mary O’Hanlon’s “Mary’s Cookie Co.” in Loughrea has become a local favourite, with queues regularly forming outside her small bakery on Main Street. Mary, who left a career in finance during the pandemic, says her home-baked cookies, brownies and cakes are inspired by family recipes handed down through generations. “I wanted to create a space where people could enjoy a treat and feel at home,” she told RTÉ News. Her business, which started from her own kitchen during lockdowns, now employs four staff and supplies baked goods to several local cafés. Mary credits the support of the Local Enterprise Office and her neighbours for her success so far.

Meanwhile, in Cork city, chef Ciarán Fitzpatrick’s “Brother Bear Doughnuts” has been stirring up a buzz with its rotating menu of gourmet doughnuts, ranging from traditional jam-filled to fillings like pistachio cream or seasonal berries. Ciarán, who was previously a sous-chef in a city centre hotel, set up shop in a converted shipping container on the Coal Quay. “Cork people love their food, and I think they appreciate something a bit different,” he says. “We get busloads of visitors at weekends, and I love seeing the smiles when people try something new.” His doughnuts have proved so popular that he now supplies orders for birthdays and corporate events, and is planning a second location for the coming year.

Further north, sisters Niamh and Aoife O’Reilly have turned their childhood love of fudge and caramel into “Sweet Republic,” an online confectionery based in Letterkenny. Using locally sourced butter and cream, the pair hand-make batches of fudge, marshmallows and honeycomb, all of which are sold through their website and at local farmers’ markets. “We want to spread some joy, especially to people who can’t get out and about,” said Niamh. Their gift boxes have become particularly popular for birthdays and special occasions, with deliveries travelling as far as France and Germany. Both sisters hope to open a bricks-and-mortar shop in Donegal in the future.

In Dublin’s Liberties, Abdi Hassan’s “Kingdom Baklava” is introducing locals to the sweet, nutty flavours of Middle Eastern and North African desserts. His small bakery on Meath Street specialises in pistachio- and walnut-filled pastries, alongside strong coffee and mint tea. Originally from Somalia, Abdi says he wanted to share a slice of his heritage with his adopted home. “People come in for the baklava, but they stay to chat and learn about the recipes,” he said. Regulars include students, local families and tourists, and now Abdi is working with a charity providing free treats to a nearby direct provision centre each week.

Despite the challenges of rising costs and changing consumer habits, all four business owners agree that connecting with their communities and creating memorable experiences for customers are key to their success. Their stories show how, with a dash of determination and a sprinkle of creativity, small Irish businesses can continue to thrive and bring a little sweetness to people’s lives.
headline: Four business owners spreading some joy with their sweet treats

text:
A police officer has been hospitalised following an assault in Co Tyrone on Tuesday evening. The incident occurred in the Moore Street area of Aughnacloy just after 8pm.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland said officers were responding to reports of a disturbance when one of their members was assaulted. The officer sustained injuries to the head and was subsequently taken to hospital for treatment. His condition is not believed to be life-threatening.

A man in his 20s has been arrested in connection with the incident and is currently being questioned by police at a local station. The PSNI said investigations are ongoing and appealed for anyone who may have witnessed the incident, or who may have relevant information, to come forward.

Chief Inspector Tate strongly condemned the attack, stating: “Assaults on officers carrying out their duty are utterly unacceptable. Our officers work to keep communities safe and any attack on them is an attack on the whole community.”

The incident comes amid ongoing concerns about violence directed at emergency service workers in the North. The PSNI has urged the public to support police efforts and respect the difficult and challenging nature of their work.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the PSNI via the 101 non-emergency number, quoting reference number 1650 of 11 June, or through Crimestoppers, which can be contacted anonymously.
headline: PSNI officer hospitalised after Tyrone assault

text:
Sean Quinn, the former billionaire businessman, has pledged in the High Court in Belfast that he will not trespass on lands at a quarry in County Fermanagh at the centre of a legal row.

The undertakings were given this morning after lawyers for a group of companies controlling the Derrylin property brought proceedings alleging Mr Quinn had entered the site without permission. Legal representatives for Mr Quinn, who was in court for the hearing, confirmed he had agreed not to enter the lands or interfere with any business there pending a further resolution of the dispute.

The quarry, operated by companies within the Mannok group, was formerly part of the vast Quinn business empire, which was broken up after Mr Quinn’s financial collapse in the wake of the 2008 banking crisis. Mannok, previously known as Quinn Industrial Holdings, has been locked in a number of legal battles with its former owner in recent years, following allegations of interference and intimidation related to company assets on both sides of the border.

During today’s proceedings, Mr Justice Scoffield was told that Mr Quinn disputes the claim that he trespassed on the property, but accepts the interim arrangements pending a full hearing. The judge welcomed the agreement as a way to keep the peace and urged both parties to avoid further escalation while legal matters are ongoing.

In a statement issued following the hearing, Mr Quinn said he is committed to complying with the court’s directive and will not enter the quarry or surrounding lands unless granted proper authorisation. He continues to maintain that he has an entitlement to access the site, but said he will pursue that claim through appropriate legal channels.

A spokesperson for Mannok welcomed Mr Quinn’s undertakings and said the company is focused on protecting its staff and assets, adding that it hopes the matter can be resolved without further disturbance or controversy.

The High Court proceedings will return later this month, when both sides are due to present further evidence. The PSNI and An Garda Síochána continue to monitor the situation amid ongoing concerns over safety and security in the border region.
headline: Sean Quinn pledges not to trespass on Fermanagh quarry

text:
A young boy from Cork living with a rare genetic condition is experiencing childhood joys many take for granted, thanks to an innovative mobility device known to his family as the "dino-cart".

Six-year-old Jack O’Donovan, from Ballincollig, has Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) Type 2, a progressive neuromuscular disorder that affects muscle strength and limits movement. Jack, who uses a wheelchair to get around, has always been fascinated by dinosaurs. His parents, Carol and David O’Donovan, wanted to find a way to help him play outside alongside his friends and siblings.

With local supports limited, Jack’s parents reached out to engineering students at Munster Technological University (MTU) last year. The students, working in collaboration with Jack’s occupational therapist from the HSE and his school, set out to design a device that would combine accessibility and fun.

After several months of planning and consultation, the students developed a custom-built mobility cart modelled on Jack’s favourite dinosaur, a triceratops. The finished device, affectionately dubbed the "dino-cart", allows Jack to sit securely while propelling himself forward using hand controls. Its wide wheelbase and sturdy frame mean it can manage grass and uneven surfaces, enabling him to join in playground games at his primary school and local park.

Jack’s mother Carol told RTÉ News: “For years, we were searching for something that would let Jack just be a child — to run around and be part of the fun, not just watching from the sidelines. The dino-cart has given him a new sort of freedom. The smile on his face says it all.”

The project was jointly funded by private donations and a grant from the Cork branch of Muscular Dystrophy Ireland. Several local businesses made in-kind contributions, including fabrication of the cart’s distinctive dinosaur body and adaptive controls.

Dr Anne O’Reilly, who supervised the MTU students, said the project was “a testament to the power of community-led innovation”. “We wanted to create something that was more than just functional — something magical that would ignite Jack’s imagination and help him socialise,” she said.

Jack has since become something of a local celebrity, with other children in his estate now asking for rides in the cart. His teachers say his confidence has soared since he started bringing it to school.

The O’Donovan family are now working with MTU and Muscular Dystrophy Ireland to share the design with other families. They hope the dino-cart can be adapted for more children living with mobility challenges across Ireland.

“We would love to see every child like Jack given the chance to play, explore, and dream,” Carol O’Donovan said. “That’s what childhood is all about.”
headline: Dino-cart invention helps boy 'to be a child'

text:
The leaders of Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael have signalled their determination to avoid a return to the kind of austerity measures implemented during the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis, despite mounting pressures on the public finances caused by the Covid-19 pandemic.

Taoiseach Micheál Martin and Tánaiste Leo Varadkar said that although the Government faces a significant budgetary challenge, its approach would not mirror the spending cuts and tax hikes seen a decade ago. Speaking after the Cabinet meeting at Government Buildings, both leaders emphasised the need for continued investment in health, education, housing and climate action.

“We are absolutely clear that austerity is not the path we will take,” Mr Martin said. “Our priority is to protect employment, support economic growth and look after those who have suffered most as a result of the pandemic.”

Mr Varadkar echoed the Taoiseach’s remarks, adding that the response to the pandemic had underlined the importance of strong public services and social supports. “We will not repeat the mistakes of the past. Recovery will be driven by investment, not retrenchment,” the Tánaiste said.

While the Department of Finance has projected a deficit of nearly €19 billion for 2021, the coalition leaders insisted that the focus must remain on supporting recovery and protecting vulnerable sectors. They pointed to the availability of low-cost borrowing on international markets, as well as the prospect of continued EU-level support, as factors that would enable the State to manage its debt burden in the medium term.

The Minister for Finance, Paschal Donohoe, is due to present an updated economic forecast to the Dáil next week, outlining the likely trajectory of government revenue and expenditure as the country continues to reopen. Both coalition parties are understood to be wary of public backlash to any suggestion of cutbacks, particularly given ongoing pressure on housing and healthcare services.

Labour Party leader Alan Kelly welcomed the Government’s commitment to avoid austerity, but warned that it must be matched by concrete measures to address inequality and rebuild public services. Sinn Féin’s Mary Lou McDonald said the coalition must go further, proposing an “ambitious investment programme” targeted at working families.

The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council has cautioned that while a short-term focus on recovery is justified, ministers will need to set out a credible plan to stabilise the public finances in the coming years. However, Government sources maintain that the priority must be “jobs, recovery, and social cohesion” for the time being.

The Opposition has pressed the Government to commit to a referendum on housing rights and to accelerate investment in health and childcare. Meanwhile, business groups have called for clarity around plans for pandemic supports such as the Employment Wage Subsidy Scheme and the Pandemic Unemployment Payment.

As the country continues its gradual exit from Covid-19 restrictions, the debate over how to balance fiscal prudence with investment in public services looks set to continue in the run-up to October’s Budget. For now, the Taoiseach and Tánaiste remain adamant: “We will not return to austerity.”
headline: FF and FG leaders keen to avoid post Covid-19 austerity

text:
A court in England has ruled that a couple who raised a child born through surrogacy are his legal parents, following a dispute which lasted more than two decades.

The case, which was heard at the High Court in London, centred on a 23-year-old man whose birth mother, a surrogate, had initially been registered as his legal parent along with her own husband, rather than the intended parents who had commissioned the surrogacy arrangement.

Mr Justice MacDonald ruled that the couple who raised the young man are now recognised as his legal parents, granting them retrospective parental rights. The man, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was present in court and welcomed the decision, stating that it affirmed the family relationships he has always known.

The couple, who are now in their fifties and live in southern England, had entered into a surrogacy agreement in the late 1990s with a surrogate mother. However, at the time, UK law automatically made the surrogate and her husband the legal parents, regardless of biological ties or the intentions of those involved. The intended parents were blocked from being officially recognised unless a formal adoption process was completed, which they were unable to do due to legal technicalities.

The legal landscape in the UK has since changed, with parental orders now available to transfer parenthood in surrogacy cases, but these were not available when the man was born. The couple argued that the absence of a legal remedy had caused years of uncertainty and distress both for themselves and their son.

Delivering the judgment, Mr Justice MacDonald said the "unique and distressing circumstances" of the case justified retrospective recognition. He noted that the man had lived all his life with the couple and regarded them as his parents in every sense other than the legal one.

Surrogacy law has faced criticism in both the UK and Ireland for lagging behind the reality faced by families involved. In Ireland, proposed reform of surrogacy arrangements and recognition of parental rights for intended parents has been the subject of ongoing debate in the Oireachtas. The Department of Health confirmed it is monitoring developments in jurisdictions such as the UK, where recent cases have exposed gaps in legal protections for children born through surrogacy.

Legal experts say the UK ruling could set an important precedent. Dr Susan Golombok of the University of Cambridge said it is a "landmark decision" that reflects the diverse ways in which families are formed in modern society.

The man and his parents said they hoped their case would provide reassurance for other families living with legal uncertainty as a result of past surrogacy arrangements.
headline: UK court rules couple are legal parents of adult son

text:
House prices in certain parts of the country have returned to levels last seen during the height of the Celtic Tiger, according to the latest figures from the Central Statistics Office (CSO) and estate agents.

Data published today show that in Dublin, average prices for second-hand homes in some southside postal districts—such as Dublin 4, Dublin 6, and parts of Dublin 14—have either matched or exceeded their 2007 peaks. In areas like Blackrock, Ranelagh and Donnybrook, three- and four-bedroom family homes are routinely commanding prices upwards of €1.2 million, with some properties selling for significantly higher after competitive bidding.

It is not just in the capital that prices have surged. In parts of Cork city and Galway, demand for well-located housing combined with tight supply has resulted in prices approaching, and in some cases surpassing, their pre-crash highs. The resurgence is particularly notable in established suburbs close to amenities, schools and transport links.

The CSO’s latest Residential Property Price Index shows a national increase of 6.7% in the year to April 2024. However, the recovery is uneven, with some regions—particularly the north-west and parts of the midlands—still lagging behind the rapid growth experienced in urban centres.

Estate agents point to a continued shortage of supply as a key driver. According to the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland, there is strong interest from both domestic buyers and returning emigrants, further intensifying competition in the market. “We are seeing a situation reminiscent of the mid-2000s in some areas,” said Mary Kelleher, a senior negotiator with a leading Dublin agency. “There are still cash buyers, and many are prepared to pay well above the asking prices for the right property.”

The Government introduced several measures in recent budgets to increase supply and support first-time buyers, including increases in the Help to Buy scheme and the introduction of the First Home Scheme. However, opposition parties argue that the pace of new housing delivery remains far too slow, with Sinn Féin housing spokesperson Eoin Ó Broin TD again calling for a major ramp-up in public housing construction.

Meanwhile, the Banking and Payments Federation Ireland (BPFI) reported mortgage approvals reaching over 5,000 for the third consecutive month, reflecting robust demand, particularly among first-time buyers. Despite higher interest rates from the European Central Bank, analysts say buyers are determined not to miss out amid fears that prices will continue to climb.

In response to rising concerns about affordability, the Taoiseach Simon Harris said the Government remains “absolutely committed” to tackling the housing crisis. “We are making progress, but we need to do more. Housing will remain the central priority for this Government,” he told the Dáil during Leaders’ Questions.

Advocacy groups such as Threshold and the Simon Community warn that rents remain at historic highs, and that spiralling house prices risk pushing more people into homelessness or out of the owner-occupier market altogether.

While there is little sign of an imminent slowdown, some economists caution that current trends may not be sustainable if interest rates remain elevated and if incomes fail to keep pace with inflation. However, for now, buyers and sellers in certain localities are once again witnessing property values reminiscent of the pre-crash boom.
headline: Houses at Celtic Tiger levels in some areas

text:
A hijacked merchant vessel in the Arabian Sea has been secured, with all crew members safe and accounted for, according to a UK maritime agency. The incident, which occurred off the coast of Somalia, had prompted international concern over the potential resurgence of piracy in the region.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said in a statement today that the vessel had been "secured" and all personnel were "reported safe." The hijacking unfolded yesterday morning when armed men boarded the ship while it was transiting through one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes.

UKMTO, which provides security guidance to commercial shipping in the region, said that naval forces had responded to the incident. Details on the identity of the vessel or the crew were not immediately available, nor has the nationality of the ship’s owners been confirmed.

International naval patrols, including those operated by the European Union’s Operation Atalanta—of which Ireland is a participant—have been monitoring the increased risk of piracy attacks in the Gulf of Aden and surrounding waters in recent months. While attacks had waned in the past decade, there has been a recent uptick in suspicious approaches and boarding attempts.

A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs said the Government was monitoring developments closely and was in contact with EU partners regarding the safety of Irish citizens and international shipping.

The motives behind the hijacking remain unclear. Authorities are investigating whether it was a targeted act of piracy or related to ongoing regional instability. The UKMTO has advised shipping companies to exercise “extreme caution” while passing through the area.

There have been no reports of injuries among the crew, and no ransom demand has been made public. The incident comes amid renewed concerns about maritime security in the region, which serves as a critical conduit for global trade, including vital energy supplies.

Irish shipping interests have previously expressed concern about the risks posed by piracy and conflict in key trade routes. The Department of Transport said it was reminding Irish-flagged vessels to adhere strictly to international security advisories.

Global maritime authorities are expected to review security measures for ships operating in the region in the wake of the latest incident.
headline: Hijacking ends in Arabian Sea, says UK agency

text:
The collapse of Stormont is “inevitable” if Westminster fails to resolve issues surrounding the Northern Ireland Protocol, a senior DUP figure has warned. The warning comes amid mounting tensions between the main unionist parties and the British government over post-Brexit trading arrangements, with concerns that the Assembly could be plunged into crisis within weeks.

Speaking to RTÉ News, the DUP’s East Antrim MP Sammy Wilson said his party is prepared to withdraw from the Executive unless “decisive and fundamental changes” are made to the Protocol, which was agreed as part of the UK’s withdrawal from the EU to avoid a hard border on the island of Ireland. He accused the British government of “dragging its feet” while unionist communities grow increasingly frustrated at what he described as an “economic border in the Irish Sea”.

“The democratic institutions in Northern Ireland cannot function with the Protocol in place in its current form,” Mr Wilson said. “If London does not act, the collapse of Stormont is not just possible but inevitable.”

The comments follow the resignation of Edwin Poots as DUP leader and ongoing negotiations involving the UK Government, EU officials, and Northern party leaders. The Protocol has been a source of political tension since its introduction, with unionists arguing it undermines Northern Ireland’s place in the UK.

Earlier this week, First Minister Paul Givan said his party would not hesitate to pull down the institutions if their concerns continue to be ignored. “Our participation in the Assembly is not unconditional,” he stated in the Assembly chamber. The Alliance Party and SDLP have criticised the DUP stance, warning that further instability could jeopardise public services and damage community relations.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin has urged all sides to engage in “calm and constructive dialogue” to resolve outstanding issues. Speaking from Dublin, he reiterated the Irish Government’s support for “practical solutions that protect the Good Friday Agreement in all its parts”. 

Meanwhile, business organisations have expressed concern about the impact of further political instability. The Northern Ireland Chamber of Commerce described the potential collapse of Stormont as “deeply damaging”, urging all parties to prioritise stability for the sake of the economy and public confidence.

Talks between the European Commission and UK Government are expected to continue over the coming weeks, but there is little sign of an imminent breakthrough. Secretary of State for Northern Ireland Brandon Lewis told reporters he remains “optimistic” a solution can be found, but stressed that “all options remain on the table”.

The European Commission’s Vice-President, Maroš Šefčovič, said the unionist concerns are “taken seriously”, but insisted that any renegotiation must respect the objectives of the Protocol and the integrity of the EU Single Market.

With the Stormont Assembly’s future in question once again, political observers are warning of the profound consequences for power-sharing and governance in the region should the current impasse persist.
headline: Stormont collapse 'inevitable' if Protocol not resolved

text:
Fourteen people availing of disability services have died after contracting Covid-19, according to new figures released by the Health Service Executive. The data, which covers the period from the beginning of the pandemic to mid-May, relate to people living in congregated settings and those receiving day or residential supports.

The HSE confirmed that 440 people in disability services have tested positive for coronavirus since March. Of those, 97 per cent were living in residential care or congregated settings.

Addressing the Oireachtas Special Committee on Covid-19 Response this afternoon, HSE officials said there are just over 8,000 individuals with disabilities in residential care, with the majority accommodated in group homes or campus-based services. Of these, 403 residents and 104 staff across 112 locations have been confirmed as virus cases.

Dr Cathal Morgan, Head of Operations for Disability Services at the HSE, told TDs that Covid-19 had posed "significant challenges" for people with intellectual and physical disabilities. He said that the relatively low mortality rate in these settings, compared to other residential care facilities, was due in part to swift action to isolate suspected cases and strict adherence to infection prevention protocols.

The HSE said it has prioritised the rollout of personal protective equipment, staff training, and comprehensive testing since the beginning of the outbreak. Dr Morgan said that, while outbreaks remain "a real and ongoing concern," the vast majority of services have not been affected.

Representatives from advocacy organisations, including Inclusion Ireland, told the committee that many families are struggling with the continued suspension of day services and respite care. They called for clear communication from the HSE regarding plans for reopening, and additional support for service users and their families in the coming weeks.

Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly said the loss of life in these settings was particularly difficult for families and communities. He pledged that the Department of Health would continue to work closely with the HSE and disability providers to ensure the highest possible level of protection for vulnerable groups as restrictions are eased.

The Department of Health said it is currently developing new guidance for the resumption of disability services in line with the Government's roadmap for reopening society and business. Service users, families and staff will be provided with further information in the coming days.
headline: 14 virus deaths among people in disability services

text:
The Association of Garda Sergeants and Inspectors (AGSI) has claimed it was excluded from key negotiations surrounding the latest public sector pay agreement, describing the process as “fundamentally unfair”.

In a statement issued today, the AGSI said it was not invited to participate in talks that led to the new pay deal, which was agreed between the Government and several public service unions earlier this week. The association, which represents over 2,500 middle-ranking Gardaí, criticised what it termed the “arbitrary and unjust exclusion” of garda representative bodies from the official negotiating table.

Antoinette Cunningham, General Secretary of the AGSI, said: “We have consistently sought to engage constructively with Government on pay and working conditions for our members. To be locked out of negotiations that have such a significant impact on the livelihoods of garda sergeants and inspectors is absolutely unacceptable.”

The AGSI has called on the Department of Public Expenditure, NDP Delivery and Reform to clarify the rationale for its exclusion and to initiate separate discussions with garda representatives. Ms Cunningham added that, while the association recognises the importance of a coherent public sector pay policy, it believes the security services have unique roles and challenges that should be directly addressed in negotiations.

The new public sector pay deal, worth an estimated €3.6 billion over the next two years, covers pay rises and other workplace improvements across the State’s public workforce. Talks concluded earlier this week after days of intensive negotiations involving unions affiliated with the Irish Congress of Trade Unions (ICTU). Gardaí, teachers and nurses have historically negotiated pay and conditions separately due to the particular nature of their work.

Speaking to RTÉ News, Ms Cunningham warned that the AGSI will now consult with its national executive and members as to what action may be taken. “We are not ruling anything out,” she said, adding that the association was also in contact with the Garda Representative Association (GRA) and the Association of Garda Chief Superintendents.

It is understood that the Department of Public Expenditure, NDP Delivery and Reform is considering how to proceed regarding pay negotiations with garda associations. In a statement, the Department said it “remains open to direct engagement with representative bodies of An Garda Síochána on issues relating to pay and conditions.”

The AGSI has previously raised concerns over ongoing recruitment and retention difficulties within An Garda Síochána, citing pay and conditions as a core factor in the challenges facing the force. The latest developments come as the Government faces increasing pressure from public sector unions to address cost-of-living and workplace reform issues.

The issue is expected to be raised in the Dáil next week, with opposition parties calling for greater transparency and engagement with all sectors of the public service.
headline: AGSI alleges exclusion from pay deal negotiations

text:
Hospital doctors and GPs remain the primary contacts for delivering Covid-19 test results to patients, according to the HSE. In most cases, those who undergo testing at community test centres or through their general practitioner will be informed of their results via a text message notification system. Positive results continue to be prioritised for urgent communication, usually by direct phone call from a GP, public health doctor or HSE contact tracer.

If a patient is tested in hospital, the treating medical team generally conveys the result in person or by telephone. For those tested through a GP referral, results are typically sent to the referring GP, who then passes on the outcome to the patient. Individuals may also receive an automated text message from the HSE, particularly in cases where the result is negative. However, if the result is positive, a member of the HSE’s Covid Care Team or a local public health official will contact the patient directly to advise on isolation, contact tracing, and any necessary care.

Public health officials emphasise that anyone who is awaiting a result should continue to self-isolate until the outcome is confirmed. The HSE has acknowledged some delays in certain areas, owing to the high volumes of testing, and has asked for the public’s patience where there are longer-than-expected waiting times.

For those who are concerned about not receiving a result within a few days of testing, the HSE advises contacting their GP or the HSE helpline. The organisation has also reiterated that no individual will be charged for their Covid-19 test result notification, following a number of reports of scam calls and text messages seeking payment for results.

As Ireland continues to expand its testing and contact tracing capacity, the HSE says keeping the public informed in a timely and accurate manner remains a central part of the national coronavirus response.
headline: Who contacts patients with the test results?

text:
The streets of Dublin were drenched in festive cheer last night as the city officially marked the beginning of the Christmas season with the annual switch-on of the Christmas lights. Thousands gathered along Grafton Street and surrounding avenues, with families and visitors braving the cold to watch the city light up in a dazzling display.

Lord Mayor of Dublin, Daithí de Róiste, performed the honours, flicking the switch shortly after 6.30pm and officially heralding the start of the countdown to Christmas. The event saw a line-up of performances by local choirs and musicians, with traders and restaurateurs reporting a surge in early evening footfall.

Speaking to RTÉ News, Lord Mayor de Róiste described the event as a "moment of togetherness" for the capital, adding: "This is a time for people to come together, to celebrate our community and look forward to the brighter days ahead. The lights bring a sense of hope after a challenging year for many."

Dublin City Council confirmed that more than one million low-energy LED bulbs have been installed across key shopping districts, from Henry Street to South William Street, as part of a city-wide installation that began in mid-October. The Council also noted efforts to reduce electricity usage, following a commitment to more sustainable festivities after a review conducted with the SEAI.

Retailers and the DublinTown business group expressed optimism that the illuminated streets will boost the local economy, with early estimates suggesting a strong start to the crucial Christmas trading period. Richard Guiney, CEO of DublinTown, said: "The city comes alive when the lights go on, and we’re hopeful this will be a real lift for traders and shoppers alike."

Gardaí maintained a visible presence throughout the evening, with additional patrols on hand to ensure safety for the large crowds. There were no reports of incidents, and traffic disruption was described as minimal, with diversions in place around the Grafton Street area until late last night.

The lighting ceremony marks the start of a busy season for the capital, with markets, concerts, and family events scheduled across the city in the coming weeks. Dublin City Council is asking members of the public to be mindful of public health guidance and to plan journeys in advance, as increased numbers are anticipated in the city centre in the lead-up to Christmas.

Visitors and residents are encouraged to take in the sights, with the Council unveiling an interactive map of all illuminated areas available on its website. The lights will remain in place until early January, ensuring the city shines bright well into the New Year.
headline: Brighter nights ahead as Dublin lights up for Christmas

text:
The Taoiseach has described the decision by a French appeal court to uphold the conviction of Irishman Robert Sheehan as "a miscarriage of justice," amid growing calls for diplomatic intervention. Mr Sheehan, a native of Co Clare, has consistently denied any involvement in the 2019 incident in Paris for which he was sentenced to six years in prison.

Speaking in the Dáil earlier today, Simon Harris expressed deep disappointment at the verdict, stating that "serious questions remain over the fairness of both the investigation and the trial process." The Minister for Foreign Affairs, Micheál Martin, also confirmed that the Department is continuing to offer consular assistance to Mr Sheehan and his family, and said the Irish Embassy in Paris is seeking urgent clarification from French authorities.

Mr Sheehan was arrested in December 2019 after police claimed he matched the description of a suspect involved in an assault near the Gare du Nord. However, the defence argued that key witness testimonies contained contradictions and that crucial CCTV evidence was missing from the prosecution’s case.

Mr Sheehan’s solicitors have criticised the handling of the investigation, pointing to what they describe as "procedural irregularities" and the absence of DNA evidence linking their client to the crime. Speaking outside the courthouse, barrister Sinéad Horgan said: "We are bitterly disappointed with this verdict. The case against Mr Sheehan was never proven beyond reasonable doubt, and we will examine all avenues for further appeal."

The Sheehan family, who have campaigned for his release since his initial conviction in 2021, said that today’s ruling was "devastating" and called on the Irish government to intensify its efforts on Robert’s behalf. "Robert has always maintained his innocence. We urge the Taoiseach and the Tánaiste to do everything in their power to ensure that justice is finally done," said his brother, Daniel Sheehan.

The issue has attracted growing attention in Ireland, with several Oireachtas members raising concerns about due process and the treatment of Irish citizens abroad. Sinn Féin's foreign affairs spokesperson, John Brady TD, said the government must prioritise the welfare of Mr Sheehan. "This is a deeply troubling case. The French authorities must be transparent and responsive to the very serious concerns raised by Mr Sheehan’s legal team," he said.

A protest in support of Mr Sheehan is being planned outside Leinster House later this week, with organisers calling on the public to show solidarity. The Department of Foreign Affairs has reiterated that it cannot intervene in the French judicial process, but will continue to monitor developments closely and provide support to Mr Sheehan and his family.

Mr Sheehan remains in custody in Paris and is considering an appeal to the French Supreme Court.
headline: French decision is miscarriage of justice

text:
Eurozone finance ministers have agreed in principle to unlock the bloc’s bailout fund to support member states tackling the economic fallout from the coronavirus pandemic. The announcement was made late on Thursday following a video conference involving the 19 eurozone countries.

The €500 billion European Stability Mechanism (ESM) is expected to provide access to funding for governments struggling with ballooning debt as a result of unprecedented public health costs and sweeping lockdown measures. The funds are intended to underpin health spending, as well as extend economic support to businesses and workers affected by restrictions.

Minister for Finance Paschal Donohoe welcomed the decision, stating that it marked “a significant step in safeguarding jobs, businesses, and public health across the euro area’s economies at this critical time.” Mr Donohoe said the Government would assess the terms of the facility, but insisted that Ireland remains in a robust position to fund its national response.

The agreement comes after several days of tense negotiations, driven by deep divisions between member states over the extent of financial solidarity required. Southern European countries, led by Italy and Spain, had pressed for so-called ‘coronabonds’—debt mutualisation backed by all eurozone members—but this was resisted by Germany, the Netherlands, and others, who feared such a move would lead to permanent transfer of liability.

Instead, the compromise focuses on making the ESM mechanism available with limited conditionality, provided the funds are directed strictly towards the direct and indirect costs of the pandemic. French Finance Minister Bruno Le Maire stressed that the deal demonstrates “the capacity of the eurozone to act together in the face of crisis.”

While the agreement is widely viewed as an important signal of solidarity, some opposition parties across the continent have criticised the outcome as insufficient. Sinn Féin’s finance spokesperson Pearse Doherty TD called for “greater ambition from European leaders” to ensure the livelihoods of citizens are protected, arguing that “more radical supports may be needed as the crisis continues.”

In Dublin, the Department of Finance estimates that the State will run a deficit of up to €23 billion this year due to falling tax receipts and the costs of emergency measures such as the Pandemic Unemployment Payment and the Temporary Wage Subsidy Scheme.

Taoiseach Leo Varadkar noted the importance of European support but said Ireland’s ability to borrow at low rates meant it would not need to immediately resort to the bailout fund. “We have strong public finances coming into this crisis and will use every available tool to protect lives and livelihoods,” he told reporters at Government Buildings.

The ESM facility remains subject to final approval by eurozone heads of government, who are expected to meet by videoconference next week. If endorsed, the money could begin to flow to member states by early May. 

Meanwhile, the latest figures from the Department of Health show the number of confirmed cases of Covid-19 in Ireland has risen to 6,574, with 263 deaths. The HSE continues to urge the public to adhere to social distancing and hygiene guidance, as preparations begin for the likely extension of current restrictions beyond Easter.
headline: Eurozone 'agrees in principle' to use bailout mechanism

text:
A much-anticipated experimental drug designed to treat Covid-19 has failed to demonstrate clinical benefit in its first large-scale human trial, dampening hopes for a new weapon against the disease as case numbers stabilise across Ireland.

The antiviral medication, developed by a US pharmaceutical firm, underwent phase three trials involving over 1,000 patients with moderate to severe coronavirus infection. Results published this morning indicate that the drug did not significantly reduce either the length of illness or mortality rates compared to standard hospital treatments.

The Department of Health said the findings were “disappointing but important in guiding future research.” HSE Chief Clinical Officer Dr Colm Henry welcomed the transparency of the results, noting that “rigorous evidence is crucial before making any treatments available to Irish patients.”

The trial, conducted in several countries including the US, Spain, and Italy, randomly assigned participants to receive the investigational drug or a placebo, in addition to routine care such as oxygen therapy and steroids. According to trial investigators, both groups showed similar recovery times, with the experimental medication producing no measurable improvement in patient outcomes.

No Irish hospital sites were directly involved in the trial. The National Virus Reference Laboratory at University College Dublin had been monitoring developments and providing updates to clinicians in association with the European Medicines Agency.

The Taoiseach, Leo Varadkar, said this afternoon that the search for effective treatments would continue “with urgency and caution,” adding that “public health measures and vaccination remain the most effective defences against severe disease and hospitalisation.”

Public health officials warned against the use of unapproved medications as anxiety around Covid-19 persists. Dr Lorraine Doherty, National Clinical Director for Health Protection, reiterated: “Novel drugs must go through a thorough evaluation process. We urge the public not to seek unauthorised sources or treatments outside the regulated health system.”

The number of patients being treated in Irish hospitals for Covid-19 remains low, with 53 currently admitted nationwide, according to the latest HSE figures. The National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET) said this week that while Ireland is in a “stable phase,” preparedness for potential new variants remains a key priority.

The failed trial is the latest in a series of setbacks for antiviral drug research, but scientists point out that negative results are part of the process towards finding effective therapies. Professor Mary Horgan, President of the RCPI, urged the public to remain confident in the research process, saying that “each study, whether successful or not, brings us closer to understanding Covid-19.”

The pharmaceutical company behind the drug said it would analyse the data further and consider whether any subgroups of patients might benefit, but that it does not plan to seek European Medicines Agency approval at this stage.
headline: Experimental virus drug fails in human trials

text:
A member of Hezbollah has been found guilty of involvement in the 2005 assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, following a protracted trial at a special court in The Hague. The court found Hassan Habib Merhi guilty of conspiracy to commit a terrorist act and the murder of Hariri, as well as the deaths of 21 others who perished in the massive Beirut bombing.

The verdict was delivered at the Special Tribunal for Lebanon, which has spent over a decade investigating and hearing evidence related to the attack. Lawyers acting for the prosecution argued that Merhi played a central role in organising the plot, which involved the use of over a tonne of explosives and led to one of the most destabilising episodes in Lebanon’s recent history.

Hariri, who had stepped down as prime minister the year before his murder, was widely regarded as a leading advocate for Lebanese sovereignty and had openly criticised the influence of Syria and Hezbollah within Lebanon. His killing sent shockwaves across the region and fuelled years of political instability in the country.

Merhi, who was tried in absentia along with three other suspects, has long been linked to Hezbollah, a powerful Shia militant and political organisation supported by Iran. Hezbollah itself has denied any involvement in Hariri's murder and has dismissed the tribunal as a politically motivated instrument of Western powers.

Throughout the trial, the court heard detailed evidence including telecommunications data, eyewitness testimony, and forensic analysis. Prosecutors outlined how mobile phone networks were used to coordinate the operation and evade detection, while also tying Merhi to the planning and execution of the bombing.

The verdict brings to a close years of legal proceedings, though the whereabouts of Merhi and the other accused remain unknown. The court has requested that Lebanese authorities cooperate in securing their arrest, but previous efforts have failed amid the country’s complex political landscape.

Reacting to the ruling, Hariri’s son, Saad Hariri, who also served as Lebanon’s prime minister, said the decision represented a measure of justice for his family and the Lebanese people. International reaction has included statements from the United Nations and European Union welcoming the verdict, and calling for accountability and respect for the rule of law in Lebanon.

The Special Tribunal for Lebanon was established by a United Nations Security Council resolution and operates outside the Lebanese judicial system. Its jurisdiction is limited to crimes related to the Hariri assassination, and it is the first international tribunal dedicated to prosecuting terrorist crimes.

The court’s ruling is expected to further strain relations between Hezbollah and its domestic rivals, as well as complicate efforts to achieve political consensus in Lebanon, which continues to grapple with economic crisis and sectarian divisions.
headline: Hezbollah suspect found guilty of 2005 Hariri murder

text:
The High Court has heard that the sister of a woman whose remains were discovered in their family home in Co Louth last year did not want to report their mother missing, despite repeated requests from concerned relatives.

Detective Garda Niamh O’Reilly told the court during the ongoing inquest into the death of 67-year-old Marie Brennan that she interviewed the deceased’s daughter, Karen Brennan, in July 2023, several weeks after Mrs Brennan’s remains were found at the family’s house in Drogheda.

The court heard that other family members, including Mrs Brennan’s son and an aunt based in the UK, had tried on numerous occasions to contact both her and Karen Brennan during the months preceding the discovery. When attempts to reach them failed, relatives asked Karen to report her mother missing, but she declined.

“We were told by Ms Brennan that she felt there was no need to make a report. She said her mother had left previously for periods of time and that she was confident she would return,” Det Garda O’Reilly told the court.

Earlier, the court was told Mrs Brennan’s body was found by Gardaí on 14 June 2023, after neighbours complained of a persistent odour coming from the property at St Laurence’s Park. Initial forensic analysis indicated the remains had been in the house for several months.

Dr Fiona Murphy, who carried out the post-mortem examination at Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital in Drogheda, told the inquest the cause of death could not be determined due to the advanced state of decomposition. However, she said there was no evidence of foul play or trauma.

The HSE had supplied social services to Mrs Brennan and her daughter, who lived together, but these visits ceased during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Under cross-examination, Karen Brennan said she was “overwhelmed” by caring duties and “just didn’t realise how much time had passed.” She told the court her mother had previously spoken about travelling to friends in Dublin and that she believed she would eventually return.

The inquest continues.
headline: Sister didn't want to report mother missing, court told

text:
Hundreds of spectators gathered at the Grand Canal Basin in Dublin today to witness the country’s first ever giant floating pumpkin relay race, an event that organisers hope will become an annual Halloween tradition.

Teams from across the city and further afield travelled to the Docklands this morning hauling enormous, specially-grown pumpkins, some weighing over 300 kilogrammes, which had been hollowed out and converted into makeshift vessels. The participants, many in elaborate costumes, took to the water after a safety briefing, paddling their pumpkins along a 200-metre stretch in a high-spirited relay.

The light-hearted contest, organised by local community group Docklands Together with support from Dublin City Council and Waterways Ireland, drew entries from schools, businesses, and sports clubs. One team from Ringsend described the intense preparation required, with months spent cultivating their pumpkin, named “The Great O’Lantern”. Another, representing a tech firm in the IFSC, revealed they had repurposed old kayak paddles and reinforced the pumpkin’s hull with recycled bike inner tubes.

The relay format saw team members complete short legs before passing a lifevest ‘baton’ to the next paddler. Several participants struggled to keep their balance, with one dramatic wobble resulting in a minor capsize, but competitors and spectators alike were in high spirits.

Organiser Siobhán Kavanagh said the event aimed to “bring people together in a fun, safe way and celebrate both Halloween and our waterways”. She added that all pumpkins used were grown without pesticides and would be composted after the race.

There was no official prize for the winning team, but a panel of local judges awarded medals for best costume and most creative pumpkin design. The Gardaí reported no incidents and praised the event’s “positive and inclusive community spirit”.

Local businesses, including cafes and market stalls, lined the quays, benefiting from the crowds. Organisers are encouraging other communities to adopt the tradition next year, noting the potential to “put an Irish stamp on Halloween festivities”.

Speaking to RTÉ News, participants said the race captured “the craic and community” of Dublin at its best, and many expressed hopes to see the event grow in the years ahead.
headline: Giant floating pumpkin relay race

text:
More than three million citizens from European Union member states have now applied to remain in the United Kingdom following Brexit, according to new figures released by the UK Home Office.

The figures relate to the EU Settlement Scheme, the process introduced by the British government to offer legal status to EU nationals and their families who have been living in the UK. Successful applicants are granted either settled or pre-settled status, allowing them to continue residing, working, and accessing public services in the UK after the Brexit transition period ends.

According to the latest statistics, by the end of January 2020, there had been over 3.1 million applications to the scheme, with Polish, Romanian, and Italian nationals topping the list of applicants. The spike in applications comes ahead of the planned conclusion of the Brexit transition, with rights and residency for EU nationals among the key issues for Ireland and other member states during recent negotiations.

Ireland accounts for a significant share, with around 40,000 Irish citizens in Britain having made applications, although Irish nationals are not obliged to do so owing to the Common Travel Area arrangement between Ireland and the UK, which predates both countries joining the EU and guarantees reciprocal rights for citizens in both jurisdictions.

However, migrant support organisations have raised concerns about some vulnerable EU nationals being left behind by the process, particularly elderly people, children in care, and victims of domestic abuse, who may struggle to provide the required documentation. Charities and legal aid groups have called for greater clarity and assistance to ensure that all those eligible can apply before the 30 June deadline.

The British government has said that the scheme is functioning well and that the majority of applicants are receiving decisions quickly, with over 2.7 million already granted status. A spokesperson for the Home Office said that efforts are ongoing to reach those who have yet to apply, including running public information campaigns and supporting community groups.

The issue of future residency rights for EU citizens in Britain—and for British citizens living in Ireland and across the EU—has been the subject of ongoing discussions between the British government, the European Commission and individual member states. The Department of Foreign Affairs has said it continues to monitor the situation closely and provide support through embassies and consulates.

The outcome is of particular interest to Ireland, given the close economic, social, and family links between the two islands, and the potential impact on Irish citizens, their families, and business links in the UK.
headline: Over three million EU citizens apply to stay in UK

text:
An organised crime group in the Indian state of Bihar operated a bogus police station for eight months, posing as legitimate officers to extort money and dupe residents, local authorities have confirmed. The illicit operation came to light this week following complaints received by the real police force in Banka district, who subsequently raided the premises.

The gang reportedly set up their fake station just 500 metres from the home of a senior police official, using the premises to collect bribes from locals in return for promises to resolve disputes, offer jobs, and fast-track paperwork. Members of the gang wore police uniforms and carried imitation firearms, using forged documentation and a counterfeit police sign to convince citizens of their authority.

Up to six people have been arrested so far in connection with the fake station, with reports suggesting that several other members of the group are currently at large. Senior officers in Banka said the fraudsters managed to collect several thousand euro from unsuspecting members of the public during their months in operation.

Police in Bihar have launched a manhunt for the remaining suspects, who fled the area shortly before the raid. It is understood the gang also issued fake appointment letters to individuals hoping to join the state police force, charging substantial “processing fees” to desperate jobseekers.

The incident has sparked embarrassment for local authorities and renewed concerns about the prevalence of corruption and impersonation scams within parts of India’s policing system. Questions have been raised as to how the fake station was able to operate for such a prolonged period in an urban area without detection.

Indian media outlets have reported that residents became suspicious after administrative irregularities emerged, prompting a formal complaint. Following investigation, the genuine local police moved in to dismantle the operation earlier this week.

The authorities have urged members of the public who may have been affected by the scam to come forward. The case remains under investigation, and further arrests are anticipated.
headline: Indian gang ran fake police station for eight months

text:
The Government is set to move forward with plans to purchase an additional 450 megawatts (MW) of electricity supply next year, in response to concerns over security of supply and the rising demands on Ireland’s national grid.

The Minister for the Environment, Climate and Communications, Eamon Ryan, confirmed today that the procurement process will begin early in 2025, following recommendations from EirGrid and the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU). The planned purchase is intended to bolster grid reliability in the face of ongoing growth in demand, particularly from the data centre sector and new housing developments.

Speaking in the Dáil, Minister Ryan said the measure was essential to ensure the stability of the national electricity system and to meet Ireland’s climate and energy targets. “While the Government remains committed to an ambitious programme of renewable energy, including offshore wind and solar, there is an immediate need to enhance system resilience and mitigate risks of potential shortfalls,” he told TDs. 

The additional 450MW will be sourced through a competitive procurement process, with a particular focus on flexible generation that can be brought online quickly. It follows warnings from EirGrid in recent months about tight margins and the risk of temporary supply shortages, especially during peak winter periods. The CRU has also highlighted the importance of securing new capacity to support the ongoing transition away from fossil fuels.

Officials from the Department of the Environment said the new capacity is likely to be provided by a mix of fast-responding gas-fired generation and battery storage, though renewable sources will be prioritised where feasible. The precise mix of technologies will depend on the outcome of the upcoming capacity auction, which is expected to open to tender in the first quarter of next year.

The ESB and several independent power producers are understood to be preparing bids for the new supply contracts, which will be awarded for an initial term of up to ten years. Early estimates put the potential cost at between €600 million and €800 million over the contract period.

Industry groups have welcomed the announcement, describing it as a necessary step to support economic growth and maintain investor confidence. However, some environmental campaigners have expressed concern at the prospect of additional fossil fuel generation, urging the Government to accelerate the rollout of renewables and grid upgrades.

The Department has said the extra capacity will be used primarily as a back-up during periods of high demand or low renewable output. It stressed that the new procurement forms part of a wider suite of measures, including increased interconnection with the UK and mainland Europe, to enhance Ireland’s long-term energy security.

Ireland’s total electricity demand is forecast to rise significantly in the coming years, driven by digitisation, electrification of transport, and an expanding population. The Government is aiming to achieve 80% renewable electricity generation by 2030, but has acknowledged the need for interim measures to prevent blackouts and maintain system stability during the transition.
headline: Govt to purchase extra 450mw of electricity next year

text:
A fundraising effort has been launched in Co Mayo after the home of two brothers was severely damaged by fire earlier this week.

The incident occurred on Monday night in the rural parish of Kilmaine, south Mayo, when a blaze broke out at the detached bungalow where the two elderly men lived. Emergency services, including units of Mayo County Fire Service from Ballinrobe and Claremorris, were called to the scene shortly after 10:30pm. It is understood the fire is believed to have started in the kitchen area, with smoke alarms alerting the brothers to the danger.

Both men, who are in their 70s, managed to escape the property without serious injury, though one was treated at Mayo University Hospital in Castlebar for smoke inhalation and later discharged. The house, which is their lifelong family home, sustained extensive smoke and heat damage, rendering it uninhabitable.

Neighbours and friends have since rallied around the brothers, setting up an online fundraising page to help with temporary accommodation and essential repairs. More than €8,000 has been raised so far, with donations coming from across the local community and beyond.

Local parish priest Fr Seán Burke described the response as "heartening" and said it reflected the strong sense of community spirit in the area. "Everyone knows the lads and they’ve always been part of the fabric here. People want to help them get back on their feet," he said.

The campaign has also received support from local GAA and community organisations, with plans for a coffee morning and auction to be held in the coming weeks.

Investigations into the cause of the fire are ongoing, but Gardaí have said they do not suspect foul play.

The brothers are currently staying with relatives while plans are made to begin restoration work on their home. Organisers of the fundraiser said all funds raised will go directly towards rebuilding efforts and supporting the brothers in the months ahead.
headline: Fundraising bid after brothers' house damaged in fire

text:
Renowned gardener and broadcaster Dermot O’Neill has died at the age of 58. A beloved figure in Irish horticulture, Mr O’Neill was well known for his work on television and radio, as well as his contributions to gardening publications and community initiatives across the country.

News of his death was confirmed by his family earlier today. Mr O’Neill had faced ongoing health challenges in recent years, having previously spoken about his diagnosis with stomach cancer in 2009.
