Tributes have since poured in from colleagues, friends, and members of the public who recalled his passion for gardening and his ability to make it accessible to all.

Best known for programmes such as RTÉ’s 'Garden Heaven' and 'Dermot’s Secret Garden', Mr O’Neill’s enthusiasm and expertise inspired a new generation of gardeners throughout Ireland. He also regularly appeared on RTÉ Radio 1, offering advice to listeners and sharing his knowledge on all things horticultural.

Colleagues at RTÉ described him as “warm, generous and endlessly enthusiastic”, with many recalling his trademark wit and down-to-earth manner. In a statement, RTÉ Director-General Kevin Bakhurst said: “Dermot’s work brought colour and joy into homes around the country. He will be sorely missed by all who had the privilege to work alongside him and by the many viewers and listeners who benefited from his wisdom and good humour.”

As an accomplished author, Mr O’Neill wrote several gardening books, and contributed to The Irish Times, The Irish Independent, and other national publications. He also played a role in various community and environmental projects, including the restoration of the walled garden at the historic Clondeglass demesne in Co Laois.

Born and raised in Dublin, Mr O’Neill developed his love of gardening from an early age, tending to his family’s back garden in Glasnevin before pursuing formal studies in horticulture. He was a longstanding member of the Royal Horticultural Society of Ireland and was frequently invited to judge at national flower shows and garden competitions.

President Michael D. Higgins expressed his condolences to Mr O’Neill’s family, calling him “a champion of Ireland’s gardens and green spaces, whose gentle manner welcomed all to share in the beauty of nature”. The Taoiseach Simon Harris noted Mr O’Neill’s “lasting legacy in communities across the country”, while the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine, Charlie McConalogue, praised his “immeasurable contribution to Irish horticulture”.

Mr O’Neill is survived by his partner, family and a wide circle of friends. Funeral arrangements are expected to be announced in the coming days.
headline: Gardener Dermot O'Neill dies aged 58

text:
The inquests into the 1974 Birmingham pub bombings opened today with a minute’s silence in memory of the 21 people killed in the attacks. Families of the victims, survivors, and members of the public gathered at Birmingham Civil Justice Centre as the long-awaited proceedings formally began, nearly fifty years after the deadly explosions shook the city.

The bombings, which occurred on the evening of 21 November 1974, targeted the Mulberry Bush and the Tavern in the Town pubs in central Birmingham. In addition to those killed, over 200 people were injured in what remains one of the worst atrocities of the Troubles on the British mainland.

Presiding coroner Sir Peter Thornton QC told the packed courtroom that the inquests would aim to seek the truth behind the attacks and give the families a chance to hear the evidence in full. “The deaths of these 21 innocent people have cast a long shadow for almost five decades,” he said. “We begin today by remembering them with silence.”

Proceedings are expected to examine new evidence on several key issues, including allegations of failings by the West Midlands Police, the emergency response on the night, and whether the attacks could have been prevented. The Irish Government and the Gardaí have offered cooperation to the coroner’s team, as has the Police Service of Northern Ireland.

Relatives of the victims, many of whom have campaigned for justice for decades, welcomed the start of the inquests but voiced frustration at the length of time taken to reach this point. Julie Hambleton, whose sister Maxine was killed at the Tavern in the Town, said, “We’ve had to fight for years just to have our loved ones’ deaths properly examined. Today is an important step, but our journey continues.”

The original inquests were halted in 1975 once criminal proceedings were brought. Six Irishmen – later known as the Birmingham Six – were wrongly convicted of the bombings and spent 16 years in prison before their convictions were quashed by the Court of Appeal in 1991.

In Dublin, the Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs, Micheál Martin, reiterated Ireland’s “deep sympathy for the families of those murdered in Birmingham and our continued support for their pursuit of truth.” The Department of Justice said it would “continue to assist the coroner as required” and stressed the importance of delivering clarity and closure for the families involved.

The inquests are set to run for several weeks, hearing from dozens of witnesses and reviewing hundreds of files. The proceedings are being livestreamed to allow wider public access, and separate arrangements have been made to accommodate families travelling from Ireland.

As the inquiry resumes tomorrow, the families say they hope finally to receive long-overdue answers about what happened that night and why their loved ones died.
headline: Birmingham bombing inquests start with minute's silence

text:
A woman has appeared before Galway District Court this morning charged in connection with a fatal hit-and-run incident that occurred in the city earlier this week.

Gardaí arrested the woman, aged in her 30s, yesterday evening after tracing the vehicle believed to have been involved in the collision. The incident took place at approximately 10.45pm on Sunday on the Headford Road, when a pedestrian, a man in his late 60s, was struck by a car that failed to remain at the scene.

Emergency services attended promptly, but the man was pronounced dead at the scene. His body was later removed to University Hospital Galway, where a post-mortem examination was carried out.

At this morning’s court sitting, the accused was charged with dangerous driving causing death and failing to stop at the scene of a collision. She was granted bail with strict conditions, including the surrender of her passport and an undertaking not to leave the jurisdiction.

Gardaí objected to bail citing the seriousness of the offence, but Judge Mary Fahy said the accused was entitled to the presumption of innocence and agreed to the defence solicitor’s application, noting the woman’s cooperation with the investigation.

The woman did not address the court and was remanded on bail to appear again before the District Court on 17 July for service of a book of evidence.

The victim has been named locally as Patrick O’Shea, a retired teacher and long-time Galway resident. His family has appealed for privacy as they continue to come to terms with the tragedy.

Gardaí have renewed their appeal for witnesses or anyone with dashcam footage from the Headford Road area between 10pm and 11pm on Sunday to contact Galway Garda Station.
headline: Woman charged over fatal Galway hit-and-run

text:
Leaders of the world’s major economies have pledged to scale up humanitarian assistance to Afghanistan amid mounting concerns over the worsening crisis in the country following the Taliban takeover.

At a virtual G20 summit held on Tuesday, heads of government, including Taoiseach Leo Varadkar, committed to increasing aid flows and ensuring access for relief organisations operating on the ground. The summit, convened by Italy, came as the United Nations warns that millions of Afghans face severe hunger as winter approaches.

Speaking after the meeting, Mr Varadkar said Ireland would continue to provide funding and support through the EU and international partners. He emphasised that the focus must remain on protecting vulnerable Afghans—particularly women, children, and minority groups—while pressing for respect for human rights.

The European Commission announced a package of over €1 billion in support for Afghans in the country and the wider region. The funding is aimed at delivering food, health care and protection services, and will be channelled through UN agencies and NGOs. However, leaders stressed the importance of keeping assistance separate from any formal recognition of the Taliban regime, which remains under international sanctions.

US President Joe Biden called on G20 nations to “stand together” to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe, while Germany’s Chancellor Angela Merkel said the world “cannot stand by and watch 40 million people descend into chaos”.

The summit took place against a backdrop of increased displacement and reports of deteriorating humanitarian conditions. According to the UN, over half the population of Afghanistan is now in need of humanitarian assistance, with the risk of famine in parts of the country.

Ireland, which holds a seat on the UN Security Council, has repeatedly urged safe and unrestricted access for aid workers. Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin noted the “huge risk” of instability in the region if urgent action is not taken.

G20 leaders also expressed concerns about the rights and freedoms of Afghan women and girls, following accounts of school closures and restrictions on employment since the Taliban took control in August. Several leaders called for an international monitoring mechanism to ensure accountability.

The G20 summit statement stopped short of any direct engagement with the Taliban, but urged the new authorities to allow unfettered humanitarian operations. The group said they would continue to review developments and coordinate closely in the coming months.

The next round of discussions is expected to focus on longer-term strategies, including possible pathways for engagement with Afghan authorities contingent upon improvements in human rights and governance.
headline: G20 leaders agree to step up Afghan humanitarian effort

text:
A forged death certificate submitted as part of a probate application has been uncovered by a keen-eyed civil servant, after a glaring typographical error cast doubt on the document’s authenticity.

The Probate Office of the High Court raised concerns this week when a death certificate, purportedly issued by the General Register Office, arrived as part of routine paperwork for an inheritance claim in Dublin. Staff noticed that the document spelled “Register” as “Registar” in the official heading—a mistake not found on any legitimate Irish death certificates.

Following the discovery, the matter was referred to the Gardaí for investigation under the Civil Registration Act. The Registrar General’s office confirmed to RTÉ News that the certificate in question was not produced by their system, and that official documentation undergoes stringent controls to prevent fraud.

It is understood the forged certificate was submitted on behalf of a supposed relative, claiming entitlement to assets from an estate in Rathgar. Gardaí from Pearse Street have launched an inquiry and are liaising with both the Probate Office and the Registrar General.

No one has been arrested in connection with the investigation. Gardaí said they are following a definite line of enquiry and have appealed for anyone with information relating to the case to come forward.

Solicitors familiar with probate procedures said that while attempted fraud is relatively rare in estate matters, the risks have increased with the growing use of online applications.

The Department of Social Protection, which oversees the Civil Registration Service, said it is reviewing measures to further strengthen verification and authentication of documents submitted in probate and other official processes.

The incident has prompted reminders from both the Law Society and the Courts Service for practitioners and the public to scrutinise official documents for any irregularities, especially in cases involving significant sums of money or disputed claims. The estate at the centre of the case is understood to be valued at over €600,000.

The forged certificate has been seized by investigating officers. The Probate Office has stressed that the attempted fraud had no impact on the administration of the estate, and that the process will continue once valid documentation is provided.
headline: Dead giveaway - typo reveals death cert a forgery

text:
Renewable energy sources in Ireland are expanding at an accelerating pace, according to the latest figures released by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI). The organisation’s annual ‘Energy in Ireland’ report, published today, indicates that renewables accounted for 42% of electricity generated in 2023, up from 38% the previous year.

The report highlights a substantial increase in onshore wind generation, supported by a growing contribution from solar projects and bioenergy. The total installed wind capacity surpassed 5,000 megawatts for the first time, following a series of large-scale wind farm completions in counties Donegal, Galway and Cork. Solar power generation, while still representing a smaller share, has doubled its output since 2021.

Minister for the Environment, Climate and Communications, Eamon Ryan, welcomed the findings, stating that Ireland is on track to meet its target of generating 80% of electricity from renewables by 2030. “The pace of progress in the sector is very encouraging. The Government’s Climate Action Plan is clearly having an impact on the ground, with more communities and businesses investing in clean, indigenous energy,” Minister Ryan said.

Emissions from the electricity sector have fallen by 9% year-on-year, aided by the growth in renewables and a reduction in coal-fired generation at Moneypoint. The ESB has confirmed plans to explore converting the Moneypoint facility into a green energy hub, with feasibility studies underway.

SEAI Chief Executive William Walsh said that while the results were positive, further investment is required to maintain momentum, particularly in grid infrastructure and offshore wind. “We have the resources and technical know-how. However, timely planning decisions and streamlined connection to the national grid will be key,” Mr Walsh said.

Despite the progress, the report warns of challenges in transport and heating, sectors which remain heavily reliant on fossil fuels. Electric vehicle adoption is rising, with over 100,000 EVs now registered, but fossil fuel cars continue to dominate Irish roads.

The environmental group Friends of the Earth Ireland described the figures as “a critical turning point,” but called for greater urgency in tackling planning bottlenecks and supporting community-led renewable projects.

Ireland’s renewable energy targets form a significant part of the Government’s climate strategy, as it seeks to comply with EU directives and reduce greenhouse gas emissions in line with the Paris Agreement. The Oireachtas Climate Committee is to convene next week to discuss further policy measures to accelerate the transition, including the rollout of new offshore wind auctions and support schemes for home solar installations.

The report concludes that a combination of government policy, industry investment and public engagement will be essential if Ireland is to realise its climate ambitions and ensure energy security in the years ahead.
headline: Renewable energy sources growing at faster rate

text:
One person has died and at least 12 others have been injured following a shooting at a supermarket in Arkansas, United States, authorities have confirmed. The incident occurred at a Mad Butcher grocery store in the town of Fordyce, around 110 kilometres south of the state capital, Little Rock, shortly after midday local time on Friday.

According to local law enforcement, the suspect opened fire both outside and inside the premises as customers sought cover amidst the chaos. Police responded to the scene within minutes and exchanged gunfire with the alleged shooter, who was subsequently detained and taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Among the injured are two police officers, said Colonel Mike Hagar of the Arkansas State Police, who addressed media shortly after the incident. One officer was grazed by a bullet, while the second sustained more significant injuries but is expected to survive. The remainder of the victims comprise supermarket employees and shoppers, some of whom required emergency medical care at the scene before being transported to nearby hospitals.

Footage shared online showed scenes of panic as people fled the area, while police vehicles and ambulances converged on the supermarket car park. Authorities praised the swift response of first responders, crediting them with limiting further casualties.

The Governor of Arkansas, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, expressed condolences to those affected and said she was “heartbroken” by the tragedy. “I am grateful to law enforcement and first responders for their quick and heroic action,” she said in a statement posted online.

The motive for the attack has not yet been established, and investigators are working to determine whether the suspected shooter had any connection to the supermarket or individuals present at the time. The Arkansas State Police has asked witnesses to come forward as they continue their inquiries.

Friday’s shooting is among the latest in a series of high-profile firearm incidents in the United States, where gun violence remains a contentious political issue. President Joe Biden has renewed calls for tighter gun control measures following a spate of recent mass shootings.

The Irish Department of Foreign Affairs is not aware of any Irish citizens being involved in the incident. The local community in Fordyce, a town of around 3,200 people, has expressed shock at the attack, with vigils planned in the coming days for the victims and their families.

The Mad Butcher supermarket is expected to remain closed for the duration of the police investigation.
headline: One dead, 12 injured in US supermarket shooting

text:
The Government is to extend the free school meal scheme during the upcoming mid-term break, it has been confirmed. The decision comes amid ongoing concerns about rising food costs and increasing numbers of families facing financial strain.

Minister for Social Protection, Heather Humphreys, announced today that schools participating in the Hot School Meals Programme will continue to receive funding over the February mid-term period. The move is expected to benefit over 230,000 primary and secondary school pupils nationwide.

Speaking outside Leinster House, Minister Humphreys said: “We recognise the critical importance of the school meals scheme in supporting children’s nutritional needs, and the pressures that many families are facing at the moment. By ensuring continuity of the scheme during the school holidays, we aim to ease the burden for parents and provide certainty for children who depend on these meals.”

Tánaiste Micheál Martin welcomed the announcement, describing it as “a vital support for families and a practical measure to combat food poverty,” while calling for continued monitoring of the scheme’s reach and effectiveness.

The scheme, first rolled out in 2019 and expanded significantly in the past year, aims to provide nutritious meals to children from disadvantaged backgrounds and promote better educational outcomes. Currently, around 1,600 schools are signed up to the programme, with the Department of Social Protection responsible for its administration.

School principals across the country have consistently raised concerns over the gap in provision during school holidays, noting the additional hardship that can create for vulnerable families. The extension of funding will allow schools to work with meal providers to distribute food parcels or arrange collection points for families over the mid-term.

The Irish National Teachers’ Organisation (INTO) has described the extension as “a common sense move” and urged the Government to examine possibilities for year-round provision. Meanwhile, the Children’s Rights Alliance said that keeping the meals scheme in place during school closures was “essential for the wellbeing of thousands of children.”

Opposition parties have generally welcomed the announcement, though Sinn Féin’s spokesperson for Social Protection, Claire Kerrane TD, said the scheme needs to be extended further, especially during longer holiday periods such as summer. She also raised ongoing concerns about delays in expanding the programme to all DEIS schools.

Funding for the mid-term extension is to come from existing Department of Social Protection budget allocations. According to figures provided to the Oireachtas Social Protection Committee, the school meals scheme’s annual cost now stands at close to €100 million.

The Department has said it will liaise with participating schools regarding arrangements for food deliveries and families are being advised to contact their school for further information.
headline: School meal scheme to continue during mid-term break

text:
There are 53 more people in hospital with Covid-19 in the State today, according to the latest figures from the Health Service Executive (HSE). This brings the total number of people currently hospitalised with the virus to 413, up from 360 reported yesterday.

The Department of Health has also been notified of 1,380 new cases of Covid-19. Of those hospitalised, 74 patients are receiving treatment in intensive care units, an increase of five compared with Monday.

Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly said the rising numbers in hospital and in ICUs are a concern and urged people to continue to follow public health guidance. “We are seeing a steady increase in Covid-19 admissions, which places additional pressure on an already stretched health service. I would again encourage all those eligible to receive their booster vaccine as soon as possible,” Minister Donnelly said.

The Chief Medical Officer, Dr Tony Holohan, advised continued caution, warning that the virus continues to circulate widely in the community. He reminded people to be vigilant for symptoms, to self-isolate and arrange a test if they feel unwell.

The HSE has also confirmed that it is dealing with a number of outbreaks in nursing homes and long-term care facilities. In an interview on Morning Ireland, HSE Chief Clinical Officer Dr Colm Henry said the majority of hospitalisations are among people who have not received a booster vaccination or who have underlying health conditions.

The latest figures come as schools across the country remain open, although the Department of Education has said it is monitoring the situation closely. The Irish National Teachers’ Organisation has called for regular antigen testing for staff and students to help mitigate the risk of outbreaks.

Public health officials reiterated the importance of mask-wearing on public transport and in crowded settings, as well as ensuring adequate ventilation in indoor spaces. The National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET) is due to meet later this week to assess the current situation and consider any further recommendations.

To date, more than 8,600 people have died with Covid-19 in Ireland, according to figures from the Central Statistics Office. The HSE says the vaccination campaign continues, with walk-in clinics open this week for all age groups eligible for booster doses.
headline: 53 more people in hospital with Covid, 1,380 new cases

text:
The number of recorded fraud offences in Ireland has seen a substantial increase in the year to June, according to new figures released by the Central Statistics Office (CSO). The data, published this morning, show that there was a 34% rise in reported incidents of fraud, deception and related offences compared to the same period last year.

A total of 18,964 fraud cases were recorded in the 12 months to the end of June 2024, representing an increase of over 4,700 cases. The CSO said the latest rise follows a general upward trend in such crimes, which began during the Covid-19 pandemic, as online activity and digital transactions surged.

The Gardaí have attributed a significant proportion of the increase to unauthorised transactions and so-called ‘smishing’ and ‘phishing’ attacks, where victims are deceived into divulging personal information through fake texts, emails or phone calls. An Garda Síochána’s National Economic Crime Bureau has repeatedly warned the public about ongoing sophisticated scams targeting bank customers and those making online purchases.

The Acting Director of the Economic Crime Bureau, Detective Chief Superintendent Pat Lordan, said that “criminals are continually coming up with new ways to target people, particularly those who may not be as familiar with digital banking or online platforms”. He urged people to remain vigilant and to never share personal or financial details with unsolicited callers or websites.

Alongside the rise in fraud, CSO figures indicate that other crime categories have experienced changes. Reports of theft have also increased by 10%, while burglary incidents have declined by 7%. The overall rate of sexual offences has remained largely unchanged.

Business groups have expressed concern over the burgeoning scale of financial crime, which they say poses a threat to consumer confidence and the wider economy. Chambers Ireland called on the Government to prioritise cyber security and consumer protection measures in the forthcoming Budget.

The Department of Justice said it is “acutely aware of the threat posed by evolving fraud schemes” and pointed to over €30 million in funding allocated for Garda cybercrime units in 2024, as well as the launch of a public awareness campaign earlier this year. Minister for Justice Helen McEntee said the increase in reported offences “reflects both the growing prevalence of fraud and an improved willingness of the public to report these crimes”.

Gardaí continue to advise members of the public to report any suspicious activity and to regularly update security settings on online accounts. They remind people that banks, State agencies or reputable companies will never ask for sensitive information through unsolicited contacts.
headline: Large increase in fraud cases in year to June

text:
Two men have been arrested in County Antrim as part of an ongoing investigation into suspected criminality linked to the Ulster Defence Association (UDA), the PSNI has confirmed.

Officers from the Paramilitary Crime Task Force detained the men, aged in their 40s, following a series of searches in the Carrickfergus area early this morning. The operation, which involved both uniformed and plainclothes personnel, saw several properties searched and a quantity of cash, suspected drugs and documentation seized for further examination.

The two men are currently being questioned at a police station in Belfast on suspicion of a range of offences including drug trafficking, money laundering and membership of a proscribed organisation. The PSNI stated that the arrests form part of a broader inquiry into organised crime activities in the region, believed to be orchestrated by elements associated with the UDA.

Detective Inspector Corrigan said the operation demonstrates the PSNI’s ongoing commitment to tackling the criminal influence of paramilitary groups in local communities. “Today’s arrests are the result of a lengthy investigation into the activities of individuals we believe are involved in drugs supply, intimidation and racketeering, which cause significant harm in communities across County Antrim,” she said.

The Paramilitary Crime Task Force, established in partnership with the National Crime Agency and HM Revenue & Customs, has been targeting groups suspected of involvement in the supply of illegal drugs, extortion and other forms of organised crime, with a particular focus on loyalist paramilitary factions.

The PSNI have appealed to anyone with information on paramilitary-linked criminality to contact them directly or to speak anonymously through the Crimestoppers service.

Investigations are continuing.
headline: Two arrested in Antrim as part of probe into UDA crime

text:
A man has appeared before Enniskillen Magistrates’ Court charged in connection with an alleged altercation at a hotel in County Fermanagh over the weekend. The incident, which occurred shortly after midnight on Saturday at a premises on the outskirts of Enniskillen, is understood to have involved several individuals attending a private function.

The accused, a 32-year-old man from the local area, was arrested by officers from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) following reports of a disturbance in the hotel bar. It is alleged that the man became involved in a heated argument with another patron, which then escalated into a physical confrontation, resulting in minor injuries.

The defendant faces charges of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and criminal damage. During Monday morning’s hearing, the court was told that CCTV footage from the premises had been obtained as part of the investigation. The PSNI said that while the injuries sustained were not life-threatening, medical attention was required for one individual.

Defence counsel requested bail for the accused, stating that he had no previous convictions and posed no flight risk. District Judge Liam McNally granted bail on the condition that the man surrender his passport and have no contact with the alleged injured party or other key witnesses until the case is concluded.

The case has been adjourned pending further police enquiries. The accused is due to appear again before Enniskillen Magistrates’ Court later this month.
headline: Man charged following altercation at Fermanagh hotel

text:
Over one hundred sea swimmers gathered on Ballyholme Beach in Bangor, Co Down this morning, braving chilly waters in an event celebrating the growing popularity of open-water swimming across the North.

From early morning, participants of all ages and abilities donned wetsuits, bathing caps and brightly coloured tow floats before wading into the Irish Sea, where water temperatures averaged a brisk 11 degrees Celsius. The majority of swimmers completed a short circuit close to shore, while some experienced enthusiasts swam longer distances parallel to the beach.

The event, organised by the Ballyholme Sea Swimming Club, aimed to highlight the health and wellbeing benefits of outdoor swimming, as well as the importance of water safety. Club chairperson Orla McCarthy said interest in sea swimming has surged in recent years, particularly during the pandemic when indoor pools were closed.

“People are realising that you don’t need fancy equipment, just a sense of adventure. The cold water is invigorating, and the sense of community is brilliant,” Ms McCarthy told RTÉ News.

Swimmers were joined by volunteers from the RNLI and representatives from the Irish Water Safety organisation, who offered advice on safe swimming practices and distributed thermal hats to newcomers. The Health Service Executive has also recently issued reminders on the risks of cold water shock and urged swimmers to gradually acclimatise.

Among those who took part was 72-year-old Patrick Donnelly from Holywood, who has swum at Ballyholme for over 40 years. “No two swims are the same. Even in the winter, once you’re in, you never regret it,” Mr Donnelly said.

Local businesses supported the event, with a nearby café providing free hot drinks and pastries to shivering participants and their families. Several swimmers travelled from as far as Derry and Newry to take part.

With plans to make the sea swim an annual fixture, organisers said they hope it will continue to draw people to the water and promote coastal tourism in Co Down. The club is planning further swims over the summer months, and has encouraged anyone interested to attend their introductory safety sessions.
headline: Sea swimmers take to the waters off Co Down

text:
A postmistress in Co Longford has welcomed reports that Cabinet is considering a new annual subvention of €12,000 for standalone post offices, in a move designed to support the future of the rural network.

Mary Farrell, who runs the post office in Ballymore, said the prospect of additional support was a "lifeline" for communities like hers, where the local post office remains a focal point for social interaction as well as business.

The proposal, which is expected to go before the Cabinet this week, would see more than 900 post offices in small towns and villages receive the payment from the Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications. It follows mounting concern over the viability of post offices amid declining transaction volumes and the loss of key State contracts in recent years.

Speaking to RTÉ News, Ms Farrell said: "Without extra support, a lot of us wouldn’t be able to keep our doors open, and that would be a disaster for the people who rely on us for pensions, social welfare, and simple things like paying bills."

The Irish Postmasters’ Union has estimated that up to a third of regional and rural post offices are at risk of closure due to falling revenues. The proposed subvention aims to bridge the gap while a government-commissioned review into the future role of An Post in community banking and new public services is ongoing.

Longford TD Joe Flaherty (Fianna Fáil), who raised the issue with Minister Eamon Ryan in the Dáil last month, said the move would be "a crucial intervention" to sustain vital rural services, acknowledging that postmasters and postmistresses have been under growing pressure.

"Post offices are about so much more than letters and parcels. They are at the heart of community life, especially for isolated and older people," Deputy Flaherty said.

An Post said it would welcome the State support package and would work with officials to ensure the funding reaches those most in need. The Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications said the details of the plan were still under consideration but that securing the future of rural post offices remained a government priority.

For Ms Farrell, the intervention cannot come soon enough. "We’re not just a business — we’re a service, a heartbeat in the middle of the village. This support would give us hope, and a fighting chance."
headline: Postmistress welcomes reports of €12k State subvention

text:
The Government has moved to quash calls for a pause in the construction of the new National Children’s Hospital, insisting there would be no interruption to the project despite ongoing concerns over spiralling costs and delays. Senior government figures, including the Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly, have reiterated their commitment to seeing the hospital delivered as planned, describing it as a “vital piece of healthcare infrastructure for future generations”.

The statement comes amid renewed scrutiny of the project after a recent report by the Oireachtas Public Accounts Committee highlighted further cost overruns, with the estimated total now set to exceed €2 billion. Opposition TDs, including Sinn Féin’s David Cullinane, have argued that the Government should pause construction to allow for a thorough reassessment of procurement and management processes. However, Mr Donnelly rejected such calls, stating that any suspension would only delay much-needed capacity and drive up costs even further.

“We are absolutely committed to delivering the National Children’s Hospital. Halting works now would serve nobody, least of all the sick children and families who desperately need these services,” Mr Donnelly told RTÉ News. “We will continue to scrutinise spending and seek accountability, but a pause is not on the table.”

The new facility, located on the St James’s Hospital campus in Dublin, is intended to centralise paediatric care currently dispersed across three Dublin hospitals—Temple Street, Crumlin and Tallaght Children’s Hospital. The HSE has repeatedly said the new hospital will offer state-of-the-art treatment and improved outcomes for children nationwide. However, construction delays and unforeseen issues with site management have led to a succession of revised completion dates.

In recent weeks, contractors BAM confirmed that while progress is being made, some sections may not be finished until late 2025, nearly a decade after the project was first approved by Cabinet. The initial estimated cost in 2016 was €983 million. Current projections now forecast a final bill of at least €2.2 billion, according to figures released to the Dáil last week.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin today defended the project on its merits, saying, “The scale of this hospital is unprecedented in the State’s history. While the cost is considerable, it’s vital we complete it rather than leave a half-finished site and a fragmented health service.”

The Department of Health has said it will continue to engage with the main contractor and that all efforts are being made to mitigate further overruns. The HSE has also confirmed that recruitment for specialist paediatric staff is ongoing in anticipation of the hospital’s eventual completion and opening.

Hospital campaigners and parent groups have called on the Government to ensure there are no further impediments to the delivery of the project, citing Ireland’s urgent need for modern paediatric healthcare infrastructure. The Children’s Health Ireland organisation welcomed this week’s assurances, saying “There has already been too much uncertainty for families. It’s critical that the project remains on course and that every euro spent is subject to robust scrutiny.”

Further hearings on the cost and governance of the hospital are expected in the Oireachtas Health Committee later this month. The Government has committed to publishing quarterly updates to keep the public informed of progress and expenditure.
headline: Govt will not entertain talk of pausing hospital build

text:
Two men have been arrested following the seizure of cocaine and a significant sum of cash during Garda operations in Galway city.

The searches were carried out yesterday as part of an ongoing investigation targeting the sale and supply of drugs in the Connacht region. Members of the Galway Divisional Drugs Unit, assisted by uniformed Gardaí, executed search warrants at two residential properties in the Ballybane and Knocknacarra areas.

Gardaí say they seized cocaine with an estimated street value of €40,000, pending analysis, along with over €15,000 in cash. Other items believed to be related to the distribution of controlled substances, including weighing scales and packaging materials, were also recovered during the searches.

The two men, both aged in their 30s, were detained at Garda stations in the city under the provisions of Section 2 of the Criminal Justice (Drug Trafficking) Act, 1996. They can be held for questioning for up to seven days.

This operation forms part of a wider strategic response by the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau in conjunction with local units to disrupt the activities of organised crime groups in Galway and beyond.

A Garda spokesperson said investigations are continuing and further arrests have not been ruled out. The seized drugs will be sent to Forensic Science Ireland for further analysis.

Anyone with information on drug-related activity in their community is urged to contact the Garda Confidential Line or any Garda station.
headline: Two held after cash, cocaine seized in Galway

text:
A member of a Dublin-based organised crime gang has pleaded guilty at the Circuit Criminal Court to hiding over €268,000 in cash in the attic of a house in west Dublin.

John O’Donnell, 37, with an address at Greenhills Road, Tallaght, admitted to possessing the criminal proceeds with intent to conceal them as part of money laundering activities. The charges arose from a search conducted by gardaí at a property in Clondalkin last year.

Detective Garda Michelle Larkin of the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau told the court that during a planned search on 15 November 2023, officers discovered bundles of banknotes wrapped in cling film and vacuum-packed bags hidden in insulation in the attic space. The total amount seized was €268,450.

O’Donnell was arrested at the scene and questioned at Clondalkin Garda Station, where he made admissions regarding his involvement. The court heard that the accused was acting on instructions from other gang members to store the money temporarily.

Defence counsel, Michael Bowman SC, said his client was not a leading figure in the organisation and had agreed to conceal the cash after experiencing “financial pressures”. Mr Bowman added O’Donnell has no previous convictions for similar offences.

Judge Martina Baxter requested a probation report and adjourned sentencing until 10 September. O’Donnell was remanded in continuing custody.
headline: Gang member pleads guilty to hiding €268k cash in attic

text:
A Japanese bullet train driver temporarily abandoned his controls to make a dash for the toilet while the train was travelling at more than 150 kilometres per hour, railway officials have confirmed. The incident occurred on Sunday, with the Nozomi Shinkansen train en route from Tokyo to Osaka, carrying approximately 160 passengers.

Central Japan Railway Company, the operator, said the driver, a man in his 30s, left the cockpit unmanned for around three minutes, asking a conductor who was unlicensed to operate the train to watch over the controls. The train was travelling at around 150km/h at that time, far exceeding typical speeds on Irish rail lines.

CCTV footage later revealed the driver had left his seat, and the man subsequently admitted to company management that he felt unwell due to abdominal pain and decided to use the toilet. He did not stop the train or notify operations control as required by company protocols.

According to the railway company, the train arrived at its destination safely and on time. No passengers were harmed and no irregularities were detected in the operation of the train during the incident.

Japanese officials said the case highlights concerns around driver fatigue and strict policies which currently prohibit drivers from leaving their posts during operations. Japanese railways are known internationally for their punctuality and safety record.

In response to the incident, the railway company issued an apology and stated that disciplinary action would be taken. The driver could face suspension or dismissal as a result of breaching company rules.

Japan’s Transport Ministry has called for an investigation and requested all railway operators to reinforce their safety protocols to prevent similar incidents in future.

Rail safety standards in Ireland differ significantly, with Irish Rail confirming that drivers here are not permitted to leave the cab while trains are in motion under any circumstances. In Ireland, intercity and commuter trains typically operate with both a driver and a train manager or guard, and are subject to oversight by the National Transport Authority and the Railway Safety Commission.

There have been no reports of similar incidents on Irish rail networks. The Japanese incident has reignited discussions on staff welfare, toilet breaks during long journeys, and the balance between safety and human needs within rail operations.
headline: Bullet train driver abandoned controls for toilet dash

text:
Minister for Defence Simon Harris donned the Defence Forces’ new ballistic body armour during a high-profile showcase at the Curragh Camp on Thursday, declaring the €16.5 million investment a “vital step” in boosting the protection of Irish personnel at home and abroad.

The new armoured vests, which are to be rolled out across all branches of the Defence Forces over the coming months, represent the most significant upgrade in personal protective equipment for soldiers since Ireland joined international peacekeeping missions in the 1960s. Designed to provide protection against rifle and handgun fire, the body armour can be adapted for varying operational environments, from UN missions in Lebanon and the Golan Heights to domestic security duties.

Minister Harris, who recently assumed his brief at the Department of Defence, arrived at the Defence Forces Training Centre to meet rank-and-file soldiers and senior officers, before being fitted with the state-of-the-art kit and taking part in a live-fire exercise. “If I’m going to understand what our troops face on a daily basis, I have to experience the gear myself,” Harris said, standing alongside Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Seán Clancy.

The €16.5 million contract, awarded last year following an EU-wide tender, covers the supply of over 6,000 sets of body armour, ballistic plates, and full modular accessories. Funding also includes maintenance and training. The Department of Defence confirmed that the new equipment complies with the highest NATO standards, a point emphasised by officials as Ireland continues to come under pressure to modernise its defence capabilities.

Harris hailed the upgrade as “long overdue” and indicated further investments are on the way. “It is unacceptable that any member of our Defence Forces would be out on patrol, whether here in Ireland or as part of a peacekeeping mission, without proper protection. This investment is just the beginning. Our soldiers deserve the very best.”

Several soldiers who trialled the new body armour said it was lighter and more comfortable than the ageing vests currently in use. “You can move about more freely, and the fit is much better for both tall and smaller people,” one corporal told The Liberal. “It’s a massive improvement.”

The move comes amid ongoing concerns about recruitment and retention across the Defence Forces, with numbers continuing to fall below government targets. The Representative Association of Commissioned Officers (RACO) has welcomed the new equipment, but said more fundamental reforms of pay and conditions are needed if the government is serious about retaining experienced personnel.

During his visit, Minister Harris said the Cabinet would shortly receive an update on progress towards the government’s goal of increasing Defence spending to €1.5 billion annually by 2028, in line with the recommendations of the Commission on the Defence Forces. However, opposition TDs have accused the government of dragging its heels, with Sinn Féin’s John Brady TD calling for “real action, not photo opportunities.”

Harris, for his part, insisted the body armour purchase is a “clear demonstration” of government commitment to the Defence Forces. “This investment will save lives, and that’s what matters.”
headline: Top Gun Harris tests Defence Forces new body armour worth €16.5 million

text:
Sinn Féin has called for the issue of Irish neutrality to be decided directly by the people, insisting that any changes to the country’s longstanding policy must go to a referendum. The party’s spokesperson on foreign affairs, Matt Carthy TD, said growing discussions at Government level about closer ties with EU defence structures have raised deep concerns among the public.

Speaking in the Dáil on Wednesday, Deputy Carthy accused the coalition of “creeping towards an abandonment of neutrality by stealth,” and demanded clarity from the Taoiseach, Simon Harris, on the Government’s intentions regarding military alliances. “Neutrality is a cherished part of our national identity and history,” Mr Carthy said. “Successive Governments have used vague language and backroom deals to erode it, but the people have never been given a real say. That must change.”

The comments come amid ongoing debate over Ireland’s participation in EU security programmes. Earlier this year, Tánaiste Micheál Martin confirmed that Ireland would take part in the European Sky Shield Initiative, a German-led programme aimed at boosting European air defences, but he denied that this constituted an entry into a military alliance.

Opponents argue that such moves are incompatible with Ireland’s traditional policy of military non-alignment. Sinn Féin and several independents have warned that public trust is being undermined by what they see as efforts to “undermine neutrality by the back door”. The party has pledged to introduce legislation that would require any substantive changes to Irish defence policy to be subject to a popular vote.

Government ministers, however, claim that Ireland’s participation in EU security and defence initiatives stops far short of NATO-style commitments, and insist that the country retains a veto on military actions. Tánaiste Martin told reporters yesterday that “Ireland’s policy of military neutrality remains intact,” adding that “no decisions have been taken to change that position.” He called the opposition’s statements “alarmist” and said that Irish involvement in peacekeeping and security operations “has always been with the consent of the Oireachtas and in the national interest.”

Recent opinion polls show that a majority of Irish people continue to support neutrality, but some polls suggest growing support for a more engaged role in European security, particularly in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Campaign groups such as the Irish Neutrality League, led by former MEP Patricia McKenna, have also joined the call for a referendum. “If the Government is so confident that the people support their direction, they should put it to the test,” Ms McKenna said. “Neutrality is not a slogan – it’s a core value that should not be given away without a real public mandate.”

The Taoiseach has not yet indicated whether the Government would allow the issue to go to a referendum, but indicated that any significant constitutional changes would require public approval. As the debate continues, Sinn Féin has vowed to keep the pressure on, stating that “only a full, free and open vote can truly decide the future of Ireland’s neutrality.”
headline: Irish neutrality should be put to a public vote, claims Sinn Féin

text:
Gardaí have called off the search for a missing man following the discovery of a body in a rural area on Saturday evening. The man, who had been the subject of a widespread search operation over recent days, was last seen in the locality earlier this week.

According to sources, the body was found shortly after 5pm by members of a volunteer search group who had joined Gardaí and other emergency services in the effort to locate the missing individual. The remains were discovered in a wooded area outside the town, some distance from where the man was last reported seen.

The scene was immediately sealed off and the State Pathologist was notified. Gardaí have stated that a post-mortem examination will be carried out to establish the cause of death, but at this stage foul play is not suspected.

Family members of the deceased have been informed, and Gardaí have thanked all those who participated in the search, including local volunteers, Civil Defence, and the Search and Rescue teams. Locals have expressed their sympathies to the bereaved family, with many taking to social media to offer condolences and pay tribute.

Investigations are ongoing, but Gardaí have indicated that they are preparing a file for the Coroner's Court, as is standard procedure. The identity of the deceased has not yet been officially released, pending formal identification and notification of extended family.

Anyone affected by this news is advised that support services are available, including local clergy and HSE helplines.
headline: Gardai end the search for missing man after a body is found

text:
Minister for Finance Jack Chambers will take centre stage this October as he delivers Budget 2025, in what sources within Government describe as a "pivotal moment" for both the young minister and the Coalition. At just 33 years of age, Chambers is set to become the youngest ever holder of the Finance portfolio to unveil the State’s annual budget plan, following the recent Cabinet reshuffle and the departure of Michael McGrath to Brussels.

Insiders have told The Liberal that Chambers, from Dublin West, is “said to be nervous” ahead of the high-profile announcement. With less than a year to the next general election, all eyes in Government Buildings are fixed on how the Fianna Fáil TD will balance demands for substantial cost-of-living supports against warnings from the Department of Finance about overheating the economy.

Jack Chambers, previously Chief Whip and most recently Minister for Transport and the Gaeltacht, is expected to walk a political tightrope. Pressure is mounting from across the Dáil for increased supports for renters, improvements in the health and education budgets, and fresh measures to tackle Ireland’s ongoing housing crisis.

Despite repeated assurances from Cabinet colleagues of a “steady hand”, recent polling shows voters are increasingly anxious about spiralling costs, hospital overcrowding, and record homelessness. Public sector unions have warned that any failure to address wages and working conditions could lead to further industrial action this autumn, particularly amongst teachers, nurses, and Gardaí.

The looming budget is also being watched closely by EU officials, given Ireland’s strong economic growth but also rising concerns around tax receipts from multinationals, which Treasury officials have repeatedly warned may not be sustainable. Chambers, a solicitor by training, faces the added challenge of juggling expectations from coalition partners Fine Gael and the Green Party, each pushing for their own priorities – from tax cuts to environmental spending.

Government sources told The Liberal that Chambers has been locked in late-night meetings in recent weeks, consulting with the Taoiseach Simon Harris, Tánaiste Micheál Martin, and Minister for Public Expenditure Paschal Donohoe on the final details.

Speaking to media on Tuesday, Minister Chambers offered few details, saying only that the budget would be “fair, responsible, and targeted at those who need it most”. When pressed about his nerves, he acknowledged the “significant responsibility” of his new role, but said he was “focused on delivering for families and communities across Ireland”.

Opposition parties have been quick to seize on the situation, with Sinn Féin’s finance spokesperson Pearse Doherty claiming that “ordinary people need real change, not more of the same failed policies”. The Social Democrats and Labour have echoed calls for sweeping investment in housing, education, and health.

Chambers, who will deliver his first budget speech in the Dáil chamber this autumn, now faces the task of convincing both his party and a sceptical public that he can rise to the occasion. The stakes could hardly be higher, with the outcome likely to shape the political landscape as the country heads into an election year.
headline: Budget 2025: “He’s said to be nervous”, 33-yr-old Jack Chambers announces the budget for the upcoming year

text:
Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael have been dealt a major blow as a new opinion poll shows support for both parties plunging to historic lows, raising fresh questions about the future of the coalition government and the leadership of Micheál Martin and Simon Harris.

According to the latest poll, conducted by Red C for The Liberal, voter backing for Fianna Fáil has slumped to 15 percent, while Fine Gael has tumbled even further, registering just 13 percent support among those surveyed. The figures represent a dramatic decline since the last general election and mark the lowest point for the two parties in decades.

The poll also indicates a surge in support for Sinn Féin, which now leads on 34 percent, leaving Mary Lou McDonald’s party well ahead of its rivals and in poll position should a general election be called in the coming months. The results come as both main coalition parties face backlash over the ongoing housing crisis, record-level hospital overcrowding, spiralling cost of living, and a series of government scandals.

Public anger over immigration policy continues to rise, with several recent protests highlighting deep concerns in communities across the country. Many voters blame the government for what they see as a failure to control Ireland’s borders and to provide adequate resources for existing citizens. The latest figures will increase pressure on the coalition to re-examine its approach ahead of next week’s Dáil sitting.

A Fianna Fáil TD, speaking anonymously to The Liberal, said there is growing unease in the party ranks: “People on the doors are not happy. There’s a real sense that we’ve lost touch with ordinary voters and are paying the price for broken promises.”

Taoiseach Simon Harris, who took over the Fine Gael leadership from Leo Varadkar earlier this year, pledged to “listen to the electorate” but dismissed suggestions of an imminent leadership challenge. Tánaiste Micheál Martin also sought to calm nerves, insisting that “there is a job of work to be done” and that the government is determined to “deliver for the people.”

Meanwhile, opposition parties and independent TDs have seized on the poll to call for a general election, claiming the coalition no longer has a mandate to govern. Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald described the result as “a clear signal that the public wants change,” while the Rural Independent Group reiterated demands for a Dáil dissolution.

With local and European elections on the horizon, the figures will worry backbench TDs and councillors, many of whom fear for their seats amid rising discontent. The government faces a crucial few weeks as it seeks to avoid further setbacks and restore public confidence.
headline: Disaster for Martin and Harris as new poll suggests nosedive for Fianna Fail and Fine Gael

text:
A significant number of gardaí assigned to Roads Policing units across the country are reportedly “completely unproductive,” according to a new report into the effectiveness of traffic enforcement in Ireland. The internal Garda report, seen by The Liberal, highlights alarming inefficiency and lack of activity among officers who are specifically tasked with tackling speeding, dangerous driving, and other road traffic offences.

The analysis, which was carried out earlier this year by a Garda inspectorate team, examined the work patterns and outputs of Roads Policing gardaí in several divisions over the course of twelve months. It found that a sizeable proportion of officers in these specialist units had failed to make a single detection for key offences such as drink or drug driving, mobile phone use, or seatbelt infractions throughout the period in question. In some divisions, as many as a third of Roads Policing gardaí were described as “entirely inactive” when it came to enforcement, issuing no fixed charge notices or summonses whatsoever.

Sources within the force said the findings have prompted concern at senior levels, especially given the recent rise in road fatalities and the Government’s commitment to halving serious injuries and deaths on Irish roads by 2030. “There is a core of officers who are doing good work, but the reality is that many others are not pulling their weight. You have a situation where some gardaí in Roads Policing could go an entire year without making a single detection,” a senior Garda source told The Liberal.

The report identified a lack of oversight by supervisory sergeants and inspectors as a key factor in the low productivity rates. It also pointed to issues with the allocation of resources, with many Roads Policing units reportedly left under-staffed at peak times, or officers regularly assigned to other duties such as public order incidents, checkpoints, or administrative work.

Garda management has pledged to address the findings as part of a wider review of traffic policing strategy, which will include measures to improve accountability and performance management within the Roads Policing divisions. “The report makes for sobering reading. There is simply no excuse for gardaí in specialist posts failing to engage in core enforcement activity,” said a spokesperson for Garda Headquarters.

The Garda Representative Association (GRA) said rank-and-file members were under immense pressure due to chronic manpower shortages, increasing paperwork, and “constant interference” from senior management. However, victims’ groups and road safety advocates have called for an urgent overhaul of Roads Policing, arguing that greater visibility and enforcement are essential to make the country’s roads safer.

According to the most recent figures published by the Road Safety Authority (RSA), 100 people have died on Irish roads since the start of this year—a significant increase on the same period last year. The Dáil’s transport committee is expected to seek clarification from the Minister for Justice on the steps being taken to ensure that all Roads Policing gardaí are delivering on their responsibilities to the public.
headline: Large numbers of Roads Policing gardaí are completely ‘unproductive’, new report says

text:
Patients across Ireland will continue to endure dangerously long waiting times and substandard care unless the State takes urgent action to increase hospital bed capacity, a senior medical expert has warned.

Dr Michael O’Connor, a consultant in emergency medicine, said the current shortage of acute and step-down beds is at the root of repeated trolley crises that have persisted for years, in spite of multiple HSE promises and government strategies. He said it was “no surprise” to see record numbers of patients on trolleys in recent weeks, given that bed capacity remains well below what is required for the country’s growing and ageing population.

“The health service in Ireland has not kept pace with demographic changes or medical advances,” Dr O’Connor said. “We have fewer hospital beds per capita than most Western European countries. Until that is addressed, patients will continue to suffer unacceptably long waits, cancelled procedures, and delays in diagnosis and treatment.”

Figures released last week by the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO) showed that more than 600 patients were without a bed on a single day, the highest number recorded so far this year. The organisation has repeatedly called for urgent investment in both acute hospital beds and community care, saying current conditions are unsafe for both patients and staff.

Despite the launch of the Sláintecare programme in 2017 and repeated government pledges to add hospital beds, progress has been slow. According to the Department of Health, just over 800 new public beds have been delivered since 2020, far short of independent estimates that an additional 5,000–6,000 beds will be needed by the end of the decade.

Dr O’Connor said that while the Government’s focus on recruiting more doctors and nurses is welcome, it will not be enough if the physical capacity in hospitals remains inadequate. “You can hire more staff, but if there’s no bed for a patient, that patient is still in a corridor,” he said. “We see frail elderly people, children, and those with complex illnesses left waiting for hours, sometimes days, for admission. It is simply not acceptable in a modern health system.”

The HSE recently announced a winter plan providing for extra funding, rapid assessment units, and support for home care in a bid to ease pressures. However, healthcare unions and frontline staff say these measures are “sticking plasters” rather than a long-term solution. 

Dr O’Connor is calling on the Taoiseach and the Minister for Health to set out a clear timeline for rapid expansion of bed numbers, saying promises must be followed with real action and transparent reporting. “Otherwise, we will be here again next winter, and the winter after that, still failing our most vulnerable patients,” he warned.
headline: Patients will continue to suffer unless bed capacity increases, says expert doctor

text:
Tensions have erupted in Co Clare as Ukrainian refugees housed in local accommodation were this week informed they must vacate their current lodgings and prepare for relocation to alternative centres. The news, delivered by Department of Integration officials, has left many families distressed, with some accusing the government of treating them as “second-class citizens”. 

Approximately 80 Ukrainians currently residing at a former hotel in Ennis said they were given less than two weeks’ notice to pack up and move on. Many voiced their frustrations at a public meeting organised on Wednesday evening, attended by members of Clare County Council, local TDs, councillors, and representatives of supporting NGOs. 

Parents, some visibly upset, told The Liberal that their children had only recently settled into local schools. One mother, who asked not to be named, said she feared for her son’s mental health after being told they might have to travel across the country to a new centre. “We thought we could start rebuilding here,” she said. “Now we are told to leave with no choice.” 

Local opposition has mounted as communities in Clare report worsening pressure on public services and housing capacity. Some residents say the government has failed to consult with locals or provide enough resources to support both newcomers and existing residents. “It’s a disgrace. They’re moving people around like cattle,” said Cllr Michael O’Callaghan. “We keep hearing about a shortage of beds, but nobody is being told straight what’s going on.”

Department sources confirmed to The Liberal that the decision is part of a nationwide reorganisation due to the ending of contracts for several emergency accommodation centres. “We recognise this is deeply unsettling for those involved, but rotation is necessary as we balance limited resources and the ongoing humanitarian response,” said a spokesperson, who insisted every effort would be made to ensure families were not split up. 

However, Ukrainian residents say the government’s assurances ring hollow, with some reporting they have received no guarantee of accommodation in their next location or clarity about transport arrangements. Several have pleaded with local TDs to intervene directly with Minister Roderic O’Gorman to halt the move or provide additional supports. 

Meanwhile, a group of locals supporting the Ukrainian families staged a small protest outside the accommodation centre yesterday, calling for compassion and stability. “It’s bad enough being uprooted by war,” said local volunteer Eileen Mahony. “They shouldn’t have their lives uprooted a second time by the Irish government’s chaos.” 

As the dispute escalates, the Department has promised to review the situation, but many in Clare believe trust has already been eroded. Concerned parents are now considering pulling their children from school rather than face the trauma of another sudden move. The issue is expected to be raised in the Dáil next week as pressure mounts on the government to provide clarity and, above all, fairness.
headline: Uproar in Clare from Ukrainians who’ve been told they have to move on

text:
The government is set to hold an emergency Cabinet meeting this Sunday in response to escalating nationwide protests over spiralling fuel prices, the Liberal has learned. Senior sources within Leinster House have said Ministers are “in panic mode” as widespread disruption and public anger continue to mount.

The special Cabinet session, confirmed late last night by sources close to the Taoiseach’s office, will bring together all senior Ministers amid growing fears that the fuel crisis could spiral out of control. It follows a week of sustained demonstrations by hauliers, taxi drivers, and ordinary citizens, who have blockaded roads, staged marches in Dublin, Cork, and Galway, and demanded immediate government action to cut fuel taxes and address the cost-of-living crisis.

Gardaí have reported significant traffic disruption in several cities, with convoys of lorries, tractors, and private vehicles descending on key thoroughfares. In Dublin, protesters gathered outside the Dáil on Friday, accusing the coalition of “ignoring ordinary families” and “punishing workers” with what they describe as punitive carbon taxes and excise duties.

A senior government source told the Liberal: “The Cabinet knows it’s a crisis and they know the country is reaching boiling point. They were hoping to sit this one out, but the public reaction has shocked them. There is real fear that the protests could get bigger, especially after payday next week.”

Opposition TDs have slammed the government’s “tone deaf” response to date, with Sinn Féin calling for an immediate reduction in excise on fuel and Social Democrats branding the current approach as “woefully inadequate”. Rural Independent TDs have warned that many small businesses and farms could face closure if fuel prices are not brought under control.

Motorists across Ireland are now paying over €2.10 per litre at some filling stations, a record high blamed by the government on global factors, including the ongoing war in Ukraine and supply chain issues. However, campaigners say the bulk of the price is still made up of government taxes and charges.

The Taoiseach is understood to be under intense pressure from backbenchers—particularly those representing rural and commuter belt constituencies—who fear a political backlash if urgent action is not taken. Calls for a temporary cut in VAT and a suspension of carbon tax increases have been growing louder, but so far no concrete measures have been announced.

Sunday’s emergency meeting will be watched closely by the thousands of protesters camped out in city centres and the millions more struggling with soaring energy bills. Demonstrators say the government must “wake up to reality” and provide immediate relief, warning that protests will escalate if their demands are not met.

A Department of Finance spokesperson indicated that “all options are on the table,” but cautioned that any tax relief measures would need to be balanced against existing commitments and EU regulations.

Public anger continues to simmer, with many telling the Liberal they feel “abandoned and betrayed” by those in power. As the clock ticks towards Sunday’s crunch meeting, the government faces what some are calling its most serious crisis since the Covid pandemic.
headline: BREAKING: “The govt is in panic mode” – Cabinet to have special meeting on Sunday to discuss fuel protest crisis

text:
Thousands of families across Ireland are facing a bleak Christmas as overwhelming demand for food vouchers has left charity organisations struggling to keep pace. The Capuchin Day Centre in Dublin has reported that all of its Christmas food vouchers were snapped up within hours of being made available, highlighting the extent of hardship faced by many in the run-up to the festive season.

Staff at the Capuchin Day Centre, a well-known fixture on Bow Street which has been serving the homeless and those in need for decades, described scenes of long queues and desperate families seeking assistance. According to Brother Kevin Crowley, founder of the Centre, the demand for support this Christmas has drastically increased compared to previous years.

“We were inundated. The vouchers were all gone in the space of a few hours. People started queueing early in the morning and the line stretched down the road,” Brother Kevin told The Liberal. “We’re seeing more working families coming to us this year, not just the homeless or people on social welfare. Rising food and energy prices are hitting everyone hard. Many just can’t manage any more.”

The vouchers, worth €50 each, were intended to help struggling households buy food for the Christmas period. While the Centre made every effort to help as many as possible, resources failed to meet the unprecedented demand, leaving many disappointed and anxious about how they will manage over the coming weeks.

Staff said that word of mouth and social media posts had spread quickly, resulting in even greater numbers turning up than anticipated. Reports of families with young children, pensioners, and people with disabilities among those seeking help have fuelled concerns that the cost of living crisis is deepening poverty and social exclusion.

The Capuchin Day Centre, which serves up to 1,000 hot meals daily, operates on donations and limited funding. “We do our best but the numbers are rising every week. The Government really needs to look at providing more direct support for the most vulnerable, especially coming up to Christmas,” said a volunteer at the Centre.

The surge in need comes as charities across the country warn of increased pressure on their services. The Society of St Vincent de Paul and Focus Ireland have also noted record requests for assistance this winter, with fuel poverty and high grocery bills cited as major factors.

Calls have intensified for the Government to introduce additional emergency measures, with opposition TDs criticising what they describe as a slow and insufficient response from the Department of Social Protection. In the Dáil this week, Sinn Féin and Labour pressed the Taoiseach to increase funding for emergency hardship schemes and ensure no family is left without basic necessities during the holidays.

Meanwhile, the Capuchin Day Centre has appealed for public donations to help meet the growing demand. “This year, more than ever, people need our help,” said Brother Kevin. “We’ll do everything we can, but we can’t do it alone.”
headline: Huge demand for Christmas food vouchers with thousands gone in hours, Capuchin Day Centre says

text:
Enoch Burke has walked free from Mountjoy Prison today, bringing to an end a marathon period of incarceration that lasted over 400 days, all the while refusing to purge his contempt of court. The controversial teacher was released on foot of a High Court order, having spent well over a year behind bars stemming from his protracted dispute with Wilson’s Hospital School and the Irish courts.

Mr Burke, who was greeted at the gates of Mountjoy by supporters and members of his family chanting “Enoch won,” exited the prison carrying a Bible and appearing visibly emotional. He made no comment to the gathered media, but his parents and siblings, who have been steadfast in their support throughout, proclaimed his release a victory for religious freedom and conscience.

The High Court’s decision to order Mr Burke’s immediate release came unexpectedly on Monday, with Mr Justice Mark Sanfey stating that the “continued detention of the respondent has ceased to operate as a coercive measure.” This means that, despite Mr Burke’s refusal to comply with court orders—specifically to stay away from Wilson’s Hospital School and to respect the school’s wishes regarding a student’s gender identity—the court found that keeping him in prison any longer would serve no further purpose.

The original case arose when Mr Burke objected to a direction from school management to use a transgender student’s preferred pronouns and name. After refusing to comply, he was suspended and subsequently barred from the campus. When he continued to attend the school regardless, the Board of Governors obtained an injunction, which Mr Burke openly defied, leading to his imprisonment for contempt of court.

Despite being offered release on multiple previous occasions if he would purge his contempt and promise to obey the court orders, Mr Burke consistently refused, citing his religious convictions and right to freedom of expression. This stance has polarised opinion in Ireland, with some viewing him as a principled defender of Christian belief, and others criticising him for disregarding both the law and the rights of the school community.

Reacting to his release, the Burke family said: “Enoch has stood firm for his beliefs against state persecution. This is a great day for Christian liberty in Ireland.” Meanwhile, LGBT+ and human rights groups have expressed concern at the message sent by Mr Burke’s release without compliance, warning it undermines the authority of the courts and the rights of transgender pupils.

Legal experts noted that while the court retains the power to sanction Mr Burke should he again breach its orders, the decision to free him—despite his intransigence—reflects the limits of coercive imprisonment as a tool for enforcement in civil matters.

The Board of Governors at Wilson’s Hospital School declined to comment but reiterated their commitment to maintaining a safe and inclusive educational environment. The Department of Education and the Minister for Education have been contacted for comment.

As Enoch Burke returns to his family home in Co Mayo, attention now turns to the ongoing legal proceedings, with several related cases still pending in the courts. The saga, which has gripped the nation and fuelled debate on religious freedom, gender identity, and the rule of law, shows no sign of abating.
headline: “Enoch won” – Enoch Burke has been released from Mountjoy Prison after over 400 days following court order without purging his contempt

text:
A 26-year-old mother has died following a horrific shark attack in Mexico while she was swimming with her daughter, according to reports emerging today.

The Irish woman, who has not been officially named, had been on holiday with her family in the resort town of Melaque, in the western state of Jalisco. Local media say the incident happened on Saturday as she was taking part in a paddleboarding tour with her five-year-old daughter, just 40 metres from the shore.

Emergency services rushed to the scene after the attack was reported, but the woman suffered catastrophic injuries to her leg and despite desperate efforts by bystanders and rescue personnel, she was pronounced dead at the scene. Her daughter was reportedly unharmed physically but is said to be deeply traumatised by the ordeal.

The tragic mother, understood to be in Mexico with her partner and two children, was attacked by what is believed to have been a tiger shark. Witnesses described chaotic scenes, with tourists and locals sprinting to get out of the water as warning calls went up.

The Irish Department of Foreign Affairs has confirmed it is aware of the case and is providing consular assistance to the woman's family. In a statement, officials said, “The Department of Foreign Affairs stands ready to provide all possible support to the family at this difficult time.” No further details have been released due to the sensitive nature of the situation and the need to respect the family’s privacy.

Authorities in Jalisco have closed a number of local beaches as a precaution while the incident is investigated. The State Civil Defence organisation issued an alert, urging people to exercise caution and follow instructions from lifeguards and officials.

The incident has understandably sent shockwaves through both the local community in Mexico and here at home. Friends and relatives are said to be devastated, describing the young woman as “devoted to her children” and “full of life”.

Shark attacks in this part of Mexico are considered rare, but local officials have promised to review safety protocols and warning systems in the area. The woman’s body is expected to be repatriated to Ireland in the coming days, supported by the Irish authorities and local diplomatic staff.

Meanwhile, messages of condolence have been pouring in on social media from friends, family, and members of the Irish community abroad, offering prayers and support to the grieving family in the aftermath of this unthinkable loss.
headline: 26-yr-old mother dies after attack by shark in Mexico while swimming with daughter

text:
