Social welfare recipients across Ireland have seen an increase in their weekly payments this week, as the measures announced in Budget 2025 have officially come into effect. The Department of Social Protection confirmed that the increases, which were outlined by Minister Heather Humphreys last October, have now been rolled out to over 1.5 million people who rely on state supports.

Under the new adjustments, weekly core welfare payments such as Jobseeker’s Benefit, Disability Allowance, Carer’s Allowance and the State Pension have all been raised by €12. The increase also applies to payments for qualified adults and children. The hike comes as part of the Government’s efforts to tackle the ongoing cost of living crisis, with inflation and rising bills continuing to put pressure on households nationwide.

There has been a mixed reaction from advocacy groups and the political opposition, with some saying that while the extra money is welcome, it does not go far enough to address the daily realities faced by those on fixed incomes. The Social Justice Ireland group said that families and individuals on welfare payments still struggle to keep up with the costs of rent, food, and energy, particularly in urban areas. Sinn Féin spokesperson on Social Protection, Claire Kerrane TD, criticised the increase as “insufficient to meet rising expenses.”

Meanwhile, the Department of Social Protection defended the move, stating it represented the largest across-the-board rise in recent years and formed part of a broader package of supports including additional lump-sum payments issued at Christmas and over the winter period. The Minister said the Government is committed to “protecting the most vulnerable in our society.”

Recipients began receiving the higher rates in their bank accounts and at post offices from Monday. The increase comes as part of a package which also includes expanded eligibility for the Fuel Allowance and increases to the Working Family Payment threshold. Pensioners, people with disabilities, lone parents and carers are among those benefitting from the measure.

The Government has signaled that further reviews of social welfare rates will take place over the course of this year, as discussions continue on measures to address poverty, child benefit and supports for those on low pay. The Department of Social Protection is due to publish a review of income adequacy later in the year.

Anyone seeking information about their payment rates or eligibility is being advised to check the Department’s website or speak to their local Intreo office.
headline: 2025 social welfare increases have kicked in with welfare recipients increasing their payments this week

text:
Dozens of new cases of the Covid Eris variant have been detected in Ireland, according to the latest figures provided by the HSE, with health officials and the mainstream media already increasing calls for more restrictions and isolation advice, prompting widespread criticism from those who believe the reaction is excessive and driven by fear rather than facts.

The detection of the Eris strain – an offshoot of the Omicron family – comes as public health experts raise the alarm about a potential increase in cases heading into the autumn and winter months. Already, the HSE has outlined updated recommended isolation rules for those with symptoms or who test positive, despite mounting evidence that the majority of cases involve mild symptoms similar to the common cold.

Symptoms attributed to the Eris variant, also known as EG.5, include a runny nose, sneezing, sore throat, and fatigue – all of which are common in other respiratory illnesses. Despite this, the hype around the new strain has prompted renewed discussion of possible restrictions, with some medical advisers even hinting that mask mandates and remote working could return should cases rise.

Many people across Ireland have reacted with scepticism, questioning the justification for ongoing restrictions and the renewed focus on Covid just as life appeared to be returning to normal. Critics have accused the health authorities and some sections of the media of stoking unnecessary panic, with concerns raised about the social and economic impact of further isolation guidelines. There are also growing fears that another round of restrictions could be used to justify more government control.

The Department of Health has insisted that the measures are based on "the latest scientific evidence" and have urged anyone with symptoms to self-isolate and avoid contact with vulnerable individuals, especially the elderly. The HSE is also considering additional vaccination campaigns in the coming months, despite the fact that large swathes of the population have either already recovered from Covid or received multiple vaccine doses.

Meanwhile, some independent medical voices have said that most people have developed a level of natural immunity and that the government should focus on supporting the health service rather than disrupting everyday life.

As debate rages in the Dáil over the government’s approach, many Irish citizens are left wondering if the rolling headlines and new isolation guidelines are truly in the public’s best interest, or if they are just the latest round in a cycle of fear-based messaging.
headline: Fear mongering continues as Covid Eris variant symptoms as Ireland confirms dozens of cases with more isolation rules outlined

text:
More than 1,200 driving tests have been cancelled so far this year as a result of insurance-related problems, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) confirmed this week. The figures, released following a parliamentary question, highlight growing concerns about access to valid learner insurance, which is increasingly being cited as a barrier for test applicants nationwide.

According to the RSA, the most common issue involves learner drivers arriving at test centres with insurance documents that are either expired, invalid for solo driving, or restricted to named drivers accompanied by a fully licensed motorist. Under Irish law, learner permit holders must be insured to drive unaccompanied only for the purpose of the driving test itself.

The cancellations come as many driving instructors and applicants report mounting confusion over insurance policy requirements, with some major insurers refusing to provide cover for unaccompanied test drives, leading to last-minute test refusals by the examiner.

A spokesperson for the RSA told The Liberal: “The safety of all road users is our paramount concern. All candidates must present valid insurance before undertaking their test. Unfortunately, a number of applicants are still unaware of the precise requirements, resulting in the growing number of cancellations.”

The number of cancellations represents a notable increase on pre-pandemic years. In 2019, less than 800 tests were cancelled due to insurance issues, while in the first five months of 2024, already over 1,200 candidates have been turned away. The RSA says the figures reflect both stricter enforcement and the increased complexity of learner permit insurance cover since Brexit and changes in the underwriting policies of some insurers.

The Motor Insurers’ Bureau of Ireland (MIBI) has previously advised all learner drivers to check with their insurance provider well in advance of the test date to ensure compliance. Some insurers, including a number of well-known names, have introduced stricter wording in their policies, adding to confusion among learners and their parents.

Driving instructors have called on the Department of Transport and the insurance industry to provide clearer guidance and standardised policy wording. The Irish School of Motoring warned that the trend is adding further delays for young people seeking to become fully licenced drivers, stretching waiting lists and increasing frustration.

Fianna Fáil TD for Dublin West, Jack Chambers, raised the issue in the Dáil, saying: “It is deeply unfair on candidates who have completed months of tuition only to have their efforts thwarted because of last-minute insurance technicalities. We need to ensure the rules are clear, communicated, and that insurance products support, not hinder, the licensing process.”

The RSA has urged candidates to double-check their insurance status before attending their scheduled test and to contact their insurer or broker in advance to request written confirmation that they are covered to sit the test alone in the vehicle. The authority added that, while the rules are not new, recent enforcement has revealed a lack of awareness among some test applicants.

The Department of Transport said it is liaising with the insurance sector to seek a resolution, but in the meantime, the responsibility remains with candidates to ensure compliance on the day. The HSE has also warned that any incident involving an uninsured driver—regardless of circumstances—could result in legal and financial penalties.

Test cancellations are recorded as ‘no test’ and candidates must reapply, further prolonging already lengthy waiting lists in many counties. The average wait time for a driving test nationally is now approaching 22 weeks, according to the most recent figures.
headline: Over 1,200 driving tests have been cancelled due to insurance issues, says RSA

text:
A judge sitting at Ennis Circuit Court has lambasted two County Clare women after dismissing what he described as “utterly fraudulent” insurance claims arising from a minor collision involving a Dublin taxi driver. Judge Gerald Keys expressed strong criticism of the plaintiffs on Monday, stating both had attempted to “pull the wool over the court’s eyes” with “exaggerated and manufactured” injuries.

The case arose from a low-speed traffic incident on the outskirts of Ennis in October 2021. The court heard that Aisling McNamara (36) of Kilmaley and Maria Reilly (41) of Ennis alleged they suffered whiplash and lasting trauma after a collision involving a Dublin taxi, driven by Mr Prakash Sharma, as they were travelling as rear seat passengers. Both women lodged personal injury claims seeking general damages totalling nearly €60,000.

Under cross-examination, glaring inconsistencies emerged between sworn testimony and medical reports provided to the court. CCTV and photographic evidence showed minimal damage to the vehicles and indicated that neither woman sought medical treatment at the scene or in the days following the incident.

Judge Keys noted that both claimants had failed to disclose previous, similar claims made in recent years, with Ms McNamara admitting to three prior settlements for whiplash injuries since 2017. Ms Reilly accepted that she had also brought two unsuccessful claims in 2020 and 2015. The judge further remarked that statements made to Gardaí and doctors “simply do not hold water” and described the injuries alleged as “the stuff of fiction”.

Rejecting both claims, Judge Keys condemned the women’s actions as a “brazen attempt to misuse the courts for personal gain” and warned that such cases contribute directly to the high cost of insurance premiums for honest motorists and businesses. He praised Mr Sharma and his insurer for vigorously defending the action and said he was “glad to see such claims exposed for what they are”.

Costs were awarded against the two women, and Judge Keys indicated he would forward his findings to the Gardaí for further investigation into possible perjury or fraudulent activity. The court was told the taxi driver, who has worked in Dublin for over a decade, had faced increased insurance costs and considerable personal distress since the claims were lodged.

The outcome was welcomed by Insurance Reform Ireland, which said it underscored the need for greater scrutiny of personal injury litigation and harsher penalties for those seeking to exploit the system. The case is the latest in a series of legal actions across the country in which exaggerated or spurious claims have been thrown out by the courts.
headline: Angered judge throws out ‘fraudulent’ insurance claims from Co Clare women against Dublin taxi driver

text:
An Irish university student who orchestrated a €16,000 scam using the popular social media app Snapchat has avoided a jail sentence, but the presiding judge imposed what he described as “severe and unequivocal” conditions during sentencing at Dublin Circuit Criminal Court today.

The 21-year-old male, whose identity cannot be published due to ongoing legal proceedings against alleged accomplices, had pleaded guilty to a series of offences under the Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001. The court heard how the student, originally from south Dublin and currently enrolled at a third-level institution in the capital, persuaded multiple victims, including two fellow students and an elderly woman, to transfer sums ranging from €250 to €4,500 after promising bogus investment returns in cryptocurrency.

Evidence presented by Detective Gardaí from the National Economic Crime Bureau revealed that the accused operated several Snapchat accounts, posting enticing stories of “guaranteed profits” through digital assets. When victims engaged with him, they were urged to lodge money to various bank accounts, which were subsequently drained via cash withdrawals from ATMs across the city.

Judge Fionnuala Ní Chúlacháin told the court that, while she acknowledged the student’s previous good character and early guilty plea, the offences “displayed a deliberate, sophisticated exploitation of trust and technical know-how that cannot go without significant consequence.”

The court was told that the accused had already refunded a substantial portion of the money, after relatives intervened and a fundraising effort was undertaken among his family and friends. The balance, totalling just over €4,000, remains outstanding, but the defence barrister said arrangements are in place for it to be repaid within the next three months.

Judge Ní Chúlacháin handed down a two-year sentence, suspended for three years, on strict conditions including full restitution within 12 weeks, ongoing engagement with the Probation Service, and a total ban on the use of all social media platforms for two years. The accused was also ordered to complete 240 hours of community service, with explicit instructions that any breach of these requirements would see the full custodial sentence imposed.

In a statement outside court, one of the victims welcomed the fact that “some accountability” had been secured, but expressed concern that “scams like this are happening to young people every day online, with too little deterrence.” 

The case comes amid mounting concern over the rise of online fraud targeting both young and elderly victims in Ireland, with the Gardaí urging the public to exercise extreme caution and never to transfer money to unknown individuals or schemes promising quick returns. 

A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said new proposals are under consideration to strengthen the law in relation to cyber-enabled fraud and to provide “better resources for education, investigation and victim support.”
headline: Irish student avoids jailtime in €16,000 Snapchat scam but judge places harsh conditions

text:
Multiple drone strikes rocked Moscow overnight and into the early hours of this morning, igniting widespread panic among residents and prompting authorities to initiate mass evacuations across several districts of the Russian capital. State media confirmed a series of explosions in at least five separate locations, with local social media channels showing dramatic footage of drones flying low over apartment blocks before detonating, sending plumes of smoke into the city skyline.

The Russian Ministry of Defence claimed to have intercepted the majority of the incoming drones, with anti-aircraft batteries lighting up the night sky. However, several devices are known to have struck residential and administrative buildings, causing substantial damage. Emergency services rushed to evacuate thousands of residents from high-rise complexes amid fears of secondary attacks and the risk of fire.

There were no immediate reports of fatalities as of this morning but at least 18 people were treated for injuries ranging from shrapnel wounds to smoke inhalation. Local hospitals are on high alert, with dozens of ambulances and fire units deployed across the affected areas.

The Kremlin accused "foreign saboteurs" of orchestrating the assault, directly linking the attacks to what it described as ongoing hostilities with Ukraine. Ukrainian officials, meanwhile, maintained their customary silence on alleged cross-border operations but insisted that such incidents are a "consequence of Russia's continued aggression".

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin called for calm and praised emergency responders for their swift action, urging residents to follow all official instructions and avoid spreading "unverified information" on social media. Nonetheless, panic buying was reported at supermarkets in several neighbourhoods, with families seeking to stockpile food and essentials as a precaution.

The attacks mark one of the most significant security breaches in the Russian capital since the start of the war in Ukraine, raising uncomfortable questions for the Kremlin about the vulnerability of its air defences. Security has been stepped up across transport hubs and government buildings, with visible patrols by armed police and soldiers.

The Irish Government this morning issued an updated travel advisory for citizens in Russia, urging anyone in the Moscow region to remain vigilant and to follow the instructions of local authorities. The Department of Foreign Affairs said it was closely monitoring the situation and in contact with the small Irish community in the city.

The Dáil is expected to debate the escalation in the region later today, with several TDs calling for a renewed diplomatic push to de-escalate the crisis and to provide humanitarian assistance where possible.

International reaction has been swift, with EU leaders condemning attacks targeting civilian areas. The United Nations Security Council is scheduled to hold an emergency session this evening to discuss the deteriorating security situation in Moscow and its potential implications for the wider European region.

Gardaí have said there is no intelligence to suggest any risk to Irish citizens at present, but have encouraged those with relatives living in Moscow to remain in contact and to register with the embassy in the event of further developments.

The Kremlin has vowed a "firm response" to what it termed an act of "terrorism" on Russian soil, sparking concerns of a further escalation in retaliatory strikes against Ukrainian targets. As tensions soar and Moscow reels from the unprecedented attack, the coming days are likely to prove critical in shaping the next phase of the conflict.
headline: Multiple drone strikes across the Russian capital cause widespread panic and spark mass evacuations

text:
A man has sadly passed away in Cork following what authorities have described as a “medical incident”.

Emergency services were called to the scene in the Ballyphehane area on Tuesday afternoon, after reports were received of a man in distress. It’s understood the man, aged in his early 40s, was found unresponsive at a private property shortly after 2pm.

Gardaí and paramedics from the National Ambulance Service attended the scene promptly. Despite efforts to revive him, the man was pronounced dead a short time later. His body has since been removed to Cork University Hospital, where a post-mortem examination will be carried out to determine the exact cause of death.

Local sources indicate that, at this stage, foul play is not suspected, but Gardaí say they are conducting standard enquiries as part of their investigation. The area was cordoned off for a number of hours to allow for a technical examination, but has since reopened.

Neighbours in the area have expressed their shock and sadness at the news. Many have described the deceased as a quiet, friendly man who kept to himself but was well-liked locally.

Gardaí have appealed for privacy for the man’s family at this difficult time. A file will be prepared for the Coroner’s Court in due course.
headline: Man sadly passes away in Cork following “medical incident”

text:
Gatwick Airport has been ranked as the second-worst airport in Europe for flight delays, according to an annual survey released this week, sparking renewed frustration among Irish holidaymakers and business travellers alike. The report, compiled by the aviation analytics firm AirHelp, examined punctuality rates across more than 130 major European airports during the peak summer period, assessing millions of scheduled flights.

The findings show that almost 41% of flights departing Gatwick experienced delays exceeding 15 minutes, with an average delay time of 27 minutes recorded. Only Lisbon Airport performed worse in the rankings. Dublin Airport, frequently the subject of passenger complaints over security queues and parking shortages, fared notably better, ranking 28th worst in Europe, with 22% of flights delayed by more than 15 minutes over the same period.

Irish passengers are all too familiar with Gatwick’s shortcomings, as it serves as a popular route to London and onward connections with Aer Lingus and Ryanair. Anecdotal reports from passengers travelling between Ireland and the UK over the summer described “chaotic” scenes at check-in and significant disruptions to both inbound and outbound services.

AirHelp cited a combination of air traffic control staff shortages, ongoing construction works, and adverse weather events for the spike in disruptions at Gatwick. The airport, which pre-pandemic was among Europe’s busiest single-runway facilities, has struggled to recover to pre-Covid performance levels despite the return of large-scale international travel.

A spokesperson for Gatwick Airport defended the facility’s efforts to improve punctuality, saying significant investments are being made in terminal upgrades and that the airport is working “closely with airlines and ground handlers to minimise delays for passengers”. The spokesperson also noted that factors outside the airport’s direct control, such as airspace restrictions and strikes among French air traffic controllers, have had a knock-on effect on UK airports.

The knockback comes as the UK’s Civil Aviation Authority faces renewed calls from consumer groups for stricter enforcement of passenger compensation regulations. Under EU law, which the UK has retained since Brexit, travellers delayed for more than three hours may be entitled to compensation of up to €600, depending on the flight distance and circumstances of the delay.

Irish travel agents have warned that persistent delays at major UK airports could affect onward travel for those connecting to long-haul destinations via London. They advise passengers to allow extra time for transfers and to check for updates in advance of travel.

The Department of Transport said it is monitoring the situation closely and is in contact with UK counterparts regarding the impact of ongoing disruptions at Gatwick. Minister for Transport, Eamon Ryan TD, has called for “greater cooperation across Europe to address aviation staffing and capacity issues that are leading to unacceptable delays for passengers”.

Passengers are advised to familiarise themselves with their rights under EU Regulation 261/2004 and to retain all relevant documentation in case a claim is necessary. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) has published updated guidance for consumers seeking redress after flight delays or cancellations.

While Gatwick’s management argues that improvements are in the pipeline, for many Irish travellers, the latest data will come as little surprise, underscoring the ongoing challenges facing the European aviation sector as it grapples with increasing demand and lingering operational issues.
headline: Gatwick Airport earns dubious honor of second-worst European airport for delays

text:
Complaints about potholes on roads nationwide have reached alarming levels, with the situation in Cork drawing particular concern. New figures reveal that over 14,000 reports of potholes were lodged in Cork County in just the past year, sparking frustration among motorists and prompting renewed calls for urgent action by local authorities.

Across the country, drivers have been voicing their anger online and contacting their local representatives, citing damage to vehicles, disruption of travel, and concerns for safety. Potholes have emerged as a major issue following the harsh winter and a series of storms, adding further strain to already stretched council repair budgets.

In Cork, the scale of the problem has reached what many residents describe as “crisis point.” Local councillors have reported being inundated with calls, emails and social media messages from frustrated constituents who say they have had enough of dangerous road surfaces. Several incidents involving burst tyres and damaged suspensions have been reported, and some road users claim they have had near misses as a result of swerving to avoid holes or debris.

The situation is mirrored in other counties, with reports rising sharply in Dublin, Limerick, Galway and Waterford. Nationally, thousands of complaints have been received by local authorities. According to data provided by Transport Infrastructure Ireland, the number of pothole-related reports has more than doubled compared to last year.

Motorists are calling on the Government to allocate emergency funding to address what is now being described as a public safety issue. “We’re paying high rates of road tax and motor insurance and yet the roads are getting worse year by year,” said one Cork driver, who had to replace two tyres in as many months. “The Government needs to step up and fix the roads before someone is seriously injured.”

The Department of Transport said it had provided local authorities with €658 million in funding for regional and local roads this year, but acknowledged the challenges posed by recent severe weather. A spokesperson said that repairs are prioritised according to road use and risk, and urged the public to continue reporting potholes via the FixYourStreet.ie portal.

Meanwhile, AA Ireland has warned that recurring pothole damage can add hundreds of euros to the annual cost of motoring and pose particular hazards for cyclists and motorcyclists. The motoring organisation has called for stronger measures to ensure councils repair reported potholes within a set period.

Opposition parties in the Dáil have accused the Government of failing to keep pace with the growing backlog of road repairs. Sinn Féin’s spokesperson on Transport, Darren O’Rourke TD, said the current situation was “entirely unacceptable” and proof that decades of underinvestment are now taking their toll on communities across Ireland.

With reports still flooding in, local authorities are facing what many describe as an uphill battle to bring the country’s roads up to standard before next winter. For many motorists, patience is running out. As one Cork resident put it, “We’d have smoother roads in rural Spain than we do here. Something has to give.”
headline: Pothole complaints surge around Ireland with 14,000 reports in Cork alone

text:
Former President Mary Robinson and rock band U2 are due to receive the European Order of Merit at a ceremony in the Belgian city of Leuven later this month. The announcement has been met with mixed reactions, with some observers questioning whether the two Irish figures are still relevant on today’s European stage.

Mary Robinson, who served as President from 1990 to 1997 before her tenure as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, has maintained a high-profile presence through her advocacy for climate action and human rights. However, critics argue her influence has waned in recent years, with some pointing to her handling of the Dubai Princess Latifa affair in 2018, which attracted controversy and calls into question her judgement.

U2, fronted by Bono, emerged from the Dublin music scene in the late 1970s and went on to achieve international superstardom. Once hailed for their anthemic music and outspoken political activism, critics now argue that the band’s relevance has diminished, with their most recent albums receiving lukewarm responses compared to their earlier successes. Detractors claim Bono’s continuous global campaigning has become increasingly out of touch, and question the band’s tax arrangements, which have attracted negative publicity in Ireland.

The Order of Merit is awarded to individuals or organisations judged to have made significant contributions to European unity and values. Previous recipients include former German Chancellor Angela Merkel and French President Emmanuel Macron. Both Robinson and the members of U2 are expected to attend the ceremony, where they will receive honorary medals.

While some in government praised the announcement, others on social media expressed scepticism, asking whether the award is a genuine recognition of Irish achievement or merely a nod to well-connected familiar faces. A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs welcomed the news, stating that "Ireland’s ongoing contribution to the European community continues to be recognised at the highest levels," but others suggested that fresh talent should be celebrated instead.

The European Order of Merit organisers defended their decision, stating that both Robinson and U2 had inspired millions across the continent. However, with calls for a new generation of Irish voices to be acknowledged on the world stage, the accolade is certain to reignite debate about the true impact of Ireland’s most famous names abroad.
headline: Two has-beens? Mary Robinson and U2 are being awarded European Order of Merit

text:
A dramatic incident unfolded at Dublin Airport yesterday evening after Gardaí stormed a Ryanair flight arriving from Manchester, following a mid-air altercation described by witnesses as a “shirt ripping brawl”.

Passengers on board flight FR553 reported scenes of chaos as a row erupted in the rear section of the aircraft approximately 30 minutes before landing. One passenger told The Liberal that shouting quickly escalated to physical violence, with “lads tearing the shirts off each other, drinks flying, and people scrambling to get out of the way”.

The pilot alerted Dublin Airport authorities to the disturbance, requesting Garda assistance on arrival. Airport Police, supported by uniformed Gardaí, met the aircraft on the tarmac upon landing at approximately 18:20. Eyewitnesses said several Gardaí boarded the plane immediately. “The guards sprinted up the steps and within minutes, they had a few of the fellas up and marched off in handcuffs,” another passenger said. “Everyone was shaken – there were kids nearby crying.”

In a statement issued late last night, An Garda Síochána confirmed that “Gardaí attended the scene of a public order incident on board a flight which landed at Dublin Airport. Two males, aged in their 20s and 30s, were arrested at the scene and detained at Ballymun Garda Station under Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act, 1984.”

No serious injuries were reported, though the HSE National Ambulance Service was called to assess a number of passengers. Ryanair confirmed the incident in a short statement, noting that “the safety and well-being of our customers and crew is our number one priority and this is now a matter for local authorities”.

It is understood the flight had been delayed on departure from Manchester, with tensions reportedly simmering among certain groups on board. Other passengers commended flight attendants for their attempts to calm the situation until Gardaí arrived, with one passenger telling The Liberal, “The crew did all they could, but it was chaos.”

Investigations are ongoing, and Gardaí are appealing for witnesses or anyone with mobile phone footage of the incident to come forward. The two arrested men remain in custody as of this morning.
headline: Gardai storm Ryanair flight in Dublin after mid air ‘shirt ripping brawl’

text:
The Government is facing renewed criticism over its handling of the accommodation crisis as significant numbers of registered tourist beds continue to be allocated to housing migrants, leaving many in the hospitality sector furious. Hoteliers, guesthouse owners and local business groups have accused officials of prolonging a ‘short-sighted’ policy that is damaging Ireland’s tourism industry and local economies.

Despite previous assurances from the Department of Integration that the reliance on tourist accommodation would be phased out, latest figures reveal that thousands of hotel, hostel, and B&B beds across the country remain contracted to the State to house asylum seekers and refugees. Industry representatives claim this is resulting in cancelled bookings, job losses, and a major hit to the summer season – typically a lifeline for rural and coastal communities.

Concerns have been voiced in popular tourist hotspots such as Killarney, Westport, and Galway, where up to half of available tourist beds are reportedly unavailable to visitors. Councillors have described it as ‘an existential threat’ to the tourism sector, while some local Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael TDs admit privately that pressure is mounting from constituents fearing for the future viability of their businesses.

Paul Gallagher of the Irish Hotels Federation said, “The ongoing commandeering of tourist accommodation is unsustainable and deeply unfair to businesses who invested in providing world-class hospitality. The government is making empty promises about ending these contracts, but in reality, very little has changed on the ground.”

Figures provided to the Oireachtas last week show over 20,000 beds originally registered for tourist use remain filled via State contracts with various accommodation providers. Industry sources warn the loss in potential revenue could run into hundreds of millions of euro, while local service businesses also report a significant decline in passing trade.

Meanwhile, community groups and opposition politicians have criticised what they describe as the Government’s lack of transparency. Sinn Féin spokesperson on Integration, Pa Daly TD, accused the Department of keeping the public in the dark: “Communities are being left to deal with the consequences of decisions made in Dublin. There is no proper consultation or planning for the pressure placed on local services and on tourism jobs.”

The Tánaiste, Micheál Martin, defended the Government’s approach, citing the unprecedented scale of arrivals and the necessity to honour Ireland’s humanitarian commitments. “We are working to expand alternative accommodation and reduce reliance on hotels and guesthouses, but this is a complex process. Our priority remains providing shelter to people fleeing war and persecution,” he told reporters.

Yet, for many in the tourism trade, patience is wearing thin. “It’s all very well to talk about compassion, but what about compassion for Irish families and workers who rely on a decent tourist trade to keep their heads above water?” said Mary O’Donoghue, who runs a family-owned guesthouse in County Clare.

With the peak tourist season now underway, calls are growing louder for the Government to accelerate the development of alternative accommodation solutions for migrants and to give clarity to the hard-pressed hospitality sector about when – or if – tourist beds will be returned to their intended use.
headline: Govt slammed as still a huge number of registered tourist beds are being used to house migrants

text:
Footage circulating widely online has sparked outrage in Wexford after a violent altercation involving groups of foreign men was filmed in the Courtown area. The incident, which took place late on Thursday night near a premises currently housing asylum seekers and refugees, has led to growing calls for public demonstrations, with concerned locals demanding action from the government.

Residents in Courtown, long a popular seaside resort in North Wexford, say they are fearful after what witnesses described as a “mob-style brawl” erupted on Main Street. Mobile phone footage, which has since gone viral on social media, shows at least a dozen men engaged in fighting, with shouting and chaos spilling onto the roadway. At least one person appeared to be armed with a stick or metal bar.

Gardaí confirmed to The Liberal that officers responded to a public order incident in the town and that an investigation is underway. They have appealed for witnesses and urged people not to share unverified reports. No arrests have yet been made, but the incident remains under active investigation.

Locals have expressed anger and frustration, claiming the government has failed to consult with or protect the community following the opening of migrant accommodation in the town. "This is not the first time we've had trouble since they started moving people in here," said one resident, who did not wish to be named for fear of reprisals. “We don’t feel safe on our own streets anymore.”

Community groups and local activists are now calling for peaceful protests outside the premises in question. Flyers and social media posts have begun circulating, encouraging townspeople to “stand up for Wexford” and demand that the government address what they say are growing security concerns linked to the increasing number of asylum seekers being housed in the region.

Wexford TDs in both government and opposition have faced mounting criticism for what some see as a lack of action and transparency. Calls have also been made for the Minister for Justice, Helen McEntee, to visit Courtown and meet directly with residents affected by recent events. In a statement, a spokesperson for the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth said that all residents in international protection accommodation are expected to comply with Irish law and that any breaches would be dealt with by the Gardaí.

The Liberal understands that the HSE and local community services have been made aware of heightened tensions and are monitoring developments. While some local groups are calling for calm and urging against any escalation, others insist that urgent action is needed to prevent further incidents and to address what they describe as “plantations” being forced upon rural Ireland without proper safeguards.

As the investigation continues, Gardaí have increased patrols in the area to reassure the public and maintain order. The situation remains tense, with local representatives urging all sides to act responsibly.
headline: Calls for protests in Wexford after footage of mob violence amongst foreign men living in migrant plantation in the Courtown goes viral

text:
Incidents of unruly passengers on board flights involving Ireland have soared to alarming levels, with new figures showing they have more than tripled in the past year. Data released by the Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) reveal a sharp rise in disruptive behaviour amongst air travellers using airports across the country.

Reports of passengers refusing to comply with crew instructions, engaging in drunken or abusive behaviour, and even physically assaulting others mid-flight have climbed steeply since the ending of most Covid-19 travel restrictions. Aviation sources say January to May 2024 saw over 130 reported cases of severe passenger disruption, compared to just 40 cases during the same period last year.

The surge in incidents has prompted calls for tougher penalties against those caught causing havoc at 30,000 feet. Under existing legislation, disruptive behaviour can result in fines of up to €5,000 or imprisonment for up to 12 months, but aviation experts warn that enforcement is patchy and convictions are rare.

One high-profile incident on a recent Ryanair flight from Dublin to Malaga forced the captain to divert to Bordeaux, where French police removed two intoxicated passengers who allegedly fought with each other and verbally abused crew. In another case reported by Aer Lingus staff, a passenger travelling from Cork to Lanzarote was restrained by crew and fellow passengers after reportedly attempting to open an emergency door mid-flight.

A spokesperson for the IAA described the rise as “deeply concerning”, noting that aggressive behaviour not only endangers crew and other passengers, but also diverts critical resources and risks costly flight diversions. “We are urging all air travellers to behave responsibly. Disruptive incidents will not be tolerated, and offenders can expect the full rigour of the law,” they said.

The Irish Airline Pilots’ Association has echoed those concerns, with union representatives saying that flight and cabin crews now face “heightened risks” due to what they call a “culture of disregard” that has emerged since the return of mass travel. “Flight crews have a duty of care for the safety of everyone on board. When passengers behave in a dangerous or threatening manner, it puts lives at risk and creates unnecessary fear and stress,” said Captain Brendan O’Sullivan of the association.

Dublin Airport Authority has confirmed it is working closely with Gardaí to ensure that unruly passengers are identified and prosecuted, and that airlines are being encouraged to share information about offenders. Gardaí at the airport say they have already increased patrols and are ready to arrest suspects on arrival, where necessary.

Justice Minister Helen McEntee has told the Dáil that she is considering proposals for new on-the-spot fines and lifetime bans for serial offenders. “Air travel must be safe for every passenger and crew member. Disruptive and violent behaviour will not be tolerated under any circumstances,” she said.

Airlines are also urging passengers to drink responsibly and to be aware that staff have a legal responsibility to refuse service when necessary. “Most people just want to get to their destination safely and without drama,” said a Ryanair spokesperson. “A tiny minority are spoiling it for everyone else.”

The IAA is urging anyone who witnesses disruptive behaviour on board to alert cabin crew immediately, and has reminded members of the public that such offences are prosecuted in Irish courts, regardless of where the incident occurs. With summer holidays underway and record numbers of Irish people travelling abroad, all eyes are now on how authorities will respond to keep Irish skies safe.
headline: Incidents of unruly passengers on airplanes have more than tripled in the past year

text:
Irish Rail is reportedly mulling over the introduction of vending machines on its inter-city train services, as part of efforts to improve on-board amenities and generate additional revenue. While the proposal remains at an early stage, sources within the company suggest that talks are underway regarding the feasibility of installing snack and beverage dispensers on popular routes, including the Dublin-Cork and Dublin-Galway lines.

At present, passengers on inter-city trains rely on trolley services for refreshments, but these have faced criticism in recent times over limited stock availability and restricted operating hours. Commenting on the reports, a spokesperson for Irish Rail confirmed that the company is “actively reviewing” various options to enhance customer experience, though no final decisions have been taken.

The potential move comes after persistent complaints from commuters about the lack of accessible food and drink, especially during busy periods or when trolley operations are suspended. In addition, Irish Rail has faced growing pressure to modernise its services in line with international rail operators, many of whom have adopted automated vending solutions for several years.

Should the plan go ahead, passengers could see machines stocked with snacks, soft drinks, tea and coffee, as well as cashless payment options. However, trade union representatives have voiced concerns over the possible impact on jobs, with fears that vending machines could eventually replace some catering staff.

There are also questions around practical issues such as machine maintenance, security, and the challenges of operating electronic devices on a moving train. Some regular users have taken to social media to voice their support for the proposal, citing the convenience and reliability of vending machines compared with the current set-up.

Irish Rail is expected to launch a public consultation in the coming months to gauge demand and seek feedback on the proposal. Any rollout of vending machines would require approval from the National Transport Authority and close coordination with staff representatives.

The move is part of a broader review of rail services nationally, as passenger numbers continue to recover following the pandemic. Irish Rail recently announced multi-million euro investments in new carriages and station upgrades, with the aim of boosting satisfaction among rail users.

The Department of Transport has declined to comment on reports regarding vending machines, but a spokesperson reiterated the government’s commitment to enhancing Ireland’s public transport offering. Further announcements from Irish Rail are anticipated later this summer.
headline: Irish Rail reportedly considering setting up vending machines on inter-city services

text:
Sales of electric cars across Ireland have taken a nosedive yet again, with the latest figures from the Society of the Irish Motor Industry (SIMI) revealing a dramatic drop in registrations for the second consecutive month. The bleak numbers come as motorists increasingly question the viability, cost, and infrastructure of electric vehicles, despite repeated government assurances and multi-million euro incentives.

Industry data shows a sharp year-on-year decline of more than 30% in electric vehicle (EV) registrations for April, marking the most significant fall since the Government launched its ambitious climate targets. In contrast, sales of traditional petrol and diesel models remain steady or are even seeing modest gains, as Irish drivers flock to more familiar, reliable options.

Motor trade insiders are pinning the blame on a host of factors, including surging vehicle prices, continued concerns about range anxiety, and a widespread lack of confidence in the public charging network. Critics say the EV rollout has been badly mismanaged, with patchy charger coverage and persistent technical issues facing those who do make the switch.

One Cork car dealer told The Liberal: “We are seeing interest fall off a cliff. People are being put off by the price and stories from neighbours about queues at chargers or home installations costing a fortune. The Government keeps pushing but ordinary people are simply not buying it – literally.”

Concerns over the real-world costs of EV ownership, including expensive insurance premiums, higher repair bills, and the looming prospect of battery replacement, have turned many prospective buyers away. Some have also raised doubts over whether the promised environmental benefits actually materialise when the full manufacturing and disposal cycle is considered.

The Department of Transport remains adamant that Ireland will hit its goal of nearly one million EVs on the road by 2030, a target described by some industry observers as “wildly unrealistic” given the current pace of uptake. This comes despite prominent public investments and grant schemes aimed at making EVs more affordable and accessible to the average motorist.

The latest figures will add to growing pressure on Minister Eamon Ryan and his Green Party colleagues, who have championed the electric revolution as central to the Government’s climate plan. However, opposition TDs are now demanding an urgent review of the policy, with Sinn Féin’s Darren O’Rourke TD calling for “a reality check instead of the same press releases and photo ops”.

Many householders are opting to hold onto their petrol and diesel cars for longer, citing ongoing concerns about the second-hand value of EVs and the uncertainty around future regulations or taxation on the vehicles.

With spring drawing to a close and the peak car-buying season looming, the slump in electric vehicle demand spells fresh trouble for the Government’s green targets, potentially derailing key promises made in the Programme for Government. For now, the road ahead for Ireland’s electric car market looks more uncertain than ever.
headline: Plummeting! Electric car sales had a massive slump again over the past month

text:
Green Party TD and Minister for Children, Roderic O’Gorman, has urged the Irish public to resist calls to support independents in the next general election, claiming that a government propped up by non-party TDs would jeopardise progress on climate action and housing.

Speaking at a party event in Dublin city centre, Minister O’Gorman cautioned that “opportunistic independents” might be tempted to prop up a coalition after the next election in exchange for localised deals and “parish pump priorities,” rather than the type of stable and coherent governance the country needs.

“We’re facing the biggest challenges of our time—climate breakdown, a housing crisis, the need for proper childcare and investment in our public services. Now, more than ever, we need leadership and clear choices, not a patchwork of independents striking side deals for their own constituencies,” he said.

The Green Minister’s warning comes as recent opinion polls suggest a significant rise in support for independent candidates, amid mounting frustration with the Government over spiralling accommodation costs, record rent levels and perceived failures to get to grips with the cost-of-living crisis. Current polling points to a fragmented Dáil after the next election, with Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil struggling to reach a majority even with their Green Party partners.

Minister O’Gorman insisted that only established parties are equipped to provide the necessary stability, and claimed that a government relying on independents “would stall the climate action agenda, put housing delivery further at risk, and lead to backroom deals instead of accountable policies.”

His comments have already been criticised by a number of high-profile independent TDs, including Roscommon-Galway’s Michael Fitzmaurice and Kerry’s Danny Healy-Rae, both of whom accused the Government of being out of touch with rural Ireland and dismissed suggestions that independents are merely looking for favours.

“This is typical scaremongering. The people know who stands up for them when it matters, and it’s not the Greens,” said Michael Fitzmaurice.

Danny Healy-Rae added that “the reason so many are turning to independents is because the parties sitting in Government have ignored ordinary people.”

Voters are expected to go to the polls within the next twelve months, with the timing now likely to shift from autumn 2024 to early 2025 following recent statements by Taoiseach Simon Harris. The Greens, meanwhile, are under pressure to show results in delivering affordable housing and hitting emissions targets amidst mounting public anger.

Minister O’Gorman finished his remarks by saying, “There are difficult decisions ahead. That’s why I’m asking the Irish people to look at who can deliver real progress, and not to be seduced by those promising easy fixes without responsibility.”

Government sources have privately conceded that the next Dáil will likely see a record number of independents returned, raising the prospect of complex negotiations to form the next coalition administration.
headline: Please don’t do it! Green’s Roderic O’Gorman warns public against independents propping up coalition

text:
Choosing to restore your floors rather than replace them is a decision more and more Dubliners are making, and with good reason. From period redbricks in Portobello to city centre cafés or the classic Georgian office buildings across Merrion Square, floor restoration services are proving essential for maintaining both the beauty and value of our capital’s properties.

Many of Dublin’s homes and businesses were built long before the era of disposable interiors. Hardwood, parquet, and traditional stone flooring are common features in older buildings, and when properly cared for, these surfaces can last generations. Over years of use, even the toughest floors show their age—scratches, dullness, and general wear can set in, leaving interiors looking tired. That’s where professional floor restoration comes in, offering not just a facelift, but a preservation of original character.

It’s not simply an aesthetic matter. For homeowners, a well-maintained floor can mean an increase in property value, especially in competitive areas where buyers are seeking authentic, high-quality finishes. For business owners, first impressions count. Whether it’s a hotel lobby or a restaurant dining area, a gleaming floor communicates attention to detail and pride in the premises, which can be crucial in attracting and retaining customers.

Professional floor restoration companies in Dublin use state-of-the-art equipment alongside traditional techniques, striking a balance between efficiency and craftsmanship. Sanding, sealing, staining, and polishing can restore wood floors to their former glory without the need for costly replacements. For natural stone and tiles, cleaning and sealing can revitalise dulled surfaces and prevent future staining. The work is often less disruptive—and cheaper—than most would expect. Many services offer flexible scheduling, including overnight and weekend work, to minimise downtime for businesses.

Sustainability is another key factor. In an era when environmental awareness is growing, retaining and rejuvenating existing floors rather than sending tonnes of material to landfill aligns with national efforts to reduce waste. Restoring old floors often uses fewer resources than installing new ones and supports the circular economy. Many specialist companies source eco-friendly oils, varnishes and polishes, ensuring a minimal impact on both indoor air quality and the wider environment.

Cost is always a consideration, but restoration can represent real value for money. The process typically costs a fraction of a new installation, and can highlight original features that simply can’t be replicated with modern materials. Government grants and incentives for heritage conservation occasionally apply, particularly in protected structures, making the process even more accessible.

The demand for these services is reflected in the number of skilled tradespeople operating across the city. From Rathmines to Drumcondra, companies cater to every need and budget, with many offering free consultations and tailored advice. It’s not uncommon to see clients marvel at the results—floors previously hidden under carpets or dulled by decades of footfall shining like new, their natural patterns and grains visible once more.

Ultimately, floor restoration is about more than maintenance; it’s about honouring Dublin’s built heritage while ensuring comfort and style in the 21st century. In a city where so much history lies underfoot, investing in professional restoration is a practical, sustainable, and aesthetically rewarding choice for homes and businesses alike.
headline: Why Floor Restoration Services in Dublin Are Essential for Homes and Businesses

text:
Russell Brand has expressed his gratitude to his supporters following what he described as a "distressing week" amid ongoing allegations against him. The British comedian and online commentator took to his social media channels over the weekend, stating he was "deeply moved" by the outpouring of support during what he called "trying times".

Brand, who has built a substantial following for his commentary and podcasting, remains at the centre of media attention in Britain and internationally after several serious allegations emerged earlier this month. The allegations, which Brand strenuously denies, have led to widespread debate online and in mainstream media, with supporters and detractors voicing strong opinions.

In a video posted to his followers, Brand claimed he was the subject of a “coordinated media campaign” and criticised what he described as a lack of due process, while reiterating his previous denials. He thanked his audience for standing by him, saying the messages of support had “made a real difference”.

The controversy has prompted further scrutiny of Brand’s past work and his public appearances, as several organisations and platforms have moved to distance themselves from him. In the UK, police confirmed they are assessing the information handed to them, but as of yet, no criminal charges have been brought.

Here in Ireland, Brand’s past shows and podcast appearances have enjoyed a sizeable audience. Social media reaction locally has mirrored the divided views seen in the UK, with #IStandWithRussellBrand trending on X (formerly Twitter) in recent days. Some Irish commentators have highlighted the need for due process and the presumption of innocence, while others have voiced support for those coming forward.

No Irish event organisers have publicly commented to date, but sources in the entertainment industry have said bookings and promotional partnerships with Brand are being "reviewed" pending further developments.

The allegations come amid growing debate over the role of influencers, online personalities, and traditional media in shaping public opinion and the reputational consequences faced by high-profile figures. Brand’s situation has again raised questions about trial by media and the balance between public interest and fair treatment.

The matter remains under investigation in the UK. Brand has said he will continue to share updates directly with his supporters and intends to “stand firm” in the face of what he terms “unprecedented” pressure.
headline: Russell Brand thanks his supporters after “distressing week”

text:
The Government has announced fresh measures to clamp down on short-term letting in larger towns and urban centres, in a move critics say is another overreach by central authorities who think “they know best” for everyone in the country. The latest regulations, which are due to come into force before the summer, will see strict limits placed on how many properties can be let for short stays on popular platforms such as Airbnb and Booking.com.

Minister for Housing Darragh O’Brien defended the plans, insisting they are needed to address the ongoing housing crisis, but opposition TDs, property owners, and local tourism operators have blasted the move as heavy-handed and anti-rural. Property owners in Galway, Limerick, Cork and other major population centres will now be required to register their properties with local authorities, apply for costly planning permission, and in many cases, limit the number of days a dwelling can be let out to tourists or visitors.

Government figures claim these steps will free up vital housing stock for long-term rental and families, but many say it is just another example of policy being dictated from Dublin that ignores the realities of life outside the capital. Local councils will be tasked with enforcing the new regime, with on-the-spot fines expected for those who break the rules.

Speaking to The Liberal, one affected homeowner in Co Cork, who did not wish to be named, described the move as “nanny state nonsense” and said it would “destroy any chance of making honest extra income from our own homes.” Small business owners in the tourism sector have also warned the restrictions could lead to a drop in visitor numbers and further damage local economies still reeling from pandemic lockdowns.

A number of opposition TDs have called for an urgent rethink of the plans, with Independent TD Mattie McGrath labelling it “social engineering dressed up as housing policy.” Meanwhile, Sinn Féin’s Eoin Ó Broin said the step would do little to solve the core issues at the heart of the housing crisis and was simply “treating the symptoms, not the disease.”

The Department of Housing maintains that compliance will be strictly monitored and that Gardaí could be called in for persistent breaches. Critics remain unconvinced, warning that genuine tourism and the rights of homeowners are being sacrificed for a one-size-fits-all approach.

As the new rules loom, concerned citizens and stakeholders are watching closely to see if the Oireachtas will bow to pressure or double down on restrictions. The debate continues as many ask if Dublin bureaucrats really do know best for the rest of the country.
headline: We know best: Govt is restricting short term letting in larger towns

text:
Met Éireann has confirmed that Ireland’s all-time May temperature record has been shattered today, with a sweltering 30.5 degrees Celsius recorded in County Clare. The figure, reached at Shannon Airport shortly after 4pm this afternoon, surpasses the previous May record of 29 degrees set just last week, which itself had beat a record standing since 1997.

Forecasters have described the exceptional temperatures as "deeply concerning", warning that the current heatwave is part of an emerging pattern of extreme weather attributed to climate change. The national forecaster has reiterated its calls for the public to take extra care, particularly vulnerable groups including children, older people, and those with underlying health conditions.

The HSE has urged the public to stay hydrated, avoid unnecessary outdoor activity during peak afternoon hours, and to check on elderly neighbours. Emergency services have reported a surge in call-outs related to heat exhaustion, dehydration, and wildfires in parts of the midlands and west. 

The Department of Housing has also raised the wildfire alert to high, with the fire services battling several blazes in Co Galway and Co Offaly over the past 24 hours. The Department has reminded landowners that it is an offence to burn land or vegetation during the closed season.

Speaking to reporters this evening, a Met Éireann spokesperson said, “Today’s temperature is unprecedented for May in Ireland. While some may enjoy the sun, this is an alarming sign of shifting weather patterns. We are monitoring the situation closely and further warnings may be issued if conditions persist.”

The Government’s Climate Action Plan aims to address such extremes, but climate campaigners have said today’s record is yet another wake-up call for more decisive measures from the Oireachtas.

The exceptional conditions are forecast to continue through the weekend, with temperatures expected to remain in the high 20s in many areas. Met Éireann has advised the public to keep updated on any further weather advisories and to remain cautious as the heatwave shows no sign of abating.
headline: BREAKING: Met Eireann concerned as Ireland’s May record broken again with 30.5c

text:
Aer Lingus has cancelled a further 25 flights due to ongoing industrial action by pilots, as the row over pay and working conditions shows no sign of resolution. Travellers across the country have been left frustrated and uncertain, with thousands facing disrupted holiday plans during what should be one of the busiest weeks of the summer.

The airline confirmed that the latest wave of cancellations affects both short-haul and long-haul routes, including services between Dublin, Cork, and Shannon airports and key European cities. Many passengers have reported receiving notification of cancellations with less than 24 hours’ notice, leaving families and business travellers scrambling to find alternatives.

The dispute centres on pay increases sought by members of the Irish Air Line Pilots’ Association (IALPA), who are demanding a 24% pay rise to reflect inflation and what they describe as pay erosion during the pandemic. The management at Aer Lingus, however, has stated that such demands are “unrealistic” and would threaten the financial stability of the company.

IALPA president Evan Cullen accused Aer Lingus management of failing to engage in meaningful negotiations and said that pilots are determined to continue their campaign until a fair deal is reached. “We have made it clear that we are willing to negotiate in good faith, but Aer Lingus has left us with no choice but to escalate our action,” Mr Cullen said. Pilots began an indefinite work-to-rule on Wednesday, refusing to work overtime or accept roster changes, which has resulted in widespread disruption to the airline’s operations.

Aer Lingus has urged affected customers to check their flight status and has offered rebooking or refunds, though some passengers have expressed frustration at the lack of suitable alternatives or clear communication from the airline. The situation has been exacerbated by high demand for summer travel and limited capacity on other airlines.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin expressed concern over the escalation and called on both sides to return to the Labour Court for fresh talks. “It is vital that all parties seek a resolution as quickly as possible to prevent further disruption to passengers, especially families planning holidays, and to protect Ireland’s connectivity,” he said.

With the peak holiday season underway, the ongoing dispute has raised fears of further cancellations in the coming days. The Department of Transport has urged Aer Lingus and IALPA to find a compromise, warning that prolonged industrial action could damage the reputation of Irish aviation and harm the tourism sector.

Passengers are advised to monitor updates from Aer Lingus and to seek compensation where applicable under EU regulations. The airline has stated that it deeply regrets the impact on customers but insists its pay offer is both fair and sustainable in the long term. Negotiations are expected to continue, but as yet there is no indication of an imminent breakthrough, leaving the travel plans of thousands of Irish consumers in limbo.
headline: Aer Lingus cancels a further 25 flights as pilots’ dispute continues

text:
A sickening case that has shocked both Ireland and the UK has concluded with Andrew Miller, a 53-year-old who abducted and sexually assaulted a young girl as she made her way to school, being sentenced to 20 years in prison. Miller, who also goes by the name Amy George, was handed the lengthy jail term at Edinburgh High Court after admitting to a string of depraved offences committed in the Scottish Borders last year.

The vile predator targeted the schoolgirl, aged just 12, as she walked alone on a February morning in 2023. Miller lured the child into his vehicle before driving her to his home, where he held her captive for more than a full day. During her harrowing ordeal, the little girl was subjected to multiple sexual assaults and deprived of food and her liberty.

The sentencing judge, Lord Arthurson, described the prolonged abuse as “planned and predatory,” declaring Miller’s actions “utterly depraved” and causing traumatic and lasting harm to his young victim. The girl’s family expressed their relief that justice had been served, but noted that their daughter’s suffering would take years to overcome.

Miller, who ran a local butcher’s shop, was a known member of the community. The revelation of his sickening actions has left neighbours and former customers reeling, with many expressing outrage that he was able to target a vulnerable child in such a calculated manner. The case has reignited concerns over child safety and the monitoring of sex offenders, with campaigners calling for tougher measures across both Ireland and the UK.

Gardaí have also been liaising with Police Scotland in recent months to ensure there are no links to any cases in Ireland, and have urged parents to remain vigilant, particularly as children travel to and from school. The HSE and various child protection agencies have increased support programmes for young people affected by sexual violence, emphasising the importance of early intervention.

Legal experts said the 20-year sentence reflected the severity of the crimes, though some victims’ advocates have argued that only a whole-life tariff would suffice for such sickening acts. The court also imposed an indefinite order restricting Miller’s contact with children and requiring lifelong registration as a sex offender.

The shocking case has prompted renewed calls from TDs and senators for greater cross-border cooperation in monitoring those convicted of sexual offences, and for improvements in the support offered to survivors and their families.

For now, Miller will begin his sentence behind bars, but the scars left by his depravity will be felt for years in the minds of his victim and her loved ones.
headline: Sicko Andrew Miller jailed for 20 years for abducting and sexually assaulting young girl on her way to school

text:
Gardaí conducted a large-scale search operation on wasteland in Dundalk, Co Louth, earlier today, in an area located near the former family home of Kyran Durnin. The operation, which involved members of the Garda Technical Bureau and local detectives, began at first light and continued throughout the day as officers meticulously combed dense scrubland off the Avenue Road.

Locals in the area reported an influx of Garda vehicles and uniformed officers in recent days, with the search focusing on undeveloped ground behind a row of houses. Gardaí erected cordons and closely guarded the scene, barring public access as specialist teams systematically examined the terrain and sifted through debris.

The search comes amid ongoing efforts to progress the investigation into the circumstances surrounding Mr Durnin, whose disappearance has sparked widespread community concern. Mr Durnin, a well-known figure in the locality, had previously lived in a nearby property before his high-profile disappearance.

A Garda spokesperson confirmed the operation this afternoon, stating that the search formed part of an “ongoing investigation” and that all lines of enquiry remained open. No further details were released. Forensic units were spotted mapping the site and using sniffer dogs in the hunt for evidence.

Residents expressed anxiety at the intensifying activity in the area. “It’s shocking to see so many guards here. We all remember what happened and hope for answers,” said one neighbour, who declined to be named.

Sources say that gardaí are acting on new information, although officials would not be drawn on whether the latest search is linked to any recent discoveries. The area searched has been described by locals as overgrown and infrequently accessed, raising questions about what may have led authorities to target the location at this time.

The investigation into Mr Durnin’s disappearance remains active, with appeals for information continuing. Gardaí have urged anyone who may have witnessed suspicious activity in the vicinity in recent months to come forward.

So far, no arrests have been announced and the results of today’s search have yet to be disclosed. An update from Garda Headquarters is expected in due course.
headline: Gardai hold major search in wasteland in Dundalk near former family home of Kyran Durnin

text:
A spokesperson for Cork Airport has urged members of the public to exercise caution if they are planning to travel to the facility over the coming days, amid warnings of continued adverse weather conditions across Munster.

The advisory comes as Met Éireann has issued a Status Yellow wind and rain warning for Cork and surrounding counties, with gusts of up to 90 kilometres per hour and persistent, heavy rain forecast to continue into the weekend. Localised flooding has already been reported in several areas, and motorists are being warned to expect dangerous driving conditions, particularly on minor roads.

In a statement released this morning, the Cork Airport spokesperson said, “We are strongly advising anyone planning to travel to or from Cork Airport to allow extra time for their journey and to check the latest travel updates before setting out. The safety of our passengers, staff, and all those travelling to the airport remains our top priority.”

Several flights have been delayed or cancelled due to the disruption, with the airport’s official social media channels providing regular updates for travellers. The spokesperson also encouraged passengers to check directly with their airline for the most up-to-date information on their flights.

Gardaí in Cork have called on all road users to drive with extreme care, reduce speed, and be alert for surface water or fallen debris on routes leading to the airport. The NRA has also asked drivers to avoid unnecessary journeys and to heed all official advice.

Cork Airport management have confirmed that additional staff have been deployed to assist passengers and ensure operations run as smoothly as possible given the challenging conditions. Extra maintenance crews are on standby to address any on-site flooding or hazards.

Passengers are reminded to adhere to all safety instructions and to consider using public transport where feasible, as several bus routes serving the airport remain operational but may be subject to delays. Weather conditions are expected to remain unsettled throughout the weekend, with further updates to be provided as the situation develops.
headline: Cork Airport spokesperson advises people to be cautious when traveling to the facility due to adverse weather conditions
