A prominent Turkish opposition figure has sparked controversy this week after alleging that major Turkish defence companies are actively supporting the Sudanese Army in its ongoing conflict. The claims were made by Özgür Özel, leader of Turkey’s main opposition Republican People’s Party (CHP), during a press conference in Ankara on Thursday afternoon.

Mr Özel stated that he had obtained “reliable evidence” suggesting Turkish-made drones, armoured vehicles, and ammunition had been supplied to the Sudanese Armed Forces over recent months, despite repeated calls from the United Nations for all countries to refrain from fuelling the violent civil war engulfing the North African nation.

The Turkish government has yet to formally respond to the allegations. However, local media in Ankara cited senior officials dismissing the claims as “unfounded”, insisting that all military exports are subject to strict oversight under current international embargoes. 

International human rights organisations have warned that the Sudanese Army and its rival paramilitary, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), have both been accused of grave abuses since fighting erupted in April 2023. The United Nations has raised particular concern about the proliferation of advanced weaponry in the theatre, and the risk it poses to civilian lives and regional stability.

In his remarks, Mr Özel claimed several Turkish defence firms—including state-linked and private manufacturers—were “turning a blind eye” to the unfolding humanitarian catastrophe in Sudan. He urged the Erdoğan government to come clean on any links between Turkish companies and parties to the Sudanese conflict, and called for an urgent investigation by the Turkish parliament.

According to Mr Özel, representatives of Turkish defence companies have travelled to Khartoum, the Sudanese capital, since the outbreak of hostilities. He cited shipping records and leaked correspondence as evidence of recent sales of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), spare parts and armoured transport.

“If proven true, this would place Turkey in direct contravention of UN resolutions and would be a stain on our country’s reputation,” Mr Özel said. “Our people do not want Turkish arms to be used in wars claiming innocent lives abroad.”

The Turkish Ministry of National Defence and the country’s largest arms producer, Aselsan, have denied involvement in arming Sudanese combatants, insisting their exports comply fully with Turkish law and international obligations. However, the allegations have drawn attention from the European Union and the United States, who both imposed arms embargoes on Sudan in response to the escalating conflict.

The Sudanese Embassy in Dublin has not commented on the issue. The Department of Foreign Affairs has said it is monitoring the situation in Sudan and supports all efforts to bring about a ceasefire and lasting peace.

The controversy has ignited debate amongst Turkish civil society groups and the expatriate Sudanese community in Ireland, with many calling for transparency and scrutiny around arms exports from EU candidate countries like Turkey. Concerns have also been raised in the Oireachtas by opposition TDs, who have demanded reassurances that Irish companies are not implicated in similar trade practices.

The Turkish parliament is expected to debate the issue in the coming weeks, as scrutiny of Turkey’s defence sector and its role in regional conflicts intensifies.
headline: Turkish Opposition Figure Accuses Turkish Defense Companies of Supporting the Sudanese Army

text:
A man originally from India has been found guilty in a Dublin court of sexually assaulting a young woman on a city-centre bus, in an incident which left the victim shaken and “very distressed”. The incident occurred on a packed Dublin Bus route last summer.

The court heard that the woman, in her early 20s, was sitting alone near the back of the bus travelling through the capital when the man, who is not an Irish national, deliberately sat beside her despite multiple empty seats being available. Eyewitnesses described the man’s behaviour as “creepy” and “persistent”, according to evidence presented.

The accused, who had come to Ireland in recent years, proceeded to grope the woman inappropriately despite her clear discomfort and attempts to move away. The woman told the court that she repeatedly asked the man to stop and tried to attract the attention of other passengers.

The judge at Dublin District Court remarked on the “serious invasion of personal space and safety” suffered by the victim. CCTV footage from the bus was shown to the court, with the judge noting that it corroborated the victim’s account.

Gardaí arrested the man after the woman managed to alert the bus driver, who notified authorities at the next stop. The perpetrator, who has been living in rented accommodation in the city, claimed it was a misunderstanding. However, the jury rejected his version of events, and he was found guilty of sexual assault.

Sentencing is due to take place early next month. The court also heard that the victim has suffered ongoing anxiety as a result of the incident and has been reluctant to use public transport alone since.

This case has sparked renewed debate over the government’s approach to migration and public safety in Dublin, with opposition TDs highlighting the failure to protect Irish women from similar attacks. Calls have been made for the Minister for Justice to introduce tougher deterrents and review the screening process for arriving migrants.

Dublin Bus and the Gardaí have urged anyone experiencing or witnessing inappropriate behaviour on public transport to report it immediately. A spokesman for Dublin Bus said they are “committed to the safety and welfare of our passengers and staff”, and that additional patrols and CCTV monitoring are being considered.
headline: ‘Creepy’ migrant from India found guilty of groping woman on bus in Dublin

text:
A migrant who launched a violent attack on a female jogger in a popular Dublin park has been exposed as a ‘genderfluid’ sex offender with a staggering 27 different aliases, it has emerged. The individual, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was apprehended by Gardaí last week following an early morning incident in the vicinity of St Anne’s Park, Raheny.

According to sources, the suspect, who presents as both male and female, initially gave Gardaí multiple false names during questioning. It was only after intensive checks involving Interpol and Europol databases that the true extent of their criminal history came to light. The person has previously been convicted of sexual offences in several European countries, including Germany, France, and the Netherlands, and is subject to a European Arrest Warrant under one of their known identities.

The DPP is understood to be considering a raft of charges, including assault and false declaration to the authorities. The attack, in which the victim sustained minor physical injuries but has spoken of “lasting trauma”, has reignited public debate around the vetting and monitoring of migrants with criminal histories entering Ireland. Locals have expressed outrage that the assailant, who was in receipt of State supports and residing in emergency accommodation in North Dublin, was able to evade detection for so long.

Calls are mounting for the Justice Minister, Helen McEntee, to explain how an individual with such an extensive criminal portfolio managed to slip through immigration and Garda vetting systems. “The safety of women and girls using our parks is not negotiable,” said one local community organiser, criticising what she called “systemic failures” in the Department of Justice’s oversight.

Gardaí have confirmed that they are liaising with police forces across Europe to clarify the full scope of the suspect’s background. The investigation remains ongoing, and further charges are expected to be brought. The female jogger is receiving support from victim services and is expected to recover physically from her ordeal. 

Opposition TDs have called for an emergency review of asylum seeker screening procedures, with some raising questions in the Dáil about the ability of State agencies to protect the public from repeat offenders. The case has stoked further tensions in communities already concerned over recent incidents involving migrants and has prompted renewed debate over government policy on refugee integration and monitoring.
headline: Migrant who attacked female jogger exposed as ‘genderfluid’ sex offender with 27 aliases

text:
A group of pro-migrant activists gathered in Dublin city centre this afternoon, vowing to fight back against what they described as a growing “anti-migrant” sentiment across Ireland. Carrying banners reading “Refugees Welcome” and chanting slogans supporting asylum seekers, the demonstrators claimed their rally was the first step in a renewed campaign to promote settlement of migrants in Irish communities.

The event, which organisers said drew several hundred people, assembled outside the GPO on O’Connell Street and included members of left-wing political parties, trade union representatives, and refugee advocates. Prominent speakers included People Before Profit TDs and figures from the Irish Refugee Council. The group accused government ministers and certain media outlets of fuelling division and scapegoating genuine refugees for social problems such as the housing crisis.

Attendees held signs with hashtags like “No Human is Illegal” and “End Direct Provision”, calling on the Government, including the Taoiseach Simon Harris and Minister for Integration Roderic O’Gorman, to accelerate the processing of asylum applications and to provide more accommodation resources. Multiple references were made to recent anti-migrant protests in small towns and rural communities, which organisers labelled as acts of intimidation orchestrated by “far-right agitators”.

One protester, Siobhán Maher from Tallaght, told The Liberal: “We’re sick of the narrative that blames people fleeing war and persecution for the problems caused by bad policy from Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael. Ireland has a proud history of emigration, and we can’t turn our backs on people in need.”

However, some bystanders voiced concern over the demonstration. “I think there needs to be an honest conversation about resources,” said a local woman who did not wish to be named. “There are plenty of Irish families on housing lists, and people feel like they’re not being listened to.”

Gardaí maintained a visible but low-key presence at the event, which passed off peacefully without incident. O’Connell Street remained open to traffic throughout the demonstration.

Organisers say today’s rally marks the beginning of a series of actions in the coming months, including planned outreach in towns where opposition to new refugee accommodation centres has been reported. They insist they will not be intimidated by what they call “the anti-migrant fringe”, and have called on more citizens to join their movement.

The Government has faced criticism over its handling of migration and accommodation shortages, with the HSE and Department of Integration under sustained pressure to find suitable solutions for both asylum seekers and the Irish homeless population. Meanwhile, the public debate continues to intensify, with further protests—both for and against the resettlement of refugees—expected in the weeks ahead.
headline: #RefugeesWelcome brigade protest in Dublin saying it’s the start of their campaign to buck anti-migrant trend

text:
A normally peaceful rural townland has been left shaken after residents reported a spate of anti-social behaviour allegedly carried out by a gang of so-called feral youths in recent weeks. Local people in the area, which is being withheld for security reasons, claim they have been terrorised by teenagers roaming the streets at night, intimidating elderly neighbours, vandalising property and causing widespread fear.

One resident, who spoke to The Liberal on condition of anonymity, described how a group of youths, ranging in age from early teens to late teens, have repeatedly gathered at a disused house at the edge of the village, lighting bonfires, drinking, and shouting obscenities late into the night. “It’s gotten completely out of hand. We can’t sleep. We’re afraid to let the young ones walk home from training or go to the shop after dark,” said the resident. “Last weekend they smashed up a neighbour’s garden wall and tried to set fire to a bin. People are living in fear.”

Locals have expressed frustration at what they see as an ongoing refusal by national media outlets and politicians to address the issue of youth crime in rural Ireland. “If this happened in Dublin there’d be uproar. But because we’re a small place, nobody cares,” another local told The Liberal. “The mainstream media seem to maintain a code of silence because it doesn’t fit the narrative. We’re just expected to put up with it.”

Attempts to contact the local Garda station were met with assurances that officers are aware of the disturbances and are stepping up patrols. However, several residents claim the response has been slow and ineffective. “They might drive by once or twice, but the kids just scatter and come back when the Gardaí are gone,” said one homeowner whose car was recently damaged.

The townland has a population of less than 500 and had previously enjoyed a low crime rate. However, locals say standards have slipped since a number of families moved to the area from outside, with some blaming changes in social housing policy and a lack of community engagement programmes. “There’s nothing for teenagers to do, no youth club or sports facilities, the council keeps cutting back,” said a concerned parishioner.

In a statement, a Garda spokesperson said: “Gardaí continue to respond to calls in the area and all incidents reported are being fully investigated. We would encourage anyone with information to come forward.” 

Despite these assurances, the sense of unease remains. “People don’t feel safe in their own homes. We want action before someone gets seriously hurt,” said another resident.

As local frustration grows, many are calling for a frank national conversation on rural crime and what they view as media reluctance to highlight such incidents outside of major cities. “We deserve the same attention and protection as any other part of the country,” a resident insisted. 

The Liberal will continue to monitor developments and provide a platform for those whose voices, they say, are too often ignored.
headline: Feral gang of youths terrorise quiet Irish townland as media maintains code of silence in face of such incidents

text:
Tributes have poured in for a woman aged in her 70s who died after getting into difficulty while swimming in the sea off the west coast over the weekend. The tragic incident occurred at a popular bathing spot near Enniscrone, Co Sligo on Sunday afternoon. Despite the swift arrival of emergency services, the woman was pronounced dead at the scene.

The alarm was raised shortly after 2pm when passers-by noticed the woman in distress in the water. Local lifeguards responded immediately, pulling her ashore and beginning CPR. The National Ambulance Service and members of the local Gardaí attended the scene, but sadly, all efforts to revive her were unsuccessful.

The woman, identified locally as a long-time resident of the area, was known for her love of the sea and daily swims. News of her sudden death has left the local community in shock, with neighbours and friends describing her as a warm, active person who was “always ready for a chat” and “a great supporter of community events”.

Cllr Tom Walsh, speaking to The Liberal, said: “This is a terrible tragedy for the family and for the whole Enniscrone community. Our thoughts and prayers are with her loved ones at this very difficult time.”

Gardaí confirmed that a file will be prepared for the Coroner’s Court in line with normal procedure, but foul play is not suspected.

The woman’s family have thanked locals and emergency responders for their efforts and support. Funeral arrangements are to be announced in the coming days.

The HSE and Water Safety Ireland have again urged the public to take precautions when swimming in open water, especially as improved weather brings more people to the coast. The organisation reminded swimmers to be aware of tide conditions and to never swim alone.
headline: Tributes paid to woman, aged in her 70s, who died after getting into difficulty in sea

text:
A fearless three-year-old boy in Australia has captured hearts worldwide after finding himself stuck inside a toy claw machine, much to the amusement of onlookers and staff alike.

The incident unfolded at a local shopping centre in the city of Brisbane, where the young adventurer reportedly squeezed through the prize chute of a claw grabber machine in pursuit of the soft toys inside. The child, who had been spending the afternoon with family, apparently saw the selection of plushies on display and decided to cut out the middleman – the claw itself.

Stunned passersby quickly raised the alarm, with staff at the amusements area initially unsure how best to free the boy without causing distress or damage to the machine. Security personnel alerted emergency services, and within minutes, local firefighters arrived on the scene to lend their expertise.

Eyewitnesses said the youngster was completely unfazed by the commotion, content to sit among the cuddly toys inside the glass cabinet. Video footage captured by shoppers showed the boy waving cheerfully to the crowd outside as his mother and arcade staff tried to reassure him through the glass.

Firefighters ultimately managed to open the back panel of the machine to safely extract the child, who emerged grinning and clutching a soft toy prize for his efforts. Neither the boy nor the machine suffered any harm in the rescue, which drew applause from relieved onlookers.

Local media reported that the child’s mother took the episode in good humour, joking that her son “certainly has a talent for getting into tight spots.” The shopping centre has since conducted a review of the machine, and operators have said they will look at ways to further secure access in order to prevent similar adventures.

No injuries were reported, and the boy is said to be “none the worse for wear” – but may have earned himself an unofficial ban from the arcade’s claw machines for the foreseeable future.
headline: Toy story! Unfazed 3-yr-old Australian boy gets rescued after he climbed into toy claw machine

text:
Gardaí have launched an investigation following a suspected arson attack in which several vehicles were set ablaze in the car park of a public house in County Meath overnight. Emergency services were called to the scene at around 2am at a well-known premises on the outskirts of Navan, after reports of multiple cars on fire.

It is understood that at least three vehicles were extensively damaged in the incident, with significant fire and heat damage sustained. Locals reported hearing loud bangs and seeing flames shooting up from the car park in the early hours of this morning, prompting a swift response from fire crews and Garda units.

A cordon remains in place at the scene as forensic specialists carry out a detailed examination. The vehicles are being removed for further technical analysis, while CCTV from the pub and surrounding area is being reviewed as part of the investigation.

No injuries have been reported, but gardaí have appealed to anyone who may have witnessed suspicious activity in the vicinity in the hours before the fires broke out to come forward. House-to-house enquiries are underway and detectives are appealing for any motorists who may have dashcam footage to contact Navan Garda Station.

Early indications suggest the fires were started deliberately, but investigators have not ruled out any line of enquiry. The motive for the attack remains unclear at this stage, and Gardaí have not confirmed whether it is linked to any local disputes or ongoing criminal activity.

The incident has caused considerable concern among residents in the area, with one local describing the act as “reckless and terrifying.” The pub remains open for business, but access to the car park is restricted as Gardaí continue their work.

Anyone with information is urged to contact the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111 or Navan Garda Station directly.

The investigation is ongoing.
headline: BREAKING: Investigation underway after a number of vehicles set alight in pub carpark in Co Meath

text:
Tánaiste Micheál Martin has praised former Dublin GAA manager Jim Gavin as an “excellent” and “wonderful” candidate for the Presidency, saying the ex-Air Corps pilot has the experience and temperament to “bring people together” in a time of division.

Speaking to reporters outside Government Buildings this morning, Mr Martin expressed strong personal support for Mr Gavin, whose name has emerged as a frontrunner to contest the Áras an Uachtaráin race next year. Mr Martin said he believes the Clondalkin native represents “the values that Irish people want in a President” and lauded his “outstanding achievements” leading the Dublin senior footballers to six Sam Maguire titles.

“All through his management of Dublin, Jim Gavin showed tremendous leadership and an ability to unite people from different backgrounds for a common goal,” said the Tánaiste. “He’s a wonderful candidate. He’s someone who has always served his country, both in the Defence Forces and in sport, and has the capacity to bring people together, which is deeply important in these times.”

Mr Gavin, 52, confirmed last week that he was considering requests to allow his name go forward for nomination to contest next year’s election, which would see Michael D. Higgins’ second term come to an end. While Mr Martin stopped short of a formal endorsement on behalf of Fianna Fáil, he said the party would “give serious consideration” to backing Gavin if he decided to run.

“He has shown real integrity and humility throughout his career. He has a deep understanding of Ireland’s history and its people,” Mr Martin said. “It’s early days but there’s no doubt he brings a unique set of skills to the table.”

The emergence of Mr Gavin as a potential candidate has thrown a new dynamic into the race, with several current and former politicians also expected to seek nominations. The Fine Gael leader, Simon Harris, declined to say whether his party would field a candidate but acknowledged Gavin’s “impressive track record”.

Meanwhile, Sinn Féin’s Mary Lou McDonald said the Presidential election should be “a contest of ideas and vision”, rather than “an establishment stitch-up”, and said her party would make an announcement in due course.

Under the Constitution, presidential candidates must secure the backing of at least 20 Oireachtas members or four local authorities. Mr Gavin has yet to indicate whether he would seek a party nomination or run as an independent.

Gavin, a qualified commercial pilot and former Commandant in the Air Corps, has been involved in several civic and voluntary organisations since stepping down as Dublin manager in 2019. Sources close to him say he is “seriously considering” entering the race, and describe him as “humbled” by the level of support from GAA circles and beyond.

The presidential election is due to be held in autumn 2025.
headline: He’s a wonderful candidate – Martin says presidential candidate Jim Gavin can ‘bring people together’

text:
RTÉ has come under renewed criticism after it emerged that the national broadcaster is set to outsource editorial research for state events, with the resulting bill to be footed by the Irish taxpayer to the tune of €180,000. The revelation has sparked outrage among viewers and taxpayers alike, many of whom have questioned why RTÉ, despite its significant public funding and licence fee, is unable to carry out such core duties in-house.

Details of the arrangement surfaced following queries to both RTÉ and the Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media. The outsourcing contract, reportedly set to run for twelve months, will cover editorial research for broadcasts of high-profile state occasions, including presidential visits, commemorations and other official ceremonies.

Critics say the move represents yet another instance of wasteful spending at the national broadcaster. Recent controversies have already put RTÉ under intense public scrutiny, with questions raised in the Dáil by several TDs about transparency and value for money. Some have called on Minister Catherine Martin to intervene and seek concrete assurances regarding the efficient use of taxpayer funds.

The sum of €180,000 is set against a backdrop of ongoing discussions around reforms to the TV licence system, which has seen declining compliance rates in the past year. Many Irish households have signalled their dissatisfaction with RTÉ’s stewardship of public money, especially in light of revelations about high executive salaries, hidden payments, and lavish expenses.

A spokesperson for RTÉ defended the decision, stating that the procurement of specialised editorial research was “essential to maintaining the highest standards of accuracy and impartiality for coverage of state occasions,” and claimed that the external expertise would help deliver programming “befitting the significance” of these national events.

However, the reasoning has done little to mollify critics, with some suggesting that qualified journalists and researchers already within RTÉ’s ranks could undertake the work as part of their existing roles, without the need for additional outside expenditure. Representatives for the National Union of Journalists have previously argued for stronger investment in in-house talent and resources.

The National Broadcaster has faced a string of crises in recent years, ranging from the payments scandal to questions over governance and accountability. The news of this latest outsourcing deal is likely to fuel further debate over RTÉ’s future, funding model, and the delivery of public service broadcasting in Ireland.

The Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media has said it will seek “full clarity” from RTÉ as to the nature of the expenditure and the selection process for the contract, but did not indicate whether any formal review or investigation would take place.

As the controversy unfolds, many are asking whether this latest instance of out-sourcing represents best practice, or yet another example of the mismanagement that has seen public trust in RTÉ erode in recent years.
headline: RTÉ to outsource editorial research for state events at a cost of €180,000 to the Irish taxpayer

text:
At least 36 people have died and dozens more have been injured after a catastrophic collision between a passenger train and a freight train in northern Greece late on Tuesday night. The crash occurred near the city of Larissa, around 380 kilometres north of Athens, and has been described by Greek authorities as the country’s worst ever rail disaster.

Emergency services worked through the night and into Wednesday morning to search the mangled wreckage for survivors, with the death toll expected to rise as rescue efforts continue. More than 80 people have been taken to hospital, several with serious injuries, according to the Greek fire service.

The passenger train, operated by Hellenic Train and carrying more than 350 people, was travelling from Athens to Thessaloniki when it collided head-on with the oncoming freight train shortly before midnight. Images from the scene show carriages derailed, twisted and engulfed in flames, with some coaches reportedly crushed almost beyond recognition.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has declared three days of national mourning and travelled to the scene to meet with emergency services and relatives of the victims. He described the crash as an “unspeakable tragedy” and vowed a full investigation into its cause. Early reports suggest that human error may have been a factor, with police detaining the stationmaster in Larissa for questioning.

Many of the passengers on board were believed to be students returning to Thessaloniki after a long holiday weekend. Survivors described scenes of chaos and terror, with some smashing windows to escape the burning carriages.

The government has set up a crisis helpline for relatives seeking information, while the Greek health ministry has made an urgent appeal for blood donations to help treat the wounded. Flags are flying at half-mast on all public buildings as a mark of respect.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has said that, at this stage, there are no reports of Irish citizens affected, but it is liaising with Greek authorities and monitoring the situation closely. The European Commission and leaders across the continent have offered condolences, with President Michael D Higgins sending a message of sympathy to his Greek counterpart.

This tragedy has raised fresh questions about Greece’s ageing rail infrastructure and the pace of modernisation efforts, with unions and transport experts warning that safety improvements have been long overdue. As rescue operations continue, the nation mourns those lost and anxiously awaits answers on how this devastating crash could have occurred.
headline: No fewer than 36 people dead following train collision in Greece

text:
World leaders are gathering in Rome today for the funeral of Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI, who died on New Year’s Eve at the age of 95. Thousands of mourners are expected to line St Peter’s Square for the historic ceremony, with senior politicians, royals, and church leaders from around the globe attending to pay their respects.

Taoiseach Leo Varadkar and President Michael D Higgins are representing Ireland at the funeral, accompanied by Tánaiste Micheál Martin and Irish Ambassador to the Holy See, Frances Collins. The Irish delegation joined mourners from across Europe, the Americas, Africa and Asia as the Vatican prepared for the rare event of a papal funeral presided over by a reigning Pope – Benedict’s successor, Pope Francis.

Crowds began arriving before dawn to secure a place, with Italian security officials estimating that over 100,000 people may be present. Gardaí have not warned of any security concerns for the Irish delegation, but the Department of Foreign Affairs continues to monitor the situation closely.

Benedict, born Joseph Ratzinger, was Pope from 2005 to 2013 before becoming the first pontiff in almost 600 years to resign. His resignation paved the way for the election of Pope Francis. Benedict’s legacy remains the subject of debate, both for his staunch defence of traditional Catholic doctrine and his handling of clerical sex abuse scandals – a topic of particular sensitivity in Ireland given the country’s own troubled history.

President Higgins issued a statement expressing condolences to Catholics in Ireland and worldwide, noting Benedict’s “intellectual contribution” to the Church. However, politicians including Labour leader Ivana Bacik TD and Social Democrats have called for continued vigilance in the protection of children and transparency within religious institutions, referencing the enduring impact of historical abuses.

The funeral Mass will include readings in several languages, prayer for global peace, and a final blessing. Pope Francis, despite recent health concerns, is expected to deliver the homily in person. Security has been tightened throughout Rome and Vatican City, with airspace restrictions and cordoned-off areas as Italian police, military and Vatican officials coordinate logistics.

Irish pilgrims and immigrants in Rome have spoken of their pride in seeing the national flag represented, with some attending the ceremony or leaving tributes at the Vatican. The Irish College Rome, which has educated priests for over four centuries, will also host a Mass of Remembrance later today.

Benedict will be interred in the Vatican crypt, alongside his predecessors. The Vatican has said the ceremony will be “solemn but simple”, in line with Benedict’s wishes. Dignitaries are expected to attend a reception afterwards, though the Department of Foreign Affairs has confirmed the Taoiseach will return to Dublin for Dáil business on Friday.

The death of Pope Benedict has prompted reflection in Ireland on the Church’s evolving role in society, with Mass attendances continuing to fall but Catholic traditions remaining deeply embedded in many communities. The Association of Catholic Priests and the Irish Bishops’ Conference have both called for prayer and dialogue in the coming days.
headline: World leaders travel to Rome for Pope Benedict’s funeral this morning

text:
It has emerged that Tánaiste Micheál Martin authorised the spending of €2,700 in taxpayer money on presents for former US President Donald Trump during an official St Patrick’s Day visit to Washington, D.C. The expenditure, charged to the Department of Foreign Affairs, reportedly included a Waterford crystal bowl and a selection of Irish craft items, presented to Mr Trump as part of the annual shamrock ceremony. 

The revelation has sparked criticism from opposition TDs and members of the public, who have questioned whether such extravagant gifts are a wise use of public funds at a time when many Irish families continue to struggle with the cost of living crisis. Speaking to The Liberal, Sinn Féin’s spokesperson for Public Expenditure, Mairéad Farrell TD, said the sum “beggars belief” and called for stricter guidelines on official gift-giving. 

According to records released under the Freedom of Information Act, the Department spent a total of €2,715.39 between the presentation bowl, a handmade piece from an Irish designer, and commemorative documents for President Trump and his team. The Department defended the purchases, citing the importance of diplomatic tradition and the “significant economic and political value” of maintaining cordial relations with the White House, particularly during the Trump administration.

However, many commentators have pointed out that the annual cost of these gifts is just one example of official excess at a time when frontline services are under pressure. The Health Service Executive has come under sustained criticism for waiting lists and funding gaps, and the government faces repeated calls to reallocate spending towards healthcare and housing. 

A source within the Department said the gifting of crystal bowls is a long-standing custom marking the strong ties between Ireland and the United States. “The bowls are considered a symbol of goodwill, but we recognise the need for careful stewardship of public money,” the source said.

The Tánaiste himself has not commented directly on the criticism, but a spokesperson for his office stressed that all spending was in line with standard protocol and approved by senior officials. The tradition of presenting shamrock to the sitting US President dates back to 1952 and is seen by many as an important opportunity to promote Irish interests in the world’s largest economy.

Nonetheless, there have been renewed calls for greater transparency in the costs associated with overseas visits by ministers and senior government officials. Deputy Peadar Tóibín of Aontú stated: “We have to ask if these traditions still fit with the spirit of public service in 2024, or if it’s time for a more modest approach.”

The Department of Foreign Affairs reiterated that all gifts presented to foreign dignitaries are “carefully considered” to reflect Ireland’s heritage and image on the world stage, but accepted that public concerns should be taken on board for future events.
headline: Martin spent €2,700 Irish taxpayer money on gifts for President Donald Trump

text:
A newly attested Garda was discovered by colleagues in a roadside ditch early this morning after abandoning their patrol car on the hard shoulder of the M1 motorway near Balbriggan, Co Dublin. The incident unfolded shortly before 3am, prompting a brief search operation involving multiple units from the local Garda station.

Motorists travelling northbound reported an unmarked Garda vehicle parked erratically with its hazard lights flashing, raising concerns for public safety. Responding officers arrived on the scene to find the vehicle unattended, with the engine still running and no sign of the driver.

A search of the area was swiftly conducted, and the rookie Garda—who only recently completed training at Templemore—was located approximately 200 metres from the car, lying in a ditch and reportedly disoriented. Emergency services attended the scene, and the individual was assessed by paramedics before being transported to Beaumont Hospital for further observation.

In a statement issued this morning, Garda Headquarters confirmed an "isolated incident involving a member of An Garda Síochána", noting that there was no evidence of criminality or threat to public safety. "The welfare of the member involved is the primary concern at this time," said a spokesperson.

Unconfirmed reports suggest the Garda may have experienced a medical episode while on patrol. Sources within the force have described the incident as "highly unusual" and have called for a review of support structures in place for probationer members, particularly those stationed in busy metropolitan divisions.

The Garda Representative Association has expressed support for the affected officer, highlighting the pressures faced by newly qualified members amid ongoing staffing shortages and increased workloads. "Our members are under enormous strain, often working in extremely challenging conditions with limited resources," a spokesperson said.

Garda management has launched an internal review and is liaising with the Health and Safety Authority as part of routine procedures. The M1 northbound was reduced to one lane for a brief period but has since fully reopened.

No injuries were reported to members of the public, and there is no indication of substance misuse or disciplinary issues. The Garda in question is currently on leave while supports are being put in place.
headline: Newbie Garda found in ditch after abandoning car on M1 motorway

text:
Met Éireann has issued a fresh nationwide weather warning this afternoon as severe weather conditions continue to intensify across the country. The forecaster is warning of heavy rainfall, strong winds, and the risk of localised flooding, urging members of the public to exercise extreme caution.

According to Met Éireann, the status yellow warning came into effect at midday and is set to remain in place until late tomorrow evening, with an orange warning possible for particularly affected western and southern counties if conditions worsen. Forecasters say persistent and, at times, torrential downpours are to be expected, with total rainfall accumulations likely to exceed 40mm in some areas.

The warning comes after several days of unsettled conditions, with parts of Munster and Connacht already experiencing flooding on roads, fallen trees, and power outages. Gardaí are urging motorists to avoid unnecessary journeys and to reduce speed, particularly on regional routes where surface water and debris pose a significant hazard.

A spokesperson for the National Emergency Coordination Group has confirmed that local authorities have been placed on high alert. Sandbags and flood defence barriers have been deployed in areas most at risk, with the Defence Forces on standby for assistance if the situation escalates further.

The Health Service Executive (HSE) has also advised vulnerable people, including the elderly and those with chronic health conditions, to remain indoors where possible and to ensure they have adequate supplies of medication, food, and heating.

Met Éireann’s Chief Meteorologist, Evelyn Cusack, said: “The current weather system is bringing a combination of high winds and intense rainfall. There is a real risk of hazardous driving conditions and flooding, particularly in low-lying and coastal areas. We ask everyone to keep up to date with the latest forecasts and heed official advice.”

Members of the public are being urged to check in on elderly neighbours and to report any emergency situations to their local Garda station. The Department of Education is monitoring the situation and has not ruled out school closures in the worst-affected counties should conditions deteriorate overnight.

In the meantime, citizens are advised to secure outdoor furniture, avoid walking or driving through floodwaters, and keep mobile phones charged in case of power disruption. For further information and regular updates, members of the public are encouraged to follow Met Éireann, the Gardaí, and the HSE on social media and local news channels.
headline: Met Eireann issues urgent new nationwide weather warning amidst deteriorating weather conditions

text:
A new report has found that overcrowding has reached critical levels in Irish prisons, prompting renewed concern over safety and rehabilitation within the State’s penal system. The Irish Prison Service’s latest figures reveal that a number of institutions are now operating well above their intended capacity, with some inmates forced to sleep on mattresses placed on cell floors.

The report shows that the national prison population has surged by more than 10% in the past year, with the most severe overcrowding observed at Mountjoy, Cloverhill, and Limerick prisons. Mountjoy, designed for 554 prisoners, routinely houses over 700, according to the figures released. Prison officers and advocacy groups have repeatedly raised the alarm about conditions, warning that cramped cells, lack of privacy, and limited access to facilities are fuelling tension and violence.

Fianna Fáil TD James Lawless said the situation was “unsustainable and unacceptable in a modern justice system,” calling on the Department of Justice to take immediate action. “The Government has been warned about this for years. We now have a situation where rehabilitation programmes are under threat because simply housing prisoners is taking priority”, he said.

Frontline staff have described fatigue and burnout from trying to manage “two to a cell or worse”, while the Irish Penal Reform Trust says that overcrowding undermines both the safety of prisoners and staff, as well as any attempts at meaningful rehabilitation. The Trust’s director, Saoirse Brady, said that “Ireland’s prisons are bursting at the seams. It is impossible to deliver services or maintain order in these conditions.”

Several TDs and Senators urged the Minister for Justice, Helen McEntee, to address the capacity issue as a matter of urgency. The Department has previously announced plans for new accommodation blocks at Limerick and Cork, but critics say these will not be complete for several years and will not keep pace with demand.

The Prison Officers’ Association has warned that the current environment breeds hostility, with assaults against both staff and prisoners rising sharply. “People are coming into an already tense atmosphere and there simply aren’t enough staff or resources to deal with the numbers. It’s a powder keg,” said one officer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission has highlighted the risk of human rights breaches if the State fails to provide adequate conditions. “Every person in custody is entitled to be treated with dignity and respect. Overcrowding, especially persistent overcrowding, puts that at risk”, its spokesperson said.

As the issue escalates, campaigners are calling on the Government to consider alternatives to custodial sentences for non-violent offences, and to invest in community-based sanctions. The Dáil Justice Committee is expected to discuss the issue further next week, with mounting pressure on the Government to take decisive action before the situation deteriorates further.
headline: Overcrowding is now a major issue is Irish prisons, report finds

text:
The Central Statistics Office (CSO) has published a new report revealing a significant income gap between Irish citizens and non-Irish nationals living and working in Ireland, with Irish citizens earning an average of €849.46 per week compared to €760.71 earned by their non-Irish counterparts – a difference of nearly €90.

The figures, drawn from the CSO’s Labour Force Survey for 2023, have sparked heated debate around issues of fairness, opportunity, and integration in Irish society. Some community activists and migrant spokespersons have described the disparity as “blatant racism,” arguing that non-Irish workers are being systematically underpaid and excluded from higher-earning jobs.

One Polish national working in Dublin told The Liberal: “I have lived and paid tax here for over a decade, and still I feel that employers see me and other immigrants as cheap labour. We work just as hard as anyone else, but we are not given the same chances to progress.”

The CSO report also detailed that the earnings gap was present across most sectors, with the most pronounced differences seen in construction, hospitality, and administrative support services. The organisation found that even when comparing people with similar experience and qualifications, the gap remained persistent.

Defending the findings, a spokesperson for the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment said: “Ireland’s labour market is regulated to ensure equal rights for all workers regardless of nationality. The Government is committed to eliminating discrimination in the workplace and continues to monitor pay disparities closely.”

However, Sinn Féin’s spokesperson on Workers’ Rights, Louise O’Reilly TD, said that the figures are “deeply concerning” and called on the Tánaiste and the Department of Social Protection to commission an urgent review into the causes of the disparity.

“The data paints a worrying picture,” Deputy O’Reilly said. “We cannot tolerate a society where people are paid less purely because of where they come from. The Government must act to ensure equal pay for equal work.”

In contrast, some employers’ groups argued that the figures may reflect differences in sectors where non-Irish nationals are predominantly employed, rather than discriminatory pay practices. A spokesman for the Irish Small and Medium Enterprises Association told The Liberal: “The wage gap could be explained by the nature of available jobs rather than direct discrimination. Many non-Irish workers are in lower-paid, entry-level positions.”

Nonetheless, campaigners have called for stronger enforcement of existing equality legislation and urged the Workplace Relations Commission to carry out audits in industries with large numbers of migrant workers.

Latest CSO figures also show that non-Irish nationals make up approximately 17% of the workforce, with Polish, Romanian, and Brazilian citizens among the largest groups. Calls for more robust action are likely to grow louder as the debate over fairness and equality in the Irish workplace continues.
headline: “It’s racism” – Irish citizens earn nearly €90 more per week than non-Irish nationals, claims CSO

text:
There are “no winners” when it comes to tariffs and trade wars, according to the US Ambassador to Ireland, Claire Cronin, who referenced the blockbuster film ‘Top Gun’ to make her point during a speech in Dublin yesterday.

Speaking at a business luncheon hosted by the American Chamber of Commerce Ireland, Ms Cronin warned that imposing tariffs and engaging in trade disputes ultimately damages both sides, echoing concerns raised by industry leaders amid ongoing global economic uncertainty.

“Much like in the movie Top Gun, where the goal is to avoid unnecessary confrontation and ensure everyone walks away safely, with trade and tariffs there are simply no winners in a trade war,” she told attendees. “Retaliation leads to escalation, and escalation leads to loss for workers, businesses, and consumers alike.”

Her comments come as renewed tensions simmer over trade policy between the United States, the European Union, and China. While Ireland has so far avoided the worst effects, Irish exporters—particularly in agriculture, pharmaceuticals, and technology—have repeatedly sounded the alarm about the potential for tariffs to threaten jobs and investment.

The Ambassador’s reference to ‘Top Gun’ drew mild amusement from the packed room at a city centre hotel, but her underlying message was clear. “We must prioritise cooperation, open dialogue, and fair competition,” she stated. “If we focus on building bridges instead of barriers, we all benefit.”

The warning arrives as the European Commission considers possible countermeasures in response to US subsidies on electric vehicles and clean energy, measures which Irish officials have said could have knock-on effects for the country’s automotive and green technology sectors.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin, speaking separately at Leinster House, said Ireland would continue to advocate for free and open trade within the EU bloc. “Irish businesses, from SMEs to multinational giants, rely on strong trading relationships,” he said. “We share the Ambassador’s view that trade wars serve no one’s interests.”

The Irish Exporters Association also weighed in, urging both sides to resist moves towards protectionism. “Irish jobs and livelihoods are at stake. Tariffs and trade barriers harm our competitiveness and undermine confidence,” a spokesperson said.

Ambassador Cronin’s remarks were also seen by some as a veiled caution to the US administration, as a presidential election looms and calls for tougher trade stances grow louder in Washington. The business community in Ireland, which hosts more than 900 US-owned firms, has long attributed much of the country’s economic growth to open markets and cross-Atlantic investment.

With the next round of EU-US trade talks scheduled for later this summer, officials in Dublin are keenly watching developments. “We must ensure Ireland’s voice is heard, and that our interests are protected in any discussions,” said a Department of Enterprise source.

For now, Ambassador Cronin’s message is being echoed by government and industry here: when it comes to trade, the only sure losers in a war are those caught in the crossfire.
headline: ‘No winners’ with tariffs or trade wars, says ‘Top Gun’

text:
Leo Varadkar has called on all political parties to include a commitment to pursue Irish unity in their manifestos ahead of the next general election. The former Taoiseach and Fine Gael leader made the suggestion during a public appearance in Dublin on Friday, urging politicians across the board to “place the vision of national unity firmly on the political agenda.”

Varadkar argued that with the changing political landscape in Northern Ireland, particularly following the restoration of power-sharing at Stormont, now is the time for the Republic’s politicians to be proactive. He contended that a cross-party pledge to work towards reunification would demonstrate unity of purpose and reflect “the aspiration of so many citizens across the island.”

“Every political party, regardless of tradition, should set out its approach to bringing about Irish unity in the lifetime of the next Dáil,” Varadkar said. “It is time to move from rhetoric to tangible political commitment. We must work together to ensure all voices are heard in planning a shared future.”

The comments have been met with a mixed reaction from other parties. Sinn Féin, which has consistently campaigned on the issue, welcomed Varadkar’s remarks as “long overdue”, with Mary Lou McDonald TD stating that “Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil have dragged their feet for too long.”

However, Fianna Fáil sources were more circumspect. One senior figure told The Liberal: “Talk of manifestos and pledges is easy. The real work is in building consensus across communities and working with all stakeholders, not just headlines.”

The Labour Party and the Social Democrats have signalled support in principle for increased discussion on unity, but stopped short of promising a formal manifesto commitment. The Green Party has yet to issue an official response.

The Tánaiste, Micheál Martin, recently established a Citizens’ Assembly on the future of the island, but has warned against “divisive deadlines or simplistic pledges,” insisting that any move towards unity should be based on dialogue and genuine reconciliation.

Varadkar’s intervention comes as polls continue to show significant support for reunification among voters in the Republic, though surveys indicate opinion north of the border remains more cautious. The question of a border poll remains contentious, with both the Irish Government and the UK Government emphasising the need for consent of the majority in Northern Ireland as set out in the Good Friday Agreement.

Meanwhile, Unionist leaders have criticised Varadkar’s comments, accusing him of “stoking tensions and playing politics with the future of Northern Ireland.” Doug Beattie, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, said: “This is a deeply irresponsible move that risks undermining the fragile trust that exists.”

Political analysts say Varadkar’s proposal could put pressure on parties to take a clear stance in the forthcoming election campaign, and could potentially reshape the debate over Irish unity in the years ahead.

The general election is expected to take place in either late 2024 or early 2025, with unity likely to feature prominently in party manifestos and public debate.
headline: Leo Varadkar wants Irish unity manifesto pledge by all parties in next election

text:
Protesters clashed with Swedish police in Malmö last night as thousands demonstrated against Israel’s participation in the Eurovision Song Contest. Several smoke canisters were ignited near the city’s Eurovision Village, enveloping the festive area in clouds of coloured smoke as crowds chanted slogans calling for an end to Israeli involvement in the international music competition.

Many protesters, including Irish supporters and diaspora, voiced their outrage at what they described as Israel’s “disproportionate response” in Gaza and accused the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) of double standards. "Letting Israel compete this year is a disgrace," said Mary O’Sullivan from Cork, who travelled to Sweden to join the rally. “When Russia invaded Ukraine, they were banned instantly. Why is Israel treated differently? They shouldn’t be allowed participate after what’s happening in Palestine.”

Swedish authorities confirmed that several hundred Gardaí-equivalent officers were deployed to maintain order as the event attracted a diverse crowd, with banners urging an immediate ceasefire and calls for a cultural boycott of Israel. At least two arrests were made after projectiles and smoke canisters were thrown towards security cordons, although no injuries were reported.

The protests coincided with a controversial performance by Ireland’s own entry, Bambie Thug, who has previously voiced support for the Palestinian people and was reportedly blocked from wearing pro-Palestinian symbols on stage due to Eurovision’s rules on political statements. Their stance has been widely supported among Irish Eurovision fans, with many criticising RTÉ for what they see as a weak response to the ongoing conflict.

In the run-up to the event, the Dáil has seen repeated calls from TDs to suspend Israel from international competitions, echoing similar actions taken against Russia in 2022. Sinn Féin’s Matt Carthy TD said: “There cannot be a double standard. We cannot allow Israel to sportswash or culture-wash their ongoing assaults on Gaza by pretending everything is normal at Eurovision.”

Meanwhile, the EBU maintains that Eurovision is a non-political event, insisting that all countries must be treated equally under its rules. However, critics argue that this neutrality benefits States accused of grave human rights violations and undermines the contest’s credibility.

The HSE has not yet reported any Irish nationals requiring medical assistance following last night’s demonstrations in Malmö, but Gardaí continue to advise Irish citizens abroad to exercise caution and remain aware of developing situations.

Eurovision organisers say that the contest will proceed as planned through the weekend, although additional security measures have been put in place in the wake of Thursday night’s protests. Israeli delegation members have reportedly been assigned increased protection amid heightened tensions.

Irish social media has seen a significant backlash against Israel’s presence at Eurovision, with #BoycottEurovision and #EurovisionApartheid trending throughout the week. As the grand final approaches, pressure is mounting on both European broadcasters and the EBU to address demands from artists and activists to hold Israel accountable for its actions in Gaza.

The fallout in Malmö is expected to continue, with further demonstrations anticipated. Many Irish Eurovision fans say they will watch the finale in solidarity with Palestine, but feel the competition’s spirit has been irrevocably tarnished.
headline: “Israel shouldn’t be allowed participate”: Smoke canisters get set off in Malmö during Eurovision protests

text:
Novak Djokovic stands on the brink of making tennis history today as he takes to the court at Roland-Garros, hoping to secure a record-breaking 23rd Grand Slam title at the French Open in Paris. The Serbian world number three is up against Norway’s Casper Ruud in the men’s singles final, with the eyes of the sporting world fixed on the historic clay courts.

Djokovic, aged 36, is already widely considered one of the greatest players the sport has ever seen, but a victory this afternoon would put him out in front of his long-time rivals Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer, who both currently sit on 22 Grand Slams apiece. The match, set to get underway at 1.30pm Irish time, has generated huge anticipation, with fans and pundits speculating about the legacy implications for men’s tennis.

Speaking ahead of the final, Djokovic said he was “motivated and inspired” by the prospect of making history, but insisted he was “fully focused” on the challenge at hand. “Every Grand Slam final is unique and special,” he told the international press, “and I always try to give my best, no matter the circumstances or what’s at stake.”

Ruud, 24, is appearing in his third Grand Slam final, having lost last year in Paris to Nadal and at the US Open to Carlos Alcaraz. The Norwegian is seen as a major underdog, but he insists he is not fazed by the magnitude of the occasion. “I know I’ll need to play my very best tennis,” he told reporters, “but I have learned from past finals and I’m ready to give it my all.”

Tennis clubs around Ireland have reported a surge in interest in the sport in recent years, especially among young players inspired by global stars such as Djokovic. Irish tennis officials are watching the build-up with keen interest, hoping an historic day in Paris will further boost participation levels, particularly among girls and boys in local clubs.

Security has been heightened at Roland-Garros for the final, following a number of protests during the tournament, with French police and private security services on high alert. There are no reports of any Irish players involved in the latter stages of the tournament, but a contingent of Irish fans have travelled to support the spectacle.

Should Djokovic clinch the title, it would strengthen his claims as the greatest men’s player in history and spark renewed debate among tennis aficionados. For now, Novak Djokovic is just one match away from standing alone atop the Grand Slam mountain, with a place in the history books awaiting the winner in Paris.
headline: Novak Djokovic aims to become the greatest of them all today by winning a 23rd Grand Slam at the French Open in Paris

text:
There has been uproar within the Ukrainian community in Ireland following confirmation that the government will withdraw State-funded accommodation for approximately 16,000 Ukrainian refugees over the coming weeks. The move, announced by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, comes amid ongoing concerns about the strain on Ireland’s overstretched resources and a chronic shortage of available accommodation.

Ukrainians who arrived in the State under the Temporary Protection Directive have been informed that their taxpayer-funded accommodation will be withdrawn once they have been in the country for more than 90 days. This policy shift follows months of mounting pressure on the government to address an ongoing crisis in the provision of beds for both asylum seekers and those fleeing the war in Ukraine.

Some Ukrainian families have described the decision as “devastating”, saying they now face homelessness and uncertainty. Representing hundreds of affected Ukrainians, community spokesperson Olena Harkusha said: “People came here fleeing war, many with nowhere else to go. Ireland showed compassion at first, but now families with young children are being told they must leave their hotel or centre with nowhere to go. It is cruel.” Ms Harkusha called on the Taoiseach, Simon Harris, and the Minister for Children, Roderic O’Gorman, to reverse the decision and honour what she termed “Ireland’s moral duty”.

A notice circulated to affected residents advises that the State will stop paying for accommodation after 90 days and that they must make alternative arrangements. The Department has stated that information and advice will be available, including help accessing social welfare payments and private rental options. However, housing campaigners have pointed out that competition for rentals remains fierce, and the cost of rent in cities like Dublin and Cork is far beyond the means of most new arrivals who do not yet have full-time employment.

There are currently more than 100,000 Ukrainian refugees residing in Ireland, the majority of whom have been accommodated in hotels, B&Bs, and emergency centres around the country at an estimated cost to the Exchequer of over €2 billion to date. In recent months, government sources have repeatedly warned that the system is unsustainable, particularly as new arrivals continue while thousands of Irish citizens remain on social housing lists.

Some Irish taxpayers and opposition TDs have expressed support for reducing State spending on refugee accommodation, citing a need to prioritise resources for citizens struggling with housing and health care. However, advocacy groups including the Irish Refugee Council and the Irish Red Cross have condemned the policy, warning that it risks pushing vulnerable families onto the streets.

A protest is planned for outside Leinster House later this week, as affected Ukrainians and their supporters vow to fight what they have called an “unjust and inhumane” decision. The Department has said it will monitor the situation closely and “continue to engage with all stakeholders”.
headline: Outrage from Ukrainians as government withdraws taxpayer-funded accommodation for 16,000 Ukrainians in Ireland

text:
The British Prime Minister, Rishi Sunak, has dismissed the prospect of any new agreement with the Irish Government regarding the return of asylum seekers, stating emphatically that he is “not interested” in striking a migrant deal with Ireland. Mr Sunak’s comments come amid escalating diplomatic tensions between Dublin and London over the return of asylum seekers from the UK, following the implementation of Britain’s controversial Rwanda policy.

Earlier this week, the Taoiseach, Simon Harris, had called for “constructive engagement” with the UK as Ireland manages an increase in the number of asylum seekers arriving from Britain. However, Mr Sunak’s remarks have poured cold water on suggestions of bilateral talks, telling British media on Friday that any difficulties faced by Ireland as a consequence of the UK’s immigration crackdown are “for Ireland to deal with”. “If Ireland wants to take them all, that’s not my problem,” Mr Sunak reportedly said, adding that his focus remains on enforcing the Rwanda deportation system.

The response from the Irish Government has been measured so far, with sources in the Department of Justice indicating that channels remain open with their British counterparts amid concerns over a loophole that allows asylum seekers to cross the border from Northern Ireland without sufficient scrutiny. Tánaiste Micheál Martin criticised Sunak’s “lack of engagement”, stating that cross-border issues “require cooperation, not political point-scoring”.

Recent weeks have seen a spike in the number of international protection applicants entering Ireland from Northern Ireland, with over 80% of new arrivals reportedly landing through the land border. According to the Department of Integration, accommodation pressures have intensified, with some local authorities warning that the system is “at breaking point”.

Several TDs have voiced concern about the lack of a formal return agreement with the UK since Brexit, as the Common Travel Area arrangements do not extend to third-country nationals seeking asylum. Sinn Féin’s spokesperson on justice, Martin Kenny TD, accused Mr Sunak of “playing politics with people’s lives”, while Fine Gael’s Alan Farrell TD called for “urgent talks to address the spiralling pressure on Irish services”.

Protests have erupted in some Dublin suburbs and provincial towns in recent days in response to the arrival of asylum seekers, with campaigners demanding “fairness for all”. The Gardaí have increased patrols at several accommodation centres after a number of incidents, while the HSE has issued reassurances concerning healthcare provision.

The controversy has also fuelled further debate about the future of Ireland’s asylum and immigration policy. The Taoiseach is expected to raise the issue in upcoming meetings with EU counterparts, with a spokesperson saying, “Ireland will continue to uphold its international obligations, but we require our neighbours to do the same.”

Meanwhile, Mr Sunak doubled down on his migration policy, telling British reporters: “No ifs, no buts – we are stopping the boats. That is what the British people expect.” 

Officials in both Dublin and London are understood to be monitoring the situation closely, but with the UK general election looming and Ireland facing its own pressures, a breakthrough appears unlikely in the immediate term.
headline: “Ireland can take them all” – Sunak says he’s “not interested” in migrant deal with Ireland

text:
Ireland’s so-called ‘lost generation’ appears to be growing by the day. The latest data paint a grim picture: never in recent memory have so many young Irish men and women packed their bags and left for foreign shores. Emigration, once regarded as an unfortunate chapter in the nation’s history, is once again a lived reality for families across the country. Figures released by the Central Statistics Office show that in 2025, a record number of people aged under 35 departed Ireland, the highest level since the dark days of the post-crash exodus a decade ago.

At the heart of this fresh bout of mass departure is a simple and uncomfortable truth: homeownership, long held as a rite of passage and a symbol of security, is now firmly out of reach for the vast majority of young people. Even those lucky enough to secure steady employment find themselves locked out of a housing market where average house prices are spiralling beyond the means of ordinary working families. The average price of a home in Dublin now stands well above €450,000, and even in smaller towns, prices and rents are shooting up, fed by chronic supply shortages and investor speculation.

Government schemes, from the Help-to-Buy to the Shared Equity initiative, have done little to ease the situation. Critics say these measures have merely stoked demand further, serving to inflate already unsustainable prices. Meanwhile, larger and larger swathes of society are left reliant on extortionate rents, fuelling anxieties that their only route to a home of their own is to leave the country entirely.

For many young Irish people, the message is clear: if you want to build a life, if you want basic security, you must go elsewhere. Traditional destinations such as Australia, Canada, and the United States beckon, and growing numbers are looking to Germany, the Netherlands and other European countries where wages are higher and rents more affordable. Social media is awash with stories of twenty- and thirty-somethings who, after years of scrambling for overpriced ‘box rooms’ or contending with derelict rentals, have finally had enough.

The consequences of this youth exodus are profound and enduring. Families are fractured, local communities lose their heartbeat, and the country faces an ageing population and looming skills shortages. Schools, hospitals, and small businesses, already stretched to their limits, will be left with a shrinking pool of young workers to support them.

The political class, meanwhile, appears paralysed. Despite mounting evidence and repeated warnings from advocacy groups, the responses from the Department of Housing and the Tánaiste ring hollow. There is little suggestion that the crisis can be solved within the current parameters. The prevailing orthodoxy, that the ‘market’ will eventually correct itself, feels increasingly out of touch with the realities of everyday life for ordinary citizens.

It is time to reckon honestly with the cost of inaction. Ireland’s future depends on its young people. Yet, by failing to provide affordable homes and a sense of security, the country is pushing them away in record numbers. Unless radical change is delivered on housing—a true commitment to building public and affordable homes, decisive action on land hoarding and investor profiteering, and meaningful reform of planning and zoning laws—the exodus will continue.

The warning signs are clear, and the cost of ignoring them will be borne for generations.
headline: Gone for good? Ireland’s youth exodus accelerates as record numbers emigrated in 2025 as homeownership remains a pipe dream

Tensions have flared within Fine Gael after Taoiseach Simon Harris reportedly instructed all party councillors to withhold support from Independent presidential candidate Conor O’Connor, prompting accusations of panic within government ranks. Sources close to Mr O’Connor’s campaign say the order is a clear sign that the establishment “are petrified Conor would win” if he secured a place on the ballot.

Mr O’Connor, who has garnered significant grassroots backing owing to his outspoken criticism of the government’s immigration policies and approach to housing, is currently seeking the necessary nominations from county and city councils to contest the presidency later this year.

Several Fine Gael councillors, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that a directive came from party headquarters earlier this week, warning local representatives not to endorse non-party candidates. Some councillors said they felt “intimidated” by pressure from senior party figures, while others expressed concern over what they described as an “attempt to stifle democracy”.

In a statement, Mr O’Connor blasted the move as “an undemocratic clampdown on the Irish people’s right to choose their own President.” He went on: “Simon Harris and his colleagues are running scared because they know people have lost faith in the old parties. If they were confident in their own candidate, they wouldn’t need to resort to strong-arm tactics.”

This is not the first time controversy has arisen around the Fine Gael leadership’s approach to political challengers. Critics say the party’s fear of an outsider campaign is reflective of a broader disconnect with the electorate, particularly on issues of immigration, rural decline, and the cost of living.

Speaking outside Leinster House on Friday, a party spokesperson said the instruction was “standard party discipline”, maintaining that Fine Gael must “stand united behind its own nominee to ensure the next President reflects the values and vision of the party.” The spokesperson dismissed claims of intimidation as “baseless” and insisted each councillor is free to make their own decisions, though added, “we expect loyalty from our members”.

Meanwhile, Mr O’Connor’s campaign has called on Fianna Fáil and Sinn Féin councillors to “stand up to the establishment” and give their support for his nomination. “Let the people decide, not the party bosses,” a campaign spokesperson argued.

Under Irish law, prospective presidential candidates require the backing of at least 20 Oireachtas members or four local authorities to secure a spot on the ballot. The deadline for nominations is expected to fall in early autumn, with campaigners warning there is now a “real risk” that only the main party candidates will be allowed contest.

The development has sparked a heated debate online, with supporters of Mr O’Connor decrying what they view as “cronyism” and “fear-mongering” from the government. Opponents, however, argue that party discipline is essential to maintain order during the nomination process.

As the presidential race gathers momentum, it remains to be seen whether mounting public pressure will force a rethink within Fine Gael, or if the party’s efforts to block outsiders like Mr O’Connor will ultimately succeed.
headline: “They’re petrified Conor would win” – Simon Harris demands all Fine Gael Councillors block Independent Presidential candidate nominations
