Five Garda trainees have been expelled from the Garda College in Templemore following an incident described by sources as a “prank” that went badly wrong, leading to the humiliation and potential endangerment of a fellow trainee.

It is understood that the incident occurred earlier this year, but the decision to dismiss the recruits was only made following a full internal investigation by senior Gardaí. According to sources familiar with the case, five probationer Gardaí forcibly handcuffed another trainee before dragging him into a communal shower and turning on the cold water.

The Gardaí involved reportedly filmed the incident on their phones, and video footage was subsequently circulated among other trainees. The victim is believed to have been left distressed and embarrassed by the ordeal, which others have characterised as “horseplay” that crossed the line.

A senior source within the Gardaí described the incident as “utterly unacceptable.” “This is not the kind of behaviour that is tolerated among members of An Garda Síochána, whether they are in training or fully qualified,” the source said.

After the matter was brought to the attention of college management, an internal disciplinary process was initiated in line with protocols for trainee misconduct. The five involved were summoned before a review board and ultimately dismissed from the training programme. All five have lost their positions as probationer Gardaí with immediate effect and have been ordered to leave the college.

A spokesperson for the Garda Press Office confirmed that “An incident involving inappropriate behaviour between students at the Garda College was thoroughly investigated, and disciplinary proceedings have concluded.” They declined to comment further, citing privacy concerns and ongoing support for the affected trainee.

The incident has sparked fresh debate over the vetting and training processes for new Garda recruits and comes at a time when public confidence in the force has been tested by a series of controversies over the past year. Garda Representative Association members have called for clear guidance on standards of behaviour, citing the need for all trainees to be held accountable to the highest standards.

Minister for Justice Helen McEntee TD has been briefed on the matter and expressed confidence that the procedures in place at the Garda College are robust. “The public has a right to expect professionalism and respect from every member of An Garda Síochána. Actions like this have no place in our police force,” she said.

It remains unclear whether any of the five dismissed trainees will appeal the decision or if other disciplinary measures may yet follow. The Garda College has indicated that support measures are being put in place for the victim, and that all protocols regarding bullying, harassment, and professional conduct will be reinforced among current and future intakes.
headline: Five trainee gardaí dismissed over ‘Prank’ that saw another garda handcuffed and thrown into a cold shower

text:
Concerns have been raised among members of the public after it emerged that Mohammad Al Shaker Al Tamimi, who is currently before the courts, is to receive a full psychological assessment funded by the taxpayer. Many have voiced frustration online and on social media, questioning why public money should be spent on such services for non-citizens, especially against the backdrop of widespread pressure on the Irish health system and continuing issues with funding for vital programmes.

Al Tamimi, who is originally from Jordan, is facing serious charges in connection with an alleged incident in Dublin earlier this year. He appeared before the Dublin District Court where his legal team requested a comprehensive psychological assessment to be carried out by specialists, at the expense of the State. The court granted the request, directing that the assessment be completed ahead of his next court appearance.

News of the decision has sparked a strong reaction among members of the Irish public, many of whom have taken to Facebook and X (formerly Twitter) to express their anger. “Irish people are waiting months or even years for mental health supports, and yet the taxpayer is expected to foot the bill for this,” wrote one commenter. Others questioned whether resources should not be reserved for Irish citizens and residents, especially at a time when the Department of Health and the HSE are warning of severe backlogs and lack of access to assessment services for children and vulnerable adults.

A number of TDs have said they have received correspondence from constituents expressing deep dissatisfaction at the use of public funds in this case. One rural TD, who asked not to be named, said, “People are understandably upset when they see headlines like this. Resources are stretched, families are under pressure trying to get assessments for their own children, and they see a person before the courts getting priority access and funding. There are serious questions for the Department of Justice to answer.”

The Gardaí have confirmed that Al Tamimi remains in custody pending further court proceedings. The psychological assessment, which is expected to cost several thousand euro, will be carried out by an independent expert and will form part of the evidence presented at the next sitting. The exact cost to the taxpayer is not yet known, but critics argue that regardless of the final figure, the principle itself is what has people most concerned.

Meanwhile, advocacy groups have pointed out that under Irish and European law, those facing serious charges are entitled to a fair trial, which may include access to assessments and expert reports where deemed necessary by the court. A spokesperson for the Irish Council for Civil Liberties said, “Ensuring due process and access to justice is a cornerstone of our legal system, irrespective of nationality or background.”

Nonetheless, public anger appears unlikely to abate soon, with many calling for greater transparency in how such decisions are made and for a review of spending priorities at a time when many Irish families are struggling to access basic public services. The next hearing in Mr Al Tamimi’s case is scheduled for later this month.
headline: Public not happy that Mohammad Al Shaker Al Tamimi is getting taxpayer-funded full psychological assessment

Pressure is mounting on both sides of the Atlantic as the United States prepares to enforce its contentious ban on TikTok, with the measure set to come into effect tomorrow unless a last-minute intervention emerges. Despite considerable lobbying and legal wrangling, US authorities are ploughing ahead with legislation that could see the popular video-sharing app barred from app stores across the country, citing national security concerns over its Chinese ownership.

TikTok, owned by ByteDance, has faced intense scrutiny in Washington, with lawmakers raising fears that the app could be used by the Chinese government to access personal data or influence public opinion in the US. The company has consistently denied these charges, insisting it stores user data outside China and has put robust safeguarding measures in place. Nevertheless, the Biden administration and Congress have pressed forward with demands that ByteDance divest itself of the app—something Beijing has signalled it would not allow.

For its part, TikTok has filed multiple legal challenges in US courts, arguing the move amounts to censorship and will harm the free speech rights of millions of Americans, particularly its estimated 170 million US users. As of today, there has been no ruling to halt the ban, meaning that, from midnight tomorrow, TikTok could disappear from the Apple App Store and Google Play for US users, though those who already have the app installed may retain access for a limited time.

The ban has reignited debate in Ireland and across the EU, where data protection and digital sovereignty are hot topics. The Data Protection Commission (DPC) and European Commission have launched their own probes into TikTok’s practices, but no ban is currently planned here. However, several European parliaments—including the Oireachtas—have restricted the use of TikTok on official devices over similar data security concerns.

Irish TikTok users and content creators are watching developments in America closely, with many expressing anger and bewilderment on social media. Business owners and influencers who rely on the platform to reach customers fear knock-on effects, as global trends often follow the lead of the US market. Some have called on the Taoiseach and Government to publicly state their position, while others argue the move sets a dangerous precedent for internet freedom.

Meanwhile, digital rights campaigners have warned that such sweeping bans could encourage a fragmented, state-controlled internet, undermining the open web. They point out that platforms like TikTok have provided a voice to young people and marginalised communities, and that blocking them could fuel resentment and distrust in government institutions.

As the clock ticks down, all eyes are now on Washington. Unless a court intervenes at the eleventh hour, the US TikTok ban will become a reality—leaving Irish users to ponder whether Europe could be next.
headline: Stop the clock on TikTok ban – US ban will go ahead tomorrow

The ongoing saga involving the Burke family escalated further this week as Martina Burke and Ammi Burke, mother and sister of suspended teacher Enoch Burke, have been warned they could face imprisonment or a substantial financial penalty after being found in contempt of court. The development comes after repeated disruptions during High Court proceedings related to Enoch Burke’s dispute with Wilson’s Hospital School.

Both women appeared visibly defiant as Mr Justice Mark Heslin addressed the court, having previously disregarded orders to maintain decorum. The judge described their conduct as “entirely unacceptable”, saying the integrity of the court must be protected against persistent interruptions and disrespect. According to witnesses present, both Mrs Burke and her daughter shouted religious slogans and levelled accusations against the judiciary during the recent hearings, echoing earlier behaviour that resulted in Gardaí being called to manage the situation.

Legal experts say the court now has the discretion to impose sanctions, ranging from a substantial fine to committal to prison, should the Burkes fail to issue an unreserved apology or undertake not to repeat the conduct in question. It’s understood that the family was given a last opportunity to purge their contempt but have thus far refused to do so, maintaining their claims that the proceedings are unjust and denouncing what they describe as an attack on their freedom of expression and religious convictions.

The initial dispute stemmed from Enoch Burke’s refusal to comply with school policy regarding the treatment of a transgender pupil, which led to his suspension and subsequent High Court action. The wider Burke family has since gained notoriety for their repeated confrontations with the courts, with multiple family members being ejected from proceedings in recent months.

Reacting to the threat of sanctions, supporters of the Burkes gathered outside the Four Courts, chanting and distributing religious pamphlets, while critics online have called on the judiciary to take a firmer stance in upholding the rule of law. Gardaí remained on standby but reported no incidents outside the building.

The matter has raised further questions about the limits of public protest and the court’s powers to enforce order in the face of what some legal observers have called “co-ordinated disruption”. With a decision on penalties expected later this week, all eyes will be on the High Court to see whether the judge will opt for financial penalties, a custodial sentence, or another sanction entirely.

Meanwhile, the Department of Education has declined to comment on the case, citing ongoing legal proceedings, while the Burke family maintain that they are being persecuted for their religious beliefs. As the legal battle continues, many are questioning how long the judiciary will tolerate such challenges to its authority.
headline: Enoch Burke’s mother and sister may face jail or a hefty fine for contempt of court

A toddler who suffered extensive burns after a cup of hot coffee was spilled on her during a Ryanair flight has been awarded nearly €19,000 in damages by the Circuit Civil Court. The court heard that the little girl, who was just 13 months old at the time, endured over three hours of pain before she could receive medical attention after the aircraft landed.

The incident occurred on a flight from Ibiza to Dublin in June 2022 when the toddler, who was seated on her mother’s lap, was accidentally scalded with hot coffee meant for her mother. It was claimed in court that a crew member handed over an uncovered cup of boiling coffee, which tipped onto the child as the tray table was being lowered.

The mother told Judge John O’Connor that her daughter screamed in agony and that she found it “impossible” to comfort her as the flight continued. She said cabin crew did their best to assist, providing cold packs and tissues, but the child remained in “visible distress” throughout the journey.

The court was told medical staff at Dublin Airport examined the toddler as soon as the flight arrived, and she was taken by ambulance to the emergency department at Temple Street Children’s Hospital. She was treated for first and second degree burns to her right thigh and lower abdomen, and required daily dressing changes for nearly two weeks.

Barrister for the family, Eoin McMahon BL, said the incident had been traumatic for both the child and her mother, who felt helpless as her daughter “cried uncontrollably” on her lap for hours with “no means for proper relief”. He said the case was settled against Ryanair DAC for €18,900, subject to court approval.

Judge O’Connor described the ordeal as “deeply upsetting for any parent” and said the settlement was appropriate given the injuries and the trauma experienced. He noted the physical wounds had largely healed but the child had been left nervous around hot drinks and “startled by sudden movements”.

The judge approved the settlement and praised the mother for her “extraordinary composure” in handling the situation. Ryanair did not contest liability.

The family declined to comment as they left court.
headline: Toddler who got scalded by hot coffee on Ryanair flight wins close to €19,000 as court hears she sat in agony for more than three hours

Protests against migrant accommodation were held in the East Wall, Sheriff Street and Five Lamps areas of Dublin on Wednesday night, with organisers describing the demonstrations as a “great success.” Hundreds of concerned residents gathered at multiple sites in the north inner city, reiterating their opposition to what they termed the “ongoing plantation” of their communities with asylum seekers and refugees.

Chanting “Ireland is full” and holding tricolours, those assembled demanded that the government immediately halt the housing of non-nationals in local facilities, claiming that their areas are already struggling with inadequate services and a lack of resources for locals. The marches, organised by local community groups and citizen activists, were peaceful and well attended, with Gardaí on hand to monitor the situation.

One protestor from East Wall told The Liberal that people in the area “feel abandoned by the government and ignored by the powers that be in the Dáil.” She accused Ministers of prioritising newcomers over Irish citizens and pointed to ongoing issues with homelessness, housing shortages and crime.

Speakers at the rallies called for increased transparency around the use of hotels and other accommodation for arrivals under the International Protection system. They voiced fears over safety, integration and the long-term impact on neighbourhoods, insisting the government should introduce an immediate pause on new arrivals and instead focus on Irish families in need.

A statement issued by protest organisers after the events said, “The people of East Wall, Sheriff Street and Five Lamps have sent a clear message to the government that our communities will not be used as dumping grounds. We are ordinary citizens standing up for our rights, and last night’s rallies were a great success in showing our unity and resolve.”

The Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth did not issue a comment in time for publication. The government’s policy of providing emergency accommodation for applicants for international protection remains controversial, with growing calls from some quarters for stricter border controls and prioritisation of Irish citizens.

No arrests were reported during the demonstrations. The protests come amid ongoing debate over migration and capacity in Irish cities, with similar rallies having taken place in other parts of Dublin and across the country in recent months.
headline: Anti plantation protests in East Wall, Sherriff Street and Five Lamps were a “great success” on Wednesday night #IrelandisFull

text:
The rapid ascent of online casinos has had a significant impact on Ireland’s economic landscape, bringing both opportunities and challenges in its wake. With a growing appetite among Irish consumers for digital entertainment and gaming, the online gambling sector has swiftly evolved from a niche pastime to a mainstream industry, reshaping employment, taxation, and regulatory debates.

The Irish online gambling market, which includes online casinos, sports betting, and lottery games, is estimated to be worth in excess of €1.1 billion annually, according to figures published by the Department of Justice. The proliferation of smartphones and high-speed broadband, even in rural pockets, has made participation more accessible than ever before. This digital shift, accelerated throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, has led to a marked increase in online casino activity, outpacing traditional betting shops and physical gambling venues.

The sector provides direct employment for thousands, with major international operators such as Flutter Entertainment (parent company of Paddy Power) and BoyleSports maintaining significant headquarters and operational centres in Ireland. As these multinational firms expand their services, spin-off benefits accrue to ancillary sectors, including digital marketing, software development, and payments technology. This has positioned Ireland as a European hub for online gambling expertise and innovation, further enhancing the country’s reputation in the tech sector.

Taxation is another vital aspect. The Irish Exchequer derives considerable revenue from the online gambling sector, primarily through betting duties and remote bookmaker’s licence fees. In 2022, government receipts from betting taxes alone reached nearly €100 million, with online casinos forming an increasing share. As discussions continue around a mooted increase in betting duty, the potential for greater public benefit remains on the political agenda.

Yet, with opportunity comes responsibility. The growth of online casinos has sparked calls for stronger regulation and greater social protections. The Oireachtas is currently progressing the Gambling Regulation Bill, a landmark piece of legislation intended to modernise Ireland’s outdated gambling laws and introduce a new authority tasked with oversight, enforcement, and prevention of gambling-related harm. Many advocacy groups have highlighted the risks of addiction and financial distress, urging a careful balance between fostering economic benefits and protecting vulnerable individuals.

Looking ahead, Ireland’s online casino market is expected to continue growing, driven by evolving technology, new game formats, and increased digital engagement, particularly among younger demographics. However, the way forward will require policymakers, industry leaders, and civil society to work in concert, ensuring innovation does not outpace necessary safeguards.

As the debate continues, most agree that regulating the sector robustly and transparently will be crucial to harness its economic potential while minimising risks. For now, the rise of online casinos stands as both a vibrant economic force and a test of Ireland’s ability to adapt to the digital age with foresight and care.
headline: The Impact of Online Casinos on the Irish Economy: Analysis and Prospects

text:
Concerns are mounting among supporters and observers alike that Enoch Burke, the controversial secondary school teacher whose steadfast refusal to use gender-neutral pronouns led to a protracted legal battle, may find himself back behind bars this Christmas.

Mr Burke, who taught at Wilson’s Hospital School in Multyfarnham, Co Westmeath, became a national figure last year after being suspended for refusing to address a transgender student by their preferred pronoun. Despite a High Court injunction ordering him not to attend the school, Mr Burke continued to do so, resulting in his imprisonment for contempt of court—a saga that garnered extensive public debate and significant media coverage.

Sources close to the case have indicated to The Liberal that the risk of Mr Burke returning to Mountjoy Prison is higher than ever, as court proceedings continue and the teacher remains unwavering in his convictions. His public statements and recent court appearances have reinforced his stance: he insists he will never call a boy “they”, citing his Christian beliefs and a refusal to comply with what he terms “dangerous, gender ideology”.

Last week, a sitting of the High Court heard evidence that Mr Burke had again breached court orders by appearing at the school premises, raising the possibility of renewed sanctions. The school’s board of management is understood to have reiterated its position, stating that the orders are necessary to ensure a safe environment for staff and students, and that compliance with the injunction is non-negotiable.

Commenting outside the Four Courts, Mr Burke claimed he was standing up not only for his own rights, but also for “freedom of conscience and freedom of speech for every Irish citizen”. Supporters gathered to back him, holding placards and reciting prayers, with some expressing their fears that the courts are “criminalising Christian beliefs”.

However, legal experts contacted by The Liberal pointed out that the judicial system has strictly maintained that the case is a matter of compliance with court orders, rather than religious freedom. “The law is clear that when a court makes an order, it must be upheld, regardless of the personal beliefs of any individual,” said retired barrister John Kilcoyne.

A statement from the Department of Education confirmed that procedures were being followed in accordance with the Education Act and employment legislation, but said they could not comment on individual cases.

With Christmas approaching, family members of Mr Burke have voiced their worry that he could once again be denied freedom at a time traditionally spent with loved ones. The dispute, which has deeply divided public opinion, shows no signs of resolution, as both sides appear entrenched in their positions.

The next phase of the legal process is expected in the coming weeks. The potential for Mr Burke’s re-imprisonment continues to be scrutinised, with many wondering whether a compromise is possible, or whether the teacher’s determination will once again see him spend Christmas behind bars.
headline: He’ll never call a boy “they” – Fears grow that Enoch Burke will be in jail again for Christmas

text:
A large anti-migrant protest is due to take place in Ballsbridge this afternoon, as demonstrators from East Wall and other communities gather with the aim of "equaling the score" with affluent areas of Dublin. Organisers say the protest, which is scheduled for 3pm near the RDS, is a response to what they allege is an unfair distribution of asylum seekers and newly-arrived migrants across the city, claiming working-class communities have borne the brunt of direct provision centres and emergency accommodation.

Crowds are expected to travel from East Wall, Ballymun, Finglas, Tallaght and other areas that have seen ongoing protests against migrant accommodation in recent months. A series of community groups and activists have called for the “burden” to be shared, with one organiser telling The Liberal: “We are not racist, we are just saying enough is enough. Let the leafy suburbs take their share. It’s time for Ballsbridge to do its bit.”

The protest follows months of tension and frequent demonstrations outside newly opened accommodation centres in various parts of Dublin. Last year, East Wall hit national headlines with nightly marches and road blockades, demanding greater consultation and claiming local services were under pressure. Similar scenes played out in Drimnagh, Inchicore, and Ballymun, leading to increased policing and heated debate in the Dáil, where some TDs accused the Government of mishandling the situation.

Today’s demonstration is seen by organisers as a symbolic escalation, intended to highlight the perceived disparity in how State accommodation for asylum seekers is distributed. Ballsbridge, one of Dublin's most affluent suburbs, has so far not seen large-scale direct provision centres established in its vicinity.

Gardaí are expected to be out in force, with a significant policing operation in place to manage crowds, commuters, and any counter-protests. While no formal counter-demonstration has been announced, anti-racism groups have previously staged spontaneous gatherings in response to similar events.

The Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, which oversees the accommodation of international protection applicants, has repeatedly said that efforts are made to locate centres wherever suitable premises can be secured, subject to planning and safety considerations. A spokesperson insisted that the distribution of asylum accommodation is “not a matter of postcode” but of availability and suitability of buildings.

The ongoing debate about Ireland’s response to refugees and asylum seekers has sharply divided opinion, with some local representatives and Government ministers denouncing what they term as “scapegoating” and “fear-mongering”. However, many locals taking part in today’s protest say they feel “left behind” and “voiceless” in the face of major changes to their communities, citing long waiting lists for housing, schools, and healthcare.

Traffic restrictions are expected in the Ballsbridge area for the duration of the protest, and the Gardaí have advised motorists to avoid the vicinity if possible. The demonstration is expected to last several hours, with further protests mooted unless locals’ concerns are addressed “at government level.”
headline: Today’s the day! Huge anti-migrant protest to take place in Ballsbridge today for #EastWall to “equal the score” with affluent communities

text:
An Irishman in his 30s has been shot dead in Australia, it has emerged this morning. The Department of Foreign Affairs has confirmed it is providing consular assistance to the man’s family following the tragic incident.

Local police in the state of New South Wales were called to a residence in the suburbs of Sydney late last night, where it is understood the Irish national was found with fatal gunshot wounds. Paramedics attended the scene but the man was pronounced dead shortly after their arrival.

Authorities in Australia have launched a full investigation and a post-mortem examination is expected to be carried out in the coming days. The man’s identity has not yet been released, but it is understood he had been living in the country for a number of years and was well known in the local Irish community.

A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs told The Liberal: “We are aware of the case and are providing consular assistance to the family.”

It is not yet clear what led to the shooting, but police in Sydney have said they are following a definite line of enquiry and have appealed for witnesses to come forward.

Irish expats in Australia have expressed shock at the news, with community groups in Sydney offering their support to the man’s friends and family.

The Department of Foreign Affairs said it would not be commenting further at this time due to the ongoing investigation and out of respect for the bereaved.

Gardaí are liaising with their Australian counterparts and assisting where possible. The situation remains under active investigation by Australian authorities. 

Further updates are expected as more information becomes available.
headline: 🔴BREAKING: An Irishman (30s) has been shot dead in Australia

text:
The funeral of six-year-old Matthew Healy, who tragically lost his life last week in County Waterford, will take place tomorrow with the local community expected to turn out in large numbers to support the grieving family.

Matthew, described by teachers and neighbours as “full of life and always smiling”, died on Thursday following a shocking incident at his family’s home. Gardaí are continuing their investigation, but do not suspect foul play. A file is being prepared for the Coroner.

His parents, Brian and Angela Healy, are said to be heartbroken as they prepare to lay their only child to rest. Family, friends, and members of the local GAA club, where Matthew had recently joined the under-8s, have rallied around the Healy family in recent days, offering meals, childcare, and messages of support.

The funeral mass will be held tomorrow morning in the Church of the Sacred Heart, Waterford city, at 11am, with burial afterwards in St. Otteran’s Cemetery. The local primary school, St. Paul’s NS, where Matthew was a pupil, will close as a mark of respect. His classmates and teachers are expected to form a guard of honour and have been encouraged to wear colourful clothing in celebration of Matthew’s short but joyful life.

An outpouring of grief from across Waterford and beyond has seen a steady stream of mourners visiting the Healy home, with a Book of Condolence set up in the Waterford City Hall and online via the County Council website. Local businesses and sports teams have expressed their condolences, with the Mayor of Waterford, Cllr. Joe Kelly, saying: “The whole city stands with the Healy family at this unimaginably difficult time.”

Gardaí have asked for the privacy of the family to be respected both at the service and in the days ahead.

In their statement, the Healy family thanked the community and emergency services for their kindness and support, asking for prayers as they face the difficult road ahead without their beloved Matthew.
headline: The funeral of little Matthew Healy will take place tomorrow in Waterford

text:
The crisis engulfing RTÉ is showing no signs of abating, as it emerged that external accountants are due to enter the broadcaster’s Donnybrook headquarters this week to conduct a further forensic review of the organisation’s finances. 

It follows months of turmoil and public anger over the ongoing revelations about financial mismanagement, undisclosed payments to top presenters, and what Oireachtas committee members have described as a “culture of secrecy” at the national broadcaster.

According to sources close to the Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media, the Government has mandated that independent forensic accountants, expected to be from one of the so-called ‘Big Four’ firms, will comb through RTÉ’s accounts in a bid to establish the full extent of undocumented transactions and off-the-books arrangements.

The move is being seen as a direct response to mounting pressure from TDs across all parties, who have expressed concern over RTÉ’s ability to properly manage the €200 million it receives annually from the licence fee and commercial revenues. The decision comes as RTÉ’s Director General, Kevin Bakhurst, faces a barrage of questions regarding his own stewardship, particularly after a further tranche of documents released last week cast fresh doubts over the broadcaster’s internal controls.

The new probe will focus on expenditure, including the now-infamous barter account and other so-called ‘grey area’ spending which TDs have accused RTÉ of using to shield luxury perks and bonuses from public scrutiny. The review is also expected to scrutinise redundancy packages, procurement processes, and the issuing of contracts to high-earning contractors.

Staff morale at Montrose is said to be at an all-time low as rank-and-file employees await word on potential job losses and departmental restructuring. Union representatives have accused senior management of “throwing ordinary workers under the bus” while attempting to save their own positions.

Meanwhile, the Government has yet to offer clarity on plans for future funding of public service broadcasting. The Minister, Catherine Martin, has signalled that significant reform is imminent but has declined to rule out job cuts or further budget reductions.

The accountant’s arrival comes as the Dáil’s Committee of Public Accounts prepares to recall both current and former RTÉ executives for questioning later this month. Several TDs have said they will be demanding answers about golden handshakes, travel expenses, and allegations of a “cosy cartel” at the top of the organisation.

The Taoiseach, Simon Harris, reiterated at the weekend that “no stone will be left unturned” in the effort to restore trust in RTÉ and ensure full accountability for past failings. However, with the facts still emerging and public confidence in the broadcaster’s leadership at rock bottom, it appears the crisis at RTÉ is far from over.
headline: RTE crisis continues as accountants to go in this week

text:
Gardaí have seized a firearm and a substantial quantity of drugs with an estimated street value in the thousands of euros following a targeted operation in north Dublin on Friday evening. The raid was conducted as part of ongoing efforts by the force to clamp down on organised crime and drug trafficking in the capital.

Members attached to the Garda Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau, supported by local units, executed a search warrant at a residential property in the Coolock area shortly after 7pm. During the course of the search, officers uncovered a handgun and a significant quantity of what is believed to be cocaine, cannabis, and ecstasy, with a combined estimated value in excess of €25,000.

A male in his mid-30s was arrested at the scene and is currently being detained at a northside Garda station under the provisions of Section 2 of the Criminal Justice (Drug Trafficking) Act 1996. Gardaí have stated that investigations are ongoing and further arrests have not been ruled out.

A spokesperson for An Garda Síochána confirmed the details of the operation, emphasising the force’s continued commitment to disrupting the activities of criminal gangs. “This seizure demonstrates the effectiveness of ongoing intelligence-led policing initiatives in tackling drug-related crime in our communities,” the spokesperson said.

The firearm recovered has been sent for forensic examination. The seized drugs will also undergo further analysis to confirm their composition and market value. Gardaí have appealed to anyone with information regarding illegal drug activity to contact their local station or the Garda Confidential Line.

The operation forms part of a broader crackdown on serious organised crime in Dublin, with Gardaí pledging to intensify actions targeting those involved in the supply and distribution of controlled substances.
headline: Gardai seize firearm and thousands of euros worth of drugs during raid in Dublin

text:
The head of Supermac’s, Pat McDonagh, has hit out at the prices being paid to Irish beef farmers, claiming they are not receiving a fair return for their work. Mr McDonagh, whose fast food chain is one of the largest buyers of Irish beef, said that farmers are shouldering the burden of rising costs while processors and retailers are not passing on enough of their profits.

Speaking to The Liberal, Mr McDonagh warned that unless action is taken, the Irish beef sector faces a serious crisis. “Beef farmers in Ireland are under savage pressure,” he said. “The price of everything they need to run their farms—diesel, fertiliser, feed—has gone through the roof. But the price they get per kilo for beef has barely shifted. It’s not sustainable.”

Mr McDonagh called on the Government and industry bodies to step up support for primary producers. “We’re proud to serve 100 per cent Irish beef in Supermac’s, but unless farmers are properly paid, the whole thing could fall apart,” he said. “The lads on the ground are working day and night and still can’t make ends meet.”

Beef farmers have staged a number of protests in recent years over low prices, including dramatic demonstrations outside meat processing plants and the offices of Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine, Charlie McConalogue. They argue that farm-gate prices have not kept pace with inflation, forcing many to consider leaving the industry.

Mr McDonagh said that while restaurants and food outlets like Supermac’s do their best to support Irish product, the real issue lies with the big processors and supermarkets. “It’s not the likes of us—that’s not where the problem is. It’s the supply chain and it’s time there was a bit of transparency. Where’s the money going after it leaves the farm gate?”

He called on Irish consumers to support local farmers by buying Irish beef where possible, but stressed that systemic reform is needed. “The big retailers are making serious profits, while farmers are getting squeezed from every end. That can’t go on.”

A spokesperson for the Irish Farmers’ Association welcomed Mr McDonagh’s remarks, saying they highlight what farmers have been saying for years. “The food producers of Ireland are at breaking point. We need action from Government and the EU to ensure fair play for farmers.”

The Department of Agriculture has said that maintaining farm incomes is a priority, with various support schemes in place, but acknowledges the ongoing challenges in the sector.

With the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation warning of volatility in global beef markets, Irish farmers say only a fair price can secure the future of the country’s beef industry.

Mr McDonagh insisted that Ireland’s rural communities depend on a thriving beef sector. “It’s time people realised, without the Irish farmer there’d be no Irish beef. We have to start looking after them before it’s too late.”
headline: Supermacs boss says Irish beef farmers are not being paid enough

text:
A man has surrendered to police in the United States after fatally shooting five people at a bank in Florida, according to authorities. The suspected gunman, named by local officials as 21-year-old Zephen Xaver, allegedly entered a branch of SunTrust Bank in the town of Sebring, central Florida, on Wednesday afternoon and opened fire.

Staff and customers inside the branch were reportedly taken hostage during the incident. Police were alerted shortly after midday, local time. After a short stand-off, officers from Highlands County Sheriff’s Office negotiated the surrender of the suspect, who was then arrested at the scene without further incident.

Sheriff Paul Blackman told media that five people had lost their lives in what he described as a “senseless act of violence.” Details about the identities of the victims have not yet been released, pending notification of next of kin. “Our hearts are broken for the families involved,” Sheriff Blackman added.

Local schools and businesses in the area were briefly put into lockdown as a precaution, but authorities later confirmed there was no further threat to the public. Eyewitnesses described scenes of panic as police and emergency services arrived at the bank, with roads quickly cordoned off and heavily armed SWAT units deployed.

US President Donald Trump and Florida’s state governor Ron DeSantis both offered their condolences to the families of those killed, while calls for tighter gun control measures have once again been raised in the aftermath of the latest mass shooting.

The FBI and state investigators have now launched a full inquiry into the tragedy. Highlands County is located around 160km south of Orlando, and the town of Sebring has a population of approximately 10,000 people.

Irish citizens concerned about relatives in the area are being advised to contact the Department of Foreign Affairs. The Irish Embassy in Washington has said it is monitoring the situation closely and liaising with US authorities.

The suspect remains in custody and is expected to appear before the local Circuit Court in the coming days, facing multiple charges of first-degree murder. The motive behind the attack remains unclear, and police have appealed for anyone with information to come forward.
headline: Gunman surrenders to police after shooting five people dead at a Florida bank

text:
The global outbreak of the coronavirus has now seen the number of confirmed infections surpass 2 million, according to figures released by health authorities around the world. The pandemic, which began late last year in China, has claimed in excess of 120,000 lives internationally as countries continue to grapple with rapidly rising caseloads and mounting death tolls.

While the virus originally centred on China’s Hubei province, it has since spread across continents, hitting Europe and the United States particularly hard in recent weeks. Italy, Spain, France, the UK, and the US remain among the worst affected, with each reporting tens of thousands of fatalities and hundreds of thousands of cases.

Ireland’s own tally has been steadily increasing, with health officials here warning that further spikes in numbers are expected in the coming days. The Department of Health reported more than 12,500 confirmed cases in the Republic, while the death toll has risen beyond 400. Northern Ireland’s numbers also continue to climb, raising concerns about cross-border transmission and the need for coordinated measures between authorities both sides of the border.

The HSE continues to urge the public to adhere strictly to social distancing guidelines and to limit travel to essential journeys only. Gardaí remain on high alert, enforcing regulations, carrying out checkpoints, and reminding people of the importance of complying with government restrictions in order to safeguard vulnerable members of the community and to stem the spread of the deadly virus.

Healthcare systems globally are under unprecedented strain, with hospitals in hotspots struggling to cope with the influx of seriously ill patients. Shortages of vital equipment, including ventilators and personal protective equipment, have been reported across multiple countries, and many governments are scrambling to ramp up supplies and expand intensive care capacity.

Research teams in several nations are working at breakneck pace to develop potential vaccines and treatments, but experts caution that it may be many months before a reliable solution is widely available. In the meantime, public health officials stress the importance of basic hygiene, handwashing, and strict adherence to recommendations from the National Public Health Emergency Team and the World Health Organisation.

The economic impact of the pandemic is also becoming increasingly evident, as businesses remain shuttered, unemployment figures soar, and governments roll out multi-billion euro rescue packages to prop up workers and enterprises facing ruin.

With no immediate end to the crisis in sight, authorities are appealing for patience, solidarity, and continued vigilance, warning that easing restrictions prematurely could lead to a renewed outbreak and even greater loss of life. As the world watches case numbers continue to rise, the coming weeks are likely to prove critical in the global fight against the coronavirus.
headline: Coronavirus: Global number of infections reaches 2m, with over 120,000 deaths so far

text:
Two courageous Irish women have spoken out about the harrowing impact stalking has had on their lives, calling urgently for more robust laws and stronger measures to protect victims. Their testimonies come amid growing pressure on the Government and the Oireachtas to prioritise tackling stalking and close what campaigners say are dangerous loopholes in current legislation.

One of the women, Sarah (not her real name), described how an ex-partner harassed her for over a year, following her to work, leaving threatening messages, and contacting her family members. Despite making multiple reports to the Gardaí, she claims little was done until the situation escalated to a physical confrontation. “It was a nightmare. I felt like I was shouting into the void and nobody was listening. The fear was constant – waiting for him to show up everywhere I went,” she said.

The second woman, Laura, detailed a campaign of intimidation that began online and quickly spilled over into her everyday life. “He found out where I lived, where my kids go to school, everything. I was terrified all the time,” she said. Laura said she faced lengthy delays waiting for Garda intervention and struggled to obtain a protection order. “You feel like you’re the one on trial, having to prove you’re not making it up,” she told The Liberal.

Both women expressed frustration at what they believe is the lack of urgency and support from authorities. They are now demanding significant updates to Irish law, including the recognition of stalking as a specific criminal offence, the introduction of stronger restraining orders, and more comprehensive supports for victims. “Ireland is so far behind other countries in this area. People’s lives are being destroyed while the system drags its feet,” Sarah said.

While the Government has promised to examine the issue, including the introduction of the Criminal Justice (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill, campaigners say clear timelines and better enforcement are needed. The women also criticised gaps in existing domestic violence legislation, which they argue fails to sufficiently protect stalking victims, especially when the perpetrator is not a former partner.

A Department of Justice spokesperson said the Minister is “committed to strengthening protections for victims of stalking” and referenced the recent establishment of a Garda Domestic Abuse Intervention Unit. However, campaigners maintain that immediate legislative change is required to prevent further suffering.

With the Oireachtas set to debate reforms in the coming months, victims like Sarah and Laura are urging TDs and Senators to listen to survivors and act decisively. “No one should have to live in fear for their safety. We need change now, not more empty promises,” Laura said.

Anyone affected by stalking or harassment is encouraged to contact the Gardaí or support services such as Women’s Aid for assistance.
headline: Two brave women spoke about their horrendous stalking experiences and what laws they want changed

text:
A 19-year-old man has died and a woman, aged 22, is fighting for her life in hospital after both reportedly took ecstasy at a gathering in Co Dublin on Friday night, according to Gardaí.

Emergency services were called to a property in the Tallaght area shortly after midnight, after it became apparent that two young people had fallen seriously ill. The pair were discovered unconscious, and efforts were made at the scene to revive them.

Both individuals were rushed to Tallaght University Hospital by ambulance, where the young man was pronounced dead a short time later. The woman remains in a critical condition, and the HSE has warned of the dangers associated with illegal drugs, particularly during the summer season when recreational use typically increases.

Gardaí are investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident and have appealed for anyone with information on the supply or distribution of illicit substances in the area to come forward. Officers are also urging anyone who was at the gathering or may have knowledge of what occurred to contact Tallaght Garda Station.

A post-mortem examination will be carried out on the deceased, while toxicology tests have been requested to determine the precise substances involved.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the HSE advised the public that the contents and strength of party drugs such as ecstasy can vary significantly, and that there is a continued risk of contamination with more potent or dangerous chemicals. The health service has urged people not to take unknown or unverified substances, and to seek urgent medical attention if they or someone they are with experiences adverse effects.

Local representatives have expressed their condolences to the family and friends of the young man, and have called for increased awareness and education in schools and communities regarding the risks associated with drug use.

Gardaí are treating the death as a tragedy and have not ruled out further arrests as their enquiries continue. The scene was preserved on Saturday to facilitate a forensic examination, and a file will be prepared for the Coroner.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Tallaght Garda Station on 01 666 6000, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.
headline: Man (19) dead and woman (22) seriously ill after taking ecstasy on Friday night

text:
The United Kingdom has recorded more than 45,100 new Covid-19 cases in the last 24 hours, raising renewed concerns about the ongoing impact of the virus across the water. British health authorities confirmed that 45,140 new infections had been identified as the pandemic continues to place pressure on the National Health Service (NHS).

While hospitalisations and deaths have not surged to the same extent as previous waves, the persistently high case numbers are prompting warnings from medical professionals and public health experts. The British Medical Association said the latest figures underline the ongoing threat posed by the virus, particularly as the winter months approach and respiratory illnesses are expected to rise.

The surge in infections comes against the backdrop of the UK government seeking to avoid reintroducing restrictive public health measures. Downing Street has so far resisted calls to implement its so-called ‘Plan B’, which would see a return to mask mandates, social distancing requirements, and potentially work-from-home guidance.

In England and Wales, the majority of new cases are believed to be the result of the Delta variant, which remains dominant. The vaccination campaign has been credited with weakening the link between infections and serious illness, but health officials are urging eligible individuals to come forward for booster shots and flu vaccines to bolster protection over the coming months.

Meanwhile, concerns remain about the situation in schools and among younger age groups, with transmission rates particularly high among children and teenagers. Teachers’ unions have urged more robust measures to ensure classrooms remain safe, including better ventilation and regular testing.

Health officials across the island of Ireland are monitoring the situation in the UK closely, amid fears that rising case numbers there could soon be reflected in increased transmission rates here. The HSE continues to encourage the public to adhere to health guidelines and to avail of vaccination where eligible.

The latest figures bring the total number of confirmed coronavirus cases in the UK since the start of the pandemic to more than 8.4 million. The official death toll stands at over 138,000, though excess mortality figures suggest the real impact is higher.

With case numbers showing no sign of significant decline, British ministers are under growing pressure to clarify their plans for managing the pandemic in the months ahead. The British government continues to urge the public to exercise caution, but critics argue that more decisive action may soon be required to protect public health and the NHS from further strain.
headline: Covid-19: UK reports just over 45,100 new coronavirus infections over the past 24h

text:
Garda checkpoints have been set up across Donegal this morning as the county officially moved to Level 3 Covid-19 restrictions at midnight. Motorists in Letterkenny, Buncrana, Ballybofey and other major towns are being stopped and questioned about non-essential travel as part of a significant policing operation initiated by An Garda Síochána.

Dozens of Gardaí are manning strategic routes into and out of the county, particularly on the N13, N14 and N15, in an effort to ensure compliance with public health measures and curb the recent surge in coronavirus cases. Checkpoints are also operating on secondary and regional roads, with officers reminding drivers and passengers that travel is now limited to within county boundaries, except for essential reasons such as work, education, or medical appointments.

Locals have expressed frustration at the sudden imposition of tighter restrictions but acknowledge that the spike in cases over recent weeks has left authorities little choice. Businesses in the hospitality sector, including pubs, cafés and restaurants, can now only offer takeaway or outdoor dining, with all indoor dining suspended for at least three weeks. Many owners fear the move will push them to the brink, while hotels are reporting mass cancellations from guests who had planned to travel for weekends or family visits.

Gardaí have warned that while the initial focus of their operation is on engagement and informing the public, enforcement powers will be used where necessary. Breaches of the rules may result in €100 fines or further penalties. Speaking this morning, Superintendent David Kelly urged people to take personal responsibility and reminded the public that unnecessary journeys put lives at risk.

The HSE says it is ramping up its testing and contact tracing programme in the county, as clusters continue to be identified, particularly in family and social settings. Health officials have attributed the rise to gatherings in homes and workplaces, and have appealed to all residents to restrict movements and follow guidelines closely.

Meanwhile, the Taoiseach has called for solidarity from all citizens and said the government will provide additional supports to businesses and workers affected by the restrictions. Opposition TDs, however, have criticised the government’s communication and warned that further local lockdowns could follow unless nationwide action is taken.

Donegal now joins Dublin as the only counties at Level 3 under the Government’s Living with Covid plan. The rest of the country remains at Level 2, but the National Public Health Emergency Team is due to meet later this week to review the situation.

Garda checkpoints are expected to continue throughout the duration of Level 3, with roadblocks operating on a rolling basis to deter cross-county travel and ensure public health advice is being followed.
headline: Garda checkpoints in force in Donegal as county moves to Level 3 restrictions

text:
The Instagram Rich List for 2019 has been unveiled, exposing the staggering sums pocketed by social media influencers and celebrities for a single post on their accounts. The annual report, compiled by Hopper HQ, shines a light on the lucrative business of turning followers into fortunes, with some stars earning enough per post to buy a Dublin city apartment outright.

Topping the global rankings, as expected, is American megastar Kylie Jenner, who reportedly commands a jaw-dropping €1.15 million for each sponsored post on her Instagram feed. Closely following are footballer Cristiano Ronaldo, pop icon Ariana Grande, and reality TV figure Kim Kardashian—each boasting enormous followings and formidable earning power.

While no Irish celebrities appear in the top ten, the trend of leveraging online popularity for income is also growing rapidly amongst Ireland’s social media scene. Home-grown influencers are increasingly partnering with brands, with some reportedly raking in thousands of euro for a single photo or story shared to their followers.

The rise of this phenomenon has prompted concerns among consumer advocacy groups and parents, who warn about the potential impact of influencer marketing on young people. The Advertising Standards Authority for Ireland (ASAI) has previously issued guidelines requiring clear labelling of sponsored content to ensure transparency for viewers.

Instagram, which remains one of the most popular platforms among young Irish users, has come under scrutiny for promoting unattainable lifestyles and blurring the lines between genuine recommendations and paid advertisements. Meanwhile, the Revenue Commissioners have also indicated an intention to keep a close eye on influencer earnings, reminding those making money online that all income must be declared.

Industry insiders say the trend shows no sign of slowing, with more Irish personalities entering the fray and foreign-based influencers continuing to raise the earning bar. For those at the top, a single photo or video is worth more than most Irish workers take home in a year, raising questions about the influence of social media and the nature of fame in the digital age.

As the Instagram Rich List captures headlines, it remains to be seen whether Irish stars will break into the global top ranks in the years to come, or if the focus on regulation and transparency will reshape the influencer landscape. For now, the message is clear: being popular online has never been more profitable.
headline: Instagram Rich List 2019 released showing stars who earn most money from each post on their account

text:
Nightlife across the country faces more upheaval as Government moves to enforce tighter controls on entry into nightclubs, as part of a last-minute clampdown to curb the spread of Covid-19. From this weekend, punters hoping to hit the dancefloor must now purchase tickets at least one hour before they arrive at the venue, under new rules set out by the Department of Health.

The decision has been met with anger and confusion among club-goers and venue operators, many of whom say they were given little notice about the dramatic change. The announcement, made by the Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly, comes just days after nightclubs reopened for the first time in 19 months. The Taoiseach yesterday defended the policy, insisting it was necessary to ensure “contact tracing and safe management” of large crowds amid rising case numbers.

However, nightclub owners have slammed the move, claiming the ticketing system will cripple trade and sow chaos at venues already struggling to stay afloat. “We spent weeks preparing to reopen under the guidelines we were given, only for this to be dropped on us at the last minute,” said Karl Sullivan, a nightclub manager in Dublin city centre. “Most of our customers are walk-ups. They’re not planning their night out hours in advance. This is just going to destroy the spontaneity.”

Under the new guidelines, tickets must be bought online or through authorised outlets a minimum of sixty minutes ahead of arrival, and names and contact details must be provided for contact tracing. Bouncers will be tasked with checking digital or printed tickets, as well as proof of Covid-19 vaccination or recovery, before granting entry. Walk-in customers will be refused.

The move comes as latest figures from the HSE show a surge in Covid-19 cases, particularly among younger age groups. The Tánaiste, Leo Varadkar, said the policy would be “reviewed constantly”, but refused to rule out further restrictions. “We are not closing nightclubs, but we need to ensure they operate as safely as possible,” he said.

Opposition TDs have labelled the Government’s handling of the situation as “a shambles”, accusing ministers of sending mixed messages to the sector. “First they said it was safe to reopen, now they’re making it impossible to operate,” said Sinn Féin’s David Cullinane.

Meanwhile, patrons attempting to enter popular venues in Cork and Galway last night described confusion at the door, with some unaware of the new ticketing rules and turned away after queuing in the cold. One reveller told The Liberal: “We were all set for a night out, got to the door, only to be told we needed tickets. Nobody knew about it. Yet another mess from the Government.”

Nightclub owners say they will struggle to enforce the measures and warn the sector could face further closures if support is not forthcoming. The Department of Health said compliance checks will be carried out by Gardaí and warned that venues could face closure for repeated breaches.

As the country braces for a winter surge of Covid-19, the nightlife sector remains in limbo, with many operators saying the mixed messaging and knee-jerk restrictions could spell the end for smaller clubs and venues. The HSE continues to urge the public to maintain caution and get vaccinated, as health officials warn that further measures cannot be ruled out if cases continue to climb.
headline: Covid-19: Punters will be forced to buy tickets for nightclubs at least one hour prior to arriving at the door

text:
The Chief Medical Officer Dr Tony Holohan has warned that the next fortnight will be "absolutely critical" in determining whether current Covid-19 restrictions can be eased or if further measures may be required. Dr Holohan expressed his growing concern about the recent rise in coronavirus cases across the country, saying the situation could deteriorate quickly if people do not strictly adhere to public health advice.

According to Dr Holohan, "We are watching the data very closely. The increase in case numbers over the past number of days is worrying and indicates that the virus remains a very real threat in our communities." He urged people not to become complacent, highlighting that every contact counts and that the actions of individuals over the coming days will have a direct impact on the trajectory of the pandemic.

"We have seen in other countries how quickly things can change, and Ireland is not immune to those risks,” he said. “If we don’t see an improvement, it will not be possible to recommend any easing of restrictions. In fact, it may be necessary to consider additional measures if the rate of infection continues to rise.”

The National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET) will review the latest figures next week, with a particular focus on the number of hospitalisations and the presence of new variants in communities. The Department of Health has also signalled alarm over outbreaks linked to household gatherings and workplace settings, with the HSE reporting increased clusters in Dublin, Donegal, and other counties.

Government sources have indicated that any decisions on easing lockdown will be based on advice from public health experts and the evolving situation in hospitals. The Taoiseach Micheál Martin said earlier this week that "nobody wants to see prolonged restrictions," but that public safety must remain the top priority.

Dr Holohan appealed to the public to continue limiting their movements, avoid unnecessary journeys, and follow the existing health guidance “to the letter.” He reiterated the importance of wearing face coverings, avoiding social visits, and supporting vulnerable members of the community.

Vaccination of priority groups is continuing, with the Department of Health stating that the rollout is on track, although some concerns over supply remain. The Tánaiste Leo Varadkar said on Thursday that the Government is “doing everything possible” to accelerate the programme, but “we cannot vaccinate our way out of this latest surge in the short term.”

With St Patrick’s Day approaching, there is further concern that any relaxation in behaviour could lead to a spike in cases. The Gardaí have said they will be increasing patrols and enforcement measures to prevent illegal gatherings and ensure compliance with regulations.

Dr Holohan concluded by emphasising that “what we do now will decide what happens next,” and called on every person in Ireland to “hold the line” for the next two weeks in the hope that the spread of the virus can be brought back under control.
headline: Holohan says that the next two weeks will determine on whether we can ease restrictions, says he’s increasingly concerned

text:
Health authorities have issued a warning to residents in Kildare, Offaly and Laois after a notable increase in Covid-19 cases over the past week. The HSE reported a cluster of outbreaks in these counties, sparking concerns about the potential for further community transmission. 

According to figures released last night, there have been more than 80 new cases identified across the three midlands counties since last Friday, prompting calls for locals to “redouble efforts” in following health guidelines. The Department of Health has confirmed that the majority of new infections are associated with outbreaks in workplaces and direct provision centres, though some community spread has also been recorded. 

Taoiseach Simon Harris has said that while there are currently no plans for a local lockdown, the situation is being monitored “hour by hour”. Speaking to RTÉ Radio One, he urged people to act responsibly and to “avoid unnecessary gatherings”, emphasising the importance of mask-wearing and hand hygiene in preventing further cases. 

Gardaí have also increased patrols in the affected areas, particularly around known congregation hotspots. Officers are reminding the public that house parties and large events are still subject to strict limits, with fines and prosecutions possible for those in breach of regulations. 

Local TDs from both Government and Opposition have appealed for calm while also expressing concern about the readiness of the local health service. Sinn Féin’s Brian Stanley said, “We need clarity from the HSE on resources and capacity in the Midlands Regional Hospital in Portlaoise.” Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly has reassured the Oireachtas that surge contingency plans are in place, should admissions rise. 

HSE Director-General Bernard Gloster stated that extra testing centres will be set up across Kildare, Offaly and Laois, with walk-in and drive-through facilities available. Contact tracing teams have been redeployed to the region in an effort to “get ahead of the curve”. 

Businesses in towns such as Newbridge, Tullamore, and Portlaoise are bracing themselves for the possibility of new restrictions. Owners say confidence is already shaken after previous lockdowns and fear any return to tighter measures would devastate the local economy. 

Public health officials are calling on anyone experiencing symptoms such as a cough, fever, or loss of taste/smell, to self-isolate and contact their GP. The HSE is also urging people who have travelled abroad in the last fortnight to be particularly vigilant. 

NPHET is expected to meet tomorrow to discuss the situation, with a further update from the Department of Health anticipated in the coming days.
headline: Kildare, Offaly and Laois warned to be on alert following rise in Covid-19 cases

text:
Approximately 1.4 million people across Ireland are set to receive a significant cash boost tomorrow as part of the Government’s latest round of social welfare support, with some recipients in line for double payments to ease the rising cost of living.

Eligible individuals will see the payment land directly in their bank accounts or at their local post office from Tuesday, following confirmation from the Department of Social Protection. The move will benefit pensioners, carers, people with disabilities, and families in receipt of various social welfare schemes.

Some will receive the standard rate while others qualify for a special double payment, known as a "double week”, designed to help offset household bills and grocery costs that have surged in recent months. The measures were announced in March as part of the spring cost-of-living package, which was unveiled by Minister for Social Protection Heather Humphreys TD.

Social Protection officials said the payment schedule covers a range of supports, including the State Pension, Disability Allowance, Carer’s Allowance, and Jobseeker’s Benefit. Those on schemes such as the Working Family Payment and the One-Parent Family Payment are also included.

Minister Humphreys said the double payment is a recognition of the ongoing challenges faced by many families. “This latest double week will provide additional breathing space to pensioners, carers, people with disabilities and low-income families right across the country. We are very conscious of pressures stemming from higher energy and grocery bills, and these targeted supports will make a meaningful difference,” she said.

Recent hikes in fuel and food prices have further impacted those on lower incomes, with advocacy groups urging the Government to provide more regular support payments. The Society of St Vincent de Paul has welcomed the announcement but warned that more permanent improvements to core social welfare rates are needed to address poverty.

Recipients do not need to apply in order to receive the additional payment, as it will be issued automatically to those eligible. The Department has urged anyone unsure of their entitlements to visit its website or contact their local Intreo office.

One pensioner from Cork, speaking to The Liberal, said the double payment would offer much-needed financial relief. “It makes a big difference at this time of year with the bills coming in,” she said.

The latest social welfare measures are part of a series of temporary supports introduced by the Government since last year. Further decisions on additional supports are expected to be discussed ahead of the Budget in October, with advocacy groups calling for increases to the overall level of social welfare payments to keep pace with inflation.
headline: 1.4 million people will receive cash boost tomorrow with some receiving double social welfare payments

text:
The Government has launched a fresh wave of Covid-19 information campaigns targeting non-Irish nationals, after admitting there is a significantly lower uptake of vaccines in some foreign communities. In a move that some critics have described as “too little, too late”, the Department of Health unveiled new resources in several foreign languages, including Polish, Romanian, Lithuanian, and Portuguese.

Officials claim these materials will “increase awareness and protect vulnerable groups”, but questions remain about why the Government waited nearly two years into the pandemic to ramp up multilingual communications.

Figures released by the HSE last week show vaccination rates lag well behind the national average among certain groups of foreign nationals living in Ireland. According to the data, some communities have take-up rates up to 20% lower than the general population, worrying public health authorities as concerns mount about further Covid surges.

A spokesperson from the Department of Health told The Liberal, “We are acutely aware that language and cultural barriers play a role in vaccine hesitancy. The new advice, available in a range of languages, will ensure everyone in Ireland has access to accurate information about Covid-19 and vaccination.”

However, TDs and campaigners have accused the Government of not doing enough to engage with communities on the ground, with some pointing to ongoing confusion around eligibility, booking systems, and misinformation spreading on social media platforms popular among foreign nationals.

One Polish community leader in Dublin said, “From the beginning there was a lack of clear information in our language. Many people didn’t understand the process, so they didn’t get vaccinated. The Government should have acted faster.”

The new information leaflets and online resources are being distributed through community groups, schools, and workplaces with large numbers of non-Irish workers. There is also a new multilingual phone line for vaccine queries.

Opposition parties have used the announcement to call for greater investment in community outreach, accusing the Department of “window dressing” and failing to address deeper issues affecting migrants’ access to healthcare. Sinn Féin spokesperson on health, David Cullinane TD, said, “We need real engagement, not just translated leaflets.”

The HSE stated that efforts are ongoing to reach all communities and that vaccination remains open to everyone living in Ireland, regardless of immigration status.

Meanwhile, with ongoing public health concerns around emerging variants, the Government is urging all residents to stay informed and consider booster jabs. However, it remains to be seen if the new campaign will have a measurable impact on vaccination rates among Ireland’s diverse foreign national communities.
headline: Government launch “foreign language” covid advice as there’s a low uptake in vaccines with foreign nationals

text:
US President Donald Trump has this evening declared a national emergency across the United States in response to the rapidly escalating coronavirus crisis, as the global outbreak continues to spread at an alarming rate. The declaration, made during a live televised address from the White House, will unlock tens of billions of dollars in federal funding to help tackle the spread of Covid-19 and to bolster the country’s under-pressure healthcare services.

The move comes as the number of confirmed coronavirus cases in the US surged past 2,000, with dozens of fatalities reported in several states. In recent days, the American response to Covid-19 has been widely criticised, with accusations of a sluggish rollout of testing and mixed messages from US authorities frustrating attempts to contain the virus.

Speaking to the American people, President Trump said: “I am officially declaring a national emergency – two very big words.” The declaration will immediately make up to $50 billion available for state and local governments to fund emergency measures, a sum equivalent to about €44 billion. The announcement comes after mounting pressure from state governors and public health officials, who have called for stronger federal action as schools have closed, sporting events have been cancelled, and public gatherings restricted in major US cities.

International shares reacted positively to the announcement, with markets clawing back some losses following the worst week since the 2008 financial crisis. President Trump also announced that the US would expand its travel ban to include the UK and Ireland, following Wednesday’s surprise move to bar entry from 26 European countries. The US Embassy in Dublin confirmed on Friday evening that these new restrictions will affect residents of Ireland from Monday onwards, though US citizens and legal permanent residents will be permitted to return home.

In Ireland, the Department of Foreign Affairs has updated its travel advice for those considering journeys to America, warning of the likelihood of further disruption as US authorities attempt to stem the spread of the virus. The HSE continues to advise Irish residents to follow public health guidance and to avoid non-essential travel.

As President Trump’s declaration was made, public health officials in the US warned that the situation could worsen in the coming weeks and urged citizens to remain calm but vigilant. The US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is continuing to recommend social distancing measures similar to those currently in place across Ireland.

Meanwhile, Taoiseach Leo Varadkar, who himself was in the US for St Patrick’s Day events earlier this week, has urged Irish citizens to “stay informed and stay safe” as the pandemic continues to disrupt life at home and abroad. The Government’s emergency measures remain in force across the country, with schools, colleges and childcare facilities closed until at least 29 March and public gatherings restricted.

The latest developments in America further highlight the global reach of the coronavirus crisis, with the number of cases worldwide now exceeding 140,000 and over 5,000 deaths reported, according to the World Health Organisation. Authorities here continue to stress the importance of personal hygiene and social distancing in combating the spread of the virus.
headline: BREAKING: Coronavirus – President Donald Trump declares national emergency in the United States

text:
Fashion retailer LK Bennett, a familiar presence on Irish high streets and a favourite with a number of high-profile clients including members of the British royal family, has entered administration, putting roughly 500 jobs in the UK at risk.

The company, which specialises in upmarket womenswear, footwear, and accessories, made the announcement on Thursday following weeks of mounting speculation about its financial stability. Despite efforts by management to secure fresh investment and reach restructuring agreements with creditors, the retailer was ultimately forced to file for administration.

The move affects the brand’s 39 shops across the UK, as well as its head office operations. There is no immediate word on the fate of LK Bennett’s international stores, including its outlet in Dublin’s Brown Thomas, but the company’s administrators have said that “all options will be explored”.

Founded in London in 1990, LK Bennett became synonymous with contemporary but classic styling and attracted a loyal following among professional women and celebrities alike. The brand found particular favour with Catherine, Princess of Wales, further elevating its profile both in Britain and internationally.

However, the retailer has faced significant challenges in recent years, including changing consumer habits, rising business rates, and intense competition from both high-street chains and online competitors. Analysts have noted that the wider retail sector, both in the UK and Ireland, continues to experience ongoing turbulence as shoppers tighten their belts and the cost-of-living crisis bites.

Administrators from EY-Parthenon have reportedly taken control of the company’s affairs and have said that stores will continue to trade for the foreseeable future while options, including a possible sale, are considered. In a statement this afternoon, administrators said: “LK Bennett has long been a much-loved British fashion brand, and we will be exploring all possibilities to secure the future of the business and safeguard jobs.”

The announcement has caused considerable concern amongst staff, with unions and employment advocates expressing fears for job security and calling for urgent action to protect affected workers. Some Irish staff who previously worked in the UK stores told The Liberal that the news is “devastating”, with “many worrying about paying their bills and mortgages.”

The development has also raised questions about the broader health of the mid-tier fashion market on both sides of the Irish Sea, with some suggesting that further closures and job losses could be on the horizon if consumer confidence does not return soon.
headline: Fashion retailer LK Bennett enters into administration, 500 UK jobs on the line

text:
