Germany, France, and Italy have taken the step of suspending the use of the AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine amid growing concerns over reports of blood clotting events thought to be linked to the jab. The three EU countries announced their decisions within hours of each other on Monday, joining a number of other European states – including Denmark, Norway, the Netherlands, and Ireland – that have halted the rollout of the vaccine temporarily as a precaution.

German Health Minister Jens Spahn stated that the pause was taken “on the basis of a current recommendation from the Paul Ehrlich Institute,” the country’s vaccine authority, which advised further investigation into possible side effects. In France, President Emmanuel Macron said administration would be suspended “as a precautionary measure” until further guidance is available from the European Medicines Agency (EMA), which is set to deliver its findings later this week. Italian authorities likewise cited the need to assess potential risks before resuming the country’s own vaccination programme.

The AstraZeneca vaccine, developed in collaboration with Oxford University, has faced mounting scrutiny after a small number of recipients developed serious thromboembolic conditions, including blood clots, after their inoculation. The EMA has so far said that there is “no indication” the vaccine caused the reported conditions, noting that the number of cases appears in line with the frequency of such events in the general population. Nevertheless, the agency has convened its safety committee to carry out a full review, with results expected in the coming days.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) also weighed in on the matter on Monday, calling on countries not to panic and stressing that the benefits of the AstraZeneca vaccine outweigh any potential risks. WHO experts said that investigations are ongoing, but no direct causal link has been established between the vaccine and blood clots.

The temporary halts mark a setback for vaccine campaigns across Europe, where the pace of inoculation has already been hampered by delays in supply and logistical challenges. AstraZeneca’s vaccine forms a central part of the EU’s vaccination strategy, with millions of doses ordered for delivery through the summer.

In Ireland, the HSE suspended the use of AstraZeneca on Sunday as a precaution following advice from the National Immunisation Advisory Committee, after a small number of cases of unusual clotting conditions were reported in Norway. The move has resulted in the rescheduling of thousands of appointments across the country.

The Taoiseach, Micheál Martin, has said that the government is closely monitoring the situation and is in constant contact with European partners. He stressed the importance of “following the science” and awaiting a clear verdict from the EMA before any further action is taken.

As health authorities conduct their investigations, the public is being urged not to lose confidence in the broader Covid-19 vaccination effort, with officials emphasising that strict monitoring and reporting systems are in place to protect safety at every stage.
headline: Covid-19: Germany, France, and Italy have temporarily halted administration of the AstraZeneca vaccine due to increasing reports of blood clotting

text:
A Status Orange rain warning issued by Met Éireann remains in effect this morning for counties Cork, Kerry and Waterford, with the alert set to continue until midday.

Residents in the affected areas have been urged to exercise caution as heavy downpours overnight have led to challenging driving conditions and a risk of spot flooding. Several roads in the south-west have already reported surface water build-up, with the Gardaí advising motorists to reduce speed and allow extra time for journeys.

Met Éireann has forecast persistent and intense rainfall amounts, particularly along coastal and mountainous regions. Rainfall totals of up to 50mm are expected in some localities. The HSE has also advised households in flood-prone areas to remain vigilant and to prepare sandbags where possible.

Emergency services in Cork, Kerry and Waterford have responded to multiple callouts since Tuesday evening, with local authorities on standby for further incidents. Some minor roads in West Cork and south Kerry were temporarily impassable earlier this morning due to waterlogging, though no major incidents or injuries have been reported.

The Department of Education is monitoring the situation, but at present all schools remain open. Parents are advised to check with individual schools regarding any localised closures or changes to bus routes.

The weather alert is part of a broader system of Atlantic fronts expected to move across the country throughout the week. A Status Yellow warning for heavy rain is also in place for several neighbouring counties, including Limerick, Tipperary and Clare, where accumulations may still cause localised disruption.

Met Éireann has advised the public to keep up to date with the latest forecasts, emphasising the continuing risk of hazardous conditions during the morning commute. The Orange alert will be reviewed before noon, with forecasters expected to downgrade to Yellow as rainfall tails off later in the afternoon.

The Office of Public Works and local council crews continue to monitor for rising river levels, and sandbagging operations are underway in flood-prone zones. Residents are encouraged to report any flooding or blocked drains to their local authority and to avoid engaging in unnecessary travel until the alert has expired.
headline: Status Orange warning for heavy rain in place for three counties until noon

text:
Kyle Rittenhouse has been found not guilty on all charges following a high-profile trial in the United States, after he fatally shot two men and injured another during Black Lives Matter protests in Kenosha, Wisconsin last year. The verdict was delivered on Friday evening by a jury following three days of deliberation, in a case that has sparked international debate surrounding issues of self-defence, gun rights, and public protest.

Rittenhouse, who was 17 years old at the time of the incident in August 2020, faced charges including intentional homicide, reckless homicide, and attempted homicide. The prosecution alleged he was a dangerous vigilante who recklessly took lives, while the defence argued he acted lawfully in self-defence after being attacked by rioters.

The trial drew intense scrutiny and widespread commentary both in the US and abroad, with political figures and commentators weighing in on the implications for American society and legal precedent. The verdict is likely to fuel further debate over the use of deadly force and the nature of protests across the United States.

In Ireland, the case has been followed closely on social media and by legal observers, with some comparing procedural aspects to self-defence laws as applied by the Irish courts. While American law differs significantly, the case has prompted questions about how similar circumstances might arise and be dealt with here.

There are no reports of large-scale protests in response to the verdict in Ireland, but the issue remains a live topic for discussion among politicians and members of the Oireachtas. The Department of Foreign Affairs has not released any comment at time of publication.

The families of the men who died, Joseph Rosenbaum and Anthony Huber, expressed disappointment and anger at the verdict, while supporters of Rittenhouse have claimed the trial demonstrates the right to defend oneself when threatened.

Rittenhouse himself was visibly emotional upon hearing the outcome, collapsing to the floor as the judge announced the not guilty verdict on all five counts.

The defence team said afterwards that the verdict proved their client’s innocence and that he should be allowed to move on with his life. Prosecutors have not yet indicated whether any further legal action will be considered.

The case is expected to remain in the headlines as reactions continue to pour in from across the world.
headline: ?BREAKING: Not guilty – Kyle Rittenhouse cleared of all charges after he shot dead two men while defending himself during Black Lives Matter protests

text:
Britain moved a significant step closer to leaving the European Union last night, as the Withdrawal Agreement Bill passed through the House of Commons with overwhelming support. The legislation, championed by Prime Minister Boris Johnson, secured a comfortable 330 to 231 majority, virtually guaranteeing that Britain will depart the EU on January 31st.

After years of political deadlock, uncertainty, and national division, the Conservative Party’s thumping General Election victory in December paved the way for Mr Johnson to drive his Brexit deal through Parliament with relative ease. Only a handful of rebels broke ranks, while Labour, the SNP and Liberal Democrats voted against the Bill in a largely symbolic gesture.

The legislation must still pass through the House of Lords, where it is likely to face some scrutiny, but with the Government’s electoral mandate and sizeable Commons majority, few expect any meaningful obstacles. If all proceeds as anticipated, Britain will officially leave the bloc after 47 years of membership, ending a turbulent chapter in both UK and EU politics.

The Taoiseach, Leo Varadkar, welcomed the clarity provided by last night’s vote, telling reporters: “We have always said that we respect the UK’s democratic decision. Our priority remains protecting the Good Friday Agreement, citizens’ rights, and Ireland’s interests.”

The Tánaiste, Simon Coveney, echoed these sentiments, but urged continued vigilance: “There is still work to be done. Negotiations on the future relationship will be complex and must safeguard Irish interests, particularly in relation to trade and the border.”

Under the terms of the Agreement, a transition period will run until the end of December 2020, during which Britain will follow existing EU rules while new arrangements are hammered out. During this period, the Irish border will continue to remain invisible, but concerns linger in border communities about future arrangements and their potential impact on trade and daily life.

Business leaders across Ireland cautiously welcomed last night’s vote, but called for urgent clarity on the post-Brexit trading relationship. Chambers Ireland chief executive Ian Talbot said: “Progress is welcome, but there remains a risk of a cliff edge if a trade deal is not reached before the end of the transition period.”

Sinn Féin President Mary Lou McDonald criticised the British government’s approach, warning that “real concerns remain for citizens in the North, whose rights must be protected.”

Meanwhile in Brussels, EU leaders said they were ready to begin talks on the future partnership, but cautioned that time is short. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated: “Decisions on our future co-operation will have to be made rapidly.”

With less than a month to go before Britain is scheduled to leave, attention now shifts to the next phase — negotiations that will determine the nature of the UK’s relationship with the EU, and with Ireland, for years to come.
headline: Brexit Withdrawal Agreement breezes through Parliament, meaning Britain will likely leave the EU for good on January 31, 2020

text:
Gardaí have launched an investigation following the discovery of a man's body in Killybegs Harbour, Co. Donegal. The remains, believed to be those of a local fisherman, were recovered from the water on Monday morning after emergency services were alerted by a member of the public who spotted something unusual near the fishing docks at approximately 8.30am.

The deceased, understood to be a man in his 50s, was pulled from the harbour by Killybegs Coast Guard personnel and the RNLI shortly after they arrived at the scene. Local reports suggest that the man's boat had been docked in the area overnight, and it is believed that he may have fallen into the water in the early hours of the morning. It is not yet clear how long the body was in the water prior to its discovery.

The scene was immediately sealed off by Gardaí and a full technical examination was carried out by the Garda Technical Bureau. The State Pathologist has been notified and a post-mortem examination is due to take place at Letterkenny University Hospital to determine the exact cause of death. Foul play is not suspected at this time, but Gardaí have confirmed that they are keeping an open mind while investigations are ongoing.

Local sources indicate that the deceased was well-known in the Killybegs fishing community, with many expressing their shock and sadness at the news. Fishing operations in the harbour were suspended temporarily as Gardaí conducted their inquiries, and the area remains under increased Garda presence.

A spokesperson for An Garda Síochána confirmed that they are appealing to anyone who was in the Killybegs Harbour area between Sunday evening and Monday morning and who may have witnessed anything unusual to contact them at Ballyshannon Garda Station or through the Garda Confidential Line.

The tragic discovery has cast a pall over the busy fishing port, with local representatives offering their condolences to the family of the deceased. The investigation is continuing.
headline: Gardai launch probe after the body of a fisherman is recovered from Killybegs Harbour in Co. Donegal

text:
Malaysian authorities are expected to release the post mortem results of Nora Quoirin later today, as investigations continue into the tragic death of the 15-year-old Irish-French teenager. Nora, who had special needs and travelled to Malaysia with her family for a holiday, was reported missing from her accommodation at the Dusun eco-resort in the Negeri Sembilan region on 4th August.

After an extensive search operation lasting over a week and involving hundreds of personnel, Nora’s body was found on Tuesday in a ravine approximately two kilometres from the resort. The discovery brought a devastating end to a case that had gripped Ireland, France, and Malaysia, with concerns voiced from the outset about the vulnerable teenager’s wellbeing.

The Malaysian police have maintained that there is no indication of foul play, but Nora’s family have repeatedly expressed their belief that she may have been abducted. The family have cited the teenager’s physical and mental difficulties, noting that she would not have wandered off alone and was highly dependent on her parents for daily care.

Irish consular officials have been in close contact with the Quoirin family and local authorities throughout the ordeal. The Taoiseach Leo Varadkar expressed his condolences to the family and thanked searchers for their efforts. President Michael D. Higgins also extended his sympathies, stating that Nora’s story had deeply affected people across Ireland.

Members of An Garda Síochána have not been deployed in the investigation, but the force has offered full assistance to Malaysian police if requested. The Department of Foreign Affairs continues to provide support to the family, who have roots in Belfast and live in London.

A post mortem was conducted yesterday by a team of pathologists in Seremban. Results, which are expected later today, are hoped to clarify the cause of death and address lingering questions about the circumstances in which Nora died. Malaysian police say that, depending on the findings, further investigations will be carried out if necessary.

Meanwhile, vigils have been held in County Kildare and Belfast in memory of Nora, with parishioners lighting candles and expressing their support for the family. The Quoirins have thanked the public for their prayers and assistance, as well as the Malaysian and Irish authorities for their support during a deeply distressing time.

With international attention focused on the results of the post mortem, Nora’s family and supporters await clarification and hope for answers in the coming hours.
headline: Malaysian authorities to release results of Nora Quoirin’s post mortem later today

text:
About 40 workers at the Stryker plant in Carrigtwohill, Co Cork, are set to lose their jobs following a company announcement on Tuesday. Staff were informed by management that a review of business operations had led to the decision to cut positions at the site, which employs around 1,200 people locally.

The US multinational, which manufactures medical devices, stated that the redundancies are “necessary to ensure long-term viability and competitiveness” in the face of what it described as “challenging global market conditions.” Stryker is one of Cork’s largest employers in the healthcare sector, with several plants across the county.

Affected staff will be offered statutory redundancy terms, and a consultation process has commenced. Some workers expressed shock at the news, as there had been no public indication of job cuts prior to the announcement. Trade union representatives are now calling for engagement with management and Government to seek assurances regarding the future of Stryker’s other Irish operations.

Local TDs have called on the Minister for Enterprise, Trade and Employment to ensure the workers are given every possible support, including access to upskilling and job placement programmes. The Department of Social Protection is preparing to offer information sessions and assistance on jobseeker supports.

Stryker’s global headquarters are based in Michigan, with the company operating in Ireland since 1998. The firm has a presence in Limerick and Belfast, as well as Cork. It is understood the job losses will take effect over the coming weeks.

Concerns are now being raised for the broader employment landscape in the Munster region, as the announcement follows recent lay-offs in other sectors. The IDA has indicated it remains in contact with Stryker and will be monitoring developments closely. 

It is not yet clear whether further redundancies are expected at Stryker’s other Irish sites.
headline: Job losses announced at the Stryker plant in Cork, about 40 people are to lose their jobs

text:
Dr Ronan Glynn, the Deputy Chief Medical Officer, has revealed that only 3% of recent Covid-19 cases in Ireland are among people over the age of 65. Speaking at the Department of Health’s daily briefing, Dr Glynn said the vast majority of new cases are being recorded in younger adults, with the median age now at just 32 years old.

According to the latest data provided by the HSE, the pattern of infection has shifted significantly since the beginning of the pandemic. Previously, older individuals were most at risk, but efforts to protect vulnerable groups and the rollout of vaccination programmes have seen the number of cases in those over 65 fall to its lowest point yet. Healthcare officials say that this trend is likely to continue as further cohorts receive the jab in the coming weeks.

Dr Glynn emphasised that, despite these positive figures for older citizens, the ongoing spread among younger people remains a source of concern. “While it is encouraging to see fewer cases in our older population, we must not become complacent. Covid-19 can still pose a serious threat to people of all ages, particularly if the virus is allowed to circulate widely in the community,” he said.

The Deputy CMO also pointed to recent clusters linked to social gatherings and workplaces, reiterating the importance of continuing to observe public health advice. “We are seeing outbreaks among people in their 20s, 30s and 40s. These cases may not result in as many hospitalisations, but the risk of transmission to more vulnerable family members and contacts remains,” he added.

Gardaí have also been urging the public to adhere to current restrictions on household visits and indoor events. With the vaccine rollout accelerating, the Government is hoping to avoid a resurgence of cases later in the year, which could put renewed pressure on the HSE and frontline staff.

Dr Glynn concluded with an appeal for ongoing vigilance: “We have made significant progress and it is thanks to the collective efforts of people across the country. If we continue to work together and follow the guidance, we can protect those most at risk and move closer to reopening society safely.”

The Department of Health has confirmed that it will continue to monitor trends closely and provide updates on the situation as it develops. The latest figures bring the total number of confirmed cases in Ireland to over 260,000, with hospitalisations and ICU admissions now at their lowest level in months.
headline: Dr Ronan Glynn says just 3% of Covid-19 cases are in the over 65s

text:
Leo Varadkar has poured cold water on speculation of a Fine Gael–Fianna Fáil grand coalition after the next general election, unequivocally stating that his party is preparing to enter opposition. The outgoing Taoiseach made the remarks today in a pointed rebuke to Tánaiste Micheál Martin’s suggestion that a post-election alliance could still be on the cards, dashing any hopes in Fianna Fáil circles of a renewed partnership.

Speaking at a press event in Dublin, Mr Varadkar was forthright: “We’ve made our position clear. Fine Gael will not be going into government after the next election. We intend to serve in opposition.” His comments come just days after announcing his intention to step down as leader of Fine Gael and as Taoiseach, a decision which has sent shockwaves throughout the party and wider Irish political landscape.

The statement is being interpreted as a direct response to whispers within Fianna Fáil, led by Mr Martin, who has recently floated the idea of continuing the current coalition arrangements in some form after the next poll. Martin’s musings had sparked speculation that the two so-called “civil war parties” might seek to keep Sinn Féin from office by renewing their alliance, despite growing public fatigue with the current government.

The comments from Mr Varadkar have upended these calculations, torpedoing what one Fine Gael source described as “Micheál’s fever dreams of a perpetual grand coalition.” Senior party figures privately acknowledge that many grassroots members are restive after years in office, with a growing mood for a spell on the opposition benches to rebuild and regroup.

Reaction from the public and among political commentators has been swift. Some have welcomed the clarity, pointing out that a clear distinction between parties and a robust opposition is vital for democratic accountability. Others have questioned whether Mr Varadkar’s stance will bind his successor, expected to be chosen at a special Fine Gael convention in the coming weeks.

For his part, Mr Martin has sought to keep his options open, insisting that “all scenarios must be considered” in the national interest. However, the Tánaiste’s overtures have found little traction with Fine Gael’s rank-and-file, weary of compromise and the electoral battering suffered in recent local and by-elections.

Attention now shifts to Fine Gael’s impending leadership contest, with Simon Harris and Helen McEntee among the front-runners. Both face the task of unifying a party facing historic uncertainty, while juggling coalition tensions in the Dáil and the prospect of a bruising campaign against Sinn Féin and a resurgent opposition.

The government’s majority remains fragile, with ongoing industrial action, the housing crisis, and cost-of-living pressures fuelling public anger. As the election looms, Varadkar’s clear signal and Martin’s hopes for a centre-ground alliance appear increasingly at odds — setting up a fierce political battle for the months ahead.
headline: Outgoing Taoiseach Leo Varadkar torpedoes Micheal Martin’s fever dreams of a grand coalition by saying that Fine Gael is headed for opposition

text:
RTÉ is set to cut up to 200 jobs, introduce pay cuts for its highest earners, and implement a pay freeze for staff in a fresh bid to stem mounting financial losses, the broadcaster confirmed today. The national broadcaster, long plagued by ongoing controversies and a deepening cash crisis, announced a sweeping cost-saving programme as it struggles to restore public trust and balance its books.

Sources within RTÉ told The Liberal that compulsory redundancies could not be ruled out as the station slashes staff numbers across departments, with voluntary redundancy schemes also on the table. The cuts are expected to be rolled out over the coming months, with management warning that drastic action is necessary to secure the organisation’s survival.

Director General Kevin Bakhurst briefed staff on the moves this morning, admitting that RTÉ must “live within its means” following a collapse in licence fee revenue and the fallout from the secret payments scandal that rocked Montrose last year. Mr Bakhurst also confirmed that presenters and executives earning over €100,000 will face pay reductions, while all staff will see their pay frozen for a minimum of two years.

“We know these are difficult messages for our staff and their families to hear, but RTÉ cannot continue as it has done,” he said, adding that the broadcaster will “act decisively” to tackle its €61 million deficit.  

Staff unions have reacted angrily to the news, with the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) condemning the lack of prior consultation and warning that the cuts will damage public service broadcasting. The SIPTU trade union said it is seeking an urgent meeting with RTÉ management and has not ruled out industrial action.

The move comes on the back of a dramatic plunge in licence fee payments, with public confidence in the station badly shaken by the Ryan Tubridy payments debacle and revelations about extravagant spending by senior executives. The Government has so far resisted calls to replace the licence fee system, with Minister for Media Catherine Martin insisting that wider reform proposals are being considered by the Oireachtas.

RTÉ has already introduced spending restrictions on travel, hospitality, and recruitment, as well as reducing programme budgets. Today’s announcement marks a significant escalation of its cost-control measures, with management warning that further cuts may be unavoidable unless public funding is increased.

Critics argue that today’s moves will hit ordinary staff hardest, while well-paid stars and managers have yet to fully shoulder their share of the pain. The broadcaster’s transparency and governance have been under fierce scrutiny since last summer, with the Public Accounts Committee and the Dáil’s Media Committee both conducting grilling inquiries.

Meanwhile, the public remains sceptical, with many calling for the abolition of the television licence fee and a root-and-branch overhaul of how the national broadcaster is funded and managed. With job losses looming and industrial unrest on the cards, the crisis at RTÉ shows no sign of abating.
headline: RTE to cut 200 jobs, introduce pay cuts and pay freeze in an effort to stop losses

text:
A controversial Covid-19 “RAT LINE” set up by Gardaí in Donegal during the pandemic has been quietly scrapped after an internal review reportedly found that up to 60 percent of reports made to the service did not relate to any breach of health regulations.

The confidential telephone line, established in early 2021, was designed to allow members of the public to report alleged breaches of Covid laws directly to local Gardaí. However, figures seen by The Liberal reveal that a majority of calls received were either unfounded, outside the scope of the regulations, or were deemed malicious.

The decision to discontinue the “RAT LINE” follows months of criticism from community groups and local representatives, who argued that the measure encouraged neighbourly distrust and was open to abuse. Several local TDs had raised concerns in the Dáil about the impact on community relations, with some describing the hotline as “draconian”.

Garda sources have confirmed that a review by senior officers found that just 4 in 10 calls led to follow-up action, with the remainder dismissed after assessment. In some cases, callers were found to have exaggerated or fabricated claims about gatherings, travel, and business activities in their locality.

Concerns were also raised about the resources required to staff and investigate calls to the hotline at a time when Garda personnel were under significant pressure due to frontline Covid enforcement and other policing duties.

In a statement to The Liberal, a spokesperson for An Garda Síochána said: “All reports of suspected breaches of public health regulations were assessed and responded to appropriately. We continue to encourage the public to report criminal activity through established channels.”

Some local business owners welcomed the decision to abandon the RAT LINE, claiming they had been unfairly targeted by anonymous reports. “It was a nightmare,” said one Letterkenny publican. “We’d have Gardaí arriving at the door after someone phoned in nonsense. It was divisive and stressful for staff and customers alike.”

The HSE has previously said it was not involved in the establishment or operation of the Garda RAT LINE in Donegal.

The move to end the controversial service comes amid ongoing controversies over the Government’s handling of pandemic restrictions and enforcement, with many calling for more transparency around the use of emergency powers.

The hotline is understood to have been shut down at the end of 2023, with notices circulated to Donegal Garda stations and relevant stakeholders. No plans have been made to reinstate the service.
headline: Donegal Gardai’s controversial Covid “RAT LINE” has been cancelled after 60% of calls were found not to be breaches of covid laws

text:
A woman in her 50s has sadly lost her life following a tragic road collision in County Kildare, adding to the growing toll of fatalities on Irish roads this year.

The incident occurred in the early hours of Monday morning on the R445 at Ballymany, near Newbridge, when a car and a lorry were involved in a devastating crash. Emergency services rushed to the scene shortly before 5am, but the woman, who was the sole occupant of the car, was pronounced dead at the scene. The driver of the lorry was uninjured.

Gardaí immediately cordoned off the area and began a full forensic examination, with local traffic diversions put in place for several hours, causing significant disruption for morning commuters. The woman’s body was removed to Naas General Hospital, where a post-mortem examination is expected to take place.

This latest fatality brings fresh grief to the local community and renewed concern about the alarming rise in deaths on Irish roads in 2024. So far, over 90 people have lost their lives in road traffic incidents, sparking calls for greater enforcement and tougher penalties for reckless driving.

Gardaí are appealing for witnesses to the collision, particularly anyone who travelled the R445 between Newbridge and the Curragh before 5am and may have dashcam footage. Anyone with information is asked to contact Newbridge Garda Station on 045 431 212, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.

Locals have expressed shock and anger at yet another life lost, with many highlighting the urgent need for road safety improvements in the area. The Government and the Road Safety Authority (RSA) have also been urging motorists to slow down and remain vigilant, as they attempt to stem the tide of what many are now calling a road carnage crisis.

Investigations are ongoing, and the victim's family are being supported by specially trained Garda officers. The Liberal will continue to follow this story and provide updates as more information emerges.
headline: Road carnage continues, after woman in her 50s dies in crash in Co. Kildare

text:
Tributes are being paid from across Ireland and the UK following the tragic death of David Amess MP, who was fatally stabbed while attending a constituency surgery in Leigh-on-Sea, Essex, on Friday afternoon. Mr Amess, a Conservative MP since 1983, was widely recognised for his gentle manner, dedicated public service, and deep commitment to his Catholic faith.

Shock and sadness have reverberated among politicians, community groups, and parishioners both in Britain and here in Ireland, with many expressing horror at the violent attack which claimed the life of the 69-year-old father of five. Mr Amess had travelled regularly to Ireland over the course of his parliamentary career, building links with Irish communities in Britain and advocating for greater ties between the two islands.

Bishop Alan Williams of Brentwood described Mr Amess as “a man of great integrity and faith” who “lived his beliefs in service to others.” Local parishioners at St Peter’s Church, where Mr Amess worshipped, remembered him as “a kind gentleman, always willing to help,” and a regular presence at Mass. One parishioner, originally from Galway, said, “He was proud of his Catholic faith. It’s a huge loss to the parish and to politics.”

Taoiseach Micheál Martin offered his condolences, calling the killing “a mindless act of brutality against a man whose sole purpose was to help his constituents.” The Tánaiste Leo Varadkar said he was “deeply saddened and disturbed” by the events, noting Mr Amess’s longstanding work with Irish community organisations in Britain, particularly those supporting emigrants and the elderly.

The Gardaí have confirmed increased liaison with their UK counterparts as part of routine cross-border security cooperation, though there is no suggestion of any Irish link to the suspect, a 25-year-old British national who remains in custody under anti-terrorism laws.

Mr Amess’s murder has raised urgent questions in both the Dáil and Westminster about the safety of elected representatives. Several Irish TDs have expressed concern for their own security and have called on the Department of Justice to review safety protocols at constituency clinics. The Ceann Comhairle, Seán Ó Fearghaíl, described the killing as “an attack on democracy itself” and said all parliamentarians must be protected as they go about their work.

As investigations continue in the UK, vigils have been held in memory of Mr Amess, with candles lit at churches and public buildings across Essex. Messages of support have poured in from Catholic churches in Ireland, as well as from President Michael D. Higgins, who said Mr Amess’s life “stood as a testament to the spirit of public service and Christian charity.”

David Amess is survived by his wife Julia and their five children. The British Prime Minister Boris Johnson led MPs in paying tribute in the House of Commons, calling the late MP “one of the kindest, nicest, most gentle people in politics.” Funeral arrangements will be announced in due course.
headline: “He was a kind gentleman” – Tributes pour in for David Amess MP, who was a practicing Catholic, after he was stabbed to death in his constituency

text:
Thousands of households across the country will begin receiving their next Fuel Allowance payment from today, as part of the social protection measures aimed at supporting vulnerable groups during the ongoing cost-of-living crisis. The Department of Social Protection has confirmed that the weekly payment, which assists people with the cost of heating their homes during the winter season, will continue to be rolled out in instalments to eligible recipients.

The Fuel Allowance is available to pensioners, people on long-term social welfare payments, and those meeting the strict means test criteria. The payment of €33 per week is typically issued from late September to April, spanning a 28-week period. Some households may have chosen to receive their full allowance in two lump sums, while most opt for the weekly payment, which lands directly into their bank account or post office account.

Minister for Social Protection Heather Humphreys has previously stated that the government is committed to supporting those most at risk of fuel poverty. "No one should have to choose between heating their home and putting food on the table," said the Minister in a recent statement to the Dáil. She reiterated that the Fuel Allowance, alongside other targeted supports, forms a central part of the government's cost-of-living package.

Recent figures indicate that over 370,000 households in Ireland are currently in receipt of the Fuel Allowance. The payment coincides with a marked increase in energy and home heating costs, with many families reporting financial strain as prices for electricity, gas, and home heating oil remain high despite recent government interventions.

Campaigners have called for further expansion of the Fuel Allowance scheme, citing a "growing cohort of working poor" who do not meet the eligibility requirements but are facing similar difficulties in affording basic home heating. Social justice groups have also criticised the means test for excluding carers and many people with disabilities.

Those unsure of their eligibility are being urged to contact their local Intreo Centre for further information or to consult the Citizens Information website for guidelines. The government has not ruled out additional measures in the upcoming Budget, but Minister Humphreys has warned that resources remain limited.

Gardaí have warned the public to be vigilant about scam messages and phone calls purporting to offer fuel allowance top-ups, reminding people that genuine payments are processed only through the official Department of Social Protection channels.

As the payments are issued this week, many households will be watching closely for further announcements from the government on additional supports to help with the mounting cost of essential utilities over the coming months.
headline: Fuel allowance payment will be issued to households from today

text:
The UK is bracing for ongoing travel disruption as rail workers embark on the largest strike in over thirty years, with services set to grind to a near halt again tomorrow after yet another round of last-minute negotiations ended without agreement. Talks between the Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers’ Union (RMT) and the rail operators stalled late this afternoon, with both sides blaming each other for the impasse.

Tens of thousands of rail staff walked off the job earlier this week, paralysing much of Britain’s rail network and causing widespread commuter chaos. The dispute centres on pay, job security, and working conditions, with unions demanding assurances and a pay rise in line with soaring inflation, which has reached a forty-year high in the UK.

Mick Lynch, RMT’s general secretary, said rail staff had “no choice” but to escalate industrial action after employers “refused to put forward a reasonable offer.” He added that “the government is deliberately prolonging this dispute by refusing to give the rail companies a mandate to negotiate.” UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak has said the government is not “in the room” and has urged both sides to reach a resolution.

Tomorrow’s strike will once again see an estimated 40,000 rail staff involved, forcing the cancellation of up to 80 percent of services across England, Scotland, and Wales. Train operating companies have urged passengers to avoid all but essential travel, warning of significant delays and overcrowding on the limited number of trains that do run. Knock-on effects are expected into Friday morning, with many early services cancelled as staff return to work.

The strike has drawn criticism from business groups and anger from stranded commuters, many of whom have turned to buses, private cars, or have been unable to travel. The Confederation of British Industry warned of “serious economic consequences” if the dispute drags on, while tourism and hospitality sectors have reported a wave of cancellations ahead of the crucial summer period.

In Ireland, the Department of Foreign Affairs has advised any Irish citizens travelling to or within Britain to check with rail operators in advance and to make alternative arrangements where possible. There have been no reports of major disruption to ferry or air services between Ireland and Britain, but longer queues were reported at airports as passengers sought alternative routes.

With no breakthrough in sight, further strikes are expected in the coming weeks, raising fears of protracted industrial unrest across the UK’s public sector. The RMT has already warned that it may coordinate walkouts with other unions, including teachers and health workers, unless the government steps in to resolve the standoff.
headline: Largest rail strike in three decades in the UK continues in the UK tomorrow, as last-ditch negotiations fail again

text:
Electric vehicles in Ireland will now be required to emit simulated engine noises, following the roll-out of new EU regulations that come into effect from today. The move applies to all newly registered electric and hybrid vehicles, which must be fitted with so-called Acoustic Vehicle Alerting Systems (AVAS) to help protect pedestrians, particularly those who are visually impaired.

The decision comes amid growing concerns that electric vehicles, which are virtually silent at low speeds, pose a heightened risk to pedestrians and cyclists. The European Commission has mandated the use of AVAS in order to address these safety issues, with the systems required to generate artificial sounds when vehicles are travelling at speeds of up to 20 km/h, or when reversing.

Transport Minister Eamon Ryan has welcomed the measure, stating that it “strikes a balance between promoting greener motoring and ensuring public safety on Irish roads.” The Department of Transport said all car manufacturers must now comply with the regulation for every new electric or hybrid model released on the Irish market.

The National Council for the Blind of Ireland (NCBI) has long campaigned for such changes, citing numerous near-misses involving people with visual impairments who could not hear approaching vehicles. “This is a critical step forward for road safety and accessibility,” said Chris White, CEO of the NCBI. “Petrol and diesel cars can be heard long before they are seen, but the silence of electric vehicles has been a real threat to our community.”

According to figures published by the Road Safety Authority, the number of electric vehicles on Irish roads has more than doubled over the past two years, with sales expected to continue rising as the Government pushes its target of one million EVs by 2030. However, concerns remain over whether retrofitting older electric vehicles with noise devices should be made compulsory, with some safety campaigners urging the Government to go further.

Motoring organisations have also raised questions about the possible impact of the artificial sounds on noise pollution levels in towns and cities. “Drivers should know that the sound generated by these devices is at a relatively low decibel level, similar to the noise of a conventional car engine at low speed,” said a spokesperson for the Automobile Association Ireland. “The aim is to alert those nearby, not to disturb the peace.”

Gardaí have indicated that enforcement of the new rule will fall under standard vehicle roadworthiness checks, with non-compliant vehicles subject to penalties in line with existing road safety legislation. The new regulation applies to both private and commercial vehicles, including taxis and delivery vans.

As the measure takes effect, the HSE has advised pedestrians to continue exercising caution when crossing roads, noting that the addition of AVAS is not a substitute for basic road safety awareness. Meanwhile, Ireland’s growing EV community has largely welcomed the change, with many drivers acknowledging the importance of making roads safer for all users.

The Department of Transport has confirmed that information campaigns will be launched in the coming weeks to raise public awareness of the new requirements, as the transition to cleaner and quieter road transport continues apace throughout the country.
headline: Electric vehicles to be fitted with noise emitting devices from today onwards

text:
Multiple reports are emerging from across the country today alleging that individuals who have lost access to their Covid passes are being openly mocked in public, with some witnesses describing scenes where the famous “Nelson laugh” from the cartoon series The Simpsons was performed at those excluded from venues.

According to readers who contacted The Liberal, incidents have been observed at cafés, restaurants, and gyms in Dublin, Cork, Waterford, and Limerick, as the enforcement of updated Covid certificate requirements comes into effect. People whose passes have lapsed or whose vaccination status is now deemed non-compliant with current booster requirements have reportedly been refused entry and, in some cases, subjected to finger-pointing and exaggerated laughter by bystanders, reminiscent of the character Nelson Muntz’s signature “Ha ha!” taunt.

Witness Maria O’Reilly, from Swords, said: “I was at a local café when a man in front of me was turned away because his pass had expired. Straight away, two lads at a nearby table pointed at him and did the Nelson laugh really loudly. Everyone was looking.”

Several other witnesses reported similar incidents outside gyms and shopping centres, with the mocking behaviour appearing to spread as word travels of individuals losing their “precious” Covid privileges due to policy changes or missing booster appointments. Social media users have also posted about the phenomenon, with some criticising the actions as childish bullying, while others suggest it is a form of “karma” for those who previously supported the pass system when it was first introduced.

The Gardaí said they have not received any formal complaints relating to harassment or intimidation over the loss of Covid certificate privileges, but a spokesperson reminded the public to treat others with respect and to avoid actions that could be deemed disorderly or harassing.

As the debate over ongoing Covid-19 restrictions and vaccine requirements continues to divide public opinion, today’s reported mockery highlights the social tensions that remain within Irish society. The Department of Health and the HSE maintain that vaccine certificates remain a crucial component in public health strategy, though opponents claim the system is divisive and increasingly outdated.

While the government has not indicated any relaxation of current certificate rules, as enforcement increases, so too does the risk of further social division. Those who find themselves excluded from daily activities without a valid Covid pass are being urged to remain patient and to report any instances of harassment to the relevant authorities.
headline: Covid-19: Multiple reports emerging nationwide of people pointing and doing the Nelson laugh at those losing their precious Covid pass privilege today

text:
The Taoiseach, the Tánaiste, and the Minister for Health are set to meet today amid mounting speculation that a fresh six-week lockdown could be imposed on the Irish public, TheLiberal.ie understands. Cabinet sources have said the three Government leaders will discuss rapidly rising case numbers and consider whether Level 5 restrictions are necessary to stem the latest surge.

The meeting comes as warnings from the National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET) intensify, with senior health officials expressing serious concerns about hospital capacity and the increased transmission seen in recent weeks. HSE chief executive Paul Reid confirmed this morning that hospitals nationwide are under severe pressure, and staff are bracing for a potential spike in admissions.

However, public patience is wearing thin, with many people expressing anger at the prospect of yet another lockdown. Small business owners in particular say they have not recovered from previous restrictions and would not survive another prolonged closure. One Dublin publican told TheLiberal.ie, “We did what we were told, closed when asked, and spent thousands making our premises safe. If they close us again, that’s it, we’re done.”

Opposition TDs have accused the Government of failing to prepare for a predictable winter wave, while members of the coalition argue that they have no choice but to follow public health advice. There have also been renewed calls for greater transparency from NPHET and the Department of Health regarding the evidence for imposing harsh restrictions on society.

As the speculation continues, Gardaí have said they are preparing contingency plans for increased enforcement if further restrictions are announced. Meanwhile, schools and childcare providers await clarification on whether they would be required to close yet again, fuelling further concerns among parents and education staff about children’s welfare and learning loss.

A Government spokesman refused to confirm whether a new lockdown decision would be made today, but acknowledged “all options are under review” given the deteriorating situation. The matter is likely to dominate the Dáil’s agenda this week, with members of the public urged to follow existing guidance as the country awaits word from its leaders.
headline: Government trio to meet today to decide whether or not the Irish public get locked down again for another 6 weeks

text:
A wave of shock and anger is sweeping across Sweden after the killing of a 12-year-old girl, who was caught in the crossfire of a gang-related shooting in southern Stockholm. The incident occurred late Sunday night on the outskirts of the Swedish capital, in an area known for recent surges in gang violence.

According to Swedish police, the young girl, who was walking her dog at the time, was struck by several bullets during a drive-by shooting outside a petrol station. She was rushed to hospital but died of her injuries shortly afterwards. Initial reports suggest the intended target was a rival gang member, but the child, described as innocent and completely uninvolved, became the tragic victim.

The case has ignited fierce debate in Sweden over the government's handling of escalating gang violence and the perceived inability of law enforcement to contain ongoing turf wars between criminal groups, many of which have links to immigrant communities. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has condemned the shooting as a "senseless act of brutality" and vowed a renewed crackdown on organised crime.

In Ireland, the violence has reignited concern about the effects of open borders across Europe and fears that similar turf wars could spill over into Irish cities. Irish authorities have, in recent years, warned about the growing reach of European gangs, and have urged vigilance in combating serious organised crime.

Swedish media report that no arrests have yet been made. The country's national police chief, Anders Thornberg, acknowledged widespread public outrage and said additional resources would be deployed to Stockholm to quell further violence. He admitted that gang-related shootings have become a “national crisis,” with dozens killed in similar attacks over the past year.

Local residents in the suburb where the shooting took place held a candlelit vigil on Monday night, demanding that politicians do more to restore safety to their communities. “This could have been anyone’s child. We are afraid to let our own children play outside,” said one woman, who had lived in the area for more than a decade.

The Swedish government is under growing pressure to introduce tougher penalties and increase police powers, amid mounting criticism that soft justice and lenient immigration policies have fuelled the growth of violent gangs. Calls for stricter law and order policies have grown louder, particularly from right-wing opposition parties, who argue that Sweden’s reputation for safety is now under severe threat.

The victim’s family have called for privacy and requested that the girl not be named in the media. Swedish police have appealed to witnesses to come forward, and the investigation remains ongoing. The killing marks the latest high-profile tragedy in a spate of shootings that has unsettled a country once ranked among the safest in Europe.
headline: Outrage in Sweden as 12-yr-old girl gets shot dead during gang war

text:
Two young girls have narrowly escaped tragedy after being swept out to sea on an inflatable airbed off the coast of County Clare yesterday afternoon. Quick-thinking members of the public and local lifeguards have been hailed as heroes after rescuing the pair from the dangerous currents.

The incident occurred at approximately 2.30pm at Lahinch Beach, a popular hotspot with families during the current spell of warm weather. Eyewitnesses told The Liberal that the girls, aged 8 and 10, had been playing on a brightly coloured air mattress near the shore when they were suddenly carried away by a strong offshore breeze. Within minutes, the inflatable had drifted some 200 metres from the shoreline, prompting panic among beachgoers.

Bystanders immediately raised the alarm, alerting lifeguards on duty and contacting the Coast Guard. Lifeguards reacted without hesitation, launching a rescue board and heading out into the open water. Members of the public also entered the water in an effort to assist, but were advised to return to shore for their own safety.

The girls were reportedly terrified but managed to hold onto the airbed as the lifeguards reached them, pulling them to safety and bringing them ashore to the applause of relieved onlookers. Paramedics assessed the girls at the scene and determined that neither required hospital treatment, though both were shaken by their ordeal.

Speaking to The Liberal, a Clare County Council spokesperson praised the swift response of the lifeguards and the vigilance of the public, emphasising the importance of following water safety advice. "This could easily have ended in tragedy. Inflatable toys are not designed for use in open water, especially in changeable weather conditions. Thankfully, thanks to the rapid action of our lifeguards and the community, the girls are safe."

The Irish Coast Guard has since issued a renewed warning to beach visitors, urging parents and guardians to keep children within sight and to avoid using inflatables in the sea. The latest incident comes amid a spike in callouts to water rescues along the west coast during the recent warm spell.

Gardaí attended the scene to take statements and to reassure those involved. The girls’ parents expressed their heartfelt gratitude to everyone who assisted, saying they "dread to think what could have happened" had it not been for the "bravery and skill" of the lifeguards.

With schools now on summer holidays and more families expected to flock to the country’s beaches, authorities are appealing for vigilance and caution. The HSE has also reminded the public to be mindful of the dangers of open water and to always swim in designated, lifeguarded areas.
headline: Hero alert: Two young girls rescued after being swept out to sea on an airbed

text:
Engineers in Florida have demolished the remaining structure of the Champlain Towers South residential block in Surfside, Miami, following the partial collapse of the building last month which resulted in at least 24 confirmed deaths. Efforts to locate further survivors among the rubble continue, but hopes have faded as the days since the disaster have grown.

The controlled demolition was carried out late on Sunday, local time, after authorities raised concerns that the standing portion of the block was unstable and posed a threat to ongoing rescue operations. Severe weather from the approaching Tropical Storm Elsa had also added pressure to bring down the building ahead of potentially hazardous winds.

Miami-Dade officials confirmed that a series of strategically placed explosives brought down the precarious remainder within seconds, sending clouds of dust billowing through surrounding streets. The move was made, officials stated, in the interests of public safety and to allow rescuers full access to areas previously deemed too dangerous to enter.

The partial collapse on June 24 drew global attention, with emergency teams from across the United States, Israel, Mexico and elsewhere converging on the scene. Family members of the missing and deceased have held daily vigils near the site, where a memorial wall to victims has grown steadily since the disaster.

Irish citizens are not believed to be among the casualties, according to the Department of Foreign Affairs. The Taoiseach, Micheál Martin, previously expressed his condolences to those affected, calling the event a “heart-breaking tragedy” and commending the rescue workers for their “heroic efforts”.

Search and recovery teams have now restarted operations as soon as the site was declared safe, with Miami-Dade Mayor Daniella Levine Cava saying authorities remain committed to finding all who are unaccounted for. “Our top priority remains the search and rescue operation, and we will not stop until all are found,” she said.

Officials continue to investigate the cause of the collapse, with structural engineers suggesting long-term deterioration and potentially significant design or construction issues may have contributed. In the meantime, other apartment complexes in Miami-Dade County are undergoing urgent reviews for safety.

The disaster has ignited fresh debate about building safety regulations in the United States, with campaigners and local politicians calling for tighter enforcement and more regular inspections of older buildings. In Ireland, some TDs have cited the Miami collapse as a reminder of the need to ensure rigorous oversight of building standards, particularly in light of ongoing concerns over defective concrete blocks and the mica scandal in the northwest.

As recovery operations progress, local officials have promised continued support for survivors and bereaved families. Emergency accommodation and counselling services remain available to those displaced by the collapse, with donations and messages of solidarity arriving from around the world.
headline: Miami tower block collapse: Engineers demolish the remains of the Champlain Tower South block

text:
Authorities in the UK have launched a major terrorism investigation after a series of suspicious packages, containing what police have described as “viable explosive devices”, were intercepted at several locations in London on Thursday. British counter-terrorism officials now believe the packages may have originated from the Republic of Ireland, raising concerns about cross-border security and the potential involvement of Irish-based groups or individuals.

The improvised explosive devices, sent in padded Jiffy bags, were discovered at transport hubs including Waterloo railway station and Heathrow Airport, as well as offices near the City of London. Met Police sources have confirmed to British media that forensic analysis of postage marks and stamps on the packages suggests they were processed through the Irish postal system, with at least two stamped at offices in Dublin.

Gardaí and the Irish Defence Forces’ bomb disposal unit are assisting UK authorities with the investigation. A spokesperson for An Garda Síochána said on Thursday evening: “We are in close contact with our UK counterparts and are providing all necessary assistance. Security operations at key airports and postal centres have been enhanced as a precaution.”

No group has claimed responsibility, though investigators are examining possible links to known dissident republican elements as well as other radical groups. Security sources told The Liberal that the sophistication of the devices suggests some level of technical expertise, raising the possibility of a coordinated campaign.

The Taoiseach, Leo Varadkar, speaking in Cork, condemned the attacks: “There is no justification for violence or intimidation, and all state resources will be made available to support our closest neighbour.” The Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs, Micheál Martin, described the incident as “deeply troubling” and urged anyone with information to contact Gardaí immediately.

British security services raised their terror alert level and have urged increased vigilance at airports, train stations, and postal centres across the UK. No injuries were reported and the devices were safely defused, but the incident has caused alarm in both jurisdictions, recalling the so-called ‘letter bomb’ campaigns of previous decades.

Irish postal workers’ union representatives expressed concern for staff safety. “Our members expect their workplaces to be secure,” said a spokesperson for the Communications Workers’ Union. “We call on management and the authorities to do everything possible to protect staff and ensure such threats are dealt with swiftly.”

The British Home Secretary has convened an emergency COBRA meeting, while Irish Justice Minister Helen McEntee briefed the Oireachtas Committee on Justice, assuring TDs that “our security services are fully engaged with their UK counterparts and all relevant intelligence is being shared”.

Gardaí are appealing to the public for any information regarding suspicious mail or unusual activity at postal facilities. The investigation is ongoing, with further updates expected from both Irish and British authorities in the coming days.
headline: London terror alert: Explosive devices were likely sent from Ireland, authorities say

text:
US President Joe Biden has tested positive for Covid-19 once again, despite being fully vaccinated and having received booster doses. The White House confirmed the news in a statement on Thursday evening, saying that the 81-year-old President was experiencing mild symptoms and would continue to carry out his duties while isolating at the residence.

The announcement comes just weeks after President Biden had previously tested negative following an earlier bout of the virus. The White House Press Secretary stated that the President is “experiencing mild symptoms, mostly fatigue and a slight cough,” and is following guidance from his medical team and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

President Biden, who is due to face a crucial election battle later this year, has been fully vaccinated and has received multiple booster shots as part of the US government’s drive to encourage vaccination among the American public. His administration previously made vaccination and booster campaigns a cornerstone of its Covid-19 response.

White House officials said that Vice President Kamala Harris and other senior staff had tested negative, and there are currently no changes to the president’s schedule apart from remote participation in planned meetings and briefings. It is understood that all close contacts are being traced and tested.

The news has reignited debate in the United States and beyond about the effectiveness of vaccine programmes, with some critics highlighting the President’s repeated infections in spite of being fully vaccinated. However, health authorities have continued to emphasise that vaccines remain effective at preventing severe illness, hospitalisation and death, particularly among older adults and those with underlying health conditions.

President Biden’s most recent public appearance was on Wednesday, when he addressed reporters outside the White House. The press office confirmed that all media present had been notified and advised to monitor for any symptoms.

The US has recorded over 100 million confirmed Covid-19 cases since the start of the pandemic, and the virus continues to circulate globally, with repeated waves due to new variants. Irish health authorities, including the HSE, continue to encourage vaccination and adherence to public health advice, particularly for vulnerable groups.

Further updates on President Biden’s condition are expected from the White House in the coming days.
headline: ?BREAKING: US President Joe Biden has tested positive for Covid-19 again even though he is full vaxxed

text:
Gardaí have arrested a man after a shocking incident in which he reportedly attempted to set a garda on fire during the early hours of this morning. The dramatic episode unfolded in Dublin city centre, when officers were responding to a call regarding a public order disturbance just after 2am.

According to sources, a male in his 30s confronted members of An Garda Síochána near O’Connell Street, becoming aggressive and brandishing a bottle believed to contain a flammable liquid. Eyewitnesses at the scene claim the man poured the substance onto a uniformed garda before producing a lighter and allegedly trying to ignite it.

Quick-thinking gardaí overpowered the suspect before any flames were struck, averting what could have been a potentially fatal attack. The targeted officer was unharmed but was taken to the Mater Hospital as a precaution and later discharged following a medical assessment. The suspect was arrested at the scene and is currently detained at Store Street Garda Station under Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act, 1984.

A spokesperson for An Garda Síochána described the incident as "an appalling act of violence against a member of the force, who was simply doing their job". The Garda Representative Association (GRA) has called for stronger protections for frontline gardaí in the wake of increasing assaults on officers, saying "incidents like this cannot and will not be tolerated".

Investigators have launched a full enquiry and are appealing for anyone who may have witnessed the disturbance or who may have mobile phone footage to come forward. The Oireachtas Justice Committee is expected to discuss the rising number of attacks on gardaí in an emergency session later this week.

No further details have been released at this stage, and investigations are ongoing.
headline: BREAKING: Man arrested after trying to set a garda on fire

text:
The National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET) has expressed fresh “concern” this evening after the Department of Health confirmed a further 1,015 new cases of Covid-19 across the Republic.

The sharp rise in cases comes amid mounting calls for clarity over the Government’s pandemic response, with renewed fears of a potential return to tighter restrictions as the country navigates the summer months.

Health officials said that as of 8am today, there are currently 72 people hospitalised with the virus, 23 of whom are in ICU. The number of daily infections has not been this high since the spring, raising alarm bells among experts and the broader public alike.

A spokesperson from NPHET urged the public to “exercise continued vigilance,” warning that the highly transmissible Delta variant is circulating widely within the community. The statement stressed the importance of adhering to public health advice, including mask-wearing and proper hand hygiene.

Meanwhile, the HSE has reiterated its call for those who have not yet received their Covid-19 vaccine to come forward and register, as vaccination centres remain open nationwide. Officials highlighted that the vast majority of severe illness and hospitalisations are among unvaccinated individuals.

The Minister for Health, Stephen Donnelly TD, faced questions in the Dáil today regarding the availability of PCR testing and the pace of the vaccine rollout, particularly among younger people. Opposition TDs criticised what they described as “mixed messaging” from the Government and called for a coherent plan to manage rising case numbers without damaging the economy further.

The Taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the Government continues to monitor the situation closely and will act on the latest advice from NPHET. He asked members of the public to “show patience and solidarity,” stating that “every effort now will help to protect our health service and keep society open.”

Gardaí have also warned against complacency as indoor gatherings and large-scale events remain subject to public health restrictions. There are growing concerns that some recent outbreaks have been linked to unregulated events and house parties.

The confirmation of over a thousand new daily cases comes at a delicate time for the State, with schools set to reopen in a matter of weeks and plans for further reopening of society under review. Public health authorities are expected to meet again in the coming days to assess the risk and advise the Government on next steps.

In the meantime, NPHET is calling on everyone to “redouble their efforts” as Ireland faces into what could be a critical phase in its ongoing response to the pandemic.
headline: ?BREAKING: NHPET ‘concerned’ as Department of Health confirms 1,015 new Covid-19 cases

text:
Met Éireann has confirmed that the country can look forward to another two days of summer-like conditions, but has warned that the weather is set to deteriorate sharply by the end of the week. 

According to the national forecaster, temperatures will continue to reach the low to mid-20s across many parts of the Republic today and tomorrow, with long sunny spells expected throughout both days. Light southerly breezes and dry conditions are set to persist, offering a brief respite from the unsettled weather that has dominated much of June so far. 

Many have taken advantage of the improved conditions, with beaches and parks around Dublin, Cork, and Galway seeing increased crowds since the weekend. Met Éireann reported peak temperatures in the Phoenix Park of 23 degrees Celsius on Tuesday, with similar readings in parts of Munster and the midlands.

Farmers and tourism operators have welcomed the dry spell, but Met Éireann is cautioning the public not to become complacent. Senior meteorologist Liz Walsh said that while the current spell feels like ‘a proper taste of summer’, it will be short-lived. “There’s a breakdown on the way,” Ms Walsh said. “By Thursday night, we’ll see increased cloud cover moving in from the Atlantic, and by Friday, heavy rain and blustery winds will spread across the country.”

The forecaster is predicting that temperatures will drop back to the mid-teens by Friday, with showers becoming widespread and persistent. There is also a risk of spot flooding in western and southern counties, with the public being advised to monitor updates and take care on the roads.

The HSE has reminded people to take sun protection measures over the next two days, particularly children, older people, and anyone working outdoors, as UV levels are expected to remain high. 

Met Éireann will continue to monitor the situation and issue localised warnings if the forecasted heavy rainfall poses any threat. Those with outdoor plans for the weekend are being urged to make alternative arrangements as conditions are likely to remain unsettled into Saturday and Sunday. 

There are no weather warnings in place at present, but the Gardaí have emphasised the need for caution on wet and slippery roads from Friday onward. 

For now, the advice from Met Éireann is to make the most of the good weather while it lasts, as another spell of wind and rain is set to arrive before the week is out.
headline: Met Eireann says that weather will remain summer-like for the next 48h, but things will take a turn for the worse by Friday

text:
Camp Bestival will proceed as planned this year, organisers have confirmed, despite ongoing concerns about Covid-19 and the emergence of new variants across Europe. The family-friendly music and arts festival, traditionally held at Lulworth Castle in Dorset, England, is set to take place from the 29th July to 1st August, with thousands expected to attend.

Authorities in the UK had previously expressed concerns about the safety of large gatherings, particularly in light of the spread of the Delta variant. However, prompted by recent easing of restrictions and the continued roll-out of vaccination programmes across both Britain and Ireland, the event will now go ahead, albeit with additional health and safety measures.

Organisers have stated that attendees will be required to provide proof of full vaccination, recent recovery from Covid-19 or a negative PCR test taken within 48 hours of arrival. Onsite testing will also be available throughout the weekend. Social distancing will be encouraged in busier areas, and hand sanitising stations will be located across the festival site.

Irish families who have travelled to Camp Bestival in previous years are already making preparations to return, although travel restrictions remain in place for those who are not fully vaccinated. The Department of Foreign Affairs has advised those intending to travel to consult the latest government guidance, including entry requirements for England, before making any arrangements.

This development comes as many in the entertainment and live events sector across Ireland continue to call on the government to provide a clear roadmap for the return of festivals and mass gatherings. While smaller pilot events have been held in Dublin and other Irish cities in recent weeks, uncertainty remains regarding the timeline for the resumption of major festivals such as Electric Picnic and Longitude.

Camp Bestival’s organisers have said they are working closely with local authorities and health officials to ensure the safety of all attendees. Headline acts this year include Fatboy Slim and Friendly Fires, with a full programme of family activities, performances and workshops promised.

As Ireland’s own festival scene remains in limbo, some in the sector have voiced frustration that large-scale events are proceeding elsewhere while strict limits remain in place at home. The Taoiseach, Micheál Martin, has previously emphasised the need for caution, citing concerns about potential spikes in Covid-19 cases.

As festival season approaches, many will be watching closely to see if Camp Bestival's approach can offer a blueprint for the safe return of live events both in the UK and Ireland.
headline: Covid-19: Camp Bestival will go ahead this year

text:
The Government has confirmed plans to house a further 230 Syrian migrants in County Tipperary despite the number of Irish people homeless reaching nearly 10,000, sparking angry reactions from locals and campaigners.

Figures from the Department of Housing show that there are 9,856 people without a home in Ireland, including more than 3,400 children, as the housing crisis continues to worsen. Yet, the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth has agreed to accommodate an additional group of Syrian nationals in a new centre in the county, as part of the State’s ongoing commitments under EU refugee resettlement programmes.

Local representatives say they were not adequately consulted about the plans. Tipperary TD Mattie McGrath criticised the Government’s priorities, saying, “It’s nothing short of a disgrace that we are expecting our own people to sleep in hotels and hostels while allocating resources and accommodation to new arrivals without even a fair discussion.”

The centre, located on the outskirts of Clonmel, is understood to be a former hotel recently refurbished for the purpose. The HSE and local Gardaí have been notified in advance, but some residents said they only learned of the development through local media and social media posts.

"This is now a weekly occurrence. People in Tipperary and Ireland as a whole are fed up. We have pensioners living out of their cars, families stuck in emergency accommodation, and yet the doors are opened again for people from outside. There’s no logic to it," said a local activist who is part of a group demanding priority for Irish citizens in housing allocations.

The Department has defended its decision, stating that Ireland has a legal and moral obligation under both EU and UN agreements to accept refugee families fleeing war and persecution. Officials said integration supports would be provided and sought to assure the community that extra resources would be made available to limit the strain on local services.

However, questions remain over the impact on public services in Tipperary, which are already overstretched. Local schools and GPs are reportedly under pressure due to increased demand.

Opposition parties and campaigners have called for increased investment in housing for Irish nationals and questioned Government transparency regarding accommodation for migrants. Some community groups have organised meetings in response, with concerns also raised about the lack of consultation and the long-term viability of the current asylum seeker accommodation system.

The Government says it remains committed to tackling homelessness through increased housing provision and reforms, but for many in Tipperary, concerns about fairness and transparency continue to grow.
headline: 10,000 of our own homeless yet Government to house another 230 Syrian migrants in Tipperary

text:
Taoiseach Simon Harris has admitted that the party’s reputation suffered as a result of the Maria Bailey compensation case, insisting lessons have been learned from the controversy. Speaking on RTÉ Radio this morning, Mr Harris, who only recently took over as Fine Gael leader, acknowledged for the first time that the fallout from the “swing-gate” saga was damaging on both a public and political level.

The Taoiseach said: “There’s no doubt that the Maria Bailey case caused reputational damage to Fine Gael. It was seen by the public as out of touch, and I absolutely recognise that.” Mr Harris emphasised that the incident “should never have happened” and expressed regret for the way it was initially handled by senior party figures.

The controversy erupted in 2019 when Ms Bailey, then a Fine Gael TD for Dún Laoghaire, lodged a personal injuries claim after falling off a swing at the Dean Hotel in Dublin. The case, and subsequent details about Ms Bailey’s activities before and after the incident, sparked outrage across the country. Public opinion turned sharply against Fine Gael, with many accusing the party of failing to take sufficient action in response to the negative publicity.

Amid mounting pressure, then-Taoiseach Leo Varadkar ordered an internal investigation. Ms Bailey was eventually deselected as a Fine Gael candidate for the 2020 general election and lost her seat as a result.

Mr Harris today admitted the saga had a lasting impact: “People expect higher standards from their public representatives, and when those standards are not met, there is a responsibility to act. We have taken steps to ensure that nothing like this happens again.”

Despite repeated questioning, the Taoiseach refused to comment on whether Ms Bailey could ever return to the party fold, stating, “That is not a matter for discussion at this time.” He said the party’s focus must remain on “delivering for the people” and re-building trust with voters.

Opposition parties have seized on the Taoiseach’s comments, with Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald accusing Fine Gael of “belated honesty” over the affair. “The government’s only coming clean now in the run-up to the local and European elections. The damage is done and the public will not forget,” Ms McDonald said.

Fine Gael sources insist the episode reinforced the need for robust candidate vetting and transparency protocols across the party. The Bailey case continues to be referenced by government critics as a symbol of perceived political privilege and a lack of accountability within the Oireachtas.
