As the general election draws closer, Mr Harris faces the challenge of convincing voters that Fine Gael has truly moved on from the controversy and is ready to learn from its mistakes.
headline: Taoiseach says Bailey case did cause reputational damage to the Fine Gael party

text:
RTÉ has come under fresh criticism after it emerged that the national broadcaster’s in-house hair and makeup team have returned to Montrose, while thousands of workers in similar sectors across the country remain shut out of their livelihoods due to ongoing Covid-19 restrictions.

Despite the Government’s roadmap prohibiting the reopening of personal care services, such as hairdressers and beauty salons, until a later phase, it has been confirmed that RTÉ presenters and on-air contributors are again availing of the services of the corporation’s style department.

A number of staff at RTÉ have quietly been allowed back on-site in Donnybrook, with sources stating that the makeup room has been operating since early in the month. Several viewers have commented on the noticeably coiffed hair and professionally-applied makeup sported by presenters on the broadcaster’s flagship news bulletins and chat shows.

This revelation has prompted anger among members of the public and industry workers who have been unable to work since last year. “It’s a joke, one rule for them, another for the rest of us,” said one Dublin hairdresser who spoke to The Liberal. “We’re told we can’t even open our doors to a single customer, but RTÉ gets to carry on as usual. Where’s the fairness in that?”

Questions are also being raised regarding compliance with public health guidelines and the operation of services deemed non-essential under Level Five restrictions. The HSE has repeatedly emphasised the risks posed by close-contact services in spreading the virus, leading to heavy fines and even prosecutions for businesses found in breach.

When contacted about the return to work of its hair and makeup artists, an RTÉ spokesperson insisted that the broadcaster continues to “follow all public health guidance,” saying: “A small number of staff providing essential support to live broadcasting have returned to work on a strictly limited and controlled basis. All necessary precautions, including social distancing and PPE, are being implemented in line with Government recommendations.”

However, the National Hairdressers Federation has called for an explanation from both the broadcaster and the Department of Communications. “How can RTÉ justify this when our salons are facing permanent closure? There cannot be a special exemption for State bodies while the rest of us are left out in the cold,” said a spokesperson.

Meanwhile, the Government has faced renewed calls in the Dáil to clarify the rules regarding the operation of such services in State institutions, with some opposition TDs accusing ministers of double standards. The Taoiseach has yet to address the controversy directly.

As tensions mount and the reopening of personal care businesses remains uncertain, many in the sector say public trust in both the Government and RTÉ has been undermined by what is widely seen as a clear case of “one rule for them and another for everyone else.”
headline: One rule for them – RTE’s hair and makeup team are back working

text:
The United States government has imposed an immediate ban on leading chipmakers Nvidia and AMD, prohibiting them from selling advanced semiconductors and related technology to China. The move, confirmed late on Thursday by the US Department of Commerce, intensifies the ongoing technology conflict between Washington and Beijing, with potential ripple effects on the global electronics industry.

In a statement, US officials cited national security concerns as the driving factor behind the order. The Biden administration alleges that certain high-performance chips, including those used in artificial intelligence and supercomputing, could be diverted for military use by China or used to bolster surveillance capabilities in ways the US deems threatening.

Both Nvidia and AMD are industry leaders in graphics processing units (GPUs) and other advanced chips. The immediate halt applies to products capable of handling complex computing workloads, specifically those used in data centres for AI training and scientific research. According to market analysts, these chips play a crucial role in powering next-generation technology, and China is a major market for both companies.

Nvidia stated on Thursday night that it is “assessing the potential impact” of the new restrictions and is “working with customers in China to comply with all legal requirements.” AMD issued a similar statement, confirming it will “fully adhere to US export controls.” However, both companies warned that their revenues could be significantly affected, with China accounting for up to a quarter of Nvidia’s data centre business in recent quarters.

Chinese authorities have condemned the US move as “unjustified economic coercion”. In an official response, China’s Ministry of Commerce accused Washington of “abusing export controls and violating the principles of fair competition.” State media outlets suggested the measure could further strain already fragile US-China relations.

Industry experts warn that the escalation could destabilise global supply chains. Many Irish technology firms, including major employers in Dublin, Cork, and Galway, either source components from US companies or directly serve Chinese clients in sectors ranging from medtech to consumer electronics. The Irish Business and Employers Confederation (IBEC) has said it is “monitoring the situation closely,” citing potential knock-on effects for Irish exports.

The new restrictions come as part of a broader US effort to limit China’s access to cutting-edge technology. The White House has also pressured its allies in Europe and Asia to adopt similar controls. In response, China has begun investing heavily in domestic chip manufacturing, but analysts note that it still lags behind US firms in critical areas.

While the Taoiseach, Simon Harris, has yet to comment publicly, Department of Enterprise officials have previously highlighted the importance of stable global trade for Ireland’s technology sector, which supports tens of thousands of jobs nationwide.

The immediate ban also comes at a sensitive time, with US and Chinese officials set to meet at the G20 summit next month. Diplomatic observers in Brussels and Washington fear the dispute could overshadow broader international efforts to address global security and economic instability.
headline: US orders Nvidia and AMD to stop selling technology to China immediately

text:
Holidaymakers from Ireland and across Europe who have not received a Covid-19 vaccination can now travel to Spain without restriction, as the Spanish government has finally removed entry requirements for unvaccinated visitors. The decision, which came into effect on Friday, reverses over two years of strict rules that saw only fully vaccinated or recently recovered travellers from non-EU countries allowed entry.

This move has been widely welcomed by Irish families who had been excluded from travelling to Spain due to their vaccination status. Travel agents are also predicting a late surge in bookings for Spanish destinations such as the Costa del Sol, the Canary Islands, and Barcelona, which remain perennial favourites among Irish tourists. Industry insiders say pent-up demand is expected to translate into a busy summer season, with many holidaymakers relieved at what they describe as “a return to common sense”.

People entering Spain will no longer be required to show proof of full vaccination or a recovery cert, nor are PCR tests needed for entry. The move brings Spain in line with several other European countries, including Portugal and Italy, which have dropped most pandemic-era travel restrictions in recent months.

The Spanish health ministry said falling Covid-19 case numbers and high levels of immunity in the population meant the measures were no longer necessary. Local businesses and tourism operators in Spain have been calling for the end of restrictions, with many reporting sharp falls in revenue due to the lower numbers of tourists from countries with lower vaccine uptake.

Irish citizens booking holidays have expressed relief that their personal medical decisions will no longer dictate whether they can access the sun holidays they have long enjoyed. “It never made sense to keep out healthy people who simply chose not to take a new vaccine,” one Dublin father told The Liberal at Dublin Airport. “We’re delighted the Spanish authorities have finally seen reason.”

However, the move has drawn criticism from some quarters, with certain public health advocates questioning the wisdom of removing restrictions so close to the peak travel season. The Department of Foreign Affairs advises Irish travellers to remain aware of the local health situation and to consult the DFA’s website for the latest updates before departure.

There are still requirements for face masks in certain indoor settings in Spain such as healthcare facilities and public transport, but for ordinary holidaymakers, the experience will feel much as it did prior to 2020. For many, Spain’s decision marks the end of a period they view as marked by unnecessary bureaucracy, with a renewed sense of normality making a welcome return. 

Ryanair and Aer Lingus both report strong demand for Spanish routes in the coming weeks. With families now able to travel together regardless of vaccine status, and no requirement for expensive tests, travel industry figures expect this summer could see a marked bounce back for Spanish tourism from the Irish market.
headline: Finally a bit of sanity returns to Spain as unvaccinated can now enter the country for holidays

text:
A Garda investigation is underway after a woman was allegedly sexually assaulted in Dublin earlier this week. The incident reportedly occurred in the early hours of Wednesday morning in the south inner city, with the precise location understood to be in the vicinity of the Grand Canal area.

It is understood that the woman, aged in her 20s, was approached by a male while walking home shortly after midnight. According to sources, the woman reported the incident to Gardaí later that morning. She received medical attention and was supported by Gardaí at a Dublin hospital.

Gardaí have established a crime scene and a technical examination has taken place. The area remained cordoned off for several hours on Wednesday as officers from the divisional protective services unit carried out door-to-door enquiries and reviewed local CCTV footage.

No arrests have been made at this stage, and the investigation is ongoing. Gardaí are appealing to anyone who may have been in the area around the time of the incident or who may have dashcam or mobile phone footage to contact Kevin Street Garda station.

A Garda spokesperson said: "Gardaí are investigating an alleged sexual assault that occurred in Dublin city centre. Investigations are ongoing and no further information is being provided at this time for operational reasons."

This latest incident comes amid ongoing concerns about safety on Dublin's streets, with several high-profile attacks reported in recent months. The Government has pledged increased resources for community policing and visible Garda patrols in the city centre.

Anyone with information is urged to contact Gardaí immediately. Support services for victims of sexual crime are available through the HSE and various voluntary organisations.
headline: Garda investigation underway after a woman is allegedly sexually assaulted in Dublin

text:
A migrant was discovered hiding in the glove box of a small vehicle as part of an apparent attempt to enter Europe, authorities in Spain have confirmed. The extraordinary incident occurred at the border checkpoint between Morocco and the Spanish enclave of Melilla, a known hotspot for attempts to cross from North Africa into European territory.

Spanish Guardia Civil officers stopped and searched a car arriving at the Beni Enzar crossing on Friday morning. During a routine inspection, officers noticed signs of tampering with the dashboard area. Upon closer examination, they prised open the glove compartment to find a young man, believed to be of sub-Saharan African origin, tightly wedged inside.

The man, who appeared disoriented and dehydrated, was extricated by emergency services. Medical staff at the scene assessed him before transferring him to a local hospital for further evaluation. His age and identity have not been released, but officials stated he is believed to be in his late teens or early twenties.

The driver of the vehicle, a Moroccan national, was arrested and is now under investigation for people smuggling. Spanish authorities say such attempts are becoming more brazen, with migrants risking their lives in increasingly dangerous conditions to reach European soil.

Local officials expressed concern over the plight of migrants seeking to enter Europe, highlighting the perilous journeys endured by many. The discovery comes amid growing pressure on Spanish border forces, who face a steady stream of attempted crossings by land and sea.

The Spanish government reiterated its commitment to upholding border security, while also calling on the European Union for more coordinated action and support in handling migration flows. Humanitarian organisations have condemned the incident as another example of desperate measures taken by those fleeing poverty and conflict, urging greater international cooperation to address the root causes driving migration.

The enclave of Melilla, along with Ceuta further to the west, represents one of only two land borders between Africa and the European Union. Security has been stepped up in recent years, but authorities acknowledge that smuggling networks continue to find new ways to circumvent controls, often at grave risk to human life.

According to a statement from the Guardia Civil, the man found in the glove box was fortunate to have survived the ordeal, with officers warning that such methods are “extremely dangerous and potentially fatal”. Investigations are ongoing into the smuggling network responsible, with further arrests expected.

An estimated 41,000 migrants have attempted to reach Spain so far this year, according to figures from the Spanish interior ministry, with many intercepted or rescued at sea. The issue continues to be a source of political debate across Europe, with calls for reform of asylum policy and greater responsibility sharing among member states.

As the migrant crisis shows little sign of abating, Irish officials have reiterated the country’s commitment to providing humanitarian assistance in line with EU agreements, with the Department of Justice stating that Ireland will continue to participate in relocation programmes where possible.
headline: Migrant desperately trying to enter Europe is found hiding in cramped car glove box

text:
The much-anticipated teaser trailer for the new James Bond film, ‘No Time To Die’, has been officially released, sparking a wave of excitement among fans of the long-running franchise across Ireland and around the world. The sneak peek offers a glimpse into Daniel Craig’s fifth and final outing as the iconic British spy, promising high-octane action, intrigue, and the trademark Bond glamour.

Running at just under a minute and a half, the teaser showcases a host of spectacular set pieces and the return of familiar faces including Léa Seydoux and Ralph Fiennes. Rami Malek, who plays the film’s enigmatic villain, is also briefly introduced, raising expectations for a dramatic showdown.

‘No Time To Die’ has been the subject of much speculation since its production was first announced, with delays and changes behind the scenes adding to the anticipation. Filming took place in multiple locations, including Italy, Jamaica, and Norway, with London also featuring prominently—a fact likely to resonate with Irish audiences familiar with the city’s iconic landmarks. The producers have promised that the film will blend the classic elements of the Bond saga with new twists for modern cinemagoers.

Irish fans, long devoted to the Bond series, will note that the trailer teases the return of MI6 stalwarts such as M, Q, and Moneypenny, along with the introduction of Lashana Lynch as a new ‘00’ agent. Social media has been abuzz since the trailer’s release, with thousands expressing their excitement and sharing their expectations for what Craig’s final performance will bring.

‘No Time To Die’ is scheduled for cinematic release in April next year, following several postponements due to the Covid-19 pandemic. Irish cinemas, which have seen a cautious reopening under current public health guidelines, are expected to see high demand for tickets as the release date approaches.

The Bond franchise has a strong following in Ireland, and speculation has already begun about who might take up the mantle of 007 after Craig’s departure. For now, the teaser has succeeded in whetting the appetite of fans eager for the return of one of cinema’s most enduring heroes.
headline: Teaser trailer of upcoming Bond movie ‘No time to die’ released

text:
Women diagnosed with advanced cervical cancer in Ireland will now have access to the groundbreaking drug pembrolizumab, widely known as Pembro, after a major policy breakthrough announced by the HSE. The move follows months of campaigning by patient advocacy groups and calls from oncologists urging the Government to make the life-extending medicine available free of charge to eligible women.

Up to now, Irish women with advanced or recurrent cervical cancer were denied public access to pembrolizumab, a precision immunotherapy that has demonstrated dramatic improvements in survival rates in clinical trials abroad. Patients without private health insurance faced considerable financial barriers, as the cost of the drug ran to tens of thousands of euro per year.

The HSE decision, described as “historic” by campaigners, was confirmed following a meeting this week of the National Cancer Control Programme. The agency said eligible patients, typically women whose cancer has spread and who have already undergone previous therapies, would be able to receive Pembro under the public health system from July.

Campaigner Vicky Phelan, a prominent voice for women affected by the CervicalCheck scandal, welcomed the announcement and described it as “a huge relief and a sign that the State is finally prioritising the lives of women with cervical cancer.” Ms Phelan added, “No woman should have to fight for access to treatment that could give her precious time with her family.”

It is understood that around 100 women per year could benefit from the new scheme. The HSE has not disclosed the total cost to the health service, citing ongoing negotiations with the manufacturer, but sources indicate that discounted pricing agreements were reached after protracted discussions.

Pembrolizumab works by helping the immune system more effectively target and destroy cancer cells. The drug has already been approved for use in a range of other cancers in Ireland, including lung and melanoma, but until now was unavailable for cervical cancer patients despite European Medicines Agency approval.

The Tánaiste, Micheál Martin, who previously served as Minister for Health, said the “long overdue decision” would help save lives. “We have listened to the voices of patients and clinicians. This is the right decision for Irish women and their families,” he said.

Critics have highlighted the delays that led to a two-tier system, with some women forced to fundraise or travel abroad for treatment. Sinn Féin health spokesperson David Cullinane TD said, “This should have been sorted years ago. Women have suffered needlessly because of bureaucracy and slow decision-making by the HSE and the Department of Health.”

The announcement comes as the CervicalCheck Tribunal continues to hear cases brought by women and their families over alleged failings in Ireland’s cervical screening programme. Campaigners say the Pembro decision is a positive step but have called for a broader overhaul of women’s healthcare and cancer services.

The HSE said further details, including criteria for eligibility and referral pathways, would be circulated to hospital oncology departments in the coming weeks. Consultants have urged women with questions to speak directly with their medical teams for guidance.
headline: Cervical cancer patients will be able to get new drug Pembro following landmark decision

text:
Authorities in Beijing have re-imposed strict travel restrictions on the Chinese capital this week amid mounting fears over a fresh outbreak of Covid-19. The move comes as the city reported a sharp increase in locally transmitted cases, sparking concern that the coronavirus, which first emerged in Wuhan in late 2019, is once again spreading within China.

Officials confirmed that dozens of new infections have been detected, many linked to a large wholesale food market in the south of the city. In response, Beijing municipal authorities have closed down several food markets, sealed off neighbourhoods, and established checkpoints to monitor movement in and out of affected districts.

Public health teams are undertaking mass testing in communities near the Xinfadi market, where the majority of recent cases have been traced. Schools in the area have been shut, and plans to resume in-person classes citywide were abruptly halted.

Residents in ‘high-risk’ zones have been ordered not to leave the city, while those in ‘medium-risk’ districts are strongly urged to forego non-essential travel. Flights, trains, and bus services out of Beijing are being curtailed, and anyone wishing to leave must first present a negative Covid-19 test result, issued within the previous seven days. Taxis and car-hailing services have also been banned from transporting passengers outside the city limits.

Restaurants and other hospitality businesses are once again prohibited from offering dine-in services, forced to revert to takeaway and delivery only. Large gatherings remain suspended, and public venues, including libraries, museums, and entertainment venues, are closed until further notice.

The developments have raised international alarm, with the World Health Organisation urging vigilance and rapid containment to avoid a repeat of the global surge experienced earlier in the pandemic. Ireland’s Department of Foreign Affairs has updated its travel advice, cautioning Irish citizens against non-essential travel to China and advising those in the region to follow local guidance.

The resurgence comes as many countries, including Ireland, grapple with the challenges of reopening societies and economies while avoiding a second wave of infections. Experts warn that even countries that appeared to have brought the virus under control may still face renewed outbreaks.

China’s government has pledged to take “decisive measures” to contain the outbreak in Beijing, which had previously reported very few new cases over several weeks. However, the new cluster has sparked fears over potential community transmission and the possibility that the virus may be more widespread than currently reported.

The situation remains fluid, with authorities on high alert and restrictions likely to remain in place for the foreseeable future. Irish citizens in China are advised to register with the local embassy and monitor developments closely.
headline: Covid-19: Travel restrictions re-introduced in Beijing, as coronavirus begins to spread again

text:
The Dublin Marathon, one of the capital’s most prestigious sporting events, has been cancelled for 2020 amid mounting concerns over the ongoing Covid-19 pandemic. Organisers announced the decision this morning, citing public health advice and the uncertainty surrounding large gatherings as the main reasons behind the move.

The marathon, which was scheduled to take place on 25 October, typically attracts over 20,000 runners from all over Ireland and abroad, along with tens of thousands of spectators who line the city’s streets. However, with the government’s current restrictions on mass gatherings and ongoing fears about the spread of coronavirus, the event’s future was thrown into doubt in recent weeks.

In a statement released today, race director Jim Aughney said: “We have taken the difficult decision to cancel the 2020 Dublin Marathon. Our primary concern must be the health and safety of our runners, volunteers, and the wider public. Given the current restrictions and the advice from the HSE and other authorities, it would not be possible to stage the event in a way that is safe for everyone involved.”

Participants who had already registered for the marathon will be offered a full refund of their entry fee or the option to roll over their place to the 2021 event. Organisers have urged runners to be patient as they process refunds, given the volume of entries to be managed.

The cancellation is likely to come as a major blow to the local economy, with hotels, restaurants, and retailers in Dublin City Centre set to lose out on much-needed business generated by the marathon weekend. Many charities and fundraising groups, who depend on the event each year, will also be affected.

Public reaction has been mixed, with some runners expressing disappointment but acknowledging the necessity of the decision in light of the ongoing risks. Others have criticised what they see as a lack of a clear roadmap for the return of large sporting events, calling on the government to provide more detailed guidance for organisers in the months ahead.

No decision has yet been made regarding other autumn sporting fixtures, with the Department of Health continuing to monitor the situation closely. In the meantime, participants are being encouraged to keep active and support each other through virtual running challenges and online communities.

This is the first time in the Dublin Marathon’s 41-year history that the event has been cancelled. Organisers have assured supporters that they are already planning for a return in 2021, provided it is safe to do so. The decision comes as the country continues to adapt to life under Covid-19 restrictions, with many public events either postponed or cancelled entirely in the interest of public safety.
headline: Covid-19: Dublin marathon canceled due to the ongoing coronavirus pandemic

text:
Gardaí have seized a significant quantity of electronic equipment as part of an ongoing crackdown on the illegal distribution of TV set top boxes across several locations in Dublin and surrounding counties. The operation, which was carried out by members of the Garda National Bureau of Criminal Investigation (GNBCI) with support from local units, targeted individuals suspected of facilitating access to premium television content without proper licences.

During a series of coordinated raids conducted in the early hours of Tuesday, Gardaí executed search warrants at both residential and commercial premises. Officers discovered a range of items, including modified set top boxes, computers, and related paraphernalia believed to be used in bypassing subscription fees for popular entertainment and sports channels.

Sources within An Garda Síochána confirmed that a small number of people were interviewed at the scene. Further arrests are expected as investigations progress and forensic analysis of the seized devices takes place.

Speaking after the operation, a Garda spokesperson highlighted the importance of such enforcement activities in protecting intellectual property rights. “This operation demonstrates our commitment to tackling the illegal streaming of television content and the associated offences,” they said. “Those found engaging in the importation, distribution or use of unlicensed set top boxes can face serious consequences, including prosecution under the Copyright and Related Rights Act.”

Revenue loss to broadcasters and legitimate service providers is believed to run into millions of euro annually, with the illegal trade in set top boxes undermining both the entertainment industry and the Exchequer. The operation comes after joint efforts with private sector partners representing media organisations, who have flagged the proliferation of these boxes in recent years.

Gardaí have urged members of the public to be wary of offers relating to suspiciously cheap TV services or devices purporting to provide free access to premium channels. “We are reminding people that using these boxes is not a victimless crime,” the spokesperson added.

Investigations are ongoing, and files will be prepared for the Director of Public Prosecutions. Anyone with information relating to the sale or distribution of illegal TV equipment is asked to contact their local Garda station or the Garda Confidential Line.
headline: Gardai seize equipment as part of an operation targeting illegal TV set top boxes

text:
The man accused of murdering Ashling Murphy is due to make his second appearance before the courts later this week, in a case that has shocked and saddened the country.

Jozef Puska, 31, with an address in Lynally Grove, Mucklagh, Co Offaly, is charged with the murder of Ms Murphy, a 23-year-old primary school teacher, who died after being attacked while out for a run along the canal bank at Cappincur, Tullamore, on 12 January. Puska was brought before Tullamore District Court last week, where the murder charge was formally put to him. He was remanded in custody to appear again at Cloverhill District Court this week.

The case has generated national grief and outrage, with hundreds attending vigils in memory of Ms Murphy across Ireland and beyond. The young teacher's funeral was attended by President Michael D. Higgins and Taoiseach Micheál Martin, and her death has sparked renewed calls for action to address violence against women.

Gardaí launched a major investigation in the wake of the attack, with support from specialist units and local communities. They have appealed to the public for information and witnesses, especially anyone who was in the area of the Grand Canal in Tullamore that afternoon. Gardaí have described the case as a "random and senseless act," and said they are continuing to appeal for anyone with dashcam or CCTV footage from the vicinity to come forward.

Ms Murphy, who taught at Durrow National School, was widely described as kind, talented and deeply committed to her pupils and local GAA club. The incident has reignited the national conversation around women's safety and prompted a review of existing policies and public awareness campaigns.

Mr Puska is expected to appear before Cloverhill District Court via videolink, where further directions from the DPP may be outlined. Legal aid has been granted in the case. The court previously ordered that the accused receive all necessary medical attention in custody. No application for bail has been made, as bail in murder cases can only be considered by the High Court.

Meanwhile, the community in Tullamore remains united in grief as they await further developments in the case. The investigation is ongoing, and the Gardaí have again stressed the importance of respecting the privacy of the Murphy family at this difficult time.
headline: Ashling Murphy murder: Accused scheduled to make second appearance in court

text:
Irish health authorities have confirmed that a total of just over 21,300 new coronavirus cases have been detected across the country in the past 24 hours. The figures, reported by the Health Protection Surveillance Centre (HPSC) on Sunday evening, represent one of the highest daily tallies seen since the onset of the pandemic.

The Department of Health also reported that there are 1,055 people with Covid-19 being treated in hospitals nationwide, with 92 of those patients receiving critical care in intensive care units. The HSE is warning that further increases in case numbers could put significant additional strain on hospital resources, as winter illnesses continue to circulate.

The majority of new cases are believed to be driven by the Omicron variant, which officials have described as highly transmissible. The National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET) has urged the public to continue observing basic public health guidelines, including mask-wearing, hand hygiene, and limiting social contacts, particularly in indoor environments.

Chief Medical Officer Dr Tony Holohan said the latest surge in cases is “a stark reminder that Covid-19 continues to pose a very real threat to public health”, and appealed for people to avail of booster vaccinations as soon as they become eligible. According to the latest HSE data, more than 2 million booster doses have been administered to date, though there have been some concerns over the pace of the rollout in certain regions.

Meanwhile, the Government has reiterated that there are no current plans to reintroduce widespread restrictions, but has not ruled out targeted measures should hospital admissions continue to rise. The Taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the situation remains “under constant review”.

The public is being advised to stay home and arrange a PCR test if symptomatic, or if they have been identified as a close contact of a confirmed case. Testing centres around the country have reported high demand, with some delays in obtaining appointments. The HSE maintains that additional capacity is being brought on-stream to cope with the surge.

In the wake of the latest figures, opposition TDs have criticised the Government for what they describe as a “lack of clarity and leadership”, pointing to ongoing issues with the contact tracing system and communications around public health advice. The Department of Health has insisted all efforts are being made to provide up-to-date information to the public as the situation evolves.

Ireland’s total number of confirmed Covid-19 cases since the pandemic began now exceeds 1.1 million, with over 6,000 deaths related to the disease recorded to date.
headline: Covid-19: Irish health authorities report just over 21,300 new coronavirus infections over the past 24h

text:
The United Kingdom has recorded a sharp surge in Covid-19 infections, with just over 93,000 new cases confirmed in the past 24 hours – the highest daily figure since the pandemic began. The new record sets alarm bells ringing across the UK and European health authorities, amid mounting concerns about the rapid spread of the Omicron variant.

Health authorities in Britain have confirmed that today’s figure has shattered all previous records, with case numbers accelerating in recent days. The steep uptick comes as the NHS faces mounting pressure, with hospitals bracing for a potential influx of patients amid warnings of staff shortages due to illness and self-isolation rules.

Public Health England has reiterated calls for people to come forward for vaccination and booster doses, as well as to observe public health guidance. Across the UK, large queues formed outside vaccination centres, with people seeking protection ahead of Christmas.

The spike in cases has led UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson to appeal to the public to exercise caution, though the British Government has so far stopped short of introducing stricter restrictions in the run-up to Christmas. Speaking at a press briefing, Johnson urged people to reduce social contact, wear masks, and use lateral flow tests before gatherings. He noted that the Cabinet continues to monitor the situation closely and will not hesitate to act if necessary.

The new figure comes just days after Ireland itself reported a sharp spike in Covid-19 cases, with the Department of Health warning of “extraordinary pressure” on the HSE and the hospital system. Although case numbers here have not reached UK levels, NPHET has advised caution amid concern about the highly transmissible Omicron variant.

The World Health Organisation has described the Omicron strain as spreading at an “unprecedented rate”, adding that it is rapidly displacing the Delta variant in several countries. EU health chiefs have recommended that member states ramp up booster campaigns and consider introducing additional measures to curb transmission.

In Northern Ireland, where public health measures differ slightly from those in the rest of the UK, the Department of Health in Stormont has signalled that further restrictions may be considered if the situation continues to deteriorate.

With the record-breaking number of cases and the Omicron threat looming large, Irish authorities are urging the public to take every precaution over the coming weeks, as millions prepare for Christmas gatherings with family and friends.
headline: Covid-19: UK reports record-busting daily coronavirus cases, with just over 93,000 new infections confirmed in the last 24h

text:
Budget airline Ryanair has announced a flash sale across its network, offering passengers a chance to snag low-cost seats from Irish airports – but the deal won’t last long as bookings must be made by midnight tonight.

With summer in full swing and travel restrictions eased, Ryanair is encouraging holidaymakers to act fast to avail of deeply discounted fares, with seats starting from just €14.99 one way for travel between 1st July and 30th September.

The company has said thousands of seats are included in the sale, covering popular sun destinations such as Spain, Portugal, and Italy, as well as city breaks to European capitals. Dublin, Cork, Shannon, Knock and Kerry airports are all included in the offer, with dozens of routes on sale for passengers keen to secure a last-minute getaway.

Ryanair’s Head of Communications, Jade Kirwan, said the airline wanted to “give Irish customers a much-needed boost” and encourage families to make the most of the remaining summer weeks. “There’s never been a better time to book a well-deserved break, but with this flash sale, you’ll need to get your skates on!” she told The Liberal.

However, the airline has reminded passengers that seats at the lowest fares are limited, and tickets are being snapped up quickly. Customers are urged to visit Ryanair’s website or app to secure the best prices before the midnight deadline.

Travel experts have warned that while the deals are attractive, would-be flyers should double-check their plans and any passport requirements, as many summer flights and hotels across the continent are already at capacity. Travellers are also advised to read the fine print regarding luggage allowances and any potential extra charges.

Ryanair’s latest sale comes amidst persistent calls from consumer groups for more transparency in airline pricing, and following the announcement this week of new routes out of Irish airports for autumn and winter.

The low-cost carrier continues to face criticism over its add-on charges but insists the headline fares remain among the cheapest available in Europe. The airline recently reported record passenger numbers taking advantage of its extensive Irish network and is projecting further growth for the remainder of the year.

With the clock ticking, those eager for a bargain break will need to act fast if they want to fly high for less this summer.
headline: Up, up and away! Ryanair launches huge sale but you must book by TONIGHT!

text:
The leader of the Irish Freedom Party, Hermann Kelly, has stepped up his campaign in the European Parliament against what he describes as “draconian and discriminatory” Covid-19 health pass requirements, vowing to fight moves which would force MEPs, employees and visitors to produce proof of vaccination or recovery.

Kelly, who founded the Eurosceptic party in 2018, travelled to Brussels this week where he held meetings with like-minded representatives and activists, pressing for the removal of all Covid-related entry restrictions within the parliament's buildings. He argued that mandatory vaccine certificates are “an affront to personal liberty, bodily autonomy and the democratic process”.

Speaking outside the parliament, he said, “Forcing elected representatives, staff and Irish citizens who want to visit the parliament to disclose their private health status is not only an attack on privacy, it effectively creates a two-tier society. There is no logical or scientific justification for continuing this divisive policy. My party stands firmly on the side of choice and freedom.”

The European Parliament had previously mandated that those entering its premises show either proof of full vaccination, a recent negative test result, or evidence of recovery from Covid-19, in line with prevailing public health advice from EU institutions. While many restrictions have eased in recent months, some controls remain in place at the discretion of parliamentary authorities.

Kelly claims that the ongoing requirement is being used as a political tool to exclude certain MEPs from full participation, especially those who object to government policies on pandemic management. He cited the example of a handful of MEPs from other countries who staged sit-ins at the entrances to parliamentary chambers last year in protest at the restrictions.

“Democracy is about debate and disagreement. When the very heart of European democracy begins excluding voices for refusing to comply with medical mandates, that's a dangerous precedent. Ireland’s voice must be heard in defence of true democracy and human rights,” Kelly said.

The Irish Freedom Party’s campaign has drawn support among some Irish constituents critical of the EU’s pandemic response, but has been dismissed by others as spreading misinformation about public health measures. Mainstream Irish political parties have largely accepted the vaccine pass system as a necessary measure during the height of the pandemic, though the government recently confirmed that all such restrictions have now been lifted in Ireland itself.

Asked if he believed his campaign had support among Ireland’s elected MEPs, Kelly insisted, “Whether they admit it or not, there are members across Europe who are deeply uncomfortable with these policies. People from all backgrounds are waking up to the reality that their rights are under threat.”

He pledged to keep up pressure on the parliament’s Bureau, the administrative body responsible for internal rules, and is calling on Irish constituents to lobby their MEPs to push for full restoration of open access to the assembly.

The European Parliament has yet to issue a formal response to Kelly’s demands, but a spokesperson noted that health and safety of all building users remains a top priority, and any measures in place are regularly reviewed in light of public health data.

Kelly concluded, “Ireland stood for freedom in the past and must stand for it now, both at home and in Europe. The right to enter public buildings and engage in the democratic process should never be conditional on medical papers.”
headline: Leader of Irish Freedom Party spearheads campaign in EU Parliament to oppose MEPs, staff and visitors having to produce a Covid-19 vaccination certificate

text:
Fast food giant KFC has announced the re-opening of 16 of its outlets across the country, much to the delight of hungry customers who have been craving their fried chicken fix. The move comes after weeks of closures due to government restrictions brought in to curb the spread of COVID-19.

The company confirmed that the selected restaurants would be offering delivery and drive-thru services only, with strict new safety protocols in place to protect staff and customers. Walk-in and sit-down dining remain off the menu for now, in line with public health guidelines.

Hungry punters flocked to social media to express their excitement at the news, with some admitting they have been counting the days since their last Zinger Burger or bucket of chicken wings. One Dublin resident told The Liberal, “I never realised how much I’d miss a proper takeaway. It’s been tough, but fair play to the staff who are getting back to work.”

The re-opened branches span Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Waterford, and other major towns, though some rural outlets remain shuttered. KFC management thanked staff members for their ongoing dedication and assured the public that measures such as contactless payments, protective screens, and rigorous cleaning regimes are in operation to minimise risk.

The re-opening comes as the Irish Government continues to gradually ease lockdown measures, allowing more sectors to return to business under controlled conditions. However, the Chief Medical Officer has urged the public to remain vigilant and adhere to social distancing, warning that such freedoms could be rolled back if the virus spreads again.

Industry insiders say the fast food sector has been one of the hardest hit throughout the pandemic, with many workers on reduced hours or temporary lay-offs. The limited re-opening is seen as a small but significant step on the road to recovery for the hospitality trade, though normal service remains a distant prospect.

KFC’s returning staff will be among those eligible for support through the Government’s Temporary Wage Subsidy Scheme. The company said it will continue to monitor public health advice and hopes to re-open more Irish outlets in the coming weeks.

For now, it seems motorists queuing at drive-thrus and delivery riders zipping through the suburbs may once again become a familiar sight, as Ireland slowly returns to some semblance of normality—one bucket at a time.
headline: Chicken run! KFC re-opens 16 Irish outlets for delivery and drive-thru

text:
Ireland faces a critical juncture in its battle against Covid-19 as the reproduction number, or R number, has risen to between 1.2 and 1.8, according to Deputy Chief Medical Officer Dr Ronan Glynn. The surge in the R number indicates that the virus is once again spreading, with every infected person now passing the disease to at least one other individual and, in many cases, nearly two.

Dr Glynn addressed the nation following the latest meeting of the National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET), warning that the country is in a "precarious position" and urging the public not to drop their guard. Citing the increase in daily case numbers and the growing rate of hospital admissions, he emphasised that the situation could escalate rapidly if people do not strictly adhere to public health guidelines.

"In the past week, we have seen a concerning upward trend in new cases across several counties, and hospitalisations are beginning to follow," Dr Glynn said. "Every effort now is required from the public to halt this trend."

The Department of Health recorded 456 new cases on Thursday, with clusters reported in Dublin, Cork, and Louth. Health officials have warned that the virus is spreading both in the community and within households, further heightening concerns ahead of the reopening of schools and workplaces.

Taoiseach Leo Varadkar has called for vigilance, stating that the Government will not hesitate to reintroduce further restrictions if numbers continue to rise. He acknowledged the impact that additional measures would have on the economy and society, but said the priority must remain public health.

Gardaí have stepped up patrols in urban areas, reminding people to maintain social distancing and wear face coverings in shops and on public transport. The HSE has increased its testing capacity, with results now being delivered within 36 hours in most cases, but officials warned that no amount of testing can compensate for complacency.

Dr Glynn’s comments come as international travel resumes on a limited basis, raising fears that imported cases could further undermine Ireland’s progress in containing the virus. The Department of Foreign Affairs continues to advise against non-essential travel to most destinations on the so-called "green list."

NPHET will review the figures again early next week, but Dr Glynn stressed that the responsibility rests with every individual. "We cannot afford to let our guard down. The decisions each of us makes in the coming days and weeks will determine the trajectory of this pandemic," he said.

The public is being urged to continue regular hand-washing, limit the number of contacts, and avoid large gatherings. The Government is monitoring the situation closely, with the Tánaiste Simon Coveney urging people to "stay the course" to prevent a return to stricter lockdown measures.
headline: Dr Glynn says Ireland is in a precarious position as R number is between 1.2 and 1.8

text:
Fans may be allowed back into sporting events from July, but only in strictly limited numbers, as government sources indicate a cautious easing of restrictions is being considered for the summer.

According to information obtained by The Liberal, the Department of Health and senior figures in the HSE are currently reviewing the possibility of permitting spectators at outdoor sporting fixtures, with initial plans likely to limit attendance to small, pre-determined groups. This would mark the first time in well over a year that supporters could return to stadiums across the country, following the blanket bans imposed during the Covid-19 outbreak.

A senior official involved in the discussions told The Liberal that the move would be “extremely cautious, gradual, and based on clear public health advice.” The official emphasised that any decision will hinge on the trajectory of the vaccine rollout, case numbers, and the presence of variants in the community.

“If the epidemiological situation continues to improve and all goes according to plan with the vaccination programme, we could see small groups of fans being allowed in from sometime in July,” the source said. “It would be heavily regulated, likely with allocated seating, mask-wearing, and social distancing in place.”

The prospective changes would be welcomed by sporting organisations such as the GAA, the FAI, and the IRFU, all of which have seen their fixtures played out in near-empty grounds since March 2020. A number of high-profile GAA matches, League of Ireland games, and rugby internationals have taken place behind closed doors, with only essential personnel present.

The Taoiseach, Micheál Martin, hinted in recent days that some restrictions could be eased over the coming months if case numbers remain low and the vaccination target is met, but warned against complacency. Speaking at a press briefing on Friday, the Taoiseach said the government would “move carefully and prudently,” noting that “we’re not out of the woods yet.”

The news comes as the latest HSE figures show steady progress in the vaccine rollout, with over 2.5 million doses administered and significant uptake among higher-risk groups. However, public health officials continue to express concern about the spread of the Delta variant, which has prompted renewed calls for caution.

No final decision has been made, and a formal announcement is expected closer to the end of June, depending on public health data. Discussions remain ongoing between the Department of Health, the National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET), and representatives from Ireland’s major sporting bodies.

The Irish Council for Civil Liberties has welcomed the potential move as “a small but important step back to normality,” but warned that continued transparency and clear communication from government would be crucial.

In the meantime, sports fans across the country remain cautiously optimistic that they may soon be able to cheer on their teams again, even if only in limited numbers, as the nation inches slowly towards recovery.
headline: Covid-19: Fans might be allowed to attend sporting events ‘in small numbers’ from July

text:
Pfizer and BioNTech are set to commence clinical trials of their Covid-19 vaccine on pregnant women, marking a significant development in the ongoing global vaccination effort. The US pharmaceutical giant and its German partner have announced that they will be enrolling expectant mothers in an international study, with Ireland likely to watch closely as it manages its own vaccination programme.

The trial is expected to involve around 4,000 healthy pregnant women, all of whom are over 18 and between 24 and 34 weeks into their pregnancies. The companies have stated that the study will take place in the United States, Canada, Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Mozambique, South Africa, Spain and the UK. No Irish sites have been confirmed, but outcomes are likely to be monitored closely by the Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) and the Department of Health.

To date, pregnant women were excluded from most Covid-19 vaccine trials due to potential risks and unknowns, despite health authorities around the world reporting increased risks associated with contracting Covid-19 during pregnancy. Ireland's current vaccine rollout, overseen by the HSE, prioritises those at highest risk including healthcare staff and the elderly, and recommendations regarding vaccination in pregnancy remain cautious.

Pfizer and BioNTech say the study will examine both safety and efficacy, with participants randomly receiving either the actual vaccine or a placebo. After childbirth, women who were in the placebo group will have the opportunity to receive the vaccine, ensuring all ultimately are offered some protection. The infants will also be monitored for up to six months to assess any transfer of immunity and other health outcomes.

Speaking about the study, Pfizer’s Vice President for vaccine clinical research, Dr William Gruber, said that “pregnant women have an increased risk of hospitalisation and severe Covid-19” and stressed the importance of gathering scientific data to inform guidance for this group.

National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC) guidance in Ireland currently recommends discussing vaccination on an individual basis with a healthcare professional, particularly for those with underlying medical conditions or a higher risk of exposure. There have been ongoing calls from advocacy groups and clinicians for clearer advice and more data on vaccine safety in pregnancy.

The results of the trial, which are not expected for several months, may play a crucial role in shaping public health policy both in Ireland and internationally. The Department of Health has yet to comment on how these trials might influence the national vaccination strategy, but sources indicate that the Government will follow the evolving evidence closely as it seeks to protect all vulnerable groups from the virus.

In total, more than 400,000 doses of Covid-19 vaccines have been administered in the Republic to date, with the rollout continuing to face logistical challenges, supply constraints and ongoing public debate about prioritisation. The forthcoming vaccine trial in pregnant women is expected to inform both public confidence and future government guidance on maternal and child health during the pandemic.
headline: Pfizer and BioNtech to start testing Covid-19 vaccine in pregnant women

text:
A Dublin Fire Brigade firefighter has been suspended after a video surfaced online reportedly showing the fireman making what has been described as an offensive ‘traveller joke’. The video, which circulated widely on social media over the past 24 hours, has sparked outrage among members of the Traveller community and prompted immediate investigation by Dublin City Council.

The firefighter in question, who is believed to be based at a northside station, is currently off duty and subject to an internal disciplinary process. Sources within the brigade told The Liberal that the video, filmed in uniform, involved a tasteless attempt at humour referencing Traveller stereotypes. The material has since been taken down but not before being widely shared.

In a statement issued this afternoon, Dublin Fire Brigade confirmed that a staff member had been placed on immediate suspension pending the outcome of a probe. “Dublin Fire Brigade is committed to the highest standards of conduct and inclusion. Any behaviour which brings the service into disrepute will not be tolerated,” the statement read.

Traveller advocacy groups have condemned the footage, calling for robust action and wider education within the emergency services on issues of racism and discrimination. Speaking to The Liberal, Martin Collins of Pavee Point said, “This type of so-called ‘banter’ has real-life consequences for Travellers, contributing to ongoing stigma and prejudice. We expect a clear response and real change.”

The Mayor of Dublin, Daithí de Róiste, has also weighed in, calling for “respect, dignity and equality from all public servants, including those serving in our fire and emergency services.”

The incident comes at a time of heightened scrutiny over social media use by public sector workers. Dublin City Council confirmed that it is reviewing social media policies for all staff. The HSE and other frontline agencies have previously issued updated guidelines following similar incidents.

Gardaí are not currently involved, but sources indicate that if further evidence of hate speech emerges, a criminal investigation could be considered under the Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act.

The firefighter’s union has declined to comment at this stage, citing the ongoing disciplinary process. The outcome of the investigation is expected within weeks, according to sources familiar with the matter.
headline: BREAKING: Dublin fire brigade suspend fireman for ‘traveller joke video’

text:
Jon Venables, one of the two men convicted of the murder of two-year-old James Bulger in 1993, is set to launch a fresh appeal for release from prison within the coming weeks, it has emerged. Venables, now in his early 40s, has already served multiple prison sentences, including his original sentence for Bulger’s brutal killing and subsequent imprisonments for offences involving indecent images of children.

The Parole Board in England is expected to consider his latest case after his legal team lodged a new application arguing for his release. Venables, who was ten at the time of the infamous crime which shocked the world, has spent a significant portion of his life under different identities provided by the British authorities. Despite being granted anonymity for his protection following his first release, he was recalled to prison twice for reoffending.

The brutal murder of James Bulger in Bootle, Liverpool, still resonates strongly throughout Ireland, with many families remembering the horrifying details of the case. The shocking nature of the crime, where the toddler was abducted, tortured and killed by Venables and his accomplice Robert Thompson, continues to provoke outrage. Campaigners representing James Bulger’s family have for years maintained their opposition to any release, arguing that Venables continues to pose a danger to society.

Venables was most recently jailed in 2017 after being caught in possession of child abuse images for a second time. His application to the Parole Board follows reports that he has engaged in therapy and rehabilitation while incarcerated. A spokesperson for James Bulger’s mother, Denise Fergus, has been quoted as saying the family would strongly oppose any effort to free Venables, and has called on the British justice system to consider the ongoing risk he might pose.

There has also been concern expressed by child protection campaigners in Ireland about the potential precedent such a release could set, particularly in terms of offenders who use new identities to evade scrutiny. Calls have been made for tighter cross-border monitoring and information sharing between the Gardaí and the relevant UK authorities, should Venables win his appeal and seek to travel or settle elsewhere, including the Republic.

The Parole Board’s decision is expected later this summer. British authorities have consistently maintained that Venables’s exact whereabouts and identity would remain secret in the interests of his safety should he be released. The case continues to fuel heated debate on both sides of the Irish Sea about justice, rehabilitation and the rights of victims’ families.
headline: Jon Venables to launch fresh appeal for freedom from jail within weeks

text:
Children aged five and over across Ireland can now be registered to receive a Covid-19 vaccine, after the HSE launched its portal for appointments for younger age groups. The move follows recommendations from the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC) and government approval, paving the way for children in the 5-11 age bracket to be vaccinated in the coming weeks.

Parents and guardians can register their children on the HSE website or by phone, with vaccine centres around the country preparing to administer the Pfizer/BioNTech Covid-19 vaccine to those who sign up. Children in this age group will receive a smaller dose than adults or teenagers, reflecting international health advice.

The HSE has said it will prioritise appointments for children with underlying health conditions or those living with vulnerable family members, but stressed that vaccine slots will be available to all in the 5-11 cohort. According to government figures, there are approximately 480,000 children in this age range in the State.

Speaking at a press briefing, Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly urged parents to consider registering their children, citing evidence from other countries where child vaccinations have already commenced. "The vaccine offers protection for our children, their families, and wider communities against the risk of serious illness,” he said.

However, the extension of the vaccine rollout to younger children has prompted debate among Irish families. Some parents have welcomed the opportunity to give their children additional protection, while others have voiced concerns over the necessity and long-term effects of vaccination for this age group. Campaigners questioning the government’s strategy have called for more transparency and access to information, with several prominent figures highlighting that the risk of severe Covid-19 outcomes in children remains low.

Schools are also being briefed on the development, with the Department of Education in contact with principals regarding any queries from parents and teachers. Unlike earlier phases of the programme, vaccines for children will not be administered on school grounds but rather in vaccination centres or participating pharmacies.

The first appointment dates for children are expected to be issued within days, and the HSE has advised parents to bring along personal identifiers, such as birth certificates or PPS numbers, when attending clinics. The government hopes to reach a high uptake rate in the 5-11 group before the return to school after the Christmas break.

Public health officials have said that while vaccination for this age group is not mandatory, it is strongly encouraged. The Chief Medical Officer, Dr Tony Holohan, reiterated that vaccination remains one of the best tools in Ireland’s ongoing response to the pandemic, particularly as the country faces continued challenges from the Omicron variant.

Parents seeking more information are encouraged to speak with their GP or visit the HSE’s official website, where a dedicated section provides details on vaccine safety, side effects, and the registration process.
headline: Is your kid getting it? Children as young as 5 can now register to get the vaccine

text:
Controversial television presenter Jeremy Clarkson has sparked a fresh storm of debate online after bluntly telling climate activist Greta Thunberg to “shut up you spoilt brat and go back to school”. The former Top Gear host made the remarks on his social media accounts this week, igniting a wave of reactions on both sides of the climate change divide.

Clarkson, never one to shy away from outspoken commentary, was responding to Thunberg’s renewed calls for urgent action at a European Union climate summit. The Swedish activist, aged 21, had criticised world leaders for “failing future generations” in a widely shared video address. Clarkson, 64, posted his response to his millions of followers, dismissing Thunberg’s warnings and urging her to return to her studies.

His comments quickly went viral, with thousands sharing both support and condemnation. Many social media users echoed Clarkson’s sentiments, criticising Thunberg for “lecturing” adults and what they see as disruptive climate protests. Others, however, accused Clarkson of bullying a young woman and dismissing the science of climate change.

The row spilled over into Irish political circles, with several TDs and senators wading into the debate. People Before Profit’s Bríd Smith called the remarks “deeply ignorant and offensive”. Fianna Fáil TD Christopher O’Sullivan said that “dismissing young people’s voices on climate is exactly why we’re in this mess”.

The exchange comes against the backdrop of increased climate activism in Ireland, with student-led protests returning to Dublin and other cities. Earlier this month, hundreds marched to the Dáil demanding more ambitious emissions targets as part of the Government’s climate action plan.

Meanwhile, Clarkson’s comments have reignited longstanding criticism of his views on environmental matters. The presenter was previously dropped by the BBC for an unrelated incident but has since found fame with his Amazon Prime show, Clarkson’s Farm. Supporters claim he is standing up for “common sense” against what they call “woke hysteria”.

Greta Thunberg has not yet directly responded to Clarkson’s outburst. Environmental groups in Ireland and abroad have rallied in her support, reiterating calls for urgent government action as Ireland continues to fall short of its own climate targets. The Department of the Environment said it is “aware of the passionate debate” but urged the public to “engage respectfully” on the issues.

Gardaí said they are monitoring online commentary but do not perceive any threat to public order arising from the dispute. As the debate continues to trend across social platforms, it appears Clarkson’s remarks have once again placed him at the centre of international controversy.
headline: Jeremy Clarkson goes viral on social media for telling Greta Thunberg to shut up you spoilt brat and go back to school

text:
Former US President Donald Trump has once again hit out at what he describes as “election shenanigans”, vowing to “fight” and bring his legal challenges to court. In a video statement released early this morning, Mr Trump accused his political opponents of “rigging” the American electoral process and insisted that he would “never surrender”.

The declaration comes after a closely fought election saw major swings in battleground states. Mr Trump, who previously held office from 2017 to 2021, has repeatedly claimed—without providing concrete evidence—that widespread irregularities and fraud have marred the integrity of the vote.

Addressing his supporters, Mr Trump said: “We are fighting. They want to silence your voice and take away your vote, but we won’t let them. We are taking this all the way to court.”

Legal teams representing the former president have already filed lawsuits in several states alleging impropriety with mail-in ballots, inconsistent counting procedures, and the alleged exclusion of Republican observers from the process. The cases are expected to be heard in courts over the coming weeks, with potential appeals all the way to the US Supreme Court.

The controversial remarks have continued to stoke division in the United States, where tensions are running high and protests are breaking out in a number of cities. Supporters of Mr Trump have gathered outside counting centres, demanding transparency, while opponents accuse the former president of undermining democracy.

The White House and the US Department of Justice have so far not commented on Mr Trump’s statements. However, election officials across several states—including both Republicans and Democrats—have insisted that the election was run fairly and that there is no evidence of widespread fraud capable of affecting the result.

The latest developments have drawn international attention, with governments across Europe—including the Irish Government—urging calm and respect for democratic institutions. Speaking in Dublin, a Government spokesperson said: “Ireland places great value on democracy, the rule of law, and the peaceful transfer of power. We encourage all parties in the US to allow their legal system to address any concerns.”

With the outcome of the American election potentially hinging on legal battles, uncertainty is likely to persist for weeks. The world’s eyes now turn to the US courts as President Trump’s legal fight gets under way.
headline: BREAKING: President Trump declares he is FIGHTING and is taking the election “shenanigans” to court

text:
The government is reportedly considering a once-off double payment of Child Benefit in response to the spiralling cost of living, sources in Leinster House have revealed. The measure, aimed at providing immediate relief to hard-pressed families, is believed to be under active discussion by senior coalition figures, with an announcement possible in the coming weeks.

Rising food, energy, and fuel prices have placed increasing pressure on households across the country, with many parents struggling to make ends meet. Campaigners and opposition TDs have been calling for urgent measures to ease the cost burden, and Child Benefit is seen as one of the most direct ways to help families cope.

If approved, the proposal would see parents receive an extra monthly payment for each child, on top of the standard rate of €140 per child. For a family with two children, this would mean an additional €280 – a significant boost during a time when many are facing higher bills and back-to-school expenses.

A spokesperson for the Department of Social Protection confirmed that a range of options is being examined as part of the government’s response to cost-of-living pressures. “Minister Humphreys is acutely aware of the difficulties facing families and is looking at targeted supports,” the spokesperson said.

Sources suggest the plan is being seriously considered as part of a broader package of measures to be unveiled before the summer recess, although no final decision has yet been made. It is understood there is support from some backbench Government TDs, who have warned that voters expect immediate action as prices continue to rise.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin refused to be drawn on the specifics of the proposal when questioned in the Dáil on Thursday, but acknowledged that “families are feeling the pinch” and that the government “will not be found wanting” in providing assistance.

Critics, however, argue that a once-off payment does little to address the underlying causes of rising costs, and have called for more permanent solutions such as increased investment in public services, rent controls, and targeted energy subsidies.

Nevertheless, for many parents, an additional Child Benefit payment would provide welcome breathing room. One Dublin mother told The Liberal, “It’s getting harder every month. Everything is going up – groceries, heating, uniform costs. Even a once-off bonus would really help.”

The government previously issued a double Child Benefit payment as part of last year’s cost-of-living package, which was widely welcomed by families. With inflation remaining stubbornly high, calls for a repeat measure have only intensified.

A final decision is expected ahead of the summer, as the coalition seeks to reassure anxious families and fend off mounting criticism over its handling of the cost-of-living crisis.
headline: Government considering a once-off double Child Benefit payment to help with rising cost of living

text:
The UK government has updated its international travel guidance by adding Malta, the Balearic Islands, and parts of the Caribbean to its so-called ‘green’ travel list, allowing British holidaymakers to visit these destinations without the need to quarantine on their return. The announcement was made by UK Transport Secretary Grant Shapps late on Wednesday, following a review by the UK authorities’ Joint Biosecurity Centre.

From 4am on 30 June, people travelling to England from Malta, Ibiza, Mallorca, Menorca, and several Caribbean islands, including Barbados, will not be required to isolate on arrival, provided they produce a negative Covid-19 test result before departure and take a PCR test on day two in Britain. The changes apply to England, but the devolved administrations in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland are expected to follow suit, as is customary.

The move is seen as a boost for the beleaguered tourism industry in those regions, as well as British travel operators and airlines, many of which have faced significant losses since the outset of the pandemic. However, the popular tourist destinations of Portugal and Spain’s mainland remain on the UK’s ‘amber list’, meaning returning travellers must still self-isolate for 10 days.

Malta, which has one of the highest Covid-19 vaccination rates in the European Union, welcomed the decision, as did tourism representatives for the Balearics. The Spanish authorities urged continued vigilance, pointing to the ongoing circulation of the Delta variant in parts of Europe.

Meanwhile, the Irish Government’s approach remains more cautious, with the Department of Foreign Affairs still advising against all non-essential international travel, except under the EU’s Digital Covid Certificate system, which is not due to be fully operational until 19 July. Irish holidaymakers currently face a mandatory hotel quarantine if arriving from countries designated as ‘high-risk’, but neither Malta nor the Balearic Islands are presently on Ireland’s mandatory hotel quarantine list.

British officials have warned that the situation remains fluid, and that countries could be removed from the green list at short notice if case numbers rise. Travellers are being urged to check the latest guidance before making bookings. The update comes as the UK reported a further rise in cases driven by the Delta variant, though hospitalisations remain relatively low, due in large part to the country’s advanced vaccination programme.

Ryanair and Aer Lingus are expected to increase capacity on routes to Malta and the Balearics in response to the announcement, while Irish travel agents reported a surge of enquiries from customers hoping for similar changes to Ireland’s travel policies in the coming weeks.
headline: Covid-19: UK adds Malta, the Balearic islands, and parts of the Caribbean to its ‘green’ travel list

text:
SuperValu has issued an urgent recall notice for one of its popular salad products after it was discovered that the item contains undeclared ingredients which may pose a risk to consumers with certain allergies. The recall, announced by the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI), affects batches of SuperValu’s Own Brand Mixed Leaf Salad.

According to the FSAI, the affected product contains mustard and celery, which were not declared on the packaging. Both ingredients are recognised allergens and may cause potentially serious or life-threatening reactions in sensitive individuals.

The batches in question bear the use-by dates of 12 June 2024 and 13 June 2024. Customers who have purchased this salad are advised not to consume it if they have allergies or intolerances to mustard or celery. The product was distributed to SuperValu stores nationwide.

SuperValu has removed the affected batches from sale and has put up recall notices in its stores across the country. The retailer is advising customers to return the product to their local store, where a full refund will be provided. No receipt is necessary for returns.

A spokesperson for the FSAI said, “The presence of undeclared allergens in food can pose a serious health risk to affected individuals. Consumers are urged to check their fridges and not to eat the affected product if they are allergic to the ingredients.”

No reports of illness linked to the product have been made at this time, according to the HSE. However, those who experience symptoms of an allergic reaction, such as difficulty breathing, swelling, or skin rashes, are advised to seek medical attention immediately.

The recall is the latest in a series of food safety alerts in recent months. The FSAI continues to remind food businesses of their responsibility to ensure accurate labelling, particularly concerning allergen information, as required under Irish and EU law.

For further information, consumers are encouraged to visit the SuperValu website or contact the SuperValu customer care line. The FSAI website also contains full details of the recall notice.
headline: Recall notice: SuperValu issues urgent recall notice for a salad product due to undeclared ingredients

text:
Italy has now overtaken China in the grim milestone of coronavirus deaths, with official figures confirming the death toll in the beleaguered European country has surpassed that of the Asian nation where the Covid-19 outbreak began.

Italian authorities reported on Thursday evening that more than 3,400 people have died as a result of the virus, pushing Italy past China’s official figure of 3,245. The number of confirmed cases in Italy has surged past 41,000, while the healthcare system is being stretched to breaking point.

Hospitals in northern regions, including Lombardy and Veneto, are reportedly overwhelmed, with medical staff working round the clock and in some cases, forced to make heart-wrenching decisions about which patients receive critical care. The Italian government extended the nationwide lockdown earlier this week, closing all non-essential businesses and urging people to stay indoors in a desperate effort to halt the rampant spread of the disease.

The news has sent shockwaves throughout Europe, with fears mounting that other countries could face similar catastrophic outbreaks if containment measures are not observed. Here in Ireland, the Department of Health has reiterated appeals for the public to follow strict social distancing guidelines and to stay at home unless absolutely necessary. An Garda Síochána have been granted additional powers to enforce restrictions as the HSE braces itself for an expected surge in cases.

Meanwhile, concerns remain about the accuracy of China’s reported statistics, with allegations that the true figures may be higher than those published. Despite this, the situation in Italy is being viewed as the most severe in the global pandemic to date.

The escalation in Italy has been attributed in part to an ageing population and the fact that the virus spread undetected for weeks before the introduction of controls. Several towns have effectively been cut off, and military vehicles have been pictured transporting coffins from the worst-hit areas due to a lack of space in local morgues.

The Taoiseach has warned that Ireland must learn from the Italian tragedy and take every possible precaution to prevent a similar outcome. The Government has indicated that measures currently in place may need to be extended if the number of cases continues to rise.

Scientists and doctors urge that strict adherence to guidelines is the only way to flatten the curve and avert a public health crisis on the scale now being witnessed in Italy.
