headline: Coronavirus: Disaster in Italy as death toll surpasses China’s, where the Covid-19 virus was first detected

text:
A well-known shopping centre in the Dublin suburbs was forced to shut early on Saturday evening, following disgraceful scenes involving groups of young thugs running riot through the premises and frightening staff and shoppers alike.

Eyewitnesses told The Liberal that packs of teenagers, many wearing dark clothing and face coverings, swarmed through the centre at around 6pm, intimidating customers and causing damage to shop displays. Several units were forced to close their doors as the situation escalated, and dozens of families were seen leaving the area in distress.

One local woman, who did not wish to be named, said: “It was absolute chaos. You could hear shouting and running, and the security staff were completely overwhelmed. People were terrified for their children.”

Video footage circulating on social media shows a number of youths jumping on benches and hurling objects at shop windows. Witnesses reported fireworks being set off inside the building. Several shoppers described a "mob mentality" and said they felt Garda resources in the area were completely inadequate for the situation.

Management at the shopping centre confirmed to The Liberal that the decision was taken to cease trading early for the safety of staff and customers. In a brief statement, they said: “Due to anti-social behaviour involving large groups of youths, the centre closed early. We are working with the Gardaí and reviewing our security protocols.”

A Garda spokesperson said officers attended the scene and dispersed groups congregating both inside the shopping centre and in the car park. No arrests were made but investigations are ongoing. Anyone with information is asked to contact their local Garda station.

The incident is the latest in a growing pattern of anti-social behaviour plaguing retail and public spaces in the capital, with business owners warning that staff are increasingly fearful for their own safety. “We can’t go on like this,” one small shopkeeper said. “If the authorities don’t get a grip, we’ll see more closures and more fear for ordinary people.”

Public representatives have called for a greater Garda presence and tougher action against those causing mayhem in communities. Calls have also been made for parents to take responsibility for the whereabouts and conduct of their children.

The shopping centre is expected to reopen as normal on Sunday, but staff say measures must be urgently put in place to prevent a repeat of such disturbing scenes.
headline: Groups of young thugs run riot around Irish shopping center, forcing early closure

text:
Tánaiste Leo Varadkar has come under fire after maintaining silence regarding a violent rampage associated with Black Lives Matter activists in his own Dublin West constituency on New Year’s Eve. The incident, which unfolded in Blanchardstown late on Sunday night, saw dozens of masked individuals swarm the main street, smashing windows, setting off fireworks, and reportedly clashing with Gardaí who struggled to contain the mayhem.

Local residents, still shaken after the night of chaos, said their calls for help went largely unanswered as emergency services were stretched thin. According to eyewitness accounts, several shopfronts were damaged and at least two vehicles were set alight while people hid indoors, fearful for their safety. Some residents claim that the group responsible displayed banners and chanted slogans associated with the BLM movement, raising further concerns about imported unrest finding its way into Irish communities.

Despite the high-profile and brazen nature of the incident, Mr Varadkar, who is also a TD for Dublin West, has yet to issue a public statement condemning the violence or offering support to those affected. This lack of response has drawn criticism from both local representatives and members of the public, who accuse the Tánaiste of selective outrage and double standards when it comes to politically sensitive issues.

“This is Varadkar’s own backyard. If this had been any other group, he’d have been first out with a statement,” said one local business owner whose premises was damaged in the attack. “People are frightened and angry, and he’s nowhere to be seen.”

The Gardaí confirmed that several arrests were made on the night and that an investigation into the events is ongoing, with CCTV footage being examined. They appealed for anyone with information to come forward, while stating that extra patrols will be in place in the area over the coming days. No serious injuries were reported, though considerable damage was done to properties and vehicles.

The silence from the Tánaiste stands in stark contrast to his previous prompt condemnation of other disturbances, raising questions about the consistency of government responses to violent disorder. As of Tuesday afternoon, calls to Mr Varadkar’s office for comment had not been returned. Local representatives are now urging the government to take a stronger stance on imported political activism that leads to violence on Irish streets.

The situation comes amid heightened tensions nationally about law and order, with public confidence in the Gardaí being tested repeatedly in recent months following similar incidents of disorder in the capital. Many residents now say they feel abandoned by their political leaders and are calling for a robust response to ensure peace and security in communities across the country.
headline: Taniste Leo Varadkar remains silent on violent BLM rampage in his own constituency on New Year’s Eve

text:
A large group of protesters breached the heavily fortified US embassy compound in Baghdad on Tuesday, in a dramatic escalation of tensions following recent US airstrikes that killed at least 25 members of an Iran-backed militia group in Iraq. The incident has raised concerns of a wider conflict breaking out in the region and drawn condemnation from both American and Iranian officials.

According to reports from international news agencies, the protest began in the early morning, with hundreds marching through the streets of the Iraqi capital, chanting anti-American slogans and carrying the flags of the Popular Mobilisation Forces, which includes the Kata’ib Hezbollah group targeted by US forces on Sunday night. The crowd forced their way through a checkpoint and set fire to a reception area at the edge of the embassy complex, while US personnel reportedly took shelter inside secure areas of the building.

No embassy staff have been reported injured, according to a statement released by the US State Department. American forces inside the compound used tear gas to disperse the protesters, while Apache helicopters circled overhead as a show of force. Iraqi security personnel were deployed to the scene and have since established a cordon around the embassy to prevent further incursions.

The US airstrikes, carried out on Sunday, targeted five sites in Iraq and Syria belonging to Kata’ib Hezbollah, after a rocket attack killed a US civilian contractor and wounded several American and Iraqi personnel at a military base in Kirkuk. American officials described the strikes as “precision defensive actions” in response to repeated attacks by Iranian-backed groups on coalition troops.

Iraqi authorities have condemned both the US airstrikes and the embassy incident, warning that the violence could threaten Iraq’s stability. The caretaker Prime Minister, Adel Abdul Mahdi, called on protesters to leave the embassy grounds and urged all sides to show restraint. The Iraqi Foreign Minister has summoned the US ambassador to express formal opposition to the American strikes, which the Baghdad government says violated Iraqi sovereignty.

Iran has also strongly denounced the US attacks, accusing the Trump administration of escalating tensions in the region. Iran’s Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, warned Washington of a “harsh response” if further “aggression” occurred. The events come at a time of heightened distrust between Washington and Tehran, with observers warning of the risk of further tit-for-tat violence.

The embassy breach is among the most serious confrontations at the US diplomatic mission in Baghdad in recent years, and follows repeated warnings from US authorities of “significant threats” to its personnel in Iraq. The incident has prompted the US Department of State to urge American citizens not to travel to Iraq, citing concerns for their safety.

The developments will be watched closely in Ireland, with the Department of Foreign Affairs advising Irish citizens in Iraq to exercise caution and follow local advice. There are no reports of any Irish nationals being caught up in the violence. The European Union has called for de-escalation and dialogue between all parties involved. 

The United States has since announced the deployment of additional military personnel to the region to bolster security at its embassy and other facilities. It remains unclear whether the situation in Baghdad will calm in the coming days, but the events mark a significant deterioration in US-Iraq-Iran relations, with fears of further violence looming as the political crisis deepens.
headline: Large crowd storms US embassy in Baghdad in protest over recent airstrikes that killed 25 fighters from an Iran-backed militia group

text:
The latest row over Irish language signage in the Six Counties tells us rather more than either side in the dispute would care to admit. It tells us, in fact, something fundamental about the incoherence at the heart of the post-Agreement settlement, and about the way in which "diversity" has become less a principle and more a weapon.

The specifics of the case are almost secondary to the broader dynamic at play. A council — in an area where Irish is not and has never been the community language — is asked to erect bilingual signage. Objections are raised, not on the grounds of hostility to the language per se, but on the grounds that the demand is political rather than practical. And immediately, the familiar machinery clicks into gear: those who object are cast as bigots, those who demand are cast as champions of inclusion, and the actual question of whether any of this serves the public good is lost entirely in the fog.

Let us be honest about what is happening here. The Irish language, in the context of the Six Counties, has been instrumentalised. This is not a controversial observation. It is a statement of plain fact that anyone with even a passing familiarity with northern politics will recognise. That instrumentalisation cuts both ways, of course. Unionism's historic hostility to the language was never really about the language itself — it was about what the language represented. And the same is true, in mirror image, of much of the current enthusiasm for Irish language provision in areas where nobody speaks it. The language is a proxy. It has been made into one by both traditions, and the people who genuinely love and use it are poorly served by the arrangement.

The deeper problem, however, is structural. The entire architecture of governance in the Six Counties is built on a model of communal balance that treats every question as a zero-sum contest between two blocs. This was, perhaps, an unavoidable feature of an agreement designed to end a conflict. But a quarter of a century on, it is worth asking whether a system designed to manage division has instead become a system that perpetuates it.

When the proponents of bilingual signage frame their case in the language of rights and diversity, they are borrowing from a liberal universalist tradition that sits very uneasily alongside the communalist logic of the institutions they operate within. You cannot simultaneously argue that Irish language signage is a matter of universal cultural enrichment — something that ought to be welcomed by all communities — and also treat it as a deliverable for one community within a power-sharing framework built on the premise that the two communities have fundamentally different and competing interests. The two arguments are incompatible, and the attempt to run them in tandem is, at best, intellectually dishonest.

This is not, it should be said, a problem unique to nationalism. Unionism plays precisely the same game with its own cultural symbols, wrapping what are plainly communal territorial claims in the language of heritage and tradition. The Twelfth is either a celebration of culture that everyone should appreciate, or it is a marker of Protestant and unionist identity in a contested space. It cannot coherently be both, and yet both arguments are routinely deployed depending on the audience.

What is remarkable is how rarely any of this is challenged.
headline: Dispute over Irish language signage exposes flaws in the scheme for a diverse Six Counties

text:
A fundraiser has been launched for the family of a young girl who tragically lost her life after getting into difficulty in a river at the weekend, with tributes pouring in describing her as a "gentle" and "kind-hearted" child.

The girl, who has not been formally named by the Gardaí, was recovered from the water after emergency services were called to the scene on Saturday afternoon. Despite the efforts of first responders and medical personnel, the child was pronounced dead a short time later.

A GoFundMe page set up to support the bereaved family has already raised thousands of euro, with organisers saying the funds would go towards funeral costs and supporting the family during what they described as an unimaginably difficult time.

Those who knew the child have spoken of their devastation at her passing. Tributes left on the fundraising page described her as a "gentle soul" who was "always smiling" and "lit up every room she walked into."

"She was the kindest, most gentle girl you could ever meet," one message read. "No family should ever have to go through something like this."

Local community figures have also expressed their shock and sadness, with one describing the incident as a tragedy that had left the entire area in mourning.

"The whole community is in shock. There are no words that can adequately describe the grief that people are feeling right now," a local representative said. "All we can do is rally around the family and make sure they know they are not alone."

The Gardaí have confirmed that the circumstances of the incident are not being treated as suspicious and that a file will be prepared for the Coroner.

Water Safety Ireland has urged the public to exercise extreme caution around waterways, particularly during the summer months when children are out of school and more likely to be in the vicinity of rivers, lakes and coastal areas. The organisation has repeatedly called for greater awareness of the dangers posed by open water, noting that drowning remains one of the leading causes of accidental death in Ireland.

The fundraiser had, at the time of publication, surpassed its initial target, a reflection of the depth of feeling within the community and beyond for a family dealing with an unthinkable loss.
headline: Fundraiser for “gentle” girl who died in River tragedy

text:
A public meeting in Co Meath is expected to hear that residents have experienced a "spiral" of crime and anti-social behaviour in their area, with locals demanding action from authorities they say have failed to adequately respond to their concerns.

The meeting, which has been organised by concerned members of the local community, comes amid growing frustration at what attendees are expected to describe as a deterioration in quality of life and a sense that the problems are being ignored or downplayed by those in positions of responsibility.

Residents in the area have spoken of a range of issues including burglaries, drug-related activity, intimidation, and persistent anti-social behaviour that they say has left some people, particularly older members of the community, afraid in their own homes.

One local, who did not wish to be named, said the situation had become "intolerable" and that the meeting was a last resort for people who felt they had exhausted other avenues.

"People are at the end of their tether," the resident said. "We've been raising these issues for a long time and nothing seems to change. If anything, it's getting worse. People are genuinely frightened."

The organisers of the meeting are expected to call for increased Garda resources in the area, as well as greater engagement from Meath County Council and other relevant agencies. Questions are also likely to be raised about the adequacy of current policing levels in the county more broadly, a concern that has been echoed by communities across rural Ireland in recent years.

It is understood that local public representatives have been invited to attend the meeting and will face pointed questions from constituents about what concrete steps are being taken to address the problems.

The issue of Garda numbers has been a recurring source of contention nationally, with the Garda Representative Association repeatedly warning that force strength remains well below what is required to adequately police communities. Despite government commitments to increase recruitment, progress has been slower than promised, and many rural and suburban areas say they have felt the impact of stretched resources most acutely.

Critics have long argued that official crime statistics do not capture the full extent of the problem, pointing to widespread underreporting driven by a belief among some members of the public that reporting incidents will not lead to meaningful action.

The meeting is the latest in a series of similar community gatherings that have taken place across the country in recent months, reflecting what many see as a growing disconnect between the lived experience of residents and the official narrative around crime and public safety.

Local representatives contacted ahead of the meeting acknowledged the concerns of residents and said they were committed to working with An Garda Síochána and other bodies to find solutions, though several admitted that the pace of progress had been frustrating.
headline: Public meeting in Meath to hear there has been ‘spiral’ of crime and anti-social behaviour

text:
A major new study has found that the overwhelming majority of young women who were administered testosterone as part of a gender transition developed pelvic floor dysfunction, raising fresh questions about the long-term physical consequences of cross-sex hormones.

The research, published in the journal *Urology*, examined 40 female patients aged between 18 and 40 who had been taking testosterone for gender transition purposes. Of those studied, 95 per cent were found to have developed pelvic floor dysfunction — a condition that can cause chronic pain, urinary incontinence, difficulty emptying the bladder, and sexual dysfunction.

The findings are likely to intensify the already heated debate around the medicalisation of gender dysphoria, particularly in young people, and will add to growing international unease about the evidence base underpinning so-called "gender-affirming care."

Pelvic floor dysfunction occurs when the muscles of the pelvic floor become too tight, too weak, or otherwise impaired. The condition can be severely debilitating, affecting basic bodily functions and quality of life. The researchers noted that testosterone causes significant changes to the vaginal and urethral tissues, including atrophy, which may contribute to the high rates of dysfunction observed.

The study's authors recommended that clinicians who prescribe testosterone to female patients should screen routinely for pelvic floor disorders and refer patients for specialist physiotherapy where necessary. The implication, however, is that a side effect of such severity and prevalence ought to factor more prominently into informed consent processes before hormones are prescribed in the first place.

The research comes amid a broader international reassessment of paediatric and young adult gender medicine. The landmark Cass Review in the United Kingdom, published last year, found that the evidence base for prescribing puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones to young people was "remarkably weak." In its wake, the NHS effectively ended the routine prescription of puberty blockers to minors, and several European countries — including Finland, Sweden, Denmark, and Norway — have moved to sharply restrict hormonal interventions for gender-dysphoric youth, favouring psychotherapy-first approaches instead.

In Ireland, however, the approach has remained largely unchanged. The HSE's National Gender Service continues to operate, and there has been little public indication that Irish health authorities intend to follow the more cautious path now being adopted by several of Ireland's European neighbours. Critics have argued that Irish policymakers and media have been slow to engage with the accumulating evidence of harm, and that young Irish patients may consequently be exposed to risks that clinicians in other jurisdictions have deemed unacceptable.

The question of informed consent is particularly pressing. If 95 per cent of young women taking testosterone develop pelvic floor dysfunction, it is reasonable to ask whether patients are being adequately warned of this near-certain outcome before beginning treatment. Advocates for a more cautious approach argue that many young people, and their parents, are not given a full picture of the potential consequences — physical, psychological, and irreversible — of medical transition.

Proponents of gender-affirming care maintain that for many patients, the benefits of transition outweigh the risks, and that withholding treatment can itself cause significant psychological harm.
headline: Study: 95% of young women on testosterone for sex change developed pelvic floor dysfunction

text:
Elon Musk has claimed that Twitter, prior to his takeover of the platform, actively interfered in elections around the world, describing the social media giant's previous management as having operated a system of political censorship on a global scale.

The billionaire owner of X, formerly Twitter, made the remarks during a wide-ranging discussion on his platform, alleging that the company's former trust and safety team had suppressed political speech in a manner that directly influenced electoral outcomes in multiple countries.

"The old Twitter was basically an arm of the establishment," Musk said, claiming that content moderation decisions were made not on the basis of neutral rules but according to the political preferences of the company's former leadership.

Musk has made similar claims in the past, most notably in relation to the suppression of the Hunter Biden laptop story in the United States ahead of the 2020 presidential election. The so-called "Twitter Files," a tranche of internal documents released after Musk's acquisition of the platform in late 2022, revealed extensive communication between Twitter staff and US government agencies regarding content moderation decisions.

However, his latest comments appear to go further, suggesting the problem extended well beyond the United States and amounted to a concerted pattern of electoral interference.

Critics have pushed back against Musk's framing, arguing that the Tesla and SpaceX chief executive has himself used the platform to amplify certain political voices and causes while adjusting the algorithm in ways that boost his own posts and those of figures he supports. Several researchers have pointed to Musk's own interventions during elections in countries including Brazil and the United Kingdom, where he has weighed in on politically charged issues, as evidence that the platform's neutrality problem has not been resolved under his ownership but has merely changed direction.

The claims come at a time when governments across Europe, including Ireland's, are grappling with how best to regulate social media platforms. The EU's Digital Services Act, which came into full effect last year, imposes obligations on very large online platforms to address systemic risks including potential interference with democratic processes. X has faced scrutiny from the European Commission under the legislation, with an investigation opened into the platform's handling of content and its algorithmic systems.

In Ireland, the issue of social media's influence on political discourse has been a growing concern. Coimisiún na Meán, the State's media regulator, has been tasked with enforcing the DSA domestically and has signalled its intention to take a robust approach to platform accountability.

Musk's remarks are likely to reignite debate about the appropriate boundaries of platform power and whether any single individual — whether a corporate executive or a government official — should hold such significant influence over the digital public square.

No evidence has yet been produced by Musk to substantiate the specific claim that Twitter's former management interfered in elections outside the United States in any coordinated fashion, and former Twitter executives have consistently maintained that their content moderation policies were applied in good faith to combat misinformation and protect users.
headline: Musk says Twitter interfered in elections

text:
Minister for Justice James O'Callaghan has pushed back against calls to introduce automatic deportation for all foreign nationals convicted and jailed in Ireland, saying such a blanket policy would not be legally feasible under current EU and international law obligations.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the minister said that while he was committed to strengthening the deportation process for serious offenders, a one-size-fits-all approach was not something he could implement without running into significant legal challenges.

"There are people who have lived in this country for many years, who have families here, who have deep roots here. You cannot simply say that every single person who is not an Irish citizen and who receives a custodial sentence will be automatically removed from the State," O'Callaghan said.

The comments come amid growing public frustration over the pace of deportations and the perceived leniency of the current system. Critics have pointed to a number of high-profile cases in which foreign nationals convicted of serious offences, including violent and sexual crimes, have been permitted to remain in the State after serving their sentences.

O'Callaghan insisted that the government was taking the issue seriously and pointed to recent legislative changes designed to expedite the removal of foreign nationals who pose a threat to public safety. However, he stressed that Ireland's obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights, EU free movement directives, and international refugee law meant that each case had to be assessed on its individual merits.

"What I will not do is promise people something that would be struck down by the courts within weeks. That would be dishonest. What I will do is make sure the system works faster, works better, and prioritises the safety of the Irish public," the minister said.

The response is unlikely to satisfy those who have been calling for a far more hardline approach. A number of figures on the political right have argued that any non-citizen who receives a prison sentence should face mandatory deportation upon completion of that sentence, with no exceptions.

Independent TD and immigration spokesman Mattie McGrath described the minister's position as "more of the same," arguing that the government was hiding behind legal technicalities rather than taking decisive action.

"The Irish people are sick and tired of being told what they can't do. They want to see action. They want to know that people who come to this country and commit serious crimes will be sent home. It's as simple as that," McGrath said.

Legal experts have noted that introducing automatic deportation without any individual assessment would almost certainly face a constitutional challenge, with Article 40 of the Constitution guaranteeing certain rights to all persons within the State, not solely citizens.

However, some have argued that the minister could do far more within the existing legal framework to speed up deportation orders and to ensure that those who are ordered to leave the State actually do so. It has been widely reported that a significant number of deportation orders issued by the Department of Justice are never enforced, with individuals either absconding or successfully challenging their removal through the courts.

O'Callaghan acknowledged the enforcement gap and said additional resources were being allocated to the Garda National Immigration Bureau to address the backlog. He also confirmed that discussions were ongoing with a number of countries regarding bilateral return agreements.
headline: O’Callaghan won’t automatically deport all jailed migrants

text:
The widely held belief that ageing populations will inevitably cripple economic growth and overwhelm public finances has been significantly challenged by a major new study, which argues that the doom-laden projections frequently deployed by policymakers are based on flawed assumptions and fail to account for a range of countervailing factors.

The research, published by economists at the National Bureau of Economic Research in the United States, finds that the standard models used to forecast the economic consequences of demographic change systematically overstate the burden of an older population by ignoring productivity gains, changes in labour force participation among older workers, and the economic benefits of lower dependency ratios among the young.

For decades, governments across the developed world — Ireland very much included — have warned that falling birth rates and rising life expectancy would combine to produce a fiscal time bomb: fewer workers supporting a growing cohort of retirees, with ballooning pension and healthcare costs threatening to swamp the public purse. It is a narrative that has underpinned arguments for everything from increased immigration to raising the retirement age to restructuring public pension entitlements.

But the study's authors contend that these projections tend to treat demographic change in isolation, as though economies are static systems incapable of adaptation. In reality, they argue, societies adjust in numerous ways that substantially offset the supposed costs of ageing. Workers remain in employment longer, particularly as the nature of work shifts away from physically demanding occupations. Older workers, far from being an economic drag, often bring experience and institutional knowledge that enhances productivity. And fewer children mean reduced spending on education and child-related services, freeing up resources that rarely feature in the headline projections about demographic decline.

The findings are particularly relevant in the Irish context, where the ageing population has become a fixture of policy debate. The Government's own projections have repeatedly warned of mounting pressures on the State pension system, the HSE, and long-term care provision as the proportion of over-65s in the population grows. The Commission on Pensions, which reported in 2021, recommended increasing the State pension age to 67 and subsequently to 68, in part on the basis of demographic forecasts suggesting the old-age dependency ratio would become unsustainable.

Those recommendations proved politically toxic, with the Government ultimately shelving the proposed increase in the pension age following significant public backlash. The debate, however, has never gone away, and demographic projections continue to be cited by the Department of Finance and other bodies as evidence that difficult choices lie ahead.

The new research does not suggest that ageing populations pose no challenges whatsoever. Healthcare costs do tend to rise with an older population, and pension systems designed in an era of higher birth rates and shorter retirements will inevitably require some adjustment. What the authors dispute is the catastrophist framing that has dominated the conversation — the suggestion that ageing societies face an existential economic crisis unless radical action is taken immediately.

They point to the experience of Japan, frequently held up as the cautionary tale of demographic decline, where GDP per working-age adult has actually grown at a respectable rate despite decades of population ageing and overall population decline.
headline: Study: Economic fears of ageing societies overblown

text:
Jim Moore, an 85-year-old man from Bangor, Co Down, has been charged with the murder of 81-year-old Patricia Aust, whose body was discovered at a property in the seaside town earlier this week.

Moore appeared before Newtownards Magistrates' Court on Saturday, where he was formally charged with the single count of murder. He spoke only to confirm his name and date of birth during the brief hearing.

The PSNI had launched a murder investigation after Ms Aust's body was found at a residential address in the Chippendale Vale area of Bangor on Wednesday evening. Officers had attended the scene following a report of concern for the welfare of a woman at the property.

A post-mortem examination was carried out, and the death was subsequently treated as suspicious before being upgraded to a murder inquiry.

Moore, whose address was given as Chippendale Vale, Bangor, was arrested shortly after the discovery and had been in police custody prior to his court appearance.

A detective inspector from the PSNI's Major Investigation Team told the court he could connect the accused to the charge. No application for bail was made, and Moore was remanded in custody.

The case has been adjourned and is expected to return to court in the coming weeks.

Ms Aust's family have been informed and are being supported by specialist PSNI family liaison officers. In a statement released through police, the family asked for privacy during what they described as an extremely difficult time.

The investigation is understood to be ongoing, with detectives continuing to carry out enquiries in the Chippendale Vale area. Police have appealed for anyone with information relevant to the case to come forward.

The killing has shocked the quiet residential neighbourhood, with local representatives expressing their sympathies to the deceased woman's family and friends.
headline: Jim Moore (85) charged with murder of Patricia Aust (81) in Bangor

text:
Independent TD Michael Fitzmaurice and former senator Pádraig Mullooly travelled to Brussels this week to voice their opposition to the EU-Mercosur trade deal, warning that the agreement poses an existential threat to Irish farming and food production standards.

The pair joined a broader protest movement that has seen farmers and rural representatives from across Europe converge on the Belgian capital as the European Commission continues to push for the finalisation of the long-delayed trade pact with the South American bloc comprising Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay.

Fitzmaurice, who represents the Roscommon-Galway constituency, has been one of the most vocal critics of the deal in the Dáil, repeatedly arguing that it would open European markets to beef and other agricultural products produced under environmental and welfare standards far below those demanded of Irish farmers.

Speaking from Brussels, the Roscommon-based TD said that Irish and European farmers were being "sold out" by a Commission that was more interested in securing market access for the automobile and pharmaceutical industries than in protecting the livelihoods of family farmers.

"The people making these decisions in Brussels have no understanding of what this will do to rural Ireland," Fitzmaurice said. "They're willing to throw agriculture under the bus to get a trade deal over the line. We're here to tell them that this is not acceptable."

Mullooly, a former Fianna Fáil senator from County Roscommon, echoed those concerns, arguing that the deal would amount to a "betrayal" of Irish farmers who have invested heavily in meeting ever-increasing regulatory requirements around emissions, water quality and animal welfare.

The EU-Mercosur agreement, which has been under negotiation in various forms for over two decades, would create one of the largest free trade zones in the world. Under its terms, significant quotas of South American beef, poultry, sugar and ethanol would gain preferential access to the EU market.

Agricultural organisations including the IFA and ICMSA have consistently opposed the deal, pointing out that Brazilian beef production in particular is linked to Amazon deforestation and that producers in Mercosur countries are permitted to use hormones, pesticides and other inputs that are banned or heavily restricted in the European Union.

The protest comes at a time of heightened tension between the farming community and policymakers in both Dublin and Brussels. Farmers across Europe have staged rolling protests over the past year, citing what they describe as an unsustainable burden of regulation combined with trade policies that undercut them by importing food produced to lower standards.

The Irish government's position on Mercosur has shifted over the years. While successive administrations have expressed "concerns" about the deal's impact on the beef sector, critics like Fitzmaurice have accused the government of failing to take a sufficiently robust stance in opposing it at European Council level.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin has previously indicated that Ireland would seek safeguards for the agricultural sector in any final agreement, but opponents of the deal argue that no amount of safeguards can adequately protect Irish farmers from the sheer scale of South American production capacity.
headline: Fitzmaurice, Mullooly protest EU-Mercosur deal in Brussels

text:
The slow death of the Gaeltacht has been foretold so many times that it has become something of a cliché, a funeral oration delivered perennially by politicians who then proceed to do absolutely nothing about it. But there is a difference between a slow decline and an active destruction, and what is happening now in Ireland's Irish-speaking communities falls squarely into the latter category.

The housing crisis — that great national affliction which successive governments have failed to address with anything resembling competence — is now reaching into the Gaeltacht areas with consequences that threaten to be terminal for the Irish language as a living, community tongue. And the most galling thing about it is that almost nobody in official Ireland seems to care.

The basic mechanics are brutally simple. Young people who grew up speaking Irish in areas like Conamara, the Kerry Gaeltacht, Múscraí, and Gaoth Dobhair cannot afford to buy or build homes in their own communities. Planning restrictions, inflated site costs, a shortage of tradespeople, and the general dysfunction of the Irish housing market have combined to make it functionally impossible for a young couple to remain in the area where they were raised. So they leave. And when they leave, the language goes with them.

Into the vacuum come two forces. The first is the short-term letting and holiday home market, which has hollowed out communities from An Rinn to Carna. Houses that once held families — families who spoke Irish at the kitchen table, who sent their children to the local Gaelscoil, who kept the language alive in the most organic and important way possible — now sit empty for ten months of the year, their owners residing in Dublin or London or further afield, their contribution to the linguistic life of the community precisely nil.

The second force is the arrival of English-speaking residents who, however well-intentioned, inevitably shift the linguistic balance of the community. This is not a criticism of any individual. People have a right to live where they choose. But it is a statement of sociolinguistic fact, well established in the academic literature, that once the proportion of daily Irish speakers in a community drops below a certain threshold, the language ceases to function as the community's vernacular. It becomes instead a prestige code, something spoken in school and at official functions, but not in the shop, not in the pub, not between neighbours. At that point, the Gaeltacht exists in name only.

The most recent data from the Central Statistics Office should alarm anyone who claims to value the Irish language. The number of daily Irish speakers in Gaeltacht areas continues to decline. In several electoral divisions that are officially designated as Gaeltacht, Irish is now a minority language in practice. The Comprehensive Linguistic Study of the Use of Irish in the Gaeltacht, first published in 2007, warned that most Gaeltacht areas would cease to be Irish-speaking within a generation without radical intervention. That generation is now almost up, and the radical intervention never came.
headline: The housing crisis threatening An Ghaeltacht

text:
It is one of the more curious corners of Christmas folklore, and one that tends to surprise people when they first encounter it: the long and surprisingly well-documented association between Santa Claus and cats. Not reindeer, not elves, but cats. The connection runs deeper than most realise, threading through centuries of European tradition and arriving, in a somewhat roundabout fashion, at the red-suited figure we know today.

The most obvious starting point is Iceland, where the Jólakötturinn — the Yule Cat — has stalked the popular imagination for centuries. This enormous, fearsome feline was said to roam the countryside during the Christmas season, devouring anyone who had not received new clothes to wear before Christmas Eve. The tradition served a practical purpose, encouraging workers to finish processing the autumn wool before the festivities began. Those who worked hard were rewarded with new garments and thus protected from the beast; the lazy were, in the folklorist's delicate phrasing, consumed.

The Yule Cat was not exactly a benevolent figure, but it operated within the same moral framework as the broader Santa Claus tradition: reward for the good, punishment for the bad. In this sense, it functioned as a kind of feline enforcer of the Christmas spirit, a role that predates the jolly gift-giver of modern commercial culture by several hundred years.

But Iceland is far from the only place where cats and Christmas overlap. In Scandinavian and Northern European folk traditions more broadly, cats were associated with the winter solstice and the returning of the light. The Norse goddess Freya, whose chariot was famously pulled by two large grey cats, was closely linked with the midwinter festival of Yule. When Christianity gradually absorbed and repurposed pagan winter celebrations, elements of Freya's mythology did not simply vanish. They were folded into the newer traditions, often in ways that were not immediately obvious.

Some historians of folklore have argued that the association between Freya's cats and the gift-giving traditions of Yule created a cultural template that persisted even as the figure of Saint Nicholas — the Christian bishop of Myra, in modern-day Turkey — was grafted onto existing northern European midwinter customs. Saint Nicholas himself had no particular connection to cats, but the traditions he was mapped onto certainly did.

In parts of France and the Low Countries, where Sinterklaas traditions remain robust to this day, cats appear in Christmas iconography with striking regularity. Medieval woodcuts from the region frequently depict cats sitting near hearths on Christmas Eve, and some scholars have suggested that the association between Santa Claus and chimneys may owe something to the older folk belief that cats served as guardians of the hearth. The hearth, of course, was not merely a source of warmth but the spiritual centre of the home in pre-modern European culture, and cats — creatures of warmth and domesticity — were its natural custodians.

There is also the rather charming Italian tradition of La Befana, the Christmas witch who delivers gifts to children on the eve of the Epiphany.
headline: Why Santa Claus is historically associated with cats

text:
A man has been charged with the murder of his parents and brother following a tragic incident that has shocked a local community.

The accused, who is in his twenties, appeared before a special sitting of the District Court on Monday evening, where he was charged with three counts of murder. He spoke only to confirm his name and address to the court.

The bodies of the three deceased were discovered at a residential property over the weekend following what Gardaí described as a "violent incident." The victims have been named locally, though Gardaí have asked media to respect the privacy of the extended family at this time.

The accused was arrested at the scene and had been detained at a local Garda station under the provisions of Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act, 1984, prior to being charged.

During the brief court appearance, a Garda inspector gave evidence of arrest, charge, and caution, telling the judge that the accused made no reply when the charges were put to him.

Legal aid was granted to the accused after the court heard he was not in a financial position to fund his own defence. His solicitor made no application for bail, and the accused was remanded in custody to appear before the court again at a later date.

The Director of Public Prosecutions has directed that the case be tried on indictment, meaning it will ultimately be heard before the Central Criminal Court.

Locals in the area have expressed disbelief at the killings, with one neighbour describing the family as "quiet and well-liked" in the community. Floral tributes have been left near the family home, which remains sealed off as a crime scene as the Garda Technical Bureau continues its examination.

Gardaí have said they are not seeking any other persons in connection with the investigation and have appealed for anyone with information to contact them.
headline: BREAKING: Son charged with murder of parents, brother

text:
The Dáil has voted to accept the final report of the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Assisted Dying, which recommends that the Government legislate to permit assisted suicide in Ireland under certain conditions.

The vote, which passed without a formal division, marks a significant step in what is likely to be one of the most contentious legislative debates in the history of the State. Critics have warned that the committee's recommendations, if enacted, would represent a fundamental shift in the State's approach to the sanctity of life and the role of medicine.

The committee's report, which was published earlier this year following months of hearings, recommends that assisted dying be made available to adults who are ordinarily resident in the State and who have a terminal illness that is likely to lead to death within a defined timeframe. It also recommends the establishment of a regulatory framework to oversee the process, including requirements for multiple medical assessments and a cooling-off period.

However, concerns have been raised about the breadth of the committee's recommendations and the speed at which the issue is being advanced. A number of TDs and Senators have expressed disquiet about the lack of adequate safeguards in the proposals, and disability rights groups have warned that the legislation could place vulnerable people at risk.

The Disability Rights Coalition has been among the most vocal opponents of the proposals, arguing that the introduction of assisted suicide in other jurisdictions has invariably led to an expansion of eligibility criteria beyond what was initially intended. In Canada, where medical assistance in dying was introduced in 2016 for those with a terminal illness, the regime has since been expanded to include those with chronic illnesses and disabilities, and a further expansion to include those suffering solely from mental illness has been proposed.

Several TDs who spoke during the debate raised concerns about the so-called "slippery slope" effect, pointing to the Canadian experience as evidence that initial safeguards are inevitably diluted over time. Others questioned whether the State should be facilitating death at a time when palliative care services remain significantly underfunded and inaccessible in many parts of the country.

The Irish Hospice Foundation has previously noted that access to specialist palliative care remains uneven across the State, with significant gaps in provision in rural areas and for non-cancer diagnoses. Critics of the committee's report have argued that the Government should prioritise investment in palliative care before considering any legislation on assisted dying.

Those in favour of the proposals have argued that the legislation is about providing choice and compassion to those who are suffering at the end of life, and that robust safeguards can be built into any legislative framework. Committee members who supported the report have pointed to the experience in Oregon, where a more restrictive model of assisted dying has been in operation for over 25 years without significant expansion of eligibility criteria.

The vote to accept the report does not commit the Government to introducing legislation, but it does increase the political pressure to do so. The Taoiseach has previously indicated that the matter is one of conscience for individual TDs and that any vote on future legislation would be a free vote, though the Government has not yet committed to a timeline for bringing forward a bill.
headline: Dáil votes to accept report recommending legislating for assisted suicide

text:
Sinn Féin has come under fire after it emerged that a party branch organised a fundraiser in aid of Mermaids, the controversial UK-based transgender charity that has faced sustained criticism over its stance on puberty blockers for children.

The fundraiser, which was promoted on social media by a local Sinn Féin cumann, drew immediate backlash from critics who accused the party of aligning itself with an organisation whose approach to gender-questioning minors has been the subject of serious concern in both Britain and Ireland.

Mermaids has long advocated for the use of puberty-blocking drugs for children who question their gender identity, a position that has become increasingly contentious following the publication of the landmark Cass Review in the UK. That independent review, led by paediatrician Dr Hilary Cass, found that the evidence base for prescribing puberty blockers to gender-questioning young people was "remarkably weak" and that children had been let down by a lack of rigorous research.

The NHS in England subsequently moved to ban the routine prescription of puberty blockers for minors outside of clinical trials, a decision that was upheld by the UK Supreme Court.

Mermaids itself has faced a string of controversies in recent years. The Charity Commission for England and Wales opened a regulatory compliance case into the organisation, and its former CEO stepped down amid questions about safeguarding practices. The charity also lost its appeal against a decision granting charitable status to the LGB Alliance, a group that has raised concerns about the medicalisation of gender-confused children.

Critics argued that Sinn Féin's association with the charity raised serious questions about the party's position on child safeguarding and the medical transitioning of minors.

"This is an organisation that has promoted an approach to vulnerable children that is now being rejected by mainstream medicine across Europe," said one commentator. "For any political party to be fundraising on their behalf at this stage is deeply irresponsible."

The backlash is the latest in a series of controversies for Sinn Féin around gender identity issues. The party has been a vocal supporter of self-identification policies and broader gender ideology, positions that have increasingly put it at odds with a growing body of medical evidence urging caution when it comes to the treatment of minors.

Several European countries, including Sweden, Finland, Denmark, and Norway, have moved to restrict or curtail the use of puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for minors in recent years, citing the lack of robust evidence for their safety and efficacy.

In Ireland, the HSE has faced questions about its own approach to gender services for young people, though the issue has received comparatively less political scrutiny than in the UK and other European nations.

Sinn Féin was contacted for comment on the fundraiser and whether the party endorses Mermaids' position on puberty blockers for children. At the time of publication, no response had been received.

The controversy highlights the growing political sensitivity around gender medicine, particularly as it relates to children, and the extent to which Irish political parties may face increasing pressure to clarify their positions as the international consensus continues to shift towards a more cautious approach.
headline: Sinn Féin slammed for Mermaids fundraiser over puberty blocker stance

text:
The latest figures from the EU Agency for Asylum make for interesting, if not entirely surprising, reading. Across the European Union, the number of people lodging asylum applications fell by 7 per cent in 2024 compared to the previous year. In Ireland, however, the trend moved decisively in the opposite direction, with applications rising sharply over the same period.

It is a pattern that has become wearily familiar. While other European countries have begun to get to grips with the scale of the challenge — tightening procedures, accelerating returns, and in some cases deploying rhetoric that would make Irish politicians blush — Ireland continues to operate as something of an outlier. The question, as ever, is why.

Part of the answer lies in policy, or rather the absence of it. For much of the past two years, the Government has lurched from crisis to crisis on the issue of immigration and asylum, seemingly incapable of getting ahead of events. Communities from Coolock to Cahersiveen have found themselves dealing with the consequences of decisions made — or not made — in Leinster House and on Merrion Street. Ministers have offered sympathetic noises, promised reviews, and commissioned reports. What they have not done, by and large, is act with anything resembling urgency.

The contrast with other EU member states is instructive. Countries that were once held up as exemplars of liberal asylum policy have quietly changed course. Germany has reimposed border controls. The Netherlands has signalled a dramatic shift in approach. Even Sweden, long the poster child for open-door migration in Europe, has reversed course in a manner that would have been unthinkable a decade ago. Applications across the bloc have fallen not by accident but because governments have made deliberate choices to reduce them.

Ireland, it seems, did not get the memo. Or if it did, it filed it somewhere between the latest HSE overspend report and the never-ending housing crisis updates.

The Government will, no doubt, point to the measures it has introduced. The International Protection Office has been given additional resources. Emergency reception centres have been stood up — and in some cases stood down again, amid local opposition. There has been talk of speeding up processing times, of increasing the rate of deportation orders, of a new returns policy that will finally have teeth. Talk, however, is cheap, and the numbers suggest that whatever has been done is not working.

There is an uncomfortable reality that few in official Ireland seem willing to confront directly. Ireland's system, as currently configured, acts as a pull factor. The combination of relatively generous welfare provisions, a slow and cumbersome processing system, and an almost non-existent returns mechanism makes this country an attractive destination for those seeking to lodge an asylum claim — including, it must be said, those whose claims may ultimately be found to have no basis.

This is not, despite what some would have you believe, a far-right talking point. It is a straightforward observation about incentive structures, the kind of analysis that would be unremarkable in any other policy area. If you design a system that is slow to process claims, reluctant to enforce negative decisions, and generous in its interim provisions, you will attract more applicants. This is not complicated. It is not xenophobic.
headline: Numbers claiming asylum across EU fall, but rise in Ireland

text:
The notion that the United States might find itself in a shooting war with Venezuela would have seemed fanciful even a few months ago. Yet here we are, with warships repositioned, diplomatic cables flying, and rhetoric from both Washington and Caracas reaching a pitch that suggests something more than mere posturing. Understanding how we arrived at this point requires looking beyond the immediate headlines and examining the deeper currents driving the confrontation.

The proximate cause is, as it so often is in American foreign policy, a combustible mixture of domestic politics and geopolitical ambition. President Trump has made no secret of his desire to reassert American dominance in the Western Hemisphere, framing the Monroe Doctrine not as a relic of the nineteenth century but as a living, breathing mandate. Venezuela, under the authoritarian rule of Nicolás Maduro, presents itself as a convenient foil — a socialist government sitting atop the world's largest proven oil reserves, allied with China, Russia, and Iran, and presiding over a humanitarian catastrophe that has sent millions of refugees streaming across the continent.

But to reduce this to a simple story of American aggression against a plucky socialist underdog, as much of the international left is inclined to do, is to miss the picture entirely. Maduro's regime is not a government in any meaningful democratic sense. It stole the 2024 presidential election from opposition candidate Edmundo González in broad daylight, ignoring results that independent observers and the country's own electoral data overwhelmingly suggested he had won. The regime has imprisoned, tortured, and disappeared political opponents on an industrial scale. That the international community, including the European Union, largely recognised González as the legitimate winner has done nothing to shift the reality on the ground.

The Trump administration's escalation has taken several forms. There are the expanded sanctions, which target not merely the regime's inner circle but Venezuela's oil exports more broadly, including threats of secondary sanctions against countries — notably China and India — that continue purchasing Venezuelan crude. There are the military deployments to the Caribbean, which the Pentagon describes as counter-narcotics operations but which carry an unmistakable signal. And there is the diplomatic offensive, with Washington pressing Latin American allies to further isolate Caracas.

Maduro, for his part, has responded with characteristic bombast, warning of an imperialist invasion and rallying nationalist sentiment in a country where anti-American feeling, carefully cultivated since the Chávez era, runs deep. He has also leaned harder into his relationships with America's adversaries. Russian military advisors remain in the country. Chinese investment continues. Iranian oil tankers have made the crossing. For a regime that defines itself primarily through opposition to Washington, the threat of American military action is, perversely, something close to a gift.

The question that ought to concern observers — and that the mainstream American media has been curiously reluctant to interrogate — is what precisely Washington's endgame looks like. Regime change is the obvious answer, but the track record of American-backed regime change, from Iraq to Libya, offers little cause for optimism.
headline: Why are America and Venezuela on the cusp of war?

There are elections, and then there are elections. What unfolded in Kildare South over the weekend was something closer to political theatre at its most gripping, a count centre drama that had veterans of the tally rooms shaking their heads and reaching for superlatives. Tom McDonnell, the Fine Gael candidate who had been written off by more than a few commentators in the early hours, somehow found a way through the wreckage of transfers and eliminations to take a seat that, by any rational analysis, he had no business winning.

And yet he did. Which tells you something about the man, something about the constituency, and quite a lot about the state of Irish politics in 2024.

McDonnell's victory was the kind of against-the-odds triumph that restores your faith in the sheer unpredictability of our PR-STV system. The proportional representation mechanism, for all its maddening complexity, occasionally throws up results that remind you why the founders of the State chose it in the first place. It rewards persistence. It rewards the candidate who has knocked on every door, attended every funeral, turned up to every community meeting in every townland from Monasterevin to Castledermot. It punishes complacency. And in Kildare South, complacency was very much on the ballot.

The so-called Battle of Newbridge — and it earned that title honestly — came down to transfers in a way that would make a mathematics professor weep with joy and a political scientist reach for the whiskey. McDonnell trailed at several stages of the count. There were moments when his team in the count centre wore the haunted expressions of people who could see the writing on the wall and didn't much care for the font. But transfers, those strange and wonderful things that turn Irish elections into elaborate puzzles, broke his way at precisely the moments they needed to.

What does this tell us? For one thing, it tells us that the ground game still matters. In an era when we are constantly told that social media has transformed politics beyond recognition, that TikTok campaigns and viral moments are what swing elections, McDonnell's victory was built on something far more old-fashioned. He ran a constituency operation of formidable discipline. His people knew their boxes. They knew where the votes were and, crucially, where the transfers would come from. This is the unsexy, grinding work of Irish electoral politics, and McDonnell and his organisation were better at it than anyone else in the field.

It also tells us something about the resilience of Fine Gael in parts of the country where the party's brand has come under sustained pressure. Kildare South is not the leafy south Dublin heartland where Fine Gael support can be taken as a given. It is a constituency in transition, with a growing commuter population that does not necessarily feel any tribal loyalty to the old Civil War parties. Sinn Féin had targeted the seat. Labour had ambitions. The Social Democrats fancied their chances. And yet it was the Fine Gael man who emerged blinking into the light with the seat secured.
headline: Tom McDonnell emerges with Tricolour flying in the nail-biting Battle of Newbridge

The European Union, never one to let a good crisis go to waste, is quietly repurposing the infrastructure it built during the pandemic for an altogether different purpose. The EU Digital Identity Wallet, a direct descendant of the Covid Digital Certificate that governed the lives of hundreds of millions of Europeans between 2021 and 2023, is being positioned as a key tool in the bloc's expanding online censorship apparatus. And if you think that sounds like conspiratorial thinking, you simply haven't been reading the Commission's own documents.

Let us recall, because memory is short and institutional memory shorter still, what we were told about the Covid pass. It was temporary. It was proportionate. It was necessary. It would sunset when the emergency ended. And yet here we are, watching its technological skeleton being fitted with new flesh, new muscle, and new purpose. The architecture of digital control, once erected, does not simply disappear. It finds new reasons to exist.

The EU Digital Identity Wallet, which member states are expected to make available to all citizens by 2026, will function as a kind of universal digital credential. It will allow — or, more precisely, require — users to verify their identity when accessing online platforms. The regulation, known as eIDAS 2.0, was revised and adopted with remarkably little public debate given the scale of what it proposes. Under its provisions, very large online platforms will be obligated to accept these wallets for user authentication.

Now, on the surface, one might argue this is simply about convenience, about streamlining access to public services, about fighting fraud. That is certainly how the Commission has framed it. But consider the context in which this tool is being deployed. The Digital Services Act, which came into full force last year, already compels platforms to remove so-called "illegal content" and to take action against what Brussels vaguely terms "disinformation." The DSA created the obligation. The Digital Identity Wallet creates the mechanism by which that obligation can be enforced against individual users, not just platforms.

Think about what this means in practice. Once your online activity is tied to a verified, government-issued digital identity, anonymity — long understood as a cornerstone of free expression, particularly for dissidents, whistleblowers, and those who simply wish to speak uncomfortable truths — effectively ceases to exist. Every comment, every post, every share becomes attributable. And in a regulatory environment where the definition of "disinformation" is whatever the Commission and its network of "trusted flaggers" say it is, that attributability becomes a tool of discipline.

This is not speculation. The European Commission has already demonstrated, repeatedly, its willingness to lean on platforms to suppress speech it finds inconvenient. During the pandemic, content that questioned lockdown efficacy, vaccine side effects, or the origins of the virus was systematically suppressed — much of it later vindicated by mainstream scientific consensus. The Twitter Files and subsequent revelations showed direct coordination between government actors and social media companies to silence dissenting voices. Commissioner Thierry Breton, before his departure, openly threatened Elon Musk with regulatory consequences if X did not moderate content to the Commission's satisfaction.
headline: EU to Use COVID Pass Sequel for Online Censorship

John Aidan Byrne, the veteran Irish-born journalist and financial commentator based in New York, joins us this week on Odeon Capital Conversations to discuss one of the most consequential yet under-examined forces shaping the global economy: demographic change.

It is a topic that rarely makes the front pages, yet the numbers tell a story that policymakers ignore at their peril. Across the developed world, birth rates are plummeting, populations are ageing rapidly, and the implications for everything from labour markets to pension systems to sovereign debt are becoming impossible to wave away.

Byrne, who has spent decades covering Wall Street and the broader American economy for outlets including the New York Post, brings a sharp transatlantic perspective to the conversation. He notes that the United States, long insulated from the worst of the demographic crunch by relatively higher birth rates and sustained immigration, is now beginning to feel the pinch. But it is in Europe and East Asia where the picture is most stark.

Ireland, of course, is not immune. Despite being one of the younger countries in the European Union for much of the past generation, the State's demographics are shifting. The total fertility rate has fallen well below replacement level, and while immigration has masked some of the economic consequences, it has introduced its own set of political and social pressures that are now firmly part of the national conversation.

What Byrne argues compellingly in this episode is that demographic decline is not simply a social curiosity — it is an economic earthquake in slow motion. Fewer workers mean lower productivity growth, reduced tax revenues, and mounting pressure on public services, particularly healthcare and pensions. The dependency ratio — the number of retirees relative to working-age adults — is moving in a direction that should alarm every finance minister in the Western world.

There is also the question of what demographic change means for asset prices, for housing markets, and for the long-term trajectory of interest rates. These are the bread-and-butter concerns of investors, but they are also deeply relevant to ordinary people trying to plan for retirement or wondering whether the State pension will still be there when they need it.

Byrne is characteristically forthright in his analysis, and he does not shy away from pointing out that many of the policy responses currently on offer — whether from Washington, Brussels, or indeed Dublin — amount to little more than sticking plasters on a structural wound.

You can listen to the full conversation above, or subscribe to Odeon Capital Conversations wherever you get your podcasts.
headline: PODCAST: John Aidan Byrne on Odeon Capital Conversations on the effect of the demographic change on the economy

The people of Kildare are about to learn a lesson that communities the length and breadth of this country have already been taught: your objections do not matter, your concerns are illegitimate, and the democratic process you were raised to believe in is a polite fiction when it collides with government immigration policy.

Plans for an asylum centre accommodating up to 950 people are set to proceed in the county despite fierce and sustained local opposition. Residents have held meetings, organised petitions, written to their public representatives, and done everything that citizens in a functioning democracy are supposed to do when they object to a decision that will fundamentally alter their community. For their trouble, they have been ignored, patronised, and — inevitably — smeared as something less than decent people.

This is now the established pattern, and it is worth spelling out plainly because the political establishment and its allies in legacy media seem determined to pretend it is not happening. A site is identified. Locals are given little or no prior consultation. When they object, they are told the decision is effectively already made. When they persist, the suggestion — sometimes whispered, sometimes shouted — is that their opposition is rooted in bigotry rather than legitimate planning, infrastructure, and community concerns.

It is a neat trick, and it has worked remarkably well for the Government. By framing every objection as a moral failing on the part of the objector, they relieve themselves of the obligation to actually engage with the substance of what is being said. Nobody in Kildare needs to be told that their local schools are already at capacity. Nobody needs a briefing document to understand that GP waiting lists in the area are stretched to breaking point. Nobody requires an expert to explain that dropping the population equivalent of a large village into an area without corresponding infrastructure is a recipe for dysfunction.

But these are precisely the arguments that officialdom refuses to hear. Instead, we get the ritual invocation of "our international obligations," as though those obligations include a requirement to treat the concerns of Irish citizens as an inconvenience to be managed rather than a democratic expression to be respected.

Consider for a moment what message this sends. The Government is telling the people of Kildare — and every other community in the same position — that their role in this process is to accept what they are given and be grateful they were informed at all. The TDs who represent them will, for the most part, make sympathetic noises in private while voting the party line in the Dáil. The county council will express "concerns" that will be duly noted and duly ignored. Integration Minister Roderic O'Gorman's department will issue a statement about the need for compassion, as though compassion is a quality that only flows in one direction.

This is not how a democracy is supposed to function. In a democracy, the people affected by a decision have a meaningful say in that decision. They do not simply get to hold a meeting that nobody in power attends or takes seriously. They do not get fobbed off with vague promises about "consultation processes" that are, in reality, information sessions where the conclusion has already been reached.

What is particularly galling is the sheer scale of what is proposed. An asylum centre for 950 people is not a modest intervention.
headline: Democracy? Kildare asylum centre for 950 will be bulldozed through despite local protests

There is a peculiar irony in the fact that we have never had more access to mental health services, more awareness campaigns, more therapeutic language woven into everyday conversation, and yet by every available metric, people seem to be getting worse. The question that polite society would prefer we not ask is whether the two phenomena might, in some way, be connected.

It is now virtually impossible to spend a day on social media without encountering someone self-diagnosing with ADHD, autism, complex PTSD, or some combination thereof. TikTok has become a diagnostic manual for a generation, with short videos confidently informing young people that their perfectly ordinary struggles with concentration, social awkwardness, or emotional turbulence are in fact evidence of a clinical condition. The algorithm, ever obliging, serves up more of the same until the viewer is fully convinced. The next step, increasingly, is a trip to the GP armed with a printout and a demand for a referral.

This is not to say that genuine mental illness does not exist, or that proper diagnosis is not life-changing for those who truly need it. Of course it is. But there is a world of difference between acknowledging that some people are genuinely unwell and accepting the current cultural premise that practically everyone is, in some fashion, broken and in need of professional intervention.

The numbers tell a striking story. In Ireland, prescriptions for ADHD medication have surged dramatically in recent years. Waiting lists for Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services are staggeringly long, not solely because of underfunding — though that is real enough — but because demand has exploded in a way that would have been unimaginable twenty years ago. Are we simply better at identifying conditions that were always there? Or has something else happened?

The honest answer is likely both, but the cultural establishment is only willing to entertain the first explanation. The suggestion that we might be over-diagnosing, over-medicalising, and over-pathologising the ordinary difficulties of human existence is treated as something close to heresy. To raise the question is to be accused of stigmatising mental illness, of telling people to simply pull themselves together, of being on the wrong side of progress. This rhetorical trap is remarkably effective at shutting down a conversation that desperately needs to be had.

The American social psychologist Jonathan Haidt has documented extensively how the rise of what he calls "safetyism" — the conviction that young people are fragile and must be protected from discomfort at all costs — has coincided with a genuine collapse in adolescent mental health, particularly among girls. His thesis, shared by the British journalist and author Abigail Shrier, is that therapeutic frameworks, when applied indiscriminately, do not merely describe suffering but actively create it. Tell a teenager that their normal anxiety about fitting in is actually a disorder, and you have not helped them — you have given them an identity built around dysfunction.

Ireland has imported this culture wholesale, as it imports most Anglophone cultural trends, with minimal critical examination. Our schools now have wellbeing programmes baked into the curriculum. The language of therapy — boundaries, triggers, trauma, toxic — has become the lingua franca of Irish public life.
headline: Therapy Culture: Do we live in an age of over-diagnosis?
