The Government has announced a new €8 million scheme aimed at attracting leading international academics to Irish universities, in a move that has drawn scrutiny over whether the funding represents value for money at a time of significant pressure on public services.

The programme, which will be administered by the Irish Research Council, is designed to lure senior researchers and scholars from institutions abroad to take up positions in Irish higher education. Officials say the initiative will bolster Ireland's reputation as a hub for research and innovation, though critics have questioned whether the money might be better directed towards retaining Irish academics who have already left the country or supporting those struggling with the cost of living at home.

Details of the scheme suggest that substantial financial packages will be offered to entice high-profile figures in various academic disciplines, with funding covering salaries, research support, and relocation costs. The programme is expected to benefit a relatively small number of individuals, raising questions about the per-head cost of the initiative at a time when Irish universities are already facing criticism over administrative bloat and the casualisation of existing academic staff.

It comes as many early-career Irish researchers continue to report difficulty securing permanent positions in the country's universities, with a significant number forced to emigrate or leave academia altogether. Postgraduate researchers have long complained of inadequate stipends, with many living below the poverty line while contributing substantially to their institutions' research output.

The Higher Education Authority has previously acknowledged the challenges facing the sector, but Government policy has consistently emphasised the importance of attracting international talent as part of broader economic strategy.

There is no indication that the scheme includes any specific provision for encouraging Irish-born academics working overseas to return, despite repeated calls from within the sector for a dedicated programme to reverse the brain drain that has seen some of the country's most promising researchers take up permanent positions in the UK, the United States, and continental Europe.

The announcement is likely to fuel an ongoing debate about priorities in Irish higher education funding, with student accommodation shortages, rising fees for postgraduate students, and questions about the governance of universities all remaining live issues. Whether spending €8 million to bring a select number of international academics to Ireland represents a sound investment or a misplaced priority will depend very much on whom you ask.
headline: €8 million to be spent bringing academics to Ireland

The Ceann Comhairle has issued a stark warning to party leaders and whips that the current impasse over speaking rights in the Dáil cannot be allowed to continue, telling them that the failure to agree new arrangements is undermining the basic functioning of the House.

Verona Murphy used the opening of Thursday's sitting to express her frustration at the lack of progress in negotiations over how Dáil time should be allocated in the 34th Dáil, which has seen an unprecedented number of TDs elected outside the traditional party structures. The stand-off has left the chamber operating on a week-by-week basis, with no settled standing orders and repeated disputes over who gets to speak and for how long.

The intervention is significant because the Ceann Comhairle has traditionally been reluctant to insert herself directly into what are essentially political negotiations between the parties and groupings in the House. Murphy's decision to go public with her concerns suggests that behind-the-scenes efforts to broker an agreement have effectively stalled.

At the heart of the dispute is the question of how to accommodate the large number of Independent TDs and smaller groupings who now make up a substantial bloc in the Dáil. Under the previous arrangements, speaking time was allocated primarily on the basis of party strength, a system which critics argued left many TDs effectively frozen out of meaningful participation in debates.

The Government side is understood to be cautious about any reforms that would significantly eat into its own speaking time or slow down the passage of legislation, while the Opposition groupings have struggled to reach a consensus among themselves about what a fair allocation would look like.

Sources familiar with the negotiations say the Technical Group arrangement, which has historically allowed Independents to pool their speaking rights, has become increasingly unwieldy given the numbers involved. Several smaller parties are also unhappy with proposals that would, in their view, give disproportionate weight to loose alliances of Independents over ideologically coherent parties that ran on a national platform.

The paralysis has had practical consequences. Several TDs have complained publicly about being unable to raise constituency matters or contribute to legislation, with some describing the situation as an affront to their mandate from voters. There have been repeated points of order and procedural objections that have consumed time that could otherwise have been used for substantive debate.

Murphy told the House that she had written to all party leaders and the leaders of recognised groupings requesting that they engage constructively with her office to find a resolution. She made clear that if agreement could not be reached voluntarily, she would consider using the powers available to her under standing orders to impose interim arrangements.

That threat is unlikely to go down well in all quarters. Some Government TDs are privately resistant to any solution that would be seen to reward what they characterise as the refusal of certain Independent deputies to organise themselves into stable, accountable groupings. On the other side, several Independents have accused the larger parties of deliberately dragging their feet in order to maintain the status quo which suits them.

The situation highlights a broader tension in Irish politics following an election that delivered a Dáil unlike any in the history of the State.
headline: Dáil paralysis: Ceann Comhairle demands progress on speaking rights

There's nothing quite like a local authority tying itself in knots to avoid saying the word "Christmas" to get the public's collective blood boiling, and Dublin City Council has managed to do just that with its rebranding of the capital's festive celebrations as "Winter Lights."

The move, which has seen the council promote its programme of seasonal events under the determinedly secular banner, has drawn a furious response from ordinary Dubliners and commentators alike, with many accusing DCC of engaging in precisely the kind of cultural cringe that makes people despair of those in charge of public life in Ireland.

The backlash has been swift and unsparing. Social media lit up with criticism from people who saw the rebrand as yet another attempt to strip the Christian identity from a holiday that remains deeply important to the vast majority of Irish people. Polling consistently shows that Ireland, while rapidly secularising in many respects, still overwhelmingly identifies Christmas as a meaningful cultural and religious occasion — not merely an exercise in switching on decorative lighting.

"It's Christmas. Just say Christmas," was the common refrain across platforms, with variations ranging from the weary to the incandescent.

Critics pointed out the peculiar irony of a council that presides over a city dotted with churches — including two Church of Ireland and one Catholic cathedral — finding itself unable to utter the name of the feast day that has shaped Dublin's cultural calendar for over a millennium. Christ Church Cathedral, after all, is not called "Winter Stonework."

Several public figures weighed in. There is a growing sense, articulated repeatedly in recent years, that Irish institutions are adopting an approach to cultural sensitivity that nobody actually asked for and that manages to be simultaneously patronising to minorities — who, for the most part, are not remotely offended by the word "Christmas" — and dismissive of the majority population.

It is worth noting that Dublin's Muslim and Jewish communities, among others, have never been known to campaign for the removal of the word Christmas from public life. The assumption that they might find it offensive says rather more about the assumptions of those in officialdom than it does about the reality of multicultural life in the capital.

Dublin City Council is, of course, no stranger to controversy. From the handling of housing to the state of the city centre, the council has faced sustained criticism on multiple fronts. But there is something about this particular row that touches a nerve beyond the usual grumbles about bins and bike lanes. It speaks to a deeper anxiety about who gets to define Irish public culture and on what terms.

The question that DCC has apparently failed to ask itself is a simple one: who, precisely, is this for? If it is intended to be more inclusive, it has achieved the opposite, alienating huge numbers of people who see it as an act of needless erasure. If it is intended to modernise the council's image, it has succeeded only in making it look ridiculous.

There is a wider pattern here, and it extends well beyond Dublin City Council. Across the public sector, there is an observable tendency to pre-emptively capitulate to a version of progressive etiquette that exists primarily in the minds of communications consultants and HR departments.
headline: It’s Christmas! Huge backlash to DCC ‘Winter Lights’

The European Commission has unveiled what it is calling a "Democracy Shield," a sweeping new package of measures it says is designed to protect the bloc's democratic institutions from foreign interference and disinformation.

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the initiative in Brussels, framing it as a necessary response to what she described as an escalating threat landscape driven by hostile state actors, particularly Russia, seeking to destabilise European democracies through information manipulation and covert influence campaigns.

The package includes proposals for a new intelligence hub to monitor foreign information manipulation, enhanced powers for EU institutions to identify and counter disinformation campaigns, and a framework for coordinating responses across member states. It also envisages expanded cooperation between tech platforms and EU authorities on content moderation.

Critics, however, have already raised concerns that the initiative amounts to a centralisation of power over public discourse under the guise of protecting democracy — a tension that has become increasingly familiar in Brussels policymaking.

Free speech advocates have pointed to the EU's existing Digital Services Act, which has already drawn accusations of enabling censorship, as evidence that the Commission's approach to "disinformation" tends to involve pressuring platforms to suppress speech that challenges official narratives rather than genuinely protecting citizens from foreign interference.

The framing of the announcement will do little to reassure sceptics. The language of "shielding" democracy carries an inherent implication that ordinary citizens require protection from information that Brussels deems harmful — a proposition that sits uneasily with the classical liberal understanding of democracy as a system in which free citizens are trusted to weigh competing claims for themselves.

MEPs from several groupings have questioned who, precisely, will define what constitutes "foreign information manipulation" as distinct from legitimate dissent or criticism of EU policy. The distinction is far from academic. Throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, positions initially dismissed by authorities as misinformation — including the lab leak hypothesis and questions about vaccine efficacy against transmission — were subsequently acknowledged as legitimate lines of inquiry.

The Commission insists the measures are targeted exclusively at coordinated foreign interference operations and will include robust safeguards for press freedom and legitimate political debate. A senior Commission official, speaking on background, said the package was "not about policing opinions" but about "protecting the information ecosystem from state-sponsored manipulation."

However, the track record of EU institutions in this space has not inspired universal confidence. The now-defunct EU Disinformation Lab was embroiled in controversy, and the European Digital Media Observatory has faced questions about the ideological composition of its network of fact-checkers.

In Ireland, the announcement is likely to reignite debate around the State's own approach to speech regulation, including the contentious Criminal Justice (Incitement to Violence or Hatred and Hate Offences) Act, which passed through the Oireachtas amid significant public opposition. The Government has broadly aligned itself with Brussels on these matters, with successive ministers expressing support for EU-level coordination on tackling disinformation.

Some Irish MEPs have expressed cautious support for the package, while others have warned it could represent another step toward what they see as an increasingly paternalistic approach by EU institutions toward their own citizens.
headline: European Commission announces ‘Democracy Shield’

Carol Nolan TD has called on the Government to urgently reassess the means test income threshold for Carer's Allowance, warning that the current system is forcing families into financial hardship while they provide essential care to loved ones at home.

The Independent TD for Laois-Offaly said that the failure to meaningfully reform the means test was penalising people who are already saving the State billions of euro each year by keeping vulnerable family members out of institutional care settings.

"The means test for Carer's Allowance is simply not fit for purpose," Deputy Nolan said. "We have a situation where people who are giving up their careers, their social lives, and in many cases their own health to care for a parent, a child, or a spouse are being told they earn too little to survive but too much to qualify for support. It is an absolute disgrace."

Deputy Nolan pointed to figures which suggest that family carers save the State an estimated €20 billion annually, yet many find themselves excluded from accessing the weekly payment due to income thresholds that have not kept pace with the rising cost of living.

"The income disregard thresholds were last adjusted in Budget 2008. That is seventeen years ago. The cost of everything — groceries, energy, mortgage repayments — has skyrocketed since then, but the thresholds have remained frozen in time. How can anyone in Government defend that?" she said.

Under the current rules, a single person caring full-time for a loved one can earn no more than €350 per week after certain deductions before their Carer's Allowance begins to be reduced. For a couple, the threshold is €750 per week combined.

Deputy Nolan argued that these figures are wholly inadequate in the context of modern living costs, particularly for families with mortgages or who are renting in the private market.

"I am dealing with constituents in Laois and Offaly who are at breaking point. They are providing round-the-clock care, they are exhausted, and they cannot even get the basic financial recognition from the State that they deserve. Many of them tell me they feel completely invisible," she said.

The Laois-Offaly TD also criticised what she described as the overly intrusive and bureaucratic nature of the means testing process itself, saying that carers are being subjected to lengthy delays and excessive paperwork at a time when they are already under enormous personal strain.

"People are being asked to provide reams of documentation, bank statements going back months, details of every asset they own. The process is demeaning and it is putting people off applying altogether. That is not how we should be treating the people who are doing some of the most important work in this country," Deputy Nolan added.

She called on the Minister for Social Protection to bring forward proposals in the next Budget to significantly raise the income disregard thresholds and to simplify the application process for Carer's Allowance.

"We need to stop paying lip service to family carers and start actually supporting them. The Government needs to act on this as a matter of urgency.
headline: “Urgent need to reassess means test income threshold for carers.” Carol Nolan

The man suspected of projecting the words "Blood on Their Hands" onto the façade of Leinster House during a pro-Palestinian demonstration late last year is understood to be a Libyan-born individual who was last known to be residing in Dublin, Gript has learned.

The dramatic stunt, which saw the inflammatory message beamed onto the front of the national parliament building during a sitting week, drew significant attention on social media and was widely shared by pro-Palestinian activist accounts. The projection was understood to be a reference to Ireland's diplomatic and trade relationships with Israel, and was intended as a direct message to members of the Oireachtas.

Gardaí launched an investigation into the incident, which raised serious questions about security at the Leinster House complex. Sources familiar with the matter have indicated that the individual believed to be responsible is a Libyan-born man who had been living in the capital. It is understood that efforts to locate the suspect have so far proven unsuccessful, with the man last seen in the Dublin area.

The incident was one of a number of escalating protest actions targeting Irish political institutions over the government's response to the conflict in Gaza. While Ireland has taken a comparatively strong stance among EU member states — including joining South Africa's genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice — activists have argued that the government has not gone far enough, particularly in relation to trade with Israel.

Security at Leinster House has been a persistent concern in recent years, with a number of incidents prompting reviews of protective measures around the Kildare Street complex. The projection incident underscored the relative ease with which individuals could carry out such actions in close proximity to the seat of government.

It is not yet clear whether the suspect remains in the State. Gardaí declined to comment on the specifics of the investigation when contacted by Gript, stating only that enquiries were ongoing.

The case has also raised broader questions about the policing of protest actions that, while not violent, are designed to cause maximum political embarrassment and may involve trespass or criminal damage considerations. Legal experts have noted that the projection of messages onto buildings without permission could potentially fall under public order legislation, though prosecutions in such cases remain rare.

Sources within government circles expressed frustration at the slow pace of the investigation, with one figure telling Gript that the incident had been "deeply embarrassing" and that there were concerns about copycat actions if no consequences followed.

The suspect's background and immigration status in Ireland remain unclear. Gript understands that the man had been known to pro-Palestinian activist circles in Dublin but was not a prominent public figure within the movement.

Anyone with information is asked to contact their local Garda station.
headline: Libyan-born ‘Blood on Their Hands’ suspect last seen in Dublin

text:
It started, as these things often do, with the best of intentions. I wanted to make the world a better place. I believed in compassion, in fairness, in standing up for the underdog. I marched, I donated, I shared the right posts, I read the right books. I was, by any reasonable measure, a good progressive. And for a long time, that felt like enough.

But somewhere along the way, the ground shifted beneath my feet. Or perhaps I simply stopped moving with it. Either way, I found myself standing in a place I no longer recognised, surrounded by people who had once been my allies but who now regarded me with something between suspicion and contempt. My crime? Asking questions. Wanting to talk about things. Believing, naively it turned out, that the principles I had signed up to — free expression, open debate, the dignity of the individual — were still the principles that mattered.

The first real rupture came during the housing protests. I had been involved for years in advocacy work, volunteering with organisations that helped families facing eviction and homelessness. I had seen the crisis at the coalface, had sat in District Court hearings with people who were terrified, had helped fill out HAP forms and ring the local authority for the hundredth time. I cared about this stuff in a way that was not theoretical. And yet, when I gently suggested at a meeting that perhaps demonising every landlord in the country was not strategically wise — that some of them were ordinary people with a single property and a tracker mortgage who were also struggling — I was met with a silence that could curdle milk.

Afterwards, a younger activist took me aside and explained, with the patience one reserves for a slow child, that I was "centering the wrong voices." I did not know what that meant then. I have since learned that it means disagreeing.

That was the beginning, but it was far from the end. Over the following years, I watched as the progressive movement I had loved became something unrecognisable. It was no longer enough to believe in equality; you had to subscribe to an ever-expanding catechism of positions that seemed to shift with the wind. You had to use the right language, affirm the right slogans, and above all, never — under any circumstances — express doubt.

I expressed doubt.

When the gender recognition debate intensified in Ireland, I made the mistake of saying, publicly, that I thought women's concerns about single-sex spaces deserved to be heard. Not prioritised. Not weaponised. Heard. I said this because I believed in listening to people, because I had spent my entire adult life arguing that marginalised voices mattered. But it turned out that some marginalised voices mattered more than others, and the hierarchy was not one you were permitted to question.

Within days, I was dropped from a panel discussion I had been invited to months earlier. A colleague I had worked with for years sent me a message saying she was "disappointed" in me. An organisation I had volunteered with for the best part of a decade quietly removed me from their mailing list. No conversation. No debate. Just erasure.
headline: No Good Deed Goes Unpunished

text:
President Michael D. Higgins is to attend the coronation of King Charles III at Westminster Abbey, it has been confirmed, in what will mark a significant moment in the ongoing relationship between Ireland and the United Kingdom.

The President's attendance at the ceremony, expected to take place in London, will be closely watched on both sides of the Irish Sea, not least given the historic sensitivities that have long characterised relations between the two countries. It is understood that the invitation was extended by Buckingham Palace and accepted following consultations between Áras an Uachtaráin and the Department of Foreign Affairs.

The decision is likely to prompt debate in Ireland, where questions surrounding the appropriate level of engagement with the British monarchy remain a live issue for many. While the State has moved to normalise relations with the UK in recent decades — most notably through Queen Elizabeth II's landmark visit to Ireland in 2011 and President Higgins's reciprocal state visit to London in 2014 — there are those who will view attendance at a coronation as a step that carries a different symbolic weight.

President Higgins has long positioned himself as a champion of human rights and post-colonial discourse, and has not shied away from critiquing aspects of British policy, particularly in relation to the legacy of empire. His decision to attend the coronation will therefore strike some observers as noteworthy, though others will frame it as a pragmatic continuation of the diplomatic thaw that has defined Anglo-Irish relations in the post-Good Friday Agreement era.

The coronation itself is expected to be a grand affair steeped in the traditions of the British monarchy, with heads of state from across the world in attendance. It will be the first such ceremony since Queen Elizabeth II was crowned in 1953, and it comes at a time when the monarchy faces its own questions about relevance and public support, both domestically and across the Commonwealth.

Government figures are understood to be broadly supportive of the President's attendance, viewing it as consistent with Ireland's mature and forward-looking approach to bilateral relations. A spokesperson for Áras an Uachtaráin confirmed that the President had accepted the invitation but declined to comment further on the arrangements.

However, the move is not without its critics. Some republican voices have already questioned whether the President of Ireland ought to be lending the prestige of his office to a ceremony that celebrates hereditary monarchy and which, in their view, remains bound up with a history of colonialism that directly affected Ireland.

Sinn Féin, for its part, has generally supported diplomatic engagement with the UK, though individual members have in the past expressed reservations about events with overtly monarchical overtones. The party had not commented on the matter at the time of publication.

The coronation will also take place against the backdrop of continuing difficulties over the Northern Ireland Protocol and the functioning of the power-sharing institutions at Stormont, issues that have at times strained relations between Dublin and London in recent years. Whether the President's presence at the ceremony helps to smooth over any of those tensions remains to be seen.

Whatever the political implications, the visit will add another chapter to a relationship that, for all its complexity, has undergone a remarkable transformation in the space of a generation.
headline: Michael D. Higgins to attend coronation of UK’s King Charles

text:
The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission has once again demonstrated precisely why enshrining a so-called "right to housing" in the Constitution would be a catastrophic mistake. Its latest intervention – backing a legal challenge on behalf of international protection applicants over accommodation standards – is a masterclass in how rights-based language gets weaponised by unelected bodies to override democratic decision-making and heap ever-greater obligations on an already buckling state.

Let's be clear about what is happening here. IHREC, a state-funded body, is using its considerable legal resources to argue that the State has enforceable obligations regarding the standard of accommodation it provides to asylum seekers. Whatever one thinks about the conditions in Direct Provision centres – and there are legitimate criticisms to be made – the implications of this kind of legal activism should alarm anyone who believes that elected representatives, not judges and quangos, should set national policy.

Now imagine this dynamic on steroids. That is precisely what a constitutional right to housing would deliver.

The campaign to insert a right to housing into Bunreacht na hÉireann has been gathering steam for years, pushed by a familiar coalition of NGOs, academics, and left-wing politicians who seem to believe that the solution to every social problem is to hand more power to the courts. The argument is superficially attractive: everyone deserves a home, so why not guarantee it? But the IHREC case lays bare the fundamental dishonesty at the heart of this project.

A constitutional right to housing would not build a single house. Not one. What it would do is create a litigation bonanza, empowering bodies like IHREC to drag the State through the courts on an essentially endless basis, arguing that this or that group's rights have been violated because their accommodation is not up to some judicially determined standard. The beneficiaries would not be families on housing waiting lists in Cork or Limerick. The beneficiaries would be lawyers.

Consider the practical reality. Ireland is in the grip of a housing crisis that successive governments have failed to resolve. There are approximately 14,000 people in emergency accommodation. Local authorities across the country have waiting lists stretching back years. The State cannot meet existing demand. Into this context, campaigners want to insert a justiciable right that would allow any individual – citizen or otherwise – to take a case arguing that the State has failed in its constitutional duty to provide them with adequate housing.

And this is where the IHREC case becomes so instructive. Because once you establish a right, you do not get to control who invokes it, or in what circumstances. The Commission is not arguing that Irish citizens sleeping rough should be prioritised. It is arguing on behalf of international protection applicants – people who have arrived in the State and are, in many cases, still having their claims assessed. If a right to housing existed in the Constitution, there would be nothing whatsoever to prevent similar cases being taken on behalf of anyone who sets foot on Irish soil.

This is not speculation. This is precisely how rights-based frameworks operate in practice. They are universal in their application, and they are interpreted and expanded by courts over time, invariably in directions that the politicians who enacted them never intended and the public never endorsed.
headline: IHREC refugee case shows why “Right To Housing” would end badly
