The HSE is set to spend €50 million this year on the development of a dedicated health care model for refugees and migrants, a figure that has drawn sharp criticism from those who argue the money would be better directed towards addressing chronic deficiencies in the public health system.

The allocation, confirmed in documentation reviewed by Gript, forms part of a broader suite of spending commitments aimed at providing tailored health services to the growing number of people entering the State through international protection and other migration pathways. The programme is understood to encompass primary care, mental health supports, and screening services specifically designed for new arrivals.

It comes at a time when record numbers of people are presenting to emergency departments across the country, with patients routinely spending days on trolleys, and when waiting lists for basic procedures continue to run into the hundreds of thousands. Critics have questioned the priorities of a health service that struggles to deliver for Irish citizens while simultaneously constructing an entirely new parallel infrastructure for non-nationals.

The HSE has maintained that providing early health interventions for refugees and migrants is both a humanitarian obligation and a sound public health strategy, arguing that unmet health needs among new arrivals can place greater strain on the system further down the line. Officials have pointed to the particular vulnerabilities of those fleeing conflict zones and the prevalence of communicable diseases that require early detection and treatment.

However, the scale of the expenditure is likely to fuel ongoing public frustration. Ordinary citizens who have spent years on waiting lists, or who cannot access a GP in their area due to chronic shortages, may struggle to understand why a bespoke health care model for those newly arrived in the country commands such significant resources.

The Government has faced sustained pressure on immigration-related spending across multiple departments, with the cost of providing accommodation alone running to billions of euro annually. Housing, education, and now health care costs associated with migration have become among the most politically sensitive issues in the State, with protests erupting in communities across the country over the past year.

No detailed breakdown of how the €50 million will be spent has been made publicly available, and there are questions about transparency and accountability in relation to the programme. It remains unclear how the HSE intends to measure the outcomes of this investment or whether any evaluation framework has been established.

Opposition TDs have called for a full accounting of the expenditure to be brought before the Dáil, with some arguing that the Oireachtas health committee should conduct a dedicated examination of how the funds are being allocated and whether they are delivering value for money.

The Department of Health did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.
headline: €50 million will be spent in 2024 to develop model of HSE refugee and migrant health care

text:
The numbers, when you sit with them long enough, begin to feel less like statistics and more like a civilisational epitaph. South Korea's total fertility rate has fallen below 0.7 children per woman. Italy and Japan are closing maternity wards faster than they can open geriatric ones. And here in Ireland, where the pram in the hallway was once as inevitable as the rain, the birth rate has quietly slipped to levels that would have been unimaginable to our grandparents.

It is fashionable in certain circles to greet this news with a shrug, or even a kind of grim satisfaction. Fewer people, we are told, means fewer carbon footprints, less pressure on housing, a lighter burden on the planet. The overpopulation anxieties of the 1970s never quite went away; they merely acquired a green veneer and a new vocabulary. But the people making these arguments tend not to dwell on what a society actually looks like when it stops replacing itself. The reality is not some serene, spacious utopia. It is decay.

Consider what is already happening. In rural Japan, entire villages have been abandoned, their schools shuttered, their shops boarded up. The Japanese government has resorted to offering substantial cash incentives to young couples willing to have children, with almost no measurable effect. In China, the sudden reversal of the one-child policy has met with a collective yawn from a generation that has grown accustomed to the freedoms and comforts of small family life. You can turn a tap off quickly, it turns out, but turning it back on is another matter entirely.

Ireland's situation is less dramatic but no less significant. Our total fertility rate now sits at around 1.5, well below the replacement level of 2.1. The Central Statistics Office figures show a pattern that has been trending downward for years, and there is precious little reason to believe it will reverse. We have, in the space of a generation, moved from being one of the most fertile countries in Europe to being squarely in the middle of the continent's demographic decline.

The consequences of this are not abstract. They are fiercely practical. The entire architecture of the modern welfare state — pensions, healthcare, social insurance — was designed on the assumption that there would always be a sufficiently large working-age population to fund the needs of those who had retired. When that assumption collapses, as it is now collapsing across the developed world, the maths becomes brutal. Fewer workers supporting more retirees means either significantly higher taxes, significantly reduced services, or both. The HSE, already buckling under existing demand, will face pressures in the coming decades that make the current crisis look manageable by comparison.

The standard progressive response to this problem is immigration. And immigration can, in the short to medium term, paper over some of the gaps. But it is worth noting that this is essentially a policy of importing other nations' children because you have decided not to have your own. It is also, in demographic terms, a temporary fix. Immigrants' birth rates tend to converge with those of their host countries within a generation or two. You cannot immigrate your way out of a fertility crisis indefinitely.
headline: Are we entering an age of decay as birth rates fall?

text:
The leader of the Liberal Democrats has insisted that a woman can "quite clearly" have a penis, in remarks that have reignited the ongoing debate over gender identity in British politics.

Sir Ed Davey made the comments during an interview in which he was pressed repeatedly on whether biological sex is binary and whether it is possible for a woman to possess male genitalia. Rather than deflecting or attempting to sidestep the question, as many politicians have become accustomed to doing, Davey leaned into the argument, stating that a woman can "quite clearly" have a penis.

The remarks drew immediate criticism from women's rights campaigners and gender-critical commentators, who accused the Lib Dem leader of denying basic biological reality in order to appease gender ideology activists within his party and the broader progressive movement.

Maya Forstater, the executive director of Sex Matters, was among those who responded, arguing that the continued insistence by political leaders that males can be women undermines sex-based rights and protections that women have fought for over generations.

The intervention is notable given the political trajectory of the gender debate in the United Kingdom, where the Labour government has found itself increasingly at odds with gender-critical feminists despite initially appearing to take a more cautious line than its predecessors. The previous Conservative government moved to block Scotland's Gender Recognition Reform Bill, a decision that was broadly popular with the public.

Polling consistently shows that a significant majority of the British public believe that biological sex is binary and immutable, making Davey's position something of an outlier not merely among political opponents but among ordinary voters, including many who might otherwise be sympathetic to the Liberal Democrats.

Critics have long argued that the reluctance of mainstream politicians to state plainly that sex is biological and immutable represents a capitulation to a small but highly vocal activist class that holds disproportionate influence within progressive political parties, media organisations, and third-sector bodies. Davey's comments, rather than representing a gaffe, appear to reflect a settled position within the Liberal Democrat party, which has consistently adopted some of the most permissive stances on gender self-identification of any major UK party.

The question of whether a woman can have a penis has become something of a litmus test in British politics, with politicians across the spectrum regularly finding themselves ambushed by the question in interviews. Former Labour leader Keir Starmer famously tied himself in knots over the issue before eventually conceding that a woman could not, in fact, possess male genitalia — a shift that was itself criticised by trans rights campaigners as a betrayal.

Davey, it appears, has no intention of making a similar course correction.
headline: Liberal Democrat party leader says a woman can “quite clearly” have a penis

text:
Irish people are among the heaviest users of cocaine in the world, ranking joint fourth globally according to a new report from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.

The findings, published in the UNODC's World Drug Report, place Ireland alongside several other Western nations at the top of the table for cocaine prevalence, a ranking that will raise further questions about the State's approach to drug policy and enforcement.

The report examines drug use patterns across dozens of countries and found that cocaine consumption in Ireland has continued to climb in recent years, reflecting a trend seen across much of Western Europe. The drug, once considered the preserve of affluent urban professionals, has become widespread across all demographics and regions of the country, including rural areas.

The data will come as little surprise to those working in frontline addiction services or in law enforcement. The Gardaí have made a series of significant cocaine seizures in recent years, with record hauls intercepted at ports and in communities across the country. Despite these efforts, the sheer volume of the drug entering the Irish market appears to have done little to dent supply or push up street prices, which have remained relatively stable.

Drugs policy has become an increasingly contentious issue in Irish public discourse. The Government's approach has broadly moved in the direction of treating drug use as a public health matter rather than a criminal justice one, a position formalised in the national drugs strategy. Critics, however, have argued that this shift in emphasis has effectively amounted to a softening of the State's stance and has done nothing to deter consumption.

The Citizens' Assembly on Drug Use, which concluded its work last year, recommended the decriminalisation of the possession of small amounts of drugs for personal use, a proposal that proved divisive. Government has yet to act decisively on the Assembly's recommendations, though Minister of State for Public Health, Wellbeing and the National Drugs Strategy Hildegarde Naughton has indicated that the recommendations are being examined.

Meanwhile, addiction services remain under significant strain. Organisations working in the sector have repeatedly warned that funding has not kept pace with the scale of the problem, and that waiting lists for treatment remain unacceptably long in many parts of the country. The HSE's addiction services have faced particular criticism for inconsistencies in provision between different regions.

The cocaine market in Ireland has also been linked to a sharp increase in drug-related violence and intimidation. Criminal gangs involved in the supply chain have become increasingly brazen, with drug debt intimidation now representing one of the most common categories of crime reported to the Gardaí in some areas. Families have been driven from their homes, and community organisations have spoken of a climate of fear in certain neighbourhoods.

Tony Duffin, CEO of the Ana Liffey Drug Project, has previously noted that Ireland's high levels of cocaine use are a reflection of broader societal factors, including disposable income, cultural attitudes towards substance use, and the relative ease with which the drug can be obtained.

The UN findings will inevitably reignite debate about whether the State is doing enough — either in terms of enforcement or harm reduction — to address what has become one of the most pressing public health and social challenges facing the country.
headline: Irish people joint fourth biggest users of cocaine globally, UN study finds

text:
A Dáil member has called for the introduction of a formal mechanism allowing the State to audit non-governmental organisations that receive public funding, arguing that taxpayers have a right to know how their money is being spent.

The call comes amid growing public concern over the scale of State funding flowing to NGOs and charities involved in areas such as immigration, housing, and social policy, with critics arguing that many of these bodies operate with insufficient transparency and accountability.

Speaking to Gript, the TD said that while NGOs play a legitimate role in civil society, the current arrangements around their funding amount to a "blank cheque" from the taxpayer, with little meaningful oversight of how hundreds of millions of euro are allocated and spent each year.

"If you are receiving public money — and some of these organisations are receiving very significant sums — then the public has an absolute right to see how that money is being used," the TD said. "That's not an unreasonable ask. That's basic accountability."

The deputy argued that the Comptroller and Auditor General, or a similar body, should be empowered to conduct full audits of any NGO in receipt of taxpayer funding above a certain threshold. At present, while NGOs are required to file accounts with the Charities Regulator, there is no standardised mechanism for the State to carry out the kind of detailed performance and value-for-money audits that would apply to government departments or State agencies spending equivalent sums.

The issue has become increasingly politically charged in recent years. A number of NGOs working in the asylum and immigration space have come under particular scrutiny, with questions raised about the level of State funding they receive and the extent to which their advocacy positions align with government policy rather than challenging it. Critics have suggested that a network of publicly funded organisations effectively operates as an arm of the State while maintaining the appearance of independence.

Defenders of the NGO sector have pushed back against such characterisation, arguing that civil society organisations perform essential services that the State itself is often unable or unwilling to deliver, and that calls for increased auditing are motivated by a desire to silence advocacy groups rather than genuine concerns about financial probity.

However, the TD rejected this framing, insisting that the demand for transparency should not be controversial regardless of one's political outlook.

"Nobody is saying these organisations shouldn't exist or shouldn't advocate for whatever cause they believe in," the deputy said. "But when they're doing it with public money, the public gets to ask questions. That's how democracy is supposed to work."

The question of NGO funding has surfaced repeatedly in the Dáil in recent sessions, with a number of TDs across the political spectrum raising concerns. Despite this, there has been little appetite from Government to introduce the kind of structural reforms being called for, with ministers generally expressing confidence in existing regulatory frameworks.

The Charities Regulator, which was established under the Charities Act 2009, has the power to investigate charities and request information about their activities and finances. However, the body has faced criticism for being under-resourced and lacking the teeth needed to provide genuine oversight of a sector that has grown enormously in both scale and influence.
headline: TD calls for State to be able to audit taxpayer-funded NGOs

text:
Mateusz Morawiecki has announced, in a dramatic escalation of the bitter dispute between the two countries over Ukrainian grain imports.

The Polish leader made the stunning declaration during a television interview on Wednesday evening, saying Warsaw would now focus on arming itself with more modern weaponry rather than continuing to transfer arms to Kyiv.

"We are no longer transferring weapons to Ukraine because we are now arming ourselves with the most modern weapons," Morawiecki told the Polsat News channel.

The announcement marks a remarkable deterioration in relations between two nations that had been among the closest of allies since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Poland had been one of the earliest and most enthusiastic backers of Ukraine's war effort, serving as a critical logistics hub for Western military aid and welcoming millions of Ukrainian refugees.

The row centres on cheap Ukrainian grain flooding into the Polish market, which Polish farmers say has devastated prices and threatened their livelihoods. Poland, along with Hungary and Slovakia, recently announced a unilateral extension of a ban on Ukrainian grain imports after an EU-wide restriction expired. Ukraine responded by filing a complaint with the World Trade Organisation, a move that infuriated Warsaw.

Morawiecki's comments came just days before a general election in Poland, leading some analysts to suggest the tough stance was at least partly motivated by domestic political considerations. The ruling Law and Justice party has been courting the rural vote and faces a serious challenge from the opposition.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky hit back at Poland during his address to the United Nations General Assembly, accusing some European countries of playing politics with the grain issue and effectively aiding Moscow. Without naming Poland directly, Zelensky said some nations were "making a thriller from grain" and that their actions demonstrated "solidarity is not given, it can be shuffled like a card in a political game."

The diplomatic spat prompted a sharp exchange, with Poland summoning the Ukrainian ambassador in response to Zelensky's UN remarks. Morawiecki accused the Ukrainian president of insulting Poles, declaring that he should "never insult Poles again."

The developments will cause concern among Western allies who have sought to maintain a united front in support of Ukraine. Poland's geographical position on NATO's eastern flank and its role as a transit point for military supplies make it a critical player in the alliance's support for Kyiv.

It remains to be seen whether the Polish position on arms transfers will hold after the October 15th election, regardless of which party or coalition emerges victorious. Opposition leader Donald Tusk, who leads the Civic Platform party, has sought to balance criticism of the government's handling of the grain dispute with continued expressions of support for Ukraine's sovereignty.

The grain dispute also has implications for Ukraine's broader aspirations toward European Union membership, a process that requires the goodwill of all existing member states. Poland had previously been among the most vocal champions of Ukrainian accession.

Brussels has attempted to mediate the dispute, with the European Commission proposing measures to address the concerns of frontline member states while maintaining broader trade liberalisation with Ukraine.
headline: Poland will no longer supply weapons to Ukraine after grain row

text:
Helen McEntee has insisted that opposition to the Government's controversial hate speech legislation is rooted in "disinformation," as she defended the bill against sustained criticism from civil liberties groups, legal experts, and members of the public.

The Minister for Justice made the remarks as the Criminal Justice (Incitement to Violence or Hatred and Hate Offences) Bill continues its passage through the Oireachtas, with the Government pressing ahead despite what critics describe as an unprecedented level of public concern about the legislation's potential impact on free expression.

McEntee claimed that much of the pushback against the bill had been driven by misleading narratives, particularly on social media, and suggested that opponents had mischaracterised the legislation's provisions. She argued that the bill contains robust safeguards and that it is narrowly targeted at genuinely hateful conduct rather than ordinary speech.

However, the Minister's characterisation of the opposition as being based on falsehoods is likely to draw a sharp response from the bill's many critics, who include senior legal academics, prominent barristers, and free speech organisations who have raised detailed and specific concerns about the legislation's text.

Among the most persistent criticisms is the bill's provision relating to material "likely to incite hatred," which opponents argue sets a dangerously low threshold that could criminalise speech based not on intent but on how a third party might interpret or react to it. The Irish Council for Civil Liberties has itself raised concerns about the legislation, a fact that sits uneasily with the Minister's suggestion that opposition is driven by bad actors spreading disinformation.

Senator Michael McDowell, a former Minister for Justice himself and a Senior Counsel, has been among the most vocal critics of the bill in the Oireachtas, arguing that its definitions are vague and that it risks creating a chilling effect on legitimate public discourse. His concerns can hardly be dismissed as the product of online misinformation.

The question of what constitutes "disinformation" in this context is itself revealing. The Government has increasingly adopted a framing in which substantive policy disagreement is recast as a problem of public misunderstanding — a tendency that critics argue is itself corrosive to democratic debate. When a Minister dismisses opposition to legislation as the product of disinformation rather than engaging with the specific legal and constitutional arguments being made, it raises questions about the Government's willingness to genuinely listen to concerns.

The bill has also attracted significant international attention, with figures such as Elon Musk weighing in to criticise the legislation. While the Government has been quick to dismiss foreign commentary, the reality is that Ireland's approach to hate speech law is being closely watched as a potential template — or cautionary tale — for other liberal democracies grappling with the same questions.

McEntee's comments come at a time when trust in political institutions is already under significant strain, and when the public is increasingly sceptical of Government attempts to regulate speech. Polling has consistently shown deep unease among the Irish public about the potential for hate speech laws to be used to suppress legitimate expression, and the Minister's decision to dismiss those concerns as the fruit of disinformation is unlikely to reassure anyone who does not already agree with her.
headline: Helen McEntee says opposition to hate speech bill based on “disinformation”

text:
A Ukrainian national has been charged in connection with the fatal assault on a man at a direct provision centre, it has emerged.

The accused, who is understood to be in his thirties, appeared before a sitting of the District Court following the incident, which occurred at an International Protection Accommodation Services (IPAS) centre earlier this week.

The deceased, also a resident of the centre, was pronounced dead at the scene after emergency services were called to the facility. It is understood that the two men were known to each other and that the incident occurred following an altercation at the premises.

Gardaí had launched a murder investigation following the discovery of the man's body, with the scene preserved for a technical examination by members of the Garda Technical Bureau.

The accused was arrested a short time after the incident and detained at a local Garda station under the provisions of Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act, 1984, before being brought before the court.

During the brief court appearance, the judge was told that the accused had been formally charged and cautioned, and that he had made no reply to the charge. A solicitor for the accused indicated that there was no application for bail at this time, and the man was remanded in custody to appear before the court again at a later date.

The fatal incident is the latest in a series of violent episodes at IPAS centres across the country, which have drawn sustained criticism from both local communities and those working in the asylum sector. Questions have repeatedly been raised about security arrangements at the facilities, with staff and residents alike expressing concerns about overcrowding and the lack of adequate vetting procedures.

The Department of Integration has faced growing pressure over conditions in the centres, with the number of people seeking international protection in Ireland having risen sharply in recent years. The Government has struggled to source sufficient accommodation, leading to the use of emergency facilities including hotels, former office buildings, and modular housing units, many of which have been the subject of local opposition.

Campaigners opposed to the Government's asylum accommodation policy have pointed to incidents of violence within centres as evidence that the current system is failing both communities and those housed within it.

A Garda spokesperson confirmed that a man had been charged in connection with the incident and that investigations are ongoing. The Department of Integration declined to comment on the specific case but said it takes the safety of all residents and staff in its accommodation centres "extremely seriously."

A post-mortem examination was carried out by the Office of the State Pathologist, the results of which are not being disclosed for operational reasons.
headline: Ukrainian charged in connection with fatal assault on man in asylum centre

text:
Disability rights groups in California have launched a legal challenge against the state's assisted suicide regime, arguing that the law fails to protect vulnerable people and effectively creates a two-tier system of healthcare in which disabled and chronically ill individuals are offered death rather than treatment.

The lawsuit, filed by a coalition including the Disability Rights Education and Defense Fund and Not Dead Yet, targets California's End of Life Option Act, which has been in operation since 2016 and was subsequently amended to make access to lethal prescriptions even easier. The groups contend that the law violates the equal protection rights of disabled people and those with terminal diagnoses, and that its so-called safeguards are hopelessly inadequate.

It is worth pausing on that claim, because it cuts against the entire narrative that has been constructed around assisted suicide in the Western world over the past two decades. Proponents of these laws — and there are many, including in Ireland, where the Oireachtas has been inching towards its own legislation — invariably frame the debate as one of autonomy, dignity, and compassion. Who could possibly object to allowing a suffering person to choose the time and manner of their own death?

Disability rights campaigners, that's who. And their objections deserve far more attention than they typically receive, particularly from a media class that tends to treat assisted suicide as an inevitability rather than a policy choice with profound consequences.

The Californian plaintiffs argue that the law has created a situation in which people who express suicidal ideation are treated in radically different ways depending on whether or not they have a qualifying diagnosis. A healthy person who expresses a wish to die will, rightly, be offered psychiatric support, intervention, and every possible resource to keep them alive. A person with a terminal diagnosis who expresses the same wish will be handed a prescription for lethal drugs, often with minimal scrutiny. The groups argue that this amounts to a judgment — whether explicit or implicit — that some lives are worth less than others.

This is not a fringe position. It is not the preserve of religious conservatives or pro-life absolutists, though both groups obviously have their own objections to assisted suicide. It is a position rooted in the lived experience of disabled people who have spent decades fighting against a society that routinely undervalues their lives, withholds resources, and treats their existence as a burden.

The amendments made to California's law in recent years are instructive. The original legislation included a requirement that patients make two oral requests for lethal medication, separated by a waiting period of fifteen days. That waiting period was subsequently reduced to forty-eight hours. The requirement for a mental health evaluation was never mandatory in the first place — it was only triggered if a physician believed the patient's judgment was impaired, a standard so subjective as to be almost meaningless. The trajectory, as it always is with these laws, has been towards fewer safeguards, faster access, and less oversight.

Readers in Ireland should pay very close attention to this case. The Oireachtas Committee on Assisted Dying reported in favour of legislating for assisted suicide in 2024, and while the political appetite for moving quickly on the issue has been somewhat tempered by the change of government, it has not gone away.
headline: Disability rights groups launch lawsuit to quash California’s assisted suicide law

text:
Irish Water has issued a Boil Water Notice affecting approximately 22,000 customers in the Wexford area, advising residents to boil their water before use until further notice.

The notice, which was put in place following consultation with the HSE, affects customers supplied by the Wexford Town and environs public water supply. Irish Water said the measure was taken as a precautionary step to protect public health after an issue was identified at the water treatment plant serving the area.

Customers in the affected area are being advised to boil water before consuming it, using it for food preparation, brushing teeth, or making ice. Boiled water should be cooled and stored in a clean, covered container in the fridge.

Irish Water said in a statement that it is "working to resolve the issue as quickly as possible" and that it would keep affected customers informed of any developments. The utility provider added that it was liaising closely with the HSE and Wexford County Council to ensure the situation is addressed and the notice lifted at the earliest opportunity.

A spokesperson for the HSE confirmed that the notice had been issued on its recommendation and that vulnerable persons, including the elderly, young children, and those with compromised immune systems, should take particular care to follow the advisory.

The disruption is likely to cause significant inconvenience for the thousands of households and businesses affected. Local representatives have expressed frustration at the state of water infrastructure in the area, with some pointing to years of underinvestment as a contributing factor.

Fine Gael councillor for the Wexford district described the situation as "unacceptable" and called for urgent investment in the local water treatment infrastructure to prevent similar occurrences in the future.

Boil Water Notices have become an increasingly common feature of Irish life in recent years, with ageing infrastructure across the country continuing to pose challenges for Irish Water. Critics of the utility provider have repeatedly called on the Government to accelerate capital investment in water services, arguing that the frequency of such notices points to systemic failures in the network.

Irish Water has said it will provide updates through its website and social media channels and has urged affected customers to contact its helpline with any queries. The company has not yet provided a timeline for when the notice is expected to be lifted.
headline: Wexford: Boil Water Notice issued for 22,000 customers

text:
The people of Ennis have spoken, and what they have to say should send a shiver down the spine of every planner, consultant, and local authority official who had a hand in the Ennis 2040 plan. But whether anyone in power is actually listening is another matter entirely.

At a packed public meeting in the town last week, local business owners lined up to deliver a withering verdict on the strategic vision document that promises to "reimagine" the Clare capital over the coming decades. The phrase that kept recurring, in various forms, was stark in its simplicity: their vision is our nightmare.

It is a sentiment that has become depressingly familiar in towns and cities across Ireland, where grand plans drawn up by consultants who parachute in for a few weeks are imposed on communities who will have to live with the consequences for generations. The pattern is always the same. Glossy brochures filled with renders of happy cyclists gliding past continental-style café terraces. References to "placemaking" and "activated streetscapes." Pedestrianisation schemes that sound wonderful in a PowerPoint presentation but which, in practice, throttle the commercial lifeblood of towns that are already struggling.

In Ennis, business owners are warning that restrictions on car access to the town centre will be the final nail in the coffin for traders who have already endured years of declining footfall, rising rates, and competition from online retail and out-of-town shopping centres. These are not people who are resistant to change for the sake of it. These are people who open their doors every morning, who employ their neighbours, who pay their rates and their taxes, and who understand, with an intimacy that no consultant ever could, what actually keeps a town alive.

The disconnect between the planning class and the people who inhabit the spaces they seek to redesign has become one of the defining features of modern Irish governance. It is not unique to Ennis, of course. Dublin's city centre has been subjected to a rolling programme of interventions — bollards, bus gates, traffic restrictions — that have coincided with, if not directly caused, an exodus of retail and a rise in vacancy rates that would have been unthinkable a decade ago. Cork, Galway, Limerick — the story is broadly the same everywhere. The planners plan. The consultants consult. The renders are rendered. And the businesses close.

What makes the Ennis situation particularly galling is the sheer presumption of it. The 2040 plan was developed through what the authorities describe as "extensive public consultation." But as anyone who has ever participated in one of these exercises knows, the consultation process in Ireland is largely performative. The decisions have already been made. The submissions are noted, filed, and quietly ignored. The workshops are designed not to gather genuine input but to manufacture the appearance of consent.

When local business owners tell you that they were not meaningfully consulted — that the plan as presented bears no resemblance to the concerns they raised — you would have to be extraordinarily naive to disbelieve them. This is how things work in Ireland now.
headline: Local businesses on Ennis 2040 plan: “Their vision is our nightmare”

text:
A new fund backed by a coalition of international philanthropic organisations is seeking to support what it describes as "marginalised" leaders working to advance "systemic reforms" across a range of policy areas, raising questions about the nature of the initiatives it intends to finance.

The fund, which has been established with significant backing from several well-known progressive foundations, says its mission is to identify and resource individuals and organisations from communities it considers underrepresented in public life. According to its own materials, the programme aims to build a pipeline of leaders who can "shape policy, shift narratives, and support systemic reforms" in their respective countries.

Among the areas of focus listed by the fund are migration, climate policy, gender identity, and racial equity — issues which have in recent years become flashpoints in public discourse across Europe and North America. Critics have previously raised concerns that such initiatives, while framed in the language of inclusion and empowerment, can serve to advance a particular ideological agenda under the guise of grassroots activism.

The fund's promotional literature emphasises the need to counteract what it terms "rising authoritarianism" and "democratic backsliding," language which has increasingly been deployed by progressive organisations to characterise populist movements and parties that have gained electoral ground in numerous Western democracies.

It remains unclear whether any Irish-based organisations or individuals stand to benefit directly from the new fund, though Ireland has in recent years seen a significant increase in the volume of philanthropic money flowing into advocacy groups working on migration, housing, and equality issues. Several such organisations have received substantial funding from international sources, including from foundations linked to billionaire George Soros's Open Society network, a pattern that has drawn scrutiny from commentators who question the transparency and democratic accountability of such arrangements.

The concept of funding "systemic reform" through third-sector organisations rather than through elected representatives and established democratic institutions is one that continues to generate debate. Proponents argue that marginalised communities require additional support to have their voices heard in policy debates, while sceptics contend that such funding structures can effectively allow wealthy donors to exert outsized influence on the political direction of sovereign nations without any democratic mandate.

In Ireland, the question of foreign-funded advocacy has taken on particular salience in the wake of the citizenship and family referendums in March 2024, when voters overwhelmingly rejected two Government-backed proposals despite near-unanimous support from the political establishment and a wide array of civil society organisations, many of which had received State or philanthropic funding to campaign for a Yes vote. That result was widely interpreted as evidence of a growing disconnect between the priorities of funded advocacy groups and the views of the general public.

The new fund's architects have not yet disclosed the full extent of its financial resources, nor have they published a complete list of intended beneficiaries. Further details are expected in the coming months.
headline: New fund aims to help “marginalised” leaders to “support systemic reforms”

text:
A call has been made for nursing home staff who are found to have physically abused residents to be permanently barred from working in the care sector, following what one TD described as a pattern of disturbing incidents that have gone largely unpunished.

The demand came from Independent TD for Kerry Michael Healy-Rae, who told the Dáil that families across the country are living in fear that their elderly relatives may be suffering mistreatment behind closed doors, with little confidence that the current regulatory framework is fit for purpose.

Speaking during Leaders' Questions, Healy-Rae said he had been contacted by a number of families who had either witnessed or uncovered evidence of violent abuse of their loved ones in residential care settings. He said the cases he had been made aware of were "absolutely sickening" and that the response from authorities had been inadequate.

"If a person is caught physically abusing an elderly person in a care setting, they should never be allowed to work in that sector again. It's as simple as that," the Kerry TD said.

He argued that the current system, whereby complaints are investigated by HIQA or referred to the Gardaí, too often results in staff being quietly moved on to other facilities rather than being held to account. He said this represented a "revolving door" that put other vulnerable residents at risk.

Healy-Rae called on the Government to introduce a statutory register for all care workers, similar to what exists for nurses and doctors, which would allow individuals found guilty of abuse to be struck off and prevented from re-entering the profession.

The issue of elder abuse in care settings has been a recurring concern in Irish public life, with a number of high-profile cases in recent years drawing attention to gaps in oversight and accountability. Advocacy groups have long argued that the absence of a mandatory registration system for healthcare assistants and care workers represents a significant blind spot in the regulatory architecture.

HIQA, which is responsible for inspecting and regulating nursing homes, has the power to impose conditions on a facility's registration or, in extreme cases, to cancel it entirely. However, critics point out that the regulator has no direct authority over individual staff members, meaning that a worker dismissed from one facility for misconduct can, in theory, take up employment in another without any impediment.

The Government has previously indicated its support in principle for the registration of healthcare assistants under CORU, the body responsible for regulating health and social care professionals. However, progress on the matter has been slow, with the relevant legislation yet to be brought forward.

Responding to Healy-Rae's intervention, the Tánaiste said the Government took the issue "extremely seriously" and that any form of abuse of elderly or vulnerable people was "completely unacceptable." He said work was continuing on the regulation of healthcare assistants and that the matter would be progressed as a priority.

However, Healy-Rae said he had heard similar assurances before and that families were tired of waiting. He said that until a robust system was in place, vulnerable people in care settings would continue to be at risk from individuals who had no business working with them.

"These are people's mothers and fathers, their grandparents.
headline: TD: Ban nursing home staff who violently abuse residents

text:
The Department of Justice has confirmed it is engaging with 19 airlines operating routes into Ireland as part of efforts to tackle the ongoing scandal of passengers arriving at Irish airports with fraudulent or no travel documents.

The revelation comes amid mounting concern over the scale of the problem, which has seen thousands of individuals arrive at Irish ports of entry each year without valid documentation, placing enormous pressure on the State's international protection system and raising serious questions about border security.

In response to queries, the Department confirmed that engagement with the airlines is focused on ensuring carriers comply with their obligations under existing legislation, which places a duty on airlines to check that passengers are in possession of valid travel documents before boarding flights to Ireland.

The scale of the issue has been a persistent source of frustration for those calling for tighter immigration controls. Critics have long argued that the destruction or disposal of identity documents mid-flight — a well-documented phenomenon — makes it effectively impossible for the State to verify the identity or nationality of those claiming international protection upon arrival.

Under Section 2 of the Carriers' Liability Act 2001, airlines can face fines for bringing passengers into the State who do not possess valid travel documents. However, questions have been raised about how rigorously these provisions have been enforced in practice, with relatively few penalties understood to have been levied against carriers in recent years despite the significant numbers arriving without documentation.

Sources familiar with the process say that while some progress has been made in terms of carrier cooperation, the fundamental problem remains that individuals who board aircraft with documents can dispose of them before landing, making it extraordinarily difficult for airlines to prevent the practice entirely.

The issue has taken on renewed political salience as the number of people entering the international protection system has surged in recent years, stretching accommodation capacity and public services to breaking point and fuelling significant public disquiet in communities across the country.

Several TDs have raised the matter repeatedly in the Dáil, pressing both the current and previous Ministers for Justice on what concrete steps are being taken to close what many describe as a glaring loophole in the State's immigration architecture.

Government figures have pointed to the introduction of electronic travel authorisation systems and enhanced pre-clearance checks as part of the solution, though critics maintain that without robust enforcement of existing carrier liability provisions, such measures will have limited impact.

The Department did not provide a breakdown of which airlines are involved in the engagement process, nor did it specify what proportion of undocumented arrivals are associated with particular carriers or routes. It also did not clarify how many fines, if any, have been issued to airlines under the Carriers' Liability Act in recent years.

Immigration control advocates have argued that the State's approach to the issue compares unfavourably with other European countries, where more stringent pre-boarding checks and carrier penalties are credited with significantly reducing the number of undocumented arrivals.

The matter is likely to face further scrutiny in the Oireachtas in the coming weeks as pressure continues to build on the Government to demonstrate that it is taking meaningful action to address what many voters regard as a fundamental failure of border management.
headline: Dept engaging with 19 airlines to address false documents scandal

text:
The political leader of Hamas, Ismail Haniyeh, has been killed in what Iranian state media described as a missile strike in the Iranian capital Tehran, in a dramatic escalation that threatens to plunge the Middle East into a wider regional conflict.

Haniyeh was reportedly killed in the early hours of Wednesday morning while staying in a residence in Tehran, where he had been attending the inauguration of Iran's new president, Masoud Pezeshkian. A bodyguard was also reported killed in the attack.

Hamas confirmed the death of its political bureau chief in a statement, describing it as a "treacherous Zionist raid" on his residence. The group vowed that the killing would "not go unanswered," while Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei declared that Tehran considered it a duty to avenge Haniyeh's death, given that he was killed on Iranian soil as a guest of the Islamic Republic.

Israel has not officially claimed responsibility for the strike, though it has long maintained a policy of targeting Hamas leadership. The Israeli military declined to comment on the reports.

The killing comes just hours after Israel carried out a strike in Beirut that killed a senior Hezbollah military commander, Fuad Shukr, in what has amounted to a devastating 24-hour period for Iran's network of regional proxies.

Haniyeh, aged 62, had served as the head of Hamas's political bureau since 2017 and was widely regarded as the more pragmatic, diplomatic face of the organisation, operating from exile — primarily in Qatar and Turkey — while the group's military operations in Gaza were directed by Yahya Sinwar. He had been a central figure in the ongoing ceasefire and hostage negotiations, and his assassination raises serious questions about the future of any diplomatic efforts to end the war in Gaza.

Western governments have been bracing for the possibility of a significant Iranian retaliation. The United States, which maintains a substantial military presence in the region, is reportedly moving additional assets into position. Washington has urged de-escalation but has not condemned the strike.

The Irish Government has consistently called for a ceasefire in Gaza and the release of hostages held by Hamas. Tánaiste Micheál Martin has previously warned against actions that could widen the conflict, while Ireland's recognition of the State of Palestine earlier this year drew sharp criticism from Israel.

The killing of Haniyeh marks one of the most high-profile targeted assassinations in the region in years and has drawn comparisons to the US killing of Iranian General Qasem Soleimani in 2020. The fact that it took place deep inside Iranian territory, in the heart of Tehran, represents a profound security and intelligence failure for the Iranian regime and is likely to make a retaliatory response all but politically unavoidable for Khamenei.

Regional analysts have warned that the coming days will be critical in determining whether the situation escalates into a direct confrontation between Israel and Iran, a scenario that both sides have thus far managed to avoid despite months of mounting tensions since the October 7th attacks and the subsequent Israeli military campaign in Gaza.
headline: Political leader of Hamas, Ishmail Haniyah, killed in Iran missile strike

text:
The author of the landmark review into children's gender services in the United Kingdom has said that young people have been "weaponised" by adults engaged in a toxic ideological battle over transgender identity.

Dr Hilary Cass, the distinguished paediatrician whose final report sent shockwaves through gender medicine when it was published earlier this year, made the remarks during a wide-ranging address in which she warned that children had become collateral damage in a culture war fought largely by grown-ups with entrenched positions on both sides of the debate.

The Cass Review, commissioned by NHS England, found that the evidence base for treating gender-distressed children with puberty blockers was "remarkably weak" and that the dramatic surge in referrals to the now-shuttered Tavistock clinic — particularly among adolescent girls — had never been adequately explained or investigated. Its recommendations led to a fundamental overhaul of how gender services for minors are delivered across the NHS.

Dr Cass has faced extraordinary levels of personal abuse since the publication of her findings, with activists accusing her of having blood on her hands and of seeking to deny care to vulnerable young people. Several professional organisations initially sought to distance themselves from the review's conclusions, though a number have since quietly walked back their criticisms as the weight of evidence has mounted.

Speaking about the hostility she has encountered, Dr Cass said the reaction demonstrated precisely the kind of toxic atmosphere that had made it so difficult to conduct sober, evidence-based medicine in the field. She noted that clinicians had told her they were afraid to raise concerns about the "affirmative" model of care for fear of being branded bigots or transphobes — a climate of intimidation that she said had actively harmed the children the services were supposed to help.

The remarks will resonate in Ireland, where the debate around gender medicine for minors has been notably muted compared with the UK. The HSE continues to operate a gender service for children and adolescents, though it has faced questions about its protocols and waiting lists. Unlike in the UK, Finland, Sweden, Denmark, and Norway — all of which have moved to restrict or fundamentally reassess the use of medical interventions for gender-questioning minors — Ireland has not conducted a comparable independent review of its own services.

Dr Cass emphasised that her concern was not with how adults choose to live their lives, but with ensuring that children and adolescents, who are by definition still developing, receive care that is grounded in robust evidence rather than ideology. She warned that the polarisation of the debate had created a false binary in which one was either entirely in favour of early medical intervention or was accused of denying the existence of trans people altogether.

"There is no other area of healthcare where we would accept this level of uncertainty about what we are doing to children," she said, adding that the young people caught up in the controversy deserved far better than to be treated as pawns in an adult argument.

The intervention comes at a time when political and medical establishments across Europe are increasingly moving towards a more cautious approach, even as some jurisdictions — including several US states — have gone in the opposite direction, enshrining access to puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for minors in law.
headline: Dr Cass: children “weaponised” by toxic trans debate

text:
A major new study has added significant weight to the growing body of evidence suggesting that common viral infections may play a far greater role in the development of neurodegenerative diseases than previously understood, with researchers identifying strong associations between certain viruses and conditions including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.

The research, published in the journal *Neuron*, analysed data from hundreds of thousands of patients across multiple countries and found that individuals who had been hospitalised with specific viral infections faced a markedly elevated risk of developing neurodegenerative conditions in subsequent years. The findings have potentially profound implications for how the medical establishment approaches both the prevention and treatment of diseases that affect tens of millions of people worldwide.

Researchers from the National Institutes of Health in the United States examined medical records from Finland and the United Kingdom, covering a combined dataset of nearly 450,000 individuals. They identified 22 pairings between viral infections and neurodegenerative diseases, with some of the strongest links emerging between viral encephalitis — an inflammation of the brain caused by viral infection — and Alzheimer's disease. Patients hospitalised with encephalitis were found to be up to 31 times more likely to develop Alzheimer's in the years following their infection.

Influenza accompanied by pneumonia was also associated with an increased risk of several neurodegenerative disorders, while intestinal infections showed links to vascular dementia. The associations held up even when researchers controlled for a range of confounding factors.

It should be stressed that the study identifies associations rather than definitive causal mechanisms. The researchers themselves have been careful to note that correlation does not equal causation, and that further work is needed to determine the precise biological pathways through which viral infections might trigger or accelerate neurodegeneration. Nevertheless, the scale and consistency of the findings across two separate national datasets lend the conclusions considerable credibility.

The implications are potentially far-reaching. If viral infections do indeed contribute to the onset of neurodegenerative diseases, it raises the possibility that vaccination programmes and antiviral treatments could serve as preventative measures against conditions like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's — diseases for which there are currently no cures and only limited treatments available.

This is not an entirely novel hypothesis. Previous research has already established a link between herpes simplex virus and Alzheimer's risk, and the connection between the Epstein-Barr virus and multiple sclerosis has gained increasing acceptance in recent years. What this latest study does is dramatically widen the scope of the inquiry, suggesting that the viral connection to neurodegeneration may be far more extensive than a handful of specific virus-disease pairings.

The findings arrive at a time when researchers are also examining whether COVID-19 infection may carry long-term neurological consequences. Several studies have pointed to an elevated risk of cognitive decline and neurological symptoms among those who experienced severe SARS-CoV-2 infection, a finding that sits comfortably within the broader framework established by this latest research.
headline: New Study: link between Alzheimer’s/Parkinson’s and viral infection

text:
The Government has spent more than €1.7 million on Garda recruitment advertising since 2019, figures obtained by Gript reveal, even as the force continues to haemorrhage members and struggles to maintain numbers anywhere close to the target of 15,000 officers long promised by successive administrations.

The expenditure, which covers campaigns across television, radio, print, digital, and social media platforms, has done little to arrest the ongoing crisis in Garda numbers, which currently stand at approximately 13,900 – well below the level repeatedly pledged by government.

The figures, released following a parliamentary question, show a steady stream of spending on glossy recruitment drives over the past five years, with campaigns intensifying even as retention problems worsened and experienced members continued to leave the force in significant numbers.

Critics have described the expenditure as throwing good money after bad, arguing that the fundamental issues driving the recruitment and retention crisis – poor pay, difficult working conditions, and low morale – cannot be papered over with advertising campaigns, no matter how slickly produced.

One serving member, who spoke to Gript on condition of anonymity, described the campaigns as "absolutely pointless" while the underlying conditions of service remained unaddressed.

"You can spend whatever you like on advertisements, but if people join and then realise the reality of the job doesn't match what was sold to them, they'll leave. And that's exactly what's happening," the member said.

The Garda Representative Association has repeatedly warned that the organisation is facing a staffing emergency, with members leaving at a faster rate than they can be replaced. Retirements, resignations, and members transferring to other careers have all contributed to a net decline in numbers that no amount of recruitment advertising appears capable of reversing.

The issue is particularly acute outside Dublin, where rural stations have seen their complement reduced to skeleton levels, with some stations effectively operating on a part-time basis despite being nominally open to the public.

It is understood that a significant proportion of the advertising spend was directed towards digital and social media channels in an effort to attract younger applicants, yet even this approach has yielded diminishing returns. Recent recruitment competitions have seen fewer applicants than in previous years, and dropout rates during the training process at the Garda College in Templemore remain a persistent concern.

The situation has been compounded by the lengthy recruitment process itself, which can take up to eighteen months from initial application to attestation, a timeline that sees many promising candidates accept other employment opportunities in the interim.

Government TDs have continued to insist that Garda numbers will reach the 15,000 target, a commitment that has been a feature of successive programme for government documents. However, there is growing scepticism, even within government ranks, that this figure is achievable within any realistic timeframe given current trends.

The Department of Justice, when contacted by Gript, pointed to ongoing recruitment campaigns and stated that the Government remained committed to increasing Garda numbers. A spokesperson said that advertising formed part of a broader strategy to attract a diverse range of candidates to the force.

However, the raw figures tell their own story.
headline: “Absolutely pointless”: €1.7m spent on Garda recruitment ads since 2019

text:
A Russian drone has struck an apartment block in a NATO member state, with footage emerging showing the moment of impact in a residential area in Romania near the Ukrainian border.

The incident, which took place in the eastern Romanian town of Plauru, has sent shockwaves through the military alliance, raising serious questions about the adequacy of NATO's air defence posture along its eastern flank.

Video circulating on social media shows the drone slamming into the upper floors of a residential building, sending debris cascading into the street below. Remarkably, no fatalities have been reported, though several residents were treated for minor injuries and shock.

Romanian authorities confirmed the strike, with the country's Ministry of National Defence stating that radar systems had tracked the object crossing into Romanian airspace from Ukrainian territory. It is understood the drone was a Russian-made Shahed-type loitering munition, the same Iranian-designed weapon that Moscow has used extensively in its aerial bombardment campaign against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.

It is not the first time Russian drones have crossed into Romanian territory. Fragments of drones have previously been found on Romanian soil, though this is believed to be the first instance of a drone directly striking a residential building in a NATO country.

The incident puts enormous pressure on the alliance, which is treaty-bound under Article 5 to treat an attack on one member as an attack on all. However, Western leaders have historically been reluctant to characterise such incidents as deliberate provocations, typically describing them as accidental or stray fire from the conflict raging across the border.

Romania's President Klaus Iohannis condemned the strike and called for an emergency meeting of the country's Supreme Council of National Defence. Bucharest has also reportedly requested urgent consultations with NATO allies under Article 4 of the treaty, which allows any member state to bring a matter of concern before the North Atlantic Council.

The Kremlin has not yet issued a formal response to the incident, though Russian officials have previously dismissed similar border violations as unintentional consequences of military operations against Ukraine.

The strike will inevitably intensify debate across European capitals about the need for bolstered air defence systems along NATO's eastern border, particularly in countries such as Romania, Poland, and the Baltic states which sit closest to the conflict zone.

It also raises uncomfortable questions for Western governments, including Ireland's, about how far the conflict in Ukraine can escalate before the alliance is forced into a more direct confrontation with Moscow. Ireland, while militarily neutral, is a member of the EU and has backed successive rounds of sanctions against Russia since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022.

For residents of Plauru, a small town that until recently had little reason to feature in international headlines, the strike is a terrifying reminder that the war in Ukraine is not a distant conflict but one unfolding on their doorstep.
headline: WATCH: Russian drone hits apartment block in NATO member Romania

Tributes have been pouring in following the passing of Scarlett Faulkner, with family, friends, and community members expressing their heartfelt condolences and sharing memories of a life that touched many.

Scarlett's family have been inundated with messages of sympathy and support since news of her death became known, with many taking to social media to pay their respects and recall the impact she had on those around her.

Those who knew Scarlett have spoken of her warmth, her kindness, and the lasting impression she made on everyone she encountered. Friends and loved ones have described her as someone who brought light into the lives of others and whose presence will be deeply missed.

Local community figures have also offered their condolences to the Faulkner family during what has been described as an incredibly difficult time. Neighbours and acquaintances have rallied around the family, offering practical support and words of comfort as they come to terms with their loss.

Floral tributes and messages of remembrance have been left in Scarlett's memory, with many expressing the view that her passing has left a void that will be impossible to fill.

The family have thanked all those who have reached out with kind words and gestures of solidarity, noting that the outpouring of love and support has been a source of great comfort during their time of grief.

Funeral arrangements are expected to be confirmed in the coming days. The family have asked for privacy as they mourn their loss.
