A bishop and at least three other people have been stabbed during a church service in Sydney, Australia, in an attack captured on a live-streamed video that has since been widely circulated online.

The incident occurred at Christ The Good Shepherd Assyrian Church in Wakeley, in Sydney's west, on Monday evening local time. The bishop, identified by parishioners as Mar Mari Emmanuel, a prominent Assyrian Christian clergyman, was delivering a sermon when a man approached the altar and allegedly stabbed him multiple times.

Footage from the church's live stream, which was being broadcast to thousands of viewers at the time, appeared to show a man lunging at the bishop before members of the congregation rushed to intervene. At least three other people were also stabbed during the ensuing chaos, according to New South Wales Police.

The attacker was restrained by parishioners before police arrived at the scene. Emergency services responded in force, with multiple ambulances dispatched to the church. The victims were transported to nearby hospitals, with the bishop reported to be in a stable condition.

The attack prompted a large crowd to gather outside the church, with tensions escalating into what police described as a "major disturbance." Officers were pelted with projectiles as hundreds of people amassed in the area, with footage showing bricks and other objects being thrown at police lines. Several officers were injured in the unrest.

New South Wales Police Commissioner Karen Webb urged calm, saying the investigation was in its early stages. Authorities have not yet confirmed a motive for the attack, though they indicated it was being treated as a potential terrorist incident.

The Assyrian Christian community in Sydney is one of the largest in the diaspora, and Bishop Mar Mari Emmanuel is widely followed online, with his sermons regularly attracting large audiences on social media platforms.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese addressed the incident, calling the scenes "disturbing" and appealing for calm in the community. He urged people not to take the law into their own hands and to allow police to conduct their investigation.

The attack comes just days after a separate stabbing incident at a shopping centre in the Sydney suburb of Bondi Junction, in which six people were killed. That attack, carried out by a lone male assailant, sent shockwaves through the country and placed the city on edge.

The proximity of the two attacks has heightened anxiety across Sydney, though police have said there is no indication the incidents are linked.
headline: BREAKING: Video captures Bishop attacked as 4 stabbed during church service

text:
There is a particular kind of sentimentality in Irish public life that makes it almost impossible to have an honest conversation about certain subjects. The case of Lisa Smith is one of them.

Smith, the former Defence Forces member from Dundalk who travelled to Syria to join Islamic State, has long been the subject of a debate that most people in this country find straightforward but which a certain class of commentator finds agonisingly complex. The ordinary person on the street has a very simple view: she made her choice, and it was a choice against us. The commentariat, predictably, would prefer we all tie ourselves in knots about citizenship rights and obligations and the danger of "statelessness."

Let us be clear about what happened. Lisa Smith was not some naive teenager swept up in an online romance. She was a grown woman, a trained member of the Irish Defence Forces, who made a conscious, deliberate decision to travel to the territory controlled by the most barbaric terrorist organisation in modern history. She pledged her allegiance to a so-called caliphate that burned men alive in cages, drowned prisoners, threw gay people from rooftops, and enslaved women and children. She did not wander into this. She chose it.

And now, as has been the pattern, we are expected to engage in a solemn discussion about her "right" to return, about reintegration, about compassion, about what Ireland "owes" her. The assumption baked into this conversation is that Irish citizenship is an irrevocable bond, something that can never be broken regardless of what a person does, regardless of the depth of their betrayal.

This is, frankly, absurd. Citizenship is not merely a legal status. It is a compact. It is a relationship of mutual obligation between a person and their country. When someone actively repudiates that compact — not by committing a crime of passion or falling into addiction or making some human error, but by swearing fealty to a foreign enemy dedicated to the destruction of everything this society represents — then the compact is broken. They broke it. Not us.

The counter-argument, always made in very serious tones, is that if we do not take her back, we are "abandoning our responsibilities." To whom? To a woman who abandoned hers? There is something almost perverse about a framework in which the person who betrayed the State is owed more consideration than the State gives to those who actually contribute to it. Try getting a hospital appointment through the HSE. Try getting a council house in Dublin. See how much the State's sense of obligation extends to you, the ordinary citizen who has never joined a genocidal death cult.

There is also the inevitable invocation of her child. This is, of course, the most emotionally manipulative element of the entire affair, and it is deployed with ruthless efficiency by those who want Smith brought back and quietly reabsorbed into Irish life. Nobody wants to see a child suffer. But the person who put that child in danger was Lisa Smith. She brought a child into a warzone, into the heart of a terrorist state. The responsibility for that child's predicament lies with her and her alone. Using the child as a moral shield is not an argument — it is emotional blackmail.
headline: Lisa Smith is not one of us, no matter how much she wants to “come home”

text:
Ireland is getting older, and nobody in power seems to have any particular problem with that. In fact, if you look at the decisions being made in Leinster House, you might conclude that the greying of the nation is not merely tolerated but actively managed, curated, and defended by a political class whose interests are perfectly aligned with those of the asset-rich over-fifties and perfectly misaligned with everyone else.

This is not, let us be clear, an attack on older people. It is an attack on a system that has arranged itself so comprehensively around the preferences of one generation that it has become, in all but name, a gerontocracy. And a gerontocracy, as history teaches us, is never at peace – not with itself, not with its young, and not with the future.

Consider the housing crisis, which at this stage has persisted for so long that calling it a crisis feels almost generous. A crisis implies something acute, something that will pass. What we have is structural. And it is structural precisely because the people who benefit from high property values – older homeowners, landlords, the already-housed – have vastly more political power than the people who are destroyed by them. Every time a rezoning is blocked, every time an objection is lodged against a development that might, God forbid, bring density to a leafy suburb, every time a politician nods sympathetically at residents' concerns about "the character of the area," what you are witnessing is the gerontocracy in action.

The average age of a first-time buyer in Ireland is now north of 35. An entire generation has spent its twenties and early thirties haemorrhaging money into a rental market that treats them as little more than revenue streams for someone else's retirement plan. They are told to save, told to be patient, told that their time will come – by people who bought their own homes for a fraction of the current cost and who have watched their net worth multiply simply by sitting in a house and waiting.

And it is not just housing. Look at healthcare. The HSE, that magnificently dysfunctional apparatus, presides over a two-tier system in which those with private insurance – disproportionately older, disproportionately comfortable – receive faster and better care than those without. Young workers, many of whom cannot afford insurance because they are paying ruinous rents, wait in emergency departments and on trolleys. The system is not broken. It is working exactly as designed, for the people it was designed to serve.

Look at pensions. The State pension is, politically, untouchable. No Taoiseach, no Tánaiste, no TD with an ounce of survival instinct would dare suggest that perhaps the single largest item of social expenditure might need reform. Meanwhile, the same political class has shown no comparable urgency about the fact that younger workers face the prospect of retiring into poverty, if they can retire at all, because the auto-enrolment pension scheme that was promised for years was delayed and diluted until it became almost beside the point.

The Dáil itself is an institution that reflects this imbalance. The average age of TDs has crept upwards.
headline: Ireland a gerontocracy will never be at peace

text:
The National Gender Service has called for the establishment of surgical facilities in Ireland to perform "affirming" mastectomies, a move that will raise serious questions about the direction of travel in this country's approach to gender medicine even as much of the rest of the world pulls back.

The revelation, contained in documentation obtained by this outlet, comes at a time when countries such as the United Kingdom, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, and Norway have all moved to restrict or entirely halt the medicalisation pathway for gender-distressed individuals, particularly minors. The Cass Review in the UK, widely regarded as the most comprehensive review of gender medicine ever conducted, found that the evidence base for such interventions was "remarkably weak." Yet Ireland, it seems, is pressing ahead regardless.

What is being described in clinical language as "affirming" surgery is, in plain terms, the removal of healthy breast tissue from individuals — overwhelmingly young women — who believe themselves to be male. There is no physical pathology. There is no disease. The breasts being removed are healthy and functioning. The only diagnosis driving the scalpel is a psychological one, and an increasingly contested one at that.

It is worth pausing to consider what would happen if any other medical service in the State proposed the elective removal of healthy organs from young people on the basis of psychological distress. One imagines there might be rather more scrutiny than has been applied here.

The National Gender Service, based at St Columcille's Hospital in Loughlinstown, has for years operated with remarkably little public oversight or political interrogation. It has functioned, in effect, as an activist-adjacent service within the public health system, adopting the language and framework of gender ideology wholesale. The word "affirming" is itself a tell. It is not a neutral clinical term. It is a political and ideological one, drawn directly from activist organisations, and it presupposes that the only appropriate clinical response to a patient presenting with gender distress is to agree with their self-diagnosis and facilitate their desired bodily modifications.

This is not medicine as it has traditionally been understood. It is something else entirely.

The demand for domestic surgical capacity also points to a practical reality that has received insufficient attention: Irish patients are already being referred abroad for these procedures, at the expense of the taxpayer, through the Treatment Abroad Scheme and the Cross Border Directive. The HSE has been quietly funding these surgeries for some time, with little public debate and even less democratic accountability. The call to bring these services "in-house," as it were, represents not a new departure but an escalation of an existing programme.

One must ask: where is the Oireachtas in all of this? Where are the TDs and Senators who might reasonably be expected to interrogate the evidence base, the ethics, and the long-term outcomes of these interventions before they become further embedded in the Irish health system? The answer, depressingly, is that most of them are nowhere to be found. The political class in this country has, with a handful of honourable exceptions, entirely abdicated its responsibility on this issue, cowed by the fear of being labelled transphobic or of attracting the ire of a small but exceptionally vocal lobby.
headline: National Gender Service calls for ‘affirming’ surgical breast removal facilities

Thousands of people have signed a petition calling on authorities to spare the life of a dog which has been ordered to be put down following an incident in which a person was bitten.

The petition, which has garnered significant traction on social media in recent days, argues that the destruction order is a disproportionate response and that alternative measures such as rehoming or behavioural rehabilitation should be explored before resorting to euthanasia.

Details surrounding the specific incident remain somewhat limited, but supporters of the campaign insist the dog poses no ongoing threat to public safety and that the circumstances of the bite have been misrepresented or taken out of context.

The case has reignited a familiar debate about how the Irish legal system deals with dogs deemed dangerous, with many questioning whether current legislation is fit for purpose. Under the Control of Dogs Act, a District Court judge can issue a destruction order if satisfied that a dog is dangerous and not kept under proper control.

Animal welfare advocates have long argued that such orders are too readily handed down and that the legislation fails to distinguish adequately between genuinely dangerous animals and dogs which may have acted out of fear, provocation, or unusual circumstances.

"The law as it stands is a blunt instrument," one animal rescue volunteer involved in the campaign told Gript. "There's very little room for nuance, and it's the dog that pays the ultimate price."

Those on the other side of the argument maintain that public safety must remain the paramount concern, and that courts do not issue destruction orders lightly. They point out that dog attacks can result in serious, life-altering injuries, particularly to children and elderly people.

The petition is understood to have been sent to the relevant local authority, with organisers also calling on the Minister for Rural and Community Development to intervene. Whether the online mobilisation will have any bearing on the legal process remains to be seen, as destruction orders are a matter for the courts rather than for political decision-making.

It is not the first time such campaigns have attracted widespread public attention in Ireland. Several high-profile cases in recent years have seen communities rally around individual dogs facing destruction, with mixed results. In some instances, courts have agreed to revisit orders where new evidence or alternative arrangements were presented.

The case is expected to return before the District Court in the coming weeks.
headline: Thousands sign petition to Save Dog from Being Put Down

text:
There is a peculiar feature of Irish public life that ought to trouble anyone who claims to value democratic discourse: the near-total absence of any serious or sustained debate about the merits and drawbacks of Ireland's membership of the European Union. It is treated, in almost every quarter, as a settled question – one that only cranks and malcontents would think to revisit. And yet, according to the most recent Eurobarometer polling, some 12 per cent of Irish people say they would vote to leave the EU if given the opportunity. That is not a trivial number. In a country of five million, it represents hundreds of thousands of citizens whose views are, for all practical purposes, unrepresented in mainstream political life.

Consider, for a moment, how Irish politics would respond if 12 per cent of the population held a strong view on literally any other major policy question. If 12 per cent of voters wanted to rejoin the Commonwealth, or abolish the Seanad, or withdraw from NATO's Partnership for Peace, there would be at least one party, one newspaper column, one regular voice on RTÉ willing to articulate and interrogate that position. There would be, at minimum, a conversation. On the question of EU membership, there is something closer to a wall of silence.

This is not, let it be said clearly, an argument for Ireland to leave the European Union. Reasonable people can and do disagree about the balance of benefits and costs that membership entails. But that is precisely the point: reasonable people do disagree, and they deserve to have their concerns aired rather than dismissed with a wave of the hand and a muttered accusation of populism.

The reasons for scepticism are not difficult to identify. Ireland's corporation tax sovereignty – long the engine of the country's economic model – has been under sustained pressure from Brussels for years. The EU Pillar Two directive on a global minimum tax rate was, in effect, imposed on Ireland over the objections of successive governments, and the celebrated "win" of maintaining a 15 per cent rate rather than something higher was less a victory than a managed retreat. The Migration Pact, agreed at EU level, will significantly constrain Ireland's ability to set its own immigration policy at a time when housing and public services are already under extraordinary pressure. The Common Agricultural Policy, once the great sweetener of Irish membership, has become increasingly oriented towards environmental compliance regimes that many farmers regard as onerous and out of touch with the realities of food production on this island.

Then there is the democratic question itself. The European Parliament remains, despite decades of institutional tinkering, a body in which Irish voters have negligible influence. Ireland elects 13 MEPs out of 720. The European Commission, which holds the sole right of legislative initiative, is not directly elected at all. For a country that fought a long and bitter struggle for self-governance, the steady transfer of sovereign competences to Brussels ought to be a subject of lively debate, not quiet acquiescence.

None of this is to suggest that the EU has not delivered genuine benefits to Ireland. It manifestly has. Structural funds transformed Irish infrastructure in the 1990s and early 2000s. The single market remains enormously valuable to Irish exporters.
headline: On EU membership, the 12% deserve a voice

text:
The energy crisis that has swept across Europe, sending household bills soaring and plunging millions into fuel poverty, did not arrive out of nowhere. It was not simply an act of God, nor was it solely the result of Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine. The truth, uncomfortable as it may be for the political establishment in Brussels and across European capitals, is that the crisis was years in the making, and the architects of it were the very politicians and bureaucrats who now claim to be solving it.

For the better part of two decades, European energy policy has been driven by a single overriding obsession: the reduction of carbon emissions. That is a goal which, stated in the abstract, few would quarrel with. But the manner in which it has been pursued has been reckless, ideological, and wilfully blind to the consequences. Policymakers chose to wage war on reliable energy sources long before reliable replacements were ready, and ordinary people are now paying the price.

Consider the trajectory. Across the continent, coal plants were shuttered. Nuclear power stations — among the cleanest and most reliable sources of baseload energy ever devised — were decommissioned or earmarked for closure, most infamously in Germany, where the decision to abandon nuclear power after Fukushima now looks like one of the great acts of energy policy self-harm in modern history. The Irish government, for its part, has never seriously entertained nuclear energy, preferring instead to place an enormous bet on wind power while importing electricity interconnected from Britain when the wind does not blow.

What filled the gap left by coal and nuclear? In large part, natural gas — much of it piped from Russia. This was the grand paradox at the heart of European green policy. Countries that congratulated themselves on closing coal plants and blocking fracking became ever more dependent on gas imports from an authoritarian regime. Germany built Nord Stream 2. Europe collectively made itself strategically vulnerable to Moscow, all while claiming the moral high ground on climate. When Russia invaded Ukraine and gas supplies were weaponised, the entire edifice came crashing down.

But the war merely accelerated a crisis whose roots lay elsewhere. The EU Emissions Trading System had already been driving up energy costs for years. Carbon taxes, while theoretically elegant, functioned in practice as a regressive levy on the poor. The rush to deploy wind and solar at scale, subsidised by the taxpayer and the bill-payer, introduced intermittency problems that required expensive backup systems and grid upgrades. None of this was free, and none of it was honestly costed to the public.

In Ireland, we have felt this acutely. The price of electricity here is among the highest in Europe. The government's response has been to hand out energy credits — funded, of course, by the taxpayer — rather than to address the structural reasons why energy costs so much. We have a carbon tax that rises every year by law, regardless of whether people can afford it. We have planning and regulatory frameworks that make it extraordinarily difficult to build new energy infrastructure of any kind, whether data centres, gas storage, or indeed wind farms. The result is a system that is simultaneously expensive, unreliable, and insufficient for the demands of a growing economy.
headline: How European green policies caused the energy crisis

text:
It would be easy to dismiss it. Another celebrity finding God, another millionaire wrapping himself in the language of redemption just as his public image needs a bit of polish. Kanye West has, after all, spent the better part of a decade testing the patience of even his most devoted fans with erratic behaviour, bizarre political pronouncements, and the kind of narcissism that would make Narcissus himself blush. So when he released an album called *Jesus Is King* and started hosting "Sunday Service" gatherings, the cynics had a field day.

But here's the thing: cynicism is easy. And what Kanye West is doing — however imperfectly, however chaotically — matters far more than the cultural gatekeepers want to admit.

The album itself is uneven, as most honest reviewers have acknowledged. It is not *My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy*. It is not even *Yeezus*, the ironically titled earlier work that now looks like an unwitting precursor to an actual conversion. But artistic quality is almost beside the point here. What matters is that one of the most famous human beings on the planet — a man whose cultural reach extends into every corner of the Western world — has publicly, unambiguously, and repeatedly declared his Christian faith. Not a vague, spiritualised, Oprah-friendly "I believe in something bigger than myself" faith. Actual, doctrinal, Jesus-Christ-is-Lord Christianity.

This is not supposed to happen. Not in 2019. Not in the entertainment industry. Not from a figure of Kanye's stature.

The Western cultural establishment has spent decades carefully constructing a world in which sincere religious belief — and specifically Christian belief — is treated as, at best, a quaint personal eccentricity and, at worst, a dangerous pathology. The acceptable posture for a public figure is one of studied agnosticism, perhaps leavened with some fashionable borrowings from Buddhism or a tasteful nod to "the universe." To declare yourself a Christian in the music industry is roughly as countercultural as it is possible to be, which is deeply ironic given that the music industry has long since stopped being countercultural about anything else.

Consider the reaction. When Kanye wore a MAGA hat, the establishment was furious but could at least contextualise it within familiar political categories. When he declared himself for Christ, something stranger happened. There was a palpable discomfort, a sense that this was somehow worse, somehow more transgressive. The political commentators didn't quite know what to do with it. The music press, overwhelmingly secular and progressive, reviewed the album with a kind of embarrassed condescension, as though a friend had started selling essential oils.

The Irish context is worth considering here, too. We live in a country that has undergone one of the most dramatic processes of secularisation in modern European history. The collapse of the Catholic Church's institutional authority — brought about largely by its own appalling failures — has been accompanied by a broader cultural shift in which religious faith itself, rather than merely its institutional expressions, has become suspect. To be young and Irish and publicly Christian is to invite a very particular kind of social sanction.
headline: Kanye West says “Jesus Is King”. Here’s why that matters

text:
It would be easy to miss, amid the weekly deluge of reports and recommendations that pour forth from Ireland's ever-expanding ecosystem of quangos and state-funded research bodies, but the latest tranche of funding awarded to the Economic and Social Research Institute deserves a moment of quiet reflection. Ten million euro. For a report.

Now, to be fair, the ESRI would likely bristle at that characterisation. They would point out that the funding covers a multi-year programme of research, that their work informs vital policy decisions, that the complexity of the issues demands rigorous and sustained analysis. All of which may well be true. But it does rather raise the question that nobody in official Ireland ever seems terribly keen on asking: at what point does the research-industrial complex become an end in itself?

The ESRI occupies a peculiar and privileged position in Irish public life. It is nominally independent, but the overwhelming majority of its funding comes from the State. It produces research that is treated with an almost reverential deference by politicians and media alike, cited as though it were holy writ handed down from an unimpeachable oracle rather than what it actually is — the work of academics whose conclusions are shaped, inevitably, by methodological choices, assumptions, and yes, institutional incentives.

And here is where things get interesting. Because when your continued funding depends on the State, there is a natural gravitational pull towards producing work that the State finds useful — which is to say, work that tends to validate the broad thrust of existing government policy. This is not to suggest anything so crude as direct political interference. It is subtler than that. It is the soft bias of institutional alignment, the way in which an organisation that depends on government contracts will, over time, tend to frame questions in ways that are congenial to government thinking.

Consider the pattern. The Government announces a policy direction. The ESRI produces a report that broadly supports that direction, perhaps with some gentle caveats and minor quibbles around the margins. The relevant Minister cites the ESRI's findings as evidence that the policy is sound. The media reports the ESRI's conclusions as objective, disinterested analysis. And the cycle continues, lubricated by a steady flow of public money.

Ten million euro buys a lot of lubrication.

The ordinary taxpayer might reasonably wonder what they are getting for their money. Ireland is not short of social research. Between the ESRI, the various university departments, the NESC, the NCCA, the growing constellation of bodies operating under the aegis of the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform, and the endless parade of consultancy firms retained by government departments, the country is practically drowning in analysis, recommendations, and strategic frameworks. What it is rather shorter on is common sense applied to obvious problems.

We do not, for instance, need a ten million euro research programme to understand why housing is unaffordable. The reasons are blindingly apparent to anyone who has spent ten minutes examining the planning system, the cost of construction, or the regulatory environment. What we need is political will to act on what is already known. But political will is harder to manufacture than another glossy report, and considerably less remunerative for those in the business of producing them.
headline: The social scientists are doing alright: ESRI get €10 million for report

text:
Michelle O'Neill has insisted she did not breach social distancing guidelines at the funeral of senior republican Bobby Storey, despite photographic evidence appearing to show mourners in close proximity during the event.

The Sinn Féin vice president faced sustained questioning over her attendance at the west Belfast funeral in June 2020, which drew widespread public anger at a time when families across Ireland, north and south, were unable to properly grieve their own loved ones due to Covid-19 restrictions.

O'Neill maintained her position that she had adhered to the rules in place at the time, a line that will strike many bereaved families as remarkably difficult to reconcile with the images that emerged from the funeral, which showed large crowds lining the route and gathering at Milltown Cemetery.

The episode remains one of the most politically toxic of the entire pandemic period, not least because ordinary people were being told they could not attend the funerals of their own parents, children, and spouses in anything approaching normal numbers. The sight of senior Sinn Féin figures appearing to disregard the very restrictions they publicly urged others to follow provoked a furious reaction that has never fully subsided.

It is worth remembering the context. At the time of the Storey funeral, regulations in the North limited funeral attendance to thirty people. While the PSNI subsequently decided not to pursue prosecutions, the Public Prosecution Service's decision not to charge any attendee did little to settle the matter in the public mind.

O'Neill's continued insistence that no rules were broken has become something of a running theme — one that requires the public to disbelieve what their own eyes told them. It is a strategy that relies on a very particular reading of the regulations and a very generous interpretation of the photographic record.

For the thousands of families who buried loved ones during lockdown — sometimes watching funerals on laptop screens from their sitting rooms, sometimes standing in car parks outside churches — the suggestion that nothing untoward occurred at Milltown Cemetery that day remains deeply insulting.

The episode speaks to a broader pattern in pandemic-era politics, where those who made the rules, or who most loudly demanded compliance with them, appeared to consider themselves exempt from the sacrifices they imposed on everyone else. It is a dynamic that corroded public trust across these islands, from Downing Street garden parties to the streets of west Belfast.

O'Neill, now First Minister in the restored Stormont Executive, has clearly calculated that the passage of time will dull public memory. Whether that calculation proves correct may depend on whether the public is prepared to accept a version of events that contradicts the evidence of their own eyes.
headline: Michelle O’Neill: No, you didn’t see me breach social distancing at that funeral

text:
The residents of a small Meath village are mobilising to oppose plans for a large-scale accommodation development for Ukrainian refugees on land adjacent to their community, arguing that the proposal would overwhelm local infrastructure and fundamentally alter the character of the area.

Locals in the village, which has a population of only a few hundred people, say they were blindsided by the plans, learning of the development not through any formal consultation process but through word of mouth and local social media channels. Several residents told Gript that they feel the government is treating rural communities as dumping grounds for a crisis that has been mismanaged at national level.

"Nobody asked us. Nobody consulted us. We found out about this the same way we find out about everything — after the decisions have already been made," one resident said, asking not to be named for fear of being labelled anti-Ukrainian. "This isn't about the Ukrainian people. We have sympathy for them. This is about a government that refuses to plan properly and then expects small communities to absorb the consequences."

The proposed development would reportedly consist of modular housing units intended to accommodate a significant number of arrivals, potentially doubling or even trebling the existing population of the village. Residents have raised concerns about the capacity of local schools, the absence of adequate public transport, the strain on water and sewage infrastructure, and the lack of any GP or medical services in the immediate area.

A community group has been established to formally oppose the plans, and members say they intend to make submissions through the planning process and, if necessary, pursue legal avenues to halt the development. They have also written to their local TDs and to the Department of Integration seeking answers about the consultation process — or lack thereof.

The situation mirrors dozens of similar standoffs that have taken place across the country since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which triggered a wave of arrivals that the State has struggled to accommodate. The government has faced persistent criticism for its approach to housing refugees, with communities from East Wall in Dublin to Coolock to villages in the rural west objecting to what they describe as a top-down imposition of large-scale accommodation without meaningful engagement.

Critics of the government's strategy, including several Opposition TDs, have argued that the absence of proper planning and consultation has needlessly stoked tensions in communities that might otherwise have been willing to welcome newcomers. The failure to invest in local services alongside accommodation has been a recurring flashpoint.

Government sources have repeatedly insisted that Ireland has an obligation under EU agreements and international law to provide shelter to those fleeing the conflict in Ukraine, and that every community must play its part. Minister for Integration Roderic O'Gorman has previously acknowledged that consultation has not always been what it should be, but has pointed to the unprecedented scale of the crisis as a mitigating factor.

However, residents in the Meath village are not mollified by such explanations. Several pointed out that the village has seen little investment in services or infrastructure in recent years and questioned why the State could find resources to build an entirely new housing development for refugees but not to address longstanding deficiencies for existing residents.

"We've been looking for footpaths, for traffic calming, for broadband, for years," another resident said.
headline: Meath village seeks to stop Ukrainian refugee village being built on its doorstep

text:
A leaked internal document has reportedly revealed that pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca is on the verge of being able to terminate its much-publicised pledge to supply its Covid-19 vaccine on a not-for-profit basis, raising fresh questions about the company's long-term pricing intentions.

The document, first reported by European media outlets, suggests that the Anglo-Swedish drugmaker has built in contractual mechanisms that would allow it to declare the pandemic phase of Covid-19 effectively over, thereby releasing it from the commitment it made at the outset of the vaccine rollout to forgo profits on doses during the crisis.

AstraZeneca had won considerable goodwill — and secured enormous public contracts — on the back of its promise that it would not seek to turn a profit from the vaccine while the pandemic persisted. The pledge was seen as distinguishing the company from rivals such as Pfizer and Moderna, both of which charged significantly higher prices per dose and generated enormous revenues from their mRNA vaccines.

However, critics had long pointed out that the definition of when the pandemic would be deemed to have ended was left largely at AstraZeneca's own discretion, a concern that appears to have been borne out by the leaked material.

The revelation is likely to fuel ongoing scepticism about the relationship between governments and pharmaceutical companies during the pandemic, a period which saw an unprecedented transfer of public funds to private drug manufacturers, often under contracts whose terms were heavily redacted before being shared with legislators or the public.

In Ireland, the Government committed billions of euro to vaccine procurement, with the bulk of spending directed towards the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna vaccines, though AstraZeneca doses were also purchased and administered, particularly in the earlier phases of the rollout. Questions about value for money and contractual transparency were raised repeatedly in the Dáil, though ministers consistently defended the procurement process as necessary given the urgency of the crisis.

The European Commission, which negotiated vaccine contracts on behalf of member states including Ireland, has itself faced sustained criticism over its lack of transparency, most notably regarding European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's personal text message exchanges with Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla, which the Commission has refused to fully disclose.

AstraZeneca has not directly commented on the leaked document but has previously indicated that it expected to begin generating a modest profit from its Covid-19 vaccine as the pandemic transitioned into an endemic phase. The company has also faced separate headaches relating to rare but serious side effects associated with its vaccine, including vaccine-induced immune thrombocytopenia and thrombosis (VITT), which led several countries to restrict or discontinue its use.

The development will do little to ease public trust in the pharmaceutical sector, which polling consistently shows has been dented rather than bolstered by the pandemic experience, despite the unprecedented speed with which vaccines were developed and deployed.

It also raises broader questions about the model of pandemic preparedness that governments, including Ireland's, intend to pursue in future — and whether commitments made by pharmaceutical companies under public pressure can be relied upon when the immediate crisis fades from view.
headline: Leaked document: AstraZeneca can end no-profit pledge soon

text:
It has become something of a received wisdom among Ireland's political and media class that the country is hopelessly addicted to the private car, and that only the most radical interventions — carbon taxes, congestion charges, bans on new registrations — can wean us off our shameful dependency. The narrative is familiar: Ireland is an outlier, a nation of petrolheads clinging to their steering wheels while the rest of Europe cycles serenely into a green utopia. There is just one small problem with this story. It isn't true.

Figures from Eurostat, the European Union's own statistical office, show that Ireland's rate of passenger car ownership per capita is, in fact, below the EU average. At roughly 462 cars per 1,000 inhabitants, Ireland sits comfortably behind countries such as Luxembourg, Italy, Poland, Finland, and Lithuania, among others. Even Germany, that great champion of public transport and green energy, has a significantly higher rate of car ownership than Ireland does.

You would not know this from listening to the discourse in Leinster House, or from reading the output of most Irish media outlets, where the car is treated less as a mode of transport and more as a moral failing. Minister Eamon Ryan and his Green Party colleagues have spent their time in government behaving as though Ireland were some kind of automotive dystopia, a country uniquely and pathologically wedded to the internal combustion engine. Policy after policy has been designed around the assumption that Irish people drive too much, own too many cars, and must be nudged, taxed, and ultimately forced into alternative arrangements — whether those alternatives actually exist or not.

And that, of course, is the crux of the matter. For people living in rural Ireland, in towns and villages with no bus service, no rail connection, and no prospect of either arriving any time soon, the car is not a lifestyle choice. It is a necessity. It is how children get to school, how workers get to their jobs, how elderly people get to their GP. To treat car ownership in such communities as a problem to be solved, rather than a reality to be acknowledged, is not progressive policy-making. It is metropolitan arrogance.

The irony is that Ireland's relatively modest car ownership rate exists despite the fact that the State has chronically underinvested in public transport for decades. People in Dublin still cannot rely on a metro system that has been promised, scrapped, redesigned, and re-promised more times than anyone can count. Bus Connects has been mired in controversy and delays. Outside the capital, the situation is considerably worse. In much of rural Ireland, public transport is essentially non-existent, and yet people are being told that they must abandon their cars for the good of the planet.

What the Eurostat figures actually demonstrate is that Irish people are, if anything, making do with fewer cars than their European counterparts, often in the face of significantly worse infrastructure. Rather than being congratulated for this, they are being lectured. Rather than being offered viable alternatives before being asked to change their behaviour, they are being punished first and promised solutions later — solutions which, based on the State's track record, may never materialise at all.
headline: Despite Climate Hysteria, figures show Ireland has low car ownership rate

text:
The Irish public, it turns out, are not exactly rushing to embrace the notion that biological males who identify as women should be competing in women's sports, according to a new poll that will make for uncomfortable reading in certain quarters.

The findings, which come amid a growing international backlash against gender self-identification policies in athletics, suggest that the relentless push by lobby groups and compliant politicians to embed transgender ideology into every facet of Irish life has not, in fact, convinced the man or woman on the street.

The poll found that a significant majority of respondents believe that biological sex, rather than gender identity, should be the determining factor when it comes to participation in competitive sport. This is, of course, the position that would have been regarded as so blindingly obvious as to not require stating aloud until approximately five minutes ago.

What is particularly notable is that the sentiment cuts across age groups, gender, and political affiliation. This is not, as activists would have you believe, a concern confined to cranky conservatives or people who spend too much time on the internet. Women, unsurprisingly, feel especially strongly about the matter, perhaps because they are the ones who stand to lose out when a six-foot biological male lines up beside them on the starting blocks.

The Irish political establishment has, characteristically, been slow to engage with the issue in any meaningful way. Most TDs would sooner chew their own arm off than say anything that might attract the ire of the extraordinarily online activist class that monitors public discourse for signs of wrongthink. The result is a bizarre disconnect between what elected representatives are willing to say publicly and what their own constituents evidently believe privately.

Sport Ireland, for its part, has issued guidance on transgender inclusion that attempts to walk a tightrope between inclusion and fairness, satisfying precisely nobody in the process. The organisation has largely deferred to individual sporting bodies, many of which have been left to navigate the issue without anything resembling political leadership from Government.

Internationally, the tide has been turning for some time. World Athletics, World Aquatics, and a host of other governing bodies have moved to restrict or ban the participation of trans-identified males in female competition, citing the overwhelming scientific evidence that male puberty confers physical advantages that no amount of hormone therapy can fully reverse. The International Olympic Committee, while stopping short of a blanket ban, has acknowledged that the issue is rather more complex than simply being kind.

None of this has prevented Irish media from largely treating the matter as settled, framing any objection to male-bodied athletes competing against women as a species of bigotry. RTÉ, in particular, has been reliably one-sided in its coverage, a fact that will surprise absolutely nobody who has been paying attention.

The poll results suggest, however, that the public are not buying what they are being sold. The Irish people have a long and storied tradition of nodding politely while being lectured by their betters before going into the polling booth and doing whatever they were going to do anyway. The marriage equality and repeal referendums are often cited as evidence of a socially liberal revolution, but it is worth remembering that both of those campaigns succeeded because they asked people to extend freedoms to others without taking anything away from anyone else.
headline: Poll: Irish public not real keen on the transgender sports stuff

text:
A Canadian member of parliament was cut off mid-sentence while attempting to raise questions about the World Economic Forum's influence on government policy, in a moment that has since gone viral on social media.

Colin Carrie, the Conservative MP for Oshawa, Ontario, was addressing the House of Commons when he began to question whether the World Economic Forum had been exerting undue influence over the Canadian government's policy direction. Carrie was attempting to read a question into the record when the feed appeared to cut out, with the Speaker citing "audio problems" as the reason for moving on to the next speaker.

The incident has drawn significant attention online, with critics arguing that the interruption was suspiciously timed given the nature of the question being posed. Supporters of Carrie have suggested that the moment exemplifies a broader reluctance among political establishments in the West to engage with legitimate questions about the role of organisations like the WEF in shaping domestic policy.

The World Economic Forum, founded by Klaus Schwab, has become a lightning rod for criticism in recent years, particularly following the publication of Schwab's book *The Great Reset*, which outlined a vision for reshaping the global economy in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic. Critics have pointed to the WEF's "Young Global Leaders" programme, which has counted numerous heads of state and senior politicians among its graduates, as evidence of an organised effort to embed a particular ideological framework within governments worldwide.

Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau has himself been identified as a graduate of the programme, a fact which has fuelled scrutiny from opposition politicians and independent media alike about the degree to which WEF priorities have been reflected in Canadian federal policy, from climate targets to digital identity initiatives.

The incident in the Canadian parliament echoes a broader pattern across Western democracies, where questions about the influence of supranational organisations on elected governments have increasingly become a feature of political debate. In the European Parliament, several MEPs have raised similar concerns about the WEF's access to and influence over EU policymakers.

Despite the growing public interest, mainstream coverage of the WEF's role in national policymaking has remained relatively limited, with much of the discussion taking place on alternative media platforms and social media channels. Critics of those raising the questions have frequently attempted to dismiss concerns about WEF influence as conspiracy theory, though the organisation itself has been quite open about its ambitions to shape global governance frameworks.

Carrie later confirmed that he had been attempting to ask about the WEF's involvement in Canadian policy and expressed frustration at being unable to complete his remarks on the floor of the House. The episode has added to calls from some quarters for greater transparency around the relationships between elected officials and international organisations such as the WEF.
headline: Canadian MP cut off in parliament while asking about WEF

text:
There is a particular kind of vindication that comes not from being proved right in one's own lifetime, but from watching the very thing one warned against unfold with an almost mechanical inevitability across the span of centuries. John Henry Newman, the great Victorian convert, Anglican clergyman turned Catholic cardinal, enjoyed no such satisfaction in his own day. He was regarded by many of his contemporaries as a reactionary, a man swimming against the tide of progress. Yet the world we inhabit now — fractured, disoriented, allergic to the very concept of settled truth — is one he described with an almost eerie precision long before it arrived.

Newman's great intellectual project, the one that animated his work from the Oxford Movement through to his later Catholic writings, was the identification and critique of what he called "liberalism in religion." It is worth pausing on that phrase, because it does not mean what a casual modern reader might assume. Newman was not railing against some political programme or party affiliation. He was describing something far more fundamental: the doctrine that there is no positive truth in religion, that one creed is as good as another, and that revealed religion is not a truth but a sentiment and a taste. "It is inconsistent with any recognition of any religion as true," he said in his famous Biglietto Speech upon being made a cardinal in 1879.

Read in its original context, the statement is remarkable enough. Read in ours, it is practically a news bulletin.

Consider the reigning assumptions of public discourse across the Western world. The idea that religious claims might be objectively true — not merely personally meaningful, not simply culturally interesting, but actually, stubbornly, non-negotiably true — is treated in most quarters as faintly embarrassing at best and dangerously fundamentalist at worst. This is not a development that happened overnight, and Newman understood the process by which it would occur better than almost anyone.

His insight was that liberalism in religion would not stop at religion. It could not. Once the principle was established that revealed truth had no binding authority, that the individual conscience unmoored from any objective standard was the final arbiter of meaning, the logic would inevitably extend itself into every domain of human life. Morality, identity, the nature of the human person — all of these would eventually be subjected to the same corrosive acid. If God has not spoken definitively, then nothing is definitive. Everything is negotiable. Everything is a matter of opinion.

And so it has proved. The contemporary West does not merely doubt particular religious propositions. It doubts the very category of proposition itself, at least when it comes to questions of ultimate meaning. We have arrived at a civilisational moment in which the assertion "this is true" is regarded as an act of aggression, unless it pertains to the hard sciences or to the particular ideological commitments that have, with no small irony, assumed the character of unfalsifiable dogmas in their own right.

Newman saw, too, that this process would not lead to the tolerant, pluralistic paradise its advocates imagined. Liberalism in religion promised freedom. What it delivered, and what Newman predicted it would deliver, was not freedom but a new and peculiarly ruthless form of conformism.
headline: Holding liberalism to account: the prescience of John Henry Newman

text:
Maria Bailey has resigned from her position as chairwoman of the Oireachtas Committee on Members' Interests, in the latest fallout from the controversy surrounding her much-publicised personal injuries claim.

The Fine Gael TD for Dún Laoghaire confirmed her decision to step down from the role on Wednesday, a move that had been widely anticipated following days of mounting pressure from within her own party and from opposition figures who argued her position had become untenable.

Bailey's chairmanship of the ethics committee had become a source of considerable embarrassment for Fine Gael, given that the committee is tasked with overseeing standards of behaviour among members of the Oireachtas. Critics had pointed to the obvious irony of a TD embroiled in a controversial personal injuries claim holding the chair of such a body.

The controversy centres on a claim Bailey took against a Dublin hotel after she fell from a swing on its premises in 2015. Details of the claim, which she subsequently withdrew, provoked a fierce public backlash when they emerged earlier this year and opened the TD up to sustained criticism and ridicule.

The affair has proven deeply damaging not only to Bailey personally but to Fine Gael more broadly, with senior party figures reportedly furious at the manner in which the saga has unfolded and the reputational damage it has caused.

Taoiseach Leo Varadkar had previously expressed his dissatisfaction with how Bailey handled the matter, and it was understood that pressure had been applied behind the scenes for her to relinquish the committee role.

The resignation from the chairmanship does not affect her position as a TD, though questions continue to be asked about whether she will be added to the Fine Gael ticket in Dún Laoghaire at the next general election. The constituency, which was reduced from a five-seater to a four-seater, is already considered a challenging prospect for the party.

Bailey is understood to have informed party whips of her decision before making it public. The vacancy on the committee will now need to be filled, with Fine Gael expected to nominate a replacement in due course.

The episode has added fuel to the broader national debate around Ireland's personal injuries culture, with the government facing continued calls to reform a system that critics say drives up insurance costs for businesses and consumers alike.
headline: Ouch: Maria Bailey resigns from chairmanship of Oireachtas ethics committee

text:
The best of traditional Irish music and the Irish language will be available from the comfort of your own home this weekend, as two of the country's most beloved cultural festivals move to online formats in response to ongoing public health restrictions.

The Patrick O'Keeffe Traditional Music Festival, which normally draws thousands of visitors to the Sliabh Luachra region of County Kerry, and Oireachtas na Gaeilge, the premier festival of Irish language and culture, are both set to offer rich programmes of events through digital platforms over the coming days.

For devotees of trad, the Patrick O'Keeffe Festival has long been a highlight of the autumn calendar. Named after the legendary Sliabh Luachra fiddle player, the festival ordinarily transforms the town of Castleisland and surrounding areas into a hub of sessions, concerts, and workshops celebrating the distinctive musical tradition of the Kerry-Cork-Limerick border region. This year, organisers have worked to ensure that the spirit of the event carries through despite the limitations imposed by the pandemic, with a programme of performances and tributes being made available online.

Meanwhile, Oireachtas na Gaeilge, organised by Conradh na Gaeilge, represents one of the most significant annual gatherings for the Irish-speaking community. The festival, which typically features competitions in sean-nós singing, storytelling, poetry, and drama, has similarly adapted to the circumstances. The sean-nós singing competitions remain among the most anticipated events of the cultural calendar, and this year's online edition will allow audiences who might not otherwise have been able to travel to attend the festival to experience these performances for the first time.

The move online is, of course, a bittersweet development. Much of what makes both festivals special is rooted in the communal experience — the impromptu session that breaks out in a pub corner, the conversations struck up between strangers united by a shared love of the language or the music. These are things that no streaming platform can fully replicate.

That said, there is something to be said for the democratising effect of bringing these events to a wider audience. For members of the diaspora, for those with mobility issues, or simply for people in parts of the country where access to live trad or Irish-language events is limited, the digital format opens doors that were previously closed. It would be no bad thing if some element of online accessibility were retained even when in-person gatherings return in full.

Both festivals deserve credit for pressing ahead rather than simply cancelling. The cultural sector has been among the hardest hit by restrictions, and the effort required to pivot established events to a digital format should not be underestimated. It is worth noting that these are grassroots cultural organisations operating without the deep pockets of major commercial festivals, making their determination to keep going all the more commendable.

For those interested in tuning in, details of the Patrick O'Keeffe Festival programme are available through the festival's social media pages, while Oireachtas na Gaeilge has information on its schedule and how to access events on its website. Both are well worth a look for anyone with even a passing interest in the living traditions that make Irish culture distinctive.
headline: Enjoy trad and sean-nós this weekend as Patrick Ó’Keeffe Festival and Oireachtas na Gaeilge move online

text:
Frustration among Ireland's farming community is reaching boiling point, with organisers now calling for thousands of tractors to descend on Dublin in what would represent a significant escalation of protests against government agricultural policy.

The call to action, which has been circulating widely on social media and through farming networks, urges farmers from every county to bring their machinery to the capital in a show of force that organisers hope will be impossible for the government to ignore. It follows months of simmering discontent over a range of issues, from the impact of environmental regulations on farm viability to what many in the sector regard as an existential threat to their livelihoods.

Sources close to the protest movement say the demonstration could dwarf previous agricultural protests, with some estimating that several thousand tractors could converge on the city if the turnout matches the level of anger being expressed at mart yards and farm gates across the country.

The escalation comes amid growing resentment at what farmers describe as a disconnect between policymakers in Leinster House and the realities of life on the land. Nitrates regulations, mandatory destocking measures, and the perceived prioritisation of climate targets over food production have all been cited as key grievances driving the movement.

One farmer involved in the organising effort told Gript that the protest is not the work of any single organisation but rather a grassroots response from ordinary farming families who feel they have been backed into a corner.

"People have had enough," he said. "We've gone through every official channel. We've engaged with the Department, we've talked to TDs, we've made submissions. None of it has made a blind bit of difference. The only language they seem to understand is when you bring the country to a standstill."

The Irish Farmers' Association has not formally endorsed the tractor protest, though individual IFA members are understood to be heavily involved. The Irish Creamery Milk Suppliers' Association has similarly stopped short of an official endorsement, while acknowledging the depth of feeling among its membership. The more recently formed farming advocacy groups, which have gained considerable traction on social media, appear to be playing a central role in the mobilisation.

There are obvious logistical and legal questions surrounding the prospect of thousands of large agricultural vehicles entering Dublin's already congested streets. The Gardaí have yet to comment publicly on whether they have been in contact with protest organisers or what arrangements, if any, are being put in place to manage such a demonstration. Previous tractor protests in Dublin, while smaller in scale, caused significant traffic disruption and drew considerable public attention.

The Minister for Agriculture has faced repeated questions in the Dáil about the government's approach to the farming sector, with opposition TDs from rural constituencies increasingly vocal in their criticism. Several have accused the coalition of treating farmers as collateral damage in the pursuit of Ireland's climate obligations, a charge the government has rejected.

A spokesperson for the Department of Agriculture said the Minister remains open to engagement with all farming representative bodies and is committed to ensuring a viable future for the sector. However, the spokesperson declined to comment directly on the planned protest.
headline: Call for thousands of tractors in Dublin: farmers’ protest escalates

text:
The Danish newspaper Berlingske, one of the oldest and most respected broadsheets in Scandinavia, has issued a remarkable public apology for what it described as its "hypnotic" adherence to official narratives during the Covid-19 pandemic.

In an editorial that has sent shockwaves through European media circles, the paper's editor-in-chief acknowledged that the publication had failed in its fundamental duty to hold power to account during the crisis, instead acting largely as a mouthpiece for government messaging and public health authorities.

The admission is striking not merely for its content but for its rarity. Major legacy media outlets across the Western world have been notably reluctant to engage in any serious self-reflection about their pandemic-era coverage, during which dissenting voices — including credentialled scientists and medical professionals — were routinely dismissed, marginalised, or outright censored.

Berlingske's apology specifically addressed the paper's failure to adequately scrutinise lockdown measures, vaccine mandates, and the suppression of debate around the origins of the virus and the efficacy of various policy responses. The editorial conceded that journalists had become too close to official sources and had allowed a climate of fear to override the professional scepticism that ought to be the hallmark of serious journalism.

The development will be watched with interest in Ireland, where similar questions about media performance during the pandemic have been raised but have largely gone unanswered. Irish legacy media outlets were, if anything, even more uniform in their adherence to government and NPHET messaging than many of their European counterparts. Dissenting perspectives were vanishingly rare across RTÉ, the Irish Times, and other major outlets during the period of restrictions.

Critics of Irish media's pandemic coverage have pointed to the almost complete absence of interrogation of lockdown harms, including the devastating impact on children's education and mental health, the backlog of medical procedures that continues to plague the HSE, and the economic damage whose effects are still being felt in the cost-of-living crisis.

The question of whether any Irish publication might follow Berlingske's lead in offering a similar mea culpa seems, for now, remote. The prevailing attitude among Irish media establishments appears to remain that their pandemic coverage was broadly appropriate and proportionate, a position that sits uneasily alongside the growing body of evidence suggesting that many of the measures they championed were at best questionable and at worst actively harmful.

Denmark has form in this area. The Scandinavian nation was among the first in Europe to roll back its Covid restrictions and was notably more willing than Ireland to revisit and revise its pandemic policies in light of emerging evidence. Its neighbour Sweden, of course, famously pursued a markedly different path from the outset, eschewing strict lockdowns in favour of voluntary measures — an approach that was relentlessly pilloried in international media at the time but which has since been substantially vindicated by comparative analyses.

Berlingske's apology also raises broader questions about the relationship between media, government, and public trust. Across the Western world, trust in legacy media has plummeted in recent years, and the pandemic period is frequently cited as a key inflection point.
headline: Danish newspaper sorry for “hypnotic” reporting of Covid narrative

text:
There is a romantic notion, one that has persisted for centuries, that suffering and creativity are inextricable bedfellows. It is a notion that deserves interrogation rather than blind acceptance, but it would be dishonest to dismiss it entirely. The history of art, literature, and music is littered with evidence that periods of profound personal or societal difficulty have produced work of extraordinary power and lasting significance.

Consider the Irish case. It is no exaggeration to say that the most celebrated period of Irish literary output coincided with some of the most turbulent decades in the nation's history. The Revival, the revolution, the Civil War, the stifling conservatism of the nascent Free State — these were not comfortable times to be alive in Ireland, and yet they gave us Yeats at his most incandescent, O'Casey's tenement tragedies, and the early, restless brilliance of Samuel Beckett. The pressure of living through upheaval did not extinguish the creative impulse. It sharpened it.

This is not to say that artists require misery in order to produce great work, a reductive and frankly cruel formulation that has been used to romanticise mental illness and excuse the neglect of creative people by the state. Nobody should have to starve in a garret for the sake of their art, and the suggestion that they should is an insult dressed up as a compliment. But there is something worth examining in the relationship between constraint and creation, between difficulty and the drive to articulate what that difficulty means.

The present moment in Ireland offers an interesting case study. The cost of living remains punishing, particularly for younger people. Housing is a disaster that successive governments have failed to resolve in any meaningful way. The cultural sector, despite warm words from politicians at every available podium, remains chronically underfunded. The Arts Council, while doing what it can within its remit, simply does not have the resources to support the volume of talented artists working in this country. Many creative people are leaving, or considering leaving, or have already left.

And yet. There is a palpable energy in Irish culture at the moment that is difficult to deny. Irish literature is enjoying what can only be described as a golden age of international recognition. Irish film and television are punching absurdly above their weight. Irish theatre continues to produce work of a standard that would be the envy of countries with ten times the population and a hundred times the funding. Something is happening, and it is happening in spite of, not because of, the conditions in which artists are working.

The question is whether the difficulty itself is generating some of that energy. There is a long tradition in psychology and philosophy of examining what is sometimes called "post-traumatic growth" — the idea that individuals who endure hardship can emerge from it with a deeper understanding of themselves and the world, and with a heightened capacity for meaning-making. This is not the same as saying hardship is good for you. It is saying that human beings have a remarkable capacity to transform painful experience into something that illuminates the human condition.

The creative person, almost by definition, is someone who processes the world through the act of making. When the world becomes more difficult to navigate, the need to process it becomes more urgent.
headline: For the creative, the worst of times can be the best of times

text:
The family of a French man with Down syndrome who was shot dead by police have expressed their devastation after the three officers involved were acquitted of all charges by a court in Toulouse.

"Killing us is ok?" asked the victim's sister, speaking outside the courthouse as the verdict was delivered. The case has reignited fierce debate in France over the use of lethal force by police and the treatment of people with disabilities.

The man, identified as Yacine, was 28 years old when he was killed in 2020. He had Down syndrome and an intellectual disability. Police were called to an incident at his home, and the encounter ended with officers firing multiple shots. The family has maintained throughout the legal proceedings that the level of force used was entirely disproportionate, given Yacine's condition and the circumstances of the confrontation.

Prosecutors had sought convictions against the three gendarmes, arguing that the shooting could not be justified. However, the court found that the officers had acted within the bounds of self-defence, a conclusion that drew audible gasps and cries from the public gallery.

The acquittal follows a pattern that campaigners say has become depressingly familiar in France, where convictions of police officers for lethal use of force remain vanishingly rare. Disability rights organisations have pointed to the case as emblematic of a broader failure to train law enforcement in how to handle encounters with vulnerable individuals.

The family's lawyer confirmed that an appeal would be lodged. "This is not justice," she told reporters. "This family has waited years, and today they have been told that the life of their son, their brother, did not matter enough."

The verdict prompted protests in several French cities, with demonstrators accusing the justice system of granting effective impunity to police. Banners bearing Yacine's name were carried through the streets of Paris, Marseille, and Toulouse itself.

France's Interior Minister has so far declined to comment on the specific case but issued a general statement affirming that police are "bound by strict rules on the use of force." Critics were quick to point out that such assurances ring hollow when acquittals are the norm rather than the exception.

The case carries echoes of other high-profile incidents across Europe in which police encounters with individuals who have mental health conditions or intellectual disabilities have ended in death. In Ireland, questions around Garda use of force and mental health training have also surfaced periodically, most notably following the publication of reports by the Garda Síochána Inspectorate recommending enhanced de-escalation training and the deployment of specialist crisis intervention teams.

For Yacine's family, however, the broader policy debates offer cold comfort. His mother, who was present throughout the trial, was too distraught to speak after the verdict. His sister's words — "Killing us is ok?" — were directed not merely at the court, but at a system the family believes failed their son at every turn, from the initial police response to the final judgment.

The appeal is expected to be heard later this year or in early 2026.
headline: “Killing us is ok?” – grief as cops who shot man with Down Syndrome acquitted

text:
It would be difficult to parody the sheer brass neck of Ireland's self-appointed arbiters of truth, but the Institute for Strategic Dialogue has managed to do something rather remarkable: in the course of lecturing everyone else about the dangers of misinformation, it has gone ahead and spread some of its own.

The ISD, for the uninitiated, is one of those well-funded outfits that has carved out a comfortable niche in the modern information ecosystem. Its business model, such as it is, relies on positioning itself as a neutral, expert body capable of identifying and flagging "disinformation" and "hate speech" online. It has received funding from a variety of governments and foundations, and its pronouncements are treated with a kind of reverential seriousness by legacy media outlets that would never dream of subjecting its claims to the same scrutiny they demand of others.

Which makes its latest intervention all the more instructive.

In a recent output, the organisation made a series of claims about transgender-related topics that are, to put it charitably, at odds with the available evidence. The kind of claims that, were they made by an ordinary citizen on social media, might well find themselves flagged, fact-checked, and suppressed by the very content moderation infrastructure the ISD itself advocates for.

The central issue is a familiar one. Organisations like the ISD have adopted, wholesale and without caveat, a set of activist claims about gender identity that are increasingly contested — not by fringe figures or anonymous accounts, but by mainstream medical bodies, courts, and governments across Europe.

The notion, for example, that there is no legitimate concern about the safeguarding implications of self-identification policies, or that puberty blockers are a settled and uncontroversial medical intervention, is now flatly contradicted by the findings of the Cass Review in Britain, by the policy reversals in Sweden, Finland, Denmark, and Norway, and by a growing body of peer-reviewed research. England's National Health Service shut down the Tavistock gender clinic precisely because of concerns about the evidence base for the interventions being offered to children. These are not opinions plucked from the wilder corners of the internet. They are the considered positions of public health authorities in some of the most progressive countries on earth.

Yet the ISD appears to treat any questioning of gender ideology as inherently suspect — as misinformation or, worse, as a vector for radicalisation. This framing is not merely wrong; it is actively dangerous. It seeks to place an entire area of legitimate public concern beyond the boundaries of acceptable debate, and to characterise anyone who raises questions — parents, clinicians, feminists, journalists — as participants in a "hate" ecosystem.

This matters enormously in an Irish context. The Government has shown itself to be remarkably susceptible to the influence of organisations like the ISD. The now-shelved hate speech legislation, which would have criminalised the possession of material deemed likely to incite hatred, was developed in an environment heavily shaped by the lobbying of precisely these kinds of groups. The Online Safety Commissioner's framework draws on the same intellectual wellspring.
headline: Anti-misinformation think-tank spreads trans misinformation

text:
There are moments in Irish politics when a single voice of dissent tells you more about the state of play than a hundred press releases ever could. Eamon Ó Cuív's declaration that he is opposed to the proposed coalition arrangement is one such moment, and it deserves to be taken seriously — not because Ó Cuív is always right, but because his willingness to say plainly what many others in Fianna Fáil are thinking privately is a quality that has become vanishingly rare in Leinster House.

Ó Cuív, of course, is no stranger to breaking ranks. The grandson of Éamon de Valera has long occupied an unusual space within Fianna Fáil — simultaneously the embodiment of the party's founding tradition and one of its most persistent internal critics. He has been a thorn in the side of successive leaderships, and he has paid the price for it in terms of preferment and influence. But he has also, on more than one occasion, been vindicated by events. When he warned that the party was drifting from its base, he was dismissed as a nostalgist. When that base subsequently collapsed, there were fewer people laughing.

His opposition to the proposed coalition should be understood in that context. This is not a man engaged in performative dissent for the sake of a headline. Ó Cuív has spent decades in the trenches of Fianna Fáil politics, and when he says publicly that a proposed government formation is wrong for the party and wrong for the country, it reflects a genuine and deeply held conviction — and, one suspects, a calculation that he is far from alone in holding it.

The question, as always, is whether anyone in the upper reaches of Fianna Fáil is listening. The party leadership has become extraordinarily adept at managing internal dissent, which is a polite way of saying that it has become extraordinarily adept at ignoring it. The mechanisms of party discipline — the whip system, the promise of ministerial preferment, the quiet threat of constituency organisation difficulties — are all designed to ensure that objections like Ó Cuív's remain isolated and ultimately ineffectual. The leadership will note his opposition, thank him for his candour, and proceed as planned.

But there is a risk in this approach, and it is a risk that Fianna Fáil has failed to learn from repeatedly. The party's great electoral collapses — in 2011 most dramatically, but the slow bleed of support over the last decade as well — have invariably been preceded by periods in which the leadership convinced itself that internal critics were out of touch, that the grassroots would fall into line, and that the public would reward pragmatism over principle. Each time, the leadership was wrong. Each time, the critics turned out to have been closer to the pulse of the ordinary voter than the strategists and advisers who dismissed them.

What Ó Cuív is articulating, whether he frames it in precisely these terms or not, is a concern that has been growing across the country: that coalition formations in modern Ireland have become exercises in elite management rather than democratic responsiveness.
