The people vote. The results come in.
headline: Eamon O’Cuiv says: I am against this proposed coalition

text:
The Great Barrier Reef has recorded its highest levels of coral cover since monitoring began nearly four decades ago, according to a new survey that will inevitably reignite debate over the true state of the world's largest reef system.

The Australian Institute of Marine Science's annual long-term monitoring programme found that two-thirds of the reef recorded the highest amount of coral cover since surveys began in 1985. Hard coral cover increased across all three regions of the reef — the northern, central, and southern sections — with particularly strong growth recorded in the northern and central areas.

The findings sit awkwardly alongside years of apocalyptic warnings from environmental groups and media outlets, many of which have spent the better part of a decade claiming the reef was on the verge of irreversible destruction due to climate change. The reef has been subjected to several mass bleaching events in recent years, each of which generated global headlines suggesting permanent, catastrophic damage.

Yet the data tells a rather different story. The reef, it appears, possesses a remarkable capacity for recovery that has been consistently underplayed in mainstream coverage. Coral bleaching, while visually dramatic and genuinely stressful for reef ecosystems, does not necessarily equate to coral death, a nuance that has often been lost in the rush to present the reef as a casualty of fossil fuel consumption.

Peter Ridd, a former professor of physics at James Cook University who was famously sacked after questioning the quality of science used to assess the reef's health, has long argued that the reef's resilience has been deliberately downplayed by institutions with a vested interest in catastrophism. Ridd fought a protracted legal battle over his dismissal, which he argued was a case of suppressing legitimate academic dissent.

The survey results are likely to prove uncomfortable for UNESCO, which has repeatedly threatened to place the Great Barrier Reef on its "in danger" list, a move the Australian government has lobbied fiercely against. Critics have accused the international body of using the reef as a political instrument to pressure Australia on emissions policy, rather than basing its assessments on the best available scientific evidence.

None of this is to suggest that the reef faces no challenges whatsoever. Crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks, cyclone damage, and periodic bleaching events remain genuine concerns for reef management. The institute itself cautioned that the gains recorded in the survey could be quickly reversed by such disturbances.

However, the consistent pattern of record coral recovery does raise legitimate questions about whether the public has been given an accurate picture of the reef's condition, or whether the narrative has been shaped more by ideological commitment than by observational science. For years, the Great Barrier Reef has served as perhaps the single most potent symbol in the climate change debate — a living, colourful shorthand for ecological collapse. The fact that it is thriving is, for some, an inconvenient piece of data.

The Australian government welcomed the findings but maintained that climate change remained the single greatest threat to the reef's long-term future, a position that allows it to simultaneously celebrate good news and maintain its commitments to emissions reduction targets.

What the survey cannot settle is the broader question of how science communicates uncertainty and complexity to the public.
headline: Great Barrier Reef has record levels of coral, says survey

text:
There is an old Irish superstition about swallows. If they nested in your eaves, it was a sign of good fortune. If they abandoned the nest, trouble was coming. It is difficult not to think of that folk wisdom when surveying the state of Irish housing in 2024, because the swallows, in a manner of speaking, have well and truly departed.

The numbers are by now so familiar that they risk losing their capacity to shock. Average rents in Dublin have surpassed €2,200 a month. House prices nationally have risen for the umpteenth consecutive quarter. The waiting list for social housing remains a source of quiet national shame, with over 60,000 households in need. Young professionals — the very people this country spent a fortune educating — are leaving in numbers that ought to alarm anyone who claims to care about the future of the State.

And yet the political class continues, with an almost admirable serenity, to insist that things are moving in the right direction. The Taoiseach speaks of "record levels of delivery." Ministers point to Housing for All targets as though the existence of a target were the same thing as hitting one. The rhetoric has become a kind of liturgy, repeated with such conviction that one suspects those reciting it have begun to believe it themselves.

The reality on the ground tells a rather different story. Commencement notices — a leading indicator of future housing supply — have been volatile at best. Planning permissions remain tangled in a system so labyrinthine that even seasoned developers describe it as actively hostile to building. An Bord Pleanála, now rechristened An Coimisiún Pleanála in one of those rebranding exercises that substitutes a new nameplate for actual reform, continues to process applications at a pace that would embarrass a medieval scriptorium. Local authorities, meanwhile, sit on landbanks of considerable size while pleading poverty and procedural constraints.

None of this is accidental. It is the predictable consequence of a system that has, over decades, been designed — whether by intention or by the accumulated weight of competing interests — to make building homes as difficult as possible. Every stakeholder in the process has a veto. Nobody has responsibility for the outcome.

Consider the extraordinary fact that it takes, on average, longer to get planning permission for a modest housing estate in Ireland than it does in almost any comparable European country. Consider that the cost of a single social housing unit delivered by a local authority can exceed €400,000. Consider that the State's response to a crisis of supply has included, with apparently no sense of irony, the introduction of yet more regulations, more compliance requirements, and more opportunities for delay.

The Government will point, correctly, to the fact that housing completions have risen. Approximately 33,000 units were completed last year, a figure that represents genuine progress from the post-crash nadir. But the figure, while welcome, is insufficient. Estimates of actual demand vary, but most credible analyses suggest the country needs somewhere between 50,000 and 60,000 units per year to address both current shortfalls and future population growth.
headline: Irish housing, and the flight of the swallows

text:
The Irish Red Cross has issued a warning to the public after reports emerged of scammers targeting elderly and vulnerable people by offering fake Coronavirus tests in exchange for €100.

The organisation said it had been made aware of individuals calling to the doors of older people, claiming to represent health authorities and offering to carry out Covid-19 tests on the spot for a fee. No such service exists, and the Red Cross stressed that legitimate testing is carried out only through the HSE and its designated testing centres.

It is understood that the scam has been reported in several parts of the country, with those behind it exploiting the widespread fear and confusion surrounding the pandemic to extract money from those most at risk. The fraudsters are said to be presenting themselves in a professional manner, in some cases wearing high-vis clothing or carrying clipboards, in an effort to appear credible.

The Red Cross urged people to be vigilant and to remind elderly relatives and neighbours that no legitimate health worker will call to their door unannounced seeking payment for a Covid-19 test. Anyone who is contacted in this way should refuse to engage and report the matter to the Gardaí immediately.

The warning comes amid growing concern about the proliferation of scams linked to the Coronavirus crisis. Since the outbreak began, fraudsters have sought to capitalise on public anxiety through a range of schemes, from phishing emails purporting to come from the HSE or the World Health Organisation to fake online shops selling personal protective equipment that never arrives.

The Gardaí have previously warned that criminals are adapting their methods to exploit the pandemic, particularly targeting older people who may be isolated and more vulnerable during the current restrictions. Garda Community Engagement offices around the country have been working to alert communities to the risks.

A spokesperson for the Red Cross said that the organisation was "deeply concerned" by the reports and appealed to the public to look out for elderly neighbours and family members who might be targeted. "These are despicable acts carried out against some of the most vulnerable people in our society at a time when they are already frightened and anxious," the spokesperson said.

The HSE has confirmed that all legitimate Covid-19 testing is arranged through a GP referral and carried out at designated centres or, in some cases, through mobile testing units. There is no charge for testing, and no health professional will call to a person's home seeking payment.

Anyone who believes they have been the victim of such a scam is urged to contact their local Garda station.
headline: Red Cross warn against Coronavirus scam charging elderly €100 for fake test

text:
Canada has finally scrapped its Covid-19 vaccine requirement for travellers entering the country, ending one of the last remaining pandemic-era border restrictions in the Western world.

The requirement, which had been in place since the early days of the pandemic response, mandated that foreign nationals show proof of vaccination against Covid-19 in order to gain entry to Canada. Unvaccinated Canadians returning home were also subject to testing and quarantine requirements at various points during the mandate's lifespan.

The move comes long after most comparable nations had already done away with similar restrictions, leaving Canada as an international outlier. Critics had for months — and indeed years — accused the Liberal government under Prime Minister Justin Trudeau of clinging to the mandate for political rather than public health reasons.

Trudeau's government faced sustained criticism over its handling of pandemic restrictions more broadly, not least during the so-called Freedom Convoy protests of early 2022, which saw truckers and their supporters descend on Ottawa to protest against vaccine mandates for cross-border travel. The government's response at the time — invoking the Emergencies Act to clear protesters and freeze bank accounts — remains deeply controversial and was subsequently found by a federal court to have been an unreasonable use of the legislation.

The vaccine border mandate had become a symbol of what opponents characterised as the Trudeau government's authoritarian tendencies during the pandemic, with civil liberties groups arguing that the restriction had long since ceased to serve any meaningful public health purpose.

It is worth noting that Ireland dropped most of its own Covid-related travel restrictions considerably earlier, with the EU Digital Covid Certificate requirement for travel having been wound down in 2022.

The Canadian decision brings the country into line with virtually every other developed nation, though it will do little to repair the political damage already sustained by the Liberal Party on the issue. Polling has consistently suggested that the mandates contributed to a significant erosion of trust in the federal government, particularly in western provinces like Alberta and Saskatchewan.

The announcement has been welcomed by travel industry groups and civil liberties advocates alike, though many have pointedly asked why it took so long.
headline: Canada finally drops Covid vaccine requirement for entry at border

text:
It is one of the great unresolved contradictions of the Covid era, and one that the Irish public has never quite been given a satisfactory answer to: if the restrictions were as necessary as we were told, why did so many of the people imposing them seem so relaxed about ignoring them?

The Oireachtas Golf Society dinner in Clifden in August 2020 was, at the time, treated as a scandal primarily because of the "optics." That was the word everybody used. The optics were bad. Phil Hogan lost his EU Commissioner post. Dara Calleary lost his ministry. Jerry Buttimer resigned as Leas-Cathaoirleach. Seamus Woulfe, a Supreme Court judge, endured months of public controversy. The fallout was real and it was severe. But in a curious way, the framing of the scandal as one of "optics" actually served to protect the establishment from the far more damaging question: did these people simply not believe the rules were justified in the first place?

Because if you genuinely believed, as the Irish public was being told every single evening on RTÉ News, that gathering indoors was a potentially lethal act — that you could kill your granny by sitting down to a meal with too many people — then you would not have attended that dinner. You would not have needed a regulation to stop you. Your own fear would have done the job. The fact that senior politicians, a European Commissioner, a judge, and various other pillars of the establishment happily gathered together in a hotel ballroom tells you something far more significant than mere hypocrisy. It tells you they did not believe the threat was what they were telling the public it was.

This is not a minor point. The Irish people made extraordinary sacrifices during the Covid period. They missed funerals. They missed births. They were separated from dying relatives. They watched loved ones deteriorate in nursing homes behind glass partitions. They cancelled weddings. They closed businesses that never reopened. They did all of this because they were told, by the very people who attended that dinner, that it was absolutely necessary.

And now we are expected to simply move on.

The RTÉgate scandal, which erupted in the summer of 2023, added another layer to the same fundamental problem. Here was the national broadcaster — the single most important institution in the communication of Covid restrictions to the public — revealed to be rotten with secret payments, undisclosed earnings, and a culture of entitlement that would make a medieval court blush. RTÉ was the organisation that broadcast public health messaging into every living room in the country. It was the organisation whose presenters sternly reminded the public of their obligations. It was the organisation that gave airtime to those who wanted restrictions tightened and largely denied a platform to those who questioned whether the approach was proportionate.

The same organisation, it turned out, could not even govern itself honestly.

Now, one might argue these are separate issues. Golfgate was about politicians breaking Covid rules. RTÉgate was about financial governance at Montrose.
headline: Golfgate and RTÉgate – clearly the elites don’t believe their own spin on Covid

text:
Hillary Clinton was heckled and branded a "war criminal" during a public appearance in Belfast, in scenes that drew a sharp contrast with the warm reception she has traditionally received on visits to the island of Ireland.

The former US Secretary of State and presidential candidate was confronted by protesters during the event, with at least one individual loudly denouncing her record in office. Video footage circulating on social media showed Clinton being called a "war criminal" as she attempted to address the audience.

Clinton has long enjoyed a broadly favourable reception in Ireland and Northern Ireland, owing in large part to the role played by her husband, former President Bill Clinton, in the Northern Ireland peace process. The couple have made numerous visits over the years and have cultivated close relationships with political figures on both sides of the border.

However, her record as Secretary of State under Barack Obama – particularly her role in the NATO intervention in Libya in 2011 and her support for military operations in the Middle East – has made her a lightning rod for anti-war campaigners. The destruction of the Libyan state following the Western-backed overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi is widely regarded as having created a humanitarian catastrophe, with the country descending into factional conflict and becoming a major route for people trafficking into Europe.

The heckling in Belfast reflects a broader trend in which establishment political figures from the United States and elsewhere are increasingly facing vocal public opposition when they appear at events in Ireland and the United Kingdom. The ongoing conflict in Gaza has further energised protest movements, with activists drawing connections between current US foreign policy and the records of figures like Clinton.

Clinton has never faced any formal legal proceedings in connection with her time in office, and her supporters maintain that her diplomatic record was one of pragmatic engagement in complex international situations. Critics, however, argue that such characterisations amount to a sanitising of policies that resulted in significant civilian casualties and the destabilisation of entire regions.

The incident is unlikely to deter Clinton from future visits to the island, where she retains significant institutional goodwill, but it underscores the extent to which public sentiment – particularly among younger demographics and those engaged in pro-Palestinian activism – has shifted in recent years.
headline: “WAR CRIMINAL” – Hillary Clinton heckled in Belfast

text:
The scale of transnational telecommunication fraud has reached a point where no single country, no matter how well-resourced, can tackle it alone. In the years since the pandemic upended daily life and pushed billions more interactions online, criminal syndicates have exploited every seam in the global digital infrastructure. They operate across borders with an ease that would make legitimate businesses envious, yet the international response remains fragmented, hampered by political considerations that have nothing to do with public safety. Taiwan's exclusion from key multilateral forums is one such consideration, and it is costing the world dearly.

The numbers speak for themselves. According to Interpol, losses from cyber-enabled fraud now run into the hundreds of billions of euro annually, with the trend accelerating sharply during and after the Covid-19 pandemic. Lockdowns drove populations online at an unprecedented rate, creating vast new pools of potential victims. Criminal networks, many of them headquartered in Southeast Asia, adapted with remarkable speed. They built industrial-scale scam compounds, trafficked workers to staff them, and targeted victims across continents with sophisticated schemes ranging from romance fraud to cryptocurrency investment scams.

Taiwan has particular expertise in this area, born partly of necessity. For years, Taiwanese citizens were lured or trafficked to operations in Cambodia, Myanmar, and Laos, where they were forced to run fraud schemes targeting victims in East Asia and beyond. Taipei responded with dedicated law enforcement units, advanced digital forensics capabilities, and bilateral cooperation agreements with several countries. Taiwan's Criminal Investigation Bureau has developed some of the most effective tools in the region for tracing the complex money-laundering chains that underpin these operations. Its financial intelligence apparatus has been credited with disrupting networks that stretched across multiple jurisdictions.

Yet Taiwan remains shut out of Interpol, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, and virtually every other multilateral body where the global anti-fraud architecture is being constructed. The reason is entirely political. Beijing insists that Taiwan cannot participate in international organisations in any capacity that might imply statehood, and most governments, including Ireland's, acquiesce to this demand as a matter of diplomatic routine. Whatever one's view on the status of Taiwan — and the position of the Irish Government, like most Western governments, is to acknowledge Beijing's position without formally endorsing it — the practical consequences of this exclusion are becoming harder to justify.

Consider the mechanics of a typical transnational fraud operation. A syndicate based in Myanmar recruits operatives from across Asia. It sets up call centres targeting victims in Europe, North America, and Australia. The proceeds are laundered through shell companies in multiple jurisdictions, converted into cryptocurrency, and dispersed through exchanges that may be registered in yet another set of countries. Disrupting such a network requires real-time intelligence sharing, coordinated law enforcement action, and compatible legal frameworks across every jurisdiction involved. When a territory with 23 million people, a highly developed technology sector, and front-line experience of these very networks is excluded from the table, the entire effort is weakened.

This is not a theoretical concern. There have been documented cases in which investigations stalled because Taiwanese authorities could not share intelligence through formal Interpol channels, or because Taiwan's exclusion from mutual legal assistance frameworks created gaps that criminals exploited.
headline: Taiwan’s participation can strengthen international cooperation to fight transnational telecommunication fraud in the postpandemic era

text:
The Chinese Communist Party is reportedly preparing to appoint a new Catholic bishop without the approval of the Vatican, in what would be a direct violation of a controversial agreement between Beijing and the Holy See that has been renewed twice since it was first signed in 2018.

According to reports in the Italian Catholic press, Chinese authorities are preparing to install a bishop in a diocese without following the process laid out in the provisional agreement, which gives both Rome and Beijing a say in the appointment of Catholic bishops in China. The move, if confirmed, would represent the latest in a series of unilateral actions by the Chinese government that critics say have made a mockery of the deal from the outset.

The agreement, the precise terms of which have never been made public, was hailed by Vatican diplomats as a historic breakthrough that would help to heal the decades-long rift between the underground Catholic Church loyal to Rome and the state-controlled Chinese Patriotic Catholic Association. Pope Francis and his Secretary of State, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, invested significant diplomatic capital in securing the deal, which was renewed in 2020 and again in 2022.

But the arrangement has faced withering criticism from senior churchmen, not least the now-retired Cardinal Joseph Zen, the former Bishop of Hong Kong, who described the agreement at the time as a "complete surrender" to the Communist Party. Cardinal Zen, who was arrested by Hong Kong authorities in 2022 on charges related to a pro-democracy fund, has been one of the most vocal critics of the Vatican's China policy, arguing that it has abandoned faithful Catholics who suffered decades of persecution for their loyalty to Rome.

The reported move has drawn sharp condemnation from Catholic commentators and China watchers. One senior Catholic source described the expected appointment as "a slap in the face" for the Vatican, though others noted that Beijing has violated the spirit and letter of the agreement on multiple occasions already, with relatively muted responses from the Holy See.

Since the deal was first signed, Chinese authorities have reportedly interfered with the appointment process on several occasions, with bishops being installed or moved without proper Vatican approval. In each instance, the Vatican's public response has been notably restrained, leading critics to accuse the Holy See of prioritising the continuation of diplomatic engagement over the defence of persecuted Chinese Catholics.

The situation for Catholics in China remains dire by any objective measure. Members of underground churches who refuse to register with the state-controlled patriotic association continue to face harassment, detention, and the destruction of church property. Crosses have been removed from churches across several provinces, and minors remain banned from attending religious services under Chinese law.

The Vatican's willingness to continue engaging with Beijing despite these ongoing abuses reflects a broader diplomatic strategy pursued under Pope Francis, who has sought to maintain open channels of communication with China even as relations between Beijing and much of the Western world have deteriorated sharply. Vatican officials have argued that dialogue, however imperfect, is preferable to the complete absence of any formal relationship, which was the status quo for decades.

However, patience with this approach appears to be wearing thin, even among those sympathetic to the Vatican's diplomatic aims.
headline: “Slap in the face”: China to reportedly betray Vatican deal

The question is not rhetorical. It demands an answer, and the answer, when it arrives, ought to disturb every person with a functioning conscience.

A report emerged this week detailing the case of a twelve-year-old girl in the United States who underwent a double mastectomy — the surgical removal of both healthy breasts — as part of so-called "gender-affirming care." The surgeon who performed the procedure did so on the basis that the child identified as transgender. The child was twelve. Let that settle for a moment.

We are not talking about a lifesaving intervention to remove cancerous tissue. We are not talking about a procedure carried out on an adult who had spent years in careful psychological assessment. We are talking about the irreversible mutilation of a child who had barely entered puberty, carried out by a medical professional who presumably took an oath to first do no harm.

There was a time, not so very long ago, when the mere suggestion that doctors might perform elective double mastectomies on children would have been dismissed as the fever dream of a conspiracy theorist. Anyone who raised the alarm was told they were exaggerating, engaging in a moral panic, or simply lying. "Nobody is doing surgery on children," we were assured, again and again, by the same activists and media organisations who now celebrate such procedures as compassionate healthcare.

The goalposts have not so much shifted as been launched into orbit.

It is worth remembering that in this country, Ireland, we are not immune to the ideological capture that has overtaken medical institutions elsewhere. The HSE has its own gender identity services. Lobby groups exert enormous pressure on politicians, educators, and clinicians alike. Any medical professional, teacher, or parent who expresses the slightest hesitation about the affirm-at-all-costs model is liable to find themselves denounced as a bigot, reported to professional bodies, or hounded on social media. The chilling effect is real and it is deliberate.

In the United Kingdom, the Cass Review — led by Dr Hilary Cass, one of the most respected paediatricians in these islands — concluded earlier this year that the evidence base for medically transitioning children is remarkably weak. The review found that young people had been let down by a lack of research, a lack of rigorous assessment, and an institutional culture in which ideology had displaced clinical caution. The Tavistock clinic, England's main gender identity service for children, was shut down on the back of its findings.

One would think that a review of this magnitude, conducted just across the water, would prompt serious reflection among Irish policymakers and clinicians. One would think that TDs might raise the matter in the Dáil, that the Minister for Health might commission an equivalent review, that the HSE might pause and take stock. Instead, the response in official Ireland has been something closer to studied silence. The Cass Review has been treated less as a wake-up call and more as an inconvenience to be managed.

This is cowardice, plain and simple.

The activists will say, as they always do, that any questioning of paediatric gender medicine is an attack on trans people. This is manipulative nonsense.
headline: What kind of doctor amputates the breasts of a 12-year-old girl?

text:
Denmark has moved to halt the administration of Covid-19 vaccines for children and young people under the age of 18, in a decision that is likely to reignite debate across Europe about the appropriateness of vaccinating younger age groups against the virus.

The Danish Health Authority confirmed the decision, stating that children and young people are at very low risk of becoming seriously ill from Covid-19 and that the virus no longer poses the kind of threat to younger populations that might justify a general vaccination programme.

The move represents a significant departure from the approach taken by many Western nations, including Ireland, where health authorities had encouraged vaccination across a broad range of age groups throughout the pandemic. The HSE's vaccination programme extended to children aged five and over during the height of the rollout, though uptake among younger cohorts was notably lower than among older age groups.

Denmark has been something of a trailblazer when it comes to scaling back Covid-era measures. It was one of the first countries in Europe to lift all domestic restrictions, and its health authorities have taken an increasingly cautious approach to continued mass vaccination, particularly for demographics considered to be at minimal risk of severe illness.

The decision will undoubtedly fuel questions about whether other European countries, including Ireland, should follow suit. To date, Irish health authorities have not indicated any plans to formally restrict access to vaccines for younger age groups, though the emphasis of the booster programme has long since shifted towards the elderly and those who are immunocompromised.

Critics of ongoing vaccination campaigns for young people have pointed to the diminishing severity of newer variants, the high levels of natural immunity in the population, and concerns about potential side effects, however rare. Proponents argue that vaccines remain a useful tool in reducing transmission and protecting vulnerable individuals through broader population immunity.

The Danish decision is unlikely to be the last word on the matter. As Covid-19 continues its transition from pandemic to endemic status, governments across Europe face difficult questions about where to draw the line on interventions that were once considered essential but are now viewed by many as increasingly disproportionate.

Whether Ireland's National Immunisation Advisory Committee will revisit its own guidance in light of the Danish move remains to be seen, but the direction of travel in Scandinavia is clear.
headline: Denmark halts Covid vaccines for under 18s

The article should reflect Gript's editorial style, which tends toward sceptical, adversarial coverage of progressive policy positions, particularly on abortion, with a focus on accountability and questioning official narratives.

---

An abortion provider who claimed to have been subjected to harassment outside a healthcare facility has failed to produce any tangible evidence to support the allegation, it has emerged.

The claim, which was widely reported and cited by campaigners pushing for the introduction of exclusion zones around facilities where abortions are carried out, was treated as established fact by much of the media and by politicians who used it to bolster the case for legislation restricting protest and prayer near such premises.

However, when pressed for specifics — including dates, locations, the nature of the alleged harassment, and whether any complaint was made to the Gardaí — no concrete details were forthcoming. No Garda report, no CCTV footage, and no corroborating witness testimony have been produced to substantiate the account.

The absence of evidence is particularly notable given the extent to which the claim was deployed in political debate. TDs and Senators referenced alleged harassment of medical professionals during Oireachtas debates on the Health (Termination of Pregnancy Services) (Safe Access Zones) Act, which was signed into law and establishes 100-metre exclusion zones around premises providing abortion services.

Critics of the legislation have long argued that the case for safe access zones was built on anecdote rather than documented evidence, and that existing public order legislation was already sufficient to deal with any genuinely threatening or harassing behaviour. Under current law, the Gardaí have extensive powers to act against harassment, intimidation, and threatening behaviour in public places.

Pro-life groups have consistently maintained that their activities outside hospitals and clinics are peaceful in nature, typically involving silent prayer or the offering of leaflets to women entering premises. They argue that the safe access zone legislation effectively criminalises peaceful assembly, free speech, and the right to pray — rights which are ostensibly protected under the Constitution.

The failure to produce evidence in this instance raises serious questions about the broader narrative that was constructed around the need for exclusion zones. Throughout the legislative process, accounts of alleged intimidation were presented in highly emotive terms, yet the Oireachtas committees examining the Bill heard relatively little testimony that was independently verifiable.

It also raises questions about the role of the media in amplifying claims without subjecting them to basic scrutiny. The original allegation was reported largely without challenge, and the absence of follow-up on whether it was ever substantiated points to a wider pattern in how abortion-related stories are covered in Ireland.

Several TDs who voted against the safe access zone legislation at the time raised concerns that the Bill was being rushed through on the basis of emotion rather than evidence. Those concerns appear, in light of this development, to have been well-founded.

The legislation as enacted provides for criminal penalties — including fines and potential imprisonment — for those found to be in breach of the exclusion zones.
headline: Abortion doctor provides no tangible evidence of harassment claim

text:
Laura Whitmore has had enough, and she wants you to know about it.

The Wicklow-born presenter, who has carved out a remarkably lucrative career in British television largely on the strength of being attractive and willing to turn up, has taken to the airwaves once more to lament the appalling treatment she has suffered at the hands of, well, everyone really.

In a new interview, Whitmore detailed the various slings and arrows that have come her way over the years — the online trolls, the tabloid scrutiny, the unsolicited opinions about her appearance, her career choices, and presumably the thread count of her Egyptian cotton bedsheets. It is, by her account, a relentless campaign of persecution that would make a lesser woman crumble.

One might gently observe that Whitmore chose a career in the public eye. Nobody forced her onto Love Island. Nobody held a gun to her head and demanded she present a programme in which aesthetically blessed young people couple up in a villa for the entertainment of millions. She did that voluntarily, and was compensated handsomely for the trouble.

This is not to say, of course, that anyone deserves genuine abuse. They don't. But there is a growing tendency among celebrities — and Whitmore is far from the only offender — to conflate actual harassment with the ordinary rough-and-tumble of public life. Criticism becomes "hate." Disagreement becomes "toxicity." A less-than-glowing review becomes evidence of systemic misogyny.

It is a rhetorical sleight of hand that serves a very particular purpose: it renders the celebrity permanently beyond reproach. If every negative word spoken about Laura Whitmore is recast as persecution, then no negative word can ever legitimately be spoken about Laura Whitmore. A convenient arrangement, if you can manage it.

The Irish media, predictably, have responded to Whitmore's complaints with the requisite sympathy. Our broadcast and print outlets have long operated on the principle that any Irish person who achieves even modest fame in Britain must be celebrated unconditionally, their every utterance treated as profound, their every grievance validated without scrutiny. It is a curious national habit, this reflexive deference to our exported celebrities, and it speaks to something rather uncomfortable about how we still measure success.

What is particularly tiresome about the Whitmore routine is how perfectly it mirrors a broader cultural trend in which victimhood has become the most valuable currency in public life. The more persecuted you can credibly claim to be, the more insulated you become from accountability. It is a dynamic that plays out across politics, media, and the corporate world, and it is corrosive to honest discourse.

Whitmore earns a reported salary that would make most people in this country weep. She lives a life of extraordinary privilege by any reasonable standard. She has a platform that reaches millions and an industry infrastructure that exists, in large part, to promote and protect her personal brand. If this constitutes persecution, then the word has lost all meaning.

None of which is to suggest that life in the public eye is without genuine difficulty. It plainly isn't.
headline: The persecution of Laura Whitmore

text:
Suicide remains the single biggest killer of young men in Ireland under the age of 25, according to the latest figures, prompting renewed calls for a fundamental overhaul of how the State approaches mental health services for young people.

The statistics, which have been described as "staggering" by mental health advocates, paint a grim picture of a crisis that successive governments have acknowledged but failed to adequately address. While Ireland has made significant strides in reducing road deaths and tackling other public health challenges, the rate at which young men are taking their own lives continues to represent a national emergency that many believe is not being treated as one.

Ireland's suicide rate among young males has consistently tracked above the European average, and the gap shows little sign of narrowing. For every high-profile awareness campaign launched and every pledge made on the floor of the Dáil, families across the country continue to be devastated by losses that experts insist are, in many cases, preventable.

The question of why Irish men in particular are so vulnerable has been the subject of extensive discussion but comparatively little concrete action. Cultural factors, including a lingering reluctance among young men to seek help or discuss emotional difficulties, are frequently cited. But campaigners argue that even when young men do reach out, the services that are supposed to catch them are often simply not there.

Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services, known as CAMHS, have been beset by well-documented problems for years. Waiting lists remain unacceptably long, with thousands of young people left in limbo at the most critical moments of their lives. A damning report into the operation of CAMHS in South Kerry revealed serious failings in the standard of care provided, including inappropriate prescribing of medication to children and adolescents. While that report led to expressions of shock and contrition from politicians, the systemic issues it exposed were far from unique to one region.

The HSE has repeatedly been criticised for its failure to recruit and retain sufficient numbers of mental health professionals, particularly in areas outside Dublin. Rural isolation compounds the problem for many young men who may already feel disconnected from support networks. The closure of local services, the decline of community infrastructure, and the ongoing housing crisis all feed into a broader sense of hopelessness that can prove fatal for those already struggling.

There is also the question of what happens when a young person ages out of CAMHS at 18. The transition to adult mental health services has been described by those who work in the area as a cliff edge rather than a bridge. Young men at a particularly volatile stage of their development can find themselves effectively abandoned by the system at the precise moment when continuity of care is most essential.

Social media and its impact on the mental health of young people is another factor that cannot be ignored. While much of the public conversation around online harms has focused on girls and young women, there is growing evidence that young men are also profoundly affected by the pressures and distortions of online life. Exposure to violent content, the proliferation of nihilistic ideologies targeting disaffected young males, and the replacement of real-world social bonds with shallow digital interactions are all contributing to a mental health landscape that is more treacherous than ever.

Alcohol and substance abuse continue to play a significant role.
headline: Suicide the biggest killer of Irish men under the age of 25

text:
Sweden has become something of a Rorschach test for the great Covid debate. Mention the Scandinavian nation in polite company and you will quickly discover where your interlocutor stands on the defining question of our age: just how much power should governments seize in the name of keeping us safe?

For those of us who watched with mounting alarm as liberal democracies across the West tore up centuries of hard-won civil liberties practically overnight, Sweden offered a tantalising counter-narrative. Here was a country that largely refused to lock down, that kept schools and restaurants and businesses open, that trusted its citizens to behave like adults rather than treating them as wayward children in need of house arrest. And the sky, contrary to the breathless predictions of every bien-pensant commentator from Dublin to Brussels, did not fall.

Now, before the usual suspects begin their ritual denunciations, let us be clear about what the Swedish experience actually showed. It was not a libertarian paradise. There were restrictions. There were recommendations. The Swedish public health authority issued guidance, and Swedes, being Swedes, largely followed it. The point is not that Sweden did nothing. The point is that Sweden did not do what virtually every other Western government did, which was to assume extraordinary, unprecedented powers over the daily lives of its citizens and then act as though this was the most natural thing in the world.

The Irish experience could hardly have been more different. We had, lest anyone forget, one of the longest and most restrictive lockdowns in Europe. We had a five-kilometre travel limit that would have made the architects of the Berlin Wall blush with its pettiness. We had Gardaí setting up checkpoints on country roads to ask people where they were going and why. We had ministers lecturing us from behind podiums about the number of people we were permitted to have in our own homes. We had, in short, one of the most extraordinary expansions of state power in the history of the State, and it happened with remarkably little resistance.

And what did we get for it? The promised land of Zero Covid? Hardly. Ireland's outcomes, when you strip away the self-congratulatory rhetoric that emanated from Government Buildings, were not dramatically different from those of comparable European nations. What we did get was an economy brought to its knees, a mental health crisis of staggering proportions, a generation of children whose educational and social development was stunted, and a political class that discovered it rather enjoyed telling people what to do.

That last point is the one that ought to concern us most. Because the machinery of control, once constructed, is never easily dismantled. The habits of obedience, once cultivated, are not quickly unlearned. And the precedent, once established, is always available for the next emergency — real or manufactured.

Consider how readily the language of lockdown has seeped into other policy areas. We are now routinely told that climate change requires the same kind of emergency response. That misinformation and disinformation require the same kind of state intervention.
headline: Does Sweden show we need a lockdown against the spread of government over-reach?

text:
The Government jet has racked up approximately 125 hours of flight time so far this year, at an estimated cost to the taxpayer of more than half a million euro, new figures have revealed.

The Learjet 45, which is operated by the Air Corps and used to transport senior government ministers and officials on state business, has been in near-constant use since January, according to details released following a parliamentary question.

The figures, which cover the period up to mid-year, suggest the aircraft is on track to match or exceed its usage in recent years, raising fresh questions about whether ministers are making appropriate use of the asset or whether commercial alternatives might offer better value for money.

At an estimated operating cost of roughly €4,000 per flight hour — a figure which accounts for fuel, maintenance, crew costs and other overheads — the 125 hours of logged flight time translates to a bill in the region of €500,000. That figure does not include the broader costs of maintaining the Air Corps fleet or the salaries of the personnel involved in its operation, which are borne by the Department of Defence regardless of how frequently the jet is used.

The Government has long defended the use of the jet on the basis that it allows ministers to attend meetings and summits, particularly in Brussels, without the scheduling constraints and security complications that come with commercial air travel. Ministers have also pointed out that the aircraft can be used for other state purposes, including air ambulance missions and security operations, when it is not being used for ministerial transport.

However, critics argue that many of the journeys undertaken could be completed just as efficiently on commercial flights at a fraction of the cost. A return commercial flight from Dublin to Brussels, for instance, can be booked for as little as a few hundred euro, compared to the thousands it costs to dispatch the Government jet for the same journey.

People Before Profit have previously called for greater transparency around the use of the jet, arguing that taxpayers deserve a full accounting of every journey undertaken, including the names of passengers and the purpose of each trip. Sinn Féin have also raised concerns, with party TDs regularly submitting parliamentary questions seeking detailed breakdowns of the aircraft's usage.

The Department of Defence, which has operational responsibility for the Air Corps fleet, has said that the jet provides a necessary capability for the State and that its use is determined by the Department of the Taoiseach in consultation with other departments.

The Learjet 45, which has been in service for over two decades, has itself been the subject of debate in recent years, with questions raised about whether the ageing aircraft should be replaced. The Government has indicated that a replacement is under consideration as part of a broader review of Air Corps capabilities, though no timeline has been confirmed.

The latest figures are likely to fuel ongoing debate about government spending priorities at a time when the public is being asked to absorb rising costs across housing, health and other essential services.
headline: Government Jet has flown for 125 hours this year, costing half a million

text:
The European Commission is set to propose a digital vaccine certificate system that would allow citizens to travel freely across the bloc in time for the summer holiday season, in a move that has already drawn sharp criticism from civil liberties advocates.

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen confirmed the proposal, which she described as a "Digital Green Certificate," would be presented in the coming weeks and would show whether a person has been vaccinated against Covid-19, received a negative test result, or recovered from the virus.

The certificates would be available in both digital and paper format and would include a QR code to ensure security and authenticity, according to Commission sources. Von der Leyen insisted the system would respect data protection and privacy, though critics have questioned how such guarantees could be meaningfully enforced across twenty-seven member states with varying approaches to civil liberties.

The proposal comes amid intense pressure from southern European member states, particularly Greece and Spain, whose economies are heavily dependent on tourism revenue and have been devastated by successive lockdowns and travel restrictions. Athens has been among the most vocal proponents of the scheme, lobbying fellow member states for months.

However, the plan has exposed deep divisions within the bloc. France and Belgium have expressed reservations, warning that the certificates could create a two-tier society in which unvaccinated citizens — many of whom have simply not yet been offered a jab due to the EU's sluggish rollout — would face effective discrimination.

The concern is far from academic. The EU's vaccination programme has been beset by supply shortages, delivery delays, and contractual disputes with pharmaceutical manufacturers, most notably AstraZeneca. With only a fraction of the bloc's adult population fully vaccinated, the prospect of tying freedom of movement to vaccination status has raised uncomfortable questions about whether the scheme is premature at best, and coercive at worst.

Civil liberties organisations have warned that the certificates represent a dangerous normalisation of health-status documentation as a precondition for the exercise of fundamental rights. Critics have pointed out that what begins as a temporary, emergency measure has a well-documented tendency to become permanent, and that once the infrastructure for digital health passes exists, its scope could easily be expanded beyond its original stated purpose.

There are also practical concerns. Questions remain about whether the certificates would be interoperable across member states, how long vaccine-derived immunity would be recognised, and whether citizens vaccinated with jabs not yet approved by the European Medicines Agency — such as Russia's Sputnik V, which Hungary has already begun administering — would be included.

Here in Ireland, the Government has indicated it would engage with the Commission's proposal, though Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly has previously cautioned against any system that could be seen to create inequalities between vaccinated and unvaccinated citizens. The issue is likely to come before the Dáil as the proposal takes shape, with Sinn Féin and other opposition parties already signalling they will scrutinise the civil liberties implications closely.

The proposal will require the backing of both the European Parliament and member state governments before it can be implemented, and negotiations are expected to be fraught. Proponents argue the system is essential to salvaging what remains of the summer tourism season and restoring free movement across the Schengen area.
headline: EU to propose vaccine passports for summer travel

The average monthly rent in Dublin has now reached almost €2,000, according to the latest figures, underlining the deepening crisis facing tenants across the capital and fuelling renewed criticism of the Government's housing strategy.

The data, which tracks asking rents on new tenancies, shows that the average monthly cost of renting a home in Dublin now stands at €1,979, representing a significant year-on-year increase and placing the capital firmly among the most expensive rental markets in Europe on a cost-to-income basis.

Outside Dublin, rents have also continued to climb sharply, with the national average now well in excess of €1,500 per month. The figures will come as little surprise to renters who have spent years competing for a dwindling supply of available properties, but they nonetheless represent a stark marker of just how far the market has moved beyond the reach of ordinary workers.

The rental crisis has been a defining political issue for the best part of a decade, and successive governments have faced accusations of failing to take the kind of decisive action needed to bring supply to a level that would meaningfully reduce costs. Rent Pressure Zones, introduced to cap annual increases, have been widely criticised as ineffective, not least because they apply only to existing tenancies and do nothing to restrain the price of new lettings entering the market.

Critics have long argued that the Government's overreliance on institutional investors and build-to-rent developments has contributed to inflated rents rather than alleviating them. The concentration of new apartment supply in the hands of large-scale landlords, many of them international funds, has meant that new stock frequently comes onto the market at the very top end of the price range, doing little or nothing for those on average incomes.

Small landlords, meanwhile, have continued to exit the market in significant numbers, citing punitive tax treatment and an increasingly complex regulatory environment as reasons for selling up. Each property sold out of the rental sector further tightens supply and puts additional upward pressure on rents for the remaining stock.

The political response has largely centred on promises to increase housing output, with the Government's Housing for All plan setting ambitious targets for new builds. However, completions have consistently fallen short of what is needed to meet demand, and the planning process continues to be identified as a significant bottleneck by developers and housing bodies alike.

For renters in Dublin, the practical consequences are severe. A couple earning the average industrial wage would now expect to spend well over a third of their combined net income on rent alone, far exceeding the threshold generally considered sustainable. For single renters, the situation is considerably worse, with many forced into house-shares well into their thirties and forties or facing lengthy commutes from more affordable areas outside the capital.

The figures are also likely to intensify the debate around immigration and housing demand. Population growth, driven in significant part by inward migration, has added to pressure on an already overstretched housing stock, and polling consistently shows that voters regard the connection between the two issues as self-evident, even as politicians have been reluctant to address the link directly.

There is little indication that relief is on the horizon.
headline: Average rent now almost €2,000 per month in Dublin

text:
Sir Chris Whitty, England's Chief Medical Officer, has said he expects another wave of Covid-19 infections to hit the United Kingdom by autumn, warning that the virus has not yet settled into a predictable seasonal pattern.

Speaking at a public event in London, Whitty cautioned against complacency, noting that while the worst of the pandemic appears to be behind the UK, the virus continues to circulate and mutate in ways that could yet cause significant disruption to health services.

"I would expect us to have another Covid surge at some point, probably in the autumn or winter," Whitty told attendees, adding that the precise timing and severity remained uncertain. He stressed that the NHS would need to remain vigilant and that booster vaccination campaigns would likely continue to play a role in protecting the most vulnerable.

The remarks come at a time when Covid has largely receded from public consciousness, with few restrictions remaining anywhere in the United Kingdom or Ireland. However, hospitalisations linked to the virus have continued at a low but persistent level throughout the year, and new variants continue to emerge globally.

Whitty's intervention is notable given the degree to which pandemic-era warnings from public health officials have become politically contentious. Critics have accused senior medical figures of overstating risks during the pandemic and enabling lockdown policies that caused enormous economic and social harm, particularly to children and younger people. The UK Covid Inquiry has heard extensive testimony about the decision-making processes behind lockdowns, with sharp disagreements about whether the restrictions were proportionate to the threat.

In Ireland, the pandemic response has similarly come under scrutiny, though no comparable formal inquiry has been established by the Government. Calls from Opposition TDs and civil liberties groups for a full public inquiry into Ireland's handling of the crisis, including prolonged school closures and restrictions on religious worship, have so far been resisted.

The question of how governments should respond to future surges remains politically fraught. While few are advocating a return to lockdowns, there is an ongoing debate about the appropriate level of public health intervention, with some arguing that the infrastructure of emergency powers built during the pandemic has never been fully dismantled.

Whitty himself acknowledged that public tolerance for restrictions had fundamentally changed, and that any future response would need to reflect that reality. He nonetheless maintained that Covid remained a serious public health concern, particularly for the elderly and immunocompromised.

Whether the predicted autumn surge materialises, and how severely it impacts hospitals on both sides of the Irish Sea, will be watched closely by health officials in Ireland, where the HSE continues to grapple with chronic capacity issues in acute hospital settings.
headline: UK CMO expects another Covid surge by autumn

text:
Russia has warned that it will deploy nuclear weapons and hypersonic missiles in its European enclave of Kaliningrad if Sweden and Finland press ahead with their bids to join NATO, in a dramatic escalation of rhetoric that has sent shockwaves through European capitals.

Dmitry Medvedev, the former Russian president who now serves as deputy chairman of the country's Security Council, said Moscow would have no choice but to bolster its military posture in the Baltic region if the two Nordic nations abandon decades of military neutrality. Medvedev, who has increasingly adopted a hawkish public persona since the invasion of Ukraine, described the potential expansion as a direct threat to Russian national security.

The warning comes as both Stockholm and Helsinki appear to be moving rapidly towards formal applications to join the Western military alliance, a seismic shift in European security architecture driven almost entirely by Russia's decision to launch a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February. Public opinion in both countries has swung dramatically in favour of membership, with polls in Finland showing support surging from around 25 per cent to well over 70 per cent in the space of weeks.

Kaliningrad, a Russian territory wedged between NATO members Poland and Lithuania on the Baltic Sea, already hosts significant Russian military assets, including Iskander ballistic missile systems. The region has long been viewed by Western defence analysts as one of the most heavily militarised areas in Europe. The deployment of nuclear-capable weapons there would represent a significant further provocation, though some analysts have noted that Russia is believed to already possess nuclear capability in the exclave.

The Kremlin's threats appear to be having the opposite of their intended effect. Finnish leaders have been remarkably unflinching in their response, with President Sauli Niinistö pointedly telling Moscow that Russia has only itself to blame for the dramatic realignment taking place across northern Europe. Sweden's ruling Social Democrats, who had long resisted any discussion of NATO membership, have also signalled a historic change of position.

The prospect of Finnish and Swedish accession would represent a massive strategic headache for Moscow. Finland shares a 1,340-kilometre border with Russia — the longest of any EU member state — and its accession would more than double NATO's border with Russia. Both countries also bring formidable military capabilities to the table. Finland maintains a wartime strength of some 280,000 troops and one of the largest artillery arsenals in Western Europe, while Sweden possesses a sophisticated defence industry and a capable navy and air force.

NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg has said both countries would be welcomed "with open arms" and that the accession process could be completed swiftly, though Turkey has raised objections related to what it describes as Swedish and Finnish support for Kurdish organisations that Ankara considers terrorist groups.

The broader pattern of Russian nuclear sabre-rattling has been a persistent feature of the conflict since its earliest days. President Vladimir Putin placed Russian nuclear forces on heightened alert in the opening week of the invasion, a move that was widely condemned by Western leaders. Since then, senior Russian officials and state media figures have made repeated references to Russia's nuclear arsenal, in what Western governments have described as reckless and irresponsible behaviour.
headline: Russia threatens to deploy nukes if Sweden & Finland join NATO

text:
The Irish Council for Civil Liberties has warned that proposed government legislation risks creating a "chilling effect on the free expression of opinion," raising serious concerns about the scope and potential impact of the Bill on ordinary citizens and public discourse.

The ICCL, one of the country's most established rights organisations, issued the warning in a detailed submission examining the legislation, arguing that key provisions are vaguely drafted and could sweep up legitimate speech and commentary in their net.

The intervention adds further weight to growing criticism from civil liberties groups, legal academics, and free speech advocates who have argued that the government's approach to the legislation is heavy-handed and poorly calibrated. It also poses a significant challenge to ministers who have insisted the Bill contains adequate safeguards and is narrowly targeted.

The civil liberties body expressed particular concern about the lack of clear and precise definitions within the text, warning that ambiguity in criminal legislation of this nature inevitably produces a chilling effect. When citizens cannot be certain whether their speech or expression falls foul of the law, the ICCL argued, the rational response is self-censorship — a result fundamentally at odds with the principles of a democratic society.

This is a point that critics of the legislation have been making for some time, but it carries additional weight coming from the ICCL, which cannot easily be dismissed as a partisan voice. The organisation has a long track record of advocating for rights across the political spectrum and has historically supported robust anti-discrimination frameworks. That it has seen fit to raise the alarm about this particular piece of legislation is notable.

The concerns echo those raised by a number of TDs in the Dáil who have questioned whether the Bill as drafted would survive a constitutional challenge. Ireland's Constitution provides strong protections for the expression of convictions and opinions under Article 40.6.1, and any legislation that encroaches on those protections must meet a high bar of justification and proportionality.

The government has maintained throughout the legislative process that the Bill is a necessary modernisation of existing law and that it targets only the most egregious forms of harmful content. Ministers have pointed to similar legislative efforts in other EU member states and argued that Ireland risks falling behind its European peers without action.

However, the ICCL's submission suggests that the comparison with other jurisdictions is not as straightforward as government figures have presented it. Different legal traditions, constitutional frameworks, and judicial oversight mechanisms mean that what works in one country may produce very different outcomes in another. Ireland's particular constitutional architecture, the organisation suggested, demands a more carefully tailored approach.

The question of enforcement has also drawn scrutiny. Critics have asked how the provisions would operate in practice, who would make the initial determination that speech has crossed the line from protected expression into criminal territory, and what safeguards exist against politically motivated or vexatious complaints. The ICCL's concerns about vague definitions feed directly into these practical questions. If the boundaries of the offence are unclear to legal experts and civil liberties organisations, there is a legitimate question about how ordinary members of the public — or indeed members of An Garda Síochána tasked with enforcement — are supposed to navigate them.

There is also the broader political context to consider.
headline: ICCL Flags “chilling effect on the free expression of opinion” in Government Bill

text:
Residents of a housing estate in Mulhuddart have expressed shock and dismay after a judge made remarks during a court hearing suggesting that "other agencies" related to children could become involved in their ongoing housing dispute.

The comments were made during proceedings in which the residents are fighting against what they describe as wholly inadequate living conditions in their homes, which they say have been plagued by serious defects including persistent damp, mould, and structural issues that have left families living in misery for years.

Several of the residents, many of whom have young children, told Gript that they were left feeling intimidated by the judge's remarks, which they interpreted as a veiled reference to Tusla, the Child and Family Agency.

"We were absolutely shocked," said one mother who did not wish to be named. "We're in court because we're trying to get proper homes for our children, trying to get the damp and the mould sorted so our kids aren't getting sick, and then to have it suggested that agencies could get involved with our children — it felt like a threat."

Another resident described the comments as "disgusting," saying that the families had been fighting for years simply to have basic repairs carried out and to be housed in conditions fit for human habitation.

"We're the ones advocating for our children here. We're the ones saying this isn't good enough. And somehow we're the ones being made to feel like we're doing something wrong," she said.

The remarks have raised serious concerns among housing campaigners, who argue that the comments reflect a broader pattern of institutional hostility towards families who challenge the State or local authorities on housing conditions.

One activist who has been working with the Mulhuddart residents described the judge's intervention as "chilling" and said it would have a deterrent effect on other families considering legal action over substandard housing.

"These are parents who are doing everything right. They're going through the proper legal channels. They're trying to vindicate their children's rights to a safe and healthy home. To have any suggestion that child protection agencies might become involved because they're living in conditions that the State itself is responsible for — that is an absolute inversion of responsibility," the campaigner said.

The housing issues in the estate have been well documented, with residents reporting that complaints to their local authority and housing body had gone unaddressed for extended periods. Families have described children suffering from respiratory issues and recurring illness which they attribute directly to the persistent damp and mould in their properties.

It is understood that the residents intend to continue with their legal action despite the remarks.

The case highlights ongoing tensions around housing standards in Ireland, particularly in developments that were built during or after the Celtic Tiger era and which have subsequently been found to have significant construction defects. Housing campaigners have long argued that tenants and residents are routinely failed by a system that places the burden on families to pursue legal remedies at their own expense and emotional cost.

Questions have also been raised about whether the judge's comments were appropriate in the context of a housing dispute, with some legal observers noting that remarks from the bench can carry enormous weight and may be perceived as threatening by litigants, particularly those unfamiliar with court proceedings.
headline: Mulhuddart protestors “shocked” as judge says “other agencies” related to children may become involved in housing case

text:
Three successive Taoisigh have refused or failed to respond to requests from victims and survivors of the Glenanne Gang to meet and discuss the campaign of collusion-linked violence that claimed the lives of over 120 people, it has emerged.

Families of those murdered by the notorious cross-border gang, which comprised members of the Ulster Volunteer Force, the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and the British Army's Ulster Defence Regiment, say they have been consistently stonewalled by the highest office in the State despite years of appeals for engagement.

The Glenanne Gang operated primarily in the border counties of Armagh and Tyrone and carried out some of the most devastating atrocities of the Troubles, including the Dublin and Monaghan bombings of May 1974, which killed 34 people — the single greatest loss of life on any day of the conflict. The gang's campaign also extended to attacks in counties Louth, Donegal, and other border areas within this jurisdiction.

Victims' representatives have confirmed that formal requests for meetings were made to Leo Varadkar, Micheál Martin, and current Taoiseach Simon Harris, with none of the three leaders agreeing to sit down with the families. The refusal to engage has been described by campaigners as a continuation of what they see as decades of institutional indifference by the Irish State towards citizens murdered in cross-border collusion attacks.

Edward Barnard, whose family were among those affected by the gang's activities, said the persistent refusal to meet was "a slap in the face" to people who had waited decades for answers. "We are Irish citizens who were murdered on Irish soil, in some cases with the involvement of agents of a foreign state, and our own government won't even meet us," he said.

The Glenanne Gang's activities were extensively documented in a report by the Pat Finucane Centre and the book *Lethal Allies* by Anne Cadwallader, which drew on historical evidence to demonstrate that a significant number of the gang's members were serving members of the British security forces. The evidence of collusion between loyalist paramilitaries and the British state has been acknowledged by multiple investigations and inquiries, yet campaigners argue that the Irish government has never adequately pursued the matter at a diplomatic level.

The issue takes on a renewed urgency in the context of the British government's Legacy Act, which effectively shut down legacy inquests and civil actions related to Troubles-era killings. Victims' groups have argued that the legislation amounts to an amnesty for perpetrators and that the Irish government has a particular obligation to its own citizens who were killed in collusion-linked attacks.

Critics have long questioned why successive Irish governments have been reluctant to press the collusion issue more forcefully with London. The Barron Inquiry, established by the Oireachtas, found evidence of collusion in the Dublin and Monaghan bombings and noted significant failures of cooperation by the British authorities. Despite the inquiry's findings, campaigners say the political follow-through has been negligible.
headline: 3 Taoisigh Have Ignored Requests to Meet with Victims and Survivors of the Glenanne Gang

text:
A seventeen-year-old girl died in hospital after testing positive for Covid-19 on a subsequent swab, having initially returned a negative result upon admission, according to details that have emerged from a review of her case.

The teenager, who had significant underlying health conditions, was admitted to hospital during one of the earlier waves of the pandemic. An initial Covid-19 test carried out at the time of her admission came back negative, but a later swab returned a positive result.

Details surrounding the precise timeline of events, including how long after admission the second test was conducted and the nature of her underlying conditions, remain limited. It is understood that the case was subject to review within the hospital system.

The case raises renewed questions about the reliability of Covid-19 testing during key periods of the pandemic, particularly regarding the sensitivity of PCR and antigen tests and the possibility of false negatives upon hospital admission. Throughout the pandemic, public health officials acknowledged that no test was one hundred per cent accurate and that false negatives could occur, particularly if a swab was taken too early in the course of an infection.

It also raises the question of whether the young woman contracted the virus in the community prior to admission — with the initial test failing to detect it — or whether she may have acquired the infection within the hospital setting itself. Nosocomial transmission, the spread of Covid-19 within healthcare facilities, was a significant and well-documented problem throughout the pandemic in Ireland, particularly during surge periods when hospitals were under severe pressure.

HIQA and the HSE both published reports during the pandemic highlighting concerns about infection control in acute hospital settings. Healthcare-acquired Covid-19 infections were linked to a number of deaths across the hospital system.

The death of a teenager in any circumstances is a tragedy, and the details of this case will likely prompt further scrutiny of the protocols that were in place at the time for testing and infection prevention within the hospital system.
headline: 17 year old girl died in hospital following a positive covid 19 swab after initially testing negative on admission.

text:
Parents from across the country packed a community hall to capacity on Tuesday night to voice their anger and frustration at the content of Relationships and Sexuality Education programmes being delivered in their children's schools, with many demanding greater transparency and parental oversight of what is being taught in the classroom.

The meeting, which was organised by a coalition of concerned parents and family advocacy groups, heard testimony after testimony from mothers and fathers who said they were shocked when they discovered the explicit nature of materials being used in RSE classes, in some cases with children as young as twelve.

One mother, who asked not to be named, told the packed room that her daughter had come home from school "confused and upset" after a class in which content was presented that the parent described as "wholly age-inappropriate." She said that when she contacted the school to raise her concerns, she was told the material was in line with the curriculum and that there was little scope for opting out.

"I couldn't believe what I was looking at when I saw the worksheets," she said. "No reasonable parent would consider this appropriate for a child of that age. And yet we were essentially told to accept it."

Several speakers raised concerns about the influence of external organisations in developing RSE content, questioning whether groups with a particular ideological perspective had been given undue access to the curriculum development process. There were calls for the National Council for Curriculum and Assessment to engage in a more meaningful consultation with parents before rolling out updated programmes.

A father of three from the midlands said that parents had been "deliberately kept in the dark" about what was being taught and accused the Department of Education of treating parental rights as an afterthought. "The Constitution recognises the family as the primary educator of the child," he said. "That is not some throwaway line. It is a fundamental right, and it is being eroded."

The meeting also heard from a secondary school teacher who said that many of her colleagues shared the concerns being raised but felt unable to speak publicly for fear of professional repercussions. She said there was a "chilling effect" on any dissent within the profession and that teachers who raised questions about the suitability of certain materials were made to feel that they were on the wrong side of the conversation.

Organisers said the event had been prompted by a growing awareness among parents of the content of RSE programmes, fuelled in part by material shared on social media. They said they had been inundated with messages from parents across the country who felt they had nowhere to turn with their concerns.

There were repeated calls throughout the evening for the Minister for Education to intervene and to ensure that parents are given a meaningful right to review and, where they see fit, withdraw their children from classes that conflict with their values. Several speakers pointed to the constitutional protection afforded to parental rights in matters of education and argued that the current system was failing to uphold those protections.

Not everyone at the meeting was in full agreement on the path forward, with some parents arguing that comprehensive RSE is necessary but should be delivered in a more age-appropriate manner, while others took the view that the State should have no role in teaching children about sexuality at all. What united the room, however, was a shared conviction that parents had been sidelined and that the current approach lacked adequate transparency.
headline: Packed meeting on explicit RSE course hears parents’ anger and concern

text:
A total of 12,776 people received a Covid-19 vaccine on Tuesday, according to the latest figures from the HSE's vaccination programme.
