The daily update from the health service shows that the rollout continues to gather pace, with the bulk of doses administered through vaccination centres, GP surgeries, and hospital sites around the country.

Of those vaccinated on Tuesday, a significant proportion received their first dose, while others attended for their second jab, completing their initial course of vaccination.

The figures bring the total number of vaccines administered in the State to date closer to the Government's revised targets, though questions remain about whether the pace of delivery will be sufficient to meet the ambitious goals set out by the Taoiseach and the Minister for Health.

The Government has repeatedly stated that the vaccination programme would accelerate significantly once supply issues with manufacturers were resolved, with a target of vaccinating up to 80 per cent of the adult population by the end of June.

However, supply constraints from pharmaceutical companies including AstraZeneca and Johnson & Johnson have caused disruption to the planned schedule on several occasions, forcing the HSE to revise its weekly allocation plans.

The HSE's online registration portal for vaccine appointments has seen strong uptake since its launch, with eligible age cohorts encouraged to register as soon as their group is opened.

Further updates on the programme are expected later this week as the rollout continues to expand to younger age groups.
headline: Vaccine Update: 12,776 vaccinated on Tuesday

text:
Willie O'Dea has called for the immediate removal of mask mandates for school children, describing the continued imposition of face coverings on young pupils as disproportionate and no longer justifiable.

The Limerick City TD and former Minister for Defence said the policy had gone on far too long and was having a tangible negative effect on children's wellbeing, their ability to learn, and their social development.

Speaking to Gript, O'Dea said he had been contacted by a significant number of parents in his constituency who were deeply unhappy with the requirement, particularly for younger children who they felt were bearing an unfair burden of public health restrictions.

"Children have sacrificed enormously throughout this pandemic," O'Dea said. "They gave up school, they gave up their sports, they gave up seeing their friends. And now, when the rest of society is largely moving on, we're still insisting that children as young as nine sit in a classroom all day with a mask on their face. It's not right."

The Fianna Fáil TD pointed out that a number of European countries had already moved to drop mask requirements in schools, and questioned why Ireland appeared to be lagging behind in this regard. He noted that jurisdictions such as the United Kingdom, Denmark, and Sweden had either never imposed such mandates on children or had removed them considerably earlier.

O'Dea also raised concerns about the lack of any clear criteria or timeline from government for when the requirement might be reviewed. He argued that NPHET and the government owed parents a transparent explanation of the evidence base for continuing the policy, particularly in light of the high levels of vaccination and immunity now present in the population.

"What are we waiting for exactly?" he asked. "If not now, when? Parents deserve to know what the metrics are and what has to happen before their children can go to school without a mask. The goalposts keep shifting and people are frustrated."

The intervention is notable given O'Dea's position within Fianna Fáil, one of the three coalition parties in government. It adds to growing pressure from across the political spectrum, with a number of TDs from various parties having raised the issue in the Dáil in recent weeks.

O'Dea rejected the suggestion that questioning mask mandates for children amounted to being anti-public health or dismissive of the virus. He said he had supported the vast majority of restrictions throughout the pandemic and had encouraged his constituents to get vaccinated. However, he insisted there was a difference between proportionate measures and those which had outlived their usefulness.

"Nobody is saying Covid doesn't exist. But we have to be honest about the fact that children are at extremely low risk of serious illness, and we have to weigh the known harms of masking children all day against the uncertain benefits. I don't think that balance is being struck correctly at the moment."

He also criticised what he described as a reluctance within government to have an honest conversation about the issue, suggesting that some politicians were afraid of being labelled as reckless if they questioned any aspect of the restrictions.

"There's a culture of fear around challenging any of these measures, even when the evidence supports doing so.
headline: Willie O’Dea TD: Mask mandates for school children must go

text:
A major study from the United Kingdom has found that rates of depression doubled during lockdown, adding to a growing body of evidence pointing to what researchers are calling a "looming mental health crisis" in the wake of pandemic restrictions.

The study, published in the journal *The Lancet*, tracked tens of thousands of adults across the UK and found that symptoms of depression surged from around 10 per cent of the population before the pandemic to more than 20 per cent during periods of strict lockdown.

Younger adults, women, and those from lower-income households were disproportionately affected, the researchers found, with some subgroups reporting rates of clinically significant depressive symptoms as high as one in three.

The findings will raise uncomfortable questions for governments across Europe, including Ireland, which imposed some of the longest and most stringent lockdown measures on the continent. At various points during 2020 and 2021, Irish restrictions matched or exceeded those in the UK, with the infamous 5km travel limit and prolonged closures of schools, hospitality, and religious services drawing significant public criticism.

Throughout the pandemic, critics of lockdown policy argued that the potential mental health consequences of prolonged isolation and economic disruption were being systematically underweighted in public health decision-making. Proponents of restrictions largely dismissed such concerns at the time, insisting that the priority had to remain the suppression of viral transmission.

The UK study's authors noted that while some recovery in mental health indicators was observed following the easing of restrictions, a significant proportion of those who developed depressive symptoms during lockdowns continued to experience them long after measures were lifted, suggesting the damage may prove lasting.

"This is not simply a case of people feeling a bit down during a difficult period," one of the study's lead researchers said. "We are looking at a clinically meaningful increase in depression that has persisted well beyond the period of restrictions themselves. The long-term implications for health services are very serious."

In Ireland, the HSE has acknowledged rising demand for mental health services in recent years, though it has consistently resisted drawing a direct causal link between lockdown measures and deteriorating mental health outcomes. Waiting lists for psychological and psychiatric services remain lengthy, with some patients waiting over a year to access treatment.

Mental Health Reform, the national coalition on mental health, has repeatedly warned that Ireland's mental health infrastructure was already under-resourced before the pandemic and is now struggling to cope with what it describes as an unprecedented surge in demand.

The question of whether lockdowns caused more harm than they prevented remains one of the most contested debates in public health. Studies such as this one are likely to fuel calls for a full public inquiry into pandemic decision-making — something that several opposition TDs have called for but which the Government has thus far declined to establish.

No comparable large-scale longitudinal study has been conducted in Ireland, a fact that critics say is itself telling, arguing that there has been little political appetite for a rigorous accounting of the collateral damage inflicted by restrictions.
headline: ‘Looming crisis’ as depression DOUBLES in lockdown: UK study

text:
There is something almost perversely enjoyable about watching a writer who died in 1936 become more relevant with each passing year. G.K. Chesterton, the rotund, paradox-loving, cape-wearing English Catholic, has been experiencing a quiet but unmistakable resurgence, and it is not difficult to see why. In an age that prizes ideological conformity and mistakes sloganeering for thought, Chesterton's insistence on actually thinking — and thinking joyfully — feels less like a throwback and more like an act of rebellion.

The revival has been building for some time. New editions of his work continue to appear. His influence is cited by an increasingly eclectic range of writers, commentators and public intellectuals, from the traditionalist right to the distributist left, from devout Catholics to agnostics who simply enjoy a well-turned argument. Online, clips and quotations from Chesterton circulate with a frequency that would have baffled the man himself, who was famously indifferent to fashion and would almost certainly have regarded social media with the same cheerful suspicion he reserved for most expressions of modernity.

What makes Chesterton so attractive to a contemporary audience, particularly one that feels alienated from the dominant assumptions of the age? Part of it is his sheer readability. Chesterton wrote with a kind of exuberant clarity that is vanishingly rare in public discourse today. He could summarise an entire philosophical position in a single epigram and then, in the next paragraph, demolish it with a joke. He wrote with the energy of a man who genuinely enjoyed the contest of ideas, who relished the chance to test his own convictions against the strongest possible objections. That is a quality conspicuously absent from much of what passes for intellectual life in 2024, where the preferred approach is to simply declare one's opponents beyond the pale and move on.

But there is more to the Chesterton revival than style. His ideas themselves have acquired a startling freshness precisely because the world has moved so decisively in the direction he warned against.

Consider his writing on the family. Chesterton defended the ordinary household not as a sentimental relic but as the fundamental unit of liberty, the one institution small enough to be genuinely free and diverse in a way that large bureaucracies and corporations never could be. He saw, long before it became obvious, that the progressive project of liberating the individual from family ties would not produce freedom but a new and more comprehensive dependency on the state and the market. That analysis looks considerably more prescient today than it did even twenty years ago, as rates of loneliness, atomisation, and state dependency climb across the Western world.

Or consider his views on what he called "the servile state" — a phrase he borrowed from his friend Hilaire Belloc but deployed with characteristic vigour. Chesterton argued that the modern world was not moving towards either genuine socialism or genuine freedom but towards a peculiar arrangement in which a small class of owners and managers would effectively administer the lives of everyone else, offering security in exchange for submission.
headline: Back to the future with G.K. Chesterton

text:
The number of hours volunteered at a Dublin-based suicide helpline has more than doubled since the onset of Covid-19 restrictions, as the service struggles to cope with an unprecedented surge in calls from people in crisis.

Volunteers with the service have stepped up dramatically, with many working additional shifts to ensure that no call goes unanswered during what staff describe as the most sustained period of demand they have ever experienced.

The figures, which have not previously been reported, paint a stark picture of the mental health fallout from successive lockdowns, with callers increasingly citing isolation, job losses, and the collapse of normal social supports as factors pushing them towards despair.

Speaking to Gript, one volunteer who asked not to be named said the nature of the calls had changed markedly since March 2020.

"Before Covid, we'd get people who were in long-term crisis. That hasn't gone away. But now we're hearing from people who never imagined they'd be ringing a helpline. People who had jobs, had routines, had lives that functioned. All of that has been pulled away from them."

The revelation raises serious questions about the adequacy of the Government's response to the mental health dimensions of the pandemic. Critics have long argued that the focus on suppressing the virus has come at a devastating cost to the psychological wellbeing of the population, with mental health services already stretched to breaking point before the crisis began.

Minister of State for Mental Health Mary Butler has repeatedly pointed to additional funding allocated in successive budgets, but frontline workers say the money has been slow to translate into tangible supports on the ground.

The HSE's own figures show that waiting lists for psychological and psychiatric services remain stubbornly long, with some patients waiting over a year for an initial appointment. Community mental health teams continue to operate well below recommended staffing levels, a problem that predates the pandemic but has been exacerbated by it.

Meanwhile, the voluntary sector has been left to pick up much of the slack. Organisations that rely heavily on fundraising have seen traditional revenue streams dry up during lockdown, even as demand for their services has surged.

"The State has essentially outsourced a significant portion of its mental health response to the voluntary sector, and then left that sector to fend for itself financially," one advocate told Gript. "It's not sustainable. These volunteers are incredible people, but you cannot run a mental health system on goodwill alone."

The issue has received relatively little attention in the Dáil, where debates on Covid-19 have been dominated by questions of public health restrictions, vaccine rollout, and economic supports. Several TDs have raised the matter, but it has struggled to gain traction in a political environment consumed by the immediate logistics of the pandemic response.

Sinn Féin's health spokesperson David Cullinane has accused the Government of treating mental health as "an afterthought," while People Before Profit TD Richard Boyd Barrett has called for emergency funding to be released to frontline services without delay.

The Government has pointed to measures including the expansion of online counselling services, the provision of a text-based support line, and additional funding for organisations such as Pieta House and the Samaritans.
headline: Dublin suicide helpline volunteers DOUBLE their hours as calls skyrocket amid lockdown

text:
A secondary school in Dublin asked a 13-year-old girl whether she had said anything racist after she was physically assaulted by a black classmate, Gript can reveal.

The girl's mother, who has asked not to be named to protect her daughter's identity, said she was left stunned when the school's response to the violent incident appeared to focus more on whether her daughter might have provoked the attack through some form of racial comment than on the assault itself.

Speaking to Gript, the mother described how her daughter came home from school visibly shaken and with marks on her body after being struck and pushed by another student during a confrontation in the school corridor.

"She was hit, she was pushed into the lockers. She came home in bits," the mother said. "And then when I went into the school to discuss it, one of the first things they asked her was whether she had said anything racist. I couldn't believe it. My daughter was the one who was assaulted."

The mother said her daughter had no prior history of disciplinary issues at the school and had never been accused of making racist remarks. She said the question left her daughter feeling as though she was being treated as the guilty party rather than the victim.

"The message it sent to my child was that somehow she must have deserved it, that there must have been a reason she was attacked. She was 13 years old and she was hit by another student. That should have been the focus."

The mother said that while the other student did receive a short suspension, she felt the school's handling of the matter was wholly inadequate and reflected a culture in which institutions are more afraid of accusations of racism than of addressing violence against children.

"If the roles were reversed, if my daughter had hit this girl, I have no doubt it would have been treated as a serious incident, possibly even a hate crime. But because my daughter was the victim, they wanted to find out if she had somehow caused it."

She said she raised her concerns with the school's principal but felt they were not taken seriously. She has since considered making a formal complaint but said she fears her daughter could face further repercussions.

"You're afraid to speak up because you'll be labelled. That's the environment now. Parents are afraid, teachers are afraid. Everyone is walking on eggshells."

The incident comes amid ongoing public debate about how schools handle issues of discipline, integration, and the competing pressures placed on them by diversity and inclusion policies. Critics have argued that such policies can sometimes create a two-tier system in which certain students are treated more leniently for fear of racial controversy, while others feel they cannot raise legitimate concerns without being accused of bigotry.

Gript contacted the school in question but received no response by the time of publication.

The Department of Education declined to comment on individual cases but said all schools are expected to follow established anti-bullying procedures under the guidelines published in 2013, which require schools to address all forms of bullying behaviour, including physical aggression.
headline: School asked student (13) if she had said anything racist after she was assaulted by black classmate

text:
The woman at the centre of a viral online campaign that has divided opinion across Irish social media has refused to comment when approached by journalists, offering only a terse "no comment" before walking away.

The so-called "SaveKim" saga has dominated online discourse for days, generating thousands of posts across X, TikTok, and Instagram, and drawing commentary from public figures, activists, and ordinary members of the public alike. Yet the woman whose situation sparked the entire furore appears determined to avoid engaging with the media frenzy that has built up around her.

When approached by Gript, the woman declined to answer any questions about the campaign, her circumstances, or the growing public debate her case has generated. She offered no elaboration beyond the two words "no comment" before departing.

The refusal to engage publicly stands in stark contrast to the volume of commentary her case has generated online, where supporters and critics alike have been more than willing to offer their views. The hashtag #SaveKim has trended repeatedly on Irish social media in recent days, with users fiercely debating the merits of the campaign and the circumstances that gave rise to it.

Supporters of the campaign have argued that the woman's situation highlights systemic failures in how the State deals with vulnerable individuals, while critics have questioned the motivations of some of those driving the online campaign, suggesting it has been exploited for political purposes.

Several TDs have been drawn into the controversy, with some calling for official scrutiny of the case and others urging caution about trial-by-social-media dynamics. To date, no formal statement has been issued by any government department in relation to the matter.

The woman's silence may well be understandable given the intensity of the public spotlight that has been trained upon her. However, it also means that much of the narrative surrounding her case continues to be shaped entirely by third parties — many of whom have their own agendas and none of whom appear to have been authorised to speak on her behalf.

What is clear is that the saga shows no signs of dying down any time soon, with or without her participation. The question of who exactly benefits from the continued amplification of the story is one that few of those involved seem inclined to answer either.
headline: “No comment” – woman in SaveKim saga refuses to speak

text:
It has become something of a ritual now. An incident occurs in one of Dublin's most disadvantaged estates, the footage circulates online, and within hours two competing narratives emerge. On one side, people point to antisocial behaviour, lawlessness, and a community that appears to have slipped beyond the reach of the State. On the other, defenders insist that the area is being unfairly stigmatised, that the vast majority of residents are decent people, and that what is really needed is more investment, more services, more amenities.

After the latest events in Cherry Orchard, this pattern has played out with almost mechanical predictability. And once again, the conversation has carefully skirted around the single most important factor in understanding what has gone wrong — not just in Cherry Orchard, but in communities like it across the country.

Let us deal first with the investment question, because it is the one most frequently raised and the one most easily addressed. Cherry Orchard is not a community that has been starved of resources. It has a dedicated community centre. It has sports facilities. It has youth programmes. It has been the beneficiary of successive rounds of government and EU funding aimed at regeneration and social inclusion. DEIS status ensures that its schools receive additional supports. Tusla, the HSE, and various community development organisations all have a presence in the area. By any reasonable measure, the State has not ignored Cherry Orchard.

And yet the problems persist. They persist because amenities, however generously provided, cannot perform the function that intact families perform. A youth club cannot replace a father. A community centre cannot replicate the structure, discipline, and emotional security that a child absorbs, almost by osmosis, in a stable two-parent household. A sports programme that runs for two hours on a Tuesday evening cannot compensate for the other 166 hours in the week during which a child may have no meaningful adult authority or guidance in their life.

This is not a moral judgement. It is a statement of sociological fact, supported by decades of research across multiple countries and across the political spectrum. Children raised in lone-parent households are, on average, more likely to experience poverty, more likely to struggle academically, more likely to encounter the criminal justice system, and more likely to replicate the pattern in the next generation. The research is so overwhelming and so consistent that it would be considered uncontroversial in almost any other context. And yet in Ireland, raising the subject in connection with communities like Cherry Orchard is treated as something close to a hate crime.

The reasons for this silence are not difficult to identify. Ireland's political and media class has absorbed, almost wholesale, a set of assumptions that originated in academic sociology departments and progressive advocacy organisations. Chief among these is the idea that all family structures are equally valid and that to suggest otherwise is to stigmatise lone parents, most of whom are women. The result is that an entire dimension of the problem — arguably the most important dimension — is simply excluded from public discussion.

Consider the language that is typically used when these incidents arise. Commentators speak of "systemic disadvantage" and "structural inequality." Politicians reference "deprivation indices" and pledge additional funding.
headline: Falling down in Cherry Orchard: lots of amenities but few intact families

text:
There is a certain kind of political actor in Ireland for whom the pandemic was not a crisis to be endured but an opportunity to be savoured. And now, as the rest of the country attempts to crawl back towards something resembling normality, these same actors are doing everything in their power to ensure that the emergency mindset never quite goes away.

You can see it in the language they use. Every policy proposal, every ## demand for new spending, every call for expanded state power is still framed in the grammar of crisis. We must act urgently. Lives are at stake. Now is not the time to return to the old ways. The implication is always the same: the lockdown proved that the state could do more, and therefore the state must do more, permanently.

It would be one thing if this were simply an argument about public health. Reasonable people can disagree about the pace at which restrictions should have been lifted, or about the ongoing management of Covid in hospitals and care homes. But that is not really what is going on here. What is going on is something much more ideological, and much more cynical.

For the Irish left — and here we are talking about Sinn Féin, the Social Democrats, People Before Profit, and a significant chunk of the commentariat that populates RTÉ panels and the opinion pages of the Irish Times — the lockdown was a proof of concept. It demonstrated that the government could, if sufficiently motivated, intervene in the economy and in daily life on a scale previously unimaginable. It could pay people to stay at home. It could close businesses by decree. It could restrict movement, suspend civil liberties, and centralise decision-making in the hands of a small number of officials, and the public would broadly accept it.

The lesson the left drew from this was not, as most normal people concluded, that such measures were extraordinary and temporary and came at a devastating cost. The lesson they drew was that the state had finally shown what it was capable of, and that this capacity should never be surrendered.

Consider the debate around housing. The eviction ban introduced during the pandemic was, by any measure, an emergency intervention. It was a response to the fact that people could not work, could not earn, and could not reasonably be expected to find alternative accommodation during a lockdown. It was not designed to be permanent. And yet, when it came time to lift it, the opposition parties howled as though the government were committing an act of cruelty. The assumption underpinning their outrage was revealing: once the state has assumed a power, it should never give it back.

Or consider the Pandemic Unemployment Payment. Again, a necessary and broadly welcome emergency measure. But the speed with which certain quarters began arguing that it should be converted into a permanent universal basic income was remarkable. The crisis had barely begun before the policy entrepreneurs were treating it as a dry run for their preferred model of society — one in which the state is the primary provider, the primary employer, and the primary decision-maker in people's lives.

This is not a conspiracy theory. It is simply an observation about how a certain kind of politics operates. The left has always understood, better than the right, that crises are moments of political opportunity.
headline: The Left wants the Lockdown to be forever

text:
The staggering potential cost of Ireland's climate ambitions has been laid bare in the Dáil, with a TD warning that achieving carbon neutrality could carry a price tag of up to €375 billion.

The figure was raised during a heated exchange on the floor of the chamber, as questions continue to mount over the economic feasibility of the State's legally binding commitment to reach net-zero emissions by 2050.

The claim underscores growing unease among some elected representatives that the full financial implications of Ireland's Climate Action Plan have never been properly communicated to the public, nor subjected to the kind of rigorous cost-benefit analysis that expenditure of such magnitude would ordinarily demand.

Ireland's Climate Action and Low Carbon Development Act, passed in 2021 with cross-party support, committed the country to a 51 per cent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 and to achieving climate neutrality no later than 2050. The legislation was celebrated by environmental groups at the time, but critics have consistently argued that the targets were agreed without adequate consideration of what they would mean for ordinary households, farmers, and businesses.

The cost of retrofitting the national housing stock alone is expected to run into tens of billions of euro, with homeowners facing bills of between €25,000 and €75,000 per dwelling depending on the age and condition of the property. The government's target of retrofitting 500,000 homes to a Building Energy Rating of B2 or better by 2030 has already been acknowledged as extremely challenging, with the pace of delivery falling well short of what is required.

Agriculture, which accounts for roughly a third of Ireland's total emissions, remains a particularly fraught area of the debate. Farmers have expressed deep frustration at what they see as an outsized burden being placed on the sector, with proposals to reduce the national herd drawing fierce opposition in rural communities. The Irish Farmers' Association has repeatedly warned that aggressive emissions targets threaten the viability of family farms and could simply result in food production being displaced to countries with lower environmental standards — a phenomenon known as carbon leakage.

Transport and energy infrastructure represent further areas of enormous expenditure. The planned expansion of renewable energy capacity, including offshore wind, along with the electrification of the vehicle fleet and the overhaul of public transport networks, will require sustained investment on a scale the State has rarely if ever undertaken.

Critics of the government's approach argue that the political class has been unwilling to level with the public about the true costs involved, preferring instead to speak in aspirational terms about green transitions and climate leadership. The concern is that by the time the full bill becomes apparent, it will be too late to change course without incurring significant penalties under EU climate governance frameworks.

Supporters of the climate agenda counter that the cost of inaction would ultimately dwarf the cost of transition, pointing to the increasing frequency of extreme weather events, rising insurance costs, and the long-term economic risks associated with continued dependence on fossil fuels. They also note that much of the required investment would generate economic activity, create employment, and reduce Ireland's exposure to volatile international energy markets.

Nevertheless, the political mood appears to be shifting.
headline: TD: Ireland going carbon neutral could cost €375 billion

text:
A Dáil debate on Irish fishing rights turned heated yesterday as an opposition TD accused the government of having permitted what he described as an "act of piracy" off the Cork coast, in a broadside that drew sharp criticism from the ministerial benches.

The charge was levelled during an exchange on the ongoing difficulties facing Ireland's coastal fishing communities, with the TD claiming that a foreign-registered vessel had been allowed to operate in Irish territorial waters in a manner that was wholly at odds with the rights of Irish fishermen and the State's obligations to protect its own maritime resources.

The deputy, speaking with evident frustration, told the chamber that the incident in question had been brought to his attention by fishermen in the Cork region who had witnessed the vessel's activities first-hand and felt utterly abandoned by the State. He argued that successive governments had shown a pattern of indifference to the sovereignty of Irish waters, dating back to the terms negotiated during accession to the European Economic Community, which he said had left Ireland with a fraction of the fishing rights it ought to enjoy in its own waters.

"What happened off the Cork coast was nothing short of an act of piracy, and this government stood by and allowed it to happen," the TD told the Dáil. He called on the Minister to explain what, if any, action had been taken in response and whether the Naval Service had been deployed to investigate.

The Minister responded by rejecting the characterisation as "inflammatory and unhelpful," insisting that the government takes the protection of Irish waters seriously and that the relevant authorities, including the Naval Service and the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority, were fully empowered to enforce compliance with both Irish and EU regulations.

However, the Minister's response did little to satisfy critics, who pointed out that the Naval Service has been operating at significantly reduced capacity in recent years owing to a well-documented recruitment and retention crisis. Several vessels in the fleet have been unable to put to sea due to a lack of personnel, a situation that has raised serious questions about the State's ability to patrol and police its exclusive economic zone, one of the largest in the European Union.

Industry figures have long argued that Ireland drew the short straw in the Common Fisheries Policy, with quotas that they say are disproportionately unfavourable given the sheer extent of the Irish fishing zone. The frustration in coastal communities has only deepened in recent years as they watch foreign super-trawlers operate in waters they consider their own, while Irish boats are tied to the pier by restrictive quotas and ever-tightening regulations.

The TD said he would be raising the matter again and called for an urgent review of the State's capacity to monitor activity in Irish waters, warning that without action, similar incidents were inevitable. He also called on the government to seek a renegotiation of Ireland's fishing quotas at European level, something that has been repeatedly dismissed as impractical by successive administrations.

It remains to be seen whether the government will provide further detail on the specific incident referenced in the Dáil, or whether, as critics suspect, it will be quietly allowed to fade from the political agenda.
headline: TD says government allowed “act of piracy” off Cork coast

text:
A TD has publicly acknowledged that gang violence is wreaking havoc in Balbriggan, describing a litany of serious criminal incidents including stabbings, arson attacks, and the effective takeover of a local shopping centre by criminal elements.

The admission comes amid growing frustration among residents in the north Dublin town, who say they have been raising the alarm for years about deteriorating conditions in what was once considered a quiet commuter town.

The TD's remarks paint a picture of a community under siege, where ordinary people feel increasingly unsafe going about their daily business. Locals have long complained that the town centre has become a no-go area at certain times, with antisocial behaviour and outright criminality making life unbearable for families and business owners alike.

The reference to a shopping centre being "taken over" will resonate with residents who have spoken repeatedly about groups congregating in commercial areas, intimidating shoppers and staff, and effectively driving footfall away from businesses already struggling in difficult economic conditions.

Balbriggan has experienced significant demographic change over the past two decades, with rapid population growth that many argue was never matched by a corresponding investment in infrastructure, services, or policing resources. Critics have long pointed to the failure of successive governments to adequately resource the area, leaving the Gardaí stretched thin and unable to maintain order.

The stabbings referenced by the TD are part of a broader pattern of knife crime that has alarmed communities across the country, with calls for tougher sentencing and greater Garda visibility repeatedly falling on deaf ears at government level.

Arson attacks, meanwhile, have become an increasingly common feature of life in certain parts of the town, with residents reporting feeling abandoned by the State.

The question now is whether this public acknowledgement by a sitting TD will translate into any meaningful action, or whether it will simply become another entry in the long catalogue of political hand-wringing that has characterised the response to Balbriggan's decline.

Residents will rightly ask why it has taken this long for their elected representatives to say publicly what everyone on the ground has known for years. They will also want to know what concrete steps are being taken to restore order and safety to their community.

The Government has faced sustained criticism for its approach to law and order issues, with opposition figures accusing Ministers of being more concerned with optics than outcomes. The situation in Balbriggan serves as a case study in what happens when rapid population growth is pursued as policy without any of the supporting architecture that communities need to function.

Whether the political establishment is prepared to confront the underlying causes of the mayhem in Balbriggan — rather than simply acknowledging its existence — remains to be seen.
headline: TD admits ‘gang violence’ causing mayhem in Ballbriggan: ‘stabbings, arson, shopping centre taken over’

text:
Iran's theocratic government, not typically a poster child for progressive family policy, has found itself grappling with a problem that would be instantly recognisable to policymakers in Dublin, Seoul, or Rome: nobody is having enough babies.

The Islamic Republic's fertility rate has plummeted from roughly six children per woman in the early 1980s to approximately 1.7 today, well below the 2.1 replacement level needed to maintain a stable population. That is a staggering demographic reversal by any standard, and Tehran is now scrambling to do something about it before the consequences become irreversible.

The Iranian parliament has in recent years rolled out a suite of pro-natalist measures that, stripped of their particular cultural context, could have been lifted from the wish list of any European family advocacy group. These include cash bonuses for newborns, subsidised housing for young married couples, extended maternity leave, and free fertility treatment. Contraceptive programmes that the state itself had enthusiastically promoted in the 1990s have been wound down. President Masoud Pezeshkian has spoken openly about the crisis, framing it in terms of national survival.

The irony is rich, of course. Iran spent decades actively suppressing its birth rate, running one of the most successful state-sponsored family planning campaigns in the developing world. It worked, perhaps too well. Now the regime finds itself in the unenviable position of trying to put the toothpaste back in the tube.

But the broader lesson here is one that transcends Iran's particular circumstances, and it is a lesson that Western governments, Ireland very much included, seem remarkably reluctant to learn.

Demographic decline is not a theoretical problem for the future. It is a concrete, measurable crisis unfolding in real time across the developed and increasingly the developing world. South Korea's fertility rate has cratered to below 0.8. Italy and Japan have been shrinking for years. China, having inflicted the one-child policy on itself for decades, is now watching its population contract at a pace that alarms even its own Communist Party planners.

And Ireland? Our total fertility rate sits at approximately 1.5, a historic low. The CSO's projections make for grim reading. We are, in the demographer's clinical language, not reproducing ourselves. The political class here acknowledges this mostly by implication, through discussions about pension sustainability and migration-driven population growth, rather than by confronting the question head on: why are Irish people having fewer children than they say they want?

Because that is the critical point. Survey after survey, in Ireland and across Europe, shows that the average desired family size remains above two children. People want families. They are simply not having them, or not having them at the size they would prefer. The gap between aspiration and reality is the gap that policy should be attempting to close.

The reasons are well documented. Housing costs in Ireland are punitive, particularly for the young couples who are precisely the cohort most likely to be starting families. Childcare remains extraordinarily expensive by European standards, despite years of government promises.
headline: Baby drought fears prompt introduction of pro-family incentives in Iran

text:
There is a particular kind of story that, when it surfaces, tells you more about the state of a country than any government press release or ministerial speech ever could. This is one of those stories.

A migrant family, newly arrived in Ireland, has been allocated a cost rental home. Cost rental, for those who haven't been following the housing crisis with the devotion of a medieval monk transcribing scripture, is supposed to be the State's answer to the affordability crisis. It is meant to provide below-market rents to working people who earn too much for social housing but too little to avoid being financially destroyed by the private rental market. It was sold to the public as a lifeline for nurses, teachers, guards, young professionals — the people who keep the country running but who cannot, in the Ireland of 2024, afford to live in it.

And yet here we are.

Now, before anyone accuses this column of being animated by hostility to migrants as people, let us be clear about what the objection actually is. The objection is not to the family. The objection is to a system that has become so distorted, so detached from the interests of the people it was ostensibly designed to serve, that it functions as a kind of Willy Wonka government — distributing golden tickets according to a logic that is incomprehensible to ordinary citizens and, when questioned, retreating behind a wall of process and jargon.

The Irish worker who has been on a housing list for a decade, who has watched rents climb past any reasonable threshold of affordability, who has done everything right — paid their taxes, stayed in employment, played by the rules — is entitled to ask a very simple question: how is this possible?

It is possible because the Irish State has constructed an immigration and housing system in which accountability is distributed so widely that it effectively vanishes. No single minister is responsible. No single department is responsible. The Housing Agency will point to the local authority. The local authority will point to the Department. The Department will point to the legislation. The legislation will point to EU directives. And around and around it goes, a bureaucratic carousel that never stops long enough for anyone to be held to account.

This is not an accident. This is design. The entire architecture of Irish governance on these questions has been constructed to ensure that no elected representative ever has to stand in front of a camera and say: "Yes, I made this decision, and here is why." Instead, decisions of enormous consequence — decisions that determine who gets housed and who does not, who gets access to scarce public resources and who is left to fend for themselves — are made in the bowels of a system that is deliberately opaque.

The Taoiseach will tell you, if pressed, that Ireland has obligations. And Ireland does have obligations. No serious person disputes that. But obligations are not a blank cheque, and the social contract is not a one-way street. A government that houses newly arrived migrants in cost rental properties while tens of thousands of Irish workers cannot find an affordable place to live is a government that has lost the plot. It is a government that has confused process with justice, and compliance with competence.
headline: The migrant, the cost rental house, and the Willy Wonka Government

text:
Ireland is now accepting Ukrainian refugees at more than twice the rate of France and the United States on a per capita basis, new figures reveal, placing the country among the most generous nations in the world in terms of its intake relative to population size.

The latest data, compiled from UNHCR and European Commission sources, show that Ireland has taken in approximately 100,000 Ukrainians since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022. For a country of just over five million people, that represents roughly one Ukrainian arrival for every 50 residents.

By contrast, France — with a population of nearly 68 million — has accepted around 65,000 Ukrainian refugees, while the United States, home to over 330 million people, has admitted in the region of 271,000 under its Uniting for Ukraine programme. On a per capita basis, Ireland's intake dwarfs both nations by a factor of more than two.

The figures raise further questions about the sustainability of Ireland's open-door approach to the crisis, which has placed enormous strain on housing, health services, and school places in communities across the country.

The Government has spent billions of euro on accommodation alone, converting hotels, repurposing former institutional buildings, and erecting modular housing units in towns and villages that were given little or no prior consultation. Tented accommodation was even deployed at various points when the system reached breaking point.

Critics have long argued that Ireland is shouldering a disproportionate burden compared to larger and wealthier EU member states, and that the Government has been unwilling to have an honest conversation with the public about the limits of what the State can provide.

Several TDs have raised the issue in the Dáil, pointing out that neighbouring countries with far greater capacity have taken significantly fewer people. There is a growing sense among some elected representatives that Ireland's generosity, while well-intentioned, has come at a tangible cost to Irish citizens who were already on lengthy waiting lists for housing and healthcare before the war began.

Defenders of the Government's position argue that Ireland has a moral obligation to assist those fleeing a war of aggression, and that the country's response has been broadly in line with EU solidarity commitments. The Taoiseach has previously stated that Ireland will continue to meet its international obligations.

However, the comparison with France is particularly striking. As one of the EU's founding members and its second-largest economy, France has the infrastructure and resources to accommodate far greater numbers than it currently does. The United States, meanwhile, despite its vast wealth and landmass, has accepted fewer Ukrainians per head of population than a small island nation on the western edge of Europe.

The issue shows no sign of receding from public debate. Polling consistently indicates that while the Irish public retains broad sympathy for Ukrainian refugees, there is mounting concern about the pace and scale of arrivals and a widespread belief that other countries should be doing more.

With local elections having already demonstrated the potency of the immigration issue at the ballot box, and with the Government continuing to struggle with accommodation capacity, the question of whether Ireland is doing more than its fair share is one that is likely to intensify rather than diminish in the months ahead.
headline: Ireland taking twice as many Ukrainian refugees as France, USA

text:
It was three years ago that Ireland voted to repeal the Eighth Amendment, and the political and media establishment would very much like you to stop thinking about it. The speed with which they moved on was, in itself, revealing. The champagne corks had barely stopped popping on the lawn of Dublin Castle before the same voices were telling us that the debate was over, settled, done. Time to move on. Nothing more to see here.

But some of us haven't moved on, and we don't intend to. Not because we're bitter, or because we can't accept a democratic result, but because we believe the consequences of that vote deserve scrutiny – the kind of scrutiny that Irish media has been almost entirely unwilling to provide.

So here, three years on, are five reasons I remain glad I voted No.

First, because the so-called "hard cases" were a Trojan horse, and everybody now knows it. We were told, relentlessly, that repeal was about fatal foetal abnormalities, about rape, about compassion for women in the most desperate of circumstances. The legislation that followed tells a very different story. Abortion is now available in Ireland on request up to twelve weeks, for any reason or no reason at all. The campaign leaned heavily on the most agonising situations to sell a policy of abortion on demand. Those of us who said this at the time were accused of scaremongering. We were right.

Second, because the promised "rare and safe" regime has proved to be nothing of the sort. The numbers have climbed steadily since the legislation was introduced. In 2019, there were 6,666 abortions carried out under the new law. By any reasonable measure, this is not the cautious, compassionate, restricted regime that was promised to the Irish people. Simon Harris, then the Minister for Health, assured voters that this would be a carefully regulated system. The reality is that Ireland now has an abortion rate that would have been unthinkable a decade ago, and it continues to rise. Nobody in government or media wants to talk about those numbers. I wonder why.

Third, because the three-year review has been entirely predictable. Rather than honestly examining whether the legislation has operated as promised, the review has been dominated by voices calling for further liberalisation – the removal of the three-day waiting period, the extension of gestational limits, the elimination of any remaining safeguards. This was always the trajectory. Those of us who warned that repeal was not an endpoint but a beginning were dismissed as conspiracy theorists. Yet here we are, three years later, and the abortion lobby is already pushing for more. The goalposts haven't just moved; they've been removed from the pitch entirely.

Fourth, because of what repeal revealed about Irish public life and the institutions that are supposed to serve the public interest. The campaign to repeal the Eighth was the most one-sided media campaign in the history of the State. RTÉ, the Irish Times, the Irish Independent, virtually every organ of mainstream media threw its weight behind repeal. Citizens' Assembly members were given presentations that were overwhelmingly weighted towards one side.
headline: Three years after repeal, here’s 5 reasons I’m glad I voted No

text:
A seventeen-year-old girl has lost the sight in one eye after she was viciously attacked in an unprovoked assault that has sent shockwaves through her community.

Alanna Idris Quinn was set upon in what her family have described as a brutal and senseless attack, leaving her with life-changing injuries including the permanent loss of vision in one eye.

The teenager's family have spoken publicly about the devastating impact the assault has had on Alanna, who now faces a lengthy physical and emotional recovery. Photographs shared by the family show the extent of the horrific injuries she sustained, prompting an outpouring of grief and anger on social media.

Gardaí are investigating the circumstances of the attack, though details surrounding the incident remain limited at this stage. It is understood that a number of lines of inquiry are being pursued.

The case has drawn widespread public attention, with many questioning whether enough is being done to tackle violent crime and protect young people on Irish streets. Calls have intensified for tougher sentencing for those convicted of serious assaults, with critics pointing to what they describe as a revolving-door justice system that fails victims.

Speaking about the attack, family members expressed their devastation at what happened to Alanna and called for justice to be served. A fundraising campaign has been established to support the family with the costs of her ongoing medical treatment and rehabilitation, which has already attracted significant donations from members of the public.

The case comes amid growing concern about the prevalence of violent assaults, particularly against young people, with victims and their families frequently expressing frustration at what they perceive as lenient treatment of offenders by the courts.

Anyone with information about the attack is asked to contact their local Garda station or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: Alanna Idris Quinn (17) loses sight in eye after vicious attack

text:
Ashton Pound, the controversial animal pound operator, has been ordered to pay €18,000 in compensation to a former employee who was dismissed after raising concerns about the treatment of animals at the facility.

The decision was handed down by the Workplace Relations Commission following a lengthy hearing into the case, which centred on allegations that the worker was let go in retaliation for reporting what they believed to be instances of animal cruelty and neglect.

The complainant, who had worked at the pound for a number of years, alleged that they had witnessed practices that caused them serious concern regarding animal welfare standards. After raising these issues internally and subsequently with outside bodies, the employee claimed they were subjected to a hostile work environment before ultimately being dismissed.

The WRC adjudicator found that the dismissal constituted penalisation under the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, which is designed to shield workers who raise legitimate concerns about wrongdoing in the workplace from suffering adverse consequences as a result.

In awarding the €18,000 sum, the adjudicator determined that the complainant had made a protected disclosure and that the termination of their employment was directly connected to their decision to speak up about animal welfare concerns.

The case will raise further questions about oversight of animal pound operations in Ireland, a sector that has faced recurring criticism from animal welfare organisations. Campaigners have long argued that the system of contracting out pound services to private operators lacks sufficient transparency and accountability, with inspections often described as inadequate.

Under Irish law, local authorities are responsible for the provision of dog pound services, though many contract these out to private operators. The Dog Breeding Establishments Act 2010 and the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013 set out standards for the care and treatment of animals, with enforcement falling to local authorities and the Department of Agriculture.

Animal welfare groups have frequently called for a centralised, publicly operated model to replace the current patchwork of private contracts, arguing that the profit motive can conflict with the best interests of animals in care.

The ruling serves as a reminder that employees who raise genuine concerns about animal welfare — or indeed any form of wrongdoing — are entitled to legal protection, and that employers who seek to punish whistle-blowers face significant financial consequences.

It is not known whether Ashton Pound intends to appeal the decision.
headline: Ashton Pound ordered to pay €18,000 to animal cruelty whistle-blower

Danny Healy-Rae has called for repeat offenders and those convicted of serious violent crimes to be sent to "isolation or Spike Island," as frustration mounts over what the Kerry TD describes as a revolving door justice system that is failing victims and communities.

Speaking in the Dáil, the Independent TD for Kerry launched a broadside at the current approach to sentencing and prison policy, arguing that too many dangerous criminals are being released back into communities where they continue to terrorise ordinary people.

"They should be sent to isolation or Spike Island," Healy-Rae declared, invoking the infamous Cork harbour island that served as a prison and penal colony for much of the 19th and 20th centuries. The facility, which once housed some of the state's most hardened criminals, was decommissioned as a prison in 2004 and has since been developed as a tourist attraction.

The Kerry TD's remarks come amid growing public concern over violent crime, with a particular focus on repeat offending and what critics see as excessively lenient sentencing by the courts. Healy-Rae has long positioned himself as a voice for rural communities who feel abandoned by the justice system, and his latest intervention will resonate with constituents who have expressed alarm at the prevalence of burglaries, assaults, and antisocial behaviour in their areas.

Healy-Rae pointed to cases where individuals with dozens of previous convictions have been handed suspended sentences or released early from prison, only to go on to commit further offences. He argued that the current system effectively rewards criminality and punishes victims, who are left to live in fear while their attackers walk free.

The call to reopen Spike Island as a prison facility is not entirely new in Irish political discourse. Various politicians and commentators have floated the idea over the years, particularly during periods of heightened public anxiety over crime. However, successive governments have shown no appetite for the proposal, and the Department of Justice has consistently pointed to its investment in modernising the existing prison estate.

The Government has faced sustained criticism from opposition TDs over its handling of law and order issues. Minister for Justice Helen McEntee has defended the Government's record, pointing to increased Garda recruitment targets and new legislation aimed at tackling certain categories of crime. However, critics like Healy-Rae argue that these measures amount to tinkering at the margins while the fundamental problem — a refusal to impose and enforce meaningful sentences — remains unaddressed.

Spike Island, located in Cork harbour, has a long and storied history in the Irish penal system. At various points it housed convicts destined for transportation to Australia, republican prisoners during the War of Independence and Civil War, and ordinary criminals throughout much of the 20th century. Fort Mitchel, as the prison was known, closed its doors almost two decades ago, and the island has since been reimagined as a heritage site, winning multiple tourism awards.

Whether Healy-Rae's call gains any traction remains to be seen.
headline: Danny Healy-Rae: ‘To isolation or Spike Island’

The question is not a complicated one, and yet it is one that the Government seems determined to avoid answering. Where, precisely, is the evidence that vaccine passports actually work to reduce the transmission of Covid-19? Because if such evidence exists, it has not been produced. And if it does not exist, then the entire policy is built on sand.

This week, the Government pressed ahead with its plan to require proof of vaccination or recovery from Covid-19 for access to indoor hospitality. Restaurants and pubs that serve food will be expected to verify the vaccination status of every customer who walks through the door. Staff, many of them young people on minimum wage, will be conscripted into the role of enforcement officers for a public health policy that nobody voted for, nobody was consulted on, and which has divided the country in a manner not seen since the early days of the pandemic.

The Taoiseach has insisted that this is the only way to reopen indoor dining safely. The Tánaiste has described it as a necessary and proportionate measure. Ministers across government have lined up to assure us that this is all being done on the basis of public health advice. But when pressed for the specific evidence underpinning the policy, what we get is waffle, deflection, and appeals to authority rather than data.

Let us be clear about what is being asked. Nobody is questioning whether vaccines work. The evidence that they dramatically reduce severe illness and death is overwhelming and beyond serious dispute. The vaccines are, by any reasonable measure, a triumph of modern science. Getting vaccinated is, for most people, the sensible and responsible thing to do. That is not the issue.

The issue is whether a system of domestic vaccine passports — which by definition creates a two-tier society, dividing citizens into those who may participate in ordinary life and those who may not — is justified by the evidence. That is a separate question entirely, and it deserves a separate answer.

Consider what we know. Vaccinated individuals can still contract Covid-19. They can still transmit it. The viral load carried by a vaccinated person infected with the Delta variant appears to be comparable, at least initially, to that carried by an unvaccinated person. Public Health England data has shown this clearly. The Centres for Disease Control in the United States revised its guidance on masking precisely because of this reality. A venue full of vaccinated people is not, therefore, a venue in which transmission cannot occur. It is simply a venue in which the people present are less likely to become seriously ill if they do contract the virus.

That is an important distinction, and it matters enormously for the logic of vaccine passports. If the purpose of the system is to create Covid-free spaces, it will fail, because vaccinated people can carry and spread the virus. If the purpose is to protect the unvaccinated from themselves, then we are in the territory of coercion rather than public health, and the Government ought to have the honesty to say so.

There is another dimension to this that has received far too little attention. The system as designed will inevitably discriminate against younger people, who through no fault of their own have not yet been offered a vaccine.
headline: Where is the evidence that vaccine passports work?

text:
It is one of the quiet ironies of intellectual history that a man who insisted he was merely transmitting the wisdom of the ancients, rather than creating anything new, should have become one of the most influential thinkers the world has ever produced. Confucius, or Kong Qiu as he was known in his own time, lived in an age of political fragmentation and moral disorder in China some five centuries before Christ. The parallels with our own era are not difficult to draw.

The West has spent the better part of the last century in a sustained project of dismantling its own intellectual and moral inheritance. We have convinced ourselves that the old ways of thinking about virtue, duty, social obligation, and the proper ordering of human relationships are at best quaint and at worst instruments of oppression. In this context, it is worth revisiting what Confucius actually taught, because much of it speaks directly to pathologies we have either refused to diagnose or lack the vocabulary to describe.

At the heart of Confucian thought is the concept of *ren*, often translated as benevolence or humaneness, but which might more accurately be understood as the quality of being fully and properly human. For Confucius, this was not an abstract philosophical category. It was something worked out in the concrete realities of daily life — in how a son related to his father, how a ruler governed his subjects, how a friend treated a friend. The human being, in the Confucian vision, is not an isolated atom of autonomous will, but a person constituted by relationships and the obligations those relationships entail.

This is, of course, deeply unfashionable. The dominant liberal framework in the West conceives of the individual as sovereign, prior to and independent of any unchosen bonds. Rights are the fundamental unit of moral discourse, and freedom is understood almost exclusively in negative terms — as the absence of constraint. The Confucian would find this baffling, and not without reason. A society of radically autonomous individuals, each pursuing their own self-defined conception of the good, is not a society at all. It is, at best, a market, and at worst, a war of all against all dressed up in the language of tolerance.

The Confucian emphasis on filial piety — *xiao* — is perhaps the element most likely to provoke modern Western discomfort. The idea that children owe their parents not merely respect but genuine reverence and obedience strikes the contemporary ear as authoritarian. And yet one might reasonably ask what the alternative has produced. The warehousing of the elderly in nursing homes, the collapse of intergenerational solidarity, the epidemic of loneliness among older people — these are not signs of a civilisation that has improved upon the Confucian model. In Ireland, we once understood something of this instinctively. The family farm passed from father to son. The elderly parent had a place by the fire. That world has largely vanished, and we are not obviously the better for its passing.

Confucius was also deeply concerned with the quality of governance, and here again his insights have a sharpness that cuts across the centuries. He believed that rulers governed primarily by moral example rather than by coercion or bureaucratic management.
headline: The lasting relevance of Confucius

A priest in Italy has died after voluntarily giving up his ventilator to a younger patient who had been struggling with the coronavirus.

Fr Giuseppe Berardelli, 72, had been serving as parish priest in Casnigo, a small town in the province of Bergamo in northern Italy — one of the regions hardest hit by the pandemic. He had been diagnosed with the virus and was being treated in hospital when he made the decision to surrender the breathing apparatus to a younger patient whom he did not know.

The ventilator had reportedly been purchased for him by members of his own parish, who had fundraised to buy the equipment when they learned of his deteriorating condition. Despite their efforts, Fr Berardelli chose to give it away, and he subsequently passed away.

The story has been shared widely on social media and has drawn tributes from across Italy and beyond, with many pointing to the priest's sacrifice as an example of extraordinary selflessness during a crisis that has pushed the Italian healthcare system to breaking point.

Italy has been the worst-affected country in Europe, with the death toll now surpassing that of China, where the virus originated. Hospitals in the Lombardy region, where Bergamo is located, have been overwhelmed, with doctors forced to make agonising decisions about which patients receive treatment and which do not, owing to a chronic shortage of ventilators and intensive care beds.

The situation in Bergamo has been particularly dire. Military trucks were photographed transporting coffins out of the city after its crematorium was unable to cope with the volume of the dead. Local obituary pages, which would normally run to a page or two, have stretched to over ten pages in recent days.

Fr Berardelli's parishioners in Casnigo reportedly applauded from their balconies and windows as his coffin was taken away — the only way they could pay their respects under Italy's strict lockdown rules, which ban public gatherings including funerals.

The priest's sacrifice has resonated particularly strongly among Italy's Catholic communities, where clergy have themselves been heavily affected by the outbreak. A significant number of priests in the Bergamo diocese have died after contracting the virus, many of them elderly men who continued to minister to the sick and dying even as the contagion spread.

Pope Francis has spoken repeatedly about the courage of priests, doctors, and nurses on the frontlines of the pandemic, describing them as "saints next door."

The story comes as governments across Europe, including Ireland, grapple with the challenge of sourcing sufficient ventilators and personal protective equipment to deal with the anticipated surge in cases. The HSE has been working to increase intensive care capacity in Irish hospitals, with the Government placing orders for additional ventilators in recent weeks.

Italy's experience has served as a stark warning to other European countries about the potential consequences of the virus if it is allowed to spread unchecked. As of this week, the country has recorded over 69,000 confirmed cases and more than 6,800 deaths, with the true figures believed to be significantly higher due to limited testing.

Fr Berardelli had served the parish of Casnigo for several years and was described by locals as a devoted and beloved figure in the community.
headline: Priest with Coronavirus gives up his ventilator to a younger patient and dies

text:
Senator Regina Doherty is at it again. The Fine Gael senator and former minister has taken to the airwaves to bemoan the so-called gender pay gap, repeating a claim that has been debunked so thoroughly and so often that its continued circulation in Irish public life amounts to something close to a deliberate deception.

Doherty, who was instrumental in pushing through gender pay gap reporting legislation during her time as Minister for Social Protection, insists that women in Ireland earn less than men for doing the same work. It is a claim that sounds shocking. It is meant to sound shocking. The only problem is that it is not true — at least not in the way it is invariably presented.

The raw gender pay gap — the figure that politicians like Doherty love to cite — simply compares the median earnings of all men with the median earnings of all women across the entire economy. It does not compare like with like. It does not account for hours worked, occupation, sector, experience, career breaks, or any of the myriad factors that actually explain differences in aggregate earnings between the sexes. When those factors are controlled for, the gap shrinks to somewhere between negligible and non-existent. Every serious economist knows this. Many of them have said so publicly. It makes no difference whatsoever to the political class.

This is not a minor methodological quibble. It is the entire ball game. Saying that women earn less than men because of discrimination, based on a raw pay gap figure, is like saying that primary school teachers are discriminated against compared to surgeons because they earn less. It ignores every relevant variable and then attributes the resulting difference to bigotry. It is intellectually dishonest, and the people pushing it either know this and do not care, or have not bothered to examine the claim they are making. Neither possibility reflects well on them.

The reality is that men and women, on average, make different choices. Men are more likely to work longer hours, to choose higher-paying but less pleasant or more dangerous occupations, to commute further, and to take fewer career breaks. Women are more likely to work part-time, to prioritise flexibility, and to take time out of the workforce to raise children. These are not signs of oppression. They are signs of freedom. In a free society, people make different choices, and different choices produce different outcomes. This is not a problem to be solved by government legislation. It is simply life.

But of course, acknowledging this reality does not allow politicians to position themselves as heroic crusaders against injustice. It does not generate headlines. It does not justify new regulations, new bureaucracies, and new compliance burdens on Irish businesses already struggling under the weight of an ever-expanding regulatory state. And so the myth persists, because it is useful.

The gender pay gap reporting regime that Doherty championed, and which is now being rolled out to companies with 50 or more employees, is a case study in performative governance. It forces businesses to publish raw pay gap figures that tell us almost nothing meaningful, but which will inevitably be used to shame those businesses in the press.
headline: Regina Doherty revives feminist pay gap myth

The question would have seemed absurd six months ago. It seems rather less absurd today. Leo Varadkar, once the undisputed master of the political stage, the man who could do no wrong in the eyes of the Dublin media class, is beginning to look distinctly vulnerable. And the whispers within Fine Gael are growing louder.

Let us be clear about what is happening here. Fine Gael's poll numbers have been sliding steadily. The party that once commanded the confidence of a broad swathe of the electorate is now struggling to hold its base together. And increasingly, the finger of blame is being pointed not at policy, not at external circumstances, but at the leader himself.

It is worth remembering that Fine Gael has form when it comes to dispatching leaders who become electoral liabilities. The party is, at its core, a ruthlessly pragmatic outfit. Loyalty counts for something, certainly, but not as much as seats. When backbenchers begin to fear for their seats, sentiment goes out the window rather quickly. Ask Enda Kenny.

The difficulty for Varadkar is that his problems are not confined to one area. The housing crisis continues to deepen, with another generation of young Irish people locked out of home ownership and trapped in a rental market that can only be described as dysfunctional. Immigration policy has become a toxic issue that the Taoiseach has conspicuously failed to get ahead of, lurching between performative announcements and administrative paralysis. The cost of living remains a grinding daily reality for ordinary families, despite government interventions that have amounted to sticking plasters on a gaping wound.

What is perhaps most damaging, however, is the growing perception that Varadkar has simply run out of things to say. The communication skills that once dazzled political correspondents now seem to produce little more than carefully rehearsed talking points and occasionally tone-deaf social media posts. There is a hollowness to the messaging that voters have begun to notice, even if much of the press gallery has been slower on the uptake.

Within the parliamentary party, the mood is uneasy. TDs in constituencies outside the Dublin commuter belt report that the Taoiseach's name comes up on the doorsteps, and not in a good way. There is a sense, articulated privately by more than one Fine Gael elected representative, that the party under Varadkar has become disconnected from the concerns of people in provincial Ireland. The charge is not merely that government policy has failed in this or that area — that is the normal cut and thrust of politics — but that the leadership does not understand, or particularly care about, the lives of people who do not inhabit the same professional-managerial social milieu as the Taoiseach and his inner circle.

This is a devastating charge for a party that has historically drawn much of its strength from rural and small-town Ireland. Fine Gael is not, despite what some of its younger strategists might wish, a socially liberal urban party in the mould of the Liberal Democrats or En Marche. Its base is farmers, small business owners, professionals in market towns, and the respectable middle class of regional cities.
headline: Is Varadkar safe as FG leader?
