Moderna, the pharmaceutical giant which became a household name during the Covid-19 pandemic, has announced it is developing an HIV vaccine using the same mRNA technology that underpinned its coronavirus jab.

The company confirmed that early-stage clinical trials are underway for the experimental vaccine, which aims to train the immune system to produce broadly neutralising antibodies against the virus that causes AIDS. It represents one of the most ambitious applications yet of the mRNA platform, which was thrust into the global spotlight when Moderna and Pfizer-BioNTech rolled out their respective Covid-19 vaccines at unprecedented speed.

HIV has long been considered one of the most difficult targets in vaccine development. Unlike SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes AIDS mutates at an extraordinarily rapid rate and has evolved sophisticated mechanisms to evade the human immune system. Decades of research using conventional vaccine approaches have failed to produce a viable candidate, despite billions of dollars in investment.

Moderna executives have expressed cautious optimism that the flexibility of mRNA technology could succeed where traditional methods have not. The approach works by instructing cells to produce specific proteins that mimic parts of the virus, prompting an immune response without exposing the recipient to the pathogen itself.

However, sceptics have urged caution, noting that the biological challenges posed by HIV are of an entirely different order to those presented by the coronavirus. Several previous HIV vaccine candidates showed initial promise in early trials only to fail at later stages.

The announcement comes at a time when mRNA technology is being explored for a wide range of applications beyond infectious disease, including cancer treatments and therapies for rare genetic conditions. Moderna itself has been investing heavily in expanding its pipeline, partly in an effort to diversify its revenue base as demand for Covid-19 boosters has declined sharply from its pandemic peak.

It also arrives against the backdrop of ongoing public debate about the safety and efficacy of the mRNA Covid-19 vaccines themselves. Critics have pointed to reports of adverse events, including myocarditis, particularly among younger males, and have questioned whether the full risk profile of the technology is yet fully understood. Regulatory agencies in multiple countries have acknowledged these signals whilst maintaining that the benefits of the Covid jabs outweighed the risks for most populations.

The question of whether public trust in mRNA technology has been dented by the controversies surrounding the pandemic-era rollout — and whether that might affect uptake of any future HIV vaccine — remains an open one.

According to UNAIDS, approximately 39 million people worldwide were living with HIV at the end of 2023, with roughly 1.3 million new infections recorded during the year. In Ireland, the HSE's Health Protection Surveillance Centre has reported a broadly stable number of new HIV diagnoses in recent years, though public health officials have emphasised that the virus remains a significant concern, particularly among certain at-risk populations.

Antiretroviral therapies have transformed HIV from a death sentence into a manageable chronic condition for those with access to treatment, and pre-exposure prophylaxis, known as PrEP, has proven highly effective at preventing transmission. A successful vaccine, however, would represent a paradigm shift in the fight against the virus, potentially offering a route to ending the epidemic entirely.
headline: Moderna developing vaccine for HIV using mRNA technology

There is, it must be said, something almost admirably brazen about the whole thing. Leo Varadkar has barely finished clearing out his desk, and already the party machinery has swung into gear to ensure that the coronation of Simon Harris proceeds without so much as a contested vote. The speed of it all should, in itself, give Fine Gael members pause. But it won't, because the party has long since abandoned any pretence that internal democracy matters more than managed transitions.

Let us be clear about what is happening here. Fine Gael, a party that has been in government now for over a decade in various configurations, is about to hand the leadership — and with it the office of Taoiseach — to a man whose primary political skill is appearing on television looking concerned. That is not a throwaway jibe. It is, if you examine his record honestly, the most charitable summary available.

Simon Harris has held a number of senior ministries. He was Minister for Health. He was Minister for Further and Higher Education. In neither role did he distinguish himself with any achievement that anyone can readily name. What he did do, consistently and with great energy, was talk. He talked on Twitter. He talked on Instagram. He talked in scrums outside Leinster House. He has, in fairness, an extraordinary ability to generate the appearance of activity whilst presiding over remarkably little of substance.

His tenure in Health was defined not by reform but by crisis management — and not particularly good crisis management at that. The trolley crisis continued. Waiting lists grew. The National Children's Hospital, which was already becoming a byword for government incompetence, metastasised into the single greatest financial scandal in the history of the State on his watch. Harris's contribution was largely to express concern, announce reviews, and move on before anyone could pin him down on outcomes. It is a strategy that has served him well personally, if not the public.

And this is the fundamental problem. Fine Gael is not choosing Harris because he has a record of delivery. They are choosing him because he is good on camera, because he has cultivated a social media following, and because the alternatives within the parliamentary party are either unwilling to run or insufficiently telegenic. That is not a basis for selecting a Taoiseach. It is a basis for selecting a spokesperson.

The party would do well to remember that the qualities which make a politician popular on social media are not the same qualities which make a leader effective in government. The Dáil is not TikTok. The Cabinet table is not a podcast studio. The decisions that face the next Taoiseach — on housing, on immigration, on the cost of living, on health, on defence — require somebody with the capacity for strategic thinking, for making difficult and unpopular choices, and for following through on commitments even when the cameras have moved on. Nothing in Harris's career suggests he possesses these qualities.

There is also the not insignificant matter of political positioning. Harris has, throughout his career, tacked relentlessly towards whatever he perceives to be the fashionable consensus.
headline: SCALLAN: Fine Gael would be mad to make Simon Harris leader

text:
It is one of those cases that lingers in the mind long after the details have been reported, not because it is exceptional in the annals of crime, but because of what it reveals about how the Irish justice system processes the very worst acts committed by the very youngest offenders.

A boy — and we must call him a boy, because he was fourteen years of age at the time — carried out a brutal rape. The details, as is so often the case, are not for the faint-hearted. The victim will carry the consequences for the rest of her life. There is no sentence a court can impose that will undo what was done to her. Everyone acknowledges this. And yet the question of what happens to the perpetrator matters enormously, because it tells us what kind of society we have decided to be.

He will be released at twenty-one. That is the practical reality of the sentence handed down. By the time most young men are finishing college, starting careers, beginning their adult lives in earnest, this individual will have served his time and will walk back out into the community. He will still be a young man. He will have his whole life ahead of him. His victim, of course, will also have her whole life ahead of her — but it will be a life shaped indelibly by what he chose to do.

Now, there are those who will argue — and they will argue with considerable force and no small amount of legal precedent behind them — that the youth of an offender must be taken into account. That rehabilitation is not merely a nice idea but a legal obligation when dealing with minors. That the Children Act exists for a reason. That locking up a child and throwing away the key is not something a civilised society does. All of this is true, as far as it goes.

But there is a growing sense among ordinary people in this country that the system has lost its balance. That the rights and prospects of the offender have come to weigh so heavily in judicial considerations that the experience of the victim has become almost secondary — a factor to be acknowledged with solemn words from the bench before the business of mitigation gets properly underway.

We have seen it time and again. The careful enumeration of the offender's difficult background. The references to a troubled childhood. The reports from psychologists and social workers attesting to the possibility of change. The quiet, almost bureaucratic, parsing of guidelines and precedent. And at the end of it all, a sentence that leaves victims and their families staring at each other in disbelief.

It is not that any of those individual considerations are wrong. Of course a fourteen-year-old is not the same as a thirty-year-old. Of course the capacity for rehabilitation is greater in a young person. Of course the law must treat children differently from adults. Nobody serious disputes any of this.

What people dispute — and what they are right to dispute — is whether the endpoint of all these considerations is proportionate. Whether a sentence that sees a violent rapist walk free at twenty-one adequately reflects the gravity of what was done. Whether the system, in its anxiety to do right by the offender, has forgotten what justice is supposed to feel like for the person who was offended against.
headline: The boy who brutally raped at 14 will be just 21 when he gets out

The Department of Justice has effectively admitted that it has no idea whether people who enter Ireland on short-stay visas actually leave when those visas expire. That is not a paraphrase. That is not an uncharitable reading. That is, in substance, what the Department has confirmed.

In response to a parliamentary question, the Department acknowledged that it does not routinely track the departure of individuals who arrive on short-stay visas, meaning there is no systematic mechanism in place to determine whether someone who was given permission to stay for 90 days, for example, has in fact departed on day 91 or is still living somewhere in the State.

Let that sink in for a moment. We have a system that processes visa applications, that ## assesses whether someone should be allowed to enter, that stamps passports at airports — and then simply loses interest in what happens next. It is the administrative equivalent of locking the front door while leaving the back door not just unlocked but removed entirely from its hinges.

This would be remarkable in any country. In Ireland, a small island nation with a limited number of entry and exit points, it is extraordinary. We are not talking about a vast land border stretching thousands of kilometres. We are talking about a handful of airports and ports. The idea that we cannot track departures in 2024 is not a resource issue. It is a choice.

And it is a choice that has consequences. Without exit checks, the State has no reliable data on how many people are overstaying their visas. Without that data, it has no reliable estimate of the undocumented population. Without that estimate, it cannot plan services, enforce immigration law, or give the public an honest accounting of who is in the country and on what basis.

This is not, as some will inevitably claim, an argument against immigration. It is an argument against incompetence. Every functioning state has a basic obligation to know, in broad terms, who is within its borders and whether they have a legal right to be there. That is not nativism. That is not xenophobia. That is sovereignty, in its most elementary form.

The political class in Ireland has developed an extraordinary habit of treating any question about immigration enforcement as inherently suspect, as though the mere act of asking whether the system works is itself a form of bigotry. This framing is not only dishonest but actively dangerous, because it provides cover for a level of administrative dysfunction that would be considered scandalous in any other policy area.

Imagine, for instance, if the Revenue Commissioners admitted they had no way of knowing whether people who owed tax had actually paid it. Imagine if the HSE said it had no system for tracking whether patients discharged from hospital had actually left the building. The response would be immediate and furious. Ministers would be hauled before committees. There would be demands for accountability, for reform, for heads to roll.

But when it comes to immigration, different rules apply. The admission that the State does not track visa overstays was met with something close to a collective shrug. A few TDs raised concerns. A handful of journalists noted it.
headline: We don’t have a clue if people leave when visas expire says Department

Hopes are growing that the fragile ceasefire between Israel and Hamas could be extended beyond its initial timeframe, as further hostages held in Gaza were released in exchanges that have brought a measure of relief to families on both sides of the conflict.

The truce, which has seen a pause in the devastating bombardment of the Gaza Strip, has allowed humanitarian aid to flow into the besieged territory, where the United Nations has warned of a catastrophic situation for civilians. In return, Hamas has released hostages taken during its October 7th attack on Israel, while Israel has freed Palestinian prisoners as part of the agreement.

Diplomatic efforts led by Qatar, Egypt and the United States have intensified in recent days, with mediators said to be cautiously optimistic that both parties could agree to a further pause in hostilities. Sources close to the negotiations indicated that discussions were ongoing but that significant obstacles remained, not least the question of how many additional hostages and prisoners would be included in any extended arrangement.

The releases have been closely watched around the world, including in Ireland, where the Government has repeatedly called for a lasting ceasefire and unimpeded access for humanitarian aid. The Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs has urged all parties to use the current pause as a foundation for a more durable peace, reiterating Ireland's longstanding support for a two-state solution.

Families of the remaining hostages have maintained pressure on the Israeli government to prioritise the safe return of their loved ones, with emotional vigils continuing in Tel Aviv. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has faced mounting domestic criticism over his handling of the crisis, with opposition figures arguing that a longer truce would provide the best chance of securing the release of all those still held captive.

In Gaza, residents have used the pause to search for relatives in the rubble, queue for food and water, and attempt to reach hospitals that remain overwhelmed. Health authorities in the territory say that thousands of people have been killed since the conflict began, with vast swathes of infrastructure reduced to ruins.

Aid agencies have warned that even with the truce in place, the humanitarian situation remains dire. Médecins Sans Frontières said its teams on the ground were struggling to cope with the volume of casualties and that medical supplies were running dangerously low.

The Irish humanitarian sector has also been active, with Irish aid organisations calling on the Government to increase its financial support for relief operations in the region. Several Irish NGOs with staff operating in the Middle East have described conditions in Gaza as among the worst they have encountered.

The prospect of an extension has been broadly welcomed by the international community, though analysts have cautioned that the underlying political and military dynamics remain deeply volatile. Any resumption of hostilities would likely see a further escalation in the scale of destruction, with civilians bearing the heaviest burden.

For now, both sides appear to be weighing their options carefully, with the world watching to see whether diplomacy can hold the line.
headline: Hopes for extension of Israel-Hamas truce as more hostages released

text:
A legal challenge has been lodged against the controversial Northern Ireland legacy legislation which effectively grants an amnesty to those involved in Troubles-related killings, it has emerged.

The case, which has been brought before the High Court in Belfast, represents the latest in a series of legal efforts to overturn provisions of the Northern Ireland Troubles (Legacy and Reconciliation) Act, which was passed at Westminster last year despite fierce opposition from victims' groups, political parties across Ireland and Britain, and the Irish Government.

The legislation established the Independent Commission for Reconciliation and Information Recovery (ICRIR) as the sole body for investigating Troubles-related deaths and serious injuries, while shutting down all existing inquests, civil actions and police investigations into incidents during the conflict.

Most controversially, the Act introduced a conditional immunity scheme under which individuals who cooperate with the commission can be granted effective amnesty from prosecution for serious offences, including murder.

The challenge is understood to focus on whether the legislation is compatible with the European Convention on Human Rights, particularly Article 2, which enshrines the right to life and imposes a duty on states to carry out effective investigations into unlawful killings.

Victims' families and their representatives have consistently argued that the legislation denies them access to justice and truth, describing it as an attempt to draw a line under the past without proper accountability.

The Irish Government has been vocal in its opposition to the legislation, with the Tánaiste Micheál Martin previously describing it as "fundamentally flawed" and at odds with the mechanisms agreed under the 2014 Stormont House Agreement. Dublin has indicated it is considering an interstate case against the United Kingdom at the European Court of Human Rights over the matter.

Political parties in Northern Ireland, including Sinn Féin, the SDLP, the DUP and the Alliance Party, have all expressed varying degrees of opposition to the Act, marking a rare moment of cross-community consensus on the issue.

Human rights organisations, including Amnesty International and the Committee on the Administration of Justice, have also condemned the legislation, arguing it undermines the rule of law and sets a dangerous international precedent for dealing with legacy issues in post-conflict societies.

The British Government under former prime minister Rishi Sunak had defended the legislation as a means of providing information to families while allowing society to move forward. However, the incoming Labour government signalled during the general election campaign that it intended to repeal and replace the Act, though a concrete timeline for doing so has yet to be confirmed.

The ICRIR, which is chaired by the former Lord Chief Justice of Northern Ireland Sir Declan Morgan, has begun preliminary work, though its operations have been hampered by the legal uncertainty surrounding the legislation and a widespread refusal by families and victims' groups to engage with it.

The case is expected to be heard in the coming months, with the outcome likely to have significant implications for how Britain addresses legacy issues from the three decades of conflict which claimed more than 3,500 lives.
headline: Legal challenge lodged over controversial Northern Ireland legacy legislation

Rita Ora has revealed she squeezed in a whistle-stop tour of Cork city before taking to the stage at Apple's Hollyhill campus, describing her brief visit to the Rebel County as memorable despite its brevity.

The pop star, who performed at a private event at the tech giant's European headquarters, took to social media to share snaps of herself exploring the streets of Cork, telling fans she wished she had more time to take in the sights.

"Short but sweet Cork," Ora wrote alongside a series of photographs posted to her Instagram account, which showed her strolling through the city centre and posing at several well-known landmarks.

The singer, who has had a string of chart hits including *I Will Never Let You Down* and *Anywhere*, appeared in high spirits as she documented her time in the city, sporting a casual but typically stylish outfit as she took in the local atmosphere.

Apple regularly hosts high-profile musical acts at its Cork campus, which serves as the company's European headquarters and employs thousands of people. The facility in Hollyhill has been a cornerstone of Cork's economy since Apple first established its presence there more than four decades ago, and private performances by major artists have become something of a tradition for staff at the site.

Ora's visit drew a warm reaction from Cork locals on social media, with many expressing delight that the star had taken time to explore the city rather than simply arriving for the gig and departing immediately afterwards. Several fans shared their own encounters with the singer, describing her as friendly and happy to pose for photographs.

The performer has a busy schedule ahead, with touring commitments across Europe in the coming months.
headline: Rita Ora spends 'short' stint exploring Cork ahead of Apple HQ gig

text:
There is a particular kind of grief that attaches itself not merely to what has been lost, but to what was once, however briefly, within reach. Raja Shehadeh knows this grief intimately. The Palestinian lawyer, writer and founder of the human rights organisation Al-Haq has spent the better part of five decades chronicling the slow, systematic erosion of a homeland — not in the language of polemic, but in the quiet, devastating prose of a man who walks his hills and watches them disappear beneath settlements and bypass roads.

When Shehadeh speaks of a time when Palestinians dared to hope for peace, he is not indulging in sentimentality. He is recalling a concrete historical moment — the early 1990s, the Madrid Conference, the Oslo Accords — when it seemed, to many on both sides, that the long nightmare might yield to negotiation, to compromise, to the ordinary dignity of two peoples living side by side. That this hope has not merely faded but been actively dismantled is the central tragedy of our time in the Middle East, and one that the international community, Ireland included, cannot claim ignorance of.

The Oslo years were intoxicating and, as it turned out, deeply misleading. The famous handshake on the White House lawn in September 1993 between Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat suggested a trajectory. A Palestinian Authority would govern, incrementally, over the occupied territories. Final status negotiations would resolve the impossibly thorny questions — Jerusalem, refugees, borders, settlements. The world exhaled. Prize committees reached for their envelopes.

But the trajectory was an illusion, or at best a possibility that required sustained political will and good faith from all parties, and received neither in sufficient measure. The settlement enterprise did not pause during the Oslo years; it accelerated. The number of Israeli settlers in the West Bank roughly doubled between 1993 and 2000. Each new housing unit, each new access road carved through Palestinian agricultural land, was a fact on the ground that made the promised final status agreement geometrically more difficult to achieve. Shehadeh, a property lawyer by training, understood this arithmetic better than most.

What has unfolded since — the collapse of Camp David, the Second Intifada, the separation barrier, the blockade of Gaza, the steady rightward shift in Israeli politics, and now the devastating military campaign in Gaza following the horrific Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023 — is not a sequence of discrete events but a continuum. Each chapter has made the next more extreme, more entrenched, more resistant to resolution. The moderates on both sides, and they do exist, have been progressively marginalised by those who profit, politically or materially, from perpetual conflict.

Ireland has a particular vantage point on this question, and Irish people have, broadly speaking, exercised it with a moral seriousness that does this country credit.
headline: Raja Shehadeh: I remember when Palestinians dared to hope for peace. How did it come to this?

text:
Leo Varadkar has said he does not believe he would have become Taoiseach were it not for the progress made on LGBT rights in the United States, crediting the American civil rights movement with helping to shift attitudes in Ireland.

Speaking during a visit to Washington DC, Mr Varadkar reflected on his own journey as the first openly gay leader of Ireland, saying the cultural influence of the US had been instrumental in changing perceptions both at home and abroad.

"I don't think I'd be here without America's work on LGBT rights," the Fine Gael leader said, pointing to landmark moments such as the legalisation of same-sex marriage by the US Supreme Court in 2015 — the same year Ireland became the first country in the world to introduce marriage equality by popular vote.

Mr Varadkar said the American experience had given courage to campaigners and politicians in Ireland who pushed for legislative change, from the decriminalisation of homosexuality in 1993 to the passage of the Marriage Equality Act.

"When you see progress being made elsewhere, it gives people the confidence that change is possible in their own country," he said. "Ireland has its own proud story to tell on equality, but we didn't get there in isolation."

The remarks come at a time of growing concern among LGBT advocacy groups in the US about a rollback of protections under the current administration. Mr Varadkar did not directly address the political situation in Washington but said Ireland must continue to be "a beacon" for rights and inclusion.

His comments drew a warm response from Irish LGBT organisations. Moninne Griffith, chief executive of BeLonG To Youth Services, said the Taoiseach's acknowledgement of the transatlantic dimension of the equality movement was "hugely significant" and reflected the interconnected nature of the struggle for rights.

However, some opposition TDs were less enthusiastic, suggesting Mr Varadkar's focus on social issues abroad risked distracting from pressing domestic concerns. Sinn Féin's spokesperson on equality said the Government needed to match its rhetoric with action, pointing to delays in implementing hate crime legislation and the slow progress on a ban on conversion practices.

Mr Varadkar has previously spoken about the deeply personal nature of his decision to come out publicly in 2015, ahead of the marriage equality referendum. He has said he wanted to be honest with the Irish public and acknowledged that the timing was influenced by the national conversation around the referendum campaign.

During his time as Taoiseach, Mr Varadkar attended a number of Pride events and was photographed with his partner, Matt Barrett, at official engagements both in Ireland and overseas.

The visit to Washington also included meetings with senior US politicians and Irish-American community leaders, with discussions understood to have covered trade, immigration reform, and the ongoing importance of the transatlantic relationship.

Mr Varadkar is expected to return to Dublin later this week ahead of a busy Dáil schedule, with opposition parties set to press the Government on the cost-of-living crisis and the state of the public health system.
headline: Leo Varadkar: I don't think I'd be here without America’s work on LGBT rights

text:
There was a time when America felt like a promise. Not a political one, though of course it was always that too, but something more personal, more intimate. It was the promise of possibility, of bigness, of a place where you could drive for days and still not reach the edge. I first went when I was nineteen, a summer spent waitressing in Cape Cod with a J1 visa and a head full of notions, and I came home transformed in the way that only nineteen-year-olds can be transformed — utterly, dramatically, and with a conviction that I had seen the future.

My children will never know that America. I don't mean this in the nostalgic, rose-tinted way of someone mourning their own youth. I mean it literally. The country I brought home in my heart, imperfect and complicated as it always was, has become something else entirely.

I was thinking about this last week as I watched yet another news clip from Washington, another executive order signed with the flourish of a man who believes he is writing history rather than unravelling it. My eldest, who is twelve, wandered into the room and watched for a moment. "Why is he allowed to do that?" she asked, and I found I didn't have a good answer. Not because the constitutional mechanics are beyond a twelve-year-old, but because the honest answer — that democratic norms are only as strong as the people willing to defend them — felt too heavy, too frightening, for a Tuesday evening in Cork.

We had been planning a family trip. Orlando, naturally, because when you have three children under thirteen, all roads lead to Disney. My husband had been pricing flights, and the children had been making lists of rides and restaurants with the earnest seriousness that children bring to matters of leisure. But something had shifted in me. I couldn't put my finger on exactly when it happened, but at some point in recent months, the idea of handing over our passports at US immigration began to feel less like a formality and more like a vulnerability.

I know I'm not alone in this. I've had the conversation with friends, at school gates and over kitchen tables, the same uneasy calculus. Is it grand? It's probably grand. But what if it isn't? What if someone looks at your phone? What if you've posted something critical on social media? What if you've written something? I write things for a living. I have opinions, publicly expressed, about the current American administration. There was a time when that would have been entirely unremarkable. Now it feels like a risk factor.

This is what authoritarianism does long before it arrives at your door. It makes you police yourself. It makes you run the calculations of safety in your head before you've even packed a bag. It doesn't need to detain every traveller or turn back every foreign journalist to achieve its effect. It just needs to make you wonder if it might.

The stories have been trickling in for months. The Columbia professor turned back at the airport. The international students with valid visas told they were no longer welcome. The reports of border agents scrolling through travellers' phones, reading their private messages, examining their social media histories.
headline: Jennifer Horgan: My children will never see America as I did

text:
Sinn Féin members have voted on a series of motions at the party's Ard Fheis, including calls to ban hare coursing, legalise cannabis for personal use, and reaffirm the party's long-standing position on political prisoners.

The motions, debated over the weekend, underscored the breadth of policy issues now occupying the party as it seeks to broaden its appeal beyond its traditional base while navigating internal tensions on a number of fronts.

A motion calling for the party to adopt a formal policy of opposing hare coursing and to campaign for a legislative ban on the practice was passed by delegates. Animal welfare campaigners had lobbied Sinn Féin members in the lead-up to the Ard Fheis, arguing that the party was out of step with public opinion on the issue. Hare coursing remains legal in Ireland under licence from the National Parks and Wildlife Service, though it has faced sustained criticism from animal rights organisations and some TDs across the political spectrum.

The debate on cannabis policy also drew significant interest from the floor, with a motion proposing the decriminalisation and regulation of cannabis for personal adult use put before members. Proponents argued that the current prohibitionist approach had failed, pointing to the experience of other jurisdictions that have moved towards regulation. Opponents within the party cautioned that the move could send the wrong message, particularly in communities already grappling with drug-related harm. The motion was ultimately carried, though the party leadership will now face questions on how it intends to translate the policy into a concrete legislative programme.

On the question of political prisoners, delegates reaffirmed the party's position calling for the release of individuals it considers to have been imprisoned in connection with the conflict in the North. The motion, which also referenced broader issues of prisoners' rights and conditions, was passed without significant opposition from the floor, reflecting the enduring significance of the issue within the party's membership.

The Ard Fheis comes at a politically sensitive time for Sinn Féin, which is seeking to rebuild momentum following a disappointing performance in last year's general election. The party's leader, Mary Lou McDonald, used her keynote address to rally members and insist the party remained the most credible alternative to the Government parties.

However, the range of motions debated over the weekend illustrated the challenge facing the leadership in maintaining unity across a membership that spans republican traditionalists and a newer cohort drawn to the party on issues such as housing, the cost of living, and social reform.

The results of the votes are not binding in the sense of compelling the parliamentary party to introduce legislation, but they do shape official Sinn Féin policy and will inform the positions taken by the party's TDs and senators in the Oireachtas in the months ahead.

Government sources indicated they would be watching closely to see whether Sinn Féin moves to table motions or legislation on any of the issues in the Dáil, particularly on cannabis regulation, which remains a divisive topic across the political landscape. A number of Private Members' Bills on the issue have been brought forward by individual TDs and senators in recent years, but none has secured sufficient cross-party support to progress.
headline: Sinn Féin members vote on hare coursing, cannabis, and political prisoners

text:
The word "immigrant" carries different weight depending on where you stand. For those who have made the journey, it is a lived reality, a daily negotiation of belonging and bureaucracy. For those born here, it has become something else entirely — a political football, a talking point, a problem to be solved. The danger now is that a raft of proposed reforms threatens to redefine the very experience of immigration in Ireland, and not necessarily for the better.

I write as someone who has been an immigrant myself. I lived abroad for years, navigated foreign systems, filled out forms in languages I barely spoke, and understood viscerally the vulnerability of being somewhere you have no automatic right to remain. That experience stays with you. It gives you a certain sympathy for the process, and a certain scepticism when governments start talking about making things "fairer" or "more efficient." Those words can mean almost anything.

What is being proposed now — tighter rules around family reunification, more restrictive pathways to residency, enhanced conditionality around welfare supports, and a general political mood that treats immigration as something to be managed rather than welcomed — represents a philosophical shift. It is not simply a matter of tweaking policy. It is an attempt to reshape the social contract between the State and those who come here to build lives.

There was a time, not so very long ago, when Ireland understood immigration from the other side. We were the ones leaving. We were the ones sending letters home, working in bars in Boston and on building sites in London, hoping for a break, hoping not to be noticed by the wrong authorities. That collective memory, which informed so much of our self-image as a compassionate, outward-looking nation, appears to be fading with remarkable speed.

The political calculus is not difficult to understand. The housing crisis has created a zero-sum mentality in which every new arrival is perceived, rightly or wrongly, as competition for an already inadequate supply of homes. Public services are under strain. There is genuine frustration in communities across the country, and that frustration has been exploited by some and ignored for too long by others. The Government, bruised by local election results and rattled by the rise of anti-immigration sentiment, has decided that the path of least resistance runs through restriction.

But there is a difference between addressing legitimate concerns about capacity and infrastructure, and fundamentally altering what it means to arrive in Ireland as a newcomer. The reforms being advanced risk doing the latter while pretending to do the former.

Consider the implications for someone arriving in Ireland today compared with even five years ago. The atmosphere has changed. The political language has hardened. Where once there was at least a rhetorical commitment to integration and inclusion, there is now an emphasis on conditionality, on proving your worth, on earning the right to be here. That shift in tone matters enormously. It filters down through every interaction a person has with the State — at the immigration office, at the social welfare counter, at the school gate.

The Taoiseach and his ministers will insist, as they always do, that Ireland remains a welcoming country. And in many respects it is. The voluntary sector continues to do extraordinary work.
headline: Colin Sheridan: New reforms risk transforming what it means to be an immigrant in Ireland

Activists involved in a humanitarian aid flotilla bound for the Gaza Strip have said that Israeli naval forces have intercepted almost half of the vessels attempting to breach the maritime blockade, raising fresh international concern over the ongoing restrictions on aid reaching the besieged Palestinian territory.

The Freedom Flotilla Coalition, an international grouping of pro-Palestinian organisations, said Israeli warships moved to intercept several of the boats in international waters as they attempted to navigate towards the coast of Gaza, where a devastating humanitarian crisis has deepened amid the ongoing conflict.

The coalition said the Israeli navy had boarded and seized control of a number of the vessels, detaining crew members and activists on board. It was not immediately clear how many people had been detained or whether any injuries had been sustained during the interceptions.

Israel has maintained a naval blockade on Gaza for years, arguing it is necessary to prevent weapons from reaching Hamas, which controls the territory. The blockade has been widely criticised by humanitarian organisations and has been a persistent source of diplomatic tension between Israel and its allies.

The attempted flotilla comes as aid agencies continue to warn of catastrophic conditions in Gaza, where access to food, clean water, medical supplies and fuel has been severely curtailed. The United Nations has repeatedly called for unimpeded humanitarian access to the territory, where the civilian population faces what officials have described as famine-like conditions.

The Irish Government has previously been vocal in its criticism of the blockade and has called for the free flow of humanitarian aid into Gaza. Ireland has long been among the most outspoken EU member states on Palestinian rights, and the issue has frequently been raised in the Dáil.

The Israeli military said it had acted in accordance with international law to enforce the blockade, describing the flotilla as a provocation rather than a genuine humanitarian effort. A spokesperson said the vessels were offered the option of diverting to the Israeli port of Ashdod, where cargo could be inspected before being transferred to Gaza through established land crossings.

Previous attempts to break the blockade by sea have ended in confrontation. In 2010, Israeli commandos boarded the Mavi Marmara, a Turkish-flagged vessel, killing ten activists in an incident that provoked international outrage and severely damaged Israel's relationship with Turkey for years.

Human rights groups have called on the international community to take concrete action to ensure humanitarian aid reaches Gaza without obstruction, warning that the situation on the ground is growing more desperate by the day.
headline: Activists say Israeli navy has intercepted almost half of Gaza aid flotilla

Paul Murphy TD has initiated High Court proceedings seeking to prevent so-called super junior ministers from attending Cabinet meetings, arguing that their presence at the table is unconstitutional.

The People Before Profit–Solidarity TD is challenging the long-standing convention whereby ministers of state are permitted to sit in on Cabinet discussions, a practice that has been a feature of coalition governments for decades as a means of ensuring smaller parties have a voice at the top table.

Mr Murphy contends that Article 28 of the Constitution is clear in limiting Cabinet membership to no more than 15 members, and that the attendance of super junior ministers at meetings effectively circumvents this cap. He argues that allowing ministers of state to participate in Cabinet discussions, even without a formal vote, amounts to an unconstitutional expansion of the Government.

The position of super junior minister has traditionally been used as a bargaining chip in coalition negotiations, offering smaller parties a seat at Cabinet without the need to allocate a full ministerial portfolio. Under the current Government, the arrangement has continued as part of the coalition agreement between Fine Gael, Fianna Fáil and the Green Party.

Speaking outside the Four Courts, Mr Murphy said the case was about "defending the Constitution and ensuring that the Government does not simply get to rewrite the rules to suit coalition arithmetic."

"The Constitution sets a clear limit on the size of Cabinet for good reason. You cannot just work around that by giving people a different title and pretending it is something other than what it is," the Dublin South-West TD said.

He argued that the presence of additional figures at Cabinet creates a situation where the deliberative process is influenced by individuals who have no constitutional mandate to be there, regardless of whether they hold a formal vote.

Legal experts have noted that the case raises significant questions about the boundaries between constitutional text and established political convention. The role of super junior minister has never been subject to a direct legal challenge of this nature, and the outcome could have far-reaching implications for how future coalition governments are structured.

The Government is expected to robustly defend the practice, with sources indicating that legal teams will argue the attendance of ministers of state at Cabinet is an administrative arrangement rather than a constitutional matter, and that their presence does not confer membership of Government as defined under the Constitution.

The arrangement dates back several decades and has been used by successive administrations. Ministers of state who attend Cabinet do not have a vote on decisions but are permitted to contribute to discussions and receive Cabinet papers.

The case has been listed for hearing before the High Court, with a date expected to be confirmed in the coming weeks. Mr Murphy has indicated he will press for the matter to be heard as expeditiously as possible, given what he described as its implications for the proper functioning of Government.

The challenge comes at a politically sensitive time, with the coalition parties already navigating tensions over policy priorities ahead of a general election that must be held by March 2025 at the latest.

Opposition figures have offered mixed reactions to the legal challenge, with some expressing sympathy for the constitutional argument while others questioned whether the courts were the appropriate forum for what is essentially a political dispute.

A Government spokesperson declined to comment in detail on the proceedings, citing the fact that the matter is now before the courts.
headline: Paul Murphy takes High Court case to block super junior ministers from Cabinet meetings

text:
At least 32 Palestinians have been killed while attempting to reach food distribution sites in Gaza, according to Palestinian health officials, in the latest deadly incident to underscore the deepening humanitarian catastrophe engulfing the besieged territory.

Dozens more were reported injured in the incidents, which took place as desperate crowds gathered near aid distribution points in the hope of securing food for their families. Details of the precise circumstances remained contested, with Palestinian officials blaming Israeli forces and Israel offering no immediate comment on the reports.

The killings come amid growing international alarm over the scale of hunger gripping Gaza, where aid agencies have repeatedly warned that famine is either imminent or already taking hold in parts of the strip. The United Nations and several humanitarian organisations have said that the delivery of food and other essential supplies has been severely hampered by ongoing Israeli military operations and restrictions on aid access.

The UN's World Food Programme has described conditions in Gaza as catastrophic, with the vast majority of the population displaced from their homes and reliant on humanitarian assistance that is arriving in quantities far below what is needed. Scenes of large crowds surging towards aid trucks have become grimly routine, with previous such gatherings having ended in bloodshed on multiple occasions throughout the conflict.

The war was triggered by Hamas's attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, in which approximately 1,200 people were killed and some 250 taken hostage. Israel's subsequent military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 45,000 Palestinians, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, figures which do not distinguish between combatants and civilians but which international observers have broadly accepted as credible.

Ireland has been among the most vocal EU member states in calling for an immediate ceasefire and unimpeded humanitarian access to Gaza. Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin has repeatedly condemned the level of civilian casualties and the obstruction of aid deliveries, while Ireland's case at the International Court of Justice supporting South Africa's genocide proceedings against Israel has drawn significant international attention.

Humanitarian workers on the ground have described an increasingly impossible operating environment, with warehouses looted, convoys delayed or denied passage, and distribution points becoming sites of chaos and danger. Several aid workers have themselves been killed during the conflict, prompting some organisations to scale back or suspend operations at various points.

The European Union has called for full compliance with international humanitarian law and for all parties to ensure the safe passage of aid to civilians. However, diplomatic efforts to secure a lasting ceasefire have so far failed to produce a durable agreement, despite intermittent negotiations mediated by Qatar, Egypt and the United States.

Human rights organisations, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, have documented what they describe as a pattern of attacks on or near sites where civilians have congregated to collect food, calling for independent investigations into each incident.

The latest deaths are likely to intensify pressure on the international community to take more decisive action to address both the immediate crisis and the broader conflict, with further emergency discussions expected at the UN Security Council in the coming days.
headline: 32 Palestinians killed ‘while trying to reach food distribution sites in Gaza’

The Government must do more to help middle-income earners navigate the growing number of barriers preventing them from purchasing their first home, the country's leading auctioneering body has urged.

The Institute of Professional Auctioneers and Valuers (IPAV) has called for a suite of targeted measures in Budget 2025 to assist average earners who find themselves locked out of the housing market despite being in steady employment.

IPAV chief executive Pat Davitt said that while significant progress has been made in increasing housing supply, a range of "impediments" continue to frustrate would-be buyers who earn too much to qualify for social housing supports but too little to compete in an increasingly expensive market.

"These are people who are working hard, paying their taxes, and doing everything right, yet they simply cannot get on the property ladder," Mr Davitt said. "The Government needs to recognise that there is a squeezed middle out there who are being left behind."

Among the measures being sought by the organisation is an extension and enhancement of the Help to Buy scheme, which provides tax rebates for first-time buyers purchasing newly built homes. IPAV has also called for a review of the Central Bank's mortgage lending rules, arguing that the current income multiples do not adequately reflect the reality of elevated property prices, particularly in Dublin and other urban centres.

The body has pointed to stamp duty, legal costs, and other transaction expenses as additional hurdles that disproportionately affect first-time buyers operating at the margins of affordability. IPAV suggested that targeted stamp duty relief for purchasers below a certain income threshold could make a meaningful difference.

The calls come against a backdrop of continued house price growth nationally. According to the latest CSO figures, residential property prices have risen by more than 8% year on year, with prices in many parts of the country now exceeding their Celtic Tiger peaks.

Mr Davitt acknowledged that the Housing for All plan has delivered improvements in planning and construction output but argued that supply alone will not resolve the affordability crisis facing ordinary workers.

"Building more homes is essential, but it is only one part of the equation," he said. "If the people these homes are intended for cannot afford to buy them, then we have a fundamental problem that requires a policy response."

The organisation also highlighted regional disparities, noting that while affordability pressures are most acute in the capital, buyers in cities such as Cork, Galway, and Limerick are increasingly encountering similar difficulties. IPAV said that greater investment in regional infrastructure and transport links would help to spread demand more evenly and open up more affordable locations for commuters.

Minister for Housing Darragh O'Brien has previously signalled that the Government remains committed to supporting homeownership and would consider further interventions where necessary. However, opposition TDs have accused the Coalition of failing to act with sufficient urgency, with Sinn Féin housing spokesperson Eoin Ó Broin describing the current situation as "untenable for an entire generation of workers."

IPAV said it would be making a formal pre-budget submission to the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage in the coming weeks, outlining its proposals in detail.
headline: Government must help average earners overcome 'impediments' to homebuying, say auctioneers

text:
There's a moment early in *Kneecap* where you realise this isn't going to be your typical music biopic. It's too irreverent, too furious, too funny, and far too alive with the chaotic energy of its subjects to settle into the comfortable rhythms of the genre. I walked out of the cinema buzzing, and I haven't stopped thinking about it since.

I should say upfront that I came to the film as a fan of the band, but not a devotee. I knew the broad strokes — three lads from west Belfast rapping in Irish, winding up loyalists, getting into trouble — but I hadn't followed every twist and turn of their story. That turned out to be the perfect vantage point, because the film, directed by Rich Peppiatt, manages to be both a love letter to its protagonists and something much more ambitious than that.

What strikes you first is the sheer velocity of it. The film moves like the band's music — relentless, stacked with layers, switching between Irish and English with the fluidity of people who genuinely live between two languages. The subtitles become part of the comedy, part of the storytelling, and there's a playfulness to the whole enterprise that feels genuinely fresh. When was the last time a film about music in these islands felt this dangerous and this entertaining at the same time?

Móglaí Bap, Mo Chara and DJ Próvaí play themselves, and they're magnetic. There was always a risk that putting the actual band members in front of the camera would feel stilted or self-conscious, but they inhabit the screen with a naturalism that would shame many professional actors. Michael Fassbender, meanwhile, is quietly superb as Arlo, the fictional schoolteacher who becomes the group's unlikely Irish language mentor and whose own past catches up with him in ways I won't spoil here.

The film has already drawn predictable controversy, of course. There are those who see Kneecap — the band and now the film — as glorifying the IRA, and it would be disingenuous to pretend the film doesn't engage with republican politics. But reducing it to that reading misses the point entirely. This is a film about language as resistance, about a generation in the North who inherited a peace they didn't negotiate and a cultural identity that powerful forces spent decades trying to extinguish. The Irish language scenes aren't window dressing. They're the beating heart of the thing.

What Peppiatt has pulled off is remarkable. He's made a film that functions as a comedy, a thriller, a coming-of-age story and a genuine piece of social commentary, all without ever feeling like it's trying too hard. The Belfast it depicts is messy and real — not the sanitised, mural-tour version, but a city of house parties and police raids, of grief and gallows humour, of people getting on with it in spite of everything.

There's a line in the film — "Every word of Irish spoken is a bullet fired for Irish freedom" — that could easily have landed as preachy or overwrought.
headline: Tom Dunne: Here's why Kneecap is already my favourite film of the year

text:
Tens of thousands of Oasis fans descended on Cardiff's Principality Stadium last night for the Gallagher brothers' long-awaited reunion, with some devotees travelling from as far as Australia to witness the band's first live performance in 16 years.

The scenes outside the venue were electric from early afternoon, as fans old and new gathered in the Welsh capital wearing bucket hats and parkas, many clutching pints and singing Wonderwall and Don't Look Back in Anger long before the doors had even opened. For a band whose acrimonious split in 2009 seemed utterly irreversible, the atmosphere carried a sense of the surreal.

Among those in the crowd were Irish fans who had missed out on tickets for the band's sold-out Croke Park dates later this summer and decided Cardiff was the next best thing. Several had travelled from Dublin, Cork and Galway, with some describing the reunion as a once-in-a-lifetime event they simply could not afford to miss.

But the prize for dedication surely went to fans who had flown in from Australia and New Zealand, with one group from Melbourne telling reporters they had booked flights within minutes of the reunion being announced last August.

The road to reunion has been anything but smooth. When Noel Gallagher walked out of a Paris dressing room in August 2009, declaring he "simply could not go on working with Liam a day longer," few believed the brothers would ever share a stage again. Years of public sniping on social media and in interviews only cemented that view.

Yet the announcement last summer that Oasis would reform for a series of stadium dates across Britain and Ireland sparked a frenzy of excitement — and controversy. The scramble for tickets became a national talking point, with dynamic pricing on Ticketmaster pushing some face-value tickets well beyond €400 and leaving fans furious. The debacle prompted the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission in Ireland and its UK counterpart to examine ticketing practices, and contributed to broader political pressure around the regulation of dynamic pricing for live events.

None of that rancour was evident last night, however, as the band took to the stage. Early reports from inside the stadium suggested Liam Gallagher's voice, a subject of considerable speculation in the build-up, held up well across a setlist heavy on the classics from Definitely Maybe and (What's the Story) Morning Glory?.

For the many Irish fans present, the countdown now begins to the Croke Park concerts, which are expected to draw more than 160,000 people across multiple nights. Dublin's hotel and hospitality sector is already bracing for a significant economic boost, with accommodation in the capital reportedly close to fully booked for the gig weekends.

Whether the Gallagher brothers can sustain their truce for the duration of a world tour remains the question on every fan's lips. But for one night in Cardiff at least, all the old feuds were forgotten, and it was just about the music.
headline: Oasis fans travel from Australia for band’s first gig in 16 years

text:
Mary Crilly, one of Ireland's most prominent campaigners against sexual violence, has announced she is to retire from her role at the Sexual Violence Centre in Cork, bringing to a close more than three decades of tireless advocacy for survivors of rape and sexual assault.

Ms Crilly, who has been the face of the centre since the early 1990s, confirmed she will step down from her position as director but was quick to emphasise that her retirement from the organisation does not signal a retreat from public life.

"I will continue to campaign and to speak out," she said. "There is still so much work to be done. The issues haven't gone away, and neither will I."

Under her stewardship, the Sexual Violence Centre on Camden Place grew from a small, under-resourced service into one of the most recognised support organisations in the country. Ms Crilly became a household name through her willingness to speak plainly and publicly about issues many found difficult to confront, from the treatment of complainants in the courts to the prevalence of domestic and sexual abuse in Irish society.

Her forthright approach occasionally put her at odds with the establishment, but she earned widespread respect across the political spectrum and among frontline service providers. She was a vocal critic of how the justice system treated victims of sexual crime and campaigned relentlessly for reform of the courts process, better Garda training, and improved access to therapeutic supports.

Throughout her career, Ms Crilly was instrumental in pushing sexual violence to the centre of public discourse in Ireland, long before movements such as #MeToo brought the conversation into the global mainstream. She worked closely with successive governments and appeared before Oireachtas committees to argue for legislative and policy changes.

Tributes have been pouring in from across the political divide and from organisations working in the sector. Many credited Ms Crilly with fundamentally changing how Ireland responds to sexual violence and with giving a voice to thousands of survivors who felt they had none.

The Sexual Violence Centre provides counselling, support, and accompaniment services to people who have experienced sexual violence in the Cork region. The organisation said it would continue to build on the foundations Ms Crilly had laid and that her legacy would endure in the work carried out every day at the centre.

Ms Crilly said she was proud of what had been achieved but remained frustrated at the pace of change.

"We have come a long way, but when I look at the statistics, when I listen to the people who come through our doors, I know we are nowhere near where we need to be," she said. "Attitudes have shifted, yes, but the system still fails too many people."

She expressed particular concern about the ongoing delays in the justice system, the attrition rate in sexual violence cases, and the lack of sufficient funding for frontline services, issues she said she would continue to raise in her retirement.
headline: Mary Crilly to retire from Sexual Violence Centre Cork but says she will continue campaigning

text:
Every June, the coastal town of Dungarvan transforms into a paradise for food lovers, and this year's Waterford Festival of Food promises to be no exception. Now firmly established as one of the premier culinary events on the Irish calendar, the festival draws thousands of visitors to the Déise each year, filling the streets with the aromas of freshly baked sourdough, locally smoked fish, and artisan cheeses that have put this corner of the southeast firmly on the gastronomic map.

What began as a modest celebration of local produce has grown into a sprawling weekend-long affair that takes over the town centre, the harbour area, and seemingly every available square metre of Dungarvan's charming streetscape. It is a testament to the depth of food talent in the region that the festival continues to attract not only loyal regulars but a growing cohort of first-time visitors eager to discover what all the fuss is about.

And there is plenty to fuss about. Waterford's food credentials are formidable. The county is home to some of Ireland's most respected artisan producers, from the celebrated Knockanore Farmhouse Cheese to the Barron family's Eunice Power Foods, and from the craft brewers at Metalman Brewing to the sea salt harvesters working the copper coast. Dungarvan itself punches well above its weight, boasting a concentration of quality restaurants, cafés, and delis that would be the envy of towns twice its size.

The festival programme typically features a mix of cookery demonstrations, tasting trails, foraging walks, and masterclasses, with some of the biggest names in Irish food making appearances alongside passionate local producers who are the backbone of the event. Previous years have seen the likes of Darina Allen, Rory O'Connell, and Catherine Fulvio take to the demonstration stages, but it is often the lesser-known artisans – the woman perfecting her chutney recipe over decades, the young farmer experimenting with heritage grain varieties – who provide the most memorable encounters.

The tasting trail remains the festival's beating heart. Armed with a booklet and an empty stomach, visitors can wander from premises to premises, sampling everything from freshly shucked Helvick oysters to handmade chocolates, craft gins to wood-fired pizzas. It is an exercise in delicious excess, and one that reveals the remarkable diversity of what is produced in this relatively small patch of Ireland.

For families, the festival has always made a particular effort to ensure younger visitors are catered for, with children's cookery workshops, face painting, and live entertainment creating a genuinely inclusive atmosphere. There is something deeply appealing about watching a seven-year-old carefully ice a cupcake with the same concentration that a Michelin-starred chef might bring to plating a tasting menu two streets away.

The economic impact of the festival on the town and wider region should not be underestimated either. Hotels, bed and breakfasts, and holiday rentals fill up weeks in advance, and local businesses report a significant uplift during the festival weekend.
headline: Delicious Déise delights: How Waterford Festival of Food brings fun to Dungarvan

text:
The second phase of a popular Douglas housing development has gone on sale, but agents report a noticeably calmer scene than the frenzied first release, with fewer buyers queueing to secure properties in what may be an early signal of a shifting market.

The Bayly development in Douglas, on Cork's southside, released its latest tranche of homes over the weekend, with prospective purchasers arriving in smaller numbers than had been the case when the first phase launched to strong demand earlier this year.

Estate agents involved in the sale said that while interest remained solid, the days of lengthy queues forming before dawn appeared to be easing, at least at this particular scheme. The development, which has proven attractive to both first-time buyers and those trading up, offers a mix of three- and four-bedroom houses in one of Cork's most sought-after suburban locations.

Douglas has long been among the most desirable addresses in the Cork metropolitan area, with its village centre, established schools, and proximity to the city centre and the South Ring Road making it a perennial draw for families. Prices at the Bayly development are understood to reflect the premium that the area commands, with three-bedroom semi-detached homes starting from around €395,000.

However, the more subdued turnout for the second phase may point to a number of factors tempering demand. Rising interest rates, tighter lending conditions, and a degree of buyer fatigue after years of intense competition for new-build stock are all thought to be playing a role.

Some prospective buyers who attended the launch said they felt less pressure to commit immediately than they might have done twelve months ago. One couple, who asked not to be named, said they had been outbid on a property in the first phase and had returned hoping for a less competitive environment this time around.

"It was still busy, but nothing like the last time," the woman said. "We felt we could actually take a breath and think about it properly, rather than being panicked into making a decision on the spot."

Property analysts have noted a broader cooling in parts of the new-homes market nationally, though supply constraints continue to underpin prices in most urban centres. The latest Residential Property Price Index from the Central Statistics Office showed that while prices continued to rise on an annual basis, the rate of growth had moderated in recent months.

Cork has not been immune to these trends, though demand in established suburbs such as Douglas, Ballincollig, and Carrigaline continues to outstrip supply in many cases. New housing completions in Cork city and county have increased year on year, but remain well below the levels that housing experts say are needed to meet demand.

The developers behind the Bayly scheme are understood to be satisfied with the level of interest in the second phase, noting that a significant number of units were reserved on the opening day. Further phases are expected to be released in the coming months as construction progresses.

Local representatives have broadly welcomed the delivery of new housing in the area, though some have raised concerns about the capacity of local infrastructure, including roads and schools, to absorb the additional population. Douglas has experienced significant residential growth in recent years, with several large-scale developments either completed or under construction in the wider area.
headline: Fewer buyers queue for Douglas homes as second phase of Bayly development goes on sale

text:
The personal papers and photographs of a key figure in the negotiations that saw Britain hand back the Treaty Ports to Ireland are set to go on public display on Spike Island for the first time, offering a rare glimpse into one of the most significant moments in the State's history.

The collection, which includes handwritten correspondence, official documents and a series of previously unseen photographs, belonged to one of the Irish officials closely involved in the diplomatic efforts that led to the return of the ports in 1938. The ports at Cobh, Berehaven and Lough Swilly had remained under British control following the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921, and their handover was a pivotal moment in Irish sovereignty.

Spike Island, situated in Cork Harbour and itself a former British military installation, is a fitting location for the exhibition, given its proximity to the former Treaty Port at Haulbowline and Cobh. The island has in recent years established itself as one of Munster's premier heritage attractions, drawing tens of thousands of visitors annually.

The material sheds light on the behind-the-scenes negotiations between the governments of Éamon de Valera and British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, which culminated in the Anglo-Irish Agreements of April 1938. The handover of the ports was widely regarded as a masterstroke of de Valera's diplomacy and proved crucial during the Second World War, allowing Ireland to maintain its policy of neutrality.

Among the items in the collection are personal letters that reveal the human dimension of the negotiations, including reflections on the political pressures faced by both sides and the sense of historic occasion that accompanied the talks. Photographs from the period capture both formal diplomatic settings and more candid moments, providing a fuller picture of the personalities involved.

John Crotty, manager of Spike Island, said the exhibition represents a significant addition to the island's offering. "These are documents of enormous historical importance, and we are delighted to be able to share them with the public. The Treaty Ports story is central to the history of Cork Harbour and to the broader story of Irish independence. To have these personal papers displayed here on Spike Island, which itself played such a role in that history, feels very appropriate."

The handover of the ports on 11 July 1938 was marked by ceremonies at each of the three locations. At Spike Island and the associated facilities in Cork Harbour, the Irish tricolour was raised as British forces departed, an event that drew large crowds and was greeted with considerable emotion locally.

Historians have noted that the return of the ports removed one of the last vestiges of British military presence in the 26 counties and marked a critical step in the assertion of full Irish sovereignty. During the Emergency, as the Second World War was known in Ireland, Winston Churchill repeatedly sought the use of the ports, but de Valera's refusal to grant access was underpinned by the 1938 agreements.

The exhibition is expected to open in the coming weeks and will run throughout the summer season. Spike Island is accessible by ferry from Kennedy Pier in Cobh, with guided tours of the island's fortifications and exhibitions available daily.
headline: Photos and letters belonging to Treaty Ports negotiator to go on display on Spike Island

text:
The head of Oxfam Ireland has urged political parties to place the crisis in Gaza at the heart of the General Election campaign, warning that Ireland's response to the conflict will define the country's standing on the world stage for years to come.

Jim Clarken, chief executive of Oxfam Ireland, said the humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in the Palestinian territory demands a far more robust response from the next government than has been offered to date, and called on candidates across the country to set out clear positions on what Ireland should do to end the suffering of civilians.

Speaking ahead of the election, Mr Clarken said the scale of destruction in Gaza is unlike anything the aid organisation has witnessed in recent memory, with hospitals, schools and refugee camps repeatedly struck and the civilian population left with nowhere safe to go.

"Ireland has always punched above its weight on issues of international justice and human rights. The people of this country expect their leaders to do more than offer words of sympathy — they expect action," Mr Clarken said.

He pointed to Ireland's seat on the UN Security Council in recent years and its historic support for Palestinian statehood as evidence that the State has both the credibility and the moral authority to play a leading role in pressing for a ceasefire and accountability for violations of international humanitarian law.

Mr Clarken called on all parties to commit to concrete measures in their election manifestos, including support for the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice in their investigations, a review of any trade or economic links that may contribute to the occupation, and a significant increase in humanitarian funding for the region.

He also urged the next government to move swiftly on the Occupied Territories Bill, which would ban trade with illegal settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories. The legislation has been the subject of lengthy delays and political controversy, with successive governments declining to advance it, citing legal advice around EU competence on trade matters.

"The Occupied Territories Bill has been sitting there for years. The Irish people support it overwhelmingly. It is time for the next Dáil to pass it without further delay," Mr Clarken said.

The Oxfam Ireland chief said the organisation's partners on the ground in Gaza are reporting desperate conditions, with clean water, food and medical supplies almost impossible to access in many areas. He described the situation as a "man-made catastrophe" and said the blocking of humanitarian aid amounts to the use of starvation as a weapon of war.

Mr Clarken acknowledged that domestic issues such as housing, health and the cost of living will inevitably dominate the campaign trail, but argued that Ireland's foreign policy commitments should not be treated as secondary concerns.

"Voters care about what is happening in Gaza. We see it in the protests, in the community fundraisers, in the letters people send to their TDs. This is not a niche issue — it is a question of basic human decency, and people want to know where their candidates stand," he said.

His intervention comes amid growing public pressure on Irish politicians to take a stronger stance on the conflict. Protests have been held in cities and towns across the country in recent months, and a number of Oireachtas members from across the political spectrum have been vocal in their criticism of Israel's military campaign.
headline: Oxfam Ireland chief calls for Gaza to be central issue in General Election campaign
