Every so often, a phrase captures the public imagination so neatly that it risks becoming a cliché before its wisdom has had time to sink in. "It takes a village to raise a child" is one such phrase, and in the context of children's digital lives it has never been more relevant.

Parents across Ireland are grappling with a challenge that no previous generation has faced: how to keep children safe in a world that fits inside their pocket. The temptation, understandably, is to reach for a technological fix — a parental control app, a screen-time tracker, a content filter. These tools have their place, but if we rely on them as our primary line of defence we are setting ourselves up for failure. Digital safety is not a software problem. It is a relational one.

I meet parents regularly who have invested in the latest monitoring software only to discover that their twelve-year-old has found a workaround within a fortnight. Children are, by their nature, resourceful. They share tips in the schoolyard, watch tutorials online, and treat any digital restriction as a puzzle to be solved. The arms race between parent and child, mediated by technology, is one the child will almost always win eventually.

What works far better — though it requires considerably more effort — is building a culture around technology use that extends beyond the four walls of the family home. This is where the village comes in.

When I speak to parents' groups around the country, the single most common frustration I hear is the feeling of isolation. A parent might decide that their ten-year-old is too young for a smartphone, only to discover that every other child in the class already has one. The pressure to relent becomes enormous, not because the parent has changed their mind about the risks but because they cannot bear to see their child socially excluded. This is a real and legitimate concern, and no app on earth can address it.

What can address it is collective action. We have seen encouraging examples of this in recent years, with parent groups in schools across Ireland coming together to agree shared guidelines on smartphone use. The idea is beautifully simple: if all the parents in a class agree to delay smartphones until a certain age, no single child is left out. The social pressure that undermines individual decisions evaporates when the community acts as one.

These initiatives work precisely because they acknowledge something that the app-based approach ignores — that children's digital lives are fundamentally social. A child does not use a phone in isolation. They use it to connect with friends, to participate in group chats, to keep up with what is happening in their peer group. Any strategy that fails to account for this social dimension is treating the symptom rather than the cause.

Schools, too, have a critical role to play. The introduction of digital literacy into the curriculum is welcome, but it needs to go beyond teaching children how to spot a phishing email. Young people need to develop what we might call digital emotional intelligence — the ability to recognise how technology makes them feel, to understand the persuasive design techniques that keep them scrolling, and to make conscious choices about their online behaviour rather than simply reacting to notifications.
headline: Colman Noctor: Digital safety needs a village, not an app

text:
The Irish fishing industry has called on the Government to intervene urgently as soaring fuel costs push vessel owners to the brink, with some warning they may be forced to tie up their boats permanently if relief is not forthcoming.

Representatives from across the sector met in Killybegs, Co Donegal, yesterday to discuss the escalating crisis, which they say threatens the viability of entire coastal communities that depend on fishing for their livelihoods.

Diesel prices for marine vessels have risen sharply in recent months, with some skippers reporting that fuel now accounts for more than half of their total operating costs. Industry figures suggest the price of marine diesel has more than doubled compared to two years ago, leaving many smaller operators unable to break even on individual trips.

Patrick Murphy, chief executive of the Irish South and West Fish Producers Organisation, said the situation had become untenable for many in the fleet. "We are at a point where fishermen are going to sea and coming back having made no money at all, or in some cases actually losing money once fuel is factored in," he said. "This is not sustainable, and without Government support we will see boats permanently removed from the water."

The industry is seeking a range of measures, including a fuel subsidy scheme, a temporary reduction in marine diesel levies, and the establishment of a dedicated support fund to help vessel owners weather the crisis. Fishing organisations have pointed to schemes introduced in France and Spain, where governments moved swiftly to cushion the blow for their fleets, and have urged the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine to follow suit.

The Irish Fish Processors and Exporters Association warned that the knock-on effects would be felt well beyond the quayside. Processing plants, transport companies, and ancillary services in ports such as Killybegs, Castletownbere, Dingle, and Howth all stand to suffer if vessels remain tied up, the association said.

Several TDs from coastal constituencies have raised the matter in the Dáil in recent weeks, calling on the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to outline what specific supports are being considered. Independent TD Thomas Pringle, who represents Donegal, described the crisis as an existential threat to the industry. "These are not large corporations. These are family-run businesses, many of them multi-generational, and they simply cannot absorb costs of this magnitude," he said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine said the Minister was aware of the difficulties facing the sector and that officials were engaged in ongoing discussions with industry representatives. The spokesperson added that any supports would need to be considered within the framework of EU state aid rules, which place limitations on the type and scale of assistance that can be offered to the fishing sector.

However, industry leaders expressed frustration at the pace of the Government's response, noting that other EU member states had already implemented emergency measures. "We are competing directly with French and Spanish vessels that are benefiting from state support while our lowers are left to fend for themselves," said Sean O'Donoghue of the Killybegs Fishermen's Organisation. "The playing field is not level, and every week of delay is costing jobs."
headline: Fishing industry seeks Government help as soaring fuel costs threaten Irish fleet

text:
The Road Safety Authority has warned that any driving test appointments booked through unauthorised third-party platforms will be cancelled, as it moves to crack down on a growing grey market in test slots.

The RSA said it had become aware of a number of websites and apps offering to secure driving test bookings on behalf of learner drivers, in some cases charging significant fees for the service. The authority stressed that its official online booking system is the only legitimate channel for scheduling a test and that any bookings made through other platforms would be identified and cancelled without refund to the third party.

It is understood that some of the platforms operate by using automated software to monitor the RSA's booking system for cancellations, snapping up available slots and then reselling them to learner drivers at a premium. In some cases, drivers have reportedly paid upwards of €100 on top of the standard €85 test fee to secure an earlier appointment.

The RSA said the practice was placing additional pressure on an already strained system and was unfair to the majority of learner drivers who book through the proper channels. Waiting times for driving tests have been a persistent source of frustration, with some test centres reporting delays of several months.

"We want to make it very clear that the only way to book a driving test is through the RSA's official booking system," a spokesperson for the authority said. "We are actively monitoring for bookings made through third-party platforms and these will be cancelled. We would strongly advise learner drivers not to pay any third party to book a test on their behalf."

The spokesperson added that the authority was working to implement additional technical measures to prevent automated systems from accessing the booking platform.

The warning comes as the RSA continues its efforts to reduce driving test waiting times nationally. The authority has previously committed to recruiting additional driver testers and increasing the number of tests carried out each week to address the backlog, which was significantly worsened during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Minister of State at the Department of Transport Jack Chambers has previously acknowledged the frustration felt by learner drivers and said he had been engaging with the RSA on the matter. The Department said it was supportive of any measures taken by the authority to ensure fair and equitable access to the booking system.

Conor Faughnan, a motoring commentator and former director of consumer affairs at AA Ireland, said the emergence of third-party booking platforms was a predictable consequence of lengthy waiting times. "When people are waiting months for a test, it's inevitable that a secondary market will spring up," he said. "But it's not a solution — it just means those who can afford to pay more get to jump the queue, and that's not right."

The RSA advised any learner driver who has already used a third-party service to book a test to contact the authority directly to discuss their situation. It also urged members of the public to report any websites or services purporting to offer driving test bookings on behalf of the RSA.
headline: RSA warns learner drivers tests booked through third-party platforms will be cancelled

text:
Robert De Niro has spoken publicly about his transgender daughter for the first time, expressing his "love and support" for the 13-year-old in a heartfelt statement that has drawn widespread praise.

The Hollywood legend, who turned 81 earlier this year, confirmed that one of his children identifies as transgender and said he wanted to make clear where he stood as a father.

"I love my daughter and I will always support her," De Niro said. "She is a brave and beautiful person, and I am proud of her."

The Oscar-winning star of Taxi Driver, Goodfellas and The Irishman is a father of seven children from several relationships. His youngest daughter, Helen Grace, was born in 2011 via surrogate with his former partner Tiffany Chen. De Niro has not specified which of his children has come out as transgender.

The actor has long been known for guarding his family's privacy fiercely, making the public statement all the more notable. In recent years, however, he has become increasingly outspoken on political and social matters, frequently criticising former US president Donald Trump and speaking candidly about the grief he experienced following the death of his grandson Leandro in 2023.

De Niro's comments come at a time of heightened political tension around transgender rights in the United States, where Republican-led state legislatures have introduced a wave of legislation restricting access to gender-affirming healthcare for minors and limiting the participation of transgender young people in school sports.

Advocacy groups welcomed the actor's remarks, with GLAAD, the US media monitoring organisation focused on LGBTQ+ representation, describing them as "powerful and important" at a moment when transgender young people and their families face increasing hostility.

"When a parent like Robert De Niro speaks openly about loving and supporting their trans child, it sends a message to families across the country and around the world," a GLAAD spokesperson said.

In Ireland, transgender advocacy organisations have similarly highlighted the importance of parental support for young transgender people. Research published by BeLonG To Youth Services has consistently shown that family acceptance is one of the strongest protective factors for the mental health and wellbeing of LGBTQ+ young people.

De Niro, who is currently promoting several forthcoming film projects, did not elaborate further on the matter but made clear he would not be drawn into any political debate about his child's identity.

"This is about my family and about love," he said. "That is all."
headline: Robert De Niro expresses ‘love and support’ for transgender daughter

text:
The HSE has launched a new app that will allow patients to access their personal health data directly from their smartphones, marking what the health service has described as a significant step in the digital transformation of Ireland's healthcare system.

The new Health Portal app, which is available to download on both iOS and Android devices, gives users the ability to view a range of their medical records, including vaccination history, referral letters, and discharge summaries, all in one place.

HSE chief executive Bernard Gloster said the app represents a "major milestone" in putting patients at the centre of their own care. "This is about empowering people to take a more active role in managing their health by giving them easy and secure access to their own information," he said.

The app uses MyGovID verification to ensure that users' data is protected, with the HSE stressing that robust security measures have been built into the platform from the outset. The health service said it had worked closely with the Data Protection Commission throughout the development process to ensure full compliance with GDPR requirements.

Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly welcomed the launch, saying it was a key deliverable under the Government's Sláintecare reform programme. "We know that when patients have access to their own health information, outcomes improve. This app is a practical example of how we are modernising our health service for the benefit of everyone," the Minister said.

The HSE acknowledged that the app will initially offer a limited range of records but said additional features and data sets would be added on a phased basis over the coming months. Future updates are expected to include access to GP visit records, diagnostic test results, and the ability to manage hospital appointments.

Patient advocacy groups broadly welcomed the development but cautioned that the app must not become a substitute for face-to-face engagement with healthcare professionals. The Irish Patients' Association said it was encouraged by the initiative but urged the HSE to ensure that older people and those without access to smartphones are not left behind.

"Digital tools like this have enormous potential, but equity of access must remain a priority," a spokesperson for the association said. "Not everyone is comfortable using apps, and alternative means of accessing health records must be maintained."

The launch comes as the HSE continues to invest heavily in its digital infrastructure following the devastating cyberattack in May 2021, which crippled the health service's IT systems and exposed significant vulnerabilities. The HSE has since committed hundreds of millions of euro to upgrading its technology and cybersecurity defences.

Health professionals have also signalled their support for the initiative, with the Irish Medical Organisation noting that better access to records could help reduce duplication of tests and improve communication between patients and their doctors.

The app is available to all adults with a verified MyGovID account and can be downloaded free of charge from the Apple App Store and Google Play Store.
headline: HSE launches app allowing patients access to their health data

text:
There is something deeply personal about the way Ireland watches American presidential politics. It is not merely the fascination of observing the world's most powerful democracy at work, nor even the hard-headed calculation of what any given administration might mean for trade, investment and the transatlantic relationship. It is something more intimate than that. When Joe Biden speaks of Ballina and the Cooley Peninsula, when he quotes Seamus Heaney and invokes the memory of the Famine ships, he is not performing for a foreign audience. He is, in a very real sense, coming home.

The 46th president of the United States has never been shy about his Irishness. From his first days in public life as a young senator from Delaware, Biden wore his ancestry not as a political badge but as a genuine marker of identity. His visits to this country, both before and during his presidency, have been marked by an emotional connection that goes well beyond the choreography of diplomatic occasions. The tears were real. The cousins were real. The pints were, by all accounts, real too.

None of this is to suggest that Ireland's relationship with the United States should be conducted on the basis of sentiment alone. It most emphatically should not. There are serious and sometimes difficult questions to be navigated — on corporation tax, on defence and neutrality, on the Middle East, on the future shape of the European Union's relationship with Washington. Ireland must always be clear-eyed in its dealings with any American administration, however warmly disposed that administration might be.

But it would be foolish to pretend that the personal dimension does not matter. In diplomacy, as in life, relationships count. Access counts. The willingness of a president to take a phone call, to raise an issue, to lean in on a question that matters to a small island on the western edge of Europe — these things are not trivial. Biden has demonstrated, time and again, that Ireland occupies a place in his thinking that cannot be explained by strategic calculation alone.

His unwavering commitment to the Belfast Agreement and to the preservation of peace on this island has been one of the most consequential features of his engagement with Irish affairs. At moments when the post-Brexit settlement threatened to unravel the delicate arrangements that underpin stability in the North, Biden and his administration made clear that American interest in the matter was not negotiable. That mattered. It mattered enormously.

The Irish diaspora in America remains a formidable force, and Biden is in many ways its most prominent standard-bearer. When he seeks the backing of the Irish — whether in America or on this island — he does so not as a stranger asking for support but as one of their own. That is a distinction with a very real difference, and it is one that the people of Ireland, instinctively and rightly, understand.
headline: Irish Examiner view: Biden will have backing of the Irish

text:
Every parent has been there — that mortifying moment when your baby reaches out and grabs a fistful of someone's hair, yanking with a surprisingly iron grip while you scramble to intervene. It can feel embarrassing, especially when the person on the receiving end is a stranger, a grandparent trying to enjoy a cuddle, or another child at a playgroup. But before you start worrying that your little one is displaying aggressive tendencies, let me reassure you: this is entirely normal developmental behaviour.

Babies are sensory explorers. From the moment they develop the ability to grasp — which typically emerges around three to four months — they want to grab, pull, squeeze and mouth everything within reach. Hair happens to be one of the most fascinating textures available to them. It moves, it has an interesting feel, and it often produces a dramatic reaction from the person whose hair is being pulled, which in itself becomes rewarding for the baby.

It is important to understand that babies under the age of about 18 months are not pulling hair to be bold or to hurt anyone. They simply do not yet have the cognitive capacity for intentional aggression. What they do have is curiosity, a developing grasp reflex, and an emerging understanding of cause and effect. When your baby pulls someone's hair and that person yelps, laughs, or makes a big fuss, your baby's brain registers this as interesting. They are learning that their actions produce reactions in other people, which is actually a significant developmental milestone — just not a particularly comfortable one for the person whose scalp is involved.

So what can you do about it? The first thing is to stay calm and avoid overreacting. If you respond with a big dramatic "No!" or even laughter, you are inadvertently reinforcing the behaviour by giving it a lot of attention. Instead, calmly and gently uncurl your baby's fingers from the hair, saying something simple and neutral like "gentle hands" while stroking the person's hair softly with your baby's open hand. This teaches them an alternative way to interact with the texture they find so appealing.

Repetition is your friend here. You will likely need to do this dozens of times before the message begins to land, and that is completely fine. Babies learn through consistent, repeated experience. Each time you guide their hand to be gentle, you are laying down neural pathways that will eventually help them regulate their own behaviour. But this takes time, and expecting a baby to remember and apply a lesson after being told once or twice is not realistic at this stage of development.

For parents who find their baby is particularly drawn to hair-pulling, it can help to offer alternative sensory experiences. Toys with different textures — soft fabric books, sensory ribbons, or toys with strands they can pull — can redirect that urge to grab and tug. You might also look at whether your baby is doing this more at particular times of day. Babies who are overtired, overstimulated, or teething may be more inclined to grab and pull because their sensory system is already in overdrive.

If the hair-pulling is happening frequently at parent-and-toddler groups or in social settings, don't let embarrassment keep you away.
headline: Joanna Fortune: My baby keeps pulling other people's hair

text:
A senior Cabinet minister has cast doubt on the Government's ability to deliver a further reduction in student contribution fees, exposing a rift at the heart of the coalition just months before the next budget.

The comments, which caught coalition partners off guard, come amid growing pressure from student organisations and opposition TDs to build on last year's modest reduction in the student contribution charge, which currently stands at €3,000.

The minister, speaking on condition of anonymity, suggested that the fiscal space available for Budget 2025 would not stretch to accommodate another cut, pointing to competing demands across health, housing and defence. "There are only so many pots of money to go around," the minister said. "People need to be realistic about what can be delivered."

The remarks drew a swift response from coalition colleagues, with sources in one of the other Government parties insisting that a further reduction in fees remained very much on the table and that no decisions had yet been taken on budgetary priorities.

Minister for Further and Higher Education Simon Harris had previously signalled his ambition to reduce the contribution charge further, describing the cost of third-level education as a significant burden on families. However, the Department of Public Expenditure is understood to have raised concerns about the cost of any additional cut, with estimates suggesting that every €500 reduction in the charge costs the Exchequer in the region of €95 million.

The Union of Students in Ireland described the apparent split as deeply concerning. USI president Joe Donnelly said students and their families could not afford to be treated as a "political football" and called on the Taoiseach to confirm the Government's commitment to reducing fees.

"Students are already under enormous financial pressure between fees, rent and the cost of living," Mr Donnelly said. "We need clarity, not mixed messages from Government."

Sinn Féin's education spokesperson Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire accused the coalition of being "all talk and no action" on the issue, arguing that the Government had failed to deliver meaningful reform of the student contribution system despite repeated promises. The Cork South-Central TD said his party would continue to push for the complete abolition of the charge.

The Social Democrats and Labour also weighed in, with both parties calling for a multi-year plan to progressively reduce the contribution to €1,500 over the lifetime of the next government.

The issue is expected to feature prominently in pre-budget discussions over the coming weeks, with the Taoiseach likely to face questions in the Dáil on whether the coalition remains united on the matter. Government sources said the three party leaders would discuss the matter as part of broader budgetary negotiations, but stressed that final decisions would not be made until the autumn.

The tension highlights the difficulty facing the coalition as it seeks to balance a wide range of spending commitments ahead of a general election that must be held by March 2025 at the latest. With housing, childcare and health all competing for additional resources, the question of student fees risks becoming a flashpoint between the coalition parties as budget negotiations intensify.
headline: Government split as minister casts doubt on further student fee cut

A man charged with the murder of a Ukrainian national in Cork city has been remanded in custody after a brief appearance before Cork District Court.

The accused, who cannot be named for legal reasons, appeared before Judge Helen Boyle on Monday morning in connection with the fatal incident, which occurred in the city centre over the weekend.

Gardaí attached to Anglesea Street Garda Station had launched a murder investigation after the victim, a Ukrainian man in his 30s, was found with fatal injuries in the early hours of Saturday morning. He was pronounced dead at the scene, and his body was removed to Cork University Hospital where a post-mortem examination was carried out by the State Pathologist's office.

Detective Garda Brian Murphy gave evidence of arrest, charge and caution, telling the court that the accused made no reply when the charge was put to him after caution at Bridewell Garda Station.

The court heard there was no application for bail, with the defence indicating that such an application would be made at a later date before the High Court.

Legal aid was granted after the court was told the accused was unemployed and had no means.

Judge Boyle remanded the accused in custody to appear again before Cork District Court via video link in two weeks' time.

The judge directed that the accused receive any necessary medical attention while in custody and also granted a request from the defence for the preparation of disclosure materials.

Gardaí have appealed for any witnesses to the incident, or anyone with information, to contact Anglesea Street Garda Station on 021 4522000, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.
headline: Man accused of murdering Ukrainian in Cork city remanded

text:
A powerful earthquake with a magnitude of 6.2 has struck central Japan, leaving several people dead and dozens more injured as rescue crews scramble to reach affected communities.

The quake hit in the early hours of the morning local time, with its epicentre located in a mountainous region of central Honshu, Japan's main island. The Japan Meteorological Agency reported that the tremor was felt across a wide swathe of the country, with intense shaking recorded in several prefectures.

Buildings were damaged and landslides were triggered in rural areas close to the epicentre, hampering efforts by emergency services to reach those trapped beneath rubble. Footage broadcast on Japanese public broadcaster NHK showed cracked roads, collapsed walls and debris strewn across residential streets, while frightened residents gathered in evacuation centres overnight.

Japanese authorities confirmed that a number of fatalities had been recorded, with the toll expected to rise as search and rescue operations continue. Hospitals in the region reported treating dozens of people for injuries ranging from cuts and bruises to more serious trauma.

Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba convened an emergency meeting of his cabinet and urged residents in affected areas to remain vigilant for aftershocks, which seismologists warned could continue for several days. The Japanese Self-Defence Forces were deployed to assist with rescue and relief operations.

No tsunami warning was issued following the quake, as the epicentre was located inland. However, authorities cautioned that weakened hillsides and infrastructure could pose ongoing dangers, particularly in the event of further seismic activity or heavy rainfall.

Japan sits on the so-called Pacific Ring of Fire and is one of the most seismically active countries in the world. The nation has invested heavily in earthquake-resistant construction and early warning systems, measures widely credited with saving lives during major tremors. Nevertheless, earthquakes continue to pose a significant threat, particularly in older buildings and rural communities where infrastructure may be less resilient.

The quake comes just over a year after a devastating 7.6-magnitude earthquake struck the Noto Peninsula on New Year's Day 2024, killing more than 200 people and causing widespread destruction.

Ireland's Department of Foreign Affairs said it was not aware of any Irish citizens affected by the earthquake but advised any Irish people in the region to follow the instructions of local authorities and to contact the department's consular assistance team if they require help.
headline: Deadly 6.2-magnitude earthquake strikes central Japan

text:
The problem**

My mother-in-law is 74 and lives alone since my father-in-law passed away three years ago. She's in reasonable health for her age but has started to slow down noticeably in the past year — she's had a few falls, she forgets things, and she's become very dependent on my husband for everything from changing lightbulbs to sorting her prescriptions.

I feel terrible even writing this, because she's a lovely woman and she's always been good to me. But I can see the way this is heading. My husband is an only child, and every conversation we have about his mother ends with him saying "we'll cross that bridge when we come to it." I'm 46, I work full-time, and we have two teenagers. I'm already stretched to my limit.

Last weekend, he floated the idea of her moving in with us "down the line." He said it casually, but I know him — he's been thinking about it for a while. I didn't say anything at the time because I didn't want a row, but inside I was panicking. I love our home the way it is. I don't want to become a full-time carer on top of everything else. I've seen it happen to other women — they give up their jobs, their social lives, their marriages even, and nobody ever thanks them for it.

Am I a terrible person for feeling this way? How do I talk to my husband about this without sounding heartless?

**Dáithí responds**

You are not a terrible person. Not even close. The fact that you feel guilty about having these worries tells me you're someone who cares deeply — about your mother-in-law, about your husband, and about your family. But caring about someone and signing up to become their full-time carer are two very different things, and you are entirely right to want an honest conversation about what lies ahead.

The reality is that this is one of the great unspoken pressures facing families across Ireland today. We have an ageing population, an overstretched HSE, home care packages that are difficult to access and often inadequate, and a nursing home system that many families simply cannot afford. Into that gap steps the family — and, more often than not, it is women who end up shouldering the burden. Research from Family Carers Ireland consistently shows that women make up the vast majority of informal carers in this country, and many of them describe feeling invisible, exhausted, and unsupported. You are not being selfish for wanting to avoid that fate. You are being realistic.

What concerns me most in your letter is not your mother-in-law's health or even your husband's suggestion that she might move in. What concerns me is the silence. You didn't say anything when he raised it. He hasn't sat down with you properly to discuss it. The two of you are circling one of the biggest decisions of your married life, and neither of you is willing to land the plane. That has to change.
headline: Dear Dáithí: I'm worried I'll end up as a carer for my mother-in-law

A man is to face criminal charges after a fire caused significant damage to the Pennsylvania governor's mansion in the US city of Harrisburg, authorities have confirmed.

The blaze broke out at the historic residence, known as the Governor's Residence, on Sunday evening, prompting a major emergency response. No injuries were reported in the incident, though the property sustained considerable damage.

Pennsylvania State Police said a male suspect was taken into custody shortly after the fire was brought under control. He is expected to face a number of charges in connection with the incident, though the precise nature of those charges has yet to be formally announced.

Governor Josh Shapiro and his family were not present at the residence at the time of the fire, according to a statement from his office. The Democratic governor said he was grateful that no one was hurt and thanked the emergency services for their swift response.

"The safety of everyone is what matters most," Mr Shapiro said. "We are working closely with law enforcement as they investigate this matter."

The Governor's Residence, situated along the Susquehanna River in the state capital, has served as the official home of Pennsylvania's governors since 1968. The Georgian-style mansion is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and is a popular destination for public tours.

Investigators were continuing to examine the scene on Monday to determine the full extent of the damage and establish the precise circumstances surrounding the fire. Authorities have not yet disclosed a possible motive.

The incident comes at a time of heightened security concerns around public officials and government buildings across the United States. Security arrangements at the residence are expected to be reviewed in the wake of the fire.
headline: Man to face charges after fire damages Pennsylvania governor’s mansion

The Cabinet has given the green light to the long-awaited M28 Cork to Ringaskiddy motorway project, with a price tag of €456 million, in a major boost for transport infrastructure in the Cork region.

The decision, confirmed by Minister for Transport Eamon Ryan, will see the existing N28 route upgraded to motorway standard, providing a critical link between Cork City and Ringaskiddy, home to one of the country's busiest port facilities and a significant pharmaceutical manufacturing hub.

The project has been in the planning pipeline for well over a decade, with local politicians, business leaders and residents along the route campaigning for the upgrade amid growing concerns about safety and congestion on the existing road.

The new motorway will run for approximately 14 kilometres and is expected to significantly improve journey times and road safety for the tens of thousands of commuters, hauliers and port users who travel the route daily. The current N28 has long been regarded as one of the most dangerous and congested national routes in the State, with heavy goods vehicles sharing the road with local traffic through built-up areas including Rochestown, Carr's Hill and Shanbally.

The Port of Cork's operations at Ringaskiddy have expanded considerably in recent years following the relocation of container and cargo services from the city centre's Tivoli terminal. The inadequacy of the road network serving the deepwater port has been repeatedly highlighted by the business community as a brake on economic development in the wider Cork region.

Cork Chamber welcomed the announcement, describing it as a transformative investment for the south of the country. The organisation said the motorway would support the continued growth of the pharmaceutical, logistics and marine sectors concentrated in the Ringaskiddy and Carrigaline areas.

Local TDs from across the political spectrum have been pressing the Government on the issue for years. Several Cork South-Central and Cork South-West representatives expressed relief that the project has finally cleared the Cabinet table, noting the frustration felt by communities who have endured worsening traffic conditions while waiting for a resolution.

Construction is expected to take approximately four years once a contractor is appointed, with enabling works anticipated to commence in the near term. The project will be delivered by Transport Infrastructure Ireland in conjunction with Cork County Council.

The approval comes as the Government continues to face scrutiny over its capital spending programme, with a number of major infrastructure projects around the country experiencing delays and cost overruns. However, ministers insisted the M28 represents a sound investment, given its strategic importance to national connectivity and the economic output of the Cork harbour area.

Community groups along the route have expressed a mixture of relief and concern, welcoming the end of uncertainty while seeking assurances about noise mitigation, environmental protections and the impact on local amenities during the construction phase. Detailed engagement with affected landowners and residents is expected to intensify in the coming months as the project moves towards the construction phase.

The Taoiseach said the approval underlined the Government's commitment to balanced regional development and to ensuring that Cork, as the State's second city, has the infrastructure it needs to compete internationally and sustain economic growth.
headline: Cabinet approves €456m M28 Cork to Ringaskiddy motorway project

The chronic shortage of long-term rental accommodation in Gaeltacht areas has been laid bare by new data revealing that short-term holiday lets outnumber permanent rental properties by a factor of 100 to one in some of the country's most linguistically vulnerable communities.

The figures, compiled from an analysis of listings on major letting platforms and cross-referenced with available long-term rental stock on Daft.ie, paint a stark picture of a housing market that campaigners say is actively undermining the survival of the Irish language in its remaining heartlands.

In parts of Connemara, west Kerry, and the Donegal Gaeltacht, researchers found hundreds of properties listed on Airbnb and similar platforms, while in many cases not a single long-term rental property was available for people seeking to live and work in the area year-round.

The data has reignited calls for the Government to introduce specific planning protections for Gaeltacht communities, where the interplay between housing scarcity and language decline has become a matter of growing urgency.

Donncha Ó hÉallaithe, a long-standing campaigner on Gaeltacht housing issues, said the figures confirmed what communities on the ground had been saying for years.

"Young people who have grown up through Irish, who want to raise their families through Irish, simply cannot find anywhere to live in their own communities," he said. "Meanwhile, every second house on the road is available for a weekend stay. You cannot sustain a living language community under those conditions."

The issue has become particularly acute in areas such as An Cheathrú Rua in Connemara and Corca Dhuibhne in west Kerry, where the tourism economy has driven significant demand for short-term accommodation. Local representatives say that while tourism provides vital income, the balance has tipped so far that it now threatens the very cultural distinctiveness that attracts visitors in the first place.

Catherine Connolly TD, who has repeatedly raised the matter in the Dáil, said the Government's response to date had been wholly inadequate.

"We have had endless reports, endless strategies, and endless hand-wringing about the future of the Irish language, but when it comes to the single most important factor — whether people can actually afford to live in the Gaeltacht — there has been a complete failure to act," she said.

Under planning regulations introduced in 2019, property owners letting their homes on a short-term basis for more than 90 days per year in rent pressure zones are required to obtain change-of-use planning permission. However, many Gaeltacht areas fall outside designated rent pressure zones, meaning the regulations do not apply. Even where they do apply, enforcement has been widely criticised as inadequate.

The Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media said it recognised the challenges facing Gaeltacht communities and pointed to the Government's housing strategy for the Gaeltacht, published as part of the broader Housing for All plan. A spokesperson said the department was working closely with Údarás na Gaeltachta and local authorities to address housing supply in Irish-speaking areas.
headline: Gaeltacht areas have 100 times more Airbnbs to let than permanent rental properties, new data shows

text:
Donald Trump has issued a fresh threat against Iran, warning the Islamic Republic to "watch what happens" if it fails to reach a deal with the United States over its nuclear programme.

The US president made the remarks on his Truth Social platform on Sunday, escalating his rhetoric as negotiations between Washington and Tehran over Iran's nuclear ambitions appear to have stalled following an initial round of talks.

"If Iran doesn't make a deal, watch what happens," Mr Trump wrote, without elaborating on what specific actions the US might take. The post came amid reports that a second round of indirect negotiations, which had been expected to take place in Oman, has yet to be formally scheduled.

The warning marks a significant ratcheting up of tensions between the two countries, which have been locked in a diplomatic standoff over Iran's nuclear programme for years. Tehran has consistently denied that it is seeking to develop nuclear weapons, insisting its programme is for peaceful energy purposes, though international inspectors have raised concerns about the country's enrichment activities.

Mr Trump withdrew the United States from the landmark 2015 Iran nuclear deal during his first term in office, reimposing sweeping economic sanctions on Tehran. Since returning to the White House, he has pursued what his administration describes as a "maximum pressure" campaign aimed at forcing Iran back to the negotiating table on terms more favourable to Washington.

Iranian officials have responded cautiously to the latest threat, with foreign ministry sources reportedly saying that Tehran would not negotiate under duress. Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, has previously expressed scepticism about the value of direct talks with Washington, arguing that the US cannot be trusted to honour its commitments.

The exchange comes at a particularly sensitive moment in the Middle East, with the region still grappling with the fallout from the conflict in Gaza and broader instability across several fronts. European allies, including France and Germany, have urged both sides to pursue diplomacy, with EU foreign policy officials expressing concern that a collapse in talks could lead to a dangerous escalation.

Analysts have noted that Mr Trump's threat could be interpreted in several ways, from the imposition of further economic sanctions to the possibility of military action. However, some foreign policy experts have cautioned against reading too much into what they describe as the president's characteristic negotiating style.

"Trump has a long track record of issuing dramatic ultimatums as a bargaining tactic," said one Washington-based analyst. "The question is whether Tehran takes this as a serious threat or simply more bluster."

Ireland's Department of Foreign Affairs has not yet commented on the latest developments, though Dublin has traditionally supported multilateral diplomatic efforts to resolve the Iranian nuclear question and has backed the EU's role in facilitating negotiations.
headline: ‘Watch what happens’ – Donald Trump issues new threat to Iran

Students who had put in consistent preparation throughout the year were rewarded with a Leaving Certificate accounting paper that, while fair and accessible, demanded a solid working knowledge of the subject, teachers have said.

The paper, which was sat by thousands of students across the country on Wednesday, was described as straightforward in places but with enough challenging elements to separate the high achievers from those who had done only surface-level revision.

Teachers said the paper was well-structured and broadly in line with expectations, with no major surprises in terms of the topics examined. However, they noted that students who were "match fit" — having completed regular practice questions and past papers — would have been best placed to perform well.

"This was a paper that suited the student who had done plenty of practice," said one experienced accounting teacher. "If you had been working through questions consistently, you would have felt very comfortable sitting down to this. But if you had left your revision late or tried to predict what was coming up, you might have found it more difficult."

The compulsory question on final accounts was described as fair and manageable, with no unexpected twists that might have thrown students off course. Teachers said the layout was clear and the figures were workable, which would have been a welcome sight for students who often find this section the most high-stakes part of the paper.

Elsewhere, the paper offered a good spread of choice, allowing students to play to their strengths across the remaining sections. Questions on interpretation of accounts, club accounts, and tabular statements were all noted as being accessible, though teachers stressed that precision and attention to detail would ultimately determine how marks were awarded.

"Accounting is a subject where you either know how to do the work or you don't — there's very little room to bluff your way through," one teacher remarked. "The students who had been diligent all year will be pleased with how today went."

The paper was also praised for being well-balanced in terms of difficulty across higher and ordinary levels, with teachers suggesting that the examining body had pitched the standard appropriately.

Student reaction was largely positive, with many taking to social media afterwards to express relief that the paper had been manageable. Some noted that certain parts required careful reading of the question, with marks potentially lost by those who rushed through without fully digesting what was being asked.

The State Examinations Commission does not comment on individual papers while the examination series is ongoing.
headline: Accounting exam suited 'match fit' students who had done 'plenty of practice'

text:
The University of Nevada, Las Vegas has confirmed that no students were among those killed in a shooting on campus, with all victims being faculty members of the institution.

The university released a statement clarifying the status of the victims following the attack, which left three people dead and a fourth critically injured. The gunman was also killed at the scene.

The shooting unfolded on Wednesday afternoon at Beam Hall, a building on the university's main campus that houses the Lee Business School. Armed police responded within minutes and engaged the shooter, identified as Anthony Polito, a 67-year-old man who was described as a professor at another institution.

UNLV president Keith Whitfield said the university community was devastated by the loss of its faculty members, whom he described as dedicated educators and valued colleagues. He said counselling services had been made available to students and staff across the campus.

The confirmation that all victims were faculty members has raised questions about whether the gunman had specifically targeted academic staff. Investigators said Polito had applied for a position at UNLV and had not been successful, though authorities cautioned that a definitive motive had not yet been established.

Police said the suspect was found carrying multiple letters addressed to university staff in several states, which are now being examined as part of the investigation.

The shooting prompted a lockdown across the sprawling campus, with thousands of students sheltering in place as police swept buildings. Classes were cancelled for the remainder of the week, and the university said it would work with the families of the victims before publicly identifying them.

The attack came during a period of final examinations, when the campus would ordinarily have been busy with students preparing for end-of-semester assessments.

It was the latest in a long succession of mass shootings across the United States, where gun violence remains a deeply polarising political issue. Las Vegas was previously the scene of one of the deadliest mass shootings in modern American history, when a gunman opened fire on a music festival from a hotel room in October 2017, killing 60 people and injuring hundreds more.
headline: No students killed in Las Vegas shooting with victims all faculty members, university says

Donald Trump is set to address a hastily convened gathering of the nation's most senior military commanders, according to a US official familiar with the matter, in what marks an unusual summoning of top brass that has raised eyebrows in Washington.

The meeting, which was organised at short notice, will see the US president speak to combatant commanders and other high-ranking Pentagon officials, though the precise agenda for the session has not been made public. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the matter publicly, offered few further details about what prompted the rapid scheduling.

The gathering comes at a time of heightened global tensions on multiple fronts, with the war in Ukraine grinding on, instability across the Middle East, and growing concerns about China's military posture in the Indo-Pacific region. It also follows a period of significant turbulence within the US defence establishment, where Mr Trump has moved aggressively to reshape the Pentagon's leadership and priorities since returning to office.

The president has made no secret of his desire to exert greater personal control over the military, having installed loyalists in key defence roles and clashed publicly with senior officers he views as insufficiently aligned with his agenda. His relationship with the military establishment has been fraught at times, with critics accusing him of politicising the armed forces while supporters argue he is reasserting necessary civilian authority over the defence apparatus.

Such meetings between a sitting president and combatant commanders are not unprecedented but are typically planned well in advance and scheduled around routine cycles of military briefings. The hastily arranged nature of this particular gathering has fuelled speculation in Washington about whether a specific security development may have prompted it, though no such event has been publicly identified.

The White House declined to comment on the meeting's specific purpose, with a spokesperson saying only that the president regularly engages with military leaders on matters of national security.

Several former defence officials expressed concern about the optics and substance of such a rapidly organised meeting, noting that it could signal either a genuine security concern or an attempt by the president to use the military as a backdrop for political messaging.

Members of Congress from both parties said they would be seeking further information about the meeting and any decisions that may flow from it, with Democratic lawmakers in particular warning against any moves that could draw the United States into new military commitments without proper congressional oversight.
headline: Donald Trump to speak at hastily called meeting of top military leaders, says official

text:
The stabbing of a woman in Dundalk by a man reportedly motivated by Islamist ideology has crossed a threshold that security analysts long warned was a matter of when, not if. Ireland has now joined the grim roster of European nations that have experienced an attack inspired by violent jihadist extremism, and the questions it raises about our preparedness, our intelligence capabilities, and our broader approach to radicalisation demand honest and urgent answers.

It is important, first, to state what this event is not. It is not an indictment of Ireland's Muslim community, the vast majority of whom will be as horrified by this act as anyone else. It is not a justification for the kind of far-right rhetoric that cynically exploits such incidents to demonise entire populations. And it is not a reason to abandon the open, tolerant values that define this country at its best. But nor should it be minimised, explained away, or buried beneath a layer of well-meaning but ultimately evasive commentary about lone actors and mental health. If the ideology mattered — and the Gardaí clearly believe it did — then the ideology must be confronted.

For years, Ireland has occupied an unusual position in the European security landscape. Our neutrality, our relatively small Muslim population, and our historical absence from military interventions in the Middle East were often cited as reasons why this country was unlikely to become a target. That analysis always contained more hope than rigour. The reality is that Islamist-inspired violence in Europe has long since moved beyond any neat calculus of foreign policy grievances. The attacks in Nice, in Würzburg, in Reading — carried out with knives, with vehicles, with whatever came to hand — were not responses to specific geopolitical provocations. They were products of a globalised ideology of hate, transmitted through online networks that respect no borders and require no passport.

Ireland's security infrastructure has been evolving to meet this reality, but the pace of that evolution is a legitimate matter of public concern. The establishment of the National Security Analysis Centre and the Strategic Threat Analysis Centre within the Department of the Taoiseach represented important steps. The Gardaí have built up counter-terrorism capabilities, and successive commissioners have acknowledged the threat posed by international terrorism. But resources remain constrained. Ireland still lacks a dedicated domestic intelligence agency of the kind that operates in most comparable European states. MI5 in Britain, the DGSI in France, the BfV in Germany — these are organisations with statutory mandates, dedicated personnel, and legal frameworks tailored specifically to the work of identifying and disrupting terrorist threats before they materialise.

The Gardaí do extraordinary work, but they are a police force being asked to simultaneously manage everything from community policing to organised crime to counter-espionage to counter-terrorism. The question of whether a standalone security and intelligence agency is now necessary for Ireland is one that successive governments have been reluctant to grasp. It is politically awkward, it is expensive, and it raises legitimate civil liberties concerns that would need careful legislative attention. But the Dundalk attack should concentrate minds. The threat environment has changed, and our institutional architecture must change with it.

There is also the thorny question of radicalisation itself.
headline: Ireland’s first Islamist-inspired knife attack raises urgent questions about extremist threats

text:
Older people in Ireland are paying significantly more for private health insurance than younger policyholders, with those aged 65 and over facing premiums that are on average 43% higher, according to new findings from the Health Insurance Authority.

The watchdog's analysis, published today, lays bare the extent to which age continues to drive the cost of cover despite Ireland's community-rated health insurance system, which is designed to ensure that insurers charge the same premium to all consumers regardless of age or health status.

Under the community rating system, a 25-year-old and a 75-year-old should be quoted the same price for the same plan. However, the Authority found that in practice, the wide array of plans available on the market means older customers tend to be clustered on more expensive policies that offer higher levels of cover, while younger consumers are more likely to opt for cheaper, more basic plans.

The result is that the average premium paid by those aged 65 and over stands at approximately €2,400 per annum, compared with roughly €1,680 for the general adult population. The disparity raises questions about whether the current system is working as intended to spread the cost of healthcare across all age groups.

The Health Insurance Authority urged older consumers to shop around and consider switching plans, noting that many could achieve equivalent levels of cover at a lower cost. The watchdog said there were often comparable plans available at significantly reduced premiums, but that consumer inertia and a reluctance to switch remained persistent barriers, particularly among older policyholders.

"Many people have been on the same plan for years and assume that switching would mean a loss of cover or waiting periods," a spokesperson for the Authority said. "In the vast majority of cases, that is simply not so. Consumers who have served their initial waiting periods will not have to re-serve them when moving to a comparable plan, even with a different insurer."

The findings come at a time when the cost of private health insurance remains a significant household expense for many families. Approximately 2.3 million people in Ireland now hold some form of private health insurance, representing around 46% of the population.

The authority also highlighted the role of lifetime community rating loadings, introduced in 2015, which impose additional charges on people who take out health insurance for the first time after the age of 34. These loadings, set at 2% for each year over 34 at the time of first taking out cover, were designed to encourage people to purchase insurance at a younger age and remain in the market.

While the loadings have been credited with stabilising the risk pool by attracting younger members, consumer advocates have raised concerns that they add a further layer of cost for those who come to private health insurance later in life, potentially compounding the affordability challenges faced by older people.

The Irish Patients' Association said the findings underscored the need for greater transparency in how health insurance plans are marketed and sold to older consumers. "There is an onus on insurers to ensure that vulnerable customers, including older people, are not left paying over the odds simply because they are unfamiliar with the options available to them," a spokesperson said.
headline: Over 65s pay 43% more for health insurance, watchdog finds

text:
Kathleen MacMahon spent two decades as a journalist with RTÉ before stepping away to write fiction full-time, and she admits there are days when she misses the newsroom terribly. "I miss the camaraderie, the buzz of a breaking story, the sense that you're right in the middle of things," she says. "But I don't miss the early mornings. I was never a morning person, and journalism is very unforgiving on that front."

Her latest novel finds her exploring territory that is at once deeply personal and universally recognisable: the complicated, tender, infuriating, irreplaceable bond between mothers and daughters. It is a relationship she knows intimately, both as a daughter herself and as a mother to her own girls, and she says it is one that fiction is uniquely placed to illuminate.

"There's something about the mother-daughter relationship that resists easy summary," she says. "It's not one thing. It's everything, all at once. It's love and resentment and guilt and fierce protectiveness and the desire to be understood and the terror of being seen too clearly. I wanted to write something that captured all of those contradictions without resolving them neatly, because in life they don't resolve neatly."

MacMahon, who grew up in Dublin and still lives in the city, published her debut novel, *This Is How It Ends*, in 2012 to considerable acclaim. It became a bestseller in Ireland and was translated into more than a dozen languages, establishing her as one of the most distinctive new voices in Irish literary fiction. Subsequent novels have cemented that reputation, and she has built a loyal readership both at home and abroad.

She acknowledges that the transition from journalism to fiction was not entirely seamless. "In journalism, you're trained to get to the point quickly, to strip away anything extraneous. In fiction, the extraneous stuff is often where the truth lives. It took me a while to give myself permission to slow down, to let a scene breathe, to trust the reader to stay with me."

That said, she believes her years in RTÉ gave her skills that serve her well as a novelist. "Listening is the big one. As a journalist, you learn to really listen to people, to hear what they're saying and also what they're not saying. That's invaluable when you're writing dialogue, when you're trying to create characters who feel real and three-dimensional."

The new novel began, she says, with an image rather than a plot. "I had this picture in my head of a woman standing in her mother's kitchen, holding a cup of tea she didn't want, and feeling simultaneously like a child and like the adult in the room. That tension between who you are and who you become when you walk through your parents' door — I think everyone knows that feeling."

She is careful to stress that the novel is not autobiographical, though she concedes that writing about mothers and daughters inevitably draws on personal experience. "You'd have to be very dishonest to write about this subject and not put something of yourself into it. But the characters are their own people.
headline: Kathleen MacMahon on missing journalism, the mother/daughter relationship and her latest novel

text:
A woman in her 30s has appeared before Carlow District Court in connection with the murder of a man in Co Carlow.

The accused, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was brought before Judge Patricia Cronin in a brief sitting on Saturday morning. She was charged with one count of murder contrary to common law.

Detective Sergeant Brian Mahon of Carlow Garda Station gave evidence of arrest, charge and caution. He told the court the accused was arrested in the early hours of Friday morning and was subsequently charged at Carlow Garda Station, where she made no reply when the charge was put to her.

The court heard the Director of Public Prosecutions has directed trial on indictment, meaning the case will ultimately be heard before the Central Criminal Court.

Defence solicitor John O'Brien applied for legal aid on behalf of his client, telling the court the accused was not in a financial position to fund her own defence. Judge Cronin granted the application.

Mr O'Brien made no application for bail, and the accused was remanded in custody to appear before Cloverhill District Court at a later date.

The brief hearing lasted only a matter of minutes, with the accused speaking only to confirm her name, address and date of birth.

Gardaí had launched a murder investigation following the discovery of a man's body at a residence in the Carlow area earlier in the week. A postmortem examination was carried out by the State Pathologist's office, the results of which are not being disclosed for operational reasons.

Investigating Gardaí have appealed for anyone with information to contact Carlow Garda Station or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: Woman, 30s, appears in court in connection with murder of man in Carlow

text:
Sara Ochs arrives on the literary scene with the kind of debut that makes you sit up and take notice. There is no tentativeness here, no sense of a writer finding her feet. Instead, what we get is a novel that reads as though it were the work of someone several books deep into a career, a strikingly assured and accomplished piece of fiction that announces a significant new talent.

The novel, which has been generating considerable buzz since its acquisition was announced, centres on a woman grappling with the aftermath of a decision that has fractured her life in ways both obvious and imperceptible. Ochs has a remarkable ability to render the interior world of her protagonist with precision and empathy, never tipping into sentimentality but never withholding compassion either. It is a delicate balance, and she maintains it throughout with an almost effortless grace.

What is most impressive about Ochs' writing is her command of pace. She understands instinctively when to linger and when to accelerate, when to let a scene breathe and when to cut away at exactly the moment of maximum tension. Too many debut novelists fall into the trap of overwriting, of labouring every point until the reader's patience frays. Ochs does the opposite. She trusts her reader, and the result is a narrative that feels both lean and deeply layered.

The prose itself is clean and direct without ever being sparse. There is a musicality to her sentences that rewards close reading, but the story never becomes subordinate to style. She writes with the kind of clarity that can only come from genuine rigour, from having worked and reworked each paragraph until every word earns its place on the page.

The supporting characters are drawn with similar care. None of them exists merely to serve the protagonist's arc. Each feels fully realised, possessed of their own motivations and contradictions, their own private griefs and small triumphs. Ochs has a particular gift for dialogue that reveals character through what is left unsaid as much as what is spoken aloud. Conversations in this novel carry the weight of history, of shared experience and mutual evasion, and they crackle with an authenticity that is genuinely rare.

There are moments in the second half where the plot takes turns that, in lesser hands, might have strained credulity. But Ochs has laid her groundwork so carefully, has built such a solid foundation of character and motivation, that even the most dramatic developments feel earned and inevitable. This is storytelling of a high order, the kind that makes you want to go back to the beginning the moment you reach the final page.

Irish readers may find particular resonance in the novel's exploration of silence and secrecy within families, of the stories we tell ourselves to survive and the truths we bury because we cannot yet bear to face them. These are themes that transcend geography, of course, but they land with a specific weight in a culture that has spent recent decades reckoning with its own long-held silences.

It would be premature to place too heavy a burden of expectation on any debut novelist, however talented.
headline: Book Review: Sara Ochs' debut is strikingly assured and accomplished

text:
A massive polio vaccination campaign has begun in the Gaza Strip, with health workers racing to inoculate hundreds of thousands of children amid the ongoing conflict and a deepening humanitarian crisis.

The World Health Organisation and the United Nations children's agency UNICEF launched the drive after polio was detected in sewage samples in the territory, raising fears of a full-blown outbreak in conditions where sanitation and clean water systems have been largely destroyed.

The campaign aims to reach more than 640,000 children under the age of ten across Gaza, a monumental logistical challenge given the scale of displacement and destruction wrought by months of Israeli military operations.

Health workers have fanned out across the territory, setting up vaccination points in shelters, hospitals and makeshift clinics. Many families have been displaced multiple times and are living in overcrowded tents and temporary shelters, making it difficult to ensure every child is reached.

The WHO has said that humanitarian pauses in fighting are essential to allow vaccinators to safely access all parts of the strip, including areas in the north that have been subject to the most intense bombardment. The organisation has called on all parties to the conflict to facilitate the campaign.

Polio, a highly infectious viral disease that can cause irreversible paralysis and is potentially fatal, had been considered eradicated in Gaza for more than 25 years. However, the collapse of the territory's health infrastructure, the displacement of nearly the entire population and the breakdown of routine immunisation programmes have created the conditions for its return.

UNICEF has warned that the reappearance of polio is a damning indictment of the humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in Gaza, where hospitals are barely functioning and access to clean water remains desperately limited.

The Irish Government has repeatedly called for greater humanitarian access to Gaza and has been among the more vocal EU member states in pressing for a ceasefire. Ireland has also contributed funding to UNICEF and other agencies operating in the territory.

International health experts have cautioned that the vaccination campaign, while critical, will need to be repeated in subsequent rounds to ensure sufficient coverage and that the virus does not gain a foothold in the population.
headline: Massive polio vaccination campaign begins in Gaza

text:
RTÉ has confirmed the identity of the new judge who will take a seat on the Dancing With The Stars panel following the departure of long-serving adjudicator Loraine Barry.

The announcement, which had been the subject of intense speculation among fans of the popular Sunday night show, brings to an end weeks of rumour about who would fill the vacancy left by Barry, who had been a fixture on the programme since its Irish debut.

Barry, a former professional ballroom dancer and World Dance Council adjudicator, had been part of the judging panel since Dancing With The Stars first aired on RTÉ One in 2017. Her departure at the end of the most recent series prompted an outpouring of tributes from viewers and former contestants alike, many of whom credited her warm but exacting critiques with raising the standard of the competition.

The show, which pairs celebrities with professional dancers in a weekly ballroom and Latin dance contest, has become one of RTÉ's most reliable ratings performers since it was adapted from the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing format. It regularly draws audiences in excess of 400,000 viewers on Sunday evenings, making it a cornerstone of the national broadcaster's entertainment schedule.

The new judge will sit alongside returning panellists Brian Redmond and Arthur Gourounlian when the programme returns for its next series. Presenter Jennifer Zamparelli is also expected to reprise her hosting duties.

RTÉ said further details about the upcoming series, including the celebrity line-up, would be announced in due course. Production on the new run is expected to get under way in the coming months, with the series traditionally airing in the first quarter of the year.
headline: Revealed: New Dancing With The Stars judge confirmed following Loraine Barry's exit

text:
Morning Ireland has retained its position as the most listened-to radio programme in the country, according to the latest Joint National Listenership Research figures published today.

The RTÉ Radio 1 flagship breakfast programme, presented by Rachael English and Mary Wilson, recorded an audience of 447,000 listeners in the latest survey period, comfortably maintaining its dominance at the top of the national listenership table.

RTÉ Radio 1 continues to lead the way as the most popular station in the State, with the latest JNLR/Ipsos figures showing it commands a market-leading share of the national audience. The station's strong daytime schedule, anchored by Morning Ireland and followed by programmes such as Today with Claire Byrne and Liveline with Joe Duffy, continues to draw significant numbers.

In Cork, Neil Prendeville has once again cemented his status as the region's most popular radio voice. The Neil Prendeville Show on Cork's RedFM topped the local listenership figures, outperforming all rivals in the market. Prendeville, who has long been a dominant force in Munster broadcasting, continues to attract a loyal and sizeable audience in the region.

The figures will be a source of considerable satisfaction for RedFM, which has consistently challenged the more established Cork stations for audience share. Prendeville's programme, which airs on weekday mornings, has proven a formidable competitor to both local and national offerings in the Cork market.

Across the wider radio landscape, the figures confirm that radio listenership in Ireland remains remarkably robust despite increasing competition from podcasts and streaming services. Some 83% of the adult population continues to tune in to radio on a daily basis, spending an average of almost four hours a day listening.

Among the national stations, Today FM and Newstalk both recorded solid performances, while local and regional stations across the country continue to command strong loyalty from listeners outside Dublin.

The JNLR figures are compiled by Ipsos and are regarded as the industry standard measure of radio audiences in Ireland. The survey is conducted over a 12-month rolling period and is published several times a year, providing broadcasters and advertisers with a detailed picture of listening habits across the State.
headline: Morning Ireland the country's most popular radio show as Neil Prendeville on top in Cork

text:
The funeral of celebrated poet Michael Longley has heard that he possessed a rare and extraordinary gift for touching the deepest parts of the human soul with the most economical use of language.

Longley, who died last week aged 85, was laid to rest in Belfast on Wednesday following a service attended by family, friends, fellow poets and admirers from across Ireland and beyond. The Belfast-born poet, widely regarded as one of the finest of his generation, had been a towering figure in Irish and British literature for more than five decades.

Mourners at the service heard tributes describing a man of immense warmth, generosity and quiet dignity, whose spare and luminous verse belied the depth of feeling contained within it. Friends spoke of his deep love of the west of Ireland, particularly Carrigskeewaun in Co Mayo, the landscape that inspired some of his most celebrated work, and of his lifelong devotion to the natural world.

His ability to compress vast emotional and philosophical weight into poems of startling brevity was repeatedly referenced during the service. Mourners were told that Longley could achieve in a handful of carefully chosen words what others struggled to convey in volumes.

Born in Belfast in 1939 to English parents who had moved to the city, Longley studied classics at Trinity College Dublin, where he met his wife, the critic and academic Edna Longley, née Broderick. The couple's partnership was one of the great literary marriages, and Edna was a constant presence and intellectual companion throughout his career.

Longley's work drew deeply on his classical education, the Troubles in Northern Ireland, the two World Wars — his father had served in and been wounded during the First World War — and the flora and fauna of the west of Ireland. His poem "Ceasefire", a reimagining of a scene from Homer's Iliad published on the day of the IRA ceasefire in 1994, became one of the defining literary responses to the Northern Irish peace process.

Over his long career, Longley received numerous honours. He was awarded the Queen's Gold Medal for Poetry in 2001 and the T.S. Eliot Prize in 2007 for his collection *Snow Water*. He served as Ireland Professor of Poetry from 2007 to 2010, a cross-border role shared between Trinity College Dublin, Queen's University Belfast and University College Dublin. He was also the recipient of the Irish Times Poetry Now Award on multiple occasions and the Hawthornden Prize.

President Michael D Higgins, himself a poet, led tributes in the days following Longley's death, describing him as a poet of "extraordinary grace" whose work had illuminated the lives of countless readers. Mr Higgins said Longley's contribution to Irish cultural life was immeasurable and that his poems had served as bridges between communities during the darkest days of the Troubles.

Longley was closely associated with a remarkable generation of Northern Irish poets that included Seamus Heaney, Derek Mahon and James Simmons, all of whom studied or taught at Queen's University Belfast during the 1960s.
headline: Poet Michael Longley touched souls with just a few words, funeral hears

text:
A man in his 20s has died following a single-vehicle crash in Co Tipperary in the early hours of this morning.

The collision occurred at approximately 2.30am on a local road outside Cahir. Emergency services attended the scene, but the man, who was the sole occupant of the car, was pronounced dead at the scene.

His body has been removed to the mortuary at University Hospital Waterford, where a post-mortem examination is due to take place.

The road has been closed to facilitate a technical examination by Garda forensic collision investigators. Local diversions are in place, and motorists are being advised to avoid the area.

Gardaí are appealing to anyone who may have witnessed the collision to come forward. They are particularly keen to hear from road users who may have travelled in the area between 2am and 3am, or anyone with camera footage, including dash cam, who was in the vicinity at the time.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Cahir Garda Station on 052 744 5630, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.
headline: Man, 20s, dies in single-vehicle crash in Tipperary

text:
Elon Musk's brain-chip startup Neuralink is under federal investigation over allegations that it used unsafe methods to transport hazardous materials, raising fresh questions about the billionaire's controversial neurotechnology venture.

The US Department of Transportation has been probing the company over claims that it failed to properly package and ship dangerous biological and chemical substances, according to reports.
