The investigation centres on whether Neuralink violated federal regulations governing the transport of hazardous pathogens and other materials linked to its animal testing programme.

The probe is understood to have been triggered by a complaint alleging that materials were moved without the appropriate containment measures, potentially putting workers, couriers and the wider public at risk. Federal rules impose strict requirements on how such substances must be labelled, packaged and documented before they can be shipped.

It is the latest in a series of controversies to engulf Neuralink, which has faced sustained criticism from animal welfare groups over the treatment of primates and other animals used in its research. The company has previously been investigated by the US Department of Agriculture's inspector general over potential animal welfare violations, with reports suggesting that rushed timelines imposed by Musk led to botched experiments and unnecessary animal suffering.

Neuralink, which is headquartered in Fremont, California, is developing a brain-computer interface designed to be implanted in the human skull. The device, roughly the size of a coin, uses tiny electrode threads to read neural signals, with the ultimate aim of allowing paralysed patients to control computers and other devices using only their thoughts.

The company reached a significant milestone last year when it received approval from the US Food and Drug Administration to begin human trials. It has since implanted its device in a small number of patients, with Musk claiming encouraging early results. However, reports have also emerged of complications, including issues with the implant's electrode threads retracting from brain tissue.

Musk, who also leads Tesla, SpaceX and the social media platform X, has made sweeping claims about Neuralink's potential, suggesting it could eventually cure blindness, treat spinal cord injuries and even enable a form of telepathy. Critics have accused him of overpromising and underplaying the risks involved in such an invasive technology.

The transportation investigation adds to the regulatory scrutiny facing the company at a time when Musk's sprawling business empire is attracting heightened attention. His prominent political role in Washington, where he has been leading efforts to slash federal spending through the so-called Department of Government Efficiency initiative established by President Trump, has drawn particular focus to potential conflicts of interest given his companies' extensive dealings with US government agencies.

Neuralink has not publicly commented on the investigation. The Department of Transportation declined to provide further details, citing the ongoing nature of the probe.
headline: Elon Musk’s brain-implant company investigated over ‘unsafe’ shipping methods

text:
A substantial Limerick farming holding has been sold for a combined sum in excess of €3.8 million, in one of the more significant agricultural land transactions to come before the market in the mid-west region this year.

The property, which was offered in lots, attracted considerable interest from both local and national buyers, with strong competition reported at every stage of the sales process. The final accumulated figure across all lots surpassed the €3.8m mark, underlining the enduring demand for quality agricultural land in Munster.

Selling agents confirmed that the holding comprised top-quality grassland, well suited to both dairy and dry stock enterprises, with the land described as being in excellent heart. The acreage, which included a range of farm buildings and supporting infrastructure, had been well maintained and was considered ready to farm from the outset.

The sale reflects a broader trend of robust prices being achieved for prime agricultural holdings across the country, particularly in the so-called Golden Vale region, where fertile limestone soils continue to command a premium. Land agents operating across Limerick, Tipperary and Cork have noted that demand has remained strong despite the wider economic uncertainty, with both established farmers seeking to expand and new entrants to the sector competing for available acres.

Industry figures suggest that the average price per acre for good-quality grassland in Limerick has continued to climb in recent years, with prime parcels regularly exceeding €15,000 per acre and, in some instances, pushing well beyond that threshold depending on location, road frontage and the availability of entitlements.

The Irish Farmers' Association has previously noted that competition for land remains particularly intense in dairying regions, where expansion ambitions following the abolition of milk quotas continue to drive purchasing activity. The availability of sizeable, contiguous blocks of land remains relatively scarce, which has further supported prices when such holdings do come to market.

Agricultural consultants have said that sales of this scale tend to generate significant local interest and can set benchmarks for land values in the surrounding area for some time afterwards. The transaction is also likely to draw the attention of the Land Price Report compiled by the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland, which tracks trends in the agricultural property market on a quarterly basis.

Details of the individual lot prices and the precise acreage involved have not been publicly disclosed by the selling agents, though it is understood the holding extended to several hundred acres in total.
headline: Limerick farm sold for accumulated sum of over €3.8m

text:
A new artwork believed to be by the elusive street artist Banksy has appeared at the base of a London skyscraper, drawing crowds of onlookers and reigniting speculation about the anonymous figure's latest statement.

The piece, which appeared overnight, was spotted by early morning commuters at the foot of the building in central London. Photographs of the work quickly circulated on social media, with street art enthusiasts and Banksy followers debating its authenticity and possible meaning.

While the artwork has not yet been confirmed as a genuine Banksy, its style and execution bear the hallmarks of the Bristol-born artist, who is renowned for his stencilled works carrying sharp social and political commentary. Banksy typically confirms his pieces through his official Instagram account or website, though as of this afternoon no such confirmation had been posted.

The appearance of the work drew significant crowds throughout the day, with some passers-by stopping to take photographs while others debated whether the building's owners or the local council would move to protect or remove it.

Banksy's works have become enormously valuable, with authenticated pieces fetching millions at auction. However, the artist's preference for placing works in public spaces has often put local authorities in a difficult position, balancing the cultural cachet of hosting a Banksy against concerns about crowd management and property rights.

The Metropolitan Police said officers attended the scene to manage the gathering crowds but that no offences were being investigated.

It is the latest in a long line of surprise appearances by the artist, whose identity remains one of the art world's most closely guarded secrets despite decades of speculation. His works have appeared on walls, bridges and buildings across the world, from the separation barrier in the West Bank to the sides of terraced houses in English seaside towns.

Local councillors said they were seeking to establish the provenance of the piece before deciding on next steps regarding its preservation.
headline: Artwork thought to be by Banksy appears at foot of London skyscraper

text:
There is something quietly devastating about watching a play set during a pandemic when the memory of our own is still so fresh. Emma Donoghue's latest stage adaptation, drawn from her own prose work examining the 1918 influenza crisis, arrives at a moment when audiences need no instruction in the particular claustrophobia of quarantine, the awful arithmetic of daily death tolls, or the way a crisis strips human relationships back to their most essential elements.

The production, staged with a kind of austere beauty that lets the text breathe, follows a small cast of characters confined together as the Spanish flu tears through their community. Donoghue, who has long demonstrated a gift for finding the universal within the enclosed — most famously in *Room* — here turns her attention to a historical catastrophe that, until recently, had been largely forgotten by the general public. The timing, of course, lends the material an almost unbearable prescience that no one could have anticipated when the project was first conceived.

What distinguishes Donoghue's approach is her refusal to treat the pandemic merely as backdrop or metaphor. The virus is not a symbol; it is a presence, as real and as ruthless as any antagonist. Characters sicken with terrifying speed. The rituals of care — the sponging of foreheads, the changing of soaked linens, the desperate brewing of remedies from whatever is to hand — become the central dramatic action. There is no cavalry coming. There is only the next hour, the next breath, the next decision about who to tend to first.

The performances are uniformly strong, with a particular standout in the role of the nurse at the centre of the action. She carries the weight of the piece with a quiet authority that never tips into melodrama, even as the bodies accumulate and the living grow more desperate. It is a physically demanding role — she is rarely still, rarely afforded the luxury of reflection — and it is played with a controlled intensity that holds the audience in something close to a shared vigil.

The director has made several intelligent choices that serve the material well. The set is deliberately sparse, suggesting both the poverty of resources and the narrowing of the world that illness imposes. Lighting shifts are subtle but effective, marking the passage of hours that blur into one another as exhaustion takes hold. There is no interval, a decision that initially seems punishing but ultimately proves essential to the cumulative emotional power of the piece. To break the spell would be to offer a reprieve that the characters themselves are never granted.

Donoghue's script is characteristically precise, her ear for dialogue evident in exchanges that manage to be both naturalistic and carefully shaped. She has a novelist's instinct for the telling detail — a character's obsessive folding of cloth, the way a window is opened and closed as a negotiation between fresh air and freezing cold — and these details accumulate into something richly textured. If there is a criticism to be made, it is that the middle section occasionally feels as though it is circling rather than advancing, the repetitive nature of crisis care threatening to become dramatically static. But this may well be the point. Monotony and terror, as we all learned not so long ago, are not mutually exclusive.
headline: Theatre review: Emma Donoghue's tale of 1918 has a renewed prescience

text:
There's no shortage of culture worth your time this week, from one of Cork's finest singer-songwriters hitting the road to a dazzling new film from one of Hollywood's most celebrated actresses. Here are five things to put on your radar.

Mick Flannery has long since cemented his reputation as one of the most compelling voices in Irish music, and fans will have the chance to catch him on a run of intimate dates across the country over the coming weeks. The Blarney native, whose songwriting has drawn comparisons with the greats of Americana and folk, continues to mine a rich seam of emotionally raw, beautifully crafted material. Whether you've followed him since his early days or are coming to his music fresh, a Flannery live show remains one of the most rewarding nights out you can have. Check local venues for dates and tickets.

Emma Stone returns to the screen in a film that has already been generating serious awards buzz on the international festival circuit. The collaboration reunites her with director Yorgos Lanthimos, and early reviews suggest it may represent some of her finest work to date. Stone has spoken in interviews about being drawn to roles that challenge audiences, and this latest outing appears to do precisely that — expect something provocative, visually striking and utterly unlike anything else in cinemas at the moment.

Book festival season is in full swing, and there are some wonderful literary gatherings taking place across the country in the weeks ahead. Ireland's festival circuit has become one of the most vibrant in Europe for readers and writers alike, offering everything from headline author events and panel discussions to workshops and children's programming. It's worth scanning the schedules carefully, as some of the most memorable encounters tend to happen at the smaller, more conversational events rather than the marquee appearances.

For theatre lovers, there is plenty to tempt you out of the house as well. The country's stages are alive with new work and bold revivals, with several productions transferring from successful runs at regional venues into Dublin. Irish theatre continues to punch well above its weight internationally, and catching a show in its early life — before the wider world discovers it — remains one of the great pleasures of the domestic arts scene.

Finally, for those after something a little different, keep an eye on what's happening in the gallery space this week. A number of striking new exhibitions have opened around the country, spanning photography, painting and mixed media. As ever, many of Ireland's publicly funded galleries offer free admission, making a midweek visit one of the best value cultural outings available. Take the time — you won't regret it.
headline: Five For Your Radar: Mick Flannery, Emma Stone film, book festival...

text:
A West Cork company has been fined a total of €18,000 after pleading guilty to six breaches of emissions regulations at its facility.

The case, brought by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), was heard at Clonakilty District Court, where the judge heard that inspections carried out at the company's premises revealed a series of violations of its industrial emissions licence conditions over a period of several months.

The EPA told the court that its inspectors had identified six separate breaches relating to the company's failure to comply with the terms of its licence, which governs the levels and management of emissions from its operations. The breaches included failures to monitor emissions adequately and to keep proper records, as well as instances where emission limits were exceeded.

Counsel for the EPA said the agency had engaged with the company on numerous occasions to bring it into compliance, but that the breaches had persisted over a sustained period, necessitating the prosecution.

A representative of the company told the court that significant investment had since been made to address the issues identified by the EPA and that the facility was now operating in full compliance with its licence conditions. The court heard that new monitoring equipment had been installed and additional staff training had been carried out.

The judge noted the seriousness of the offences and the importance of environmental regulations in protecting the health of local communities and the wider environment. However, the court also acknowledged the steps the company had taken to rectify the situation.

A fine of €3,000 was imposed in respect of each of the six charges, bringing the total to €18,000. The judge also directed the company to pay a contribution towards the EPA's costs in bringing the prosecution.

Speaking after the hearing, an EPA spokesperson said the case demonstrated the agency's commitment to enforcing environmental legislation and holding companies to account where licence conditions are not met.

"Compliance with emissions licences is not optional," the spokesperson said. "These regulations exist to protect public health and the environment, and we will not hesitate to take enforcement action where breaches are identified."
headline: West Cork company fined for six breaches of emissions regulations

text:
The launch of auto-enrolment on 30 September will mark a genuine watershed in how Ireland treats retirement savings. For the first time, hundreds of thousands of workers who have never had access to an occupational pension will be nudged — firmly, by default — into building one. And while the policy is gender-neutral on its face, its greatest impact will fall disproportionately on women. That alone makes it worth celebrating. But celebration should not be confused with complacency, because the gender pension gap in Ireland remains a chasm that auto-enrolment, however welcome, cannot bridge on its own.

The numbers are stark and well-rehearsed. According to the CSO, just 35% of women in employment have supplementary pension coverage, compared with roughly 50% of men. When women do have pensions, the accumulated value tends to be significantly lower. By the time they reach retirement, Irish women receive, on average, substantially less pension income than their male counterparts. The European Commission has estimated the gender pension gap across the EU at around 30%, and Ireland sits comfortably — or rather, uncomfortably — within that range.

Auto-enrolment will help. It will capture women working in the retail, hospitality and care sectors — industries where employer-sponsored pension schemes have historically been thin on the ground. The "opt-out rather than opt-in" design leverages behavioural economics in precisely the right way, overcoming the inertia that has left too many workers, and particularly women, without any private retirement savings at all. The matching state contribution is a further incentive. For a woman earning €30,000 a year in a job that never offered a pension scheme, this is transformative.

Yet the architecture of auto-enrolment also reveals its limitations. To be enrolled, a worker must be aged between 23 and 60, earning at least €20,000 a year. That €20,000 threshold is not negligible. Many women working part-time — and women still account for the overwhelming majority of part-time workers in Ireland — will fall below it. A woman working 20 hours a week at the minimum wage, for example, will not automatically qualify. She is precisely the kind of worker who most needs a pension safety net, and she will remain outside it.

Then there is the contribution rate. Auto-enrolment begins with a modest 1.5% of gross earnings from the employee, matched by the employer and topped up by the State. This will rise gradually to 6% over a decade. It is a cautious, politically pragmatic approach — designed to minimise resistance from employers and to avoid sticker shock for workers — but the sums involved, particularly in the early years, will not generate pension pots large enough to close the gap meaningfully. A woman who enters the system at 35 on a modest salary will still face a significant shortfall at 66.

The deeper structural issues lie well beyond the reach of any auto-enrolment scheme. The gender pension gap is, in large part, a downstream consequence of the gender pay gap, which in turn reflects the unequal distribution of unpaid care work.
headline: Ireland’s pension auto-enrolment is a turning point for women but it's not the whole story

text:
The Taoiseach has made a direct pitch to American business leaders to deepen their investment in Ireland, insisting the country remains one of the most attractive locations in Europe for US companies looking to expand their operations.

Speaking at a business roundtable event in New York as part of a wider trade mission, the Taoiseach told senior executives from the technology, pharmaceutical and financial services sectors that Ireland's pro-enterprise environment, highly educated workforce and continued commitment to the 15 per cent global minimum corporation tax rate made it an ideal base for transatlantic growth.

"Ireland has been a gateway to Europe for American companies for decades, and that relationship has never been more important than it is today," the Taoiseach said. "We are not resting on our laurels. We are investing in infrastructure, in housing, in skills — all of the things that matter to companies when they are deciding where to locate."

The trade mission, supported by IDA Ireland and Enterprise Ireland, comes at a time of heightened uncertainty in global trade, with the impact of US tariff policy continuing to weigh on business confidence on both sides of the Atlantic. The Taoiseach acknowledged those concerns but stressed that Ireland's open economy and deep ties with the United States provided a degree of stability that few other European countries could match.

Ireland is home to more than 900 US companies, which between them employ approximately 210,000 people. The IDA has consistently pointed to the depth of the existing relationship as one of its strongest selling points when courting new investment, though competition from other EU member states has intensified in recent years.

Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin, who is also travelling as part of the delegation, held separate meetings with representatives from the financial services industry and emphasised Ireland's role as a key hub for fund management and fintech within the European Union.

"Our membership of the EU, our common law legal system, our English-speaking workforce — these are real, tangible advantages," the Tánaiste said. "But what sets Ireland apart more than anything is the quality of the people. That is what American companies tell us time and again."

Opposition TDs were quick to point out that the Government's pitch abroad must be matched by action at home. Sinn Féin's finance spokesperson argued that chronic underinvestment in housing and public transport infrastructure risked undermining Ireland's competitiveness, warning that many multinational employees were struggling with the cost of living.

"You can make all the speeches you like in New York, but if workers cannot find an affordable place to live in Dublin or Cork, that is a problem no trade mission can fix," the TD said.

The Social Democrats echoed those concerns, calling on the Government to publish a comprehensive workforce planning strategy to ensure Ireland could meet the skills demands of an expanding foreign direct investment base without placing further strain on public services.

Business groups gave the mission a cautious welcome. Ibec said sustained engagement with US firms was essential but urged the Government to accelerate capital investment in energy infrastructure, noting that the availability of reliable, competitively priced power was becoming a decisive factor for companies considering data centre and advanced manufacturing investments.
headline: Taoiseach urges US firms to expand operations to Ireland

text:
There is a quiet crisis unfolding in homes across this country, one that rarely makes the front pages but is felt in every county, every community, and behind every door where a parent or family member has set aside their own life to care for a child with complex needs.

On Saturday, thousands of family carers will take to the streets of Dublin in what organisers are calling a march for recognition, for dignity, and for the basic supports that the State has long promised but consistently failed to deliver. If ever there was a march that deserved the full-throated support of the Irish public, this is it.

The numbers alone should shame us. There are more than 500,000 family carers in Ireland, and a significant proportion of them are caring for children with disabilities, chronic illnesses, and additional needs. They save the State an estimated €20 billion a year — a figure so staggering that it bears repeating. Twenty billion euro. That is not a typo. That is the economic contribution of people who are, in many cases, surviving on a Carer's Allowance of €236 a week, means-tested to within an inch of its life, and hedged about with conditions that seem designed to discourage rather than support.

Let us be honest about what family caring actually looks like in Ireland in 2025. It looks like a mother who hasn't slept through the night in six years because her son requires round-the-clock supervision. It looks like a father who gave up a career he loved because no suitable respite care was available. It looks like a grandmother raising a grandchild with profound disabilities because the system simply could not cope. It looks like exhaustion, isolation, financial hardship, and a gnawing sense that nobody in power is listening.

I have spoken to dozens of family carers over the past year, and the same themes emerge again and again. The waiting lists that stretch into years. The therapies that are technically available but practically inaccessible. The Children's Disability Network Teams that were supposed to revolutionise services but have, in too many cases, left families worse off than before. The respite services that vanished during Covid and never fully returned.

One mother in Cork told me she waited 18 months for an occupational therapy assessment for her daughter, only to be told that the recommended supports would require a further wait of indeterminate length. "They assess you," she said, "and then they leave you." That single sentence encapsulates the experience of thousands of families who exist in a permanent state of limbo, identified and categorised and then abandoned to get on with it.

The reorganisation of children's disability services under the Progressing Disability Services programme has been, by almost any measure, a disaster. The intention was laudable enough — to move away from a diagnosis-led model to one based on need, and to ensure that no child fell between the cracks. In practice, it has meant that children who previously had access to services through specific organisations found those services withdrawn, with nothing adequate put in their place. Staff shortages, recruitment difficulties, and a lack of clinical oversight have left many teams operating well below capacity. The HSE's own internal reviews have acknowledged as much, yet the pace of reform remains glacial.
headline: Jennifer Horgan: For the sake of Ireland's children, let's march in solidarity with their carers

text:
A Cork-based mental health author who was blackmailed online has spoken of her disappointment at what she described as a victim-blaming response when she reported the crime.

SarahOnal, who has written extensively about mental health and wellbeing, revealed she was targeted by an online blackmailer who threatened to release intimate images unless she paid a sum of money. She refused to pay and instead reported the matter to the Gardaí, but said the experience of coming forward left her feeling re-victimised.

Ms Onal said she was "disappointed but not entirely surprised" by some of the responses she received, both from individuals and from the system more broadly, which she said placed undue focus on her own behaviour rather than on the criminal actions of the perpetrator.

"There is still this undercurrent of 'well, what did you expect?' when someone comes forward with something like this," she said. "It's incredibly damaging, and it's exactly the reason so many people don't report these crimes."

She said she decided to speak publicly about her ordeal in the hope of encouraging others who find themselves in similar situations to come forward, and to challenge what she sees as a culture that too often holds victims to account rather than offenders.

Image-based sexual abuse, which includes the non-consensual sharing or threatening to share intimate images, was criminalised under the Harassment, Harmful Communications and Related Offences Act 2020, commonly known as Coco's Law. The legislation provides for penalties of up to seven years' imprisonment for the most serious offences.

Despite the legal protections now in place, campaigners and support organisations have consistently warned that enforcement remains patchy and that victims frequently encounter attitudes that discourage them from pursuing complaints.

Ms Onal said she believed there was a particular stigma attached to victims of online sexual crimes that does not apply in the same way to other forms of criminal activity.

"If someone broke into your house, nobody would say, 'well, you shouldn't have had a front door,'" she said. "But when it comes to online crimes of a sexual nature, there is still this reflex to question the victim's judgement rather than to focus on the person who committed the offence."

She acknowledged that the Gardaí have made efforts in recent years to improve their handling of such cases, but said there was still a significant gap between policy and the lived experience of victims who present at Garda stations.

A Garda spokesperson said An Garda Síochána takes all reports of online crime seriously and encouraged anyone who is the victim of blackmail or image-based abuse to contact their local Garda station. The spokesperson said members receive ongoing training in dealing sensitively with victims of such offences.

Ms Onal said she would continue to advocate for better supports for victims and for a shift in public attitudes. She urged anyone experiencing online blackmail not to engage with the perpetrator and to seek help immediately.

"The shame does not belong to the victim," she said. "It belongs entirely to the person who chose to exploit and threaten another human being."
headline: Cork mental health author blackmailed online 'disappointed by victim-blaming'

text:
United Nations Secretary General António Guterres has said that people around the world are looking to their leaders to find a way out of the "mess" created by escalating conflicts, deepening inequality and the accelerating climate crisis.

Speaking at the opening of the UN General Assembly's high-level debate in New York, Mr Guterres delivered a stark assessment of the state of global affairs, warning that multilateral institutions are under unprecedented strain and that trust between nations has eroded to dangerous levels.

"People are looking to you, their leaders, for a way out of this mess," Mr Guterres told the assembled heads of state and government. He urged world leaders to set aside narrow national interests and embrace collective action to address what he described as a confluence of crises threatening to overwhelm the international order.

The Secretary General pointed to the ongoing wars in Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza as evidence of the failure of diplomatic mechanisms to prevent and resolve conflict. He reiterated his call for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza and the unconditional release of all hostages, while also demanding unimpeded humanitarian access to civilians caught up in the fighting.

Mr Guterres was particularly pointed in his criticism of the UN Security Council, which has been repeatedly paralysed by vetoes from permanent members. He said the body's inability to act decisively had undermined the credibility of the entire United Nations system and left vulnerable populations without protection.

On the climate emergency, the Secretary General said the world was "playing Russian roulette with our planet," noting that global temperatures continue to break records and that extreme weather events are becoming more frequent and more destructive. He called on wealthy nations to honour their financial commitments to developing countries bearing the brunt of climate change.

The address also touched on the growing gap between rich and poor nations, with Mr Guterres warning that developing countries are being crushed by unsustainable debt burdens while struggling to recover from the economic fallout of the Covid-19 pandemic.

The high-level debate, which brings together leaders from the organisation's 193 member states, is expected to continue throughout the week, with the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine dominating discussions on the sidelines.
headline: UN chief says people are looking to leaders for way out of ‘mess’

text:
The future of the Black Sea grain deal remains shrouded in uncertainty as the agreement approaches yet another renewal deadline, with Ukraine, Russia and the United Nations locked in fraught negotiations that carry enormous implications for global food security and, closer to home, for Irish farmers grappling with volatile input costs.

The initiative, brokered by the UN and Turkey in July 2022, was designed to allow the safe passage of Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea following Russia's full-scale invasion, which had effectively blockaded one of the world's most important breadbaskets. Ukraine had long been a major supplier of wheat, maize, sunflower oil and barley to global markets, and the sudden disruption sent shockwaves through commodity prices worldwide.

For Irish tillage farmers, the ramifications were felt almost immediately. Ireland imports significant quantities of grain and animal feed ingredients, and the spike in global prices fed directly into already-soaring input costs for livestock and dairy producers. Feed costs, which represent the single largest variable expense on most Irish farms, were driven to unprecedented levels, squeezing margins that were already under pressure from rising energy and fertiliser bills.

The grain deal has been renewed several times since its inception, though never without considerable brinkmanship. Russia has repeatedly threatened to withdraw, arguing that its own agricultural exports and fertiliser trade have not been sufficiently facilitated under a parallel memorandum of understanding. Moscow has complained that Western sanctions, while not directly targeting Russian food and fertiliser exports, have created a chilling effect on shipping, insurance and banking services that has hampered its ability to trade.

The UN has sought to address those concerns, with Secretary-General António Guterres personally engaging in diplomatic efforts to keep both sides at the table. However, progress has been painstaking, and each renewal period has brought fresh anxiety to grain markets.

The deal's importance to developing nations in Africa, the Middle East and Asia cannot be overstated. The World Food Programme has sourced significant quantities of grain through the corridor for humanitarian operations, and any collapse in the agreement would likely trigger a fresh surge in food prices that would hit the world's most vulnerable populations hardest.

But the consequences would also ripple through European and Irish agriculture. Teagasc has noted that global grain price movements have a direct bearing on the Irish market, given the country's reliance on imported feedstuffs. Ireland's tillage sector, while relatively small by European standards, is also affected by the price signals emanating from international markets. Higher global prices can benefit Irish grain growers in the short term, but the knock-on effects for the much larger livestock sector — which depends on affordable feed — tend to be negative overall.

The Irish Farmers' Association has consistently called for greater market stability and has urged the Government and the European Commission to take a more proactive role in ensuring food supply chains remain resilient. IFA president Francie Gorman has highlighted the need for Europe to reduce its dependence on volatile global commodity markets by investing in domestic production capacity and supporting tillage farmers through properly funded CAP measures.

At EU level, the European Commission has been navigating its own tensions around Ukrainian grain.
headline: Against the grain: What's the latest with the UN's grain deal?

text:
Former US president Donald Trump was injured but said he was "fine" after an apparent assassination attempt at a campaign rally in Pennsylvania on Saturday evening, in a shocking incident that sent shockwaves through American politics and prompted widespread condemnation.

Mr Trump was addressing supporters at an outdoor rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, when what sounded like gunfire rang out, causing the former president to clutch his right ear before dropping to the ground as Secret Service agents swarmed the stage.

Dramatic footage showed Mr Trump being helped to his feet by agents, his face visibly bloodied, before he raised his fist to the crowd and appeared to mouth the words "fight, fight, fight" as he was rushed to a waiting vehicle.

The Secret Service confirmed that a suspect had fired multiple shots from an elevated position outside the rally venue and had been "neutralised" by agents. One rally attendee was killed and two others were critically injured, according to authorities.

Mr Trump was taken to a local medical facility where he was treated for a wound to his right ear. In a post on his Truth Social platform, the 78-year-old said he had been "shot with a bullet that pierced the upper part of my right ear" and thanked the Secret Service and law enforcement for their rapid response.

"I knew immediately that something was wrong in that I heard a whizzing sound, shots, and immediately felt the bullet ripping through the skin," Mr Trump wrote. "I want to thank the United States Secret Service, and all of Law Enforcement, for their rapid response on the shooting that just took place in Butler, Pennsylvania. Most importantly, I want to extend my condolences to the family of the person at the Rally who was killed, and also to the family of another person that was badly injured."

US president Joe Biden said he had been briefed on the incident and condemned the violence in the strongest terms. "There's no place for this kind of violence in America. We must unite as one nation to condemn it," Mr Biden said in a statement.

The incident prompted an outpouring of reaction from political leaders across the globe. Taoiseach Simon Harris said he was "deeply shocked" by the events in Pennsylvania and wished Mr Trump a full recovery.

"Political violence is an attack on democracy itself and can never be justified," Mr Harris said.

The FBI said it was leading the investigation and had identified the suspected shooter, who was killed at the scene by Secret Service counter-snipers. The suspect was later identified as Thomas Matthew Crooks, a 20-year-old man from Bethel Park, Pennsylvania.

Questions immediately arose about how a gunman was able to position himself with a clear line of sight to the former president at an outdoor event. The incident is expected to prompt a thorough review of security protocols for campaign events.

The shooting marks the most serious assassination attempt on a US president or presidential candidate since Ronald Reagan was shot and wounded in Washington DC in 1981. Mr Trump, who is the presumptive Republican nominee for the November presidential election, said he would not be deterred from campaigning.

Security has been stepped up at political events across the United States in the wake of the incident, with the Secret Service saying it had implemented enhanced protective measures.
headline: Trump injured but ‘fine’ after attempted assassination at rally

text:
Migrants living in Ireland are more likely to be in employment than their Irish-born counterparts but face significantly higher rates of poverty and deprivation, according to new research published by the Economic and Social Research Institute.

The study, which draws on Census data and large-scale survey evidence, paints a complex picture of the migrant experience in Ireland, challenging simplistic narratives around immigration and welfare dependency while highlighting persistent inequalities that researchers say demand policy attention.

According to the ESRI findings, migrants in Ireland have higher employment rates overall than the Irish-born population, a trend that has been consistent across recent years. The pattern is particularly pronounced among migrants from EU accession states, many of whom came to Ireland during the Celtic Tiger era and have remained in the workforce since.

However, despite their strong attachment to the labour market, migrants are more likely to experience poverty and material deprivation. The research points to lower wages, concentration in sectors with poor working conditions, and difficulties in having qualifications recognised as key factors driving this disparity.

"The finding that migrants can be both more likely to work and more likely to experience poverty underlines the importance of looking beyond employment rates alone," said one of the study's authors. "It tells us something important about the quality of work available to migrants and the barriers they continue to face."

The report notes significant variation between different migrant groups. Migrants from western and northern European countries tend to have outcomes comparable to or better than Irish-born workers, while those from outside the EU, particularly African nationals, face the steepest challenges in terms of income, housing and social inclusion.

Language barriers, discrimination in the labour market, and limited access to social networks were all identified as contributing factors. The research also found that migrants are disproportionately represented in lower-paid roles in sectors such as food processing, accommodation, cleaning and caring, even where they hold third-level qualifications.

Housing emerged as a particular pressure point. The study found that migrants are far more likely to live in the private rental sector and to spend a greater proportion of their income on accommodation, leaving them more exposed to the current housing crisis. Overcrowding rates are also notably higher among migrant households.

The ESRI researchers said the findings have clear implications for Government policy, particularly in the areas of integration, recognition of foreign qualifications and access to public services. They called for a more targeted approach to ensuring that employment translates into adequate living standards for all residents.

Immigrant advocacy groups said the research confirms what many in the sector have long observed. "People come here to work and they do work, often in jobs that are essential to the functioning of our economy," said one representative. "But working hard is not enough if the system doesn't provide fair wages, secure housing and equal treatment."

The study comes at a time of heightened public debate around immigration in Ireland, with the issue featuring prominently in recent political discourse. Integration Minister Roderic O'Gorman has previously acknowledged the need for improved supports for migrants already living and working in the State.

The ESRI said further research is needed to track outcomes over time, particularly for migrants who arrived during the recent increase in international protection applications, and to assess whether second-generation migrants fare better than their parents in the Irish labour market and education system.
headline: Migrants more likely to work but face higher poverty rates, ESRI study finds

text:
It was a phone call that changed everything. When Sarah Byrne's aunt was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2019, the Galway woman's first instinct was to be there for her family. She never imagined that her aunt's diagnosis would ultimately save her own life.

"My aunt Margaret was always the healthiest person in the family – she walked every day, ate well, never smoked," says Byrne, now 41. "When she found a lump, none of us could believe it. It just didn't seem possible."

Margaret Byrne was 58 when she was diagnosed with stage two breast cancer. She underwent surgery, chemotherapy and radiation at University Hospital Galway and is now in remission. But it was a conversation during her treatment that would prove pivotal for her niece.

"Margaret sat me down one day and said, 'Promise me you'll get checked. Don't wait.' She was very direct about it. She told me that our family history meant I needed to be vigilant."

Sarah had been putting off a routine check-up for months. Like so many women, life got in the way – work, children, the general busyness of the everyday. But her aunt's words stayed with her.

"I kept hearing her voice in my head. So I rang my GP and made an appointment. I honestly thought it would be a box-ticking exercise."

It was anything but. Sarah's GP referred her to BreastCheck, the HSE's national breast screening programme, for further investigation. Within weeks, she received a diagnosis that floored her: stage one breast cancer.

"I remember sitting in the car park afterwards, just staring at the steering wheel. I couldn't process it. I was 37, I had two small children, and I had breast cancer. But then I thought of Margaret, and I thought, 'She caught this for me. She saved me.'"

According to the National Cancer Registry Ireland, breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in this country, with approximately 3,700 new cases diagnosed each year. When detected early, the five-year survival rate exceeds 90 per cent, making awareness and screening critically important.

Dr Fiona Murphy, a consultant breast surgeon based in Cork, says Sarah's story illustrates a pattern she sees regularly in her practice.

"Family history is one of the most significant risk factors for breast cancer, and we know that when one family member receives a diagnosis, it can prompt others to come forward for screening," she explains. "That ripple effect genuinely saves lives. I would always encourage women to know their family history and to engage with their GP about their individual risk."

Dr Murphy stresses that while BreastCheck currently invites women aged 50 to 69 for free mammograms every two years, women of any age who notice changes in their breasts should seek medical advice without delay.

"There is sometimes a perception that breast cancer is something that only affects older women. That simply isn't the case. We see women in their 30s and 40s with diagnoses, and the message has to be that vigilance matters at every age."

For Sarah, the treatment journey was gruelling but ultimately successful.
headline: My aunt's breast cancer diagnosis saved me

text:
A young chef died after falling and striking his head off a tumble dryer during a night out, an inquest has heard.

The coroner's court was told that 26-year-old Daniel Hartigan, who worked in a well-known restaurant in Limerick city, sustained fatal head injuries following the incident in the early hours of the morning.

The inquest, held at Limerick Coroner's Court, heard that Mr Hartigan had been socialising with friends on the night in question before returning to a friend's house in the early hours. While at the property, he lost his balance and fell, striking his head against a tumble dryer in the utility area of the house.

Friends who were present at the time initially believed Mr Hartigan had simply fallen and would recover. However, when he failed to regain consciousness, emergency services were contacted. Paramedics attended the scene and Mr Hartigan was rushed to University Hospital Limerick, where he was pronounced dead a short time later.

A post-mortem examination carried out by the State pathologist's office found that the cause of death was a traumatic brain injury consistent with blunt force trauma to the head sustained in a fall. The toxicology report indicated that Mr Hartigan had consumed a significant quantity of alcohol on the evening in question, which was found to be a contributing factor in the fall.

Evidence was given by a number of witnesses, including friends who had been with Mr Hartigan on the night. One friend, who asked not to be named, described Mr Hartigan as "the life and soul of every room he walked into" and said he was a talented and passionate chef who was beloved by his colleagues and customers alike.

The Gardaí confirmed that a full investigation had been carried out and that there were no suspicious circumstances surrounding the death. A liaison officer had been appointed to support the Hartigan family throughout the process.

Mr Hartigan's mother, speaking outside the court, paid tribute to her son, describing him as a kind and generous young man who had a bright future ahead of him in the culinary industry. She urged young people to take care of one another on nights out.

The coroner extended his sympathies to the Hartigan family and returned a verdict of death by misadventure, noting that the consumption of alcohol had been a significant contributing factor in the fall that led to Mr Hartigan's untimely death.

Originally from Co Clare, Mr Hartigan had been living and working in Limerick city for a number of years and was well regarded in the local hospitality scene. Colleagues at the restaurant where he worked described him as a dedicated professional with an infectious enthusiasm for his craft.
headline: Chef, 26, died after falling and hitting his head off dryer

text:
We've all been there, or at least most of us have. You do someone a favour — a generous, no-strings-attached favour — and it comes back to bite you. In this case, the favour was lending a family holiday home, and the bite was discovering it had been returned in a condition that would make a student flat after Rag Week look like the Merrion Hotel.

The letter that landed on my desk this week came from a reader I'll call Siobhán, and her frustration was palpable even through the page. Her parents own a lovely cottage down in West Cork, the kind of place that's been in the family for decades, kept in beautiful condition, full of memories and carefully chosen bits and pieces. A relative — let's say a cousin — asked to borrow it for a long weekend with friends. The parents, being the decent sort of people they are, said of course.

What Siobhán's parents found when they next visited would turn your stomach. Stained carpets. Broken crockery. A burn mark on the kitchen counter. Bins overflowing. The garden furniture left out in the rain. And, the pièce de résistance, a mysterious crack in the bathroom sink that nobody has owned up to.

Now, Siobhán wants to know: how do you raise this without starting a family civil war?

Here's the thing about family and property — it's a combination more combustible than petrol and a match. Money and blood relations have been a toxic cocktail since Cain and Abel were arguing over who got the better field. The Irish dimension makes it worse, of course, because we are a people who would sooner chew our own arm off than have a direct confrontation. We'd rather seethe silently at Christmas dinner for the next forty years than say, "You left the place in a heap and we'd like you to pay for the damage."

But seethe you must not, Siobhán. Because that way lies madness, and the kind of slow-burning resentment that poisons every family gathering from here to eternity.

My advice? Your parents need to have the conversation, not you. This is crucial. If you wade in on their behalf, you become the villain of the piece, the one who "caused trouble," and your cousin will spend the rest of their natural life telling anyone who'll listen that you were always a bit much. Your parents lent the house. Your parents found the damage. It needs to come from them.

And it needn't be nuclear. A phone call. Keep it calm, keep it factual. "We found a few things when we went down to the cottage. The sink is cracked, there's a burn on the counter, and the place was left in a bit of a state. We're sure it wasn't intentional, but we'd appreciate if you could cover the cost of putting it right." No accusations. No drama. Just a statement of fact and a reasonable request.

Will the cousin be embarrassed? One would hope so. Will they be defensive? Almost certainly.
headline: Dear Dáithí: A relative left our parents' lovely holiday home in an awful state

text:
Sir – I write as a concerned citizen who has had recent cause to interact with the HSE at various levels, and I must say that while many frontline staff are dedicated and hardworking, the system itself is being let down by a cohort of employees who are simply not fit for purpose.

I am not referring to the nurses, doctors, and healthcare assistants who work punishing hours under impossible conditions. These people deserve nothing but praise. I am referring instead to a layer of administrative and managerial staff who appear to operate without accountability, without urgency, and without any meaningful connection to the patients they are supposed to serve.

My elderly mother waited 14 months for what was described as a "routine" outpatient appointment. During that time, letters went unanswered, phone calls were met with indifference, and on one occasion a member of staff openly told me that there was "nothing they could do" and suggested I contact my local TD. Since when did accessing a public health service require political intervention?

When I eventually lodged a formal complaint, it took the HSE's own complaints process a further three months simply to acknowledge receipt. This is not a system under pressure. This is a system in which certain individuals have grown comfortable in the knowledge that their performance will never be scrutinised and their positions will never be at risk.

The public service agreement and various employment protections are important, but they were never intended to shield people from basic standards of competence and courtesy. The HSE employs more than 130,000 people and has a budget running into billions of euro. The taxpayer is entitled to expect that every single person drawing a salary from that organisation is contributing meaningfully to its mission.

Until there is a genuine culture of accountability – one in which underperformance has real consequences – the HSE will continue to fail the very people it exists to help.
headline: Letters to the Editor: Some HSE workers are not fit for purpose

text:
Ronan Keating has spoken publicly about the devastating loss of his older brother Ciaran, describing the months since his death as "the hardest time" of his life.

The Boyzone singer, who lost Ciaran in a road traffic collision in Co Mayo in January, opened up about his grief in an emotional social media post shared with his followers over the weekend.

Ciaran Keating, 57, died after the car he was travelling in was involved in a collision with a lorry near Swinford on January 15. He was pronounced dead at the scene. The driver of the lorry was uninjured.

Ronan, 47, said the pain of losing his brother had been overwhelming and that his family had been leaning on one another through the difficult period.

"It's been the hardest time. There's no way to prepare for something like this," the Dublin-born singer wrote. "I miss him every single day. He was the best of us."

The singer, who is currently based in Australia where he co-hosts a breakfast radio show on Magic FM, said he had been grateful for the outpouring of support from fans and well-wishers both at home and abroad.

At the time of Ciaran's death, Ronan paid tribute to his brother, describing him as his "best friend" and saying the family was "broken hearted."

Ciaran, who lived in Co Mayo, was one of five siblings in the Keating family. He was well known and respected in his local community, with tributes pouring in from across the west of Ireland following his passing.

Ronan had travelled home from Australia to attend the funeral, which took place at the Church of the Holy Rosary in Castlebar, with large crowds turning out to pay their respects.

The former Late Late Show performer has previously spoken about the close bond he shared with his older brother, crediting Ciaran and the wider Keating family with keeping him grounded throughout his years in the spotlight.
headline: ‘It’s been the hardest time:’ Ronan Keating shares update following death of his brother

text:
The Department of Health and hospital consultants are locked in an increasingly bitter war of words over responsibility for growing waiting lists, with each side accusing the other of failing to address what patient advocacy groups have described as a national crisis.

Figures released this week show that more than 900,000 people are now waiting for outpatient appointments, inpatient procedures, or diagnostic tests across the public hospital system, representing a record high and a sharp increase on the same period last year. The numbers have prompted renewed calls for urgent reform from opposition TDs and from organisations representing patients and frontline medical staff.

The Department has pointed to what it described as significant additional investment in recent years, including the allocation of more than €400m in dedicated waiting list funding since 2020. A spokesperson said the Government had provided unprecedented resources to the HSE and that it expected to see measurable improvements in access to care.

"The level of investment in tackling waiting lists has never been higher," the spokesperson said. "We have funded additional capacity, extended operating hours, and supported the expansion of community diagnostics. We expect hospital groups and individual consultants to deliver on the commitments made in their service level agreements."

However, the Irish Hospital Consultants Association hit back sharply, accusing the Department of deflecting blame onto clinicians who are working in a system that remains chronically understaffed and under-resourced. Professor Robert Lóránt, president of the IHCA, said consultants were seeing more patients than ever before but were being asked to do so in facilities that were not fit for purpose.

"Our members are working flat out, often in overcrowded hospitals with insufficient theatre capacity and inadequate diagnostic infrastructure," Professor Lóránt said. "It is deeply unfair and fundamentally dishonest to suggest that the problem lies with the doctors rather than with decades of underinvestment and poor workforce planning."

The IHCA pointed to ongoing difficulties in recruiting and retaining consultants, noting that approximately 900 approved consultant posts remain either vacant or filled on a temporary basis. The association has long argued that the failure to restore pay parity following cuts introduced under the Financial Emergency Measures in the Public Interest legislation has made Ireland uncompetitive internationally, with many Irish-trained specialists choosing to remain abroad rather than return to work in the public system.

The Irish Medical Organisation also weighed in, with its consultant committee chair warning that waiting lists would continue to grow unless fundamental structural issues were addressed. The IMO said that bed capacity in Irish hospitals remained among the lowest in the OECD on a per capita basis, and that no amount of additional funding could compensate for the physical constraints facing clinicians.

In the Dáil, Sinn Féin health spokesperson David Cullinane accused the Minister for Health of presiding over a system in freefall. "People are waiting years — not months, but years — for basic procedures and diagnostic tests," he said. "The Minister needs to stop hiding behind press releases about investment and start delivering actual results for patients."
headline: Department of Health and hospital doctors at odds over growing waiting lists

text:
Met Éireann is forecasting an unusually mild spell for the coming weekend, with temperatures expected to reach highs of 15C in parts of the country — well above the seasonal average for this time of year.

The national forecaster said that a plume of warm air moving in from the south will push temperatures several degrees above normal, with the mildest conditions expected across the south and west of the country on Saturday and Sunday.

Daytime highs of between 12C and 15C are forecast, compared with the typical average of around 8C to 10C for the time of year. Overnight temperatures are also expected to remain unusually elevated, staying above 7C in many areas.

A Met Éireann spokesperson said the conditions are being driven by a southerly airflow bringing mild subtropical air across Ireland, a pattern that has become more frequently observed in recent years.

"It will be a notably mild weekend for the time of year, with temperatures well above average across much of the country," the forecaster said. "The mildest conditions will be felt in Munster and along the Atlantic seaboard, though all areas will benefit from the warmer-than-usual spell."

However, the mild weather is expected to come with a trade-off, as cloud cover and patchy rain are likely to accompany the warmer air mass. Friday night will see rain spreading from the west, clearing to scattered showers on Saturday before a drier and brighter spell develops on Sunday, particularly in the east and midlands.

Professor John Sweeney, a climate scientist at Maynooth University, said that while individual weather events should not be attributed directly to climate change, the increasing frequency of mild spells during the cooler months is consistent with broader warming trends observed in Ireland's climate data.

"We are seeing a clear pattern of milder winters and more frequent above-average temperature events," Prof Sweeney said. "Ireland's average temperatures have risen by approximately one degree over the past century, and that shift is becoming increasingly evident in these kinds of episodes."

The mild conditions are expected to be welcomed by those planning outdoor activities over the weekend, though farmers have expressed mixed feelings about the unseasonably warm weather, with concerns that it could disrupt the dormancy cycles of certain crops and encourage premature growth.

The Irish Farmers' Association said it would be monitoring the situation, noting that prolonged mild spells can create difficulties for tillage farmers in particular.

Met Éireann said the milder-than-usual conditions are expected to persist into the early part of next week before temperatures gradually return closer to seasonal norms by midweek.
headline: Unusually mild temperatures predicted for weekend, with highs of 15C forecast

text:
A major international fundraising appeal has been launched after catastrophic flooding in eastern Libya left thousands dead and entire neighbourhoods swept into the Mediterranean Sea.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said it was seeking emergency funding as the death toll from the disaster climbed sharply, with more than 5,300 people feared dead and thousands more still missing.

The coastal city of Derna bore the brunt of the devastation after Storm Daniel brought torrential rains that caused two dams upstream of the city to burst, sending a wall of water through the urban centre in the early hours of the morning. Entire residential quarters were washed away, with buildings, cars and debris carried out to sea.

Survivors described scenes of utter horror as the floodwaters tore through the city without warning, giving residents little or no time to evacuate. Rescue teams have been pulling bodies from the mud and rubble, while others have been recovered from the shoreline and from the sea itself.

Tamer Ramadan, head of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies delegation in Libya, said the scale of the disaster was staggering. "The situation in Derna is catastrophic. Entire neighbourhoods have been wiped out. The needs are overwhelming," he said.

The Libyan Red Crescent has mobilised volunteers to assist with search and rescue operations, but access to the worst-hit areas has been severely hampered by the destruction of roads and bridges. Communications infrastructure has also been badly damaged, making it difficult to establish the full extent of the catastrophe.

The United Nations said it was coordinating with partners on the ground to deliver emergency assistance, including shelter, clean water, food and medical supplies. The World Health Organisation warned of the risk of waterborne diseases as floodwaters contaminated drinking water sources across the affected region.

The disaster has laid bare the vulnerabilities of Libya's infrastructure, much of which has deteriorated during more than a decade of conflict and political instability since the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011. The country remains divided between rival administrations in the east and west, complicating relief efforts.

Engineers had reportedly warned for years that the two dams above Derna were in a dangerous state of disrepair, but maintenance work was never carried out. Questions are already being raised about whether the scale of the tragedy could have been mitigated had those warnings been heeded.

Several countries, including Turkey, Egypt and the United Arab Emirates, have pledged to send aid and rescue teams to the stricken region. The European Union said it stood ready to assist, while the Irish government expressed its condolences and said it was monitoring the situation closely.

The flooding also affected other cities across eastern Libya, including Benghazi, Sousse and Al-Bayda, though Derna was by far the worst hit. Across the affected areas, tens of thousands of people have been displaced from their homes.

Aid agencies have warned that the final death toll is likely to rise significantly as rescue teams reach areas that have so far been inaccessible.
headline: Fundraising appeal launched as 5,300 feared dead in flood-hit eastern Libya

text:
Parents of children attending a primary school in East Cork are calling for a comprehensive safety audit of the school bus fleet after a driver was injured in an incident that has raised fresh concerns about the condition of vehicles used on daily routes.

The incident occurred on Tuesday morning when the driver of a bus serving a school in the Midleton area sustained injuries after a mechanical fault reportedly caused the vehicle to lurch unexpectedly while stationary. The driver, a man in his 50s, was treated at Cork University Hospital for what are understood to be non-serious injuries and has since been discharged.

No children were on board at the time of the incident, which took place as the driver was preparing for the morning collection run. However, parents who were informed of the matter through the school's messaging system have expressed alarm at what they describe as a pattern of maintenance issues with buses serving the route.

A group of parents have now written to Bus Éireann, the Department of Education and their local TDs seeking an independent safety audit of all vehicles operating under the School Transport Scheme in the Cork region.

"We've had concerns for some time about the age and condition of some of these buses," said one parent, who asked not to be named. "This incident could have been far worse. If children had been on board, we'd be having a very different conversation today. We want reassurance that every vehicle on these routes is fit for purpose."

The parent said the group had documented a number of issues over the current school year, including buses breaking down on route, heating systems failing during cold weather, and seatbelts that were not functioning properly.

A spokesperson for Bus Éireann said the organisation takes the safety of all passengers "extremely seriously" and that the vehicle involved had been immediately withdrawn from service pending a full inspection.

"All vehicles operating under the School Transport Scheme are subject to rigorous maintenance schedules and must hold a valid roadworthiness certificate," the spokesperson said. "We are investigating the circumstances of this incident and will take whatever action is necessary."

The Department of Education, which oversees the School Transport Scheme, said it had been made aware of the incident and the concerns raised by parents. A spokesperson said the department was engaging with Bus Éireann on the matter but declined to comment further while the investigation was ongoing.

Fine Gael TD David Stanton, who represents the Cork East constituency, said he had been contacted by several parents and intended to raise the matter with the Minister for Education.

"Parents need to have absolute confidence that their children are travelling safely to and from school every day," Deputy Stanton said. "I will be seeking a full account of what happened and assurances that every bus operating in Cork meets the highest safety standards."

The Road Safety Authority, which is responsible for the roadworthiness testing regime for commercial vehicles including school buses, declined to comment on the specific incident but confirmed that all buses used for school transport are required to pass an annual commercial vehicle roadworthiness test.

The incident comes amid broader national concerns about the School Transport Scheme, which has faced sustained criticism over capacity issues, eligibility rules, and the age profile of the fleet. A review of the scheme published last year recommended significant investment in modernising the fleet, though parents' groups have argued that progress has been too slow.
headline: Parents call for fleet safety audit after Cork school bus driver injured

text:
The cruelty is not a bug. It is the architecture. When Donald Trump and his administration take aim at public health infrastructure, food assistance programmes, and medical research funding simultaneously, the effect is not merely a series of unfortunate budget decisions. It is a strategy, one that keeps vulnerable populations preoccupied with survival rather than resistance.

This is worth stating plainly, because the instinct in political commentary is often to treat each cut, each executive order, each institutional gutting as a discrete event. The slashing of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's budget is reported on one day. The proposed cuts to Medicaid are discussed the next. The chaos unleashed on the National Institutes of Health by Elon Musk's so-called Department of Government Efficiency gets its own news cycle. But to analyse these moves in isolation is to miss the forest for the trees.

Consider what has unfolded in the opening months of Trump's second term. The administration has moved to impose work requirements on food stamp recipients that would strip millions of their access to basic nutrition. It has targeted the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP, which feeds roughly 42 million Americans, a programme whose bureaucratic unglamourousness belies its role as one of the most effective anti-poverty measures the United States has ever devised. Simultaneously, the administration has sought to kneecap Medicaid, the programme that provides healthcare to low-income Americans, pregnant women, and people with disabilities. The proposed per-capita caps and block grants are the kind of policy mechanisms that sound technocratic but function as slow strangulation.

Then there is the war on medical research. The NIH, which funds studies into cancer, Alzheimer's, diabetes, and infectious diseases, has seen grant freezes and funding clawbacks that have thrown laboratories across the country into disarray. Researchers have described decades of work being jeopardised overnight. Clinical trials have been paused. Early-career scientists have been told, in effect, that the country no longer considers their work a priority.

For Irish observers, this might seem a peculiarly American dysfunction, the predictable consequence of a political culture that has never fully committed to the idea that healthcare is a right rather than a commodity. But it would be a mistake to view it with comfortable detachment. Ireland's own health system, for all the progress made through Sláintecare and the expansion of free GP care, remains deeply fragile. The HSE's waiting lists, the recruitment crises in nursing and general practice, the persistent inequalities in access between urban and rural communities — these are reminders that the social contract around health is never as secure as we might like to believe. What is happening in the United States is an extreme manifestation of a tendency that exists in every wealthy democracy: the temptation to balance budgets on the bodies of those least able to object.

And that is the crucial point. People who are hungry are not organising. People who are sick are not marching. People who are terrified of losing their health coverage are not making trouble for their elected representatives — or if they are, they are doing so from a position of such desperate vulnerability that they are easily dismissed. There is a long and well-documented history of this dynamic.
headline: Trump's targeting of health keeps people hungry, sick and less likely to fight back

text:
There is a particular kind of ache that comes with watching your child do something for the very last time. The trouble, of course, is that you rarely know it's the last time until the moment has already passed. The last time they reach for your hand crossing the road. The last time they ask you to read *Room on the Broom* before bed. The last time they fall asleep on your shoulder. These moments slip away quietly, without ceremony, and it is only in the rearview mirror that you realise they have gone.

It is one of the great paradoxes of parenting that we spend so much of the early years willing time forward — longing for unbroken sleep, for the end of nappies, for the start of school — and then spend the years that follow wishing we could claw some of it back. We are caught, always, between exhaustion and nostalgia, and the distance between the two is often no more than a single afternoon.

But milestones, the ones we do see coming, offer us something rare: the chance to pause. To mark a moment while we are still in it.

This is the time of year when milestones come thick and fast. Communions, confirmations, end-of-year concerts, sports days, graduations from crèche and preschool and primary school and secondary school. The calendar fills up with dates circled in pen, outfits bought and altered, relatives summoned, tables booked. There is a great machinery to it all, and it can feel, in the thick of the organising, more like logistics than love.

And yet. When your child walks up to the altar, or crosses the stage, or stands in the back garden in an outfit they will grow out of by September, something catches in your chest. You feel the weight of all the ordinary days that led to this one. The school runs. The lunchboxes. The homework battles. The Wednesday evenings spent sitting in a car park outside training. All of it, quietly accumulated, has brought you here.

It is worth saying that milestones do not have to be grand to matter. We have become very good, in the age of social media, at documenting the big occasions — the professional photographs, the balloon arches, the elaborate party bags. There is nothing wrong with any of that, but it can create a pressure that squeezes the joy out of the very thing you are trying to celebrate. Some of the most meaningful milestones are the ones that would never make it onto Instagram. The first time your child makes their own breakfast. The evening they come home and tell you about a problem they solved themselves. The moment you realise they no longer need you to check under the bed.

Dr Malie Coyne, a clinical psychologist based in Galway and author of *Love In, Love Out*, has spoken often about the importance of what she calls "micro-moments of connection" — the small, daily interactions that build a child's sense of security and belonging. These are the building blocks of memory, she argues, far more than any single event. A child is unlikely to remember the exact details of their sixth birthday party, but they will carry with them the feeling of being celebrated, of being seen.
headline: Marking milestones and making memories

text:
A stark new survey has revealed that a significant majority of Defence Forces personnel would not recommend a career in the military to their friends or family members, in what has been described as a damning indictment of conditions within the organisation.

The findings, which emerged from an internal climate survey conducted among serving members, paint a troubling picture of morale across the Army, Naval Service and Air Corps at a time when the Defence Forces are already struggling with a severe recruitment and retention crisis.

According to the survey results, officers overwhelmingly indicated they would not encourage those close to them to pursue a career in uniform, citing concerns over pay, working conditions, and a perceived lack of career progression opportunities. Enlisted personnel expressed similarly negative sentiments, with many pointing to the impact of military life on their families and personal relationships.

The results are likely to increase pressure on the Government to accelerate implementation of the recommendations contained in the Commission on the Defence Forces report, which was published in 2022 and set out a sweeping programme of reform intended to modernise the organisation and improve conditions for its members.

RACO, the representative association for commissioned officers, said the findings reflected a deep malaise that had taken root over many years of underfunding and neglect. A spokesperson said the survey confirmed what the association had been warning about for some time and called on the Minister for Defence to treat the matter with the urgency it demanded.

PDFORRA, which represents enlisted personnel, echoed those concerns and said the Government's response to the retention crisis had been far too slow. The association has repeatedly called for Defence Forces members to be granted full trade union rights, arguing that the current representative structures are inadequate to address the scale of the problems facing serving members.

Staffing levels across the Defence Forces have fallen well below the establishment figure of 9,500, with numbers dropping to fewer than 8,000 in recent years. The Naval Service has been particularly badly affected, with ships forced to remain tied up at Haulbowline due to a shortage of trained crew.

The Department of Defence said the Minister was committed to ensuring the Defence Forces remained an attractive career choice and pointed to a number of measures already introduced, including pay increases and improvements to military allowances. A spokesperson said the Government had accepted the vast majority of recommendations made by the Commission on the Defence Forces and that implementation was ongoing.

However, critics have argued that the pace of reform has been glacially slow and that many of the commission's most significant recommendations, including the proposed move to a level of ambition that would see defence spending increase substantially, have yet to be meaningfully acted upon.

Speaking in the Dáil recently, several TDs from across the political spectrum raised concerns about the state of the Defence Forces, with some warning that Ireland's ability to defend its sovereignty and meet its international obligations was being compromised by the ongoing personnel crisis.
