Security analysts have also noted that the survey findings come at a particularly sensitive time, with the war in Ukraine having prompted a reassessment of defence and security policy across Europe. Ireland, despite its tradition of military neutrality, has faced growing questions about the adequacy of its defence capabilities, particularly in relation to the protection of critical undersea infrastructure off the Atlantic coast.
headline: Officers would not recommend Defence Forces career to friends or relatives, survey shows

text:
Two brothers from Cork are lacing up for one of the most gruelling charity challenges ever undertaken in Ireland, hoping their extraordinary feat of endurance will raise more than €1m for dementia research.

Sean and Kevin O'Sullivan plan to run 33 marathons in 33 consecutive days, a punishing schedule that will see them cover more than 1,390 kilometres across the country as they seek to shine a spotlight on a condition that has touched their family deeply.

The brothers, who grew up in Ballincollig, were inspired to take on the mammoth challenge after watching their grandmother's decline with dementia over several years. They say the experience left them feeling helpless and determined to do something meaningful to support research into the disease.

"Anyone who has seen a loved one go through dementia knows how devastating it is — not just for the person but for the entire family," Sean said. "We wanted to do something that matched the scale of the problem. Dementia doesn't take a day off, so neither will we."

The pair, both experienced distance runners, have been training intensively for months under the guidance of a sports physiotherapist and nutritionist. Each marathon will cover the standard 42.195 kilometres, with routes planned through towns and communities across Ireland to maximise public engagement and local fundraising efforts.

According to the Alzheimer Society of Ireland, there are currently more than 64,000 people living with dementia in the country, a figure projected to more than double by 2045. Despite the growing prevalence, campaigners argue that research into the condition remains significantly underfunded compared to other major illnesses.

Kevin acknowledged that the physical toll would be immense but said the brothers had prepared for every eventuality. "We know there will be days when our bodies are screaming at us to stop. But when you think about what people with dementia and their families endure every single day, running a marathon feels like the least we can do."

The funds raised will be directed towards dementia research programmes in Ireland, with the brothers working alongside established charities to ensure the money is channelled into projects with the greatest potential for impact.

Local businesses and community groups along the planned route have already begun pledging their support, with several offering to provide accommodation, meals and medical assistance to the brothers as they make their way through each stage.

The challenge has also attracted attention on social media, where the brothers have been documenting their training journey and sharing information about dementia awareness. Their fundraising page has already seen a significant surge in donations since they announced the attempt.

"The response has been overwhelming," Sean said. "People from all over Ireland have been getting in touch with their own stories about dementia. That tells you just how many families are affected. If we can raise over €1m and get people talking about this disease, then every blister and every aching muscle will have been worth it."

The brothers are encouraging supporters to join them for sections of each marathon along the route, turning the challenge into a community event that they hope will foster a national conversation about dementia care and research funding in Ireland.
headline: Brothers hope running 33 marathons in 33 days will raise over €1m for dementia research

text:
There is something about the pop of a Champagne cork that signals celebration like nothing else can. As we prepare to ring in another new year, it seems only fitting to revisit the world's most famous sparkling wine – a drink that has been synonymous with festivity, elegance and sheer joie de vivre for centuries.

Champagne, of course, comes exclusively from the Champagne region in northeastern France, a fact fiercely protected by French and European Union appellation laws. Everything else, no matter how delicious, is sparkling wine. And while Ireland has developed a wonderful appreciation for Prosecco, Cava and our own increasingly impressive domestic craft offerings, there really is no substitute for the real thing when the clock strikes midnight.

What makes Champagne so special is the painstaking method behind its production. The méthode traditionnelle – or méthode champenoise, as it was once more commonly known – involves a secondary fermentation in the bottle, a process that creates those impossibly fine, persistent bubbles and a complexity of flavour that is extraordinarily difficult to replicate. The chalky soils of the region lend a distinct minerality, while the cool climate ensures the grapes retain a bracing acidity that gives Champagne its remarkable freshness and ageing potential.

Most Champagne is non-vintage, meaning it is a blend of wines from multiple years. This is not a shortcoming – far from it. The art of blending, or assemblage, is one of the great skills of the Champagne houses, and the consistency they achieve from year to year is genuinely remarkable. The three principal grape varieties – Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier – each bring something different to the final cuvée. Chardonnay offers elegance and citrus finesse, Pinot Noir contributes structure and red fruit depth, while Pinot Meunier adds roundness and approachability.

For those looking to splash out this New Year's Eve, vintage Champagne – produced only in exceptional years – offers a step up in complexity and depth. These wines are typically aged for longer on their lees, developing toasty, brioche-like notes that mingle beautifully with the fruit. Prestige cuvées such as Dom Pérignon, Krug Grande Cuvée or Louis Roederer Cristal represent the pinnacle of the art, though they come with price tags to match. You would be looking at well north of €150 for most of these, and considerably more in some cases.

The good news for those of us watching the pennies – and who isn't these days – is that there is superb Champagne to be had at far more accessible prices. The own-brand Champagnes from the major supermarkets and wine retailers in Ireland have improved enormously in recent years and regularly perform well in blind tastings. Many are made by the same prestigious houses that produce the big-name labels, and they represent outstanding value, often coming in at around €25 to €35 a bottle.
headline: Wine with Leslie: Toast the New Year with time-tested Champagne

text:
The DSPCA is appealing for the public's help in identifying a man who was caught on CCTV shoving an injured dog under the gates of the animal welfare charity's shelter in Rathfarnham.

The organisation said the incident, which occurred in the early hours of the morning, left staff deeply concerned for the welfare of the animal, which was found with visible injuries when workers arrived on site.

CCTV footage shows a man forcing the dog beneath the entrance gates of the DSPCA's premises on Mount Venus Road in Dublin before walking away from the scene.

The charity said while it understands that people may feel desperate when an animal is in distress, it urged anyone in such a situation to contact them directly rather than abandoning an animal outside the facility, particularly in a manner that could cause further injury.

"We would ask anyone who recognises this individual to please get in touch with us," a DSPCA spokesperson said. "We need to establish the circumstances surrounding this dog's injuries and how it came to be in this condition."

The organisation confirmed that the dog is now receiving veterinary treatment and is being cared for by DSPCA staff. The full extent of the animal's injuries is being assessed.

The DSPCA operates a 24-hour emergency service and said members of the public can contact them at any time if they encounter an animal in distress. The charity stressed that abandoning animals outside their gates, particularly during unsociable hours when no staff are present, puts the welfare of the animal at serious risk.

Anyone with information about the man's identity or the circumstances of the incident is asked to contact the DSPCA directly.

The incident comes at a time when animal welfare organisations across the country continue to report increasing pressure on their services, with rising numbers of animals being surrendered or abandoned.

Under the Animal Health and Welfare Act 2013, it is an offence to abandon an animal or to cause unnecessary suffering to an animal, with penalties including fines of up to €250,000 or imprisonment for up to five years on indictment.
headline: DSPCA looking to identify man who shoved injured dog under their gates

text:
A woman who had been sexually abused as a child was attacked by a stranger in Cork city centre in what a court heard was a traumatic incident that compounded years of suffering.

The accused man, who cannot be named for legal reasons, pleaded guilty at Cork Circuit Criminal Court to assault causing harm to the woman during the incident, which occurred in the early hours of the morning.

The court heard the woman had been walking alone through the city centre when she was approached by the accused, who was unknown to her. Without provocation, the man struck her and knocked her to the ground, leaving her with facial injuries and significant bruising.

Sergeant Michael O'Connell told the court the victim had been left deeply distressed by the assault and that it had triggered memories of the sexual abuse she had endured as a child. He said the woman had been receiving counselling for the childhood abuse and that the unprovoked attack had set back her recovery considerably.

In a victim impact statement read to the court, the woman said she had spent years trying to rebuild her life after the abuse she suffered as a child. She said the assault had left her afraid to leave her home and that she now struggled to sleep at night. She told the court she felt she had been robbed of the progress she had made in dealing with her past trauma.

Counsel for the accused told the court his client had been heavily intoxicated at the time of the assault and had no recollection of the incident. He said the man, who had a number of previous convictions, had expressed genuine remorse for what he had done and wished to apologise to the victim.

The barrister said his client had a difficult background and had struggled with alcohol addiction for a number of years. He asked the court to take into account the man's early guilty plea and his cooperation with the Gardaí during the investigation.

Judge Helen Boyle said it was an entirely unprovoked and cowardly attack on a vulnerable woman who had already endured significant trauma in her life. She said the court had to take into account both the physical injuries inflicted and the profound psychological impact the assault had on the victim.

The judge noted the accused's guilty plea and his expression of remorse but said the aggravating factors in the case were significant. She adjourned the matter for the preparation of a probation report to assist the court in determining the appropriate sentence.

The accused was remanded on continuing bail with strict conditions, including that he have no contact whatsoever with the injured party and that he sign on three times weekly at his local Garda station. The matter is due to come back before Cork Circuit Criminal Court for sentencing at a later date.
headline: Woman who was sexually abused as child attacked by stranger in Cork city

text:
Gardaí are appealing to the public for assistance in tracing the whereabouts of a man who has gone missing from Co Meath.

The man, who has not been named publicly at this stage, was reported missing from the Navan area, and there is growing concern for his welfare among investigating officers.

Gardaí at Navan Garda Station are leading the search and have urged anyone with information on his whereabouts to come forward. Officers are particularly keen to hear from anyone who may have seen the man or had any contact with him in recent days.

A Garda spokesperson confirmed that enquiries are ongoing and that all available resources are being deployed to locate the missing man. Search efforts are being coordinated in the wider Meath area, with members of the local community also assisting.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Navan Garda Station on 046 903 6100, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.

Gardaí have reminded the public that if they encounter a missing person, they should contact their nearest Garda station immediately.

More to follow.
headline: Gardaí concerned for welfare of missing Meath man

text:
A man who pointed an imitation firearm into the face of a van driver during a road rage incident has been sentenced at Cork Circuit Criminal Court.

The court heard that the incident occurred on a busy stretch of road in Cork city when the accused, who cannot be named for legal reasons, became involved in an altercation with the driver of a delivery van after a minor traffic dispute.

The victim told the court he had been making his usual deliveries when the accused pulled up alongside him, rolled down his window and produced what appeared to be a handgun, pointing it directly into his face from close range.

"I genuinely thought I was going to die," the van driver told the court in his victim impact statement. "I froze. I couldn't move. I have never experienced fear like that in my life."

The court heard that the victim suffered significant psychological trauma following the incident and had been unable to return to work for a number of weeks. He continues to attend counselling and has experienced ongoing anxiety and difficulty sleeping.

Gardaí launched an investigation and the accused was subsequently identified and arrested. When his vehicle was searched, officers recovered an imitation firearm which was found to be a replica weapon. The accused made admissions during interview at the Garda station.

Counsel for the defence told the court that his client was deeply remorseful for his actions and had entered an early guilty plea to a charge of possession of an imitation firearm with intent to cause fear. The court heard the accused had no previous convictions of a similar nature and had been dealing with personal difficulties at the time of the offence.

Judge Seán Ó Donnabháin said the offence was an extremely serious one and that the victim had been subjected to a terrifying ordeal. He noted that the use of imitation firearms was a growing concern and that the courts had a duty to send a clear message that such behaviour would not be tolerated.

The judge imposed a sentence of three years' imprisonment, suspending the final 18 months on condition that the accused enter a bond to keep the peace and be of good behaviour for a period of three years following his release. He also directed that the imitation firearm be destroyed.

Speaking outside the courthouse, the investigating officer said the case highlighted the serious consequences of brandishing imitation weapons in public. "From the victim's perspective, there was no way of knowing this was not a real firearm," the Garda said. "The trauma caused was every bit as real as if a loaded weapon had been used."
headline: Man pointed imitation gun into van driver's face

text:
Gardaí have arrested a man following a burglary at a pharmacy in Cork city in the early hours of this morning.

The incident occurred at approximately 3.15am when the alarm was raised at the premises on the northside of the city. Gardaí from Mayfield station responded to the scene within minutes and discovered that entry had been forced through a side door of the pharmacy.

A man in his 30s was arrested a short distance from the premises after he was observed by gardaí leaving the area on foot. A quantity of pharmaceutical products and a small sum of cash were recovered at the scene.

The suspect was taken to Mayfield Garda Station where he is currently being detained under Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act, 1984. He can be held for up to 24 hours.

It is understood that significant damage was caused to the interior of the pharmacy during the break-in. The scene was preserved overnight and a technical examination was carried out this morning by members of the Garda Technical Bureau.

Investigating gardaí are appealing for anyone who was in the area in the early hours of this morning and who may have witnessed any suspicious activity to come forward. They are also seeking dashcam or CCTV footage from the vicinity.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Mayfield Garda Station on 021 455 8510, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any garda station.

Investigations are ongoing.
headline: Man arrested following burglary at Cork pharmacy

text:
The Russian ambassador to Ireland has rejected accusations that he has lied to the Irish public about the war in Ukraine, insisting that Moscow's position has been "consistent and transparent" throughout the conflict.

Ambassador Yuri Filatov was responding to sustained criticism from Irish politicians and commentators who have accused him of repeatedly making misleading and false statements about Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which began in February 2022.

Speaking to reporters, Mr Filatov denied that he or the Russian Embassy in Dublin had spread disinformation, claiming instead that Western media and governments were engaged in a "one-sided propaganda campaign" against Russia.

"We have never lied to the Irish people. We have presented the Russian perspective, which is our duty as diplomats," Mr Filatov said. "It is unfortunate that in today's climate, any view that does not conform to the Western narrative is immediately labelled as disinformation."

The comments drew a sharp rebuke from several TDs and senators, who pointed to a catalogue of claims made by the ambassador and the embassy's social media accounts that have been widely debunked.

Fine Gael TD and chair of the Oireachtas Joint Committee on Foreign Affairs and Defence, Charlie Flanagan, said Mr Filatov's denial was "brazen and insulting" to the intelligence of the Irish public.

"The Russian Embassy in Ireland has been a vehicle for Kremlin propaganda since day one of this illegal invasion," Mr Flanagan said. "The ambassador has stood in front of cameras and repeated falsehoods about civilian massacres, about the origins of this war, and about Russia's intentions. To now deny this is simply extraordinary."

The issue of the Russian Embassy's continued operation in Dublin has been a recurring source of political debate since the onset of the full-scale invasion. In early 2022, then-Taoiseach Micheál Martin said Ireland would not expel the ambassador, though four senior Russian diplomats were expelled in March of that year on the advice of the Gardaí and intelligence services after being identified as undeclared intelligence officers.

Sinn Féin foreign affairs spokesperson Matt Carthy said the ambassador's remarks were "predictable but no less galling," adding that "the evidence of Russia's war crimes in Bucha, Mariupol, and countless other Ukrainian cities speaks for itself."

The Ukrainian Ambassador to Ireland, Larysa Gerasko, has previously called on the Government to downgrade diplomatic relations with Moscow, arguing that the Russian Embassy serves primarily as a platform for disinformation rather than genuine diplomacy.

The Department of Foreign Affairs declined to comment directly on Mr Filatov's remarks but reiterated Ireland's "unwavering support for Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity" and its condemnation of Russia's "illegal and unprovoked aggression."

Ireland has committed over €200m in humanitarian and non-lethal support to Ukraine since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, and more than 100,000 Ukrainian refugees have arrived in the State under the EU's Temporary Protection Directive.
headline: Russian ambassador to Ireland denies lying to public over Ukraine

text:
Fine Gael poured more than €1m into its European Parliament election campaign last year, comfortably outspending all other major parties in the contest, according to new figures published by the Standards in Public Office Commission.

The party's expenditure on the June 2024 elections across the three European constituencies came to €1.03m, more than double the amount spent by its coalition partner Fianna Fáil, which recorded a total outlay of just under €490,000.

Sinn Féin, which endured a bruising election night that saw it fail to win a seat despite high expectations, spent approximately €380,000 on the campaign, the returns show.

The figures offer a stark illustration of the financial firepower Fine Gael was able to deploy in a contest that ultimately returned four of its candidates to the European Parliament, consolidating the party's position as the dominant Irish force in the EPP grouping in Brussels and Strasbourg.

Labour, the Social Democrats, the Green Party and a host of independents and smaller groupings spent considerably less, with none breaching the €200,000 mark across all three constituencies.

Under electoral law, candidates and parties are required to furnish detailed spending returns to the Standards in Public Office Commission within a set period after an election. The spending limits for European elections are significantly higher than those applying to Dáil contests, reflecting the larger geographical size of the constituencies involved.

Fine Gael's investment appeared to pay dividends on the night, with the party securing seats in each of the three constituencies — Ireland South, Midlands-North-West, and Dublin — a result that exceeded many pre-election predictions and underscored the party's organisational strength on the ground.

Political analysts have long noted the correlation between campaign spending and electoral outcomes, though the relationship is far from straightforward. Sinn Féin's relatively substantial spend failed to translate into seats, while some independents managed to mount competitive campaigns on far more modest budgets.

The European election results were widely interpreted at the time as a significant setback for Sinn Féin and a show of strength for Fine Gael, a dynamic that carried forward into the general election held later in the year.

The detailed breakdowns of candidate-by-candidate spending are available on the commission's website, with expenditure covering items such as advertising, printed materials, posters, social media promotion, and staff costs associated with the campaign period.

A Fine Gael spokesperson said the party had invested heavily in the European elections because it believed strongly in Ireland's role at the heart of the European Union. "We make no apology for running professional, well-resourced campaigns that bring our message to voters in every corner of the constituency," the spokesperson said.

Fianna Fáil said its spending reflected a targeted and disciplined approach, while Sinn Féin declined to comment on the figures beyond confirming that its returns had been submitted in full compliance with the relevant legislation.
headline: Fine Gael's €1m European election spend outstrips other parties

text:
Everyone dreams of a smooth getaway, but the reality is that holidays can and do go wrong — from cancelled flights and lost luggage to accommodation that bears no resemblance to the glossy brochure photos. The good news is that Irish and European consumer law offers a robust set of protections, and knowing your rights before you travel can make all the difference when things go south.

If your flight is cancelled or significantly delayed, EU Regulation 261/2004 remains the cornerstone of air passenger rights for anyone departing from an EU airport or arriving into one on an EU-based carrier. Under the regulation, passengers may be entitled to compensation of between €250 and €600 depending on the distance of the flight and the length of the delay. Airlines must also provide meals, refreshments, and hotel accommodation where an overnight stay becomes necessary due to a cancellation or long delay.

Crucially, airlines cannot simply wash their hands of responsibility by citing "extraordinary circumstances" without justification. While genuine events such as severe weather or air traffic control strikes may exempt carriers from paying compensation, mechanical faults discovered during routine maintenance generally do not. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) advises passengers to always request written confirmation of the reason for any cancellation or delay, as this can prove invaluable if a claim is later disputed.

For those who have booked a package holiday — defined under the EU Package Travel Directive as a combination of at least two travel services such as flights and accommodation — the protections are even more comprehensive. The directive, transposed into Irish law, places the organiser firmly on the hook for the performance of all services included in the package. If the hotel is not as described, or a promised excursion fails to materialise, the tour operator is obliged to remedy the situation or offer an appropriate price reduction.

Should significant elements of a package not be provided as agreed, the organiser must arrange suitable alternative arrangements at no extra cost to the consumer. If those alternatives are of a lower quality than what was originally booked, a price reduction must follow. In extreme cases where the holiday is fundamentally different from what was promised, the consumer may be entitled to terminate the contract and receive a full refund along with compensation for any additional expenses incurred.

Lost or damaged luggage on flights is covered under the Montreal Convention, which sets a maximum liability of approximately €1,400 per passenger. Airlines are obliged to compensate passengers for the reasonable cost of essential items — toiletries, clothing, and the like — purchased while waiting for delayed bags. It is important to keep all receipts, and passengers should file a property irregularity report at the airport before leaving the arrivals hall, followed by a formal written claim to the airline within seven days for damage or 21 days for delayed luggage.

Travel insurance, while not a legal requirement, is strongly recommended by the CCPC and the Department of Foreign Affairs. A good policy can cover medical emergencies, trip cancellations due to illness, and other scenarios that fall outside the scope of EU consumer protections.
headline: What you're entitled to if your holiday goes wrong

text:
Businesses on both sides of the Irish Sea could face costs of up to €1.5bn as a result of what industry figures have described as a "chaotic" Brexit transition process, with firms warning that a lack of clarity from both London and Brussels is leaving them unable to plan for the months ahead.

The stark figure, drawn from analysis by cross-border trade bodies and logistics groups, accounts for additional customs declarations, regulatory compliance, supply chain restructuring and the hiring of specialist staff needed to navigate new trading arrangements. Small and medium-sized enterprises are expected to bear a disproportionate share of the burden, according to those familiar with the findings.

Business groups have expressed mounting frustration at the pace of negotiations and the absence of detailed guidance on how new checks and procedures will operate in practice. Several sectors, including agri-food, pharmaceuticals and retail, have flagged particular concern about the potential for disruption at ports and the knock-on effects for consumers.

Ibec, the group that represents Irish business, said companies were being forced to prepare for multiple scenarios simultaneously, driving up costs at a time when many were still recovering from the economic fallout of the pandemic. A spokesperson said the situation was "deeply unsatisfactory" and called on the Government to provide additional supports for affected firms.

"The reality is that businesses cannot plan in a vacuum," said one senior industry figure who asked not to be named. "What we are seeing is a chaotic process that is costing real money and real jobs. Companies need certainty, and they need it now."

The Government has committed significant resources to Brexit preparedness, with the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment overseeing a range of supports including the Brexit Adjustment Reserve, which provides funding for sectors and communities most affected by Britain's departure from the EU. However, critics argue that the supports have been slow to reach those who need them most, and that the scale of the challenge has been underestimated.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin acknowledged in the Dáil this week that the transition had created "real and ongoing difficulties" for businesses, particularly those engaged in east-west trade. He said the Government was in regular contact with the European Commission to ensure that Irish concerns were reflected in any further negotiations on implementation.

The issue is particularly acute for firms operating along the border, where supply chains have long been integrated across both jurisdictions. Cross-border trade bodies have warned that additional friction, even of a relatively minor nature, can have an outsized impact on smaller operators with tight margins.

Freight Transport Association Ireland said its members were reporting increased delays and costs associated with new documentary requirements, with some consignments held up for days rather than hours. The organisation said the situation had improved somewhat since the early weeks of the new arrangements but remained far from satisfactory.

In the agri-food sector, which accounts for a substantial portion of Irish exports to Britain, processors and exporters said they were grappling with a complex web of sanitary and phytosanitary requirements that had added both time and expense to every shipment. Meat Industry Ireland said the cumulative effect of the new procedures was significant and called for further simplification.
headline: Businesses could face €1.5bn costs amid ‘chaotic’ Brexit transition

text:
The national organisation supporting older people, ALONE, is set to hold its first ever Donation Day in Dublin this weekend, calling on members of the public to drop off essential items for vulnerable older people across the country.

The charity said the event, which will take place at its premises in Dublin, aims to collect a range of practical items that can be distributed directly to older people who are struggling with the cost of living or experiencing isolation and loneliness.

ALONE provides a range of services to older people, including befriending, practical support, and housing, and works with thousands of individuals each year who may be living alone or in difficult circumstances.

The organisation said it has seen a significant increase in demand for its services in recent years, with more older people reaching out for help than ever before. Rising costs of energy, food, and other essentials have placed additional pressure on many older people, particularly those living on fixed incomes such as the State pension.

Speaking ahead of the event, ALONE CEO Seán Moynihan said the Donation Day represents a new way for the public to get involved and make a tangible difference in the lives of older people in their communities.

"We know that people want to help, and this Donation Day gives them a very practical way to do that," Mr Moynihan said. "The items we collect will go directly to older people who need them most."

The charity said it would provide further details on the specific items being sought and the exact times for the Donation Day on its website and social media channels.

ALONE operates a national support line for older people who may need assistance, which can be reached at 0818 222 024.
headline: ALONE holding first ever 'Donation Day' in Dublin

text:
Phil Hogan's reported interest in the role of director-general of the World Trade Organisation has set tongues wagging in political and diplomatic circles on both sides of the Irish Sea and across the Continent. The former EU Trade Commissioner, whose tenure in Brussels was cut short in controversial circumstances during the Golfgate affair in 2020, appears to be positioning himself for a return to the international stage. Whether this amounts to a serious candidacy or merely the kite-flying that so often characterises the early stages of such contests remains to be seen, but it raises questions worth examining.

There is no doubt that Hogan possesses a formidable CV for the post. His time as Agriculture Commissioner and subsequently as Trade Commissioner gave him deep experience of the multilateral trade architecture that the WTO oversees. He is well known in Geneva, Washington and Beijing, and his reputation as a tough and effective negotiator is widely acknowledged, even by those who found his style abrasive. In terms of sheer competence and knowledge of the brief, few candidates from any country could claim to match his credentials.

Yet competence alone does not secure such positions. The manner of his departure from the European Commission continues to cast a long shadow. Hogan's attendance at the now-infamous Oireachtas Golf Society dinner in Clifden, and his handling of the fallout, damaged not only his own standing but caused significant embarrassment to the Government and to Ireland's reputation in Brussels. Any candidacy would inevitably reopen those wounds, and his opponents would not hesitate to exploit them.

There is also the broader question of whether the Irish Government would be willing to expend diplomatic capital backing such a bid. The WTO director-general role is one that requires the active and sustained support of a candidate's home government, and the current coalition would need to weigh carefully whether championing Hogan serves the national interest or merely invites unwelcome controversy at a time when Ireland faces no shortage of diplomatic challenges, from the fallout of global trade tensions to the continuing complexities of our post-Brexit trading arrangements.

The WTO itself is an organisation in crisis, struggling with relevance in an era of rising protectionism, bilateral deals, and the effective paralysis of its dispute-settlement mechanism. Whoever takes the helm will need not just technical expertise but extraordinary political skill and, crucially, the confidence of member states across the developed and developing world. It is a role that demands consensus-building of the highest order.

Hogan has never lacked ambition, and ambition in public life is no vice. Ireland, as a small, open economy utterly dependent on rules-based international trade, has a profound interest in the effective functioning of the WTO. Having an Irish figure at the top of that organisation would, in theory, be a considerable prize. But the path from here to there is strewn with obstacles, not least of Hogan's own making. The Government would be wise to consider the question carefully before committing itself one way or the other.
headline: The Irish Examiner View: Hogan’s hat in the WTO ring?

text:
There is a certain irony in the fact that the more access we have to skincare information, the more confused many of us seem to be about what actually works. Social media has democratised beauty advice to an extraordinary degree, but it has also created a Wild West of misinformation, where a celebrity endorsement can carry more weight than decades of dermatological research.

It is worth stating plainly: celebrities are not skincare experts. They are, in many cases, extraordinarily good-looking people with access to the best facialists, dermatologists, and cosmetic procedures money can buy. When they attribute their luminous complexion to splashing cold water on their face each morning or rubbing a high-street moisturiser into their skin, they are often leaving out several rather significant steps — and several rather significant invoices.

This is not to suggest that every famous person who launches a skincare line or shares their routine is being deliberately dishonest. Many genuinely believe in the products they promote. The problem lies in the gulf between their experience and ours. A celebrity who swears by a particular cleanser may also be having regular microneedling, LED therapy, and prescription-grade retinoids administered by a top-tier skin specialist. The cleanser is the least interesting part of the equation, yet it is the part that gets packaged and sold.

The Irish skincare consumer is becoming increasingly savvy, and rightly so. We have access to brilliant dermatologists, skin therapists, and aestheticians in this country who take an evidence-based approach to skin health. The rise of skin clinics and qualified professionals offering consultations — many of whom have spent years studying the science of the skin — means there is no shortage of trustworthy guidance available.

Yet the pull of celebrity culture remains powerful. When a well-known face appears on Instagram or TikTok crediting a single product for their transformation, it creates a surge in demand that no amount of reasoned professional advice can match. We have seen it time and again: a product sells out overnight not because clinical trials have demonstrated its efficacy, but because someone with millions of followers held it up to a ring light.

The issue becomes more concerning when celebrities promote practices that are actively harmful. Over the years, we have seen famous figures advocate for everything from excessive exfoliation to entirely unregulated supplements, from DIY chemical peels to the complete abandonment of sunscreen. In a country like Ireland, where our skin is particularly vulnerable to UV damage — yes, even under cloud cover — dismissing sun protection on the basis that a Hollywood actress finds it unnecessary is genuinely dangerous.

Ingredients matter, and understanding them does not require a chemistry degree. However, it does require more than a cursory glance at a celebrity's sponsored post. Retinoids, niacinamide, hyaluronic acid, vitamin C — these are ingredients with robust evidence behind them, but they need to be used correctly, in appropriate concentrations, and as part of a routine that suits your individual skin type and concerns. What works for a twenty-three-year-old model in Los Angeles may be entirely wrong for a forty-five-year-old in Cork dealing with rosacea and perimenopause.

There is also the question of transparency.
headline: The Skin Nerd: Coming clean- celebrities don’t always know best

text:
Nagasaki has marked the 76th anniversary of the US atomic bombing that killed more than 70,000 people, with the city's mayor renewing calls for nuclear disarmament and urging world leaders to do more to rid the planet of such weapons.

Mayor Tomihisa Taue led a ceremony at the Nagasaki Peace Park on Monday, where survivors, their relatives and a small number of foreign dignitaries gathered to observe a minute's silence at 11.02am local time — the exact moment the bomb was dropped on August 9th, 1945.

The ceremony was scaled back for a second consecutive year due to the Covid-19 pandemic, with the number of attendees reduced to roughly 500, compared with the thousands who would typically gather at the park.

In his peace declaration, Mr Taue called on the Japanese government to sign and ratify the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which came into force in January of this year. Japan, the only country to have suffered atomic attacks, has so far declined to join the treaty, citing its security alliance with the United States.

Mr Taue warned that the risk of nuclear weapons being used was growing rather than receding, pointing to the modernisation of arsenals by nuclear-armed states and the development of smaller, more "usable" weapons.

"I call on the government of Japan to sign, ratify and become a party to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons," he said. "To do so would manifest the will of the only nation to have suffered atomic bombings in war."

Three days before the Nagasaki bombing, the US had dropped the world's first atomic bomb on Hiroshima, killing around 140,000 people. Japan surrendered on August 15th, 1945, bringing the Second World War to an end.

Prime Minister Yoshihide Suga also attended the ceremony but stopped short of expressing support for the nuclear weapons ban treaty, saying instead that Japan would serve as a "bridge" between nuclear and non-nuclear states.

His remarks drew criticism from survivors' groups, who accused the government of hiding behind diplomatic language while refusing to take meaningful action.

The average age of the survivors of the two bombings, known as hibakusha, is now over 83, adding urgency to efforts to record their testimonies and pass on their experiences to future generations.

Nagasaki was not the original target on that August morning in 1945. The industrial city of Kokura had been selected, but heavy cloud cover forced the B-29 bomber Bockscar to divert to its secondary target instead, altering the course of history for both cities.
headline: Nagasaki marks 76th anniversary of US atomic bombing

text:
Four new cases of coronavirus have been confirmed in the west of Ireland, bringing the total number of cases in the region to 23, the HSE has confirmed.

The National Public Health Emergency Team (NPHET) announced the new cases this evening, with all four individuals understood to have had close contact with previously confirmed cases. Three of the cases are in Co Galway and one is in Co Clare.

It is understood that contact tracing is under way in respect of each of the new cases, with the HSE's public health teams in the west working to identify and notify all close contacts of the individuals involved.

The Department of Health confirmed this evening that the four cases are included in the national figures announced today by the Chief Medical Officer Dr Tony Holohan. The individuals are being managed in line with HSE guidelines, and those who require hospitalisation are being treated at University Hospital Galway.

Dr Holohan urged the public to continue to follow public health advice, including regular handwashing, respiratory hygiene, and social distancing measures.

"We are asking people to take personal responsibility for their actions and to follow the public health advice. This is how we will slow the spread of this virus and protect the most vulnerable in our society," Dr Holohan said.

A spokesperson for the HSE West confirmed that the public health department is continuing to monitor the situation closely and that additional supports have been made available to GP practices and community services across the region.

The HSE has advised anyone experiencing symptoms of coronavirus — including cough, fever, shortness of breath, or breathing difficulties — to phone their GP and to self-isolate immediately. Members of the public are advised not to attend GP surgeries, pharmacies, or emergency departments without first making telephone contact.

Saolta University Health Care Group, which manages University Hospital Galway, said it has robust plans in place to deal with any increase in cases across its hospital network in the west and north-west.

The latest cases come amid growing concern about community transmission of the virus, with public health officials warning that the coming weeks will be critical in determining the trajectory of the outbreak in Ireland.
headline: Four new coronavirus cases confirmed in west of Ireland

text:
Micheál Martin has been urged to "come out of hiding" and address mounting confusion over the formation of the next government, as talks between the prospective coalition parties continue behind closed doors with little indication of when a deal might be finalised.

The Fianna Fáil leader, who is widely expected to return as Taoiseach, has faced criticism from opposition TDs and political commentators for what they describe as a lack of transparency around the negotiations process. Sinn Féin's Mary Lou McDonald accused Mr Martin of keeping the public in the dark at a time when the country faces pressing challenges on housing, health, and the cost of living.

"The people voted weeks ago and they deserve to know what is going on," Ms McDonald said. "Micheál Martin needs to come out of hiding and tell the public what kind of government he intends to lead, what commitments are being made, and when the Dáil will be in a position to vote on a programme for government."

The criticism comes as negotiations between Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael, and potential coalition partners have stretched on longer than many had anticipated. While both larger parties have publicly expressed confidence that a deal can be reached, the lack of visible progress has fuelled frustration among TDs on all sides of the House, including some within the prospective coalition's own ranks.

Several Independent TDs who are understood to be in discussions about supporting a government have privately expressed unease at the pace of talks, with some suggesting that a clearer timeline is needed. One Independent TD, speaking on condition of anonymity, said there had been "radio silence" from the negotiating teams in recent days.

Labour leader Ivana Bacik echoed calls for greater clarity, saying the protracted nature of the talks was "unacceptable" given the scale of the crises facing the State. "People are on hospital trolleys, families cannot find a home, and we have a caretaker government that cannot make decisions. The public deserve better than this," she said.

A Fianna Fáil spokesperson said the negotiations were proceeding in a "constructive and serious manner" and that Mr Martin would address the public at the appropriate time. The spokesperson added that it was important to allow space for the talks to conclude without a "running commentary" that could undermine progress.

Fine Gael sources similarly played down concerns, insisting that the complexity of forming a stable government required careful negotiation. "These things take time if they are to be done properly," one senior party figure said. "Nobody benefits from a rushed programme for government that falls apart six months down the line."

Political analysts have noted that while coalition formation talks in Ireland have historically taken several weeks, the current period of uncertainty is testing public patience. Dr Eoin O'Malley of Dublin City University said the longer the talks drag on without visible progress, the greater the risk of political disillusionment among voters.

"There is a balance to be struck between getting the details right and keeping the public informed," Dr O'Malley said. "At some point, the party leaders need to step forward and give people a sense of where things stand. Otherwise, you risk the perception that deals are being done in back rooms with no accountability."
headline: Micheál Martin urged to 'come out of hiding' amid Government formation confusion

text:
Jacinda Ardern is on course for a commanding victory in New Zealand's general election, with early results suggesting her Labour Party will secure enough seats to govern alone for the first time under the country's proportional representation system.

With more than half of votes counted on Saturday evening, Labour was polling at around 49 per cent, a result that would hand Ms Ardern a decisive mandate and represent a stunning endorsement of her leadership during a tumultuous term marked by the Christchurch mosque shootings, a deadly volcanic eruption and the Covid-19 pandemic.

The incumbent prime minister, who first came to global prominence when she took the reins of a struggling Labour Party just weeks before the 2017 election, cast her ballot earlier in the day in Auckland, where she told reporters she felt "positive" about the campaign her party had run.

Her main rival, National Party leader Judith Collins, was facing a bruising night, with her centre-right party tracking at roughly 27 per cent — a historically poor showing that would represent a dramatic collapse from the 44 per cent it secured at the last election under former leader Bill English.

Ms Collins conceded defeat and telephoned Ms Ardern to congratulate her, telling supporters at National's election night event in Auckland that she had wished the prime minister well.

The result, if confirmed once special votes are tallied in the coming weeks, would mark the first time any single party has won an outright majority since New Zealand adopted its mixed-member proportional system in 1996. Under the MMP system, which bears similarities to the Additional Member System used in some European parliaments, voters cast two ballots — one for a local electorate MP and one for a party.

Ms Ardern's first term in office saw her forge a coalition with the populist New Zealand First party, led by the veteran politician Winston Peters, and a confidence-and-supply arrangement with the Green Party. Early results suggested New Zealand First was struggling to reach the five per cent threshold needed to return to parliament, a result that would spell the end of Mr Peters' lengthy political career.

The Greens appeared set to clear the threshold, however, leaving open the possibility that Ms Ardern could choose to bring them into a coalition arrangement even if Labour secures enough seats to govern without them.

New Zealand went to the polls after a campaign dominated by the country's response to the pandemic. Ms Ardern won widespread international praise for her government's elimination strategy, which involved closing the country's borders early and imposing one of the strictest lockdowns in the world. New Zealand has recorded just 25 deaths from Covid-19, a figure that stands in stark contrast to the devastating tolls seen across Europe and the Americas.

The election had originally been scheduled for September but was postponed by a month after a fresh cluster of cases emerged in Auckland, forcing the city back into lockdown.

Two referendums were also held alongside the general election, with New Zealanders asked to vote on whether to legalise recreational cannabis and whether to permit assisted dying for the terminally ill. Results of those votes are not expected for several weeks.
headline: Ardern heading for big win as votes counted in New Zealand poll

text:
Jerry Harris, the star of the hit Netflix docuseries *Cheer*, has been sentenced to 12 years in federal prison after pleading guilty to sex crimes involving minors, telling the court "I am not an evil person" before the sentence was handed down.

The 22-year-old, who rose to fame as the breakout star of the cheerleading documentary, was sentenced in a Chicago courtroom on Wednesday after having pleaded guilty earlier this year to two counts of receiving child sexual abuse imagery and one count of travelling with the intent to engage in illegal sexual conduct with a minor.

In an emotional address to the court before sentencing, Harris apologised to his victims and insisted he was not defined by his crimes. "I am not an evil person. I am not the person that they probably see me as," he told the judge. "I want them to be able to live their lives freely and not have to worry about me."

Prosecutors had sought a 15-year sentence, while Harris's defence team had argued for a term of six years, pointing to his troubled childhood and the sexual abuse he himself suffered as a young person.

US District Judge Manish Shah ultimately settled on a 12-year prison term, followed by eight years of supervised release. The judge acknowledged Harris's difficult upbringing but said the seriousness of the offences demanded a substantial sentence.

Harris first came to public attention in 2020 when *Cheer* premiered on Netflix, following the competitive cheerleading squad at Navarro College in Texas. His exuberant personality and infectious catchphrase made him an instant fan favourite, leading to appearances on talk shows and even a spot on the red carpet at the Academy Awards.

However, his meteoric rise was cut short just months later when he was arrested by the FBI in September 2020 following allegations that he had solicited sexually explicit photographs and sex from minors. The investigation was prompted by a report filed by twin brothers who alleged Harris had repeatedly harassed them for explicit images and videos beginning when they were 13 years old.

Court documents revealed that Harris admitted to soliciting explicit material from at least 10 minors and to engaging in sexual conduct with a 15-year-old at cheerleading competitions.

The case sent shockwaves through the cheerleading community and raised serious questions about safeguarding within the sport, which has a large population of young participants. It also prompted renewed scrutiny of the institutions and organisations responsible for overseeing competitive cheerleading in the United States.

The victims' families released a statement following the sentencing expressing relief that the legal process had concluded but noting that the impact of Harris's crimes would be felt for years to come.

Harris will be required to register as a sex offender upon his release from prison.
headline: Jerry Harris says ‘I am not an evil person’ as he receives 12-year sentence

text:
There was a time, not so long ago, when the phrase "fashion for all" might have been dismissed as little more than a well-meaning slogan. But a growing cohort of Irish fashion enthusiasts, designers and content creators are working to ensure those words carry real weight, championing inclusivity in an industry that has long been criticised for its narrow definition of who gets to look and feel good.

From size-inclusive styling to adaptive clothing for people with disabilities, and from celebrating diverse skin tones to making fashion accessible at every price point, the message from Ireland's most passionate fashion advocates is clear: style has no prerequisites.

Among those leading the charge is Cork-based stylist and content creator Stephanie O'Connell, who has built a loyal following by showcasing how to put together outfits that flatter a range of body types, rather than just the sample sizes traditionally favoured by the industry. "For so long, the conversation around fashion was really about aspiration in a very exclusionary way," she says. "You were supposed to aspire to be thinner, taller, younger. What we're saying now is that you can aspire to express yourself exactly as you are."

It is a sentiment echoed across the Irish fashion landscape. Dublin designer Sinéad Burke, who stands three feet, five inches tall due to achondroplasia, has been a powerful voice on the world stage for adaptive and inclusive fashion. Her advocacy has opened doors not just in Ireland but internationally, forcing major fashion houses to reconsider who their garments are designed for and how those garments function in the real world.

The shift is also visible on the high street. Irish retailers have been gradually expanding their size ranges, though advocates note there is still considerable ground to cover. Many Irish brands now extend their offerings to a size 24 or beyond, but critics point out that extended sizes are frequently available only online, denying plus-size customers the in-store experience their straight-size counterparts take for granted.

"It's not enough to simply produce the sizes," says Galway-based fashion blogger and body positivity advocate Laura010. "If you can't walk into a shop on Grafton Street or Patrick Street and try something on, you're still being told that fashion isn't really for you. The fitting room experience matters."

The conversation around inclusivity extends well beyond size. Irish fashion creators from diverse ethnic backgrounds have spoken openly about the difficulty of finding foundations, hosiery and even so-called "nude" clothing that matches their skin tones. Nigerian-Irish model and activist Bashir Otukoya has highlighted how the Irish fashion scene, while improving, still has blind spots when it comes to racial diversity on runways and in campaigns.

Sustainability, too, has become intertwined with the inclusivity conversation. Advocates argue that fast fashion's relentless churn disproportionately affects those on lower incomes, who may feel pressured to keep up with trends but lack the means to invest in quality pieces. The growing popularity of charity shops, clothing swaps and rental services in cities like Dublin, Cork, Limerick and Galway has offered an alternative, making fashion more democratic in the process.
headline: The Fitting Room: Irish fashionistas advocate fashion for all

text:
Emilie Pine first announced herself as a literary force with *Notes to Self*, the essay collection that landed in 2018 like a depth charge and went on to win the An Post Irish Book of the Year award. In those pages, she wrote about addiction, infertility, sexual violence and family with a candour that felt almost radical in its refusal to look away. Now, with her debut novel, she proves that the same unflinching gaze and emotional intelligence translate seamlessly into fiction.

*Ruth & Pen* follows two women across a single Dublin day — a structure that inevitably invites comparisons to Virginia Woolf and, closer to home, to the long shadow of Joyce. But Pine wears those influences lightly, and the novel is very much its own creature. Ruth is a married academic whose carefully constructed life is beginning to fracture under the weight of things left unsaid. Pen is a young woman navigating the city with a rawness and vulnerability that will be achingly familiar to anyone who has ever felt unmoored in their own skin.

The two women do not know each other, yet Pine weaves their narratives together with a deftness that reveals unexpected resonances between their interior lives. Both are grappling, in different ways, with questions of identity, belonging and the stories we tell ourselves to keep going. It is testament to Pine's skill that neither storyline feels subordinate to the other; each is given room to breathe, and each earns its emotional payoffs honestly.

What distinguishes Pine from many of her contemporaries is her capacity for empathy without sentimentality. She writes about pain — psychological, physical, relational — with precision and care, never exploiting her characters' suffering for dramatic effect but never shying from it either. There is a generosity in her prose that extends to even the most flawed decisions her characters make. She seems genuinely interested in understanding why people do what they do, rather than sitting in judgment.

The Dublin that emerges in these pages is vividly rendered, not the postcard version but the living, breathing city of bus routes and coffee shops, of housing anxiety and casual kindness. Pine has a keen ear for the rhythms of contemporary Irish life, and the novel is peppered with small, perfectly observed details that anchor its emotional drama in the everyday.

If there is a criticism to be made, it is that the novel's structure occasionally works against its momentum. The alternating chapters mean that just as one narrative builds to a pitch of intensity, the reader is pulled away into the other. For the most part, Pine manages this tension skilfully, but there are moments in the middle section where the pacing falters slightly.

These are minor quibbles, however, in what is an accomplished and deeply felt debut. Pine has spoken in interviews about the years it took to write this novel, about the difference between the exposure of memoir and the freedom of fiction, and that careful gestation shows on every page. This is not a book that was rushed into existence on the back of a successful essay collection; it is a work that stands confidently on its own merits.
headline: Book review: Emilie Pine's debut novel reinforces her reputation as an empathetic writer

text:
British forces are prepared to launch air strikes against Islamic State terrorists operating in Afghanistan, the UK's defence secretary has confirmed, as the threat posed by the group's regional affiliate continues to grow.

John Healey said the RAF stands ready to carry out strikes against Islamic State Khorasan Province, or IS-K, which has established a significant foothold in Afghanistan since the Taliban's return to power in 2021. The group has been responsible for a series of devastating attacks across the region and is believed to be plotting operations further afield, including against Western targets.

Speaking to journalists during a visit to the Middle East, Mr Healey said Britain would not hesitate to act where there was a direct threat to national security, adding that military planners had drawn up options for targeted strikes should they be deemed necessary.

"We will take whatever action is required to keep the British public safe," the defence secretary said. "Islamic State Khorasan remains a serious and growing threat, and we are prepared to act decisively."

The comments mark a notable escalation in rhetoric from the Labour government regarding the terror threat emanating from Afghanistan, a country from which Western forces withdrew in chaotic scenes in August 2021. Since then, IS-K has exploited the security vacuum, carrying out attacks not only in Afghanistan but also in neighbouring Pakistan and, according to intelligence assessments, directing or inspiring plots in Europe.

The group claimed responsibility for the devastating attack on Moscow's Crocus City Hall concert venue in March of last year, which killed more than 140 people and underscored its capacity to strike well beyond its traditional area of operations.

British intelligence officials have repeatedly warned that Afghanistan has once again become a breeding ground for international terrorism, with IS-K regarded as the most potent threat. MI5 director general Ken McCallum said last year that the threat from Islamist terrorism had "not gone away" and that groups operating out of Afghanistan and the surrounding region remained a priority for the security services.

The prospect of British air strikes in Afghanistan would raise significant legal and diplomatic questions, not least because the Taliban, who are not recognised as the legitimate government by London or any Western capital, nominally control the territory. Any military action would likely require careful legal justification under international law, with the UK expected to invoke the right of self-defence.

There are also practical considerations. Unlike during the 20-year military campaign in Afghanistan, Britain no longer has bases or a significant military footprint in the country or the immediate region. Strikes would likely need to be carried out using long-range aircraft or assets based in the Gulf, where the RAF maintains a presence.

The development will be watched closely in Dublin, where the Government has been monitoring the evolving terrorism threat landscape in Europe. While Ireland faces a considerably lower threat level than the UK, security officials have cautioned that no European country can consider itself entirely immune from the reach of groups like IS-K.

Opposition politicians at Westminster pressed Mr Healey on the criteria that would need to be met before strikes were authorised, with some expressing concern about the risk of civilian casualties and the potential for mission creep. The defence secretary insisted that any action would be "proportionate, legal and targeted" and would be taken only on the basis of robust intelligence.
headline: British forces prepared to launch air strikes to target Islamic State terrorists in Afghanistan

text:
A man has been hospitalised after being stabbed during an attack on St Stephen's Day in what Gardaí are treating as a serious assault.

The incident occurred in the early hours of December 26 when the victim, a man in his 30s, was set upon in circumstances that are still being established by investigating officers.

Emergency services attended the scene and the injured man was rushed to hospital, where he was treated for stab wounds. His injuries are understood to be serious but not life-threatening, and he remained in hospital last night in a stable condition.

Gardaí have launched an investigation into the attack and are appealing for witnesses to come forward. Officers have been carrying out door-to-door enquiries in the area and are examining CCTV footage from the vicinity in an effort to establish the sequence of events leading up to the stabbing.

It is understood that Gardaí are following a definite line of enquiry and are confident of making progress in the investigation. No arrests have been made at this stage.

A Garda spokesperson confirmed that investigations are ongoing and appealed for anyone who may have witnessed the incident or who has information that could assist the investigation to contact their local Garda station or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.

The attack has caused concern among locals, with residents describing the area as generally quiet and expressing shock at the level of violence on what is traditionally a family occasion.

Anyone with information is asked to come forward.
headline: Man stabbed in St Stephen's Day attack

text:
Boris Johnson has warned his Cabinet that a "huge spike" of Omicron cases is on its way, as the British government faces mounting pressure to introduce fresh restrictions to curb the spread of the new variant.

The Prime Minister delivered the stark assessment during a virtual Cabinet meeting on Tuesday, telling ministers that the country must brace itself for a significant wave of infections driven by the highly transmissible Omicron variant in the coming weeks.

Mr Johnson, who chaired the meeting remotely after being identified as a contact of a confirmed Omicron case, said the government would not hesitate to take further action if necessary to protect the National Health Service from being overwhelmed.

The warning came as the UK recorded a sharp rise in confirmed Omicron cases, with health officials cautioning that the true number of infections is likely to be significantly higher than official figures suggest. Scientists have warned that the variant could be spreading at a doubling rate of between two and three days, raising the spectre of a fresh crisis for hospitals already under considerable strain.

Downing Street confirmed that no new restrictions were agreed at the Cabinet meeting, but ministers discussed the latest data and were told to keep the situation under constant review. The Prime Minister is understood to have stressed the importance of the booster vaccination programme in providing a wall of defence against the variant.

However, several senior Tory backbenchers have signalled fierce opposition to any further curbs on freedoms, warning that the economic and social costs of additional restrictions would be devastating. The resistance within Mr Johnson's own party threatens to complicate any attempt to introduce new measures, even as scientific advisers urge caution.

The Plan B measures already introduced in England — including guidance to work from home where possible, mandatory face coverings in most indoor public settings, and the use of Covid passes for large events — are expected to remain in place for the foreseeable future.

Labour leader Sir Keir Starmer called on the government to be "straight with people" about the scale of the threat and accused Mr Johnson of being too slow to act in the face of a rapidly evolving situation.

The development will be closely watched on this side of the Irish Sea, where the Government has already moved to introduce a series of restrictions in response to the Omicron threat, including the early closure of hospitality venues and limits on household gatherings.
headline: Johnson warns ‘huge spike’ of Omicron cases on way at virtual Cabinet

text:
Paschal Donohoe has said that whoever forms the next government will face the enormous task of restoring the Irish economy in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic, warning that the scale of the challenge ahead should not be underestimated.

The Minister for Finance said the crisis had fundamentally altered the fiscal landscape, with the State's finances having been transformed from a position of relative strength to one of significant strain in a matter of weeks.

Mr Donohoe said the incoming administration — regardless of its composition — would need to chart a careful course back to economic stability, balancing the need to support workers and businesses with the imperative of returning the public finances to a sustainable footing.

"The next government, whatever form it takes, is going to be a government that will be very concerned with how we restore and rebuild our economy," Mr Donohoe told reporters.

The Fine Gael TD for Dublin Central acknowledged that the pandemic had forced the Government to deploy unprecedented levels of State support, including the Temporary Wage Subsidy Scheme and the Pandemic Unemployment Payment, which between them are supporting hundreds of thousands of workers at a cost of billions of euro.

The minister cautioned that while such emergency measures were necessary to prevent an even deeper economic collapse, they could not be sustained indefinitely. He indicated that any transition away from these supports would need to be handled with great care to avoid undermining the recovery.

His comments come amid ongoing negotiations between Fine Gael, Fianna Fáil and the Green Party on the formation of a coalition government, with the economic fallout from Covid-19 looming large over the talks.

Mr Donohoe said the Exchequer figures painted a stark picture, with tax revenues falling sharply and expenditure rising dramatically as the State moved to cushion the blow of the pandemic. He noted that the borrowing requirement for this year would be significantly higher than anything envisaged before the crisis struck.

The minister also pointed to the considerable uncertainty that remained about the trajectory of the virus and its economic impact, saying this made planning for the recovery all the more difficult. He stressed the importance of Ireland maintaining its credibility with international markets and investors, noting that the State's ability to borrow at favourable rates had been crucial in funding the emergency response.

"We went into this crisis with our public finances in good order and that has made a real difference to our capacity to respond," he said. "We need to be mindful of ensuring that we can maintain that position as we come through this."

Mr Donohoe also highlighted the particular vulnerability of certain sectors, including hospitality, tourism and retail, which he said would require continued support as the economy gradually reopened. He acknowledged that some businesses would not survive the crisis and that the labour market would take considerable time to recover.

Opposition TDs have called for a more ambitious stimulus package, arguing that the Government's response, while welcome, has not gone far enough to protect jobs and businesses. Sinn Féin's finance spokesperson Pearse Doherty has repeatedly pressed for additional supports, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises struggling with cash flow and mounting debts.
headline: Donohoe: Next government will be concerned with restoring economy after Covid-19

text:
A close associate of the former US congressman Matt Gaetz has pleaded guilty to sex trafficking charges, in a case that has cast a long shadow over the controversial Florida Republican's political career.

Joel Greenberg, a former tax collector in Seminole County, Florida, entered his guilty plea in a federal court in Orlando, admitting to a string of offences including sex trafficking of a minor, identity theft, and wire fraud. The plea deal is expected to require Greenberg to cooperate with federal investigators, raising the prospect that he could provide testimony against others caught up in the sprawling investigation.

Greenberg, who had been indicted on more than 30 federal charges, agreed to plead guilty to six counts as part of the deal reached with prosecutors. In court, he admitted to paying women and an underage girl for sex, and to using a state database to look up information about his victims.

The case has drawn intense scrutiny because of Greenberg's well-documented ties to Gaetz, who has himself been the subject of a federal investigation into whether he had a sexual relationship with a 17-year-old girl and paid her to travel with him. Gaetz has strenuously denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with any crime. He has described the investigation as a politically motivated smear campaign and has insisted he has never paid for sex.

During the plea hearing, Greenberg's defence lawyer Fritz Scheller told reporters outside the courthouse that his client was prepared to assist prosecutors, remarking pointedly that he was "sure Matt Gaetz is not feeling very comfortable today."

The guilty plea marks a significant escalation in a case that has already upended political life in Florida. Greenberg, once a rising figure in local Republican circles, was first arrested in 2020 on charges of stalking a political opponent. The investigation subsequently widened dramatically to encompass allegations of sex trafficking, fraud, and the exploitation of his public office for personal gain.

Under the terms of the plea agreement, Greenberg faces a minimum mandatory sentence of 12 years in federal prison, though prosecutors could recommend a reduced sentence depending on the extent and value of his cooperation.

Legal analysts in the United States have noted that cooperation agreements of this nature are frequently used by federal prosecutors to build cases against higher-profile targets, and the deal has fuelled intense speculation in Washington about whether charges against Gaetz or other individuals could follow.

Gaetz, who represented Florida's first congressional district, had been one of the most prominent allies of former president Donald Trump during his time in Congress and was known for his combative style and willingness to court controversy. The ongoing investigation has nonetheless complicated his standing within the Republican Party, even as he has continued to maintain a visible public profile.

The US Department of Justice has declined to comment on the broader investigation or on whether additional charges are being considered.
headline: Matt Gaetz associate pleads guilty to sex trafficking charges

text:
The Department of Health has confirmed 53 additional cases of Covid-19 in the Republic, with no new deaths recorded.

The total number of confirmed cases now stands at 25,842, while the death toll remains at 1,764.

Of the cases notified today, 30 are men and 23 are women, with 71% aged under 45 years of age. The median age is 31.

A total of 24 cases are located in Dublin, with 7 in Kildare, 5 in Limerick, 4 in Donegal, and the remaining 13 cases spread across nine other counties.

As of 2pm today, 6 confirmed cases of Covid-19 are hospitalised, of which 1 is in ICU. There have been no new admissions in the past 24 hours.

Dr Ronan Glynn, Acting Chief Medical Officer at the Department of Health, urged the public to continue following public health advice as the country moves through the reopening phases.

"We are seeing clusters of the disease emerge in a number of settings. I would urge everyone to continue to practise hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette and physical distancing," Dr Glynn said.

"If you have any symptoms consistent with Covid-19, self-isolate and contact your GP without delay."

The HSE is working to identify any contacts of the confirmed cases to provide them with information and advice to prevent further spread.

Professor Philip Nolan, chair of the NPHET Irish Epidemiological Modelling Advisory Group, said the five-day moving average of new cases has stabilised but cautioned that vigilance remains essential.

"The disease has not gone away. We must continue to suppress the virus through our individual and collective actions," Prof Nolan said.

Meanwhile, validation of data at the HPSC has resulted in the denotification of two previously confirmed cases. The figures above reflect this.

The Government continues to monitor the situation closely as restrictions are eased under the roadmap for reopening society and business.
headline: Covid-19: 53 additional cases with no new deaths recorded

text:
The North's chief medical officer has urged the public to prepare for the possibility of a second lockdown as coronavirus cases continue to rise across the region.

Dr Michael McBride said that while nobody wanted to see a return to the severe restrictions imposed earlier this year, it would be irresponsible not to plan for such a scenario. He warned that the coming weeks would be critical in determining whether the spread of the virus could be brought under control without resorting to the most drastic measures.

"We need to be honest with people," Dr McBride said. "A second lockdown remains a possibility and we must be prepared for that eventuality, even as we work to avoid it."

His comments came as the North recorded a further sharp increase in confirmed cases, with health officials expressing particular concern about transmission rates in the Belfast, Derry and Strabane areas. The seven-day rolling average of new cases has climbed steadily in recent weeks, placing renewed pressure on the health service.

The North's Executive has already introduced a series of localised restrictions in an effort to curb the spread, including limits on household gatherings and the early closure of pubs and restaurants in certain areas. However, Dr McBride indicated that these measures may not prove sufficient if the public does not adhere to the guidance.

First Minister Arlene Foster and Deputy First Minister Michelle O'Neill have both acknowledged the gravity of the situation, though they stressed that any decision on a full lockdown would be taken only as a last resort. Ms O'Neill said the Executive was keeping all options under review and urged the public to take personal responsibility for following the rules.

"Nobody wants to go back to where we were in March," Ms O'Neill said. "But people need to understand that their actions in the coming days and weeks will determine what happens next."

The warning comes amid growing concern on both sides of the border about a resurgence of the virus. The Republic has also seen a significant uptick in cases, with the National Public Health Emergency Team recommending enhanced restrictions in several counties.
