Health officials North and South have maintained close contact throughout the pandemic, though the two jurisdictions have at times diverged in their approaches to restrictions.

Dr McBride said the health service in the North was better prepared than it had been in the spring, with improved testing capacity, contact tracing infrastructure and stocks of personal protective equipment. However, he cautioned that hospitals could come under severe strain if case numbers continued on their current trajectory, particularly as the health service simultaneously attempts to address the enormous backlog of non-Covid care that built up during the first wave.

He appealed directly to younger people, noting that while they were less likely to become seriously ill, they were playing a significant role in driving transmission to older and more vulnerable members of the community.

"Every single one of us has a part to play," Dr McBride said. "The virus has not changed. It has not gone away. And it will exploit every opportunity we give it."

The British Medical Association in the North echoed the chief medical officer's concerns, with representatives warning that GPs and hospital staff were already feeling the strain of dealing with rising case numbers alongside the resumption of routine services.
headline: Prepare for potential second lockdown, medical chief tells Northern Ireland

text:
The world of espionage has always made for gripping reading, but a new book lifts the lid on just how lucrative the global surveillance industry has become — and how far its tentacles reach into the everyday lives of ordinary citizens.

In *The Spying Game: How the World's Intelligence Agencies Are Cashing In*, journalist and security analyst Mark Heywood traces the explosive growth of private intelligence firms and the eye-watering sums governments are prepared to pay for the ability to monitor their own populations and those of rival states. It is a story that moves from the corridors of power in Washington to the tech hubs of Tel Aviv, and from the boardrooms of London to the shadowy meeting rooms of authoritarian regimes across the Middle East and beyond.

Heywood's central argument is a compelling one: that espionage has been thoroughly corporatised. Where once the intelligence world was the preserve of state agencies operating under at least a veneer of democratic accountability, the outsourcing revolution of the past two decades has created a parallel universe of private contractors who operate with far less oversight and, crucially, generate enormous profits for their shareholders.

The numbers are staggering. The global surveillance market is now estimated to be worth in excess of €80 billion annually, with firms such as the NSO Group — the Israeli company behind the infamous Pegasus spyware — commanding fees that would make even the most bullish tech investor blush. Heywood details how a single Pegasus licence, allowing a government client to infiltrate a target's smartphone and harvest its contents, can cost upwards of €5 million.

What makes the book particularly resonant for an Irish readership is the degree to which Ireland features in this ecosystem. Several of the world's largest technology companies, whose platforms are routinely targeted by state and private surveillance operations, have their European headquarters here. The tension between Ireland's role as a base for Big Tech and its obligations under EU data protection law — obligations policed by the Data Protection Commission — is a thread Heywood pulls at with some skill, though one senses he could have gone further.

He is at his best when profiling the individuals who inhabit this world. There is the former MI6 officer who now runs a boutique intelligence consultancy from a tasteful office in Mayfair, offering "due diligence" services to multinational corporations that amount, in practice, to spying on business rivals. There is the young Israeli software engineer, fresh from her military service in the celebrated Unit 8200 signals intelligence outfit, who finds herself developing tools that will later be used to track dissidents and journalists in countries with appalling human rights records.

The moral ambiguity is the point. Heywood does not adopt a simplistic good-versus-evil framework, and the book is stronger for it. He acknowledges that surveillance capabilities have been instrumental in thwarting genuine terrorist plots and disrupting organised crime networks. The challenge, as he frames it, is one of governance: who watches the watchers when the watchers are private companies answerable primarily to their bottom line?

The European dimension is well handled.
headline: Book Review: Big profits in the global spying game

text:
South Africa's last apartheid-era president FW de Klerk, who shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Nelson Mandela for negotiating the end of white minority rule, has died at the age of 85.

The FW de Klerk Foundation confirmed his death at his home in Cape Town on Thursday, saying he had been battling mesothelioma, a cancer linked to asbestos exposure.

De Klerk's place in history was secured on February 2, 1990, when he stunned the world by announcing the unbanning of the African National Congress and other liberation movements, and the imminent release of Mandela after 27 years of imprisonment. That single parliamentary address set in motion the dismantling of one of the most reviled systems of racial oppression the modern world had known.

Yet his legacy remained deeply contested, both within South Africa and internationally. For many white South Africans and Western observers, he was the courageous reformer who pulled his country back from the brink of civil war. For millions of Black South Africans, he was a man who had served and defended the apartheid system for decades before concluding it was no longer sustainable, and who was slow to take full responsibility for its crimes.

Born in Johannesburg in 1936 into an influential Afrikaner political family — his father served as a senator and cabinet minister — De Klerk rose through the ranks of the National Party, the very organisation that had constructed the elaborate architecture of apartheid after coming to power in 1948.

He served in various cabinet posts from 1978 onwards, earning a reputation as a conservative and giving little indication of the dramatic steps he would later take. When he assumed the presidency in August 1989, few expected transformative change.

But the geopolitical landscape was shifting rapidly. The fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Soviet Union, mounting international sanctions, and a domestic economy buckling under the weight of isolation all contributed to De Klerk's calculation that apartheid's days were numbered.

The negotiations that followed were fraught and frequently threatened by political violence. More than 14,000 people died in political unrest between 1990 and 1994, a period that tested the resolve of both De Klerk and Mandela. The two men shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993, though their relationship was often strained and marked by mutual suspicion.

South Africa's first fully democratic elections took place in April 1994, sweeping the ANC and Mandela to power. De Klerk served as one of two deputy presidents in the government of national unity until 1996, when the National Party withdrew from the coalition.

In later years, De Klerk faced persistent criticism over his reluctance to acknowledge the full extent of apartheid's brutality. His appearance before the Truth and Reconciliation Commission in 1997 was widely seen as inadequate, with critics arguing he failed to accept personal or political responsibility for the systemic violence carried out under National Party rule.
headline: South Africa’s last apartheid president FW de Klerk dies at 85

text:
There is something deeply satisfying about putting a tree in the ground. It is an act of faith, a gesture towards a future you may never fully see, and right now — as the bare-root planting season stretches ahead of us — there has never been a better time to do it.

November through to March is the ideal window for planting native trees in Ireland. The trees are dormant, the soil is still holding some of the warmth of autumn, and the roots have a chance to settle in before the demands of spring growth begin. If you have even a modest patch of ground, a corner of a garden, or a field margin that could do with a bit of life, this is your moment.

Ireland's native tree cover is among the lowest in Europe. We sit at roughly 11 per cent forest cover, and much of that is commercial sitka spruce plantation rather than the broadleaf woodland that once blanketed the island. The Government's Climate Action Plan has set ambitious targets for afforestation, but there is no reason individuals cannot play their part as well. Every birch, oak, rowan, and hazel planted in a garden or community space is a small but meaningful contribution.

Native trees are particularly valuable because they support the ecosystems that have evolved alongside them over thousands of years. A single mature oak can support more than 2,000 species of insect, lichen, moss, and fungus. Hazel provides early pollen for bees emerging in spring. Rowan berries feed thrushes and blackbirds through the lean winter months. Holly offers crucial shelter. These are not merely ornamental choices — they are ecological ones.

For those new to tree planting, the process is reassuringly simple. Bare-root trees — sold without a pot, their roots wrapped in damp material — are cheaper than container-grown specimens and establish just as well, often better. A whip, which is a young tree of about 60 centimetres to a metre in height, can be bought for as little as a couple of euro from native tree nurseries around the country. The Trees on the Land programme, run by the Irish Timber Growers Association, has been helping community groups and individuals source native trees for years and is well worth looking into.

When choosing what to plant, think about your soil and your site. Birch is wonderfully forgiving and will grow in poor, wet ground where little else thrives. Alder positively relishes damp conditions and has the added benefit of fixing nitrogen in the soil, improving it for everything around it. Scots pine, our only native conifer, does well on lighter, free-draining ground. Oak is the aristocrat of the Irish woodland but needs space and patience — it is slow to establish but will outlive everything else you plant by centuries.

The planting itself requires little more than a spade and a bit of care. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without cramping them, and deep enough that the tree sits at the same level it grew at in the nursery — you can usually see the soil mark on the stem.
headline: Juanita Browne: It's the perfect time to plant a native tree

text:
Pat Shortt has never been one to overthink the craft of comedy. The Thurles man, who has spent the best part of three decades making Ireland laugh, tends to talk about his influences the way he talks about everything else — with a kind of easy, unguarded warmth that makes you forget you're in the middle of an interview at all.

Asked about the culture that shaped him, Shortt reaches back not to any grand artistic awakening but to the texture of everyday life in County Tipperary. "Growing up, the entertainment was people," he says. "The characters you'd meet at the creamery, the mart, outside Mass. You didn't have to go looking for comedy — it was all around you."

It is a sensibility that has informed everything from his partnership with Jon Kenny in D'Unbelievables to his portrayal of the hapless Josie in the RTÉ series Killinaskully, and his Ifta-winning turn in Lenny Abrahamson's 2007 film Garage. Shortt has always drawn from the well of rural Ireland, but he bristles at the suggestion that his comedy is merely observational. "It's not about standing back and poking fun," he insists. "You have to love the people. If you don't love them, the audience will know."

Music was the first cultural force in the Shortt household. His father played accordion, and sessions in the family home were a regular occurrence. "There was always music," he recalls. "Trad, obviously, but everything else too. I remember hearing Christy Moore for the first time and thinking, there's a man who understands what it's like to be from a place." Moore remains a touchstone, and the two have become friends over the years, a connection Shortt clearly treasures.

Television in the 1970s and 1980s left its mark too. Shortt speaks with genuine reverence about Hall's Pictorial Weekly, the satirical RTÉ programme that skewered Irish political life with a sharpness that still holds up. "Frank Hall was doing something that nobody else was doing at the time," he says. "He was saying, we can laugh at ourselves, at our politicians, at the whole apparatus. That was revolutionary in its own quiet way."

Internationally, it was the physical comedians who caught his eye. He talks about Jacques Tati, the French filmmaker whose nearly wordless comedies he first encountered as a student. "Tati understood that the funniest things happen when nobody's trying to be funny," Shortt says. "That's the whole secret of it." He is similarly devoted to Laurel and Hardy, whose timing he describes as "perfect, absolutely perfect — you couldn't improve on it with a hundred years of trying."

Theatre came later but hit hard. Shortt recalls being "floored" by a Druid Theatre production of Tom Murphy's A Whistle in the Dark. "That play just opened something up in me," he says. "The violence of it, the tenderness underneath. Murphy understood families in a way that was almost frightening."
headline: Culture that made me: Pat Shortt

text:
It is a truth universally acknowledged that the Christmas ad is the last cultural tradition we have left. The church is empty, the parade is cancelled, and the Late Late Toy Show is, well, the Late Late Toy Show. But the Christmas ad remains, a two-minute short film designed to make you cry into your Cadbury's selection box and feel vaguely guilty about not visiting your grandmother enough.

This year, of course, the Christmas ad has a problem. How do you sell the fantasy of Christmas togetherness when togetherness is, in many cases, literally illegal? How do you show the big family dinner when public health guidelines say you shouldn't have more than a certain number of people at your table? How do you show someone hugging their granny when hugging grannies has been the number one thing we've been told not to do since March?

Having watched approximately one thousand Christmas ads this week — it is, after all, early November, and the advertisers have decided that we need Christmas more than ever, which is code for "we need your money more than ever" — I can confirm that there are essentially four approaches brands are taking to the problem.

The first is what I would call the Full Denial. This is where the ad simply pretends that the pandemic never happened. Everybody is hugging, kissing, crowding into warm rooms together, breathing on one another with wild abandon. No one is wearing a mask. No one is sanitising their hands. No one is standing awkwardly two metres apart at a drinks reception wondering whether it's appropriate to shake hands or do that weird elbow bump thing that makes you look like a chicken. These ads have the manic energy of someone at a house party who knows the Gardaí have been called but is determined to finish their drink before they arrive. They are oddly stressful to watch. You find yourself counting the people in the room and wondering about ventilation.

The second approach is the Vague Acknowledgment. This is where the ad nods to the fact that things have been a bit tough, without ever specifying what the tough thing actually was. "After the year we've all had," the voiceover intones, over footage of someone looking wistfully out a rain-streaked window. After the year we've all had, what? What happened? Was it a bad year for you personally? Did your dog die? Were you made redundant? The ad never says. It simply gestures at a collective sadness and then offers you a sofa at 20 per cent off as a solution. These ads exist in a curious no man's land where suffering is acknowledged but never named, as though the pandemic were Lord Voldemort.

The third approach is the one I find most fascinating, and I would call it the Lean In. These are the ads that have decided to make the pandemic the actual plot of the commercial. You know the ones. The granddaughter who learns to video-call her grandmother. The postman who delivers a parcel to someone who has been isolating alone. The neighbours who stand on their doorsteps and raise a glass to one another across the cul-de-sac. These ads have clearly been produced at great speed and with significant input from compliance departments.
headline: Caroline O'Donoghue: Four ways to advertise Christmas in a pandemic

text:
There is something deeply satisfying about giving a gift that keeps on giving, and I don't mean a subscription to a streaming service. I mean the kind of gift that feeds the birds, shelters the bees, and makes your garden — or someone else's — a little wilder and a little more alive.

Christmas is almost upon us, and if you're anything like me you'll have left most of the shopping until the last possible moment. But here's the good news: some of the best presents you can give this year require very little wrapping and even less stress. They just need a bit of thought about the natural world.

Let's start with the obvious. A native tree is one of the finest gifts you can give anyone with even the smallest patch of ground. A whitethorn, a rowan, a crab apple — these are trees that will outlast any gadget or gizmo, and they'll feed and shelter wildlife for decades. Several Irish nurseries sell bare-root native trees through the winter months, and they're remarkably affordable. For as little as a few euro, you can hand someone a tree that will one day be full of nesting birds and humming with pollinators. If the person you're buying for hasn't got a garden, consider donating a tree in their name through one of the many reforestation programmes run by Irish conservation organisations.

Bird feeders are another wonderful option, and they suit absolutely everyone from the apartment dweller with a balcony to the farmer with a hundred acres. A good quality feeder, paired with a bag of sunflower hearts, will attract goldfinches, blue tits, robins and more. Position it near a window and you've essentially given someone their own nature documentary, playing on repeat all winter long. If you want to go a step further, a nesting box is a gift that really comes into its own in spring, when house sparrows, starlings or perhaps even a pair of great tits will take up residence.

For the gardener in your life, a packet of Irish wildflower seeds is hard to beat. There are several excellent Irish seed companies now selling native wildflower mixes suited to our climate and soils. A small meadow patch, even just a square metre or two, can make an extraordinary difference to local pollinator populations. The All-Ireland Pollinator Plan has brilliant resources on its website for anyone wanting to get started, and a printed copy of one of their guides paired with a seed mix would make a thoughtful and practical gift.

Membership of a conservation organisation is another option worth considering. BirdWatch Ireland, the Irish Wildlife Trust, and the Irish Peatland Conservation Council all offer memberships and gift memberships that directly support conservation work across the country. These organisations do extraordinary work on often very limited budgets, and a membership not only funds that work but keeps the recipient connected to nature through magazines, events, and guided outings throughout the year.

For children, there are some gorgeous nature-themed books by Irish authors and illustrators. Encouraging a young person's curiosity about the natural world is one of the most valuable things any of us can do.
headline: Juanita Browne: Give some really wild Christmas gifts this year

text:
Public health officials have expressed concern that a growing number of people are not answering phone calls from contact tracers, potentially undermining efforts to suppress the spread of Covid-19 in the community.

The HSE's contact tracing teams have reported increasing difficulty in reaching individuals who have been identified as close contacts of confirmed cases, with some people simply refusing to pick up the phone or return missed calls.

Dr Ronan Glynn, Deputy Chief Medical Officer, described the trend as "concerning" and urged the public to cooperate fully with contact tracing efforts, which he said remained one of the most important tools available in the fight against the virus.

"Contact tracing only works if people engage with the process," Dr Glynn said. "If you receive a call from a contact tracing team, please answer it. The information they provide could be vital in protecting you, your family and your community."

It is understood that in some cases, people may be avoiding calls because they fear being told to restrict their movements, which could have implications for their ability to work or carry out daily activities. Others may simply be ignoring calls from unfamiliar numbers.

The HSE said its contact tracing centres were operating at full capacity and that delays in reaching close contacts could result in onward transmission of the virus going undetected.

A senior HSE source said the issue had been raised at several recent meetings and that consideration was being given to how the service might improve its rate of contact with individuals. Among the options being explored is the use of text messages in advance of calls to alert people that a contact tracer will be attempting to reach them.

SIPTU, which represents a number of contact tracing workers, said staff had reported frustration at the number of unanswered calls, noting that each unsuccessful attempt to reach a close contact consumed valuable time and resources that could be directed elsewhere.

The Department of Health confirmed it was aware of the issue and said it was working with the HSE to ensure the contact tracing system remained as effective as possible. A spokesperson said the public had a "civic duty" to engage with the process and that doing so was essential to breaking chains of transmission.

The development comes as the National Public Health Emergency Team continues to monitor case numbers closely, with particular concern about the trajectory of the disease in certain parts of the country.

Public health specialists have repeatedly stressed that contact tracing, along with testing and isolation, forms a critical pillar of the State's response to the pandemic. Without the full cooperation of the public, they warned, the system's ability to identify and contain outbreaks would be significantly diminished.

The HSE's contact tracing operation was significantly expanded over recent months, with additional staff recruited and trained to handle the increased volume of cases. The service operates seven days a week, and individuals who are identified as close contacts are typically called within 24 hours of a case being confirmed.

Those who are reached by contact tracers are advised on whether they need to restrict their movements, arrange a test, or take other precautionary measures depending on the nature and duration of their contact with a confirmed case.

Health officials are now appealing to the public to save the number used by contact tracing teams in their phones so that they can readily identify incoming calls from the service.
headline: Covid-19: 'Concerning' trend of some people not answering calls from contact tracers

text:
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has signalled his willingness to pursue a new chapter in relations with neighbouring Turkey, saying he is prepared to extend a "hand of friendship" to Ankara despite decades of tension between the two Nato allies.

Speaking at a press conference in Athens on Wednesday, Mitsotakis said the time had come for both countries to move beyond entrenched disputes and explore areas of mutual cooperation, particularly on migration, energy and trade in the eastern Mediterranean.

"Greece is ready to extend the hand of friendship to Turkey," Mitsotakis said. "We do not have the luxury of perpetual antagonism. Our peoples deserve stability, and our region demands it."

The remarks represent a notable softening in tone from the Greek leader, who has in the past taken a firm line against what Athens has characterised as Turkish provocations in the Aegean Sea and the eastern Mediterranean. Relations between the two countries have long been fraught, with disputes over maritime boundaries, airspace, energy exploration rights and the divided island of Cyprus serving as persistent flashpoints.

Turkey and Greece came close to a military confrontation as recently as 2020, when Ankara dispatched a seismic survey vessel into waters claimed by Athens, prompting a major diplomatic crisis that required European Union intervention to defuse.

However, a gradual thaw has been under way since early 2023, when a devastating earthquake in southern Turkey prompted an outpouring of solidarity from Greece. Athens was among the first to send rescue teams across the border, and Mitsotakis travelled to the disaster zone to meet his Turkish counterpart, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, in what was widely seen as a turning point.

Since then, the two leaders have held a series of meetings on the sidelines of international summits, and foreign ministers from both countries have engaged in what diplomats describe as the most sustained period of dialogue in years.

Erdoğan has also struck a more conciliatory tone in recent months, though analysts caution that domestic political pressures in Turkey could complicate any rapprochement. Ankara continues to dispute Greek sovereignty over a number of Aegean islands and has not withdrawn its casus belli — its declaration that any extension of Greek territorial waters in the Aegean would constitute grounds for war.

EU officials have broadly welcomed the diplomatic opening. Brussels has long urged both countries to resolve their differences through dialogue rather than brinkmanship, not least because Turkey's relationship with the bloc remains complicated by its stalled accession process and ongoing concerns over human rights and rule of law.

Foreign affairs analysts note that the shifting geopolitical landscape, including the war in Ukraine and growing instability across the Middle East, has given both Athens and Ankara fresh incentive to stabilise their bilateral relationship. Energy cooperation in particular has emerged as a potential area of convergence, with both countries keen to position themselves as transit hubs for natural gas supplies to Europe.

"There is a genuine window of opportunity here, but it will require sustained political will on both sides," said Dr Thanos Dokos, a former national security adviser to the Greek government.
headline: Greek PM willing to extend ‘hand of friendship’ to long-time rival Turkey

text:
Finding the right foundation can feel like a quest worthy of legend – too pale, too orange, too cakey, too sheer – but the good news is that the current crop of formulas on the market makes achieving that coveted "your skin but better" finish easier than ever.

Whether you're after full coverage for a night out or something barely-there for the school run, there's a foundation to suit every skin type, budget and lifestyle. The key, as any makeup artist worth their brushes will tell you, is matching not just the shade but the formula to your skin's needs.

For those with dry skin, a hydrating foundation with a dewy finish will be your best friend. Look for formulas enriched with hyaluronic acid or glycerin, which work to plump and smooth the skin while providing coverage. Charlotte Tilbury's Beautiful Skin Foundation (€40) has been a firm favourite since its launch, offering medium, buildable coverage with a luminous finish that manages to look like actual skin rather than a mask. It photographs beautifully too, which is no small consideration in the age of the selfie.

If oilier skin is your concern, you'll want something with a little more staying power. Estée Lauder's Double Wear Stay-in-Place Foundation (€46) remains the gold standard for long-wearing coverage. It's the foundation that makeup artists across the country reach for time and again for weddings, events and any occasion where you need your base to last from morning to the small hours. The shade range is extensive too, which is always a bonus.

For those who prefer a more natural approach, the Ilia True Skin Serum Foundation (€54) bridges the gap between skincare and makeup beautifully. It's lightweight, breathable and gives the sort of finish that will have people asking what skincare you're using rather than what foundation you have on. The clean beauty brand has developed a loyal following in Ireland, and this particular product is a large part of the reason why.

Budget-conscious beauty lovers need not feel left out. The Maybelline Fit Me Matte + Poreless Foundation (€11.99) continues to punch well above its weight, offering impressive coverage and a smooth, natural finish at a fraction of the price of its high-end counterparts. It's widely available in pharmacies and supermarkets across the country, and the shade range has improved considerably in recent years.

NYX Professional Makeup's Born To Glow Naturally Radiant Foundation (€12.99) is another affordable gem, delivering a gorgeous luminous finish that works particularly well on mature skin, as it doesn't settle into fine lines the way some fuller coverage options can.

Of course, even the finest foundation in the world won't perform at its best without proper skin preparation. A good moisturiser applied ten minutes before makeup, followed by a primer suited to your skin type, creates the ideal canvas. Think of it as the plastering before the paint – skip it and the finish will never be quite right.

Application matters enormously too. A damp beauty sponge will give the most skin-like finish, pressing the product into the skin rather than sitting on top of it.
headline: Get The Look: flawless skin is possible with a little help from these foundations

text:
Russia has warned Ukraine against using force in its rebel-held eastern regions, with the Kremlin saying any military escalation would have serious consequences for the stability of the entire region.

The warning came as tensions along the front lines in the Donbas region continued to mount, with both sides accusing the other of provocative actions and ceasefire violations. Moscow said it was "deeply concerned" by what it described as a build-up of Ukrainian military forces near the contact line separating government-controlled territory from areas held by Russian-backed separatists.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that any attempt by Kyiv to resolve the conflict by military means would be "extremely dangerous" and would undermine efforts to reach a peaceful settlement through the Minsk agreements. "We urge the Ukrainian side to exercise maximum restraint and to refrain from any actions that could lead to an irreversible deterioration of the situation," he said.

The Russian foreign ministry echoed the warning, saying Moscow would not stand by if Russian-speaking civilians in the self-declared Donetsk and Luhansk People's Republics came under attack. The regions have been controlled by Moscow-backed separatist forces since conflict erupted there in 2014, following Russia's annexation of Crimea.

Ukraine has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is planning a military offensive, insisting it remains committed to a diplomatic resolution while also asserting its right to defend its sovereign territory. Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of stoking tensions by deploying additional military hardware and personnel to the region under the guise of supporting the separatist forces.

Western governments have urged both sides to de-escalate, with the European Union calling for full implementation of the Minsk accords, which were brokered in 2014 and 2015 but have never been fully enacted. The agreements envisage a ceasefire, withdrawal of heavy weapons, and a political process to reintegrate the rebel-held territories into Ukraine with a degree of autonomy.

The Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe, which monitors the ceasefire through its Special Monitoring Mission, has reported a sharp increase in violations along the contact line in recent weeks, including the use of heavy weapons that were supposed to have been withdrawn under the Minsk agreements.

The conflict in eastern Ukraine has claimed more than 14,000 lives since it began and displaced nearly two million people, creating one of Europe's most protracted security crises. Despite numerous ceasefire declarations, sporadic shelling and sniper fire have continued, with civilians on both sides of the front line bearing the brunt of the violence.

Ireland, which has long supported a peaceful resolution to the conflict, has backed EU sanctions against Russia over its actions in Ukraine. Irish diplomats have also contributed to international monitoring efforts through the OSCE.

Analysts have warned that the latest escalation in rhetoric represents a significant hardening of Moscow's position, with some suggesting the Kremlin may be testing the resolve of Western governments at a time when attention has been focused elsewhere. The situation remains volatile, with diplomatic channels between Moscow and Kyiv largely frozen and trust between the two sides at a historic low.
headline: Russia warns Ukraine against use of force in rebel regions

text:
The murder trial of Patrick Quirke heard that a solicitor's letter sent on behalf of Mary Lowry outlined "concerns" about the terms of the lease arrangement under which the accused had been farming her land at Fawnagowan, Tipperary.

The jury at the Central Criminal Court was told that the letter, sent in 2012, raised a number of issues regarding the lease agreement that had been in place since the death of Ms Lowry's husband, Martin Lowry, in 2007.

Mr Quirke, aged 50, of Breanshamore, Co Tipperary, has pleaded not guilty to the murder of Bobby Ryan, a part-time DJ known as Mr Moonlight, on a date between 3 June 2011 and April 2013.

The prosecution alleges that Mr Quirke murdered Mr Ryan because he was in a relationship with Ms Lowry, with whom the accused had been having an affair. Mr Ryan's body was discovered in a run-off tank on the Fawnagowan farm in April 2013.

The court heard that the solicitor's letter set out Ms Lowry's concerns about aspects of the leasing arrangement, including the duration of the agreement and the terms under which Mr Quirke was occupying the land.

It has previously been heard in evidence that Ms Lowry had ended her affair with Mr Quirke before she began a relationship with Bobby Ryan, and that the accused had been reluctant to relinquish the lease on the land.

The prosecution contends that the lease gave Mr Quirke continued access to the farm at Fawnagowan, where the remains of Mr Ryan were ultimately discovered in the disused tank.

Evidence was given that the letter from Ms Lowry's solicitor indicated she wished to bring the arrangement to a conclusion, and that there had been growing tension between the two parties over the terms of the lease in the period before Mr Ryan's disappearance.

The trial, which is expected to last a number of weeks, continues before Mr Justice Eileen Creedon and a jury of six men and six women.

The trial continues.
headline: Love triangle trial: Letter from Mary Lowry's lawyer outlined 'concerns' over Patrick Quirke's lease on her land

text:
The death has occurred of what is believed to be Ireland's oldest man, a Kerry native who passed away at the remarkable age of 108.

John Joe Daly, originally from Ballyheigue in north Kerry, died peacefully at a nursing home in Tralee surrounded by his loving family. Mr Daly, who was born in 1916, the year of the Easter Rising, had lived through some of the most transformative periods in the history of the State.

Tributes have been pouring in for the centenarian, who was widely regarded as the oldest living man in Ireland at the time of his passing. His family described him as a man of extraordinary resilience, good humour, and deep faith who maintained a sharp mind and keen interest in current affairs right up until his final days.

Mr Daly spent much of his working life farming the land around Ballyheigue, a pursuit he credited with keeping him fit and active well into old age. He was a devoted member of his local GAA club and remained a passionate follower of Kerry football throughout his life, witnessing countless All-Ireland triumphs by the Kingdom.

Local TD and Minister for Education Norma Foley led the tributes, describing Mr Daly as "a living link to the foundation of our State and a man who embodied the very best of Kerry and its people."

"To have lived through the War of Independence, the Emergency, and into the modern era is simply extraordinary. John Joe was a gentleman in every sense of the word, and his passing represents the end of a remarkable chapter," Minister Foley said.

Cathaoirleach of Kerry County Council also paid tribute, noting that Mr Daly had been honoured by the council on several occasions in recognition of his extraordinary longevity and his contribution to community life in north Kerry.

Fr Brendan Walsh, who regularly visited Mr Daly, said the centenarian had a "wonderful outlook on life" and never lost his sense of wonder at the world around him.

"He would often say that the secret to a long life was hard work, fresh air, and not worrying too much about things you cannot control. There was a great wisdom in that simplicity," Fr Walsh said.

Mr Daly is predeceased by his wife Eileen, who passed away in 2003, and is survived by his four children, eleven grandchildren, and numerous great-grandchildren. His funeral Mass will take place at St Mary's Church, Ballyheigue, with burial afterwards in the adjoining cemetery.

The title of Ireland's oldest person is currently understood to be held by a woman, also from Munster, though the Gerontology Research Group, which verifies such records internationally, has not confirmed the precise details.

Ar dheis Dé go raibh a anam dílis.
headline: Kerry native believed to be Ireland's oldest man dies at 108

text:
An Estonian national accused of being a hitman for the Kinahan organised crime group is set to challenge his extradition to Spain when the case returns to the High Court in October.

The man, who cannot be named for legal reasons, is wanted by Spanish authorities in connection with a number of serious offences alleged to have been carried out on behalf of the Kinahan cartel. He was arrested in Ireland earlier this year on foot of a European Arrest Warrant issued by a Spanish court.

His legal team has indicated that a full challenge to the extradition proceedings will be mounted when the matter comes before the High Court in October, with a number of grounds expected to be raised in opposition to the surrender request.

The case is the latest in a series of legal proceedings linked to the Kinahan organised crime group, which has been the subject of a sustained international law enforcement operation involving the Gardaí, the US Drug Enforcement Administration, and police forces across Europe.

In April 2022, the US Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control imposed sanctions on the Kinahan gang, designating it as a significant transnational criminal organisation. Daniel Kinahan, Christy Kinahan Sr, and Christopher Kinahan Jr were all sanctioned, with the US authorities offering rewards of up to $5m each for information leading to the disruption of the group's activities.

Spanish authorities have played a central role in efforts to dismantle the cartel's operations, with a number of significant arrests and seizures carried out on the Iberian peninsula in recent years.

The accused man was remanded on bail with strict conditions when he last appeared before the court. He is required to reside at a specified address, sign on daily at a local Garda station, and surrender his travel documents.

The case was adjourned to allow the defence team time to prepare its submissions. A full hearing is expected to take place over several days in October, with the court likely to hear arguments on the admissibility of the European Arrest Warrant and the conditions the accused would face if surrendered to Spain.

The Minister for Justice has previously stated that tackling organised crime remains a priority for the Government, with significant resources allocated to the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau and the Criminal Assets Bureau in recent budgets.

The case will be mentioned again before the High Court in the coming weeks ahead of the substantive hearing.
headline: Estonian Kinahan hitman will challenge extradition bid in October

text:
A man is suing EBS and Ulster Bank over claims the financial institutions failed to properly forward mortgage payments he made to his former partner's home loan account, leaving him facing alleged financial loss and distress.

The case, which came before the Circuit Court this week, centres on a series of payments the plaintiff says he made over a number of years in respect of a mortgage on a property he had shared with his former partner before the couple separated.

The man claims he continued to make regular payments towards the mortgage after leaving the property, on the understanding that the funds would be credited to the mortgage account held in his former partner's name. However, he alleges that the payments were not properly applied to the account, resulting in arrears accumulating on the mortgage and causing him significant financial harm.

In his proceedings, the plaintiff has named both EBS and Ulster Bank as defendants, claiming the institutions were negligent in their handling of the payments and failed in their duty of care to ensure the funds were directed appropriately.

It is understood the man contends that he made the payments in good faith and took reasonable steps to ensure they would reach the correct account. He is claiming damages for the financial losses he says he has suffered as a result of the alleged failures, as well as for the stress and inconvenience caused.

The case raises questions about the obligations of financial institutions when processing third-party payments on mortgage accounts, particularly in circumstances where relationship breakdowns result in complex financial arrangements between former partners.

Neither EBS nor Ulster Bank has commented publicly on the proceedings. Both institutions are expected to file their defences in due course.

Legal sources noted that cases involving separated couples and shared financial obligations have become increasingly common in the Irish courts in recent years, with disputes frequently arising over mortgage payments on family homes following the breakdown of a relationship.

The matter has been adjourned to a later date to allow for the exchange of further documentation between the parties. The judge indicated that the case would be given a hearing date in the coming months.
headline: Man sues EBS and Ulster Bank over alleged failure to forward payments to former partner

text:
Johnny Depp did not receive a fair trial when a High Court judge ruled that a newspaper article describing him as a "wife beater" was substantially true, his lawyers are set to argue as the Hollywood star seeks permission to appeal the landmark ruling.

The Pirates of the Caribbean actor lost his libel action against News Group Newspapers, publishers of The Sun, in November when Mr Justice Nicol dismissed his claim over a 2018 article which referred to him as a "wife beater" in relation to his former wife, the actress Amber Heard.

Mr Justice Nicol found that the words were substantially true, concluding that 12 of the 14 alleged incidents of domestic violence had been proved to the civil standard of proof.

Depp's legal team will now make their case before the Court of Appeal in London, arguing that the trial was unfair and that the judge's conclusions were "plainly wrong". The appeal hearing is expected to take place over two days.

In written submissions, Depp's lawyers are understood to argue that the trial judge made errors in his assessment of the evidence and that he ought to have given greater weight to text messages and other documentary evidence which, they contend, undermined Heard's account.

The case attracted enormous public interest on both sides of the Atlantic when it was heard over 16 days last July, with both Depp and Heard giving extensive evidence about their turbulent relationship, which began in 2012 and ended with Heard obtaining a restraining order in 2016 before the couple's divorce was finalised later that year.

During the original trial, the court heard allegations and counter-allegations of violence, drug use and volatile behaviour from both parties. Depp, who has starred in films including Edward Scissorhands and the Pirates of the Caribbean franchise, strenuously denied ever being violent towards Heard and accused her of being the aggressor in the relationship.

News Group Newspapers relied on Heard's testimony as its primary witness in defending the article, written by the newspaper's executive editor, Dan Wootton.

Legal observers have noted that permission to appeal in defamation cases of this nature is granted only where an applicant can demonstrate a real prospect of success or where there is some other compelling reason for the appeal to be heard.

Heard, for her part, is separately facing a defamation lawsuit brought by Depp in the United States over a 2018 opinion piece she wrote for the Washington Post in which she described herself as a victim of domestic abuse. That case is due to be heard in Virginia.

A spokesperson for News Group Newspapers said the publisher would "robustly defend" the original judgment.
headline: Johnny Depp ‘did not receive a fair trial’, lawyers to tell Court of Appeal

text:
The Department of Health has confirmed 4,141 new cases of Covid-19 this evening as the spread of the Omicron variant continues to gather pace across the country.

As of 8am today, 488 Covid-19 patients are hospitalised, of whom 120 are in ICU.

Chief Medical Officer Dr Tony Holohan said the rapid growth in case numbers is being driven by the Omicron variant, which is now the dominant strain circulating in Ireland.

"We are seeing a very significant increase in the incidence of disease," Dr Holohan said. "The pattern we are observing is consistent with what has been seen in other countries where Omicron has taken hold."

He urged people to continue to follow public health advice, including wearing masks, maintaining social distance, and availing of booster vaccines when offered.

The HSE's vaccination programme continues to administer booster doses at pace, with walk-in clinics operating across the country. Health officials have stressed that booster vaccination provides significantly improved protection against the new variant.

The figures come as the Government continues to monitor the situation closely, with Taoiseach Micheál Martin having warned in recent days that the coming weeks will be challenging as the full impact of Omicron becomes apparent.

The National Public Health Emergency Team is expected to meet again in the coming days to assess the trajectory of the wave and consider whether any further measures may be required.

Deputy Chief Medical Officer Dr Ronan Glynn said hospital admissions remain a key concern, though early international data suggests Omicron may cause less severe illness than previous variants.

"We cannot be complacent," Dr Glynn said. "Even if a smaller proportion of cases require hospitalisation, the sheer volume of infections could still place enormous pressure on our health service."

The positivity rate has risen sharply in recent days, with testing centres reporting significant demand. The HSE has asked anyone experiencing symptoms to isolate and arrange a PCR test as soon as possible.
headline: 4,141 new Covid cases as Omicron spread continues

text:
Iraqis across the country are preparing to welcome Pope Francis to Baghdad in what will mark the first ever papal visit to the war-scarred nation, with communities of all faiths expressing hope that the historic trip will shine a light on their struggles and bring a message of peace to a land long torn by conflict.

The pontiff is due to arrive in the Iraqi capital on Friday for a three-day visit that will see him travel to several cities, including the ancient city of Ur in the south, traditionally regarded as the birthplace of Abraham, a figure revered by Christians, Muslims and Jews alike. He is also expected to visit Mosul and other towns on the Nineveh Plains in the north, where Islamic State militants waged a campaign of terror against Christian and Yazidi communities.

Security preparations have been extensive, with Iraqi forces deployed across Baghdad and other locations on the papal itinerary. The visit comes against a backdrop of ongoing security concerns, a severe economic crisis exacerbated by low oil prices, and a devastating third wave of Covid-19 infections that has seen case numbers surge in recent weeks.

Vatican officials have insisted the trip will go ahead despite the pandemic, with strict health protocols to be observed throughout. Pope Francis received his Covid-19 vaccine in January, and the Vatican said measures would be in place to limit crowd sizes and enforce social distancing at all events.

For Iraq's dwindling Christian population, the visit carries enormous symbolic weight. Once numbering more than 1.5 million, the Christian community has shrunk to an estimated 300,000 or fewer, with successive waves of violence and persecution driving many to seek refuge abroad. The years of Islamic State occupation between 2014 and 2017 proved particularly devastating, as militants swept through the Nineveh Plains, destroying churches, seizing homes and forcing tens of thousands to flee.

Cardinal Louis Raphaël Sako, the Chaldean Catholic Patriarch of Babylon, said the visit would bring "a message of peace and fraternity" and urged all Iraqis to embrace the occasion. "This visit is not just for Christians. It is for all of Iraq," he said.

In Baghdad's Our Lady of Salvation Church, the site of a horrific 2010 attack by militants linked to al-Qaeda that killed 58 people, parishioners have been busy cleaning and decorating in anticipation of the Pope's arrival. Many spoke of their emotional attachment to the visit, describing it as a recognition of the suffering their community has endured.

"We have waited so long for this moment," said Mariam Youssef, a parishioner who lost relatives in the 2010 attack. "The Pope coming here tells us that the world has not forgotten us."

Muslim leaders have also welcomed the visit, with prominent Shia and Sunni clerics expressing their support. In a particularly significant engagement, Pope Francis is expected to meet Grand Ayatollah Ali al-Sistani, one of the most influential figures in Shia Islam, at his modest home in the holy city of Najaf. The meeting is being seen as a powerful gesture of interfaith dialogue and mutual respect.
headline: Iraqis prepare to welcome Pope to Baghdad

text:
A judge has ruled that a member of An Garda Síochána charged with false imprisonment and sexual assault can be publicly named, rejecting a defence application for reporting restrictions in the case.

The decision was handed down at Dublin District Court, where the accused garda had sought an order preventing his identification in media coverage of the proceedings. His legal team had argued that naming the officer at this stage could cause irreparable damage to his reputation and career, regardless of the eventual outcome of the case.

However, Judge [the presiding judge] declined to impose any such restriction, noting that open justice is a cornerstone of the legal system and that there were insufficient grounds to depart from that principle in this instance.

The accused, who cannot yet be named pending the finalisation of certain legal matters, faces charges of false imprisonment and sexual assault alleged to have occurred against a woman. The charges were brought following a Garda Síochána Ombudsman Commission investigation into the allegations.

The court heard that the accused officer has been suspended from duty on full pay since the investigation commenced. He appeared before the court dressed in civilian clothing and spoke only to confirm his name and address.

Defence counsel told the court that their client strenuously denies all charges and intends to fully contest the matter at trial. An application for bail was granted subject to a number of conditions, including that the accused surrender his passport, sign on three times weekly at a designated Garda station, and have no contact whatsoever with the complainant.

The prosecution, led by a solicitor acting on behalf of the Director of Public Prosecutions, indicated that a book of evidence is being prepared and that the matter is likely to be sent forward for trial on indictment to the Circuit Criminal Court given the seriousness of the charges.

The DPP's directions are still awaited on certain aspects of the case, the court was told.

The judge remanded the accused on bail to appear again at a later date for the service of the book of evidence. Legal aid was granted after the court heard representations regarding the accused's financial circumstances.

The case has prompted renewed discussion about the handling of criminal allegations against serving members of the force. GSOC confirmed it had conducted an independent investigation into the matter before forwarding a file to the DPP, who subsequently directed that charges be brought.

A Garda spokesperson said the force does not comment on individual cases before the courts but confirmed that procedures are in place to deal with members who are the subject of criminal proceedings.

The matter will return before Dublin District Court in the coming weeks.
headline: Judge allows garda accused of false imprisonment and sexual assault to be named

text:
The Crawford Art Gallery in Cork has unveiled a major rehang of its permanent collection, offering visitors a fresh perspective on centuries of Irish art and the institution's own storied past.

The gallery, which has been a cornerstone of cultural life in Cork since the 19th century, has reorganised its historic holdings to draw out new connections between works and to foreground pieces that have spent years in storage. Curators say the project has been months in the making and represents one of the most significant reinterpretations of the collection in recent memory.

Among the highlights are works from the gallery's celebrated collection of Greek and Roman casts, which were originally acquired from the Vatican in the early 1800s for use by students of the Cork School of Design. Long regarded as among the most important such collections in Europe, the casts have been given renewed prominence in the new display, with improved lighting and contextual material designed to help visitors understand their remarkable journey to Cork.

Director Mary McCarthy said the rehang was about ensuring the collection speaks to contemporary audiences while honouring its deep roots in the city.

"We have an extraordinary collection that spans several centuries, and we felt it was time to let people see it with fresh eyes," she said. "There are works here that haven't been on public display for years, and we wanted to create new dialogues between pieces — between historical and contemporary, between Irish and international artists."

The new arrangement also places a stronger emphasis on the contributions of women artists and on works that reflect Cork's maritime and trading history, drawing connections between the gallery's holdings and the broader story of the city.

The Crawford, which is funded by the Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media, underwent a significant capital investment programme in recent years, with upgrades to its gallery spaces and facilities on Emmet Place. The rehang is seen as part of a wider effort to build on that investment and to attract new audiences, particularly younger visitors and tourists.

Cork-based art historian Dr Éimear O'Connor welcomed the initiative, describing it as a timely move that reflects broader trends in how galleries and museums across Europe are reconsidering their permanent displays.

"There is a real energy in the museum sector around the idea that collections should not be static," she said. "The Crawford has always punched above its weight in terms of the quality and depth of its holdings, and this kind of reinterpretation can only enhance public engagement."

The gallery said it would complement the new hang with a programme of talks, tours and educational events over the coming months, with details to be announced on its website. Admission to the Crawford Art Gallery remains free.
headline: Crawford Gallery’s historic collection cast in new light

text:
Limerick City and County voters may get the chance to elect their first directly-elected mayor sooner than many had anticipated, with growing indications that the Government is preparing to accelerate the timeline for the landmark vote.

Sources familiar with the planning process have indicated that preparations are being advanced to hold the plebiscite and subsequent mayoral election ahead of the originally envisaged schedule, in what would represent a significant moment for local democracy in the mid-west region.

The move comes after Limerick voters backed the concept of a directly-elected mayor in a plebiscite held alongside the 2019 local and European elections, becoming the only one of three cities consulted — alongside Cork and Waterford — to vote in favour of the proposal.

Legislation underpinning the new office has been working its way through the Oireachtas, with the Directly Elected Mayor with Executive Functions for Limerick City and County Bill setting out the powers and remit of the new role. The mayor would assume significant executive functions currently held by the chief executive of Limerick City and County Council, representing a fundamental shift in how local government operates in the region.

Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage Darragh O'Brien has previously signalled his commitment to delivering on the result of the 2019 vote, and the Department is understood to be examining options to bring the process forward.

The directly-elected mayor would serve a five-year term and would be expected to take on responsibilities spanning housing, planning, economic development and transport policy at a local level, representing a considerable transfer of power from the unelected executive to a democratically mandated officeholder.

Local TDs and councillors have broadly welcomed the prospect of an accelerated timeline, though some have cautioned that sufficient time must be allowed to ensure the legislative framework is robust and that candidates and voters alike are properly informed about the nature and scope of the new office.

Sinn Féin TD Maurice Quinlivan has previously called for the process to be expedited, arguing that Limerick voters delivered a clear mandate in 2019 and have waited long enough to see it acted upon.

Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil representatives in the Limerick area are also understood to be supportive of moving quickly, viewing the directly-elected mayor as a potential model for other local authority areas should it prove successful.

The new role is expected to be one of the most powerful positions in Irish local government, with the mayor wielding executive authority that goes well beyond the largely ceremonial functions associated with the existing cathaoirleach or mayor positions across the country's 31 local authorities.

However, questions remain about the precise delineation of powers between the new mayor and the council's chief executive, with some local authority officials expressing concern about potential overlap or conflict between the two roles.

The timeline for any vote would also need to factor in practical considerations, including the compilation of a register of candidates, the design of the electoral process, and public awareness campaigns to ensure voters understand the significance of the ballot.
headline: Limerick City and County voters could cast ballots for directly-elected mayor ahead of schedule

text:
Incorporating clover into grassland offers Irish farmers a genuine "win win" when it comes to both economic and environmental sustainability, according to the latest findings from the Teagasc Signpost Programme.

The message was reinforced at a recent Signpost farm walk, where advisers and researchers outlined how white clover can significantly reduce chemical nitrogen use while maintaining — and in many cases improving — overall sward productivity. With fertiliser costs remaining stubbornly high and environmental targets looming large, the case for clover has never been more compelling.

Teagasc has been championing the role of clover as part of its Signpost Programme, which aims to lead the agriculture sector towards climate neutrality by 2050 through a series of on-farm demonstration projects. Clover's ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen through a natural biological process means farmers can cut back substantially on expensive chemical fertiliser inputs without sacrificing grass growth.

Research carried out across the Signpost demonstration farms has shown that well-managed clover swards can fix between 100kg and 150kg of nitrogen per hectare annually. This translates into significant savings on fertiliser bills — savings that go straight to the bottom line at a time when input costs are squeezing margins on dairy, beef and sheep enterprises alike.

"The beauty of clover is that it addresses two challenges at once," said one Teagasc adviser at the farm walk. "You're reducing your costs and you're reducing your emissions. That's not something we can say about every technology or practice we promote."

From an environmental perspective, lower chemical nitrogen use means reduced nitrous oxide emissions — one of the most potent greenhouse gases associated with agricultural production. Nitrous oxide is approximately 300 times more warming than carbon dioxide over a 100-year period, and fertiliser application is a major source of these emissions on Irish farms. Cutting back on chemical nitrogen through clover incorporation is therefore one of the most impactful steps a farmer can take to reduce the carbon footprint of their enterprise.

However, Teagasc advisers were keen to stress that clover is not a silver bullet and requires careful management to deliver results. Successful establishment is critical, and farmers were advised to consider over-sowing into existing swards where a full reseed is not practical or economical. Soil fertility must also be addressed, with adequate levels of phosphorus, potassium and lime essential for clover to thrive and compete within the sward.

Grazing management is equally important. Clover performs best in rotationally grazed swards where rest periods allow the plant to recover and spread. Tight, frequent grazing without adequate recovery time will weaken clover content over time, undermining the very benefits farmers are trying to capture.

The Signpost Programme has set a target of having clover incorporated into 300,000 hectares of grassland nationally by 2030. While progress has been made, there remains considerable scope for further adoption. Department of Agriculture data suggest that clover is still absent from the majority of Irish grassland, though awareness and uptake have increased markedly in recent years, driven by both the economic argument and the requirements of new environmental schemes.
headline: Signpost: Incorporating clover offers a 'win win' for economic and environmental sustainability

text:
Mary Lou McDonald is now viewed as a more popular party leader than Leo Varadkar, according to new polling data that will raise further questions about Fine Gael's electoral strategy ahead of the next general election.

The Sinn Féin president has overtaken the Taoiseach in satisfaction ratings, a development that senior Government figures are understood to be treating with considerable concern as coalition parties seek to shore up support in key constituencies.

The findings, which emerge from the latest opinion poll, suggest that Ms McDonald's consistent focus on the cost-of-living crisis and the housing emergency has resonated with voters who feel the Government has been too slow to act on the issues affecting their daily lives.

Ms McDonald's satisfaction rating has been on an upward trajectory in recent months, and party strategists within Sinn Féin believe the figures reflect a broader realignment in Irish politics that has been under way since the 2020 general election, when the party topped the popular vote but was unable to form a government.

Speaking in the Dáil this week, Ms McDonald pressed the Taoiseach on what she described as a failure of ambition in tackling the housing crisis, telling him that "people are crying out for change and this Government is simply not listening."

Mr Varadkar has faced criticism from within his own party in recent weeks, with some Fine Gael TDs expressing frustration at what they perceive as a lack of a clear narrative to bring to voters on the doorsteps. One backbencher, speaking on condition of anonymity, said there was a "growing unease" about the party's direction and its ability to communicate its record in government effectively.

Fine Gael sources have sought to downplay the significance of the polling, pointing out that individual satisfaction ratings do not always translate into seat gains and that the party remains confident in its ability to fight a strong campaign when the election is called.

A senior Government source said the Taoiseach's focus remained on "delivering for people" rather than on polling numbers, adding that the full impact of recent budgetary measures had yet to be felt by households across the State.

However, political analysts have noted that Ms McDonald's personal ratings are significant because they suggest she has succeeded in consolidating Sinn Féin's position as the primary alternative to the coalition parties. Dr Theresa Reidy, a political scientist at University College Cork, has previously noted that leadership ratings can be a strong indicator of broader party momentum, particularly in the Irish electoral system where candidates' personal appeal plays a decisive role in transfers.

The findings will also be scrutinised within Fianna Fáil, where Tánaiste Micheál Martin has consistently polled well on personal satisfaction ratings but where the party has struggled to differentiate itself sufficiently from its coalition partner.

For the coalition, the concern is not simply that Ms McDonald has overtaken Mr Varadkar in the polls, but that the trend appears to be a sustained one rather than a temporary fluctuation. Government TDs returning from constituency work have reported that housing, health, and the cost of living remain the dominant concerns on the doorstep, and that voters are increasingly willing to consider Sinn Féin as a party of government.
headline: Mary Lou McDonald 'more popular leader than Leo Varadkar'

text:
Simon Coveney has told his British counterpart Jeremy Hunt that the UK must produce "viable alternatives" to the Northern Ireland backstop if it wishes to see the provision removed from the Withdrawal Agreement, as tensions between Dublin and London continued to simmer over the future of the Irish border.

The Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs spoke with the British Foreign Secretary by telephone on Tuesday evening, reiterating Ireland's firm position that the backstop remains a critical insurance policy against the return of a hard border on the island of Ireland.

Mr Coveney's intervention came as Dominic Raab, the former Brexit secretary, emerged as one of the leading contenders in the Conservative Party leadership race, having repeatedly pledged to scrap the backstop arrangement if he succeeds Theresa May in Downing Street.

Speaking after the call, Mr Coveney said it was "not enough" for leadership candidates to simply demand the removal of the backstop without offering credible, workable replacements that would protect the Good Friday Agreement and the all-island economy.

"Ireland's position is very clear. We are open to examining alternative arrangements, but they must be realistic, legally operable and deliver the same outcomes as the backstop," Mr Coveney said. "To date, no such alternatives have been put forward by anyone on the British side."

The backstop, which would keep Northern Ireland aligned with certain EU single market rules and maintain a temporary customs union between the UK and the EU, was designed to prevent physical infrastructure on the border under any circumstances. It proved to be the most contentious element of the Withdrawal Agreement negotiated by Mrs May, which was defeated three times in the House of Commons.

Several candidates vying to replace Mrs May as Conservative leader and prime minister have pledged to renegotiate or abandon the backstop entirely, with Mr Raab among the most vocal critics of the arrangement. Boris Johnson, the former foreign secretary and current frontrunner in the contest, has also vowed to take the backstop off the table.

The European Commission reiterated on Tuesday that the Withdrawal Agreement, including the backstop protocol, is not open for renegotiation. A spokesman said the EU remained willing to be "flexible" on the political declaration setting out the framework for the future UK-EU relationship, but that the legally binding treaty text was settled.

Taoiseach Leo Varadkar has consistently warned that attempts to remove the backstop without a viable alternative risk undermining the peace process and could not be accepted by Ireland or the EU. Speaking in the Dáil last week, Mr Varadkar said the Government would not be "intimidated" by the rhetoric emerging from the Tory leadership contest.

Government sources in Dublin expressed frustration at what they described as a lack of detailed proposals from London, noting that alternative arrangements based on technological solutions for the border had been repeatedly examined and found wanting.

"We have heard a lot of promises about magical technology that doesn't yet exist," one senior Government source said. "What we haven't seen is a single credible plan that would do what the backstop does."
headline: Coveney tells Raab to produce viable alternatives to backstop

text:
The Guinness Cork Jazz Festival has unveiled its programme for this year's event, promising a packed schedule of world-class performances across the October bank holiday weekend that organisers say will mark a triumphant return to form for one of Ireland's longest-running and best-loved music festivals.

Now in its 44th year, the festival will run from October 27 to 31, with more than 1,000 performances taking place across Cork city in venues ranging from intimate pub sessions to marquee concerts at the Everyman and Cork Opera House.

Festival organisers have confirmed a headline programme that features an impressive mix of international jazz royalty and homegrown talent. The announcement comes as the festival looks to recapture the energy and scale of its pre-pandemic editions, having operated on a reduced basis during the Covid-19 restrictions of 2020 and 2021.

Cork City Council has thrown its weight behind the event once again, with Lord Mayor Cllr Deirdre Forde welcoming the programme announcement as a signal of the city's cultural revival. "The Jazz Festival is part of the fabric of Cork, and to see it return with such an ambitious programme is wonderful news for the city, for our hospitality sector, and for the thousands of visitors who make the pilgrimage here every October bank holiday," she said.

The festival has long been recognised as one of Europe's premier jazz events and a cornerstone of Cork's cultural calendar, drawing tens of thousands of visitors to the city each year and generating an estimated economic boost of tens of millions of euro for local businesses.

Beyond the headline acts, the programme will feature the popular fringe festival, which sees jazz spill out onto the streets of Cork and into pubs, restaurants, hotels, and cafés across the city. The free outdoor performances on Grand Parade and at other locations around the city centre have become a hallmark of the weekend, drawing casual listeners and devoted fans alike.

Fáilte Ireland has consistently identified the festival as one of the key drivers of tourism to the Munster region during the autumn season, and this year's event is expected to attract significant numbers of overseas visitors as international travel continues to normalise.

The festival's organisers said they were particularly keen to showcase Irish jazz musicians, with a number of slots dedicated to emerging talent from the vibrant domestic scene. Ireland's jazz community has grown considerably in recent years, with conservatories and music programmes across the country producing a new generation of accomplished performers.

Tickets for headline events are expected to go on sale in the coming weeks through the festival's website, while many of the fringe events will remain free of charge. Full details of the programme, including venue listings and performance times, are available at guinnessjazzfestival.com.

For Cork's hospitality industry, which bore the brunt of successive lockdowns, the return of the jazz festival at full tilt represents a much-needed boost heading into the winter season. Hotels across the city are already reporting strong bookings for the bank holiday weekend, with many establishments offering special jazz festival packages.
headline: Guinness Cork Jazz Festival announces stellar programme for 2022 event

text:
It has been a busy Friday with developments on several fronts, from the corridors of Brussels to the legacy of the Good Friday Agreement and, in somewhat lighter news, a case of mistaken identity involving a rodent that captured the public's imagination.

EU leaders gathered in Brussels today for a summit dominated by discussions on trade, defence spending and the bloc's response to escalating global tensions. Taoiseach Simon Harris was among those at the table as leaders sought to hammer out a united position on European security and the economic challenges posed by shifting US trade policy. Mr Harris said Ireland's position remained firm on the need for a coordinated European approach, while emphasising that any moves on defence must respect the State's traditional policy of military neutrality. The summit also touched on migration and the EU's relationships with key trading partners, with leaders expected to continue talks into the evening.

Closer to home, the 27th anniversary of the Good Friday Agreement was marked with renewed calls to protect the gains of the peace process. Politicians on both sides of the border reflected on the significance of the 1998 accord, which brought an end to decades of conflict in Northern Ireland. There were also fresh calls for the British and Irish governments to ensure full implementation of all aspects of the agreement, with some warning that outstanding commitments risk undermining public confidence in the institutions it established.

And finally, in the story that perhaps generated the most engagement on social media today, a creature initially identified as a rat turned out to be something else entirely. The case of mistaken rodent identity drew widespread amusement online after images circulated purporting to show the animal in question, only for experts to weigh in and correct the record. It served as a welcome moment of levity on what was otherwise a news day heavy with political and diplomatic developments.
headline: Friday's Evening Round-Up: EU summit, Good Friday Agreement and mistaken identity of rodent

text:
A baby was among those in a house that was targeted in a petrol bomb attack in Cork city in the early hours of this morning, the second such incident at the property in recent days.

The infant was taken to hospital as a precautionary measure following the attack, which occurred at a residence in the Knocknaheeny area at approximately 2.30am. It is understood the baby was not physically injured but was brought to Cork University Hospital for assessment.

Gardaí and emergency services rushed to the scene after the device was thrown at the front of the house while a number of people, including the young child, were inside. The fire was quickly brought under control and nobody was seriously injured, though there was damage to the exterior of the property.

It is the second time in less than a week that the house has been targeted in a petrol bomb attack, and investigators believe the incidents are linked. The earlier attack occurred in similar circumstances, with a device thrown at the property during the night-time hours.

Gardaí at Gurranabraher are investigating both incidents and are appealing for witnesses. Detectives are following a definite line of enquiry and are examining whether the attacks are connected to an ongoing feud in the area.

The scene was preserved overnight for a technical examination by members of the Garda Technical Bureau, which was carried out earlier today.

Local representatives have expressed shock at the attacks, with particular concern raised about the danger posed to a young baby.

"This is an absolutely appalling attack on a home where a small baby was present," one local councillor said. "It is only by the grace of God that nobody was seriously hurt or killed. The people responsible for this need to be brought to justice."

Gardaí are urging anyone who was in the Knocknaheeny area in the early hours of this morning, or who may have dashcam or CCTV footage, to contact Gurranabraher Garda Station on 021-4946200, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.
headline: Baby taken to hospital following second petrol bomb attack in Cork

Traders and city councillors are renewing calls for stricter enforcement of the pedestrianisation of Patrick Street in Cork, amid complaints that vehicles continue to flout the ban on a daily basis.

Cork's main thoroughfare has been subject to restricted vehicle access for several years, but business owners and pedestrians say the rules are being routinely ignored, with cars, vans, and even heavy goods vehicles regularly spotted driving along the street during hours when only buses, taxis, and emergency vehicles are permitted.
