Fine Gael councillor Shane O'Callaghan said the lack of enforcement was undermining the entire purpose of the pedestrianisation scheme. "People are genuinely frustrated. You have families with young children, elderly people, and tourists trying to enjoy the street, and they're having to dodge vehicles that simply shouldn't be there," he said.

"We need to see proper bollard infrastructure and camera enforcement put in place. Other European cities have managed this successfully, and there's no reason Cork can't do the same."

The issue was raised at a recent meeting of Cork City Council, where members heard that while the Gardaí have the power to enforce traffic restrictions, resources are often stretched. A spokesperson for the Gardaí confirmed that enforcement operations are carried out "on a regular basis" but acknowledged that competing demands across the city can affect the frequency of dedicated patrols on Patrick Street.

Local traders, many of whom were initially cautious about pedestrianisation, say they have come to support the concept but feel its benefits are being diluted by the failure to keep unauthorised traffic off the street. Kevin McCarthy, who runs a retail business on Patrick Street, said the situation had become "a bit of a free-for-all" at certain times of the day.

"Early morning and late afternoon are the worst. You'll see delivery vans parked up on the street well outside the permitted delivery hours, and private cars just driving straight through as if the restrictions don't exist," he said. "It sends out the message that the rules don't really apply."

Cork City Council said it is examining a number of options to improve compliance, including the installation of automatic number plate recognition cameras and retractable bollards at entry points to the street. A council spokesperson said a review of the current traffic management arrangements on Patrick Street is under way and that any proposed changes would be subject to public consultation.

Sinn Féin TD Thomas Gould, who represents Cork North-Central, said the issue spoke to a broader need for investment in Cork's urban infrastructure. "Pedestrianisation only works if it's done properly. Half measures just create confusion and leave everyone unhappy — drivers, pedestrians, and businesses alike," he said.

The issue comes as Cork City Council continues to progress plans for wider improvements to the city centre, including enhanced public realm works and the expansion of pedestrian-friendly zones. Supporters of the Patrick Street scheme say its full potential will only be realised when enforcement catches up with ambition.
headline: Calls for more enforcement of Cork's Patrick St car ban

text:
There are operas that audiences leave humming, and then there are operas that audiences leave in a state of stunned, electrified silence. Richard Strauss's *Elektra* belongs firmly in the latter category, and Irish soprano Máire Flavin knows it.

"It's not a work you can take lightly," Flavin says, speaking ahead of her upcoming performance in the role of Chrysothemis, Elektra's sister, in a new production that promises to bring the full visceral force of Strauss's score to Irish audiences. "The emotional intensity is relentless. You can't coast through it. The music demands everything from you — physically, vocally, psychologically."

First staged in 1909, *Elektra* remains one of the most challenging works in the operatic repertoire. Based on Hugo von Hofmannsthal's adaptation of Sophocles' tragedy, it tells the story of Elektra's obsessive desire to avenge the murder of her father, Agamemnon, at the hands of her mother Clytemnestra and her mother's lover. It is an opera drenched in blood, madness and grief, scored with an orchestral ferocity that can feel almost overwhelming in the theatre.

Flavin, who has built a formidable reputation on international stages, is no stranger to demanding roles. The Limerick-born soprano has performed with companies across Europe and has long been recognised as one of Ireland's finest vocal talents. But she acknowledges that the Strauss repertoire occupies a particular place in her artistic life.

"Strauss writes for the voice in a way that is simultaneously glorious and punishing," she says. "The vocal lines soar above this enormous orchestra, and you have to find a way to ride that wave without being swallowed by it. Chrysothemis is often described as the 'lighter' sister, the one who wants a normal life — marriage, children, escape from this cursed house. But vocally, there is nothing light about it. The writing is huge."

The role of Chrysothemis serves as a dramatic counterweight to the title character. Where Elektra is consumed by vengeance, Chrysothemis yearns for domesticity and freedom. It is a contrast that Flavin finds endlessly compelling.

"There's something deeply human about Chrysothemis. She's living in this nightmarish household, surrounded by violence and paranoia, and all she wants is to get out, to live. Some people see that as weakness, but I think it takes extraordinary courage to insist on hope in those circumstances. She refuses to be defined by the trauma around her."

Flavin is thoughtful about the opera's darker themes, which include matricide, psychological torment and what modern audiences might recognise as post-traumatic stress. She believes that *Elektra* speaks to contemporary concerns in ways that Strauss and von Hofmannsthal could scarcely have anticipated.

"When this opera was written, Freud was publishing his theories about the unconscious, about repression and hysteria. You can feel that in the libretto and in the music.
headline: Máire Flavin: Irish soprano on her role in Elektra, Strauss's famously dark opera

text:
Nurses and midwives are paying up to €110 per day for childcare following the scrapping of a pandemic-era scheme that had provided them with subsidised care, the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation has said.

The INMO has called on the Government to introduce a dedicated childcare support scheme for healthcare workers, warning that the prohibitive cost of childcare is driving nurses and midwives out of the profession or forcing them to reduce their hours at a time when the health service can ill afford to lose staff.

The union said the withdrawal of the Government's Covid-19 childcare scheme, which had been introduced to support frontline healthcare workers during the pandemic, has left many of its members struggling to cover costs that in some cases exceed their daily take-home pay.

INMO general secretary Phil Ní Sheaghdha said the situation was "completely unsustainable" and was compounding the recruitment and retention crisis in nursing and midwifery.

"We have members who are effectively paying to go to work once childcare costs are factored in. When a nurse or midwife is paying €110 a day for childcare, and they look at what they are bringing home after tax, it simply does not add up," Ms Ní Sheaghdha said.

"This is not just a personal financial issue for our members — it is a workforce planning crisis. We are losing experienced nurses and midwives because the State has failed to recognise that affordable childcare is essential infrastructure for a functioning health service."

The INMO said the problem was particularly acute for those working shift patterns, including nights, weekends and bank holidays, as standard childcare services do not cater for non-traditional working hours. Members in Dublin and other urban centres reported the highest costs, though the issue was described as nationwide.

The union pointed out that many other countries with comparable health systems provide dedicated childcare supports for healthcare workers, recognising the atypical hours they are required to work.

The Government's National Childcare Scheme, which provides subsidies based on household income, was described by the INMO as inadequate for meeting the specific needs of nurses and midwives, particularly those on rotating shift patterns who require flexible or extended-hours care.

The HSE currently employs more than 40,000 nurses and midwives, though staffing shortages remain a persistent challenge across the acute hospital system, community care and disability services.

The Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth said the National Childcare Scheme was designed to be a universal and progressive system of financial support and that it was open to all eligible families. A spokesperson said the scheme had seen significant investment in recent budgets.

The INMO said it intended to raise the matter directly with the Minister for Health and would seek engagement with the Department of Children on the development of a tailored childcare solution for healthcare workers.
headline: INMO: Some nurses paying €110 per day for childcare as govt scheme scrapped

text:
A North Yorkshire-based fertiliser company is eyeing significant international expansion after securing a series of deals that could see its products distributed across Europe, the Americas and beyond.

Harrogate-based YaraTera, which specialises in water-soluble crop nutrition products, has reported a sharp uptick in demand from growers seeking more efficient and environmentally sustainable alternatives to traditional fertiliser applications. The company says its range of fully soluble fertilisers, designed for use in fertigation and foliar feeding systems, has attracted interest from large-scale agricultural operations in markets as diverse as Brazil, Mexico and southern Europe.

The firm's managing director, speaking at a recent industry event, said the growing global focus on precision agriculture and water conservation had created a favourable climate for products that allow farmers to deliver nutrients directly to the root zone with minimal waste.

"There is a clear shift happening in how growers think about crop nutrition," he said. "The old model of broadcasting granular fertiliser and hoping for the best is giving way to much more targeted approaches, and that plays to our strengths."

The development will be of particular interest to Irish tillage and horticulture farmers, many of whom have increasingly adopted fertigation techniques in recent years, particularly in the protected crops sector. Teagasc has previously highlighted the potential for such systems to reduce nutrient run-off, a matter of growing regulatory concern here as the State seeks to meet its obligations under the EU Nitrates Directive.

Irish growers operating in the mushroom, soft fruit and vegetable sectors have been among the earliest adopters of water-soluble fertiliser technology on these shores, though uptake in mainstream arable farming remains comparatively limited.

Industry figures suggest that the global water-soluble fertiliser market is projected to be worth in excess of €18 billion by the end of the decade, driven in large part by expansion of irrigated agriculture in water-stressed regions and the intensification of greenhouse production worldwide.

For Irish farmers watching input costs with an increasingly anxious eye, the promise of products that deliver more precise nutrition with less waste will hold obvious appeal, though the higher unit cost of soluble fertilisers compared with conventional granular products remains a barrier for many.

The company said it planned to increase its production capacity at its Yorkshire facility over the coming 18 months and was in advanced discussions with distributors in several new markets. It declined to comment on the specific financial value of the contracts under negotiation.
headline: Global success beckons for North Yorkshire fertiliser

text:
The board of the National Paediatric Hospital Development Board was informed of significant cost overruns on the new children's hospital project as far back as last June, it has emerged, raising fresh questions about when senior government figures became aware of the escalating budget.

The revelation comes as the controversy surrounding the spiralling costs of the flagship project at St James's Hospital campus in Dublin continues to dominate political debate. The hospital, originally estimated to cost approximately €800 million, has seen its projected final bill rise to €1.73 billion, with some estimates suggesting it could climb even higher.

It is understood that board members were briefed on rising costs at a meeting last June, months before the issue entered the public domain and became the subject of intense Oireachtas scrutiny. The timeline has prompted opposition TDs to demand answers about what information was passed to the Department of Health and to the then minister for health, Simon Harris, and when.

Sinn Féin's health spokesperson has called for full transparency on the matter, insisting that the Dáil deserves a complete account of who knew what and when. Labour and the Social Democrats have echoed those calls, with both parties pressing for a full independent review of the governance failures that allowed costs to escalate so dramatically before the public was informed.

The Taoiseach, Leo Varadkar, has previously stated that he only became aware of the full extent of the overruns in November.

Meanwhile, more than 37,000 nurses and midwives represented by the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation are engaged in their third day of strike action in an ongoing dispute over pay and staffing levels. The industrial action has caused widespread disruption across the health service, with the HSE confirming that thousands of outpatient appointments and elective procedures have been cancelled.

Picket lines were mounted at hospitals and healthcare facilities across the State, with nurses reporting strong public support for their campaign. The INMO has said its members are seeking pay parity with other allied health professionals and has warned that the recruitment and retention crisis in nursing is placing patient safety at risk.

The HSE's emergency management structures remain in place, with contingency plans activated to ensure that emergency departments, critical care units and other essential services continue to operate. However, health officials have acknowledged that the cumulative impact of repeated strike days is placing considerable strain on an already stretched system.

Efforts to resolve the dispute through the Workplace Relations Commission and the Labour Court have so far failed to produce a breakthrough, though both sides have indicated a willingness to engage in further negotiations. The Government has maintained that any resolution must fall within the terms of the Public Service Stability Agreement, a position the INMO has rejected as inadequate to address what it describes as a deepening crisis in the nursing profession.
headline: Bulletin: Children's hospital board told of rising costs last June; Over 37,000 nurses in third day of strike action

text:
Leo Varadkar has said he does not want to live in a country where politicians are forced to retreat behind layers of security, even as concerns mount over the safety of public representatives in the wake of a series of intimidation incidents.

The Taoiseach was speaking after it emerged that a number of TDs and senators have been subjected to threats, harassment and aggressive confrontations in recent months, with some elected representatives reporting that abuse has escalated sharply since the Dublin riots last November.

Mr Varadkar acknowledged that the current climate posed challenges but insisted that accessibility to politicians remained a cornerstone of Irish democracy.

"I don't want a country where politicians live in a security bubble, where we can't go to the local shop, where we can't walk down the street, where we can't meet constituents," Mr Varadkar said.

"That's not the kind of country I want to live in, and I don't think it's the kind of country most people want to live in either."

The Taoiseach said he believed the vast majority of people engaged with their public representatives in a respectful manner, but he accepted that a small minority had sought to exploit tensions around issues such as immigration and the housing crisis to target politicians.

He confirmed that the Gardaí continued to monitor threats against elected representatives and that additional security measures had been put in place for some officeholders where necessary. However, he stressed that he was reluctant to see a situation develop where politicians became remote from the communities they serve.

The issue has been raised repeatedly in the Oireachtas in recent weeks, with TDs from across the political spectrum describing incidents of intimidation at their constituency offices and at public events. Several have reported criminal damage to their property, while others said their family members had also been targeted.

Minister for Justice Helen McEntee said the Government took the safety of all public representatives extremely seriously and that any threats or acts of intimidation would be fully investigated by An Garda Síochána.

"People have every right to protest and to disagree with their politicians — that is democracy," Ms McEntee said. "But there is a line, and when that line is crossed into threats, harassment or criminal behaviour, it will not be tolerated."

Garda Commissioner Drew Harris has previously indicated that the force keeps the security of public representatives under ongoing review and works closely with those who report threats.

Opposition parties have called for a more structured approach to the issue, with some suggesting that a formal risk assessment process should be introduced for all members of the Oireachtas. Sinn Féin's justice spokesperson Pa Daly said there needed to be a broader conversation about the coarsening of public discourse and its real-world consequences for those in public life.

The Labour Party leader Ivana Bacik said that while robust political debate was healthy, the normalisation of abuse and intimidation risked deterring people — particularly women — from entering politics.

"We need to be very clear that this kind of behaviour is not acceptable in a democratic society," Ms Bacik said. "If we allow it to continue unchecked, we will end up with a poorer democracy."
headline: Varadkar: 'I don't want a country where politicians live in a security bubble'

text:
RTÉ has withdrawn its appeal against a Workplace Relations Commission ruling that found the national broadcaster liable for ageist and sexist remarks made to a former employee, with the challenge collapsing at the Labour Court this week.

The case centred on a woman in her fifties who had alleged she was subjected to discriminatory comments by a senior colleague, including remarks about her age and gender, during her time working at the Donnybrook-based organisation. The WRC had found in her favour and ordered RTÉ to pay compensation, a decision the broadcaster initially moved to challenge.

However, the appeal was withdrawn before a full hearing could take place at the Labour Court, effectively leaving the original ruling and compensation award intact.

The complainant, who cannot be named for legal reasons, had told the WRC that she was made to feel unwelcome and marginalised in her role after a colleague made repeated references to her age and made remarks she described as sexist. She said the comments left her feeling humiliated and had a significant impact on her wellbeing and her ability to carry out her work.

In its original determination, the WRC adjudicator found that the remarks amounted to discrimination on the grounds of both age and gender under the Employment Equality Acts, and that RTÉ had failed to take adequate steps to prevent the behaviour or to address it when it was brought to the attention of management.

The adjudicator noted that employers have a duty of care to ensure workplaces are free from discriminatory conduct and that the broadcaster had not demonstrated it had discharged that duty in this instance.

RTÉ had lodged the appeal arguing that the WRC's findings did not reflect the full circumstances of the case. The broadcaster did not comment publicly on the reasons for the withdrawal of the appeal.

A spokesperson for RTÉ said the organisation does not comment on individual employment matters but added that it is committed to maintaining a workplace culture that is respectful and inclusive for all staff.

The collapse of the appeal is likely to attract further scrutiny of workplace culture at RTÉ, which has faced sustained public and political pressure in recent years over a range of governance and internal conduct issues. The broadcaster has been the subject of intense Oireachtas committee hearings and public debate since controversies over undisclosed payments emerged in 2023, prompting broader questions about management practices and accountability within the organisation.

Employment law solicitors have noted that the case underscores the obligations on all employers, including State and semi-State bodies, to have robust policies in place to deal with workplace discrimination and to act swiftly when complaints are raised.

Under the Employment Equality Acts, the WRC and Labour Court can award compensation of up to two years' remuneration or, in cases where the complainant is not an employee, up to the maximum of €40,000 for the effects of discrimination.

The exact amount of compensation awarded in this case has not been publicly disclosed.
headline: RTE challenge against compensation ruling collapses over 'ageist and sexist' remarks

text:
Traffic-calming measures and improved footpath connectivity must be central to the planning of future housing developments in Cork, local representatives have insisted, as concerns mount over pedestrian safety in rapidly expanding suburban and rural communities.

The call came at a recent meeting of Cork County Council, where councillors raised persistent complaints from residents living in estates where basic infrastructure has failed to keep pace with the volume of new homes being built.

Councillors from across the political spectrum voiced frustration that developers are being granted planning permission for sizeable residential schemes without adequate provision for safe pedestrian routes, cycle lanes, or measures to slow traffic through built-up areas.

Cllr Deirdre O'Brien said residents in several estates in her area have been left with no safe way to walk to local schools, shops, or bus stops, describing the situation as "an accident waiting to happen".

"We are building houses at pace, which is welcome, but we cannot keep bolting on developments without thinking about how people are going to move around safely on foot," she said. "Footpath connectivity isn't a luxury — it's a must."

She pointed to several developments where footpaths simply end abruptly, forcing pedestrians, including parents with buggies and children walking to school, onto busy roads with no hard shoulder.

Council officials acknowledged the concerns and said the local authority is working to strengthen requirements around pedestrian infrastructure and traffic calming as part of the development management process. They noted that conditions attached to planning permissions increasingly stipulate the provision of footpaths, pedestrian crossings, and traffic-calming features such as ramps, chicanes, and raised tables.

However, councillors argued that enforcement remains a significant issue, with some developers failing to complete promised infrastructure or delivering it to a substandard quality before estates are taken in charge by the council.

Cllr Alan Coleman said the council needs to take a firmer line with developers who do not deliver on their commitments. "There is no point having conditions on paper if they are not being followed through on the ground," he said. "Residents are the ones who suffer, and it's the council that ultimately picks up the tab when remedial work is needed."

The issue of taking estates in charge has long been a source of contention in Cork, with dozens of developments across the county still awaiting completion to a standard that would allow the council to assume responsibility for roads, footpaths, lighting, and open spaces.

Councillors also highlighted the particular challenges facing rural villages and smaller towns where new housing has been developed along regional and local roads that were never designed to accommodate significant pedestrian traffic. In these areas, the absence of footpaths and public lighting creates serious safety risks, particularly during the darker winter months.

There were also calls for greater investment in retrofitting traffic-calming measures in older estates where the original design did not anticipate current traffic volumes. Several councillors said they are inundated with requests from residents for speed ramps and other interventions, but that funding for such works remains limited.

Council management said a programme of traffic-calming works is under way across the county, prioritised on the basis of traffic surveys and accident data, but acknowledged that demand far outstrips available resources.
headline: Traffic-calming measures and footpath connectivity 'a must' for future Cork housing developments

text:
The Russian military intelligence unit blamed for hacking the Democratic National Committee ahead of the 2016 US presidential election is attempting new cyber intrusions against targets in the United States and Europe, according to security researchers and Western intelligence officials.

The group, widely known as Fancy Bear or APT28 and linked to Russia's GRU military intelligence agency, has been detected launching fresh phishing campaigns and exploiting vulnerabilities in email systems and virtual private networks, cybersecurity firms have warned.

Microsoft and other major technology companies have been tracking the renewed activity, which appears to target political organisations, government agencies, think tanks and defence contractors across several Western nations.

The revelation comes amid heightened tensions between Moscow and Western capitals over Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine, and will raise fresh concerns about the security of democratic processes ahead of upcoming elections in the US and across Europe.

In 2016, Russian operatives successfully breached the servers of the Democratic National Committee and the email account of Hillary Clinton's campaign chairman John Podesta. The stolen material was subsequently published by WikiLeaks in a drip-feed that caused significant political damage during the presidential race ultimately won by Donald Trump.

US intelligence agencies later concluded with high confidence that the Kremlin had orchestrated the operation to interfere in the election, an assessment that led to sanctions against Russian entities and the indictment of several GRU officers by special counsel Robert Mueller's investigation.

Western security officials have cautioned that the latest intrusion attempts demonstrate that Russian cyber capabilities remain a persistent and evolving threat, despite years of public exposure and diplomatic consequences.

The Kremlin has consistently denied any involvement in state-sponsored hacking, dismissing the allegations as politically motivated and anti-Russian.

Cybersecurity analysts have noted that the group's tactics have grown more sophisticated since 2016, with operatives now employing more advanced methods to disguise their activities and avoid detection by security systems.

The warnings are likely to intensify calls from security experts for governments and political organisations to bolster their cyber defences ahead of what is expected to be a particularly sensitive period for democratic institutions worldwide.
headline: Russian group blamed for hacking Democrats in 2016 ‘attempting new intrusions’

text:
The former president of Waterford Institute of Technology has lost his High Court action against the college's governing body over its decision not to reappoint him to the role for a second term.

Professor Willie Donnelly had taken the legal challenge against the governing body of WIT, claiming the decision not to offer him a second term as president was unlawful and in breach of fair procedures.

Prof Donnelly, who served as president of WIT from 2014, had argued that he had a legitimate expectation of being reappointed and that the governing body had failed to follow proper procedures when it decided not to extend his tenure.

However, Mr Justice David Barniville dismissed the proceedings, finding that the governing body had acted within its powers and had followed the appropriate procedures in reaching its decision.

The judge said the governing body was entitled to decide whether or not to reappoint the president and was not obliged to offer a second term. He found that there was no basis for the claim that Prof Donnelly had a legitimate expectation of reappointment.

The court heard that under the relevant legislation, the governing body had the authority to appoint the president for a specified term and that any reappointment was a matter for the governing body to determine.

WIT subsequently merged with IT Carlow in 2022 to form the South East Technological University, one of several new technological universities established across the State in recent years.

The case had been closely watched in the higher education sector, where questions around the governance of technological universities and the tenure of senior academic leaders have become increasingly relevant as the sector undergoes significant restructuring.

Legal costs in the case are expected to be addressed at a later hearing, with the respondents likely to seek their costs against Prof Donnelly, in line with the usual practice following an unsuccessful action.
headline: Former WIT president loses High Court action over college's decision not to reappoint him

text:
It was a long day of counting in the RDS, but as the first count concluded in the Dublin constituency, one thing was clear: Ciaran Cuffe of the Green Party had topped the poll, yet no candidate managed to reach the quota in a hotly contested race for the capital's four European Parliament seats.

Mr Cuffe, a former TD and sitting Dublin city councillor, secured 95,958 first-preference votes, placing him well ahead of the field but still short of the quota of 125,876. The result underscored the remarkable surge in support for the Green Party, which has been a defining feature of both the local and European elections this weekend.

Fine Gael's Frances Fitzgerald, the former Tánaiste, came in second with 82,935 first preferences, while Fianna Fáil's Barry Andrews secured 55,036 votes to place third. Independent candidate Clare Daly, running on a strong left-wing platform, took fourth position with 50,731 votes.

The high quota, a consequence of a large turnout and a crowded field of candidates, meant that even Mr Cuffe's impressive haul was not sufficient to see him elected on the first count. With 19 candidates in the race for four seats, votes were widely dispersed across the field, making it virtually impossible for any single candidate to clear the threshold without the benefit of transfers.

Speaking at the count centre, Mr Cuffe said he was "humbled and delighted" by the level of support shown to him and to the Green Party. He acknowledged that the party's message on climate action had resonated strongly with Dublin voters, many of whom he said had expressed frustration at the lack of urgency from government on environmental issues.

The result represents a significant personal achievement for Mr Cuffe, who lost his Dáil seat in the 2011 general election when the Green Party was decimated at the polls following its time in coalition government with Fianna Fáil. His topping of the poll in Dublin is perhaps the clearest signal yet of the party's rehabilitation in the eyes of the electorate.

For Ms Fitzgerald, the second-place finish will be seen as a solid if unspectacular performance. The former Minister for Justice had been considered a strong contender following her nomination by Fine Gael, though her candidacy was not without controversy given the circumstances surrounding her departure from cabinet during the Sergeant Maurice McCabe controversy.

Mr Andrews, son of former Fianna Fáil minister David Andrews, will be hoping that transfers from eliminated candidates can propel him towards one of the four seats, though he faces stiff competition from a number of candidates positioned behind him.

The battle for the remaining seats is expected to be a protracted affair, with Ms Daly, sitting MEP Lynn Boylan of Sinn Féin, and Labour's Alex White all in contention. Ms Boylan received 30,832 first-preference votes, a significant drop from the party's performance in the 2014 European elections, reflecting the broader difficulties Sinn Féin has encountered in these elections.
headline: #Elections2019: Ciaran Cuffe tops the poll but nobody reaches quota in Dublin

text:
A pensioner who was left shaken after being knocked to the ground and robbed of her handbag in broad daylight has spoken of her disbelief at the brazenness of the attack, asking: "What is the world coming to?"

Margaret Hennessy, 74, was walking home from her local shop in Ballincollig, Co Cork, shortly after 2pm on Tuesday when a young man approached her from behind, shoved her to the pavement and grabbed her bag before fleeing on foot.

Ms Hennessy, who suffered bruising to her hip and grazed hands in the fall, told the Irish Examiner she was "in total shock" and could not understand how someone could target a woman of her age.

"I was just walking along minding my own business, carrying a few bits from the shop. The next thing I knew I was on the ground. I didn't even see him coming," she said. "There was nothing of any great value in the bag — a few euro, my bus pass, my reading glasses. But it's not about what was in it. It's the fright of it. What is the world coming to when you can't walk down the road in the middle of the afternoon?"

A passing motorist stopped to help Ms Hennessy and called an ambulance. She was treated at Cork University Hospital and later discharged.

Gardaí in Ballincollig have confirmed they are investigating the incident and are appealing for witnesses. CCTV footage from the area is being examined, and investigators believe they may be able to identify the suspect from the recordings.

A Garda spokesperson said: "We are investigating an incident of robbery from a person that occurred on Tuesday afternoon in the Ballincollig area. No arrests have been made at this time. We would appeal to anyone who may have witnessed the incident or who may have dashcam footage from the area between 2pm and 2.30pm to contact Ballincollig Garda Station."

Ms Hennessy's daughter, Karen, said the family were "disgusted" by the attack and that her mother had been left afraid to leave the house on her own.

"She's a strong woman, she's independent, she walks everywhere. Now she's afraid to go out the front door. That's what this person has taken from her — her confidence, her sense of safety. That's worth more than anything that was in that bag," Ms Karen Hennessy said.

Local Fine Gael councillor Derry Canty described the incident as "absolutely appalling" and said it had caused widespread anger in the community.

"Ballincollig is a safe, close-knit community and people here are shocked and angry that something like this could happen. An attack on a vulnerable, elderly woman in broad daylight is about as low as it gets," Cllr Canty said. He called for increased Garda visibility in the area and said he would be raising the matter at the next meeting of the Cork City joint policing committee.
headline: 'What is the world coming to?'

text:
With the back-to-school season upon us, the humble cheese sandwich remains the undisputed champion of the lunchbox. But not all cheddars are created equal, and with the cost of living still squeezing household budgets, parents want to know which block delivers the best combination of flavour, texture and value. We put eight widely available supermarket cheddars through a blind taste test to find out which ones deserve a place in your trolley – and which ones might be better left on the shelf.

The rules were simple. We selected own-brand and branded cheddars available in the major Irish supermarkets – Tesco, Dunnes Stores, SuperValu, Aldi and Lidl – all in the mild to medium range, since that's what most children will actually eat. Each cheese was tasted at room temperature, both on its own and in a plain white bread sandwich with butter, to replicate lunchbox conditions. Our panel included two adults and, crucially, three children aged between five and eleven, because there is no more honest food critic than a seven-year-old with a firm opinion.

Starting from the bottom, in eighth place was a mild cheddar that our testers found bland and rubbery, with a texture one panellist compared to "chewing an eraser." It melted oddly in the mouth and left behind very little flavour. At around €3.50 for 200g, it represented poor value as well.

Seventh place went to a block that was perfectly inoffensive but entirely forgettable. It did the job in a sandwich but inspired no enthusiasm whatsoever. The children ate it without complaint but also without any indication they were enjoying it, which tells its own story.

In sixth place, we had a cheese that started promisingly – a decent golden colour and a pleasant, slightly tangy aroma – but fell down on an oddly crumbly texture that made it difficult to slice neatly, a genuine consideration when you're assembling four lunchboxes at half seven in the morning.

Fifth place was claimed by Aldi's Emporium Irish Cheddar, which offered a surprisingly full flavour for a mild cheese and sliced cleanly. It lost marks only because the children found it "a bit strong," which is the sort of feedback that divides households. For adults, this would rank considerably higher.

The fourth spot went to Lidl's Coolmore Irish Cheddar, a reliable all-rounder that ticks every box without excelling in any particular area. It's creamy, mild, slices well, and at its price point represents solid value. A dependable workhorse of a cheese.

In third place, Dunnes Stores Simply Better Mature Irish Cheddar punched above its weight. Yes, it's labelled as mature rather than mild, but it was smooth enough that even the younger testers approved. It has a depth of flavour that elevates a simple sandwich into something genuinely enjoyable, and the quality of the cheese is evident from the first bite. It's pricier than some options here, but you get what you pay for.
headline: Top 8: Supermarket cheddars put to the taste test for school lunches

text:
Victims of domestic abuse are being effectively trapped in dangerous living situations because of the financial ties binding them to shared mortgages, a leading advocacy group has warned.

Safe Ireland, the national organisation supporting domestic violence services, said it is hearing from growing numbers of women who feel unable to leave abusive partners because they cannot afford to walk away from jointly held mortgages or fear losing their homes entirely.

The organisation said the housing crisis has compounded what was already a deeply difficult situation for victims, with the shortage of available rental properties and the cost of alternative accommodation making it all but impossible for many to contemplate starting over.

"We are seeing women who are quite literally trapped," said a spokesperson for Safe Ireland. "They have a mortgage with the person who is abusing them, and they face an impossible choice — stay and endure the abuse, or leave and face homelessness."

The issue was raised in the Dáil this week, with several TDs calling on the Government to introduce specific financial protections for domestic abuse victims who are tied into mortgage agreements. There were calls for a dedicated scheme that would allow victims to buy out their abuser's share of a property or to be facilitated in accessing alternative housing without financial penalty.

Under current legislation, the Domestic Violence Act 2018 provides for safety and barring orders that can remove a perpetrator from the family home. However, advocates say that in practice, the financial entanglement of a shared mortgage creates a web of complications that the legal system is not adequately equipped to address.

In many cases, even where a barring order is granted, the abusive partner retains a financial interest in the property, meaning victims must continue to engage with their abuser over mortgage repayments or risk falling into arrears.

"The legal protections are there on paper, but the financial reality is very different," the spokesperson added. "A barring order does not resolve who pays the mortgage. It does not resolve the question of ownership. And it certainly does not resolve the fear and anxiety that comes with being financially bound to someone who has caused you harm."

The issue is particularly acute for women with children, who may be reluctant to uproot their families from schools and communities but who face ongoing danger by remaining in the family home.

Sinn Féin's spokesperson on housing called on the Minister for Housing to engage directly with mortgage lenders and the Central Bank to develop a protocol for cases involving domestic abuse. "The banks need to be part of the solution here," the TD said. "We cannot have a situation where financial institutions are inadvertently facilitating the entrapment of abuse victims."

The Banking and Payments Federation Ireland said its members treat cases involving domestic abuse with sensitivity and that customers in such circumstances are encouraged to contact their lender directly to discuss their options. However, it acknowledged that there is no industry-wide protocol specifically tailored to domestic abuse situations.

Threshold, the national housing charity, said it has also seen cases where victims of abuse in the private rental sector face similar difficulties, particularly where both partners are named on a lease.

Women's Aid, which operates the national freephone helpline for victims of domestic abuse, said the housing and mortgage issue is among the most frequently cited barriers to leaving an abusive relationship.
headline: Domestic abuse victims 'trapped' in dangerous homes by mortgages

text:
The stabbing of author Salman Rushdie at a literary event in New York state has drawn a mixture of celebration and unease in Iran, where hardline newspapers praised the attack while moderates expressed concern about the diplomatic fallout for the Islamic Republic.

Rushdie, who has lived under the shadow of a death sentence for more than three decades, was stabbed multiple times on Friday as he prepared to deliver a lecture at the Chautauqua Institution in western New York. The 75-year-old novelist was placed on a ventilator and is likely to lose an eye, his agent confirmed.

The attack has revived memories of the fatwa issued against Rushdie in 1989 by Iran's then-supreme leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, who called for the author's death over his novel *The Satanic Verses*, which many Muslims consider blasphemous. The current supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, has never rescinded the edict, and a semi-official Iranian religious foundation has offered a bounty of more than $3 million for Rushdie's killing.

Hardline Iranian newspapers made little effort to conceal their approval. The Kayhan daily, whose editor-in-chief is appointed directly by Khamenei, praised the attacker and declared that "a thousand bravos" were owed to the man who assaulted Rushdie. "Let us kiss the hand of the one who tore the neck of the enemy of God with a knife," the newspaper wrote in an editorial.

Other ultra-conservative outlets carried similar sentiments, with some describing the attack as divine retribution long overdue.

However, the reaction was far from uniform. Iranian reformist and moderate commentators warned that the incident could further isolate Tehran on the world stage at a particularly delicate moment, with negotiations over the revival of the 2015 nuclear accord at a critical juncture. Several moderate Iranian journalists and analysts took to social media to express concern that the attack would be used to undermine the already fragile diplomatic efforts.

Iran's foreign ministry struck a careful tone, stating that Tehran should not be blamed for the attack. A spokesman said Iran had no connection to the assailant, identified as Hadi Matar, a 24-year-old New Jersey man of Lebanese descent. The ministry added, however, that Rushdie had "exposed himself to popular anger" by insulting Islam and its sacred figures.

The carefully worded response reflected a familiar balancing act for Iran's government, which must navigate between the hardline clerical establishment and the pragmatic demands of international diplomacy. Analysts noted that while the fatwa remains technically in force, successive Iranian governments have sought to distance themselves from it without explicitly revoking it — a step that would be politically impossible given the supreme leader's authority.

Western leaders roundly condemned the attack. US President Joe Biden praised Rushdie's "refusal to be intimidated or silenced" and described the assault as a reminder of the ongoing threats faced by writers and journalists around the world.
headline: Salman Rushdie attack provokes both praise and anxiety in Iran

text:
She is barely a teenager, but Cork native Aoife Brennan has already caught the attention of some of the most discerning eyes in Irish fashion, earning praise for her remarkably assured sense of design and a maturity of vision that belies her 13 years.

The Midleton secondary school student first came to wider notice after winning a national young designers competition run by the Design & Crafts Council Ireland earlier this year, impressing judges with a collection of upcycled garments that married sustainability with genuine flair. Since then, she has been invited to showcase her work at a number of events, including a pop-up exhibition at Cork's Crawford Art Gallery and a youth design showcase during this year's Cork Fashion Week.

"I've always loved making things — even when I was really small I'd be cutting up old clothes and trying to put them back together in different ways," Aoife told the Irish Examiner. "My mam would come home and find the kitchen table covered in fabric and thread. She was very patient about it."

That patience appears to have paid off handsomely. Aoife's mother, Sinéad, said the family has been taken aback by the level of interest in her daughter's work. "We always knew she had a creative streak, but to see other people recognise it too has been wonderful. We're just trying to keep her feet on the ground and make sure school comes first."

Industry figures have been quick to note the young designer's potential. Celia Holman Lee, one of Ireland's most respected names in fashion, said she was struck by the sophistication of Aoife's work when she encountered it at an event in Limerick.

"You see a lot of young people with enthusiasm, and that's great, but what sets Aoife apart is that she already has an eye — a real understanding of shape and colour and how fabric moves," Holman Lee said. "At 13, that's extraordinary. She is absolutely a name to watch."

Aoife draws inspiration from a wide range of sources, citing the Japanese-influenced minimalism of Issey Miyake alongside the bold textures of Irish knitwear traditions. She is particularly passionate about sustainable fashion, a concern she says was sparked by learning about the environmental impact of fast fashion in school.

"It made me really angry, actually," she said. "There's so much waste. I wanted to show that you can make beautiful things from what people throw away."

Her competition-winning collection featured jackets constructed from discarded curtain fabric, a dress fashioned from vintage linen tablecloths, and accessories made using offcuts donated by a Cork-based upholstery business. The judges described the work as "inventive, polished, and remarkably well-executed for a designer of any age."

Despite the attention, Aoife remains refreshingly grounded. She is a keen camogie player with her local club and says she has no intention of abandoning her studies, though she hopes eventually to pursue a degree in fashion design, with the National College of Art and Design in Dublin and the Crawford College of Art and Design among her preferred options.
headline: A name to watch in fashion at just 13 years old

text:
The Minister for Education has announced a new €1m fund to provide free schoolbooks to primary school pupils, in a move that has been broadly welcomed by parents' groups and teaching unions alike.

The initiative, which will be rolled out on a phased basis from the next academic year, is aimed at easing the financial burden on families at a time when the cost of living continues to place significant pressure on household budgets.

Under the scheme, funding will be allocated directly to primary schools to purchase textbooks and workbooks for pupils, removing the need for parents to cover the often substantial cost of book lists at the start of each school year.

Speaking at Leinster House, the Minister said the fund represented a "significant step" towards ensuring that no child is disadvantaged in their education because of their family's financial circumstances.

"We know that the cost of sending children back to school each September can be a real source of stress for families right across the country," the Minister said. "This fund is about making sure that every child has the books they need to learn and to thrive, regardless of their background."

The Irish National Teachers' Organisation welcomed the announcement, describing it as a positive development that would make a tangible difference in classrooms. An INTO spokesperson said the union had long campaigned for such a measure and urged the Department of Education to ensure the funding is sufficient to meet demand across all schools.

The National Parents Council Primary also expressed its support, though it cautioned that €1m may not stretch far enough given the number of primary schools and pupils in the State. There are approximately 3,200 primary schools and more than 560,000 primary school pupils nationally.

"While we absolutely welcome this announcement, we would urge the Minister to view this as a starting point rather than the finished article," a spokesperson for the council said. "The reality is that book costs represent only one part of the back-to-school expense that families face each year."

Sinn Féin's education spokesperson said the fund was "long overdue" but questioned whether the allocation was adequate, calling on the Government to commit to a fully funded free schoolbooks scheme for all primary and secondary school pupils.

The Department of Education confirmed that details of how schools can apply for funding under the scheme will be issued in the coming weeks. Priority will be given to schools in areas of socioeconomic disadvantage under the DEIS programme, though all primary schools will be eligible to apply.

The announcement comes amid broader political debate about the cost of education, with several Opposition TDs raising the issue repeatedly in the Dáil in recent months. A recent survey by the Irish League of Credit Unions found that the average back-to-school cost for a primary school pupil now exceeds €380, a figure that many families struggle to meet.
headline: Education Minister announces €1m fund for free books in primary schools

text:
Tensions at meat processing plants around the country have continued to simmer, with reports of renewed disruptions at a number of factory gates, despite what had appeared to be a breakthrough agreement earlier this week to stand down pickets and remove the threat of legal injunctions.

Farmers in several counties have defied calls from farm organisation leaders to step back from protests, insisting that the deal brokered between stakeholders does not go far enough to address the chronic crisis in beef prices that has left many suckler and beef farmers operating at a significant loss.

The protests, which began several weeks ago with farmers blockading the gates of major meat processors, had been paused after an agreement was reached involving the main farming bodies, Meat Industry Ireland, and the Department of Agriculture. A central element of that deal was the withdrawal of High Court injunction proceedings taken by processors against individual farmers and protest organisers.

However, frustration on the ground has boiled over once more, with farmers at a number of locations in the midlands and the south-east returning to factory gates in significant numbers. Those involved say they feel the agreement was weighted too heavily in favour of the processors and that the fundamental issue — the price paid per kilo for beef at the factory gate — has not been adequately addressed.

"We were told to go home and wait, but waiting is what has us in this mess in the first place," one Tipperary farmer said. "Lads are losing money on every animal they bring in. You can't keep asking people to produce food at below the cost of production and expect them to stay quiet."

The Irish Farmers' Association and the Irish Cattle and Sheep Farmers' Association have both urged calm, with representatives warning that a return to protest action could jeopardise the fragile framework for talks that had been agreed. There are concerns that any renewed blockades could prompt processors to return to the courts seeking fresh injunctions, potentially exposing individual farmers to significant legal costs and penalties.

The Minister for Agriculture has appealed for all sides to engage constructively with the process and has indicated that a beef taskforce, established as part of the agreement, must be given time and space to deliver meaningful reform. The taskforce is expected to examine a range of issues including pricing transparency, the bonus and penalty grid system applied by factories, and the market specification requirements that many farmers regard as overly restrictive.

Meat Industry Ireland has said its members remain committed to the agreed framework but warned that any illegal blockading of processing facilities causes significant economic damage and puts jobs at risk. A spokesperson said the industry was willing to engage on all issues raised but that this must happen through dialogue rather than disruption.

The escalation is a sign of the depth of anger in rural Ireland over what farmers describe as years of declining returns. Many point to the widening gap between retail beef prices and what producers receive, arguing that the margin is being absorbed further up the supply chain by processors and retailers.

Independent TDs from rural constituencies have called on the Government to take a more active role in mediating the dispute, with some suggesting that the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission should be tasked with examining pricing practices in the beef sector.

The coming days are likely to prove critical.
headline: Beef price protests escalate in some areas despite agreement to remove legal threat

text:
Two people have been killed and at least eight others wounded after a gunman opened fire in a busy area of Tel Aviv, Israeli police and emergency services have confirmed.

The shooting took place in a central district of the city, with witnesses describing scenes of panic as people fled for cover. Emergency responders rushed to the scene, where they treated casualties before transporting the wounded to nearby hospitals. Two of those injured are understood to be in a serious condition.

Israeli police said the attacker was "neutralised" at the scene, though they did not immediately confirm whether the gunman had been killed or apprehended. Authorities launched a wide search of the surrounding area to determine whether any additional attackers were involved.

The incident sent shockwaves through the Israeli commercial capital, with a heavy security presence quickly established across the city. Roads in the vicinity were closed off as forensic teams began examining the scene.

Magen David Adom, Israel's national emergency medical service, said its paramedics had arrived within minutes of the first reports and had treated multiple casualties with gunshot wounds.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was briefed on the attack and was monitoring the situation, his office said. Security forces were placed on heightened alert across the country in the immediate aftermath.

The shooting comes amid an already volatile security environment in the region, with tensions running high as the war in Gaza continues and violence in the occupied West Bank persists.

Ireland's Department of Foreign Affairs has advised Irish citizens in the area to exercise extreme caution, follow the instructions of local authorities and to monitor updates from the embassy.

No group had immediately claimed responsibility for the attack at the time of publication. Israeli security services said an investigation was under way to establish the full circumstances and motivation behind the shooting.
headline: Two killed and eight wounded in Tel Aviv shooting

text:
Dublin Zoo and Fota Wildlife Park are to receive emergency State funding of €1.1m to help stave off the threat of closure brought about by the devastating impact of Covid-19 restrictions on their revenues.

The Minister for Public Expenditure Michael McGrath confirmed the allocation, which will be split between the two popular visitor attractions, with Dublin Zoo receiving €900,000 and Fota Wildlife Park in Co Cork set to benefit from €200,000 in emergency support.

Both facilities had warned in recent weeks that they were facing an existential crisis, with the prolonged closure of their gates to the public during successive lockdowns leaving them struggling to meet the enormous costs associated with the care and feeding of thousands of animals.

Dublin Zoo, which is home to more than 400 animals and has been a fixture in the Phoenix Park since 1831, launched a public fundraising campaign late last year after warning it was in serious financial difficulty. The campaign struck a chord with the public, raising more than €3m in donations in a matter of weeks, in what was widely seen as a reflection of the deep affection in which the zoo is held by generations of Irish families.

Fota Wildlife Park, which is operated by the Zoological Society of Ireland, similarly found itself under severe financial pressure, with the Cork attraction heavily reliant on gate receipts to fund its operations.

Minister McGrath said the Government recognised the vital role both institutions play, not only as major tourist attractions but as centres for conservation, education and biodiversity research.

"Dublin Zoo and Fota Wildlife Park are national treasures. They are home to endangered species and play an important role in international conservation programmes. The Government was not going to stand by and allow these institutions to face closure," Mr McGrath said.

The funding will be drawn from the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform and is intended to cover essential animal welfare costs, including veterinary care, feeding and habitat maintenance, during the period in which the facilities remain closed or operating at significantly reduced capacity under public health restrictions.

The Zoological Society of Ireland welcomed the announcement, describing it as a "lifeline" that would help ensure the continued care of animals at both parks. A spokesperson said the organisation remained grateful for the extraordinary generosity shown by the public through donations but stressed that the ongoing costs of maintaining the collections were substantial and that State support was essential to bridge the gap until normal visitor numbers could resume.

TDs from across the political spectrum had called on the Government to intervene, with several raising the matter in the Dáil in recent weeks. Labour TD Duncan Smith said the funding was "welcome but overdue," adding that the Government needed to put in place a longer-term plan to ensure the financial sustainability of both institutions beyond the pandemic.

Sinn Féin's spokesperson on public expenditure, Mairéad Farrell TD, said her party supported the emergency allocation but questioned whether it would be sufficient given the scale of the challenges facing the two parks.

The announcement comes as the Government continues to grapple with the wider economic fallout from Covid-19 restrictions, with a range of sectors from hospitality to the arts seeking additional State support to survive the crisis.
headline: Emergency €1.1m fund to help prevent closure of Dublin Zoo and Fota

text:
Larry King, the legendary American broadcaster whose unmistakable voice and signature braces became synonymous with talk show television for more than half a century, has died at the age of 87.

King, who hosted CNN's flagship programme *Larry King Live* for 25 years, passed away on Saturday morning at Cedars-Sinai Medical Centre in Los Angeles, his production company Ora Media confirmed. The cause of death was not immediately disclosed, though King had been hospitalised earlier this month after contracting Covid-19.

Born Lawrence Harvey Zeiger in Brooklyn, New York, in 1933, King rose from humble beginnings to become one of the most recognised broadcasters in the world. Over a career spanning six decades, he conducted an estimated 50,000 interviews with presidents, world leaders, celebrities and ordinary people whose stories captivated audiences.

His interviewing style — conversational, curious and notably devoid of confrontation — earned him both admirers and critics, but it was a formula that drew guests who might otherwise have shied away from the spotlight. Every sitting US president from Richard Nixon to Barack Obama sat across from King at his famous desk.

"I've never learned anything while I was talking," King was fond of saying, a philosophy that underpinned his approach to broadcasting throughout his remarkable career.

King's personal life was as eventful as his professional one. He was married eight times to seven women, and is survived by three of his five children. He endured significant health challenges over the years, including a major heart attack in 1987 and a diagnosis of lung cancer in 2017.

After departing CNN in 2010, King continued broadcasting through his programme *Larry King Now* on Ora TV and RT America, proving that his appetite for conversation remained undimmed well into his eighties.

Tributes poured in from across the worlds of media, politics and entertainment, with many noting that King's brand of long-form, respectful interviewing had become increasingly rare in the modern media landscape.
headline: Legendary talk show host Larry King dies aged 87

text:
The beat goes on in Cork this weekend with a packed programme of events set to keep music lovers, culture enthusiasts and families entertained across the city and county.

Leading the charge is the long-running Cork Jazz Festival, which continues to draw thousands of visitors to venues across the city centre, with sessions spilling out from pubs, hotels and concert halls in what has become one of the most anticipated weekends on the Munster social calendar. Organisers have reported strong ticket sales across the board, with several headline acts already sold out.

The festival, which has been a cornerstone of Cork's cultural identity for decades, brings an estimated economic boost of millions of euro to the local economy each year, with hoteliers and restaurateurs reporting a surge in bookings. Cork City Council has worked closely with event organisers to ensure the smooth running of proceedings, with additional Gardaí deployed across the city centre to manage the expected crowds.

Beyond the jazz, there is plenty more to keep Leesiders occupied. A number of community events and markets are taking place across the county, offering something for those looking for a quieter alternative to the main festival programme.

Transport arrangements have been bolstered for the weekend, with Bus Éireann and Iarnród Éireann laying on additional services to cope with the influx of visitors travelling to the city. Cork City Council has also reminded motorists of temporary traffic management measures in place around key venues.

Local publicans and venue owners have spoken of their delight at the return of bumper crowds, noting that the weekend represents one of the busiest trading periods of the year. Many establishments have invested in refurbishments and expanded their offerings in anticipation of the weekend rush.

For those yet to make plans, organisers have encouraged people to check individual venue listings, as a number of free events and pop-up performances are scheduled throughout the weekend across the city.
headline: Beat goes on for busy weekend in Cork

text:
A man has been charged in connection with the seizure of drugs worth an estimated €6.5 million at Rosslare Europort in Co Wexford.

The drugs were discovered by Revenue officers during a routine search of a commercial vehicle that arrived at the port on a ferry service from continental Europe. The seizure, which was carried out with the assistance of detector dogs, involved a large quantity of cannabis herb.

The man, who is aged in his 30s, was arrested at the scene by officers from the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau (GNDOCB), who had been conducting the operation in conjunction with Revenue's Customs Service.

He was detained at a Garda station in the Wexford district under the provisions of Section 2 of the Criminal Justice (Drug Trafficking) Act 1996.

The accused was brought before a special sitting of Wexford District Court, where he was charged with offences under the Misuse of Drugs Act. He was remanded in custody to appear before the court again at a later date.

Gardaí said investigations into the matter are ongoing.

The seizure is the latest in a series of significant drug interceptions at Rosslare Europort, which has seen increased volumes of direct freight traffic from mainland Europe in recent years. Revenue has stepped up its enforcement operations at the port, deploying additional scanning technology and detector dog teams to target drug smuggling through the route.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: Man charged over €6.5m drug seizure at Rosslare Europort

text:
A viable pipe bomb has been made safe by Army Technical Officers after being discovered in Co Down earlier today.

The device was found in the Drumaness Road area of Ballynahinch this morning, prompting a major security alert in the area.

Police Service of Northern Ireland officers cordoned off the scene and a number of nearby properties were evacuated as a precautionary measure while the device was examined.

An Army Technical Officer attended the scene and carried out a controlled explosion on the device, which was later confirmed to have been a viable pipe bomb.

Residents who had been moved from their homes were permitted to return once the device had been made safe and the security operation had concluded.

The Drumaness Road was closed for a number of hours during the alert, causing disruption for motorists and local residents. It has since been reopened to traffic.

PSNI detectives are now investigating the circumstances surrounding the discovery of the device and have appealed for anyone with information to come forward.

Detective Sergeant Michael Forsythe said the discovery of such a device in a residential area was reckless and could have had serious consequences for the local community.

"This was a viable device which posed a real threat to life," he said. "We are fortunate that no one was injured as a result of this incident."

He urged anyone who noticed any suspicious activity in the area in recent days to contact detectives at the PSNI's non-emergency number 101, quoting the reference number for the incident. Information can also be provided anonymously through the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.
headline: Pipe bomb defused after being found in Co Down

text:
The man convicted of the murder of Ashling Murphy has been granted legal aid to appeal his conviction.

Jozef Puska, a Slovakian national who had been living in Mucklagh, Co Offaly, was found guilty by a Central Criminal Court jury in June 2023 of the murder of the 23-year-old primary school teacher as she jogged along the canal bank at Cappincur, Tullamore, on 12 January 2022.

Puska, who is 33, was sentenced to the mandatory term of life imprisonment following the unanimous verdict.

The Court of Appeal today granted Puska legal aid to pursue his appeal against the conviction. The court heard that Puska has no means to fund his own legal representation.

Ms Murphy's murder sent shockwaves through the country and prompted widespread vigils and calls for greater action on violence against women. The young teacher, who was also a talented traditional musician, was attacked in broad daylight along a popular walking and running route beside the Grand Canal.

During the trial, which lasted several weeks, the jury heard extensive forensic and DNA evidence linking Puska to the attack. The prosecution case included CCTV footage tracking his movements on the day of the murder, as well as testimony from witnesses who encountered him in the hours before and after the killing.

Puska had denied murdering Ms Murphy. His defence team argued at trial that the forensic evidence was not sufficient to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

The grounds on which Puska intends to appeal his conviction have not yet been made public. A date for the full hearing of the appeal has not been set.

The Director of Public Prosecutions was represented at today's brief hearing and indicated that the State would be opposing the appeal.
headline: Puska granted legal aid to appeal murder conviction

text:
A dramatic video has emerged showing a US military aircraft plunging from the sky over Kuwait before crashing to the ground in a fireball.

The footage, which has been widely shared on social media, captures the moment the plane nosedives sharply before disappearing behind a cluster of buildings. A large plume of black smoke can then be seen rising from the crash site.

The United States military confirmed the incident, stating that the aircraft went down during what it described as a routine training mission. It said an investigation into the cause of the crash has been launched.

It is understood the aircraft was operating out of one of the US military installations in Kuwait, which hosts thousands of American troops as part of Washington's broader presence in the Middle East.

Reports from the region indicate that the crew managed to eject before impact, though the extent of any injuries remains unclear. The US military has not yet confirmed the condition of those on board.

Kuwait has long served as a key staging ground for American military operations in the region, hosting several bases that support missions across the wider Middle East. The Gulf state has maintained close defence ties with Washington since the 1991 Gulf War, when a US-led coalition liberated the country following Iraq's invasion.

Local authorities in Kuwait said the crash site had been secured and that there were no reports of civilian casualties on the ground.

The US military said further details would be released as its investigation progresses.
headline: Watch: US military plane plummets from sky in Kuwait

text:
North Korea has vowed to deploy new weapons systems along its border with South Korea, in a move that threatens to further escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

The announcement came through the country's state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), which said the regime would bolster its military capabilities in areas close to the demilitarised zone (DMZ) that has divided the two Koreas since the end of the Korean War in 1953.

Pyongyang said the deployments were a response to what it described as provocative military exercises carried out by South Korea and the United States in the region. The North Korean military said it would take "practical and offensive" steps to defend its sovereignty, without specifying the exact nature of the weapons to be stationed along the border.

South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said it was closely monitoring developments and maintaining a state of military readiness. The South Korean military urged the North to cease actions that raise tensions and to return to dialogue.

The United States, which maintains roughly 28,500 troops in South Korea, said it remained committed to the defence of its ally. A spokesperson for the US Department of Defense said Washington was aware of the reports and was coordinating closely with Seoul.

The latest sabre-rattling comes amid a prolonged breakdown in diplomatic efforts to denuclearise the Korean Peninsula. Talks between Washington and Pyongyang have been stalled for some time, with North Korea continuing to develop its nuclear and missile programmes in defiance of United Nations Security Council resolutions.

Relations between the two Koreas have deteriorated sharply in recent times, with Pyongyang scrapping several inter-Korean agreements and declaring South Korea its "principal enemy." North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has repeatedly ruled out the possibility of reunification, marking a significant departure from decades of official rhetoric on both sides of the border.

Analysts say the planned deployments could include tactical nuclear weapons, short-range ballistic missiles or new artillery systems, all of which would pose a direct threat to the South Korean capital, Seoul, which lies just 50 kilometres south of the DMZ.

The Irish Department of Foreign Affairs has not yet commented on the developments. Ireland, which has served on the UN Security Council and has historically supported multilateral efforts towards denuclearisation, has previously called on all parties to pursue diplomatic solutions to the crisis.
headline: North Korea vows to deploy new weapons at border

text:
Financial services firm BNY has confirmed it will close its facility in Wexford, with the loss of a significant number of jobs in the south-east.

The company, formerly known as BNY Mellon, informed staff at its Wexford office of the decision today. It is understood that approximately 100 employees will be affected by the closure, which is expected to take place over the coming months.

In a statement, BNY said the decision was part of a broader review of its global operations and was aimed at consolidating its footprint to drive greater efficiency. The firm said it would work closely with affected employees to provide support, including exploring redeployment opportunities at other BNY locations where possible.

BNY has maintained a presence in Ireland for a number of years, with operations also based in Dublin and Cork. The company said its commitment to Ireland as a key location for the firm remained strong despite the Wexford closure.

The news will come as a blow to the Wexford economy, where the facility has been a notable employer in the region's financial services sector. Local representatives expressed concern at the announcement and called for supports to be put in place for those who will lose their positions.

Sinn Féin TD for Wexford Johnny Mythen described the closure as "devastating news" for the workers and their families, and called on the Government and the IDA to urgently work to attract replacement investment to the area.

The Tánaiste and Minister for Enterprise has been briefed on the situation, according to a Government spokesperson. The Department of Enterprise said it would engage with the relevant State agencies, including IDA Ireland and the local enterprise office, to support affected workers and explore alternative employment opportunities in the region.

IDA Ireland said it was aware of the announcement and would continue to work to win new investment for Wexford and the wider south-east.

BNY is one of the world's largest financial services companies, providing investment management, investment services and wealth management services to institutions and individuals globally. The firm employs more than 50,000 people worldwide.
headline: Financial services firm BNY to close its Wexford facility

text:
A man arrested as part of the investigation into the murder of Sean Fox has been released without charge.

The man, aged in his 30s, was detained by Gardaí on Tuesday morning and was questioned at a Garda station in Belfast's commuter belt. He has since been released without charge, and a file is being prepared for the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Mr Fox, who was in his 40s, was found dead at a property in Co Louth in the early hours of last Thursday morning. Gardaí and emergency services attended the scene, where Mr Fox was pronounced dead a short time later.

A post-mortem examination was carried out at Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital in Drogheda, the results of which are not being released for operational reasons.

The scene was preserved for a forensic examination by members of the Garda Technical Bureau, and the investigation is being led by detectives attached to Dundalk Garda Station.

Gardaí have renewed their appeal for anyone with information in relation to the killing to come forward. They are particularly keen to speak to anyone who was in the area in the hours leading up to the discovery of Mr Fox's body, or anyone who may have dashcam or doorbell camera footage from the vicinity.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Dundalk Garda Station on 042 938 8400, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.

Investigations are ongoing.
headline: Man released in Sean Fox murder investigation

text:
Sir Keir Starmer has acknowledged he was wrong to appoint Lord Mandelson as Britain's ambassador to the United States, in a remarkable admission from the prime minister that marks a significant climbdown.

Speaking to reporters, Mr Starmer said the decision to nominate the veteran Labour figure for the Washington role had been a mistake, conceding that the appointment had become a distraction at a time when the UK's relationship with the Trump administration is of critical importance.

Lord Mandelson had faced sustained criticism over his past business links to China, which drew sharp rebukes from senior figures in Washington. The former European Commissioner's consultancy work had included advising clients with Chinese connections, a fact that proved deeply problematic given the Trump administration's hawkish stance on Beijing.

The admission is a bruising moment for the British prime minister, who had personally championed Lord Mandelson for the post, viewing the twice-resigned cabinet minister's diplomatic experience and extensive contacts book as ideal credentials for navigating the unpredictable terrain of Donald Trump's White House.
