However, the backlash was swift and came from both sides of the Atlantic. Republican figures close to the Trump administration made clear their displeasure, while Conservative MPs at Westminster accused Mr Starmer of a serious misjudgement.

The episode raises broader questions about the judgment of the prime minister's operation in Downing Street, with opposition figures likely to seize on the reversal as evidence of a government struggling to find its footing on the international stage.

It remains unclear who will now be put forward for the ambassadorial role, which is seen as one of the most consequential diplomatic postings in British foreign policy, particularly given the ongoing trade tensions between Washington and its allies.

The UK has been engaged in delicate negotiations with the Trump administration over tariffs, and the vacancy in Washington comes at a particularly sensitive juncture for the so-called special relationship.
headline: Starmer says he was wrong to name Mandelson as US envoy

text:
Tributes have been pouring in for Joey Forker, a well-known and beloved figure in the Donegal community, who has been described as "larger than life" by those who knew him.

Mr Forker, who was widely recognised across the county for his warmth, good humour and community spirit, passed away in recent days, prompting an outpouring of grief and affection from friends, neighbours and community organisations.

Local councillors, sports clubs and community groups have all paid tribute to a man who, by all accounts, left an indelible mark on those fortunate enough to have crossed his path.

"Joey was one of those people who lit up a room the moment he walked in," said one close friend. "He was larger than life in every sense — generous to a fault, always ready with a story or a joke, and the first to put his hand up when anyone needed help."

Mr Forker was deeply involved in local life in Donegal, giving his time to a range of causes and organisations over many years. His contribution to the community was described as immeasurable by those who worked alongside him.

Local representatives also spoke of the deep sense of loss felt across the area. One local councillor said Mr Forker embodied everything that is good about community life in Donegal and that his passing leaves a void that will be difficult to fill.

"He was the heartbeat of so many things that happened around here," the councillor said. "Whether it was organising events, supporting local causes or simply being there for people, Joey gave everything he had."

Friends and well-wishers have taken to social media in large numbers to share memories and express their condolences to the Forker family.

His funeral is expected to be a significant occasion, with large numbers anticipated to turn out to pay their final respects to a man who touched so many lives.

Mr Forker is survived by his loving family, to whom sympathy has been extended from across the county and beyond.
headline: Tributes to 'larger than life' Joey Forker in Donegal

text:
The death toll from a devastating fire at a ski resort hotel in northwestern Turkey has risen to 76, authorities have confirmed, making it one of the deadliest such disasters in the country's recent history.

The blaze tore through the Grand Kartal Hotel in the popular Kartalkaya ski resort in the Bolu province during the early hours of the morning, when many guests were asleep. Dozens more were injured, with some in a critical condition in hospital.

Rescue teams worked through the night and into the following day to recover victims from the charred remains of the multi-storey timber-clad building, which was reported to have been near full capacity at the time of the fire.

Harrowing footage shared on social media showed guests attempting to escape the flames by climbing from windows and using makeshift ropes fashioned from bedsheets. Emergency services said some of those who died had jumped from upper floors of the building in desperate attempts to flee.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan visited the scene and declared a period of national mourning. He vowed that those responsible for any negligence would be held to account, saying the nation shared in the grief of the victims' families.

Prosecutors have launched an investigation into the cause of the fire and whether the hotel met fire safety regulations. Several people, including the hotel's management, have been detained for questioning as part of the inquiry.

Reports in Turkish media suggested the building may have lacked adequate fire escapes and that its alarm systems may not have functioned properly. Questions have also been raised about the speed of the emergency response, given the hotel's remote mountain location.

The resort, situated in the Köroğlu mountains at an altitude of roughly 2,000 metres, is one of Turkey's most popular winter tourism destinations, drawing large crowds particularly during the holiday season.

The Turkish government has ordered inspections of hotels and accommodation facilities at ski resorts across the country in the wake of the tragedy.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has said it is not aware of any Irish citizens having been affected by the fire.
headline: Death toll in Turkish ski resort fire jumps to 76 people

text:
Firefighters are battling a significant wildfire on the Fanad Peninsula in Co Donegal this evening, with crews working to prevent the blaze from spreading to nearby homes and farmland.

The fire, which broke out earlier today, has been burning across a wide area of upland terrain on the peninsula, sending plumes of smoke visible from several kilometres away.

Donegal County Council's fire service has deployed multiple units to the scene, with crews from surrounding stations called in to assist in tackling the blaze.

It is understood that strong winds in the area have hampered efforts to bring the fire under control, with gusts fanning the flames across dry gorse and heathland.

Local residents have been urged to exercise caution and to keep windows and doors closed due to heavy smoke in the surrounding area.

There are no reports of injuries at this stage, and no properties are believed to have been damaged, though firefighters remain on high alert as conditions continue to pose challenges.

The cause of the fire has not yet been established, though Gardaí are understood to be aware of the situation.

It comes during a period in which fire services across the west and north-west have dealt with a number of gorse and wildfire incidents, a recurring issue during spells of dry weather in spring and early summer.

The Department of Agriculture has previously warned landowners that the illegal burning of vegetation poses serious risks to wildlife habitats and can result in penalties, including reductions in farm payments.

Coillte and the Irish Wildlife Trust have also raised concerns about the environmental damage caused by uncontrolled fires, particularly in areas of ecological sensitivity such as blanket bog.

Crews are expected to remain at the scene on the Fanad Peninsula into the night as they continue to monitor the situation.
headline: Firefighters tackling wildfire on Fanad Peninsula

text:
There is a peculiar irony in the timing. As the Dáil broke for the Christmas recess, with TDs scattering to constituencies armed with talking points about the cost of living and the housing crisis, a familiar spectre settled over Leinster House — the uncomfortable sense that we have been here before.

The Ghost of Christmas Past, in this instance, wears many faces. It looks like the tail end of 2007, when a government flush with revenue insisted the fundamentals were sound. It looks like the pre-election scramble of 2020, when promises multiplied faster than hospital beds. And it looks, most uncomfortably of all, like the budgetary choices of recent months, where the sheer volume of one-off spending packages has begun to blur the line between fiscal prudence and political expediency.

The Government will, of course, bristle at any comparison with the Celtic Tiger era. And in fairness, the macroeconomic picture is genuinely different. Corporation tax receipts, however volatile, have delivered surpluses that Bertie Ahern could only have dreamed of. The rainy day funds exist. The debt-to-GDP ratio, even allowing for the well-documented distortions in Irish GDP figures, is manageable. The Department of Finance has been at pains to stress that the spending increases announced in Budget 2025 are, in their view, sustainable.

But sustainability and wisdom are not always the same thing, and this is where the ghost begins to rattle its chains.

Consider the pattern. Across successive budgets now, the Coalition has relied heavily on once-off measures — energy credits, double child benefit payments, lump-sum social welfare bonuses — rather than embedding structural reforms into the system. Each individual measure can be defended on its merits. Taken together, they create an expectation among the public that the State will always be there with a cheque when times are difficult. That expectation becomes extraordinarily hard to unwind, as anyone who remembers the medical card controversies of 2008 and 2009 can attest.

The political logic is obvious. One-off payments do not permanently increase the spending base, which means they do not bind future governments in the way a permanent welfare increase or a new universal service would. They allow Ministers to appear generous at Budget time without, technically, compromising the fiscal position. It is clever politics, but it stores up a different kind of problem: a public that feels perpetually under-supported despite receiving billions in additional transfers, because nothing has structurally changed about the cost of housing, childcare, or health.

This is where the ghost's message becomes pointed. The lessons of Ireland's recent economic history are not solely about profligate spending, though that was certainly part of the story. They are about the failure to use periods of plenty to fix things that are broken. In the 2000s, we had the resources to build a health service fit for purpose, to create a sustainable housing model, to invest in public transport beyond the M50. We chose instead to cut taxes and inflate a property bubble.

Today, the failures are different in character but rhyme in their essence.
headline: Leinster House visited by Ghost of Christmas Past

text:
It has become something of a ritual in Irish politics: a new housing plan lands with a fanfare, ministers line up to insist that this time things will be different, and the rest of us are left to sift through the detail for signs of genuine ambition or familiar repackaging. The Government's latest intervention follows that well-worn script in some respects, but there are elements that deserve closer scrutiny. Here are five key takeaways.

**The targets are ambitious — but ambition is not the same as delivery**

The headline figures are undeniably striking. The Government is committing to a significant uplift in the number of new homes to be built annually, with social and affordable housing given particular prominence. On paper, the numbers represent a step-change from previous plans. But Ireland has been here before. Housing for All, Rebuilding Ireland, and their predecessors all came laden with targets that were subsequently missed. The critical question, as always, is whether the State has the capacity — in terms of skilled labour, planning throughput, and available serviced land — to translate projections into bricks and mortar. Without a credible pathway to delivery, targets risk becoming little more than political decoration.

**Planning reform is finally being treated as a bottleneck**

Perhaps the most significant signal in the plan is the acknowledgement that the planning system itself is part of the problem. Proposals to streamline An Bord Pleanála processes, reduce judicial review delays, and fast-track applications for large-scale residential developments suggest the Government has absorbed criticism that has been mounting for years. Industry figures have long argued that the time and cost involved in navigating the planning system acts as a powerful deterrent to building at scale. Whether the reforms go far enough remains to be seen — and any changes will inevitably face legal and political challenges — but the direction of travel is notable.

**Local authorities are being asked to do more, with an open question about whether they can**

A recurring theme in the plan is the enhanced role envisaged for local authorities, both as direct builders of social housing and as enablers of private development through the provision of serviced sites and infrastructure. This represents a welcome return, in principle, to the era when councils were significant housing providers in their own right. The difficulty is that many local authorities have spent decades shedding precisely the kind of in-house expertise and capacity they are now being asked to redeploy. Staffing shortages, procurement constraints, and the sheer complexity of modern construction mean that ramping up local authority output will not happen overnight. The plan nods to this challenge but is less convincing on how quickly it can be overcome.

**The affordability question remains thorny**

For many younger people and families locked out of the housing market, the central issue is not simply the volume of homes being built but whether they can afford to buy or rent them. The plan includes measures aimed at improving affordability — from shared equity schemes to cost-rental initiatives — but critics will argue that these interventions risk being overwhelmed by the broader dynamics of a market where demand continues to vastly outstrip supply. There is a tension, too, between measures designed to support buyers and the risk that such supports simply feed into higher prices.
headline: 5 takeaways from Government's housing plan

text:
Gardaí came under sustained attack during hours of violent unrest in Dublin city centre last night, following a stabbing incident in which a number of people, including children, were seriously injured.

The disorder erupted on Thursday evening after a man attacked several people on Parnell Square East shortly after 1.30pm. Three children and a woman were among those injured in the stabbing, with some of the victims understood to have been taken to hospital in a serious condition.

The suspect was apprehended at the scene by a member of the public and subsequently detained by gardaí. He was taken to hospital for treatment of injuries sustained during his arrest.

In the hours that followed, large crowds gathered in the city centre and scenes of significant disorder broke out across several locations. Gardaí in riot gear were deployed to O'Connell Street, Parnell Square and surrounding areas as groups attacked officers, set fire to vehicles, looted businesses and caused widespread damage to property.

A Luas tram was set alight on O'Connell Street, while a Dublin Bus was also torched. Fires were started at multiple locations and a number of businesses, including several shops and fast food outlets, were smashed and looted.

Garda Commissioner Drew Harris described the violence as scenes not witnessed in Dublin in decades. He said the disorder was driven by a "complete lunatic, hooligan faction" fuelled by far-right ideology and social media agitation.

Taoiseach Leo Varadkar condemned the rioting in the strongest terms, saying those involved had brought shame on Dublin and on Ireland. He said the violence was not in response to the earlier stabbing but was rather driven by people who sought to exploit a terrible tragedy.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin echoed the condemnation, describing the scenes as "an attack on the rule of law" and on the people of Dublin.

The Garda Public Order Unit was deployed in significant numbers throughout the night, with reinforcements drawn from across the Dublin Metropolitan Region and surrounding divisions. Water cannon, which had not been used in the State in living memory, were also deployed to disperse crowds.

A significant number of arrests were made during the course of the night, with gardaí confirming that more were expected in the coming days as CCTV footage and other evidence was reviewed.

Lord Mayor of Dublin Daithí de Róiste said the city had been "desecrated" and that the actions of those involved bore no resemblance to any legitimate expression of concern for the victims of the stabbing.

Business owners arrived to scenes of devastation on Friday morning, with shopfronts smashed and premises ransacked along O'Connell Street and surrounding areas. Dublin City Council said a major clean-up operation was under way.

The injured children were being treated at Temple Street Children's University Hospital, while the woman was taken to the Mater Hospital. Medical staff described some of the injuries as serious but not life-threatening.

Gardaí have appealed for anyone with information about the disorder, including video footage, to come forward. Investigations into both the stabbing and the subsequent rioting are ongoing.
headline: Gardaí attacked during violent unrest after stabbing

text:
Twenty-seven people have been sentenced in what has been described as the biggest tax fraud case in Northern Ireland's history, following a complex investigation spanning several years.

The sentences were handed down at Belfast Crown Court in connection with a sophisticated fraud scheme that cost HM Revenue and Customs tens of millions of pounds in lost revenue.

The case centred on a large-scale operation involving the laundering of illicit fuel and the evasion of excise duty and VAT. The defendants, who ranged in age and came from various parts of Northern Ireland and the border region, played different roles in the criminal enterprise.

Sentences varied significantly depending on the level of involvement of each defendant, with some receiving custodial terms and others given suspended sentences or community-based orders.

The presiding judge said the scale of the fraud was exceptional and had deprived the public purse of substantial sums that could otherwise have been used to fund public services.

The Public Prosecution Service for Northern Ireland described the outcome as a landmark result, while HMRC said the sentencing sent a clear message that organised tax fraud would not be tolerated.

The investigation involved cooperation between a number of agencies on both sides of the border, including Revenue Commissioners in the Republic, reflecting the cross-jurisdictional nature of fuel fraud in the border region.

Such schemes have long been a concern for authorities in both jurisdictions, with criminal gangs exploiting the difference in fuel duty rates and using elaborate laundering plants to remove markers from rebated diesel before selling it at full price.

The case is understood to have required the analysis of vast quantities of financial records and surveillance material before charges were brought against the defendants.

Welcoming the sentences, HMRC said its officers remained committed to pursuing those involved in organised fraud and bringing them before the courts.
headline: 27 people sentenced in biggest tax fraud case in NI

text:
The Archbishop of Canterbury is facing mounting pressure to step down from his position following revelations about his handling of a major abuse scandal that has rocked the Church of England.

Justin Welby has come under intense scrutiny after an independent review found he could and should have taken action to stop a serial abuser connected to the Church. The review, published this week, examined the case of John Smyth, a prominent barrister and volunteer at Christian summer camps, who is alleged to have carried out horrific physical and sexual abuse against more than 100 boys and young men over a period spanning several decades across the UK, Zimbabwe and South Africa. Smyth died in 2018 before facing any criminal charges.

The Makin Review, led by Keith Makin, concluded that the Church of England's response to the allegations amounted to a catastrophic failure. It found that Archbishop Welby was first made aware of the allegations against Smyth in 2013, shortly after taking office, but failed to ensure the matter was properly reported to the police or that adequate safeguarding measures were put in place.

Senior clergy, abuse survivors and campaigners have called on the archbishop to consider his position, arguing that his continued leadership is untenable in the circumstances. Several members of the General Synod have publicly stated that his resignation is necessary to restore confidence in the Church's commitment to safeguarding.

Archbishop Welby has issued a public apology to the survivors, describing the abuse as "horrendous" and acknowledging personal responsibility for failing to act with sufficient urgency. However, he has so far resisted calls to resign, stating that he intends to continue working to improve the Church's safeguarding procedures.

The scandal has drawn comparisons with institutional abuse failures in other organisations and jurisdictions, including in Ireland, where decades of clerical abuse prompted extensive state investigations and led to fundamental changes in how the Catholic Church operates.

Survivors' groups have expressed frustration at what they describe as a pattern of institutional self-protection, arguing that meaningful accountability requires leadership change at the highest level. Several prominent voices within the Church have echoed those sentiments, suggesting that the archbishop's position has become a distraction from the urgent reforms needed.

The Church of England has said it accepts all recommendations contained in the Makin Review and has committed to implementing them in full.
headline: Archbishop of Canterbury urged to resign over scandal

text:
Parents and health professionals are calling on TikTok to take greater responsibility for the proliferation of extreme diet content on its platform, as concerns mount over the so-called "SkinnyTok" trend that has been linked to disordered eating among young people in Ireland.

The trend, which promotes rapid weight loss and glorifies extremely thin body types, has gained significant traction on the social media platform in recent months. Content tagged with related hashtags has amassed billions of views globally, with Irish advocacy groups warning that vulnerable teenagers are being exposed to dangerous messaging around food and body image.

Bodywhys, the Eating Disorders Association of Ireland, said it has seen a notable increase in contacts to its helpline from young people who reference content they have encountered on TikTok. The organisation's chief executive, Jacinta Hastings, said the platform's algorithm bears particular responsibility.

"What we're hearing from young people and their families is that once a user engages with even one piece of this type of content, the algorithm serves up more and more of it. It creates an echo chamber that can be incredibly harmful, particularly for adolescents who may already be struggling with body image," she said.

A number of TDs have raised the issue in the Dáil in recent weeks, with calls for the Government to ensure that Coimisiún na Meán, the media regulator established under the Online Safety and Media Regulation Act, uses its full powers to hold platforms to account.

Sinn Féin's spokesperson on mental health said the Government needed to move beyond "warm words" and take concrete action to protect children online. "We know that these platforms are designed to maximise engagement, and unfortunately that often means amplifying the most extreme and harmful content. Irish children deserve better," the TD said.

Fine Gael Senator Regina Doherty, who has been vocal on online safety issues, said she would be writing to TikTok's European trust and safety team, which is based in Dublin, to seek a meeting on the matter.

TikTok has previously stated that it removes content that promotes or glorifies eating disorders and that it redirects users who search for related terms to support resources. A spokesperson for the company said it takes the issue "extremely seriously" and is continually working to improve its enforcement of community guidelines.

However, researchers at Dublin City University's Anti-Bullying Centre, who have been studying harmful content on social media platforms, said moderation efforts remain inadequate. Dr Tijana Milosevic, an assistant professor at DCU, said much of the content that falls under the SkinnyTok umbrella does not explicitly promote eating disorders but instead normalises restrictive eating in ways that are difficult for automated systems to detect.

"The content is often framed as wellness or fitness advice, which makes it harder to moderate. But the cumulative effect of consuming this material, particularly for a young person, can be devastating," Dr Milosevic said.

The HSE's national clinical programme for eating disorders has also expressed concern. Figures published earlier this year showed that referrals to eating disorder services have increased significantly since the pandemic, with clinicians noting that social media is frequently cited as a contributing factor by patients and their families.
headline: Calls for TikTok accountability over 'SkinnyTok' trend

text:
Six children are currently waiting for a place in one of the State's special care units, the Minister for Children has confirmed, amid renewed concerns about the capacity of the system to meet the needs of the most vulnerable young people in care.

Special care units provide secure residential placements for children who are deemed to be at serious risk to themselves or others, and who cannot be safely managed in other care settings. Placements are ordered by the High Court.

The figures were disclosed in response to a parliamentary question tabled by a member of the Oireachtas, who described the situation as deeply concerning and called for urgent action to address capacity shortfalls.

Tusla, the Child and Family Agency, operates three special care units nationally, with a combined capacity of seventeen places. However, not all of those places are available at any given time due to staffing difficulties and the complex needs of children already resident in the units.

A Tusla spokesperson said the agency was working to ensure that children awaiting placement were being supported in the most appropriate alternative settings available, including high-support residential care and bespoke community-based arrangements. The spokesperson added that every effort was being made to expedite placements as they became available.

However, advocacy groups have warned that delays in accessing special care can have serious consequences for children who are already in crisis. Empowering People in Care, a national advocacy organisation for those who have experience of the care system, said the waiting list pointed to a chronic underinvestment in services for the most at-risk children.

"These are children whose needs have been assessed by the High Court as requiring a secure placement. Every day they spend waiting is a day in which they remain at significant risk," a spokesperson for the organisation said.

The issue of special care capacity has been a recurring concern. Reports from the Health Information and Quality Authority, which inspects the units, have repeatedly highlighted challenges around staffing, with recruitment and retention of qualified social care workers proving particularly difficult.

The Minister said the Government remained committed to ensuring that sufficient special care places were available and that work was ongoing to address workforce challenges in the sector. Additional funding had been allocated to Tusla in the most recent budget to support residential care services, the Minister added, though no specific timeline was given for when the waiting list might be cleared.

The Children's Rights Alliance has called for a comprehensive review of the State's special care provision, arguing that a long-term strategic approach is needed rather than what it described as a reactive response to recurring crises.
headline: Six children waiting for special care unit place

text:
The United States government has filed a lawsuit against the state of California, alleging that its animal welfare regulations have driven up egg prices across the country and violated interstate commerce protections.

The legal action, brought by the Department of Justice, targets California's Proposition 12, a voter-approved measure that sets minimum space requirements for egg-laying hens, breeding pigs and veal calves. The law, which took full effect in 2024, requires that all eggs sold in California — regardless of where they are produced — must come from cage-free hens housed in compliance with the state's standards.

Federal officials argue that the regulation has effectively forced egg producers in other states to overhaul their operations at significant cost in order to access the massive California market, which accounts for roughly one in eight eggs consumed in the United States. The lawsuit contends this amounts to an unconstitutional burden on interstate commerce.

The move comes amid heightened public frustration over soaring egg prices in the US, which have been driven in large part by a severe avian influenza outbreak that has decimated flocks across the country. The average price of a dozen eggs in the US has exceeded $6 in recent months, more than double what consumers were paying two years ago.

California officials have defended the law, arguing that it reflects the democratic will of voters and promotes humane treatment of farm animals. Governor Gavin Newsom's office said the state would vigorously contest the lawsuit, describing it as politically motivated.

"California voters spoke clearly when they passed Proposition 12, and we will defend their right to set standards for the food sold in our state," a spokesperson for the governor said.

The legal challenge marks the latest flashpoint in an ongoing dispute between the federal government and California, which has frequently found itself at odds with Washington on issues ranging from environmental regulation to immigration policy.

The US Supreme Court previously weighed in on Proposition 12 in 2023, ruling in National Pork Producers Council v Ross that the law did not violate the Commerce Clause of the US Constitution. However, the current administration appears to be mounting a fresh challenge on different legal grounds, arguing that the cumulative economic impact of the regulation on producers and consumers nationwide warrants federal intervention.

Agricultural economists have offered mixed assessments of the law's impact on egg prices. While some analysts say the cage-free requirements have added to production costs, others note that the avian flu crisis remains the primary driver of price increases and that California's regulations account for a relatively modest share of the overall rise.

The Irish poultry sector has not been directly affected by developments in the US market, though industry figures have noted with interest the debate over animal welfare standards and their economic implications. The European Union has its own regulations governing hen welfare, including a ban on conventional battery cages that took effect in 2012, and the European Commission has been considering further reforms under its Farm to Fork strategy.

The case is expected to take months to progress through the federal courts and could ultimately return to the Supreme Court if lower courts issue conflicting rulings.
headline: US government sues California over egg prices

text:
The Irish Farmers' Association has said that the European Commission's own impact assessment of the EU-Mercosur trade deal effectively undermines the case for the agreement, describing the findings as a vindication of long-standing concerns raised by Irish farmers.

The IFA was responding to the publication of an updated sustainability impact assessment commissioned by the Commission, which the association says highlights significant risks to European agriculture, particularly in the beef and poultry sectors.

IFA president Francie Gorman said the assessment confirms what farmers have been warning about for years. "This report, commissioned by the EU itself, lays bare the damage this deal would do to Irish and European farmers," he said. "It undermines the very case the Commission has been trying to make in favour of the agreement."

Mr Gorman said the findings show that increased imports of beef, poultry and sugar from Mercosur countries — Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay — would place enormous downward pressure on prices for European producers, with Ireland particularly exposed given the importance of the beef sector to the national economy.

The IFA has consistently opposed the deal, arguing that it would allow large volumes of agricultural products into the EU market from countries that do not meet the same environmental, animal welfare and food safety standards required of European farmers.

The association said the assessment also raises serious concerns about deforestation in South America and the environmental consequences of expanding agricultural production in the Mercosur bloc.

The European Commission has maintained that the deal, which has been under negotiation in various forms for more than two decades, would deliver significant economic benefits to the EU through increased access to the South American market for European goods and services.

However, the agreement has faced strong opposition from farming organisations across Europe, as well as from several member states, including Ireland. The Government has previously expressed reservations about the agricultural provisions of the deal and has sought additional safeguards for sensitive sectors.

Minister for Agriculture Charlie McConalogue has repeatedly stated that Ireland would not support a deal that undermines Irish farmers or fails to uphold EU production standards.

Mr Gorman called on the Government to use the findings to press for the deal to be blocked at Council level. "There can be no ambiguity now. The evidence is there in black and white. This deal cannot proceed in its current form," he said.

The Irish Cattle and Sheep Farmers' Association and Macra na Feirme have also voiced opposition to the agreement in its current form, with concerns centring on the potential for an influx of cheaper South American beef onto the European market.

The EU and Mercosur reached a political agreement on the trade deal in 2019, but ratification has been stalled amid opposition from several quarters. Efforts to finalise the agreement have intensified in recent months, with the Commission keen to conclude what would be one of the largest trade deals in EU history.
headline: IFJ probe 'undermines' EU-Mercosur trade deal, says IFA

text:
The cost of the IT system underpinning the State's student grant scheme has significantly exceeded its original budget, with the final bill coming in well above initial projections, according to new figures released to the Oireachtas.

The SUSI online grants system, which processes applications from tens of thousands of students each year, was developed to replace the previous patchwork of local authority-administered grant schemes with a single centralised platform. However, the project has been dogged by cost overruns that have drawn scrutiny from TDs and senators alike.

Figures provided to members of the Oireachtas Public Accounts Committee show that the total expenditure on the IT infrastructure far outstripped the budget allocated when the system was first commissioned. The overspend has raised questions about project management and oversight within the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science.

The SUSI system, operated by City of Dublin Education and Training Board on behalf of the Department, was intended to streamline the grants process and deliver efficiencies. While it has succeeded in centralising the application process, the escalating costs have prompted concern among public representatives about value for money.

Speaking in the Dáil, several TDs called for a full accounting of how the overspend occurred and whether adequate controls were in place during the development and rollout phases. Opposition deputies questioned whether the Department had been sufficiently vigilant in monitoring expenditure as the project progressed.

A spokesperson for the Department acknowledged that costs had risen beyond the original estimates but said the system had delivered significant improvements in how student grants are administered across the State. The spokesperson pointed to faster processing times and greater consistency in decision-making as key benefits of the centralised approach.

The Comptroller and Auditor General is understood to have examined aspects of the spending, and the matter may be subject to further review by the Public Accounts Committee in the coming weeks.

Student representatives have expressed frustration that the focus on IT costs risks overshadowing ongoing concerns about the adequacy of the grants themselves. The Union of Students in Ireland has repeatedly called for increases to SUSI maintenance grant rates, arguing that they have failed to keep pace with the rising cost of living, particularly accommodation costs in Dublin and other university cities.

The controversy comes at a time when the Government is under pressure to demonstrate prudent management of public finances, with several large-scale State IT projects having attracted criticism for cost overruns in recent years. The National Children's Hospital, while primarily a construction project, has heightened public sensitivity to any perception of runaway costs in State-funded initiatives.

The Minister is expected to address the matter further when appearing before the relevant Oireachtas committee in the coming sitting period.
headline: Significant overspend in cost for SUSI IT system

text:
The World Health Organisation has declared the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo a public health emergency of international concern, its highest level of alert, prompting renewed questions about the virus, the risks it poses and what the declaration means in practice.

The move comes after the disease spread from the DRC's eastern provinces to neighbouring countries, raising fears of wider regional transmission. It is only the second time an Ebola outbreak has triggered such a declaration, the first being the devastating 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa that claimed more than 11,000 lives.

So what exactly does the declaration mean, and should people in Ireland be concerned?

A public health emergency of international concern, or PHEIC, is the WHO's most serious designation. It signals that an outbreak poses a risk to other countries through international spread and requires a coordinated global response. The declaration is made by the WHO Director-General on the advice of an independent emergency committee of experts.

Crucially, the designation does not mean the disease is spreading uncontrollably across the globe. Rather, it is designed to galvanise international attention and resources, and to encourage countries to step up surveillance and preparedness measures without resorting to unnecessary trade or travel restrictions.

Ebola is a severe, often fatal viral illness. It spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person or with contaminated surfaces and materials. Symptoms include fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. The fatality rate varies between outbreaks but has historically ranged from 25 to 90 per cent.

The current outbreak has been particularly challenging owing to the security situation in eastern DRC, where armed conflict and community mistrust have hampered the response. Health workers have faced attacks, and some communities have resisted vaccination and treatment efforts.

Despite the elevated alert, the risk to Ireland and the wider European Union remains very low, according to both the HSE's Health Protection Surveillance Centre and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. Ireland has no direct flights to the affected region, and robust surveillance systems are in place at ports and airports.

The Department of Health has said it is monitoring the situation closely in coordination with European and international partners. The HSE has protocols in place for the identification, isolation and treatment of any suspected cases, and designated facilities are on standby should they be needed.

Ireland has contributed funding to the international response through Irish Aid, the Government's overseas development programme, which has directed resources to the WHO and to non-governmental organisations working on the ground in the DRC. Minister of State for Overseas Development Aid has previously indicated that Ireland would continue to support efforts to contain the outbreak.

Vaccines have played a significant role in the current response. An experimental Ebola vaccine, rVSV-ZEBOV, has been administered to tens of thousands of people in the DRC, including frontline health workers and contacts of confirmed cases. Studies suggest the vaccine is highly effective at preventing infection, and its deployment has been credited with helping to slow transmission.

However, experts caution that vaccines alone cannot end the outbreak. Effective contact tracing, safe burial practices, community engagement and access to treatment centres remain essential pillars of the response.
headline: Explained: WHO's high-risk Ebola emergency

text:
A major wildfire burning through forest land on the outskirts of Athens has forced the evacuation of several communities as firefighters battle to contain the blaze amid strong winds and soaring temperatures.

Greek authorities ordered residents in a number of areas northeast of the capital to leave their homes as the fire, which broke out in the early hours, spread rapidly through pine forest and scrubland. Thick plumes of smoke were visible across the Athens skyline, and residents reported ash falling in parts of the city centre.

The fire service said dozens of firefighters backed by water-dropping aircraft and helicopters had been deployed to tackle the blaze, which was being fanned by gusts of wind and dry conditions that have left much of the region parched.

Emergency alerts were sent to mobile phones in affected areas urging people to evacuate immediately, while police closed several roads to allow emergency vehicles through and to facilitate the movement of residents fleeing the flames.

Civil protection authorities said a number of people had been treated for respiratory problems linked to the heavy smoke, though no serious injuries or fatalities had been reported at this stage.

Greece has been gripped by an intense heatwave in recent days, with temperatures exceeding 40 degrees Celsius in parts of the country. Meteorologists have warned that the combination of extreme heat, low humidity and strong winds has created highly dangerous fire conditions across much of southern Europe.

The Greek government has placed the country's fire service on its highest level of alert, with authorities warning that the risk of further outbreaks remains critical in the coming days.

Climate scientists have pointed to a clear link between rising global temperatures and the increasing frequency and severity of wildfires across the Mediterranean region. Greece suffered one of its worst ever wildfire seasons in recent years, with blazes devastating vast tracts of forest and claiming lives.

The European Union's Copernicus Emergency Management Service has been activated to provide satellite mapping of the affected area, while neighbouring countries have offered assistance should the situation deteriorate further.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said the government was mobilising all available resources to protect lives and property, and urged residents in at-risk areas to heed evacuation orders without delay.
headline: Greece forest fire forces evacuations near Athens

text:
A man has been sentenced to seven years in prison for the fatal shooting of another man in Ballymun, Dublin, in 2021.

The Central Criminal Court heard that the accused, who is now in his late twenties, shot the victim at close range during an altercation at a flat complex in the area on the night of 14 August 2021.

The victim, who was in his early thirties, was pronounced dead at the scene after sustaining multiple gunshot wounds. Emergency services had attended the scene within minutes, but efforts to revive him proved unsuccessful.

The accused had initially been charged with murder but pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of manslaughter, which was accepted by the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Passing sentence today, Mr Justice handed down a seven-year prison term, backdated to the date of the accused's first remand in custody.

The court heard that the accused had no previous convictions of a violent nature, though he had a number of minor convictions. A probation report presented to the court assessed him as being at moderate risk of reoffending.

In his sentencing remarks, the judge said the use of a firearm in any circumstance represented an extremely grave matter and that the court had to reflect the seriousness of the offence in the sentence imposed.

The court heard victim impact statements from several family members of the deceased, who spoke of the devastating and permanent impact the loss has had on their lives. His mother told the court that she has been unable to return to the area where her son was killed.

Defence counsel told the court that his client had expressed genuine remorse for what had occurred and had cooperated with Gardaí during the investigation. Counsel said his client had experienced a troubled upbringing and had been involved in drug use from a young age.

The judge noted the mitigating factors, including the guilty plea, which he said had spared the family the ordeal of a lengthy trial. However, he said these had to be balanced against the aggravating factors, most notably the use of a firearm resulting in the loss of a human life.

Gardaí have said they are not looking for anyone else in connection with the investigation.
headline: Man jailed for seven years over fatal Ballymun shooting

text:
Thames Valley Police has confirmed it has received a number of "non-recent" allegations against the comedian and actor Russell Brand, following media reports detailing serious accusations of sexual assault and rape.

The force said it had received allegations relating to offences that are said to have taken place in the Thames Valley area, though it declined to provide further detail on the nature or number of complaints. A spokesperson confirmed that officers are working with other police forces and agencies as part of their enquiries.

The Metropolitan Police has also confirmed it has received a report of an alleged sexual assault said to have taken place in London in 2003. The force said it is assessing the information provided.

The development comes after a joint investigation by The Times, The Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches programme aired allegations from four women, who accused Brand of rape, sexual assault and emotional abuse between 2006 and 2013.

Brand, who rose to fame as a presenter on Channel 4 and BBC Radio 2, has strenuously denied the allegations. In a video posted to his social media channels before the investigation was broadcast, he said that all of his relationships had been "always consensual" and described the allegations as part of a "coordinated attack."

Since the allegations emerged, Brand's live tour dates have been paused, and his former agency, Tavistock Wood, said it had cut ties with the performer. YouTube has also moved to demonetise his channel, which has millions of subscribers.

Channel 4 said it was "deeply concerned" by the allegations and committed to investigating any complaints relating to Brand's time at the broadcaster.

The organisation Women's Aid has encouraged anyone who has experienced sexual violence to come forward to the Gardaí or their local police force, noting that specialist support services are available.
headline: 'Non-recent' allegations against Brand made to police

text:
The United States has deployed additional warships to the Caribbean amid growing fears of a potential military conflict involving Venezuela, in a significant escalation of tensions between Washington and Caracas.

The Pentagon confirmed the naval deployment, which includes guided-missile destroyers and other vessels, saying the move was intended to bolster security in the region. Officials said the ships would be used to support counter-narcotics operations, though analysts have noted the scale of the deployment goes well beyond what would typically be required for such missions.

The move comes against a backdrop of deepening political crisis in Venezuela, where President Nicolás Maduro continues to face international criticism over his government's record on democracy and human rights. The administration of US President Donald Trump has taken an increasingly hawish stance towards the Maduro government, with senior officials refusing to rule out military options in recent weeks.

Speaking at the White House, Trump said "all options remain on the table" with respect to Venezuela, without elaborating on what specific actions the US might consider. The comments echo similar language used by the president on previous occasions when discussing the South American nation.

Venezuela's foreign ministry condemned the deployment as a "provocation" and an act of "imperial aggression," calling on the international community to reject what it described as US interference in the region's affairs. Maduro has accused Washington of attempting to orchestrate a coup against his government.

The European Union has urged restraint on all sides, calling for a diplomatic resolution to the crisis. Several Latin American nations have also expressed concern about the prospect of military action, warning that any conflict could trigger a fresh wave of migration in a region already struggling to absorb millions of Venezuelan refugees.

Ireland's Department of Foreign Affairs has not yet issued a specific statement on the latest deployment, though the Government has previously expressed concern about the humanitarian situation in Venezuela and has supported EU calls for free and fair elections in the country.

The crisis has been compounded by Venezuela's ongoing economic collapse, which has seen hyperinflation, severe shortages of food and medicine, and the displacement of more than seven million people since 2014, according to United Nations figures.

Military analysts have cautioned that any armed confrontation would carry enormous risks, not least for the civilian population already enduring what the UN has described as one of the worst humanitarian emergencies in the region's recent history.

The deployment is expected to be discussed at the UN Security Council in the coming days, where divisions between Western nations and Venezuela's allies, including Russia and China, are likely to be laid bare once again.
headline: US deploys warships amid fears of Venezuela conflict

text:
The outcome of ongoing trade negotiations between the European Union and the United States remains far from guaranteed, a senior government figure has cautioned, as fears continue to mount over the potential impact of tariffs on Irish exporters.

Speaking after a meeting of EU trade ministers in Brussels, Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin said that while there had been "constructive engagement" between both sides, significant differences remained and it would be premature to assume a deal was within reach.

"The outcome is not certain," the Tánaiste said. "There is a willingness to engage, but the gap between the EU position and what the US administration is seeking is still considerable. We need to be realistic about that."

Ireland, with its heavy reliance on transatlantic trade, is considered particularly exposed to any escalation in tariff measures. The agrifood sector, the pharmaceutical industry and the technology sector have all been identified as vulnerable should negotiations break down.

The Taoiseach Simon Harris had earlier spoken with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to stress the importance of securing a resolution that would protect Irish and European economic interests. A Government spokesperson confirmed that Ireland's specific concerns, including the depth of its trade relationship with the US, had been communicated clearly to the Commission's negotiating team.

Enterprise Ireland has been working with exporters to assess their exposure and explore potential market diversification strategies, though industry representatives have warned that the US market cannot easily be replaced for many Irish firms.

Ibec, the business lobby group, said uncertainty alone was already having a chilling effect on investment decisions. "Irish businesses need clarity," said its head of trade policy. "Prolonged uncertainty is almost as damaging as the tariffs themselves."

Opposition TDs have pressed the Government on its contingency planning. Sinn Féin's spokesperson on enterprise called for a dedicated support package for affected businesses, while Labour accused the Government of being too slow to prepare for what it described as a foreseeable crisis.

In the Dáil, Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke said the Government was monitoring the situation "hour by hour" and was in constant contact with Brussels. He said any support measures would be calibrated to the final outcome of the talks and warned against premature interventions that could send the wrong signal to either side.

EU officials have indicated that the next round of technical discussions is expected to take place within the coming days, with a political-level meeting possible before the end of the month. The European Commission has maintained that it is negotiating from a position of unity among the 27 member states, though diplomatic sources have acknowledged that internal differences over the pace and scope of concessions remain.

The euro weakened slightly against the dollar on the back of the continued uncertainty, while Irish-listed stocks with significant US revenue exposure saw modest declines in early trading.
headline: Outcome of EU-US tariff talks 'not certain'

text:
A bitter dispute has erupted in the French countryside after an unlikely pairing of wolves was spotted roaming farmland in a region where the predators had not been seen for more than a century, reigniting tensions between conservationists and the agricultural community.

The two wolves — believed to be a male that dispersed from an Alpine pack and a female whose origins remain unclear — were confirmed by French wildlife authorities to have established a territory in the hills of the Aveyron département in southern France. It is the first known breeding pair in the area since wolves were hunted to local extinction in the late 19th century.

Livestock farmers in the region have reacted with alarm, with several reporting attacks on sheep flocks in recent weeks. The French farmers' union FNSEA has demanded immediate intervention, calling for the pair to be culled before they produce offspring and the local population becomes established.

"We cannot allow what happened in the Alps to repeat itself here," said one sheep farmer, who asked not to be named. "We are already struggling to make a living. Wolves will finish us off."

France's wolf population has grown steadily since the animals naturally recolonised the Alps from Italy in the 1990s. There are now an estimated 1,100 wolves across the country, a recovery that environmental groups have hailed as a conservation success story but which has provoked fury in rural communities where sheep farming remains a cornerstone of the local economy.

The French government compensated farmers for more than 12,000 animals killed by wolves last year, at a cost of several million euro. Under a strictly regulated protocol, authorities can authorise the lethal removal of individual wolves in areas where attacks on livestock are particularly severe, though the species remains protected under both French and EU law.

Environmental campaigners have urged calm, arguing that the arrival of wolves in new territories is a natural and ecologically beneficial process. France Nature Environnement, the country's largest federation of environmental organisations, said the focus should be on helping farmers adapt through the use of guard dogs, improved fencing and shepherding support rather than resorting to killing.

"Every time wolves appear somewhere new, we hear the same calls for extermination," said a spokesperson for the organisation. "But coexistence is possible if the political will is there."

The row echoes similar debates playing out across Europe, including in Ireland, where the question of rewilding and the potential reintroduction of apex predators has surfaced periodically in public discourse. While there are no plans to reintroduce wolves to Ireland, conservation groups here have pointed to the French experience as evidence of both the possibilities and the complexities involved in restoring species to landscapes from which they were long ago driven out.

The Irish wolf was hunted to extinction by the late 18th century, and any discussion of its return tends to provoke strong reactions from farming organisations such as the IFA, which have consistently argued that the realities of modern Irish agriculture are incompatible with the presence of large predators.

In France, the standoff in Aveyron shows no sign of resolution.
headline: Unlikely wolf pair sparks row in rural France

text:
Gardaí seized nine mobile phones from the home of a well-known public figure during the execution of a search warrant, a court has heard.

Details of the seizure emerged during a hearing at Dublin District Court, where a legal challenge to the retention of the devices is being mounted on behalf of the individual, who cannot be named for legal reasons.

The court was told that members of An Garda Síochána attended the property in the greater Dublin area on foot of a warrant issued under the Criminal Justice (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act. During the search, officers removed nine mobile phones along with a number of other electronic devices, including a laptop and a tablet.

A solicitor acting for the individual told Judge Mary O'Leary that the seizure was "wholly disproportionate" and had caused significant disruption to their client's personal and professional life. The solicitor argued that several of the phones were no longer in active use and contained no material relevant to the Garda investigation.

"The retention of nine separate devices, many of which are legacy phones with no bearing whatsoever on the matters under investigation, is excessive by any standard," the solicitor submitted.

However, a Garda sergeant gave evidence that the phones were seized as part of an ongoing investigation and that digital forensic examination of the devices was required to establish their relevance. The sergeant told the court that the examination process was continuing and that it would be premature to return any of the devices at this stage.

The sergeant added that all seized items had been properly catalogued and stored in accordance with Garda procedures and that the investigation was being conducted as expeditiously as possible.

Judge O'Leary noted the submissions from both sides and said she was satisfied that the Gardaí had acted within the scope of the warrant. However, she urged that the forensic examination be completed "without unnecessary delay" and said she would revisit the matter if there were unreasonable hold-ups.

The case was adjourned to a date next month to allow for an update on the progress of the forensic analysis.

The nature of the investigation has not been disclosed, and no charges have been brought. The individual at the centre of the case has not commented publicly on the matter.
headline: Gardaí 'seized nine phones' from celebrity's home

text:
Israel goes to the polls today in what has become one of the most consequential and bitterly fought elections in the country's history, with the political future of former prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu — and the very character of Israeli democracy — hanging in the balance.

It is the fifth time in less than four years that Israeli voters have been asked to cast their ballots, a remarkable cycle of political deadlock that has left the country without a stable government for extended periods and exhausted an electorate weary of repeat trips to polling stations.

At the centre of the contest, as has been the case for more than a decade, is Netanyahu himself. The longest-serving prime minister in Israeli history is fighting to reclaim the office he lost in 2021, when a fragile coalition of ideologically disparate parties united with the sole purpose of ousting him from power. That coalition, led first by Naftali Bennett and then by Yair Lapid, eventually collapsed under the weight of its own contradictions, triggering the latest election.

For Netanyahu, the stakes could hardly be higher. The 73-year-old Likud leader is currently standing trial on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust — allegations he strenuously denies. A return to power could open the door to legislation that would grant him immunity from prosecution, a prospect that has alarmed his opponents and drawn warnings from legal experts about the erosion of judicial independence.

Opinion polls in the final days of the campaign have consistently suggested that Netanyahu's right-wing bloc, which includes far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties, holds a narrow advantage over the rival camp led by Lapid, the caretaker prime minister. However, the margins are tight enough that the outcome remains genuinely uncertain, and much will depend on turnout and the performance of smaller parties hovering near the electoral threshold.

What has drawn particular international attention is the composition of Netanyahu's likely coalition partners. Itamar Ben Gvir, leader of the far-right Jewish Power party, and Bezalel Smotrich of the Religious Zionism alliance are expected to demand senior cabinet positions in any Netanyahu-led government. Both men have advocated hardline policies towards Palestinians, including the annexation of parts of the occupied West Bank and the weakening of the judiciary.

Their potential elevation to positions of power has prompted concern among Western allies, including the European Union, and within Israel's own security establishment. Several former military and intelligence chiefs have spoken out publicly against a government that would include the far-right factions, warning it could destabilise the region and damage Israel's international standing.

For the Irish Government, which has consistently called for a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, the election result could have significant implications. A right-wing Israeli government committed to settlement expansion would likely deepen tensions with Dublin, which has been among the more vocal EU member states on Palestinian rights. Ireland's Occupied Territories Bill, which would ban trade with illegal settlements, remains a point of contention in Irish-Israeli relations.

On the other side of the political divide, Lapid has sought to present himself as a unifying figure capable of preserving Israel's democratic institutions and maintaining relationships with Western partners.
headline: What's at stake in Israel's elections?

text:
A man accused of assaulting a tourist in Dublin city centre has been refused bail after a judge heard he posed a flight risk and had a number of previous convictions.

The 32-year-old appeared before Dublin District Court this morning charged with assault causing harm, contrary to Section 3 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997.

The court heard the alleged incident took place on O'Connell Street in the early hours of Saturday morning. Gardaí told the court that the accused allegedly struck the victim, a 45-year-old Italian national who was visiting Dublin on holiday, in an unprovoked attack.

The tourist was taken to the Mater Misericordiae University Hospital, where he was treated for facial injuries including a fractured cheekbone. He has since been discharged.

Detective Garda Sarah Brennan told the court she objected to bail on a number of grounds. She said the accused had 14 previous convictions, including several for public order offences and two for assault. She told the judge she believed the accused was a flight risk, noting that he had failed to appear in court on two previous occasions in relation to other matters.

Det Gda Brennan also expressed concerns that the accused could interfere with witnesses if released, telling the court that the injured party had provided a statement to gardaí and was cooperating with the investigation from abroad.

A solicitor for the accused told the court his client was willing to abide by any conditions the court saw fit to impose, including signing on daily at his local Garda station and surrendering his passport. He said his client had a fixed address in the Dublin 1 area and strong ties to the community.

However, Judge Michael Collins said he was not satisfied that any conditions would adequately address the concerns raised by the prosecution. He remanded the accused in custody to appear again before the court next week.

The judge directed that the Director of Public Prosecutions be furnished with a file in relation to the matter.

The accused, who cannot be named for legal reasons, spoke only to confirm his name and address during the brief hearing.
headline: Man in court for assault on tourist in Dublin denied bail

text:
The Government has announced a further expansion of the free contraception scheme, extending eligibility to additional age groups as part of its ongoing commitment to improving access to reproductive healthcare across the country.

The scheme, which was first introduced in August 2022 for women aged 17 to 25, has now been broadened to include women up to the age of 35. The expansion had been signalled in recent months and was confirmed today by the Minister for Health.

Speaking this afternoon, the Minister said the move represented a "significant step forward" in removing financial barriers to contraception and supporting women in making informed choices about their reproductive health.

"We know that the cost of contraception can be a real obstacle for many women, and this expansion ensures that a much larger cohort will now be able to avail of free services," the Minister said.

Under the scheme, eligible women can access a range of contraceptive options free of charge, including the contraceptive pill, long-acting reversible contraceptives such as implants, injections and intrauterine devices, as well as the costs associated with fitting and removal. The services are provided through participating GPs and pharmacies nationwide.

The Irish Family Planning Association welcomed the announcement, describing it as a "positive and progressive" development, while calling on the Government to commit to eventually making the scheme available to all women of reproductive age regardless of their age bracket.

Since its introduction, the scheme has seen strong uptake. Figures from the HSE indicate that hundreds of thousands of claims have been processed, suggesting significant demand existed for publicly funded contraceptive services.

The expansion is expected to cost the Exchequer an additional sum in the region of tens of millions of euro annually, though the Department of Health has indicated that the measure is likely to deliver savings in other areas of the health service over time.

Opposition TDs have broadly supported the policy but have questioned the pace of the rollout, with several calling for the scheme to be extended to all women without age restrictions and for greater investment in sexual health services more broadly.

The Irish College of General Practitioners said its members had reported positive feedback from patients since the scheme's inception and that the expansion would be welcomed in practices around the country, though it stressed the importance of ensuring adequate resourcing and staffing to meet anticipated increased demand.

Women who wish to avail of the scheme are advised to contact their GP or a participating healthcare provider to discuss their options. A full list of participating providers is available through the HSE website.
headline: Government expands free contraception scheme

text:
The European Court of Justice has rejected the Irish Government's argument that it is not bound by certain EU obligations regarding the reception conditions of asylum seekers, in a ruling that could have significant implications for how the State treats those seeking international protection.

The Luxembourg-based court found that Ireland cannot selectively opt out of provisions under the EU's recast Reception Conditions Directive while remaining part of the Common European Asylum System. The Government had argued that, due to Ireland's unique opt-in protocol under EU treaties, it was not obliged to comply with all aspects of the directive.

The case centred on the standards of housing, healthcare and access to the labour market that EU member states are required to provide to people who have applied for international protection. Ireland had maintained that its position under Protocol 21 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union afforded it greater discretion in how it implemented these measures.

However, the ECJ ruled that once Ireland opted into the directive, it was required to transpose and apply it in its entirety, and could not cherry-pick which elements to implement.

The ruling is likely to intensify pressure on the Government at a time when it is already facing significant challenges in providing accommodation and services to asylum seekers. The Department of Integration has been struggling to secure sufficient capacity, with thousands of people in emergency accommodation and some left without any State-provided shelter.

Opposition TDs were quick to seize on the judgment, with several calling on the Government to outline how it intends to bring Ireland into full compliance with the directive. Sinn Féin's spokesperson on immigration said the ruling exposed what they described as a pattern of the Government failing to meet its legal obligations to some of the most vulnerable people in the State.

The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission welcomed the decision, saying it affirmed the rights of asylum seekers under EU law and underscored the need for Ireland to uphold the standards to which it had committed.

A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said the Government was studying the judgment carefully and would take whatever steps were necessary to ensure compliance. The spokesperson declined to comment further while the legal implications of the ruling were being assessed.

Legal experts said the decision could also open the door to further legal challenges from asylum seekers who believe their reception conditions have fallen below the standards required under EU law. Dr Liam Thornton, a lecturer in law at University College Dublin who specialises in asylum and immigration law, said the ruling sent a clear message that Ireland could not operate outside the framework it had voluntarily signed up to.

The case had been referred to the ECJ following proceedings in the Irish High Court, where the issue of Ireland's obligations under the directive had arisen in the context of a challenge brought by an asylum seeker regarding their living conditions.

The Government is expected to bring a memo to Cabinet in the coming weeks setting out how it plans to respond to the judgment.
headline: ECJ rejects Govt's claim over asylum seeker obligations

text:
The Irish husband of a woman who died from suspected botulism poisoning in France remains in hospital as investigations continue into the source of the contamination.

The man, who is understood to be in his 50s, is being treated at a hospital in Bordeaux where his condition is described as serious but stable. His wife, who held dual Irish and French citizenship, died last week after the couple fell ill following a meal at their home in the south-west of France.

French health authorities have been working to establish the precise source of the botulism, with initial investigations focusing on preserved food products consumed by the couple. Botulism is a rare but potentially fatal illness caused by toxins produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum, which can develop in improperly preserved or canned foods.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has confirmed it is providing consular assistance to the man's family. A spokesperson said the department does not comment on the details of individual cases but confirmed it was aware of the situation and was in contact with the family.

The couple's adult children have travelled to France to be at their father's bedside. Family members in Ireland have asked for privacy during what they described as an extremely difficult time.

Botulism cases, while rare across Europe, can occur in clusters linked to contaminated food products. French authorities are understood to be examining whether any commercially produced items may be linked to the case, though no public health alert has been issued to date.

The Food Safety Authority of Ireland said it was monitoring the situation but noted there was currently no indication of any risk to consumers in Ireland.

Medical experts say that botulism requires urgent treatment with an antitoxin, and that delays in diagnosis can significantly affect outcomes. Symptoms typically include difficulty swallowing, muscle weakness, and paralysis, and can appear between 12 and 36 hours after consuming contaminated food.

The man's family are understood to be in regular contact with the Irish Embassy in Paris, which is liaising with French medical and investigative authorities on their behalf.
headline: Irish husband of botulism victim remains hospitalised

text:
As Pope Francis marks another milestone in a pontificate that has reshaped the Catholic Church in ways few could have predicted, it is worth reflecting on the moments that have come to define his papacy.

From the very first moments after his election in March 2013, it was clear that Jorge Mario Bergoglio intended to do things differently. When he stepped onto the balcony of St Peter's Basilica and greeted the crowd with a simple "Buonasera" — good evening — before asking them to pray for him, the tone was set. He eschewed the traditional red papal mozzetta in favour of the plain white cassock, a visual signal of the humility that would become his hallmark.

His decision to live in the Casa Santa Marta guesthouse rather than the Apostolic Palace was another early marker. By choosing a modest suite over the grand papal apartments, Francis signalled a desire to remain close to ordinary people and avoid the isolation that can come with high office. It was a decision that resonated strongly with Catholics in Ireland and around the world who had grown weary of perceived excess within the Church hierarchy.

The publication of Evangelii Gaudium in November 2013, his first major apostolic exhortation, laid out a vision for a Church that was missionary, merciful and unafraid to engage with the messiness of the modern world. In it, he delivered a stinging critique of unfettered capitalism, describing trickle-down economics as a theory that "has never been confirmed by the facts" and declaring that the current economic system was one of exclusion and inequality. The document electrified progressive Catholics and drew sharp criticism from free-market advocates.

His 2015 encyclical Laudato Si', on care for the environment, was arguably the most significant papal document in a generation. Published months before the landmark Paris climate agreement, it framed environmental destruction as a moral and spiritual crisis, coining the phrase "integral ecology" and calling for urgent action on climate change. The encyclical was widely credited with helping to build momentum for the Paris accord and established Francis as a leading global voice on the environment, a role he has continued to embrace.

The declaration of the Extraordinary Jubilee Year of Mercy in 2015 was a moment that captured the essence of Francis' theological vision. By placing mercy at the centre of Church life, he sought to reorient Catholicism away from what he saw as an excessive focus on doctrine and rules and towards accompaniment and compassion. The image of the Pope opening the Holy Door at St Peter's Basilica became one of the defining symbols of his papacy.

His visit to Ireland in August 2018 for the World Meeting of Families was a moment of profound significance for the Church in this country. Arriving into a vastly changed Ireland from the one that had welcomed Pope John Paul II in 1979, Francis acknowledged the "open wound" of clerical sexual abuse and met with survivors. The visit, while historic, also laid bare the scale of the challenge facing the Church in Ireland, with attendance at the closing Mass in the Phoenix Park falling well short of the numbers that had gathered nearly four decades earlier.
headline: 10 notable moments from Francis' pontificate so far

text:
The United Nations has demanded a "prompt" and independent investigation into an Israeli military strike near a hospital in Beirut, which left several people dead and dozens more injured.

The strike, which hit in the vicinity of a medical facility in the Lebanese capital, drew immediate condemnation from UN officials, who said attacks near hospitals and other protected sites may constitute violations of international humanitarian law.

The UN's human rights office said it was "deeply alarmed" by the incident and called on all parties to respect their obligations under the laws of war, including the protection of medical infrastructure and civilian lives.

"There must be a prompt, thorough, independent and transparent investigation into this strike," a spokesperson for the office said, adding that those responsible for any violations must be held accountable.

Lebanon's health ministry confirmed casualties from the attack, though precise figures remained subject to revision as rescue workers continued to search through rubble at the scene. Footage shared on social media showed significant damage to buildings surrounding the hospital, with emergency crews working to evacuate patients and staff.

Israel's military said it was targeting Hezbollah infrastructure and accused the Iran-backed group of deliberately embedding its operations in civilian areas, including near hospitals. Hezbollah has previously denied such allegations.
