The Irish Government has repeatedly called for restraint in the region and for full compliance with international humanitarian law. Ireland, which holds a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council, has been among the most vocal European nations in pressing for accountability over civilian casualties in both Lebanon and Gaza.

The World Health Organisation has warned that attacks near medical facilities have a devastating ripple effect, discouraging civilians from seeking urgent care and undermining an already strained healthcare system. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said hospitals must never be used as targets or as shields.

The latest strike comes amid an intensification of Israeli military operations in Lebanon, which have displaced more than a million people since hostilities escalated in recent months. Diplomatic efforts to broker a ceasefire have so far failed to produce a breakthrough, though talks are understood to be continuing behind the scenes.

Human rights organisations, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, have echoed the UN's call for an independent probe, warning that a pattern of strikes near civilian infrastructure demands urgent international scrutiny.
headline: UN demand 'prompt' probe into strike near Beirut hospital

text:
Kieran Cuddihy has been named as the new presenter of RTÉ Radio 1's Liveline, taking over the reins of one of the most iconic programmes in Irish broadcasting.

The Today FM presenter will succeed Joe Duffy, who announced earlier this year that he would be stepping down from the long-running phone-in show after more than two decades at the helm.

Cuddihy, who currently co-presents The Last Word on Today FM, is well known to Irish radio audiences and has built a reputation as a sharp and engaging interviewer. His appointment was confirmed by RTÉ on Wednesday.

Speaking about his new role, Cuddihy said he was honoured to be entrusted with a programme that holds such a special place in the hearts of listeners across the country.

"Liveline is more than a radio programme – it is a national institution. Joe Duffy made it his own, and I have enormous respect for what he built over the years. I'm looking forward to bringing my own energy to the show while staying true to what makes it so important to so many people," he said.

RTÉ's head of Radio 1, Peter Woods, said the organisation was delighted to welcome Cuddihy to the station.

"Kieran is an outstanding broadcaster who understands the power of letting people tell their own stories. We are confident he is the right person to lead Liveline into its next chapter," he said.

Liveline has been a staple of the RTÉ Radio 1 afternoon schedule for decades, giving ordinary members of the public a platform to discuss the issues affecting their lives. Under Joe Duffy's stewardship, the programme became one of the most listened-to shows in the State, regularly setting the national agenda and prompting political and social debate.

Duffy, who took over the programme in 1999, confirmed his departure earlier this year, describing it as the right time to move on. He received widespread tributes from across Irish public life for his contribution to broadcasting.

Cuddihy is expected to take up his new position in the coming weeks. His departure from Today FM, which is owned by Bauer Media Audio Ireland, will leave a significant gap in that station's schedule, though no announcement has yet been made regarding his replacement.
headline: Kieran Cuddihy named as new Liveline presenter

text:
A renowned Northern Irish mountaineer has died after successfully reaching the summit of one of the world's highest peaks in the Himalayas.

Noel Hanna, who was from Dromara in Co Down, died during his descent from Annapurna, the tenth highest mountain in the world, which stands at 8,091 metres.

The experienced climber, who was in his mid-50s, had summited Mount Everest a number of times and was widely regarded as one of Ireland's most accomplished high-altitude mountaineers.

Reports from Nepal suggest that Mr Hanna encountered difficulties during the descent from the summit, which is considered one of the most dangerous peaks in the Himalayas due to its avalanche-prone slopes and unpredictable weather conditions.

Annapurna has one of the highest fatality-to-summit ratios of any 8,000-metre peak, with climbers facing significant risks from avalanches, crevasses and extreme weather even after reaching the top.

Mr Hanna had built a formidable reputation in the mountaineering world over many years, having scaled numerous peaks across the globe. He had previously spoken publicly about the risks involved in high-altitude climbing but said his passion for the mountains continued to drive him forward.

Tributes have been pouring in from the climbing community both in Ireland and internationally. Fellow mountaineers described him as an inspirational figure who had encouraged many others to take up the sport.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has said it is aware of the case and is providing consular assistance.

Mr Hanna is survived by his family in Co Down, who have asked for privacy at this difficult time.
headline: NI climber Noel Hanna dies after scaling Himalayan peak

text:
Belarus has agreed to host Russian tactical nuclear weapons on its territory following what Western officials describe as sustained pressure from Moscow, in a move that has drawn sharp condemnation from Kyiv and its allies across Europe.

The development, confirmed by Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko during a televised address, marks a significant escalation in the militarisation of the region since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Lukashenko framed the decision as a necessary step to protect Belarus from what he characterised as growing threats from NATO.

However, Western intelligence assessments suggest the Belarusian leader had little choice in the matter, with Moscow exerting considerable diplomatic and economic leverage over Minsk to secure the arrangement. Belarus is heavily dependent on Russian energy supplies and financial support, and Lukashenko owes his continued hold on power in large part to the Kremlin's backing during the mass protests that swept the country in 2020.

Russian President Vladimir Putin first announced plans to station tactical nuclear weapons in Belarus last year, drawing comparisons with the United States' long-standing practice of hosting nuclear warheads in several European NATO member states. Moscow has insisted the weapons will remain under Russian operational control, though the precise details of command arrangements have not been made public.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the deployment, calling it an attempt to hold the entire region hostage. Speaking at a press conference, he urged the international community to respond with further sanctions against both Russia and Belarus.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte described the move as dangerous and irresponsible, though he stressed that the alliance had not observed any change in Russia's nuclear posture that would require a shift in NATO's own nuclear deterrence stance.

The development is likely to feature prominently in discussions at the next meeting of EU foreign affairs ministers, where Ireland's position on the broader security implications for Europe will come under scrutiny. Ireland, while militarily neutral, has been a strong supporter of EU sanctions against both Russia and Belarus since the outbreak of the war.

Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin has previously described Russia's nuclear sabre-rattling as deeply destabilising and has backed calls for a robust European response. A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs said Ireland remains firmly opposed to any actions that undermine the global non-proliferation regime.

Arms control experts have warned that the stationing of nuclear weapons in Belarus effectively collapses one of the last remaining pillars of the post-Cold War security architecture in Europe. Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union, Belarus, along with Ukraine and Kazakhstan, had voluntarily given up nuclear weapons stationed on its territory, a decision that was seen at the time as a landmark achievement in non-proliferation.

The move also raises questions about the security of the weapons themselves and the risk of miscalculation in an already volatile region. Belarus shares borders with three NATO and EU member states — Poland, Lithuania and Latvia — all of which have expressed alarm at the deployment.

Poland's government has called for an emergency consultation under Article 4 of the NATO treaty, which allows any member to raise concerns about threats to their territorial integrity or security.
headline: Belarus to hold Russian nuclear arms after 'pressure'

text:
A rare Roman coin bearing the image of Marcus Junius Brutus, one of the most infamous figures in ancient history, is set to go under the hammer at auction in Geneva later this month.

The gold aureus, which dates to 42 BC, depicts Brutus on its obverse and is considered one of the finest surviving examples of its kind. Auction house specialists have estimated the coin could fetch in excess of €500,000 when it goes to sale, though some numismatic experts believe it could far exceed that figure given the intense interest it has already attracted from private collectors and institutions worldwide.

Brutus is best known as one of the leading conspirators in the assassination of Julius Caesar on the Ides of March in 44 BC, a moment that would alter the course of the Roman Republic and eventually give rise to the Roman Empire. The coin is believed to have been struck to pay Brutus's legions in the period following the assassination, as he and fellow conspirator Cassius waged war against the forces of Mark Antony and Octavian.

Coins from this period bearing Brutus's likeness are exceptionally scarce. The most famous of these is the so-called "Eid Mar" denarius, which depicts two daggers flanking a cap of liberty on its reverse, a direct reference to Caesar's killing. While the coin being offered in Geneva is not of the Eid Mar type, experts say its rarity and historical significance place it among the most important Roman coins ever to come to market.

"This is a piece that transcends numismatics," said one specialist at the Geneva auction house. "It is a tangible connection to one of the most dramatic episodes in Western history."

The auction comes amid a period of surging demand for ancient coins among wealthy collectors, with several high-profile sales in recent years setting new records. In 2020, an Eid Mar aureus sold for a record-breaking sum in excess of €3.2 million at auction in London.

The sale is scheduled to take place on 28 November at the Geneva auction rooms, with bidding also available online.
headline: Rare Roman coin featuring Brutus up for auction in Geneva

text:
Mark Rutte has barely had time to settle into his office at NATO headquarters in Brussels before confronting what may be the most daunting set of challenges any Secretary General has faced since the alliance's founding in 1949. The former Dutch prime minister, who took over from Jens Stoltenberg in October, must navigate a dramatically shifting transatlantic landscape in which the two most consequential figures — Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin — are pulling the alliance in radically different directions.

The return of Trump to the White House in January has injected fresh uncertainty into the very foundations of the transatlantic compact. During his first term, the former and now current US president repeatedly questioned the value of NATO, publicly mused about withdrawing from the alliance, and berated European members for failing to meet the two per cent of GDP defence spending target. Now back in power, Trump has shown little sign of softening that stance, and his unpredictable approach to diplomacy has left European capitals scrambling to demonstrate their commitment to collective defence.

Rutte, widely regarded as a skilled consensus-builder after more than 13 years leading coalition governments in The Hague, will need every ounce of that political dexterity to manage the Trump relationship. The Dutchman is said to have cultivated a personal rapport with Trump during his time as prime minister, reportedly using a combination of flattery and directness that few European leaders have managed to master. Whether that rapport can survive the pressures of office remains to be seen.

The challenge from the east is no less formidable. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now grinding through its third year, continues to dominate the alliance's strategic calculus. Putin has shown no meaningful willingness to negotiate an end to the conflict on terms that Ukraine or its Western backers could accept, and Russian forces have made incremental gains in the Donbas region in recent months. NATO must continue to support Kyiv while simultaneously preparing for the possibility that the war could escalate or spill beyond Ukraine's borders.

The question of Ukraine's eventual membership of the alliance remains one of the most divisive issues among the 32 member states. While countries on NATO's eastern flank, particularly Poland and the Baltic states, have pushed aggressively for a concrete pathway to Ukrainian accession, others have urged caution, wary of provoking Moscow further or making commitments that cannot be honoured while active hostilities continue. Trump, for his part, has expressed scepticism about continued US support for Ukraine, raising fears in European capitals that Washington could seek to broker a deal over Kyiv's head.

Defence spending represents another acute pressure point. The two per cent target, once considered aspirational, is now widely viewed as a floor rather than a ceiling. Trump has gone further, suggesting that allies should be spending three per cent or even more. While several European nations have dramatically increased their defence budgets since Russia's invasion of Ukraine — with Poland leading the way at approximately four per cent of GDP — others continue to lag behind. Rutte must find a way to maintain pressure on laggards without fracturing alliance unity.

The new Secretary General also inherits a NATO that is grappling with challenges far beyond Europe's eastern frontier.
headline: Trump to Putin: what key challenges face Rutte at NATO?

text:
The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has released its first full-colour images of the cosmos, offering an unprecedented glimpse into the deep universe as part of a mission to map the largest-ever survey of the sky.

The images, which were unveiled at a press event today, showcase the telescope's remarkable ability to capture vast swathes of the sky in extraordinary detail, a capability that scientists say will be crucial in the quest to understand the mysterious forces of dark matter and dark energy that make up roughly 95% of the universe.

Among the first images released are stunning views of galaxy clusters, nebulae and distant star-forming regions, each demonstrating Euclid's unique capacity to observe both visible and infrared light across enormous areas of sky in a single observation.

ESA's director of science, Professor Carole Mundell, described the images as "breathtaking" and said they represented a significant milestone for the €1.4 billion mission, which launched from Cape Canaveral in Florida in July aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.

"These are just the first steps, but already we can see the incredible potential of Euclid to transform our understanding of the cosmos," Prof Mundell said.

Over the next six years, Euclid will survey more than a third of the sky, cataloguing billions of galaxies stretching back some 10 billion light years. By mapping the shapes, positions and movements of these galaxies with extraordinary precision, scientists hope to build the most detailed three-dimensional map of the universe ever constructed.

The central aim of the mission is to shed light on why the expansion of the universe appears to be accelerating, a phenomenon attributed to dark energy but which remains one of the deepest puzzles in modern physics. The telescope will also help researchers trace the distribution of dark matter, the invisible substance believed to act as a kind of cosmic scaffolding holding galaxies together.

Irish researchers are among those contributing to the Euclid mission. Scientists at several Irish universities have been involved in the broader Euclid Consortium, a collaboration of more than 2,000 researchers from 300 institutes across 13 European countries, as well as the United States, Canada and Japan.

Professor Peter Gallagher of the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies has previously highlighted the importance of Irish involvement in ESA missions, noting that Ireland's membership of the agency provides researchers and Irish industry with opportunities to participate in cutting-edge space science.

Ireland contributes to ESA through its annual membership fees, which are administered by Enterprise Ireland on behalf of the Government. The country's investment in ESA has grown in recent years, reflecting a broader ambition to expand Ireland's role in the European space sector.

Euclid is now positioned at the second Lagrange point, a gravitationally stable spot roughly 1.5 million kilometres from Earth, where it orbits alongside the James Webb Space Telescope. While Webb is designed to observe individual targets in extraordinary detail, Euclid's strength lies in its ability to survey enormous portions of the sky, making the two telescopes complementary rather than rivals.

Scientists involved in the project say the initial images exceeded their expectations and that the telescope's instruments are performing superbly.
headline: Europe's Euclid space telescope releases first images

text:
A new e-scooter sharing scheme is set to be trialled in Waterford city, even as safety concerns continue to dominate the debate around the use of the electric vehicles on Irish streets.

Waterford City and County Council confirmed it is working with a private operator to roll out a docked e-scooter programme in the city centre, with designated pick-up and drop-off points planned for key locations including the Quays, the Viking Triangle and Waterford Institute of Technology.

The initiative comes after the Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023 provided a legal framework for e-scooters, which had previously occupied a grey area in Irish traffic law. Under the legislation, users must be at least 16 years of age, e-scooters are limited to a maximum speed of 20 kilometres per hour, and riders are not permitted to use them on motorways or footpaths.

However, the announcement has drawn a mixed response from locals and advocacy groups. Waterford councillors heard representations from residents who expressed concern about the potential for collisions with pedestrians, particularly older people and those with visual impairments.

The Irish Wheelchair Association has previously called for robust enforcement of any regulations governing e-scooters, warning that irresponsible use poses a serious risk to vulnerable road users.

Cllr Joe Kelly said the council is taking the concerns seriously. "We want to offer people a sustainable transport option, but not at the expense of pedestrian safety. The docking system is specifically designed to prevent the kind of pavement clutter you see in other European cities," he said.

The Gardaí in the Waterford division said they would be monitoring compliance with the new regulations closely and warned that riders found in breach of the rules could face fixed charge penalties.

A spokesperson for the council said a public consultation period will be held before the scheme is formally launched, with a view to having the e-scooters operational by early summer. The council added that the programme would be reviewed after an initial six-month period, with data on usage patterns and any reported incidents to be assessed before a decision is made on its continuation.

The Road Safety Authority has urged all e-scooter users to wear helmets, remain visible and exercise caution, particularly at junctions and in areas with heavy foot traffic.
headline: Waterford e-scooter initiative amid safety concerns

text:
A man is due to appear before a sitting of the District Court today in connection with an investigation into human trafficking.

The man, who is aged in his 30s, was arrested by members of An Garda Síochána yesterday as part of an ongoing investigation into suspected human trafficking for the purposes of labour exploitation.

He was detained at a Garda station in Dublin under the provisions of the Criminal Law (Human Trafficking) Act 2008 and was questioned by investigating gardaí over the course of yesterday evening.

It is understood the investigation has been under way for a number of months, with gardaí working alongside the Garda National Protective Services Bureau (GNPSB), which has lead responsibility for investigating human trafficking offences in the State.

The arrest follows a search operation carried out at a premises in the greater Dublin area, during which a number of items were seized for forensic examination.

Gardaí have said investigations into the matter are ongoing and have appealed to anyone with information to contact their local Garda station or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.

Human trafficking remains a significant concern for law enforcement agencies across Ireland and Europe. According to the Department of Justice, Ireland has identified a growing number of suspected victims of trafficking in recent years, with labour exploitation accounting for an increasing proportion of cases.

Support services for victims of human trafficking are available through the HSE's anti-human trafficking team and a number of non-governmental organisations operating in the State.

No further details are being released at this time as the matter is now before the courts.
headline: Man due in court in human trafficking investigation

text:
The latest episode of RTÉ News's podcast examines US President Donald Trump's claim of credit for the ceasefire agreement in Gaza, as the deal to pause hostilities between Israel and Hamas took effect over the weekend.

Trump has been vocal in praising the agreement as a personal diplomatic achievement, telling supporters that the deal would not have happened without his involvement. The president, who took office just days after the ceasefire was announced, has sought to position himself as the driving force behind negotiations that had in fact been under way for months under the Biden administration.

The ceasefire, which includes a phased release of hostages held by Hamas in exchange for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails, has brought a fragile calm to the devastated Gaza Strip, where months of bombardment have killed tens of thousands of people and displaced the vast majority of the territory's population.

In the podcast, RTÉ's reporters and analysts unpack the claims and counterclaims around who deserves credit for the deal, examining the role played by mediators Qatar, Egypt and the United States under both the Biden and Trump administrations. They also consider what the agreement means for the people of Gaza, who face a humanitarian catastrophe of extraordinary proportions, with much of the territory's infrastructure reduced to rubble.

The discussion also explores the wider geopolitical implications, including what Trump's approach to the Middle East may mean for Ireland and the European Union, and whether the ceasefire can hold long enough to develop into a more lasting peace.

Ireland has been among the most vocal EU member states in calling for a permanent ceasefire and has recognised the State of Palestine, a move that drew sharp criticism from Israel. The Taoiseach has repeatedly called for accountability for what he has described as the collective punishment of the Palestinian people.

The podcast episode also considers the domestic political dimensions in the United States, where Trump has sought to use the Gaza deal to burnish his credentials as a dealmaker on the world stage, contrasting his approach with that of his predecessor.

Listeners can find the full episode on all major podcast platforms and on rte.ie.
headline: Podcast: Trump praises his peace deal for Gaza

text:
The Government has been accused of taking a "wait and see" approach to protecting households and businesses from rising energy costs, with opposition TDs calling for immediate intervention ahead of the winter months.

During heated exchanges in the Dáil, the Taoiseach defended the Government's record on energy supports, insisting that measures would be brought forward "at the appropriate time" and that the situation was being closely monitored.

However, Sinn Féin's leader accused the Government of being slow to act, arguing that families across the country were already struggling with bills and could not afford to wait for decisions to be made at the eleventh hour.

"People are worried right now," the Sinn Féin leader told the chamber. "They don't have the luxury of a wait-and-see approach. They need certainty, and they need it now."

The exchange comes amid growing concern about the trajectory of wholesale energy prices and the knock-on effects for consumers. While prices have fallen from the extraordinary peaks seen during the worst of the energy crisis, they remain significantly above pre-pandemic levels, and there are fears that any volatility in international markets could quickly feed through to household bills.

The Government has previously introduced a series of energy credits to help offset rising costs, with several rounds of payments applied directly to electricity accounts. However, there has been no confirmation as to whether further credits will be issued, with Ministers indicating that any decision would depend on market conditions and the fiscal position.

The Minister for the Environment, Climate and Communications said the Government remained committed to supporting households but stressed the importance of acting in a "targeted and fiscally responsible" manner. The Minister pointed to longer-term measures, including investment in renewable energy infrastructure and retrofitting programmes, as evidence of the Government's commitment to reducing energy costs on a sustainable basis.

The Social Democrats described the Government's position as "kicking the can down the road," while Labour called for a comprehensive energy affordability strategy rather than what it termed "ad hoc interventions."

The Society of St Vincent de Paul has echoed concerns, noting that its members continue to encounter significant levels of energy poverty, particularly among older people and those living in poorly insulated homes. The organisation called on the Government to outline its plans well in advance of winter so that vulnerable households could plan accordingly.

Energy experts have noted that Ireland's continued reliance on imported natural gas leaves the country particularly exposed to international price fluctuations. The Commission for Regulation of Utilities is due to publish updated guidance on energy price trends in the coming weeks, which is expected to inform Government deliberations.

Business groups, including ISME and Ibec, have also urged clarity, warning that uncertainty over energy costs is making it difficult for small and medium enterprises to budget effectively and is undermining competitiveness.

The Taoiseach told the Dáil that the Government would not be found wanting and that any supports deemed necessary would be delivered in a timely fashion. He said the Government's track record demonstrated its willingness to act decisively when circumstances required it.

The issue is expected to feature prominently in budget discussions in the coming months.
headline: Govt taking 'wait and see' approach to energy protection

text:
With the bank holiday weekend approaching, water safety organisations are urging the public to take extra care around rivers, lakes and coastal areas.

Water Safety Ireland has issued an appeal for people to exercise caution, particularly as warmer weather is expected to draw large numbers to beaches, waterways and other outdoor swimming spots over the coming days.

The organisation said that drownings remain one of the leading causes of accidental death in Ireland, with a significant number of incidents occurring during the summer months and around bank holiday weekends when more people are enjoying the outdoors.

Roger Sweeney, chief executive of Water Safety Ireland, said that while it is important for people to enjoy the water, basic precautions can make the difference between life and death. He urged swimmers to use lifeguarded beaches and bathing areas where possible and to always swim within their ability.

"We would ask people to be aware of the dangers, to never swim alone, and to always let someone know where you are going and when you expect to return," Mr Sweeney said. "Cold water shock, rip currents and changing tidal conditions can catch even experienced swimmers off guard."

The Irish Coast Guard echoed the appeal, reminding the public to call 112 and ask for the Coast Guard in the event of a coastal emergency. A spokesperson said additional resources would be deployed at key locations around the country over the weekend.

The RNLI, which operates lifeboat stations and lifeguard services around the Irish coast, said its volunteer crews and seasonal lifeguards would be on heightened alert throughout the bank holiday period. The charity advised beachgoers to check tide times and weather forecasts before heading out and to supervise children closely near water at all times.

Parents and guardians are being particularly urged to remain vigilant around open water, with Water Safety Ireland noting that young children can get into difficulty in a matter of seconds, even in shallow water.

The organisation also highlighted the dangers of consuming alcohol before or during swimming, saying it remains a contributing factor in a number of drowning incidents each year.

Local authorities across the country have been asked to ensure signage and safety equipment, including ring buoys, are in place and in good condition at known swimming and water recreation areas.

Anyone who notices missing or damaged ring buoys is asked to report it to their local authority immediately.
headline: Appeal for safety around water ahead over bank holiday

text:
A major conservation programme aimed at protecting Ireland's dwindling curlew population has recorded its most successful breeding season to date, offering fresh hope for one of the country's most endangered bird species.

The Curlew Conservation Programme, overseen by the National Parks and Wildlife Service, has reported a significant increase in the number of chicks fledged this year, marking what conservationists are describing as a genuine breakthrough after years of painstaking effort.

Ireland's curlew population has suffered a catastrophic decline over recent decades, falling from an estimated 5,000 breeding pairs in the 1980s to fewer than 150 in recent years. The bird, once a familiar sight and sound across Irish bogs and farmland, had been on a trajectory towards national extinction.

The programme, which works closely with landowners and farming communities across several counties, focuses on locating curlew nests and protecting them from predation and disturbance during the critical breeding months. Nest protection measures, including temporary fencing and targeted predator management, have proved central to the improved results.

Minister of State with responsibility for nature and heritage Malcolm Noonan said the results demonstrated that "dedicated, science-led conservation, delivered in partnership with rural communities, can make a real difference."

"The curlew is an iconic species, deeply woven into our landscape and culture. Its loss would be felt profoundly, and these results show that we can turn the tide," the Minister said.

Farmers participating in the scheme receive payments through agri-environment measures in recognition of their role in managing land sympathetically for curlew nesting. Several participants have spoken of their pride in contributing to the bird's recovery, with some families recalling a time when the curlew's distinctive call was a hallmark of the Irish countryside.

BirdWatch Ireland, which has been closely involved in monitoring efforts, welcomed the results but cautioned that sustained investment and political commitment would be essential if the gains are to be maintained.

"This is enormously encouraging, but we must be clear-eyed about the scale of the challenge," a spokesperson for the organisation said. "We are still dealing with a critically small population, and one bad breeding season could undo much of this progress. Long-term funding and expanded habitat restoration are absolutely vital."

Conservationists have pointed to the loss of suitable nesting habitat, particularly through drainage of wetlands and changes in farming practices, as the principal driver of the curlew's decline. Predation by foxes and hooded crows has also been identified as a significant factor, particularly for ground-nesting birds in fragmented landscapes.

The programme currently operates across a number of key sites in counties including Donegal, Mayo, Roscommon, Sligo, Monaghan and Leitrim, with plans to expand its reach in the coming years.

The Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage confirmed that funding for the programme would be continued and said it was examining options to scale up conservation measures as part of Ireland's broader commitments under the EU Biodiversity Strategy.

Experts have noted that Ireland's experience mirrors challenges faced across Europe, where curlew populations have declined sharply.
headline: Curlew conservation scheme makes breakthrough

text:
The Football Association of Ireland has issued a formal apology to a number of former female international players who came forward with accounts of mistreatment and neglect during their time representing the country.

The apology comes after an RTÉ Investigates programme broadcast detailed testimony from several former players who described systemic failures in how the women's international programme was managed over a period spanning more than a decade.

Among the issues raised were inadequate medical support, substandard travel and accommodation arrangements, a lack of basic kit and equipment, and what players described as a pervasive culture of disregard for the women's game within the association.

In a statement, the FAI said it "sincerely apologises to those former players who have bravely spoken about their experiences" and acknowledged that "the standards they were subjected to fell far below what they deserved as international athletes representing their country."

The association said it recognised that the treatment described by the players was "unacceptable" and that it was committed to ensuring such failings would not be repeated.

Several of the former players who contributed to the investigation said they had been left feeling like an afterthought within the organisation, with one describing how the women's team had been made to feel they were "a nuisance" rather than valued representatives of Irish football.

Another former international recalled being expected to fund her own travel to training camps and being provided with men's jerseys that did not fit because women's kit had not been ordered.

The revelations have drawn sharp criticism from across the political spectrum. Speaking in the Dáil, the Minister for Sport expressed concern at the accounts and said the Government expected the FAI to demonstrate through concrete actions that the culture within the organisation had fundamentally changed.

Several TDs called for the Oireachtas Committee on Tourism, Culture, Arts, Sport and Media to invite the FAI to appear before it to answer questions about the treatment of female players, both historically and in the current set-up.

The FAI said it has undertaken significant reforms in recent years, including increased investment in the women's and girls' game, the appointment of dedicated staff to the women's programme, and the introduction of improved minimum standards for international teams.

However, some of the former players who spoke to RTÉ Investigates said they remained sceptical about whether the changes went deep enough, arguing that meaningful cultural reform required more than additional funding.

Vera Pauw, who managed the Republic of Ireland women's senior team before her departure, had previously raised concerns about resourcing and support structures during her tenure. Her comments at the time were seen as highlighting ongoing tensions between the ambitions of the women's programme and the resources allocated to it.

Sport Ireland, which oversees the distribution of Government funding to national governing bodies, said it had engaged with the FAI on the matter and would continue to monitor the association's progress in delivering on its commitments to the women's game.

The players who came forward said they hoped their testimony would serve not only as a record of what they endured but as a catalyst for lasting change, ensuring that the next generation of female footballers in Ireland would be treated with the respect and professionalism they deserve.
headline: FAI apologises to female former players who have spoken out

text:
The Minister for Justice is set to publish a long-awaited review of the laws governing sex work in Ireland, a move that has been welcomed by advocacy groups on all sides of the debate.

The review examines the operation of Part 4 of the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences) Act 2017, which criminalised the purchase of sexual services while decriminalising those who sell sex. The so-called Swedish model was introduced with the stated aim of reducing demand for prostitution and tackling human trafficking.

It is understood the review has been completed for some time but its publication had been subject to repeated delays, prompting criticism from opposition TDs and civil society organisations who argued the lack of transparency was hampering efforts to protect vulnerable people.

Speaking ahead of the publication, the Minister said the review would provide an evidence base for any future policy decisions and that the Government remained committed to tackling exploitation in all its forms.

"This is an important piece of work that examines how the legislation has operated in practice since its introduction," the Minister said. "It is right that we take stock of how these laws are functioning and whether they are achieving their intended objectives."

The review is expected to draw on submissions from An Garda Síochána, the HSE, NGOs working with sex workers, and anti-trafficking organisations, as well as international research on different legislative models.

Advocacy groups have been sharply divided on the question of how sex work should be regulated. Organisations such as the Immigrant Council of Ireland, which campaigned for the 2017 legislation, have argued that the criminalisation of buyers is essential to combating trafficking and exploitation. They point to the law as sending a clear signal that the purchase of another person's body is unacceptable.

However, groups representing current and former sex workers, including Sex Workers Alliance Ireland, have long argued that the legislation has made conditions more dangerous for those selling sex. They contend that criminalising clients pushes the trade further underground, making it harder for sex workers to screen potential buyers or negotiate safer conditions.

Several TDs have raised concerns in the Dáil about the delay in publishing the review, with some calling for a broader public debate about whether the current framework is fit for purpose. Labour and Social Democrats TDs have previously pressed the Minister on the timeline, arguing that policy in this area should be guided by evidence rather than ideology.

An Garda Síochána has reported a relatively low number of prosecutions under the purchase provisions since the law came into effect, a fact cited by critics who question whether the legislation is being adequately enforced. Gardaí have maintained that the law is one tool among several used to target trafficking networks and that investigations in this area are complex and resource-intensive.

The review is also expected to address the intersection of sex work legislation with immigration policy, given that a significant proportion of those involved in the sex trade in Ireland are migrants, some of whom may have insecure immigration status.

It is anticipated the Minister will bring the findings to Cabinet before any legislative amendments are considered. The publication is likely to reignite a highly charged public debate about the balance between protecting individuals from exploitation and respecting the agency of those who say they choose to engage in sex work.
headline: Minister to publish review of sex work legislation

text:
Kamala Harris has sharply criticised the direction of the United States under President Donald Trump, describing his administration's approach as "self-serving" and warning that it is undermining America's standing on the world stage.

The former vice president, who lost to Mr Trump in last year's presidential election, made the remarks during a public appearance in which she offered her most pointed critique of her successor's policies since leaving office.

Ms Harris said the current administration was pursuing an agenda that prioritised narrow political interests over the wellbeing of ordinary Americans and the country's traditional alliances abroad.

"What we are seeing is a presidency that is self-serving, that is not about the people of our country, and that is certainly not about strengthening the relationships that have kept the world safer for generations," she said.

Her comments come at a time when the Trump administration has faced growing international criticism over its trade policies, including sweeping tariffs that have rattled markets and strained relations with longstanding allies, including the European Union.

The EU, of which Ireland is a member, has been engaged in tense negotiations with Washington over tariff arrangements that have caused significant concern among Irish exporters and multinational firms based here.

Ms Harris did not outline any plans to re-enter electoral politics but suggested she would continue to speak out against policies she believes are damaging to American democracy and global stability.

"I will not be silent when I see our democracy being undermined and our values being abandoned," she said.

The White House has not yet responded directly to Ms Harris's remarks, though President Trump has previously dismissed criticism from his former rival as politically motivated.

Her intervention is likely to fuel speculation about the future direction of the Democratic Party as it seeks to regroup following its defeat in the 2024 election and to position itself as a credible opposition to the Trump administration's agenda both at home and abroad.
headline: Trump's America is 'self-serving', says Kamala Harris

text:
A meatball made using DNA from the woolly mammoth has been unveiled by an Australian cultured meat company at a science museum in Amsterdam.

Vow, the start-up behind the creation, said the project was designed to spark conversation about the future of food and the role cultivated meat could play in addressing the climate crisis.

The firm used publicly available genetic information from the mammoth — an animal that roamed the earth thousands of years ago before going extinct — and filled in gaps in the DNA sequence using genetic material from the African elephant, the mammoth's closest living relative.

The resulting protein, myoglobin, was then grown in a laboratory using cultured sheep cells, producing enough material to form a single large meatball, which was presented under glass at the NEMO Science Museum in the Dutch capital.

However, nobody has yet tasted the mammoth meatball. The company said that because the protein had not been consumed for thousands of years, there was no way to know how the human immune system might react to it.

"We wanted to get people talking about what the future of food could look like," said Tim Noakesmith, co-founder of Vow. "The mammoth is a symbol of loss, and we chose it because we don't want the same thing to happen to the species we rely on today."

Cultured meat — sometimes referred to as lab-grown or cell-based meat — is produced by taking cells from an animal and growing them in a controlled environment, bypassing the need to raise and slaughter livestock. Proponents argue the technology could dramatically reduce the environmental footprint of meat production, which is a significant contributor to greenhouse gas emissions, deforestation and water use globally.

The sector has attracted considerable investment in recent years, though regulatory approval for commercial sale remains limited. Singapore became the first country to approve the sale of cultured meat in 2020, and the United States granted approval to two companies last year.

Professor Ernst Wolvetang of the Australian Institute for Bioengineering at the University of Queensland, who helped with the project, said the work demonstrated the remarkable possibilities of cellular agriculture but stressed that it was intended primarily as a talking point rather than a commercial product.

The unveiling comes as debate around sustainable food systems intensifies, with organisations including the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation calling for urgent transformation of how the world produces and consumes food.
headline: Meatball made with mammoth DNA unveiled in Amsterdam

text:
Several hundred people gathered in Dublin city centre this afternoon to demand an end to the ongoing conflict in Gaza, with organisers describing the turnout as a reflection of growing public frustration over the humanitarian crisis in the region.

The demonstration, which began at the GPO on O'Connell Street before proceeding to the Dáil on Kildare Street, saw protesters carrying Palestinian flags and placards calling for an immediate ceasefire and an end to the bombardment of civilian areas in the besieged territory.

Speakers at the rally criticised the international community's response to the crisis and called on the Irish Government to take stronger diplomatic action, including the full implementation of the Occupied Territories Bill and the expulsion of the Israeli ambassador.

Among those addressing the crowd was Niamh Ní Bhriain of the Ireland-Palestine Solidarity Campaign, who said the Irish public had consistently shown solidarity with the Palestinian people and urged the Government to match that sentiment with concrete political action.

"People are watching in horror as hospitals, schools and refugee camps are being bombed," she told the crowd. "Ireland has a proud tradition of standing up for oppressed peoples, and we are calling on our Government to lead, not follow, on this issue."

A number of TDs from across the opposition benches attended the protest, with several calling on the Taoiseach to use Ireland's voice at EU and UN level to push for accountability and an end to what they described as collective punishment of the Palestinian population.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has previously stated that Ireland supports a two-state solution and has consistently called for adherence to international humanitarian law by all parties. Ireland was among the first EU member states to formally recognise the State of Palestine.

The Gardaí said the protest passed off peacefully, with rolling traffic restrictions in place for a period along the route through the city centre.

Saturday's demonstration was the latest in a series of large-scale protests that have taken place in Dublin and other Irish cities since the conflict escalated, with organisers vowing to continue weekly actions until there is a lasting ceasefire.
headline: Dublin protesters call for end to Gaza conflict

text:
At least 61 people have drowned after a boat carrying migrants capsized off the coast of Libya, in one of the deadliest shipwrecks in the Mediterranean this year.

The vessel, which was believed to be heading towards Europe, went down in waters off the western Libyan coast, according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) and the UN refugee agency, UNHCR.

Survivors were brought ashore by the Libyan coastguard, with reports suggesting that a number of those rescued were in a critical condition and required immediate medical attention. The nationalities of those on board have not yet been confirmed, though the IOM said the passengers were believed to include men, women and children from sub-Saharan African countries.

The precise circumstances of the sinking remain unclear, but aid organisations said the vessel was overcrowded and unseaworthy, as is typical of boats used by smuggling networks operating out of Libya.

The IOM's chief of mission in Libya described the tragedy as "devastating but sadly not surprising," calling on the international community to take urgent action to address the root causes of irregular migration and to establish safe, legal pathways for those seeking protection.

The Central Mediterranean route, which runs from North Africa to Italy and Malta, remains one of the most dangerous migration corridors in the world. More than 20,000 people are estimated to have died or gone missing attempting the crossing since 2014, according to the IOM's Missing Migrants Project.

Human rights organisations have repeatedly criticised the European Union's policy of supporting the Libyan coastguard to intercept migrant boats and return passengers to detention centres in Libya, where they face well-documented abuses including torture, extortion and forced labour.

UNHCR reiterated its call for an end to returns to Libya, describing the country as an unsafe place for refugees and asylum seekers.

The tragedy comes as the number of attempted crossings has risen sharply in recent months, driven by deteriorating conditions in countries of origin and transit, as well as favourable weather conditions in the Mediterranean.

Italy's far-right government, led by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, has taken an increasingly hardline stance on migration, striking deals with North African governments to curb departures and introducing tougher penalties for NGO rescue ships operating in the region.

Ireland's own engagement with the migration crisis has come under renewed scrutiny in recent months, with the Government facing questions over its capacity to process and accommodate international protection applicants arriving in the State.
headline: 61 migrants drown after shipwreck off Libya

text:
Israel's defence minister has threatened to annex parts of the Gaza Strip, in a significant escalation of rhetoric that is likely to draw widespread international condemnation.

Israel Katz, who was appointed defence minister last year, said Israel could move to permanently seize territory in northern Gaza if Hamas does not agree to release all remaining hostages held in the territory.

The comments mark one of the most explicit statements yet from a senior Israeli government figure suggesting that parts of Gaza could be permanently absorbed into Israeli-controlled territory, a move that would be considered a violation of international law by the vast majority of states and international legal bodies.

Mr Katz said that Israel would "act to annex" areas in the north of the strip, where the Israeli military has been conducting intensive operations for months. He framed the threat as a direct response to what he described as Hamas's refusal to negotiate in good faith over the release of hostages taken during the 7 October 2023 attacks.

The comments were swiftly condemned by Palestinian officials, with the Palestinian Authority describing the threat as evidence of Israel's long-term ambitions to permanently occupy and colonise Gaza. Hamas, for its part, said the remarks demonstrated that Israel was not genuinely interested in reaching a ceasefire agreement.

The international community has broadly opposed any permanent Israeli presence in Gaza. The United States, while maintaining its strong support for Israel's military campaign, has repeatedly stated that it does not support the reoccupation or reduction in the territory of Gaza. The European Union has also warned against any moves that would alter the status of the territory.

The Taoiseach has previously been vocal in criticising Israel's conduct of its military campaign in Gaza, and Ireland has been among the most outspoken EU member states in calling for an immediate ceasefire and the protection of Palestinian civilians.

Ireland formally recognised the State of Palestine last year alongside Spain and Norway, a move that drew sharp criticism from the Israeli government.

The war in Gaza has killed more than 46,000 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, since Israel launched its military offensive in response to the 7 October attacks in which approximately 1,200 people were killed and around 250 taken hostage.

Humanitarian organisations have warned repeatedly of catastrophic conditions in the strip, with widespread displacement, famine-like conditions, and the near-total destruction of civilian infrastructure including hospitals and schools.

The threat of annexation is likely to further complicate already stalled negotiations over a potential ceasefire and hostage deal, with mediators in Qatar and Egypt having struggled for months to bridge the gap between the two sides.

Under international law, the annexation of territory acquired by force is prohibited under the United Nations Charter. Israel's existing annexation of East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights is not recognised by the vast majority of the international community.
headline: Israeli defence minister threatens to annex parts of Gaza

text:
Labour leader Ivana Bacik has accused the Government of throwing students' budget plans into "disarray" following confirmation of an increase in the student contribution charge.

Speaking in the Dáil, Ms Bacik said the fee hike would place an unacceptable burden on families already struggling with the cost of living, and called on the Government to reverse the decision.

"Students across the country have been making their plans for the academic year ahead, and now those plans have been thrown into complete disarray," the Dublin Bay South TD said. "This is a Government that talks about supporting young people but consistently fails to put its money where its mouth is."

Ms Bacik said the increase would disproportionately affect students from lower and middle-income backgrounds, many of whom are already working multiple part-time jobs to fund their education. She argued that the move ran counter to the Government's stated commitment to widening access to third-level education.

The Labour leader also pointed to the experience of other European countries where tuition fees have been reduced or abolished entirely, and said Ireland was "going in the wrong direction" on the issue.

In response, the Minister for Further and Higher Education said the Government had delivered a significant package of financial supports for students in recent budgets, including reductions in the student contribution in previous years and increases to the SUSI grant. The Minister said the Government remained committed to making higher education accessible and affordable, and pointed to record levels of investment in the sector.

However, Ms Bacik dismissed these assurances as insufficient, arguing that piecemeal supports could not compensate for a policy that placed the cost of higher education squarely on the shoulders of students and their families.

The Union of Students in Ireland has also criticised the fee increase, describing it as a "retrograde step" and warning that it would force some students to reconsider their plans to attend or remain in college. USI president said the organisation would be engaging with TDs across all parties to seek a reversal of the measure.

Sinn Féin's education spokesperson echoed concerns about the impact on students, saying the party would oppose the increase and press the issue in the Oireachtas in the weeks ahead.

The student contribution charge, which currently stands at €3,000, is one of the highest such charges in Europe. Critics have long argued that it represents a significant barrier to participation in higher education, particularly for students from disadvantaged backgrounds who may not qualify for the full SUSI grant.

The issue is expected to feature prominently in Dáil exchanges in the coming days as opposition parties seek to build pressure on the Government ahead of the next budget.
headline: Bacik: Student's budget plans in 'disarray' over fee hike

text:
Scientists have for the first time detected microplastics in the exhaled breath of bottlenose dolphins, raising fresh concerns about the pervasive spread of plastic pollution in marine environments and its potential impact on the health of some of the ocean's most iconic species.

Researchers from the College of Charleston in South Carolina collected breath samples from wild bottlenose dolphins living in two coastal locations — Sarasota Bay in Florida and Barataria Bay in Louisiana. Using a modified version of a technique originally developed to study respiratory health in the animals, the team captured the dolphins' exhalations in specially designed petri dishes held above their blowholes as they surfaced to breathe.

The results, published in the journal PLOS ONE, revealed that every single dolphin sampled had at least one type of microplastic particle present in its exhaled breath. Across the 11 animals tested, researchers identified a range of synthetic polymers including polyester, polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and nylon — materials commonly found in clothing, plastic bottles and fishing gear.

The findings suggest that dolphins are not only ingesting microplastics through contaminated prey and seawater but are also inhaling the particles directly from the air at the ocean's surface, where they breathe. This is significant because inhaled microplastics can potentially penetrate deep into lung tissue, where they may cause inflammation or other damage over time.

"Dolphins are spending their entire lives in these environments, breathing in whatever is at the surface," said Dr Miranda Dziobak, the study's lead author. She noted that the air just above the water's surface can contain high concentrations of microplastic particles, which are lofted into the atmosphere from wave action and sea spray.

The research adds to a growing body of evidence highlighting the ubiquity of microplastics — defined as plastic fragments smaller than five millimetres — across virtually every ecosystem on Earth. Previous studies have found the particles in human blood, lung tissue, placentas and breast milk, as well as in deep ocean sediments and Arctic ice.

Marine conservation groups have described the findings as deeply troubling. Microplastics have already been documented in the digestive systems of a wide range of marine species, from tiny zooplankton to large whales, but the discovery that they are present in the respiratory systems of air-breathing marine mammals represents what researchers called a "new pathway of exposure" that warrants further investigation.

Ireland's own coastal waters are home to a significant population of bottlenose dolphins, most notably the resident group in the Shannon Estuary, which is protected under EU habitats legislation. The Irish Whale and Dolphin Group has previously highlighted concerns about pollution threats to cetaceans in Irish waters, and the new research is likely to intensify calls for stronger action on plastic waste entering the marine environment.

The study's authors acknowledged that their sample size was small and said larger-scale research is needed to understand the full health implications. However, they cautioned that because dolphins are long-lived apex predators, they may be particularly vulnerable to the cumulative effects of microplastic exposure over their lifetimes.
headline: Microplastics discovered in dolphin breath

text:
Donegal County Council has unanimously backed calls for a full public inquiry into the Creeslough explosion, which claimed the lives of ten people in October 2022.

Councillors from across all parties and none supported a motion at Monday's plenary meeting in Lifford, calling on the Government to establish an independent public inquiry into the tragedy, which devastated the small north Donegal community.

The explosion at the Applegreen service station and residential building on 7 October 2022 was one of the deadliest incidents in the State in recent decades. Ten people, ranging in age from five to 59, lost their lives, while a number of others were seriously injured.

Speaking after the vote, councillors said the families of those who died and those who were injured deserve full transparency and accountability regarding the circumstances surrounding the explosion.

The motion echoes growing pressure on the Government to go beyond existing investigations and establish a public inquiry with the power to compel witnesses and evidence. Families of the victims have been vocal in their calls for such an inquiry, expressing frustration at the pace of progress in establishing the full facts of what happened.

An Garda Síochána investigation into the cause of the explosion remains ongoing, while a separate Health and Safety Authority inquiry has also been under way. However, campaigners have argued that only a full public inquiry can provide the comprehensive, transparent account that the bereaved families and the wider Creeslough community need.

Several councillors spoke emotionally during the debate, recalling the impact the tragedy had on the tight-knit community and the broader county. Independent councillor Michael McClafferty, who represents the local electoral area, said the people of Creeslough have shown extraordinary dignity and patience but that they now need answers.

The Taoiseach has previously indicated the Government would consider the question of a public inquiry once the Garda investigation had concluded, but bereaved families and their supporters have argued that the two processes need not be sequential and that further delay is causing additional distress.

Donegal County Council now joins a growing chorus of voices, including members of the Oireachtas and community organisations, urging the Government to act without further delay. The council confirmed it will write formally to the Taoiseach, the Tánaiste, and the relevant Government ministers conveying the unanimous position of the elected members.
headline: Donegal councillors back Creeslough public inquiry

text:
Gardaí are appealing for witnesses following the death of a man in the early hours of this morning.

The incident occurred at approximately 2.30am on the Ennis Road in Limerick city. The man, who was in his 40s, was pronounced dead at the scene. His body has been removed to University Hospital Limerick where a post-mortem examination is expected to be carried out later today.

The results of the post-mortem will determine the course of the Garda investigation.

The scene has been preserved and is currently being examined by members of the Garda Technical Bureau. Local diversions are in place and motorists are being advised to avoid the area where possible.

Gardaí at Henry Street Garda Station are appealing to anyone who may have been in the Ennis Road area between 1am and 3am this morning to come forward. They are particularly keen to hear from anyone who may have dashcam or doorbell camera footage from the area during that time.

A Garda spokesperson said investigations are ongoing and that no further information is available at this time.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Henry Street Garda Station on 061 212 400, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.
headline: Gardaí appeal for witnesses following death of man

text:
With just weeks to go before voters across the European Union head to the polls, candidates in Ireland's three European Parliament constituencies are stepping up their campaigns as they jostle for position in what is shaping up to be a fiercely competitive contest.

The European elections, scheduled for 7 June, will see Ireland elect its allocation of MEPs across the Dublin, Midlands-North-West and South constituencies, with a number of high-profile figures vying for seats alongside a raft of newcomers hoping to make a breakthrough.

Sitting MEPs are facing stiff challenges from party colleagues and rivals alike, with recent opinion polls suggesting several seats could come down to the wire and the final transfers proving decisive.

Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil are both targeting gains, while Sinn Féin is hoping to build on its strong showing in recent domestic polls by securing additional European Parliament seats. The Green Party, Labour and a number of prominent independents are also in the mix, adding further uncertainty to the outcome.

The contest in Midlands-North-West is widely regarded as the most unpredictable, with a crowded field of candidates competing for a limited number of seats. In Dublin, the battle is equally intense, with several well-known political figures fighting to distinguish themselves from their rivals.

Campaign strategists across the parties acknowledge that turnout will be a critical factor, with European elections historically attracting lower voter participation than general elections or even local elections. Parties are investing heavily in get-out-the-vote operations, particularly in urban areas where turnout tends to lag behind rural constituencies.

The European Parliament elections will be held on the same day as the local elections, a factor that could boost overall turnout but also complicates the picture for candidates who must compete for attention with hundreds of local authority hopefuls canvassing the same doorsteps.

Issues such as the cost of living, housing, immigration and Ireland's role in EU defence and security policy have dominated the campaign trail, with candidates seeking to frame the European election around matters of direct concern to Irish voters.

Taoiseach Simon Harris has urged voters to consider the European elections carefully, describing them as an opportunity to shape the direction of the EU at a time of significant geopolitical uncertainty. Opposition leaders have similarly stressed the importance of the vote, with Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald arguing that Ireland needs MEPs who will challenge the status quo in Brussels.

As the campaign enters its final stretch, party leaders are expected to increase their visibility on the trail, lending their support to candidates in key constituencies where every vote and every transfer could prove decisive.
headline: Candidates jostle for position ahead of Euro Parl vote

text:
Met Éireann has confirmed that a temperature of 28.6 degrees Celsius was recorded at Shannon Airport today, smashing the previous May temperature record for Ireland.

The reading, taken at the Co Clare station, surpassed the long-standing record of 28.4C which had been set at Kilkenny in May 1947. It marks the highest temperature recorded in Ireland so far this year and is exceptional for the time of year, according to forecasters.

Met Éireann said the remarkable warmth was driven by a plume of hot air tracking northwards from the Iberian Peninsula and continental Europe, bringing unseasonably high temperatures to much of the country throughout the day.

Several other weather stations also reported temperatures well above seasonal norms, with readings in excess of 25C recorded at a number of locations across the midlands and the west. However, it was Shannon that claimed the headline figure, benefiting from its sheltered position along the estuary.

Climatologist and Met Éireann forecaster Séamus Walsh said the record was "truly remarkable" and noted that temperatures of this magnitude in May are "very rare in an Irish context."

"To exceed 28 degrees at any point during the Irish summer would be noteworthy, but to do so in May is highly unusual," he said. "It speaks to the broader pattern of more frequent extreme weather events that we are observing in line with climate change."

The warm spell brought thousands of people to beaches and parks across the country, with the Irish Water Safety organisation urging the public to exercise caution around water. A number of local authorities issued notices reminding people to stay hydrated and to check on elderly and vulnerable neighbours during the warm conditions.

The HSE also issued guidance advising people to apply sunscreen, seek shade during the hottest hours of the day, and to be mindful of the risks of heat exhaustion, particularly for young children and older people.

Met Éireann has indicated that temperatures are expected to ease somewhat over the coming days as the high-pressure system gradually weakens and more typical Atlantic conditions reassert themselves. However, forecasters said conditions are likely to remain warm and largely dry through the early part of the week, with highs of 20 to 24 degrees expected in many areas.

The record comes amid growing attention to the frequency with which temperature records are being broken both in Ireland and across Europe. Data from Met Éireann shows that the last decade has seen a notable increase in the number of days where temperatures have exceeded 25C, a threshold once considered unusual in Ireland.
headline: 28.6C reached at Shannon, breaking May temperature record

text:
The use of Bloody Sunday footage in a Conservative Party political broadcast has been condemned as "disgusting" by relatives of those killed on the day and by politicians on both sides of the Irish border.

The broadcast, which aired on British television, featured archive footage from the 1972 atrocity in Derry as part of a wider montage depicting periods of civil unrest. The images showed scenes from Bloody Sunday, in which 13 people were shot dead by members of the British Army's Parachute Regiment during a civil rights march. A fourteenth person died later from injuries sustained on the day.

Relatives of those killed expressed outrage at the inclusion of the footage, describing it as deeply hurtful and an exploitation of their grief for party political purposes.

The Taoiseach said the use of the footage was deeply insensitive and showed a lack of understanding of the pain still felt by the families of the victims. He said the British government had itself acknowledged, through the Saville Inquiry, that the killings were unjustified and unjustifiable, making the use of the images in a party political context all the more inappropriate.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin described the broadcast as "crass and offensive," adding that it demonstrated a troubling disregard for the suffering of victims and their families.

Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald TD called on the Conservative Party to withdraw the broadcast immediately and to issue an apology to the Bloody Sunday families. She described the decision to include the footage as "beneath contempt" and said it was indicative of a broader attitude within elements of the Tory party towards events during the Troubles.

The SDLP and Alliance Party in the North also strongly criticised the broadcast. SDLP leader Colum Eastwood said the footage had been used recklessly and without any consideration for the families who had spent decades campaigning for truth and justice.

The Saville Inquiry, which reported in 2010, found that the soldiers had fired on unarmed civilians and that none of the victims had posed a threat. Then British prime minister David Cameron described the killings as "unjustified and unjustifiable" and issued a formal apology on behalf of the British government.

Despite that apology, the families of those killed have continued to campaign for accountability, with efforts to prosecute individual soldiers having largely stalled in recent years.

The Conservative Party has not yet responded to the criticism or indicated whether it intends to withdraw the broadcast.
headline: Tories' use of Bloody Sunday footage 'disgusting'

text:
More than 30 dogs have been rescued from a property in England after their owner was found dead inside the home.

The RSPCA said the animals were discovered living in squalid conditions at the house in Lincolnshire, with many of them suffering from severe neglect and health problems.

Officers from the animal welfare charity were called to the property after the owner's body was discovered by local police. The circumstances of the death are not being treated as suspicious.

The charity said the dogs, a mix of breeds including several small terrier types, were found in a state of significant distress. Many were matted, underweight and had not received veterinary care for some time. Some of the animals were found in crates and confined spaces within the property.

An RSPCA inspector who attended the scene described the conditions inside the home as "heartbreaking" and said it was clear the owner had been struggling to cope with the number of animals for some time.

"This is a situation we sadly see all too often, where someone's love of animals has spiralled beyond their ability to care for them properly," the inspector said. "The welfare of these dogs had clearly deteriorated significantly."

The dogs have been taken to RSPCA centres across the region where they are receiving veterinary treatment and being assessed. The charity said it was hopeful that many of the animals would eventually be rehomed once they had recovered.

Neighbours told local media they had been aware of a large number of dogs at the property but had not realised the extent of the situation inside.

The RSPCA urged anyone concerned about animal welfare in their community to contact the charity's helpline rather than ignore potential signs of neglect.
headline: 30 dogs rescued from home in UK after owner found dead

text:
James Watson, the American molecular biologist who shared the Nobel Prize for his role in discovering the double helix structure of DNA, has died at the age of 97.

Watson, along with Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962 for what has been described as one of the most important scientific breakthroughs of the 20th century.

Their discovery in 1953 of the twisted ladder structure of deoxyribonucleic acid — the molecule that carries the genetic instructions for life — transformed the fields of biology and medicine and paved the way for advances in genetics, forensics and the treatment of inherited diseases.

However, Watson's legacy was deeply tarnished in his later years by repeated racist remarks, including claims that intelligence was linked to race. Those comments led to Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory in New York, the prestigious research institution he had led for decades, severing ties with him in 2019 and stripping him of his honorary titles.

Born in Chicago in 1928, Watson was a prodigious student who entered the University of Chicago at just 15 years of age. He went on to earn his doctorate in zoology from Indiana University before travelling to the Cavendish Laboratory at the University of Cambridge, where he began his collaboration with Crick.

Their work built significantly on X-ray crystallography images produced by Rosalind Franklin and Wilkins at King's College London. Franklin's crucial contribution to the discovery was for many years insufficiently recognised, a fact that has prompted considerable debate among scientists and historians. Franklin died of ovarian cancer in 1958 at the age of 37 and was not included in the Nobel Prize.

Watson served as the first director of the Human Genome Project at the National Institutes of Health from 1990 to 1992, helping to launch the ambitious international effort to map the entirety of human DNA.

In 2007, he told The Sunday Times that he was "inherently gloomy about the prospect of Africa" because "all our social policies are based on the fact that their intelligence is the same as ours, whereas all the testing says not really." The remarks drew widespread condemnation from the scientific community.

He repeated similar views in a 2019 documentary, prompting Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory to revoke his remaining honorary titles. The laboratory said his comments were "reprehensible" and "unsupported by science."

Watson is survived by his wife Elizabeth and his sons Rufus and Duncan.
headline: DNA pioneer James Watson dies aged 97

text:
More than half the homes that have been inspected under the Defective Concrete Blocks Grant Scheme require additional remediation work beyond what was initially anticipated, according to new figures released by the Department of Housing.

The data, which was provided to the Oireachtas Housing Committee ahead of a meeting today, reveals that of the approximately 3,200 properties that have undergone detailed engineering assessments, some 1,650 require more extensive interventions than their owners had originally expected.

The scheme, which was established to support homeowners whose properties were built with defective concrete blocks containing excessive amounts of the mineral mica or pyrite, has been a source of ongoing frustration for affected families, particularly in Donegal and Mayo.

Housing Minister Darragh O'Brien said the Government remained committed to ensuring that every homeowner affected would have their home restored to a proper standard. "We have always said that this scheme would be responsive to the needs of homeowners, and where additional work is identified through the engineering process, that work will be covered," the Minister said.

However, campaigners expressed concern that the findings would lead to further delays in a process that many families have described as already painfully slow. Paddy Diver, a prominent campaigner for affected homeowners in Donegal, said the figures confirmed what families on the ground had been saying for years.

"People are living in homes that are literally crumbling around them. They don't need more reports and more assessments — they need their homes fixed," he said.

Several TDs raised the issue during today's committee session, with Sinn Féin's housing spokesperson Eoin Ó Broin describing the pace of the scheme as "completely unacceptable." He called on the Minister to streamline the approvals process and ensure that additional remediation costs would not result in homeowners facing shortfalls.

Independent TD for Donegal Thomas Pringle said constituents in his area were growing increasingly disillusioned. "There are families who applied to this scheme in good faith and are still waiting to see any meaningful progress.
