The bureaucracy is overwhelming people who are already under enormous stress," he said.

The Department confirmed that the enhanced grant scheme, which provides a maximum grant of €420,000 for a full demolition and rebuild, would cover the cost of additional works where they are deemed necessary following a professional assessment. Officials told the committee that efforts were under way to reduce processing times, including the recruitment of additional staff to handle applications.

To date, more than 6,500 applications have been received under the scheme, with the vast majority coming from counties Donegal and Mayo. However, only a fraction of applicants have progressed to the construction phase, a point that has drawn repeated criticism from opposition TDs and campaign groups.

The Government has earmarked more than €2.7 billion for the scheme over the coming years, making it one of the most significant State-funded remediation programmes in the history of the State.

The Mica Action Group said it would continue to press for faster delivery and warned that any attempt to cap or limit additional remediation costs would be met with further protests.
headline: Half of homes in defective blocks scheme need more work

text:
It was one of those stories that cut through the noise of a turbulent year and reminded people of the simple, healing power of the bond between a child and their pet.

Cian's Kennels, the volunteer-run initiative that allows children receiving treatment in hospital to spend time with their beloved animals, captured hearts across the country in 2022 and became one of the most shared and talked-about good news stories of the year.

The project, which provides free, temporary foster care for the pets of families whose children are undergoing long-term hospital treatment, was born out of a deeply personal experience. When a child is diagnosed with a serious illness, the upheaval affects every corner of family life — and for many families, the heartbreak of having to rehome or surrender a pet on top of everything else can feel like one loss too many.

Cian's Kennels stepped into that gap, offering not just practical support but something more profound: the chance for sick children to be reunited with their dogs, cats, and other pets during what are often the most difficult days of their young lives. Volunteers foster the animals for as long as needed and bring them to visit the children, whether in hospital or at Ronald McDonald House facilities.

The emotional reunions, often shared on social media, struck a chord with the public and drew widespread attention both at home and internationally. Videos of children's faces lighting up as their pet bounded towards them were viewed millions of times online, prompting an outpouring of support and donations.

The organisation also highlighted a gap in support services for families dealing with childhood illness that many people had never previously considered. For parents already juggling hospital appointments, caring for other children, and managing the financial strain that serious illness brings, the worry over a pet's welfare can be an additional source of stress and guilt.

Volunteers with Cian's Kennels said they were overwhelmed by the response throughout the year, with offers of foster care, fundraising, and assistance coming from every county in Ireland. The initiative also inspired similar projects in other countries, with enquiries coming from as far afield as the United States and Australia.

Health professionals noted the well-documented therapeutic benefits of animal-assisted interaction for children in medical settings, pointing out that the comfort a familiar pet provides can reduce anxiety, lift mood, and even aid recovery.

In a year that saw the continuing fallout from the pandemic, a cost-of-living crisis that squeezed households across the State, and the ongoing horror of the war in Ukraine, the story of Cian's Kennels offered something increasingly rare — a moment of uncomplicated warmth. It served as a reminder that, amid the grand sweep of national and international events, the stories that resonate most deeply are often the most human ones.

As 2022 drew to a close, the organisation said it was looking ahead to expanding its services and ensuring that no family facing a child's illness would have to face the additional heartbreak of losing their pet. For the children and families it has already helped, the difference it made was immeasurable — measured not in policy or politics, but in wagging tails and tearful, joyful embraces.
headline: Cian's Kennels reunites sick children with their pets

text:
The National Lottery has issued an urgent appeal to Lotto players in the midlands to check their tickets after a prize worth €1 million remains unclaimed more than three weeks after the draw.

The life-changing sum was won on a Lotto Plus 1 ticket purchased in Co Westmeath, but the lucky ticket holder has yet to come forward to claim their winnings.

The winning ticket was sold at Dunnes Stores in the Harbour Place Shopping Centre in Mullingar for the draw on Saturday 24 May. The National Lottery has confirmed that the ticket was a quick pick purchase.

A spokesperson for the National Lottery said they were "eager" to unite the winner with their prize and urged anyone who bought a ticket in the Mullingar area around that time to carefully check their numbers.

"We are appealing to all our players, particularly those in the Westmeath area, to rummage through their pockets, handbags, car consoles and kitchen drawers to check if they have the winning ticket," the spokesperson said.

"This is a massive, life-changing amount of money and we would hate to see it go unclaimed."

The winning Lotto Plus 1 numbers for the draw were 2, 9, 17, 23, 31 and 40, with a bonus number of 12.

Under National Lottery rules, winners have 90 days from the date of the draw to claim their prize. That means the deadline to come forward in this case falls in late August.

The National Lottery advised that the winner should sign the back of their ticket, keep it in a safe place and contact the prize claims team on 1800 666 222 or email claims@lottery.ie.

It is not the first time a significant Lotto prize has gone unclaimed for a prolonged period. In recent years, the National Lottery has made several public appeals to trace winners of large sums, with some prizes ultimately going unclaimed after the 90-day deadline passed. Any unclaimed prize money is returned to the National Lottery fund, which supports Good Causes projects across the country.

Staff at Dunnes Stores in Harbour Place said there had been considerable excitement in the shop since the win was announced, with many regular customers checking and rechecking their tickets at the counter.

"Everyone who comes in is talking about it," one staff member said. "We'd love to know who it is. Hopefully they find the ticket before it's too late."
headline: Appeal to find winner of unclaimed €1m Lotto prize

text:
The number of children living in emergency accommodation has reached what housing charities are calling a "deeply alarming" milestone, prompting renewed calls for urgent government intervention to address the escalating crisis.

New figures from the Department of Housing show that the number of homeless children has continued to climb in recent months, with families now accounting for a significant and growing proportion of those relying on emergency accommodation across the State.

Focus Ireland has expressed major concern over the pace at which child homelessness is increasing, warning that the current trajectory suggests the situation will worsen considerably before any meaningful improvement is felt.

Pat Dennigan, chief executive of Focus Ireland, said the organisation is seeing families presenting in circumstances of acute distress, with many having exhausted every available option before turning to emergency services.

"Behind every one of these statistics is a child whose education, health and emotional development is being profoundly affected," Mr Dennigan said. "The pace at which these numbers are rising should be a source of deep concern for every member of the Oireachtas."

The Simon Communities of Ireland echoed the concerns, noting that the lack of available social housing and the pressures in the private rental market are the primary drivers pushing families into homelessness. The organisation said that notices to quit remain one of the leading causes of family homelessness, despite legislative measures introduced in recent years to strengthen tenant protections.

The Government has pointed to its Housing for All plan as the framework through which the crisis will be addressed, with the Taoiseach stating that record levels of investment are being directed towards social and affordable housing delivery.

However, opposition TDs have questioned whether the pace of housing delivery is sufficient to meet demand. Sinn Féin's housing spokesperson said the figures represent a "damning indictment" of government policy and called for an emergency response specifically targeting families with children.

The Society of St Vincent de Paul said its members are encountering families in emergency accommodation who are struggling to meet basic needs, including adequate nutrition and access to consistent schooling for their children. The charity called for an increase in the Housing Assistance Payment limits and greater investment in family-specific supports.

The HSE has acknowledged that prolonged periods in emergency accommodation can have significant impacts on children's physical and mental health, with access to primary care and community health services often disrupted for families who are moved between different locations.

Children's rights groups, including the Children's Rights Alliance, have urged the Government to adopt a child-centred approach to homelessness policy, arguing that the particular vulnerabilities of young people in emergency accommodation require dedicated and targeted interventions.

The Department of Housing said it is continuing to work with local authorities and approved housing bodies to increase the supply of long-term housing solutions and to reduce reliance on emergency accommodation for families.
headline: Major concern over pace of child homelessness

text:
Two people have been killed and at least 10 others have been taken to hospital following a series of explosions at a steel manufacturing plant in the United States.

The blasts occurred at the facility in the early hours of this morning, with emergency services rushing to the scene amid reports of thick black smoke billowing from the site.

Local fire crews and hazardous materials teams were deployed to tackle the resulting fires, which took several hours to bring under control.

The two workers who died were pronounced dead at the scene. Of those hospitalised, several are understood to be in a critical condition, with injuries including severe burns and smoke inhalation.

Authorities have not yet released the names of the deceased, pending notification of their families.

The plant, which employs several hundred workers, has been shut down pending an investigation into the cause of the explosions. The US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) confirmed it has launched a probe into the incident.

Workers at the facility described scenes of chaos as the first explosion ripped through a section of the plant, followed by secondary blasts moments later.

"It was like nothing I've ever experienced," one worker, who asked not to be named, told local media. "The ground shook and then there was just fire everywhere. People were running in every direction."

Local residents in the surrounding area were briefly advised to shelter in place as a precaution while air quality monitoring was carried out. That advisory has since been lifted.

The governor's office issued a statement expressing condolences to the families of those killed and said the state would offer its full support to the investigation.

Trade union representatives have called for a thorough inquiry, raising concerns about safety standards at the plant. They said they would be seeking full access to the findings of any investigation.

The steel industry in the US has faced increased scrutiny in recent years over workplace safety, with OSHA recording a number of serious incidents at manufacturing facilities across the country.
headline: Two dead, 10 hospitalised after US steel plant explosions

text:
The iconic Pompidou Centre in Paris is set to close its doors later this year for an extensive five-year renovation programme, with the landmark modern art museum not expected to reopen until 2030.

French authorities confirmed that the building, one of the most visited cultural institutions in Europe, will shut to the public in the autumn to allow for a major overhaul of its ageing infrastructure, including the replacement of asbestos insulation and a complete upgrade of its electrical, heating and ventilation systems.

The Centre Pompidou, which opened in 1977 and is renowned for its radical inside-out architectural design by Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers, attracts more than three million visitors annually. Its brightly coloured exposed pipes, ducts and escalators on the building's exterior have made it one of the most recognisable structures in the French capital.

The renovation is expected to cost in the region of €262 million, with the French state covering the bulk of the expense. Officials have acknowledged that the building's mechanical systems, many of which are original, have reached the end of their functional lifespan and require comprehensive replacement.

During the closure, parts of the Pompidou's vast collection of modern and contemporary art — which includes works by Picasso, Kandinsky, Matisse and Duchamp — are expected to be loaned to partner institutions across France and internationally.

The extended closure has drawn some criticism, with concerns raised about the impact on the surrounding Beaubourg neighbourhood, which relies heavily on the footfall generated by the centre. Local business owners have expressed worry about the economic consequences of losing such a significant cultural anchor for half a decade.

However, supporters of the project argue that the renovation is long overdue and essential to preserving the building for future generations. The centre has undergone only one previous major refurbishment, a two-year project completed in 2000.

The reopening is being targeted for early 2030, though large-scale public building projects in France have historically been subject to delays and cost overruns.
headline: Pompidou Centre in Paris to close for 5-year renovation

text:
The Government has announced that all departments and State agencies will be required to accept cash payments from the public as part of a new national strategy aimed at safeguarding the future of physical currency in Ireland.

The move comes amid growing concern that the increasing shift towards digital payments is leaving behind older people, those in rural areas, and individuals who rely on cash for budgeting purposes.

Minister for Finance Jack Chambers is expected to bring the strategy to Cabinet shortly, with the plan setting out a series of commitments to ensure that cash remains widely accepted across the economy.

Under the new framework, every government department and public body that deals directly with members of the public will be obliged to offer a cash payment option. The requirement is intended to guarantee that citizens who cannot or choose not to use card or digital payments are not excluded from accessing public services.

The strategy is understood to also include measures to protect access to ATMs and bank branches, particularly in towns and villages that have seen significant closures in recent years. It is expected to involve engagement with the banking sector and An Post to ensure adequate cash infrastructure is maintained nationwide.

Consumer groups and advocacy organisations for older people have broadly welcomed the announcement. Age Action said the commitment was an important recognition that not everyone has embraced digital banking, and that a significant minority of the population continues to depend on cash for everyday transactions.

The issue has been raised repeatedly in the Dáil and at Oireachtas committee level, with TDs from across the political spectrum highlighting the difficulties faced by constituents in areas where bank branches have closed and ATMs have been removed.

Social Democrats co-leader Catherine Murphy TD, who has campaigned on the issue, said the strategy was a step in the right direction but warned that implementation would be critical. She called on the Government to set clear timelines and ensure that departments comply with the new requirements.

Sinn Féin's finance spokesperson Pearse Doherty TD said the announcement was overdue and called for the strategy to go further by introducing legislation compelling all businesses above a certain size to accept cash.

The Central Bank of Ireland has previously noted that while the use of cash in day-to-day transactions has declined markedly since the pandemic, it remains an important means of payment for a substantial portion of the population. Research conducted by the bank found that cash was still the preferred payment method for roughly one in four adults in the State.

The Retail Excellence group said its members were broadly supportive of maintaining cash acceptance, though it cautioned that the costs of handling and lodging cash had risen significantly as bank branches have closed.

The strategy is also expected to address the role of the euro as legal tender and to consider whether legislative underpinning may be needed in the longer term to ensure cash acceptance across the wider economy, not just within the public sector.

A spokesperson for the Department of Finance said the Government was committed to ensuring that no one was left behind in the transition to a more digital economy, and that cash would continue to play a vital role in Irish life for the foreseeable future.
headline: All Govt depts to accept cash under new strategy

text:
Thousands of people took to the streets of Budapest on Saturday for a Pride march that went ahead despite attempts by the Hungarian authorities to ban it, in what organisers described as one of the largest turnouts in the event's history.

Police had sought to prohibit the parade on security grounds, but a court overturned the ban just days before the march was due to take place, clearing the way for participants to walk through the centre of the Hungarian capital.

Organisers estimated that more than 30,000 people joined the march, which wound its way along the banks of the Danube past some of the city's most prominent landmarks. Participants waved rainbow flags and carried placards calling for equal rights and an end to discrimination against LGBTQ+ people in Hungary.

The march took place against a backdrop of increasingly restrictive legislation targeting LGBTQ+ rights under the government of Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. In 2021, Hungary passed a controversial law that banned the depiction of homosexuality and gender reassignment to under-18s, drawing sharp condemnation from the European Commission and several EU member states.

The European Commission launched legal proceedings against Hungary over the legislation, which critics have compared to Russia's so-called "gay propaganda" law. The European Court of Justice subsequently ruled that the law violated EU principles, though Budapest has shown little inclination to repeal it.

A heavy police presence was visible along the route, with officers deployed to keep marchers and a smaller number of counter-protesters apart. There were no reports of significant incidents or arrests during the event.

Several European diplomats and ambassadors attended the parade in a show of solidarity, with some embassies flying rainbow flags from their buildings in Budapest throughout the week.

Speaking at the event, one of the organisers said the turnout demonstrated that Hungarian civil society would not be intimidated. "Every attempt to silence us only makes us louder," they told the crowd gathered near the finish point at the city's Városliget park.

Human rights organisations, including Amnesty International, praised the marchers and called on the Hungarian government to reverse what they described as a sustained rollback of LGBTQ+ rights in the country.

The Irish Council for Civil Liberties, which has previously expressed concern about the erosion of democratic norms in Hungary, said the march was "a powerful reminder that Pride is, at its core, a protest movement."

Hungary's government has not commented publicly on the march.
headline: Thousands march in banned Budapest Pride parade

text:
A man who died following a road traffic collision in Co Mayo yesterday has been described as a "lovely guy" by those who knew him.

The man, aged in his 40s, was fatally injured when the car he was driving was involved in a single-vehicle collision on the N5 near Westport in the early hours of Sunday morning.

He has been named locally, though Gardaí have not yet formally released his identity pending notification of all family members.

The collision occurred at approximately 2.30am, and emergency services attended the scene shortly afterwards. The man was pronounced dead at the scene. No other injuries were reported.

The road was closed for a number of hours to facilitate a technical examination by Garda forensic collision investigators, with local diversions put in place. It has since fully reopened.

Tributes have been paid to the deceased by friends and members of the local community, who spoke of their shock at his sudden passing.

One friend, who asked not to be named, told RTÉ News that the man was a "lovely guy who would do anything for anyone" and said his death had left the community in a state of disbelief.

"He was one of those people that everybody knew and everybody liked. This is just devastating for his family and for everyone who knew him," the friend said.

Local councillors have also expressed their sympathies to the man's family, describing the loss as a terrible tragedy for the area.

Gardaí at Westport are appealing for witnesses to the collision. Anyone who was travelling on the N5 in the area at the time, particularly those with dashcam footage, is asked to contact Westport Garda Station on 098 50230, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.
headline: Man who died in Mayo collision was 'lovely guy'

text:
Russia launched one of its largest aerial assaults on Ukraine on Monday, killing at least 36 people and striking a children's hospital in Kyiv in a wave of missile attacks that drew immediate international condemnation.

The Okhmatdyt children's hospital, one of the largest paediatric facilities in Ukraine, was badly damaged in the daytime strikes, with rescuers pulling casualties from the rubble as desperate parents carried injured children from the building. At least two people were killed at the hospital, according to Ukrainian officials, with dozens more injured.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attack was proof that Russia "cannot be left to do as it wishes" and renewed his calls for additional air defence systems from Western allies. "Russia cannot claim ignorance of where its missiles are flying," he said in an address posted to social media.

The strikes hit multiple cities across Ukraine, with missiles targeting residential buildings, infrastructure and medical facilities. In Kyiv alone, at least 22 people were killed, while further casualties were reported in Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih, Sloviansk and Pokrovsk.

The Russian defence ministry has not commented directly on the hospital strike, though Moscow has previously denied deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure.

The Taoiseach Simon Harris condemned the attacks, describing them as "horrific and unconscionable" and reiterating Ireland's support for Ukraine. Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin said the strikes on a children's hospital represented "a new low, even by the standards of this brutal war," and called for full accountability.

The United Nations Secretary General António Guterres said the attack on the hospital was "particularly shocking" and called for an independent investigation.

Ukraine's air force said Russia fired more than 40 missiles of various types in the barrage, including Kh-101 cruise missiles and Kinzhal hypersonic missiles. Officials said a number of the missiles were intercepted, but those that got through caused devastation across the country.

Emergency workers continued to search through the wreckage of the Okhmatdyt hospital into the evening, with authorities warning the death toll could rise. The facility had been treating children with cancer and other serious illnesses, and efforts were under way to transfer young patients to other hospitals.

The European Union's foreign policy chief Josep Borrell said the strikes were "a stark reminder of the urgent need to continue supporting Ukraine" and called on member states to accelerate deliveries of air defence equipment.

The attacks came ahead of a NATO summit in Washington this week, where Ukraine's allies are expected to discuss further military support for the country. President Zelensky said the timing was not coincidental and urged world leaders to respond with concrete action rather than words.

Ireland, which has maintained its military neutrality, has provided over €200 million in non-lethal aid to Ukraine since the full-scale Russian invasion began in February 2022. A number of Ukrainian refugees who have resettled in Ireland expressed horror at the latest strikes, with community groups organising vigils in Dublin and other cities.
headline: 36 dead, Kyiv hospital hit in Russian strikes on Ukraine

text:
Members of the public are being asked to avoid the area around An Earagail in Co Donegal over the coming days as helicopter operations get under way on the mountain.

The National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) confirmed that specialist aerial work will be carried out on the peak, one of the most popular hillwalking destinations in the northwest, beginning this week and expected to continue for several days depending on weather conditions.

The work is understood to involve the airlifting of materials as part of ongoing conservation and path restoration efforts on the mountain, which has seen significant erosion in recent years due to increasing footfall.

An Earagail, which rises to 752 metres and is the highest peak in Donegal, attracts thousands of walkers each year, with numbers growing steadily since the expansion of the Wild Atlantic Way tourism route.

The NPWS said the helicopter operations will require a temporary exclusion zone around parts of the mountain for safety reasons and urged hillwalkers and climbers to respect the restrictions while the work is ongoing.

"We are asking the public to co-operate with us by avoiding the area during these operations," a spokesperson said. "The safety of both the public and those carrying out the work is our primary concern."

Local mountain rescue volunteers have also been made aware of the planned operations. Donegal Mountain Rescue Team said it supported the request and encouraged walkers to choose alternative routes in the area while the work continues.

Signage has been erected at key access points to the mountain advising of the restrictions, and further updates will be provided through the NPWS and local authority social media channels.

The path restoration programme on An Earagail forms part of a broader national effort to repair upland trails that have suffered damage from erosion, with similar projects already completed or under way at a number of locations across the country, including in Kerry and Wicklow.

Anyone seeking further information is advised to contact the NPWS regional office in Donegal.
headline: Public asked to avoid An Earagail during helicopter work

text:
Nicaraguan police have arrested two more opposition figures who had been seeking to challenge President Daniel Ortega in the country's November elections, deepening a crackdown that has drawn international condemnation.

Félix Maradiaga and Juan Sebastián Chamorro were detained in separate operations on Tuesday, bringing to four the number of potential presidential candidates arrested in the space of a week. Both men had been openly critical of the Ortega government and had declared their intention to contest the presidency.

Maradiaga, a political analyst and civil society leader, was taken into custody at a police checkpoint in Managua shortly after leaving the offices of the public prosecutor, where he had been summoned for questioning. Chamorro, an economist and prominent opposition figure, was arrested at his home in the capital later the same evening.

Police said both men were being investigated under a controversial law passed last year that targets those it accuses of "undermining national sovereignty" with the backing of foreign powers. Critics say the legislation has been used as a tool to silence dissent and dismantle any credible challenge to Ortega's grip on power.

The arrests follow the detention last week of Cristiana Chamorro, a journalist and frontrunner in opinion polls, who was placed under house arrest on money laundering charges her supporters say are politically motivated. Another would-be candidate, Arturo Cruz, was also detained in recent days.

The European Union called the latest detentions "arbitrary" and urged Nicaraguan authorities to guarantee the rights of all citizens to participate in the democratic process. The United States said it was considering further sanctions against members of the Ortega government.

Costa Rica's president also expressed concern, while the Organisation of American States said the arrests represented a serious escalation against democratic norms in the region.

Ortega, a former revolutionary leader who has held power since 2007, is widely expected to seek a fourth consecutive term. His government has dismissed the international criticism, characterising those arrested as agents of foreign interference seeking to destabilise the country.

Nicaragua's opposition coalition has called for mass protests, though public demonstrations have been effectively banned since a wave of unrest in 2018 that left more than 300 people dead.
headline: Nicaraguan police arrest two more opposition contenders

text:
Three men have appeared before the Special Criminal Court in Dublin in connection with the fatal shooting at the Regency Hotel in 2016.

The men, who are aged in their 30s and 40s, were brought before the three-judge, non-jury court this morning following their arrests by Gardaí earlier this week. Each of the accused was charged with offences related to the gun attack, which took place during a boxing weigh-in event at the north Dublin hotel in February 2016.

David Byrne, a 33-year-old from Crumlin, was killed during the attack, which saw a number of gunmen, some dressed in Garda-style tactical uniforms, open fire in the lobby of the hotel. Two other men were injured in the incident, which sent shockwaves through the country and marked a dramatic escalation in an ongoing gangland feud.

The Director of Public Prosecutions directed trial on indictment, meaning the cases will be heard before the Special Criminal Court. The non-jury court is typically used for cases involving organised crime and paramilitary activity, where there are concerns about potential jury intimidation.

Each of the three accused spoke only to confirm their names and addresses during the brief hearing. Legal aid applications were made on behalf of all three men.

The accused were remanded in custody and are due to appear before the court again at a date to be fixed.

Gardaí have said the investigation into the Regency Hotel attack remains ongoing, and further arrests have not been ruled out.

The shooting at the Regency Hotel was widely regarded as a pivotal moment in the Kinahan-Hutch gangland feud, which has claimed a number of lives on both sides in the years since.
headline: Three men in court in connection with Regency shooting

text:
A man has escaped injury after a suspected petrol bomb was thrown at a property in the early hours of this morning.

The incident occurred at a house in a residential area, with Gardaí and emergency services called to the scene shortly after the device was thrown.

The man, who was inside the property at the time of the attack, was not injured in the incident.

Gardaí have confirmed they are treating the incident as a case of criminal damage by arson and have launched an investigation.

The scene was preserved overnight and a technical examination of the area was carried out earlier today by members of the Garda Technical Bureau.

It is understood that investigators are examining CCTV footage from the area as part of their enquiries and are appealing for anyone who may have witnessed the incident or noticed any suspicious activity in the vicinity to come forward.

Local residents have expressed shock at the attack, describing the area as generally quiet and peaceful.

One neighbour, who did not wish to be named, said they heard a loud noise during the night and saw the emergency services arrive shortly afterwards.

"It's very frightening to think something like this could happen on your doorstep," they said. "You just don't expect it in an area like this."

No arrests have been made at this stage and Gardaí say their investigations are ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact their local Garda station or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: Man uninjured after suspected petrol bomb attack

text:
Gardaí have issued a public appeal for help in tracing a man who has gone missing from Dundalk, Co Louth.

The man was reported missing from the town, and investigators are seeking the public's assistance in establishing his current whereabouts.

Anyone with information on his location is asked to contact Dundalk Garda Station on 042 938 8400, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.

Gardaí have said that investigations are ongoing and have appealed to anyone who may have seen the man or who has any information that could assist in locating him to come forward.
headline: Appeal issued to trace man missing from Dundalk

text:
Ken Starr, the former independent counsel whose dogged investigation into President Bill Clinton led to only the second presidential impeachment in American history, has died at the age of 76.

His family confirmed that Starr died on Tuesday at a hospital in Houston, Texas, due to complications from surgery. He had been in ill health in recent months.

Starr became one of the most recognisable figures in American politics during the 1990s, when his wide-ranging investigation into the Whitewater real estate dealings of Bill and Hillary Clinton expanded to encompass the president's sexual relationship with White House intern Monica Lewinsky.

His final report to Congress in September 1998, which contained explicit details of Clinton's encounters with Lewinsky, was released to the public and became an instant sensation. The report concluded that there were grounds for impeachment, citing perjury, obstruction of justice and abuse of power.

The House of Representatives voted to impeach Clinton in December 1998, but the Senate acquitted him on all charges the following February, falling well short of the two-thirds majority needed for conviction.

Critics accused Starr of conducting an overzealous and politically motivated prosecution, while supporters argued he was simply following the evidence wherever it led. The investigation, which lasted more than four years and cost in excess of $70 million, deeply polarised American public opinion and shaped the country's political landscape for years to come.

Born in Vernon, Texas, in 1946, Starr studied at George Washington University and Duke University School of Law before clerking for Chief Justice Warren Burger at the US Supreme Court. He served as a federal judge on the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit before being appointed Solicitor General under President George H.W. Bush.

In later years, Starr served as president and chancellor of Baylor University in Texas but was removed from the presidency in 2016 over his handling of sexual assault allegations against members of the university's football team. He subsequently resigned as chancellor.

More recently, Starr served on the legal defence team for President Donald Trump during his first impeachment trial in 2020, arguing against the use of impeachment as a political weapon — a position some commentators noted was strikingly at odds with his earlier role in the Clinton affair.
headline: Ken Starr, who investigated Clinton, dies at 76

text:
Tourists and business travellers from Ireland and across Europe are preparing to return to the United States after more than 18 months of pandemic-related travel restrictions were finally lifted.

The US reopened its borders to fully vaccinated international travellers today, marking the end of one of the longest and most contentious travel bans imposed during the Covid-19 crisis. The restrictions, first introduced in March 2020, had barred most non-US citizens who had recently been in Ireland, the UK, the EU's Schengen zone, and several other countries from entering the United States.

Under the new rules, foreign nationals aged 18 and over must show proof of full vaccination with a vaccine approved or authorised by the US Food and Drug Administration or listed for emergency use by the World Health Organisation. Travellers must also present a negative Covid-19 test taken within three days of departure.

There were emotional scenes at Dublin Airport this morning as families separated for months, and in some cases years, prepared to reunite with loved ones across the Atlantic. Several airlines, including Aer Lingus and United Airlines, had reported a surge in bookings on transatlantic routes in the weeks leading up to the reopening.

Aer Lingus said it had significantly increased its capacity on US routes to meet the anticipated demand, with services operating to destinations including New York, Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles, and Washington DC.

The Irish American community had been among the most vocal in campaigning for the lifting of the ban, with many families unable to visit relatives on either side of the Atlantic for prolonged periods. Irish American groups and politicians on Capitol Hill had lobbied the Biden administration extensively to ease restrictions.

The Tourism Ireland chief executive said the reopening of the US market represented a hugely significant moment for the Irish tourism industry. The US has traditionally been one of Ireland's most valuable source markets for overseas visitors, with American tourists contributing an estimated €1.6 billion to the Irish economy annually before the pandemic.

The Minister for Transport said the Government had worked closely with the US administration to ensure a smooth reopening and welcomed the return of transatlantic connectivity, which he described as vital for trade, tourism, and the deep personal connections between Ireland and the United States.

However, some concerns remain about the complexity of the documentation required for travel. Passengers must upload vaccination records and contact tracing information through airline systems before boarding, and there have been warnings of potential delays at check-in desks as staff verify paperwork.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has also confirmed that fully vaccinated travellers will no longer be required to quarantine upon arrival, though they are advised to get tested three to five days after their journey.

The travel industry had been pressing for the reopening for months, arguing that the blanket ban was no longer proportionate given the widespread availability of vaccines. Business groups including the American Chamber of Commerce Ireland and IBEC had highlighted the damage to commercial relationships and foreign direct investment caused by the prolonged restrictions.

Dublin Airport Authority said it expected passenger numbers on transatlantic routes to recover steadily in the coming months, though it cautioned that a full return to pre-pandemic levels of traffic was unlikely before next year at the earliest.
headline: Tourists prepare to return to US as travel ban lifted

text:
The Department of Health has confirmed 7,333 new cases of Covid-19 in the Republic today, with 410 patients currently hospitalised with the virus.

Of those in hospital, 88 are being treated in intensive care units, according to the latest figures.

Chief Medical Officer Dr Tony Holohan said the ongoing high level of transmission across the country continues to place significant pressure on the health service and urged people to follow public health advice.

"We are continuing to see very significant levels of disease in the community," Dr Holohan said. "It is vital that people who have symptoms isolate immediately and arrange a PCR test."

He appealed to those who have not yet come forward for vaccination, or who are eligible for a booster dose, to avail of the opportunity as soon as possible.

The HSE has said that hospitals in several parts of the country are experiencing considerable strain, with some emergency departments particularly affected by the current wave of infections.

As of this morning, there were 410 Covid-positive patients in hospitals across the State, an increase on yesterday's figure. The number in ICU has remained relatively stable in recent days.

Meanwhile, the vaccination programme continues to be rolled out, with the booster campaign now extended to further age groups. The latest figures show that more than 94% of the eligible adult population is fully vaccinated.

The National Public Health Emergency Team has urged continued vigilance, particularly around household mixing and social gatherings. People are reminded to wear masks in indoor settings, maintain social distancing where possible, and ensure good ventilation in shared spaces.

The Department noted that anyone experiencing symptoms such as a cough, fever, shortness of breath, or loss of taste or smell should self-isolate and contact their GP or arrange a test through the HSE's online portal.
headline: Covid-19: 7,333 cases, 410 patients in hospital

text:
Renewed calls have been made for the construction of a new pier on Great Blasket Island, with local representatives and tourism operators warning that the current landing infrastructure is no longer fit for purpose and is putting lives at risk.

The existing slip on the island, which has remained largely unchanged for decades, has long been a source of concern for boat operators who ferry thousands of visitors to the remote Kerry island each summer. Landing conditions are heavily dependent on weather and tidal movements, and operators say passengers and crew are regularly exposed to dangerous situations when disembarking.

Councillor Breandán Fitzgerald, who has raised the issue at Kerry County Council on multiple occasions, said the time for action is long overdue. "We have been talking about this for years and years, and nothing has been done," he said. "The Great Blasket is one of the most iconic cultural and heritage sites in Ireland, and yet we cannot guarantee safe access to it. That is simply not acceptable."

The island, which was permanently evacuated in 1953, has become one of the most popular tourist destinations in the south-west, drawing visitors from around the world who are drawn by its literary heritage, dramatic landscape and abundant wildlife. The island's former residents produced some of the most celebrated works in the Irish language, including Tomás Ó Criomhthain's *An tOileánach* and Peig Sayers' memoir.

During peak season, several hundred visitors a day can travel to the island from Dún Chaoin pier on the Dingle Peninsula. However, boat operators say there are frequent days when crossings must be cancelled or cut short because of conditions at the island's landing point, resulting in significant economic losses for local businesses.

One boat operator, who did not wish to be named, said there had been a number of near-misses in recent years. "People are jumping from boats onto wet, slippery rocks. It's only a matter of time before there is a serious accident or worse," he said.

The Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, which has responsibility for harbour and pier infrastructure, said it is aware of the calls for improved landing facilities on the island. A spokesperson said any proposed development would require detailed environmental and planning assessments, given the island's status as a Special Area of Conservation and a National Monument.

The National Parks and Wildlife Service, which manages much of the island, has previously expressed concerns about the potential environmental impact of any construction on the island, particularly on nesting seabird populations.

However, local representatives have argued that a sensitively designed pier could be developed without causing significant environmental damage. They point to similar projects on other island communities along the western seaboard which have been completed in recent years.

Ciarán Mac an Bhaird, a heritage officer with links to the island, said it was possible to balance conservation with practical necessity. "Nobody wants to damage the Blasket's environment or heritage. But we have a duty of care to the people who visit and the people who bring them there. A properly designed pier would actually help manage the island better," he said.

Kerry TDs have also backed the campaign, with calls made in the Dáil for ring-fenced funding to be allocated for a feasibility study as a first step.
headline: Renewed calls for a new pier on Great Blasket Island

text:
The Indonesian navy has confirmed that the submarine which went missing last week has been found broken into three parts on the sea floor, with all 53 crew members on board declared dead.

The KRI Nanggala-402 was located at a depth of more than 800 metres in waters north of Bali, far beyond the vessel's survivable depth limit of around 500 metres. Indonesian military chief Hadi Tjahjanto said the submarine had been positively identified with the help of underwater rescue vehicles deployed by neighbouring Singapore and Australia.

"With this authentic evidence, we can declare that all 53 crew members have passed," Mr Tjahjanto told reporters at a press conference in Bali. "We hereby lift the status from submissed to sunken."

The discovery brings to an end a desperate four-day search that had captivated the region and drawn international assistance from dozens of countries. Contact with the submarine was lost on Wednesday during a torpedo drill in the Bali Strait.

Indonesian President Joko Widodo expressed his condolences to the families of the crew and declared all 53 personnel as national heroes. "They were doing their best duty for the defence and sovereignty of our country," he said.

An oil slick and debris, including prayer mats and a grease bottle for the submarine's periscope, had been found on the surface in the days before the wreckage was located, raising fears the vessel had suffered a catastrophic failure.

Defence analysts have pointed to the age of the German-built submarine, which was constructed in 1978 and underwent a refit in South Korea in 2012, as a possible factor. Indonesia has long faced questions about the readiness of its ageing military equipment, and the disaster is likely to intensify pressure on Jakarta to modernise its fleet.

The cause of the sinking remains under investigation. Indonesian navy officials said a crack in the hull, possibly triggered by the submarine exceeding its dive limit, may have led to a catastrophic implosion. The vessel's three sections were found scattered on the seabed, along with other debris.

Recovery of the wreckage is expected to prove extremely difficult given the depth at which the submarine was found. Mr Tjahjanto said the military would make every effort to retrieve the remains of the crew but acknowledged the significant technical challenges involved.

The disaster is one of the worst submarine incidents in recent decades and has drawn messages of sympathy from governments around the world. Several nations, including the United States, India and Malaysia, had contributed ships and aircraft to the search effort.
headline: Sunken Indonesian submarine found broken in three

text:
The Road Safety Authority is set to recruit 80 new driving testers in a bid to address a significant backlog that has left thousands of learner drivers facing lengthy waiting times for their test.

The RSA confirmed the recruitment drive following sustained pressure from public representatives and motoring groups who have highlighted the growing delays across the country. At present, some test centres are reporting waiting times of more than 20 weeks, well in excess of the RSA's target of ten weeks.

Minister for Transport Eamon Ryan welcomed the announcement, saying the additional testers would make a "real and tangible difference" to the waiting times experienced by learner drivers. He said the Government was committed to ensuring the driving test system operated efficiently and that no one was left waiting an unreasonable length of time.

The RSA said the new positions would be spread across test centres nationwide, with priority given to locations where the backlog is most acute. Dublin, Cork and Galway are understood to be among the centres experiencing the greatest demand.

It is expected the recruitment process will be managed through the Public Appointments Service, with the first tranche of new testers expected to be in place within a number of months. The RSA said all new recruits would undergo a comprehensive training programme before being assigned to test centres.

Several TDs have raised the issue of driving test delays in the Dáil in recent months, with some describing the situation as unacceptable. Sinn Féin's transport spokesperson Darren O'Rourke said the recruitment was overdue and called on the RSA to set out a clear timeline for reducing waiting lists to an acceptable level.

The backlog has been attributed to a combination of factors, including increased demand following the pandemic, retirements among existing testers, and a surge in applications from those who had deferred their tests during Covid-19 restrictions.

Motoring groups, including the AA, said the delays had created knock-on difficulties for learner drivers, many of whom need a full licence for employment purposes. The AA said it hoped the additional testers would bring waiting times back within the RSA's own targets by the end of the year.

The RSA currently employs approximately 130 driving testers and conducts in the region of 200,000 tests annually. The addition of 80 new testers would represent a substantial increase in capacity.

The authority also noted that it continues to offer an online service allowing applicants to check waiting times at their nearest test centre and to avail of cancellation slots where they arise.
headline: 80 driving testers to be hired to tackle backlog

text:
The Japanese ambassador to Ireland has made an impassioned appeal for the global elimination of nuclear weapons, warning that the threat of their use remains as pressing today as it was nearly eight decades ago.

Ambassador Norio Maruyama made the remarks at a commemorative event in Dublin marking the anniversary of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, which killed an estimated 210,000 people by the end of that year and left countless others suffering the effects of radiation for generations.

Speaking to an audience that included members of the Oireachtas and representatives of civil society organisations, the ambassador said Japan's experience as the only country to have suffered nuclear attack in wartime carries with it a profound responsibility to advocate for disarmament.

"The hibakusha — the survivors of the atomic bombings — are ageing, and their numbers are dwindling," Ambassador Maruyama said. "It falls to all of us to carry forward their testimony and to ensure the world never again witnesses the devastation that nuclear weapons bring."

He praised Ireland's longstanding commitment to nuclear disarmament, noting the State's early advocacy at the United Nations and its role in championing the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. Ireland was also among the first countries to sign and ratify the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which entered into force in 2021.

The ambassador acknowledged that the current geopolitical landscape, including heightened tensions in several regions and nuclear sabre-rattling by some states, has made the path to disarmament more challenging. However, he argued that these developments made the cause more urgent, not less.

Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs Micheál Martin has previously described nuclear disarmament as a cornerstone of Irish foreign policy. The Government has consistently called on nuclear-armed states to engage meaningfully in multilateral disarmament efforts.

Several TDs and Senators attended the event, with cross-party support evident for the disarmament message. Senator Alice-Mary Higgins, who has been a vocal advocate for the nuclear weapons ban treaty, described the ambassador's address as a timely reminder of the humanitarian consequences at the heart of the debate.

Campaign groups including the Irish Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament welcomed the ambassador's intervention, saying it reinforced the moral imperative to pursue a world free of nuclear weapons.

The event also featured a display of origami cranes, a symbol of peace inspired by Sadako Sasaki, a young girl who developed leukaemia as a result of the Hiroshima bombing and who famously folded paper cranes in the hope of recovery.
headline: Japanese ambassador appeals for end to nuclear weapons

text:
A man has died while climbing a mountain in Co Kerry.

The man, who is understood to be in his 50s, got into difficulty while ascending Carrauntoohil, Ireland's highest peak, on Saturday afternoon.

Kerry Mountain Rescue Team was alerted to the incident at approximately 2pm and deployed a team to the location. The HSE National Ambulance Service and the Irish Coast Guard helicopter based at Shannon were also tasked to the scene.

Despite the efforts of rescue personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene. His body was recovered from the mountain and brought to University Hospital Kerry in Tralee, where a post-mortem examination is expected to be carried out in due course.

The man's identity has not been released, and it is understood his family has been notified.

Gardaí in Killarney are investigating the circumstances of the death, which is being treated as a tragic accident. A file will be prepared for the Coroner's Court.

Kerry Mountain Rescue Team, which is a voluntary organisation, has urged climbers to take all necessary precautions when heading into mountainous terrain, including checking weather conditions in advance and ensuring they carry appropriate equipment.

Carrauntoohil stands at 1,038 metres and attracts thousands of hillwalkers each year. It is situated in the MacGillycuddy's Reeks range on the Iveragh Peninsula.
headline: Man dies while climbing Kerry mountain

text:
Paris is set to become the first major European capital to ban rental electric scooters from its streets, after residents voted overwhelmingly in favour of removing the vehicles in a landmark referendum.

The city's mayor, Anne Hidalgo, who championed the vote, said the result sent a clear message that Parisians had grown tired of the chaos caused by the tens of thousands of rental scooters cluttering pavements and contributing to a rising toll of injuries and deaths.

Nearly 90 per cent of those who cast a ballot backed the ban, though turnout was notably low, with fewer than eight per cent of the city's 1.3 million eligible voters taking part. Critics of the referendum have pointed to the modest participation as evidence that the result may not reflect the true will of Parisians, but Hidalgo dismissed such concerns, insisting the outcome was decisive.

The three operators currently licensed to run rental scooter fleets in Paris — Lime, Dott and Tier — will see their contracts expire on 1 September, after which no new permits will be issued. The companies collectively operate around 15,000 scooters across the French capital and have argued that the vehicles offer an environmentally friendly alternative to car journeys.

The decision in Paris will be closely watched by other European cities grappling with similar questions about how to manage the rapid proliferation of shared micro-mobility services. In Dublin, e-scooters have occupied a regulatory grey area for some time, with legislation only recently providing a framework for their use on public roads. The Road Traffic and Roads Act 2023 paved the way for regulations governing e-scooters in Ireland, though questions remain about enforcement and safety standards.

Opponents of the Paris ban argue that removing scooters will simply push commuters back towards cars, worsening congestion and air pollution in a city that has made ambitious commitments to reducing emissions. Lime said it was "disappointed" by the outcome and warned that the ban would be a step backwards for sustainable urban transport.

However, safety campaigners have long raised the alarm about the dangers posed by rental scooters, which are frequently ridden on pavements, left strewn across pedestrian walkways and involved in collisions with both pedestrians and motorists. According to French authorities, accidents involving e-scooters have risen sharply in recent years, with several fatalities recorded in Paris alone.

Hidalgo, who has reshaped Paris's streetscape during her time in office by expanding cycle lanes and pedestrianising sections along the Seine, framed the ban as the latest step in reclaiming public space for residents. She acknowledged that privately owned e-scooters would remain legal but said the sheer volume of rental vehicles had become unmanageable.

The move comes as cities across Europe continue to experiment with different regulatory approaches. Some, including London, have trialled rental scooter schemes in limited areas with strict speed and parking controls, while others have imposed caps on fleet sizes or introduced designated parking zones.

For Paris, the ban marks a significant turning point in the debate over who controls the urban streetscape — and whether the convenience of new mobility technology should take precedence over concerns about safety, accessibility and the quality of public space.
headline: Paris aims to put the brakes on scooter proliferation

text:
Eight people have died after a private plane crashed in a mountainous area of northern Italy, according to local emergency services.

The aircraft, a twin-engine turboprop, went down in a wooded area near the town of San Candido in the South Tyrol region close to the Austrian border. The crash occurred shortly after midday local time on Sunday.

Italian authorities confirmed that all eight people on board the aircraft were killed in the incident. There were no survivors.

Emergency crews, including mountain rescue teams, firefighters and medical personnel, were dispatched to the remote crash site, which was described as difficult to access due to the steep and densely forested terrain. A helicopter was used to reach the wreckage.

The cause of the crash is not yet known, and Italian aviation authorities have opened an investigation into the incident. Weather conditions at the time of the crash are among the factors being examined, with reports suggesting there was low cloud cover in the area.

The identities of those on board have not yet been publicly released, pending notification of next-of-kin. Italian media reported that the aircraft had departed from a regional airport earlier that morning, though its intended destination has not been confirmed.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has said it is aware of the incident and is making enquiries to establish whether any Irish citizens were involved. A spokesperson said consular assistance would be made available if required.

Italy's transport minister expressed condolences to the families of those who lost their lives and said the government would ensure a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding the crash.
headline: Eight die after private plane crashes in Italy

text:
Small and medium-sized enterprises across the State have lost billions of euro in revenue as a result of Covid-19 restrictions, according to a new report that lays bare the devastating financial toll the pandemic has taken on Irish businesses.

The study, carried out by the Small Firms Association in conjunction with economists at University College Dublin, found that SMEs collectively suffered losses in excess of €12 billion during the various phases of public health restrictions imposed since March 2020.

The findings show that businesses in the hospitality, retail and personal services sectors were among the hardest hit, with many experiencing revenue declines of between 60% and 80% during periods of Level 5 restrictions.

Speaking at the launch of the report, SFA Director Sven Spollen-Behrens said the figures underline the scale of the challenge facing small business owners as they attempt to rebuild.

"These are not just numbers on a page. Behind every statistic is a business owner who has poured their life savings, their time and their energy into building something, only to see it brought to its knees by circumstances entirely beyond their control," he said.

The report also highlights that one in five SMEs took on significant additional debt to survive the pandemic, with the average level of Covid-related borrowing standing at approximately €120,000 per firm.

Minister for Enterprise, Trade and Employment Leo Varadkar acknowledged the enormous pressures facing the sector and said the Government remains committed to supporting businesses through the recovery phase.

"We have put in place a range of supports, including the Employment Wage Subsidy Scheme, the Covid Restrictions Support Scheme and tax warehousing measures, and we will continue to work with businesses to ensure they can get back on their feet," the Tánaiste said.

However, opposition TDs have criticised the Government's response as insufficient. Sinn Féin's spokesperson on enterprise Louise O'Reilly TD said many small business owners feel abandoned and called for a more comprehensive package of measures, including the extension of commercial rates waivers and greater access to low-cost finance.

"The Government needs to wake up to the reality that SMEs are the backbone of the Irish economy. They employ over one million people in this country, and if we allow them to fail, the consequences for local communities and the wider economy will be catastrophic," Deputy O'Reilly told RTÉ News.

The Irish Small and Medium Enterprises Association echoed those concerns, warning that many businesses remain in a precarious financial position despite the easing of restrictions. ISME CEO Neil McDonnell said cash flow remains the single biggest issue for the majority of its members.

The report recommends a series of measures to support the sector's recovery, including the introduction of a targeted grant scheme for the worst-affected businesses, further extensions to the tax debt warehousing arrangement and investment in digitalisation programmes to help SMEs adapt to changing consumer behaviour.

According to the Central Statistics Office, there are approximately 270,000 SMEs operating in the State, accounting for more than 99% of all active enterprises and employing roughly 68% of the private sector workforce.
headline: SMEs lose billions due to Covid-19 restrictions

text:
The DUP has been urged to engage constructively in efforts to find workable solutions to the challenges posed by post-Brexit trading arrangements, as frustration mounts over the party's continued opposition to the Northern Ireland Protocol.

Senior political figures on both sides of the border have called on the party to move beyond its entrenched position and join what one government source described as "the serious work of making things better for people and businesses in Northern Ireland."

The appeal comes as the European Commission and the British government continue technical discussions aimed at easing the operation of the protocol, which governs the movement of goods between Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The protocol, agreed as part of the Brexit Withdrawal Agreement, effectively keeps Northern Ireland aligned with EU single market rules for goods, creating checks on some products arriving from Britain.

The DUP has consistently opposed the protocol, arguing that it undermines Northern Ireland's place within the United Kingdom's internal market and creates a trade border in the Irish Sea. The party has refused to re-enter the power-sharing Executive at Stormont until its concerns are addressed, leaving the institutions in a state of paralysis.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin said that while the Irish Government understood the concerns of unionists, the current impasse was not serving the interests of anyone in Northern Ireland. He said there was "a genuine willingness" on the part of the EU to find practical solutions but that progress required all parties to engage in good faith.

"The protocol is there to protect the Good Friday Agreement and to ensure there is no hard border on the island of Ireland," Mr Martin said. "But there is significant flexibility being shown, and the DUP would do well to be part of those conversations rather than standing outside them."

A number of business groups in Northern Ireland have expressed growing impatience with the political deadlock, noting that the protocol also affords Northern Ireland unique dual-market access to both the EU single market and the UK market — a position some firms have described as a competitive advantage.

The British government has continued to press Brussels for further easements, particularly around the movement of food products and parcels from Great Britain to Northern Ireland. However, London has also faced criticism for its threat to invoke Article 16 of the protocol, a safeguard mechanism that would allow either side to unilaterally suspend parts of the arrangement.

Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald TD said the DUP's refusal to engage was "holding the people of the North to ransom" and called on the British government to do more to encourage the party back to the table.

"The protocol is a direct consequence of Brexit — a Brexit that the people of the North voted against," Ms McDonald said. "Solutions are there to be found, but only if everyone is prepared to roll up their sleeves."

SDLP leader Colum Eastwood echoed those sentiments, saying that businesses and ordinary families were paying the price for political posturing. "People need their elected representatives working for them, not blocking progress for the sake of political positioning," he said.

Alliance Party leader Naomi Long said there was an onus on all political leaders to demonstrate maturity and pragmatism.
headline: DUP urged to join search for post-Brexit solutions

text:
A Conservative MP has accused Stanley Johnson, the father of former prime minister Boris Johnson, of touching her inappropriately on two separate occasions.

Caroline Nokes, who chairs the Women and Equalities Committee, told Sky News that Mr Johnson had smacked her on the backside at the 2003 Conservative Party conference and had grabbed her thigh at a similar event in 2014.

Ms Nokes said she had decided to speak out after watching an interview in which Mr Johnson was asked about allegations made by journalist Ailbhe Rea, who had accused him of touching her inappropriately at the 2019 Conservative conference.

In a clip that aired on Sky News, Mr Johnson appeared to laugh off the allegation, saying he could not "remember" the incident.

Ms Nokes said she had been "astounded" by his response. "I watched the interview with Stanley Johnson and just thought, here is a man who has been called out for inappropriate behaviour towards a young woman and thinks it's funny," she told Sky News.

"And I thought, 'I'm not having that.' It happened to me and I'm not prepared to let that lie."

The MP for Romsey and Southampton North said she had not reported the incidents at the time, describing the culture within politics as one where such behaviour was often dismissed.

A spokesman for Mr Johnson said he had "no recollection" of the incidents described by Ms Nokes but added that he would "naturally apologise" if he had "inadvertently offended anybody."

The allegations come amid a wider reckoning over behaviour within Westminster, with several MPs and political figures facing accusations of misconduct in recent years.
headline: MP accuses Stanley Johnson of inappropriate touching

text:
A young schoolboy from Co Cork has discovered a whole new world of imagination after a local literacy programme helped him fall in love with reading through the works of Roald Dahl.

Nine-year-old Cian McCarthy, a pupil at Scoil Mhuire in Ballincollig, had struggled with reading for much of his early school years and was at risk of falling further behind his classmates. But a targeted intervention programme run through his school, with support from the Department of Education, has transformed his relationship with books.

His mother, Áine McCarthy, said the change has been remarkable. "He wouldn't have picked up a book six months ago. Now he's devouring everything Roald Dahl ever wrote. He started with *Charlie and the Chocolate Factory* and he hasn't stopped since. We can't get him to put the books down at bedtime," she told RTÉ News.

Cian said *Matilda* is his favourite so far. "She loves reading just like me now, and she has magic powers. I don't have magic powers but I think reading is kind of magic," he said.

His teacher, Sarah Brennan, said Cian's progress has been extraordinary. "When a child finds the right author, the right story that speaks to them, it can be completely transformative. Cian has jumped two reading levels in a matter of months, and his confidence across all subjects has improved as a result," she said.

The programme, which pairs children with trained literacy support workers for one-to-one reading sessions, has been operating in a number of schools across Cork and is part of a broader initiative aimed at improving literacy outcomes among primary school pupils. The Department of Education has committed to expanding similar programmes nationwide as part of its literacy and numeracy strategy.

Research published earlier this year by the Economic and Social Research Institute found that one in ten children in Irish primary schools continues to experience significant difficulty with reading, with boys disproportionately affected.

Ms Brennan said the key is finding material that captures a child's imagination. "Roald Dahl has that wonderful ability to speak directly to children, to make them feel like they're in on the joke. For reluctant readers, that can make all the difference," she said.

Cian, meanwhile, has already set himself his next target. "I want to read every single Roald Dahl book. Then maybe I'll write my own," he said.
headline: Schoolboy enjoys new chapter reading Roald Dahl books

text:
Maternity hospitals across the country have been celebrating the arrival of the first babies of the New Year, with a number of little ones making their entrance into the world in the early hours of 1 January.

The Rotunda Hospital in Dublin welcomed its first baby of 2025 just moments after midnight, with staff describing scenes of joy and excitement on the ward. The hospital, one of the busiest maternity units in Europe, said both mother and baby were doing well.

At the National Maternity Hospital on Holles Street, the first arrival came shortly after midnight, continuing a long-standing tradition that sees staff eagerly awaiting the stroke of twelve to see which baby will claim the coveted title.

University Maternity Hospital Limerick also reported an early arrival, with a healthy baby born in the opening minutes of the New Year. Cork University Maternity Hospital and University Hospital Galway were among the other units to welcome new additions in the small hours.

The HSE said maternity services operated as normal throughout the holiday period, with midwives, obstetricians and support staff working through the night to ensure safe deliveries across the country.

Staff at several hospitals took to social media to share their congratulations with the new families, posting photographs with the permission of parents and describing the special atmosphere on the wards as the clock struck midnight.

The first babies of the year are always a source of particular celebration for hospital staff, many of whom volunteered to work the New Year's Eve shift in the hope of being part of the occasion.

Ireland sees approximately 55,000 births each year, according to the Central Statistics Office, with numbers remaining relatively steady in recent years.

The new parents and their families were wished well by hospital management and staff as they began the New Year with the newest members of their families.
headline: Hospitals welcome first babies of the New Year

text:
President Michael D Higgins has officially switched on the Christmas lights at Áras an Uachtaráin, marking the beginning of the festive season at the historic residence in the Phoenix Park.

The President was joined by his wife, Sabina Higgins, for the ceremony, which saw the grounds of the Áras illuminated with thousands of lights as darkness fell over Dublin.

The annual event has become a much-loved tradition, signalling the start of Christmas celebrations at the official residence of the head of state. Members of the public who had gathered at the Phoenix Park were treated to the spectacle as the lights were switched on, casting a warm glow across the façade of the building and its surrounding gardens.

Speaking at the event, President Higgins reflected on the importance of community and togetherness during the Christmas period, and extended his thoughts to those who may be experiencing hardship or loneliness at this time of year. He also paid tribute to those working over the festive season in hospitals, emergency services and other essential roles.

The lighting display at Áras an Uachtaráin is expected to remain in place throughout the Christmas period and into the new year. The Phoenix Park itself has become an increasingly popular destination for Dubliners and visitors during the festive season, with families often making the trip to see the lights at the presidential residence.

The President and Mrs Higgins have traditionally used the Christmas period to host a number of receptions at the Áras, welcoming community groups, charities and organisations working with vulnerable people across the country.

The switching on of the lights at Áras an Uachtaráin follows similar ceremonies in towns and cities across Ireland in recent weeks, as communities around the country prepare for the festive season.
headline: President turns on Áras an Uachtaráin Christmas lights

text:
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control has warned that a newly identified mutation of the coronavirus could potentially reduce the effectiveness of vaccines currently being rolled out across the EU.

In a risk assessment published today, the ECDC said the variant, which has been detected in a growing number of member states, carries mutations in the spike protein that may allow the virus to partially evade the immune response generated by existing vaccines.

The agency stressed that while vaccines remain the most important tool in combating the pandemic, ongoing genomic surveillance is critical to identifying and tracking variants of concern as they emerge.

"There is laboratory evidence to suggest that certain mutations may reduce neutralising antibody activity," the ECDC said in its assessment. "However, it is too early to draw definitive conclusions about the real-world impact on vaccine effectiveness."

The warning comes as Ireland continues to accelerate its vaccination programme, with the HSE confirming that more than one million doses have now been administered across the State. The Department of Health said it is closely monitoring the situation in conjunction with European partners.

The National Public Health Emergency Team has been briefed on the ECDC's findings, and NPHET is expected to discuss the implications at its next scheduled meeting.

Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly said the Government is taking the development "very seriously" and that Ireland's genomic sequencing capacity has been significantly expanded in recent months to detect new variants circulating in the community.

"We have always said that this virus will continue to evolve, and we must remain vigilant," the Minister said. "Our sequencing programme is now among the most comprehensive in Europe, and we are working closely with the ECDC and our EU colleagues to assess any emerging threats."

Professor Philip Nolan, chair of NPHET's Irish Epidemiological Modelling Advisory Group, said the development underscores the importance of maintaining public health measures even as the vaccine rollout progresses.

"Vaccination alone will not end this pandemic overnight," Prof Nolan said. "We need to suppress transmission to reduce the opportunity for the virus to mutate further. Every person who follows public health advice is contributing to that effort."

The ECDC has recommended that member states enhance their sequencing efforts and share data rapidly through European surveillance networks. It also urged manufacturers to begin preparatory work on adapted vaccines that could target emerging variants if necessary.

Infectious disease specialists in Ireland have echoed the ECDC's call for caution but have also sought to reassure the public that current vaccines are still expected to provide significant protection against severe illness and hospitalisation, even in the presence of new variants.

Dr Cillian De Gascun, director of the National Virus Reference Laboratory at UCD, said that while reduced vaccine effectiveness against certain variants is a concern, the vaccines are designed to generate a broad immune response.

"Even where we see some reduction in neutralising antibody levels in laboratory studies, that does not necessarily translate into a complete loss of protection," Dr De Gascun said. "The immune system has multiple lines of defence, and current evidence suggests that vaccinated individuals remain well protected against the most serious outcomes of infection."
