The ECDC said it will continue to update its risk assessment as further data becomes available and urged all EU citizens to avail of vaccination when offered.
headline: ECDC: Virus mutation could hamper vaccine effectiveness

text:
The Government has launched a new Seafood Sector Taskforce to address the significant challenges facing Ireland's fishing and seafood industries in the aftermath of Brexit.

The taskforce, which will be chaired by Aidan Cotter, former chief executive of Bord Bia, will examine the impacts of the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement on the Irish seafood sector and recommend measures to support those most affected.

Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine Charlie McConalogue said the establishment of the taskforce reflects the Government's recognition that the Brexit agreement has had a "disproportionate impact" on Ireland's fishing communities.

"Our fishing fleet and coastal communities have borne a significant burden as a result of the outcome of the Brexit negotiations," the Minister said. "This taskforce will engage directly with those affected and develop a comprehensive response to the challenges they face."

Under the terms of the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement, EU member states were required to transfer a proportion of their fishing quotas in UK waters to Britain. Ireland, given its heavy reliance on fishing in UK waters, was among the most affected member states, with the sector facing quota reductions of approximately 15% of the total value of fish taken from UK waters, to be phased in over a period of five and a half years.

The taskforce will consult with industry representatives, fishing organisations and coastal communities to assess the full extent of the economic and social impacts. It is expected to make recommendations on supports including potential fleet restructuring, diversification opportunities and investment in coastal communities that are heavily dependent on the fishing industry.

The Irish fishing industry has long argued that it was unfairly disadvantaged by the Brexit deal, with representatives pointing out that Ireland accounts for a significant share of the EU quota reductions despite being a relatively small member state.

The taskforce is expected to report back to the Minister with its findings and recommendations within a number of months. The Government has indicated that funding from the Brexit Adjustment Reserve, the €5 billion EU fund established to help member states cope with the fallout from Britain's departure, could be used to support measures arising from the taskforce's work.

Industry groups have broadly welcomed the initiative, though some have expressed concern that action has not come sooner. The Irish Fish Processors and Exporters Association said it hoped the taskforce would lead to "tangible and meaningful supports" for a sector that has been under severe pressure.

The establishment of the taskforce comes as the broader agri-food sector continues to navigate the new trading reality with the UK, which remains one of Ireland's most important export markets for food and drink products.
headline: Seafood Sector Taskforce launched in wake of Brexit

text:
When the first lockdown drill of the school year was announced over the intercom, Aoife Brennan didn't flinch. The Cork native, who has been teaching in a public elementary school in Massachusetts for the past six years, simply guided her young pupils to the corner of the classroom, switched off the lights, and locked the door.

"It's just part of life here," she told RTÉ News. "You do fire drills, you do lockdown drills. The children know the routine. They know to be quiet, to stay low, to move away from the windows. It's heartbreaking when you think about it, but in the moment, you just go into autopilot."

Ms Brennan's experience reflects a reality that remains largely alien to teachers in Ireland but is deeply embedded in the American education system. In the wake of repeated mass shootings at schools across the United States, lockdown drills — in which students and staff practise responding to an armed intruder — have become as routine as fire safety exercises in the vast majority of American schools.

According to the National Centre for Education Statistics, more than 95 per cent of public schools in the US now conduct lockdown drills at least once a year, with many holding them several times throughout the academic year.

Ms Brennan, who grew up in Ballincollig and studied education at University College Cork before emigrating in 2018, said the drills were one of the biggest culture shocks she encountered when she began teaching in the US.

"In Ireland, the worst thing you'd be preparing for is maybe a storm or a power cut. Here, you're preparing children — some of them five and six years old — for the possibility that someone could come into their school with a gun. It took me a long time to come to terms with that."

She said the school where she teaches holds lockdown drills roughly every two months, and that staff receive regular training on how to respond to an active shooter situation. The training includes instructions on barricading doors, identifying escape routes, and, as a last resort, confronting an attacker.

"There's a protocol called 'Run, Hide, Fight' that we're trained on. It's surreal. You're sitting in a staff meeting discussing lesson plans one minute and the next you're being told how to barricade a door with furniture."

Ms Brennan said that while the drills can be distressing, particularly for younger children, schools have become more thoughtful in how they conduct them. "When I first started, the drills were quite intense. There'd be someone rattling the door handle to simulate an intruder. They've moved away from that now, at least in our district, because of the trauma it was causing. Now it's more about practising the procedure calmly."

The issue of school safety in the US has once again come to the fore in recent months, with several high-profile incidents reigniting the debate over gun control. Despite widespread public support for stricter firearms legislation, efforts to pass comprehensive gun reform at the federal level have repeatedly stalled in Congress.

Ms Brennan said the political paralysis on the issue is a source of deep frustration for many teachers.
headline: Lockdown drills 'part of life' for Irish teacher in US

text:
The British government is set to relax immigration requirements for overseas care workers in an effort to address chronic staffing shortages across the social care sector in England.

Under the revised rules, care providers will find it easier to recruit workers from abroad, with the UK Home Office confirming that the care worker role will be added to the shortage occupation list. This means employers will be able to offer lower salaries than would typically be required under the points-based immigration system introduced after Brexit.

The move represents a significant policy shift for a government that had made reducing net migration a central plank of its post-Brexit agenda. Ministers have acknowledged, however, that the care sector faces an acute recruitment crisis, with tens of thousands of vacancies threatening the delivery of services to elderly and vulnerable people across England.

Care sector representatives have broadly welcomed the announcement, describing it as a pragmatic recognition of the workforce pressures that have intensified since the end of free movement from the European Union. Before Brexit, many care homes and domiciliary care providers relied heavily on workers from EU member states, including a significant number of Irish citizens.

The decision is likely to be closely watched on this side of the Irish Sea. The care sector in the Republic has faced similar staffing difficulties, and there have been ongoing concerns about competition for workers between the two jurisdictions. Irish care providers have previously warned that any easing of UK immigration rules could draw potential workers away from Ireland, where the sector already struggles to fill vacancies.

The HSE and private care providers here have been grappling with recruitment challenges of their own, with advocacy groups calling on the Government to do more to make the sector attractive to both domestic and international workers.

Trade unions in Britain have cautioned that while overseas recruitment may provide short-term relief, it must not be used as a substitute for improving pay and conditions in a sector long characterised by low wages and precarious employment. Unison, one of the largest unions representing care workers in the UK, said the government must ensure that migrant workers are not exploited and that their rights are properly protected.

The changes are expected to come into effect in the coming months, subject to final approval from the UK Home Secretary.
headline: UK to ease immigration rules for care workers

text:
The National Public Health Emergency Team had considered the possibility that indoor dining might have had to remain closed well beyond September, it has emerged, as the country continues to navigate the complex reopening of society.

Senior health officials discussed the potential for a prolonged shutdown of indoor hospitality at several meetings earlier this year, amid concerns about the trajectory of the Delta variant and its potential to derail the vaccination programme.

It is understood that NPHET modelling had examined scenarios in which indoor dining would not have been feasible until a significantly larger proportion of the adult population had been fully vaccinated, potentially pushing any reopening into the autumn or even later.

The revelation underscores the degree of caution that characterised deliberations within the public health advisory body, even as political and industry pressure mounted to reopen the sector.

Indoor dining resumed in late July under a system that required proof of vaccination or recovery from Covid-19, a compromise that proved deeply controversial and posed significant logistical challenges for the hospitality industry.

The Restaurants Association of Ireland had repeatedly warned that further delays to reopening would have proved catastrophic for thousands of businesses already on the brink of collapse after more than a year of restrictions.

Speaking on RTÉ's Morning Ireland, a senior Government source said ministers had been acutely aware of the more pessimistic scenarios outlined by NPHET but had ultimately opted to proceed with a phased reopening tied to the vaccination programme.

"There was always a tension between what was epidemiologically ideal and what was sustainable for society and the economy," the source said. "The vaccination cert system was the mechanism that allowed us to bridge that gap."

Chief Medical Officer Dr Tony Holohan has consistently maintained that NPHET's advice is guided solely by public health considerations, and that decisions on the pace of reopening are ultimately a matter for Government.

The Tánaiste, Leo Varadkar, had previously acknowledged that the Government and NPHET did not always see eye to eye on the timeline for easing restrictions, describing the relationship as one of constructive but sometimes difficult engagement.

Opposition TDs have called for greater transparency around the modelling and advice that informed key reopening decisions. Sinn Féin's health spokesperson David Cullinane said the public deserved a full account of the deliberations that shaped the country's pandemic response.

"People in the hospitality sector went through enormous hardship," he told the Dáil. "They are entitled to know what scenarios were being discussed and what evidence underpinned those discussions."

Meanwhile, the HSE's vaccination programme continues to make significant progress, with more than 88% of the adult population now fully vaccinated. Health officials have said this level of coverage has provided a substantial degree of protection against severe illness and hospitalisation, even as case numbers remain elevated.

NPHET is expected to meet again next week to review the latest epidemiological data ahead of further decisions on the easing of remaining restrictions in October.
headline: NPHET: Indoor dining could have closed beyond September

text:
The United States has threatened to impose sweeping new tariffs on a range of European Union exports including cheese, pork and whiskey, in a significant escalation of trade tensions between Washington and Brussels.

The warning, which came from senior US trade officials, could have serious implications for Irish exporters, given the country's heavy reliance on the American market for dairy and spirits in particular.

Ireland exported more than €2 billion worth of food and drink products to the US last year, with dairy and beverages among the largest categories. The Irish Farmers' Association said any new tariffs on cheese and pork would be "deeply damaging" to producers already contending with rising input costs and market volatility.

The threat is understood to be linked to ongoing disputes over EU regulatory standards and what Washington has characterised as unfair trade barriers to American agricultural products entering European markets. The US has long complained that EU protections for geographically indicated products, such as certain cheeses and spirits, effectively shut American competitors out of the European marketplace.

The European Commission said it stood ready to engage in dialogue but would "respond firmly and proportionately" to any unilateral measures that breach World Trade Organisation rules.

The Tánaiste and Minister for Enterprise, Trade and Employment said the Government was monitoring the situation closely and had been in contact with EU counterparts. "Ireland's trading relationship with the United States is of enormous strategic importance, and we will work through the EU to ensure that Irish exporters are not unfairly penalised," he said.

The Irish Whiskey Association warned that tariffs could set back years of growth in the American market, which now accounts for a substantial share of Irish whiskey sales globally. The US is the single largest export market for Irish whiskey, with sales there having grown significantly over the past decade.

Ibec, the business representative group, called on the EU to prioritise a negotiated settlement. "A tit-for-tat tariff war would be in nobody's interest, least of all small, open economies like Ireland that depend on transatlantic trade," a spokesperson said.

The threat echoes a similar episode in 2019 when the US imposed tariffs on a range of EU goods, including Irish whiskey and cheese, as part of a dispute over aircraft subsidies to Airbus. Those tariffs caused significant disruption before being suspended in 2021.

Brussels is expected to discuss the latest developments at a meeting of EU trade ministers later this week, with the Irish Government set to push for a de-escalation in rhetoric and a return to formal negotiations.
headline: US threatens tariffs on EU cheese, pork and whiskey

text:
Sinn Féin has confirmed Martina Anderson as its candidate for the Northern Ireland constituency in the European Parliament elections.

The former MEP, who represented the North in the European Parliament from 2012 until Brexit took effect in 2020, was selected at a party convention held in Belfast on Saturday evening.

Ms Anderson said she was "honoured and delighted" to have been chosen by party members and pledged to work to ensure that the voices of people in the North are heard in Brussels and Strasbourg.

"I have the experience, the track record and the determination to represent the people of the North of Ireland on the European stage," she said. "I know how the European Parliament works and I'm ready to hit the ground running."

Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald congratulated Ms Anderson on her selection, describing her as a "proven champion" for Irish interests in Europe.

"Martina brings unrivalled experience to this election. She has a strong record of delivering for people across the North during her time as an MEP and she will do so again," Ms McDonald said.

The selection comes as part of the new arrangements under the Windsor Framework, which provide for the North to once again have representation in the European Parliament given the continued application of certain EU single market rules there.

Ms Anderson, a former MLA for Foyle, is well known within republican circles and served a lengthy prison sentence in the 1980s before becoming a prominent figure in the peace process.

Other parties are expected to confirm their candidates for the Northern Ireland European constituency in the coming weeks, with the election set to be closely watched as a barometer of political sentiment in the region.
headline: Anderson confirmed as Sinn Féin's NI Europe candidate

text:
Countries around the world must significantly raise their ambitions on climate action or risk catastrophic consequences, the United Nations has warned in a stark assessment ahead of the next round of international negotiations.

The UN's latest report on nationally determined contributions found that current pledges from governments fall far short of what is needed to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, the target set under the Paris Agreement.

Speaking at the launch of the report, UN Secretary General António Guterres said the findings should serve as a "wake-up call" for every nation, urging leaders to treat the climate crisis with the same urgency as any other threat to global security.

"We are running out of time," Mr Guterres said. "The window to act is narrowing, and the costs of inaction are mounting with every passing year."

The report found that even if all current pledges were fully implemented, the world would still be on course for warming of approximately 2.5 to 2.9 degrees by the end of the century, a level that scientists say would trigger devastating and irreversible changes to the planet's climate systems.

Small island developing states and vulnerable nations expressed deep frustration at the pace of progress, with several delegates warning that their very existence is under threat from rising sea levels and increasingly severe weather events.

The findings come as Ireland continues to grapple with its own climate targets. The Government has committed to halving emissions by 2030 under the Climate Action Plan, but progress across several sectors, particularly agriculture and transport, has been slow. Ireland has previously faced criticism for lagging behind its European counterparts on emissions reductions.

Minister for the Environment Eamon Ryan has repeatedly stressed the need for Ireland to meet its obligations, warning that failure to do so could result in billions of euro in fines under EU regulations.

Environmental groups, including Friends of the Earth Ireland, said the UN report underscored the need for the Government to accelerate its efforts domestically while pushing for stronger commitments at the international level.

The next UN climate summit, COP29, is expected to be a critical juncture in global efforts to address the crisis, with countries due to submit updated climate plans that reflect greater ambition. Developing nations are also pressing wealthier countries to deliver on long-standing promises of climate finance, arguing that those most responsible for historical emissions must bear a greater share of the burden.

Analysts have warned that without a dramatic shift in policy direction from the world's largest emitters, including China, the United States, and the European Union, the Paris Agreement targets will remain out of reach.
headline: Countries must be more ambitious on climate goals: UN

text:
New South Wales authorities have announced tighter restrictions across Greater Sydney as the state grapples with what officials have described as a "stubborn" Delta variant outbreak that has continued to grow despite weeks of stay-at-home orders.

Premier Gladys Berejiklian said the existing lockdown, which has been in place since late June, was not doing enough to curb the spread of the virus, with case numbers continuing to climb. The state recorded another sharp rise in daily infections, prompting the government to act.

Under the new measures, construction sites across Greater Sydney will be shut down for at least two weeks, while retail outlets will be limited to click-and-collect services only. Masks will be mandatory whenever a person leaves their home, and exercise will be restricted to within a five-kilometre radius of a person's residence.

Ms Berejiklian acknowledged the frustration felt by residents who have already endured several weeks of restrictions but said the highly transmissible Delta variant had proven far more difficult to contain than previous strains.

"This is a very stubborn variant and we need to throw everything at it," she told reporters at a press conference in Sydney. "I know this is not the news people want to hear, but we need to do more."

Chief Health Officer Dr Kerry Chant said a significant number of new cases were being detected among people who had been active in the community while infectious, undermining efforts to bring the outbreak under control. She urged anyone with even the mildest of symptoms to come forward for testing immediately.

The tightened restrictions come as Australia's vaccine rollout continues to face criticism for its slow pace. Only a fraction of the country's adult population has been fully vaccinated, leaving large swathes of the community vulnerable to the Delta variant.

Prime Minister Scott Morrison said the federal government would increase vaccine supplies to New South Wales, which he described as the "epicentre" of the national outbreak. However, he stopped short of imposing a nationally coordinated response, maintaining that pandemic management remained primarily a matter for state and territory governments.

The situation in Sydney stands in stark contrast to the approach taken earlier in the pandemic, when Australia was widely praised for its swift border closures and aggressive suppression strategy. The country had largely avoided the mass outbreaks seen in Europe and North America, but the arrival of the Delta variant has exposed vulnerabilities in the nation's defences.

Several other Australian states have closed their borders to travellers from New South Wales in an effort to prevent the variant from spreading further. Queensland, Victoria and South Australia have all imposed strict entry requirements, with some banning arrivals from the state altogether.

Business groups have warned that the extended and deepening lockdown will have a devastating economic impact, particularly on small businesses and casual workers who lack access to adequate government support payments. The federal government has faced calls to expand its disaster payment scheme to provide more comprehensive assistance.

Ms Berejiklian said the restrictions would remain in place until case numbers showed a sustained decline but declined to set a specific end date, saying only that the government would review the situation on a week-by-week basis.
headline: Sydney tightens lockdown amid 'stubborn' outbreak

text:
China has revoked the press credentials of three reporters working for The Wall Street Journal, in what represents one of the most significant expulsions of foreign journalists from the country in recent years.

The move was announced by China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which said the decision was taken in response to a column published by the Journal's opinion section that Beijing deemed racist and demeaning.

The opinion piece, published earlier this month under the headline "China Is the Real Sick Man of Asia," drew sharp criticism from Chinese officials, who called it insulting to the Chinese people, particularly as the country grapples with the deadly coronavirus outbreak.

The three journalists ordered to leave the country within five days are deputy bureau chief Josh Chin and reporters Chao Deng and Philip Wen. None of the three were involved in writing or editing the opinion column that provoked Beijing's ire.

The Wall Street Journal's publisher, William Lewis, said the newspaper was "deeply disappointed" by the decision and called on the Chinese authorities to reconsider. The Foreign Correspondents' Club of China condemned the expulsions as an "unprecedented form of retaliation" against foreign media.

The move comes at a time of heightened tensions between Washington and Beijing, with the United States recently designating five Chinese state-run media organisations as foreign government missions, effectively treating them as extensions of the Chinese state rather than independent news outlets.

The Trump administration described China's decision as an affront to press freedom. US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo said Washington condemned the expulsions and called on Beijing to respect the vital role of a free press.

Press freedom organisations, including Reporters Without Borders, have criticised the move as part of a broader pattern of tightening controls on foreign media operating in China. The country currently ranks near the bottom of global press freedom indices.

It is understood that the expulsions mark the first time since 1998 that China has revoked the credentials of multiple foreign journalists from a single news organisation simultaneously.
headline: China revokes press credentials of three WSJ reporters

text:
Iceland will cease all whale hunting from next year, the country's food minister has confirmed, bringing to a close a practice that has drawn sustained international criticism.

Svandís Svavarsdóttir said there was no longer sufficient economic justification for the continuation of whaling, and that the industry's days were effectively numbered.

"There is little to justify the authorisation of whale hunting beyond 2024," Ms Svavarsdóttir told the Icelandic broadcaster RÚV. "The economic benefits are negligible."

The announcement means Iceland will join the vast majority of nations that have already turned their backs on commercial whaling. Only Norway and Japan continue to hunt whales commercially, though Japan withdrew from the International Whaling Commission (IWC) in 2019 to do so.

Iceland had been a member of the IWC moratorium on commercial whaling, which came into effect in 1986, but resumed fin whale hunting in 2006 and minke whale hunting in 2003, citing scientific reservations about the moratorium.

In practice, however, the industry had already been winding down considerably. Only one company, Hvalur hf, owned by the veteran whaling magnate Kristján Loftsson, had continued to hunt fin whales in recent years, and its operations were suspended for much of the past several seasons amid tightening animal welfare regulations.

The Icelandic government temporarily halted this summer's whaling season in June after an independent review found that the hunting methods used did not comply with the country's animal welfare laws. Inspectors found that many of the whales killed took too long to die, raising serious ethical concerns.

Environmental organisations welcomed the decision. The International Fund for Animal Welfare described it as "a momentous day for whale conservation," while campaigners expressed hope that the move would increase pressure on Norway and Japan to follow suit.

Whale watching has become a significant tourism industry in Iceland in recent decades, with operators arguing that living whales are worth considerably more to the economy than dead ones. The sector generates tens of millions of euro annually and has grown steadily, even as the whaling industry has contracted.

The decision is expected to be formalised when Iceland's current whaling permits expire at the end of this year, with no new licences to be issued thereafter.
headline: Iceland to end whale hunting from 2024, says minister

text:
Shannon Airport Managing Director Robert Dowers is to leave his role, it has been confirmed.

Mr Dowers, who has served as managing director of Shannon Group's airport operation, will depart the position in the coming weeks, the company said in a statement.

During his tenure, Mr Dowers oversaw significant efforts to rebuild passenger numbers at the mid-west airport following the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on the aviation sector. He also played a key role in securing new route announcements and strengthening Shannon's position as a transatlantic gateway.

Shannon Group confirmed the departure, thanking Mr Dowers for his contribution to the airport and wishing him well in his future endeavours.

The news comes at a pivotal time for Shannon Airport, which has been working to attract additional airlines and expand its route network as the aviation industry continues its recovery. The airport has been a focal point for regional connectivity in the west of Ireland, serving as a key economic driver for Clare, Limerick and the wider mid-west region.

It is understood that a process to appoint a successor will get under way in due course.

Shannon Airport, which handles both commercial and transatlantic traffic, has long been regarded as strategically important to the region's tourism and business sectors. Politicians across the mid-west have consistently called for greater investment in the facility and more government support to help it compete with larger airports in Dublin and Cork.

Shannon Group, which also oversees Shannon Commercial Properties, declined to comment further on the reasons for Mr Dowers' departure.
headline: Shannon Airport Managing Director is to leave his role

text:
A motorcyclist in his 20s has been taken to hospital after a collision in Co Offaly this afternoon.

The incident occurred on the R420 at Ballinagar shortly before 3pm when the motorcycle was involved in a collision with a car.

The injured man was treated at the scene by emergency services before being transported to Midland Regional Hospital, Tullamore, where his injuries are understood to be non-life-threatening.

The driver of the car, a woman in her 40s, was uninjured in the collision.

Gardaí have closed the road to facilitate an examination of the scene by forensic collision investigators, and local diversions are in place. Motorists are being advised to avoid the area and seek alternative routes.

Gardaí at Tullamore are appealing for witnesses to come forward. Any road users who were travelling on the R420 in the Ballinagar area between 2.30pm and 3pm this afternoon and who may have dashcam footage are asked to make it available to investigating gardaí.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Tullamore Garda Station on 057 932 7600, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.
headline: Motorcyclist, 20s, injured in Offaly collision

text:
A locum general practitioner is appearing before the Medical Council's fitness to practise committee over concerns about the care provided to a patient.

The inquiry, which opened in Dublin on Monday, relates to allegations of professional misconduct against the doctor in connection with a consultation at a general practice. The committee is examining whether the standard of care provided fell below that which could reasonably be expected of a competent medical practitioner.

The Medical Council's legal team outlined the background to the case, telling the committee that concerns had been raised about the manner in which the patient was assessed and treated during the consultation. It is alleged that the locum GP failed to carry out an adequate clinical examination and did not arrange appropriate follow-up care.

The committee heard that the patient subsequently required further medical attention. Details of the specific clinical issues involved were outlined to the hearing, though the Medical Council has asked media not to identify the patient.

A locum GP is a doctor who provides temporary cover at a practice, typically filling in for a permanent general practitioner who is on leave or otherwise unavailable. Such doctors are required to meet the same professional standards as any registered medical practitioner in the State.

The fitness to practise committee has the power to make a range of findings following its inquiry, from dismissing the complaint to recommending sanctions including conditions on the doctor's registration, suspension, or removal from the medical register.

The Medical Council, which is the regulatory body for doctors in Ireland, is obliged to hold public inquiries into complaints where there is sufficient cause for concern about a practitioner's conduct, performance or health.

The hearing is expected to continue over the coming days, with a number of witnesses due to give evidence. The committee will hear from medical experts as well as those directly involved in the patient's care.

The doctor, who is legally represented, is expected to respond fully to the allegations during the course of the inquiry.
headline: Locum GP before Medical Council over care of patient

text:
Four entrepreneurs from across the country are proving that there is always room for something sweet, each carving out a niche in the competitive world of confectionery, baking and desserts.

From artisan chocolates to custom celebration cakes, these business owners share a passion for quality ingredients, creativity and putting a smile on their customers' faces. Here, they tell us how they turned their love of all things sweet into thriving enterprises.

Sarah Kearney set up her chocolate business, Wildly Delicious, from her kitchen in Co Cork during the first lockdown in 2020. What started as a hobby quickly snowballed when friends and family began placing orders, and she soon realised she had the makings of a proper business on her hands.

"I had always loved working with chocolate, but it was during lockdown that I really had the time to experiment and develop recipes," she said. "I started posting pictures on Instagram and the response was overwhelming."

Kearney now operates from a purpose-built production kitchen and supplies a number of independent retailers across Munster. She credits her participation in the Local Enterprise Office's mentoring programme with helping her to scale up in a sustainable way.

"The mentoring was invaluable. It helped me get my head around the financial side of things and understand what I needed to do to grow without overextending myself," she said.

Her range includes hand-painted bonbons, chocolate bars made with locally sourced ingredients such as West Cork sea salt and Highbank Orchard syrup, and seasonal collections that have become particularly popular as gifts.

"People are really willing to spend that bit more on something that is genuinely handmade and uses quality ingredients. There has been a real shift towards supporting local and buying Irish, and I have definitely benefited from that."

Meanwhile, in Co Galway, David and Emma Nolan have built a loyal following for their custom celebration cakes through their business, Nolan's Cake Studio. The couple, who are both self-taught bakers, launched the venture in 2018 after years of making cakes for family occasions.

"Every single cake we make is designed from scratch with the customer," Emma Nolan said. "We sit down with them, talk about what the occasion means to them, and create something completely unique. That is what sets us apart."

The business has grown steadily through word of mouth and social media, and the couple now produce between 15 and 20 bespoke cakes each week. They have also expanded into offering workshops, which have proved enormously popular.

"The workshops were something we introduced almost by accident. People kept asking us to teach them, so we gave it a go, and now they are a really important part of the business," David Nolan said. "It is a different revenue stream, but it also brings people through the door who then come back to order cakes."

The couple said the cost of ingredients has been one of their biggest challenges in recent years, with the price of butter, sugar and eggs all rising significantly.

"We have had to adjust our pricing, and we were nervous about that, but customers have been very understanding," Emma Nolan said.
headline: Four business owners spreading some joy with their sweet treats

text:
A PSNI officer has been taken to hospital after being assaulted while on duty in Co Tyrone.

The incident occurred in the Dungannon area on Saturday evening, with the officer sustaining injuries that required hospital treatment. The officer has since been discharged.

Police have confirmed that a man in his 30s was arrested at the scene in connection with the assault and remains in custody assisting officers with their enquiries.

PSNI Superintendent Michael Greer condemned the attack, describing it as "totally unacceptable" and saying that no officer should face violence while carrying out their duties to keep the community safe.

"This officer came to work to serve and protect the public and has ended up in hospital as a result of being assaulted," he said. "We will not tolerate attacks on our officers, and I would appeal to anyone with information about this incident to come forward."

The Police Federation for Northern Ireland has also spoken out about the assault, with a spokesperson saying the attack highlights the dangers officers face on a daily basis.

"Every shift our members put on their uniforms not knowing what they will encounter. Attacks like this are a stark reminder of the risks involved in policing," the spokesperson said.

Anyone with information about the incident is asked to contact the PSNI on the non-emergency number 101, quoting the reference number provided. Information can also be given anonymously through the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.
headline: PSNI officer hospitalised after Tyrone assault

text:
Sean Quinn has pledged to the High Court that he will not trespass on a quarry in Co Fermanagh formerly owned by his family, as part of an undertaking to resolve a long-running legal dispute.

The 77-year-old businessman gave the undertaking to Mr Justice Garrett Simons during proceedings brought by Quinn Industrial Holdings, which now operates the quarry at Derrylin. The company had sought an injunction restraining Mr Quinn from entering the site without permission.

Mr Quinn's legal team told the court that their client was willing to give a voluntary undertaking not to enter the lands in question and that there was no need for the court to grant an injunction.

The quarry was once the cornerstone of the Quinn Group empire, which at its height employed thousands of people across the border region. The business was taken from Mr Quinn's control following the collapse of his financial interests during the economic crash, and subsequent receivership proceedings.

Quinn Industrial Holdings, which took over the running of the manufacturing and quarrying operations, has had a fraught relationship with the Quinn family and its supporters in the years since. The region was rocked by a campaign of intimidation against company executives, which included the abduction and assault of then director Kevin Lunney in 2019. Four men were subsequently convicted in connection with the attack.

The undertaking given by Mr Quinn to the court is binding and any breach could be treated as contempt of court, carrying potentially serious sanctions.

Outside court, Mr Quinn made no comment on the proceedings. His solicitor confirmed the undertaking had been given on a voluntary basis and that the matter was now resolved to the satisfaction of all parties.

The case was struck out with no order as to costs.
headline: Sean Quinn pledges not to trespass on Fermanagh quarry

text:
A young boy with a rare genetic condition is experiencing the joy of independent movement for the first time, thanks to an ingenious invention by a team of students and engineers who transformed a simple go-kart into a dinosaur-themed mobility cart.

Four-year-old Cillian O'Sullivan, who has a condition that severely limits his mobility, had been unable to move around freely or keep up with other children his age. But a specially designed cart, built to look like a friendly green dinosaur, has changed everything for the Meath youngster.

The project was the brainchild of a group of engineering students at TU Dublin who volunteered their time and expertise to design and build the custom cart. Working closely with Cillian's family and his occupational therapist, the team spent months perfecting the design to ensure it met his specific physical needs while also capturing the imagination of a child who, like so many his age, is mad about dinosaurs.

"He just lights up when he sees it," his mother Sinéad told RTÉ News. "For the first time, he can move around on his own, he can play with other kids in the park, he can just be a child. That's all we ever wanted for him."

The cart is operated using simple hand controls that Cillian can manage independently, and it has been fitted with safety features including a harness and a speed limiter. The dinosaur head at the front, complete with googly eyes and felt teeth, was added at Cillian's own request.

His occupational therapist said the impact of the device on Cillian's development has been remarkable. Beyond the obvious physical benefits, she noted significant improvements in his confidence, social interaction and emotional wellbeing since he began using the cart several weeks ago.

The cost of specialised paediatric mobility equipment remains a significant barrier for many Irish families. Standard powered wheelchairs suitable for young children can cost thousands of euro, and waiting lists for HSE-funded equipment are often lengthy. Cillian's family had been on a waiting list for more than a year before the university project intervened.

The engineering team said they hoped the project could serve as a model for similar initiatives around the country, and they have made their designs freely available online so that other groups might replicate the work.

"It's not rocket science in terms of the engineering," said final-year student Aoife Brennan, who led the project. "But the impact it has on a child's life is absolutely enormous. Every child deserves the chance to explore the world around them."

The family said they have been overwhelmed by the response since sharing videos of Cillian racing around in his dino-cart on social media, with parents of children in similar situations reaching out from across Ireland and beyond.
headline: Dino-cart invention helps boy 'to be a child'

text:
The leaders of Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael have signalled their determination to avoid a return to the kind of austerity measures that defined Ireland's response to the financial crash, as the country begins to chart a course through the economic fallout of the Covid-19 pandemic.

Taoiseach Leo Varadkar and Fianna Fáil leader Micheál Martin both stressed the need for a fundamentally different approach to the post-pandemic recovery, drawing a clear distinction between the current crisis and the banking collapse that led to years of painful spending cuts and tax increases.

Speaking separately, both leaders acknowledged that the State's finances have been placed under enormous strain by the emergency supports rolled out during the crisis, but argued that the path to recovery should be built on investment rather than retrenchment.

Mr Varadkar said the Government was conscious that the mistakes of the past should not be repeated, noting that the circumstances of the current downturn were entirely different to those that preceded the bailout programme. He pointed to the fact that the public finances had been in a relatively strong position before the pandemic struck, with the State running a budget surplus and the national debt falling as a proportion of national income.

Mr Martin echoed those sentiments, saying that any new government would need to prioritise protecting public services and stimulating economic activity. He said there was broad consensus among economists that an austerity-driven response would be counterproductive and risked deepening the recession.

The comments come as the two parties continue negotiations on forming a coalition government, with the Green Party also involved in talks. The shape of any programme for government will be heavily influenced by the scale of the economic challenge ahead, with the Department of Finance warning that the cost of emergency measures including the Temporary Wage Subsidy Scheme and the Pandemic Unemployment Payment is running into billions of euro.

The Exchequer figures have laid bare the extent of the damage, with tax revenues falling sharply and expenditure rising dramatically as the State moved to support businesses and workers through the lockdown period.

However, both leaders pointed to the historically low cost of borrowing as a factor that would allow the State to spread the burden of the crisis over a longer period, rather than imposing immediate cuts. Ireland's borrowing costs remain at near-record lows, in part due to the European Central Bank's massive bond-buying programme, which has helped to keep yields on Irish government debt subdued.

Sinn Féin's Mary Lou McDonald said the commitment to avoid austerity would be judged on actions rather than words. The Sinn Féin leader said her party would be watching closely to ensure that any incoming government did not impose cuts to public services or social welfare payments by stealth.

Labour leader Alan Kelly also warned against any erosion of workers' rights or conditions as the economy reopens, calling for a recovery that puts ordinary workers at its centre.

The Social Democrats co-leader Róisín Shortall said the pandemic had exposed deep inequalities in Irish society, particularly in areas such as housing, healthcare and childcare, and that any recovery plan must address these structural deficiencies rather than simply restoring the status quo.
headline: FF and FG leaders keen to avoid post Covid-19 austerity

text:
A UK court has ruled that a couple are the legal parents of their adult son, in what is believed to be the first case of its kind.

The man and woman, who cannot be named for legal reasons, had raised their son from birth but had never been formally recognised as his legal parents due to the circumstances of his conception through a surrogacy arrangement.

The case was heard in the High Court in London, where Mr Justice Poole granted a parental order in respect of the couple's son, who is now in his twenties.

Under UK law, parental orders are typically sought within six months of a child's birth in surrogacy cases, transferring legal parenthood from the surrogate to the intended parents. However, the couple in this case had not applied within that timeframe.

The judge acknowledged that the case raised novel legal questions, given that the subject of the parental order was no longer a child but a fully grown adult. Nevertheless, he concluded that granting the order was both lawful and in the public interest.

In his ruling, Mr Justice Poole said the absence of a legal relationship between the couple and their son had caused practical difficulties and emotional distress over many years. He noted that the family unit had functioned as any other, with the couple having raised their son and supported him throughout his life.

The court heard that the son himself supported the application and wished to have his legal parentage formally recognised.

Legal commentators said the ruling could open the door for other families in similar situations to seek retrospective parental orders, particularly those involving older surrogacy arrangements where parents may not have been aware of the legal requirements at the time.

Surrogacy law in the UK has long been regarded as outdated by campaigners and legal professionals alike. The Law Commission of England and Wales has previously recommended reforms to simplify the process of establishing legal parenthood in surrogacy cases, though legislation has yet to be brought forward.

The ruling has no direct implications for Irish law, where surrogacy remains largely unregulated, though the Health (Assisted Human Reproduction) Act 2024 is expected to provide a statutory framework for surrogacy arrangements in this jurisdiction once commenced.
headline: UK court rules couple are legal parents of adult son

text:
House prices in parts of the country have now returned to or even surpassed the peak levels reached during the Celtic Tiger era, according to new data that underscores the deepening affordability crisis facing prospective buyers.

The latest figures from the Central Statistics Office show that residential property prices in several urban and commuter-belt areas have matched or exceeded the highs recorded in 2007, before the crash that plunged the State into economic turmoil.

Dublin, in particular, has seen prices in certain postcodes climb back to levels not witnessed since the height of the boom, while commuter counties such as Meath, Kildare and Wicklow have also experienced sharp increases that bring them into line with pre-crash valuations.

The trend is being driven by a persistent shortage of supply, strong demand fuelled by population growth, and the continued difficulty many first-time buyers face in competing with institutional investors and cash purchasers.

The Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland said the figures reflected a market that remained fundamentally constrained by a lack of new housing stock. Its members reported that bidding wars have become commonplace in sought-after areas, with properties routinely selling well above their asking prices.

Minister for Housing Darragh O'Brien acknowledged the challenge but pointed to the Government's Housing for All plan, which aims to deliver 33,000 homes per year by 2030. He said the pipeline of new builds was increasing and that measures such as the Help to Buy scheme and the First Home shared equity scheme were assisting buyers in getting on the property ladder.

However, opposition TDs were sharply critical. Sinn Féin's housing spokesperson said the figures were a damning indictment of Government policy and called for greater investment in public housing and stronger regulation of institutional landlords. Social Democrats TD Cian O'Callaghan described the situation as "a crisis of the Government's own making" and said reliance on the private market to deliver affordable homes had comprehensively failed.

Economists have cautioned that while the nominal price levels may mirror Celtic Tiger peaks, the comparison is not entirely straightforward. When adjusted for inflation, current prices in many areas remain below their 2007 highs in real terms. Earnings have also risen in the intervening years, though not at the same pace as house prices, meaning affordability has nonetheless worsened significantly for many households.

The Banking and Payments Federation Ireland noted that mortgage drawdowns have increased in recent quarters, suggesting sustained demand. However, the Central Bank's macroprudential lending rules, introduced in 2015 to prevent a repeat of the reckless lending that characterised the boom years, continue to place limits on how much buyers can borrow relative to their income and the value of the property.

For those locked out of the purchase market, the rental sector offers little respite. Rents nationally are at record highs, with the latest Residential Tenancies Board data showing average monthly rents exceeding €1,800 in Dublin and climbing steadily in regional cities such as Cork, Galway and Limerick.

Housing charities, including the Simon Communities and the Peter McVerry Trust, warned that rising prices were pushing more people towards homelessness.
headline: Houses at Celtic Tiger levels in some areas

text:
A hijacking incident aboard a commercial vessel in the Arabian Sea has ended, according to a United Kingdom maritime security agency.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) confirmed that the vessel, which had been seized by armed individuals, was no longer under the control of its hijackers. The agency said the ship and its crew were now safe, though full details of how the incident was resolved remained unclear.

The episode is the latest in a series of security incidents in waters around the Arabian Peninsula, where commercial shipping has faced heightened threats in recent months. Houthi rebels in Yemen have launched repeated attacks on vessels in the Red Sea and surrounding waters since November, in what they say is a campaign in solidarity with Palestinians during the war in Gaza.

The UKMTO, which acts as the primary point of contact for merchant vessels in the region, had earlier issued an alert warning ships in the area of the incident. Naval forces from several countries, including the United States and European nations, have been deployed to the region in an effort to protect international shipping lanes.

The attacks on commercial shipping have caused significant disruption to global trade, with many shipping companies rerouting vessels around the southern tip of Africa rather than risk passage through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. The diversions have added considerable time and cost to journeys, with knock-on effects for supply chains and consumer prices worldwide.

Ireland has no naval vessels deployed to the region, though the Government has previously expressed concern about the disruption to international shipping and the threat to seafarers.

It is understood that international naval forces in the area are continuing to monitor the situation closely, with further details of the hijacking expected to emerge in the coming hours.
headline: Hijacking ends in Arabian Sea, says UK agency

text:
The collapse of the Stormont institutions is "inevitable" if the issues surrounding the Northern Ireland Protocol are not resolved, the DUP has warned.

Speaking ahead of fresh talks with the British government, senior party figures said the current arrangements are undermining Northern Ireland's place within the United Kingdom and eroding cross-community support for the devolved institutions.

The warning comes amid growing frustration within unionism over the trade barriers effectively placed in the Irish Sea as a result of the post-Brexit arrangements. The Protocol, which was agreed as part of the Brexit Withdrawal Agreement, keeps Northern Ireland aligned with EU single market rules for goods, meaning checks are required on products arriving from Britain.

DUP leader Sir Jeffrey Donaldson said his party had been "clear and consistent" that the Protocol must be replaced with arrangements that respect Northern Ireland's constitutional position. He said the party would not countenance a situation where the current trading arrangements remain in place indefinitely.

"If the Protocol is not resolved in a way that restores Northern Ireland's place fully within the United Kingdom internal market, then the institutions of the Belfast Agreement, which are founded on the principle of consent, cannot survive," Sir Jeffrey said. "That is not a threat — it is a statement of political reality."

The comments were described as unhelpful by several parties at Stormont. Sinn Féin vice president Michelle O'Neill accused the DUP of "holding the institutions to ransom" and said the people of the North needed a functioning Executive to deal with pressing issues including health waiting lists and the cost of living.

Alliance Party leader Naomi Long said it was "reckless in the extreme" to threaten the collapse of power-sharing over an issue that requires negotiation between London and Brussels.

The SDLP's Colum Eastwood urged all parties to focus on making the Protocol work rather than using it as a political weapon. He said there were real opportunities for the North's economy if the dual market access afforded by the Protocol was properly harnessed.

The British government said it remained committed to finding a resolution and that talks with the European Commission were ongoing. A spokesperson said the government recognised the "genuine concerns" within the unionist community and was working to find practical solutions that addressed disruption to trade.

The Irish Government has consistently maintained that the Protocol is the best available mechanism to avoid a hard border on the island of Ireland while respecting the integrity of the EU single market. The Taoiseach has previously said that any solutions must be found within the framework of the existing agreement.

The European Commission has put forward a package of measures aimed at reducing the impact of the Protocol on everyday life in the North, including significant reductions in checks on retail goods, medicines and parcels. However, the DUP has dismissed these proposals as insufficient, insisting that nothing short of the removal of the Irish Sea border will satisfy unionist concerns.

Political observers have noted that the DUP's increasingly firm stance may be linked to electoral pressure from the Traditional Unionist Voice party, which has called for an immediate withdrawal from Stormont.

The situation has raised concerns in Dublin, London and Brussels about the stability of the power-sharing institutions, which have already endured several periods of collapse since the Belfast Agreement was signed in 1998.
headline: Stormont collapse 'inevitable' if Protocol not resolved

text:
The HSE has confirmed that 14 people with disabilities living in residential care settings have died after contracting Covid-19.

The figures, which were disclosed following queries from RTÉ News, highlight the significant toll the virus has taken on some of the most vulnerable people in the State's care.

It is understood that the deaths occurred across a number of residential centres operated by both the HSE and Section 38 and Section 39 organisations. The HSE said it was working closely with disability service providers to manage outbreaks and protect residents and staff.

Disability services have received considerably less public attention than nursing homes during the pandemic, despite caring for thousands of people in congregated settings where the virus can spread rapidly.

There are approximately 8,000 people with disabilities living in residential centres across the country, many of them in older, congregated facilities where residents share bedrooms, bathrooms and communal living areas.

Inclusion Ireland, which advocates for people with intellectual disabilities, said the deaths were deeply concerning and called for greater transparency around the impact of the virus on disability services.

"These are people who were in the care of the State, and their families deserve answers about what happened and what is being done to prevent further deaths," the organisation said.

The HSE's National Director for Disability Services said infection prevention and control teams had been deployed to support residential centres experiencing outbreaks. Testing of residents and staff had been carried out in affected facilities, and additional personal protective equipment had been supplied.

However, concerns have been raised by staff and family members about the adequacy of the response in some centres. Several sources told RTÉ News that staffing shortages had made it difficult to isolate residents who tested positive, particularly in older congregated settings where the physical layout of buildings was not suited to cocooning measures.

HIQA, which has responsibility for inspecting residential centres for people with disabilities, said it had been engaging with providers throughout the crisis and was monitoring the situation closely.

The Government has faced repeated calls to publish detailed data on Covid-19 cases and deaths in disability services, similar to the information that has been made available in relation to nursing homes. To date, such data has not been published on a routine basis.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health said the Minister was aware of the challenges facing disability services during the pandemic and that additional funding had been made available to support the sector's response.

Sinn Féin's spokesperson on disability, Pauline Tully TD, said the lack of transparency was unacceptable and called on the Government to ensure that disability residential services received the same level of attention and resources as nursing homes.

"People with disabilities in residential care are every bit as vulnerable as nursing home residents, and they deserve the same level of protection," she said.
headline: 14 virus deaths among people in disability services

text:
The Association of Garda Sergeants and Inspectors has alleged that it has been excluded from key negotiations on the latest public sector pay agreement, claiming the move undermines the role of middle-ranking Garda management.

AGSI General Secretary Antoinette Cunningham said the organisation was not afforded a meaningful seat at the table during recent discussions, despite representing a significant cohort of sworn members of An Garda Síochána.

Ms Cunningham described the situation as "deeply disappointing" and said it raised serious questions about the Government's commitment to genuine engagement with all representative bodies in the public service.

"Our members are the backbone of frontline policing in this country. They supervise and manage the day-to-day operations of An Garda Síochána, and yet their voice has been sidelined in a process that will directly affect their pay, conditions and morale," she said.

The AGSI has long argued that its members occupy a unique position within the public service, carrying significant legal responsibilities under the Garda Síochána Act while often being grouped in with broader public sector negotiations where their specific concerns can be overlooked.

It is understood the organisation has written to the Department of Public Expenditure seeking clarification on how future negotiations will be structured and requesting a formal commitment that AGSI representatives will be included at all stages of the process.

The Department said it was committed to engaging with all recognised staff associations and that the pay agreement process remained open and transparent. A spokesperson said discussions were ongoing and that all parties would have an opportunity to contribute.

The Garda Representative Association, which represents rank-and-file gardaí, declined to comment on the AGSI's claims but confirmed it had been involved in the negotiations.

The row comes at a time of significant pressure on Garda resources, with ongoing challenges around recruitment and retention. AGSI has repeatedly warned that inadequate pay and conditions for sergeants and inspectors are contributing to difficulties in attracting members to apply for promotion.

Speaking ahead of the organisation's annual conference, Ms Cunningham said the exclusion issue would be a central topic of discussion among delegates and warned that the matter could escalate if not addressed promptly.

"We are not seeking special treatment. We are seeking fair and equal treatment in a process that affects every one of our members. If that is not forthcoming, we will have to consider what options are available to us," she said.
headline: AGSI alleges exclusion from pay deal negotiations

text:
The question of who actually delivers a Covid-19 test result to a patient has become a source of confusion for many people awaiting news after being tested, with some unsure whether to expect a phone call, a text message, or contact from their GP.

The HSE has confirmed that the process differs depending on whether the result is positive or negative, and the system has evolved considerably since the early days of the pandemic when testing capacity was far more limited.

For those who test positive for Covid-19, the result is communicated by a member of the HSE's contact tracing team, who will phone the patient directly. During this call, the patient will be advised on the steps they need to take, including how long they must self-isolate and what to do if their symptoms worsen. The contact tracing team will also begin the process of identifying close contacts who may need to be tested themselves.

A negative result, on the other hand, is delivered by text message to the mobile number provided at the time of testing. The HSE has urged anyone who is tested to ensure they give the correct phone number, as delays and confusion have arisen in cases where contact details were inaccurate or incomplete.

GPs do not generally deliver test results themselves, though they may follow up with patients in certain circumstances, particularly where a referral for testing was made through the practice and a clinical assessment is ongoing.

The HSE has acknowledged that there have been delays in communicating results during periods of high demand, with some patients waiting considerably longer than the target turnaround time. Officials have said that efforts are being made to reduce waiting times and that additional resources have been allocated to both laboratory processing and contact tracing operations.

Public health officials have stressed that anyone awaiting a result should continue to self-isolate until they hear back, regardless of how long the process takes. Those who have not received a result after seven days are advised to contact the HSE helpline or their GP for further guidance.

The Department of Health has said the testing and tracing infrastructure remains under constant review and that improvements are being made on an ongoing basis to ensure the system can cope with fluctuations in demand as the country continues to manage the pandemic.
headline: Who contacts patients with the test results?

text:
The capital is set to sparkle once again as Dublin's Christmas lights are officially switched on this evening, marking the unofficial start of the festive season for the city.

Tens of thousands of people are expected to line the streets of the city centre as the annual lights display is illuminated along Grafton Street, Henry Street and O'Connell Street, with a programme of live entertainment accompanying the switch-on.

Dublin City Council, working alongside Dublin Town, has invested significantly in this year's display, which organisers say will be the most impressive yet, with new installations and energy-efficient LED lighting designed to reduce the environmental footprint of the festivities.

Lord Mayor of Dublin Daithí de Róiste will perform the official switch-on ceremony, joined by a host of well-known faces from the worlds of entertainment and sport.

Speaking ahead of the event, the Lord Mayor said the lights represent "a moment of joy and togetherness" for the people of Dublin. "After what has been a challenging year for many families, the Christmas lights remind us that brighter days — and nights — are ahead," he said.

Dublin Town chief executive Richard Guiney said the festive illuminations are vital not just for morale but for the local economy, with retailers hoping the lights will draw shoppers back into the city centre in the crucial weeks before Christmas.

"The switch-on traditionally signals a major uplift in footfall across the city," Mr Guiney said. "Our members rely on this period, and the lights play a real role in creating the kind of atmosphere that encourages people to come into town, spend time here and support local businesses."

This year's display will extend beyond the traditional shopping thoroughfares, with festive lighting also planned for areas including South William Street, Capel Street and parts of the Docklands. New animated projections on a number of landmark buildings are also expected to feature prominently.

Transport arrangements have been put in place to accommodate the large crowds expected this evening. Dublin Bus, Luas and DART services will operate extended timetables, while An Garda Síochána has confirmed that additional resources will be deployed in the city centre to ensure public safety.

A number of rolling road closures will be in effect around Grafton Street and O'Connell Street from late afternoon, and motorists are being advised to avoid the city centre where possible and to use public transport.

The lights will remain in place until early January, with Dublin City Council confirming they will be illuminated each evening from approximately 5pm.

The switch-on forms part of a wider programme of seasonal events across the capital, including the return of festive markets at several locations and a series of free family-friendly performances scheduled throughout December.
headline: Brighter nights ahead as Dublin lights up for Christmas

text:
The conviction of Gisèle Pelicot's former husband and dozens of other men in the mass rape trial that gripped France and the wider world has been widely welcomed, but serious questions are now being raised about the sentencing, with critics arguing the punishments handed down represent a miscarriage of justice.

Dominique Pelicot, the principal defendant, was sentenced to 20 years in prison — the maximum term — after being found guilty of drugging his then-wife over the course of a decade and recruiting strangers to rape her while she was unconscious. However, of the 50 co-defendants convicted alongside him, the majority received sentences significantly below the maximum, prompting outrage from campaigners and legal commentators both in France and internationally.

Several of the men convicted of aggravated rape received sentences of as little as three years, with some of those terms partially suspended. The disparity has drawn fierce criticism from women's rights organisations, who argue the court failed to reflect the gravity of the crimes committed against Ms Pelicot.

Speaking in Dublin, the Rape Crisis Network Ireland said the sentencing sends a "deeply troubling message" to survivors of sexual violence across Europe. "When a court acknowledges that these acts took place but then hands down sentences that amount to a fraction of what the law allows, it undermines public confidence in the justice system's capacity to protect victims," a spokesperson said.

Ms Pelicot, who waived her right to anonymity in a decision that was praised globally for shining a light on the realities of sexual violence, said she was "disappointed" by several of the sentences. Her courage throughout the trial transformed her into a symbol of resistance for survivors, with her image carried at protests from Paris to Dublin.

French prosecutors had sought sentences of between 10 and 18 years for the co-defendants, making the final outcomes all the more difficult to reconcile with the evidence presented during the months-long trial in Avignon. Legal analysts noted that the court appeared to have given weight to mitigating factors that many observers found difficult to comprehend, given the nature of the offences.

The case has reignited debate in Ireland too about how sexual violence cases are handled within the criminal justice system. Noeline Blackwell, chief executive of the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, said the French verdicts should prompt reflection closer to home. "We know from our own experience in Ireland that sentencing in sexual violence cases can leave survivors feeling that the system has not truly recognised the harm done to them," she said.

In France, tens of thousands of people took to the streets in protest at the perceived leniency of the sentences. Demonstrations were held in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities, with many carrying placards bearing Ms Pelicot's name and the slogan "La honte doit changer de camp" — shame must change sides — which became a rallying cry during the trial.

The French government has faced calls to review sentencing guidelines for sexual offences in light of the case. President Macron acknowledged the trial had been a "moment of reckoning" for French society but stopped short of commenting directly on the individual sentences.

Irish politicians have also weighed in.
headline: French decision is miscarriage of justice

text:
Eurozone finance ministers have agreed in principle to use the European Stability Mechanism to help member states cope with the economic fallout of the coronavirus pandemic, according to sources close to the talks.

The agreement, reached after marathon discussions among the Eurogroup, would allow countries to access credit lines from the ESM bailout fund to cover direct and indirect healthcare costs related to the Covid-19 crisis.

It is understood that the credit lines could amount to up to 2% of a member state's gross domestic product, which in Ireland's case could mean access to billions of euro in emergency funding.

However, significant disagreements remain over the conditions that would be attached to such lending, with a number of southern European countries, including Italy and Spain, insisting that any credit lines must come without the kind of strict austerity-linked conditionality that marked the eurozone debt crisis a decade ago.

Minister for Finance Paschal Donohoe, who participates in the Eurogroup meetings, had previously signalled Ireland's openness to using the ESM as part of a broader European response to the pandemic.

The ESM has a lending capacity of €410 billion and was originally established during the financial crisis to provide assistance to eurozone countries in severe financial difficulty. Ireland itself exited its ESM-predecessor programme in December 2013 after receiving €67.5 billion in troika funding.

The proposal to deploy the mechanism for pandemic-related spending represents a significant shift in the fund's traditional mandate and underscores the extraordinary nature of the economic crisis facing Europe.

Countries hardest hit by the virus, particularly Italy and Spain, have been pushing for a more ambitious collective fiscal response, including the issuance of joint debt instruments — sometimes referred to as "coronabonds" — but this proposal has met with firm resistance from the Netherlands, Germany, Austria and Finland.

The European Commission has already relaxed its fiscal rules to allow member states to spend freely to combat the crisis, and the European Central Bank has launched a €750 billion bond-buying programme to stabilise financial markets.

Any final agreement on the ESM credit lines will need to be endorsed by eurozone leaders before it can take effect. Further talks are expected in the coming days to resolve outstanding differences on the terms and conditions of the lending facility.

The discussions come as economies across the eurozone face unprecedented contractions, with millions of workers laid off or placed on temporary wage subsidy schemes as lockdown measures continue to suppress economic activity.

In Ireland, the Government has committed to spending billions of euro on emergency supports, including the Temporary Wage Subsidy Scheme and the Pandemic Unemployment Payment, which is currently being claimed by more than 500,000 people.
headline: Eurozone 'agrees in principle' to use bailout mechanism

text:
An experimental antiviral drug that had shown promising results in laboratory settings has failed to demonstrate significant benefit in human clinical trials, dealing a setback to efforts to expand the arsenal of treatments available against Covid-19.

The drug, developed by a US-based pharmaceutical company, had generated cautious optimism after early-stage testing suggested it could reduce viral replication in infected cells. However, results from a large-scale Phase III trial involving more than 1,200 participants across several countries found no statistically significant difference in recovery times or hospitalisation rates between patients who received the drug and those given a placebo.

Researchers said the findings, while disappointing, were not entirely unexpected given the well-documented difficulty of translating laboratory results into effective clinical treatments.

"The gap between what works in a petri dish and what works in a human body remains one of the great challenges in drug development," said one of the lead investigators involved in the trial. "We have to be honest about what the data is telling us."

The setback comes as health authorities in Ireland and across Europe continue to monitor the evolving nature of the virus. The HSE has consistently emphasised the importance of vaccination as the primary line of defence against severe illness, while acknowledging the need for effective therapeutic options, particularly for immunocompromised patients who may not respond as well to vaccines.

In Ireland, antiviral treatments such as Paxlovid remain available for eligible patients, though access has at times been a source of concern among GPs and patient advocacy groups. The failure of the experimental drug underscores the limited pipeline of new treatments coming to market.

The World Health Organization noted that several other candidate drugs remain in various stages of clinical testing globally and urged continued investment in research. A spokesperson said it was important that individual trial failures did not discourage the broader effort to develop next-generation antivirals.

Infectious disease specialists here said the results serve as a reminder that there are no shortcuts in the development of safe and effective medicines.

"Every failed trial still teaches us something valuable," said Dr Cillian De Gascun, director of the National Virus Reference Laboratory. "The scientific process is working as it should — filtering out treatments that don't meet the bar."

The pharmaceutical company behind the drug said it would review the full dataset before deciding whether to pursue any modified version of the treatment or redirect its resources toward other candidates in its pipeline.
headline: Experimental virus drug fails in human trials

text:
A United Nations-backed tribunal has found a Hezbollah suspect guilty of the 2005 assassination of former Lebanese prime minister Rafik Hariri, in a landmark verdict delivered more than 15 years after the devastating Beirut bombing.

The Special Tribunal for Lebanon, sitting in The Hague, convicted Salim Ayyash in absentia of conspiracy to commit a terrorist act, the murder of Hariri and 21 others, and the attempted murder of a further 226 people who were injured in the massive car bomb attack.

However, the tribunal acquitted three other Hezbollah-linked defendants — Hussein Oneissi, Assad Sabra and Hassan Merhi — citing insufficient evidence to convict them. All four men had been tried in absentia, with Hezbollah refusing to hand them over to the court.

Hariri was killed on 14 February 2005 when a suicide bomber detonated a van packed with explosives as his motorcade passed through central Beirut. The blast left a massive crater in the seafront road and damaged buildings across a wide area of the Lebanese capital.

The assassination sent shockwaves through the Middle East and triggered the so-called Cedar Revolution, a series of mass protests that ultimately led to the withdrawal of Syrian troops from Lebanon after nearly three decades of military presence.
