Hezbollah has consistently denied any involvement in the killing, and it remains unclear whether Ayyash will ever serve any sentence imposed by the tribunal. The group, which is designated a terrorist organisation by the European Union and several other countries, wields significant political and military power in Lebanon.

The verdict comes at a particularly sensitive time for Lebanon, which is grappling with its worst economic crisis in decades and the aftermath of the catastrophic explosion at Beirut port in August, which killed more than 200 people and caused widespread destruction across the city.

The tribunal was established by the UN Security Council in 2007, and the trial proceedings began in 2014. The court's work has cost more than €600 million, funded partly by the United Nations and partly by the Lebanese government.

Hariri's son, Saad Hariri, who himself served multiple terms as Lebanese prime minister, had long campaigned for justice over his father's killing.
headline: Hezbollah suspect found guilty of 2005 Hariri murder

text:
A woman's sister did not want to report their mother as missing because she was afraid of what might be found, a court has heard.

The detail emerged during a hearing at the Central Criminal Court, where a man is on trial charged with the murder of the woman, who had not been seen for several weeks before her remains were discovered at a property in Co Tipperary.

The accused, who is in his late 40s and cannot be named for legal reasons, has pleaded not guilty to the charge.

Giving evidence on the second day of the trial, the deceased woman's eldest daughter told the jury that she had become increasingly concerned about her mother's welfare after being unable to reach her by phone over a period of weeks.

She said she had contacted her sister to discuss reporting their mother as a missing person to the Gardaí, but her sister had been reluctant to do so.

"She said she didn't want to ring the guards because she was afraid of what they'd find," the witness told the court.

The witness said she had ultimately made the decision to contact Gardaí herself, as she felt something was seriously wrong. She described her mother as someone who would always return calls and who kept in regular contact with her children.

Under cross-examination by counsel for the defence, the witness agreed that her mother had periods during which she could be difficult to reach, but she insisted that the length of silence in this instance was unprecedented and deeply troubling.

The court also heard evidence from a member of An Garda Síochána who attended the scene after a welfare check was requested. The garda described gaining entry to the property and discovering the woman's remains in a bedroom.

A pathologist's report, which was read into the record, indicated that the woman had sustained significant injuries consistent with a violent assault.

The trial, which is expected to last up to three weeks, continues before Mr Justice Michael White and a jury of seven men and five women.
headline: Sister didn't want to report mother missing, court told

text:
It may not be the most conventional vessel to take to the water, but dozens of competitors did just that over the weekend, climbing inside hollowed-out giant pumpkins and paddling their way across a lake in a relay race that has become one of the more unusual fixtures on the autumn calendar.

The event, held annually in the Belgian city of Kasterlee, sees teams of intrepid racers take turns navigating the waterway in enormous gourds, each one carefully selected and carved to serve as a makeshift boat. Competitors kneel or sit inside the pumpkins, using small paddles to propel themselves forward, though staying upright proved to be the greater challenge for many participants.

Organisers said this year's crop of pumpkins was among the largest they had worked with, with some of the specimens weighing in excess of 400 kilograms before being hollowed out. Growers spend months cultivating the giant varieties specifically for the race, and there is considerable local pride attached to producing a pumpkin both large enough and sturdy enough to carry a fully grown adult across the water without sinking.

The relay format added an extra layer of difficulty, as competitors were required to clamber out of their pumpkins at designated changeover points before their teammates took over. More than a few ended up in the water during the handover, much to the delight of the large crowd that had gathered along the banks to watch.

The event has been running for over a decade and continues to draw growing numbers of spectators and participants alike, with organisers reporting that teams from neighbouring countries have begun entering in recent years.

While Ireland has yet to send a team, the country's own giant pumpkin growing community has been steadily expanding, and enthusiasts say it may only be a matter of time before Irish growers produce specimens large enough to compete on the European stage — or at least large enough to float.
headline: Giant floating pumpkin relay race

text:
More than three million European Union citizens have applied to remain in the United Kingdom under the government's EU Settlement Scheme, according to new figures released by the Home Office.

The milestone figure underscores the sheer scale of the administrative exercise undertaken by British authorities as they seek to regularise the status of EU nationals living in the UK following Brexit. The scheme, which allows EU citizens and their family members to apply for settled or pre-settled status, has now received 3.1 million applications since it opened in March 2019.

Of those applications processed so far, the majority have been granted settled status, which gives holders indefinite leave to remain, while a significant proportion received pre-settled status, allowing them to stay for a further five years before needing to reapply.

The figures are of particular interest in Ireland, given the significant number of Irish citizens living in the UK. However, Irish nationals are in a unique position among EU citizens, as their rights to live and work in the UK are protected under the Common Travel Area arrangements, which predate and are separate from EU membership. Irish citizens are therefore not required to apply under the settlement scheme, though some have chosen to do so.

Campaigners and advocacy groups have expressed concern about those EU citizens who may have failed to apply before the deadline, warning that individuals who miss the cut-off risk losing their right to work, rent property, or access public services. Charities working with vulnerable populations, including elderly EU nationals and those with limited English, have called on the British government to ensure that no one falls through the cracks.

The Home Office said it would take a "pragmatic approach" to late applications where individuals had reasonable grounds for missing the deadline.
headline: Over three million EU citizens apply to stay in UK

text:
A criminal gang in India operated a bogus police station for eight months, duping locals into believing it was a legitimate outpost of the law, authorities have confirmed.

The fake station, complete with uniforms, a signboard and official-looking paperwork, was run from a rented building in the northern state of Bihar, one of India's most populous and poorest regions. The gang allegedly used the setup to extort money from unsuspecting members of the public who came seeking help with disputes or to file complaints.

Police said the operation came to light after a tip-off led officers to raid the premises in the Banka district, where they discovered the elaborate ruse. Several suspects have been arrested in connection with the scheme.

According to local police officials, the gang members dressed in khaki uniforms resembling those worn by genuine officers and even held court-style proceedings, issuing fines and collecting payments from people who believed they were dealing with real law enforcement.

The men allegedly settled land disputes, family disagreements and minor criminal complaints, charging fees for their so-called services. In some cases, they are accused of threatening individuals with arrest if they refused to pay.

Senior police officials in the district said the fake station had been operating since early in the year and had built up a considerable local reputation before being uncovered.

The case has drawn attention to the challenges of policing in rural India, where legitimate police stations can be thinly spread across vast areas, leaving communities vulnerable to such deceptions. Bihar, home to more than 100 million people, has long struggled with law and order issues, and the incident has prompted calls for greater oversight and more resources for policing in remote districts.

Authorities said an investigation is ongoing and that further arrests are expected.
headline: Indian gang ran fake police station for eight months

text:
The Government is set to purchase an additional 450 megawatts of electricity capacity next year in a bid to shore up the national grid and stave off the risk of power shortages during peak demand periods.

The move, confirmed by the Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications, comes amid growing concerns over the security of Ireland's electricity supply as data centre expansion and increased electrification place unprecedented strain on the system.

EirGrid, the State's grid operator, has repeatedly warned in recent years that Ireland faces a tight outlook for power generation, particularly during cold winter evenings when demand surges and wind generation can drop off.

The additional 450mw will be procured through emergency temporary generation contracts, supplementing existing capacity on the system. It is understood the power will come from a combination of gas-fired and battery storage sources, though the precise mix will depend on the outcome of the procurement process.

Minister for the Environment Eamon Ryan said the purchase was a necessary step to ensure the lights stay on while Ireland transitions to a greater share of renewable energy.

"We have to be pragmatic about where we are right now," the Minister said. "This additional capacity gives us the insurance we need while we continue to build out our renewable infrastructure at pace."

The Commission for Regulation of Utilities, which oversees the energy market, has been closely involved in the planning. The CRU noted that while new renewable generation capacity is coming on stream, it will take time before it fully offsets the retirement of older, less efficient plants.

Opposition TDs have criticised the Government's approach, arguing that the need for emergency generation reflects a failure of long-term energy planning. Sinn Féin's spokesperson on energy said the repeated reliance on temporary measures was costing taxpayers dearly and called for a comprehensive review of energy security policy.

The Industrial Development Authority has previously flagged the tight power supply situation as a potential impediment to attracting foreign direct investment, particularly from large technology firms seeking to establish or expand data centre operations in Ireland.

EirGrid's most recent generation capacity statement indicated that while the system is expected to meet demand in most scenarios over the coming winters, the margin of safety remains slim. The additional 450mw would go some way towards widening that margin and reducing the likelihood of controlled disconnections during extreme weather events.

The procurement process is expected to get under way in the coming weeks, with contracts due to be finalised before the end of the year to ensure the additional capacity is available for the winter of next year.
headline: Govt to purchase extra 450mw of electricity next year

text:
A fundraising campaign has been launched to support two brothers whose home was badly damaged in a fire in Co Galway.

The blaze broke out at the property in the early hours of the morning, leaving the house extensively damaged and the brothers unable to return to their home.

Units of the fire service responded to the incident and brought the fire under control, but not before significant damage had been caused to the structure and contents of the house.

The two men, who are understood to have lived together in the property for a number of years, escaped the fire without serious injury. However, they have been left without many of their personal belongings and are currently staying with relatives in the area.

Friends and neighbours have since rallied around the brothers, setting up an online fundraising page to help them get back on their feet. Organisers of the campaign say the response from the local community has been overwhelming, with donations coming in from across the region and beyond.

"These are two men who would do anything for anyone, and the community just wanted to give something back," one of the organisers said. "The support has been incredible and it really shows what a tight-knit community we have here."

The funds raised will go towards helping the brothers with immediate living costs as well as repairs to the property, which they hope to eventually move back into.

Local representatives have also been in contact with the brothers to offer assistance, and Galway County Council has been made aware of the situation.

Anyone wishing to contribute to the fundraising effort can do so through the online campaign page, which has been shared widely on social media in recent days.
headline: Fundraising bid after brothers' house damaged in fire

text:
Dermot O'Neill, one of Ireland's best-known gardening experts and a familiar face to television audiences for more than two decades, has died at the age of 58.

The popular horticulturist, who was a regular contributor on RTÉ programmes including RTÉ Today and Nationwide, passed away surrounded by his family, it has been confirmed.

Originally from Dublin, O'Neill built a reputation as one of the country's most accessible and enthusiastic advocates for gardening, inspiring generations of Irish people to get outdoors and into their gardens regardless of experience or expertise.

He was widely regarded for his warm personality and his ability to make gardening approachable for beginners, while also offering expert-level advice that earned respect across the horticultural community.

O'Neill was a regular presence at Bloom, the Bord Bia gardening festival held annually in the Phoenix Park, where he was a firm favourite with visitors. He also contributed gardening columns and advice to a number of Irish publications over the years.

Tributes have been pouring in from across the gardening world and beyond, with colleagues and fans remembering him as a generous, kind-hearted man who was passionate about sharing his love of plants and the outdoors.

RTÉ's Maura Derrane, who worked alongside O'Neill on RTÉ Today, described him as a wonderful colleague and a true gentleman who brought joy to everyone he met.

President Michael D Higgins led tributes, praising O'Neill's contribution to Irish life and his role in encouraging people across the country to connect with nature.

He is survived by his family, to whom deepest sympathies have been extended.
headline: Gardener Dermot O'Neill dies aged 58

text:
The long-awaited inquests into the 1974 Birmingham pub bombings opened today with a minute's silence in honour of the 21 people who were killed in the attacks.

The hearings, which are being held at Birmingham and Solihull Coroner's Court, represent a significant moment for the families of the victims, many of whom have campaigned for decades for a full account of the circumstances surrounding the deaths of their loved ones.

On the evening of 21 November 1974, two bombs exploded in the Mulberry Bush and the Tavern in the Town pubs in Birmingham city centre, killing 21 people and injuring more than 200 others. The attacks remain among the deadliest carried out during the Troubles on the British mainland.

The coroner, Sir Peter Thornton QC, invited all those present to stand for a minute's silence before proceedings began. He told the court that the inquests would seek to establish the circumstances in which each of the 21 victims came to their deaths.

Six men were wrongly convicted of the bombings in 1975 and sentenced to life imprisonment. The so-called Birmingham Six had their convictions quashed by the Court of Appeal in 1991 after spending 16 years in prison, in one of the most notorious miscarriages of justice in British legal history.

No one has ever been successfully prosecuted for carrying out the attacks, which have been widely attributed to the Provisional IRA, though the organisation never formally claimed responsibility.

The families of the victims have long argued that the original inquests, held in 1975, were inadequate and failed to properly examine the full circumstances of the bombings, including questions about whether the security services had prior intelligence that could have prevented the attacks.

The resumption of the inquests follows years of legal battles by relatives, who have pressed for a fuller investigation into the events of that night. Campaigners have said they hope the process will finally deliver the answers they have been seeking for more than four decades.

The hearings are expected to examine a range of issues, including the emergency response on the night of the bombings and whether any warnings were given before the explosions. The inquests are expected to last several weeks.
headline: Birmingham bombing inquests start with minute's silence

text:
A woman has been charged in connection with a fatal hit-and-run incident in Co Galway that claimed the life of a pedestrian earlier this week.

The woman, who is in her 40s, was arrested by Gardaí yesterday evening and was detained at a garda station in the Galway division under Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act, 1984.

She has since been charged and is due to appear before Galway District Court this morning.

The incident occurred on Tuesday night on a road on the outskirts of Galway city. Emergency services attended the scene, but the pedestrian, a man in his 60s, was pronounced dead at the scene. His body was removed to University Hospital Galway where a post-mortem examination was carried out.

The vehicle involved in the collision failed to remain at the scene, prompting a significant garda investigation. Gardaí attached to the Galway Garda Division launched an appeal for witnesses and sought dashcam footage from motorists who may have been travelling in the area at the time.

It is understood that the investigation involved an examination of CCTV footage from the surrounding area, which assisted Gardaí in identifying the vehicle and its registered owner.

The road where the incident took place was closed for a period to allow a technical examination by Garda Forensic Collision Investigators and has since reopened.

Gardaí have said investigations into the circumstances of the collision are ongoing and have renewed their appeal for anyone with information to contact them.
headline: Woman charged over fatal Galway hit-and-run

text:
G20 leaders have agreed to step up humanitarian efforts in Afghanistan, pledging to channel aid through international organisations to avert what many fear could become a devastating humanitarian catastrophe in the war-torn country.

The agreement came at an extraordinary virtual summit convened by Italian Prime Minister Mario Draghi, who holds the rotating G20 presidency, with the leaders of the world's largest economies joining the call to address the rapidly deteriorating situation on the ground.

The leaders committed to ensuring that aid reaches the Afghan people without passing through the Taliban government, which seized power in August following the chaotic withdrawal of US and allied forces. The Taliban have not been formally recognised by any G20 member state.

Mr Draghi said the summit had achieved a "united response" to the crisis, adding that the international community had a duty to prevent Afghanistan from sliding into famine and economic collapse.

"We must not look away," he said. "Millions of Afghans, including women and children, face hunger and deprivation as winter approaches."

The United Nations has repeatedly warned that more than half of Afghanistan's population — some 23 million people — face acute food insecurity, with the country's economy in freefall since the Taliban takeover. International funding, which once accounted for roughly 75% of public spending, has largely been frozen.

Under the agreement, aid will be funnelled through UN agencies and other multilateral bodies to ensure it reaches those most in need. Leaders also stressed the importance of maintaining pressure on the Taliban to uphold human rights, particularly the rights of women and girls to education and employment.

However, the question of whether and how to engage directly with the Taliban administration remains a deeply divisive issue among G20 members. Several leaders emphasised that any future engagement must be conditional on the Taliban meeting international expectations on human rights and counter-terrorism commitments.

European Council President Charles Michel said the EU was ready to increase its humanitarian support but insisted that broader engagement with the Taliban would depend on concrete actions, not promises.

US President Joe Biden reiterated Washington's commitment to humanitarian assistance while maintaining that the Taliban must demonstrate a genuine commitment to safe passage for those wishing to leave the country and to combating terrorism.

China and Russia, both of which have maintained diplomatic channels with the Taliban, urged the international community to release Afghanistan's frozen assets, arguing that economic collapse would only deepen the crisis and fuel instability across the region.

The summit also addressed the threat of terrorism emanating from Afghan territory, with leaders underlining the need for the Taliban to ensure the country does not once again become a safe haven for militant groups.

Aid organisations operating on the ground have cautioned that pledges alone will not be sufficient, calling for urgent and sustained action to prevent what the UN has described as a humanitarian disaster of historic proportions.
headline: G20 leaders agree to step up Afghan humanitarian effort

text:
A man's attempt to fraudulently obtain a death certificate was undone by a single spelling mistake that immediately aroused the suspicion of staff at a registry office, a court has heard.

The forged document, which purported to certify the death of a woman in her 40s, contained a glaring typographical error in the name of the hospital where she had allegedly died. Staff at the civil registration office spotted the mistake and contacted the Gardaí.

The case, which came before Dublin District Court, heard that the accused had presented the document in an effort to settle financial and legal matters connected to the woman, who was in fact alive and well.

Judge Sarah Brennan was told the forgery was of a sufficiently poor quality that it would not have withstood even cursory scrutiny, with the typo in the hospital name being only the most obvious of several irregularities.

Sergeant Declan Murphy told the court that when gardaí arrested the man at his home in Dublin, he initially denied any knowledge of the document before later admitting he had sourced it online.

"It was a remarkably clumsy attempt," Sgt Murphy said. "The misspelling was a dead giveaway, if you'll pardon the expression."

The accused, who is in his 50s and cannot be named for legal reasons, pleaded guilty to a charge of uttering a forged instrument. His defence solicitor told the court his client had been under considerable personal and financial pressure at the time and had acted out of desperation rather than any calculated intent to defraud.

The solicitor asked the judge to take into account his client's early guilty plea, his lack of previous convictions, and the fact that no financial loss had ultimately been suffered by any party as a result of the attempted fraud.

Judge Brennan said the offence was a serious one that struck at the integrity of the State's civil registration system. She adjourned the case for the preparation of a probation report, warning the accused that all sentencing options remained open.

The General Register Office confirmed that safeguards are in place to detect fraudulent documents, and that any suspected forgeries are referred to the Gardaí as a matter of course. A spokesperson said instances of forged death certificates, while rare, are treated with the utmost seriousness.

The case is due to return before the court next month.
headline: Dead giveaway - typo reveals death cert a forgery

text:
Renewable energy sources are now growing at a faster rate than previously anticipated, according to new figures that suggest Ireland's transition away from fossil fuels is gathering momentum.

Data published by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland show that wind, solar and other clean energy technologies accounted for a greater share of electricity generation in the first quarter of this year compared with the same period last year, with wind energy alone responsible for more than 30 per cent of all power produced on the grid.

The findings come as the Government faces continued pressure to meet its climate targets under the Climate Action Plan, which commits Ireland to achieving a 51 per cent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 and reaching net zero by 2050.

Minister for the Environment Eamon Ryan said the figures were encouraging but cautioned that significant challenges remain, particularly in the areas of planning and grid infrastructure.

"We are making real progress, but we need to accelerate further if we are to meet our legally binding targets," Mr Ryan said. "The pace of renewable energy deployment must continue to increase, and we need to ensure the planning system and grid connections can keep up with demand."

The growth has been driven in large part by new onshore wind farms and a sharp increase in solar panel installations, both at commercial scale and among households availing of grants through the SEAI's home energy upgrade schemes.

Industry figures say the expansion of offshore wind will be critical to meeting Ireland's target of generating 80 per cent of electricity from renewable sources by the end of the decade. Several major offshore projects are currently progressing through the planning process, though some have faced delays.

The Irish Wind Energy Association welcomed the latest data but warned that bottlenecks in grid connections and lengthy planning timescales risk undermining progress. A spokesperson for the organisation said EirGrid and ESB Networks must be adequately resourced to deliver the infrastructure needed to support the additional capacity.

Opposition TDs have also raised concerns in the Dáil about the speed of the transition, with some arguing that communities hosting renewable energy projects need to see greater direct benefits. Sinn Féin's climate spokesperson called on the Government to introduce stronger community benefit provisions for all new developments.

Meanwhile, the Environmental Protection Agency has noted that while emissions from the electricity sector have fallen in recent years, other sectors including agriculture and transport continue to pose significant challenges to Ireland's overall climate ambitions.

The Government is expected to publish an updated assessment of progress against its carbon budgets later this year.
headline: Renewable energy sources growing at faster rate

text:
At least one person has been killed and 12 others injured after a gunman opened fire at a supermarket in the United States.

The shooting took place at a busy grocery store, with emergency services rushing to the scene after reports of gunfire. Police confirmed that the suspected gunman was among those who died, though authorities have not yet clarified whether the attacker was killed by responding officers or died by a self-inflicted wound.

Several of the injured are understood to be in a critical condition and have been transported to nearby hospitals for emergency treatment. The ages and identities of the victims have not yet been released, as authorities work to notify families.

Witnesses described scenes of panic as shoppers fled the store or sought shelter in back rooms and storage areas when the shooting began. Some described hearing what they initially thought were fireworks before realising shots were being fired.

Law enforcement officials said they responded within minutes of the first emergency calls. A large police presence remained at the scene for several hours as investigators worked to piece together the sequence of events.

The motive for the attack remains unclear, and authorities said they were examining the suspect's background as part of the ongoing investigation. Federal agencies, including the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), have been called in to assist with the probe.

The incident is the latest in a long line of mass shootings across the United States, which continue to fuel an intense national debate over gun control. Despite repeated calls for tighter firearms legislation, efforts to pass comprehensive reform at the federal level have repeatedly stalled in Congress.

The US has seen hundreds of mass shooting incidents so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which tracks such events. The organisation defines a mass shooting as one in which four or more people are shot, not including the gunman.

President Biden has previously described gun violence as an "epidemic" in the country and has urged lawmakers to take action, though legislative progress remains limited.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has confirmed that there are no reports of any Irish citizens being among those affected.
headline: One dead, 12 injured in US supermarket shooting

text:
The Government has confirmed that the school meals programme will continue to operate during the upcoming mid-term break, ensuring thousands of children across the country do not go without a hot meal during the holiday period.

Minister for Social Protection Heather Humphreys announced the extension, saying it was important that vulnerable children continued to receive nutritional support even when schools were closed.

The Hot School Meals Programme, which currently provides free meals to pupils in over 1,500 schools nationwide, has been one of the Government's flagship initiatives in tackling food poverty among children. Under the temporary extension, schools participating in the programme will be able to arrange for meals to be provided to pupils over the mid-term period.

Speaking this morning, the Minister said the decision reflected the reality facing many families across the country who were struggling with the cost of living.

"We know that for some children, the meal they receive in school is the most nutritious meal they will have in the day. It is only right that we ensure these children are not left without that support simply because schools are closed for a week," Ms Humphreys said.

The move has been broadly welcomed by opposition TDs, though several have called on the Government to make the extension permanent for all school holiday periods, including the summer months.

Sinn Féin's spokesperson on social protection said the announcement was a positive step but argued it did not go far enough. The party has repeatedly called for a universal free school meals programme that would cover every primary and secondary school in the State.

The Society of St Vincent de Paul also welcomed the decision, noting that demand for its services had increased significantly over the past two years as families continued to grapple with rising food, energy and housing costs.

The organisation said it had seen first-hand the difference the school meals programme made to children's wellbeing and educational outcomes, and urged the Government to consider a year-round approach.

The Department of Social Protection said details on the logistical arrangements for the mid-term extension would be communicated directly to participating schools in the coming days. It is understood that schools will have flexibility in how they organise the provision, with some expected to offer collection points for families while others may arrange delivery.

The hot meals programme was significantly expanded during the lifetime of the last government, with the aim of eventually making it available to all primary schools. It currently covers pupils in DEIS schools and a growing number of non-DEIS schools that have been brought into the scheme on a phased basis.
headline: School meal scheme to continue during mid-term break

text:
The number of people being treated in hospital for Covid-19 has risen by 53 over the past 24 hours, the Department of Health has confirmed, as a further 1,380 cases of the virus were notified this evening.

There are now 612 patients with the disease in hospitals across the country, of whom 116 are in intensive care units.

The latest figures represent a significant increase in hospitalisations compared to recent days, though health officials have cautioned that daily fluctuations are to be expected.

The Health Service Executive said that the pressure on hospitals remains a serious concern, with a number of facilities operating at or above capacity. Several hospitals have been forced to postpone elective procedures in recent weeks as they attempt to manage the surge in admissions.

Chief Medical Officer Dr Tony Holohan said the trajectory of the disease remains a cause for concern and urged the public to continue to follow public health guidelines.

"We are asking people to reduce their contacts as much as possible and to follow the basic measures we know work — wearing masks, maintaining social distance, practising good hand hygiene and ensuring adequate ventilation in indoor settings," Dr Holohan said.

The five-day moving average of cases now stands at 1,256, and health officials said the positivity rate among those tested remains elevated.

Dr Holohan also appealed to anyone who has not yet come forward for vaccination to do so, noting that the vast majority of those in intensive care are either unvaccinated or not fully vaccinated.

The HSE confirmed that as of this morning, more than 7.1 million doses of Covid-19 vaccine have been administered in the State, with over 3.5 million people now fully vaccinated.

Separately, NPHET is due to meet later this week to review the current epidemiological situation and to advise the Government on any further measures that may be required.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health said the figures underline the importance of continued vigilance as the country navigates the latest wave of infections.
headline: 53 more people in hospital with Covid, 1,380 new cases

text:
The number of fraud cases recorded by the Gardaí has risen sharply in the year to the end of June, according to new figures from the Central Statistics Office.

The CSO data shows a significant increase in fraud, deception and related offences compared with the same period last year, continuing a trend that has alarmed both law enforcement and consumer advocates.

The figures, published as part of the quarterly recorded crime statistics, reveal that fraud offences have become one of the fastest-growing crime categories in the State. The increase is understood to be driven in large part by a surge in online and cyber-enabled fraud, including phishing scams, invoice redirect fraud and identity theft.

Gardaí have pointed to the growing sophistication of criminal gangs, many of them operating from outside the jurisdiction, who target individuals and businesses through increasingly convincing digital methods. Older people and small businesses have been identified as particularly vulnerable to such schemes.

The Garda National Economic Crime Bureau, which leads the investigation of complex fraud cases, has seen its caseload grow substantially. A spokesperson for An Garda Síochána said the force continues to invest in its capacity to tackle economic crime and urged members of the public to remain vigilant.

The Minister for Justice said the Government is aware of the growing threat posed by fraud and is committed to ensuring that the Gardaí have the resources and legislative tools necessary to respond. The Department of Justice has been working on updated legislation to address gaps in the criminal law around online fraud and digital crime.

The Banking and Payments Federation Ireland has also expressed concern at the rising figures, noting that its member institutions have invested heavily in fraud prevention and detection systems. It called on consumers to take care when sharing personal or financial information online and to verify any unexpected requests for payments or account details.

The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission reiterated its advice to the public, warning that if an offer or communication seems too good to be true, it almost certainly is. The commission encouraged anyone who believes they have been the victim of fraud to report the matter to their local Garda station without delay.

Opposition TDs have criticised the Government's response, arguing that resources dedicated to tackling fraud remain insufficient given the scale of the problem. Sinn Féin's justice spokesperson said the figures demonstrate that the State is failing to keep pace with criminals who are exploiting technology to steal from ordinary people.

The CSO noted that changes in recording practices and increased public awareness may have contributed to some of the recorded increase, as more victims come forward to report offences that might previously have gone unreported. However, the office said the scale of the rise strongly suggests a genuine increase in the level of fraudulent activity.
headline: Large increase in fraud cases in year to June

text:
Two people have been arrested in Co Antrim as part of an ongoing investigation into criminality linked to the Ulster Defence Association.

The arrests were made by detectives from the Police Service of Northern Ireland on Wednesday morning as part of what the PSNI described as a proactive operation targeting organised crime connected to the loyalist paramilitary grouping.

A man and a woman, both in their 30s, were detained at separate addresses in the greater Antrim area during planned searches carried out in the early hours. They have been taken to a police station in the region for questioning.

During the course of the operation, officers also seized a quantity of suspected Class A drugs, a sum of cash, and electronic devices, which will now be subject to forensic examination.

The PSNI said the arrests form part of a wider investigation into the activities of the UDA in the area, including drug dealing, extortion and intimidation within local communities.

Detective Inspector Karen Moore said the operation demonstrated the PSNI's commitment to tackling the criminal enterprises of paramilitary organisations.

"These groups claim to act in the interests of their communities, but the reality is that they exploit and control vulnerable people for their own financial gain," she said.

"We will continue to work to bring those involved in this type of criminality before the courts and to disrupt the activities of these groups at every opportunity."

The PSNI has urged anyone with information about paramilitary activity or organised crime to contact police on 101 or to pass information anonymously through the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

The arrests come amid a renewed focus on paramilitary-linked crime across Northern Ireland, with the PSNI and partner agencies continuing to target the influence of loyalist and republican groupings in communities across the region.

The UDA, which declared a formal end to its campaign in 2007, remains a proscribed organisation. Despite its ceasefire, security sources have consistently assessed that elements within the organisation remain heavily involved in criminal activity, particularly the drugs trade.
headline: Two arrested in Antrim as part of probe into UDA crime

text:
A man has been charged following an altercation at a hotel in Co Fermanagh over the weekend.

The PSNI said officers were called to the incident at the hotel in Enniskillen in the early hours of Sunday morning.

It is understood the altercation involved a number of individuals and that one person sustained injuries during the incident. The injured party was treated at the scene by paramedics from the Northern Ireland Ambulance Service but did not require hospital treatment.

A man in his 30s was arrested at the scene and was taken to a custody suite for questioning. He has since been charged with a number of offences, including assault occasioning actual bodily harm and disorderly behaviour.

He is due to appear before Enniskillen Magistrates' Court at a date to be confirmed.

The PSNI has appealed for anyone who witnessed the incident or who may have footage of what happened to contact them on the non-emergency number 101, quoting the reference number provided.

Alternatively, information can be passed anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.
headline: Man charged following altercation at Fermanagh hotel

text:
Dozens of hardy sea swimmers braved the chilly waters off the Co Down coastline on Saturday morning as part of a growing community tradition that has taken on a life of its own in recent years.

The group gathered at Ballyholme Beach in Bangor shortly after dawn, with air temperatures hovering around seven degrees and the Irish Sea offering little more warmth, estimated at roughly nine degrees by those who ventured in.

Organisers said the turnout was one of the largest they had seen in months, with swimmers of all ages and abilities wading into the water in wetsuits, swimming costumes and, in some cases, little more than determination.

"There's nothing like it for clearing the head," said one regular participant, who has been swimming year-round at the beach for the past three years. "Once you get past the first thirty seconds, it's pure magic."

The popularity of open-water and sea swimming has surged across the island of Ireland since the pandemic, when outdoor activities became one of the few social outlets available. What began as a coping mechanism for many has since become a firmly established part of weekly routines for communities along the coast.

In Co Down, groups now meet regularly at spots including Crawfordsburn, Tyrella and Newcastle, with social media pages helping to coordinate swims and attract newcomers.

Health professionals have pointed to the potential benefits of cold-water swimming for both physical and mental wellbeing, though they also urge caution, advising swimmers never to enter the water alone and to be mindful of currents and cold-water shock.

Saturday's swim concluded, as is tradition, with hot drinks and conversation in the car park — a ritual participants say is nearly as important as the swim itself.

"You come for the water, but you stay for the community," one swimmer said, towel wrapped tightly around her shoulders. "It's become the highlight of my week, honestly."

Further swims are planned throughout the spring, with organisers encouraging anyone curious to come along and give it a try.
headline: Sea swimmers take to the waters off Co Down

text:
A rural postmistress has welcomed reports that the Government is considering a new annual subvention of €12,000 for post offices across the country, describing the measure as a potential lifeline for small communities.

Margaret Daly, who has run the post office in Knockmore, Co Mayo, for more than 20 years, said the reported payment would go some way towards ensuring the survival of offices that have been under severe financial pressure in recent years.

"It would make a huge difference to offices like mine," Ms Daly told RTÉ News. "We've seen our income drop steadily over the years as more services have moved online. A subvention like this would at least give us a fighting chance of keeping the doors open."

Reports emerged over the weekend that the Department of Social Protection is examining a proposal to provide the annual payment to postmasters and postmistresses to help sustain the network, which has seen hundreds of closures over the past two decades.

The Irish Postmasters' Union has long campaigned for a State subvention, arguing that post offices provide essential services in rural areas, particularly for older people who rely on them to collect social welfare payments and access basic financial services.

General secretary Ned O'Hara said the union would reserve full judgement until the details of any scheme were confirmed but described the reports as encouraging. "Post offices are the last remaining piece of State infrastructure in many villages and townlands. Once they close, they don't reopen," he said.

Minister for Social Protection Heather Humphreys has previously expressed her commitment to maintaining the post office network. A spokesperson for her department said the Minister was engaged in ongoing discussions with An Post and other stakeholders regarding the future sustainability of the network but declined to comment on the specifics of any proposed subvention.

An Post confirmed it was in discussions with the Government about supports for the network but said it would not be appropriate to comment further at this stage.

There are currently around 900 post offices operating across the State, down from more than 1,900 at the turn of the century. Rural TDs from across the political spectrum have repeatedly raised the issue of post office closures in the Dáil, warning that each closure diminishes the social fabric of the communities affected.

Ms Daly said her post office serves as far more than a place to collect payments or post letters. "People come in here for a chat, to check in, to feel connected. For some of the older people in this area, it's their only reason to leave the house on a given day. You can't put a price on that."
headline: Postmistress welcomes reports of €12k State subvention

text:
The Government has firmly rejected any suggestion that construction of the new National Children's Hospital should be halted, insisting the project will be seen through to completion despite further cost escalations.

Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly said the priority now must be delivering the hospital at St James's campus in Dublin as quickly as possible, and that pausing the build would only add to the final bill.

"Nobody in Government is entertaining the idea of stopping or pausing this project," the Minister told RTÉ News. "Every independent assessment we have received makes clear that stopping now would cost the taxpayer more, not less, and would delay the delivery of world-class paediatric care for children across the country."

The comments come amid renewed political pressure following confirmation that the estimated cost of the hospital has risen again, prompting sharp criticism from opposition TDs who have described the project as a monument to Government mismanagement.

Sinn Féin's health spokesperson David Cullinane said the latest overrun was "utterly scandalous" and called for full accountability, while Labour leader Ivana Bacik said families had been waiting far too long and deserved answers about when the facility would actually open its doors.

The National Paediatric Hospital Development Board has maintained that significant progress is being made on site, with construction now well advanced. However, the project has been dogged by controversy since costs began spiralling beyond the original budget approved by the Oireachtas.

The Taoiseach, speaking during Leaders' Questions in the Dáil, acknowledged public frustration but said the Government remained fully committed to delivering the hospital. He said it would transform children's healthcare in Ireland for generations and that walking away at this stage was simply not an option.

The Public Accounts Committee is expected to examine the latest cost projections in the coming weeks, with senior officials from the Department of Health and the HSE due to appear before members.

Independent TD Cathal Berry said that while he accepted the hospital needed to be finished, there had to be consequences for how the project had been managed. "You cannot simply keep writing blank cheques and expect the public to accept it," he said.

When completed, the new children's hospital will replace three existing paediatric facilities — at Temple Street, Crumlin, and Tallaght — bringing all services together on a single site. Satellite urgent care centres at Connolly Hospital in Blanchardstown and at Tallaght University Hospital are already operational.

Construction unions have indicated that work on site is proceeding at pace, with thousands of workers currently employed on the project. Any pause, they warned, would risk the loss of skilled tradespeople to other developments and make it significantly harder to resume at the same intensity.

The Department of Health said a revised timeline for the hospital's completion would be published in due course.
headline: Govt will not entertain talk of pausing hospital build

text:
Gardaí have arrested two people following the seizure of cash and cocaine during a search operation in Galway.

The operation was carried out by members of the Galway Divisional Drugs Unit, assisted by local Gardaí, as part of an ongoing investigation into the sale and supply of drugs in the Galway area.

During the course of a search at a premises in the city, Gardaí seized a quantity of cocaine, which is subject to analysis but is believed to have an estimated street value of a significant sum. A sum of cash was also recovered during the search.

Two individuals, a man and a woman, both aged in their 30s, were arrested at the scene and taken to a Garda station in Galway, where they were detained under the provisions of Section 2 of the Criminal Justice (Drug Trafficking) Act 1996.

Both individuals have since been released without charge, and a file is being prepared for the Director of Public Prosecutions.

Gardaí said the operation forms part of their continued efforts to disrupt the supply of controlled drugs across the western region. Further searches in the area have not been ruled out.

Investigations are ongoing.
headline: Two held after cash, cocaine seized in Galway

text:
A member of an organised crime gang has pleaded guilty to concealing more than €268,000 in cash in the attic of a house in Dublin.

The man, who is in his early 30s, entered his plea at Dublin Circuit Criminal Court today after being charged with possession of the proceeds of crime.

The court heard that gardaí from the Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau (DOCB) carried out a search of the property in west Dublin in the early hours of a morning last year as part of an ongoing investigation into the activities of the criminal gang.

During the search, officers discovered a large holdall bag hidden in the attic space containing €268,400 in cash, made up of various denominations. The money was vacuum-packed in several bundles, which the prosecution said was consistent with the proceeds of drug trafficking.

A detective sergeant told the court that the accused was present in the house at the time of the search and that he made no comment when cautioned. The officer said the accused is a known associate of a criminal organisation operating across the greater Dublin area, which is primarily involved in the sale and supply of controlled drugs.

Defence counsel told the court that his client wished to enter an early guilty plea and asked that this be taken into account at sentencing. Counsel said a number of matters would be raised in mitigation at the appropriate time.

The judge adjourned the case for the preparation of a probation report and a victim impact assessment. Sentencing has been scheduled for a date in the coming weeks.

The accused was remanded on continuing bail with strict conditions, including that he sign on daily at his local Garda station and surrender his passport.
headline: Gang member pleads guilty to hiding €268k cash in attic

text:
A bullet train driver in Japan left his controls unattended while the high-speed service was carrying more than 150 passengers, after he was forced to dash to the toilet mid-journey.

The driver of the Tokaido Shinkansen service, which was travelling at speeds of up to 150 kilometres per hour, left the cockpit for approximately three minutes to use the onboard lavatory. The train continued on its route without anyone at the controls during the absence.

West Japan Railway Company confirmed the incident and said the driver had been experiencing stomach pains during the journey. Rather than reporting his condition to the operations centre and requesting a replacement or an emergency stop, he instead asked the onboard conductor to briefly take over — though the conductor was not qualified to operate the train.

The railway operator said the driver's actions were in breach of its safety regulations, which strictly prohibit the cockpit from being left without a qualified operator at any time. Company officials bowed in apology at a press conference, a customary gesture in Japan when organisations acknowledge failings.

Japan's bullet train network, known as the Shinkansen, is renowned worldwide for its extraordinary safety record and punctuality. The system has operated since 1964 without a single passenger fatality caused by a derailment or collision. Services famously run with such precision that delays of even a minute are considered noteworthy.

The incident has prompted the railway company to review its protocols around driver welfare during journeys, including how staff should report health issues while operating services. It said it would consider measures to ensure drivers have adequate opportunities for comfort breaks before departing on routes.

Japan's transport ministry has also been notified and is understood to be examining the circumstances surrounding the breach.
headline: Bullet train driver abandoned controls for toilet dash

text:
Taoiseach Simon Harris has been photographed testing out the Defence Forces' new body armour, in what critics might describe as a Top Gun moment for the Fine Gael leader.

Harris visited the Defence Forces this week to inspect the new personal protective equipment, which forms part of a €16.5 million investment in upgraded body armour for members of the Irish military.

The Taoiseach was pictured wearing the new armour system, striking a pose that drew inevitable comparisons to politicians who have previously attempted to burnish their security credentials through carefully staged photo opportunities.

The investment in new body armour has been flagged as a key element of the Government's commitment to modernising the Defence Forces, which have faced years of criticism over underfunding, poor equipment, and a recruitment and retention crisis that has seen numbers fall well below the establishment strength of 9,500.

The €16.5 million procurement programme will see the new protective equipment rolled out across the Army, Naval Service, and Air Corps, replacing older systems that personnel and representative organisations had long complained were outdated and inadequate for modern operational requirements.

Defence spending has become an increasingly prominent political issue in Ireland, with pressure mounting from both domestic commentators and EU and NATO partners for the State to significantly increase its military expenditure. The Government has committed to moving towards a target of 2 per cent of GDP on defence, though Ireland remains among the lowest spenders in Europe on a per capita basis.

The Commission on the Defence Forces, which reported in 2022, recommended sweeping reforms and a substantial increase in funding to address what it described as critical capability gaps. The Government accepted the majority of the commission's recommendations, though opposition TDs and military representative bodies have argued that implementation has been far too slow.

Whether Harris's hands-on approach to showcasing the new equipment will translate into the kind of sustained investment the Defence Forces say they need remains to be seen. For now, the Taoiseach appears content to suit up and demonstrate that the Government is taking the issue seriously — one photo opportunity at a time.
headline: Top Gun Harris tests Defence Forces new body armour worth €16.5 million

text:
Sinn Féin has called for any change to Ireland's long-standing policy of military neutrality to be put to the people in a referendum, accusing the Government of attempting to quietly shift the country's defence posture without proper democratic oversight.

The party's defence spokesperson made the remarks during a heated exchange in the Dáil, where TDs debated the findings of the Consultative Forum on International Security Policy and Ireland's evolving relationship with European defence structures. Sinn Féin argued that neutrality is a core value held by the Irish public and that no government should have the authority to alter it without an explicit mandate from voters.

The intervention comes amid growing pressure on Ireland to deepen its participation in EU defence initiatives, particularly in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine and broader geopolitical instability. The Government has consistently maintained that Ireland's policy of military non-alignment remains intact, but critics have pointed to increased engagement with EU battlegroup arrangements and PESCO projects as evidence of a gradual erosion of the principle.

Sinn Féin's position puts it at odds with coalition parties, who have argued that enhanced cooperation with European partners does not amount to abandoning neutrality but rather represents a pragmatic response to an increasingly dangerous world. A Government spokesperson reiterated that Ireland's triple lock mechanism — requiring UN authorisation, Government approval, and Dáil approval for overseas military deployments — remains firmly in place.

However, Sinn Féin dismissed this assurance as insufficient, arguing that the triple lock itself could be undermined by legislative changes that would not require a public vote. The party pointed to recent polling suggesting that a significant majority of Irish people continue to support neutrality and would oppose joining any formal military alliance such as NATO.

The debate has exposed deep divisions within the Oireachtas on the issue. Some TDs from across the political spectrum have expressed sympathy with the idea of a referendum, arguing that the question is of such constitutional significance that it demands direct public input. Others have cautioned that a binary referendum question would oversimplify a complex policy area and could tie the hands of future governments in responding to emerging security threats.

Political commentators have noted that the issue could become a significant fault line ahead of the next general election, with Sinn Féin likely to use its pro-neutrality stance to distinguish itself from Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil. The party has long positioned itself as the most vocal defender of Irish neutrality in the Dáil, and its call for a referendum is seen as an attempt to force the coalition parties into a politically uncomfortable public position.

The Tánaiste has previously acknowledged that a "mature conversation" about Ireland's security posture is necessary but stopped short of endorsing a referendum, suggesting instead that the matter could be addressed through Oireachtas deliberation and public consultation.

Defence analysts have warned that Ireland's current defence capabilities remain significantly underfunded regardless of the neutrality debate, with the Defence Forces continuing to face serious recruitment and retention challenges. A report from the Commission on the Defence Forces recommended a substantial increase in spending, but implementation has been slow, drawing criticism from opposition TDs and military representative organisations alike.
headline: Irish neutrality should be put to a public vote, claims Sinn Féin

text:
Gardaí have stood down the search for a missing man after a body was discovered earlier today.

The remains were found in circumstances that are not being treated as suspicious, according to Garda sources. While formal identification has yet to take place, the family of the missing man has been notified of the development.

Gardaí had issued a public appeal for assistance in locating the man, and a search operation had been under way involving local units and specialist resources.

A post-mortem examination is expected to be carried out in due course, and the results will determine the course of any further investigation.

Gardaí have confirmed that no further action is required from the public at this time, and have thanked all those who assisted in the search effort and responded to appeals for information.

A Garda spokesperson said the matter remains under investigation and that no further comment would be made at this stage.

The identity of the deceased is not being released publicly at this time, in line with standard Garda procedure pending the completion of formal identification and notification of all family members.

Anyone who may be affected by issues raised in this article can contact the Samaritans on freephone 116 123 or by emailing jo@samaritans.ie. Pieta House can be reached on 1800 247 247.
headline: Gardai end the search for missing man after a body is found

text:
Jack Chambers, the 33-year-old Minister for Finance, rose in the Dáil today to deliver Budget 2025, becoming one of the youngest politicians in the history of the State to announce the annual fiscal package. Sources close to the minister had suggested in the days leading up to the announcement that he was feeling the weight of the occasion, with one senior Fianna Fáil figure remarking: "He's said to be nervous, but he's well prepared."

Chambers, who took over the finance brief from Michael McGrath following the latter's appointment as European Commissioner, faced the unenviable task of delivering what is widely expected to be the last budget before a general election. The pressure to produce a crowd-pleasing package while maintaining fiscal credibility was evident throughout the speech, which ran to well over an hour.

The budget comes at a time when the State's coffers are flush with corporation tax receipts, largely driven by a small number of multinational firms headquartered in Ireland. The government has been under sustained pressure from opposition TDs and advocacy groups alike to use the windfall to address the housing crisis, the creaking health service, and the rising cost of living that continues to squeeze households across the country.

Standing at the front bench, Chambers outlined a package that the government will hope strikes a balance between once-off cost-of-living measures and longer-term structural investment. The Tánaiste and senior coalition figures watched on from the government benches as the minister laid out adjustments to income tax bands, social welfare increases, and a series of targeted supports aimed at families and lower-income workers.

Opposition TDs were quick to respond. Sinn Féin's finance spokesperson accused the government of engaging in pre-election politics, describing the package as a "scattergun approach" designed to buy votes rather than fix systemic problems. The Social Democrats and Labour similarly criticised what they characterised as an over-reliance on temporary measures that would do little to address the structural deficits in housing and healthcare.

The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council had warned in the weeks prior to the budget that the government risked overheating the economy with excessive spending, a concern that Chambers acknowledged in his speech but sought to assuage by pointing to the establishment of future-proofing funds designed to insulate the State against potential economic shocks.

Whether the budget will achieve its obvious electoral purpose remains to be seen. With a general election widely expected before the end of the year, the coalition parties will be hoping that voters feel the benefit of today's measures in their pockets sooner rather than later. For Chambers personally, the delivery of his first and potentially only budget as Minister for Finance represents a significant milestone in what has already been a remarkably rapid political career.

The full details of the budget will be scrutinised in the coming days as the Finance Bill makes its way through the Oireachtas, with further debate expected in both the Dáil and Seanad over the weeks ahead.
headline: Budget 2025: “He’s said to be nervous”, 33-yr-old Jack Chambers announces the budget for the upcoming year

text:
A devastating new opinion poll has delivered a hammer blow to the coalition parties, with both Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael suffering sharp drops in support that will send shockwaves through Government Buildings.

The poll, which will make for grim reading in the offices of Taoiseach Micheál Martin and Tánaiste Simon Harris, suggests the two establishment parties are haemorrhaging support at an alarming rate, with voters increasingly turning away from the traditional pillars of Irish politics.

Fianna Fáil has seen its numbers fall significantly, a result that will raise serious questions about Martin's leadership and the party's ability to connect with an electorate that appears to be growing ever more disillusioned with the status quo. The party, which has long traded on its reputation as the natural party of government, now finds itself struggling to maintain relevance with a public that seems to have had enough.

Fine Gael's figures are no less catastrophic. Harris, who was installed as party leader with great fanfare and was supposed to inject fresh energy and appeal into the party's brand, appears to have singularly failed to arrest the decline. The notion that a new face at the top would be enough to win back voters now looks hopelessly naive.

The results will inevitably fuel speculation about whether the coalition partners can realistically expect to return to power together after the next general election, or whether the political landscape is shifting in ways that neither party is equipped to handle.

Sinn Féin, along with a host of smaller parties and independents, stand to benefit from the continued erosion of support for the two-party system that has dominated Irish politics for a century. The growing fragmentation of the vote suggests that the Irish electorate is no longer willing to simply rotate between the two Civil War parties and accept more of the same.

The poll numbers will be particularly concerning given the vast sums of public money the Government has been spending in what critics have described as a transparent attempt to buy voter goodwill ahead of an election. If billions of euro in giveaway budgets and spending packages cannot shore up support, it is difficult to see what Martin and Harris can do to turn the tide.

For ordinary voters struggling with the housing crisis, creaking public services, and an immigration system that remains a source of deep public frustration, the poll may simply confirm what they have long suspected — that the current Government is out of touch and out of ideas.

The question now is whether this represents a temporary dip or the beginning of a more permanent realignment in Irish politics. If it is the latter, then both Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael have far more to worry about than one bad poll.
headline: Disaster for Martin and Harris as new poll suggests nosedive for Fianna Fail and Fine Gael

text:
Large numbers of gardaí assigned to Roads Policing Units across the country are delivering little to no measurable output, according to a damning new report that raises serious questions about the effectiveness of traffic enforcement nationwide.

The report, which examined the productivity of officers within dedicated Roads Policing Units, found that a significant proportion of gardaí in the units were recording virtually no detections, checkpoints or engagements over extended periods, effectively rendering them unproductive in their assigned roles.

The findings are likely to intensify scrutiny of An Garda Síochána at a time when road fatalities remain a persistent concern and when the organisation is under pressure to demonstrate value for the considerable public resources it receives.

According to the report, the disparity between the most active and least active members within Roads Policing Units was stark, with some gardaí recording high volumes of Fixed Charge Notices, mandatory intoxicant testing checkpoints and other enforcement activity, while colleagues in the same units recorded figures that were negligible or, in some cases, practically non-existent.

The findings will be particularly uncomfortable for Garda management given that Roads Policing Units are specialist assignments. Officers in these roles are specifically tasked with traffic enforcement and road safety duties, meaning low productivity cannot easily be attributed to competing demands from other policing functions.

Sources familiar with the report indicated that the problem was not confined to any single Garda division or region but was instead a national issue, suggesting systemic failures in supervision, accountability and performance management within the organisation.

The Road Safety Authority has repeatedly highlighted the critical role that visible and active roads policing plays in deterring dangerous driving behaviour. Research consistently demonstrates that the perceived risk of detection is one of the most powerful factors influencing driver behaviour, making the productivity gaps identified in the report all the more concerning from a public safety perspective.

It is understood that the report has been shared with senior Garda management. However, it remains unclear what specific steps, if any, will be taken to address the failings identified.

The revelations come against a backdrop of continued frustration among road safety advocates, who have long argued that Ireland's roads policing capacity has been allowed to decline significantly since the dedicated Garda Traffic Corps was effectively disbanded and its functions absorbed into broader divisional structures several years ago.

At its peak, the Traffic Corps had in excess of 1,200 members. Numbers in Roads Policing Units have fluctuated considerably since, and campaigners have consistently argued that the reorganisation led to a dilution of focus and expertise.

The Policing Authority, which provides independent oversight of Garda performance, has on multiple occasions raised concerns about roads policing numbers and activity levels, urging the Garda Commissioner to prioritise the area.

A spokesperson for An Garda Síochána did not directly address the specific findings of the report but said the organisation was committed to ensuring that all members performed their duties effectively and that roads policing remained a priority.

The Department of Transport, which has policy responsibility for road safety, declined to comment on the operational matters of An Garda Síochána but pointed to the Government's Road Safety Strategy, which sets ambitious targets for reducing deaths and serious injuries on Irish roads.
headline: Large numbers of Roads Policing gardaí are completely ‘unproductive’, new report says

text:
Patients across the country will continue to face unacceptable levels of suffering unless the Government commits to a significant and sustained increase in hospital bed capacity, a leading doctor has warned.

The stark assessment comes amid ongoing overcrowding in emergency departments, with hundreds of patients routinely left waiting on trolleys in hospital corridors for hours and sometimes days before being admitted to a ward.

The doctor, speaking at a health policy forum in Dublin, said that Ireland's ratio of hospital beds per capita remains among the lowest in the European Union and that years of underinvestment have left the system unable to cope with rising demand from a growing and ageing population.

"We can talk all we like about reform and efficiency, but the fundamental problem is that we simply do not have enough beds," the expert said. "Until that changes, patients will continue to suffer. People are being left in wholly inappropriate settings, without dignity, without privacy, and without the standard of care they deserve."

The Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation has consistently highlighted the trolley crisis, with figures regularly showing more than 500 admitted patients waiting for beds on the worst days. The problem is particularly acute at hospitals outside Dublin, where capacity constraints are compounded by difficulties in recruiting and retaining staff.

The HSE's own winter plan acknowledged the need for additional capacity, but critics have argued that the pace of delivery falls far short of what is required. The Government has committed to delivering thousands of additional acute and community beds under the Sláintecare programme, but progress has been slow, with construction delays and planning difficulties hampering several key projects.

Opposition TDs have repeatedly raised the issue in the Dáil, accusing the Government of failing to treat the crisis with sufficient urgency. Sinn Féin's health spokesperson said the situation amounted to a "systemic failure" that was costing lives, while Labour called for an emergency capital investment programme to fast-track new bed capacity in the worst-affected regions.

The Department of Health said in a statement that significant investment had been made in recent years and that bed capacity had increased, pointing to the opening of new units at several hospitals around the country. A spokesperson said the Government remained committed to the full implementation of Sláintecare and that further capacity would come on stream in the coming years.

However, the expert doctor cautioned that even the planned increases may not be sufficient given demographic trends, warning that the number of people over 65 in Ireland is projected to double in the coming decades. Without a longer-term plan that accounts for this reality, the health service risks lurching from one crisis to the next, the doctor said.

"This is not a problem that can be solved with sticking plasters or seasonal surge plans," the doctor added. "It requires a fundamental commitment to building the infrastructure our health service needs. Every week we delay, more patients pay the price."
headline: Patients will continue to suffer unless bed capacity increases, says expert doctor

text:
There has been uproar among Ukrainian refugees in County Clare after a number of families were informed they would have to relocate from their current accommodation, with some given just days' notice to prepare for the move.

Residents at a number of sites across the county have expressed anger and distress at the decision, which they say has come with little warning and scant regard for the lives they have begun to build in their local communities. Several of those affected have children enrolled in nearby schools, have registered with local GPs, and have taken up employment in the area.

One woman, who asked not to be named, said she was "devastated" at being told she would have to uproot her family once again. "We came here with nothing. We have tried so hard to settle, to learn English, to make friends. My children are happy in school for the first time since the war started. Now they tell us we must go somewhere else. It feels like we are starting from zero again," she said.

The relocations are understood to be linked to ongoing capacity pressures within the International Protection Accommodation Services (IPAS) system and changes to contracts with accommodation providers. The Department of Integration has been managing an unprecedented demand for emergency accommodation since the outbreak of the war in Ukraine in February 2022, with more than 100,000 people having arrived in Ireland seeking temporary protection.

Local representatives in Clare have been inundated with calls from concerned residents and community groups who have rallied around the Ukrainian families since their arrival. Independent councillor PJ Kelly said the situation was "completely unacceptable" and called on the Government to show greater sensitivity in how it manages the process.

"These people have been through enough. They fled a war zone, they came here in good faith, and many of them have integrated beautifully into communities across Clare. To pull the rug from under them now, with minimal notice, is cruel and unnecessary," he said.

Community volunteers who have been working closely with the families echoed those sentiments. Local groups had organised English language classes, social events and school supplies for the children, and say the sudden announcement has left both refugees and their supporters feeling blindsided.

It is understood that some of those being moved have been offered alternative accommodation in other parts of the country, though specific details of where they would be sent were not immediately made available to the families concerned. That lack of clarity has only added to the anxiety, according to those on the ground.

A spokesperson for the Department of Integration confirmed that "some movements of beneficiaries of temporary protection are necessary from time to time due to contractual and operational requirements" but insisted that every effort is made to minimise disruption. The spokesperson added that the Department was "committed to ensuring that all those in the system are provided with appropriate accommodation and supports."

However, that assurance has done little to calm tensions locally. Several of the affected families have said they intend to resist the move, and there are suggestions that a public meeting may be organised in the coming days to allow residents to voice their concerns directly.

The situation in Clare is not an isolated one. Similar complaints have emerged from other parts of the country in recent months as the Government continues to grapple with the logistical and financial pressures of housing tens of thousands of displaced people.
headline: Uproar in Clare from Ukrainians who’ve been told they have to move on

text:
The Government is set to hold an extraordinary Cabinet meeting on Sunday as the fuel protest crisis continues to escalate, with blockades now affecting supply chains across the country and mounting pressure on the coalition to act.

It is understood the Taoiseach convened the emergency session after a day of fraught discussions with senior ministers and officials, as hauliers and ordinary motorists maintained rolling blockades at key fuel depots and along major arterial routes for a third consecutive day.
