A Government source confirmed the meeting would take place on Sunday afternoon, with the Department of Transport and the Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications expected to present options to ministers. The source said all options were "on the table" but declined to elaborate further.

Opposition TDs were quick to seize on the development as evidence that the coalition had lost control of the situation. Speaking to The Liberal, one prominent opposition figure said the decision to召 a Sunday Cabinet meeting spoke volumes.

"The Government is in panic mode," the TD said. "They have completely misread the mood of the country on this. People are genuinely struggling with the cost of filling their cars and heating their homes, and the response from Government has been utterly inadequate."

The protests, which began on Thursday evening, have seen convoys of trucks, tractors and private vehicles slow traffic to a crawl on motorways around Dublin, Cork, Limerick and Galway. Demonstrators are demanding an immediate reduction in excise duty on petrol and diesel, as well as a reversal of the latest carbon tax increase, which they say is crippling households and businesses already stretched to breaking point.

Fuel prices have surged in recent months, with the average cost of a litre of petrol now exceeding €2 at many forecourts. Diesel prices have risen even more sharply, prompting particular fury among haulage operators who say their margins have been wiped out entirely.

The Gardaí have maintained a largely hands-off approach to the blockades thus far, with Garda management understood to be keen to avoid any confrontation that could inflame tensions further. However, there are growing concerns about the impact on essential supply lines, with some retailers reporting difficulty receiving deliveries and several filling stations in the greater Dublin area running dry on Friday evening.

The Irish Road Haulage Association said it understood the frustration of its members but stopped short of formally endorsing the blockades, calling instead for "immediate and meaningful engagement" with Government on the fuel cost crisis.

Tánaiste's efforts to calm the situation on Friday appeared to have had little effect, with protesters dismissing assurances that the Government was "acutely aware" of the pressure on households and businesses as hollow rhetoric.

Several Government TDs have privately expressed alarm at the speed with which the protests have gathered momentum, with one backbencher telling The Liberal that their constituency office had been "inundated" with calls from constituents supporting the demonstrators.

"There is a real anger out there that I haven't seen in a long time," the TD said. "People feel they are being squeezed from every direction – energy costs, mortgage rates, the cost of the weekly shop – and fuel is the one that has finally tipped them over the edge."
headline: BREAKING: “The govt is in panic mode” – Cabinet to have special meeting on Sunday to discuss fuel protest crisis

text:
The Capuchin Day Centre has said it has been overwhelmed by demand for its Christmas food vouchers, with thousands of the vouchers snapped up within hours of becoming available.

The centre, which operates from its base on Bow Street in Dublin's north inner city, said the speed at which the vouchers were claimed underscores the depth of the cost-of-living crisis still facing families across the country.

Brother Kevin Crowley, who has long been the public face of the centre's work, said the level of demand was staggering but unfortunately not surprising given the financial pressures many households continue to endure.

"People are struggling. They are choosing between heating and eating, and at Christmas time that pressure only intensifies," he said. "We see it every single day, but the speed at which these vouchers went is something that should give everyone pause for thought."

The vouchers, which allow recipients to purchase food for the Christmas period, are a crucial lifeline for families who might otherwise go without a proper meal over the festive season. The centre confirmed that thousands were distributed in a matter of hours, with demand far outstripping supply.

The Capuchin Day Centre provides meals, food parcels, and other essential supports to people experiencing poverty and homelessness throughout the year. It has consistently highlighted the growing number of working families turning to its services, a trend that has accelerated sharply since the onset of the cost-of-living crisis.

Social Democrats co-leader Holly Cairns has previously called on the Government to do more to address food poverty, describing it as "a stain on a wealthy country." Similar calls have come from charities and opposition TDs who argue that existing State supports are not keeping pace with the rising cost of essentials.

The Society of St Vincent de Paul has also reported a significant increase in requests for help in the lead-up to Christmas, with the charity warning that many families are facing impossible choices as bills mount and incomes remain stretched.

The Government has pointed to a range of measures introduced in recent budgets, including increases to social welfare payments and the provision of one-off cost-of-living supports, as evidence of its commitment to helping those most in need. However, organisations working on the front line say the supports, while welcome, are not sufficient to meet the scale of the problem.

The Capuchin Day Centre has urged anyone in a position to donate to do so, saying that every contribution helps ensure that no family in Ireland goes hungry at Christmas. It also called on the Government to treat food poverty as a matter of urgency, rather than a seasonal concern.

"This isn't just a Christmas problem," Brother Kevin said. "People need help all year round. But if the response to these vouchers tells us anything, it's that the need out there is enormous and it's growing."
headline: Huge demand for Christmas food vouchers with thousands gone in hours, Capuchin Day Centre says

text:
Enoch Burke, the secondary school teacher who became one of the most polarising figures in Irish public life, has been released from Mountjoy Prison after spending more than 400 days behind bars for contempt of court, without ever purging that contempt.

Burke walked free from the north Dublin prison following a court order, prompting his family to declare that "Enoch won" in a statement posted to social media. The release brings to a close one of the longest and most unusual contempt of court detentions in the history of the State, though the broader legal saga involving Burke and his former employer, Wilson's Hospital School in Multyfarnham, Co Westmeath, appears far from over.

The Church of Ireland secondary school suspended Burke in 2022 after he refused to use the preferred name and pronouns of a transitioning student, a stance he said was rooted in his sincerely held religious beliefs. When he continued to attend the school premises despite the suspension, the school obtained a court order barring him from doing so. Burke's repeated refusal to comply with that order led to his committal to Mountjoy for contempt of court.

Throughout his imprisonment, Burke steadfastly refused to purge his contempt — the standard mechanism by which a person detained for civil contempt secures their own release by agreeing to comply with the relevant court order. His continued detention became a cause célèbre among certain religious conservative and free speech groups, both in Ireland and internationally, while critics maintained he was simply refusing to follow a lawful court order and that no principle of conscience was engaged.

The Burke family, who have been vocal and visible throughout the entire affair, framed the release as a vindication. In their statement, they characterised the outcome as a victory not only for Enoch Burke personally but for the principles of religious liberty and freedom of conscience. The family have consistently argued that no teacher should be compelled to use language that contradicts their religious beliefs and that Burke's treatment amounted to persecution by the State and the school authorities.

Legal observers have noted the significance of Burke's release without purging his contempt. In the ordinary course, civil contempt is regarded as coercive rather than punitive — the detained person is said to hold the keys to their own cell. The fact that Burke was released without yielding raises questions about the practical limits of civil contempt as a remedy when the contemnor is prepared to endure indefinite imprisonment rather than comply.

The court order that led to his release is understood to reflect a recognition that continued detention was no longer serving its coercive purpose, a consideration that has arisen in other jurisdictions where individuals have been held for extended periods for civil contempt without any realistic prospect that further imprisonment would secure compliance.

Burke's case has drawn attention well beyond the specific facts of the dispute with Wilson's Hospital School. It has become entangled with broader debates about transgender rights, religious freedom, the limits of employer authority, and the role of the courts in adjudicating conflicts between competing rights. His supporters have drawn comparisons with cases of conscience and civil disobedience, while his detractors have argued that the case is fundamentally about an employee's refusal to abide by workplace policies and lawful court orders.
headline: “Enoch won” – Enoch Burke has been released from Mountjoy Prison after over 400 days following court order without purging his contempt

text:
A young mother has died after being attacked by a shark while swimming with her daughter off the coast of Mexico, according to local authorities.

The 26-year-old woman, who has not yet been publicly named, was swimming in the waters near Melaque, a coastal town in the western state of Jalisco, when she was bitten by the shark. Her young daughter, who was in the water at the time of the attack, was not injured in the incident.

Emergency services rushed to the scene after witnesses raised the alarm, and the woman was pulled from the water with serious injuries to her lower body. She was transported to a nearby hospital but was pronounced dead shortly after arrival, local media reported.

Authorities in Jalisco confirmed the fatal attack and said they had closed the beach to swimmers in the aftermath while an investigation into the incident was carried out. Officials have urged beachgoers in the region to exercise extreme caution and to heed any warnings issued by lifeguards and local civil protection agencies.

Shark attacks in Mexican waters, while not unheard of, remain relatively rare. The country's Pacific coastline has seen a number of incidents in recent years, though fatalities are uncommon.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has not indicated that any Irish citizens were involved in the incident. The department routinely advises Irish travellers abroad to check its travel advice and to register their details with the nearest embassy or consulate when travelling overseas.

The woman's family are understood to be devastated by the tragedy. Further details regarding the circumstances of the attack are expected to be released by Mexican authorities in the coming days.
headline: 26-yr-old mother dies after attack by shark in Mexico while swimming with daughter

text:
The full suite of social welfare increases announced in Budget 2025 have now taken effect, with welfare recipients across the country seeing higher payments in their accounts this week.

The increases, which were confirmed by Minister for Social Protection Heather Humphreys last October, mean that most weekly social welfare payments have risen by €12 per week. The higher rates applied from the first week of January, meaning that those in receipt of jobseeker's payments, disability allowance, carer's allowance, the state pension and a range of other schemes are now benefitting from the uplift.

For pensioners, the full rate of the contributory state pension has increased to €289.30 per week, while the non-contributory pension has risen to €266 per week. The increase brings some relief to older people who have been among those hardest hit by the cost of living crisis in recent years.

Working-age recipients on payments such as Jobseeker's Allowance and Disability Allowance will now receive €232 per week at the full rate, up from €220. Qualified adult dependant rates have also been increased in line with the changes.

The qualified child increase has also been raised, going up to €54 per week for children aged 12 and over, and €46 for those under 12. The increases are intended to provide additional support to families relying on social welfare.

Carer's Allowance, which has long been a point of contention for advocacy groups who argue the means test is too restrictive, has also risen by €12 to €248 per week for those caring for one person, and to €372 for those caring for two or more people.

The Living Alone Allowance, paid to people aged 66 and over who live by themselves, has increased by €12 to €34 per week, a measure which the government said was targeted at addressing the particular vulnerability of older people living alone to poverty.

The changes come alongside a number of other cost of living measures that were rolled out over the Christmas period and into the new year. A double payment of Child Benefit was made in December, while lump sum payments were also issued to recipients of the fuel allowance, living alone allowance, and carer's support grant during the final quarter of 2024.

However, opposition TDs and social justice organisations have cautioned that the increases, while welcome, may not be sufficient to keep pace with the rising cost of essentials. The Society of St Vincent de Paul noted before Christmas that demand for its services remained at unprecedented levels, with housing costs, energy bills, and food prices continuing to place enormous strain on low-income households.

Sinn Féin's spokesperson on social protection had argued during the budget debate that the €12 increase would be quickly eroded by inflation, and that more structural reform of the social welfare system was needed to genuinely lift people out of poverty.

The Department of Social Protection has urged anyone who believes they may be entitled to a payment, or who has not yet seen the increase reflected in their account, to contact their local Intreo centre for assistance.
headline: 2025 social welfare increases have kicked in with welfare recipients increasing their payments this week

text:
The familiar drumbeat of Covid alarm has sounded once again as health authorities in Ireland confirmed dozens of cases of the Eris variant, prompting fresh calls for vigilance and a renewed emphasis on isolation protocols that many had hoped were firmly in the rearview mirror.

The variant, officially designated EG.5.1 and nicknamed Eris, has been detected in increasing numbers across the country in recent weeks, with the HSE confirming that cases have been identified in multiple regions. Yet the response from official channels has followed a well-worn playbook that critics argue leans heavily on stoking public anxiety rather than providing measured, proportionate guidance.

Symptoms associated with the Eris variant are, by all accounts, virtually indistinguishable from those of previous Omicron subvariants. They include a runny nose, sore throat, headache, cough, fatigue, and in some cases a loss of taste or smell. In the vast majority of cases, particularly among the vaccinated and those who have had previous infections, the illness is mild and self-limiting. Hospital admissions linked to the variant remain low, and there is no evidence to suggest that Eris causes more severe disease than its predecessors.

Despite this, messaging from public health officials has once again placed considerable emphasis on isolation rules and behavioural restrictions. Those who test positive are being advised to isolate for at least five days and to avoid contact with vulnerable individuals for a further period thereafter. The guidance, while framed as advisory rather than mandatory, carries an unmistakable echo of the more restrictive measures that defined the pandemic years and imposed enormous social, economic, and psychological costs on the population.

The question that many are now asking is whether this level of response is warranted or whether it represents an institutional reluctance to move beyond a crisis footing that has served certain interests well. Throughout the pandemic, Ireland maintained some of the longest and most stringent lockdown measures in Europe, with significant consequences for mental health, small businesses, children's education, and civil liberties. The suggestion that the country should now return to a posture of heightened alarm over a variant that is causing predominantly mild illness has understandably been met with scepticism in many quarters.

Professor of immunology at Trinity College Dublin Luke O'Neill has previously noted that the population now possesses significant levels of immunity through a combination of vaccination and natural infection, a wall of protection that renders the threat posed by new variants considerably less acute than it was in 2020 or 2021. Yet this context is frequently absent from official communications, which tend to foreground case numbers and isolation protocols rather than the reassuring reality of population-level immunity.

The World Health Organisation classified Eris as a variant of interest in August, a designation that sits below the more serious variant of concern category. The WHO has not recommended any additional public health measures in response to the variant, a fact that makes the tone of domestic messaging appear somewhat disproportionate.

In the Dáil, there has been limited scrutiny of the government's approach to ongoing Covid communications, with opposition TDs largely declining to challenge the prevailing narrative.
headline: Fear mongering continues as Covid Eris variant symptoms as Ireland confirms dozens of cases with more isolation rules outlined

text:
The Road Safety Authority has confirmed that more than 1,200 driving tests have been cancelled in recent months due to issues with candidates' motor insurance, raising fresh concerns about the backlog in the testing system and the costs being imposed on learner drivers.

The RSA said the cancellations arose because candidates presented for their test in vehicles that did not have valid insurance cover, or where the insurance policy did not adequately cover the vehicle for the purposes of a driving test. Under the rules, a candidate must present a vehicle that is taxed, insured and roadworthy on the day of the test, and the insurance must cover the driver for the test itself.

The figures, which were released in response to a parliamentary question, have prompted criticism from opposition TDs who argued that the cancellations are placing an unnecessary burden on learner drivers already facing lengthy waiting times. Several TDs called on the Minister for Transport to intervene and work with the insurance industry to ensure that policies are clearer about what cover is required for a driving test.

Sinn Féin's transport spokesperson said the situation was "completely unacceptable" and accused the Government of failing to address systemic problems in the driving test system. "These are people who have waited weeks, sometimes months, for a test appointment, only to be turned away on the day through no real fault of their own," the TD said. "The insurance industry needs to be far more transparent about what is and isn't covered, and the RSA needs to do more to communicate the requirements to candidates well in advance."

The RSA, for its part, said it does notify candidates of the documentation and vehicle requirements ahead of their test date, including the need for appropriate insurance cover. A spokesperson for the authority said candidates are urged to check with their insurer well before the date of the test to confirm that their policy covers them for the purpose of undertaking a driving test.

"It is the responsibility of the candidate to ensure that the vehicle presented on the day meets all the necessary requirements," the RSA spokesperson said. "We would strongly encourage all candidates to contact their insurance provider in advance to confirm they have the appropriate level of cover."

Insurance Ireland said that the vast majority of learner driver policies do provide cover for driving tests, but acknowledged that some policies may carry specific exclusions or conditions. The industry body said it would encourage any learner driver who is unsure about their cover to contact their provider directly.

The issue has shone a light on the broader difficulties facing learner drivers in Ireland, who have long complained about the cost and complexity of obtaining a full licence. Between the expense of lessons, insurance premiums that can run into thousands of euro, and waiting times for test appointments, the process remains a source of significant frustration for many young drivers and their families.

The average waiting time for a driving test currently stands at several weeks in most test centres, though in some parts of the country the wait can stretch considerably longer. The RSA has been working to reduce the backlog by recruiting additional driver testers, but motoring groups say progress has been too slow.

The Alliance for Insurance Reform said the cancellations highlighted a wider problem with transparency in the motor insurance market.
headline: Over 1,200 driving tests have been cancelled due to insurance issues, says RSA

text:
A judge has thrown out what he described as "fraudulent" personal injury claims brought by two women from Co Clare against a Dublin taxi driver, expressing anger at the attempt to deceive the court.

Judge John O'Connor, sitting at Dublin Circuit Court, dismissed the cases after finding that the two claimants had grossly exaggerated their injuries and presented misleading evidence in pursuit of insurance payouts.

The women, who are understood to be from the same family, had each sought significant damages following a minor road traffic incident involving a taxi in Dublin city centre. They claimed to have suffered debilitating soft tissue injuries that left them unable to carry out everyday tasks and affected their quality of life over an extended period.

However, the defence produced surveillance footage and social media evidence that directly contradicted the women's accounts of their injuries. The footage showed both claimants engaging in physical activities entirely inconsistent with the level of disability they had described to the court.

Judge O'Connor did not hide his frustration during the proceedings, telling the court that cases of this nature were a blight on the legal system and contributed directly to the insurance crisis that has burdened honest motorists and businesses across the country for years.

He remarked that the taxi driver, who had been put through considerable stress by the proceedings, should never have been subjected to the ordeal of defending claims that were without foundation.

The judge said claims such as these drive up premiums for every driver and every business in the State, describing them as an abuse of process that wastes court time and resources.

Insurance fraud has remained a persistent concern in Ireland, with industry bodies and successive governments pointing to exaggerated and fabricated claims as a key factor behind the country's stubbornly high insurance costs. The Government's Insurance Reform Action Plan, which was introduced to tackle the issue, has led to the establishment of revised personal injuries guidelines and greater judicial scrutiny of claims.

Alliance for Insurance Reform spokesperson Peter Boland has previously called for more judges to follow suit in calling out fraudulent claims, arguing that robust judicial responses serve as an essential deterrent.

The taxi driver, who was represented in court and had his costs covered by his insurer, is understood to have welcomed the outcome. Speaking through his legal team, he expressed relief that the matter had been resolved and that the court had seen through what he had always maintained were bogus claims.

It is not yet clear whether the matter will be referred to the Director of Public Prosecutions for consideration of criminal charges. Under legislation strengthened in recent years, making a fraudulent insurance claim can carry serious penalties, including fines and imprisonment.

The cases are the latest in a growing number of personal injury claims to be struck out by the courts amid increased vigilance around insurance fraud. Legal professionals have noted a shift in recent years, with judges increasingly willing to penalise claimants who are found to have misled the court, including through orders for costs against unsuccessful plaintiffs.
headline: Angered judge throws out ‘fraudulent’ insurance claims from Co Clare women against Dublin taxi driver

text:
An Irish student who orchestrated a sophisticated scam through Snapchat, defrauding victims of more than €16,000, has narrowly avoided a custodial sentence after a judge opted instead for a suspended term with a series of stringent conditions.

The young man, who cannot be named for legal reasons, appeared before the court after pleading guilty to multiple counts of fraud and deception. The court heard that the accused had used Snapchat to lure victims into parting with money through a scheme in which he promised goods and services that were never delivered.

The scam, which ran over a period of several months, targeted a number of individuals, many of them young people themselves, who transferred funds electronically after engaging with the accused on the social media platform. Some victims handed over relatively modest sums, while others lost several thousand euro in a single transaction.

A Garda investigation was launched after a number of complaints were filed, and detectives were able to trace the transactions back to accounts controlled by the accused. When arrested and questioned, the student made admissions and cooperated with the investigation.

In court, the defence counsel argued that the accused was a young man who had made a serious error of judgement and pointed to his previously clean record, his age, and the fact that he was engaged in full-time education. The court was told the student had expressed genuine remorse and had already begun making efforts to repay the money owed to victims.

The judge acknowledged the seriousness of the offending, noting that the breach of trust involved in online fraud causes significant harm not only to direct victims but to public confidence in digital commerce more broadly. However, the judge said that given the accused's youth, his lack of previous convictions, and his early guilty plea, a custodial sentence was not warranted at this stage.

Instead, the judge imposed a suspended sentence with what legal observers described as notably harsh conditions. The accused was ordered to repay the full €16,000 to his victims within a specified timeframe, perform a substantial number of community service hours, and remain under the supervision of the Probation Service for an extended period.

Additionally, the judge placed strict restrictions on the student's use of social media, effectively barring him from using Snapchat and similar platforms for the duration of the suspended sentence. He was also warned in the strongest possible terms that any breach of the conditions, or any further offending of any nature, would almost certainly result in the activation of the custodial term.

The case has drawn attention to the growing prevalence of social media-based fraud in Ireland, particularly among younger demographics. The Gardaí have repeatedly urged the public to exercise caution when engaging in financial transactions through social media platforms and to report any suspicious activity.

Victim advocacy groups have expressed mixed reactions to the outcome, with some welcoming the restitution order and others questioning whether a suspended sentence sends a sufficiently strong deterrent message to would-be fraudsters operating online.

The student left court without making any comment.
headline: Irish student avoids jailtime in €16,000 Snapchat scam but judge places harsh conditions

text:
Multiple drone strikes hit Moscow in the early hours of this morning, causing widespread panic across the Russian capital and triggering mass evacuations from several residential districts as air raid sirens sounded for hours in what Ukrainian officials have described as one of the largest aerial attacks on the city since the full-scale invasion began.

Russian authorities confirmed that at least a dozen drones targeted locations across Moscow and the surrounding oblast, with several penetrating the city's air defence systems and striking buildings in residential areas. Emergency services were dispatched to multiple sites, with footage circulating on social media showing plumes of smoke rising from at least three districts and long queues of traffic as residents attempted to flee affected neighbourhoods.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said in a statement on Telegram that air defence units had intercepted a number of the incoming drones but acknowledged that debris and at least some direct hits had caused damage to civilian infrastructure. He urged residents to remain calm and follow instructions from emergency services, though his appeal appeared to do little to quell the sense of alarm gripping parts of the city.

Russian state media initially downplayed the scale of the attack, describing it as a "terrorist provocation" that had been largely repelled. However, independent Russian media channels and eyewitness accounts painted a markedly different picture, with reports of shattered windows across entire apartment blocks, fires breaking out in at least two locations, and scenes of considerable distress among residents who were roused from sleep by explosions.

The Russian Ministry of Defence said it was investigating the origins of the drones but placed responsibility squarely on Ukraine, warning of "severe consequences" for what it termed an escalation against civilian targets. Ukraine has not formally claimed responsibility for the strikes, though a senior adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky said in remarks widely interpreted as an oblique acknowledgement that "Russia is learning what it means to live under the constant threat of aerial attack."

The strikes represent a significant escalation in Ukraine's capacity to project force deep into Russian territory. While Moscow has been targeted by drones on several occasions since the war began in February 2022, previous incidents were largely limited in scope and were often intercepted before causing substantial damage. The scale of this morning's assault, and the evident failure of Russian air defences to prevent multiple hits, marks a notable shift that military analysts say will have both strategic and psychological ramifications.

Dr Rob Lee, a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute in Philadelphia, said the attacks demonstrated that Ukraine's domestically produced long-range drone programme had matured considerably. "The ability to simultaneously strike multiple targets across a city as heavily defended as Moscow is a significant capability milestone," he said. "It fundamentally challenges the Kremlin's narrative that this war is something happening far away and poses no direct threat to ordinary Russians."

The psychological impact was immediately apparent. Videos posted to social media showed chaotic scenes at metro stations as residents sought shelter underground, while others documented bumper-to-bumper traffic on roads leading out of the city despite the pre-dawn hour. Several schools and public buildings in affected districts were closed for the day, and hospital emergency departments reported treating patients for injuries sustained during evacuations as well as from debris.
headline: Multiple drone strikes across the Russian capital cause widespread panic and spark mass evacuations

text:
A man has sadly passed away in Cork following what has been described as a "medical incident."

Emergency services were called to the scene, where the man was treated before being transported to hospital. Despite the best efforts of medical personnel, he was pronounced dead a short time later.

The circumstances surrounding the incident are not being treated as suspicious at this time, and it is understood that the Gardaí are not seeking any further information in connection with the matter.

The identity of the deceased has not been released, and it is understood that his family have been notified.

A Garda spokesperson confirmed that the man had experienced a medical episode and that a file would be prepared for the Coroner's Court, as is standard procedure in such cases.

Local representatives in the area have expressed their sympathies to the man's family and friends during what they described as an incredibly difficult time.

No further details are available at this stage, and it is expected that additional information may be released in due course following the completion of a post-mortem examination.

The thoughts of the community are with the man's loved ones as they come to terms with their loss.
headline: Man sadly passes away in Cork following “medical incident”

text:
Gatwick Airport has been crowned the second-worst airport in Europe for delays, according to new data that will do little to reassure the millions of holidaymakers who pass through its gates each year.

The London hub, which serves as a key departure point for Irish travellers heading to destinations across the continent, was found to have one of the poorest punctuality records among major European airports, with a significant proportion of flights departing or arriving behind schedule.

The analysis, which examined performance data from airports across the continent, placed Gatwick behind only one other facility in the unenviable rankings. The findings have prompted renewed criticism of the airport's capacity constraints and operational management, with passenger advocacy groups calling for urgent improvements.

Gatwick, which operates with a single operational runway — making it the busiest single-runway airport in the world — has long struggled with congestion issues that critics say inevitably lead to cascading delays, particularly during peak travel periods.

The airport has faced increasing pressure in recent years as passenger numbers have rebounded sharply following the pandemic-era slump. Capacity issues that were temporarily masked by reduced demand have now returned with a vengeance, leaving travellers facing lengthy waits and disrupted itineraries.

For Irish passengers, the data serves as a timely reminder to consider alternatives when booking connecting flights through London. Dublin Airport, which has faced its own well-publicised difficulties with queuing and staffing in recent times, will nonetheless take some quiet satisfaction from its absence near the top of the European delay charts.

Gatwick's operator said it was committed to improving the passenger experience and pointed to ongoing investment programmes aimed at enhancing capacity and reducing disruption. However, industry observers noted that without a second runway — a prospect that remains politically fraught — the airport's structural challenges are unlikely to be resolved in the near term.

The rankings come at a particularly sensitive time for the aviation sector, as airports across Europe grapple with staffing shortages, air traffic control limitations, and the knock-on effects of increasingly unpredictable weather patterns linked to climate change.
headline: Gatwick Airport earns dubious honor of second-worst European airport for delays

text:
Pothole complaints have surged across Ireland, with local authorities inundated by reports from frustrated motorists and residents struggling with deteriorating road surfaces, according to new figures that lay bare the scale of the country's road maintenance crisis.

Cork County Council alone has received more than 14,000 pothole-related reports, a staggering figure that underscores the extent of damage inflicted on the road network by recent severe weather and years of what critics describe as chronic underinvestment in maintenance.

The figures, compiled from local authority records and complaints lodged through the Fix Your Street platform, reveal that the problem is far from confined to any single region. Councils in Dublin, Galway, Limerick, and Donegal have all reported significant increases in the volume of complaints from the public, with many areas seeing numbers double or even triple compared to previous years.

Motorists have taken to social media in droves to document the damage caused to their vehicles, sharing images of buckled wheels, burst tyres, and damaged suspension systems. Several have reported being left with repair bills running into hundreds or even thousands of euro after encountering particularly severe potholes on both national and local roads.

The issue has drawn sharp criticism from opposition TDs, who have accused the Government of failing to adequately fund local authorities for essential road repairs. Sinn Féin, Labour, and the Social Democrats have all called for emergency funding to be released to councils to address what they describe as an escalating public safety hazard.

Local representatives across the country have echoed those concerns, with councillors in rural areas warning that secondary and tertiary roads have been left in a dangerous state. In many cases, temporary repairs carried out by council crews have proven inadequate, with potholes reappearing within weeks due to the underlying condition of the road surface.

Engineers Ireland has previously warned that the country's road infrastructure requires sustained and significantly increased investment if the network is to be maintained to an acceptable standard. The organisation has pointed to the cumulative effect of freeze-thaw cycles, increased traffic volumes, and insufficient capital spending as the primary drivers of the deterioration.

Transport Infrastructure Ireland, which oversees the national road network, has said it continues to work with local authorities to prioritise repairs on the most heavily trafficked routes. However, the vast majority of Ireland's road network falls under the remit of local councils, many of which say they simply do not have the resources to keep pace with the volume of damage.

The Department of Transport has indicated that funding allocations for road maintenance are kept under ongoing review, but has stopped short of committing to the kind of emergency supplementary budget that many local authority officials say is desperately needed.

For ordinary road users, the practical consequences are felt daily. Commuters in both urban and rural areas report having to navigate obstacle courses of crumbling tarmac, with some stretches of road described as virtually impassable without risking vehicle damage. Cyclists and motorcyclists are considered particularly vulnerable, with advocacy groups warning that poorly maintained surfaces pose a serious risk of injury.

The Irish Road Haulage Association has also raised concerns, noting that damaged road surfaces increase wear and tear on commercial vehicles, driving up costs that are ultimately passed on to consumers.
headline: Pothole complaints surge around Ireland with 14,000 reports in Cork alone

text:
It says something about the European establishment's fondness for familiar faces that the latest recipients of the European Order of Merit are Mary Robinson and U2, two names that have been trading on past glories for longer than most would care to admit.

The former president and the Dublin rock band are to receive the honour from the European Council, joining a rarefied club of laureates who have supposedly made an outstanding contribution to European unity and values. Robinson, now 81, is being recognised for her decades of work in human rights and climate activism, while Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton and Larry Mullen Jr are being lauded for their humanitarian efforts and cultural contribution to the continent.

One might reasonably ask: what have either done lately that merits fresh applause from Brussels?

Robinson has spent the years since leaving the presidency and her role as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights accumulating board positions, giving speeches at international conferences, and lecturing ordinary people about climate change whilst maintaining a carbon footprint that would make most Irish families blush. Her transformation from the trailblazing president who lit a candle in the window of Áras an Uachtaráin into a fully paid-up member of the global NGO circuit has been one of the more predictable journeys in Irish public life.

As for U2, the band has become something of a punchline in recent years, better known for tax arrangements that saw them shift part of their business to the Netherlands than for any music that has troubled the cultural conversation. Bono's relentless activism and fondness for hobnobbing with world leaders and corporate executives has long since overshadowed whatever credibility the group once had as rock and roll outsiders from Dublin's northside. The band's last album of any real consequence is now the better part of two decades old, and their most memorable recent achievement was forcing their music uninvited onto every iPhone on the planet, a stunt that generated more irritation than admiration.

The European Order of Merit itself is, of course, precisely the sort of bauble that the EU loves to bestow upon reliably on-message public figures. It costs nothing, offends nobody of consequence, and generates a day's worth of favourable headlines. Robinson and U2 are safe, comfortable choices, the kind of recipients who will say all the right things about European solidarity and cooperation without ever challenging the orthodoxies of the Brussels establishment.

There was a time when Robinson genuinely represented something radical in Irish life. Her election as president in 1990 was a watershed moment, a signal that the country was ready to move beyond the stifling conservatism of the previous decades. But that was 35 years ago. Since then, she has become the very embodiment of the international elite class, utterly disconnected from the concerns of ordinary people in Ireland or anywhere else.

Similarly, there was a time when U2 mattered, when their music spoke to something real and urgent. The Joshua Tree and Achtung Baby were genuine cultural events. But the band has long since become a legacy act, coasting on nostalgia and Bono's apparently inexhaustible appetite for self-promotion.

None of this is to say that Robinson and U2 have not made genuine contributions over the years.
headline: Two has-beens? Mary Robinson and U2 are being awarded European Order of Merit

text:
Gardaí boarded a Ryanair flight at Dublin Airport on Sunday evening after a violent altercation broke out between passengers mid-flight, with witnesses describing a chaotic brawl that left at least one person with their shirt ripped from their body.

The incident occurred on a flight arriving into Dublin from Lanzarote, with passengers reporting that a confrontation between two men escalated rapidly into a physical fight as the aircraft was still airborne. Fellow travellers described scenes of panic as punches were thrown and cabin crew struggled to intervene and restore order.

One passenger, who asked not to be named, told The Liberal that the confrontation appeared to stem from a dispute over seating and legroom that had been simmering for much of the flight. "It kicked off about 40 minutes before landing. One fella just lost it and grabbed the other lad by the shirt. Next thing you know the shirt was literally torn off him and they were swinging at each other in the aisle," the witness said.

"The cabin crew were trying to get between them but it was fairly rough for a few minutes. There were families with small children absolutely terrified. It was disgraceful behaviour."

Crew members are understood to have alerted Dublin Airport authorities while the aircraft was still in the air, and Gardaí were waiting on the tarmac when the plane touched down. Officers boarded the aircraft and removed at least two men from the flight. Passengers were held on board for a period while Gardaí dealt with the situation.

A Garda spokesperson confirmed that officers attended an incident at Dublin Airport on Sunday evening. "Gardaí attended the scene of an incident on board an aircraft at Dublin Airport on the evening of Sunday. Two males, both aged in their 30s, were arrested in connection with a public order incident. Both men were taken to a north Dublin Garda station where they were detained. Investigations are ongoing," the spokesperson said.

Ryanair confirmed the incident in a brief statement, saying the airline would not tolerate unruly or disruptive behaviour on its flights. "The crew of this flight from Lanzarote to Dublin requested Garda assistance upon landing at Dublin Airport after a disruptive incident involving passengers on board. The matter is now in the hands of An Garda Síochána," a Ryanair spokesperson said.

The airline added that it would pursue the fullest possible legal proceedings against any passengers found to have engaged in disruptive or violent behaviour.

It is understood that neither of the two men involved in the altercation required hospital treatment, though one is reported to have sustained minor facial injuries.

The incident is the latest in a growing number of disruptive passenger events on flights in and out of Ireland. Aviation authorities across Europe have flagged increasing concerns about mid-air altercations, with alcohol consumption frequently cited as a contributing factor. Under Irish law, disruptive behaviour on board an aircraft can result in criminal prosecution and significant fines.

Gardaí have confirmed that a file will be prepared for the Director of Public Prosecutions in relation to the incident.
headline: Gardai storm Ryanair flight in Dublin after mid air ‘shirt ripping brawl’

text:
The Government has come under renewed fire over the continued use of thousands of registered tourist beds to accommodate international protection applicants, with critics warning that the practice is hollowing out Ireland's hospitality sector and damaging local economies across the country.

New figures confirm that a significant proportion of hotel and guesthouse rooms originally designated for tourists remain block-booked by the State to house asylum seekers and refugees, despite repeated promises from ministers to wind down the reliance on commercial accommodation.

The Irish Hotels Federation has long sounded the alarm over the arrangement, arguing that the diversion of tourist stock is costing the sector hundreds of millions in lost revenue each year while simultaneously driving up prices for domestic and international visitors. Tourist boards in some of the worst-affected areas say the knock-on effects are being felt by restaurants, pubs, shops and activity providers who depend on a steady flow of guests through local hotels and B&Bs.

Opposition TDs have accused the Government of failing to deliver on its commitment to develop purpose-built accommodation centres, leaving hotel owners locked into State contracts and entire communities without adequate tourism infrastructure. Several rural towns that previously relied heavily on seasonal tourism have reported sharp declines in visitor numbers, with some businesses warning they may not survive another year of reduced footfall.

A spokesperson for the Department of Integration said the Government remained committed to reducing its dependence on commercial accommodation and pointed to ongoing efforts to source and develop alternative facilities. However, the spokesperson acknowledged that the scale of arrivals into the international protection system had made it difficult to transition away from hotels and guesthouses as quickly as had been hoped.

Sinn Féin's immigration spokesperson said the figures represented a damning indictment of Government inaction, accusing ministers of lurching from one crisis to the next without any coherent long-term strategy. The party called for an accelerated programme of purpose-built reception centres and a clear timeline for returning tourist beds to the hospitality market.

Independent TDs from rural constituencies were equally scathing, with several pointing out that their communities had been left to shoulder a disproportionate burden while receiving little or no additional investment in services or infrastructure to cope with increased demand.

Fáilte Ireland has previously estimated that the loss of tourist accommodation is undermining the State's capacity to meet its tourism targets, which envisage the sector generating in excess of €5 billion in overseas revenue annually. Industry figures say Ireland's reputation as a destination risks being tarnished if visitors continue to encounter reduced availability and inflated room rates during peak season.

The Government has insisted it is making progress, pointing to the opening of a number of dedicated accommodation centres in recent months and the establishment of a new unit within the Department tasked with sourcing alternative sites. Ministers have also highlighted the challenges posed by the housing crisis more broadly, arguing that the shortage of available properties across the State has made it virtually impossible to move people out of hotel accommodation at the pace originally envisaged.

However, critics say the continued reliance on tourist beds years into the crisis suggests a fundamental failure of planning and political will. Several local authority members have called for greater transparency around the contracts being signed between the Department and accommodation providers, arguing that communities deserve to know how much public money is being spent and for how long the arrangements are expected to remain in place.
headline: Govt slammed as still a huge number of registered tourist beds are being used to house migrants

text:
Calls are mounting for a public demonstration in Wexford after disturbing footage emerged online showing a violent altercation amongst a group of foreign nationals accommodated in the Courtown area, with the video rapidly gaining traction across social media platforms.

The footage, which began circulating over the weekend, appears to show a large-scale brawl involving several men reportedly residing in International Protection Accommodation Services (IPAS) accommodation in the north Wexford seaside village. The clip, which has been viewed tens of thousands of times, shows what witnesses described as mob violence, with multiple individuals engaged in a chaotic and aggressive confrontation in a public area.

Local residents have expressed alarm at the scenes, with many taking to social media to voice their frustration at what they say is a deteriorating situation in the once-quiet coastal community. Courtown, a popular holiday destination for families from Dublin and across the southeast, has seen significant numbers of asylum seekers and migrants placed in accommodation in the area over recent months as part of the government's ongoing dispersal programme.

Organisers are now calling for a peaceful protest in the area, with details expected to be confirmed in the coming days. Several community groups have indicated their intention to attend, citing concerns about public safety, the strain on local services, and what they describe as a complete lack of consultation with residents before large numbers of foreign men were placed in the locality.

One local woman, who did not wish to be named, told The Liberal that families in the area no longer feel safe allowing their children to play outdoors unsupervised. "This is a small community. People came here for the quiet life, and now you have scenes like this playing out on our doorstep. Nobody asked us. Nobody consulted us. We were just expected to accept it," she said.

Another resident said the footage confirmed what locals had been warning about for months. "We were told we were being alarmist. We were called every name under the sun for raising legitimate concerns. And now this is there for everyone to see," he said.

The government has faced sustained criticism over its handling of the migration crisis, with communities across the country pushing back against what many view as a plantation policy, whereby towns and villages are expected to absorb disproportionate numbers of International Protection applicants with little or no additional resources provided to support the increased population.

Local representatives have been contacted for comment. A spokesperson for the Department of Integration said they do not comment on individual incidents and that any criminal matters should be referred to An Garda Síochána.

Gardaí confirmed they are aware of the footage circulating online and that enquiries are ongoing. No arrests have been made at the time of publication.

The situation in Courtown mirrors growing tensions seen in communities across the country, from East Wall in Dublin to Killarney in Kerry, where residents have staged demonstrations against the placement of large numbers of asylum seekers in their localities without prior engagement or adequate planning.

Critics of the government's approach argue that the current system is unsustainable and is fuelling community resentment, while integration groups have cautioned against conflating the actions of individuals with the broader migrant population.
headline: Calls for protests in Wexford after footage of mob violence amongst foreign men living in migrant plantation in the Courtown goes viral

text:
Incidents of disruptive and unruly behaviour on commercial flights have surged dramatically, with new figures revealing the number of reported cases has more than tripled over the past twelve months.

The alarming rise has prompted renewed calls from airline staff representatives and aviation authorities for tougher penalties and greater enforcement against passengers who abuse cabin crew, endanger fellow travellers, or refuse to comply with safety instructions during flights.

Industry data compiled by the International Air Transport Association shows that reports of unruly passenger behaviour have escalated at a pace that has caught many in the sector off guard, even as airlines had anticipated some degree of increased tension following the return to pre-pandemic passenger volumes. The figures encompass a range of offences from verbal abuse and refusal to follow crew instructions to physical assaults and attempts to interfere with aircraft operations.

Irish airlines have not been immune to the trend. Sources within the sector confirmed that carriers operating out of Dublin, Cork and Shannon airports have all recorded notable increases in incidents over the period, with alcohol consumption before and during flights cited as a significant contributing factor.

The Irish Air Line Pilots' Association has expressed serious concern, warning that such behaviour poses a genuine safety risk and places an unacceptable burden on cabin crew who are already managing demanding working conditions. Representatives have called on the Government to examine whether existing legislation is sufficient to act as a meaningful deterrent.

Under current Irish law, endangering the safety of an aircraft or assaulting crew members can result in criminal prosecution, with cases typically heard before the District or Circuit Courts depending on severity. However, critics argue that fines and sentences handed down have too often failed to reflect the seriousness of offences committed at 35,000 feet.

Fórsa, the trade union representing many aviation workers in Ireland, said its members have reported a noticeable deterioration in passenger behaviour and called for a zero-tolerance approach. A spokesperson said cabin crew should not have to endure threats, intimidation or violence as part of their working lives and urged the Irish Aviation Authority to work with airlines on more robust reporting and follow-through mechanisms.

The Dublin Airport Authority confirmed it has been working closely with the Gardaí and airline partners to address issues related to passenger behaviour, including the responsible service of alcohol in terminal bars and restaurants. DAA introduced a voluntary code of conduct for alcohol retailers at Dublin Airport several years ago, but questions remain about whether voluntary measures go far enough.

Speaking on the issue, a spokesperson for the Department of Transport said the Minister is aware of the international trend and is monitoring the situation closely. The spokesperson added that Ireland remains committed to its obligations under the Montreal Protocol of 2014, which strengthened the legal framework for dealing with unruly passengers on international flights, though they acknowledged that ratification and enforcement across jurisdictions remains uneven.

Aviation analysts suggest the spike in incidents is driven by a confluence of factors, including post-pandemic travel stress, increased alcohol consumption, longer security queues and a general erosion of social norms that has been observed across many public-facing industries. Some point to the proliferation of budget travel, which has brought more first-time and infrequent flyers into an environment with strict behavioural expectations that may not be fully understood.
headline: Incidents of unruly passengers on airplanes have more than tripled in the past year

text:
Irish Rail is reportedly considering the introduction of vending machines on its inter-city services, in what would mark a significant shift in how passengers access food and drink on board trains.

The move is understood to be under consideration as the semi-state company examines ways to improve the reliability and availability of onboard catering, which has long been a source of frustration for commuters and long-distance travellers alike.

Reports suggest that vending machines could be installed on certain inter-city routes where the traditional trolley service has proven difficult to maintain consistently. Passengers on services between Dublin and cities such as Cork, Galway, and Limerick have frequently complained about the absence of any catering option on journeys that can last upwards of two and a half hours.

The catering service on Irish Rail has faced persistent staffing challenges in recent years, with the trolley service often unavailable on scheduled services. The company has previously come under fire from passengers who have boarded long-distance trains only to discover that no food or beverages were available for purchase during their journey.

It is understood that vending machines could offer a range of hot and cold drinks, snacks, and light refreshments, potentially providing a more consistent service than the current trolley-based model, which is dependent on staff availability.

Irish Rail has not yet publicly confirmed the plans. The company currently operates its onboard catering through a contract with an external provider, and any introduction of vending machines would likely require modifications to existing rolling stock.

The proposal comes at a time when Irish Rail is investing significantly in its fleet and infrastructure, with new carriages and expanded services planned as part of broader efforts to encourage greater use of public transport across the State.

Consumer groups have broadly welcomed the idea, noting that any measure which ensures passengers can reliably access refreshments on longer journeys would be a positive development. However, some have raised concerns about the potential impact on existing catering staff, who could see their roles diminished or eliminated should vending machines prove successful.

Trade unions representing workers in the transport sector are expected to monitor developments closely, particularly regarding any implications for employment.
headline: Irish Rail reportedly considering setting up vending machines on inter-city services

text:
Electric vehicle sales have taken yet another bruising hit, with new registration figures painting a grim picture for the Government's ambitious climate targets and raising fresh questions about whether motorists are being asked to make a switch they simply cannot afford.

New figures from the Society of the Irish Motor Industry show that battery electric vehicle registrations fell sharply again last month, continuing a trend that has left the sector well off the pace needed to meet Ireland's target of having nearly a million EVs on the road by 2030.

The slump comes despite generous grants and tax incentives designed to coax Irish drivers into going electric, and industry figures are warning that the current trajectory suggests the Government's targets are now little more than fantasy.

It is a pattern that has been repeated month after month throughout this year, with consumers increasingly opting for hybrid models or sticking with traditional petrol and diesel cars rather than committing to fully electric vehicles. The cost of purchasing an EV remains a significant barrier for many households, with even the most affordable models still carrying a price tag that puts them out of reach for average earners.

Charging infrastructure, or the lack of it, continues to be cited as a major deterrent, particularly for those living in apartments or terraced housing where installing a home charger is not a practical option. Rural drivers have also expressed concern about range anxiety and the sparse network of public charging points outside major urban centres.

The motor industry has pointed the finger squarely at Government policy, arguing that the current suite of incentives is not cutting through with consumers and that more radical intervention is needed if there is to be any hope of hitting the 2030 targets. Some dealers have reported that customers who were initially interested in making the switch have been put off by the total cost of ownership, insurance premiums, and uncertainty about resale values.

Meanwhile, critics have accused the Government of pursuing an ideological agenda that ignores the financial realities facing ordinary families already squeezed by the cost of living crisis. There are growing calls for a more pragmatic approach that acknowledges hybrid vehicles as a realistic stepping stone rather than insisting on a full leap to battery electric.

The figures will make for uncomfortable reading in Government Buildings, where the climate action plan has positioned transport electrification as a cornerstone of Ireland's emissions reduction strategy. With the 2030 deadline now just a handful of years away, the gap between ambition and reality appears to be widening rather than narrowing.

Transport commentators have noted that Ireland is not alone in experiencing an EV slowdown, with similar trends visible across several European markets. However, the scale of the Irish decline is particularly stark given how far the country still has to travel to meet its own stated goals.

The question now facing policymakers is whether to double down on incentives, accept that targets will be missed, or fundamentally rethink the strategy altogether. What seems increasingly clear is that hoping consumers will simply come around is not working.
headline: Plummeting! Electric car sales had a massive slump again over the past month

text:
Roderic O'Gorman has issued a stark warning to the public against allowing independent TDs to prop up the next government, arguing that such arrangements lead to unstable coalitions driven by parochial interests rather than national policy.

The Green Party leader, who is fighting to keep his party relevant ahead of the general election, made the plea during a campaign event in which he sought to contrast the Greens' record in government with what he described as the transactional nature of independent politicians.

O'Gorman argued that independents who enter coalition arrangements inevitably prioritise local projects and constituency-level deals over coherent national policymaking, warning that the public would pay the price for such arrangements in the long run.

"I would really urge people, please don't do it," O'Gorman said. "We have seen what happens when governments are dependent on independents to survive. You get a situation where national policy is held hostage to local demands, and the country suffers as a result."

The Green Party leader pointed to his own party's time in government with Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael as evidence that smaller parties, rather than independents, provide a more stable and policy-driven foundation for coalition. He highlighted the Greens' role in delivering climate legislation, public transport investment, and renewable energy targets as examples of what a programmatic approach to government can achieve.

His comments come as polling suggests that a significant number of independent candidates could win seats in the next Dáil, potentially making them kingmakers in coalition formation talks. The current government has itself relied on independent support at various points during its term, a reality that has not been lost on commentators.

O'Gorman's intervention is widely seen as an attempt to carve out a distinct space for the Greens in an increasingly crowded electoral landscape, where smaller parties risk being squeezed between larger coalition partners and a rising tide of independent and smaller-party candidates.

However, critics have pointed out a certain irony in the Green Party leader's position, noting that the Greens themselves have faced accusations of abandoning key policy commitments in order to remain in government. The party's polling numbers have struggled significantly since entering coalition, with many of its core supporters expressing disillusionment over compromises made on environmental and housing policy.

Independent TDs have been quick to reject O'Gorman's characterisation. Several sitting independents have argued that they provide a vital voice for communities that feel underserved by the larger parties, and that their presence in government arrangements ensures a more diverse range of perspectives at the cabinet table.

The question of who will form the next government remains wide open, with Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael both expected to seek coalition partners after the election. Whether that partner ends up being a smaller party like the Greens, Labour, or the Social Democrats — or a grouping of independents — may ultimately come down to the numbers returned on election night.

For O'Gorman, the message is clear: voters should think carefully before lending their support to independent candidates who may end up wielding outsized influence in a fragmented Dáil.
headline: Please don’t do it! Green’s Roderic O’Gorman warns public against independents propping up coalition

text:
Floor restoration has quietly become one of the most sought-after services in Dublin, as homeowners and business operators alike recognise the value of preserving what lies beneath their feet rather than ripping it all out and starting from scratch. It is a trend driven by a combination of practical economics, environmental awareness, and a growing appreciation for the character that original flooring can bring to a property.

Walk into any period home in Rathmines, Ranelagh, or Drumcondra and there is a reasonable chance you will find original hardwood floors that have survived a century or more of daily life. These floors, typically crafted from oak, pine, or mahogany, were built to last in a way that modern laminate alternatives simply cannot replicate. Yet decades of wear, water damage, and ill-advised carpet coverings have left many of them looking worse for wear. Restoration specialists working across the capital are now breathing new life into these surfaces, sanding back years of grime and applying modern finishes that protect the wood while preserving its original grain and warmth.

The appeal is not limited to residential properties. Commercial premises across Dublin, from restaurants and hotels to retail units and office spaces, are increasingly turning to professional floor restoration as a cost-effective alternative to full replacement. With commercial rents in the capital remaining at a premium and fit-out costs continuing to climb, restoring an existing floor can represent a significant saving. For businesses operating in older buildings, particularly in areas such as the Liberties, Temple Bar, and the Georgian quarter around Merrion Square, restored original flooring can also serve as a distinctive design feature that sets a premises apart.

The economics are straightforward. A full floor replacement in a standard three-bedroom Dublin home can run to several thousand euro, factoring in materials, labour, and the disposal of the old surface. Restoration, by contrast, typically comes in at a fraction of that cost, and the finished product often looks better than anything that could be bought new. For businesses, the calculation is even more compelling when one considers the reduced downtime involved. A restoration project can often be completed in a matter of days, whereas a full replacement may require a premises to close for considerably longer.

Beyond the financial argument, there is an environmental dimension that resonates with a growing number of Dublin property owners. Ireland has committed to ambitious climate targets, and the construction and renovation sector is under increasing scrutiny for its contribution to waste. The Environmental Protection Agency has repeatedly highlighted the volume of construction and demolition waste generated nationally. Restoring a floor rather than replacing it keeps materials out of landfill and reduces the demand for new timber, much of which is imported. For property owners who are conscious of their environmental footprint, it is a relatively painless way to make a difference.

The range of services available has expanded considerably in recent years. Where once floor restoration in Dublin meant little more than a basic sand and varnish job, specialists now offer everything from intricate parquet repair and tile regrouting to stone floor polishing and the restoration of terrazzo surfaces, a material that was once common in Dublin's commercial buildings and is now enjoying something of a revival. Some firms have also begun offering maintenance programmes, providing regular upkeep that extends the life of a restored floor and prevents the need for more intensive work down the line.
headline: Why Floor Restoration Services in Dublin Are Essential for Homes and Businesses

text:
Russell Brand has thanked his supporters after what he described as a "distressing week" following allegations of rape, sexual assault and emotional abuse made against him by several women.

The comedian and actor posted a video on his social media channels in which he expressed gratitude to those who had rallied behind him since the allegations were first aired in a joint investigation by The Times, The Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches programme.

Brand, who has denied all the allegations against him, said the past week had been "very, very distressing" but that he had been buoyed by the response from his fanbase.

"I've been through a very, very distressing week but what has been amazing to me is your incredible support," he said in the video, which was posted to his YouTube channel and other platforms.

He reiterated his denial of the allegations, insisting that all of his relationships had been consensual. The 48-year-old had initially responded to the allegations before they were broadcast, releasing a video in which he characterised the encounters as "always consensual."

Since the investigation was published, Brand has seen significant consequences in his professional life. YouTube suspended monetisation on his channel, while his publisher halted sales of his books. His talent agency, Tavistock Wood, also dropped him as a client.

The Metropolitan Police in London has said it is investigating allegations of sexual offences reported in the wake of the media investigation, though it has not confirmed whether Brand is a suspect. Brand has not been arrested or charged with any offence.

The allegations span a period from 2006 to 2013, during which Brand was at the height of his mainstream fame, presenting on BBC Radio 2 and Channel 4 and appearing in Hollywood films.

Brand has in recent years reinvented himself as an online commentator and conspiracy theorist, amassing millions of followers across social media platforms. Some of his supporters have framed the allegations as a coordinated attack on Brand because of his anti-establishment views, a narrative he appeared to encourage in his initial response video.

The story has prompted renewed debate about the culture within the entertainment industry and the duty of care owed by broadcasters and production companies to staff and members of the public who come into contact with high-profile presenters.
headline: Russell Brand thanks his supporters after “distressing week”

text:
The Government is pressing ahead with plans to restrict short-term letting in Ireland's larger towns and cities, insisting the measures are necessary to free up housing stock — but critics say the approach is heavy-handed and risks damaging tourism and property rights.

Under regulations that have been tightened in recent years, property owners in designated rent pressure zones are required to secure planning permission before listing homes or apartments on platforms such as Airbnb and Booking.com. The restrictions, which initially applied to Dublin and a handful of other urban centres, have been progressively expanded to cover larger towns across the country, with the Government signalling its intention to go further still.

The rationale is straightforward enough on paper: every property used for short-term tourist lets is one fewer home available for long-term renters in areas where housing supply is already critically tight. Minister for Housing Darragh O'Brien has repeatedly argued that the balance must tip in favour of permanent residents, particularly in towns where workers and families are being priced out or simply cannot find anywhere to live.

Yet the policy has drawn sustained criticism from property owners, tourism operators, and those who see in it yet another example of the State's instinct to regulate first and ask questions later. Small-scale landlords — many of whom let a room or a second property to supplement their income — say the planning permission requirement is disproportionate, costly, and deliberately discouraging. Several have simply withdrawn their properties from the market altogether, choosing to leave them vacant rather than navigate what they describe as a bureaucratic maze.

The tourism industry has also raised concerns. Fáilte Ireland has acknowledged the importance of short-term letting platforms in providing visitor accommodation, particularly in areas where hotel capacity is limited. In many towns, Airbnb-style properties are not competing with the long-term rental market so much as filling a gap that traditional hospitality simply does not cover. Restricting supply risks pushing up the cost of tourist accommodation and making parts of Ireland less attractive to visitors at a time when the sector is still consolidating its post-pandemic recovery.

There is a broader philosophical objection, too. Property owners argue that the Government's approach amounts to telling people what they can and cannot do with assets they own, all in pursuit of a housing policy that has manifestly failed to deliver adequate supply through other means. The State has consistently underperformed on its own social and affordable housing targets, yet rather than address the root causes of the crisis — planning delays, construction costs, land hoarding — it has found it politically easier to impose restrictions on individual owners.

The data on whether the policy is actually working remains thin. There is little compelling evidence that restricting short-term lets has led to a significant increase in long-term rental supply in the areas where the rules apply. Some properties have indeed returned to the long-term rental market, but many others have simply been sold, left idle, or taken off all letting platforms entirely. The net effect on housing availability is, at best, marginal.

Meanwhile, enforcement has been patchy. Local authorities have been tasked with policing compliance, but resources are stretched and the platforms themselves have been slow to cooperate fully with regulatory requirements. The result is a system that penalises those who attempt to comply while doing relatively little to catch those who do not.
headline: We know best: Govt is restricting short term letting in larger towns

text:
Met Éireann has expressed concern after Ireland's all-time May temperature record was shattered once again, with a reading of 30.5 degrees Celsius recorded today in what meteorologists are calling an "extraordinary and unprecedented" event for this time of year.

The record-breaking temperature, which surpassed the previous May high by a significant margin, was recorded at one of Met Éireann's synoptic weather stations, sending climate scientists scrambling to put the figure into context.

A spokesperson for Met Éireann said the organisation was "deeply concerned" by the reading, noting that temperatures of this magnitude in late spring are far outside the normal range for Ireland's maritime climate and represent a worrying departure from historical norms.

"This is not something we would expect to see in Ireland in May, or indeed at any point during the summer months," the spokesperson said. "A temperature of 30.5 degrees would be remarkable in July or August. To record it in May is, frankly, alarming from a climatological perspective."

Ireland's climate has traditionally been characterised by mild temperatures year-round, with summer highs rarely exceeding the mid-twenties. The previous all-time national temperature record of 33.3 degrees, set at Kilkenny Castle in June 1887, has stood for well over a century, and May records have historically sat considerably lower.

The Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications said it was monitoring the situation closely, while the HSE issued guidance urging the public, particularly older people and young children, to take precautions against heat exposure, stay hydrated and avoid prolonged periods in direct sunlight.
