Climatologists have pointed to the reading as further evidence that Ireland is not immune to the accelerating effects of climate change, with the country warming at a rate consistent with broader European trends. Data from Met Éireann's own records show that average temperatures across Ireland have risen measurably over recent decades, with several of the warmest years on record occurring since 2010.

The Green Party called the record "a stark warning" and urged the Government to redouble its efforts on emissions reduction targets, which Ireland has consistently struggled to meet. A spokesperson for the party said it was "no longer possible to treat climate action as something that can be kicked down the road" in light of increasingly extreme weather events on Irish soil.

Government TDs from the coalition parties acknowledged the significance of the reading but stressed that Ireland's Climate Action Plan remained on track, pointing to recent investments in renewable energy and retrofitting programmes.

Sinn Féin's environment spokesperson said the record should serve as "a wake-up call for a Government that has been far too slow to act" on climate commitments, and called for an emergency debate in the Dáil on climate preparedness.

Met Éireann has indicated that while temperatures are expected to ease somewhat in the coming days, the broader pattern of warmer-than-average conditions is likely to persist through the remainder of the week. The organisation urged the public to check its website and app regularly for updated forecasts and any weather warnings that may be issued.
headline: BREAKING: Met Eireann concerned as Ireland’s May record broken again with 30.5c

text:
Aer Lingus has been forced to cancel a further 25 flights as the ongoing dispute with its pilots shows no sign of resolution, leaving thousands of passengers stranded and frustrated at the height of the summer travel season.

The airline confirmed on Wednesday that the latest round of cancellations would affect services across its European and UK network, with routes to and from Dublin Airport bearing the brunt of the disruption. The cancellations come on top of dozens of flights already scrapped in recent days as members of the Irish Air Line Pilots' Association (IALPA) continue their work-to-rule action in pursuit of a significant pay increase.

Aer Lingus said it "deeply regrets" the impact on customers and urged affected passengers to check the status of their flights on its website. The carrier said it was working to rebook passengers on alternative services where possible, though options remain limited given the peak holiday period.

The dispute centres on IALPA's demand for a pay increase of over 20 per cent for its members, which the union argues is necessary to bring pilot remuneration into line with European competitors and to account for the cost-of-living crisis. Aer Lingus has described the claim as excessive and unsustainable, offering instead what it has characterised as a fair and reasonable package.

Efforts to broker a resolution through the Labour Court have so far failed to produce a breakthrough, with both sides accusing the other of intransigence. The Government has called on both parties to return to talks and engage meaningfully, though ministers have stopped short of direct intervention in what they describe as an industrial relations matter between a private company and its employees.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin said the situation was "deeply concerning" for passengers and for Ireland's reputation as a well-connected island economy. He urged both Aer Lingus management and IALPA to show flexibility and to prioritise reaching a settlement.

The disruption has drawn sharp criticism from passenger advocacy groups and the tourism sector, with industry figures warning that prolonged cancellations risk causing lasting damage to inbound tourism at a critical time of year. Several hotel and hospitality operators reported a spike in cancellations from international visitors unable to secure reliable flights into Ireland.

Passengers caught up in the disruption have expressed anger and exasperation on social media, with many complaining of long delays in reaching Aer Lingus customer service lines and a lack of clarity about rebooking options and compensation entitlements. Under EU passenger rights regulations, travellers affected by cancellations may be entitled to re-routing, refunds, and in certain circumstances, additional compensation, though airlines are not obliged to pay compensation where disruption is caused by extraordinary circumstances, a category that can include strike action.

The Irish Travel Agents Association called the situation untenable and said its members were inundated with queries from worried holidaymakers. It urged both sides to resolve the matter without further delay, warning that consumer confidence in booking with Aer Lingus was being eroded with each passing day.

IALPA, which represents the vast majority of Aer Lingus pilots, has insisted that its members remain open to negotiation but said the airline has failed to table a credible offer.
headline: Aer Lingus cancels a further 25 flights as pilots’ dispute continues

text:
A predator who snatched a young girl off the street as she walked to school before subjecting her to a horrifying sexual assault has been jailed for 20 years.

Andrew Miller, a convicted sex offender with a string of previous convictions, carried out the attack in broad daylight, leaving the child with devastating physical and psychological injuries.

The court heard how Miller, who had been prowling the area in his vehicle, pulled up alongside the girl before dragging her inside and driving her to a secluded location where he carried out the sickening assault.

The child, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, was found distressed and alone after Miller dumped her some distance from where she had been taken. She was rushed to hospital where she was treated for her injuries.

Detectives launched a major investigation and were able to track Miller down through CCTV footage and forensic evidence recovered from the scene. He was arrested a short time later and initially denied any involvement before being confronted with overwhelming evidence against him.

The sentencing judge described Miller as a "dangerous predator" who had targeted a completely innocent and defenceless child in one of the most disturbing cases to come before the court. The judge said the sentence reflected the extreme gravity of the offences and the need to protect the public from a man who posed a serious and ongoing risk.

Miller showed no emotion as the sentence was handed down.

The victim's family, who were present in court, said in a statement read on their behalf that their daughter's life had been "changed forever" by what happened to her. They said she continued to suffer nightmares and had been unable to return to her normal routine since the attack.

A spokesperson for the investigating police force said they hoped the lengthy sentence would provide some measure of comfort to the victim and her family, and praised the bravery of the young girl in helping officers to bring her attacker to justice.

Miller was also placed on the sex offenders register indefinitely.
headline: Sicko Andrew Miller jailed for 20 years for abducting and sexually assaulting young girl on her way to school

text:
Gardaí have carried out a major search operation on a patch of wasteland in Dundalk, close to the former family home of missing boy Kyran Durnin, as investigators continue their efforts to establish what happened to the child.

The search, which involved specialist units, took place on an area of scrubland in the town and is understood to have been planned in advance as part of the ongoing investigation into the disappearance of the eight-year-old, who has not been seen alive for a number of years.

Sources have confirmed that the wasteland is situated in close proximity to the property where Kyran previously lived with his family in Dundalk, Co Louth. It is understood that the area was examined by members of the Garda Technical Bureau alongside other specialist search teams.

The case of Kyran Durnin has gripped the nation since it emerged that the young boy, who would now be aged eight, was reported missing in August but is believed not to have been seen alive for a considerably longer period. Gardaí have said they believe Kyran is dead, though no remains have yet been recovered.

A number of searches have been conducted at various locations as part of the investigation, which remains active and ongoing. Gardaí have appealed to anyone with information about Kyran's whereabouts or circumstances to come forward.

The boy's mother, Dayla Durnin, was previously charged with offences in connection with the case. She appeared before the courts and the matter remains before the criminal justice system.

Investigators are understood to be pursuing a number of lines of enquiry and have not ruled out further searches at additional locations in the coming weeks.

A Garda spokesperson confirmed that a search operation took place but declined to comment further, stating that the investigation is ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Dundalk Garda Station or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: Gardai hold major search in wasteland in Dundalk near former family home of Kyran Durnin

text:
Cork Airport has urged passengers and those dropping off or collecting travellers to exercise caution when making their way to the facility, as adverse weather conditions continue to affect the region.

A spokesperson for Cork Airport issued the advisory amid ongoing disruption caused by poor weather, reminding the public to allow extra time for their journeys and to check road conditions before setting out.

"We would advise all passengers and those travelling to Cork Airport to take extra care on the roads due to the current weather conditions," the spokesperson said. "We recommend checking the latest travel updates and allowing additional time for your journey."

The advisory comes as Met Éireann has warned of difficult conditions across Munster, with low temperatures, ice, and reduced visibility all posing potential hazards for motorists. Road users have been advised to be particularly vigilant on secondary routes and elevated stretches approaching the airport, which sits on a hilltop south of Cork city.

Cork Airport confirmed that it is continuing to monitor the situation closely and is working to ensure operations at the airport remain as normal as possible. Passengers have been encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest information on flight schedules, as some services may be subject to delays or alterations depending on how conditions develop.

AA Roadwatch has also reminded drivers heading to the airport to reduce speed and maintain safe stopping distances, particularly on roads that may not yet have been treated.

Passengers can find real-time updates on arrivals and departures through the Cork Airport website and social media channels.
headline: Cork Airport spokesperson advises people to be cautious when traveling to the facility due to adverse weather conditions

text:
The Turkish opposition has levelled serious accusations against Ankara's defence industry, claiming that Turkish military companies have been actively supporting the Sudanese Armed Forces amid the country's devastating civil war.

Ümit Özdağ, leader of the Victory Party and a prominent figure in Turkish opposition politics, has publicly alleged that Turkish defence firms have been supplying military equipment and support to the Sudanese army in its ongoing conflict against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. The claims, which have circulated widely on Turkish social media and opposition-aligned outlets, add a new dimension to the international debate over foreign involvement in Sudan's brutal internal conflict.

Özdağ, who has positioned himself as a nationalist critic of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's foreign policy, suggested that the support extended by Turkish defence companies is not merely a commercial arrangement but reflects a broader strategic alignment between Ankara and the Sudanese military leadership under General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan. He accused the Turkish government of pursuing an interventionist agenda in Africa that serves narrow political and economic interests rather than promoting stability.

Turkey's defence exports have grown dramatically in recent years, with the country emerging as one of the world's most prominent arms exporters. Turkish-made Bayraktar drones, in particular, have become fixtures of conflicts from Libya to Ukraine, and Ankara has aggressively courted African nations as customers for its expanding catalogue of military hardware.

The Sudanese civil war, which erupted in April 2023, has created one of the world's worst humanitarian catastrophes. The conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces has displaced millions of people, triggered widespread famine, and led to allegations of atrocities committed by both sides. International humanitarian organisations have repeatedly warned that the flow of arms into the country from various foreign backers is prolonging the suffering and making any prospect of a ceasefire increasingly remote.

Several nations have faced scrutiny over their involvement in the Sudanese conflict. The United Arab Emirates has been widely accused of backing the Rapid Support Forces, while Egypt and Iran have been linked to support for the Sudanese army. Turkey's alleged role, if substantiated, would place Ankara among a growing list of foreign powers accused of fuelling the violence.

The Turkish government has not issued a detailed public response to Özdağ's specific allegations, though Ankara has historically defended its defence exports as legitimate commercial activity conducted within the framework of international law. Turkish officials have previously emphasised that the country's defence industry operates under strict regulatory oversight and that exports are subject to end-user agreements.

Özdağ's accusations come at a time of heightened political tension within Turkey itself. The opposition remains fractured following its failure to unseat Erdoğan in the 2023 presidential election, and figures like Özdağ have sought to carve out distinct political identities by challenging the government on foreign policy and national security matters. Critics of Özdağ have suggested that his claims are politically motivated and lack sufficient evidentiary backing, though observers note that Turkey's expanding military footprint across Africa and the Middle East has attracted growing international concern.
headline: Turkish Opposition Figure Accuses Turkish Defense Companies of Supporting the Sudanese Army

text:
A man from India has been found guilty of sexually assaulting a woman on a Dublin bus after he groped her during a journey in the capital.

The incident, described as "creepy" by the victim, took place when the man sat beside the woman and began touching her inappropriately without her consent.

The woman told the court she had been left shaken and distressed by the encounter, which occurred in broad daylight on a busy route. She described how the man had deliberately positioned himself next to her despite other seats being available on the bus.

The accused, who came to Ireland from India, denied the charges but was found guilty following a trial at Dublin District Court.

The victim told the court she had initially tried to move away from the man but he persisted in making unwanted physical contact. She described his behaviour as "creepy" and said she felt trapped in her seat during the ordeal.

Fellow passengers intervened after noticing the woman's visible distress, and the driver was alerted. Gardaí were called and the man was arrested at the scene.

CCTV footage from the bus was presented as evidence during the trial and was said to have corroborated the victim's account of events.

Judge adjourned the matter for sentencing at a later date, with a probation report requested in advance of that hearing. The accused was granted continuing bail in the interim.

The conviction comes amid growing public concern about safety on public transport in Dublin, with women's advocacy groups calling for increased security measures on buses and other services operated by Dublin Bus and other providers.
headline: ‘Creepy’ migrant from India found guilty of groping woman on bus in Dublin

text:
A migrant who violently attacked a female jogger in the United States has been exposed as a convicted sex offender who identifies as "genderfluid" and has used at least 27 different aliases to evade law enforcement, it has emerged.

The case has reignited fierce debate around border security, sex offender registries, and the exploitation of gender identity policies within the criminal justice system, with critics arguing that authorities on both sides of the Atlantic are failing to adequately protect women and girls from known predators.

The individual, who was arrested following the brutal assault on a woman jogging alone in a public park, was found upon booking to have an extensive criminal history spanning multiple states. Law enforcement officials confirmed that the suspect had used dozens of false names, dates of birth, and identifying details over a period of years to avoid detection and evade registration requirements as a convicted sex offender.

According to reports, the suspect had previously been convicted of serious sexual offences but had repeatedly absconded from monitoring by adopting new identities. The discovery that the individual had claimed to be "genderfluid" — and had at various times presented as male or female to authorities — has raised serious questions about how identity claims are being recorded and managed within the justice system.

Critics argue that the case illustrates how self-identification policies can be manipulated by predatory individuals seeking to exploit the system, particularly when it comes to housing in detention facilities and placement on sex offender registries. Women's rights campaigners have long warned that such policies, if implemented without adequate safeguards, pose a direct risk to vulnerable women and girls.

The case carries resonance on this side of the Atlantic, where similar debates around self-identification and its implications for women's safety have been playing out in Ireland and across Europe. Concerns have been raised repeatedly about the Irish government's approach to gender recognition legislation and the potential for its exploitation by bad actors, though such concerns are frequently dismissed by advocacy groups as fearmongering.

In Ireland, questions around the management of sex offenders and the robustness of the Sex Offenders Act 2001 have been raised on numerous occasions, with victims' advocates arguing that the system is not fit for purpose even without the added complication of multiple identities and self-declared gender changes.

The attack on the jogger has been described as particularly violent, with the victim sustaining significant injuries. Local law enforcement said the arrest was made possible through CCTV footage and witness testimony, and that it was only after the suspect was taken into custody that the full extent of their criminal history and use of aliases became apparent.

Immigration authorities confirmed that the individual had no legal right to be in the country at the time of the attack, further fuelling calls from conservative lawmakers for stricter border enforcement and more rigorous screening of those entering the country.

The case has drawn widespread attention on social media, where many have expressed outrage that a convicted sex offender was able to operate under so many false identities without being detected. Others have pointed to it as a cautionary tale about the unintended consequences of policies that prioritise self-declared identity over biological reality in criminal justice settings.
headline: Migrant who attacked female jogger exposed as ‘genderfluid’ sex offender with 27 aliases

text:
The organisers behind a renewed pro-refugee movement took to the streets of Dublin on Saturday afternoon, declaring that their demonstration marked the opening salvo in a sustained campaign to push back against what they described as a rising tide of anti-migrant sentiment across the country.

Several hundred people gathered at the Garden of Remembrance on Parnell Square before marching through the city centre, carrying placards bearing slogans such as "Refugees Welcome," "Ireland Against Hate" and "No Room for Racism." The protest was organised by a coalition of activist groups, trade unions and NGOs who say they are alarmed by the increasingly hostile tone of public discourse around immigration and asylum seekers.

Speakers at the rally insisted that Ireland has a proud tradition of emigration and solidarity with displaced peoples, and accused far-right agitators of hijacking legitimate concerns about housing and public services to stoke division. One organiser told the crowd that Saturday's march was "only the beginning" and promised a rolling programme of demonstrations, community events and political lobbying in the weeks and months ahead.

The demonstration comes against a backdrop of heightened tensions around the issue of migration in Ireland. In recent months, protests against the housing of asylum seekers in various communities around the country have become a regular occurrence, with several planned accommodation centres abandoned following local opposition. There have also been incidents of arson and intimidation at properties earmarked for use by International Protection applicants.

The Government has come under pressure from multiple directions on the issue, with opposition TDs and community groups on one side demanding tighter controls on immigration and faster processing of asylum claims, while refugee advocacy organisations on the other accuse Ministers of capitulating to mob rule by pulling back from planned accommodation sites.

Critics on social media were quick to point out that the turnout at Saturday's march, while respectable, was dwarfed by some of the anti-immigration protests that have taken place in Dublin and other towns in recent months. Others questioned whether the organisers, many of whom are drawn from established left-wing activist networks and publicly funded NGO sector bodies, truly represent grassroots opinion on the matter.

Several commentators noted that the protest appeared to be largely composed of the usual coalition of activist groups and that the challenge for the movement would be broadening its appeal beyond those already sympathetic to its message. Polling has consistently shown that public concern about immigration has risen sharply over the past two years, with a significant proportion of voters now ranking it among their top issues ahead of any general election.

The organisers, however, remained bullish. Speaking after the march, one of the leading figures behind the event said they were confident that what they termed the "silent majority" of Irish people remained welcoming and compassionate, and simply needed to be given a platform and the confidence to speak up.

"The narrative has been captured by a small but very loud minority who want to drag Ireland down a dark path," they said. "We're here to say that's not who we are, and we're not going away."

Whether the movement can sustain momentum and translate street protest into meaningful political influence remains to be seen. For now, at least, the battle for the soul of Ireland's immigration debate shows no sign of quieting down.
headline: #RefugeesWelcome brigade protest in Dublin saying it’s the start of their campaign to buck anti-migrant trend

text:
The residents of a small rural townland have spoken of their terror after a gang of youths descended on their community in a spree of antisocial behaviour that left property damaged, locals intimidated, and serious questions hanging over the response of both the authorities and the mainstream media.

The incident, which took place over the course of several evenings in recent weeks, saw a group of up to a dozen young people gather in the area, reportedly arriving from outside the locality. Residents described scenes of open intimidation, with youths roaming through private land, shouting abuse at householders, throwing objects at vehicles, and engaging in wanton vandalism of fences, letterboxes, and garden furniture.

One elderly resident, who asked not to be named for fear of reprisal, told The Liberal that she was "absolutely petrified" to leave her home after dark. "I've lived here for over fifty years and never experienced anything like it," she said. "They have no respect for anyone or anything. You feel completely abandoned."

Another local described how his car was struck with stones as he drove through the area, cracking the windscreen. He said he reported the matter to the Gardaí but was told resources were stretched and that patrols would be increased "when possible." Weeks later, he said, he has seen no discernible increase in Garda presence.

Local representatives say they have raised the issue with both the Garda Síochána and the relevant local authority but have been met with what one described as a "wall of indifference." A county councillor for the area, speaking to The Liberal, said the situation was "completely unacceptable" and that residents were being "left to fend for themselves."

"These are decent, law-abiding people who pay their taxes and expect a basic level of safety in their own homes," the councillor said. "They are not getting that. The system is failing them."

Perhaps equally troubling, however, is the near-total silence from Ireland's legacy media on incidents of this nature. Despite the frequency with which such episodes are now reported anecdotally across rural and suburban Ireland, they rarely if ever make the pages of the national newspapers or the bulletins of the State broadcaster. Residents in the affected area expressed frustration that their ordeal appeared to be of no interest whatsoever to RTÉ or the major print titles.

The reluctance of mainstream outlets to report on what communities across the country describe as a growing crisis of youth disorder has become a story in itself. Critics argue that a de facto code of silence operates in Irish media when it comes to antisocial behaviour, particularly when reporting on the perpetrators might raise uncomfortable questions about policy failures in areas such as justice, integration, or youth services.

This studied avoidance stands in stark contrast to the lived experience of ordinary people in communities from Donegal to Waterford, who increasingly feel that their concerns are being deliberately ignored or minimised by a media class more interested in managing narratives than reflecting reality.

The Garda Press Office, when contacted by The Liberal, confirmed that it was "aware of reports of antisocial behaviour in the area" and that "appropriate action" was being taken, though no further details were provided. No arrests have been made.
headline: Feral gang of youths terrorise quiet Irish townland as media maintains code of silence in face of such incidents

text:
Tributes have been paid to a woman, aged in her 70s, who died after getting into difficulty while swimming in the sea off the coast of Co Waterford on Wednesday afternoon.

Emergency services were alerted shortly after 2pm when the woman got into difficulty in the water at Bunmahon Beach, near the village of Bunmahon on the Copper Coast.

The alarm was raised by fellow swimmers, and the RNLI, the Irish Coast Guard, and paramedics from the National Ambulance Service all responded to the scene. The woman was recovered from the water and efforts were made to resuscitate her on the beach before she was transferred by ambulance to University Hospital Waterford, where she was later pronounced dead.

The woman, who has not been formally named, is understood to have been a local resident and a regular swimmer at the beach. She was well known in the tight-knit community, and neighbours and friends expressed their shock and sadness at her passing.

Local councillor Séamus O'Donnell described the incident as a tragedy for the entire community. "She was a woman who was full of life and was known to everyone around here. The whole parish is in shock. Our hearts go out to her family at this incredibly difficult time," he said.

Bunmahon Beach is a popular bathing spot along the Copper Coast, which is a UNESCO Global Geopark. The beach is not currently staffed by lifeguards, as the seasonal lifeguard service operated by Waterford City and County Council had not yet commenced for the summer season.

Water Safety Ireland has urged swimmers to exercise caution and to always swim at lifeguarded beaches where possible. A spokesperson reminded the public to be aware of the risks associated with cold water shock, particularly in the early summer months when sea temperatures remain low.

The Gardaí have confirmed that they are treating the death as a tragic incident, and a file will be prepared for the Coroner's Court. A post-mortem examination is expected to be carried out in due course.

Ar dheis Dé go raibh a hanam.
headline: Tributes paid to woman, aged in her 70s, who died after getting into difficulty in sea

text:
A three-year-old Australian boy had to be rescued by emergency services after he managed to climb inside a toy claw machine, in a story that has captured hearts and raised eyebrows in equal measure.

The young lad, whose name has not been released, somehow wriggled his way into the arcade-style grabber machine, presumably deciding that the direct approach was far more efficient than feeding coins into the slot. Rather than being distressed by his predicament, the boy appeared entirely unfazed by the ordeal, happily sitting among the stuffed toys as if he had found exactly where he wanted to be.

The incident occurred in a shopping centre in Queensland, where the child's parents reportedly took their eyes off him for just a moment before discovering he had taken matters into his own hands. Emergency services were called to the scene to extract the boy from the machine after staff were unable to free him themselves.

Footage and images of the rescue quickly went viral on social media, with users around the world charmed by the boy's remarkably calm demeanour throughout the whole affair. Several commenters noted that the child appeared far less bothered about the situation than the adults attempting to get him out.

Fire crews carefully dismantled part of the machine to free the youngster, who emerged unscathed and, by all accounts, thoroughly unbothered by the entire experience.

Queensland police confirmed that the boy was uninjured and was reunited with his relieved parents shortly after the rescue. No charges were filed, though one could argue the lad deserves credit for initiative if nothing else.

The incident has prompted renewed discussion about the safety of claw machines and similar arcade equipment, with some calling for better safeguards to prevent curious children from gaining access to their interiors.

It is far from the first time a child has found their way inside a claw machine, with similar incidents reported across the United States and Asia in recent years. The machines, which typically feature a small prize chute, can apparently provide just enough of an opening for a determined and sufficiently small adventurer.
headline: Toy story! Unfazed 3-yr-old Australian boy gets rescued after he climbed into toy claw machine

text:
Gardaí are investigating after a number of vehicles were set alight in the carpark of a pub in Co Meath in the early hours of this morning.

The incident occurred at approximately 3am when emergency services were alerted to a fire involving several cars parked outside the premises, which is understood to be located in the south of the county.

Units from Meath County Fire and Rescue Service attended the scene and brought the blaze under control, but not before significant damage was caused to a number of vehicles. It is understood that at least three cars were badly damaged in the fire.

Gardaí arrived at the scene shortly after the alarm was raised and the area was cordoned off to allow for a technical examination to be carried out. The results of that examination are expected to assist investigators in determining the exact cause and circumstances of the fire.

While investigations are at an early stage, it is understood that Gardaí are treating the fire as a case of suspected criminal damage. Officers are examining CCTV footage from the premises and surrounding area as part of their enquiries.

A Garda spokesperson confirmed that an investigation is underway. "Gardaí are investigating an incident of criminal damage by fire that occurred in the carpark of a licensed premises in Co Meath in the early hours of this morning. No injuries were reported. Investigations are ongoing," the spokesperson said.

Gardaí are appealing for anyone who may have been in the area at the time, or who may have dashcam or other footage, to contact their local Garda station. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: BREAKING: Investigation underway after a number of vehicles set alight in pub carpark in Co Meath

text:
Micheál Martin has thrown his weight firmly behind Jim Gavin's presidential bid, describing the former Dublin GAA manager as a "wonderful candidate" with a unique ability to unite people from all walks of life.

The Taoiseach was speaking at a Fianna Fáil event on Saturday where he offered a full-throated endorsement of Gavin, who is seeking to succeed Michael D. Higgins in the Áras later this year.

"He's a wonderful candidate," Martin told reporters. "Jim has a capacity to bring people together, and I think that's what the country needs right now in a president."

Martin pointed to Gavin's distinguished record both on and off the pitch as evidence of his suitability for the role. The Dubliner led the capital's senior footballers to an unprecedented six All-Ireland titles, including the historic five-in-a-row between 2015 and 2019, but has also enjoyed a successful career as a commercial pilot and served with the Defence Forces.

The Taoiseach suggested that Gavin's combination of leadership experience, military service, and sporting achievement gave him a profile that could resonate with voters across the political spectrum and beyond.

"He understands what it means to lead, to bring diverse groups of people together and to get the best out of them," Martin said. "That's exactly the kind of person we want representing Ireland on the world stage."

Gavin, who has kept a relatively low public profile since stepping down as Dublin manager in 2020, has been gradually increasing his visibility in recent weeks as the presidential race begins to take shape. He has been endorsed by Fianna Fáil and is expected to formally launch his campaign in the coming weeks.

The endorsement from Martin is significant, though hardly unexpected given that Gavin is running with the backing of the Taoiseach's own party. However, the warmth and enthusiasm of the remarks suggest that the Fianna Fáil leadership sees Gavin as a candidate who can appeal well beyond the party's traditional base.

The presidential election is expected to be held in the autumn, with several other potential candidates understood to be considering entering the race. Any candidate not nominated by at least 20 members of the Oireachtas must secure the backing of four county or city councils to get on the ballot paper.

Gavin's candidacy has already attracted some debate, with critics questioning whether his association with Dublin GAA — a team whose dominance proved divisive in some quarters — could prove a liability outside the capital. Supporters, however, argue that his leadership qualities and personal integrity transcend county rivalries.

Martin dismissed such concerns, insisting that Gavin's appeal was national rather than parochial. "People respect achievement, and they respect decency," the Taoiseach said. "Jim Gavin has both in abundance."
headline: He’s a wonderful candidate – Martin says presidential candidate Jim Gavin can ‘bring people together’

text:
RTÉ is set to spend €180,000 of public money outsourcing editorial research for state events, a move that has drawn criticism from those who question whether the national broadcaster should be farming out what many consider a core journalistic function.

The contract, which covers research for coverage of major state occasions and commemorations, was confirmed through public procurement documents. It will see an external provider tasked with preparing background material, historical context and editorial briefing notes for RTÉ's coverage of events such as state funerals, presidential inaugurations and national commemorative ceremonies.

The decision comes at a time when RTÉ remains under intense public scrutiny over its financial management and governance in the wake of the controversies that engulfed the broadcaster in recent years. Questions around how the organisation spends licence fee revenue and public funding have become a persistent feature of political debate in the Dáil, with TDs across the political spectrum demanding greater accountability and transparency from Montrose.

Critics will argue that editorial research is precisely the kind of work that a well-resourced national broadcaster, employing hundreds of journalists and researchers, ought to be capable of handling in-house. The outsourcing of such a function raises legitimate questions about how RTÉ allocates its existing resources and whether the organisation has allowed its internal capacity to erode to the point where it must pay external contractors to perform fundamental editorial tasks.

RTÉ receives substantial public funding each year, a figure that has been the subject of considerable political wrangling since the Government moved to reform the television licence system. The broadcaster has repeatedly made the case that it requires additional resources to fulfil its public service mandate, yet decisions such as this contract will do little to reassure either the public or their elected representatives that the money is being spent wisely.

The procurement of external research services for state events is not without precedent in broadcasting, and RTÉ would likely argue that specialist knowledge is sometimes required for historically complex occasions. However, the scale of the expenditure — €180,000 is a significant sum by any measure — will inevitably invite scrutiny, particularly given the organisation's stated commitment to reform and efficiency in the aftermath of its recent financial and governance scandals.

It also raises a broader question about the direction of public service broadcasting in Ireland. If RTÉ cannot draw on its own editorial teams to research and prepare for the coverage of national events — occasions that sit at the very heart of its public service remit — then what precisely is the licence fee funding?

Members of the Oireachtas Media Committee have previously expressed frustration at what they perceive as a lack of cost discipline within RTÉ. This latest expenditure is likely to feature in future committee hearings, where the broadcaster's leadership can expect pointed questions about why this work could not have been undertaken internally.

RTÉ did not provide a detailed response when asked to justify the expenditure, though the broadcaster has previously maintained that all procurement decisions are made in accordance with proper procedures and represent value for money.

Whether the Irish taxpayer agrees remains another matter entirely.
headline: RTÉ to outsource editorial research for state events at a cost of €180,000 to the Irish taxpayer

text:
No fewer than 36 people have been killed and scores more injured after two trains collided head-on in central Greece late on Tuesday night, in what is being described as one of the deadliest rail disasters in the country's history.

The collision occurred near the city of Larissa, in the Tempi valley, when a passenger train travelling from Athens to Thessaloniki crashed into an oncoming freight train at around 11.30pm local time. Emergency services rushed to the scene, where several carriages were derailed and at least two caught fire, hampering rescue efforts through the night.

Greek authorities confirmed the death toll had risen to at least 36 by Wednesday afternoon, though officials warned the figure could climb further as rescue crews continued to search through the wreckage of the mangled carriages. Dozens of the injured were taken to hospitals in Larissa and surrounding areas, with several reported to be in a critical condition.

The passenger train was carrying an estimated 350 people at the time of the crash, many of them young people and university students returning to Thessaloniki after a long holiday weekend.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis declared three days of national mourning and travelled to the scene on Wednesday morning. Speaking to reporters, he described the disaster as "an unspeakable tragedy" and vowed a full investigation into how the two trains came to be travelling on the same stretch of track.

The country's transport minister, Kostas Karamanlis, tendered his resignation in the wake of the disaster, saying he felt a moral obligation to step down even before the full circumstances of the collision had been established.

Greek rail workers' unions have long raised concerns about chronic underinvestment in the country's rail infrastructure, pointing to outdated signalling systems and staffing shortages as persistent safety hazards. Questions were immediately raised about how the two trains were permitted to travel on the same line in opposing directions, with the local stationmaster at Larissa reportedly taken into custody for questioning.

The disaster prompted an outpouring of grief across Greece, with spontaneous vigils held in Athens and Thessaloniki on Wednesday evening. Protesters also gathered outside the headquarters of Hellenic Train, the railway operator, demanding accountability and systemic reform.

The European Commission offered its condolences and said it stood ready to assist Greek authorities. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the crash as "devastating" and expressed solidarity with the victims and their families.

It is understood that international teams have offered technical assistance in the investigation, which is expected to examine both human error and potential systemic failures in Greece's rail network.

The disaster has drawn comparisons to previous fatal rail accidents in Europe and has reignited a broader debate about the state of transport infrastructure across southern European nations that were subject to severe austerity programmes during the eurozone debt crisis. Critics argue that years of budget cuts left critical public services, including rail safety systems, dangerously underfunded.

Rescue operations at the crash site were continuing on Wednesday evening, with heavy machinery brought in to lift overturned carriages. Authorities have established a dedicated helpline for families seeking information about passengers who were on board the train.
headline: No fewer than 36 people dead following train collision in Greece

text:
World leaders from across the globe have travelled to Rome this morning for the funeral of Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI, who died on New Year's Eve at the age of 95.

The ceremony, presided over by Pope Francis, is taking place in St Peter's Square before an expected congregation of tens of thousands of mourners who have gathered to pay their final respects to the first pontiff to resign in almost 600 years.

President Michael D Higgins is representing Ireland at the funeral, with the President's office confirming his attendance earlier this week. Taoiseach Leo Varadkar offered his condolences following Benedict's death, describing him as a man of "great intellect and faith" who had made an enormous contribution to the Catholic Church during a period of significant challenge.

Among the other heads of state and senior dignitaries in attendance are Italian President Sergio Mattarella, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, and King Philippe of Belgium. Germany, as Benedict's homeland, has sent a particularly large delegation to the Vatican. Several other European leaders and representatives from nations across Africa, Asia and the Americas have also made the journey to Rome.

Born Joseph Ratzinger in Marktl am Inn, Bavaria, in 1927, Benedict served as pope from 2005 until his historic resignation in February 2013, when he cited declining health and a lack of the strength required to fulfil the demands of the papacy. He spent his final years living quietly in a converted monastery within the Vatican grounds.

His papacy was marked by considerable controversy, not least the ongoing clerical sexual abuse crisis that had caused such devastation in Ireland and elsewhere. His 2010 pastoral letter to Irish Catholics, in which he acknowledged the "shame and humiliation" brought about by the abuse, drew a mixed response from survivors, many of whom felt it did not go far enough in accepting institutional responsibility.

Pope Francis, who succeeded Benedict and who has himself grappled with the abuse crisis, is leading the relatively simple funeral liturgy in keeping with the wishes of his predecessor. Benedict had requested a ceremony that would be solemn but not elaborate, reflecting his status as pope emeritus rather than a reigning pontiff.

The funeral marks only the second time in the modern history of the Church that a sitting pope has celebrated the funeral Mass for his predecessor in such circumstances, underscoring the extraordinary nature of Benedict's decision to step down from the papacy.

Vatican officials have said that Benedict will be laid to rest in the papal grottoes beneath St Peter's Basilica, in the tomb previously occupied by Pope John Paul II before his remains were moved following his beatification.

Flags are flying at half-mast at government buildings across Ireland as a mark of respect.
headline: World leaders travel to Rome for Pope Benedict’s funeral this morning

text:
Micheál Martin spent €2,700 of Irish taxpayer money on gifts for US President Donald Trump during his St Patrick's Day visit to Washington, according to figures released by the Department of the Taoiseach.

The Taoiseach's official gift-giving during the traditional White House visit included a selection of Irish-made items presented to Trump as part of the annual shamrock ceremony, a diplomatic occasion that successive Irish leaders have used to strengthen ties between Dublin and Washington.

Details of the expenditure were confirmed following queries about the cost of the gifts, which were sourced from Irish artisans and manufacturers. The Department of the Taoiseach has historically used the St Patrick's Day visit as an opportunity to showcase Irish craftsmanship, with gifts typically including crystal, fine art and other luxury items produced on the island.

The €2,700 figure will nonetheless raise eyebrows among some taxpayers at a time when households across the State continue to grapple with the cost of living crisis. Opposition TDs have previously questioned the scale of spending on diplomatic gift-giving, arguing that the tradition could be maintained at a lower cost to the exchequer.

However, Government sources have defended the outlay, pointing to the enormous economic significance of the Irish-American relationship. The United States remains one of Ireland's most important trading partners, with bilateral trade worth tens of billions of euro annually. More than 900 US companies operate in Ireland, employing approximately 210,000 people, while Irish firms in the US support a further 110,000 jobs.

The St Patrick's Day visit to the White House is regarded by officials in Merrion Street as one of the most valuable diplomatic engagements on the Irish calendar, offering unparalleled access to the sitting US president at a time when other world leaders must compete for face time.

This year's visit carried particular weight given the Trump administration's aggressive tariff policies, which have caused significant uncertainty for Irish exporters and US multinationals based in Ireland. Martin used the visit to press Ireland's case on trade and to discuss immigration matters, with the status of undocumented Irish citizens in the United States remaining a long-standing concern.

The tradition of presenting a bowl of shamrock to the US president dates back to 1952, when then-Taoiseach John A. Costello sent the gift to President Harry Truman. It has since evolved into a broader diplomatic engagement involving gifts, bilateral meetings and high-profile receptions.

The Department of the Taoiseach did not provide a full itemised breakdown of the gifts presented to Trump but confirmed the total expenditure figure. It is understood that the gifts were selected to reflect Irish heritage and contemporary Irish design.
headline: Martin spent €2,700 Irish taxpayer money on gifts for President Donald Trump

text:
A newly qualified Garda was discovered lying in a ditch at the side of the M1 motorway after abandoning a patrol car on the busy route, it has emerged.

The incident, which has caused considerable embarrassment within Garda management, occurred when the probationary member left the official vehicle on the motorway and was subsequently found by colleagues in a state of distress in a nearby ditch.

It is understood the young Garda, who had only recently been attested from the Garda College in Templemore, was on duty at the time of the incident. The patrol car was left unattended on the M1, creating a potential hazard for other motorists until it was recovered by fellow members.

Sources within the force have indicated that the member had been struggling with the pressures of the job in the period leading up to the incident. The Garda was taken to receive medical attention following the discovery and has not returned to active duty since.

The incident has reignited concerns about the level of support provided to newly qualified Gardaí as they transition from training in Templemore to frontline policing. The Garda Representative Association has repeatedly raised issues about the welfare of younger members, arguing that many feel overwhelmed and underprepared when they begin operational duties.

A Garda spokesperson confirmed that the organisation was aware of the incident and said the welfare of all members remains a priority. "An Garda Síochána provides a range of supports to all personnel, including access to counselling services and peer support programmes," the spokesperson said.

It is understood that a welfare check has been carried out on the member and that they are receiving ongoing support. No disciplinary proceedings are believed to have been initiated at this stage, with senior management said to be treating the matter as a welfare concern rather than a disciplinary issue.

The GRA has called for a review of the mentoring structures in place for probationary members, with a particular focus on ensuring that newly attested Gardaí are not left isolated during their initial period of service. A spokesperson for the association said the incident highlighted the need for more robust support systems across all Garda divisions.

The M1 motorway was not closed during the incident and no injuries to members of the public were reported.
headline: Newbie Garda found in ditch after abandoning car on M1 motorway

text:
Met Éireann has issued an urgent new nationwide weather warning as deteriorating conditions sweep across the country, with heavy rain, strong winds and plummeting temperatures expected to cause significant disruption in the coming days.

The national forecaster has put the entire country on alert, with a Status Yellow warning in effect for all 26 counties. Forecasters have warned that the worst of the conditions are expected to hit the western seaboard first before tracking eastward, bringing with them the potential for localised flooding, fallen trees and hazardous driving conditions on roads across the State.

Met Éireann meteorologist Aisling Ní Chonghaile said the weather system moving in from the Atlantic is "particularly vigorous" and urged members of the public to take appropriate precautions. "We are looking at a period of very unsettled weather that will affect the entire country over the next 48 to 72 hours," she said. "Rainfall accumulations could be significant, particularly in upland areas, and gusts of up to 110 kilometres per hour are possible along exposed coasts."

Local authorities across the country have activated their severe weather protocols, with council crews on standby to respond to any incidents of flooding or storm damage. The Office of Public Works has said it is monitoring river levels closely, particularly along catchments that have already seen elevated water levels in recent weeks.

The Road Safety Authority has urged motorists to exercise extreme caution, particularly on secondary roads and in rural areas where surface water and debris may accumulate quickly. Drivers have been advised to reduce speed, maintain greater distances from vehicles ahead and to avoid unnecessary journeys during the worst of the conditions.

The Irish Coast Guard has also issued a warning to the public to stay away from exposed coastal areas, piers and cliff walks during the period of the warning, noting that the combination of high tides and strong onshore winds could generate dangerous wave surges.

The ESB has said it has additional crews at the ready to deal with any power outages that may arise as a result of the severe weather. During previous storms, tens of thousands of homes and businesses were left without electricity, some for extended periods, and the utility company said it was taking no chances with the incoming system.

The HSE has advised members of the public, particularly older people and those with underlying health conditions, to ensure they are prepared for the deteriorating conditions by keeping adequate supplies of medication and food in their homes. Emergency departments across the country have been placed on a heightened state of readiness.

Transport services are also expected to face disruption, with Irish Rail, Bus Éireann and Dublin Bus all warning of potential delays and cancellations should conditions worsen beyond current projections. Passengers have been advised to check for updates before travelling. A number of ferry services on routes along the west coast have already been suspended as a precautionary measure.

Met Éireann has indicated that there is a possibility the warning could be upgraded to Status Orange for certain counties as the weather system develops and its track becomes clearer. Forecasters are continuing to monitor the situation and have said they will issue further updates as new data becomes available.
headline: Met Eireann issues urgent new nationwide weather warning amidst deteriorating weather conditions

text:
Overcrowding has become a significant and pressing concern across the Irish prison system, according to a new report that paints a stark picture of conditions behind bars and raises serious questions about the State's capacity to house its growing inmate population.

The report, published by the Inspector of Prisons, found that a number of facilities are now operating well beyond their intended capacity, with some prisons holding substantially more inmates than they were designed to accommodate. The findings point to a system under considerable strain, with the knock-on effects being felt by both prisoners and staff alike.

According to the report, the total number of people in custody has risen sharply in recent years, driven in part by longer sentences, an increase in committals, and a slowdown in the use of alternative sanctions such as community service orders. The prison population now stands at levels not seen in over a decade, and the trajectory shows little sign of reversing.

The Inspector noted that overcrowding is contributing to a deterioration in living conditions, with inmates in some institutions forced to share cells designed for single occupancy. In certain cases, prisoners are sleeping on mattresses on the floor. The report highlighted that such conditions undermine not only the dignity of those in custody but also the ability of the Irish Prison Service to deliver meaningful rehabilitation programmes.

Healthcare provision within the prison system is also being stretched thin as a result of the increased numbers. The report found that access to mental health services, addiction supports, and general medical care has become more difficult, with waiting times growing and resources being spread across a larger population than originally planned for.

Staff welfare was another area of concern flagged in the report. Prison officers are working in increasingly pressurised environments, the Inspector warned, with higher prisoner numbers leading to greater tensions on landings and a heightened risk of violent incidents. The Irish Prison Officers' Association has repeatedly raised concerns about the impact of overcrowding on the safety and wellbeing of its members.

The Minister for Justice has acknowledged the challenges outlined in the report and indicated that the Government is examining a range of measures to address the situation. These include the potential expansion of existing facilities and a review of sentencing policy to ensure that imprisonment is reserved for the most serious offences.

However, opposition TDs have accused the Government of failing to act with sufficient urgency. Speaking in the Dáil, several members called for an emergency response to what they described as a crisis that has been allowed to develop over successive governments. There were also calls for greater investment in community-based alternatives to custody, which critics say have been chronically underfunded.

Penal reform advocates have long warned that Ireland's reliance on imprisonment as a primary response to offending is unsustainable. The Irish Penal Reform Trust said the report's findings, while deeply concerning, were entirely predictable given the lack of strategic planning and investment in the criminal justice system over many years. The organisation called for a comprehensive review of how the State uses detention and urged policymakers to look at evidence-based approaches that have proven effective in other European jurisdictions.

The report also drew attention to the particular difficulties facing certain categories of prisoner.
headline: Overcrowding is now a major issue is Irish prisons, report finds

text:
Irish citizens are earning nearly €90 more per week than their non-Irish counterparts, according to new figures from the Central Statistics Office, prompting accusations of systemic racism in the Irish labour market.

The CSO's latest data on earnings and labour costs reveals a significant disparity between what Irish nationals and non-Irish nationals take home each week, with the gap standing at almost €90 in median gross weekly earnings. The figures have reignited debate about whether Ireland's much-vaunted multiculturalism extends to the workplace, or whether structural barriers continue to hold back workers from migrant backgrounds.

The data, drawn from the CSO's Earnings Analysis using Administrative Data Sources, shows that while Irish citizens recorded higher median weekly earnings, non-Irish nationals were disproportionately concentrated in lower-paid sectors such as accommodation and food services, administrative and support services, and wholesale and retail trade. These sectors have long been associated with precarious working conditions and limited opportunities for advancement.

Campaigners and migrant advocacy groups have pointed to the figures as evidence that non-Irish workers are being funnelled into low-wage employment regardless of their qualifications or experience. Several organisations working with migrant communities have described the pay gap as reflective of a broader pattern of discrimination that permeates hiring practices, promotion opportunities, and workplace culture across the State.

The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission has previously flagged concerns about racial discrimination in employment, noting that people of African descent and other ethnic minorities face particular barriers when seeking work commensurate with their skills and education. Research has consistently shown that job applicants with non-Irish names are less likely to be called for interview, even when their CVs are otherwise identical to those of Irish applicants.

Trade union representatives have called on the Government to take more decisive action to address the earnings gap, arguing that existing equality legislation is not being adequately enforced. The Irish Congress of Trade Unions has said that stronger protections are needed for workers in sectors where exploitation is most prevalent, and that labour inspections by the Workplace Relations Commission should be significantly increased.

Some economists have cautioned that the raw earnings gap does not necessarily indicate direct wage discrimination, noting that factors such as language barriers, non-recognition of foreign qualifications, and the concentration of non-Irish workers in part-time or temporary roles all contribute to the disparity. However, critics argue that these structural factors are themselves products of a system that fails to adequately support the integration of migrant workers into the Irish economy.

The Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment has said the Government is committed to ensuring fair treatment for all workers regardless of nationality, pointing to initiatives under the Migrant Integration Strategy. However, that strategy has itself come in for criticism from advocacy groups who say it lacks teeth and has not been adequately resourced.

The figures come at a time of heightened public debate around immigration and integration in Ireland, with the issue featuring prominently in political discourse across the Oireachtas. Several TDs have raised the matter in the Dáil, calling for a comprehensive review of how non-Irish nationals are treated in the labour market and whether current policy frameworks are fit for purpose.
headline: “It’s racism” – Irish citizens earn nearly €90 more per week than non-Irish nationals, claims CSO

text:
There are "no winners" in trade wars or tariff disputes, the head of the International Air Transport Association has said, warning that escalating protectionism poses a serious threat to global aviation and the economies that depend on it.

Willie Walsh, the Dublin-born director general of IATA and former chief executive of Aer Lingus and British Airways, issued the stark warning as airlines around the world grapple with the fallout from US President Donald Trump's sweeping tariff regime.

Walsh, who has earned the nickname "Top Gun" over a career spanning decades in the aviation industry, said the imposition of tariffs and the retaliatory measures they provoke risk undermining the connectivity that underpins international trade and tourism.

"There are no winners with tariffs or trade wars," Walsh said. "History has shown us time and again that protectionism damages economies, reduces consumer choice and drives up costs. Aviation is a global industry by its very nature, and anything that fragments that global system is bad news for airlines, for passengers and for the economies we serve."

His comments come at a particularly sensitive time for Ireland, where the aviation sector is a cornerstone of economic activity. Ireland is home to major aircraft leasing firms controlling a significant share of the world's commercial fleet, while airlines such as Ryanair and Aer Lingus connect the island to hundreds of destinations worldwide.

The potential impact of tariffs on aircraft manufacturers such as Boeing and Airbus could have knock-on effects for Irish-based lessors and carriers alike, with increased costs for new aircraft ultimately being passed on to consumers through higher fares.

Walsh also pointed to the broader economic risks for small, open economies like Ireland's, which are disproportionately reliant on trade and foreign direct investment. Any disruption to the free flow of goods, services and people across borders could have outsized consequences for such economies, he cautioned.

The IATA chief's intervention echoes concerns raised by figures across Irish industry and government. The Taoiseach has previously stressed the importance of free trade to Ireland's economic model, while business groups including Ibec have warned of the potential damage a prolonged transatlantic trade dispute could inflict on Irish exporters.

Walsh urged governments on all sides to step back from the brink and pursue negotiated solutions rather than escalatory measures. "We need cool heads and pragmatic thinking," he said. "The answer to trade disputes is diplomacy, not tariffs that punish your own consumers and businesses."

The former Aer Lingus boss, who began his career as a cadet pilot with the Irish flag carrier before rising through its management ranks, has long been regarded as one of the most forthright voices in global aviation. His willingness to speak bluntly on politically charged issues has defined his tenure at IATA, where he has consistently advocated for reduced regulation and greater liberalisation of air travel markets.

Industry analysts have noted that the current trade tensions come at a difficult moment for the aviation sector, which is still navigating the aftereffects of the pandemic alongside rising fuel costs and pressure to decarbonise. The addition of tariff-related uncertainty, they say, creates yet another headwind for an industry operating on notoriously thin margins.
headline: ‘No winners’ with tariffs or trade wars, says ‘Top Gun’

text:
Leo Varadkar has called on all political parties to include a commitment to Irish unity in their manifestos ahead of the next general election, arguing that the issue should be treated as a shared national objective rather than the preserve of any single party.

The former Taoiseach and Fine Gael leader made the remarks at an event in Dublin on Wednesday evening, where he outlined his vision for how preparations for a potential border poll should be advanced in the coming years. Varadkar said that while the question of when a referendum might be held remained open, the principle of working towards a united Ireland should be embraced across the political spectrum.

"I think it would be a powerful statement if every party contesting the next general election included in their manifesto a commitment to Irish unity as a long-term objective and a willingness to begin serious preparations for that eventuality," Varadkar said. "This shouldn't be something that belongs to one tradition or one party. It belongs to all of us."

The intervention marks a notable shift in emphasis for Varadkar, who during his time as Taoiseach was often cautious on the unity question, warning against rushing towards a border poll without adequate preparation. He now appears to be positioning himself as a more vocal advocate, though he stressed that any move towards reunification must be consensual and must take account of unionist concerns.

His comments come against the backdrop of ongoing demographic and political change in the North, where Sinn Féin holds the position of First Minister and where census data has shown a growing nationalist population. Polling on both sides of the border has consistently shown significant support for a unity referendum within the next decade, though opinion remains divided on the timing and terms.

Varadkar said that the Government should establish a dedicated unit within the Department of the Taoiseach to begin planning for unity, including examining the constitutional, economic and social implications of bringing together two systems of governance, healthcare, education and taxation.

"We need to do the homework," he said. "People are entitled to know what a united Ireland would look like in practice — how it would affect their public services, their pensions, their taxes, their identity. We can't ask people to vote for something undefined."

The call is likely to be welcomed by Sinn Féin, which has long campaigned for a border poll and has repeatedly urged the Government to establish a citizens' assembly on the matter. Mary Lou McDonald has previously accused successive governments of a lack of ambition on the question, and her party will likely view Varadkar's intervention as validating their long-standing position.

However, the proposal may prove more complicated for other parties. Fianna Fáil, while constitutionally committed to Irish unity, has traditionally been cautious about the pace of any such process. The party's current leadership under Micheál Martin has emphasised the need for dialogue and reconciliation over any fixed timeline. Fine Gael itself remains divided on how prominently the issue should feature, with some TDs wary of alienating moderate voters who see more pressing domestic concerns.

Labour, the Social Democrats and the Greens have all expressed openness to the concept of unity in various forms, but none has made it a centrepiece of their political offering.
headline: Leo Varadkar wants Irish unity manifesto pledge by all parties in next election

Smoke canisters were set off in the streets of Malmö on Thursday evening as thousands of protesters descended on the Swedish city to demonstrate against Israel's participation in this year's Eurovision Song Contest.

The protests, which had been building throughout the week, reached a fever pitch as the second semi-final of the competition got underway, with demonstrators chanting slogans and waving Palestinian flags in the city centre. Swedish police confirmed that several smoke canisters were deployed by protesters, though no injuries were reported in the immediate aftermath.

Organisers of the demonstration said they had gathered to send a clear message that Israel should not be permitted to take part in the contest while its military offensive in Gaza continues. Among those protesting were Irish fans who had travelled to Sweden for the event.

"Israel shouldn't be allowed participate, full stop," one Dublin woman told reporters at the scene. "You can't have a song contest celebrating unity and togetherness while this is going on. It's a disgrace that the EBU hasn't acted."

The European Broadcasting Union, which organises Eurovision, has repeatedly resisted calls to exclude Israel from the competition, maintaining that the contest is a non-political event. The stance has drawn sharp criticism from campaigners and several national broadcasters across Europe.

Swedish police had deployed significant resources in Malmö ahead of the contest, with thousands of officers drafted in from across the country in anticipation of large-scale protests. Barriers were erected around the Malmö Arena, and protest zones were designated at a considerable distance from the venue itself.

Climate activist Greta Thunberg was among those who joined the demonstrations earlier in the week, adding her voice to calls for Israel's exclusion.

The scenes in Malmö were echoed on social media, where the hashtag #BoycottEurovision2024 trended across multiple European countries throughout the evening. Several Irish politicians, including a number of TDs, had previously called on RTÉ to take a stronger stance on the matter, though the national broadcaster confirmed Ireland's participation would proceed as planned.

The controversy has drawn inevitable comparisons to the exclusion of Russia from the contest following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, with critics accusing the EBU of applying a double standard.

Malmö police said they were monitoring the situation closely and that further protests were expected ahead of Saturday's grand final.
headline: “Israel shouldn’t be allowed participate”: Smoke canisters get set off in Malmö during Eurovision protests

text:
Novak Djokovic stands on the brink of history today as he takes to the clay at Roland Garros with the chance to claim a record-breaking 23rd Grand Slam singles title and cement his place as the greatest tennis player of all time.

The Serbian maestro, who has already shared the all-time record of 22 major titles with Rafael Nadal, will face Casper Ruud of Norway in the French Open final, with the weight of sporting history resting squarely on his shoulders.

Should Djokovic prevail on the Parisian clay this afternoon, he will stand alone at the summit of men's tennis, surpassing Nadal's tally and putting what many would consider a definitive end to the greatest-of-all-time debate that has consumed the sport for the better part of two decades.

At 36 years of age, Djokovic has shown no signs of slowing down, powering through the draw at Roland Garros with a series of commanding performances. His run to the final has been all the more remarkable given that the French Open has traditionally been Nadal's domain, with the Spaniard having claimed the title a staggering 14 times.

Djokovic's journey to this point has been one of extraordinary resilience and longevity. While his great rivals Nadal and Roger Federer have battled injuries and the inevitable toll of time, the Belgrade native has continued to compete at the very highest level, defying the ageing process in a manner that has left commentators and fellow professionals alike shaking their heads in disbelief.

The significance of today's final extends beyond mere numbers. A victory would give Djokovic at least three titles at each of the four Grand Slam tournaments, a feat of consistency across different surfaces that arguably no other player in the history of the sport can match.

Ruud, for his part, will be desperate to spoil the party. The Norwegian reached last year's French Open final, where he was beaten by Nadal, and also finished runner-up at the US Open. He will be eager to ensure that his third Grand Slam final is not another case of being a supporting actor in someone else's coronation.

However, the bookmakers and the vast majority of tennis analysts expect Djokovic to get the job done. His record in Grand Slam finals is formidable, and his ability to rise to the biggest occasions has been one of the defining characteristics of his extraordinary career.

For Irish tennis fans, many of whom will have grown up watching the epic battles between Djokovic, Nadal and Federer, today's final represents something of a watershed moment. The so-called Big Three era, which has produced some of the most thrilling sporting contests of the 21st century, is drawing to a close, and Djokovic appears determined to have the final word.

Play is scheduled to begin at Roland Garros this afternoon, with coverage available across several broadcasters. Whatever the result, tennis fans are in for a spectacle, but the smart money is on Djokovic writing himself into the record books once more.
headline: Novak Djokovic aims to become the greatest of them all today by winning a 23rd Grand Slam at the French Open in Paris

text:
The Ukrainian community in Ireland has reacted with fury after the Government confirmed it will withdraw taxpayer-funded accommodation for approximately 16,000 Ukrainians currently living in the State, in a move that ministers say is necessary to bring Ireland's approach into line with other EU member states.

The Department of Integration announced that Ukrainians who have been in Ireland for over two years and are currently in employment will be expected to source their own accommodation from early next year, with a phased withdrawal of State-provided housing beginning in the coming months.

The decision has provoked an angry backlash from Ukrainian nationals and advocacy groups, who say the move will leave thousands of people in an impossible position given the severity of Ireland's housing crisis. Many Ukrainians have argued that even those in full-time employment cannot hope to secure private rental accommodation in a market where supply remains critically constrained and rents continue to reach record highs.

Speaking outside a direct provision centre in Dublin, one Ukrainian woman who has been living in Ireland since the early weeks of the Russian invasion said the decision amounted to a betrayal. "We were told we were welcome here. We have been working, paying taxes, contributing to this country. Now they tell us to find somewhere to live when Irish people themselves cannot find housing. Where are we supposed to go?"

The Government has maintained that the Temporary Protection Directive, under which Ukrainians were granted the right to live and work across the EU, was never intended to provide indefinite accommodation at the expense of the taxpayer. A spokesperson for the Department said the State had spent in excess of €2.5 billion on accommodation and supports for Ukrainian refugees since 2022, and that a managed transition towards independent living was both reasonable and overdue.

The Irish Refugee Council has expressed concern about the timeline, warning that without adequate notice and transitional supports, the policy risks pushing vulnerable families into homelessness. The organisation called on the Government to ensure that no individual or family is left without a roof over their head as a result of the change.

Tánaiste Micheál Martin, speaking to reporters in Leinster House, acknowledged the difficulties but said the current arrangement was unsustainable. "Ireland has been extraordinarily generous, and I think that is recognised internationally. But we have to be realistic about what the State can continue to provide. People who are working and who have been here for a considerable period of time need to begin the process of transitioning to independent living."

The backlash has been particularly vocal on social media, where Ukrainian community groups have organised online campaigns and petition drives calling on the Government to reverse the decision. Several demonstrations have been planned for Dublin and Cork in the coming weeks.

Not all reaction has been sympathetic, however. A significant number of Irish commentators and members of the public have pointed out that the State's obligations to its own citizens — many of whom are themselves struggling with housing insecurity — must take priority. Some TDs have privately welcomed the announcement, noting that the issue of indefinite State-funded accommodation for Ukrainians has become a growing source of frustration among constituents.

Sinn Féin's spokesperson on integration said the party supported a transition towards independent living in principle but criticised the Government for failing to build sufficient housing stock to make such a transition viable.
