headline: Outrage from Ukrainians as government withdraws taxpayer-funded accommodation for 16,000 Ukrainians in Ireland

text:
Rishi Sunak has dismissed the prospect of striking any deal with Ireland over the movement of asylum seekers across the border, declaring bluntly that he is "not interested" in entering negotiations on the matter and suggesting sarcastically that Ireland should simply accept all comers.

The British Prime Minister's remarks came amid mounting tensions between Dublin and London over what the Irish Government says is a significant increase in the number of asylum seekers entering the State via Northern Ireland, a trend Ministers here have directly linked to the UK's controversial Rwanda deportation policy.

Speaking to reporters, Sunak was unapologetic. "Ireland can take them all," he said, before adding that his sole focus was on making the Rwanda scheme operational and reducing the number of people crossing the English Channel in small boats. "I'm not interested in doing a deal with Ireland on this. My focus is on stopping the boats."

The comments are likely to cause significant irritation in Government Buildings, where both the Taoiseach and the Tánaiste have repeatedly raised the issue of cross-border migration flows in recent weeks. Simon Harris has previously said that the Rwanda policy is having a "direct impact" on Ireland and called on the UK to engage constructively on the matter.

The Minister for Justice Helen McEntee has pointed to figures suggesting that a substantial proportion of those arriving into the international protection system have entered via Northern Ireland, travelling across the border which, under the Common Travel Area, remains open and largely unpoliced.

The Government has already moved to introduce emergency legislation allowing the State to return asylum seekers to the UK if it can be established that they travelled through it before arriving in Ireland. However, the UK has so far refused to accept any such returns, arguing that there is no bilateral readmission agreement in place and that it is under no obligation to take people back.

Opposition TDs have accused the Government of being naive in its approach to the issue, with Sinn Féin's justice spokesperson saying that Ministers should have anticipated the consequences of the Rwanda policy long before the current situation developed. Others in the Dáil have questioned whether the emergency measures announced by McEntee are legally robust enough to withstand challenge in the courts.

The diplomatic row represents a notable low point in Irish-British relations, which had already been strained by years of disagreement over post-Brexit trading arrangements for Northern Ireland. The Common Travel Area, which predates both EU membership and the Good Friday Agreement, has long been regarded as one of the cornerstones of the relationship between the two states, and there are concerns in Dublin that the migration dispute could undermine the cooperative framework that underpins it.

Legal experts have also raised questions about whether Ireland's proposed return policy is compatible with EU law and the European Convention on Human Rights, particularly given that the UK is no longer an EU member state and its asylum system operates on fundamentally different principles to those in place across the Union.

For his part, Sunak appears content to let the matter rest, calculating that being seen to refuse concessions to Ireland plays well with voters in Britain who regard immigration as a priority issue. The Prime Minister is under enormous pressure from the right of his own party and from Reform UK to demonstrate that his Rwanda policy is delivering results, and picking a public fight with Dublin costs him nothing domestically.
headline: “Ireland can take them all” – Sunak says he’s “not interested” in migrant deal with Ireland

text:
It is a truth universally acknowledged in modern Ireland that a young professional in possession of a decent salary must be in want of a flight out of the country. The latest emigration figures paint a picture that is as depressing as it is predictable: record numbers of Irish-born citizens, disproportionately aged between 25 and 35, packed their bags and left in the year to April 2025. They did not leave because they wanted adventure, though some will dress it up that way on Instagram. They left because Ireland, for all its gleaming GDP figures and multinational headquarters, has made itself unliveable for an entire generation.

The Central Statistics Office numbers are stark, but numbers alone do not capture the particular cruelty of what is happening. These are not unskilled workers fleeing a collapsing economy, as was the case in the 1980s. These are nurses, engineers, teachers, software developers — the very people the State spent tens of thousands of euro educating, only to watch them board Ryanair flights to cities where a one-bedroom flat does not consume seventy per cent of a take-home salary. The irony would be amusing if it were not so ruinous.

At the heart of this exodus lies the housing crisis, a phrase so overused it has lost almost all capacity to shock, yet one that continues to define and distort every aspect of Irish life. Homeownership, once considered a near-birthright in this country, has become a fantasy for the majority of young workers. The average house price nationally now sits at a level that requires a deposit so large it might as well be denominated in a fictional currency. In Dublin, the situation is farcical. A couple, both working full-time in professional roles, diligently saving for years, will still find themselves outbid by institutional investors or priced out of catchment areas where they might actually want to raise a family. The Help to Buy scheme and various other government initiatives have functioned less as meaningful interventions and more as sticking plasters on a severed artery, occasionally useful for headlines but structurally inadequate.

The rental market offers no refuge. Ireland's rents are among the highest in Europe, and the protections afforded to tenants remain laughably weak by continental standards. The Residential Tenancies Board does what it can, but enforcement is patchy and the structural imbalance between supply and demand renders regulation almost beside the point. Young people are not merely struggling to buy homes; they are struggling to find anywhere to live at all. When the choice is between paying €2,200 a month for a house-share in Dublin 8 or paying €900 for a well-appointed apartment in Amsterdam or Berlin — cities that also happen to offer better public transport, better healthcare access, and a functioning work-life balance — the calculation is not difficult.

What makes this iteration of Irish emigration particularly insidious is its voluntary invisibility. There are no coffin ships, no American wakes. There are WhatsApp groups and video calls. The emotional distance is compressed by technology in a way that allows politicians to pretend the problem is less severe than it is.
headline: Gone for good? Ireland’s youth exodus accelerates as record numbers emigrated in 2025 as homeownership remains a pipe dream

text:
Simon Harris has moved to shut down any possibility of Fine Gael councillors lending their signatures to independent presidential candidates, issuing a directive that members of the party at local authority level must refuse all nomination requests ahead of a potential contest.

The Taoiseach's intervention comes amid growing speculation that several high-profile independents are seeking the 20 local authority signatures required to secure a place on the presidential ballot paper, with particular concern within Fine Gael circles about the prospect of Conor McGregor entering the race.

Speaking to The Liberal, a senior party source said the directive was unambiguous. "They're petrified Conor would win," the source said. "The instruction has gone out clearly – no Fine Gael councillor is to sign a nomination paper for any independent candidate. Full stop."

Under the Presidential Elections Act, a candidate who does not have the backing of 20 members of the Oireachtas must instead secure nominations from at least four local authorities, with each county or city council passing a resolution in support. Alternatively, a candidate can gather the signatures of 20 sitting councillors from across the country to be formally proposed. This latter route has become the most viable path for independent hopefuls, making the cooperation of councillors from the larger parties essential.

Fine Gael, which holds a significant number of council seats following last year's local elections, represents a critical bloc in this process. By ordering its councillors to withhold their signatures, Harris has effectively narrowed the pathway for any independent candidate hoping to mount a credible challenge.

The move has drawn sharp criticism from opposition figures and democracy campaigners, who argue that councillors hold a constitutional role in the presidential nomination process and should not be whipped into refusing to facilitate candidates who wish to stand.

One independent councillor, who declined to be named, described the directive as "deeply anti-democratic" and accused Harris of attempting to control who the Irish people are permitted to vote for. "Councillors have a duty to the democratic process, not to party headquarters," the councillor said. "If a credible candidate wants to put their name forward, the people should decide – not Simon Harris."

The spectre of a McGregor candidacy has loomed over political discussions for several months. The former UFC champion has cultivated a significant social media following and has made increasingly political interventions on matters ranging from immigration to housing. Polling, while limited, has suggested he could command a notable share of first-preference votes in a presidential contest, a prospect that has alarmed the established parties.

Fine Gael is understood to be particularly anxious about a scenario in which a populist independent candidate draws votes away from any establishment-backed nominee, potentially handing the presidency to a figure outside the mainstream political consensus. The party has not yet confirmed whether it intends to run its own candidate or back a consensus figure should President Michael D. Higgins' second term conclude with a contested election.

Sinn Féin and Fianna Fáil have not issued similar formal directives to their councillors, though sources in both parties indicated that informal pressure has been applied to discourage members from facilitating nominations that could complicate the political landscape.
headline: “They’re petrified Conor would win” – Simon Harris demands all Fine Gael Councillors block Independent Presidential candidate nominations

text:
Five trainee gardaí have been dismissed from the Garda College in Templemore after an internal investigation found they had handcuffed a fellow recruit and forced him into a cold shower in what they described as a "prank."

The incident, which took place at the Co Tipperary training facility several weeks ago, came to light after the victim made a formal complaint to college authorities. It is understood the trainee was restrained using a pair of handcuffs before being dragged into a shower block and doused with cold water, leaving him shaken and distressed.

Sources familiar with the matter said the five recruits initially attempted to characterise the episode as harmless horseplay, but senior management at the college took a dim view of the behaviour, determining that it fell well below the standards expected of those training to become members of An Garda Síochána.

A Garda spokesperson confirmed that a number of student gardaí had been dismissed from the training programme following a breach of the code of conduct at the Garda College. The spokesperson declined to comment further on the specifics of the case, citing the privacy of those involved.

It is understood that the matter was also referred to the Gardaí for assessment as to whether any criminal offence may have been committed, though no arrests have been made at this stage. The victim is understood to have been offered welfare supports through the college.

The dismissals have reignited discussion around the culture within the Garda College, which has faced scrutiny in recent years over a number of controversies. In 2016, an internal audit uncovered significant financial irregularities at the Templemore facility, while separate concerns have been raised periodically about the welfare of recruits undergoing training.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, one serving garda said the decision to dismiss the five trainees sent "a clear message" that such behaviour would not be tolerated. "There was a time when that kind of thing might have been brushed under the carpet, but the organisation has changed," the source said. "If you can't treat a colleague with basic respect during training, you've no business putting on the uniform."

Garda Representative Association officials declined to comment on the matter, noting that student gardaí are not yet full members of the force and do not fall under their representation.

The Irish Council for Civil Liberties said the incident, if the reported details were accurate, raised serious questions. "Restraining someone against their will and subjecting them to a degrading experience is not a prank — it is an assault," a spokesperson said. "It is reassuring that the Garda College appears to have acted swiftly, but it is important that the criminal dimension is also properly investigated."

The five dismissed recruits are understood to have the right to appeal the decision through the college's internal processes, though it is not yet clear whether any of them intend to do so.
headline: Five trainee gardaí dismissed over ‘Prank’ that saw another garda handcuffed and thrown into a cold shower

text:
The public has reacted with anger to the revelation that Mohammad Al Shaker Al Tamimi, the man charged in connection with the knife attack on children and a crèche worker in Parnell Square in November 2023, is to receive a full psychological assessment funded by the State.

Al Tamimi, an Algerian national, was charged with three counts of attempted murder and one count of assault causing harm following the incident, which left three young children and a woman seriously injured outside a crèche on Parnell Square East in Dublin city centre. The attack prompted widespread public outrage at the time and led to rioting in Dublin city centre on the evening of the incident.

It has now emerged that the accused is to undergo a comprehensive psychological assessment, the cost of which will be borne by the Irish taxpayer through the legal aid system. The development has sparked a fresh wave of public frustration, with many questioning why State resources are being directed towards the accused rather than towards the victims and their families.

Social media users were quick to voice their displeasure at the news, with many pointing out that ordinary Irish citizens often face lengthy waiting lists and significant out-of-pocket expenses when seeking psychological and psychiatric services through the HSE. Critics argued that there is a deep unfairness in a system where an individual charged with such serious offences can access a full psychological assessment at public expense while many people across the country struggle to access basic mental health supports.

The waiting lists for psychological services in Ireland have long been a source of public frustration. According to recent figures, thousands of children and adults remain on waiting lists for mental health assessments and treatment through the public system, with some waiting well over a year for an initial appointment. The contrast between the availability of services for the accused and the experience of ordinary citizens has not been lost on the public.

Several commentators have also raised broader questions about the legal aid system in Ireland, which provides State-funded legal representation and associated services to individuals who cannot afford to pay for their own defence. While the right to a fair trial and legal representation is a cornerstone of the justice system, critics have long argued that the legal aid system is overly generous and lacks sufficient oversight regarding the costs incurred by the State.

It is understood that the psychological assessment has been requested as part of the defence's preparation for the case, which is proceeding through the courts. Such assessments are not uncommon in serious criminal cases and can be used to establish a defendant's mental state at the time of the alleged offence or their fitness to stand trial.

The victims of the Parnell Square attack, including a five-year-old girl who suffered serious injuries, have received widespread public sympathy and support. A number of fundraising efforts were launched in the aftermath of the attack to support the injured children and the crèche worker who intervened to protect them.

The case remains before the courts.
headline: Public not happy that Mohammad Al Shaker Al Tamimi is getting taxpayer-funded full psychological assessment

text:
The controversial ban on TikTok in the United States is set to take effect tomorrow, with the Supreme Court upholding legislation that would force the Chinese-owned social media platform to either divest from its parent company ByteDance or cease operations in the country.

The decision, which has sent shockwaves through the tech world and raised serious questions about digital rights and free expression, will see the app removed from American app stores and effectively cut off from its estimated 170 million users in the US if no last-minute deal is struck.

President-elect Donald Trump has signalled he may seek to delay enforcement of the ban once he takes office, suggesting he could issue an executive order to pause the legislation. However, legal experts have cast doubt on whether such a move would be within his authority, given that the ban was passed with overwhelming bipartisan support in Congress and has now been affirmed by the highest court in the land.

The implications for Ireland and Europe are significant. TikTok's European operations are headquartered in Dublin, where the company employs over 3,000 people. The platform's data centre in the capital handles European user data, and the Irish Data Protection Commission serves as TikTok's lead regulator within the EU under GDPR.

There are concerns that a US ban could embolden calls for similar action in Europe, though EU officials have so far taken a regulatory rather than prohibitive approach to the platform. The Digital Services Act, which came into full effect last year, already imposes stringent obligations on TikTok and other large platforms operating in the European market.

The Irish tech sector will be watching developments closely. Ireland's position as a European hub for major tech companies means any significant shift in the global regulatory landscape has the potential to affect jobs and investment here. Industry figures have warned that an outright ban sets a dangerous precedent that could be replicated by governments around the world seeking to restrict platforms they view as national security threats.

Civil liberties groups on both sides of the Atlantic have expressed alarm at the decision. The Irish Council for Civil Liberties has previously raised concerns about governments using national security justifications to curtail digital freedoms, and the TikTok case is likely to intensify that debate.

ByteDance has consistently denied that it shares user data with the Chinese government or that the platform poses a security risk, but these assurances have failed to satisfy American lawmakers. The company now faces an extraordinarily tight deadline to find a buyer for its US operations or face being shut out of its largest Western market.

For the millions of young people who have built livelihoods and communities on the platform, the ban represents more than a geopolitical chess move. Content creators, small businesses, and musicians who rely on TikTok for their income face an uncertain future, with no guarantee that alternative platforms will offer the same reach or revenue.

As the clock ticks down, all eyes are on Washington to see whether political intervention can delay what now appears to be an inevitable collision between national security concerns and the realities of the modern digital economy.
headline: Stop the clock on TikTok ban – US ban will go ahead tomorrow

text:
Enoch Burke's mother and sister could be facing imprisonment or a substantial fine after a judge found them in contempt of court for disrupting proceedings at the High Court.

Martina Burke and Ammi Burke were found to be in contempt following incidents during a hearing related to the long-running legal saga involving the Burke family and Wilson's Hospital School in Co Westmeath.

The court heard that the pair had engaged in disruptive behaviour during proceedings, with the judge warning that such conduct would not be tolerated. The matter has been adjourned to allow the court to consider what sanctions should be imposed, with the possibility of a custodial sentence or a significant financial penalty remaining firmly on the table.

The Burke family have become well known in Ireland for their numerous legal battles, many of which stem from Enoch Burke's dismissal from his teaching position at Wilson's Hospital School. Burke was originally suspended and later dismissed from the Church of Ireland school after refusing to use the preferred pronouns of a transgender student. He was first jailed in September 2022 for breaching a court order barring him from attending the school, and has since been imprisoned on multiple occasions for contempt of court.

The family have been vocal in their opposition to what they describe as an attack on their religious beliefs, and various members of the Burke family have appeared before the courts on numerous occasions in connection with related matters.

The contempt findings against Martina and Ammi Burke represent the latest chapter in a series of legal proceedings that have drawn significant public attention. Legal experts have noted that contempt of court is treated as a serious matter by the judiciary, with judges possessing broad powers to impose sanctions intended to uphold the authority and dignity of the courts.

The case is expected to return before the court in the coming weeks, when a decision on the appropriate penalty will be handed down. Both women will have the opportunity to address the court before any sanction is imposed, in keeping with standard legal procedure.

The Burke family have consistently maintained that their actions are motivated by sincerely held religious convictions and have shown no indication of stepping back from their various legal disputes. Whether the threat of jail or a hefty fine will alter that stance remains to be seen.
headline: Enoch Burke’s mother and sister may face jail or a hefty fine for contempt of court

text:
A toddler who was scalded by hot coffee during a Ryanair flight sat in agony for more than three hours before the plane landed and she could receive medical treatment, a court has heard.

The young girl, who was just 14 months old at the time of the incident, has been awarded close to €19,000 in damages after the case was heard before Dublin's Circuit Civil Court.

The court heard that the child was sitting on her mother's lap during the flight when a cup of hot coffee was knocked over, spilling onto the toddler and causing scalding burns to her skin. The little girl was left screaming in pain, and despite the efforts of cabin crew, there was little that could be done to properly treat the burns at altitude.

The family were forced to endure the remainder of the flight with the distressed child in considerable discomfort, with no adequate medical facilities available on board the aircraft. It was more than three hours before the plane touched down and the toddler could be brought for proper medical attention.

The child sustained scald burns that required medical treatment upon landing, and the court heard evidence regarding the pain and suffering she endured both during the flight and in the period afterwards as the injuries healed.

Ryanair, which was the defendant in the case, did not contest liability. The airline had previously acknowledged its responsibility in the matter.

The judge awarded damages of close to €19,000 to the child, taking into account the nature of the injuries sustained, the pain and distress suffered during the flight, and the subsequent period of recovery.

The settlement will be held in court until the child reaches the age of 18, as is standard practice in cases involving minors.
headline: Toddler who got scalded by hot coffee on Ryanair flight wins close to €19,000 as court hears she sat in agony for more than three hours

text:
The anti-plantation protests held across three inner-city Dublin locations on Wednesday night have been hailed as a "great success" by organisers, as residents continue to voice their opposition to the housing of asylum seekers and migrants in their communities.

Demonstrations took place simultaneously in East Wall, Sheriff Street and the Five Lamps area, with large crowds gathering despite the cold weather to make their feelings known. Residents say they were not consulted before decisions were made to house significant numbers of international protection applicants in their neighbourhoods, and they have had enough.

The protests, which have become a regular fixture in these communities in recent months, saw locals carrying Irish tricolours and holding placards with slogans such as "Ireland is Full" and "House Our Own First." Organisers said the turnout was among the strongest yet and showed no signs of waning.

"The people of these communities have spoken loud and clear once again," one organiser told The Liberal. "We were told this would fizzle out, that we'd get tired and go home. But the opposite is happening. More and more people are joining us every week because they can see with their own eyes what is happening to their areas."

Residents have repeatedly stressed that their objections are not rooted in racism but in what they describe as a chronic failure by the Government to manage immigration policy and to provide adequate resources for communities already under pressure. Many point to existing problems with housing, healthcare and school places that they say have only been exacerbated by the arrival of large numbers of new residents without any prior engagement with the local population.

The Government has faced sustained criticism over its handling of the accommodation crisis for international protection applicants, with the Department of Integration coming under particular fire for what communities describe as a policy of presenting them with fait accompli decisions. Ministers have repeatedly called on locals to show compassion, but such appeals have done little to quell the anger on the ground.

Critics of the protests, including several opposition TDs and NGOs, have accused some participants of using inflammatory language and have warned about the involvement of far-right agitators. However, protest organisers reject this characterisation entirely, insisting the movement is community-led and organic.

"These are mothers, fathers, grandparents — people who have lived here their whole lives," said one local woman who has attended every protest since they began. "To call us far-right is an insult and it's designed to shut us up. It won't work."

The Gardaí maintained a visible presence at all three locations on Wednesday evening. The protests passed off without any significant incident, with organisers praising participants for their discipline and conduct.

The demonstrations show no sign of abating, with further protests already being planned for the coming weeks. Organisers say they will continue to take to the streets until the Government engages meaningfully with their concerns and reverses what they describe as a policy of "plantation" — the placing of large numbers of migrants into settled communities without consent or consultation.

The situation in Dublin's inner city reflects a broader national trend, with similar protests having taken place in towns and villages across the country in recent months as communities push back against Government accommodation plans for asylum seekers.
headline: Anti plantation protests in East Wall, Sherriff Street and Five Lamps were a “great success” on Wednesday night #IrelandisFull

text:
The gambling landscape in Ireland has undergone a quiet but profound transformation over the past decade, with online casinos emerging as a significant economic force that policymakers, regulators and industry observers are only now beginning to fully reckon with.

Once the preserve of high-street bookmakers and a handful of physical casino operations, the Irish gambling market has shifted decisively towards digital platforms. Irish players now wager billions of euro annually through online casinos, sportsbooks and virtual gaming sites, generating substantial revenue streams that ripple through the broader economy in ways both visible and less immediately apparent.

According to industry estimates, the Irish online gambling market is now worth in excess of €8 billion annually in total wagers, with gross gaming revenue — the amount retained by operators after winnings are paid out — running into hundreds of millions of euro. The sector supports thousands of jobs directly, from software development and customer service roles to compliance and marketing positions, many of them based in Ireland thanks to the country's favourable corporate environment and its established reputation as a European technology hub.

The tax contribution, however, has long been a point of contention. Ireland's betting duty regime, which levies a one per cent tax on turnover for bookmakers and two per cent for betting intermediaries, has been criticised by some economists and advocacy groups as insufficient relative to the scale of the industry. Comparisons with other European jurisdictions — where point-of-consumption taxes on gross gaming revenue can reach 20 per cent or higher — suggest that the Exchequer may be leaving significant revenue on the table.

The passage of the Gambling Regulation Bill, which has wound its way through the Oireachtas over several years, represents the most significant attempt in a generation to modernise Ireland's regulatory framework for the sector. The legislation, which provides for the establishment of a dedicated gambling regulator, Údarás Rialála Cearrbhachais na hÉireann, is intended to bring coherence to a patchwork of outdated laws, some dating back to the Gaming and Lotteries Act of 1956. For online casino operators, the new regime promises both greater legitimacy and greater scrutiny, with enhanced licensing requirements, advertising restrictions and player protection obligations all forming part of the regulatory architecture.

Industry figures broadly welcome the prospect of a well-regulated market, arguing that clear rules create a more stable operating environment and help to distinguish licensed operators from the unregulated offshore platforms that currently capture a not insignificant share of Irish custom. A regulated market, proponents contend, benefits the Exchequer through improved tax compliance, benefits consumers through stronger safeguards, and benefits legitimate operators through reduced competition from unlicensed rivals.

The economic footprint of online casinos extends well beyond the operators themselves. Ireland's thriving technology sector has proven a natural partner for the gambling industry, with Dublin and other urban centres hosting a growing ecosystem of companies specialising in payment processing, cybersecurity, data analytics and software development for gaming platforms. Several multinational gambling technology firms have established European headquarters in Ireland, drawn by the same combination of an educated English-speaking workforce, EU single market access and competitive corporate tax rates that have attracted the broader tech sector.
headline: The Impact of Online Casinos on the Irish Economy: Analysis and Prospects

text:
The spectre of another Christmas behind bars looms large over Enoch Burke, the secondary school teacher who has become the most prominent figure in Ireland's ongoing culture wars, after he made clear he will not comply with a court order requiring him to use a transgender student's preferred pronouns.

Burke, who has already spent more than 400 days in Mountjoy Prison for contempt of court, told reporters outside the Four Courts last week that his position remains unchanged and that he would "never" refer to a male student using "they/them" pronouns, describing any such requirement as a violation of his religious beliefs.

The case, which has dragged on since 2022, centres on Burke's refusal to address a student at Wilson's Hospital School in Multyfarnham, Co Westmeath, by their preferred pronouns. Burke was initially suspended from his teaching post and subsequently jailed for breaching a court order barring him from attending the school or interfering with its operation.

His family, who have been vocal supporters throughout the saga, have again raised concerns that the teacher could find himself spending the festive season in a prison cell. Burke's mother, Martina, has previously described her son's imprisonment as a "grave injustice" and an attack on Christian values.

The Burke family, well known for their deeply held evangelical Christian beliefs, have framed the case as a fundamental question about religious liberty and freedom of conscience. Enoch Burke himself has repeatedly insisted he is being jailed for his beliefs rather than for any act of wrongdoing, telling supporters that no teacher should be compelled to affirm an ideology that contradicts their faith.

However, the courts have consistently maintained that Burke's imprisonment is not about his religious views but about his repeated refusal to comply with lawful court orders. Mr Justice Max Barrett has previously stressed that the teacher "holds the keys to his own cell" and could walk free at any time simply by undertaking to abide by the terms of his suspension.

Legal observers have noted that contempt of court cases of this duration are virtually unprecedented in the history of the State. The question of how long a person can be held for civil contempt — which is designed to coerce compliance rather than punish — has itself become a matter of legal debate.

Wilson's Hospital School, a Church of Ireland boarding school, has largely sought to avoid public comment on the matter, though its board of management has stood by its decision to suspend Burke. The school had introduced a policy of accommodating the transitioning student's wishes, which Burke refused to follow.

The case has drawn significant attention from conservative and religious groups both in Ireland and internationally, with some commentators drawing parallels with similar disputes in the United Kingdom and North America over the intersection of transgender rights and religious freedom.

Burke's supporters argue that the case exposes a fundamental tension in Irish law between anti-discrimination protections and the constitutional right to freedom of religion. Critics, meanwhile, contend that Burke has manufactured his own martyrdom by refusing to comply with reasonable workplace policies and lawful court orders.

As matters stand, Burke faces a return to Mountjoy if he continues to defy the court's instructions.
headline: He’ll never call a boy “they” – Fears grow that Enoch Burke will be in jail again for Christmas

text:
Today's the day! Huge anti-migrant protest to take place in Ballsbridge today for #EastWall to "equal the score" with affluent communities

Organisers behind the ongoing East Wall anti-immigration protests have announced a significant demonstration set to take place in Ballsbridge today, with campaigners vowing to bring their message directly to one of Dublin's most affluent neighbourhoods.

The protest, which has been widely promoted across social media channels under the #EastWall hashtag, is being framed by organisers as an attempt to "equal the score" by highlighting what they describe as a disparity in how asylum seekers and refugees are being housed across different communities in the capital.

Campaigners from working-class areas including East Wall, which has become a focal point for anti-immigration sentiment in recent months, argue that disadvantaged communities have shouldered a disproportionate burden when it comes to accommodating new arrivals, while wealthier parts of Dublin have largely been unaffected.

The decision to stage the protest in Ballsbridge, home to some of the most expensive real estate in the State and the location of several foreign embassies, represents a deliberate escalation in tactics by protest organisers who have until now largely concentrated their efforts in their own localities.

Gardaí are understood to be aware of the planned demonstration and are expected to maintain a visible presence in the area throughout the day. A Garda spokesperson confirmed that appropriate policing arrangements would be in place to facilitate peaceful protest while ensuring public order.

The East Wall protests first gained national attention late last year when residents objected to the use of a former ESB office building on the East Wall Road to house several hundred international protection applicants. The community argued it had not been consulted by the Department of Integration before the facility was opened, a complaint that has since been echoed in towns and villages across the country.

Since then, similar protests have sprung up in locations from Fermoy to Finglas, with demonstrators objecting to what they characterise as a failure by Government to properly plan or consult with local communities before designating accommodation centres for asylum seekers.

The Government has maintained that Ireland has a legal and moral obligation to provide shelter to those seeking international protection, particularly in the context of the ongoing war in Ukraine and rising numbers of arrivals from other conflict zones. Minister for Integration Roderic O'Gorman has repeatedly acknowledged the pressures on the system but has called for communities to respond with compassion rather than hostility.

Critics of the protest movement, including a number of civil society organisations and anti-racism campaigners, have accused some elements within the demonstrations of promoting far-right ideology and xenophobia under the guise of legitimate community concerns. Counter-protests have been organised in several locations in response.

However, many of those involved in the East Wall campaign reject such characterisations, insisting their concerns are rooted in genuine issues around housing, resources and the lack of consultation with communities already under significant pressure.

Today's demonstration in Ballsbridge is expected to draw significant numbers, with organisers using social media platforms to encourage supporters from across Dublin and beyond to attend. The protest is scheduled to begin this afternoon, though the precise route and duration remain unclear.
headline: Today’s the day! Huge anti-migrant protest to take place in Ballsbridge today for #EastWall to “equal the score” with affluent communities

text:
An Irishman in his 30s has been shot dead in Australia, it has been confirmed.

The incident is understood to have occurred in the early hours of this morning local time, with emergency services responding to reports of a shooting at a property in a suburban area.

The Department of Foreign Affairs has confirmed it is aware of the case and is providing consular assistance to the man's family. In a statement, a spokesperson said: "The Department of Foreign Affairs is aware of the case and is providing consular assistance. As this is a consular case, we cannot comment further."

Australian police have launched a major investigation into the fatal shooting, with officers cordoning off the scene and conducting door-to-door enquiries in the surrounding area. Detectives are understood to be reviewing CCTV footage from the vicinity and are appealing for witnesses to come forward.

The identity of the deceased has not yet been publicly released, pending formal identification and notification of all next of kin. It is understood the man had been living in Australia for a number of years.

The Irish community in Australia has been left reeling by the news, with several Irish community organisations expressing shock and offering support to those affected.

A spokesperson for Australian police confirmed that an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the death is ongoing and that no arrests have yet been made. They urged anyone with information to contact local police or Crime Stoppers.

The Taoiseach's office has been contacted for comment.

More to follow.
headline: 🔴BREAKING: An Irishman (30s) has been shot dead in Australia

text:
The funeral of little Matthew Healy, the four-year-old boy who tragically lost his life in a road traffic incident in Waterford earlier this week, will take place tomorrow in the city where he was known and loved by so many.

Matthew, described by his family as a "beautiful, happy little boy" who lit up every room he entered, died following the incident which occurred on Tuesday evening in the Dunmore Road area of the city. The Gardaí and emergency services attended the scene, and the child was rushed to University Hospital Waterford, where he was later pronounced dead.

His heartbroken family have been surrounded by the support of their local community in the days since the tragedy, with neighbours and friends rallying around them during what has been described as an unimaginably difficult time.

According to a notice published on RIP.ie, Matthew's funeral Mass will be celebrated tomorrow at the Church of the Sacred Heart in Waterford city, with burial afterwards. The family have asked that those attending respect their privacy during this deeply painful period, though they have expressed their gratitude for the overwhelming outpouring of sympathy and support they have received.

Local representatives in Waterford have spoken of the profound sense of shock and grief that has enveloped the community. One local councillor described the mood in the area as one of "absolute devastation," noting that the tragedy has touched every family in the neighbourhood.

The Gardaí have confirmed that investigations into the circumstances surrounding the incident remain ongoing, and they have appealed for any witnesses who have not yet come forward to contact Waterford Garda Station.

Tributes have continued to pour in for the young boy, with flowers and soft toys left at the scene of the incident in the days since his passing. Staff at the local crèche Matthew attended described him as a "ray of sunshine" who was adored by his classmates and carers alike.

The Mayor of Waterford extended his deepest sympathies to the Healy family, saying the entire city was mourning alongside them. "There are no words adequate to describe the loss of a child," he said. "Our thoughts and prayers are with Matthew's parents, his family, and all who knew and loved him."

Counselling services have been made available to those affected by the tragedy, with the HSE confirming that supports are in place for the local community and for the emergency service personnel who responded to the incident.
headline: The funeral of little Matthew Healy will take place tomorrow in Waterford

text:
The crisis engulfing RTÉ showed no signs of abating over the weekend as it emerged that external accountants are set to enter the broadcaster's Donnybrook campus this week to begin a forensic examination of its finances.

The move comes amid growing political pressure on the national broadcaster following revelations about undisclosed payments to its former star presenter Ryan Tubridy, with senior figures across all parties demanding full transparency over how the payments were structured and why they were kept off the books.

It is understood that the accountancy firm will be tasked with conducting a root-and-branch review of RTÉ's financial practices, including the use of so-called barter accounts and other mechanisms that allowed significant sums to be moved without appearing in the organisation's published accounts.

The development was confirmed by Government sources who indicated that ministers had lost patience with the drip-feed of information coming from Montrose. The Taoiseach has repeatedly stressed that full accountability is required, while the Tánaiste has described the situation as deeply damaging to public trust in the institution.

TDs from across the Oireachtas have called for those responsible to be held to account, with several members of the Public Accounts Committee signalling that further hearings will be required once the accountants have completed their initial work.

RTÉ's board, which has itself come under intense scrutiny, is expected to cooperate fully with the external review. However, questions remain about the extent of knowledge at board level regarding the off-the-books payments, which are reported to have amounted to hundreds of thousands of euro over several years.

The broadcaster has already seen the departure of its director general, Dee Forbes, and several other senior executives in the wake of the scandal. Staff morale at the organisation is understood to be at an all-time low, with rank-and-file employees expressing anger that the actions of a small number of senior figures have brought the entire organisation into disrepute.

Trade unions representing RTÉ workers have called for protections for staff who had no involvement in the financial irregularities, warning that any cuts to services or jobs as a result of the crisis would be wholly unjust.

The crisis has also reignited the long-running debate about the television licence fee, with some TDs questioning whether the public can be expected to continue funding the broadcaster until a full accounting has been provided. The Government had been preparing legislation to reform the licence fee collection system, but those plans have now been effectively shelved until the current controversy is resolved.

Opposition parties have accused the Government of failing to exercise adequate oversight of RTÉ, pointing out that the broadcaster receives significant public funding and should have been subject to more rigorous scrutiny. Sinn Féin's spokesperson on media called for an independent commission of investigation, arguing that internal reviews and committee hearings alone would not be sufficient to get to the bottom of the matter.

There are also growing calls for the Garda to examine certain aspects of the financial arrangements at RTÉ, though no formal criminal investigation has yet been opened. Legal sources have indicated that the question of whether any criminal offences were committed will depend on the findings of the forensic review now getting under way.
headline: RTE crisis continues as accountants to go in this week

text:
Gardaí have seized a firearm and thousands of euro worth of drugs during a planned search operation at a premises in Dublin.

The raid, which was carried out as part of an ongoing investigation into the sale and supply of controlled substances in the capital, resulted in the discovery of a quantity of suspected cocaine and cannabis herb, understood to be worth several thousand euro pending analysis.

A firearm was also recovered during the course of the search, along with a quantity of ammunition. The weapon has been sent for ballistic examination.

The operation was led by members of the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau (GNDOCB), supported by local detective units and the Armed Support Unit (ASU).

A man in his 30s was arrested at the scene and was detained at a Dublin Garda station under the provisions of Section 2 of the Criminal Justice (Drug Trafficking) Act 1996. He has since been charged in connection with the seizure and is expected to appear before the Dublin District Court at a later date.

Gardaí said the operation forms part of a wider intelligence-led strategy targeting drug dealing networks operating across Dublin. Investigations are ongoing, and further arrests have not been ruled out.

In a statement, a Garda spokesperson said that the seizure represents a significant disruption to the activities of those involved in the supply of illegal drugs in the local community.

Anyone with information is asked to contact their local Garda station or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: Gardai seize firearm and thousands of euros worth of drugs during raid in Dublin

text:
Pat McDonagh, the founder and owner of Supermacs, has said that Irish beef farmers are simply not being paid enough for their produce and has called for a fairer deal for the sector.

Speaking at an event in Galway, the Galway-based businessman said he believed the price being paid to farmers at the factory gate does not reflect the quality of Irish beef or the work that goes into producing it.

"Irish beef is among the best in the world, and yet the farmers who produce it are struggling to make a living," McDonagh said. "That's not right, and it's not sustainable."

McDonagh, who sources Irish beef for his chain of restaurants across the country, said he has long been a supporter of Irish agriculture and believes the supply chain needs to be restructured so that primary producers receive a greater share of the final retail price.

The Supermacs boss said that while consumers are paying significant prices for beef in supermarkets and restaurants, too little of that money is making its way back to the farming families who rear the cattle.

His comments come amid ongoing tensions between beef farmers and meat processors over pricing, with farming organisations such as the IFA and the ICMSA repeatedly calling for greater transparency in how prices are set along the supply chain.

The issue of beef prices has been a source of considerable frustration in rural Ireland for years, with many suckler farmers in particular arguing that the cost of production frequently exceeds what they receive per kilo at the factory. Protests at meat processing plants in 2019 brought the issue to national attention, and farming representatives say the underlying problems have never been adequately addressed.

McDonagh, who built Supermacs from a single outlet in Ballinasloe in 1978 into the largest Irish-owned quick-service restaurant chain in the country, has frequently spoken out on issues affecting rural Ireland and the agri-food sector. He has previously criticised what he described as an over-reliance on multinational chains and has championed the use of locally sourced ingredients throughout his business.

The Department of Agriculture has previously pointed to various support schemes available to beef farmers, including payments under the Common Agricultural Policy and specific environmental and welfare programmes. However, farming groups have argued that direct supports, while welcome, are no substitute for a viable market price.

Minister for Agriculture Charlie McConalogue has said the Government is committed to ensuring a fair price for farmers, but critics argue that progress on the issue has been far too slow.
headline: Supermacs boss says Irish beef farmers are not being paid enough

text:
A gunman has surrendered to police after shooting five people dead inside a bank in the US state of Florida.

The suspect, identified as Zephen Xaver, 21, walked into a SunTrust Bank branch in the city of Sebring and opened fire on Wednesday afternoon before calling the emergency services himself to report the shooting.

When officers from the Sebring Police Department arrived at the scene, Xaver initially barricaded himself inside the building. After negotiations, a SWAT team eventually entered the bank and the gunman surrendered without further incident.

Sebring Police Chief Karl Hoglund confirmed that five people had been killed in the attack but did not immediately release the identities of the victims, saying families were still being notified. All five victims are believed to have been women.

"Today has been a tragic day for the city of Sebring," Chief Hoglund told reporters at a press conference. "We've suffered a significant loss at the hands of a senseless criminal doing a senseless act."

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis travelled to Sebring in the aftermath of the shooting and offered his condolences to the families of those killed.

"This is a terrible day for Sebring, for Highlands County and for the state of Florida," the governor said. "We don't want to ever see an act of violence like this."

The suspect had no apparent connection to the bank and investigators said they were still working to establish a motive for the attack. Xaver had previously worked as a prison guard trainee at a correctional facility but had been employed there for only a brief period.

Sebring, a city of roughly 10,000 people, is located about 130 kilometres south of Orlando in central Florida.

The shooting is the latest in a long series of gun violence incidents across the United States, where the debate over firearms regulation remains one of the most divisive political issues. It comes less than a year after the massacre at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, where 17 people were killed in February 2018.
headline: Gunman surrenders to police after shooting five people dead at a Florida bank

text:
The global number of confirmed coronavirus cases has surpassed two million, with more than 120,000 people now known to have died from the disease, according to the latest figures compiled by Johns Hopkins University.

The grim milestone was reached on Wednesday evening, just two weeks after the worldwide tally passed one million infections, underscoring the rapid spread of the virus despite unprecedented lockdown measures imposed across much of the world.

The United States remains the worst-affected country by a significant margin, accounting for more than 600,000 confirmed cases and in excess of 25,000 deaths. Spain, Italy and France each have recorded more than 100,000 cases, while the United Kingdom has seen a sharp rise in both infections and fatalities in recent days.

Here in Ireland, the Department of Health has continued to report significant daily increases in confirmed cases, with the total number of infections in the State continuing to climb. The HSE has been scaling up testing capacity in recent weeks, though questions remain about whether the system is keeping pace with demand.

Chief Medical Officer Dr Tony Holohan has repeatedly urged the public to continue adhering to the restrictions currently in place, warning that any relaxation of social distancing measures could lead to a dramatic resurgence in cases and place further strain on an already stretched health service.

The Government extended its stay-at-home order and the closure of non-essential businesses in an effort to slow the rate of transmission, with Taoiseach Leo Varadkar acknowledging that the measures have come at an enormous economic and social cost but insisting they remain necessary to protect lives.

Globally, there have been some cautious signs of progress. Several European countries that were among the first to be hit hard by the pandemic have begun to see a tentative flattening of their infection curves, prompting tentative discussions about how and when restrictions might be eased. In Spain, some non-essential workers have been permitted to return to their jobs, while Denmark has begun a phased reopening of schools.

However, the World Health Organisation has cautioned against moving too quickly, with Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus warning that lifting restrictions prematurely could lead to a "deadly resurgence" of the virus. He urged governments to ensure that robust testing and contact-tracing systems are in place before any significant easing of lockdown measures is considered.

The pandemic has also laid bare stark inequalities in health systems across the world, with developing nations particularly vulnerable to the spread of the virus. Concerns are mounting over the potential impact of the disease in parts of Africa, South America and South Asia, where healthcare infrastructure is often limited and social distancing measures are difficult to enforce in densely populated communities.

The economic fallout from the crisis continues to deepen, with the International Monetary Fund warning this week that the world faces its worst downturn since the Great Depression. In Ireland, the Government has committed billions of euro to support workers and businesses affected by the shutdown, including the Temporary Wage Subsidy Scheme and the Pandemic Unemployment Payment, which has been claimed by hundreds of thousands of people who lost their jobs as a result of the restrictions.
headline: Coronavirus: Global number of infections reaches 2m, with over 120,000 deaths so far

text:
Two women who endured years of relentless stalking have spoken publicly about their ordeals in the hope of pushing the Government to strengthen Ireland's laws around harassment and obsessive pursuit.

Speaking to The Liberal, both women described experiences that left them living in constant fear, unable to trust their surroundings, and frustrated by a legal system they say is not fit for purpose when it comes to protecting victims of stalking.

Laura, whose name has been changed to protect her identity, described how a former partner subjected her to a campaign of terror that lasted more than three years. He would appear at her workplace, follow her car, and send dozens of messages a day from different phone numbers. She obtained a safety order through the District Court, but said it made little practical difference to her daily reality.

"He'd stand across the road from my house, just watching. He knew the order meant he couldn't come to the door, so he'd stay just far enough away. The Gardaí were sympathetic, but they told me there wasn't much they could do unless he actually breached the order in a very clear way," she said.

The second woman, Karen, who also asked that her real name not be used, was stalked by a man she had briefly dated. The stalking escalated from unwanted contact on social media to him turning up at her home, her gym, and even her parents' house. She said the experience left her with severe anxiety and post-traumatic stress.

"People don't understand what it does to you. You stop sleeping. You stop going out. You feel like a prisoner in your own life, and the person doing it to you is walking around free as a bird," Karen said.

Both women are calling for the introduction of a standalone stalking offence in Irish law. Currently, stalking is dealt with primarily under Section 10 of the Non-Fatal Offences Against the Person Act 1997, which covers harassment. Campaigners and legal experts have long argued that this provision is inadequate, as it requires a pattern of behaviour to be established and does not fully capture the range of tactics employed by stalkers, including surveillance, cyber-stalking, and the use of tracking devices.

Laura said she wants to see stalking recognised as a distinct and serious crime, with penalties that reflect the devastating impact it has on victims.

"What happened to me wasn't just harassment. It was a sustained, deliberate campaign to control me and make me feel unsafe every single moment of the day. The law needs to call it what it is," she said.

Karen echoed those calls and added that she would like to see the introduction of stalking protection orders, similar to those available in England and Wales since 2019. These civil orders can be sought by Gardaí on behalf of a victim and can impose specific conditions on the accused, such as prohibiting them from contacting the victim or entering certain areas. Breach of such an order would be a criminal offence.

"The safety order system isn't designed for stalking. We need something specific, something that the Gardaí can use quickly to put protections in place before things escalate further," Karen said.
headline: Two brave women spoke about their horrendous stalking experiences and what laws they want changed

text:
A 19-year-old man has died and a 22-year-old woman remains seriously ill in hospital after both are believed to have taken ecstasy tablets on Friday night.

The man, who has not yet been named, was pronounced dead at a hospital in Dublin in the early hours of Saturday morning after becoming unwell at a social gathering in the south of the city. The woman, who was also present at the gathering, was rushed to hospital in a critical condition and is understood to remain in a serious but stable condition.

Gardaí have launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the man's death and have appealed for anyone with information to come forward. A post-mortem examination is expected to be carried out in the coming days, the results of which will determine the course of the Garda investigation.

It is understood that both individuals consumed what they believed to be ecstasy tablets at some point during Friday evening. Emergency services were called to the scene after the man collapsed, and paramedics attempted to revive him before he was transported to hospital by ambulance.

A source close to the investigation confirmed that a quantity of tablets was seized at the scene and has been sent for analysis. Gardaí are working to establish the precise composition of the substance involved and whether a particular batch of tablets may pose a heightened risk to the public.

The HSE has urged anyone who may have consumed similar substances in recent days and who feels unwell to seek immediate medical attention. Drug outreach services have also warned of the dangers of consuming unregulated substances, noting that tablets sold as ecstasy frequently contain unknown and potentially lethal adulterants.

Friends of the deceased man have taken to social media to express their shock and grief, describing him as a "kind and gentle soul" who was well-liked in his local community. His family is being supported by specialist Garda liaison officers.

The incident comes amid ongoing concerns about the strength and unpredictability of illicit drugs circulating in Ireland. Earlier this year, the Health Research Board published data showing a notable increase in drug-related deaths across the State, with MDMA and related substances featuring prominently.

Anyone with information is asked to contact their local Garda station or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: Man (19) dead and woman (22) seriously ill after taking ecstasy on Friday night

text:
The United Kingdom has recorded just over 45,100 new confirmed cases of Covid-19 in the latest 24-hour reporting period, according to official government data released on Tuesday.

The figures, published by the UK's Department of Health and Social Care, come as health authorities across Britain continue to monitor the trajectory of the virus amid ongoing efforts to accelerate booster vaccination programmes.

A further 147 deaths were also reported within 28 days of a positive test, bringing the total number of fatalities recorded on that measure since the beginning of the pandemic to well above 145,000.

Hospital admissions have continued to place significant pressure on the National Health Service, with NHS trusts across England warning of staff shortages driven by illness and self-isolation requirements. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each reported their own figures separately, contributing to the overall UK-wide tally.

The latest infection numbers represent a slight fluctuation on the figures recorded in recent days, with public health officials cautioning against reading too much into single-day data and instead urging the public to focus on broader trends.

British Prime Minister Boris Johnson has faced renewed calls from opposition parties and some public health experts to introduce further restrictions, though Downing Street has so far resisted imposing additional measures beyond the Plan B guidelines currently in place in England.

The situation north of the border in Northern Ireland, which shares a land frontier with the Republic, remains a matter of close attention for Irish public health officials. The Department of Health in Belfast has maintained regular contact with its counterparts in Dublin as both jurisdictions continue to coordinate elements of their pandemic response.

Here in the Republic, health authorities have continued to stress the importance of vaccination and booster uptake as the primary line of defence against severe illness. The HSE's booster programme has been significantly expanded in recent weeks, with additional capacity brought online at vaccination centres nationwide.

The World Health Organisation has repeatedly warned that the pandemic is far from over, with new variants continuing to pose a risk to global public health efforts.
headline: Covid-19: UK reports just over 45,100 new coronavirus infections over the past 24h

text:
Garda checkpoints are now in operation across Donegal as the county moves to Level 3 Covid-19 restrictions, with residents being urged to limit their movements and avoid non-essential travel in and out of the county.

The heightened measures came into effect at midnight, following a sharp rise in coronavirus cases in the north-western county over recent weeks. Donegal has seen its 14-day incidence rate climb well above the national average, prompting the government to act swiftly in imposing the additional restrictions.

Gardaí have confirmed that a significant number of checkpoints have been established on main routes into and out of the county, with officers stopping motorists to determine the nature of their journeys. Those travelling without a reasonable excuse, such as work or medical appointments, are being asked to turn back.

Speaking about the operation, a Garda spokesperson said that the checkpoints are part of a broader policing plan designed to support public health measures and ensure compliance with Level 3 guidelines. The spokesperson added that the vast majority of people have been cooperative and understanding of the need for the restrictions.

Under Level 3, residents of Donegal are being asked not to travel outside the county, while people from other parts of the country are urged not to travel into Donegal unless absolutely necessary. Visits to other households are restricted, and indoor gatherings outside of the home are significantly curtailed.

Restaurants and cafés are permitted to remain open for takeaway and outdoor dining only, while wet pubs must remain closed. Organised indoor events are not permitted, and attendance at weddings is limited to 25 guests.

Local TDs have expressed concern about the impact of the restrictions on businesses and communities in the county, particularly those in the hospitality sector who had only recently begun to recover from the initial lockdown. However, there has been broad acknowledgement that the measures are necessary to prevent a further escalation of cases.

The HSE has ramped up testing capacity in the county, with additional testing centres opened in recent days to meet demand. Contact tracing teams are also working to identify and contain clusters of infection.

Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly said the government would continue to monitor the situation in Donegal closely and that every effort was being made to bring case numbers back under control. He appealed to residents to adhere to the guidelines and to limit their social contacts as much as possible.

The National Public Health Emergency Team is expected to review the situation in the coming weeks to determine whether the restrictions are having the desired effect or whether further measures may be required.

Community leaders in Donegal have called for patience and solidarity, noting that compliance with the restrictions now would give the county the best chance of returning to lower-level measures as quickly as possible. Local organisations have mobilised to support vulnerable residents and those who may be isolated as a result of the renewed restrictions.
headline: Garda checkpoints in force in Donegal as county moves to Level 3 restrictions

text:
The annual Instagram Rich List for 2019 has been released, revealing just how much the world's biggest celebrities are earning from a single sponsored post on the social media platform.

The list, compiled by scheduling tool Hopper HQ, ranks the highest-paid Instagram stars across the globe, and the figures involved are nothing short of staggering.

Reality television star and beauty mogul Kylie Jenner has once again claimed the top spot, earning an estimated $1.27 million (approximately €1.13 million) for each sponsored post she shares with her 141 million followers. The 21-year-old, who was named the world's youngest self-made billionaire by Forbes earlier this year, has seen her per-post earnings rise significantly from last year's figure.

Singer and actress Ariana Grande has climbed the rankings to take second place, commanding around $996,000 (€888,000) per post, while footballer Cristiano Ronaldo sits in third position with an estimated $975,000 (€869,000) per post. Ronaldo remains the most-followed person on the platform, with over 170 million followers.

Kim Kardashian West, who topped the very first Instagram Rich List, now sits in fourth place, earning approximately $910,000 (€811,000) per sponsored post, followed by singer Selena Gomez in fifth with $886,000 (€790,000).

The list underlines the enormous commercial power of social media influencing, which has rapidly become one of the most lucrative forms of advertising available to brands. Industry analysts estimate that the influencer marketing sector is now worth in excess of €6.5 billion globally and is expected to continue growing at pace.

Notably, the list features a significant number of sports stars alongside entertainment figures. Brazilian footballer Neymar, former footballer David Beckham and basketball star LeBron James all feature prominently in the upper reaches of the rankings.

The findings will be of particular interest to Irish businesses and marketing agencies, many of whom have increasingly turned to influencer marketing as a means of reaching younger demographics. While Ireland's own influencer scene operates on a considerably more modest scale, the global figures illustrate the trajectory of the industry and the potential returns available to those who manage to build substantial followings.

Hopper HQ noted that engagement rates, follower counts and the broader commercial profile of each celebrity were all taken into account when compiling the estimated earnings figures. The company also pointed out that many of the highest earners use their Instagram platforms to promote their own business ventures in addition to paid brand partnerships, making the true commercial value of their accounts even higher than the list suggests.
headline: Instagram Rich List 2019 released showing stars who earn most money from each post on their account

text:
Nightclub-goers will be required to purchase their tickets at least one hour before arriving at a venue under new Covid-19 regulations being drawn up by the Government.

The measure is one of several conditions being attached to the reopening of nightclubs, which have been shuttered for the best part of two years since the onset of the pandemic. The requirement is understood to be aimed at reducing queuing and crowding at venue entrances, as well as facilitating contact tracing efforts should an outbreak be linked to a particular premises.

Under the planned rules, walk-ups on the night will not be permitted, meaning punters will have to plan their evenings out well in advance. The ticketing requirement will also effectively place a firm cap on numbers inside venues, as only those who have pre-purchased a ticket will be granted entry.

It is understood that the regulations will also require attendees to present a valid EU Digital Covid Certificate at the door, proving they are either fully vaccinated or have recovered from the virus within the previous six months. Venue operators will be expected to verify certificates against a form of photographic identification.

The hospitality industry has given the proposals a cautious welcome, though some nightclub owners have privately expressed concern about the practicality of enforcing the one-hour ticket rule, particularly for venues that have traditionally relied on spontaneous footfall in the late-night economy.

The Licensed Vintners Association and the Restaurants Association of Ireland have both called for clarity on the specifics of the regulations, with some in the sector warning that overly burdensome requirements could make reopening economically unviable for smaller operators already struggling after nearly two years of enforced closure.

The new rules are expected to be confirmed by the Government in the coming days ahead of the planned reopening date. Ministers have stressed that the measures are designed to allow nightlife to resume in as safe a manner as possible, while acknowledging that the situation remains under constant review given the emergence of the Omicron variant.

Opposition TDs have questioned whether the regulations are workable in practice. Sinn Féin's health spokesperson David Cullinane said the party supported the safe reopening of nightclubs but called on the Government to engage more meaningfully with the sector before imposing conditions that could prove "impossible to implement on the ground."

NPHET is understood to have recommended the ticketing measure as part of a broader suite of public health advice provided to the Government in recent weeks. The public health advisory body has consistently urged caution around the resumption of activities involving large numbers of people in indoor settings, where the risk of transmission is considered to be highest.
headline: Covid-19: Punters will be forced to buy tickets for nightclubs at least one hour prior to arriving at the door

text:
Dr Tony Holohan has said that the next two weeks will be critical in determining whether the country can begin to ease Covid-19 restrictions, adding that he is growing increasingly concerned about the trajectory of the virus.

The Chief Medical Officer made the comments at this evening's press briefing from the Department of Health, where he urged the public to continue to adhere to the measures currently in place.

Dr Holohan said that while there had been some encouraging signs in recent weeks, the situation remained fragile and that any premature relaxation of restrictions could undo the progress that has been made.

"The next two weeks are going to be very important in terms of determining whether we are in a position to ease restrictions," he said. "I have to say, I am increasingly concerned about some of the trends we are seeing."

He pointed to a number of indicators that were causing him worry, including the rate of close contacts per confirmed case, which he said had been rising in recent days. He also expressed concern about the level of socialisation that appeared to be taking place, warning that people may be letting their guard down too early.

The CMO said that the behaviour of the public over the coming fortnight would be the decisive factor in whether NPHET would be in a position to recommend any easing of the current measures to Government.

It comes as the Department of Health confirmed a further number of cases of Covid-19 in the Republic this evening. The HSE has continued to ramp up testing capacity across the country, with a number of testing centres now operational nationwide.

Dr Holohan acknowledged the enormous sacrifice that people across the country have been making in adhering to the restrictions but stressed that now was not the time for complacency.

"I know this is extremely difficult for people. I know the restrictions are having an enormous impact on people's lives, on their livelihoods, on their mental health. But we need people to stay the course," he said.

He added that the experience of other countries had shown how quickly the situation could deteriorate if restrictions were lifted too soon, and he urged people to continue to follow public health advice by staying at home, washing their hands regularly, and maintaining social distancing when they do need to leave the house.

The Taoiseach has previously indicated that any decision on easing restrictions would be guided by the advice of the public health experts, and that the Government would take a cautious and phased approach to reopening society and the economy.
headline: Holohan says that the next two weeks will determine on whether we can ease restrictions, says he’s increasingly concerned

text:
Residents across Kildare, Offaly and Laois are being urged to exercise heightened vigilance following a notable increase in Covid-19 cases across the three counties in recent days.

Public health officials have expressed concern at the rising numbers, warning that the trend could worsen if people do not adhere strictly to existing guidelines on hand hygiene, social distancing and the wearing of face coverings.

The National Public Health Emergency Team confirmed the uptick in cases, with a significant proportion linked to clusters in workplaces and community settings. Several meat processing plants in the midlands region have been identified as particular areas of concern, with outbreaks affecting workers and their close contacts.

Acting Chief Medical Officer Dr Ronan Glynn said the situation was being monitored closely and appealed to people living in the affected counties to limit their social interactions as much as possible.

"We are asking people in Kildare, Offaly and Laois to be particularly careful at this time," Dr Glynn said. "If you are living in these counties, please pay close attention to any symptoms you may develop and contact your GP promptly if you have any concerns."

The HSE has ramped up testing capacity in the region, with additional resources deployed to facilitate widespread screening of workers in affected facilities. Contact tracing teams are working to identify and reach all close contacts of confirmed cases as quickly as possible.

Local TDs have called on the Government to ensure adequate supports are in place for communities and businesses that may be impacted by any restrictions that could follow. There are growing fears that localised measures may be necessary if the trajectory of cases does not improve in the coming days.

The Taoiseach Micheál Martin said the Government was monitoring developments carefully and would not hesitate to take action if required to protect public health.
