"We have always said that we would act swiftly and decisively where clusters emerge," the Taoiseach said. "The situation in these three counties is a reminder that this virus has not gone away and that we must all remain vigilant."

The Irish Farmers' Association and trade union representatives have both called for enhanced protections for workers in the meat processing sector, including improved social distancing measures on factory floors and better access to testing.

Public health authorities are reminding people across the three counties to avoid large gatherings, to work from home where possible, and to restrict their movements if they develop any symptoms associated with the virus, including a cough, fever, shortness of breath or loss of taste or smell.

The coming days are expected to prove critical in determining whether the outbreaks can be brought under control through targeted interventions or whether broader restrictions will be required for the region.
headline: Kildare, Offaly and Laois warned to be on alert following rise in Covid-19 cases

text:
More than 1.4 million people across the State are set to receive a welcome cash boost tomorrow as a series of social welfare increases come into effect, with some recipients in line to receive double payments.

The increases, which were announced as part of Budget 2025, will see a €12 weekly rise applied across a range of social welfare payments from tomorrow. The boost applies to recipients of jobseeker's payments, disability allowance, carer's allowance, the State pension, and a host of other weekly payments administered by the Department of Social Protection.

For pensioners, the increase means the maximum weekly rate of the contributory State pension will rise to €289.30, while the non-contributory pension will increase to €266. The qualified adult rate for pensioners aged 66 and over will also see a corresponding increase.

Those in receipt of jobseeker's allowance, jobseeker's benefit, disability allowance, and illness benefit will see their maximum weekly personal rate rise to €232.

Some recipients are set to benefit from what effectively amounts to a double payment, as the increases are being backdated to take account of the period since the Budget was announced. This means certain claimants will see a larger-than-usual payment landing in their accounts tomorrow as arrears are included alongside the new weekly rate.

Carers are among those set to benefit significantly, with the weekly rate of carer's allowance also increasing by €12. The income disregard thresholds for carer's allowance were also adjusted, meaning more people may now qualify for the payment.

The Department of Social Protection confirmed that the increases will be applied automatically and that recipients do not need to take any action to receive the higher rate.

Minister for Social Protection Heather Humphreys had previously described the Budget package as one that would provide meaningful support to those who need it most, particularly pensioners and carers.

Working family payment thresholds have also been adjusted upward, which is expected to bring additional families into the net of the support or increase the amount received by those already claiming.

The increases come at a time when many households continue to grapple with the elevated cost of living, with the price of groceries, energy, and housing remaining a significant burden for families and individuals on fixed incomes across the country.
headline: 1.4 million people will receive cash boost tomorrow with some receiving double social welfare payments

text:
The Government has come under fire after launching what it described as a "foreign language" information campaign aimed at boosting Covid-19 vaccine uptake among foreign nationals living in Ireland, with critics questioning why the initiative took so long to materialise.

Figures obtained by the HSE indicate that vaccination rates among non-Irish nationals remain significantly lower than the general population, with particular concern around communities where English is not the primary language spoken at home. The disparity has prompted health officials to roll out translated materials and targeted outreach in a bid to close the gap.

The campaign will see vaccine information made available in a range of languages including Polish, Romanian, Portuguese, Arabic, and Mandarin, among others. The HSE confirmed it is also working with community organisations and religious groups to disseminate the materials and encourage uptake in areas where foreign nationals are concentrated.

A Government spokesperson said the initiative recognises that language barriers have played a significant role in lower vaccination rates among migrant communities and that the campaign is designed to ensure "nobody is left behind" in the national vaccination programme.

However, opposition TDs were quick to criticise the timing of the rollout, arguing that multilingual health advice should have been a feature of the vaccination programme from the very beginning. Social Democrats TD Holly Cairns said it was "frankly astonishing" that it had taken this long for the Government to address what she called an obvious gap in public health communications.

"We have known from the outset that Ireland is a diverse, multilingual country. The idea that translated materials are only now being produced beggars belief," she said.

Sinn Féin's health spokesperson David Cullinane echoed the criticism, telling the Dáil that the delay demonstrated a lack of forward planning on the part of the Government and the HSE. He called for a more comprehensive strategy that goes beyond simply translating existing materials and instead engages directly with community leaders and healthcare workers embedded in migrant communities.

Integration advocates have also raised concerns that the framing of the campaign risks further stigmatising foreign nationals at a time when anti-immigrant sentiment has been on the rise. Several organisations working with migrant communities pointed out that low vaccine uptake is not unique to foreign nationals and that socioeconomic factors, access to healthcare, and historical distrust of state institutions all play a role.

Dr Fidèle Mutwarasibo, who has long advocated for migrant inclusion in Irish public policy, noted that many foreign nationals in Ireland work in sectors such as meat processing, direct provision, and healthcare where exposure to the virus has been disproportionately high. He said any outreach effort must be accompanied by practical measures, including walk-in clinics in accessible locations and flexible appointment times for those in precarious employment.

The HSE confirmed that pop-up vaccination clinics are being planned for areas with high concentrations of foreign-born residents, including parts of Dublin, Cork, and several midlands towns. Officials said they are also exploring the use of social media platforms popular among specific diaspora communities to spread the message.

The Department of Health said it is monitoring the data closely and will adjust the campaign as needed.
headline: Government launch “foreign language” covid advice as there’s a low uptake in vaccines with foreign nationals

text:
President Donald Trump has declared a national emergency in the United States as the country scrambles to contain the spread of Covid-19, freeing up billions of dollars in federal funding to combat the growing crisis.

Speaking from the Rose Garden at the White House on Friday afternoon, the President said the declaration would open up $50 billion in emergency relief funds and give states and territories access to additional resources to fight the pandemic.

"To unleash the full power of the federal government in this effort today, I am officially declaring a national emergency," Mr Trump told reporters. "Two very big words."

The move comes as the number of confirmed coronavirus cases in the US continues to climb sharply, with more than 1,600 infections and over 40 deaths recorded across the country at the time of the announcement. The World Health Organisation declared the outbreak a pandemic earlier this week.

Mr Trump said the emergency declaration would allow the government to waive a number of federal regulations and bureaucratic hurdles, including giving hospitals greater flexibility in how they treat patients. He also announced a partnership with private sector companies to dramatically expand testing capacity, which has been a source of significant criticism of the administration's response to date.

Major US retailers including Walmart, Target and Walgreens will make portions of their car parks available as drive-through testing sites, the President said, though details on the timeline for rolling out these facilities remained sparse.

The declaration marks a significant shift in tone from the President, who had for weeks downplayed the severity of the outbreak, comparing it to seasonal flu and predicting the virus would simply disappear. As recently as last week, Mr Trump suggested the number of cases in the US was "going very substantially down, not up."

The emergency declaration was broadly welcomed on both sides of the political aisle, though Democratic leaders in Congress said it was long overdue and that the administration had squandered valuable weeks in its response.

The developments in Washington come as Ireland continues to grapple with its own response to the virus. The Government here announced the closure of all schools, colleges and childcare facilities earlier this week, with the Taoiseach Leo Varadkar making the announcement from Washington DC, where he had travelled for the traditional St Patrick's Day engagements.

Stock markets on Wall Street rallied sharply following Mr Trump's announcement, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average surging more than 1,500 points in the final hour of trading, though analysts cautioned that significant volatility was likely to continue in the weeks ahead.

The emergency declaration gives the Federal Emergency Management Agency, known as FEMA, a central role in coordinating the government's response, a move that mirrors the approach taken during natural disasters such as hurricanes and wildfires.

Mr Trump also said he would be asking every hospital in the country to activate its emergency preparedness plan, as health officials warned that the US healthcare system could come under severe strain if the virus continues to spread at its current pace.

The President said he had also taken a test for the coronavirus himself, following concerns about his contact with members of a Brazilian delegation at his Mar-a-Lago resort last weekend, several of whom subsequently tested positive. Results of the test were expected in the coming days, the White House said.
headline: BREAKING: Coronavirus – President Donald Trump declares national emergency in the United States

text:
The British fashion retailer LK Bennett has entered into administration, putting approximately 500 jobs at risk across the United Kingdom as the brand becomes the latest high street name to succumb to challenging trading conditions.

Ernst & Young has been appointed as administrator for the luxury womenswear chain, which operates 41 stores across the UK. The company, known for its shoes, dresses and accessories, has long been a favourite of the British royal family and was famously worn by Catherine, Princess of Wales, on numerous public engagements.

The brand's founder, Linda Bennett, who launched the company in 1990 with a single store in Wimbledon, had attempted to buy the business back in recent months but was ultimately unable to secure a deal that would have kept the retailer afloat.

Joint administrator Dan Hurd of Ernst & Young said the firm would continue to trade the business while seeking a buyer, adding that all stores would remain open for the time being. He urged interested parties to come forward as quickly as possible.

The collapse marks another blow for the British high street, which has seen a string of well-known retailers fall into difficulty in recent years amid rising costs, shifting consumer habits and the relentless growth of online shopping. Names such as Debenhams, Topshop and House of Fraser have all faced similar fates in what commentators have described as a retail apocalypse.

LK Bennett had attempted to restructure its operations in previous years, closing a number of underperforming stores and investing in its online presence, but the measures proved insufficient to reverse the company's fortunes.

The retailer does not operate any standalone stores in Ireland, though its products have been available through selected stockists and online. It remains unclear whether any Irish-based suppliers or partners will be affected by the administration process.

Industry analysts said the brand's positioning in the mid-to-premium market segment left it particularly vulnerable, as consumers increasingly gravitated towards either budget-friendly fast fashion or ultra-luxury labels, leaving those in the middle ground struggling to justify their price points.

Trade unions have called on the administrators to prioritise the interests of employees, many of whom now face an uncertain future. Staff have been told to continue reporting for work as normal while the search for a potential buyer continues.
headline: Fashion retailer LK Bennett enters into administration, 500 UK jobs on the line

text:
Germany, France, and Italy have all moved to temporarily suspend the rollout of the AstraZeneca Covid-19 vaccine amid growing concerns over reports of blood clotting in some recipients, dealing a significant blow to Europe's already troubled vaccination programme.

The decisions, announced in quick succession on Monday, came despite the European Medicines Agency (EMA) insisting that there was no indication the vaccine was responsible for the clotting events and that the benefits of the jab continued to outweigh any potential risks.

German Health Minister Jens Spahn said the decision to pause the rollout was taken on the advice of the country's vaccine regulator, the Paul Ehrlich Institute, which called for further investigation into a small number of cases involving blood clots in the brains of recently vaccinated individuals. Spahn described the move as a "precautionary measure" and stressed that the suspension was temporary in nature.

French President Emmanuel Macron confirmed shortly afterwards that France would follow suit, suspending use of the AstraZeneca vaccine for at least a day pending a ruling from the EMA, which was expected to issue updated guidance on Thursday. Italy's medicines regulator, AIFA, also announced a precautionary ban on the vaccine across the country.

The three nations join a growing list of European countries that have paused their use of the Oxford-AstraZeneca jab, including Denmark, Norway, Ireland, the Netherlands, and Bulgaria. Ireland's National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC) recommended a temporary suspension of the vaccine here on Sunday, a move that was quickly adopted by the HSE.

The EMA said it was reviewing reports of blood clotting disorders but maintained its position that the number of thromboembolic events reported in vaccinated individuals was no greater than the number observed in the general population. The agency noted that as of 10 March, 30 cases of thromboembolic events had been reported among nearly five million people who had received the AstraZeneca vaccine across the European Economic Area.

AstraZeneca itself issued a statement pointing to an internal review of safety data covering more than 17 million people vaccinated across the EU and the United Kingdom, which it said had found no evidence of an increased risk of pulmonary embolism, deep vein thrombosis, or thrombocytopenia.

The World Health Organisation urged countries not to halt their vaccination campaigns, with spokesperson Margaret Harris telling reporters that there was no link established between the vaccine and the reported clotting events. "We do not want people to panic," she said, adding that the WHO's advisory committee on vaccine safety was reviewing the available data.

The suspensions have nonetheless cast a further shadow over Europe's vaccination drive, which has already faced criticism for its slow pace compared to the programmes in the United Kingdom, Israel, and the United States. The moves are also likely to deepen public hesitancy around the AstraZeneca vaccine, which had already faced scepticism in several EU member states over questions about its efficacy in older age groups.
headline: Covid-19: Germany, France, and Italy have temporarily halted administration of the AstraZeneca vaccine due to increasing reports of blood clotting

text:
Met Éireann has issued a Status Orange rainfall warning for three counties, with significant accumulations expected to cause disruption before the alert lifts at noon today.

The warning, which covers counties Cork, Kerry and Waterford, came into effect in the early hours of this morning and is set to remain in place until 12pm. Forecasters have cautioned that rainfall totals of between 40mm and 60mm are expected in some areas, with higher amounts possible on elevated ground.

Met Éireann has warned that the heavy and persistent rain brings a risk of localised flooding, difficult driving conditions and possible river flooding in vulnerable catchments. Road users have been urged to exercise caution, particularly on secondary routes where surface water may accumulate quickly.

A Status Yellow rainfall warning is also in place for much of the rest of Munster and parts of south Leinster, though the conditions are not expected to be as severe as in the three counties covered by the Orange alert.

Local authorities in the affected areas have said their emergency response crews are on standby and have been clearing drains and culverts in preparation for the worst of the rainfall. Cork City Council confirmed that flood defence measures along the River Lee have been activated as a precautionary step.

The Gardaí have appealed to motorists to slow down and to avoid driving through flooded roads, noting that even relatively shallow standing water can be deeper than it appears and can cause vehicles to lose control.

AA Roadwatch has reported a number of spot flooding incidents on routes in Co Kerry and west Cork this morning, with some minor road closures already in effect. Motorists have been advised to check local conditions before setting out and to allow extra time for journeys.

ESB Networks has said it is monitoring the situation and has crews available to respond should power outages occur as a result of the adverse weather. Customers experiencing supply issues have been encouraged to report them through the PowerCheck app or by calling 1800 372 999.

Met Éireann has indicated that conditions are expected to improve through the afternoon as the band of rain clears eastward, with drier and brighter spells developing from the west. However, forecasters have noted that river levels may continue to rise even after the rain eases, and communities in flood-prone areas should remain vigilant.

The rainfall comes after what has already been a notably wet spell across much of the south and southwest, with some weather stations recording well above average precipitation for the month so far. Soil saturation levels remain high, increasing the risk of surface water flooding even from moderate additional rainfall.

Further updates are expected from Met Éireann later this morning, with the possibility that warnings could be extended or adjusted depending on how the situation develops.
headline: Status Orange warning for heavy rain in place for three counties until noon

text:
Kyle Rittenhouse has been found not guilty on all charges after shooting dead two men and wounding a third during Black Lives Matter protests in Kenosha, Wisconsin in the summer of 2020.

The jury returned its verdict on Friday after close to four days of deliberations, clearing the now 18-year-old of two counts of homicide, one count of attempted homicide, and two counts of recklessly endangering safety.

Rittenhouse, who was 17 at the time of the shootings, broke down in tears and collapsed as the verdict was read out in the Kenosha County Circuit Court. The young man had maintained throughout the trial that he acted in self-defence after being attacked by rioters during unrest that gripped the city following the police shooting of Jacob Blake, a Black man, in August 2020.

The case became one of the most politically divisive trials in recent American history, drawing sharp reactions from both sides of the political spectrum. Supporters of Rittenhouse argued he was a young man exercising his right to bear arms and defend himself, while critics contended he was a vigilante who had no business travelling across state lines with a semi-automatic rifle to insert himself into a volatile situation.

During the protests, which saw widespread property destruction and looting in Kenosha, Rittenhouse armed himself with an AR-15-style rifle and said he had gone to the city to protect businesses and offer medical aid. On the night of 25 August 2020, he shot and killed Joseph Rosenbaum, 36, and Anthony Huber, 26, and wounded Gaige Grosskreutz, now 28.

The prosecution had argued that Rittenhouse was the aggressor who had created a dangerous situation by bringing a powerful weapon into an already tense environment. However, the defence successfully made the case that each of the three men Rittenhouse shot had posed an imminent threat to his life, with video evidence playing a central role in the proceedings.

Rosenbaum was shown on footage chasing Rittenhouse across a car park before the teenager opened fire. Huber had struck Rittenhouse with a skateboard as he lay on the ground, and Grosskreutz admitted under cross-examination that he had pointed his own handgun at Rittenhouse before he was shot in the arm.

Judge Bruce Schroeder, who presided over the trial, had already dismissed a charge relating to Rittenhouse's possession of the weapon as a minor, following a legal challenge by the defence team.

The verdict prompted immediate reaction across the United States. Former President Donald Trump praised Rittenhouse, saying the verdict proved he had acted in self-defence, while President Joe Biden said he stood by the jury's decision despite saying the outcome left many Americans "feeling angry and concerned."

Protests erupted in several American cities in the hours following the acquittal, with demonstrators expressing outrage at the outcome. Civil rights organisations condemned the verdict, with some arguing it set a dangerous precedent for armed individuals attending protests.
headline: ?BREAKING: Not guilty – Kyle Rittenhouse cleared of all charges after he shot dead two men while defending himself during Black Lives Matter protests

text:
The Brexit Withdrawal Agreement has passed through the House of Commons with a comfortable majority, all but guaranteeing that Britain will formally leave the European Union on January 31, 2020, bringing to a close more than three and a half years of political turmoil that has consumed Westminster and reverberated across the Irish Sea.

MPs voted 330 to 231 in favour of the Withdrawal Agreement Bill at second reading, handing Prime Minister Boris Johnson a decisive victory and delivering on his promise to "get Brexit done." The margin of victory reflects the commanding majority Johnson secured in last week's general election, which saw the Conservatives win 365 seats and effectively neutralise the parliamentary arithmetic that had thwarted his predecessor Theresa May at every turn.

The bill will now proceed through its remaining parliamentary stages in the new year, though with such a substantial majority there is little prospect of it being derailed. Johnson has set an ambitious timetable, aiming to have the legislation fully passed before the January 31 deadline.

For Ireland, the passage of the bill brings a measure of certainty but also raises fresh questions about what comes next. The Withdrawal Agreement includes the revised Northern Ireland protocol, which will see the North remain aligned with EU single market rules for goods, effectively creating a regulatory border in the Irish Sea. The protocol was designed to avoid a hard border on the island of Ireland, a key priority for the Irish Government throughout the negotiations.

Taoiseach Leo Varadkar welcomed the progress, noting that the passage of the agreement provides clarity after years of uncertainty. However, he cautioned that the more difficult phase of negotiations lies ahead, with the future relationship between the UK and the EU yet to be hammered out. Under the terms of the Withdrawal Agreement, a transition period will run until December 31, 2020, during which the UK will continue to follow EU rules while both sides attempt to negotiate a comprehensive trade deal.

Trade experts and senior EU figures have warned that negotiating such a deal within eleven months is extraordinarily ambitious, if not unrealistic. Johnson has insisted he will not seek an extension to the transition period, a pledge he has now written into law, raising the spectre of another cliff-edge scenario at the end of next year.

Tánaiste Simon Coveney said the Irish Government would be working closely with the European Commission and fellow member states to ensure that Irish interests, particularly in areas such as agriculture, fisheries, and trade, are protected in the next phase. Ireland exports billions of euro worth of goods to the UK each year, and any disruption to trade flows could have significant consequences for the Irish economy.

The Democratic Unionist Party, which had opposed the Withdrawal Agreement due to the Northern Ireland protocol, voted against the bill. DUP leader Arlene Foster reiterated her party's concerns that the protocol would create barriers between Northern Ireland and the rest of the United Kingdom, undermining the constitutional integrity of the union. However, with Johnson's comfortable majority, the DUP's opposition carried none of the leverage it had wielded in the previous parliament, when Theresa May depended on the party's ten MPs for her working majority.
headline: Brexit Withdrawal Agreement breezes through Parliament, meaning Britain will likely leave the EU for good on January 31, 2020

text:
Gardaí have launched an investigation after the body of a fisherman was recovered from the waters of Killybegs Harbour in Co. Donegal.

The man's remains were discovered in the harbour earlier today, with emergency services called to the scene shortly afterwards. The deceased has been identified locally as a man in his middle years who was well known in the fishing community in the area.

The body was recovered from the water by members of the emergency services and taken to Letterkenny University Hospital, where a post-mortem examination is expected to be carried out in due course.

Gardaí at Killybegs Garda Station are leading the investigation into the circumstances surrounding the man's death. While foul play is not suspected at this stage, Gardaí have said they are keeping all lines of enquiry open pending the results of the post-mortem.

The scene at the harbour was preserved for a period to allow for a technical examination to be carried out by Garda forensic specialists.

Killybegs, one of Ireland's most prominent fishing ports, is home to a large fleet of trawlers and the fishing industry remains central to the town's economy and identity. The news of the man's death has sent shockwaves through the tight-knit community, with local representatives expressing their sympathies to the deceased's family.

Local councillors and community figures have spoken of the deep sadness felt across the town and wider Donegal.

Gardaí are appealing to anyone who may have information, or who may have been in the vicinity of Killybegs Harbour in recent days and noticed anything unusual, to contact Killybegs Garda Station or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: Gardai launch probe after the body of a fisherman is recovered from Killybegs Harbour in Co. Donegal

text:
Malaysian authorities are expected to release the results of a post mortem examination carried out on the body of Nora Quoirin later today, more than a week after the Irish-French teenager went missing from a jungle resort in the southeast Asian country.

The body of the 15-year-old, who had special needs, was discovered on Tuesday near the Dusun eco-resort in Negeri Sembilan state, roughly 2.5 kilometres from where she had been staying with her family. Malaysian police confirmed that the remains were positively identified as Nora's through fingerprint analysis.

Nora, who was born in London and held both Irish and French citizenship, disappeared from her family's accommodation at the resort on 3 August, a day after arriving for what was meant to be a two-week holiday. Her family, including her mother Meabh Quoirin, who is originally from Belfast, had reported her missing after discovering she was not in her bedroom and that a window had been left open.

The teenager's disappearance prompted a massive search operation involving hundreds of personnel, including members of the Malaysian police, fire and rescue teams, and local volunteers. Specialist trackers and helicopters equipped with thermal imaging technology were also deployed in the dense jungle terrain surrounding the resort.

Malaysian police have been treating the case as a missing persons investigation, though Nora's family have consistently maintained that they believe she was abducted, stating that the teenager would not have wandered off on her own due to her learning and developmental disabilities.

The Lucie Blackman Trust, which has been assisting the Quoirin family, confirmed that the post mortem was being carried out at a hospital in Seremban and that results were anticipated to be made public later in the day. The outcome of the examination is expected to shed light on the cause and circumstances of Nora's death, which remain unclear.

The case has attracted significant attention both in Ireland and internationally, with the Tánaiste and Minister for Foreign Affairs Simon Coveney confirming that the Irish Embassy in Malaysia has been providing consular assistance to the family. French authorities have also been involved, given Nora's dual nationality.

The family released a statement following the discovery of Nora's body, describing her as "the heart of our family" and expressing devastation at the outcome of the search.

"Nora has been the heart of our family. She is the most gentle, innocent and loving person in our lives," the family said. "Her presence and love define our family."

The Irish Department of Foreign Affairs has said it continues to provide all possible consular assistance and that its thoughts are with the Quoirin family at this deeply difficult time.
headline: Malaysian authorities to release results of Nora Quoirin’s post mortem later today

text:
The medical devices giant Stryker has confirmed that approximately 40 jobs are to be lost at its manufacturing facility in Cork, in what the company has described as part of a restructuring of its operations.

The announcement, which was confirmed on Wednesday, has come as a blow to workers at the plant, many of whom have been employed there for a number of years. Staff were informed of the decision at a meeting earlier in the day.

Stryker, which is one of the world's largest medical technology companies, has had a significant presence in Cork for several decades. The American multinational employs thousands of people across multiple sites in Ireland, with operations in Cork, Limerick, and Carrigtwohill among other locations.

In a statement, the company said the decision was not taken lightly and that it would work closely with affected employees to provide supports during the transition period. It is understood that redundancy packages are being offered to those impacted.

The job losses are understood to be linked to a reorganisation of certain production lines and operational efficiencies rather than any broader pullback from the Irish market. The company stressed that it remains committed to its Irish operations and to continued investment in the country.

Local representatives have expressed concern about the impact on the workers and their families. It is expected that efforts will be made to redeploy some of the affected staff to other roles within the company where possible.

Tánaiste and Minister for Enterprise Micheál Martin is understood to have been briefed on the situation. The IDA, which has long supported Stryker's investment in Ireland, said it is engaging with the company.

Trade union sources indicated that they would be seeking the best possible terms for those facing redundancy and called on the company to ensure all proper consultation processes are followed.

Stryker currently employs in the region of 4,000 people across its Irish operations, making it one of the largest employers in the medical devices sector in the country. Ireland has long been a hub for the medtech industry, with Cork playing a particularly prominent role in attracting and retaining multinational investment in the sector.
headline: Job losses announced at the Stryker plant in Cork, about 40 people are to lose their jobs

text:
Dr Ronan Glynn, Acting Chief Medical Officer, has said that just 3% of Covid-19 cases currently being recorded in the State are among those aged 65 and over, a figure he described as a testament to the success of the vaccination programme among older and more vulnerable cohorts.

Speaking at a press briefing this evening, Dr Glynn said the dramatic shift in the age profile of those contracting the virus demonstrated the clear impact of the rollout, which has now seen the vast majority of over 65s fully vaccinated.

"When we look at where the disease is now, it is overwhelmingly in younger age groups," Dr Glynn said. "Just 3% of cases are in the over 65s, and that is a very significant change from where we were earlier in the pandemic."

He noted that at earlier stages of the crisis, older people had accounted for a far greater proportion of confirmed infections, hospitalisations and deaths. The shift, he said, was directly attributable to the high uptake of vaccines among those age groups.

However, Dr Glynn cautioned against complacency, warning that the virus continued to circulate at significant levels in the community, particularly among younger people who had not yet been offered or had not yet taken up the offer of vaccination.

He urged those who were eligible and had not yet come forward to do so as soon as possible, stressing that vaccination remained the most effective tool available in reducing the impact of the disease.

The latest figures come as the National Public Health Emergency Team continues to monitor the spread of the Delta variant, which has become the dominant strain in Ireland and is known to be significantly more transmissible than previous variants.

Dr Glynn acknowledged that the coming weeks would be critical as the country continued to reopen, and he appealed to the public to continue to follow basic public health advice, including mask-wearing, hand hygiene and maintaining social distance where possible.

The HSE's vaccination programme has been proceeding at pace in recent weeks, with registration now open to all adults aged 18 and over. Latest figures indicate that more than 4.5 million doses have been administered to date, with the programme on track to meet its targets for the summer months.
headline: Dr Ronan Glynn says just 3% of Covid-19 cases are in the over 65s

text:
Leo Varadkar has put paid to any lingering hopes Micheál Martin may have harboured of stitching together a grand coalition, declaring in no uncertain terms that Fine Gael is heading for the opposition benches.

The outgoing Taoiseach, who led his party through a bruising general election that saw Fine Gael haemorrhage seats, made the announcement in what amounted to a decisive intervention in the fevered post-election horse-trading. His statement effectively torpedoes the Fianna Fáil leader's ambitions of reassembling something resembling the outgoing coalition arrangement, albeit with new junior partners.

Varadkar's declaration will come as a bitter blow to Martin, who has been quietly working the phones in an effort to build a viable coalition majority. The Fianna Fáil leader, fresh from topping the poll in Cork South-Central, had been understood to favour a continuation of the so-called "grand coalition" model that saw the two traditional Civil War parties govern together since 2020 — an arrangement that proved historically unpopular with the electorate of both parties.

But Varadkar, reading the room rather more astutely than his counterpart across the aisle, has evidently concluded that Fine Gael's interests are better served by a spell in opposition. The logic is not difficult to follow. After more than a decade in government — first under Enda Kenny, then under Varadkar himself, and latterly in the rotating Taoiseach arrangement with Martin — Fine Gael is a party in desperate need of renewal. Continuing to prop up a Fianna Fáil-led administration would likely only accelerate the erosion of its support base.

The move also carries a certain strategic ruthlessness. By consigning Fine Gael to opposition, Varadkar — or more precisely, whoever succeeds him as party leader — can sit back and watch Martin attempt to cobble together a workable majority from the fractured Dáil arithmetic. That is no small task. The numbers as they stand would likely require Fianna Fáil to court Sinn Féin, the Labour Party, the Social Democrats, or some combination of Independents, each option carrying its own political toxicity.

For Martin, the implications are severe. A grand coalition was always the path of least resistance — ideologically undemanding, operationally familiar, and requiring minimal concessions on policy. Without Fine Gael, every available coalition formula becomes exponentially more complicated and more politically costly.

There is, of course, a delicious irony in the spectacle. For years, critics of the Fianna Fáil-Fine Gael coalition argued that it was an affront to democratic accountability, denying voters a meaningful choice between the two largest parties and hollowing out the political centre. Varadkar has now, at the eleventh hour, conceded the point — though whether this owes more to principle or to self-preservation is a question his allies would prefer not to dwell upon.

The reaction from within Fine Gael has been largely supportive, with several TDs who lost their seats reportedly welcoming the decision as long overdue.
headline: Outgoing Taoiseach Leo Varadkar torpedoes Micheal Martin’s fever dreams of a grand coalition by saying that Fine Gael is headed for opposition

text:
RTÉ is set to cut around 200 jobs over the next two to three years as part of a sweeping cost-reduction plan aimed at stemming the national broadcaster's mounting financial losses.

The revised strategy, announced by RTÉ's Director General Dee Forbes, will also see pay cuts imposed on the organisation's highest earners and a pay freeze for all other staff. Those earning over €150,000 will face a 15 per cent reduction in salary, while employees earning between €100,000 and €150,000 will see their pay cut by 10 per cent.

The measures form part of a broader effort to close a projected deficit that has seen RTÉ post significant losses in recent years, with the broadcaster warning that without urgent action its financial position would become unsustainable.

RTÉ said the job losses would be achieved through a combination of voluntary redundancies, natural attrition and the non-renewal of contracts. The broadcaster currently employs approximately 1,800 staff, meaning the planned cuts would amount to a reduction of more than 10 per cent of its workforce.

The announcement is likely to prove deeply controversial, not least among staff and trade unions who have already expressed concerns about the impact of cost-cutting on programme quality and working conditions. The National Union of Journalists and SIPTU, which represent the majority of RTÉ employees, are expected to seek urgent talks with management over the proposals.

RTÉ's financial difficulties have been well documented, with the broadcaster pointing to a decline in commercial revenue and the failure to reform the television licence fee system as key factors behind its worsening position. The organisation has repeatedly called on the Government to address the issue of licence fee evasion, which costs the broadcaster an estimated €50 million annually, and to consider alternative funding models.

The Government has faced sustained pressure to act on the issue, with a report commissioned by the then Minister for Communications recommending a move towards a device-independent broadcasting charge. However, successive administrations have been slow to implement the recommendation, leaving RTÉ increasingly reliant on cost-cutting to balance its books.

Forbes said the measures were necessary to ensure the long-term viability of RTÉ as a public service broadcaster, adding that the organisation had no choice but to live within its means while continuing to deliver quality content to audiences.

The planned pay cuts for top earners will inevitably draw attention once again to the salaries commanded by some of RTÉ's best-known presenters. The broadcaster's annual report has consistently revealed that a number of on-air personalities earn salaries well in excess of €200,000, a source of ongoing public debate about the use of licence fee payers' money.

Opposition TDs were quick to respond to the announcement, with several calling on the Government to outline its long-term plan for public service broadcasting in Ireland. Sinn Féin's communications spokesperson said the situation at RTÉ reflected years of Government inaction on the funding model, while Labour described the job losses as a blow to workers who had already endured years of uncertainty.
headline: RTE to cut 200 jobs, introduce pay cuts and pay freeze in an effort to stop losses

text:
The controversial so-called "rat line" established by Gardaí in Donegal to allow members of the public to report suspected breaches of Covid-19 regulations has been quietly scrapped after it emerged that the majority of calls received did not relate to genuine breaches of public health guidelines.

The dedicated phone line, which was set up by the Donegal Garda Division during the height of pandemic restrictions, had drawn significant criticism from civil liberties advocates and members of the public who argued it encouraged a culture of informing on neighbours and community members.

An analysis of calls received by the line found that approximately 60 per cent of reports made did not constitute actual breaches of Covid regulations, raising serious questions about the effectiveness and proportionality of the measure. Many of the calls were believed to relate to personal grievances and disputes between neighbours rather than genuine public health concerns.

The phone line had been widely condemned on social media, with many drawing uncomfortable historical parallels and expressing concern that it was fostering division in communities across the county. Critics argued that encouraging citizens to report on one another was a disproportionate response that risked undermining trust between the Gardaí and the communities they serve.

It is understood that Garda resources were being diverted to follow up on reports that ultimately proved to be unfounded or did not meet the threshold for enforcement action under the public health regulations. The volume of spurious calls effectively meant that Gardaí were spending significant time investigating complaints that had no basis in law.

The decision to cancel the line will be welcomed by those who had raised concerns about the erosion of civil liberties during the pandemic. Throughout the period of restrictions, there was considerable public debate about the balance between public health measures and individual rights, with some arguing that certain enforcement mechanisms went beyond what was necessary or appropriate.

Donegal was not the only area where such reporting mechanisms drew controversy, but the dedicated phone line had become something of a lightning rod for broader frustrations about the policing of pandemic restrictions.

The Gardaí have not commented publicly on the precise reasons for discontinuing the service, though it is understood that the high proportion of calls that did not relate to actual breaches was a significant factor in the decision.

The episode raises wider questions about the appropriateness of such measures and whether lessons will be learned for any future public health emergencies. The fact that the majority of reports turned out not to involve breaches of regulations suggests that the line may have served more as an outlet for community tensions than as a genuine tool for public health enforcement.
headline: Donegal Gardai’s controversial Covid “RAT LINE” has been cancelled after 60% of calls were found not to be breaches of covid laws

text:
A woman in her 50s has died following a road traffic collision in Co. Kildare, as the grim toll on Irish roads continues to mount.

The fatal crash occurred on Tuesday evening, with Gardaí and emergency services responding to the scene. The woman was pronounced dead at the scene, and her body was removed to the mortuary at Naas General Hospital, where a post-mortem examination is expected to be carried out in due course.

The road was closed for a period to allow Garda forensic collision investigators to carry out a technical examination of the scene. Local diversions were put in place, and motorists were asked to avoid the area.

Gardaí are now appealing for any witnesses to the collision to come forward. They are particularly keen to hear from road users who may have been travelling in the area at the time and who may have dashcam footage.

The woman's death marks yet another fatality on Irish roads in what has been a deeply concerning period for road safety. The Road Safety Authority has repeatedly urged drivers to exercise caution, particularly on rural roads where the majority of fatal collisions occur.

So far this year, the number of people killed on Irish roads remains a source of serious concern for authorities, with families and communities across the country left devastated by the ongoing loss of life.

Anyone with information is asked to contact their local Garda station or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: Road carnage continues, after woman in her 50s dies in crash in Co. Kildare

text:
Sir David Amess, the long-serving Conservative MP for Southend West, has been stabbed to death while holding a constituency surgery at Belfairs Methodist Church in Leigh-on-Sea, Essex. He was 69 years old.

The father of five was attacked on Friday afternoon while meeting with constituents, a routine part of any MP's work. Emergency services rushed to the scene, but despite the best efforts of paramedics, Sir David was pronounced dead at the location. A 25-year-old man was arrested at the scene on suspicion of murder, and a knife was recovered. Essex Police said they were not looking for anyone else in connection with the incident.

Tributes have poured in from across the political spectrum, with colleagues and friends remembering Sir David not only as a dedicated parliamentarian but as a man of deep personal faith. A practising Catholic, he was known for his consistent advocacy on pro-life issues throughout his 38 years in the House of Commons, having first been elected as MP for Basildon in 1983 before moving to the Southend West constituency in 1997.

British Prime Minister Boris Johnson led the tributes, describing Sir David as one of the kindest and most gentle people in politics. "He had an outstanding record of passing laws to help the most vulnerable," Mr Johnson said.

Former prime minister Sir John Major called Sir David "a gentle and sincere man" with "a great love of Essex."

Speaker of the House of Commons Sir Lindsay Hoyle said the killing had left the House "united in grief" and ordered flags at Westminster to be flown at half-mast.

Several colleagues spoke specifically of Sir David's Catholic faith as a guiding force in his public life. He was widely regarded as one of the most prominent Catholic voices in Parliament, consistently raising issues of conscience and championing causes rooted in his beliefs. He had been a member of the All-Party Parliamentary Group on the Holy See and had spoken warmly of his audiences with successive popes.

Cardinal Vincent Nichols, the Archbishop of Westminster, said he was "deeply shocked and saddened" by the killing and paid tribute to Sir David's faith and service. "He was a man of deep Catholic conviction," Cardinal Nichols said. "His faith drove his compassion and his commitment to public service."

"He was a kind gentleman," said one constituent who had known Sir David for years, a sentiment echoed repeatedly throughout the day as tributes continued to flow.

Sir David had a particular fondness for Ireland, having campaigned for years on issues relating to the Irish community in Britain. He was a long-standing officer of the British-Irish Parliamentary Assembly and was known for his warm relationships with politicians on both sides of the Irish Sea.

The killing has reignited serious concerns about the safety of MPs meeting their constituents, following the murder of Labour MP Jo Cox in 2016. Home Secretary Priti Patel said she had asked police forces across the country to review security arrangements for all MPs with immediate effect.

MPs from all parties spoke of the difficult balance between accessibility and security, noting that constituency surgeries are a cornerstone of British parliamentary democracy.
headline: “He was a kind gentleman” – Tributes pour in for David Amess MP, who was a practicing Catholic, after he was stabbed to death in his constituency

text:
The fuel allowance payment will begin landing in the accounts of eligible households from today, providing a crucial boost to those struggling with the ongoing cost of heating their homes.

The Department of Social Protection confirmed that the weekly payment of €33 will be issued to qualifying recipients as part of the national fuel allowance scheme, which runs for a 28-week season from late September through to April.

The allowance is paid to people who are dependent on long-term social welfare payments and who are unable to provide for their own heating needs. It is available to those living alone or with other qualifying adults, and is subject to a means test.

Recipients can choose to receive the payment in weekly instalments of €33 or as a lump sum of €924 paid in two instalments over the course of the fuel season. Those who opt for the lump sum arrangement will receive their first instalment at the start of the season.

To qualify for the fuel allowance, applicants must be in receipt of a qualifying social welfare payment, satisfy a means test, and live alone or only with other qualifying persons. The household must also be the applicant's sole residence, and the applicant must not be availing of the allowance as part of another household.

The payment is designed to assist with the cost of heating for those on fixed incomes, at a time when energy prices remain elevated despite some reductions from peak levels seen in recent years.

Minister for Social Protection Heather Humphreys has previously encouraged anyone who believes they may be entitled to the payment to contact their local Intreo centre or citizens information office to check their eligibility.

The fuel allowance has been a significant feature of public debate in recent budgetary discussions, with opposition TDs and advocacy groups calling for the payment to be increased further and for the eligibility criteria to be broadened to cover more households experiencing fuel poverty.

Organisations such as the Society of St Vincent de Paul and Age Action have consistently highlighted that many older people and those on low incomes continue to face impossible choices between heating and eating, particularly during the coldest months of the year.

Anyone wishing to apply for the fuel allowance can do so through their local Intreo centre or online through MyWelfare.ie.
headline: Fuel allowance payment will be issued to households from today

text:
Commuters across Britain face another day of severe disruption tomorrow as the largest rail strike in more than thirty years rolls on, with last-ditch talks between unions and rail operators once again collapsing without agreement.

Members of the Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers' union have brought much of the British rail network to a standstill this week, with only around one in five services operating on strike days. The industrial action, which has already caused chaos for millions of passengers, is set to continue after negotiations broke down late this evening with both sides trading accusations of intransigence.

RMT general secretary Mick Lynch said the union had entered talks in good faith but accused Network Rail and the train operating companies of failing to bring a serious offer to the table. "Our members are not going to accept a deal that means thousands of job cuts, attacks on their terms and conditions, and a real-terms pay cut during a cost-of-living crisis," Lynch told reporters outside the talks.

The British transport secretary Grant Shapps has refused to involve himself directly in negotiations, insisting it is a matter for the employers and unions to resolve between themselves. Labour has criticised the government's approach, with shadow transport secretary Louise Haigh accusing ministers of "pouring petrol on the fire" by declining to facilitate a resolution.

The dispute centres on pay, job security and proposed changes to working practices. Network Rail has proposed cutting some 2,500 maintenance roles as part of a modernisation programme, while workers are seeking a pay increase that keeps pace with inflation, which in the UK is currently running at its highest level in four decades.

The knock-on effects have been considerable. Services that do operate are running on drastically reduced timetables, typically only between half seven in the morning and half six in the evening, leaving early-morning and late-night travellers with no rail options whatsoever. Many commuters have been forced onto already congested roads, while others have had to work from home or cancel plans entirely.

The disruption has also had a ripple effect on the wider economy, with hospitality and retail businesses in city centres reporting sharp drops in footfall on strike days. The Centre for Economics and Business Research has estimated that each day of strike action costs the British economy in the region of £91 million.

For Irish travellers heading to Britain, the strikes have caused significant headaches. While flights and ferry services are unaffected, onward rail connections from airports and ports have been severely curtailed. Passengers arriving into Holyhead, Liverpool and other ports popular with Irish travellers have found themselves with limited or no rail options on strike days.

The dispute has drawn comparisons with the bitter industrial conflicts of the Thatcher era, though analysts note that public sympathy for the strikers appears to be more evenly divided than it was during the miners' strike of the 1980s. Polling suggests that while a slim majority of the British public oppose the strikes, a significant proportion believe the workers' grievances are legitimate given the current economic pressures.

The RMT has not ruled out further action if a settlement cannot be reached, with Lynch warning that the union is prepared for "as long a campaign as is necessary." Further strike dates could be announced in the coming weeks if talks remain deadlocked.
headline: Largest rail strike in three decades in the UK continues in the UK tomorrow, as last-ditch negotiations fail again

text:
Electric vehicles and hybrid cars sold in the European Union must now be fitted with acoustic warning systems as new regulations come into effect from today.

The requirement, which applies to all new electric and hybrid vehicles, means that cars which are virtually silent at low speeds will now emit an artificial sound to alert pedestrians, cyclists and other road users to their presence.

The regulation has been a long time coming. The EU first signalled its intention to introduce the measure several years ago amid growing concerns about the danger posed by near-silent electric vehicles, particularly to visually impaired people and other vulnerable road users.

Under the new rules, all electric and hybrid vehicles must be equipped with an Acoustic Vehicle Alerting System, or AVAS, which will produce a continuous sound when the vehicle is travelling at speeds below 20 kilometres per hour. The system must also operate when the car is reversing.

The sound emitted must be similar to that of a conventional combustion engine vehicle, and drivers will not be permitted to deactivate the system.

Road safety campaigners in Ireland have broadly welcomed the move. The National Council for the Blind of Ireland had previously raised concerns about the risks posed by silent-running vehicles to people with visual impairments, who rely heavily on auditory cues when navigating streets and crossing roads.

Electric vehicle sales in Ireland have grown significantly in recent years, driven by government incentives and a broader push towards decarbonisation of the transport sector. The number of electric vehicles on Irish roads has increased substantially, with the government targeting one million EVs on Irish roads by 2030 as part of its Climate Action Plan.

The Society of the Irish Motor Industry has said its members are fully prepared for the regulation, noting that many manufacturers had already begun fitting the devices to newer models on a voluntary basis in advance of the deadline.

The Gardaí have confirmed they will enforce the new requirement as part of routine roadside checks, though a period of adjustment is expected as the regulation beds in. Vehicles already on the road before today's deadline are not affected by the new rules, though retrofitting of the devices is encouraged.

The Road Safety Authority has said the measure represents an important step forward in protecting all road users as Ireland transitions towards a greener vehicle fleet. The authority noted that electric and hybrid vehicles, while significantly better for the environment, do present unique challenges in terms of road safety precisely because of their quiet operation.

Consumer groups have pointed out that the addition of the acoustic systems is unlikely to add any significant cost to new vehicles, with most manufacturers having already factored the technology into their production processes.

The regulation is part of a broader suite of EU vehicle safety measures that have been gradually introduced in recent years, including mandatory automatic emergency braking systems and intelligent speed assistance technology.
headline: Electric vehicles to be fitted with noise emitting devices from today onwards

text:
It was a scene repeated in towns and cities across the country this afternoon as the clock struck midnight on Ireland's Covid pass system, with multiple reports flooding social media of gleeful citizens pointing at former pass-holders and delivering their best Nelson Muntz impressions.

The distinctive "Ha-ha!" from The Simpsons' resident bully was heard echoing through the streets of Dublin, Cork, Galway and beyond as the Government's Covid pass regime finally met its unceremonious end, and those who had wielded their digital certificates like golden tickets found themselves suddenly stripped of their precious privilege.

One Dublin man, who asked not to be named, told The Liberal he had been "saving up this moment for months" and had even practised his Nelson impression in the mirror every morning since the passes were first introduced.

"I just walked up to a fella outside a café in Temple Bar who spent the last year scanning himself into everywhere like he was some sort of VIP at an exclusive nightclub, pointed right at him, and gave him the full Nelson," he said. "It felt magnificent, in fairness."

The Covid pass system, which required individuals to show proof of vaccination or recovery to access hospitality venues and events, had drawn sustained criticism from civil liberties advocates who argued it created a two-tier society and coerced people into medical decisions they might not otherwise have made.

Throughout the pandemic, those who questioned the pass system were routinely dismissed as cranks and conspiracy theorists, despite raising concerns that legal scholars and human rights organisations in other jurisdictions took rather more seriously.

Reports on social media suggested the Nelson laugh phenomenon was not confined to urban areas. A woman in Sligo described witnessing "at least three separate Nelsons" in her local town centre before lunchtime, while a man in Kilkenny claimed an entire table outside a pub had spontaneously broken into synchronised pointing when a regular patron arrived and reflexively reached for his phone to produce a pass that was no longer required.

The scenes will no doubt irritate those who insisted throughout the pandemic that the pass system was a perfectly reasonable public health measure and not, as critics maintained, an instrument of social control designed to pressure the non-compliant into compliance through exclusion from ordinary life.

Government TDs were notably quiet on the matter today, with none appearing eager to mark the occasion or reflect on whether the system had been proportionate, effective, or indeed necessary in its later stages when it was abundantly clear to anyone paying attention that vaccination did not prevent transmission.

The irony of a system ostensibly built on "the science" lingering well past its scientific justification was not lost on those doing the pointing today.

Whether the Nelson laugh phenomenon represents a healthy moment of collective catharsis or something less edifying is, of course, a matter of perspective. But for those who spent months being told they were selfish, dangerous, and undeserving of participation in public life for exercising bodily autonomy, one suspects the "Ha-ha!" felt rather well earned.
headline: Covid-19: Multiple reports emerging nationwide of people pointing and doing the Nelson laugh at those losing their precious Covid pass privilege today

text:
The three coalition party leaders are set to meet today to thrash out whether the country will be plunged into another lengthy lockdown, with speculation mounting that Level 5 restrictions could be reimposed for a period of up to six weeks.

Taoiseach Micheál Martin, Tánaiste Leo Varadkar and Green Party leader Eamon Ryan will sit down to consider the latest public health advice from NPHET, which is understood to have recommended the most severe restrictions be brought back in amid surging case numbers.

The prospect of yet another lockdown has drawn fury from business owners, publicans and ordinary members of the public who say they have already sacrificed enough and cannot endure another prolonged period of closures. Many have taken to social media to express their frustration, questioning whether the strategy of repeated lockdowns is sustainable or even effective in the long term.

It is understood that there are differing views within the coalition on the severity and duration of any new restrictions, with some figures in Fine Gael believed to be reluctant to shut down the economy once more. However, sources close to the discussions suggest that the pressure from public health officials may prove difficult to resist.

The hospitality sector, which has been decimated by successive rounds of restrictions, has warned that another six-week closure could be a death sentence for thousands of businesses already on the brink. Representatives from the Restaurants Association of Ireland and the Vintners' Federation of Ireland have called on the government to consider targeted measures rather than a blanket shutdown.

The Irish public, many of whom have dutifully followed restrictions for months on end, are growing increasingly weary of what critics describe as a cycle of lockdowns that appear to offer no clear exit strategy. Questions continue to be raised about the government's overall plan and whether there is any endpoint in sight for the restrictions that have upended daily life across the country.

A decision is expected to be announced later today or tomorrow, with any new measures likely to take effect within days. The three leaders are also expected to discuss the economic supports that would accompany any renewed restrictions, with the PUP and EWSS schemes likely to be extended if a lockdown is confirmed.

TDs across the opposition benches have criticised the government's handling of the crisis, with several calling for the Dáil to be recalled to debate any new measures before they are imposed. Sinn Féin, Labour and the Social Democrats have all insisted that elected representatives should have a say rather than leaving the decision solely in the hands of three party leaders.

The country now waits to see whether the government trio will once again ask the Irish people to put their lives on hold.
headline: Government trio to meet today to decide whether or not the Irish public get locked down again for another 6 weeks

text:
A 12-year-old girl has been shot dead in Sweden in what police believe was a gang-related attack, sparking widespread outrage and renewed calls for tougher action against organised crime in the Scandinavian country.

The child was struck by gunfire in the Botkyrka area south of Stockholm late on Thursday night and was rushed to hospital, where she was later pronounced dead. Swedish police said the girl was not the intended target of the shooting and is believed to have been caught in the crossfire of a dispute between rival criminal gangs.

Sweden's Prime Minister Stefan Löfven described the killing as an attack on the whole of Swedish society, saying the country would not rest until those responsible were brought to justice. "A 12-year-old girl has been shot to death. This is every parent's worst nightmare. We will do everything we can to turn this development around," he said.

The shooting has reignited a fierce debate in Sweden over the country's escalating problem with gang violence, which has seen a dramatic rise in shootings and bombings in recent years, particularly in the suburbs of major cities such as Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö. Critics have long argued that successive Swedish governments have failed to adequately address the root causes of gang criminality, including issues around integration, social exclusion and the drugs trade.

Sweden has recorded a sharp increase in gun violence over the past decade, with the country now reporting one of the highest rates of fatal shootings per capita in Europe, a stark contrast to its long-held reputation as one of the safest nations on the continent.

Opposition politicians were quick to seize on the tragedy, with the leader of the centre-right Moderate Party demanding emergency measures to combat gang crime, including harsher sentencing and expanded police powers. The Sweden Democrats, the country's right-wing populist party, linked the violence to what it described as decades of failed immigration policy, a claim strongly rejected by the ruling Social Democrats.

Police have launched a major investigation into the shooting and have appealed for witnesses to come forward. Several individuals have reportedly been taken in for questioning, though no formal arrests had been confirmed at the time of writing.

The killing has drawn comparisons to high-profile cases in other European countries where innocent bystanders, including children, have been killed as a result of gang feuds. In Ireland, the issue of gangland violence and its impact on communities has similarly been a source of public concern, particularly in the wake of the Regency Hotel shooting in 2016 and the subsequent Hutch-Kinahan feud, which claimed multiple lives.

Swedish community leaders in the Botkyrka area have called for calm while also demanding greater investment in social programmes and youth services to steer young people away from criminal gangs. Vigils have been held in the neighbourhood where the girl was killed, with residents expressing a mixture of grief and anger at the senseless loss of a young life.
headline: Outrage in Sweden as 12-yr-old girl gets shot dead during gang war

text:
Two young girls have been rescued after being swept out to sea on an inflatable airbed off the coast of Co Waterford in what has been described as a terrifying ordeal for their family.

The incident occurred on Saturday afternoon at Tramore beach, where the two children, believed to be aged around seven and nine, were playing on the inflatable when a strong offshore breeze carried them rapidly away from the shoreline.

Beachgoers raised the alarm as the airbed drifted further from the strand, with the girls' parents described as frantic on the shore. The rescue came thanks to the quick thinking and bravery of two members of the public who were swimming nearby and managed to reach the children before they were carried any further out.

The Irish Coast Guard confirmed it had been alerted to the incident and that Tramore RNLI's inshore lifeboat was launched, but by the time the crew arrived on scene the two swimmers had already brought the girls safely back to shore.

Both children were assessed by paramedics at the scene but were found to be uninjured, if understandably shaken by the experience.

A spokesperson for the Irish Coast Guard praised the actions of the two rescuers but also issued a reminder to the public about the dangers of using inflatables in open water. "Inflatable airbeds, dinghies and toys can be carried offshore very quickly, even in what seems like a light breeze," the spokesperson said. "They are not designed for use in the sea and can create a very dangerous situation in a matter of moments."

The RNLI has also urged beachgoers to exercise caution as temperatures rise and more families head to the coast, advising that inflatables should only ever be used in swimming pools or sheltered, supervised environments.

Water Safety Ireland has repeatedly warned that inflatable toys and airbeds are among the most common factors in coastal rescue callouts during the summer months, with children particularly at risk.

The identities of the two swimmers who carried out the rescue have not been made public, though locals in Tramore have hailed them as heroes for their swift and selfless actions.
headline: Hero alert: Two young girls rescued after being swept out to sea on an airbed

text:
The remains of the partially collapsed Champlain Towers South condominium in Surfside, Florida, have been brought down in a controlled demolition, as authorities raced to resume search and rescue operations ahead of the approaching Tropical Storm Elsa.

Engineers carried out the demolition late on Sunday night local time, bringing down the portion of the 12-storey beachfront tower that had remained standing since the catastrophic collapse on 24 June. The decision to demolish the structure had been taken after officials warned that the remaining section posed a serious danger to rescue crews working in the rubble pile below and could topple in an uncontrolled manner as the tropical storm bore down on the region.

Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava confirmed that the demolition went according to plan and that search and rescue teams were able to return to the site within hours. She said the operation would allow crews to access areas of the debris field that had previously been too dangerous to reach, including sections beneath and adjacent to the standing portion of the building.

"We are continuing our search and rescue operation around the clock," Levine Cava told reporters. She stressed that the mission remained one of rescue rather than recovery, although hopes of finding survivors had dimmed considerably in the days since the collapse.

At the time of the demolition, the confirmed death toll stood at 24, with more than 120 people still unaccounted for. Relatives of those missing had endured an agonising wait for news, gathering daily at a reunification centre established by authorities near the scene.

The cause of the initial collapse remains under investigation, though attention has focused on a 2018 engineering report that identified "major structural damage" to the concrete slab beneath the pool deck and "abundant" cracking and crumbling of columns in the car park beneath the building. Questions have been raised about whether the building's condominium association acted swiftly enough in response to the warnings, and about the adequacy of building inspection and recertification processes in the region more broadly.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis had signed an emergency order to facilitate the demolition, and President Joe Biden approved an emergency declaration for the state, unlocking federal resources to assist with the response.

Tropical Storm Elsa was forecast to bring strong winds and heavy rain to the southern Florida coast in the days following the demolition, raising fears that gusts could have caused the unstable remains to collapse onto the rescue site had the structure not been brought down. Officials said that the approaching storm had lent additional urgency to an already fraught operation.

The collapse of Champlain Towers South, which was built in 1981, has sent shockwaves through coastal communities across Florida, with authorities ordering emergency inspections of similar ageing high-rise buildings. In the town of North Miami Beach, a 156-unit condominium was evacuated after an audit deemed it structurally and electrically unsafe.

The tragedy has also prompted renewed discussion at state and federal level about the regulation of older residential towers and the responsibilities of condominium associations to maintain ageing infrastructure.
headline: Miami tower block collapse: Engineers demolish the remains of the Champlain Tower South block

text:
British and Irish authorities are working closely together after investigators concluded that a series of suspicious packages sent to major transport hubs in London last year were likely dispatched from addresses in the Republic of Ireland.

The Metropolitan Police confirmed on Tuesday that forensic analysis of the devices, which were discovered at Heathrow Airport, London City Airport, and Waterloo station in March 2019, pointed strongly towards an Irish origin. The small improvised explosive devices, concealed in A4-sized postal bags, were capable of igniting a small fire and were described at the time as designed to cause significant harm.

Counter-terrorism officers from the Met have been liaising with the Gardaí and the Irish postal service, An Post, as part of a joint investigation that has been under way for several months. A spokesperson for Garda Headquarters in the Phoenix Park said that Irish authorities were providing "full cooperation and assistance" to their British counterparts but declined to comment further on operational matters.

The revelation is likely to raise fresh questions about postal security protocols on both sides of the Irish Sea. An Post said it takes security "extremely seriously" and had been cooperating fully with investigating authorities since the incidents first came to light.

No group has claimed responsibility for the devices, though British counter-terrorism police initially investigated possible links to dissident republican organisations. Sources familiar with the investigation cautioned that no definitive connection to any paramilitary grouping had been established and that other lines of inquiry remain active.

The packages were intercepted before causing any injuries, though the discovery of the first device at Heathrow prompted a significant security response and caused widespread disruption to travel services across the British capital. A controlled explosion was carried out on one of the packages by specialist army bomb disposal officers.

The Irish Department of Justice said it was aware of the ongoing investigation and that the Minister had been briefed on developments. A spokesperson stressed that Ireland's security services continued to monitor any potential threats and maintained close working relationships with partner agencies in the United Kingdom and across the European Union.

Security analysts noted that the apparent use of the ordinary postal system to transport explosive devices across international borders highlighted persistent vulnerabilities. Dr Karen Murphy, a security studies lecturer at Dublin City University, told The Liberal that the case underscored "the difficulty of screening every single item that passes through the postal network, particularly when devices are specifically designed to evade detection."

British Home Secretary James Cleverly said authorities on both sides were treating the matter with the "utmost seriousness" and praised the cooperation between the two countries' police and intelligence services.

No arrests have been made in connection with the investigation, which remains ongoing. The Metropolitan Police appealed to anyone with information to come forward through the confidential anti-terrorism hotline.
headline: London terror alert: Explosive devices were likely sent from Ireland, authorities say

text:
US President Joe Biden has tested positive for Covid-19, the White House has confirmed, marking yet another bout with the virus for the 81-year-old despite being fully vaccinated and boosted.

The president, who has previously contracted the virus on multiple occasions, is said to be experiencing mild symptoms and will be isolating at the White House in line with guidance from his physician. He has been administered Paxlovid, the antiviral treatment he has taken during previous infections.

White House press secretary Karine Jean-Pierre confirmed the positive test result, stating that the president is "in good spirits" and will continue to carry out his duties while in isolation. Biden has received multiple vaccine doses, including the most recent updated booster, yet the latest positive test underscores the ongoing reality that vaccination does not prevent infection, though health officials maintain it significantly reduces the risk of severe illness and hospitalisation.

The news will reignite debate around the efficacy of repeated boosters, particularly for elderly and immunocompromised individuals. Critics have long questioned the messaging around Covid-19 vaccines, pointing to breakthrough infections among high-profile fully vaccinated individuals as evidence that public health communications overpromised on the jabs' ability to prevent transmission and infection.
