Biden's age and health have been subjects of intense scrutiny in the United States, with opponents questioning whether he is fit to serve. Each bout of Covid-19 has amplified those concerns, though his medical team has consistently maintained that the president remains in robust health for a man of his age.

The positive test forced the cancellation of several scheduled engagements, with aides scrambling to rearrange the president's diary. Officials confirmed that close contacts have been notified and are being tested as a precautionary measure.

Ireland's own experience with breakthrough infections among vaccinated individuals has been well documented, with public health officials here similarly emphasising that the primary purpose of vaccination remains the prevention of serious illness rather than infection itself.
headline: ?BREAKING: US President Joe Biden has tested positive for Covid-19 again even though he is full vaxxed

text:
A man has been arrested after allegedly attempting to set a member of An Garda Síochána on fire in what has been described as a shocking attack.

The incident occurred earlier today and is understood to have left the garda shaken but without serious physical injuries. The member, who was on duty at the time, was targeted in what colleagues have described as a completely unprovoked assault.

It is understood the suspect used a flammable liquid in the attack before attempting to ignite it. Colleagues at the scene intervened quickly to prevent the situation from escalating further, and the garda was given immediate medical attention as a precautionary measure.

The suspect, a man in his 30s, was arrested at the scene and is currently being detained at a garda station in the area under the provisions of Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act, 1984. He can be held for up to 24 hours without charge.

Gardaí have confirmed that an investigation into the incident is ongoing and that a file will be prepared for the Director of Public Prosecutions.

The attack has drawn widespread condemnation, with the Garda Representative Association calling on the courts to take a hardline approach to assaults on members of the force.

A GRA spokesperson said members are increasingly being subjected to violent and dangerous attacks while carrying out their duties and that such incidents are becoming far too common.

"Our members go to work every day to protect the public, and they deserve to be able to do so without fear of being attacked in this manner," the spokesperson said.

The injured garda has since been released from hospital and is recovering at home. Gardaí are appealing for any witnesses to the incident to come forward.
headline: BREAKING: Man arrested after trying to set a garda on fire

text:
The National Public Health Emergency Team has expressed concern as the Department of Health confirmed 1,015 new cases of Covid-19 this evening.

As of midnight, the department also confirmed that a further three people with the virus have sadly passed away, bringing the total number of deaths to date in the State to a figure that continues to weigh heavily on communities across the country.

In a statement issued this evening, a spokesperson for NPHET said the team remained "concerned" by the trajectory of case numbers and urged the public to continue adhering to public health guidelines.

The latest figures mean the five-day moving average of cases has risen sharply, with health officials warning that the pattern of transmission is being driven by a combination of household mixing and workplace outbreaks.

Of the cases notified today, the median age is 34 years old, with the majority of cases concentrated in younger age cohorts. Dublin continues to account for the largest share of new infections, followed by Cork and Limerick.

As of this morning, there are 268 Covid-19 patients hospitalised across the State, of whom 57 are being treated in intensive care units. The HSE has said it is closely monitoring hospital capacity, particularly in a number of acute settings where pressure on beds remains a cause for concern.

The Chief Medical Officer, Dr Tony Holohan, said in a statement that the current level of disease represents a "significant concern" and called on the public to redouble their efforts in following basic public health measures, including hand hygiene, wearing face coverings, maintaining social distance and reducing the number of people they meet on a daily basis.

"We are asking people to hold firm," Dr Holohan said. "The vaccination programme is progressing well, but we are not yet at a point where we can rely on vaccination alone to suppress the virus. Every effort each person makes contributes to reducing transmission in the community."

The Minister for Health, Stephen Donnelly TD, echoed the call for vigilance, noting that the Government was keeping all options under review as it monitors the epidemiological situation.

The latest figures come as the HSE's vaccination programme continues to be rolled out across the country, with over two million doses now administered. However, concerns remain over the pace of the rollout and the potential impact of emerging variants on vaccine efficacy.

NPHET is due to meet again later this week to assess the latest data and provide updated advice to Government on the public health situation.
headline: ?BREAKING: NHPET ‘concerned’ as Department of Health confirms 1,015 new Covid-19 cases

text:
Met Éireann has confirmed that Ireland is set to enjoy a continuation of the current spell of warm, settled weather over the next two days, but forecasters are warning that conditions will deteriorate sharply as the week draws to a close.

The national forecaster says temperatures will remain well above seasonal norms through Wednesday and Thursday, with highs of 22 to 25 degrees expected in many parts of the country. Long spells of sunshine are forecast, particularly across the midlands and the east, with light southerly breezes keeping conditions pleasant.

It marks a welcome run of genuinely summer-like weather that has seen people flock to beaches, parks and outdoor dining spots in recent days. Water safety groups have reminded the public to exercise caution around waterways, particularly at unguarded bathing spots, as the fine weather draws larger crowds than usual.

However, Met Éireann is cautioning that the settled spell will be short-lived. A significant change in the weather pattern is expected to arrive by Friday, with an Atlantic front pushing in from the west bringing widespread rain and a notable drop in temperatures.

"We're looking at a fairly dramatic shift by Friday," a Met Éireann forecaster said. "Temperatures will fall back considerably, and there will be persistent and at times heavy rain moving across the country. It will feel much more like a typical Irish summer day."

Friday's rain is expected to be heaviest across Connacht and Munster initially before spreading to all areas through the afternoon and evening. Temperatures are forecast to drop back to between 14 and 17 degrees, a considerable fall from the highs earlier in the week.

The weekend outlook remains uncertain, though current indications suggest unsettled conditions will persist, with further spells of rain and breezy conditions expected through Saturday and into Sunday.

Met Éireann has advised anyone planning outdoor events or activities later in the week to keep a close eye on forecast updates. The current Status Green conditions mean no weather warnings are in place, but the forecaster has not ruled out issuing advisories as the incoming front becomes clearer in the forecast models.

The fine weather this week has been driven by high pressure building from the Azores, a pattern that has kept the typical Atlantic weather systems at bay. That high pressure is expected to retreat southward by Thursday evening, opening the door for the low-pressure systems that are more characteristic of Irish summers.

For now, though, the message from Met Éireann is to make the most of the next 48 hours while conditions remain favourable.
headline: Met Eireann says that weather will remain summer-like for the next 48h, but things will take a turn for the worse by Friday

text:
Organisers of Camp Bestival have confirmed that the family-friendly music festival will go ahead this summer, marking a significant milestone in the return of live events in Britain.

The festival, which takes place at Lulworth Castle in Dorset, is scheduled to run from 29 July to 1 August, with organisers expressing confidence that the UK government's roadmap out of lockdown will allow large-scale outdoor events to resume by that date.

Rob da Bank, co-founder of the festival, said the team had been working closely with public health authorities to ensure the event could proceed safely. "We've been planning for every eventuality and we're so excited to finally be able to say that Camp Bestival is happening this year," he said.

The announcement comes as festivals and live events across Europe and beyond continue to grapple with the uncertainty posed by the pandemic. In Ireland, the live events sector has been among the hardest hit by restrictions, with major festivals such as Electric Picnic having faced repeated cancellations over the course of the crisis. Industry figures here have repeatedly called on the Government to provide a clearer timeline for the resumption of large-scale outdoor gatherings.

Camp Bestival, which has been running since 2008, typically attracts around 30,000 attendees and is known for its programme of music, comedy, and family entertainment. Organisers said enhanced safety measures would be in place, though specific details regarding capacity limits or testing requirements had yet to be finalised.

The UK's roadmap has earmarked 21 June as the earliest date by which all legal limits on social contact could be removed, subject to the satisfactory progression of the vaccine rollout and the continued suppression of case numbers.

Festival promoters on this side of the Irish Sea will be watching developments closely, with many hoping that a successful reopening of large events in Britain could build momentum for similar moves here in the months ahead.
headline: Covid-19: Camp Bestival will go ahead this year

text:
The Government has confirmed plans to accommodate approximately 230 Syrian migrants in County Tipperary, a move that has drawn sharp criticism from locals who point to the more than 10,000 men, women and children already without a home across the State.

The decision, which is understood to involve the use of a facility in the town, has prompted anger among residents who say they have watched housing waiting lists grow longer year after year while successive governments have failed to deliver on promises to tackle the crisis.

Local representatives say they were given little or no meaningful consultation before the announcement, a complaint that has become a familiar refrain in communities across Ireland where international protection applicants and programme refugees have been placed in recent years.

Ireland's homelessness figures have remained stubbornly above the 10,000 mark for months, with families trapped in emergency accommodation and single individuals sleeping rough in towns and cities nationwide. The latest figures from the Department of Housing show no sign of a significant downward trend, despite billions in State spending on housing programmes.

Critics argue that the Government's approach amounts to a two-tier system in which newly arrived migrants are fast-tracked into accommodation while Irish citizens who have spent years on council waiting lists are left behind. Supporters of the resettlement programme counter that Ireland has legal and humanitarian obligations to those fleeing conflict, and that the housing crisis is the result of decades of underinvestment rather than migration.

Residents in the Tipperary area have expressed concern about the capacity of local services, including schools, GP practices and public transport, to cope with the additional demand. Several have said they have nothing against the Syrian families themselves but feel their own community has been neglected and taken for granted by politicians in Dublin.

A spokesperson for the Department of Integration confirmed that the facility would be used to house refugees arriving under the Irish Refugee Protection Programme but declined to comment further on the specific arrangements.

Sinn Féin and Independent TDs have called on the Government to publish a clear plan showing how it intends to address the needs of both homeless Irish citizens and incoming refugees without pitting one group against the other. To date, no such plan has been forthcoming.

The controversy is the latest in a series of flashpoints around the country over the placement of asylum seekers and programme refugees in local communities, an issue that shows no sign of abating as the Government struggles to find accommodation for record numbers of arrivals while presiding over what housing charities have described as the worst domestic housing crisis in the history of the State.
headline: 10,000 of our own homeless yet Government to house another 230 Syrian migrants in Tipperary

text:
The Taoiseach has acknowledged that the Ian Bailey case did cause reputational damage to Fine Gael, marking a notable shift in tone from previous party responses to the controversy.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Simon Harris said the party had to accept that the handling of the case and its surrounding controversies had not reflected well on Fine Gael, though he stressed that individual actions should not be taken as representative of the party as a whole.

The remarks come amid renewed scrutiny of the connections between Fine Gael figures and the long-running saga surrounding the murder of French filmmaker Sophie Toscan du Plantier in west Cork in 1996. Ian Bailey, the former journalist who was the chief suspect in the case but was never charged in Ireland, died last year.

The case has dogged Fine Gael for years, with questions raised about the conduct of certain party-linked individuals and their interactions with key figures in the investigation. Former TD Ian Conway and the party's links to individuals in west Cork who featured in the Bailey narrative have periodically resurfaced in political discourse.

Harris's comments represent a departure from the more defensive posture adopted by previous Fine Gael leaders when questioned on the matter. The Taoiseach appeared keen to draw a line under the affair while simultaneously conceding that the party's reputation had taken a hit.

Opposition TDs have long pressed Fine Gael on the issue, arguing that the party was slow to address uncomfortable questions about the conduct of its members and associates in relation to the case. Sinn Féin and other opposition parties have previously called for greater transparency around any political interference in the Garda investigation.

The Bailey case remains one of the most controversial and extensively examined criminal investigations in the history of the State, having been the subject of multiple Garda reviews, a high-profile French trial in absentia, and several documentaries that attracted international attention.

Harris said he believed the party had learned lessons from the episode and that Fine Gael today was focused on accountability and transparency in public life. He did not elaborate on what specific aspects of the case he believed had caused the most reputational harm.

The Taoiseach's remarks are likely to be welcomed by those who have long argued that Fine Gael needed to more forthrightly address the Bailey controversy rather than treating it as a peripheral matter. However, critics may argue that the acknowledgement, while overdue, falls short of the full reckoning they believe is necessary.
headline: Taoiseach says Bailey case did cause reputational damage to the Fine Gael party

text:
It was only a matter of time before the curtain was pulled back on yet another example of the cosy arrangements that continue to define life inside RTÉ, even as the national broadcaster insists it has turned over a new leaf.

While ordinary workers across the public sector have been told to tighten their belts, to do more with less, and to accept that the era of excess is over, RTÉ's hair and makeup team are back at work as though nothing ever happened. One rule for them, it seems, and another for everyone else.

The revelation will do little to restore public confidence in an organisation that has spent the better part of two years trying to claw back credibility following a series of scandals that rocked Montrose to its foundations. From the Ryan Tubridy payments controversy to the eye-watering revelations about spending culture at the station, the Irish public has been given every reason to view RTÉ with deep suspicion. And yet, here we are again.

It is worth remembering that the hair and makeup provision was one of the issues that drew particular public ire during the various controversies. For many taxpayers, struggling with the cost of living and watching their licence fee money being spent in ways that bore no resemblance to their own daily reality, the notion that presenters required a dedicated team of stylists at public expense was difficult to stomach.

The argument from RTÉ's defenders has always been that television is a visual medium and that on-screen presentation matters. That is true, as far as it goes. But it does not go nearly far enough when you consider the financial mess the broadcaster has found itself in, the bailout it required from the exchequer, and the promises made to the Oireachtas and the public that a new culture of fiscal responsibility would take hold.

The Dáil heard repeated assurances from RTÉ leadership that lessons had been learned. Members of the Oireachtas Media Committee were told that root-and-branch reform was underway. The new board, we were assured, would bring proper governance. The days of entitlement were behind us.

And yet the hair and makeup team are back working.

One has to ask what signal this sends to the thousands of people working across the public service who have been denied resources, who work in understaffed hospitals under the HSE, in overcrowded classrooms, and in Garda stations that are falling apart. Those workers do not have the luxury of dedicated grooming teams. Many of them can barely get their employers to replace a broken chair.

The Government, which ultimately holds the purse strings and which authorised a significant funding package for RTÉ, has questions to answer here too. Were Ministers aware that this service was being restored? Did anyone in the Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media raise an eyebrow, or has the political establishment simply accepted that Montrose operates by its own rules?

It is not that hair and makeup artists are undeserving of work. They are skilled professionals, and nobody begrudges them their livelihoods. The issue is one of priorities and optics at a time when RTÉ can ill afford to get either wrong.
headline: One rule for them – RTE’s hair and makeup team are back working

text:
The United States government has ordered American chipmakers Nvidia and AMD to immediately halt the sale of advanced artificial intelligence technology to China, in a dramatic escalation of the ongoing technology war between Washington and Beijing.

The directive, which took effect without the usual grace period afforded to companies adjusting to new export restrictions, represents one of the most aggressive moves yet by the US administration to curtail China's access to cutting-edge semiconductor technology. Both companies confirmed they had been informed of the new restrictions and were complying with the order.

Nvidia, the world's most valuable chipmaker and a linchpin of the global AI boom, said it had received a letter from the US Department of Commerce instructing it to cease exports of its most advanced AI chips to China and several other countries with immediate effect. The company had previously designed stripped-down versions of its chips specifically to comply with earlier rounds of export controls, but the latest order appears to close those workarounds.

AMD confirmed it had received a similar directive covering its MI-series AI accelerators, which compete with Nvidia's products in data centres used to train and run large artificial intelligence models.

Shares in both companies fell sharply in after-hours trading following the announcement, with Nvidia dropping several percentage points as investors digested the potential revenue impact. China has been a significant market for both firms, and the loss of access to Chinese buyers is expected to cost billions of dollars in annual sales.

The move comes amid growing concern in Washington that advanced AI chips sold to China, even in their less powerful variants, could be repurposed for military applications or used to accelerate Beijing's ambitions in autonomous weapons systems, surveillance infrastructure, and advanced computing.

Beijing responded swiftly, with a spokesperson for the Chinese Ministry of Commerce condemning the restrictions as "technological bullying" and warning that China would take "all necessary measures" to protect the legitimate rights of Chinese companies. The Chinese government has previously retaliated against US chip restrictions by imposing its own export controls on critical minerals used in semiconductor manufacturing.

The escalation is likely to reverberate well beyond the two countries directly involved. European and Asian chipmakers will be watching closely to see whether the restrictions create opportunities or whether Washington extends pressure to allies to impose similar curbs. Ireland, home to significant operations for several major US technology firms, could feel indirect effects if the technology decoupling between the world's two largest economies continues to deepen.

Industry analysts said the order marked a clear signal that the US administration views AI supremacy as a matter of national security and is willing to impose significant costs on its own companies to prevent China from closing the gap.

"This is no longer about targeted restrictions on specific end users," said one semiconductor industry analyst. "This is a blanket approach that says the US does not want China to have access to frontier AI hardware, full stop."

The restrictions also raise questions about the future of globalised supply chains in the technology sector, which have for decades relied on the relatively free flow of components and intellectual property across borders. With both Washington and Beijing now actively pursuing technological self-sufficiency, the fracturing of those supply chains appears set to accelerate.
headline: US orders Nvidia and AMD to stop selling technology to China immediately

text:
It will come as welcome news to the many Irish holidaymakers who have had Spain struck off their list for the past few years. The Spanish government has at long last dropped its requirement for visitors to show proof of Covid-19 vaccination, meaning that unvaccinated travellers can now enter the country without restriction for the first time since the pandemic era began.

The move, which has been quietly implemented in recent weeks, effectively brings Spain into line with the vast majority of European countries that had already done away with such entry requirements. For a country so heavily dependent on tourism revenue, many observers have questioned why it took Madrid so long to abandon a policy that was increasingly out of step with the rest of the continent.

Spain had been one of the last holdouts in Europe, stubbornly maintaining its vaccination entry requirement long after the justification for doing so had evaporated. The policy had been a source of considerable frustration for Irish families and individuals who, for whatever personal or medical reason, had chosen not to take the Covid-19 vaccine and found themselves effectively barred from one of Ireland's most popular holiday destinations.

It is worth remembering that throughout the pandemic period, those who raised even mild objections to vaccine mandates and travel restrictions were routinely dismissed as cranks or conspiracy theorists. Yet here we are, with governments quietly rolling back the very policies they once insisted were absolutely essential, with little fanfare and even less in the way of acknowledgement that the critics may have had a point.

The Spanish tourism industry had been crying out for the change. Visitor numbers from several key markets had been noticeably affected, with many tourists simply opting for destinations that did not demand they present medical papers at the border. Portugal, Greece and Croatia were among those that benefited from the diversion of holidaymakers who would ordinarily have headed for the Costas.

Irish travel agents have reported a noticeable uptick in bookings for Spanish destinations since the requirement was lifted, suggesting there was significant pent-up demand among those who had been effectively locked out. The Canary Islands and the Costa del Sol remain perennially popular with Irish sunseekers, and the removal of the last remaining barrier is expected to see numbers recover further in the months ahead.

The broader question, of course, is why any of these restrictions persisted as long as they did. It became abundantly clear, even to the most ardent advocates of Covid-19 vaccination, that the vaccines did not prevent transmission of the virus. Whatever case could be made for their role in reducing severe illness on an individual basis, the argument for using vaccination status as a gateway to international travel had long since collapsed.

In Ireland, the government's own Covid cert system was a source of deep division, creating what amounted to a two-tier society in which access to restaurants, pubs and public life was determined by one's vaccination status. That system too was eventually abandoned, though the social and political scars it left behind have not fully healed.

The Spanish decision is a reminder that, given enough time, common sense does tend to reassert itself. It would be gratifying, however, if those in positions of authority could bring themselves to admit that the restrictions went too far, lasted too long, and caused real harm to real people.
headline: Finally a bit of sanity returns to Spain as unvaccinated can now enter the country for holidays

text:
A Garda investigation is underway after a woman was allegedly sexually assaulted in Dublin.

The incident is understood to have occurred in the south inner city area, with Gardaí confirming they are investigating the reported assault.

The woman, whose age has not been disclosed, is believed to have reported the alleged attack to Gardaí, who have since launched a full investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident.

A Garda spokesperson confirmed the investigation is ongoing, stating: "Gardaí are investigating an alleged sexual assault that occurred in Dublin. Investigations are ongoing and no further information is available at this time."

It is understood that no arrests have been made at this stage, though Gardaí are following a number of lines of enquiry as part of their investigation.

The woman is being provided with support from specialist services, as is standard in cases of this nature. The Dublin Rape Crisis Centre operates a 24-hour national helpline for anyone affected by sexual violence, which can be reached at 1800 77 8888.

Gardaí are appealing for anyone who may have information in relation to the incident to come forward. Anyone with information is asked to contact their local Garda station or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: Garda investigation underway after a woman is allegedly sexually assaulted in Dublin

text:
A migrant desperate to reach Europe was discovered by border police hiding inside the cramped glove compartment of a car attempting to cross into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco.

Stunning images released by Spain's Guardia Civil show the man folded into an almost impossibly small space behind the vehicle's dashboard, his limbs contorted to fit inside the tiny compartment. Officers made the discovery during routine checks at the Tarajal border crossing, one of only two land borders between Africa and the European Union.

The driver of the vehicle, a Moroccan national, was immediately arrested on suspicion of human trafficking. The migrant, whose nationality has not been disclosed, was taken to a local reception centre for medical assessment and treatment.

It is not the first time that migrants have been found concealed in extraordinarily confined spaces in vehicles attempting to cross into the Spanish territories of Ceuta and Melilla on the North African coast. In recent years, border agents have discovered people hidden inside car dashboards, hollowed-out seats, specially constructed compartments beneath vehicle floors, and even inside suitcases.

The two enclaves have long served as flashpoints in Europe's migration crisis, with thousands of people each year attempting to cross their heavily fortified perimeters. Spain has invested heavily in fencing, surveillance technology and increased police patrols to stem the flow of irregular crossings, but smuggling networks continue to devise ever more inventive and dangerous methods of moving people across the border.

Human rights organisations have repeatedly raised concerns about the conditions driving people to take such extreme risks, pointing to conflict, poverty and persecution across sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East as root causes of the migration flows.

The incident comes amid broader tensions across the Mediterranean region over migration policy, with several EU member states pressing for tighter external border controls and increased cooperation with North African nations to prevent crossings.
headline: Migrant desperately trying to enter Europe is found hiding in cramped car glove box

text:
The first teaser trailer for the highly anticipated James Bond film *No Time to Die* has been released, giving fans a glimpse of Daniel Craig's final outing as the iconic British spy.

The trailer, which dropped online this morning, offers a tantalising look at the 25th instalment in the long-running franchise, featuring high-octane car chases, sweeping international locations and the kind of suave action sequences that have become synonymous with the series.

Craig, who has played 007 since *Casino Royale* in 2006, is seen coming out of retirement in the clip after being approached by his old ally Felix Leiter, played by Jeffrey Wright, for help in rescuing a kidnapped scientist. The mission puts Bond on the trail of a mysterious new villain armed with dangerous new technology.

Oscar-winner Rami Malek, who took home the Academy Award for his portrayal of Freddie Mercury in *Bohemian Rhapsody*, appears as the film's antagonist Safin, though the trailer keeps much of his character shrouded in mystery. The brief glimpses of Malek in the footage suggest a villain every bit as menacing as some of Bond's most memorable adversaries.

The film also stars Léa Seydoux, who reprises her role as Madeleine Swann from *Spectre*, alongside newcomers Lashana Lynch and Ana de Armas. Ben Whishaw and Naomie Harris return as Q and Moneypenny respectively, while Ralph Fiennes is back as M.

American filmmaker Cary Joji Fukunaga, best known for directing the first season of HBO's critically acclaimed *True Detective*, takes the helm after original director Danny Boyle departed the project over what were described as "creative differences."

The film's release has been the subject of considerable speculation, with production having been beset by a number of setbacks including an on-set injury sustained by Craig during filming in Jamaica.

*No Time to Die* is expected to be Craig's swansong in the role, bringing to a close a tenure that has spanned five films and redefined the character for a modern audience. His portrayal has been widely credited with bringing a grittier, more emotionally complex edge to the franchise, beginning with the stripped-back reinvention seen in *Casino Royale*.

The film is due for release in cinemas in April, and anticipation is already building among fans eager to see how Craig's era as Bond will be brought to a close.
headline: Teaser trailer of upcoming Bond movie ‘No time to die’ released

text:
Cervical cancer patients in Ireland will now have access to a breakthrough immunotherapy drug following a landmark reimbursement decision that has been welcomed by patient advocates and medical professionals alike.

Pembrolizumab, commonly known as Pembro, has been approved for reimbursement by the HSE for the treatment of cervical cancer, marking a significant step forward in the treatment options available to women diagnosed with the disease in this country.

The decision means that eligible patients will be able to access the drug through the public health system, removing what had been a significant barrier for many women who could not afford to access the treatment privately or through other means.

Pembrolizumab is an immunotherapy treatment that works by helping the body's own immune system to identify and attack cancer cells. It has already been approved for use in a number of other cancer types in Ireland and internationally, and clinical trial data has demonstrated significant improvements in survival outcomes for cervical cancer patients.

Cervical cancer remains a serious health concern in Ireland, with approximately 300 women diagnosed with the disease each year. While screening programmes and the HPV vaccine have contributed to earlier detection and prevention efforts, treatment options for those diagnosed with advanced or recurrent cervical cancer have historically been limited.

Patient advocacy groups have long campaigned for the drug to be made available, arguing that Irish women were being left behind compared to their counterparts in other European countries where the treatment was already accessible.

The decision was made following an assessment by the National Centre for Pharmacoeconomics, which evaluates the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of new medicines before they can be approved for reimbursement through the community drugs schemes.

Medical oncologists specialising in gynaecological cancers have described the approval as a genuinely meaningful development for their patients, noting that Pembro represents a real advance in the standard of care available and offers hope to women who may previously have had few remaining treatment options.

The HSE confirmed that arrangements are being put in place to ensure the drug is made available to eligible patients as quickly as possible through the relevant hospital treatment centres around the country.
headline: Cervical cancer patients will be able to get new drug Pembro following landmark decision

text:
Authorities in Beijing have re-introduced sweeping travel restrictions after a fresh cluster of coronavirus cases emerged in the Chinese capital, raising fears of a significant second wave of infections in the country where the pandemic began.

The city government moved swiftly to lock down several residential compounds and shut a major wholesale food market after dozens of new cases were linked to the Xinfadi market in the south-western Fengtai district. Officials confirmed scores of new locally transmitted infections over recent days, marking the most serious resurgence Beijing has seen since the early stages of the outbreak.

All flights out of the city have been cancelled, communities surrounding the market have been placed under strict quarantine measures, and residents in affected areas have been told not to leave Beijing. Schools that had only recently reopened have been closed once again, whilst sporting events and other large gatherings have been suspended indefinitely.

The Xinfadi market, which supplies the vast majority of the capital's fresh fruit and vegetables, was shut down after the virus was reportedly detected on chopping boards used to handle imported salmon. Thousands of people who worked at or recently visited the market are being traced and tested.

Chinese health authorities said they had launched a "wartime emergency" response, deploying mass testing across the city and dispatching teams of epidemiologists to trace the source of the outbreak. Nucleic acid testing stations have been established across Fengtai and neighbouring districts, with officials aiming to test tens of thousands of residents in the coming days.

The development is a significant setback for China, which had largely brought the virus under control through aggressive lockdown measures and had been gradually reopening its economy. Beijing had gone more than fifty days without reporting a single locally transmitted case before the new cluster was identified.

The resurgence has also prompted concern among international health experts, who have warned that the easing of restrictions in countries that appeared to have suppressed the virus could lead to dangerous new outbreaks. The World Health Organisation has repeatedly cautioned that the pandemic is far from over and that nations must remain vigilant even as case numbers decline.

The fresh outbreak in Beijing will be closely watched by governments around the world as they grapple with their own strategies for easing lockdown measures whilst preventing a resurgence of the virus. It serves as a stark reminder of how quickly the situation can deteriorate, even in a country that has deployed some of the most aggressive containment measures seen anywhere in the world.

China's National Health Commission urged the public not to panic but said the situation remained "extremely severe" and called on residents to cooperate fully with testing and contact tracing efforts. Travel restrictions between Beijing and other provinces have also been tightened, with several neighbouring regions requiring arrivals from the capital to undergo mandatory quarantine and testing.
headline: Covid-19: Travel restrictions re-introduced in Beijing, as coronavirus begins to spread again

text:
The Dublin Marathon has been cancelled for the second consecutive year as organisers confirmed the event cannot proceed due to the ongoing coronavirus pandemic.

The marathon, which typically draws tens of thousands of runners through the streets of the capital each October, was called off after organisers said they could not guarantee the safety of participants, volunteers and spectators under current public health guidelines.

Dublin Marathon organisers said the decision had been taken with "great reluctance" but that the logistical challenges of staging a mass participation event of this scale remained insurmountable given the continued uncertainty surrounding Covid-19 restrictions.

"We explored every possible option to try to make this year's event happen, but ultimately the health and safety of everyone involved has to come first," a spokesperson for the organising committee said. "We are bitterly disappointed, as are the thousands of runners who have been training in the hope of taking part."

The cancellation is a significant blow to the capital's hospitality and tourism sectors, which have traditionally benefited from the influx of runners and their supporters from across Ireland and abroad. The event is estimated to generate tens of millions of euro for the Dublin economy each year.

It also represents another setback for the broader running community, which has seen virtually all large-scale events shelved since the pandemic began in March 2020. Many runners had been holding out hope that the easing of restrictions over the summer months would pave the way for a return to organised racing.

The Government has been gradually relaxing public health measures in recent months, with the roadmap for reopening society offering some encouragement to event organisers. However, concerns around large crowd gatherings and the potential for new variants of the virus have continued to complicate planning for mass participation events.

Athletics Ireland acknowledged the difficulty of the decision and urged runners to maintain their training in anticipation of a return to competition when circumstances allow.

Several smaller running events around the country have managed to proceed in modified formats, with staggered start times, reduced fields and strict social distancing protocols. However, organisers of the Dublin Marathon said the sheer scale of the event, which regularly attracts more than 20,000 participants, made such adaptations impractical.

Runners who had already entered the race will be offered the option of deferring their entry to next year's event or receiving a refund, the organisers confirmed.

The marathon was first held in 1980 and had taken place every year without interruption until the pandemic forced its cancellation. Organisers expressed confidence that the event would return and said planning for next year's race was already under way.
headline: Covid-19: Dublin marathon canceled due to the ongoing coronavirus pandemic

text:
Gardaí have seized a significant quantity of equipment as part of a targeted operation cracking down on the sale and distribution of illegal TV set top boxes across the country.

The operation, which was carried out in recent days, saw officers confiscate a number of devices believed to have been modified or configured to provide unauthorised access to premium television channels and streaming services without a valid subscription.

The investigation is being led by Gardaí working in conjunction with industry representatives and is understood to focus on individuals and networks involved in the sale of so-called "fully loaded" set top boxes, which allow users to access paid content from major broadcasters for a fraction of the legitimate cost — or in many cases, for a one-off payment.

The sale and use of such devices has become increasingly widespread in Ireland in recent years, with sellers often advertising openly on social media platforms and online marketplaces. The devices typically use internet protocol television (IPTV) technology to illegally stream content from providers such as Sky, BT Sport, and various international broadcasters.

While purchasing a set top box is not in itself illegal, modifying or selling one that is pre-loaded with access to pirated content constitutes a criminal offence under Irish and EU law. Those found guilty of selling or distributing such devices can face substantial fines and potential prison sentences.

A Garda spokesperson confirmed that the seized equipment is currently being examined and that investigations are ongoing. No arrests have been made at this stage, though Gardaí indicated that a number of individuals have been identified as part of the inquiry and further action is expected in the coming weeks.

The operation forms part of a broader effort by An Garda Síochána to tackle intellectual property crime, which costs the entertainment and broadcasting industry millions of euro annually. Industry bodies have long called for more robust enforcement action, arguing that the proliferation of illegal streaming devices undermines legitimate businesses and puts jobs at risk.

A spokesperson for one industry group welcomed the Garda operation, stating that the illegal streaming market deprives content creators, broadcasters, and sporting organisations of vital revenue. They urged consumers to be aware that using such devices is not a victimless crime and that those who purchase them may also be exposing themselves to legal risk.

Gardaí are appealing to anyone with information about the sale or distribution of illegal streaming devices to contact their local Garda station or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
headline: Gardai seize equipment as part of an operation targeting illegal TV set top boxes

text:
The man charged with the murder of primary school teacher Ashling Murphy is scheduled to make his second appearance before the courts today.

Jozef Puska, aged 31, with an address at Lynally Grove, Mucklagh, Co Offaly, was charged with the murder of the 23-year-old, who was killed while out jogging along the canal bank at Cappincur, Tullamore, Co Offaly, on 12 January.

Mr Puska first appeared before Judge Catherine Staines at a special sitting of Tullamore District Court last week, where he was remanded in custody to Cloverhill Prison.

The accused, who required the assistance of a Slovak interpreter during his initial court appearance, made no application for bail at that hearing. Legal aid was granted after the court heard that Mr Puska was not in a position to fund his own legal representation.

The brief hearing saw Detective Sergeant Christopher Mangan give evidence of arrest, charge and caution. The court was told that when the charge was put to the accused, he made no reply.

Ms Murphy, a talented traditional musician and a teacher at Durrow National School, was attacked and killed as she exercised along the banks of the Grand Canal on a popular walking route in broad daylight. Her death sent shockwaves across the country, prompting vigils in towns and cities throughout Ireland and abroad.

The young woman's funeral Mass took place at St Brigid's Church in Mountbolus, Co Offaly, where mourners heard tributes to her warmth, her dedication to teaching and her love of music. President Michael D Higgins and Taoiseach Micheál Martin were among those who expressed their condolences to the Murphy family.

The investigation into Ms Murphy's death was led by detectives at Tullamore Garda Station, with significant resources deployed in the days following the killing.

It is expected that today's hearing will be brief, with the case likely to be adjourned for further preparation of a file for the Director of Public Prosecutions.
headline: Ashling Murphy murder: Accused scheduled to make second appearance in court

text:
Irish health authorities have confirmed just over 21,300 new cases of Covid-19 in the past 24 hours, as the latest wave of the virus continues to place significant pressure on the health service.

The figures, reported by the HSE, come amid growing concern over hospital admissions, with the number of patients being treated for the virus in acute settings remaining elevated. As of this morning, there were several hundred Covid-positive patients in hospitals across the State, with a number requiring intensive care treatment.

Chief Medical Officer Dr Tony Holohan and senior public health officials have urged the public to continue exercising caution, particularly in light of the highly transmissible variants currently circulating. The National Public Health Emergency Team has been closely monitoring the situation and is understood to be keeping all options under review.

The latest case numbers represent a continuation of the trend seen in recent days, with daily infections remaining stubbornly high despite the country's strong vaccination uptake. The booster programme has been credited with helping to keep the number of seriously ill patients lower than might otherwise have been expected, though officials have cautioned that the sheer volume of cases still poses a real challenge for the health system.

The HSE has appealed to anyone experiencing symptoms to isolate and follow public health guidelines. Those who have not yet availed of their booster dose are being strongly encouraged to do so at the earliest opportunity.

Minister for Health Stephen Donnelly said the Government continues to monitor the situation closely and that additional supports remain available to hospitals dealing with increased demand. Speaking to reporters, the Minister acknowledged the fatigue felt by the public but stressed that basic protective measures, including mask-wearing and hand hygiene, remain important tools in limiting transmission.

The situation in hospitals has prompted renewed calls from opposition TDs for more to be done to protect frontline healthcare workers, with Sinn Féin's health spokesperson describing staffing levels in some facilities as "critically stretched."

The figures will be reviewed by NPHET in the coming days as authorities assess whether any additional public health measures may be warranted.
headline: Covid-19: Irish health authorities report just over 21,300 new coronavirus infections over the past 24h

text:
The United Kingdom has recorded its highest ever daily tally of coronavirus cases since the pandemic began, with 93,045 new infections confirmed in the space of just 24 hours, as the Omicron variant continues to sweep across the country at an alarming pace.

The staggering figure, released by the UK government on Friday, smashes through the previous record and underscores the sheer speed at which the new variant is spreading through communities, particularly in London and the south-east of England, where Omicron has become the dominant strain.

A further 111 deaths were also recorded within 28 days of a positive test, while hospitalisations have begun to creep upward, raising fresh concerns about the capacity of the National Health Service to cope over the winter period.

The record-breaking case numbers come despite the British government's accelerated booster programme, which has seen millions of additional doses administered in recent weeks. Prime Minister Boris Johnson has urged the public to come forward for their booster jabs as the best line of defence against the variant, though he has so far resisted calls to impose further restrictions in England beyond the so-called Plan B measures already in place, which include mask-wearing in most indoor settings and the introduction of Covid passes for large venues.

The situation stands in contrast to the approaches taken in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, where devolved administrations have introduced tighter restrictions on household mixing and the hospitality sector in a bid to slow the spread of Omicron.

The figures will be watched closely on this side of the Irish Sea, where the Government has already moved to impose an 8pm closing time on hospitality venues and reintroduce restrictions on household gatherings. Ireland has itself seen a sharp rise in Omicron cases in recent days, with public health officials warning that the variant is set to become dominant here in the coming period.

The World Health Organisation has warned that Omicron's rapid transmissibility poses a significant risk to health systems globally, even if early data suggests the variant may cause less severe illness than the Delta strain. However, scientists have cautioned that even a small proportion of serious cases among vastly larger infection numbers could still translate into considerable pressure on hospitals.

British health officials said the true number of infections is likely to be significantly higher than the confirmed figure, given the constraints on testing capacity and the number of asymptomatic cases that go undetected. The UK Health Security Agency has warned that the country could see daily case numbers rise further still in the days ahead, with the peak of the Omicron wave not yet in sight.

The latest data showed that more than 31 million booster doses have now been administered across the UK, as authorities race to extend protection to as many people as possible before the full impact of the wave is felt in the new year.
headline: Covid-19: UK reports record-busting daily coronavirus cases, with just over 93,000 new infections confirmed in the last 24h

text:
Ryanair has launched a massive flash sale on flights across its European network, but bargain hunters will need to act fast as the deal expires at midnight tonight.

The budget carrier is offering seats from as little as €16.99 on a raft of routes from Dublin, Cork, Shannon and Knock airports, with travel dates stretching from now through to the end of March. Destinations covered in the sale include popular sun spots such as Málaga, Faro and Lanzarote, as well as city break favourites like Milan, Barcelona and Lisbon.

The airline confirmed the sale is available exclusively through its website and app, and urged customers not to delay in snapping up the discounted fares.

"We're giving Irish holidaymakers the chance to book their winter and early spring getaways at unbeatable prices," a Ryanair spokesperson said. "But these fares won't last — customers need to book before midnight tonight to avail of these incredible offers."

The sale comes as the airline industry enters one of its busiest booking periods, with January traditionally seeing a surge in demand as travellers look to lock in plans for the months ahead after the Christmas break.

Ryanair has been steadily expanding its Irish operations in recent years and currently operates more than 230 routes from Irish airports. The carrier transported over 183 million passengers across its network last year, cementing its position as Europe's largest airline by passenger numbers.

Consumer groups have advised anyone looking to take advantage of the sale to remain mindful of additional charges for checked baggage, seat selection and priority boarding, which can add significantly to the headline fare. Passengers are also encouraged to double-check travel insurance arrangements before booking.

The sale is live now on ryanair.com and closes at midnight tonight.
headline: Up, up and away! Ryanair launches huge sale but you must book by TONIGHT!

text:
Hermann Kelly, the leader of the Irish Freedom Party and a long-standing figure in European Parliament circles, has been at the forefront of efforts to block a requirement for MEPs, parliamentary staff and visitors to present a Covid-19 vaccination certificate in order to access the European Parliament's buildings.

Kelly, who previously served as a press officer in the European Parliament for a number of years, has been vocal in his opposition to what he describes as a fundamental breach of civil liberties and bodily autonomy. The campaign has drawn support from a number of MEPs across various political groupings who share concerns about the imposition of vaccine certification as a condition of entry to the parliament's premises in Brussels and Strasbourg.

The Irish Freedom Party leader has argued that requiring elected representatives to show proof of vaccination in order to carry out their democratic mandate sets a dangerous precedent, effectively creating a two-tier system within the very institution that is supposed to uphold democratic principles across the European Union.

"No MEP should be prevented from representing their constituents because of their private medical decisions," Kelly stated, framing the issue as one that transcends traditional political divides.

The European Parliament had introduced various Covid-related access measures during the pandemic, including the EU Digital Covid Certificate, which critics argued amounted to coercive pressure on individuals to undergo a medical procedure in order to participate in public life.

Kelly's campaign has resonated with a broader movement across Europe that has questioned the proportionality of pandemic-era restrictions and the use of vaccine passes in institutional settings. Opponents of the certificates have consistently maintained that such measures represent an overreach of authority and an infringement on fundamental rights, including the right to medical privacy and informed consent.

The Irish Freedom Party, which Kelly founded in 2018, has positioned itself as a voice against what it characterises as the erosion of national sovereignty and individual freedoms by EU institutions. The party has consistently opposed Covid-19 restrictions both domestically and at European level, arguing that many of the measures introduced during the pandemic were disproportionate and lacked adequate democratic scrutiny.

Supporters of the vaccination certificate requirement within the parliament have argued that the measures were necessary to protect the health and safety of all those working in and visiting the buildings, particularly given the large number of people who pass through the parliament on a daily basis.

However, Kelly and his allies have countered that such justifications cannot override the fundamental democratic right of elected representatives to access their place of work, nor should they be used to create barriers for citizens wishing to engage with the democratic process by visiting the parliament.

The campaign has highlighted the broader tension that has existed throughout the pandemic between public health imperatives and the protection of individual rights, a debate that has played out not only in the European Parliament but in national parliaments across the continent, including the Dáil.
headline: Leader of Irish Freedom Party spearheads campaign in EU Parliament to oppose MEPs, staff and visitors having to produce a Covid-19 vaccination certificate

text:
KFC has reopened 16 of its Irish restaurants for delivery and drive-thru orders, as the fast food chain becomes the latest major outlet to resume limited operations during the Covid-19 restrictions.

The company confirmed that locations across the country are now back up and running, though with a reduced menu and strict new safety protocols in place for both staff and customers. Dining areas remain closed in line with public health guidelines, meaning customers can only access their food through drive-thru lanes or via delivery platforms such as Deliveroo and Just Eat.

Among the outlets reopening are branches in Dublin, Cork, Limerick and Galway, with the company indicating that further locations could follow in the coming weeks depending on how the initial phase goes.

KFC said it had introduced a range of measures to protect workers, including temperature checks at the start of shifts, enhanced cleaning regimes, perspex screens at service points, and limits on the number of staff working in kitchens at any one time. Employees have also been provided with personal protective equipment including gloves and face coverings.

The menu has been stripped back to focus on the chain's most popular items, a move the company said was necessary to allow for social distancing in kitchen areas while still keeping service running smoothly.

The reopening comes as a number of fast food and restaurant chains have begun tentatively resuming operations, with many in the sector exploring ways to trade safely while the broader hospitality industry remains largely shuttered under government restrictions.

Customer reaction on social media was predictably enthusiastic, with some joking that the reopening was the best news they had received in weeks. Others, however, raised concerns about the safety of workers in fast food environments where social distancing can be difficult to maintain.

The company stressed that it would take a cautious approach and would not hesitate to close any outlet again if it felt safety standards could not be maintained.
headline: Chicken run! KFC re-opens 16 Irish outlets for delivery and drive-thru

text:
Dr Tony Holohan's deputy has warned that Ireland finds itself in a precarious position as the reproduction number of the virus continues to climb, with the R number now estimated to be between 1.2 and 1.8.

Speaking at this evening's briefing from the National Public Health Emergency Team, Acting Chief Medical Officer Dr Ronan Glynn said the figures are a cause for serious concern and urged the public to redouble their efforts in adhering to public health guidelines.

Dr Glynn said the rising R number means that each person infected with the virus is now passing it on to more than one other person on average, leading to an acceleration in the spread of the disease across the country.

"We are in a precarious position," Dr Glynn told reporters. "The R number is now estimated to be between 1.2 and 1.8. This means the disease is growing in the community, and if we do not act collectively and individually, we will see a continued deterioration in the situation."

The warning comes as NPHET reported a further increase in confirmed cases of Covid-19 in the State, with clusters continuing to emerge in a number of settings including households, workplaces and amongst close contacts of confirmed cases.

Dr Glynn stressed that the situation is not yet beyond retrieval but said it will require a sustained national effort to bring the R number back below one, the critical threshold at which the virus begins to retreat rather than spread.

He appealed to younger people in particular to be mindful of their social interactions, noting that a significant proportion of recent cases have been among those in younger age groups. While younger people are less likely to become seriously ill from the virus, Dr Glynn cautioned that they can and do transmit it to more vulnerable members of their families and communities.

The Acting CMO reiterated the importance of basic public health measures including regular hand washing, maintaining a two-metre social distance where possible, wearing face coverings in appropriate settings and limiting the number of people with whom one has close contact.

NPHET has been closely monitoring the trajectory of the virus in recent weeks as case numbers have trended upwards. There has been growing concern within the team that the gains made during the lockdown period could be eroded if compliance with public health advice continues to slip.

The Government has faced calls from some quarters to reimpose restrictions in areas where outbreaks have been most pronounced, while others have cautioned against a return to widespread lockdown measures given the devastating economic and social consequences of the initial shutdown.

Dr Glynn said NPHET would continue to monitor the data on a daily basis and would not hesitate to make recommendations to Government if the situation required it. He noted that the experience of other European countries, where surges in cases have forced the reimposition of strict measures, should serve as a cautionary tale for Ireland.

The HSE's testing and tracing capacity has been significantly expanded in recent months, and health officials have said the system is well placed to respond to further increases in demand. However, concerns remain about turnaround times for test results in some parts of the country, with delays potentially undermining the effectiveness of contact tracing efforts.
headline: Dr Glynn says Ireland is in a precarious position as R number is between 1.2 and 1.8

text:
The Government is examining the possibility of allowing fans to return to sporting events "in small numbers" from as early as July, as the country continues to ease Covid-19 restrictions in line with the revised roadmap.

Minister for Sport Shane Ross indicated that discussions are ongoing between his department and the major sporting bodies, including the GAA, FAI, and IRFU, about how spectators might safely be accommodated at matches and events in the coming weeks.

Speaking on Wednesday, the Minister said that while the return of competitive sport behind closed doors had been a welcome step, the absence of supporters remained a significant concern for organisations that rely heavily on gate receipts.

"We are looking very carefully at how we might allow fans back in small numbers, in a safe and controlled manner," Minister Ross said. "Nobody wants to see empty stadiums any longer than is absolutely necessary, but public health must remain the priority."

Under the current roadmap for reopening, outdoor gatherings are being permitted on a phased basis, with numbers allowed to increase gradually provided the epidemiological situation continues to improve. It is understood that any initial return of spectators would likely be limited to outdoor venues where social distancing can be more easily managed.

The GAA, which has seen its calendar thrown into disarray by the pandemic, has already begun planning for a restructured inter-county championship later in the year and has indicated it would welcome even a limited number of supporters at games.

NPHET will continue to advise the Government on the public health implications of any such move, and a final decision is expected to depend on the trajectory of the virus in the weeks ahead. The Department of Health confirmed that any plans to admit spectators would be subject to strict protocols, including social distancing requirements, limits on capacity, and the likely prohibition of alcohol sales at venues.

Opposition TDs have urged the Government to provide greater clarity to sporting organisations, many of which are facing severe financial difficulties as a result of the prolonged shutdown. Labour's spokesperson on sport, Aodhán Ó Ríordáin, said clubs at grassroots level were "crying out for a clear timeline" and warned that some faced an existential threat without a return of some revenue streams.

The potential return of fans, even in restricted numbers, would represent a significant psychological boost for a country that has endured months of lockdown restrictions. However, health officials have repeatedly cautioned against complacency, noting that the virus remains a threat and that any easing of measures must be carefully monitored.

Ireland's Covid-19 case numbers have continued to trend downwards in recent weeks, with the death toll and daily case counts falling considerably from their peak. As of Wednesday evening, the Department of Health reported a small number of additional confirmed cases, bringing the total number of cases in the Republic to date beyond 25,000.
headline: Covid-19: Fans might be allowed to attend sporting events ‘in small numbers’ from July

text:
Pfizer and BioNTech have announced plans to begin a global clinical trial to evaluate the safety and efficacy of their Covid-19 vaccine in pregnant women, a move that could pave the way for wider immunisation of a group that has so far been largely excluded from vaccination campaigns.

The pharmaceutical giants said the trial would involve approximately 4,000 healthy pregnant women who are between 24 and 34 weeks of gestation. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive either two doses of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine or a placebo, administered 21 days apart. The study will be conducted across sites in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Brazil, Chile, Mozambique, South Africa and Spain.

The trial will monitor the safety of the vaccine in pregnant women and will also assess whether protective antibodies are transferred from mother to infant, potentially offering newborns some level of protection against the virus in their early months of life.

Pregnant women were excluded from the initial clinical trials of the vaccine, as is standard practice in the early stages of drug development. However, mounting evidence has suggested that pregnant women who contract Covid-19 face a higher risk of severe illness and complications, including preterm birth.

The World Health Organisation has said that pregnant women may receive the vaccine where the benefits outweigh the potential risks, though it has stopped short of issuing a blanket recommendation due to the limited data available.

In Ireland, the National Immunisation Advisory Committee has advised that pregnant women in high-risk groups may be offered the vaccine following a discussion with their healthcare provider, though the absence of trial data specific to pregnancy has made many women and clinicians cautious.

Dr Özlem Türeci, co-founder and chief medical officer of BioNTech, said the company was committed to generating robust evidence to support informed decisions about vaccination during pregnancy. She described the planned trial as an important step in addressing the significant gap in data.

Pfizer said the first participants were expected to be enrolled in the coming weeks, with initial results anticipated later this year. The companies noted that women who become pregnant during the ongoing main trial, or during the booster study, are being monitored and that no safety concerns have been identified to date.

The announcement has been broadly welcomed by medical professionals and public health experts, who have called for more comprehensive data to guide policy on vaccinating pregnant women. Several countries, including the United States and the United Kingdom, have already begun offering the vaccine to pregnant women on the basis of real-world evidence and animal studies that showed no adverse effects on fertility or foetal development.
headline: Pfizer and BioNtech to start testing Covid-19 vaccine in pregnant women

text:
Dublin Fire Brigade has suspended a firefighter after a video circulated online in which the man is alleged to have made derogatory remarks about members of the Traveller community.

The video, which was widely shared across social media platforms over the weekend, appears to show the uniformed firefighter delivering what has been described as a "joke" targeting Travellers. The clip drew immediate condemnation from Traveller advocacy groups and prompted a swift response from Dublin Fire Brigade management.

Dublin City Council, which operates Dublin Fire Brigade, confirmed that the individual has been suspended pending the outcome of a full disciplinary investigation. A spokesperson said the organisation "does not tolerate any form of racism or discrimination" and that the matter was being treated with the "utmost seriousness."

"Dublin Fire Brigade is committed to providing a service to all members of the public without prejudice," the spokesperson said. "The behaviour displayed in this video does not represent the values of our organisation or the vast majority of our personnel."

The Irish Traveller Movement said the video was "deeply hurtful" and reflective of a broader culture of anti-Traveller racism that persists across Irish society. A spokesperson for the organisation said they welcomed the suspension but called for the investigation to be conducted transparently and for meaningful consequences to follow.

"This is not simply a matter of a joke in poor taste. Anti-Traveller racism has real and lasting consequences for members of our community, and when it comes from a public servant in uniform, it carries even greater weight," the spokesperson said.

Pavee Point, the Traveller and Roma rights organisation, also condemned the video and said it had been in contact with Dublin City Council regarding the matter. Director Martin Collins said the incident highlighted the need for mandatory anti-racism and cultural awareness training across all public services.

"We see time and again that Travellers are considered fair game when it comes to so-called humour. This kind of behaviour from someone employed to serve and protect all citizens is simply unacceptable," Collins said.

The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission has previously identified Travellers as one of the groups most frequently subjected to discrimination in Ireland. Under the Equal Status Acts and the Employment Equality Acts, discrimination on the basis of membership of the Traveller community is explicitly prohibited.

Several serving firefighters, speaking anonymously, told The Liberal that the suspended individual's behaviour was not reflective of the service as a whole and expressed frustration that the actions of one person could damage the reputation of the brigade.

SIPTU, which represents many firefighters, declined to comment on the specifics of the case but confirmed it was providing representation to the individual through the disciplinary process, as is standard procedure.

The suspended firefighter has not made any public comment on the matter. It is understood he could face sanctions ranging from a formal warning to dismissal, depending on the outcome of the investigation.

Dublin City Council said it expected the disciplinary process to be concluded "as expeditiously as possible" but would not be providing a specific timeline.
headline: BREAKING: Dublin fire brigade suspend fireman for ‘traveller joke video’

text:
Jon Venables, one of the killers of toddler James Bulger, is set to launch a fresh bid for release from prison within weeks, according to reports in Britain.

Venables, who along with Robert Thompson abducted and murdered two-year-old James in Liverpool in 1993 when both boys were just ten years old, is understood to be preparing a new application to the Parole Board. The case remains one of the most shocking crimes in British legal history and continues to provoke intense public debate about justice, rehabilitation and the protection of children.

Now in his early forties and living under a permanent new identity, Venables has been recalled to prison twice since his original release on licence in 2001. He was sent back to jail in 2010 after being found with indecent images of children and was recalled again in 2017 on similar charges. He pleaded guilty in 2018 to possession of indecent images and was sentenced to three years and four months in prison.

His previous bid for parole was rejected, with the board determining that he continued to pose a risk to the public. It is understood that his legal team now believes sufficient time has passed and that Venables has engaged with rehabilitation programmes in custody to a degree that warrants a fresh hearing.

James Bulger's mother, Denise Fergus, has long campaigned against any release, arguing that Venables has repeatedly demonstrated that he remains a danger to children. She has previously called for his anonymity order to be revoked, a request that has been refused by the courts on multiple occasions on the grounds that revealing his identity could put his life at risk.

The case has raised profound questions about whether individuals who commit the most serious offences as children can ever be truly rehabilitated, particularly where subsequent offending has occurred.

The Parole Board is expected to consider the application in the coming weeks. Any decision to release Venables would be subject to strict licence conditions, and he would continue to live under his assumed identity for the remainder of his life.

Thompson, who has not reoffended since his release in 2001, continues to live anonymously in the community.
headline: Jon Venables to launch fresh appeal for freedom from jail within weeks

text:
Parents across Ireland can now register children as young as five to receive a Covid-19 vaccine, the HSE has confirmed, in what health officials are describing as a significant step in the national vaccination programme.

The online registration portal opened this week for children aged five to eleven, with the HSE urging parents and guardians to consider booking their child in for the jab as soon as possible. The paediatric dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine, which is one-third of the adult dose, has been approved for use in this age group by the European Medicines Agency.

It is a move that has divided opinion among parents, with some expressing relief that their younger children can finally receive a level of protection against the virus, while others have raised concerns about the speed at which the vaccine was developed and whether it is truly necessary for children who are statistically at very low risk of serious illness from Covid-19.

The HSE has been keen to stress that the vaccine is safe and effective for children in this age group, pointing to clinical trial data and the experience of other countries such as the United States, where millions of children in the same age bracket have already been vaccinated. Chief Medical Officer Dr Tony Holohan has encouraged parents to speak with their GP if they have any questions or concerns about the vaccine for their children.

Vaccinations for the five-to-eleven age group will be administered at HSE vaccination centres around the country, with appointments available to book through the online portal at hse.ie. Children will require parental or guardian consent before receiving the vaccine, and the HSE has said that a parent or guardian must accompany the child to their appointment.

The Irish Medical Organisation has broadly welcomed the development, though some GPs have privately acknowledged that convincing hesitant parents will not be straightforward. There remains a cohort of parents who feel strongly that vaccinating healthy young children against a virus that poses minimal risk to them is unnecessary, particularly when the long-term effects of the vaccine in this age group are not yet fully understood.

The National Immunisation Advisory Committee recommended the vaccine for this cohort, noting that while severe illness in children remains rare, vaccination would help reduce transmission in households and schools and offer protection to those children who are immunocompromised or have underlying health conditions.

The programme comes at a time when case numbers among school-age children have remained stubbornly high, with outbreaks in primary schools continuing to cause disruption throughout the academic year. Schools have been among the settings most affected by Covid-19 transmission, and the Department of Education has faced sustained criticism over ventilation and mitigation measures in classrooms.

Parents wishing to register their child can do so through the HSE's online booking system, where they will be asked to provide their child's PPS number and date of birth. Walk-in clinics for children in this age group may also be made available in the coming weeks, the HSE has indicated.

The debate around vaccinating young children is likely to continue in the weeks ahead, but for now, the option is there for parents who want to avail of it. As with so much of the pandemic response, the decision ultimately rests with individual families weighing up the evidence and making the choice they feel is right for their children.
headline: Is your kid getting it? Children as young as 5 can now register to get the vaccine

text:
Jeremy Clarkson has once again found himself at the centre of a social media storm after a clip resurfaced of the former Top Gear presenter telling climate activist Greta Thunberg to "shut up" and calling her a "spoilt brat" who should "go back to school."

The outspoken broadcaster, who has never been one to shy away from controversy, made the remarks during an appearance that has since been shared tens of thousands of times across platforms including X, TikTok and Facebook, drawing a sharply divided reaction from the public.

Clarkson, who now runs a farm in the Cotswolds and stars in his own Amazon Prime series Clarkson's Farm, has long been a vocal critic of what he sees as heavy-handed environmental activism. His comments about the Swedish campaigner, who first rose to prominence as a teenager staging school strikes outside the Swedish parliament, have proven to be catnip for culture war debates online.

Supporters of Clarkson flooded the comments sections praising him for "saying what everyone is thinking," while critics accused him of bullying a young woman who has dedicated her life to raising awareness about the climate crisis.
